# A.D. 491–512

## Paschasius the Deacon

[Col. 0009]

# Prolegomenon

*(From Cave.)*

[Col. 0009A] Paschasius, a deacon of the Roman Church, was prominent at the beginning of this century, in the year 501. When the Roman schism was raging in 498, he vigorously defended the party of Laurence against Symmachus, and stubbornly championed its cause until his death. He died in 512.

On this occasion Gregory—or whoever was the author of the *Dialogues*—relates to us a thoroughly amusing story about Paschasius’s soul, consumed in the flames of purgatory. There exists a letter of Paschasius to Eugyppius, prefixed to the *Life of St. Severinus*, in Surius, January 8, and in Baronius under the year 496.

There are also two books on the Holy Spirit, against Macedonius, published at Cologne in 1539, in octavo, at Helmstedt in 1613, and in volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 806. Casimirus Oudin emphatically denies that these books are by Paschasius and argues [Col. 0009B] that they should be attributed to Faustus of Riez. Certainly his arguments do not seem wholly contemptible; they may be found in his *Supplement*, page 107. Nevertheless, since these highly polished and lucid books—to use Gregory’s words—rest on the testimony of Gregory, who expressly attributes them to Paschasius the deacon (and Oudin himself certainly acknowledges that the authority of the *Dialogues* is very great in this matter), they should not rashly be taken away from our Paschasius. Nor are we deterred by the titles of certain manuscripts, which, having been added through the carelessness of copyists, frequently mislead unwary readers—especially since Gennadius reports that Faustus wrote a book on the Holy Spirit (chapter 85).

Trithemius himself, whom Oudin cites as a witness on his side, clearly ascribes these very books mentioned by Gregory to our Paschasius, although, while occupied with another matter, he incautiously attached the opening words of this work to the single book which Faustus wrote on the subject. [Col. 0010A]

[Col. 0009B]

# Two Books of Paschasius the Deacon on the Holy Spirit

*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 0009]

# Preface

[Col. 0009B] The catholic faith was spread throughout the whole world through patriarchs, prophets, and dispensers of grace, with the Holy Spirit making it known. As apostolic diligence and perfection had extended it through the sacred pages, so it gathered it together with marvelous brevity in the saving Creed, arranging it like various kinds of remedies into a single body and, as it were, preparing from countless spices a precious ointment whose fragrance, through the power of its spiritual intensity, filled every region of the earth, so that in this ascent of the whole universe the power of truth might appear.

And since it is necessary that, as though addressing children who are wandering and ignorant, we should repeat the elementary principles of the first Christian tradition (on this see Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 3, and Prudentius’s *Psychomachia* [“Battle of the Soul”]), in this perfection of the Creed both unity is plainly revealed and the Trinity is revealed, since the confession repeated three times—to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—renders a single act of belief.

In these words also the sacred number of the three hundred and eighteen priests condemned the emerging errors of Arius and Macedonius, saying: “I believe in God the Father. I believe in his only Son, our Lord. I also believe in the Holy Spirit.” For even if the weakness of a few departed from this number, it did not dissolve the mystery of the universal number.

And therefore we called it a sacred number because three hundred, by the Greek system of numeration, displays the sign of the cross, while eighteen displays the venerable name of Jesus. Thus, in this number and mystery, in which holy Abraham also triumphed over countless nations, the piety of the elders confounded the enemy of the faith under the one proclamation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

From this it must also be understood that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit under eternal condemnation were either baptized without professing the Creed or lied in the Creed itself and at the font, before every person renouncing the devil confesses: “I also believe in the Holy Spirit.” I say, “I also believe in the Holy Spirit.”

Let us recognize the privilege of the Word himself. Any human being may believe him; but you must know that you ought to believe *in* him only as you believe in the divine Majesty. Yet this too is a distinction: it is one thing to believe that God exists, another to believe in God. The devil too is said, according to the Apostle, to believe that God exists: “For even the demons believe and tremble.”

But no one is approved as believing in God unless he has placed his hope piously in him. To believe in God, therefore, is to seek him faithfully; it is to pass wholly into him through love. “I believe in him”—that is, I say: I confess him, I worship him, I adore him; I hand and transfer my whole self into his right and dominion. In the reverence of this profession are contained all the acts of service owed to the divine name.

# Book One

[Col. 0011]

## Chapter I  
### That We Must Believe the Catholic Church, Not “in the Church” as We Believe in the Holy Spirit; the Preposition Must Be Removed

[Col. 0011A] But you object and say that God cannot immediately be shown to be meant in the words, “I also believe in the Holy Spirit,” because there follows: “I believe in the holy catholic Church.”

First, I do not know how Macedonius dares to name the catholic Church, since he is an exile outside the catholic Church, excluded from salvation and made one of those concerning whom it is said: “The wicked walk about on every side.”

So you say: “I believe in the holy catholic Church.” By inserting a small word—indeed, a single syllable—you attempt to weave beneath it a vast darkness. We believe the Church as the mother of regeneration; we do not believe *in* the Church as the author of salvation.

For when the whole Church confesses this concerning the Holy Spirit, can it also believe in itself? Therefore, since belief *in* the Trinity alone is specifically required, and since the teaching of the Fathers already mentioned, celebrated throughout the world, confirms this, either remove this syllable from the name of the Church, or at least prove by explicit confession from the Scriptures, teach by testimonies, and establish by divine utterances—removing the presumption of your own words—that you believe in the Church.

Let us take from the sacred books whatever must be believed; from their fountain the sequence of the Creed itself has flowed. Whoever believes in the Church believes in a human being. For it was not a human being who originated from the Church; rather, the Church began from a human being.

Depart, therefore, from this blasphemous persuasion, lest you think that you ought to believe in some human creature, since one ought not to believe even in an angel or an archangel.

The words that follow the name of the Holy Spirit in the Creed are received at the conclusion of the Creed with the preposition removed, so that we believe the holy Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. We believe in God—that is, we acknowledge that these things have been deposited by God and subsist in God.

For the ignorance of certain people has dragged and snatched this preposition, as though from the immediately preceding and neighboring sentence, into what follows, and unwisely added it unnecessarily. But in none of the canonical books on which the text of the Creed depends have we learned that we ought to believe in the Church as we believe in the Holy Spirit and the Son.

And therefore, since every creature is excluded from this honor, he in whom we are commanded to believe is God. [Col. 0011D] The Lord and Savior’s own speech specifically assigns this word to divinity, saying: “Believe in God, and believe in me.” And again: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John XIV, 10 and 12).

## Chapter II  
### Christ Was Not Begotten but Created by the Holy Spirit, Since the Spirit Is God

Since the catholic Church confesses, “He was conceived by the Holy Spirit,” the Macedonians must be asked at this point whether they consider the Holy Spirit the creator or the Father of the Redeemer.

If they should perhaps answer “the Father,” then, since at the beginning of the Creed they have already said, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” they will confusingly admit that Christ has two fathers.

But if they assert, as the truth requires, that the Spirit is the creator, they will necessarily be compelled to declare with us that he is God.

And therefore, through the prophet Isaiah, speaking as through his own trumpet and from his own temple, while foreshadowing two substances in Christ, he says: “Drop down, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the righteous one; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior. I, the Lord, created him” (Isaiah XLV).

For the human being assumed from Mary was the work of the Holy Spirit, not a portion of him; he was not begotten by the Spirit but created. He was conceived by power, not by substance; by operation, not by participation; by virtue, not by generation.

## Chapter III  
### On Establishing Unity through Prophetic Testimonies

[Col. 0012B] The catholic faith venerates a threefold Majesty under the confession of one divinity. Receive from the sacred books the testimony to one divinity.

“Hear, O Israel: The Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy VI). And: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.” In the Psalms: “You are God alone, doing wonders.” Again: “You alone are the Most High over all the earth.”

Also through Isaiah: “God of Israel, who sits upon the cherubim, you are the only God of all the kingdoms of the earth” (Isaiah XLV).

Again: “I am the Lord; I am the first and the last” (Isaiah XLI).

Again: “I am the Lord; this is my name. I will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah XLII).

To know that this testimony—“the first and the last”—belongs to Christ, he said of himself elsewhere: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII).

Again: “Before me there was no God, and after me there shall be none. I am the Lord, and there is no Savior besides me” (Isaiah XLIII). This specifically pertains to Christ, the Savior of the human race.

Again: “Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer and your Former from the womb: I am the Lord, making all things, stretching out the heavens, establishing the earth alone, and there is no one with me” (Isaiah XLIV). This pertains to Jesus and properly concerns him as Maker and Redeemer. Of him the evangelist recalls: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Again: “There is no God besides me, and there is no Savior apart from me” (Isaiah XLV).

Again: “I am the first and the last; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens” (Isaiah XLVIII).

As Jesus Christ clearly asserts elsewhere about himself, saying: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation XXI).

In these testimonies the Holy Spirit too is contained. In them the unity of the whole substance must be confessed in such a way that the distinct property of the persons and their undivided plurality are also believed to be present.

## Chapter IV  
### On the Trinity, and on How Even the Liberal Disciplines Have Treated of the Three Persons

Since we have shown the one divinity of the Word, let us now teach that there are three in the one Divinity: three names, not three kingdoms; three designations, but not three powers; three hypostases or subsistences, but not three substances.

Even secular wisdom has understood that the entire multitude of secular disciplines is contained within the account of three persons. What are these three? “I,” “you,” and “he.”

Thus, as we have said, even the liberal studies, borrowing instruction from spiritual disciplines, have perceived that there are only three persons in reality. It became evident to them that a second person does not satisfy perfection and that a third cannot be surpassed, because the fullness extending toward the number three proves duality to be incomplete, while perfection completed in three rejects a fourth.

Having passed over these matters with a brief reminder, let us support with sacred testimonies the Trinity as subsisting in unity “by change” (*mutatione*, reading uncertain).

But you say: “Why do you offer me the terms ‘unity’ and ‘Trinity,’ which you do not find in the canonical reading?”

It is not surprising that one who is not worthy to enter the inner sanctuary of salvation is frightened and recoils even from the testimony of truth. For what could be nearer, more natural, or more proper than that, concerning one, unity, and concerning three, Trinity, should first be named by catholic definitions?

Words that depend upon what precedes should not be examined in isolation, nor is it reasonable to declare foreign those terms that arise from “one” and “three,” that is, from the proper meaning of an evident beginning.

Notice that both these expressions are not presumptuous but derivative. Antiquity found these terms from the time of the primitive Church; authority brought them forth; long usage established them.

## Chapter V  
### When the Face of the Father Is Called the Son, He Is Acknowledged as Coeternal with the Father

Receive the Trinity from the sacred books.

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis I).

The Father is the author; the coeternal Beginning; the Holy Spirit is poured over the waters. The Spirit was borne over the waters as the eminence of the One who rules. Even then, I believe, he was symbolizing the gifts of baptism.

In the making of the human being, a threefold repetition of the Godhead demonstrates that the work belongs not to one person but to three. For we read:

“God said, ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.’”

Notice the sentence: simple in its proposal, multiple in its response.

“God said, ‘Let us make the human being.’”

What else does this mean but that the substance of unity speaks and the power of the Trinity acts?

Observe how the name of God is uttered three times in the creation of the human being. Thus we have in Genesis:

“God said, ‘Let us make the human being.’”

And again:

“God created the human being.”

And third:

“God blessed him.”

God said; God made; God blessed. On account of the three persons, the one divinity is repeated three times. Understand clearly at this point the mystery of the Trinity as well.

Behold, the image and likeness of God are given to each human being by three, and yet are recognized as one.

“God said, ‘Let us make.’”

Pay close attention: while one speaks and not one acts, and while again he mingles the plural with the singular, he does not say “according to our images and likenesses,” nor, on the other hand, “according to my image and likeness.” By singularity he commends unity; by plurality, the Trinity.

Thus, in saying, “Let us make the human being according to our image,” the number of the persons is expressed; in saying “according to the image and likeness” in the singular, the undivided divinity is gathered into one substance.

When God appeared to Abraham at the entrance of the tent (Genesis XVIII), and from one three presented themselves wondrously to his eyes, he, conscious of the Majesty, worshiped the One in the three.

In the Psalm also, unity is plainly designated in its persons: “Do not cast me away,” he says, “from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm L).

The Son is understood as the image of the Father and likewise as the face of the Father. Therefore we read: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV).

And again: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?”

Observe here the mystery of the perfect confession of faith in the Trinity. The prophet speaks to the Father; by the Father’s face he confesses the Son of the Father; and he also confesses the Holy Spirit, diffused through all things.

The Lord also speaks to Moses concerning the Son: “My face shall go before you” (Exodus XXXIII). This name—“face”—belongs both to the unity of substance and to the eternity of the Majesty.

But what of those who consider him lesser because he was born? What is it for God to be born from God except to exist naturally from God?

But you say: “If he is from him, he is younger.”

Consider: an arm is born from a body, and a face from its own body; yet the face is not thereby established as lesser than its head, nor the arm as later than its body.

If, therefore, any head has ever been found to be more ancient, then presume to assert that the Father is more ancient than his image, which consists in the perfect likeness and equality of Christ.

Thus the Son cannot be distinguished from the Father either in power or in time, just as the face cannot be separated from the head, nor can it in any way be found younger than its head.

## Chapter VI  
### The Spirit of the Father Is the Holy Spirit Himself

But you say: “Show me that the Holy Spirit subsists in his own essence. Whenever or wherever I read either ‘the Spirit of the Father,’ or ‘my Spirit,’ or ‘the Spirit of God,’ I see, you say, that it must refer not to the person of the Holy Spirit but to the person of the Father.”

First, such people heap blasphemy upon their own impiety when they say that one of two things must be believed: either that the Holy Spirit of God is a creature, or that he is the Father himself.

Deservedly, those who do not confess the Holy Spirit descend in their confused mind even to an insult against the Father. If he is a created work, he cannot belong to the substance of the Father. But if you think he is the Father’s power, how dare you abase him to the indignity of a created work?

We, however, shall demonstrate by clear testimonies that “the Spirit of God” is not spoken of the Father but properly of the Holy Spirit.

We read in Isaiah that the Holy Spirit of the Lord descended upon the Lord Jesus: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isaiah XI).

Concerning this Spirit of the Lord, who descended upon the Savior in a sacred visitation, the Son says through Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isaiah LXI).

And the evangelist Matthew says: “Behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove” (Matthew III).

That this Spirit of God, whom the Savior received in baptism, is clearly the Holy Spirit, the evangelist Luke fully demonstrated when he said: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke III).

We read in the prophet Joel: “In those days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II). The phrase “my Spirit” plainly refers to the Holy Spirit, because when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles at the sacred feast of Pentecost, the Apostle Peter asserted that this testimony had been spoken by the prophet.

The evangelists taught that this Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself, using different wording but with harmonious truth.

For when Matthew had said: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Acts II), Mark openly explained that this Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit, saying: “Whatever is given to you, that you shall speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.”

Luke likewise demonstrated that this Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit, saying: “Do not be anxious about how or what you should say. For the Holy Spirit will teach you at that hour what you ought to say.”

Accordingly, whenever you read either “the Spirit of the Father” or “the Spirit of God,” you must confess—once your error has been set aside—that the expression specifically refers to the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah also announced the one Holy Spirit in the glory of the Trinity when he says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, and the seraphim stood, and they cried out to one another: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth’” (Isaiah VI).

And afterward he says: “I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Go and say to this people: Hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; seeing you shall see and shall not see.’”

Who this Lord of Sabaoth was, who was seen by the prophet in an assumed form or who spoke through the prophet, the Apostle Paul showed in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers: ‘Hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; seeing you shall see and shall not see’” (Acts, final chapter).

Let us at least believe Paul, that most renowned herald of truth: the Holy Spirit was that God of hosts whom Isaiah saw and who spoke through Isaiah.

But since he resounds with a threefold repetition of “Holy, holy, holy,” let us see whether this honor refers to the Trinity.

When Isaiah says, “I saw the Lord of Sabaoth,” he is understood by the Jews to be proclaiming the Father.

The evangelist John is clearly shown to assert the Son, saying: “Therefore they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart’” (John XII; Isaiah VI). “Isaiah said these things when he saw the grace of the Son of God and spoke about him.”

But when the same Isaiah says, “I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Go and say to this people: Seeing you shall see, and shall not see,’” the Apostle Paul, as we have said, confirms that this Lord is the Holy Spirit.

You see, therefore, that the voice “Holy, holy, holy” celebrates the whole Trinity.

And just as in these three words there is no unlikeness and no difference, so in the truth of the Trinity there can be no disagreement.

## Chapter VII  
### On the Finger of God

But you say: “The Holy Spirit is recognized as lesser because he is called the finger of God.”

That is not so. When you hear it said concerning the Holy Spirit, “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God,” or “by the finger of God,” understand that the unity of substance, not a diminution of grace, is being demonstrated; it is not a discrepancy of honor but an agreement of work.

What then? Because the Holy Spirit is sometimes called a finger, is he therefore sometimes believed to be lesser than the Son and the Father?

Flee the error of this persuasion. See whether, in the designation “finger,” the Father and the Son are not also included on several occasions.

We remember that the reference is not to a single finger when we read: “For I see your heavens, the works of your fingers.”

But you say that in “fingers” only the Son and the Holy Spirit are signified, under a certain duality.

Do not attempt to assert this of two persons. Elsewhere Isaiah speaks in the plural number of fingers, saying—and thereby naming the Trinity: “Who hung the mass of the earth upon three fingers?” (Isaiah IV).

What could be more evident concerning the unity of the Trinity? What could be clearer? Did he not here weigh, on a certain scale of mystery, the equality of one power in three fingers?

Therefore, as has been said, since you have already been instructed concerning the fellowship of work, do not doubt the equality of power when he says: “Who hung the mass of the earth upon three fingers.”

At this point they specifically wish to speak of cooperation in power and unity of substance, which is proved to be one and the same in the three fingers.

Nevertheless, in Isaiah observe the distinct person of the Holy Spirit under the distinction of the Trinity.

Where the Son asserted concerning himself, saying, “I am the first, and I am the last,” he added immediately afterward: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah XLVIII).

The Lord the Father is therefore one person, and the Spirit of God the Father another. Thus, while the Son is read to have been sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit, it is clearly revealed under the name of three persons that the Holy Spirit subsists from himself, just as in another passage the same writer distinguishes the proper essence of the Trinity.

“Behold my servant; I shall receive him; my chosen one, my soul has been pleased with him; I have given my Spirit upon him” (Isaiah XLII).

The Father calls him his beloved servant, upon whom he gave his Spirit. Concerning him Jesus Christ testifies in his own voice: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke IV).

And so that this too might be evident to the nations, he says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew, final chapter).

Here, under the three persons, he asserts one work and one name, an undivided Majesty.

As has been said, according to Luke we have: “When Jesus had been baptized, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased’” (Luke III).

The Son is therefore declared in the body, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and the Father in the voice. But at this point we must understand the form of the dove as passing, not as a substance that remains.

## Chapter VIII  
### The Divinity of the Holy Spirit Is Not Impaired by the Fact That He Appears to Be Neither Begotten nor Unbegotten

But while in these matters we demonstrate the proper person of the Holy Spirit, confess the Father to be unbegotten, and recognize the Son as only-begotten, you ask me whether the Holy Spirit should be confessed to be unbegotten, begotten, or something else.

The sacred Scriptures speak of the power and divinity of the Holy Spirit; but whether he ought to be called begotten or unbegotten, they do not say.

See what darkness of unbelief such a person creates for himself. You do not wish to know what Scripture did not wish to leave unknown, and you wish to know what it did not command to be investigated.

It did not call him begotten, lest you believe him to be the Son; it did not call him unbegotten, lest you think him to be the Father. But, to distinguish his essence, it testified that he proceeds from the Father, as we read: “The Paraclete who proceeds from the Father.”

Since this is so, recognize at least in this way that the Holy Spirit possesses his own person. The difference of name proves him to be a third distinct from the other two; the unity of Majesty shows that, proceeding from God, he is not third in order or rank.

For he who proceeds from the inner being of God is proved to be not a creature of God but the substance of God.

Do not investigate how God is, when it is manifest that he is God. Here reason is hidden; truth is not hidden.

Why do you ask how he is the companion and equal of the King, when it is established that he belongs to the King’s honor and lineage?

Inquiry concerning the name is superfluous where there is no reason to doubt the sublimity.

Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; for this reason it says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

And elsewhere: “He breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’”

You ask whether he is unbegotten or begotten. The sacred utterances have sung nothing about this. It is impious to break through the divine silences.

What God did not consider necessary to disclose in his Scriptures, he did not wish you to disclose or know through superfluous curiosity. He indicated that what ought to reach your conscience is what pertains to your salvation.

Let us consult the sacred utterances concerning what you ought to believe about the Holy Spirit.

Would you dare to call it wrong that the Son was begotten, unless you had learned it from the heavenly testimony of the Scriptures? Or would you presume to assert that Christ the Lord was produced from a Virgin or begotten from a coeval and coeternal Father, unless you had drawn this from your reading, unless you had questioned the divine utterances concerning God?

And therefore, to know how you ought to agree concerning the Holy Spirit, you must return to the apostles and the Gospels, with whom and in whom you do not doubt that God has spoken.

To return, then, to your pointless proposition: what difference does it make for the grace or substance of the Holy Spirit whether he is proved unbegotten or begotten?

Nor does it detract anything from the Son that he is not read to be unbegotten, nor from the Father that he is not held to be begotten.

In such expressions there is a property of designation, not a difference of power or Majesty. “Begotten” and “unbegotten” express a difference of person, not of nature.

When, therefore, you have spoken or heard useless and unnecessary things about begotten and unbegotten matters—things suited only to accusations—will you be content to stop at this point?

Certainly you will go on to ask whether he is God.

Once you have accepted from what is written that he is true God, you will have nothing further to ask, because when you have begun to recognize things strong and complete, you will have no need to investigate things empty and vain.

Therefore, wherever the principle of usefulness and the fullness of truth are understood to be present, let your attention for salvation hang there.

## Chapter IX  
### The Holy Spirit Is the Perfecter and Bestower of Spiritual Gifts
The very name itself declares the Holy Spirit to be the giver of heavenly charisms and the dispenser of sanctifications. His magnificence is also manifest in the Old Testament. For there his grace was granted only to certain persons—namely, to patriarchs as well as prophets, and to holy and chosen men—so that through the perfection of the gifts themselves you might understand the dignity of the giver.

Yet, as is most clearly discerned in the sacred Scriptures, the Father himself works some things directly, others specifically through the Son, and still others through the Holy Spirit, although under the prerogative of a common power. That we exist seems properly to be referred to the Father, in whom, as the Apostle says, “we live and move and are.” But that we are capable of reason, wisdom, and justice is specially attributed to him who is reason, wisdom, and justice—that is, to the Son. But that we are called and regenerated, regenerated and renewed, renewed and sanctified, is plainly ascribed by the divine utterances to the person of the Holy Spirit.

Yet the sacred pages speak in this way with a distinction within the undivided Trinity, so that everyone may see a diversity of action in the individual persons while the unity of will nevertheless remains in all three. Thus both gentiles and catechumens participate in the dispensation of the Father and the Son, but they do not readily participate in the sanctification and infusion of the Holy Spirit unless they have already attained the most blessed state, been purified and made spiritual, and even become apostolic, prepared in their whole spirit for martyrdom.

And in the midst of all this, will he still be judged by the impious to be a creature who, within the indivisible Trinity, receives the more magnificent gifts and the more perfect blessings in the ordering of human salvation? But perhaps you will say: “The Holy Spirit is greater, because his works are greater.” It is not so. For it is the custom of the Trinity that, to whichever person it entrusts the office of administering a matter, to that person it ascribes the accomplishment; and although the work may perhaps be distinct, the purpose is common. Although something special is performed by each, the general plan remains in all three. Therefore, although they have a distinct task in the execution, they nevertheless maintain one agreement in the ordering.

After the Lord’s ascension, the Holy Spirit is described as having descended to increase and complete his benefits. Concerning him the Savior himself speaks through the Gospel according to John: “That Spirit of truth whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV). “The Father will send him,” he says, “in my name”—plainly referring to the Trinity. Of what creature have we ever read or heard that it came into this world in God’s name?

Therefore he of whom Christ the Lord God says, “Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John XVI), is without doubt God, since he is sent in the place of God to confirm God’s gifts. In these two statements, with the Trinity distinguished, the person of the Holy Spirit is also declared absolutely.

Not without reason, therefore, this too is referred to the equality of the Godhead: just as the Son, so also the Holy Spirit is called “Paraclete” in the Scriptures. And how shall we be able to prove this? Certainly by the authority of the apostle John, when he says: “If anyone among us should sin, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John I). The word *Paraclete*, that is, “advocate,” which refers to the person of the Son—or “comforter,” which refers to the Holy Spirit—is expressed by one Greek term and signifies both.

In John’s Gospel we read: “And I,” he says, “will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John XIV): “another Paraclete,” that is, one of similar power, glory with the Father, and the same nature.

“And another Paraclete.” If you think that the Holy Spirit is one of the creatures, it is unworthy that a creature descending with the same benefits which the Creator bestowed should confirm them, as though the Maker’s power were ineffective and the effect of the completed work were reserved for some creature—however excellent, but still merely a creature.

You therefore curse the Holy Spirit with the reproach of calling him a creature, although the Son of God has equated himself with him by divine testimony and by his own pronouncement: “And another Paraclete.” Here you will recognize a twofold meaning and a distinction of persons.

For this reason Christ appears to have equated himself with the Holy Spirit under the title “Paraclete.” For, according to you, Christ is the material of God’s work and a creature, since Jesus is proved to have been created from Mary; because of this unbelieving assertion, the argument is exceedingly weak.

For if you think that Christ was likened to the Paraclete according to his humanity, this too is inconsistent with charity. For he was made a little lower than the angels and became one of us; according to your claim, he could not rightly have been compared with the first and more excellent heavenly creature.

But if Christ spoke this according to the form of God, then it is certain that a work should not be compared with its maker. And if a human being equates himself with this more excellent creature, there is the arrogance of the lesser; if God does so, there is an insult to the greater.

Since, therefore, this comparison cannot be understood as consistent within the condition of creatures, it remains that both should be believed to be God and that the equality of divinity should be compared between them.

For when the Savior speaks through John—“And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (ibid.)—he who can be given to the whole world is manifestly the God of the world.

Here too recognize the triune power: the Father is the one indicated as being asked; the Son is the one understood to be asking; and the Holy Spirit is the one promised as to be sent by the Father.

Observe the person of the Holy Spirit: he is not, as you claim, associated merely with creatures akin to himself, but is joined in every work to the Trinity and equated with it in power.

## CHAPTER X. In the Acts of the Apostles the affirmation of the Trinity is repeated, and Christ is asserted to have been sent to grant repentance against the Novatians.

In the Acts of the Apostles, Peter, speaking about the Lord Jesus Christ, says: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this one whom you see and hear” (Acts II).

In “the right hand” the Son is designated; in “God the Father,” the Father; and in the distinctive name of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit. And in what follows we read: “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healed’” (Acts IV).

Here too perceive the distinction of the Trinity expressly set forth: Peter bears the Holy Spirit within himself, speaks of the Son dying in the flesh, and speaks of the Father raising him, in a further apostolic repetition.

“Everyone was filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts II). Observe also that in this passage the Holy Spirit is contained within the Trinity. In the prayer, the Father is asked; in the word of God, the Son is recognized; in the apostles’ steadfastness, the Spirit of fire is at work.

“Everyone,” he says, “was filled with the Holy Spirit.” It is the mark of manifest majesty to be able, through the subtlety of incorporeal divinity, to infuse many at once and to remain wholly intact without diminution.

Likewise, when the apostles had said of Jesus, “God exalted him by his right hand as prince and Savior, to grant repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins,” they add: “We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him” (Acts I).

Understand here, within the order of the Trinity, that the Son is sent by the Father not only to preach but also to grant repentance, while the Holy Spirit is infused into those who obey, to reward their obedience.

At the moment of his passion, Stephen is filled with the Holy Spirit, and when the gates of righteousness are opened, the Son is revealed at the Father’s right hand, as he himself declares when filled with the Holy Spirit: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

See how, under the spectacle of the Trinity, he displayed the gifts of his passion.

Peter addresses the centurion Cornelius, saying: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.” “God anointed him”—that is, power filled him, blessing infused him, divinity penetrated him. “How God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.”

These three clearly demonstrate their own properties: the gift, the giver, and the recipient of the gift; the anointer, the anointed, and the anointing. As the divine word says in another passage: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.”

In the man assumed by God, God is anointed and God anoints; and under the descent of the heavenly dove, the power of the Father is recognized. It is not permissible to believe that the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ the man is now filled with the Son of God, is anything other than God.

For if he were a creature, how could he penetrate a bodily nature while himself penetrating all things? The Trinity is capable of mutual indwelling, as it is said: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV). And again: “The Spirit searches even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. II). Likewise: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John XV).

Unless this Spirit were from the Father and naturally dwelt infused in the Father’s eternity, he could not proceed from the Father. But you ask whether the Spirit always proceeds from the Father. He is always with him, always from him; just as heat comes from fire, so he is continually brought forth in such a way that he knows how to go forth but does not know separation.

For if the procession of the Holy Spirit were not eternal, his substance would appear to be local. If one did not penetrate the other without mixture, through the incorporeal unity of their brightness, the divinity would be confused. Mixture removes the distinct property of the threefold essence; mutual infusion, however, displays a distinct essence, which may be seen as lying between substance and persons.

To substance belongs that which subsists; to persons belongs that by which each subsists in its own proper way.

Paul addresses his disciples, saying: “I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God. Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.”

How clearly the whole Trinity is designated through its persons! He announces the counsel of God the Father; he confirms that bishops have been ordained by the Holy Spirit; and he demonstrates that Christ is God, by whose blood the Church was acquired.

In the Epistle to the Romans, the Trinity is likewise arranged under the distinct properties of its names: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII).

The Father raises; the Son is raised; and because of the indwelling Spirit, life is promised for the resurrection of mortal bodies.

And in what follows: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”

When he says “the Spirit of God,” and subsequently “the Spirit of Christ,” observe that here he designates the person of Christ under the title “God.”

Or if here he signifies the Father, whose Spirit it is, under the designation “God,” behold: through the unity of substance, the Holy Spirit is declared to be the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. He is therefore rightly recognized as proceeding from both, and is seen to possess a distinct person within the bond of the Trinity. Moreover, whoever does not have the Holy Spirit is shown not to have Christ.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is God; and when he is denied, Christ too is denied, for he said: “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Whoever is empty of the Holy Spirit does not belong to Christ and loses the way by which one reaches the Father.

## CHAPTER XI. It is proper to God to sanctify the creature.

The First Epistle to the Corinthians says: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. VI).

Here too, under the expression “our God”—that is, under the mention of the Father—the Holy Spirit sanctifies the faithful Corinthians with Christ cooperating.

No creature can wholly sanctify another creature. The bestowal of sanctification is the munificence of majesty alone. In the words “in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God,” recognize three persons.

The Second Epistle to the Corinthians says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be always with you all” (2 Cor. ult.).

The grace of Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit plainly express three persons.

Again, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “But he who confirms us with you in Christ, and he who anointed us, is God; he also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. I).

Thus, in these works, he confirms the unity of the indivisible Trinity: he seals us specifically through Christ, and, intending to give himself, already gives the Holy Spirit in the present as a pledge.

In earthly transactions, the amount of earnest money is a certain portion of the contract for which it has been given. But the nature of a pledge exceeds the value of the thing for which it appears to be deposited. Here, however, since the pledge cannot be considered inferior to the majesty, it must necessarily be equal to it. For nothing perfect can be surpassed.

Therefore the Father grants the Holy Spirit as his pledge. Nothing in the Holy Spirit, then, should ever be thought half-full or more than full; he is to be thought full, because he is compared with fullness. For he who is given in the place of God as a pledge cannot rightly be believed to be anything other than God.

Again, to Titus: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ” (Titus III).

Here too, under the Trinity, the Father plainly poured out the abundance of the Holy Spirit through the Son. And what must especially be observed is that he ascribes to the Holy Spirit himself the power of regeneration and renewal.

Peter too, in his Epistle, explains the invincible Trinity in its persons, saying: “According to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ: grace and peace be multiplied to you” (1 Pet. I).

In foreknowledge, the Father is shown; in sanctification, the Spirit; in the sprinkling of blood, Christ.

## CHAPTER XII. The Holy Spirit is not local.

Let us demonstrate from his powers and works that the Holy Spirit is God. Every creature, just as it is subject to the beginnings of time, is known to be local, circumscribed by definite spaces and boundaries. The Holy Spirit is not confined by any limits like a created thing; by the very freedom of his diffused majesty, he must be regarded as God.

The voice of the Lord and Savior to the apostles says: “The Father will give you,” he says, “the Spirit of truth, that he may be with you forever.” If he is local and remained perpetually among them, he could certainly not be elsewhere.

Let us see whether his nature is to be defined by local boundaries. The Lord says to the apostles: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I).

After his ascension, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them.

Let us see why they were first granted blessings in different languages: clearly, so that they might be made capable of instructing the peoples of the faithful. But the fact that he is remembered as having rested upon each individual has this purpose: that it may be understood that he was not divided among the many, but remained wholly in each.

It is the nature of burning fire—as we know—that however many look toward it, however many gaze upon the crest of its purple radiance, to that many it imparts the use of its light and grants the service of its gift, while nevertheless remaining intact in itself.

Thus, however much the power of the Holy Spirit may flow out, however abundantly the divine grace of his generosity may overflow among the many, just as he is proved to receive no measure, so he experiences no expenditure.

Recognize God from the excellence of his works. The apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit and about to distribute the treasures of salvation throughout the whole world, carry this heavenly gift within themselves and transfer it to others by the laying on of hands. It is given to those who receive it without loss to the giver. It is handed over whole to believers and possessed whole by those who hand it over. By its infusion the whole world is filled; it expands without being diminished and is distributed without division.

On that most sacred night of regeneration, from east to west, from the rising of the sun to its setting, from the north and from the sea—in every place—the same Spirit, one and complete, works. He is present everywhere, believed in through invocation and experienced through blessing. Countless multitudes are washed in one baptism and, as the Apostle said, “drink of one Spirit”; they are reborn into the one embrace of the one who adopts them.

And therefore God said: “In those days I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh.” Observe that he said, “I will pour out from my Spirit,” and did not say, “I will pour out my Spirit”—that is, he dispenses from him as much as the world is able to receive.

You see that he proceeds from the Father, yet is not separated from the Father; he is sent forth, yet not lost; he is poured out, yet retained. And in the fact that he is said to be poured out, the greatness of his fullness is declared.

The Book of Genesis testifies at the beginning of the sacred volume: “But the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters; he was borne,” it says, “over the waters” (Gen. I). The expression itself appears to assign the abundance of one who fills all things and the supremacy of one who rules.

It celebrates this same distinctive magnificence of his, circumscribed by no spaces, with equal testimony, saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Ps. CXXXVIII)—that is, “Where shall I hide myself from the sight of him whom I do not doubt to be present everywhere, both within and without; whose eye, penetrating the depths, I dread within the secrets of my heart; whose presence I know to be subject to all that he created?”

Since he is a consuming fire, understand clearly what has been said: “There is no one who can hide from his heat” (Ps. XVIII). His ineffable greatness enters, fills, and surpasses the depths of the underworld, the expanses of the waters, the breadth of the earth, and the heights of heaven.

He is said to be sent by the Father and the Son, to proceed from their substance, and to perform one work with them; and therefore the Son says of him: “The Paraclete who proceeds from the Father” (John XV).

He did not say, “who was created by the Father,” but “who proceeds from the Father”—that is, from the fellowship of the Father’s power and from the property of his nature.

But from the very statement that he is said to proceed from the Father, it is shown that he does not have a beginning together with the Father.

What, then, is the distinction between the Son’s being said to be born from God the Father and the Holy Spirit’s being signified as proceeding? If you ask what differs between one who is born and one who proceeds, the difference is plainly this: the one is born from one, while the other proceeds from both.

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, this displays three privileges of divinity in him: that he is proved to subsist in his own person, to remain without any interval of time, and to exist wholly from the substance of the Father.

When he is therefore said to proceed, he is understood, by the very property of the expression, not to be circumscribed by any laws of time but to lack both beginning and end.

And because we read, “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me” (Exod. III), the same is indicated by “he proceeds.” For being and proceeding express one and the same eternity.

Therefore procession itself, touching neither a first nor a final point, is understood to be subject neither to any beginning nor to any limit.

We do not, then, believe that he is local merely because we have learned from Scripture that he is sent by the Father. For we also read of the Father and the Son that, as if by a certain movement, they descend and come.

Let us see where. “I,” he says, “and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). And again, when the giants were attempting to raise a tower to heaven, the person of the Father speaks: “Come, and let us confuse their languages” (Gen. XI).

Here, therefore, through the sounds of our words, the efficacy of realities is demonstrated to our senses. But divine power does not undergo local movement: it does not arrive through an advancing course, nor depart through a retreating motion. Since it surpasses all things, where could it withdraw?

From the reading of Scripture we have learned concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Church throughout all Judea had peace, walking in the fear of the Lord, and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit” (Acts IX).

How, then, does anyone presume to assert that he is a local creature, when he is proved to fill the Church of an infinite multitude, so that what the Apostle says may also clearly pertain to him: “The Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (1 Cor. I)?

We have in the Psalm: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV). What is this rushing of the river except that of which the Lord speaks through John: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly for the one who believes in me”? The Lord Jesus said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were about to receive (John I).

Observe the magnificence of his majesty. He is granted on earth to the Church of God, yet he makes glad in heaven the city of God—that is, the citizens of the heavenly kingdoms, the peoples of the heavenly host, principalities, powers, and dominions. He waters them with ineffable joys according to their consciousness of eternal blessedness, drenches them still more abundantly with the overflowing richness of joy, and awakens heaven’s harmony in exultation through the torrent of his sanctification.

If you think that these things can be bestowed through some creature, you leave nothing proper to divine power. If, I say, you suppose that these things are accomplished through some creature, you move toward an insult to the angels and archangels, since you think that such great and such gifts are bestowed through the generosity of a fellow servant.

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER I. No rational creature can be infused into a creature akin to itself.

We read concerning the overflowing outpouring of the Holy Spirit: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.” Who, then, could fill the one who fills all things, unless he were of the same fullness?

The divine word reports concerning the apostles: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with confidence.” And shortly afterward:

For he is also shown to fill entire nations, and to remain inexhaustible and full in himself.

If the Spirit was created, of what angel or archangel has it ever been read that he infused himself into any soul by being received inwardly? Tell me whether you have ever read of any power or force among created things that fills and possesses many at once and, what is more, remains undiminished and undivided.

It is impossible for a spiritual and rational creature ever to be infused into a nature akin to itself. Thus a material thing does not know how to penetrate a material substance.

God alone—in whom the Holy Spirit is also understood—simple, subtle, and pure, enters by the power of incorporeal divinity into either an angelic or a human creature. He alone penetrates his own work and enters the hidden places of the human heart.

But no heavenly creature can infuse or fill a human being to such an extent that it can know the hidden thoughts of the human mind. And therefore we read of God alone: “You alone know the hearts of human beings” (Prov. VI). And again: “He himself knows how to discern hidden things.” If this is proper to divinity, how much more is searching the deep things of the Most High God, in the person of the Holy Spirit, a mark of majesty?

This privilege is owed to the Creator alone: that he can enter the secret conscience.

A soul can be joined to a soul, and an angel to an angel, but it cannot be infused into one, because such classes of creatures are capable only of the Spirit—that is, of God alone. For they are vessels of their potter; they can be filled only by him by whom they were made from nothing and without whom they are perceived to be empty.

Thus the substance of the soul, being corporeal matter, does not know how to be infused into another rational creature at all. Compared with the thickness of the external human being, the soul may be called incorporeal; but when referred to its Creator, to whom its matter is comprehensible and its workmanship tangible, it can be enclosed and bound within the body and handed over to eternal fire, as we read: “They will go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

To this undoubted Creator belongs what the corrupt reading appears to mean by *perfectoris in re corporea est* (“[the work] of one who perfects in corporeal reality”); the precise syntax is uncertain.

But perhaps you say: “It is evident that the intrusive violence of demons also frequently infuses itself into human beings whom it has received for testing.” It is not so. For they can enter the hiding places of the body, but they cannot reach the interior of the soul.

It must therefore be understood that the deceitful subtlety of spiritual wickedness disturbs by its assault those parts of the limbs that are sometimes exhausted by excessive wine or inflamed by the burning of fever.

Thus the hostile temptation knows how, through wickedness, to creep into the perceptions of the soul, but by nature it does not know how to flow into the soul’s inner recesses.

Therefore such unclean spirits do not seize human minds and hearts by an infusion of their natures; rather, they are conceived there through the perversity of wills.

It is thus clear that they cannot penetrate the substances of souls, whose consciences they cannot know. And if it has occasionally happened that demons have come to know something about us, this results from an association with perdition, not from the power of their nature.

Therefore divine power alone—which is also in the Holy Spirit—is infused into and mingles with rational creatures, as it rested in a singular way, through overflowing grace, in the body of that Lordly man received from Mary his mother, just as the Son says of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke IV).

If the Holy Spirit were a creature subject to the created order, as they claim, it would be both impossible and unworthy of God for any creature to fill a soul or body in which the Son of God, that is, God, was already present, in which, as the Apostle says, “the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II).

If the Holy Spirit is a creature, how can corruption possess incorruptibility, or a fragile created condition possess that which is capable of majesty?

If the Holy Spirit is one of the common mass of created things, how can a creature be presumed to be equated with the Creator—that is, with the Son of God? How can a servant share one dwelling in the Savior’s soul with the Lord, as though the presence of the author were not sufficient in him and a servant had to be added to increase his sanctification?

It is not so. But in reality he recognizes as his companion the heavenly fellowship that is his temple. Nor is it surprising that, in that illustrious and blessed body and soul, the Son and the Holy Spirit receive one dwelling, since heaven too is acknowledged to be common to them.

## CHAPTER II. Whether, according to the opinion of the ignorant, the Holy Spirit was incarnated like the Son, since he too came upon Mary; or whether only the Son was born from the Virgin.

But it is said: “If the Holy Spirit dwelt in the body and soul of the redeemed, then he too will appear to have assumed an incarnation.”

It is not so. For before the beginnings of creation, Mary’s body is filled by the Holy Spirit; and at the beginnings of creation the Virgin’s Son is conceived with the Holy Spirit cooperating. But the Holy Spirit is possessed for nine months specifically in relation to the person of the Son, and is infused as the Son himself proceeds into the light. The person of the Holy Spirit does not share that period within the secret place of the virgin womb.

The Holy Spirit entered the human being whom the Son of God assumed from the very beginning not as one who assumed him, but as one who sanctified him. The one is born; the other is infused.

The soul or flesh of the Virgin’s Son may personally and specifically be called the soul or flesh of the Son of God. But the Holy Spirit can in no way be called soul or flesh.

For this reason the Son is called “the God of glory crucified”; it cannot in any way be said that the Holy Spirit suffered crucifixion in him.

Therefore the works are diverse, not the substances. For just as we cannot say that the Father descended in the form of a dove, or that the Son spoke in the Father’s voice when he said, “This is my Son” (Matt. III), so you cannot assert that the Holy Spirit was born from the Virgin, or dwelt specifically in the flesh of the Redeemer, or was crucified in his passion, or was restored to the body in the resurrection, or was exalted to heavenly things in the ascension.

These things necessarily and properly belong to the work and person of the Son. To ascribe them to the Holy Spirit, while preserving the unity of will, is nevertheless improper.

In the midst of all this Macedonius asserts that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Let him therefore show where he begins, provided that he does not presume to accomplish anything by his own words, nor go beyond the holy pages in his argument, but, if he can, produce authority in every respect from testimonies that prevail against the faith of the whole world both in number and in force.

Without doubt, great, abundant, and exceedingly clear proofs are required for anyone to establish that he is one of the creatures whom all the kingdoms of the earth, together with the Father and his Son, celebrate with the same honor and glory, and whom the Catholic Church, regenerated in him, recognizes as her Creator.

And rightly: when she sees him as her restorer, she does not hesitate to believe him her author.

## CHAPTER III. Macedonius’ objection, by which he impiously asserts the Holy Spirit to be a more excellent creature.

“I say that he is a creature,” he says, “but more excellent than all creatures.”

We have already stated that we should base our argument not on personal persuasions but on catholic testimonies. Therefore, as we discuss God, let the prophet, the apostle, and the evangelist answer.

You say that he is a creature more excellent than all creatures. Show in which books you have read such words about the Holy Spirit. I do not think you will teach this from the ancient books, nor from the new ones.

Since, then, you cannot produce such evidence, while you fail to explain your own position, we confirm ours. By failing to establish that he is a creature, even while we remain silent you demonstrate that he is the Creator.

Therefore, since this assertion of yours does not belong to catholic understanding and does not belong at all to Christian teaching, recognize it as a device of the devil. When he sees the soul empty of the Holy Spirit, he begrudges the soul its gift, as though it belonged to hostile guests of sevenfold wickedness.

Whoever excludes him receives this one.

That more excellent creature existed in the one who, shining with heavenly brightness and conscious of his own rank but ignorant of his Creator, saw that he possessed but did not understand that he had received. Therefore he lost, through exaltation, the glory that he did not understand in blessedness, saying: “I will ascend above the stars of the clouds; I will place my seat upon the throne, and I will be like the Most High.”

He therefore had no one superior to himself among creatures, as I suppose; he saw no one between himself and God against whose rivalry he might rise, driven on by the spur of pride. And so, seeing no one standing before him in the order of the heavenly host, he presumed to make himself equal to the very Lord of all things.

If he had discovered anyone superior to himself, unable to endure a greater in the heavenly joy, he would have tried either to associate himself with that one or to place himself above him.

There are two in the heavenly realm: the one who rules and those who are ruled. No third kind existed between these, greater than the second and lower than the highest.

Perhaps you can say that the more excellent creature was one of the archangels, although they surpass the others more in rank than in nature. But the archangels too serve the Holy Spirit; one of them, as his minister, announced his blessed coming to Mary.

But you say: “Behold where the prophet Amos clearly identifies the Holy Spirit as a creature, saying: ‘Behold, I am the one who establishes thunder and creates spirit’” (Amos IV).

First, the word “spirit” can by no means always be referred to the person of the sanctifying Spirit unless you add either “Spirit of God,” or “Holy Spirit,” or “the spirit blows where it wills”—that is, unless you add either the dignity of the work or of the proper name.

Furthermore, if you consider the order of the passage, this more excellent creature, as you assert, is shown to be held in very low esteem. For Amos described it as coming after the creation of thunder. It would therefore be inconsistent with your interpretation for him to subordinate this principal work of God to an irrational element or to associate it with such an element.

I will not speak of the person of an angel, but it would be unworthy to believe this even of any righteous person.

It is therefore more reasonable and more consistent to understand, after the thunder, the blasts signified by the winds, as in the Psalms: “The spirits of storms that do his word” (Ps. CXLVIII); or: “Sulfur and the spirit of storms” (Ps. X); or: “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. XLVII).

“Spirit” is understood in different ways when it is not specially designated with its own privileges.

But setting these matters aside, consult the truth of the Hebrew translation, and there you will discover the manifest error of your confused argument. For there you will find that it is said: “Behold, I am the one who forms the mountains and creates the wind.”

See how little you believed, with words nakedly opposed to God and wholly empty. See with what great an argument you armed yourself against the power of majesty; and after that, you are not afraid to cling to so weak a twig, hanging over so dreadful a precipice.

## CHAPTER IV. Macedonius, asserting a duality, denies that the Holy Spirit has a distinct person.

[Col. 0028D] Next you introduce duality and say that the Holy Spirit does not possess a distinct person, nor do you realize that you have forfeited the grace of regeneration, since you are moving toward an offense against regeneration. Divine truth declares him united with the Father and the Son in majesty and power, saying:

“Go,” he says, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” “In the name,” he says, “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. ult.). The singularity of the name speaks of unity; the diversity of the designations speaks of the Trinity. Thus, there is one in name, but in the distinction of persons, not one.

What is the prerogative of one name in three persons except the undivided harmony of the Godhead? Advance, if you can, to the point where, with God himself bearing witness, you find nothing other than the One. You hear “three,” lest Sabellian impiety mingle and confuse the unity. You hear “one,” lest Arian perversity divide the Trinity. You hear “Holy Spirit,” so that the expressly distinctive propriety of the name may pierce Macedonius.

Therefore the work being carried out is not that of a creature but of the Creator, where the abolition of sins and release from guilt are bestowed. Yet within this indivisible embrace of majesty, in the propriety of person, the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; but in unity there is no otherness. Indeed, if he were not God, he could not possess a distinct person alongside the Father and the Son.

Accordingly, when the Word passes into flesh, and God assumes the form of a human being, and “his tent is round about him,” and he wraps his splendor in the darkness of our weakness, and “makes darkness his hiding place” [Col. 0029B], there is indeed a twofold substance of God and man, but nevertheless one person. Why is this? Because, when God takes the form of a servant and is joined to a servant, the humility of the lesser is hidden within the reverence due to the greater, and is consumed by the light of the superior, who has emptied himself; thus humanity does not retain the propriety of person when divinity overshadows or surpasses it.

Equality of persons can therefore exist wherever there is equality of merits and dignities. For this reason, know that the Holy Spirit possesses, with the Father and the Son, the one privilege of majesty, while you see him possessing the distinct right of a person.

But if someone objects and says, “If in Christ, God and man alike, we speak of two substances, why should we not similarly believe in two persons?”—the matter is not so. For whoever makes two persons in Christ introduces the impiety of a quaternity [Col. 0029C], which the nature of things utterly rejects.

From two rational and different substances—especially those of God and man, of Creator and creature—one substance cannot be made; but from two persons one can be made, just as we read that the head and the body, Christ and the Church, constitute one person: “The two shall be one flesh.” And just as among us human beings a son has no position as a distinct person alongside the father of the household, nor a servant alongside his master, so in God and man there is indeed a twofold substance but not a twofold person, because person can absorb person, whereas substance cannot absorb substance. For person is a matter of legal status, while substance is a matter of nature.

At this point it seems necessary to assert, by testimonies, both the one person of Christ the Lord, God and man alike, and his two substances [Col. 0029D]. Grant the one person of the Redeemer, God and man. The Apostle says: “For if they had known the wisdom of God, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

If you ask how the inviolable one could suffer and the incomprehensible one be crucified, the unity of person makes it possible for what the man endured to be believed to have been endured by God.

Likewise, when the Evangelist recalls, “No one has ascended except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven,” how does he here say that the Son of Man descended from heaven before the day of his passion, resurrection, or ascension, and assert that he remains in the heavenly realms, unless the reasoning of truth resolves this through the unity of person?

Similarly, the person of the head and body is joined when we read: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” [Col. 0030A]. What does the unity of person say? The man is fed, and God is refreshed. The foot is treated, and the head declares that it feels the soothing care.

He therefore says, “They would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” And conversely: “No one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” See how, through the unity of person, human things are mingled with divine and divine things with human. God is crucified, and the man is remembered as descending from heaven and remaining in heaven.

Since this is so, let us discern from the sacred books the distinction of the twofold substance. Blessed Moses says: “You shall eat it with its head and its feet, and you shall devour its entrails” (Exod. XII). Let us believe that humanity is signified in the feet and majesty in the head. Thus, while by searching faith we recognize what lies hidden within the letter [Col. 0030B], we take in the fire of the entrails—that is, the hidden things of the mysteries. For the zeal of searching signifies an eagerness to devour.

Likewise, elsewhere the same revealer of the sacraments indicates the explanation of the twofold substance, saying: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). This means that deceitful heresies and dark or aerial powers have established seats for themselves in human hearts through profound condemnation. But they do not believe that I, who see the man in the flesh, am God hidden within the man. For “dens” and “nests” designate not transient and momentary dwellings, but habitations founded upon a lasting and secure possession, which multiply the nourishment of serpent-like vices.

The Apostle, removing the obscurity of the mystery, clearly added the two substances, saying: “The fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever.”

But you say: “The Apostle confesses only two persons throughout his writings,” as when he speaks to the Corinthians: “Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God.” And to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” And again: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him.”

On this basis you say that no mention is made of the Holy Spirit. To put it briefly, you have forgotten that the Apostle, full of the Holy Spirit, proclaimed these things about the Father and the Son under the Spirit’s inspiration [Col. 0030D]. Therefore, when he spoke of the operation of the Father and the Son, the one who dictated what was to be spoken was not absent, according to the statement: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

You see, then, that whoever is going to believe in, confess, or preach Christ must first have the Holy Spirit within him. Do not therefore commend your argument merely because the Father is sometimes mentioned together with the Son without mention of the Holy Spirit. Often, with the Father’s name suppressed, the operation of the Son and the Holy Spirit is proclaimed.

Saint Ananias says to Paul: “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, sent me so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Here the connection of two persons is plainly evident. Paul is struck blind by Christ, illuminated and filled by the Holy Spirit, and no mention of the Father is inserted here.

Likewise, when Paul questioned certain disciples, asking, “In what were you baptized?”—it was established that after the Lord’s ascension they had been baptized in John’s baptism. After the baptism of the Trinity had been preached, it was also shown that the mystery in which John was accustomed to baptize, namely, baptism into the one who was to come, had been omitted from their baptism. The Apostle Paul says: “John indeed baptized, but into the one who was to come” (Acts XIX). That is to say: You were not baptized in this manner.

When Paul asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”—these men, who had indeed been rightly baptized after the Savior’s baptism through the laying on of hands, confessed. But they replied: “We have not even heard whether there is a Spirit.” On hearing this, they were baptized [Col. 0031B] in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.

Observe that, when they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, they afterward receive the Holy Spirit and prophetic power through invocation of the Paraclete. Truly he is God who, after God’s gift, places the proof of fullness upon it.

Behold: although two persons are signified in baptism, the Father is not read to have been invoked, but only—as must be believed—to have acted with the Son and the Holy Spirit in unity of power and Godhead. Sacred Scripture has not denied that he was present.

When the Holy Spirit came upon them, they then spoke in tongues and prophesied. See how great is the power of the Holy Spirit. In baptism the remission of sins is granted; at the coming of the Holy Spirit the gifts of virtues are bestowed [Col. 0031C], and by those who have been confirmed the miracles of signs are performed.

Those who are strangers to the truth are accustomed to attack even syllables. For although we know that it was said absolutely of the Trinity, “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. VIII), they assert that “from him” signifies something greater than “through him,” and likewise that the preposition “through” possesses a greater prerogative than “in him.”

But if they think that “in him,” when said of the Holy Spirit, implies a diminution of power, let them hear the magnificence of this preposition and recognize that, even according to their own assertion, it must be understood of the Holy Spirit. “In him,” it says, “we live and move and are” (Acts XVII). And rightly do we live, move, and exist in him in whom we have been restored and regenerated.

But we also acknowledge that “through him” must be referred to the Holy Spirit, as you have it: “To one, through the Spirit, is given the utterance of wisdom; to another, the utterance of knowledge” (I Cor. XII). Likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God.” And again: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”

For if we understand this also of the Father, we find that “from him” and “from the Holy Spirit” are similarly spoken, as we have in the Gospel of John: “What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the Spirit is spirit” (John III). And at the conclusion of the chapter: “So is everyone who is born from the Spirit.”

Thus the Holy Spirit is not prejudiced when the works of the Father and the Son are mentioned with his name suppressed, just as the Father and the Son are not denied when the work [Col. 0032A] and power of the Holy Spirit are specifically asserted, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts I).

Likewise, in the Gospel, concerning the singular person of the Holy Spirit, it is stated: “Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III). Should the Father and the Son be thought to have been absent from this great and divine gift merely because they are not named here? It is not so. For unquestionably, while they are joined in mysteries and benefits to the Holy Spirit, with whom they have one substance, they are present not by mention but by unity of devotion and operation.

## CHAPTER V. Objection that the saying we read—“Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit”—also testifies that water and the Holy Spirit are creatures

[Col. 0032B] But you say: “The Holy Spirit is so much a creature that, according to the Gospel sentence mentioned above, he appears to be joined to the element of water, which is placed first in order: ‘Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God’ (ibid.).”

It is clear that the person who says this knows not only nothing of the divine power in the Holy Spirit but also nothing of the meaning of baptism.

The Apostle says: “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ” (Rom. VI). But if you ask how we can die and rise with Christ, pay attention.
