All who are submerged in the sacred font imitate the death and burial of the Redeemer, as the same Apostle says [Col. 0032C]: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. IX).

As he was laid in the tomb for three days by death, so we, deposited within the water—that is, within the substance of a related creature—are buried when we descend through the threefold immersion and raised when we emerge. Through water, therefore, the imitation of burial is celebrated; through the Holy Spirit, the reality of life and the hope of eternal salvation are bestowed.

Finally, let the invocation of the Holy Spirit be removed, and let us see whether the pouring of that water alone can accomplish anything. The creature, then, provides the service of burial; God is the one who grants the benefit of rebirth. Recognize, therefore, that the one whom you see as the parent of restoration is himself the author of resurrection.

Of him the prophet foretells and speaks to the Father: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. CIII). What difference is there between the operation of water and that of the Holy Spirit? Through water we seem to be led into the tomb; through the Holy Spirit we seem to be prepared for the kingdom.

## CHAPTER VI. Where it is asked whether the designation “Holy Spirit” should be considered a surname or a name

But amid these matters you think it necessary to ask whether the designation “Holy Spirit”—whom it is necessary to call God—is a name or perhaps a surname. Recognize, however, that what we customarily add to a human name does not suit the majesty of God. In his name, whatever it is, there is nothing adventitious; it is unquestionably eternal by nature.

Even grammatical instruction calls some names common, that is, appellative, and others particular, that is, proper. Let us see whether we can find something similar in our present subject.

Grant a particular or proper name in God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These are so proper that the Son cannot be called Father, nor is the Holy Spirit readily read as being called Father. Likewise, grant as proper names “unbegotten” and “proceeding from both.”

Now, in turn, grant a general and common name: majesty, immensity, fullness, one, alone, God. But when you hear “one,” number does not begin here; rather, infinite perfection is gathered together. What is “one” except an incommunicable name, which admits neither a later nor an earlier? What is “one” except a simple, uncompounded, and undivided substance? What is “one” except something incommunicable and unequal, always the same, which can never be different from itself?

Thus the common designation expresses unity. When you say “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit,” you have equally explained the persons of each. When you say “one God,” you have demonstrated the common substance and common glory of the Trinity.

Here, then, ignorance has covered itself with the night of error, because, suppressing the term for majesty, it thinks that the Holy Spirit is designated only by the name that, as we have said, is proper to him, rather than by what he shares with the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER VII. That the Holy Spirit specially fills the prophets and is proved, by clear testimonies, both to be believed and to be called God

When it is reported that the Holy Spirit specifically spoke through Moses, David, Isaiah, and the other prophets, the divine utterances declare that God spoke, as is frequently found in the Pentateuch: “The Lord spoke,” it says, “to Moses, saying.”

Let us inquire more carefully whether the Holy Spirit specifically speaks in the prophets. We have, as we said above, in the Acts of the Apostles, Paul reproving the Jews: “Well,” he says, “did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah to our fathers: ‘You shall hear with hearing and shall not understand’” (Acts ult.).

And in the same reading: “Brothers, it was necessary that the Scripture should be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David” (Acts I). And in Peter’s Epistle we read: “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke through the Holy Spirit” (II Pet. I).

Let us recognize that prophetic grace clearly belongs to the power of the Holy Spirit. Concerning a psalm of David, we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice’” (Ps. XCIV). Here too it most openly testifies that the Holy Spirit spoke through David.

Let us see, however, whether this one through whom all prophecy is remembered as inspired is God. Luke asserts that it is the Lord God who spoke through the prophets, saying: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.” And he added: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from the beginning.”

The Gospel oracle expressly celebrates the Holy Spirit who inspired the prophets as the Lord and God of Israel [Col. 0034A]. And later Simeon, full of the Holy Spirit, says: “He received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord” (Luke II).

When he had seen him and taken him into his arms, he blessed God—that is, the one from whom he appeared to have received the answer. He blessed God and said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.” He plainly calls the Holy Spirit, by whose word and answer he had received the promise that he would see Christ, the Lord God.

You see that the Holy Spirit must be understood specifically when it is said in the prophets: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken”; and, “I shall hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. XLIX).

Here, in this name, that is, “Lord,” by whose word and answer he had received that he would see Christ, you see that the Holy Spirit must specifically be understood when it is said in the prophets: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken”; and, “I shall listen to what the Lord God speaks within me.”

Here, recognize that this name, “Lord God,” must be referred to the person of the Holy Spirit, who spoke in David—or else recognize in the one God the will, power, and substance of the three. For when you say “Father,” one person is understood; when you say “God,” the whole Trinity is designated.

We also receive in the Acts of the Apostles the unequivocal statement that it was God who foretold Christ’s sufferings through the prophets, when it says: “But God, who announced through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, thus fulfilled his Christ” (Acts III), that is, the one infused with the gift of his anointing.

And again: “God, who spoke through the mouth of his holy ones” (Luke I). “His holy ones,” because sanctification properly belongs to the Holy Spirit.

We read in Jeremiah: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jer. XXVI). Who is this Lord who says through Jeremiah that he fills heaven and earth, except the Holy Spirit, who also infused Jeremiah himself with prophetic power and the Spirit of truth?

If, then, through the prophetic dispensation—and likewise, most especially, through the grace of the second birth—the will of the Trinity assigns this work to the Holy Spirit, as it says in John: “What is born from the flesh is flesh, and what is born from the Spirit is spirit”; and if elsewhere the power of renewing humanity is recorded as belonging to the Holy Spirit: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now” [Col. 0034D]; and, as was said above, “Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit”; and in Titus: “He saved us through the bath of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit”—let us see who this one is whose children we become through the grace of adoption.

“He gave them,” it says, “the power to become children of God.” And again: “Who were born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God.” You see most clearly that this Holy Spirit in whom we are reborn is God, whose fatherhood is bestowed upon us.

He himself assigns this elsewhere even more clearly: “I shall be their father, and they shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord almighty” (Titus I). Rightly is he called almighty: he erases the record of sin, loosens the bonds of consciences, strips the person who believes in him of the filth of corrupt nature, adorns him with the garment of innocence, the beauty of righteousness, and the robe of immortality, and enrolls his children, through loving fatherhood, among the angelic order.

Let no one think that the Holy Spirit should be associated with creatures. He is outside the condition of servitude, since he can grant eternal freedom. For the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, and that Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VI).

Without doubt he is God who, through the remission of sins, makes human beings children of God. It is established that the whole creation, including angels and archangels, was subject to sin; yet their obedience, diligence, and love toward God were founded upon the ruin of the transgressors. Their humility in submission became confirmation of stability; recognition of weakness became the Holy Spirit.

Unless he were free above all, he could not make the enslaved free. For if he were a creature, even though he might confer the grace of holiness, the consciousness of indebtedness would nevertheless remain. Therefore it says: “No one can forgive sins except God alone” (Mark II; Luke V).

Whoever he is, let him choose which he wishes: either let him confess that the Holy Spirit, who forgives sins, is God in every respect, or, if he does not believe that forgiveness of sins can be granted through him, let him empty out in himself the benefit of regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.

To God alone, therefore, belongs the power to release what is bound, restore what is corrupted, and cleanse what is stained. And so, conscious of our weakness and his majesty, we cry out to him with a groan: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. L), Lord, who alone are not held under the law of sin, who alone are not subject to it—not merely in action but by nature—and therefore alone can absolve debtors, since you alone are free from debts, and what you possess you have not borrowed elsewhere but possess in fullness from yourself.

No one gave to you first; you are not watered by virtues derived from elsewhere, nor has any infusion been transferred into you from another. You yourself are the fountain of your stream, and your glory is your nature. Just as you know no messenger, so you have received nothing from one who preceded you (John XIV; Rom. VIII; Luke XVII).

## CHAPTER VIII. Where it is demonstrated that the temple of God is the temple of the Holy Spirit

The sacred writings specifically define the Holy Spirit as the inhabitant of the human heart: “The Father,” it says, “will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever” (I Cor. III; I Cor. VI). And to the Romans: “He will give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.”

Therefore we rightly understand the following to have been written about the Holy Spirit: “The kingdom of God is within you.” Those who deserve to obey him are indeed the kingdom of God; they are the temple of God, not of a creature.

Hear through the Apostle the voice of our inhabitant: “You are,” he says, “the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.” And elsewhere, as God says: “I shall dwell in them, and walk among them, and I shall be their God.”

Behold: the one who inhabits the temple of the human heart declares himself to be God.

Ananias is recognized as having promised his offering to God among those who, honoring God, sold their possessions from their righteous labors and laid them at the apostles’ feet; yet he is accused of lying to the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle Peter says: “Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts III). He continued and added: “You have not lied to men, but to God.”

What does this mean? He sins against the Creator, and Scripture so diminishes his sin that, according to the impious interpretation, it makes him guilty against a creature and condemns him as a debtor to the lesser on account of an insult against the greater? It is not so.

The divine power is manifestly present in the one against whom the sacrilegious offense is directed. Of him it says elsewhere: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XI).

Therefore, since through transgression he had tempted God, he is said to have deceived the Holy Spirit. Recognize, then, that the Holy Spirit and God have one cause, one glory, and one reverence.

And so he concludes most clearly, in the following words concerning the Holy Spirit: “You have not lied,” he says, “to men, but to God.”

When Peter was speaking to Cornelius, the faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations (Acts X).

You see that the Holy Spirit bestowed this from what was his own, not from another’s. If you ask who it was who gave them grace: God. The one whom he previously identified as the giver of grace—the Holy Spirit—he here specifically declared to be God. There, the confession is repeated under a proper name; here, under a common name.

When he says that the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the nations, he himself is God by nature, the author of grace. To God alone it belongs to bestow gifts of spiritual endowments from what is his own, so that the Apostle also seems to have said of him: “I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV).

Rightly is he declared to be God, since he is the dispenser of grace and human salvation. And Peter added: “Who was I that I could hinder God?” (Acts XI)—that God, namely, who poured out upon the nations, or upon Cornelius, the impulse of his overflowing grace.

## CHAPTER IX. Where, against the Novatians, it is shown that God gave the Gentiles repentance leading to life, and that this God is the Holy Spirit, as the order of the reading itself demonstrates

Observe how, in the person of the Holy Spirit, who suddenly filled Cornelius and his companions, the name of God is celebrated through repeated testimony.

“After hearing these things,” it says, “they were silent and glorified God, saying: ‘Then God has also given repentance leading to life to the Gentiles’” (Acts XI).

At this point, against the Novatians, one must observe that God is said to grant repentance, which he certainly bestows only through the ministry of his servants. When, therefore, it says, “Who was I that I could hinder God?” and again, “Then God has also given repentance leading to life to the Gentiles,” the interpretation that must be made clear in manifest matters is one that should satisfy even the ignorant or unbelieving, in view of the repeated confession of the divine name at the coming of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER X. Where, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God through the distribution of spiritual gifts

[Col. 0037A]

Receive the testimony from the Corinthians, which alone could suffice to establish the divinity of the Holy Spirit. He says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “God also bearing witness by signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will” (Heb. II).

Let us ask the Apostle himself whether this distributor of spiritual gifts is one of the creatures. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians we have: “I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’ And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII).

Observe how he has stated with complete clarity that the Spirit of God is the Holy Spirit: in the preceding statement he had named the Spirit of God, and here he calls him the Holy Spirit [Col. 0037B]. The words that follow testify most clearly that he is God and Lord:

“There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God.”

It is as though the blessed Apostle had been asked about the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Having said “the same Spirit,” he clearly adds concerning him: “The same God, who works all things in all.”

He could not work all things if he were one among all; here the Holy Spirit is either expressly named in his own designation, as Lord and God, or is certainly shown to belong to the Trinity.

But here, in the division of gifts, divine speech is understood to have designated the Holy Spirit more particularly, because above we learn that the grace of distribution belongs to the Holy Spirit through a special dispensation.

As for the words, “the same Lord, and the same God,” the following chapter shows that they are to be referred to the Holy Spirit, saying:

“To one, through the Spirit, is given the utterance of wisdom; to another, the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills.”

He is subject to no one; rather, he is the heavenly Lord who, by his own will and by the right of his power, bestows heavenly gifts.

## CHAPTER XI. It must be observed that, just as he says there is one God, so he says there is one Holy Spirit; this could in no way be said of a common creature, nor of one who distributes to each as he wills

You see that, just as there is one Father and one Son, so there is one Holy Spirit, as he subsequently states: “For in one Spirit we were all given to drink.”

If he were one from the common people or from the multitude of creatures, he could not be called “one” at all. And when you have the words, “To another,” he says, “faith is given in the same Spirit” (Rom. XII), who gives this faith? The same Apostle declares in the Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “To each one as God has allotted the measure of faith” (Hebr.).

You see that he unequivocally declares this distributor of faith to be God. Although, in the abundant bestowal of so many gifts, the very magnificence of the work itself speaks of the power of its author, he nevertheless concluded concerning him:

“But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills.”

Likewise, elsewhere: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.” And again: “According to the distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will” (I Cor. XII).

He is therefore not subject to the servitude of ministry, but possesses the freedom of sovereign power; in distributing heavenly goods, the fullness of supreme generosity has been poured out.

How does he say that this distributor of the Holy Spirit’s distributions—that is, this divider—is God? He teaches it in the Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “There are divisions of operations, but the same God.”

We read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God” (Acts XX).

The one who placed bishops in the Church is declared by the Apostle, the chosen vessel, to be God in the Epistle to the Corinthians, as he says: “God has placed some in the Church.”

Who is this except the Holy Spirit, whose office is shown by the distribution of graces, as the immediately following passage makes clear?

“God,” he says, “has placed in the Church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues.”

“Some,” he says, “God has placed in the Church.”

That he here spoke of the Holy Spirit as God is made clear by the very dispensation of sanctifications and powers, which belongs to the Holy Spirit. He enriches the mouths of the prophets, dispenses remedies of healing, and multiplies the adornments of spiritual gifts. As he flows into the apostles, the miracles of signs and the diverse kinds of tongues proclaim him to be the God of the whole universe [Col. 0038C].

## CHAPTER XII. Where he says that those who have become the temple of the Holy Spirit must progress in such a way that they may deserve to bear God in their bodies

The Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Spirit?”

That the temple of the Holy Spirit is the temple of God is clearly suggested by the preceding passages of the same Epistle, where it says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God? And the Holy Spirit dwells in you”; and again: “The Spirit of God dwells in you.”

Who could doubt that they are the temple of that God whose dwelling place they are shown to be?

And after saying, “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” he concluded the chapter with splendid truth:

“Glorify,” he says, “and bear God in your body” [Col. 0038D].

Therefore, whoever diligently prepares a temple for the Holy Spirit in his heart through purity bears God in his body through chastity and the mortification of the flesh. He must bear bodily the one by whom he is spiritually possessed.

Therefore, recognize that the one whom you see to be worthy of a temple must be worshiped with divine honors, celebrated with vows, and honored with sacrifices.

The teacher of the nations therefore speaks to the universal Church: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?”

This is possible for no creature; it is the distinctive mark of divine majesty to fill peoples individually through each person and nevertheless remain in the immensity of its fullness. It is, he says, the singular and proper nature of God to be present everywhere, to enter into all things, and to contain all things [Col. 0039A].

It is peculiar to God, he says, to strip the children of perdition of the debts imposed by nature, renew them once their consciences have been cleansed, make them children of God, and raise them to the glory of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0040A].

[Col. 0039A]

# PASCHASIUS’S LETTER TO EUGIPIUS (C, S)

[Col. 0039A] To the holy and always most beloved Eugipius, presbyter: Paschasius, deacon, a brother most beloved in Christ.

Although, considering the bitterness and manifold occupations of sinners, you disdain to treat holy men despite the eloquence of your learning and the good fortune of leisure, I endure the loss of modesty through contemplation of your affection. You sent a memorandum to which the eloquence of learned men could add nothing; and in a brief summary you opened up a work that the whole Church could review, when you more truthfully explained the life and character of blessed Severinus, who dwelt in the neighboring provinces of Pannonia, and committed to the memory of posterity the miracles that divine power worked through him and that will endure through the ages. The deeds of the devout do not perish with the world: thus all may possess the present man and, in a certain way, feel him dwelling among them, when the report of their reading has brought him to them. And therefore, since you have expressed more simply and explained more easily these things that you asked me to narrate, we have believed that nothing should be added to your labor by our diligence. For we recount what we have heard in one way, and bring forth what we have experienced in another. The virtues of teachers are more easily expounded by their disciples—virtues repeatedly suggested by the conduct of those who teach—which, inspired by divine gifts, are cultivated in the good minds of the saints.

How much benefit the deeds of the saints confer, how much ardor they impart, how much purity they pour forth: on this subject the authority of the apostolic voice, becoming more widely known, says at length (1 Peter 5): “Become examples to the flock.” And blessed Paul commands Timothy (2 Timothy 2) to be an example to the faithful. Hence the same apostle (Hebrews 13), composing the catalogue of the righteous with the utmost brevity, beginning with Abel, proceeds to recount the virtues of illustrious men. Thus that most faithful Mattathias, already drawing near to his most glorious death, distributed to his sons, as an hereditary right, the examples of the saints, so that, stirred more famously by their admirable struggles, they might disdain their lives in the fervor of holiness for the sake of the everlasting laws. Nor did the father’s instruction deceive his children. For the deeds of their ancestors, once recalled, benefited them so greatly that, with open faith, they drove away the armed rulers, overcame the sacrilegious camps, demolished far and wide the rites and altars of demons, and, adorned by everlasting achievements, secured a civic crown for their radiant homeland. Therefore we too rejoice that, through fraternal service, something is provided for the adornment of Christ’s bride—not because, as I believe, the more illustrious life of our ancestors has ever been lacking, but because it is fitting that the house of the great King should possess the standards of many triumphs. True virtue is not excluded by the multitude of victors; rather, through desired successes, it is enlarged.

## A.D. 498–514. Pope Symmachus

## Notice

*(From the Liber Pontificalis.)*

### I

**I.** Symmachus, a Roman by nation,* son of Fortunatus, held the see for fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-six days. He lived in the time of King Theodoric and of the Augustus Anastasius, from the tenth day before the Kalends of December until the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was ordained on the same day as Laurentius, amid a dispute: Symmachus in the Constantinian basilica, Laurentius in the basilica of blessed Mary. For this reason the clergy became divided,* and the senate too was divided: some with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. After the dispute, the parties decided* that both should go to Ravenna, to the judgment of King Theodoric. When both had entered Ravenna, they found this judgment of equity: that whoever had been ordained first, or wherever the larger party was recognized, should sit in the apostolic see. In the end equity found this in Symmachus,* through the recognition of the truth. And Symmachus was made bishop.

### Marginal Notes

* C, B, Sardus. — B, eight months less four days, from the consulships of Paulinus and Scytha to that of M. Aurelius Cassiodorus. — * See Baronius under the year A.D. 498. — * C, “they arranged”; * “so that both parties.” — * C, “and the recognition.”

### Variant Readings of Holstenius and Schelestr

He lived in the time of King Theodoric and of the Augustus Anastasius, from the tenth day before the Kalends of December until the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August. He was ordained on the same day as Laurentius, amid a dispute: Symmachus in the Constantinian basilica, Laurentius in the basilica of blessed Mary. For this reason the clergy became divided, and the senate too was divided: some with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. After the dispute the parties decided that both should go to Ravenna, to the judgment of King Theodoric. When both had entered Ravenna, they found this judgment of equity:* that whoever had been ordained first, or wherever the larger party was recognized,* should sit in the apostolic see. In the end* equity found in Symmachus the recognition of the truth, and Symmachus was made bishop.

### Marginal Notes

The manuscripts Cass., Flor., Romualdus, and Deusdedit read *Sardus. — * Seven months: Flor., Cas., Vat. — * Flor. and Vat., “he found.” — * Flor. adds “to favor.” — * The same, “nevertheless.”

### II

**II.** At the same time Pope Symmachus convened a synod and, out of consideration for mercy, appointed Laurentius bishop of the city of Nuceria.* Four years later, certain members of the clergy and others of the senate, especially Festus and Probinus, moved by zeal, accused Symmachus and suborned false witnesses. They sent these witnesses to Ravenna to King Theodoric, accusing blessed Symmachus; and they secretly recalled Laurentius, after a petition had been drawn up at Rome, and caused a schism, so that the clergy was again divided. Some communicated with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. Then the senators Festus and Probinus sent a report to the king and began to press him to appoint a visitor for the apostolic see. The king then appointed Peter,* bishop of the city of Altinum, although the canons forbade this. At the same time blessed Symmachus convened one hundred and fifteen bishops; and when the synod had been held, he was cleared of the false accusation. Peter,* the usurper of the apostolic see, and Laurentius of Nuceria were condemned, because, while Bishop Symmachus was alive, they had seized his see. Then blessed Symmachus was restored to the apostolic see by all the bishops, priests, deacons, the entire clergy, and the people,* so that he might sit as bishop with glory beside blessed Peter.

See Baronius under A.D. 499. — * C, “in the city of Nuceria.” — See Baronius under A.D. 502. — * D, Altinae (“of Altinum”); “Symmachus was cleared in the synod”; * Altinensis (“of Altinum”). — * C, “was restored.”

### III

**III.** At the same time Festus, former consul and head of the senate, and Probinus, former consul, began to fight within the city of Rome with the other senators, especially with Faustus, former consul.* Slaughters and murders were committed among the clergy out of envy. Those who rightly communicated with blessed Symmachus were publicly killed with the sword whenever they were found within the City. Even consecrated women and virgins, driven from their monasteries or dwellings, were stripped of their female clothing and, battered by blows, were wounded; every day they carried on fighting against the Church in the middle of the city. They also killed many priests, among them *Dignissimus and Gordianus, priests at the shrine of the chains of the holy apostle Peter and at that of Saints John and Paul,* whom they killed with clubs and the sword, as well as many other Christians, so that no member of the clergy could safely walk through the city by day or night. Faustus alone, the former consul, fought on behalf of the Church. After all this, blessed Symmachus discovered Manichaeans in the city of Rome. He burned all their images and books together before the doors of the Constantinian basilica and banished the Manichaeans themselves into exile. This occurred from the consulship of Paulinus until the consulship of Senator.

### Marginal Notes

* “Among them Gordianus, the most distinguished priest, at the shrine of the chains.” — * “Whom they killed with clubs and the sword.” — See Baronius under A.D. 503, at the end: the Manichaeans’ books were burned.

### IV

**IV.** He built the basilica of the holy apostle Andrew beside the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, where he made a silver *canopy* and a confessionary, weighing 120 pounds. He made three silver arches, each weighing 60 pounds. He made an oratory of the holy apostle Thomas of silver, weighing 300 pounds;* in the confessionary, twenty pounds. He made a silver arch weighing sixteen pounds. He made the confessionary of Saint Cassianus and of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus of silver, weighing twenty pounds. He made a silver arch weighing twelve pounds. He made an oratory of Saint Apollinaris of silver, with a confessionary and arch of silver, weighing thirty pounds. He made an oratory of Saint *Sossius of silver in the confessionary, weighing twenty pounds. Likewise, at the fountain in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, he made an oratory of the holy cross of silver, a confessionary, and a cross of gold with gems, in which he enclosed the Lord’s wood; the golden cross itself weighed ten pounds. He also made two oratories, one of Saint John the Baptist and one of Saint John the Evangelist, and placed in their confessionaries silver arches weighing thirty pounds.* He constructed all these chambers completely from the foundations. He adorned the basilica of the blessed Peter with marble. He adorned the cantharus of blessed Peter and its four-sided portico with marble, and with mosaic he adorned it with lambs, crosses, and palms.* He fitted together the entire atrium. He enlarged the steps before the doors of the basilica of blessed Peter. He also built other steps beneath the roof, on the right and left. In the same place he made episcopal residences on the right and left. Beneath the steps in the atrium he also placed another cantharus outside, in the open field, and made it for human bodily needs. He also made other steps for those ascending to blessed Andrew and placed a cantharus there. He built the basilica of Saint Agatha the martyr on the Via Aurelia, on the estate of Lardum, constructing it from the foundations together with a fountain, and placed there two silver arches. At the same time he built the basilica of Saint Pancratius, where he also made a silver arch weighing fifteen pounds. In the same place he built a bath. Likewise, at the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul, he restored the apse, which was threatening to collapse, and adorned it with paintings behind the confessionary. He made a vaulted chamber and a matroneum, and above the confessionary he placed a silver image of the Savior with the twelve apostles; they weighed 120 pounds. Before the doors of the basilica he made steps in the atrium and a cantharus; behind the apse he introduced water, and there too he built a bath from the foundations.

### V

**V.** Within the city of Rome he constructed from the foundations the basilica of Saints Silvester and Martin beside the Baths of Trajan. There too, above the altar, he made a silver *canopy weighing 120 pounds, twelve silver arches, each weighing ten pounds, and a silver confessionary weighing fifteen pounds. At the church of Saints John and Paul he made steps behind the apse. Likewise, at the Archangel Michael he enlarged the basilica, made steps, and introduced water. Likewise, at Saint Mary he built from the foundations an oratory of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Also, on the Tiburtine Way, at the twenty-seventh milestone from the city of Rome, at the request of *Alvinus and Glaphyra, illustrious persons who were building at their own expense, he dedicated a basilica to blessed Peter on the estate of Pacinianus. Likewise, at blessed Peter, blessed Paul the apostles, and Saint Lawrence the martyr, he built dwellings for the poor. At blessed Peter he made twenty silver canthari, each weighing fifteen pounds, and twenty-two arches, each weighing twenty pounds. He repaired the basilica of Saint Felicitas,* which was already threatening to collapse. He restored the apse of blessed Agnes, which was threatening to collapse, and renovated the entire basilica.

### VI

**VI.** He established that every Sunday, or on the birthdays of martyrs, the angelic hymn should be sung, that is, “Glory to God in the highest.” He improved the cemetery of the Jordanians for the sake of the body of Saint Alexander. Every year, through Africa or Sardinia, he supplied money and clothing to bishops who had been confined in exile. He redeemed captives throughout Liguria, through Milan, and through various provinces* with money, multiplied his gifts, and released them. He carried out four ordinations in the city of Rome during the months of December and February: ninety-two priests, sixteen deacons, and 107 bishops in various places.* He too was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days; he also died in peace as a confessor.

### Marginal Notes

* “With money.” — * C, B, 17.

### L. V. Fabrotti, from Freher’s Manuscripts A and B

No. VI, line 13: A, B, 117. Line 14: B, “of the Apostle,” the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

### From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuanus Manuscripts

Lines 1–3: “He established that every Sunday, or on the birthdays of martyrs, the hymn ‘Glory to God in the highest’ should be sung.” Line 6: “money.” Lines 7–8: “through Liguria and Milan.” Lines 8–9: “he redeemed them with money.” Lines 10–12: “during the month of December, ninety-two priests.” Lines 13–15: “117 (M, 114), who also died in peace as a confessor and was buried in the basilica of blessed Peter on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, and so forth; the episcopate was vacant for seven days.”

### From another Thuanus Manuscript

Line 8: “with money.” Line 13: “117.” Lines 14–15: “of the Apostle, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days; he who also in peace, as a confessor, was laid to rest on the nineteenth day of July.”

### Variant Readings of Holstenius and Schelestr

He established that every Sunday, or on the birthdays of martyrs, the angelic hymn should be sung, that is, “Glory to God in the highest.” He improved the cemetery of the Jordanians for the sake of the body of Saint Alexander. Every year, through Africa or Sardinia, he supplied money and clothing to bishops who had been confined in exile. He redeemed captives throughout Liguria, through Milan, and through various provinces with money, multiplied his gifts, and released them. He carried out four ordinations in the city of Rome during the month of December and February: *92 priests, sixteen deacons, and 107 bishops in various places. He too was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter,* and the episcopate remained vacant for seven days; he also died in peace as a confessor.

### Marginal Notes

* The manuscripts Codd. have 22. — * Flor., “127 bishops.” — * Flor. adds “the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.”

### Variant Readings of Penia, from the Cavensis Manuscript

Lines 12–13: “117 bishops in various places.”

## Fragment

*[Note: From the Verona manuscript, published by the distinguished Joseph Blanchini in the work entitled *Commentary of the Pseudo-Athanasius*.]*

### A Second Life of the Same Pontiff, Written by a Certain Contemporary Schismatic

Symmachus held the see for fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. At that time Laurentius, a priest of the Roman Church, had been ordained bishop; and so savage a discord invaded the Roman clergy and people that neither consideration of God nor fear of the king restrained the parties from their mutual clash. Then both—Symmachus, that is, and Laurentius—were compelled to seek the royal court, in order to submit to the king’s judgment. There Symmachus prevailed through large sums of money; Laurentius was sent to govern the Church of Nuceria, a city of Campania, compelled by numerous threats and promises.

After some years Symmachus was accused before the king on many charges. Under the pretext of Easter, because he had not celebrated it with the entire community, the king summoned him to the court . . . [lacuna] . . . to render an account . . . [lacuna] . . . of the disagreement concerning the festival; and had him reside at Ariminum. While he remained there for some time with several of his clerics, walking along the seashore in the afternoon, he saw women passing by, with whom he was accused of having committed a crime,* and who, by royal command, were able to go to the court. Pretending, therefore, not to know what he had seen, in the middle of the night, while everyone was asleep, he fled with only one confidant and returned to Rome, shutting himself within the enclosure of the blessed apostle Peter.

Then the priests and deacons, as well as the other clerics whom he had brought with him, approached the king and testified that Symmachus had fled without their knowledge. Through them the king sent commands both to the senate and to the clergy concerning his condemnation, so to speak. He was also accused by the entire Roman clergy of having squandered ecclesiastical estates contrary to a decree observed by his predecessors, and of having thereby entangled himself in the bonds of anathema. During the Easter days, almost everyone requested from the king the venerable man Peter, bishop of Altinum, as visitor of the Roman Church. After the holy festival, a synod assembled in the city of Rome, at the king’s command and according to the will of the senate and clergy, to judge his offenses.

Some bishops and senators attempted to prevent Symmachus from being subjected to a hearing [lacuna]. When certain men publicly shouted in his defense that no Roman pontiff could be heard by anyone, even if he were such as he was accused of being, the more distinguished bishops nevertheless judged that, both out of regard for religion and because of the royal command, the business of so serious a matter, already widely publicized, could in no way be abandoned without examination. Since, amid this disagreement, the synod provided further fuel for discord between the parties, it finally decided that the petition offered by Symmachus’s accusers should be received and solemnly published among the official acts.

When this had been done, Symmachus was immediately summoned by the bishops to appear for judgment. But when the clerics who were in attendance on him denied that he was present, he was admonished a second and a third time by the bishops, according to the rules, to attend the synodal hearing; yet he did not deign to give any answer. Then some bishops, seeing that they were accomplishing nothing in the case, warned once and again the clergy that had withdrawn from Symmachus’s fellowship to return to him, setting aside the examination. They replied that they could by no means do this before he, accused of such great crimes, had either been acquitted by a canonical investigation, if innocent, or, if found guilty, had been deposed from the priesthood.

But when the bishops saw that the delays of the [lacuna] increasingly enlarged the party spirit of division, they established what seemed useful to them for Symmachus’s person, and thus abandoned the city in the utmost confusion. The clergy, therefore, and the more distinguished members of the senate who had avoided Symmachus’s fellowship, sent a petition to the king on behalf of Laurentius, who at that time was staying at Ravenna to escape Symmachus’s violence and persecution, asking that he himself should preside over the Roman Church, where he had formerly been ordained supreme pontiff. For this, they argued, was also fixed by the canons: that each man should remain where he had first been consecrated bishop; or, if he had been removed from there by some contrivance, that he should be recalled by every means.

Thus Laurentius came to the city and governed the Roman Church for approximately four years. What civil wars were fought or how many murders were committed during that period need not be disclosed in the present account. While the parties clashed with one another in mutual disagreement and repeatedly sought royal protection for their respective causes, Symmachus finally sent a petition to the king through Dioscorus, a deacon of Alexandria, asserting that he was suffering great prejudice, especially concerning the titles of the churches that Laurentius controlled within the city.

Moved by this representation, the king’s mind was softened, and he sent commands to Patricius F. [lacuna], instructing him that all the church titles should be restored to Symmachus and that the king should permit there to be only one pontiff at Rome. When Laurentius learned of this, he did not wish the city to be troubled by a prolonged struggle; of his own accord he immediately withdrew to the estates of the aforementioned Patricius Festus, and there, under conditions of great self-restraint, he met the end of his life.

Although Symmachus afterward emerged victorious, rumor nevertheless stained him in many matters, most shamefully and especially concerning the woman whom the common people called the “conditaria.”* He was also accused concerning ecclesiastical orders, which he openly sold after accepting money. Because of these matters the Roman Church remained in schism until the end of his life. He built and adorned the church of blessed Martin beside Saint Silvester with the money of the illustrious man Palatinus, and, at that man’s insistence, dedicated it. He also restored several cemeteries, especially that of Saint Pancratius, and built many new structures there as well.

## Letters and Decrees of Pope Symmachus

*(C)*

### First Letter *(formerly II)*

#### To Aeonius, Bishop of Arles

That he and the bishop of Vienne should send trustworthy men to Rome, instructed in their disputes, to present what ought to be laid before the apostolic see.

**Symmachus to his most beloved brother Aeonius.**

What your communication disclosed has certainly moved us: namely, that, contrary to the rules of ecclesiastical order and against the teaching of the venerable canons, the bishop of the Church of Vienne has culpably obtained something by deception from the apostolic see, while our predecessor was presiding there. If the complaint is true, what has been frivolously obtained cannot be securely possessed; nor will anything new be capable of being established by us except what has clearly been determined in this matter by our fathers and predecessors.

Nevertheless, lest we appear to have made any prejudicial decree too readily in the absence of the other party, we have judged it preferable to order that your Fraternity, at a suitable time, should not delay sending someone properly instructed in ecclesiastical procedure concerning the whole case, who may competently present the truth of the matter before us, so that, after everything has been examined, what must be established may be confirmed with the strength of deliberation.

We also command your Affection to do the following: send a messenger and a letter to admonish our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the city of Vienne, so that he too may send, on the appointed days, a representative of his own who can competently set forth the arguments of his party. Thus, after the submissions of both sides have been brought forward, we may more securely determine what must be observed forever. For a judge always appears suspect when he chooses to decide under the lamentation of what seems to be only one party.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, after the consulship of Paulinus, a most distinguished man (A.D. 499).

### Second Letter *(formerly III)*

#### To Liberius, Patricius

Concerning the bishop elected at Aquileia, whose election he approves.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to the patrician Liberius, greetings.

Since, in the matter of the election of the bishop of Aquileia, you direct words of a reverent conscience (Ennodius, first book, book V), and a tongue consecrated to divine worship serves what must be consecrated, our diligence has been held by the bonds of unfamiliar discourse; for nothing surpasses judgments whenever a proven person has brought something forward. What room does the opinion of followers leave, when it obeys justice, whose decision is not summoned for examination? You act according to a good conscience, something that would scarcely be denied to your authority.

Among the arbitrators, the venerable Marcellinus’s colleague Maximus, a man exalted by his humility, appeared; and, so that favor might not be ascribed to power through indirect interpreters, he joined to the honorarium what he had composed from his own ability. You dealt with a matter of moderate importance, so that the praise of what was exceedingly great would not be suspect; the testimony of the most illustrious men is restrained, so that the heights may acquire strength.

Happy the priesthood before which a full mind of light has carried a torch. Blessed the conduct that was brought into discussion for this reason: that, with so great a man supporting it, it might prevail—although it would never have learned the taste of victory had it not been subjected to uncertainties. Adversity has always brought glory to the innocent; moderate opposition provides the strongest defenders.

But why have I extended the limits of the letter through loquacity, overstepping pages constrained by convention in human composition? I too join myself to your most distinguished fathers [or: to your most distinguished parties], according to the measure of my own smallness, in agreement with you, while heaven favors you; and—something considered marvelous among human beings—I am drawn by regard for you toward love. Affection inspired in me through another pleases me, while charity remains implanted in my inmost heart. Though the person is absent, may heavenly grace nevertheless join itself as a companion to his desires; and, while you desire it, may the result be granted: either the good of the episcopate may come, or may bring it about.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth indiction (in the year of Christ 499).

## LETTER III (formerly I). POPE SYMMACHUS TO AEONIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

He orders that, after the things which his predecessor Anastasius had innovated in the controversy concerning Vienne have been rescinded, the ancient decrees of the Apostolic See be observed.

To his most beloved brother Aeonius, Symmachus.

We have received the letter of Your Affection, together with the instructions conveyed by our son Crescentius, a presbyter acting as intermediary. From them it is clear that some conflict has arisen between the Church of Arles and the Church of Vienne concerning the ordination of bishops in neighboring cities. This has happened because our predecessor Anastasius, of holy memory, while dealing with the confusion of the province, ordered certain things to be observed contrary to ancient custom, transgressing—although he ought not to have done so—the ordinance of his predecessors under whatever necessity.

For, just as there is one priesthood through different bishops, after the pattern of the Trinity, whose power is one and undivided, how could the ordinances of earlier men fittingly be violated by those who came later? Moreover, we believe that the avoidance of variation in judgments belongs to the very holy Catholic religion: all its power is undermined unless everything once established by the priests of the Lord is perpetual. Otherwise this could happen if a successor did not grant firmness to the acts of his predecessor and, by strengthening what had been done, did not make his own actions valid.

For how great a reverence will be judged due to the vicars of the blessed apostle Peter if the commands they issue in their priestly office are dissolved as soon as they themselves have passed away? Therefore, rereading the ordinances of the ancient bishops concerning this matter, with which the ecclesiastical archive is burdened, we earnestly admonish Your Affection that, in ordaining priests throughout the individual cities, the venerable antiquity of the established practice be preserved, and that no new enactment diminish the strength of an ancient sanction. Concord will not otherwise be able to be preserved among you unless reverence for antiquity, through wiser counsel, imposes a limit upon new ambitions.

May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Kalends of October, again after the consulship of Paulinus, the younger, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 500).

[Note: The word “younger” should be deleted, having been inserted by some ignorant person, since Paulinus cannot be called “the younger” in the year 498, when he was ordinary consul, because no one of the same name had preceded him in the consulship. Pagius, under the year of Christ 499, no. 13.]

Dominical Easter: the eighth day before the Kalends of April [or: the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 501].

## LETTER IV (formerly XII). TO AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: See Avitus’s letter to Symmachus in vol. LIX of the *Patrologia*, cols. 243 and 248. Ennodius’s letters to the same pope will be reprinted among his works at the beginning of the following volume. — Editor.]

Why he refused to judge an unheard case, and that laws must sometimes be relaxed.

To his most beloved brother Avitus, Symmachus.

[Note: From the papers of the Reverend Father Hieronymus Vignerius, p. 583, vol. V of the *Spicilegium*.]

Your Charity ought not to have been offended by what we recently wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Aeonius. For, dearest brother, your right was not prejudiced when we replied that we could not judge without hearing the other party and without a competent presentation of the case. Therefore it remains open to Your Fraternity to allege whatever you think ought to be alleged and to propose whatever you see ought to be proposed.

For although we said that the confusion of the province had been brought about by our predecessor, Bishop Anastasius of holy memory, contrary to the custom of the Church and the ancient ordinances of our predecessors, and that it ought not to be tolerated, nevertheless, if Your Fraternity demonstrates that what he did was done reasonably, we shall rejoice that he attempted nothing contrary to the canons. For what is done outside the rule, provided it is done for a just reason, does not violate the rule; only obstinacy and contempt for antiquity harm it.

For although the statutes established by the fathers must be guarded with careful observance and observant diligence, nevertheless, for the sake of some good, something is relaxed from the strictness of the law—something which the law itself would have guarded against, had it foreseen the circumstance. Often it would be cruel to insist upon the law when it appears that its observance would prejudice the Church, since laws were enacted with the intention that they should benefit, not harm.

Therefore continue to send us the reasons that moved our predecessor to deal with the aforesaid confusion, so that we may know what ought to be established and may rejoice in the Lord that Anastasius, of blessed memory, did nothing requiring revocation.

May God preserve you safe, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Avienus and Pompeius (in the year of Christ 501).

## LETTER V (formerly IV). TO MAXIMINUS OF PADUA

[Note: In Mansi’s edition this was incorrectly printed, “To Laurentius of Milan.” — Editor.]

In which his virtues are described.

To his most beloved and dearest brother Maximinus, bishop of the Church of Padua, Bishop Symmachus, greetings in the Lord.

The vow of a religious conscience comes forth, and a mind devoted to the praises of bishops. It is an assertion of ability to devote what we say to those who obey God; in their praises, our speech may perhaps reveal its narrowness and inexperience, yet if we refrain from speaking, it reveals our childishness. Who would judge a poor narrative impoverished when vows enrich it? Often the stream of a speaker’s praise is found poor in the gifts of eloquence, while, conversely, the treasure of the heart sheds light amid poverty of words.

He who judges in God’s place does not desire embellished speeches [picta alloquia; alternatively colloquia, “conversations”], but those which an unadorned brilliance of intellect commends; for in the former eloquence flatters even without love, whereas in the latter naked truth commends its own splendor. Everything dictated by affection is without ornament. Those things are fashioned with meticulous care which we want to have not so much the appearance of what is right as its likeness.

But I am speaking of you, venerable and most excellent bishop, whose virtue began with your name together with the testimony of your merits; in you, the deed speaks through the name it calls forth. The prudent diligence of your parents wished you to be chosen before you were tested [eligi, “to be chosen”; alternatively eligere, “to choose”]. Once attached to secular titles, you were refined by military exertion, and the adverse side strengthened you for the governance of the Church, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16).

The sacred judge found you worthy to be his companion in counsel and in labor. Well did you choose, when you were to be initiated into the venerable altars, what was sacred even in your lay conduct. You were found to be a guardian of chastity at an age when even the law gives way to desires. For it is enough that the arrogance of childhood, which license supports, should be shunned [horreri; alternatively horrere]. Christ seeks soldiers whom he may raise to the position of leaders amid hostile battle lines.

Once admitted to the Church, you filled the office of bishop by your conduct before you possessed the dignity of the title. Your kindness was not something foreign to you: resting upon the roots of your nature, it displayed a shoot from an hoary flower. For everything that is fabricated is temporary; what matures with age is lasting. We believe that the priesthood came to you not as a gift but as a reward.

Others are commended by the seduction of popular favor [alternatively: “Another wins the mouths of the crowd by common favor”]; in your case, strict discipline toward the guilty produced affection. You possess singular wisdom, which, although generally desirable, is nevertheless indispensable in a teacher. In vain does one assume the role of an admonisher if he cannot appreciate the weight of the office imposed upon him. Unless he surpasses others in knowledge and holiness, he who is superior in honor must be compared with the most worthless.

Judgment, not favor, gave you the highest place. The love worthy of a bishop is that which discipline wins. The character [or: intellect] of an instructor is disfigured when he wishes to please through favor alone. Instructed and formed by these gifts of heaven, you will educate the people more by doing than by teaching. Those admonitions educate the consciences of disciples which are confirmed by example. He who has himself pursued innocence invites others to it without shame.

Those who intend to sin fear you as though you were a witness within the secrets of their inner chambers. Your fear and reverence prevent faults from coming to birth [effectum, “effect”; alternatively affectum, “affection”]. You confront vices at their beginnings, remove the opportunity for falls, and cleanse the source of desire.

I have dedicated these words briefly to your blessedness as a recommendation from my tongue. If the success of my life smiles upon me through your prayers, I shall consecrate myself by a full account of your deeds, so that what is known to all may be preserved in writings destined to endure, for the future age to rejoice.

## COPY OF THE PETITION PRESENTED BY BISHOP CAESARIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS

Just as the episcopate takes its beginning from the person of the blessed apostle Peter, so it is necessary that Your Holiness clearly show the individual churches what they ought to observe through appropriate disciplines.

In the province of Gaul, ecclesiastical estates are being alienated by certain persons under various titles. The result is that each person, according to his own will, diminishes the resources devoted by pious donors to the needs of the poor. We ask that the authority of the Apostolic See prohibit this from being done, unless perhaps something should be granted to monasteries out of consideration for piety.

We also request with equal supplication that no one who has served in the individual offices of judges as a layman, or who has governed provinces under some authority, be ordained a cleric or bishop unless he has long beforehand undertaken the proper way of life and had his conduct examined.

We ask also that widows who have already for a long time assumed religious dress, and women consecrated to God who have already remained for a long time in monasteries, be protected, so that no one may have the freedom either to join himself to them in marriage against their will or to carry them off against their will on the pretext of marriage.

We further submit in humble prayer that no one be permitted to approach the episcopate through canvassing, nor should powerful men be enlisted as supporters through the payment of money. And, so that these matters may more easily be guarded, let clerics or citizens not presume at all to draw up or subscribe to a decree without the knowledge or consent of the metropolitan.

Forbid all these things through the penalty of Your severity, so that discipline friendly to good conduct may be preserved both in Your Church and in the province mentioned above.

## LETTER VI (formerly V). TO CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

[Note: In the Isidorian Collection: “The decrees of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, begin.” In the canon headings found in the manuscript Dionysian Collection at the Jesuit College in Paris, this enactment is called that of the second council under Symmachus: “On preserving the property of the Church.” — Hardouin.]

He responds to the consultations of Caesarius.

1. That the property of the Church not be alienated.  
2. That no one obtain office through rewards.  
3. That laymen advance to the priesthood by stages.  
4. That abductors of widows or virgins be expelled from communion with the Church.  
5. That widows or virgins who have professed continence not marry.  
6. That no one approach the episcopate through canvassing.

To his most beloved brother Caesarius, Symmachus.

The fairness of your request urges us gladly to assent to the desire of Your Fraternity concerning each of the matters for which you petition—or, in another reading, request—concession from the Apostolic See, since this does not differ from the caution and provision of the Fathers. And although ecclesiastical rules encompass almost everything, we nevertheless do not think it superfluous to repeat again [denuo; alternatively nunc, “now”] what has often been prohibited.

### I. That the property of the Church not be alienated

[Note: From this it becomes clear what the origin of ecclesiastical benefices was. Since clerics were accustomed to receive from the Church, through the bishop, their due stipend each month, as we stated above in the notes on the councils held in the time of Cyprian, it later happened that some of them were granted by the bishop the possessions of the Church for as long as they lived. These began to be called benefices because, as Symmachus says, they could be granted only to those who had merited well. — Severus Binius.]

We therefore do not permit possessions which anyone has given or left to the Church’s own discretion to be alienated under any title or contract—or, in another reading, transferred—or under any pretext whatsoever, unless perhaps necessity or consideration of the merits of clerics, religious concern for monasteries, or the needs of pilgrims should urge that they be granted. Even then, however, the recipients are to enjoy these possessions not perpetually but temporarily, only for as long as they live.

### II. That no one obtain office through rewards

We strongly admonish that those who attempt to approach the priesthood not through the grace of God but through promised rewards [praemiis; alternatively promissa, “promises”] consisting of ecclesiastical property be deprived of—or, in another reading, restrained from—the fulfillment of such desires. Let them know that they will without doubt be subjected to the penalties of the canons, whether they restrain themselves from such an intention or not [the alternative reading runs: “But those who do not restrain themselves from such an intention are to know that they will be subjected to penalties,” and so forth].

### III. That laymen advance to the priesthood by stages

Concerning lay persons, we decree that they not be readily permitted to approach the priesthood. Periods and stages have been established for them, through which they ought to aspire to this dignity. For whoever is promoted without the prescribed order does not easily escape blame, and no one can obtain the judgment of a valid election without having been tested.

### IV. That abductors of widows or virgins be expelled from communion

We detest the abductors of widows or virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing with particular severity those who attempt to join virgins consecrated to God to their marriage, whether the women are willing or unwilling. Because of the atrocious wickedness of so heinous a crime, we order that such men be suspended from communion.

### V. That widows or virgins who have professed continence not marry

We do not permit widows to pass to marriage if they have remained for a long time in a religious commitment through prolonged observance. Similarly, we prohibit virgins from marrying if they have spent many years of their life in monasteries.

### VI. That no one approach the episcopate through canvassing

No one, therefore, is to be permitted to approach the honor of the episcopate through canvassing. Since such misconduct is condemned in lay conduct, who doubts that it brands religious persons and those who serve God with disgrace [inurat; alternatively inducat, “brings upon” opprobrium]?

If anyone desires the episcopate, let him not employ powerful persons as supporters by giving money; nor let him compel clerics or citizens to subscribe to a decree made for him by using fear of any kind, nor encourage them with rewards. No one is to draw up a decree without the presence of the visitor, whose testimony can establish the unanimity of the clerics and citizens.

We therefore exhort all that, out of regard for the Catholic religion and for the peace of the Churches, they preserve these things with faithful and devoted minds. For there is no doubt that, according to the venerable canons, those who violate such prohibitions must suffer the loss of their own communion. We nevertheless wish these matters to be brought to the knowledge of all bishops.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Probus, a man of illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 502).

[Note: The letter of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, beginning “The fairness of your request urges us,” cannot be connected with the year of Christ 502, because it bears this subscription: “Given on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Probus, a man of illustrious rank.” Otherwise Symmachus would either have mentioned the western consul Avienus by name alone or would have mentioned both consuls. Since he does not call Probus “the younger,” it is clear that the letter was given to Caesarius in the year 513.

The same year of Christ must also be assigned to the copy of the petition presented by Bishop Caesarius to Pope Symmachus, beginning “Just as the episcopate takes its beginning from the person ...,” because Symmachus’s letter contains six replies to the six requests of Caesarius expressed in that petition. Labbe connected this copy of the petition presented by Caesarius to Pope Symmachus with the year 499, but Symmachus’s replies with the year 502. This error will have to be corrected in the second edition of the councils. — Anthony Pagius.]

## LETTER OF THE EASTERN BISHOPS TO SYMMACHUS

They ask him to aid the Eastern Churches, which are suffering from schism, and to receive them into communion. They profess the Catholic faith and condemn heresies.

The Eastern Church to Symmachus, bishop of Rome.

Our good Lord Jesus Christ, lover of humanity, who, because of his goodness, inclined the heavens toward us and descended to the earth, daily cries out through the immaculate Gospels:

“It is not those who are strong who need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9);

“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2).

Moreover, wishing to reveal more fully the works of his mercy, he added shortly afterward:

“What man among you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he places it joyfully upon his shoulders; and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost’” (Luke 15).

And, so that what he said might become clearer, he immediately added the parable of the woman who had found the drachma she had lost, joining both parables together and saying:

“Truly I say to you, so there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.”

We have said these things, most holy father, daring to make our supplication not for the loss of one sheep, nor for the loss of one drachma, but for the salvation dear to us—not merely of the Eastern regions, but of almost three quarters of the inhabited world. These are not people redeemed from the empty way of life handed down by their parents with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of the Lamb of God, as the blessed prince of the glorious apostles taught (1 Peter 1).

Christ, the good Shepherd, entrusted his chair to Your Blessedness. He came seeking and liberating what had perished, and giving his life as a ransom for many. Imitating him, most holy and most blessed father, hasten to help us, just as your teacher, the blessed Paul, once hastened to the aid of the Macedonians (Acts 16). He, indeed, learned in a vision that the Macedonians were in danger and hurried in reality to help them.

But you, a father full of affection for your children, seeing with spiritual eyes—not through visions, but in reality—those who are perishing through the transgression of our father Acacius, do not delay. Rather, as I may put it in the words of the prophet, “do not sleep, but hasten to deliver us” (Psalm 120). For power has been given to you not only to bind but also to loose those who have long been bound, in imitation of the Master; not only to uproot or destroy but also to plant and build, according to the blessed Jeremiah—and still more according to Christ, the Savior of the world, of whom Jeremiah was a type. You have power not only to hand people over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, but also to form them in charity after they have been cast down by a long estrangement, lest, God forbid, you be seen to have suffered a greater loss because we were swallowed up by Satan in our grief.

For you are not ignorant of his character. Each day you are taught by your sacred teacher Peter to feed the sheep of Christ entrusted to you throughout the entire inhabited world, not compelling them by force but willingly. Together with the learned Paul you cry out to those subject to you and say:

“We do not lord it over your faith, but we work together for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1).

Therefore we implore you to tear up our new document of indebtedness, just as Christ our Savior and leader tore up the old one on the cross, so that after the washing of regeneration we may no longer be subject to the guilt of our sins, but so that, according to the prophecy of the blessed Ezekiel (chapter 18), the sour grape may set on edge the teeth of the one who ate it.

Since the Savior fulfilled this parable in truth by his saving coming, why, most holy and most blessed father, have our teeth—who are the children of Acacius, the one who ate the sour grape of disobedience—been set on edge through so long a course of years? If one man sinned, why does divine anger through an anathema weigh upon the whole synagogue—or rather upon the entire inhabited world? Where, then, is the promise of God which says:

“Children shall not bear the sins of their parents, nor parents those of their children, but each one shall die in his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24; Ezekiel 18)?

If Acacius was anathematized because of his friendship with the Alexandrians—or rather the Eutychians—who reject and anathematize the most holy and most blessed Pope Leo, as well as the synod held at Chalcedon, why are we judged heretics by you, and why are we under anathema, when we embrace that letter alone and what was said in the holy synod? Because of the preaching of your sound doctrine we are attacked daily and anathematized as heretics by those who agree with Eutyches.

Do not judge through the one who judges the whole earth, lest you destroy the righteous with the wicked; let not the righteous be treated by you as the wicked. Let the orthodox and the heretics not be judged equally by you—nor those who anathematize the aforementioned holy letter and your holy and orthodox synod together with those who, along with you, are anathematized by them, and those who pray daily that they may die for the sound faith which is preached by you.

Jesus son of Nave, indeed, rescued the uncircumcised Gibeonites, servants of idols who had fled to him with a lie, when they were attacked by Abimelech and the other four princes who were with him. Because they had taken refuge with him, God cooperating, he defended them bravely, lest the name of their God be blasphemed as though he were unable to help them (Joshua 10).

But you, most holy men, disciples of Jesus, the great God and Savior, and imitators of him who assumed the form of a servant in order to make us free from the sin that reigned in us—when you see us attacked and put to death, do not despise us or continue to scorn us, pious fathers. We are not uncircumcised Gibeonites but, together with you, circumcised with the circumcision of Christ; nor are we servants and devotees of idols, but, although sinners, Christians who, together with you, understand all things in Christ.

As the most blessed Jesus son of Nave not only received those men but also placed Rahab the prostitute before them because she had received the two spies (Joshua 16), so you too, with vigilance and God’s help, receive us because of the tradition of the two natures that was sent by you, through the letter of Pope Leo, established among the saints, against the ravings of Eutyches.

Rahab, when she received the spies, hid them in the flax tow of her house. We, however, having received the confession of your sound faith, do not hide it in our hearts; rather, by the mercy of God, we proclaim it with authority in the doctrines of the Churches.

When she was questioned, she denied through fear that she had them. We, however, pray that we may never deny the truth of our sound doctrine through human fear; and we will stand for it even to the shedding of blood, if necessary [or: if that should happen].

Therefore, do not grow weary of helping us, nor hate us because of communion with our adversaries. Many of them, hindered by their possessions and lacking concern for the multitude of souls, have suspended themselves from this communion. Those, however, to whom the care of many souls has been entrusted communicate in the Churches committed to them, having no one who communicates with them in opposition, and fearing to leave the sheep to wolves because of the voice of the Lord, who says:

“The hired servant, who is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. He flees because he is a hired servant and has no concern for the sheep” (John 10).

Your fatherhood will henceforth be able to learn that many priests do this not because they are captivated by love of life, but because they care for the salvation of the sheep, with God showing mercy.

Some of those who have been established in the priesthood, seeing [alternatively sperantes, “hoping”] orthodox presbyters and holy men being sent into exile, and wishing to withdraw from their Churches at their own discretion without necessity and to follow them, did not cease to urge them to remain in the holy Churches entrusted to them, for the protection of the orthodox people, taking upon themselves what was regarded as those men’s separation.

Just as Rebecca once said to Jacob, “Let your sin be upon me, my son” (Genesis 27), so they said to those who voluntarily wished to depart from the Churches entrusted to them:

“Let the guilt of your separation fall upon us. Only do not, without necessity, leave the sheep of Christ to the wolves, lest heretics enter your places and the wolves tear the sheep apart.”

Or, at least, those who were driven from their own sheep because of the sound faith—and those who were not driven out but wished voluntarily to depart so as not to communicate with any of their adversaries—spoke with this faith:

“Do you think that these men are doing this out of love of life or out of love of souls?” They acted in imitation of their Lord, the first Shepherd, Jesus Christ, the great God and Savior of our hope, who laid down his life for his sheep.

In every way, therefore, both those who appear to communicate as orthodox and those who abstain from communion await, after God, the light of your visitation and reception. Therefore hasten to help the East, from which the Savior sent you Peter and Paul, the two great lights of the day, for the illumination of the whole world.

Repay it, then, with the good recompense which it itself gave you. Illuminate it with the light of the sound faith, just as through it he once illuminated you with the light of divine knowledge.

For when the whole world was sick with sins, weakened by the offense of one man, the disciples of that good physician, calling upon the heavenly physician and chief Shepherd, their teacher, to attend to the illness, sometimes said:

“Lord, bow down your heavens and descend” (Psalm 143);

and again:

“O Shepherd of Israel, attend; you who sit upon the cherubim, appear. Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Psalm 79).

So now we, cast down by the sickness of the new transgression of our father, cry out to Your Blessedness, so that, as an imitator of the Son of God, you may come in response to supplication to our love [alternatively: to our abasement], imitating your heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous (Matthew 5).

Hasten to our aid, knowing, most holy father—as was said at the beginning—that “the healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9).

If the illness were small, perhaps we would run to our spiritual physician, so that we might both honor the sufferings of good physicians—that is, of the glorious disciples of Christ and your teachers—and adore your holy footsteps, receiving from your holy mouth both the medicine of our transgression, the loosening of our bonds, and the remission of our sin.

But it is not an ulcer, a blemish, or a swollen wound; rather, it is wholly ulcerous from the feet to the head (Isaiah 1), as the blessed Isaiah said while lamenting the ancient transgression.
