Therefore, you good physicians, and most reliable planters of that true physician or of his good disciples, hasten to treat the members of the ecclesiastical body that have been dislocated, so that you may raise our weakened hands and loosened knees and make straight paths for our feet. Let what is lame not be further dislocated, but rather be healed through your vigor and excellent diligence.

For when the Lord stood beside our teacher, the glorious apostle Paul, because of certain unbelievers, while Paul was weary of speaking the word of the Lord in Corinth, he said:

“Speak and do not be silent, because I have many people in this city” (Acts 18).

So now his kindness says to Your Blessedness:

“Hasten, and do not delay, to help the East—indeed, the greater regions of the inhabited world—for know that, after God, your healing is awaited not only by the one hundred and twenty thousand who once lived in the great city of Nineveh, but by a far greater number.”

If Leo, the archbishop established among the saints who preceded Your Blessedness, did not consider it unworthy to run personally to Attila, then an errant barbarian, to correct bodily captivity—not only of Christians but also, as is credible, of Jews and pagans—how much more does it belong to your holiness to hasten, not for the correction and conversion of bodily captivity caused by war, but for the correction and conversion of souls that have been taken captive or are daily being taken captive?

Between the two diabolical paths of error, those of Eutyches and Nestorius, show us more clearly a third path—or rather the middle path—the path of the true and sound doctrine.

Our sins have made this path uncertain, with some people thinking that no middle way of salvation can be found between Nestorius and Eutyches, but that everyone must necessarily belong to one or the other.

For this reason, hasten, after God, to help us. Just as the most holy Fathers showed the middle way of truth between Arius, who divided and separated the one nature and substance of the Godhead, and Sabellius, who confused the persons and diminished the number of the Trinity—demonstrating one substance, nature, and power in the confession of divinity, and, against Sabellius, three persons and one truth of equal power—so now, most holy and most blessed fathers, illuminate us with the light of your spiritual knowledge.

That true confession of the sound faith stands between the position of Eutyches, who, in imitation of Sabellius, confuses natures and substances, and that of Nestorius, who, in imitation of Arius, divides persons and substances. It was handed down to us by Pope Leo, established among the saints, and by the holy Fathers, his disciples at Chalcedon: the unity of the two substances—or natures—in one and the same person and substance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

They themselves taught us from the divine Scriptures that, in the one person and substance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, one nature of the flesh is visible, tangible, and capable of suffering, while the other nature is invisible, incapable of suffering, and incomprehensible.

One comes from the substance and nature of the mother, from the seed of David, Abraham, and Adam, born according to the flesh; the other was begotten from the substance and nature of the Father, from the womb, before the Morning Star.

But lest those who think according to Nestorius again seize upon the occasion of the two natures and substances of the immaculate birth and wrongly introduce two persons, two sons, or two Christs, those holy and blessed Fathers taught us to acknowledge one person and the inseparable unity of the substances from two substances and natures, and in the two substances and natures of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

For we, most holy and most blessed Symmachus, consider him to be the same one from two natures and in two natures. We do not confess—as they say—that from two natures there is one nature after the union, while refusing to confess him in two subsisting natures with their unity. By doing so, they show themselves to be imitators of the Arians, who say that the Father is glorified through the Son but refuse to say that he is glorified together with the Son.

But just as your most holy brothers, the Fathers, taught against them that we should say “through whom” and “with whom” equally, because “through whom” signifies the humanity and “with whom” the divinity of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, so now, when they say “from two natures” but do not confess “in two,” we say equally “from two” and “in two.”

For when we say “from two,” we mean the two from which the unity subsists. When we say “in two,” we confess the two in which he was seen, touched, and taken up after his passion and resurrection, and in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Col. 0061B] For naked divinity could neither be touched nor crucified for the life of the world; nor could mere humanity, subjected to death, by dying confound him who held the power of death, that is, the devil. Therefore, after the resurrection, the Word of God and our God, seen in his immaculate flesh, said to all his disciples: “See my hands and my feet, because I myself am he; touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24). He said “have,” so that he would not be thought to have been changed in that flesh, but would be believed truly to have assumed it.

To blessed Thomas, who doubted, he also cried out: “Put your finger here and see my hands; and give me your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 10). Therefore, when he was taken up, two men appeared to the disciples in white garments and cried out, saying: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). He will come altogether in the glory of the Father with the holy angels on the terrible day of righteous judgment. [Col. 0061C] Thus the unbelieving Jews will see the one whom they pierced, and with them also our sinners, when they see the one who had mercy on them and freed them, yet was neglected by them. But according to you, the holy and righteous will see the one whom their soul loved, and they will rejoice with ineffable and glorious joy, receiving the completion of their faith for the salvation of their souls, and hearing his most sweet voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (Matthew 25). May Christ our Lord deem us, together with your blessedness, worthy of that blessed voice in every respect, most holy father.

## LETTER VII (FORMERLY VIII), TO THE EASTERNERS, ETC.

[Col. 0061D] We plainly desire this to happen, if what we write is fulfilled. Let no one be astonished that we have now broken the silence hitherto maintained, since this saying of the most prudent Solomon resounds: “A time to speak, and a time to be silent” (Ecclesiastes 3). For the present time defeats silence; among the other things that are occurring, to be silent and not to be stirred by the goads of faith is certainly a sign of great indifference. Indeed, when reverence for religion and the highest things are shaken, it is appropriate, according to divine Scripture (Luke 22), to say that those who are meek ought to be fighters. For there is also a kind of spiritual struggle acceptable to God; from this comes the praise of those who endure everything, so that no one may be separated from divine love. Yet for you to teach what you teach is a heavy burden of shame, though it is necessary [Col. 0062A] and useful to admonish such people. For it is not fitting to bring the doctrines of religious discipline to those from whom the complete perfection of that very instruction is expected.

But we shall touch briefly upon what is clear. Who is unaware of the contagion of Nestorius with which the Church of Constantinople suffered? I mean Nestorius, who, like a rotten limb of the body, was cut off from the fellowship of Catholic communion. Where in the world is the assembly of the holy Council of Chalcedon not proclaimed, which condemned Eutyches and Dioscorus—two famous names of great treachery—as accomplices in iniquity, pursuing with one spirit things opposed to the divine doctrines, with the integrity of a single judgment? Who was unaware of Peter and Timothy, the aforesaid lackeys, champions of their chosen cause, who in savage error surpassed their own authors and teachers? [Col. 0062B] We are speaking of that Timothy, the patricide, who, while Proterius of holy memory was still alive, not only occupied the church without legitimate authority, but also added the shedding of pious blood to the crime of seizure. The voice of the universal Church pronounced his condemnation, stripping him even of the name and honor of Christian. The many sufferings of the orthodox made his follower Peter known; through them he exulted in displaying the strength of his spirit. Ephesus knows this man, together with the whole faction of Dioscorus, where it became known that, with the aforesaid author of sin, he brought about the end of holy Flavian.

[Col. 0062C] The evils at Antioch must be passed over in silence, where, through the unspeakable mockeries of another Peter, the venerable name of the priesthood was ridiculed. Who could lament with worthy grief the groans of Apamea and Tyre, comparable to tragic crimes, even if he had leisure for nothing else? What of Acacius? As though burdened by the fascination of his own supposed goodness, he was almost caught in a novel example of speaking judgment against himself: with a changed will, defending those whom he had previously thought it glorious to condemn [alternative: reject], and laboring to join to the faithful those whom he had earlier shown by manifest treachery to be heretics. For this reason above all he must be avoided and reckoned with the band of those condemned above, dissolving the very things by which he had been proved faithful, and mingling with those through whom the general injury of the Church occurred.

[Col. 0062D] If reason advises that the doctrines of the Fathers must be preserved against these men, consider whether they can be trampled underfoot by any greater transgression than they now are by those who in your regions revive the doctrines of Eutyches, restored to life [alternative: revived anew]. But if, as though established on infirm foundations, they are neglected without guilt, then the whole substance of our belief remains without any strength, since new things are always succeeding and dissolving ancient decrees. For whenever the discoveries of the ancestral rules are despised, and the firmness of what was rightly established is not defended, impieties of this kind must overtake the faith. For where the reasonable constitution of things is easily dissolved, there every form of holiness is corrupted, Christ is attacked, and—what believer could patiently endure it?—the venerable institutions of the Fathers are trampled underfoot. And who would not, by a just choice, prefer death to life? Where is the worshipful reverence of the Catholic faith? [Col. 0063A] Where are the doctrines established through the much blood of the saints? Where is the faithful authority of the ancient teachers? Where is that astonishing endurance of religious minds, content to be stripped of their own possessions lest they fall from the hope of an eternal inheritance, embracing every kind of suffering lest they be judged unworthy of that incorruptible good? For there are no greater proofs of faith than when the circumstances of the time urge one to subject life to suffering. Therefore, whoever has deserved to undergo the danger of persecution for its sake has shown himself worthy of the heavenly service. Christ purchased us by the precious price of his blood, granting the freedom of grace, since human works found nothing worthy to offer in exchange for so great a payment. And therefore, wherever religion is injured, every affection must be surpassed by love of the faith.

[Col. 0063B] Let each person therefore regard exiles and wanderings as home and fatherland, lest, held back by human desires, he be deprived of fellowship with Christ. Behold the time when faith calls back its soldiers and summons to its defense those who have obtained the fervor of grace. Let us judge faith itself to be speaking: Behold the desirable time; behold the longed-for gathering of the fruits of the faithful. Let great gifts compensate for small sufferings.

We would desire to exhort your charity at greater length in accordance with the charge entrusted to us. But what need is there of the goads of speech where we are taught to endure sufferings magnanimously for Christ by the examples of the apostles and the Fathers, who through the losses of earthly things displayed to us the evidence [alternative: increase] of heavenly virtues? Therefore let us proclaim without fear the distinguished disciplines of the Church [Col. 0063C] with great confidence. Far from us be the saying of the prophet: “And the priests concealed the truth” (Lamentations 2). For who is unaware that knowledge must be required of disciples by their teachers? And what harms followers when it is not proclaimed is plainly dangerous to those who remain silent. Truth must labor among those in whose presence what is hidden beneath the appearance of truth is falsehood, providing great strength to those who attack the faith so long as the judgments pronounced against them are not manfully asserted.

But I wish to say better things about you: that what has been confused through wicked men may through you receive the remedy of correction. It is not so harsh for someone to be deceived as it is to persist in error after being deceived. This evil is more grievous than all other evils, when members dissent from their own body. [Col. 0063D] For even if weakness does not individually seize upon every feature, nevertheless, according to the apostolic saying, the whole body must be weighed down in part.

Therefore the communion of those condemned must be avoided, according to the blessed Apostle: “Let no one be ashamed of the proclamation of the faith; for it is a power for every believer” (Romans 1). Let us shun the sacrilegious error of Eutyches, agreeing with Manichaean wickedness; and with equal resolve let us also avoid the communion of those who were formed by such men, who are now attempting to creep into the Churches of your regions like disease and contagion. Let no one separate himself together with the aforesaid men and pretend to endure the storm, until, separated from their communion, he enters the harbor of the true faith [the wording is internally difficult].

[Col. 0064A] I give this warning in love, not accusing them in hatred. For one who censures what deserves blame but supplies nothing useful shows rather the zeal of an accuser than the affection of one who loves. But one who exhorts to what is beneficial more clearly marks out the image of a good purpose, inviting people to seek useful things more fervently.

For this reason, brothers, desiring the unity of that good Church and confidently anticipating the blessed beauty of holy concord, let us say with holy David: “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132). And, as the apostle Paul said of you: “But you are all brothers in one Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). For as long as unity does not return, let no one doubt that what recently happened in the Church of Constantinople will eventually happen again [alternative: the same thing will nevertheless come]. [Col. 0064B] Concerning these matters I must both groan and remain silent. For those who thought the admonition of the apostolic see should be disregarded deservedly fell into what usually befalls those deprived of consolation.

Therefore, if anyone, considering his own salvation, wishes to preserve the apostolic judgments, once he has separated himself from the stain of the aforesaid men, let him know that he is without doubt a participant in our communion. For if he does not remove himself from the fellowship of those whom the apostolic see has condemned, let him know that by no pretext, fiction, or ecclesiastical cunning can he insinuate himself into the Church’s protection. For just as we gladly embrace those who separate themselves from the poisons of the aforementioned men—Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy, Peter, and Acacius—so our care and vigilance concerning their followers is always alert, lest they be able to creep in.

And in another hand: [Col. 0064C] May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October [October 8] (in the year of Christ 512), after the consulship of Felix, a man of most illustrious rank.

## LETTER VIII (FORMERLY IX), TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL [Col. 0064D]

Confirms the division of the province between the Churches of Vienne and Arles established by Pope Leo.

To our dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Gaul, Symmachus.

The institutions of the apostolic see demand proclamation, so that with unceasing care we may attend to the concord of the universal Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. This concord then grows especially and more effectively when a succeeding generation reverently observes what was established by the Fathers. For our brother and fellow bishop Caesarius, priest of the metropolitan city of Arles, having presented himself at the threshold of the Church of blessed Peter, requested that what had previously been established concerning the privileges of the Churches be renewed by our words. Therefore, the faithful instruction of the Roman Church declares everything that our predecessor, Pope Leo of blessed memory, ordered in this matter between the Churches of Arles and Vienne.

[Col. 0065A] And so, lest forgetfulness—which is always a rival of truth—be able to claim something for itself, and lest the force of the former decree grow old through the long passage of time, we judged it necessary to bring what was formerly promulgated back into the light through our utterances. Accordingly, just as our predecessor Pope Leo, after examining the arguments of the parties, determined long ago the number or extent of the parishes to be assigned to the bishops of Arles and Vienne, so we decree that no one’s usurpation may exceed it. Rather, as we stated above, in accordance with the concession of the aforesaid pontiff, let the bishop of Vienne claim as belonging to his jurisdiction the towns of Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble; and let him not presume to claim anything more than what was once granted to him by the apostolic see. Let the bishopric of Arles, for its part, defend all the other parishes or dioceses in their privileges and honor throughout the continuation of time. For neither observance nor reverence for antiquity is preserved if priestly glory is raised higher through an excess of humility.

Therefore, dearest brothers, [Col. 0065B] let each of you be content with the distribution of his own honor, and let no one, either through secular patronage or under any pretext of excuse, exceed the boundaries of the power granted to him by unlawful presumption. Each person ought to devote himself to the duty of devotion more out of grace than ambition, lest he provoke both the displeasure of our Lord and human envy against himself. The rights of the charge entrusted to us do not permit us to remain silent about these matters, so that we may rejoice over those who obey the ecclesiastical rules and persevere in the concord of the apostolic see, while those who cease to obey Catholic disciplines may show themselves alienated from the grace and love of the Church.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers. Given on the Ides of November [November 13], in the consulship of Probus, a man of most illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 502 [Note: [Col. 0066] The year 513, as is clear from Pagi’s observation cited above at Letter 7.]).

## COPY OF THE PETITION [Col. 0065C] PRESENTED TO POPE SYMMACHUS BY ABBOT AEGIDIUS AND THE NOTARY MESSIANUS, CONCERNING THE PRIVILEGES OF THE CHURCH OF ARLES

Just as the apostolic see claims primacy for itself among all the bishops of the Churches spread throughout the whole world, and just as its authority surpasses them, strengthened by synodal decrees, so it ought, through the foresight of its own power, to preserve unshaken what it once granted from itself, so that the Church of Arles may enjoy its privileges. This Church now presents through Bishop Caesarius the sequence of its petition and asks that the authority of your office confirm the power it has hitherto possessed, so that what the venerable see once ordered to be guarded by perpetual sanction, and what was specifically decreed in pragmatic constitutions, your blessed authority may now also confirm by its commands.

[Col. 0065D] Command also that the bishop of the city of Aix be admonished by the regulations of your holiness: whenever he has been summoned by the metropolitan bishop of the Church of Arles to a synodal council, or whenever divine religion requires him and he is requested for some matter of ordination, he must not fail to come. Thus what the authority of the ancients established through long ages may be preserved inviolate by you bishops for the present and future generations. Given by Abbot Aegidius and the notary Messianus.

## LETTER IX (FORMERLY X), [Col. 0066A] TO CAESARIUS OF ARLES

Responds to the preceding letter.

To our dearest brother Caesarius, Symmachus.

He who guards the venerable statutes of the Fathers shows himself a friend of complete religion; and he who takes care that no opportunity for excesses remain demonstrates that he thinks about the good of grace. It is reasonable that the holy Church of Arles should enjoy its own privileges; and what antiquity granted and the authority of the Fathers strengthened ought not to be violated by a new presumption. This must nevertheless be done in such a way that the privileges acquired over time by the other Churches do not waver, since what injures the whole cannot be firm in part.

[Col. 0066B] Since the things which the constitutions of the Fathers granted to each Church remain in force, we decree that, concerning matters arising both in the provinces of Gaul and in those of Spain in connection with religion, the vigilance of your fraternity must be watchful. If reason requires the presence of bishops, each one, after being summoned by the authority of your affection and in accordance with custom, must assemble. And if, with God’s help, the controversy that has arisen can be cut off, let us attribute this to his merits. Otherwise, let the nature of the existing matter reach the apostolic see through your report, so that, once everything has been carried out in its proper order, the enemy of goodness may find no place in which to flatter himself.

Therefore, as we said above, let the benefits that have long been preserved in each Church continue to be preserved. And if the bishop of the Church of Aix, or anyone else, summoned according to the definition of the canons by the metropolitan pontiff, should refuse to obey, let him know that he will be subjected—which we do not wish—to ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0066C] In this matter we especially wish you to be vigilant: if anyone from the regions of Gaul or Spain, belonging to the ecclesiastical order and office, is compelled to come to us, let him undertake his journey with the knowledge of your fraternity, so that his honor may not suffer any insult through ignorance and, once uncertainty has been removed, he may be admitted by us into the grace of communion with a secure mind.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother. Given on the third day before the Ides of June [June 11], in the consulship of Flavius, a senator and man of most illustrious rank (in the year of Christ 514).

## LETTER X (FORMERLY VI), AN APOLOGY AGAINST THE NOTORIOUS PETITION [Col. 0066D] OF THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS, IN WHICH HE ATTACKED THE PONTIFF BECAUSE OF THE SENTENCE OF EXCOMMUNICATION PRONOUNCED AGAINST HIM

Blessed Ambrose replied in eight books to the letter of the emperor Gratian, Your August Majesty, because he did not disdain to proclaim the Catholic faith at length, and Gratian was glad to receive it [the Latin appears corrupt: *hic non fastidivit gratanter accipere*]. I say this so that, if I have gathered the substance of the petition by setting it forth, I may not be thought to have spoken what I ought not.

If, emperor, I had to speak for the Catholic faith before foreign kings, and kings ignorant of the whole divinity, I would argue even at the cost of death for whatever agreed with its truth and reason. “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9); and it is better to incur the loss of this present life than to be punished with everlasting condemnation.

[Col. 0067A] But if you are a Roman emperor, you ought also to admit the embassies of barbarian nations with clemency. If you are a Christian ruler, you ought patiently to hear the voice of whatever apostolic bishop addresses you. As for the insults you have poured out against me, emperor—insults which you yourself weigh under divine judgment—I confess that I cannot conceal them, whether for my sake or for yours.

For my sake, recalling the Lord’s promise, which says: “When they persecute you and speak every evil against you for righteousness’ sake, rejoice” (Matthew 5). For yours, because I would not wish my glory to arise in such a way as to burden you not a little. And I, instructed by the Lord’s and the apostles’ teachings, strive to return blessing for your curses, honor for your insults, and love for your hatred.

[Col. 0067B] But take care, I ask, lest from the one who says, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Romans 12), as much as is remitted by me, so much more abundantly be demanded from you. What Christ says concerning those who scandalize even the least—perhaps, “the very least”—of those who believe in him, let the Gospel relate; let it not be spoken by my voice.

But perhaps you say, emperor, that you are rather the least because you believe in Christ, and that this should more properly be understood of you, while I am scandalizing your faith. Christ, therefore, is truly and wholly God, and wholly man: thus conceived, thus living in the world, thus suffering, thus among the dead, thus raised again, thus appearing with his disciples, thus lifted up into heaven, thus thereafter said to be coming, and thus even today remaining in the region of heaven. The Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2), and certainly he says of him what he now is.

[Col. 0067C] Therefore that person is the least who has believed thus in Christ. But the person who believes in Christ in this way believes in the whole Christ, not in a half-Christ—and therefore not in Christ, because Christ is only whole. And he is whole only in this way. It is of such a person believing in him that he says: he is his least and little one. What he promised concerning the one who was scandalized is better shown, as has been said, by his own words.

Perhaps you say, emperor: “But I too believe in such a Christ, and therefore I am rightly numbered among his least.” This is more serious if, while believing in such a Christ, you mingle in communion with those who do not believe in him. “Not only those who do such things,” says the Apostle, “but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1). Is sharing communion with such people not consenting to them? Therefore either declare that the others do not exist, or—much more seriously, as has been said—act against the truth known to you.

[Col. 0067D] As for the insults, emperor, which you think are directed against my person, would that, just as they are glorious for me, they could not weigh upon you! Some said to my Lord: “You have a demon; you are a glutton” (John 8); “You were born of fornication” (Matthew 11). Do you think, then, that I ought to grieve over such things? What protection is there for one who utters such things, both under divine and under human laws? “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matthew 18). [Col. 0068A] What will you do, emperor, when what is false has been proved before both a human court and a human judge examining you? What will you do at the divine judgment? Do you think that because you are emperor there is no judgment of God?

I say nothing of the fact that it is not fitting for an emperor to be an accuser. Finally, according to the same divine and human laws, no one can be both accuser and judge. Will you plead your case under another’s judgment? Or will you stand as accuser?

You say that I am a Manichaean. Am I therefore an Eutychian, or do I defend the Eutychians, whose madness gives the greatest support to the error of the Manichaeans? Rome bears witness for me, and the archives testify whether, after coming from paganism and receiving the Catholic faith at the see of blessed Peter the apostle, I have deviated from it in any respect. Let someone come forward and convict me by any argument; otherwise these are insults, not proofs of crimes.

[Col. 0068B] I do not know whether those against whom a falsehood is alleged, or the false accusers who speak hostile things when they say that I was not consecrated in due order, are at fault [the Latin construction is incomplete]. I escaped whole amid showers of stones; God judged. Do you think, because you are emperor, that the divine judgment may be disregarded?

But perhaps you will say that even an angry God often permits harmful things. It is written: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7). Show, then, what you think ought to be accused, so that you may demonstrate that an exceedingly angry God permitted things that ought not to have happened.

Is it because I do not in any way yield to the Eutychians? These things do not wound me, but they openly and clearly demonstrate that I have thought to reject the honor which blessed Peter imposed through his intervention. Because you are emperor, do you strive against Peter’s authority? And while you receive Peter of Alexandria, do you attempt to trample blessed Peter the apostle in whatever representative of his he may have? Would I have been acting rightly if I favored the Eutychians? If I shared communion with the name of Acacius? It cannot be hidden why you advance these pretexts.

[Col. 0068C] Let us compare the honor of the emperor with the honor of the pontiff. The difference between them is as great as that between one who cares for human affairs and one who administers divine affairs. You, emperor, receive baptism from the pontiff, receive the sacraments, request prayer, hope for blessing, and ask for penance. Finally, you administer human things, while he dispenses divine things to you. Therefore, not to say superior, his honor is certainly equal.

Do not think that you surpass him by the pomp of the world: “For what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1; the citation in the source reads “II Cor. II”). Therefore consider what befits you. Yet when you have burst into accusation, you stand with me on equal ground under both divine and human laws. In this matter, if I am to be deprived of the highest honor because you wish it, once convicted through your accusation, you likewise will lose your rank if you are not able to convict me.

[Col. 0068D] Let this be a judgment in the world, with God and his angels looking on; let us be a spectacle to the whole age, so that either a priest of good life or an emperor of religious moderation may provide an example. For the human race is governed chiefly by these two offices, and neither ought to exist in such a way as to offend the divinity, especially since both honors appear to be perpetual and the human race is served through each of them.

[Col. 0069A] I ask you, emperor—let me say this with your peace—remember that you are human, so that you may use the power divinely granted to you. For even if these matters have been brought before a human judgment, they must necessarily be examined under divine scrutiny. Perhaps you will say that it is written that we ought to be subject to every authority (Romans 13). We accept human authorities in their proper place, until they raise their wills against God. But if every authority is from God, then that authority which has been appointed over divine matters is all the more so.

Give God his due in us, and we will give God his due in you. But if you do not give God his due, you cannot use the privilege of the one whose laws you disregard.

You say that I excommunicated you with the senate conspiring with me. In this I certainly follow my predecessors, since what they did was unquestionably done reasonably. You say that the Roman senate treats you badly. If we treat you badly by urging you to withdraw from heretics, do you treat us well when you wish to join us precipitately [Col. 0069B] to heretics?

“What is it to me,” you will say, “what Acacius did?” Then withdraw, and it will have nothing to do with you. For if you do not withdraw from him, it concerns you also. Let us both leave the dead man alone. This is precisely what we ask: that what Acacius did have nothing to do with you. You make us charge it against you by wishing what Acacius did to concern you. We avoid what Acacius did; you too should avoid it. Then what Acacius did concerns neither of us, so that you may be joined to what concerns us without the things Acacius did, and may be joined to our communion without Acacius.

We did not excommunicate you, emperor, but Acacius. Withdraw from Acacius, and you withdraw from his excommunication. Do not mix yourself with his excommunication, and you are not excommunicated by us. If you mix yourself with it, you are excommunicated not by us but by yourself. Thus, in either case—whether you withdraw or do not withdraw—you are not excommunicated by us.

[Col. 0069C] Catholic rulers have always sent letters ahead to the apostolic bishops whom they recognized as appointed, and, like good sons, have sought that special confession and faith which they knew had been entrusted by the mouth of the Lord Savior himself with care for the whole Church, doing so with the affection of due piety. Because your tranquility is thought perhaps to have passed this over on account of public circumstances, and lest I be judged to seek my own honor rather than concern for the Lord’s flock, I did not cease to appeal to you through my own voluntary conversations.

[Col. 0069D] You indicate that it has been made public that Your Serenity, having directed military force, was compelling those who had chosen for many years to abstain from the contagion of the faithless to enter by force and arms the detestable fellowship of a corrupted communion. Here, as ruler of human affairs, I do not cease to challenge you in my voice, as a representative of the apostolic see in whatever capacity: remember that you are human, however much worldly power supports you, and consider all those who from the beginning of Christian doctrine have attempted, with different purposes, to persecute or afflict the Catholic faith.

Consider how those who inflicted such things, by pursuing devastation and by the destruction they brought about, have themselves failed, while orthodox truth has prevailed all the more precisely when it was thought to have been oppressed. Just as truth is shown to have grown under its persecutors, so it is known to have crushed those who pursued it.

[Col. 0070A] I am astonished if human understanding does not perceive this, especially the understanding of one who wishes now to be called by the Christian name. Such a person must certainly be counted among those who have attempted to attack the right confession and Christian communion by various superstitions, while they themselves in every way strive to assail it.

For what difference is there between a pagan and one who—what is worse—under the Christian name attempts to weaken the true and pure tradition of the apostolic rule, and rushes into such blindness that, while all the opinions of every heresy in those regions have public license to profess themselves, only the freedom of Catholic communion is thought by those who consider themselves religious to be in need of subversion?

If it is considered an error—which is not permitted—let it be allowed to exist along with the other errors that have the freedom to act there. But if it is judged to be integrity, then it ought rather to have been followed than devastated by violent persecution. Nor could they have been proved to pursue it unless they were following what was perverse. But lest they themselves be convicted of error, they decided to repel that by which, as erring persons, they were wavering, preferring not to follow what is just, but rather to remove the means by which they would be taught that they were unjust.

[Col. 0070B] Thus God has withdrawn from human minds, so that they do not perceive a will obstinately set against right, even though in this world divine judgment cannot be absent, and after the course of this life that fearsome examination will not be absent either. Under it, the purposes of destructive actions will be examined in every way, exposed, and, once exposed, punished—unless there are those who altogether do not believe these things or who confidently suppose that they can commit them with impunity.

[Col. 0070C] But we do not cease to summon the conscience of the human race, with whatever voice we can, declaring that almighty God will in no way fail to act according to his own judgments, and that, however great human presumption or power may be, under the divine will the judgment of this atrocity will unquestionably be exacted. For we do not believe that such an act of daring will escape here, and in that great judgment of God it will receive what divine retribution owes to such audacity.

Let it suffice that we have by no means kept silent about these matters. When heavenly vengeance follows, human understanding must recognize that we spoke the truth, that we did not proclaim the coming punishment in vain, and that we placed before it a form of warning by which people might thereafter restrain themselves from such precipices.

[Col. 0070D] Certainly, if you determine that such people should therefore be left to their own judgment because it is not fitting for Christians to harass those who confess Christ under whatever title, nor appropriate for Romans to tear apart people living under Roman law, it follows that anyone who attacks Roman men, of whatever Christian profession, can in no way be called either Christian or Roman.

Therefore, either they ought to have been rejected, or no one at all ought to have been attacked. What you judge must be removed in one category, reject in every category if you prevail. If everything is to be allowed, no one at all should be excluded. Otherwise, while you are a friend to every error by sparing them all, it is proved that you alone are displeased by what is true.

All Catholic rulers, whether they assumed the reins of government with imperial authority or recognized that new apostolic bishops had been appointed, immediately sent their letters to that see, thereby showing that they were its companions. Those who did not do this therefore profess themselves alienated from it. We could establish this even from your own documents, unless we were avoiding you as a rival, defendant, enemy, and judge.

[Col. 0071A] It is no wonder that the patrons of the Manichaeans persecute Catholics, since falsehood cannot help persecuting truth. It is no wonder that they rage against the orthodox, since they can agree with every heresy and, being friends to every error, can be enemies only to those who do not err.

If it is error, it must be refuted. But if it is not error, recognize that you lack the truth, since you persecute what you profess to be error [alternative: what you are convicted of as error]. But an accomplice of wickedness can do nothing except persecute the one who is an enemy of wickedness.

## LETTER XI (FORMERLY VII), OF POPE SYMMACHUS—or AT LEAST WRITTEN IN HIS NAME BY THE DEACON ENNODIUS—TO THE CONFESSOR BISHOPS

[Col. 0071B] Deported to Sardinia and the other islands.

To our dearest brother bishops of Africa, Symmachus.

The enemy might perhaps have considered it a gain if, amid the dangers he imposed upon Christians, he had subdued the minds of believers, and, with the Lord’s flock scattered in different directions, there had remained no one—even among the few—by whom he could be trampled underfoot through steadfast faith. Yet he still reigns in your number, he who took pleasure not so much in multitude as in devotion.

For it is written (Luke 22) that Satan was given power to sift the servants of Christ, so that whatever could be found of wheat might be joined to the granaries, while whatever was chaff might pass over to fuel for the fires. To you especially it was said: “Do not fear, little flock; for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0071C] The sword of the faithless came among you, cutting away the withered members of the Church and leading the healthy to heavenly glory. The contest shows whom Christ has as his soldiers; through wars it is known who deserves triumph.

Do not fear that they have taken away from you the insignia of your episcopal rank. With you is that priest—or victim—who has been accustomed to rejoice not so much in honors as in minds. The rewards of confession are greater than the gifts of proclaimed dignity. Human favor often leads persons of lesser merit to the latter; the former is granted only by heavenly grace. For he himself fought and conquered in you, the one whom faith deserves to have joined to it even amid the torments inflicted by human beings.

There is no need for lengthy conversations to kindle heavenly fervor in you. The fire of divine virtue has its own growth. There is no need to exalt with praises those already placed upon the trophy [Col. 0071D], who conquered without an adviser: whatever flatteries of proclamation they receive burden the Christian conscience. What you have done is indeed a work of virtue, but it must be surpassed by the restoration of the highest reward. Nevertheless, what you hoped for when you sent letters to our son N. Ennodius [Note: The name Ennodius is absent in the manuscript codex, in which not N. but II. is read, “lest the relics of the holy martyrs be sent.” LAB.], the deacon, asking for the blessing of the blessed Nazarius and Romanus, [Col. 0072A] we do not deny to the faithful. Receive the venerable patronage of unconquered soldiers, since the emperor has now recognized your devout faith in battle. God will grant you to complete the gifts of confession happily, when it pleases him to restore peace to the Churches; and he will console with the sweetness of peace the grief that adversity has brought upon you.

## EPISTLE XII (FORMERLY XI), TO THEODORE, ARCHBISHOP OF LAURIACUM, TO WHOM HE GRANTS THE USE OF THE PALLIUM

[Note: From the appendix to the Reichersberg Chronicle and from Hondius’s Salzburg metropolitan collection.]

Symmachus, bishop by the grace of God of the holy apostolic see, to his most reverend and most holy brother Theodore, archbishop of the Church of Lauriacum.

For the days of your life we have willingly granted, in accordance with the custom of our predecessors, the use of the pallium which you appropriately requested from the apostolic see, both for the adornment of the priestly office and to display the unanimity which, together with the blessed apostle Peter, the entire flock of the Lord’s sheep—whose care has also been entrusted to you—is unquestionably to possess. Since the Church was founded by those same apostles, we have gladly granted this in accordance with ancient custom, to show that you are a teacher and archbishop, and that your holy Church of Lauriacum is the metropolitan see of the province of Pannonia.

Therefore, concerning the pallium which we send to you out of apostolic charity, we earnestly admonish you—and at the same time wish you to understand—that you must use it according to the custom of your Church. For the vestment with which you are adorned for the solemn celebration of Mass displays the sign of the cross; and through this sign know that you must suffer together with your brothers and be crucified inwardly in your affections to the allurements of the world. Accordingly, when you wear this insignia outwardly, consider inwardly in your heart that it is more a burden than an honor. While God shields your heart, restrain it from desire for this world in such a way that you strive both to carry out the governance entrusted to you and to be worthy—by integrity of conduct, alertness of diligence, and the guardianship of an unimpaired faith—of the dignity you have attained and the office by which you are exalted. Thus may you yourself deserve to obtain from God, the rewarder of all good things, the grace of blessing and eternal life. Amen.

## COPY OF THE DECREE MADE BY LORD POPE SYMMACHUS CONCERNING THE ABROGATION OF THE LAW OF KING ODOACER, WHICH OPPOSED ECCLESIASTICAL LIBERTY IN THE ELECTION OF THE PONTIFF, AND CONCERNING THE PRESERVATION OF THE PROPERTY OF THE CHURCH

[Col. 0072D] [Note: Manuscript Lucensis 125, Flavio.]

With Flavianus Avienus, a most distinguished younger man, as consul, on the eighth day before the Ides of November [alternative: the ninth], in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, while the venerable man Pope Symmachus was seated together with the venerable men [Note: In the same manuscript, “and bishops” is absent.] and bishops [Note: Manuscript Lucensis 125 lists Laurentius, Petrus, Aemilianus, Felix, Acresconius, Benignus, Innocentius, Maximus, Johannes, Eulalius, Fortunatus, Eustatius, Jocundus, Fortunatus, Euticius, Aprilis, Mercurius, Fortunatus, Asellus, Stephanus, Maximus, Laurentius, Frigidus, Cassianus, Pacannanus, Rurifinus, Johannes, Stephanus, Serenus, Proculeianus, Laurentius, Martianus, Candidus, Fortunatus, Eutychius, Aprilis, Mercurius, Fortunatus, Asellus, Stephanus, [Col. 0073C] Paschasius, Memor, Hylarus, Innocentius, Colonius, Maximinianus, Felix, Elpidius, Innocentius, Hylarus, Concordius, Innocentius, Gecontius, Vitalis, Seretinus, Regeneriosus, [Col. 0073D] Castus, Silvinus, Aresto, Severinus, Martyrius, Sebastianus, Vindemius, Victor, Mercurius, Servus Dei, Asterius, Felix, Augustus, Chrysogonus, Rusticus, Sallustius, Brobus, Cando, Bassalius, Florentius, Venantius, Propinquus, Valentinus, Romanus, Dulcitius, Ursus, Asellus, Adeodatus, Martinianus, Eusebius, Projectus, Venantius, Projectus, Martinianus, Epiphanius, Sebastianus, Servus Dei, Epiphanius, Abundantius, Paulinus, Marcellus, Benedictus, Paschasius, Severus, Adeodatus, Timotheus, Hylarus, Marcus, Venantius, Petrus, Victorius, Tinulus, Fortunatus, Octavianus, Anastasius, Vincomalus, Julianus, Agatho, Arescentianus, Julianus, Paulinus, Johannes, Laurentius, Adeodatus, Stephanus, Petrus, Chrysogonus, and Chrysogonus, and Maximinus, presbyters, being present, etc.] Laurentius, Maximus, Petrus, Laurentius, Aemilianus, [Note: Dionysius reads Trigidius. HARD.] Tigridius, Felix, Bassianus, Cresconius, Pacatianus, Benignus, Rufentius, Innocentius, [Col. 0073A] Johannes, Maximus, Stephanus, Johannes, Serenus, Eulalius, Proculeianus, Fortunatus, Laurentius, [Note: Dionysius reads Eustasius. HARD.] Eustathius, Martianus, Jocundus, Candidus, Fortunatus, Felix, Eutychius, Elpidius, Aprilis, Innocentius, Mercurius, Hilarius, Fortunatus, Concordius, Asellus, [Note: The manuscript reads Innocensus. HARD.] Innocentius, Stephanus, Gerontius, Paschasius, Vitalis, Memor, Severinus, Hilarius, Veneriosus, Innocentius, Castus, Colonicus, Silvanus, Maximilianus, Aristone [alternative: Ariste], Severinus, Propinquus, Martyrius, Valentinus, Sebastianus, Romanus, Vindemius, Vindemius, Victor, Dulcitius, Ursus, Mercurius, Asellus, Servus Dei, Adeodatus, Asterius, Martinianus, Felix, Eusebius, Augustus, Projectitius, Chrysogonus, Venantius, Rusticus, Sallustius, Probus, Amandus [alternative: Anantius], Basilius, and Florentius.

The presbyters Projectitius, Martinus, Epiphanius, Sebastianus, [Col. 0073B] Servus Dei, Octavianus, Anastasius, Abundantius, Vincomalus, Paulinus, Julianus, Marcellus, Agatho, Benedictus, Crescentianus, Paschasius, Julianus, Severus, Paulinus, Adeodatus, Johannes, Timotheus, Laurentius, Hilarius, Adeodatus, Marcus, Stephanus, Venantius, Petrus, Chrysogonus, Litorius, and Chrysogonus, Tinulus or Maximus [alternative: Maximinus], and Fortunatus were also seated; and the deacons Anastasius, Hormisdas, Johannes, and Agapetus were present. Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

### I

Your fraternity has indeed obeyed the ecclesiastical laws and, in fear of the divine judgment, has defined what had to be established, reaching the summit of justice [alternative: bringing it to completion], since it embraces everything sufficiently [Col. 0073C] and its fullness requires no addition—especially concerning the clerics whom the love of domination has seized and caused to reject the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline, and who, as has become clear among you [alternative: among us], have therefore created a schism. Yet you did not deny them the mercy which God commands to be extended to all, as was fitting, provided that the hardness of their hearts does not procure punishment for them by despising the remedies offered, although it is difficult to recount their excesses.

There is one matter, however, which has occurred to me, and I shall not delay in bringing it to the attention of your venerable order. [Note: These were evidently the schismatics, who had taken this deceitful and fraudulent material, already wholly obsolete, not from the archives of the Roman Church—into which it had never been brought—but perhaps from the praetorian headquarters at Sirmium, after eighteen years. SEV. BINIUS.]

Among other things they said that a certain document had been written by Basil, of illustrious memory, [Col. 0074A] supposedly out of love for the substance of the Church, in which no bishop of the Roman Church had either taken part or subscribed, through whom it could have acquired legitimate validity. But so that I may not argue the matter myself, [Note: The manuscript reads “from which it can.”] and so that your council may be able to judge, let it be brought forward and presented [alternative: laid down] in the midst, so that by reading it you may recognize what sort of substance it can possess.

The holy synod answered: Let it be brought forward into the midst, so that its character may be recognized.

As he was saying this, the deacon Hormisdas recited:

### II

When the exalted and most eminent man, the prefect of the praetorium and patrician, also acting as deputy of the most excellent [Note: What sort and kind of king Odoacer was, I have discussed above under Simplicius. SEV. BINIUS.] King Odoacer, had sat together with others at the blessed apostle Peter, Basil said:

[Note: Basil, the prefect of the praetorium, should not be considered a different man from that Caecina Basilus, the highly distinguished consul at Rome, in whose praise Sidonius has much to say in Book I, Letter 9, to Heronius, and elsewhere. SEV. BINIUS.]

Although it is in the interest of our zeal and religious duty that concord should above all be preserved in the Church during the election of a bishop, lest, through the occasion of sedition, the condition of the state [alternative: city] be thrown into doubt, nevertheless [Note: The claim that Pope Simplicius wanted no pontiff to be elected without the consent of the king of Italy is fabricated. He may perhaps have asked that, in order to suppress disturbances and avoid dissension, the king not refuse to be present at the election of his successor. Baronius, under the aforementioned year 483, no. 11. SEV. BINIUS.] at the admonition of our most blessed [Note: In the same manuscript, “man” is absent.] Pope Simplicius—a warning which we must always keep before our eyes—you remember that we were commanded under oath that, because of that disturbance and the injury to the venerable Church, if it should happen that he passed from this life, no election of anyone should be celebrated without consultation with us. [Note: The manuscript reads “of any.”]

When Cresconius, bishop of the Church of the city of Tuder, was reading this, he rose from his seat and said:

Let the holy synod weigh this carefully: that, setting aside the religious persons whose chief concern is such a great pontiff, they have placed the election of a layman under their own control, which is plainly contrary to the canons. [Note: In the same manuscript, “the election of a layman” is absent.]

Then the deacon Hormisdas read:

For when the venerable Church was suffering every kind of confusion and loss—we are astonished that, although we were passed over, anything was attempted [alternative: testified]; since our priest was still alive, nothing ought to have been undertaken without us. [Note: In the same manuscript, “without us” is absent.]

Therefore, if it pleases your eminence and holiness, let us preserve intact, with religious honor [alternative: veneration], everything that concerns the election of a future bishop, giving special precedence to this law, which we establish for ourselves and our heirs out of Christian devotion.

Let no estate—whether rural or urban—nor any ornaments or ecclesiastical equipment now existing, or which may come to the rights of the Churches under any title, be alienated under any title or pretext by the man who is now to be ordained bishop by common election, or by those who will follow in future ages. If anyone should wish to alienate any of these things, let it be judged ineffective and void; and let the one who does it, consents to it, or receives it be anathema.

Maximus, bishop of the Church of Blera [alternative: Bleda], said:

Let the holy synod now declare whether it was permissible for a layman to pronounce an anathema within the ecclesiastical order. Or whether a layman could pronounce an anathema against a priest and establish, contrary to the canons, something that did not belong to his authority. Tell me what you think: was it permissible for a layman to give me a law? The holy synod said: It was not permissible.

And it added: Read what follows.

The deacon Hormisdas read:

And whoever has acquired a rural or urban estate belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction must know that he is protected by no law or prescription [alternative: prescription of law]. But whether the person who alienated it, or the person who subsequently attempts, against the contrary will, to reclaim an estate alienated in this way, let him restore it together with its fruits, whoever acquired it.

As he was reading, Stephanus, bishop of the Church of Venusia, rose from his seat and said: Let it be read through.

The deacon Hormisdas read:

### III

It was also decided that this penalty should apply to the heirs and successor-heirs of the recipient. In this matter every cleric must have the freedom to contradict. For it is unjust, and akin to sacrilege, that whatever each person has contributed to the venerable Church for the salvation or repose of his soul, or has at least left for the sake of the poor, should be transferred into alien ownership by those whose chief duty it was to preserve these things. [Note: The manuscript reads “in altercation.”]

Whatever objects among gems, gold, silver, or clothing appear less suitable for the Church’s use or adornment, and cannot be preserved or endure for long, should be sold at a fair valuation and applied to religious distribution.

When this had been read, Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, said:

This document could not bind any pontiff of the Roman city, because it was not permitted [alternative: it was not approved] for a layman to possess any power of establishing anything in the Church apart from the Roman pope; the necessity is to obey [alternative: follow] him, not the authority to command—especially since neither the Roman pope subscribed to it nor is the assent of any metropolitan recorded according to the canons. [Note: The manuscript reads “of following.”]

Petrus, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, said:

It is clear that the document circulated in our assembly cannot stand by any force [alternative: cannot be upheld], because it does not agree with the canons and appears to have been composed by a lay person [alternative: now by a lay person], especially since no prelate of the apostolic see is shown to have taken part in it or confirmed it by his own subscription.

Eulalius, bishop of the Church of Syracuse, said:

The document read aloud in the priestly council is shown by the clearest evidence to be invalid. First, it appears to have been made contrary to the rules of the Fathers by laymen, even though they were religious persons, to whom no authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources is ever recorded as having been granted. Second, it is shown not to have been confirmed by the subscription of any prelate of the apostolic see.

And if the holy Fathers have decreed that, when priests of any province hold a council within their own boundaries, anything they attempt without the authority of their metropolitan or bishop [Note: The manuscript reads “has been testified.”] must be void, how much more must that be without force—and in no way be counted among ecclesiastical statutes—which is known to have been presumed by laymen, even though some bishops consented, [Col. 0076B] when it was undertaken at the apostolic see in the absence of the bishop who, by the prerogative of the merits of the blessed apostle Peter, holds the primacy of the priesthood throughout the world and is accustomed to confer validity upon synodal decrees? [Note: Explain this passage as the preceding council explained these words: “The merit of the apostle Peter first belongs to his see,” and so forth. SEV. BINIUS.] Those bishops, moreover, could not prejudice the pontiff by whom they are known to have been consecrated.

The holy synod said:

It is clear, according to the statement of our venerable brothers Laurentius, Petrus, Eulalius, Cresconius, Maximus, and Stephanus, and it is not uncertain among us, that this same document is entirely without force. Even if it could in some way subsist, it ought in every respect to be weakened and annulled by the prudent judgment of your blessedness in the synodal assembly, lest it remain as an example encouraging any laymen, however religious or powerful, to decree anything in any city concerning ecclesiastical resources by any means whatsoever. The care of disposing of these resources, we are taught, has been entrusted by God exclusively and unquestionably to priests.

Bishop Symmachus said:

Now, since God has granted me your desired presence on this occasion, I wish, if it pleases you, to make firm a matter which I believe accords with the interests of ecclesiastical resources, so that all those whom empty fury has stirred up against me may recognize that I strive for nothing more than that what has been entrusted to me by God under stewardship may remain safe. It ought also to be pleasing to all who fear God, and it belongs to the preservation of the Church’s patrimony.

The holy synod said:

We know that your provision is devoted to necessary matters, and therefore it is in your power to arrange what ought to be followed.

Symmachus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

Great reverence is indeed owed to a venerable and priestly purpose, which is concerned to arrange what is right out of diligence, not necessity. But since avarice, the mother of vices, when certain people ask for what belongs to others, rejects the barriers of decency and thinks everything permissible expedient, it abuses the patience of heavenly piety while it gapes for plunder. Those awaiting correction, under the governance of heaven, think themselves not subject to judgment, although it is clear that, among certain people, the delay of the divine sentence proceeds as an opportunity for plunder.

But we, whom pastoral care and ecclesiastical responsibility bind, must render an account of the substance entrusted to our stewardship. We must extend our concern not only to the present but also to future ages, lest it result in the ruin of our souls if those who could owe innocence to the statutes, presuming upon their freedom, should offend, when they can be supported by the religious authority both of ourselves and of our successor, while serving the ecclesiastical laws.

### IV

Therefore, having weighed these matters, and with the decree to remain in force under the consideration of our God, we establish that from this day forward no prelate of the apostolic see may transfer to another’s rights, under perpetual alienation or exchange, any rural estate, however great or small it may be, so long as, by the Lord’s disposition, the saving doctrine of the Catholic faith remains. Nor may anyone excuse himself on the pretext of necessity, since what we are discussing is not a personal matter; nor may any cleric or layman defend himself by appealing to this occasion.

Nor may it be permissible to grant such estates to anyone under a usufructuary right, or to retain estates so granted, except in the case of clerics, captives, and foreigners, lest an opportunity for bad administration be provided, since other paths remain open for that generosity. [Note: The manuscript reads “rural estates in usufruct.”]

### V

Only houses established in any cities, whose condition necessarily requires maintenance at considerable expense, may plainly be exchanged [alternative: lent], with the revenues received—if it should happen that they are offered—at a fair valuation [Note: The manuscript reads “valuation”], and with fear of the divine judgment. [Note: The manuscript reads “they shall be entrusted.”]

### VI

We likewise wish the custodians of the churches throughout all the titles of the Roman city—whether they are presbyters or whoever they may be—to be bound by this law. For it is unspeakably wrong that a person of the second order in the Church should not be held by the same obligation by which the supreme pontiff binds himself through the charity of Christ.

If anyone so bound, forgetful of God and of this decree by which we wish the priests of the Roman city to be tied by religious bonds, should, by violating the present constitution, attempt in any way to alienate any property belonging to the titles or to the aforementioned Church under perpetual right—except gold, silver, gems, and clothing, if there are any, or if any movable objects should be added that do not in any way belong to divine adornment—except also the houses under the condition stated above, let the donor, alienator, and seller be punished by loss of his rank. [Note: The manuscript reads “forgetful.”]

### VII

Moreover, whoever asks for or receives such property, or whoever among the presbyters, deacons, or defenders signs on behalf of the donor, shall be struck with an anathema by which God strikes souls in anger. Let the recipient or signatory among the persons mentioned above—that is, those whom we have judged should be struck with anathema—be subject to the penalty previously set out for the alienator, while the established penalty for accomplices is preserved. Unless, perhaps, the alienator, when he seeks its return, and the recipient, by prompt restitution, should take precautions for themselves.

### VIII

But if anyone, with insufficient concern for his soul, should perhaps neglect the remedy offered, then, in addition to the kinds of punishment written above, any document drawn up contrary to justice shall be rendered ineffective by every means, although it possessed no force from the beginning. [Note: The manuscript reads “shall be made effective,” apparently corrupt.]

It shall also be lawful for any ecclesiastical persons to raise a voice of contradiction and to be supported by ecclesiastical authority, so that they may reclaim the alienated property together with its fruits. Nor may anyone who scatters, without any consideration of piety and contrary to justice, what religious souls left for the support of the poor fortify himself with any obstacle before the tribunal of Christ.

We wish the law of this constitution to be observed only in the apostolic see; in all the Churches throughout the provinces, let it be observed according to the consideration of souls and in the manner which their rulers judge appropriate to the purpose of religion.

## SUBSCRIPTIONS

I, Caelius Symmachus, bishop of the Roman Church, have subscribed this constitution made by us.

I, Caelius Laurentius, bishop of the holy Church of Milan, have subscribed this constitution made by the venerable Pope Symmachus.

I, Petrus, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of Ravenna, have subscribed this constitution made by the venerable Pope Symmachus.

[Note: In the Acts of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, the following is said about Eulalius: “Eulalius was a man of outstanding holiness, admirable hospitality, and perfect charity. In his heart the treasure of spiritual wisdom was hidden, and through the trading of the Lord’s talents he enriched many. Distinguished above all by the virtue of discernment, he loved the profession of the monks above all else,” and so forth. SEV. BINIUS.]

## DECREE OF POPE SYMMACHUS

(From Gratian, 30, question 1, canon 8.) An equal penance is imposed upon anyone shown to have violated his spiritual daughter and his own female penitent.

All whom we receive in penance are our spiritual sons, just as those whom the sacred baptismal water regenerates, whether they are received by us or immersed by us under the name of the threefold immersion. Sylvester, teaching and admonishing, also instructs every priest that no one should approach his female penitent for the sake of fornication, because it is written: all whom we receive in penance are our sons, just as those received in baptism. Therefore, if anyone commits this crime, let him not only lose the honor of his dignity, but also submit himself to perpetual penance until the end of his life. [Note: The same words are attributed under the name of Symmachus in the Roman Penitential edited by Antonio Augustinus, title 8, chapter 3.]

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 513. PETRUS THE DEACON

[Col. 0079]

[Col. 0079C]

## PROLEGOMENON

(From Galland.)

### I

Petrus the deacon follows Hesychius, the presbyter of Jerusalem. At the beginning of the sixth century he came from the East to Rome with others in the cause of the faith. His little book On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ, addressed to Fulgentius and the other African bishops exiled in Sardinia, is extant in collections of orthodox writers and in the libraries of the Fathers, as well as in the appendix to volume X of the works of Saint Augustine [Note: Augustine’s works, volume II in the appendix, p. 146.], with four chapters on the Incarnation omitted; finally, it has often been printed among the works of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe.

Concerning this work Possevinus writes [Note: Possevinus, Sacred Apparatus, volume II, p. 252, Cologne edition]: “This little book was discovered not very many years ago in a Parisian monastery of the Premonstratensian order in the district of Louvain.”

But the distinguished editor of Saint Fulgentius’s works [Note: Preface to Saint Fulgentius’s works, p. 8, and note 1 to the book On Faith.] rightly observes, and after him the most learned editors of Saint Augustine’s works [Note: The Blessed Editors, appendix to volume VI of Saint Augustine’s works, p. 17 in the admonition.], that our author must not be confused with Petrus, to whom Saint Fulgentius dedicated his excellent treatise On Faith. For he was not a deacon, as Norisius supposed [Note: Norisius, History of Pelagianism, Book II, chapter 19, works volume I, p. 492.], nor a monk, as Blondellus mistakenly believed [Note: Blondellus, On the Primacy, p. 411.], but apparently a military man. When he had decided to travel to Palestine and had learned that numerous heresies were spreading throughout that province, he therefore requested a rule of faith from the most holy as well as most learned bishop of Ruspe, so that no sense of heretical depravity might creep into him.

### II

Now, when we are about to speak about the little book of Petrus the deacon and the occasion for its composition, we shall follow in the footsteps of learned men, whom we freely acknowledge to have gone before us in explaining this matter.

In the year 518, at the beginning of the reign of Justin, the Scythian monks, whose leader and supporter was John Maxentius, believing that the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies could not be eradicated at the root unless it were asserted that one of the Trinity had suffered, stirred up enormous disturbances at Constantinople, and within a short time the whole world was inflamed by them.

It is reported that the matter was first brought before the legates of the apostolic see residing at Constantinople, and shortly afterward was referred to Hormisdas himself, the Roman pontiff. But when the delegation of the monks sent to Rome, whose chief was Petrus the deacon, discovered that this new formula of expression was being strongly challenged, they took refuge with the African bishops exiled in Sardinia.

Accordingly, as the year 520 was ending or 521 beginning, a profession of faith, composed in the form of a letter, was delivered to Saint Fulgentius and the other confessors who had been deported to Sardinia by Thrasamund, the Arian king of the Vandals. It was issued in the name of Petrus the deacon and his companions. Among them the aforementioned Petrus the deacon stood out, and he also subscribed the little book first.

Since we have noticed that, through the carelessness of the printer, the subscriptions of these legates were omitted from our edition, we have therefore decided at least to transcribe them here. They are as follows:

Petrus, deacon by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

Johannes, monk by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

Leontius, monk by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

Johannes the lector, by the mercy of God, has subscribed.

### III

These envoys, sent by the Scythian monks, brought to the exiled African Fathers a little book arranged in eight chapters. In the first chapters—namely, the second through the fifth—they set out their own faith concerning the Incarnation; in the remaining three, from the sixth to the end, they explain what they believe concerning grace and free will.

Yet they are mistaken, as the most learned Norisius observes [Note: Norisius, History of Pelagianism, Book II, chapter 19, works volume I, p. 485.], when they attribute this testimony to Pope Innocent in his letter to the Council of Milevis:

“All the efforts, all the works, and all the merits of the saints are to be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than from what he himself has bestowed.”

I say, they are mistaken in attributing this testimony to Innocent, for it is found in Pope Celestine’s Letter 21 to the bishops of Gaul [Note: Celestine, Letter 21, chapter 8, p. 1190 and following, Coutant edition.]—not in the letter to the Council of Milevis. [Note: Petrus the deacon, little book On the Incarnation, chapter 8, below, column 90.]

When such a little book had been brought to Sardinia in the name of the Scythian monks, the African Fathers did not shrink from expressing their own judgment on the questions proposed. Nor did they, to speak with Norisius [Note: Norisius, cited work, p. 486.], merely commend the faith of those monks in its entirety; they themselves also produced another volume with the same title, On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ. In it they approved all the opinions of the Scythians and fortified them with still stronger arguments.

There were fifteen bishops, whose names are listed at the beginning of the book. Yet we understand from the author who recorded the deeds of Fulgentius that the volume was composed under the title of Fulgentius alone, bishop of Ruspe. For he says [Note: Life of Saint Fulgentius, chapter 20.]:

“Whenever the bishops were questioned by letters from overseas concerning the faith or various questions, all imposed upon Fulgentius the task of answering on behalf of everyone.”

In that work, says the editor of Fulgentius’s works [Note: Preface to Saint Fulgentius’s works], “Fulgentius indeed argues brilliantly and subtly concerning the Incarnation; but concerning the formula ‘One of the Trinity suffered,’ he is less incisive, since in its place he uses, as though expressing the same meaning, the phrase ‘One person of the Trinity was crucified’” [Note: Fulgentius, On the Incarnation, chapter 10.].

But just as the writing of the Scythian monks was devoted for the most part to explaining the mystery of grace and predestination, so Fulgentius’s response contains much material confirming and strengthening those same chapters.

IV. Furthermore, although the African Fathers, exiled in Sardinia, had from the very beginning commended the Scythian faith in Fulgentius’s writing in these words [Note: [Col. 0082D] Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation*, ch. 1]: “At once we gladly recognized both your faith and your welfare; indeed, in the recognition of faith, your welfare became known to us,” nevertheless the great father of ecclesiastical annals considered the opinion of the Scythian monks concerning “one of the Trinity suffered” to be rejected, and consequently thought that their embassy to the African Fathers should be viewed with suspicion, and even that their faith should be dulled and disparaged [Note: [Col. 0082D] Baronius, under the year 519, §§ 111 ff.].

But those same monks found a vigorous patron—Noris, I mean—who therefore declares that he cannot accept the judgment of that most learned cardinal [Note: [Col. 0082D] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, ch. 18, *Works*, vol. I, pp. 483 ff.]: “Not [Col. 0082D] because I think that the most learned man, whom I both acknowledge and revere as the leading authority in ecclesiastical history, should receive little deference; but because that honor is owed to truth, so that no one should be preferred to it in love” [Note: [Col. 0082D] The same, preface to the *History of Pelagianism*.].

Thereafter the same distinguished author undertook the defense of those monks more extensively elsewhere, both in the *History of the Controversy concerning One of the Trinity Who Suffered* [Note: [Col. 0083A] Noris, *History of the Controversy*, etc., *Works*, vol. III, pp. 775 ff.] and in the *Apology for the Scythian Monks, Vindicated from the Scruples of an Anonymous Writer* [Note: [Col. 0083A] The same, *Apology for the Monks*, ibid., pp. 879 ff.]. To compose here a fuller account of Noris’s advocacy on behalf of the Scythian monks is not appropriate. Let the reader consult that eminent author, in whose writings, I confidently promise, he will find much pleasure and very great benefit as he reads through them.

Moreover, we believe that Baronius later displayed a milder opinion concerning the Scythian monks’ doctrine of “one of the Trinity who suffered”; indeed, he should rightly be considered to have laid aside the harsher statements he had made against them, since afterward we understand him to have approved the same doctrine in Ferrandus the deacon [Note: [Col. 0084A] Baronius, under the year 533, § 28.].

Finally, in printing both treatises we followed the excellent edition of the works of Saint Fulgentius published at Paris in 1684, which the distinguished Lucas Urbanus Mangeant prepared with diligent care and scholarship, as we are informed by learned men [Note: [Col. 0084A] Goujet, *Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. III, p. 17; the *Bibliotheca* in the appendix to vol. VI of the works of Saint Augustine, p. 17.].

[Col. 0083B]

**BOOK OF PETER THE DEACON AND THE OTHERS WHO WERE SENT FROM THE EAST BY THE GREEKS TO ROME IN THE CAUSE OF THE FAITH, ON THE INCARNATION AND GRACE OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, ADDRESSED TO FULGENTIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF AFRICA.** (C, S)

[Col. 0083]

[Col. 0083B] To the most holy lords, worthy to be named with every expression of reverence, Datianus, Fortunatus, Albanus, Orontius, Boethus, Fulgentius, Januarius, and the other bishops, distinguished in their confession of Christ: the humble deacon Peter [Note: [Col. 0083D] Ant.: “deacon.”], John, Leontius, another John, and the other brothers sent to Rome in the cause of the faith.

### CHAPTER I. The agreement of the Churches in faith; the confirmation of the faithful

We believe it useful and most necessary, and especially beneficial to the holy Churches of God, to bring to your holiness the things that all the holy Churches of the East defend with us concerning the Incarnation and the divine dispensation against the heretics—who do not cease to disturb the ancient faith of the Church with depraved and wicked arguments—and humbly to obtain from your blessedness agreement concerning them.

For we believe that your holy and glorious confession differs in nothing [Note: [Col. 0083D] The manuscript reads: “we believe that your glorious confession differs in nothing.”] from ours, especially since we have no doubt that the holy Church of God is everywhere enlivened by one Spirit. For the Easterners will all be filled with no small—indeed, rather great—joy if they learn that your holiness agrees with their own, or rather with the catholic, doctrines in every respect.

Therefore we earnestly ask and implore your blessedness to examine carefully what follows and, as befits true and fearless preachers of Christ, to command that your judgment be made known to us in writing [Note: [Col. 0083D] The manuscript reads: “that you command it to be made known.”]. Thus, if—by God’s favor—our exposition before you is found, as we do not doubt it will be, to accord with the catholic faith and the apostolic traditions, fortified by the authority of so many excellent and most approved priests, we may easily silence the mouths of those who speak wickedly; and, persevering in the faith of the holy Fathers, we may give thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0083D] The printed editions read: “who glorified us.” But the manuscript’s reading, “who glorified you,” seems better, since the bishops are being addressed as those glorified in exile for the divinity of Christ.] who has glorified you by your confession of his holiness, most holy and God-worthy lords [Col. 0084C]. We now ask you to examine what follows.

### CHAPTER II. In Christ the two natures are united without confusion in one person

According, then, to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we confess our Lord Jesus Christ in two united and unconfused natures—that is, in the nature of divinity and of humanity—in one person or subsistence [Note: [Col. 0084D] The printed editions of Leuven, 1556, and Basel read *sive substantia* (“or substance”).].
