We neither agree with those who, proclaiming one incarnate nature of God the Word, reject the faith of the venerable Council of Chalcedon, nor admit those who deceitfully proclaim two natures but by no means confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, judging this contrary to the profession of two natures—as though “one incarnate nature of God the Word” signified anything other than two natures ineffably united.

The blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, writes in this way in his second letter to Succensus, bishop of Diocaesarea [Note: [Col. 0084D] These words are absent from the printed editions of the second letter but are found in the manuscript]:

“For if, when saying ‘one nature of God the Word,’ we had remained silent and had not added ‘incarnate,’ but had rather seemed to reject the dispensation, their statement might perhaps have appeared not unreasonable, while they pretended to ask: Where is perfection in the humanity? Or how does our substance subsist? But since both the perfection that is in the humanity and the manifestation of our essence have been introduced through the statement ‘incarnate,’ let them now cease putting a reed-like staff beneath themselves” [Note: [Col. 0085D] Another reading: “let them cease.”].

### CHAPTER III. The Blessed Virgin is properly the Mother of God

We believe that the blessed virgin Mary is properly and truly Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*), that is, “Mother of God,” not because of the dignity of that man who was born from her—for certain impious persons do not fear to proclaim that he became God by grace and not by nature—but because she truly and properly bore God the Word incarnate and made man, essentially, or naturally, united to flesh.

For this reason we also confess in every respect that the union of the natures was made essential, or natural; not as do those who claim that God the Word operated in Christ as in a prophet [Note: [Col. 0085D] The manuscript reads this way; the editions have “the word of the Lord.”].

The blessed Gregory of Nazianzus refutes them in his letter to Cledonius, saying:

“If anyone says that God the Word operated in Christ according to grace, as in a prophet, and does not confess that the union was made essential, let him be deprived of the better operation, or rather let him be filled with the worse.”

Nor do we agree with those who attempt to establish the union of the natures according to illumination, love, affection, personal or subsistential union, or according to authority, power, or equality of honor.

The blessed Cyril, mentioned above, anathematizes them when he says against Nestorius [Note: [Col. 0085D] Cyril, *Anathemas*, 3]:

“If anyone divides the substances in the one Christ after the union, connecting them only by an association according to dignity, authority, or power, and not rather by the conjunction that is according to natural unity, let him be anathema” [Note: [Col. 0085D] The editions read “after the unity”; the manuscript reads “after the union.”].

For God the Word, not in an empty name, not as a part of himself, but by nature God, as great as the Father, equal in every respect to the Father except only that the one is Father and the other Son, united himself to human nature and became man.

Hence, too, our Lord Christ is proclaimed by the holy Fathers as composed of divinity and humanity through their union. Because Paul of Samosata was unwilling to confess this, he was condemned by the Council of Antioch. Malchion, a presbyter of that same Church of Antioch, a man thoroughly learned and chosen by all the priests who had then assembled against Paul, took up the supreme contest of debate on behalf of the council and refuted the same heretic among other things as follows:

“Certainly what is simple becomes composite, as in Christ Jesus, who was made one from God the Word and the human body, which is from the seed of David, subsisting thereafter not by any division but in unity. You, however, seem to me unwilling on this account to acknowledge composition, so that the Son of God may not be substance in him but wisdom according to participation. For you said this because wisdom would suffer loss and therefore could not be composite. You do not consider that divine wisdom, just as it remained undiminished before it emptied itself, so also in this emptying which it mercifully undertook remained undiminished and unchangeable. You also say that wisdom dwelt in him as we dwell in houses, as one in another [Note: [Col. 0086D] The editions of Leuven and Basel read: “as one in another.”]. But neither are we a part of the house, nor is the house a part of us.”

Similarly, the blessed Athanasius, in the treatise entitled *That Christ Is One*, refuting the vanity of the heretics, after approving their superfluous inquiries concerning the divinity of the Son of God, continues as follows:

“So,” he says, “they also inquire concerning the Incarnation: ‘How,’ they ask, ‘is God incarnate? How does he become embodied? How is the uncontainable joined to a small body? How is the uncreated united to the created, the unbounded to the bounded? Or how is that great, immense, and indivisible one divided? If that greatness has been contracted into a small place, either the small has become great, or a part, and not the whole divinity, has been united to the flesh—which it is impious to believe.’

“And from this they have fallen into saying: ‘How?’ and ‘In what manner?’ Through this opinion and impiety they too have imagined indwelling in place of Incarnation, human operation in place of unity and composition, two subsistences and two persons in place of the one substance of our Lord Jesus Christ, and, indecently and impiously, a quaternity in place of the holy and ineffable Trinity” [Note: [Col. 0086D] The edition reads “operation.”].

Again, the blessed Gregory says in his sermon *On the Son*:

“In one chapter of mine,” he says, “assign the higher things to the divinity and to that nature which is shown to be superior to sufferings and the body; but assign the lower things to the composite one, who for your sake emptied himself and became incarnate.”

Therefore we rightly believe that God the Word, full and perfect, suffered no increase or diminution even after assuming flesh; indeed, through his union he bestowed ineffable glory upon the nature he assumed.

### CHAPTER IV. The Incarnation did not produce a quaternity in the Godhead

For this reason the Trinity remained the Trinity even after the mystery of the Incarnation, because the same God the Word, even with his own flesh, is one of the Trinity—not because his flesh is of the substance of the Trinity, but because the flesh belongs to God the Word, who is one of the Trinity.

For he himself, and no other, ascended into heaven who descended from heaven: the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3:13). Therefore, according to the blessed Cyril [Note: [Col. 0086D] Cyril, *Anathemas*, 13], we also confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and was buried in the flesh. Cyril says:

“If anyone does not confess that God the Word suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, since he is life and, as God, the giver of life, let him be anathema.”

Similarly, we call Christ man the Word, in accordance with the blessed John:

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have touched, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1).

For the Word could not, according to the nature of his divinity, be handled by human hands unless he became man.

There is also no doubt that the child whom the blessed Virgin bore, whom she wrapped in swaddling clothes, whom she placed in a manger, whom she circumcised on the eighth day, whom the just man Simeon embraced in his own arms, and whom the evangelists report to have been subject to his parents (Luke 2:51), whom they attest to have advanced in age and wisdom, was by nature God—the one through whom all visible and invisible things were made, the only-begotten and firstborn, in whom all things consist, according to the Apostle Paul (Col. 1:16).

The prophet Isaiah also proclaims this very thing in clear words:

“A child is born to us, and a Son is given to us; whose power is upon his shoulder, and he shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6).

Therefore we do not at all believe that we should yield to those who assert that the Mighty God was united to that child, but do not believe that the child himself is the Mighty God—especially since the Psalmist testifies that the throne belongs altogether not to someone else but to the very one who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and baptized in the Jordan by John in order to sanctify the waters [Note: [Col. 0087D] This passage is mutilated in the printed editions. We have restored it from the manuscript of Portus, from the words “forever and ever” through “God forever.” In the Basel edition, however, it reads: “but may his throne altogether . . . be forever and ever: a rod of righteousness,” etc.]:

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of righteousness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

But how could God be anointed, whose throne is forever and ever, unless he became man?

### CHAPTER V. God became man; man did not become God

Accordingly, in keeping with this saying of the prophet, Christ is God who became man, not Christ who became God, as the heretics say, who dare to assert that Christ is God through advancement and not through nature. For God was anointed because he himself became man; it is not that one is God and another man, but the same one is God and the same one is man.

For he who is the natural son of the Virgin is the natural Son of God.

Therefore we believe and confess two births of God the Word: one before the ages, from the Father according to divinity [Note: [Col. 0088D] Another reading: “in the Father.”], and the other in the last days, from the holy Virgin according to the flesh. We execrate those who deny the birth of the Word of God according to the flesh.

They also refuse to acknowledge the wonders and sufferings of one and the same Son of God, which the whole Church of God confesses.

We also accept four councils according to the meaning of this exposition of ours: Nicaea, of the three hundred and eighteen bishops; Constantinople, of the one hundred and fifty who condemned the impious Pneumatomachi; also the First Council of Ephesus, presided over by the most blessed bishops Celestine of Rome and Cyril of Alexandria; and the holy and venerable council celebrated at Chalcedon.

We likewise embrace the letters of the blessed Leo, anathematizing all who hold opinions contrary to the doctrines of the Church, as well as all the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia and of his disciple Nestorius, and all who think like them together with Nestorius; likewise all the writings opposed to the twelve chapters of the blessed Cyril, which he issued against Nestorius. To these we add Eutyches and Dioscorus with their associates, and all whom the apostolic see has justly and canonically condemned.

### CHAPTER VI. What kind of man was created, and what kind he and his posterity became through sin

After this it follows that we should also explain to your blessedness what we think concerning the grace of Christ, by which he rescued us from the power of Satan, according to what has been handed down to us; for in this matter also your authority is greatly necessary to us.

We therefore believe that Adam was made good by God, the creator of all things, and endowed with great freedom, so that he had it in his own power to do good and, if he wished, could admit evil. In a certain sense, death and immortality were placed within the freedom of his choice. For he was capable of either outcome: if he kept the commandment, he would become immortal without experiencing death; but if he despised it, death would immediately follow.

Thus, corrupted by the serpent’s cunning, he voluntarily became a transgressor of the divine law. Therefore, according to what had been foretold to him, he was condemned by God’s just judgment to the punishment of death; and he was wholly changed for the worse—that is, both in body and in soul—and, having lost his own freedom, was enslaved to the service of sin.

From that time onward no human being is born who is not bound by the chain of this sin, except the one who, in order to break this chain of sin, was born by a new mode of generation: the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5).

For what else could or can be born from a slave but a slave? Adam did not beget children when he was free, but after he had become a slave of sin. Therefore, just as every human being comes from him, so through him every human being is a slave of sin.

Hence the Apostle also says: “From one came condemnation upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:18). And again: “Through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (ibid., 12).

Those who say that only death, and not sin, passed into the human race are therefore completely mistaken, since the Apostle testifies that both sin and death were brought into the world through him.

No one at all, therefore, is freed from this condemnation and death except by the grace of the Redeemer. Although he was Lord, as God, in order to free us from perpetual slavery and from the power of the devil and to restore us to true freedom, he became a slave, taking the form of a slave (Phil. 2:7).

Hence he says to the Jews: “Then you will truly be free, if the Son makes you free” (John 8:36). For they thought themselves truly free, although with utterly futile zeal they were slaves to human occupations.

Thus, in order that false freedom might become [Note: [Col. 0089D] The printed editions have “true freedom”; that is, “so that human freedom might become.” These words have been substituted from the manuscript.] true freedom—that is, so that human freedom might become Christian freedom—that same freedom needed a liberator, through whose grace it might be turned away from human occupations and enabled to think about and desire the things that pertain to eternal life.

Without this grace a person can indeed think about and desire human things, but cannot think, will, or desire divine things. The first and chief foundation, and in a certain sense the threshold or origin of all good things, is to believe in the Lord of glory who was crucified (1 Cor. 2:8).

This does not arise from the freedom of natural choice, because it is not flesh and blood that reveals this, but the heavenly Father (Matt. 16:17), drawing whomever he wills to true freedom—not by violent compulsion, but by infusing sweetness through the Holy Spirit—so that believers immediately say, “Jesus is Lord” (1 Cor. 12:3), which no one can say through the natural freedom of choice except in the Holy Spirit.

They therefore babble in vain who say: “It is mine to will to believe; it belongs to God’s grace to help,” since the Apostle also testifies that belief itself—which is giving consent to the truth—is given to us by God, saying: “To you it has been granted by Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29).

### CHAPTER VII. God makes some believe through his goodness and abandons others by a just but hidden judgment

But they say: If God makes unwilling people willing to believe, while no one is naturally able, as you say [Note: [Col. 0089D] The printed editions read: “is able to believe in the Son of God.” The manuscript reads: “is able to believe or to will,” and omits “in the Son of God.”], to believe or to will anything good that pertains to eternal life, why then does he not make everyone willing? For there is no partiality with God, especially since it is written of him: “He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4).

Either he wills it and cannot, or divine Scripture lies. If it is impious to think either of these things, it remains that he does not awaken the human will but waits for it from the human being, so that there may be a just reward among those who will and a just condemnation among those who do not will.

If matters are as the heretics boast, the inscrutable and incomprehensible judgments of God have been grasped by them. For if, as they themselves wish, he condemns the unwilling and saves the willing, there is absolutely nothing further to investigate. As far as they are concerned, divine Scripture is false when it declares God’s judgments incomprehensible (Rom. 11:33).

But we, believing and demonstrating that God’s judgments are incomprehensible, say that from one mass of perdition some are saved by the goodness and grace of God, while others are abandoned by a just and hidden judgment.

Otherwise let those who consider this contrary to divine justice and goodness say, if they can, why he who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth performed so many miracles in Chorazin and Bethsaida, yet did not wish to perform any of them in Tyre and Sidon, where, as he himself testifies, if they had been performed, they might perhaps have repented in ashes and sackcloth (Matt. 11:21).

Or why did he forbid the Apostle to proclaim the word of salvation in Asia and Bithynia (Acts 16:6–7)?

If these things cannot be understood, let them return to themselves and, recognizing that they are human beings, cease asking why he saves some by a gratuitous gift and abandons others by a just and hidden judgment—he who has power from the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21).

Let them cry out with us, or rather with the Apostle:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33–36).

Clearly, then, the person who says, “Unless I first will, grace does not come to me,” resists not us but the Apostle himself. For this is nothing other than saying that one must first give something to God so that God may repay him.

### CHAPTER VIII. Every movement of a good will is from God

But, following the same Apostle, we say that the origin of all good thoughts, their agreement [Note: [Col. 0090D] The printed editions have “and their confession,” but the manuscript’s “and their agreement” is more correct.], and the will come from God and through God and in God. He releases and corrects the perverse wills of human beings, entangled in earthly actions, through the infusion and inner operation [Note: [Col. 0090D] Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “and operation.”] of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint).

Hence the blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea, says in the prayer of the sacred altar, which nearly the whole East recites, among other things:

“Grant, O Lord, strength and protection. We ask you: make the wicked good; preserve the good in goodness. For you can do all things, and no one can resist you. For when you will, you save, and no one resists your will.”

See how briefly and decisively that distinguished teacher once brought this controversy to an end, teaching through this prayer that wicked people are made good not by themselves but by God, and that they persevere in goodness not by their own power but by the help of divine grace.

Similarly, the blessed Innocent, bishop of the apostolic see, says in his letter to the Council of Milevis [Note: [Col. 0090D] See in Celestine, ch. 8.]:

“All the endeavors, all the works, and all the merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him from any other source than what he himself has given.”

The African councils explain this more carefully and clearly in their letter to Pope Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0091D] The printed editions read “to the Roman pope”; the manuscript reads “to Pope Zosimus.”], repeating and explaining the pope’s own statement:

“But that which you placed in the letter which you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying:

‘Nevertheless, by the prompting of God—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—we have referred everything to the awareness of our brothers and fellow bishops’—

we understand this statement to mean that you swiftly cut down, with the sword of truth, those who exalt the freedom of choice against God’s help. For what have you attributed to free choice more than referring everything to the awareness of our humility? Yet you faithfully and wisely saw, and truthfully and confidently said, that this was done by God’s prompting, precisely because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord’ (ibid.), and because the Father himself touches the hearts of his children by paternal inspirations so that they may do something good: ‘For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God’ (Rom. 8:14).

“Thus we neither feel that our choice is absent nor fail to recognize that his grace precedes every individual movement of human will toward good things. God works in the hearts of human beings and in free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we are able to do something good; without him we can do nothing.”

In agreement with this, the most blessed Celestine says in the letter sent to the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0091D] Celestine, ch. 2.]:

“For when the bishops of holy congregations carry out the commission entrusted to them before the divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0091D] The printed editions read “fulfill”; the manuscript has the present reading.], they plead the cause of the human race. With the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their unbelief; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may recover through receiving the catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and, finally, that when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.

“That these things are not asked of the Lord carelessly or in vain is shown by the outcome of the things themselves [Note: [Col. 0091D] Thus the manuscript and the printed editions except Basel, which reads: “that these things are not asked of the Lord carelessly or in vain, but effectively, is shown by the result of the prayers themselves.”]. For from every kind of error he deigns to draw very many people, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1:13), and making vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath (Rom. 9:22–23).

“This is perceived to be so entirely the work of God that thanksgiving and an acknowledgment of praise are always rendered to God, who accomplishes these things, for the illumination or correction of such persons.”

Again, a little later:

“By these ecclesiastical rules, therefore, drawn from divine authority and testimony, we have been so confirmed, with the Lord’s help, that we profess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all endeavors and virtues by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. We do not doubt that every human being’s merits are preceded by his grace, through which it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good.

“By this help and gift of God free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked straight, what was weak healthy, and what was imprudent prudent.”

The same teacher brings this letter to an end and concludes it as follows [Note: [Col. 0092D] The same, ch. 13.]:

“Because we believe that whatever the writings of the apostolic see have taught us according to the rules set forth above is sufficient for confessing the grace of God, from whose work and favor nothing at all must be subtracted, we therefore absolutely do not consider anything catholic that appears contrary to the judgments established above.”

Most holy lords, we have judged it useful to insert these words in this little book of ours—not as though we were suggesting them to those who do not know them, but for the refutation of the madness of those who reject them as new doctrines and as things wholly unheard-of in the Churches [Note: [Col. 0092D] Another reading: “almost unheard-of.”].

Instructed by the teachings of all these holy Fathers, we anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, and likewise Julian of Eclanum and all who hold opinions similar to theirs—especially the books of Faustus, bishop of Gaul, who advanced from the monastery of Lérins. There is no doubt that these books were written against the doctrine of predestination.

In them he not only comes into conflict with all these holy Fathers, but also, contrary to the tradition of the Apostle himself [Note: [Col. 0092D] Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “contradiction.”], subordinates grace’s assistance to human labor and, utterly emptying Christ’s grace, impiously declares that the ancient saints were saved not by the grace by which we too are saved, according to the teaching of the blessed Apostle Peter (Acts 15:11), but by the possibility of nature.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 518. VIGILIUS OF TAPSA.**

[Col. 0093]

[Col. 0093]

## NOTICE FROM CAVE

[Col. 0093A] Vigilius, an African by nationality, bishop of Tapsa or Tapsus in the province of Byzacena, flourished in the year 484. In that year, summoned to Carthage by order of King Hunneric to give an account of his faith, he subscribed to the profession of faith of Eugenius of Carthage and, together with him, steadfastly fought for the catholic faith.

When the Arian Vandals were raging against the Catholics, he appears to have abandoned his homeland. Theodulf of Orléans and Aeneas of Paris report that he went to Constantinople and composed books there against Eutyches. It can indeed be gathered unmistakably from the first book of this work that Vigilius eventually lived among the Greeks.

He was wrongly confused with Vigilius of Trent; knowledge of the writers of this and the preceding age long eluded scholars. Certainly his writings lay hidden among the works of others, perhaps published and falsely attributed under other names by Vigilius himself, at least for this reason, as Chiffletius accurately conjectures: to escape the hatred and hostility of the Arians and, by sheltering behind such prestigious names, to secure authority for his writings.

At last, Franciscus Chiffletius, mentioned above, collected his works, sought out everywhere, and restored to their author, arranging them in the following order.

*Five Books Against Nestorius and Eutyches in Defense of the Council of Chalcedon*, which appeared several times under the name of Vigilius of Trent: at Zurich in 1539; afterward edited by Cassander at Cologne in 1575, in octavo, and among Cassander’s works, p. 514; and in a more corrected and expanded form edited by Josias Simler at Basel in 1571, as well as elsewhere.

*Disputation under the Name of Athanasius against Arius*, or *Two Dialogues Held at the Council of Nicaea between Athanasius and Arius, with Probus as Judge*.

*Three Dialogues or Disputations Held by Athanasius against Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus before Probus as Judge.*

This should be considered the same work as the preceding one, distinguished only by the following difference: the earlier work was written in Africa by Vigilius while he still feared the Vandals and did not wish to be recognized by them; after he had left Africa, it was revised, its preface mutilated, many passages polished, and it was enlarged by the entire third book, which contains the judgment of Probus.

Georg Cassander published both works joined into one under the name of Vigilius of Trent, together with the books against Eutyches, at Cologne in 1575 and among his own works, p. 460. The first two dialogues commonly occupy, improperly, a place among the works of Athanasius.

[Col. 0093D] *On the Trinity, or On the United Trinity of the Godhead, Twelve Books against the Arian Marivadus.*

These books were written at Naples in Campania and falsely attributed to Athanasius. Under his name the first seven books also appeared in the Heidelberg edition of Athanasius. All twelve appeared in the Paris edition, though they were incorrectly divided into eleven books, the two final books having been combined into one.

[Col. 0094A] *Book on the Unity of the Trinity, Addressed to Optatus*, or *Dialogue between Saint Augustine and Felicianus the Arian*, fabricated by Vigilius. It is commonly counted among the works of Augustine.

Three books *On the Trinity against Varimadus*—or, by transposition of letters, Marivadus—who was a deacon of the Arian sect and highly favored by King Hunneric. Vigilius formerly published these under the name of Idacius Clarus, and they were frequently printed under the same name.

The book against Palladius, the Arian bishop, consists of two parts. The first is presented in the collections of councils published after the year 1550 among the acts of the Council of Aquileia held in 381; the second has two editions, both apparently published by Vigilius. The first is identical with Ambrose’s book *On Faith*, or *On the Consubstantiality of the Son with the Father*; the second, which is more extensive, is identical with Gregory of Nazianzus’s *Oration 59*. Appended to the work are two letters of the Council of Aquileia, one to the bishops of Gaul and the other to the emperors Gratian and Valentinian; these should be counted among the acts of the council. As for the first part, Chiffletius argues, by a long array of conjectures rather than arguments, that Vigilius fabricated this disputation under the title of the acts of the Synod of Aquileia. This, however, seems to me by no means plausible; nor are the little arguments he adduces so weighty that we should linger over refuting them. Certainly no one will dispute the genuineness of these Acts of the Council of Aquileia without thereby making it possible, by the same reasoning and nearly the same arguments, to call the Acts of other synods into question.

*Solutions of the objections of the Arians*, which Chiffletius conjectures Vigilius appended to the first Dialogue under the name of Athanasius, *Against the Arians*, before undertaking a second edition of these dialogues.

Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius collected the works listed above into one volume and published them, supplied with notes and dissertations, at Dijon in 1664, in quarto. They have since been included in *Bibliothecae Patrum*, volume VIII, p. 722.

The *Disputation, or Dialogue, of Saint Augustine with Pascentius the Arian before the judge Laurentius*, fabricated by Vigilius and first brought to light by the Benedictine Fathers who edited the latest edition of Augustine’s works, was appended to the appendix of his letters.

The Creed circulated under Athanasius’s name and published among his works. We think it should be attributed to Vigilius—without, as we believe, doing violence to the truth. See further under Athanasius.

Furthermore, Cassiodorus reports that a certain Vigilius, an African bishop, composed a lucid treatise on the interpretation of the thousand years foretold in the Apocalypse (*Divine Readings* I.9). Whether this was our Vigilius is entirely uncertain. This much is certain: whatever the work may have been, it has perished.

Finally, one may well wonder what Casimir Oudin means when, in more than one place, he attributes to our Vigilius the conflict of Arnobius the Younger with Serapion—without, so far as I know, being guided by any reason or supported by any authority. On this matter the often-mentioned Chiffletius, who gathered together all of Vigilius’s works, has not even a γρῦ—“a jot”—although Oudin appears willing to enlist him on his side.

[Col. 0095]

# FIVE BOOKS OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSA AGAINST EUTYCHES. (C, S)

[Col. 0095]

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0095B] 1. I. We have learned that a great and serious danger to the faith is spreading through many of the Churches of the East. It can neither easily be perceived nor easily avoided by most people, since it is concealed beneath the appearance of piety. It is defended with such persistent obstinacy of mind that neither the traditions of the ancient Fathers nor the severe enactments of religious rulers can or could cut it off. For when the human ear has been forestalled by the error of a false opinion, it proves stubborn and exceedingly difficult to bring to an understanding of the truth, however many witnesses may press it. A person prefers to defend, with still greater perversity, the judgment of the corrupt doctrine with which he has once been infected, rather than beneficially to change it after it has been refuted by the authority of so many divine and human laws.

This, then, the deadly and fatal plague of a pernicious crisis, ravages everything within the venerable gates of the Church with such ferocity that it does the more harm the less its capacity to harm is understood. For, trained under the instruction of that most loathsome serpent, it has stretched the double snares of its ambushes to right and left, leaving for travelers a very narrow and exceedingly difficult path. If you try to set your steps even slightly toward either side, you will immediately be caught.

II. Between the sacrilegious doctrine of Nestorius, once the ruler—or rather the destroyer—of the Church of Constantinople, not a shepherd but a plunderer, and the wicked and detestable 2 sect of Eutyches, the cunning of the serpent’s advance has so adjusted itself that many cannot avoid one without danger from the other. If someone condemns the perfidy of Nestorius, he is thought to succumb to the error of Eutyches. Again, when someone destroys the impiety of the Eutychian heresy, he is accused of setting up the doctrine of Nestorius.

But these clouds of empty accusations are chiefly spread by those who are either sick with the defect of ignorance or afflicted by the disease of contentiousness. While they raise themselves up with the arrogance of a wanton spirit, they despise the rules of faith handed down from ancient times by the Fathers for the sole purpose of introducing their ill-conceived novel opinions into the Church. For this reason they also set before us, as though we were teachers of dialectical skill rather than true disciples of Christ, the unavoidable syllogism of an equivocal response, supposing that by these snares of propositions they can hunt down Christian souls.

Yet the Church’s strength experiences nothing new or foreign in such things, having been shaken by almost all heretics through such whirlwinds of questions, and having gained triumph over adversaries and immovability amid opposition. For when she armed herself for battle against Sabellius, she defended the real existence of the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit: one is he who begets, another he who is begotten; one proceeds, another is the one from whom he proceeds; one sends, another is sent; one is God the Word who is born of the Virgin, another is the Father who always remains unbegotten; one, through the dispensation of the flesh, fulfills all the functions of our frailty, another is the Father who remains without any of these things.

You will immediately see Arius, as though he had received the material for a triumphal victory, insolently exulting and seeking to subject the necks of the faithful beneath the detestable yoke of his perfidy. “Recognize,” he says, “that the one who sends is superior to the one who is sent; that the one who obeys is inferior, and that the one to whom generosity is shown is more worthy.”

III. Likewise, when I am pressing Manichaeus concerning the truth of the Lord’s body—that it was assumed not through deceptive pretense and certain conjuring tricks of illusion—I point to the swelling womb of the Virgin; I indicate the delays of the awaited time, which he spent longer within the lodging of his mother’s womb, until the proper day of birth; 3 I mention the cradle of the newborn, the infant’s cry, the progress of age, and finally the mockeries of the Passion, the cross’s gibbet, the piercing of the nails, the blood and water from his opened side, his descent, burial, resurrection, and also what the Lord himself says: “Do you wish to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John 8:40). And the Apostle says: “As through one man came death, so through one man came the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:21). And again: “One mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

While I am arguing these points against Manichaeus, Photinus tries to swallow them all like food prepared for him, with the more eager jaws of his perfidy. Again, when I have armed myself against him with the weapons of life-giving Scripture and have hurled many shafts of testimony declaring that the Son of God is true God, I must also bring forward among other passages the statement that he was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2:7). At this point Manichaeus strangles me and shouts, with the full exultation of a triumphant spirit, that I have returned to his side.

But it is tedious and exceedingly laborious to review such snares of argument, by which the fraudulent stealth of heretical contrivance seeks to enslave the freedom of the Catholic faith.

IV. And since our predecessors have argued fully against all these plagues of the heretics—for even if no books had been composed for the destruction of their error, the mere fact that they have been declared heretics would itself suffice for the security of the orthodox—let us now consider those whose minds that most loathsome serpent has so corrupted with respect to the purity of faith that is in Christ Jesus that it has armed their shamelessness with a brow hardened for the open adultery of wicked preaching, so that the prophetic oracle may rightly rebound upon them: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute” (Jeremiah 3:3).

For if this is not so, what else does it mean that they yield neither to such numerous decrees of councils nor to the opinions of so many ancient Fathers? They accuse us, then, when we confess Christ in both natures, as though, in accordance with the unspeakable error of Nestorius, we appeared to assert two Christs—one God and the other human being—through a duality of nature.

But we confess one God, that same one the Son of God and the Son of man, not two. And we confess that the Word sowed within the secrets of the Virgin’s womb the beginnings of flesh for himself—that is, that he became incarnate—in such a way that the nature of the Word was nevertheless not changed into flesh. Likewise, the nature of the flesh passed through its union with the one who assumed it into the person of the Word, yet it was not thereby consumed in the Word.

Both remain: the nature of the Word and the nature of the flesh. From these two, which remain to this day, there is one Christ and one person. Who could be so foolish, clothed in sacrilegious opinion? Who could cast himself into so precipitous an abyss of error as to deny that the Son of God, without his own flesh—which he united to himself in the sacred Virgin’s womb through an ineffable communion and union, so that the Word became human and the human being became God, the same one and one person without any change in the kinds of nature—now sits at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead, when he knows that the Lord himself said: “When the Son of man comes in the glory of his Father” (Matthew 16:27)?

For, as we have often said, it is not that one is the Son of man and another the Son of God. Rather, he wished to show so clearly that the nature of our race had not been consumed through the indivisible unity of the union that, even while situated in heaven, he calls himself the Son of man, so that through the use of the true name you may recognize the reality of the nature that remains. If, therefore, the undefiled nature of the Word remains to this day, so too remains the unimpaired nature of humanity, which the same Word assumed without change in himself.

V. How is it defended today that there is only one nature of Christ? If this is so, then one has certainly been abolished from the two. Which one, then? If it is the human nature, only the nature of the Word remains, and it will be false that Christ Jesus will come in the manner in which he was seen to go into heaven. For the same Lord appeared bodily to the eyes of those who looked upon him, in the form of our race; and again, in the same bodily form, he will reveal himself to the eyes of those who pierce him at the consummation of time.

For if one of these two has been extinguished—or rather consumed—and one alone has been left, it will follow that the Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed most impiously either only God and not also the same human being, or only a human being and not also the same God.

We must not, therefore, through this madness of foolish preaching, cancel the mystery of his condescension and dignity. His condescension, that is, because God deigned to become human; his dignity, because, while the nature of the Word remains unchangeable in its union with flesh, the same human being is God through the mystery of one person.

This Catholic understanding accepts the coming-together of the natures, not their union into one nature: from two united natures, both of which remain, Christ is believed to be one God and the same human being. For according to those who insist that there is only one nature, either the nature of the Word was changed into flesh so that there might be one nature, or the flesh was consumed in the Word so that, losing its existence through its own abolition, it could no longer exist at all and only the one nature of the Word might remain.

How impious and sacrilegious this is seems perfectly clear to anyone who follows apostolic teachings rather than human inventions. Since the same God is human and the same human being is God, subsisting from both and lacking neither, it is evident that he is of both natures, because he can lose neither.

VI. Why, and in what manner, do these people reject the name of property in both natures? I do not know whether they are so completely covered by the veil of perfidy that they neither see nor understand that one thing is appropriate to his divinity and another to his humanity, although both are common to the same person.

For he says to his disciples: “If you loved me, you would rejoice because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). And again: “It is advantageous for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7).

Certainly the Word of God, the power of God, and the wisdom of God was always with the Father and in the Father, even when it was with us in our midst. For when he mercifully dwelt on earth, he did not withdraw from his heavenly dwelling. With the Father he is wholly everywhere, possessing an equal divinity, which no place contains. Everything is full of the Son, and no place is empty of the presence of his divinity.

From where, then, and to where does he say that he is going? Or how does he claim that he will proceed to the Father, from whom he plainly never departed? But this was his going to the Father and his departure from us: to take away from this world the nature 6 that he had assumed from us.

You see, then, that it belonged properly to this same nature that it should be taken away and depart from us, although it is to be restored to us at the end of time, according to the testimony of the angels: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Observe the miracle; observe the mystery of the property of both natures. According to his humanity, the Son of God departed from us; according to his divinity, he says to us: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

If he is with us, how did he depart? If he is with us, how did he say: “The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of man, and you will not see it” (Luke 17:22)? Yet he is both with us and not with us. For those whom he left and from whom he departed in his humanity, he did not leave or abandon in his divinity.

Through the form of a servant, which he took from us into heaven, he is absent from us; through the form of God, by which he does not depart from us, he is present to us on earth. Nevertheless, the one and same person is both present and absent from us.

VII. Hear another property of both natures. We all read, believe, and equally proclaim that the Son of God was buried; no Christian dares to doubt it. Let us now, if it pleases us, examine the matter in peaceful moderation: what of him could have been buried—whether the Word, the soul, the body, or all things together?

But it would be utterly absurd to say that either the Word or the soul was wrapped in linen cloths. It remains, therefore, that only the lifeless body, which was also carried by the hands of those who buried him, was wrapped in a shroud and placed in the recess of the tomb.

There is no need to argue here, where the truth itself reveals the matter with such clarity. The Word of God did not need the rites of burial; the soul could not be buried; therefore the flesh alone underwent the service of burial. Yet apostolic authority has taught that the Lord Jesus Christ was buried.

You see, then, that there is something proper to the flesh that cannot belong to the Word; yet for that very reason it also belongs to the Word, because that flesh is the flesh of the Word, to which all these things more appropriately apply.

VIII. The Gospels certainly report that the Lord Jesus 7 Christ grew through the stages of life and reached the robust limbs of youthful maturity. O you who wish nothing to be proper to the flesh: do you suppose that the Word, together with the flesh in which he was born from the Virgin, grew equally through the succession of ages and the increase of his limbs, and was solidified into a larger bodily mass?

Do not, I beg you, quibble; choose whichever one you wish. To whom does this growth and maturation of the Lord Jesus Christ belong, and his reaching full youthful age—to the Word or to the flesh? I know what narrow straits you suffer and amid what heats you gasp.

If you say that it is proper to the flesh, you admit the property of its nature. If you say that it belongs both to the flesh and to the Word—which is indeed true through the unity of the person, not through the property of nature—if, I say, you say that this increase of age belongs to the Word, you introduce a mutable and changeable Word of God.

Perhaps some portion of the Word had filled the Virgin’s womb, and therefore this small portion experienced increase together with its body, while the larger portion that remained and had not filled the Virgin’s womb gradually joined itself to the portion it possessed in the human being through the growth of that body. In this way, according to you, God was born not whole and perfect but in a small measure, and through the successive stages of age became great.

But if it is impious and detestable either to speak of a portion of the Word or to believe that the Word experienced any increase in its nature, it is nevertheless clear that the Lord Jesus Christ had a development of age. Who does not see that what grew belonged to the flesh, not to God, who assumed the flesh of our race?

If in that most glorious Passion the Lord Jesus Christ had been struck on the head or punished by any other amputations of his limbs, would these people have said that one part of the Word had been amputated with the head and another part mutilated with the hands? And since he was circumcised, care must be taken lest they suppose that part of the Word was likewise amputated with that removal of a portion of the member—something that no one with sounder and more correct judgment would say even of mutilated human beings today.

For it is not permissible to suppose that when a human being’s hands are cut off, a portion of the soul is cut off at the same time. This visible light, too, may be taken away from a human being through various afflictions of the eyes; 8 yet the light is not thereby taken away from the soul by which it is able to distinguish between justice and iniquity. One thing belongs to the body, another to the soul.

IX. Above all, this must be carefully considered: if the nature of God were of such a condition that it could, by itself and in itself, be subjected to certain kinds of suffering, there would certainly have been no necessity of assuming a human body. For what need was there for God to take upon himself the nature of mortals, if his own nature could be subjected to the laws of death?

But because death, which had entered through the transgression of disobedience, had to be destroyed by death, as the Lord himself had foretold when he said, “I shall be your death, O death” (Hosea 13:14), the Son of God needed, by the deeper and more profound plan of his dispensation, to assume a body of a suffering nature, since he himself is impassible by nature.

In this body he was to be afflicted with insults and sufferings to such an extent that, reaching the cost of death through a nature subject to death, he might destroy death in its own dwelling places; and, plundering all the rights of hell through the triumph of a victorious encounter, return to the heavenly realm.

You see, therefore, that God permitted himself to die in our nature for no other reason than that his nature is not held at all by the condition of mortality. Thus there is one thing proper to Christ that belongs to his divinity and another that belongs to his humanity, although, because of the unity of the person, death is referred to his divinity and immortality to the humanity of that same God.

X. We must certainly fear that those who, out of a most empty fear, refuse to accept the property of both natures lest they appear to introduce two Christs may likewise raise some question for us concerning the Trinity. For there are certain properties of the Father that belong neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit; certain properties of the Son that belong neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit; and certain properties of the Holy Spirit that are shown to belong neither to the Father nor to the Son. Will they therefore accuse Catholics of worshiping three gods separated from one another?

But lest you be disturbed by an unexpected question, consider the matter one point at a time. The dispensation of the assumed flesh belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Son alone; for it was the Son, not the Father, who was born of the Virgin.

Again, the voice heard over him—“This is my beloved Son” 9 (Matthew 3:17; 17:5)—belongs neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Father alone. Likewise, the form of a dove that appeared in the Jordan, and the distribution of the fiery tongues divided among many, are shown properly to belong to the person of the Holy Spirit.

But lest you still doubt these properties, hear the matter more plainly. It is proper to the Father to have begotten; it is proper to the Son to have been born; it is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed. What is specially proper to each person does not at all pass over into another person.

If, then, these three persons, each possessing their own properties—which distinguish them more clearly but do not separate them—are one God, how is the Son not one Christ while the property of both natures remains intact?

[Col. 0101B] XI. In a human being, too, if we wish to argue more subtly, you will find many things so distinctly separated by a certain property that, if you wish to bring accusations there as well, you would make many human beings out of one person.

Everyone knows that the human being consists of five senses through the ordered distinctions of the bodily members. These senses naturally possess the property of their own function in such a way that they can have nothing in common with one another and cannot claim for themselves anything belonging to another’s property.

To mention each one in detail: sight performs the distinctive function of its ministry in such a way that it cannot hear, smell, taste, or touch anything. Hearing performs the function of its nature in such a way that it does not undertake the function of seeing, smelling, tasting, or touching. The sense of smell likewise carries out the service of its office in such a way that it neither hears nor sees nor tastes nor touches anything.

Taste neither sees nor smells nor hears nor touches. Finally, touch, which is the last of the senses, enjoys neither sight, nor perceives hearing, nor receives smell, nor distinguishes taste.

Although all these kinds of bodily members are so different and so distinct, established through such natural properties that they have no communion or association with one another, but fulfill the service of their own function by a certain private and solitary right, there is nevertheless one and the same human being. Since this human being consists of five bodily senses differing from one another through a fivefold property, he ought, according to the ravings of these people, to have five persons, so that the number of persons would equal the number of properties of the senses.

Furthermore, to suffer hunger and eat, to thirst and drink, to sit and walk, to lie down and rise from sleep, to endure cold and burn with heat—although the body undergoes or performs these things not without the soul’s participation—belong properly to the flesh.

Likewise, to perceive, understand, forget, recall to memory, be lifted up with joy, be cast down by sorrow, grow gentle through kindness, become savage through fury and anger, and many similar things that it would be tedious to pursue—although these occur in the soul not without the body—belong properly to the soul.

Yet no one has dared, or dares, to say that a human being has two persons, although he sees so many differences of properties present in him.

[Col. 0102A] XII. But the rashness of these people, who introduce a diversity of persons in proportion to the number of natures, must be broken and utterly crushed by apostolic authority.

The Apostle certainly knew that Christ was of both natures when he proclaims him both human and God, and the same one person. He proclaims him human when he says: “One mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). And again: “As through one human being came death, so through one human being came the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:21). And concerning his Son he says: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). And: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David according to the flesh” (2 Timothy 2:8).

He proclaims him God when he says: “From them is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5). And there are many similar passages, which it would be tedious to recall.

Since, then, he who proclaimed this same person both God and human being showed Christ to be one from both natures, I am astonished that he did not fear these outstanding calumniators of our age when he ascribed one person to Christ, saying: “And if I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

XIII. They also regularly criticize, with their customary rashness, what they hear Catholics say: “God and human being,” supposing that the insertion of this conjunction could signify two persons. But listen to how foolish their opinion is.

For what is “God and human being” except the one who is God and was also made human—not relinquishing what he was, but assuming what was ours? When, in our confession, we place “God” first and follow it by saying “and human being,” we assert not only that he remains God but also that the same person subsists as a human being, so that neither the divinity departs from itself nor humanity perishes in divinity.

Let us nevertheless see whether this conjunction may have been inserted by divine authority. For we read: “And he is human, and who will understand him?” (Jeremiah 17:9, according to the Septuagint). And again David says: “The mother of Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Psalm 86:5).

Why, then, did he not simply say, without placing this conjunction first, “A human being was made in her,” but instead prefaced it by saying, “And a human being was made in her”? Or, in the other prophecy, why did he put “and” first? According to these people, he ought to have said: “He is human, and who will understand him?” Unless the meaning is this: the one whom you confess as God, you must not deny, by a similar confession, to have also been made human.

XIV. It is said of these people—if it is true—that they confess Christ to possess two natures until his resurrection, but after the resurrection they admit that he is of one nature. How absurd and foolish this is is demonstrated by the truth of the matter itself.

After the resurrection, to demonstrate the reality of his body, he both ate and drank and offered himself to the disciples to be touched, saying: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

But perhaps, while he was still on earth, he possessed both natures; afterward, when he ascended into heaven, he began to be only of the divine nature. What, then, is the name “Son of man” doing there, if the nature of humanity is not there? How can an empty name be assigned to something that does not exist? How does the truth of the name remain if the property of the nature is absent?

Finally, he says: “When the Son of man comes in the glory of his Father.” And again: “As lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of man” (Mark 8:38). And again: “When the Son of man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Matthew 14:27). Daniel also says: “Behold, the Son of man was coming in the clouds of heaven” (Luke 18:8; Daniel 7:13).

If, then, the nature of humanity has been lost, why has its name been retained? Was a name needed while the reality signified by the name was to be rejected as unnecessary? Let those who are ashamed of none of their error or foolishness rave in this way.

But the Lord Jesus Christ, to show that the nature of our race had not been consumed, truly calls himself the Son of man. According to this same nature he also intercedes with the Father for us, in accordance with the words of the Apostle John: “If we sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus. He himself intercedes for our sins” (1 John 2:1).

Tell us, then, O illustrious teachers: when the Son today intercedes with the Father, does he plead according to his divinity, or does he petition according to the dispensation of his humanity?

But insofar as the intention of your perfidy reveals itself—for by destroying human nature you assert that only the divine nature exists—he intercedes according to his divinity, performs the office of advocate according to his divinity, fulfills the ministry of priest according to his divinity, and even according to his divinity will be subject to the Father at the last, when all things have been subjected to that same Son.

XV. For a long time we were waiting; we had waited patiently to discover from where the stream of your error derives its origin and in what direction it flows. At last we have found that the Eutychian heresy, derived from the most bitter spring of Apollinaris, travels through turbid channels toward the muddy abyss of Arius. It is joined to that abyss by such a bond of perfidy that it refers everything to an insult against divinity that Christ either said or did according to the dispensation of the flesh, while it insists that there is only one nature—that of divinity.

Therefore we exhort all who follow this wicked perfidy: while life remains and repentance is possible, change your judgment concerning your error. Instead, follow the teaching concerning the property of both natures given by Gregory and Basil, and also by Theophilus and John, that most celebrated bishop of the city of Constantinople, as well as by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and by many others who flourished in the Church in ancient times. We offer their opinions on this matter from elsewhere for you to read through.

In the meantime, I ask the reader not to despise altogether the poverty of our style, since perhaps the discourse could have been embellished more eloquently. But we have moderated our style so that we might commend the subject rather than the words to our readers. Above all, this work ought not to be inflated with the buskin of swelling eloquence, lest there be any need to translate it into Greek. For it is more difficult to preserve the integrity of meaning in another language with an equal elegance of expression.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103C] I. A varied and diverse error of heretical depravity has nevertheless emerged from one source. For the worst hinge and origin of the evils that have produced the occasions of every impiety from themselves is this: the force of heavenly sayings, corrupted by the fault of those who misunderstand them, is not weighed according to the quality of its meaning but is diverted, at the reader’s discretion and will, toward other matters, contrary to what the truth requires.

Anyone can very easily detect this in the inventions of all the heretics. There is also another occasion of impiety, which excessive piety has provided, in a remarkable manner, for those who are less cautious. And it is greatly and sufficiently lamentable that the evil of deadly perfidy becomes impious from the very source from which another person becomes pious; that from the very place where the power of freedom is acquired, others receive the miserable hardships of captivity; that people become entangled in errors where every error of ignorance is absolved; that one becomes perfidious from the very source from which another is faithful; and that one is blinded by the same light by which another is most brilliantly illumined.

To make this clear through more evident proofs, let us compare the doctrines of the opinions of Sabellius and Arius, Manichaeus and Photinus, Nestorius and Eutyches. We find that they were so opposed to one another that—what is even more astonishing—their error bears witness to the truth, and the discordant opinions of the perfidious harmonize into one 14 pattern of right faith, while their empty struggles produce a trophy of our victory.

II. The perfidy of Sabellius condemns the error of Arius. Again, the error of Arian doctrine excludes the impiety of Sabellius.

Sabellius, deceived by the plausible confession of one nature, supposed that the Trinity had one person, so that from the fact that the three have one nature it might be understood that there is one person.

Arius, on the other hand, accepting three subsistent and distinct persons, as they truly are, believed that their natures were dissimilar. What pertains to distinction he referred to the inequality of those persons; therefore he dared to define them as widely unequal both in merit and in rank.

Let this error of his, then, serve to refute the impiety of Sabellius. Let Sabellius hear that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons to such an extent that Arius dares to profess them different in power and diverse in nature.

Let this same Arius hear, in turn, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one power and one nature to such an extent that Sabellius says they are one person.

Therefore, Arius, correct your evil through his evil, and let him correct his evil through your evil, so that the good that both of you hold with us may be common to you. For it is good that you, Arius, say that there are three persons; but it is evil that you separate them so widely in rank and nature.

Likewise, Sabellius, it is good that you say there is one nature; but it is evil that the truth of one nature compels you to confess one person.

I bring a concise resolution to your dispute. Indeed, it is not I but Christ who, as the most just judge, decreed that the controversies of your disputes should be settled by a single sentence of the Word, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

By saying “I and the Father,” he distinguished what Sabellius wrongly confuses. By adding “are one,” he united what Arius wrongly distinguishes, so that “one” may serve the unity of nature, while “are” serves the distinction of persons.

The same is expressed in the words: “Baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), indicating, in the one name of the three, that the divine nature is one.

Thus the best Judge pronounced a saving judgment amid the harmful and deadly disputes of Christians, 15 so that the one who sets aside the judge’s sentence may perish through his own fault.

### III

Likewise, Manichaeus, when he observes the miracles of such great powers that the Son of God performed, does not wish to confess Him to be human. Photinus, when he considers in Him the nature of our body, does not judge Him to be God. The former, to fortify his position, rehearses the manifestations of divine power; the latter, the weaknesses of humanity. The former is recalled from confessing humanity by the majesty of so great a name; the latter is held back in confessing only a human being by the humility of the insults that he sees to be unworthy of God. Miracles draw the former away; sufferings impede the latter. The former is deceived by divinity; the latter is offended by humanity. The former [Col. 0105C] says, “He is God”; the latter says, “He is human.” It is a great miracle that truth should be confirmed by its own refutation, and that each should speak truly while each is lying.

Listen, then, Manichaeus: when you say that He is God, you speak truly; when you say that He is not also human, you are mistaken. Listen, Photinus: He truly is human, as you assert, although not in the manner you assert; but He is also God, which you impiously refuse to acknowledge. He is so truly God that Manichaeus denies Him to be human; He is so truly human that you do not believe Him to be God. Since, then, you are both opposed to one another, you both act with us: you are far separated, and in the middle lies the way that you have abandoned. One of you on this side, the other on that—come here to us, and you will find one another. Let one pass over into the opinion of the other, but in such a way that he does not abandon his own. Let what each of you possesses privately become common to you: let him confess the human being, and you confess God; and at last depart from your respective error through the truth proper to each.

### IV

Let us now come to Nestorius and Eutyches, who have striven to overshadow the serenity of the Catholic faith throughout the entire East with the dark clouds of impiety. Although their criminal doctrine has been refuted together with its authors, their wicked followers, having found an abundant opportunity in the passage of time, spread the poisonous and deadly venom of their savage teaching so widely that what the attack of its authors could not accomplish, the disease of their pestilential assertion, raging everywhere, has wounded almost the whole Church.

Since I have already answered them appropriately in a single treatise, I shall now briefly and concisely expose their empty anxieties and futile fears. It is certain, according to the Catholic faith and the declarations of Scripture, that the Lord Jesus Christ has two births: one from the Father, without time; the other from His mother, without seed. Possessing the nature of both these births—namely, the nature of God, by which He was born from the Father, and the nature of a human being, by which He was begotten from His mother—the one and same Christ is both God and human being.

For the twofold birth gave the one Christ a twofold nature: He who is God from the Father is also human from His mother. These natures, therefore, which He has from both parents, the Apostle calls two forms when he says of Him: “Although He was in the form of God, He did not consider equality with God something to be grasped; but He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6).

Concerning these forms—both the one that He has from God the Father and the one that He received from a human mother—the prophetic oracle gives an even clearer testimony. Isaiah, speaking of His servant-form, which appeared in a certain sense unseemly because of the degradation of His passion, says: “His appearance will be without honor among men, and His form among the children of men” (Isa. LII, 14). And again: “We saw Him, and there was in Him neither appearance nor beauty; but His form was despised and deficient beyond the children of men” (Isa. LIII, 2).

Isaiah spoke these words about the servant-form in which He endured every injury of the passion. But David sang more explicitly of the form of His divinity, which, retaining its beauty through its impassibility, could not be disfigured although it was struck by the injuries of passion: “Beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

Do you see that in the one person of Christ the mystery of both forms—that is, of both natures—is contained? The form of a servant is unseemly and despised; the form of God in Him is proclaimed beautiful and most beautiful. Let another take these matters in whatever way he wishes; for the present, by prophetic and apostolic proclamation, we have shown that Christ has two forms. Now let us show that in both He is one and the same and has one person.

The Apostle says: “And whatever I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done so in the person of Christ” (II Cor. II, 10). It is therefore clear that Christ subsists from two enduring natures in the union of one person.

### V

Let us now see by what error Nestorius and Eutyches were deceived. Nestorius, introducing two natures, thought that there were two persons as well; and for this reason, by his sacrilegious doctrine, he supposed that he was introducing two Christs. Eutyches, considering one person, judged that there was one nature; and for this reason he dared to deny the human nature. [Col. 0106D]

Since in Christ there is both the distinct property of the natures and the union of the person, Nestorius, attending to the distinct properties of the natures, fell away from the union of the person and thought that there were two Christs—one passible, the other impassible. Eutyches, concentrating on the one person, departed from the distinct property of the natures and asserted that divinity itself had suffered.

Thus, there are not two Christs or two persons to such an extent that Eutyches believes there to be one nature. Conversely, there is not one nature but two, to such an extent that Nestorius thinks there are two Christs and two persons.

Accordingly, to fortify the impiety of his doctrine, by which he wants one Christ to be understood in the passion and another, Nestorius uses the testimony of the Apostle, who writes as follows to the Hebrews: “We saw Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor, so that apart from God He might taste death for all” (Heb. II, 9).

Eutyches, in turn, in order to subject divinity to suffering, likewise produces the Apostle as a witness, who says of the rulers of this age, who did not know the wisdom of God: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 9).

You see what great danger is involved either in refusing to believe that Christ has one person or in refusing to confess that He has two natures. On both sides great snares of ambush are set out, which Solomon, speaking in the prophetic spirit, more cautiously commanded to be avoided: “Remember,” he says, “that you walk in the midst of snares” (Eccli. IX, 20).

For on one side Eutyches stands armed, and on the other Nestorius, with the drawn swords of unbelief. While I defend against Nestorius the one person of Christ, I am thought, in the manner of Eutyches, to deny the human nature. While against Eutyches I assert two natures, I am thought, in the manner of Nestorius, to confess two persons, because he believed that two Christs and two persons were to be assigned to the two natures.

### VI

But in order to refute, in a Catholic understanding, their impious and detestable errors, let us discuss both the mystery of the distinct property of each nature and the hidden reality of the one person.

There is one Christ, the same God and the same human being, possessing in His words and deeds one thing that belongs to the nature of His humanity and another that belongs to His own divinity, although both together belong to His one person or substance. It is said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1).

And when He Himself says, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58), this cannot be referred to the nature of His humanity, which began from the Virgin.

Again, what is said of Him—“The child grew and was strengthened, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon Him” (Luke II, 40)—and: “When He was twelve years old, He went up with His parents to Jerusalem”; and what follows, “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and men”—cannot correspond to the nature of His divinity. For divinity neither undergoes advancement in age nor experiences any increase; it is not subject to the course of time and is not reckoned by a number of years.

To put everything briefly: although Christ has one person, it is not one nature for Him both to call the Father His equal and to assert that He is less than the Father; both not to have a beginning and to subsist from a beginning. This is the distinct property of the natures, from which the one Son of God, the same Christ who is also the Son of a human being, subsists, possessing and bearing only one person.

Therefore this one and same Christ is equal to the Father according to His divinity, and inferior to the Father according to the nature of His humanity. Thus He has no beginning because He is God, and He has a beginning because the same God is human. If, then, you ask me whether Christ has a beginning or does not have one, I shall answer you: He both has one and does not have one. He has one according to His humanity; He does not have one according to His divinity.

When I say, “He has” or “He does not have,” this pertains to the union of the person. When I say, “according to His divinity” and “according to His humanity,” this pertains to the distinct property of the natures. To make this understanding clear through more obvious proofs, let us set forth still more evident examples.

### VII

We believe that the Word of God descended from heaven without flesh, without the designation of a human being, yet in such a way that He did not abandon heaven. This Word was incarnate in the virginal womb, not changed into flesh, and became and was called the Son of a human being. If anyone believes otherwise, he is undoubtedly anathema. If anyone says that a human being—that is, flesh—descended from heaven, he is certainly anathema.

What, then, does the same Lord’s statement mean: “No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13)? And again: “If you see the Son of Man ascending to where He was before” (John VI, 63)?

Behold, the Son of Man is read to have descended from heaven, although it is established that only the Word—that is, naked, without flesh and without the designation of a human being—descended from heaven. Behold, the flesh—that is, the Son of Man—is read to have been in heaven at that time, although it never descended from there and had not yet ascended there.

But this is the mystery of the one person; this is the sacramental mystery of the one Christ subsisting from both; this is the hidden reality of the distinct property of both natures. For the Word is united with the flesh in such an inexplicable manner that the Word Himself is called flesh, although He is not flesh, since He was not changed into flesh; and the flesh is called God, although it was not changed into the nature of divinity. Rather, the Word is human because of His flesh, and the flesh is God because of the Word; whatever is proper to the Word is shared with the flesh, and whatever is proper to the flesh is shared with the Word, because the Word and the flesh are one Christ and one person.

Therefore, because of this communion—which, while preserving the distinct property of the natures, is furnished by the union of the person—the Word with the flesh, that is, the Son of Man, is read to have descended from heaven, although only the Word descended without the flesh. And God is read to have been buried and to have lain in the tomb for three days, although only the flesh was buried.

Thus, according to the distinct property of the nature, only the Word descended from heaven, not the flesh; according to the union of the person, the flesh also descended together, because the person of the flesh is in the Word that descended. Again, according to the distinct property of the nature, only the flesh experienced death and only the flesh underwent burial; but according to the union of the person, God died and was buried, because the person of the Word is in the flesh, which experienced the loss of life.

Therefore, according to the distinct property of the nature, the Word descended from heaven, not the flesh; according to the distinct property of the nature, the flesh died, not the Word. Again, according to the union of the person, both the flesh descended from heaven and the Word died and was buried.

### VIII

When, therefore, we say that God suffered and died, let Nestorius not be alarmed, because we say this according to the union of the person. Again, when we say that God neither suffered nor died, because He is altogether impassible, let Eutyches not be afraid, because we say this according to the distinct property of the nature; indeed, it is not we who say it, but the Scriptures speak.
