For the authority of the Creed holds that the Lord suffered, and the Apostle handed this down when he said: “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8). Again, the teaching that God did not suffer is likewise conveyed by apostolic authority, when Paul speaks thus to the Hebrews: “We saw Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor, so that apart from God He might taste death for all” (Heb. II, 9).

What does it mean to taste death “apart from God,” except that the Word is immortal and that the suffering occurred according to the flesh? Hence the Apostle Peter also says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh” (I Pet. IV, 1).

Suffering, then, properly belongs to the flesh according to nature, but to the Word according to the person, because the Word and the flesh have one and the same person. Consequently, God both suffered and did not suffer: He suffered according to the union of the person, and He remained impassible according to the distinct property of the nature.

[Col. 0109B] IX

And so that this very point may become still clearer, let us establish it with more evident testimonies. It is established that the Lord Jesus Christ was crucified on Friday, descended into hell on that same day, lay in the tomb on that same day, and said to the thief on that same day: “Today you will be with Me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

The flesh, therefore, was not in paradise on that day, nor in hell, but lay lifeless in the tomb. The soul was in hell throughout those three days, not in the tomb. Yet we rightly say that the Lord Jesus Christ lay in the tomb—but in the flesh alone; and that the Lord Jesus Christ was not abandoned in hell—but in the soul alone.

Although Christ is in all these things and Christ is in each of them individually, there is nevertheless one Christ. Something belonging to Him was in the tomb and something else in hell, yet He Himself, one and whole, was everywhere, since He distributed Himself separately among the places.

Therefore we say that God lay in the tomb, but in the flesh alone; and that God descended into hell, but in the soul alone. Just as we say that a human being heard a voice, but with the ears alone, and saw light, but with the eyes alone, so we say that God suffered, but in the flesh alone, and that God did not suffer, but in His divinity alone.

Consequently, because Christ is one God, He suffered according to what He is as a human being, and remained impassible according to what He is as God. I shall conclude this in a brief statement: God suffered in the union of the person; He did not suffer in the distinct property of the nature.

Indeed, divinity itself also endured the injuries of the passion, but only His flesh actually experienced the suffering. Just as we rightly say that a sunbeam or the substance of a flame can indeed be cut by a sword, but cannot be severed, so we rightly say that the Word of God endured the injuries of the passion, but did not in any way experience the suffering itself.

I shall state it still more clearly. Divinity was fastened with nails, but it could not itself be pierced, as His flesh could, since the flesh, being opened to the wound, made room for it; for the divinity remained indivisible and impenetrable. Thus, by receiving sufferings without yielding to their effects, God the Word is shown to have suffered impassibly.

But because His flesh not only endured all these things but also felt them and yielded to them, we rightly and properly say that God was sensibly affected by all these conditions of suffering in His flesh, without sensation or change in His divinity. Therefore, enduring suffering belongs to both natures; but yielding to suffering does not belong to both natures, although both belong to one and the same person.

### X

Many orthodox Christians, paying insufficient attention to these matters—or unwilling or unable to pay attention and distinguish them—have divided themselves into two groups, not by a difference of opinion but by their verbal confession. They fear to express in the same way what they understand in the same way: an entirely useless and superfluous fear, so that the prophetic statement may rightly be applied to them: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII, 5).

For many orthodox Christians, although they explain and retain the meaning of both natures in a Catholic manner, nevertheless refuse to say “two natures,” lest they appear to confess two persons according to Nestorius. They withdraw from the confession of both natures not in their hearts but only in their speech.

They use a certain circumlocution in their exposition, so as to show that they believe in two, but do not pronounce “two” in plain speech. For when they believe and confess that it was not a human being but the Word who descended from heaven, and that He was so incarnate in the Virgin’s womb—that is, so assumed flesh—that He was not changed into flesh; when they believe that the Word became human in such a way that He remained true God; when they believe that He assumed our nature in such a way that He neither changed nor cast off His own; and when they believe that God became human and a human being became God in such a way that neither was nevertheless consumed—who does not see that by this understanding two natures are plainly asserted and demonstrated?

What is gathered by the true exposition of the faith and retained by the judgment of the mind—why is it silenced in verbal confession through a needless fear?

Again, others, fearing that they might fall into the doctrine of Apollinaris and Eutyches, refuse to say that the Lord suffered and died, although they believe Him to have one person and confess that this same one is both God and human being. If He is one, as He is, why are you afraid to say that He suffered, when you are not afraid to say that He is one, and you do not dare to say that He is another according to the impious understanding of Nestorius?

These, then, are utterly empty fears and vain anxieties, which have caused orthodox Christians to hurl the names of heretics at one another, since they trample underfoot in speech what they proclaim more clearly in their hearts. Those who wish to confess with their mouths the one person whom they defend in their exposition of the faith are thought to be Eutychianists, although they are not. Likewise, those who publicly confess the two natures of the one Christ are thought to be Nestorians, although they are not.

And you may see them accusing one another, amid certain mournful insults deserving of every lamentation, in the name of heresy: “You,” he says, “are an Eutychianist, and you are a Nestorian.” They have entirely forgotten the apostolic statement: “See to it that, when you accuse one another, you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. V, 15).

I ask you: if you are sound in understanding, why do you rage in your speech? Why do you go astray through a perverse fear of words, when you stand firm in the confession of faith through the stability of a right mind? Why are you afraid to say “two natures,” when the Apostle was not afraid to say “two forms”—one in which He is God, the other in which the same one is God and human being?

Why are you afraid to say “two natures,” which Athanasius, approved by the judgment of all ecclesiastical men, declared? In this confession of faith, all the interpreters of the Greek language, whom I mentioned in the preceding treatise, [Col. 0111A] and all the apostolic men of Latin speech—that is, Hilary, Eusebius, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome—imbued with heavenly teachings, agree together and with one accord.

And why are you afraid to say that God suffered, when apostolic proclamations everywhere bear witness to this? Weigh carefully the exposition of this little treatise, and do not fear to confess with your mouths what it is clear that you feel in your hearts. For it is of no benefit to believe with the heart for righteousness unless confession is also made with the mouth for salvation (Rom. X, 10).

Hence the Prophet says: “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Ps. XXXIX, 11). Confess, therefore, with your mouths what you hold in your hearts, so that the divine humanity and human divinity may be gracious to you.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0111]

### I

Since the Eutychian heresy has fallen into such impiety that it believes not only that the Word and the flesh have one nature, but also says that this same flesh was not assumed from the sacred body of the Virgin Mary, but was brought down from heaven, according to the unspeakable error of Valentinus and Marcion; and since it so stubbornly asserts that the Word became flesh that He appears to have passed through the Virgin as water passes through a pipe, without anyone believing that He assumed anything from the Virgin belonging to our race—I judged it best to destroy this aspect of their impiety also by an assertion of the truth, and utterly to dispel all the murky darkness of their gloomy doctrine.

This is especially necessary because it greatly advances the truth of the confession of both natures to establish by divine testimonies that the Son of God assumed a human body from the flesh of the Virgin.

### II

Since, then, these people, following the more correct path of the Catholic faith and the authority of the Council of Nicaea, confess that the Son of God was begotten not from outside, not from nothing, but from the Father, and that He is of the same nature as the Father, [Col. 0111C] they should be reminded, according to this rule of confession, that this same Son, born from the Virgin, certainly possessed the nature of that Virgin’s flesh. In this matter, let the Arian heresy not hold them bound by the insoluble snare of its question, employing this syllogism of objection:

“If the Son of God, born from a human mother, had nothing from her that belonged to human nature, then without doubt, being born from the Father, He had nothing from Him that could be of the same nature as the Father. For if you truly assert,” it says, “that the Son was born from the Virgin without possessing the nature of His mother’s body, grant me also, who make the same claim, that the same Son, born from the Father, cannot possess the Father’s nature.”

Why, then, O Eutychianists, do you submit your necks to such powerful objections of unbelief and pass from one falsehood to another, so that you confess that the Son, begotten from the Father, is foreign to the nature of the Father’s divinity, just as you confess that the same Son, begotten from His mother, did not possess the nature of His mother—that is, of a human body?

Why, if you possess any wisdom, do you not rather destroy falsehood by the truth, so that, just as you believe—and truly believe—that the Son, born from the Father without time, possesses the Father’s nature, so you may believe that the same Son, born from His mother without seed, possesses the nature of a human body?

### III

For what did the angel say to Mary? “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

He did not say “what will be born through you,” as though indicating that the Word merely passed through the Virgin; rather, he said “what will be born from you,” in order to declare more clearly that He would assume the reality of a body from the Virgin.

For what reason was there for the Word of God to pass through the Virgin’s womb if He sought to assume nothing from it? Or how is He believed to have been born or made from David’s seed if He is denied to have assumed a body from his lineage?

Finally, the Apostle Paul says: “Concerning His Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3). And again, to the Galatians: “God sent His Son, made from a woman” (Gal. IV, 4).

How did the One who already was come to be made, since it is ordinarily proper to be made to one who had never previously subsisted? Only because He was made what He was not—namely, a human being—and assumed flesh from no other source than the human race, from which He was made what He had not been.

Hence the Son Himself also speaks through Isaiah of being formed from the womb, saying: “And now the Lord says, who formed me from the womb as a servant for Himself” (Isa. XLIX, 5).

What, then, do you understand to have been formed from the womb—the Word or the flesh? If the Word, then either He was formless or did not exist at all, so that His formation either gave Him essence, enabling Him to subsist, or advanced Him from an already subsisting formlessness into a better condition, so that He might appear perfect and complete.

Since it is impious and sacrilegious to suppose this, it unquestionably remains that the flesh was formed from the body of the virginal womb. According to this flesh, because of the union of the person, although He is God, He became a servant of the Father.

Hence the Psalm says to Him: “O Lord, I am Your servant and the son of Your handmaid” (Ps. CXV, 16). And again: “From the womb of my mother, You are my God” (Ps. XXI, 11). If He had received nothing from the womb of His handmaid mother, the condition of a servile nature would not hold Him within the designation of a servant.

### IV

But let us now see what prophetic figures are used to show that He assumed the true nature of flesh from the reality of His mother’s body.

Isaiah says: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a branch will rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him” (Isa. XI, 1).

Who would doubt that a branch receives the form of its subsistence from the nature of the very shrub from which it springs? Or who would deny that the branch of any tree propagates the shoots of its own nature?

Both customary examples of things and the authority of the divine writings testify that each tree produces not something different from itself but the form of its own kind. Thus Scripture speaks in Genesis: “And God said: Let the earth bring forth green grass, producing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree producing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth. And it was so” (Gen. I, 11).

If, then, trees produce from themselves shoots of their own kind and nature, and fruit of their own proper quality, there is no doubt that the shoot of the Jessean root—namely, blessed Mary—brought forth from the material of her own flesh the shoot of her nature, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ.

The mystery of this glorious sacrament was also signified in the rod of the priest Aaron. Placed in the tabernacle of the covenant, without the work or assistance of earthly cultivation and without the customary and lawful nourishment of rural labor, it blossomed, clearly and openly indicating that the Virgin Mary would give birth to Christ the Lord without the activity of earthly—that is, human—seed.

This is also shown in Daniel by a sure foreshadowing of the future mystery (Dan. II, 34), when a stone appears to be cut from the mountain without hands. This signifies that Christ would be born from the Virgin’s body without the work of human intercourse.

Who could be so foolish and so alien in mind as to believe that a stone was cut from the mountain without hands and yet not believe that Christ was born from the Virgin’s body without seed, when the former was seen only in a vision but the latter truly took place?

For so that what was wondrously to occur in Christ might be believed, a wondrous image of the same event preceded it: just as a stone could be cut from the mountain without hands, and just as a rod could blossom without turf, so Christ could be born from the Virgin without seed.

Jacob also declares this in his blessings, when, under the person of Judah, he adapts and directs the prophecy toward Christ, saying: “You have risen for me from a shoot” (Gen. XLIX, 9). He did not say “from seed,” but “from a shoot”—clearly that rod which arose from the root of Jesse and, by a new kind of miracle, blossomed forth Christ the Lord.

### V

Let us consider also the other comparisons by which it is shown that Christ assumed the nature of flesh from the human race.

Heretics themselves do not dare deny that the same Lord is called a calf or ox, a lamb, and a kid. Let them therefore read and they will find it at the beginning of Leviticus (I, 2), where, as a mystery of the future passion, a calf is commanded to be sacrificed at the door of the tabernacle of testimony. It is not simply called a calf, but a calf “from cattle.”

Through this the prophet demonstrates that Christ did not, as the heretics wish, bring down a body from heaven, but assumed flesh from the human race. For it would have been sufficient to say “calf”; why was it necessary to add “from cattle”? Who would not know that a calf is born from cattle? It was added only to show that Christ would have flesh from human beings.

Abraham too, not ignorant of this mystery, is described as having chosen a calf from the herd (Gen. XVIII, 7), which he is understood to have killed as a type of the Lord’s passion.

Moreover, the synagogue is commanded to offer a lamb from sheep and a kid from goats. Through this, the Holy Spirit, wishing to remove opportunities for unbelief, declared more openly and explicitly, by these additions of words, that Christ’s flesh was to be assumed from human beings.

Yet, wishing to show that this flesh would come from the human race, Isaiah says, “Send forth the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XVI, 1). Thus, in the command that this lamb be taken from sheep, the reality of human nature is recognized; but in the command that the same lamb be sent forth from the rock, any suspicion of human intercourse and seed is removed.

Thus he says “a lamb from sheep,” “a kid from goats,” and “a calf from cattle,” as though he were saying “a human being from human beings.”

Moses said the same thing more plainly elsewhere: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in everything he says” (Deut. XVIII, 15). And again: “A star will rise from Jacob, and a human being will arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV, 17).

And the Apostle says: “It is evident that our Lord arose from Judah” (Heb. VII, 14). And He Himself says through the prophet: “Woe to them, because my flesh is from them!” (Amos IX, 12).

### VI

A sheaf of firstfruits from the crops is also commanded to be offered and consecrated to the Lord (Lev. XXIII, 10). Who could doubt that this sheaf of firstfruits is the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the Law says: “Everything that opens the womb, the firstborn, shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. XIII, 2)?

Hence the angel says to Mary: “Therefore that which will be born from you will be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

This sheaf, taken from the harvest of the Jewish people, was offered to God the Father through the passion of death. Of it the Apostle says: “Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (I Cor. XV, 20). And again: “Christ the beginning; afterward, those who are Christ’s” (ibid., 23).

Joseph also indicated the beginning of the resurrection of this offered sheaf in his vision, saying: “I saw us binding sheaves in the field, and my sheaf rose up, and your sheaves bowed down to my sheaf” (Gen. XXXVII, 7).

We see this fulfilled most clearly in the Gospel, when the Lord, rising from the dead, is read to have been worshiped by His disciples (Matt. XXVIII, 9). Likewise, at the consummation of the age—which is signified by the harvest of that field—He is to be worshiped and seen by all in the form of a servant, whose image the sheaf bore (Matt. XXIV, 30).

There are many other things fashioned in figures and comparisons that indicate that Christ possessed the nature of flesh from human beings. But lest Photinus and those like him attempt to seize upon this as an opportunity for nurturing unbelief—since these testimonies appear to declare only the one nature of Christ’s flesh—I consider it necessary, as the faith requires, also to repeat and bring forward those testimonies that teach that both natures, divine and human, exist in the one Christ.

### VII

The Apostle says, then, that all the promises of blessing contained in prophecy and the Law pertain to the mystery of Christ. For he says: “However many the promises are, they are in Him” (II Cor. I, 20).

Let us therefore see how all these blessings of the promises are applied to Christ in mystical figures; there we shall find the mysteries of both natures shining forth as clearly as light. For the promise of blessing could not be valid and firm unless it contained the hidden mystery of the perfect faith by which Christ, God and human being, was to be announced.

Thus the patriarch Isaac, blessing his sons Jacob and Esau, spoke to Jacob as follows: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field which God has blessed. May the Lord give you dew from heaven and abundance of the richness of the earth, of grain, wine, and oil” (Gen. XXVII, 27).

But to Esau he said: “Your blessing will be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven” (ibid., 39).

What could be brought forward more openly or more clearly concerning the two natures of Christ? For the dew of heaven is shown to signify the Word, while the richness of the earth signifies His flesh.

That Jacob and Esau represent figuratively the peoples of the Gentiles and the Jews, I think no Christian can doubt. Accordingly, the first people of the Gentiles, whose image Jacob prefigured, having received the grace of blessing from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth—that is, from Christ, who is God and human being—was filled with an abundance of grain, wine, and oil; that is, it was consecrated through the mystery of Christ’s body and blood and His chrism.

David also commemorates the manifold grace of this triple blessing in a sacred song: “From the time of their grain, wine, and oil they have been multiplied” (Ps. IV, 8).

Esau, however, who had been born first according to the flesh and who most plainly bore the type of the Jewish people, while lingering longer in the field of the Law and devoting himself to the wandering and fleeting hunting of carnal senses, or serving the transient shadows and images of the Law, came as a servant to grace (Gen. XXV, 27).

He is that elder son in the Gospel who, while occupied with the work of the countryside—that is, of the Law—was overtaken by the more energetic industry of the younger son and was deprived of the flesh of the fattened calf (Luke XV).

Wearied, then, by exhausting himself through fruitless and empty labor, he hears from the father: “In vain are you occupied with all these things, and beyond the appointed time you busy yourself with the doctrines of legal decrees” [Cod. Reg.: “constitution,” instead of “condition”], thinking that you can obtain the grace of blessing from the Law; although the time appointed for observing the carnal Law has passed, and, because of the impossibility of fulfilling what the Law commands, transgressors of that same Law receive not so much blessing as a curse.

For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the Law” (Deut. XXVII, 26).

Therefore, you must know that your future blessing will be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven—that is, in Christ.

## VIII

Jacob also, when blessing his son Joseph, did not depart from the mystery of this sacrament, saying: “May he bless you with the blessings of heaven above, and with the blessings of the earth possessing all things” (Gen. 49:25). What is the blessing of heaven except the Word who descended from heaven? And what is the blessing of the earth possessing all things except Christ’s flesh, which was taken from the earth—that is, from the earthly body of the Virgin—in whom the truth of all spiritual graces overflows and the fruit of every blessing abounds?

In this fruit, which is undoubtedly Christ, the blessing of all the faithful is brought to completion, as David says: “The earth has yielded its fruit. May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (Ps. 66:7). What is the earth that yielded the fruit of blessing except Mary, to whom it is said: “Blessed are you, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42)? And in Genesis: “The blessings,” he says, “of breasts and womb” (Gen. 49:25). And in the Psalms: “Children are a reward, the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126:3). And again: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131).

Concerning this fruit, the same author of the sacred song sings elsewhere in another psalm: “Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven. For the Lord will give goodness, and our earth will yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:12). In this passage he plainly proclaims the confession of both natures and silences the mouths of the faithless, asserting that truth arose from the earth and that righteousness looked down from heaven. For Christ, possessing substance from both: from heaven, since he was begotten from the Father; and from earth, since he was also born from his mother, possesses and bears the nature of both parents.

“His going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. 18:7). For the summit of heaven is the Father. “And his procession is like that of a bridegroom” (ibid., 6), from the chamber of the virginal womb. Isaiah also, disclosing this mystery of both natures through the same signs—plainly signs of heaven and earth—spoke as follows: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8).

## IX

See with what harmonious statements truth is fortified by prophetic authority. What David says, “Righteousness has looked down from heaven,” Isaiah says in this way: “Let the clouds rain the Just One.” And what David adds, “Our earth will yield its fruit,” Isaiah adds in these words: “Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior.” He used a sufficiently clear and evident—indeed, the proper—name of the Son of God, so that no one could dare doubt that the fruit and shoot of the earth, so often named in prophecy, signifies Christ’s birth from Mary.

Isaiah still speaks concerning this shoot or fruit, saying: “On that day the shoot of the Lord will be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth will be exalted” (Isa. 4:2). Is any room for doubt left, when it is clear that by the name of shoot and fruit Christ is most plainly signified—he who has been exalted in such glory and magnificence that in his name every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father?

Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. 2:9). And now the prophet, saying, “The fruit of the earth will be exalted,” most clearly intended that what was taken from the earth—that is, from Mary—was exalted and glorified. But what is from the Father was always exalted.

## X

Nor is there any opportunity for doubt that the dew of heaven is placed as a figure of the Word of God, since Isaiah himself said: “Let the clouds rain the Just One” (Isa. 45:8). Elsewhere, in an even clearer passage, he described the Father as comparing his Word to heavenly rain. For he says in his person:

“As rain or snow descends from heaven and does not return there—[but] drenches the earth and makes it bring forth—so shall be the Word that goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:10–11).

In such open and utterly unambiguous clarity of divine proclamation, who would not behold the light of truth? Behold, the Word of God is said to flow like rain upon the earth—that is, into the womb of Mary’s bosom—and to make her, made fruitful by the intoxication of the Holy Spirit, burst forth in the shoot of the Lord’s birth and produce the most precious fruit of her swelling womb.

Because this Word, having been made incarnate—that is, having put on flesh—willed to be human, he could not return naked and empty to the Father by whom he had been sent; rather, in the same body with which he had been clothed, he entered the heavenly places. Therefore the Father says that he cannot return to him empty, because it would be impious, once he had descended into the Virgin’s earth, to confess him as naked and empty of humanity—that is, to assert that he possessed only divinity, without the nature of a human body. For it is an equal and identical danger either to confess only his divine nature or only his human nature, since one without the other does not contribute to salvation.

## XI

The Lord himself also teaches this most plainly in the Gospel under such a comparison: “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When someone finds it, he hides it, and for joy goes away, sells all that he has, and buys that field” (Matt. 13:44).

Does it not seem to you that the finder of this treasure acted with insufficient prudence? What necessity or obstacle was there to prevent him from immediately taking the treasure away from the field, since he could certainly have removed it during that very period of leisure and secrecy in which he had found it, and thus, with such an easy shortcut, avoided the need to purchase the field at the cost of his own possessions?

But the very prudent man understood that possession of this treasure without the field was ineffective and useless—indeed, dangerous. For observe that, just as he had found it hidden, so he himself hid it; and, not daring to strip or empty the field of its treasure, he hastened to sell all that he had, so that by lawful right he might obtain both the treasure and the field.

Thus the treasure hidden in the field is God, concealed in his flesh. Hear the Apostle speaking of Christ: “In him,” he says, “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2:3). Therefore every confession is altogether useless and impious if it confesses the Lord Jesus Christ as only God and not also man, or as man alone and not also God.

## XII

That the field is figuratively called Christ’s flesh is indicated both by the present passage and by the testimonies cited above. Isaac especially prophesied concerning this field in his blessings: “Behold,” he said, “the scent of my son is like the scent of a field which God has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

The Lord’s body gives off the fragrance of great and varied virtues, and by the sweetness of its scent brings the weak to life. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ to God, from life to life, for those who are being saved” (2 Cor. 2:15). Drawn by the sweetness of this outstanding and saving fragrance, the Church says to him in the Song of Songs: “We will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3).

He himself also speaks of the beauty of this field in Psalm 49: “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. 49:11). On account of the glory of this field, the Church adjures her companions in the aforementioned book of Solomon, saying: “I adjure you by the glory and virtues of the field” (Song 2:7; 3:5).

That strong and wise woman herself, namely the Church, is introduced in Solomon’s Proverbs as having purchased this field; for it is said of her: “She saw a field and bought it” (Prov. 31:16).

The possession of this field is precious, for it retains within itself the deity hidden in Christ. Christ is of a twofold nature, and therefore, as I said, no one can possess either the treasure without the field or the field without the treasure.

For Manichaeus and Eutyches, who wish to possess the treasure without the field—that is, to confess divinity alone without flesh—each refusing to confess both natures in Christ, are cast far away and excluded from this possession, regarded as disinherited outsiders. Photinus and those like him, who wished to possess only the field and not its treasure—that is, to confess Christ’s humanity but not his divinity—have likewise been deprived of this possession.

## XIII

Therefore, deservedly, the woman alone in Proverbs is considered worthy of the praise of blessedness who, having purchased this field, is described as having made two cloaks for her husband. In the cloaks, the honor of confession is understood—namely, of both natures. For her husband would not deign to accept from her a single cloak of confession, whether only of his divinity or only of his humanity; to offer one of these without the other is not an honor but the greatest insult.

Rejecting such gifts, which are not at once twofold and distinct through the confession of both natures, and divided according to time and mystery, he says to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4:7).

For he alone divides rightly who does not fail to understand in what respect the Son is equal to the Father, and in what respect he is less than the Father; in what respect he suffered and died, and in what respect he remained equally immortal and incapable of suffering. For guilt consists not only in confusing things, but also in failing to divide them rightly. In the one case the impiety of Eutyches is condemned; in the other, that of Nestorius, since what the former confused improperly, the latter distinguished most wickedly.

Concerning the difference between these doctrines, which oppose one another, I have expressed what I was able to do with the limited capacity of my intellect in the two preceding books. And since in this third book also we have taught—by the irrefutable, as I believe, authority of divine Scripture—that the Son of God has, just as from the Father the nature of divinity, so also from his mother the nature of humanity; and since we have likewise demonstrated with an invincible and evident assertion that he was called the dew of heaven and the shoot or fruit of the earth on account of both natures, let us now turn the work of our pen to the defense of Leo’s letter and of the Council of Chalcedon, and let us show, by refuting the objections of heretics, that a catholic and apostolic meaning shines forth in them.

But to demonstrate these matters, we must begin from other principles. And therefore let this finally be the end of this work.

# BOOK FOUR  
## DEFENSE OF THE LETTER OF SAINT LEO THE POPE TO FLAVIAN OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0119]

## I

Certain men of perverse mind and desirous of empty glory, knowing neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:7), possessing the appearance of piety but denying its power, indignant at the doctrines of truth and unable to tolerate the ecclesiastical rules of faith, thought that the letter of the most blessed Leo, written according to the meaning of apostolic tradition, and the decree of the Council of Chalcedon, ought to be opposed with wicked contradictions. They spewed forth unspeakable inventions in a horrible nausea of words.

Since these things seem to raise some scruple of doubt in the minds of the simpler, I have undertaken, at the urging of the holy brethren and with the help of the Lord our God, to examine and refute them. First, in a single volume, I shall dissolve the objections brought against Leo’s letter. This is the first chapter that a certain person—I do not know who—set before himself:

“The whole body of the faithful professes that it believes in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord” (Leo, Letter 10, no. 2).

This man criticizes the chapter on the ground that Leo did not say “in one God the Father, and in one Jesus Christ, his Son,” in accordance with the decree of the Council of Nicaea. But at Rome, even before the Nicene Synod convened, from the time of the apostles until now, and under Celestine of blessed memory, to whom this man bore witness concerning the right faith, the creed has been handed down to the faithful in this form. Words are not prejudicial when the meaning remains unimpaired.

Indeed, this profession of faith agrees more closely with the saying of the Lord Jesus Christ: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1). He did not say, “in one God the Father, and in one me.” For who does not know that there is one God the Father and one Jesus Christ, his Son?

## II

I nevertheless marvel at how this man marked this passage and omitted the one in which the same blessed Leo mentions the only Son, saying: “The same eternal Only-begotten of the eternal Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary” (Letter 10, no. 2).

It is also astonishing that, with similar madness, he did not criticize the statement: “Who was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary,” since the Nicene Synod did not include this wording; and, according to his preference, we ought to profess only what we find written there.

He impiously slanders Leo by claiming that he believed in one author and true Son of God, the Word, and in another man, conceived and glorified from Mary. But it cannot be proved that he thought or taught this. Rather, he confessed one and the same person when he called Christ the Son of God and man: “For there is one and the same Son of God and of man” (no. 4). And again: “One and the same mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (no. 3).

With astonishing shamelessness you also considered this passage worthy of censure, in which he says: “The Word, of course, performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh; one of these shines with miracles, the other submits to insults” (no. 4).

First, it must be noted that he did not say, as you ignorantly slander him: “One of these shines with miracles, and another submits to insults.” Such wording would have seemed, without ambiguity, to signify two separate individuals or two persons. Rather, he says: “One of these and another of these,” because “one”—that is, this and that—demonstrates not a difference of persons but a distinction of kind, namely, of the Word and the flesh.

## III

Leo also said: “For he who is true God is the same one who is true man; and there can be no falsehood in this unity, since in him there are both the humility of man and the loftiness of deity” (no. 4).

With your customary malice, you twisted this into another meaning, claiming that he introduced two separate individuals, each performing in turn what properly belonged to him, whereas he wished to demonstrate that loftiness and humility—that is, both natures—remain in the one Christ as two realities, not as two individuals.

I wonder how, on this interpretation, you have not also accused the Apostle Paul, since he too said that there are two realities in one human being, each performing what properly belongs to it and striving against the other—namely, spirit and flesh. “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these oppose one another” (Gal. 5:17).

Just as there is one human being in whom two realities remain in one another, each performing what properly belongs to it, and he cannot be called one person when he thinks and acts according to the flesh and another when he lives according to the spirit, but is the same individual in both, possessing both within himself—so also Christ, while possessing within himself one reality in which he submits to weaknesses and another in which he radiates and shines with virtues, namely, flesh and Word, is plainly shown to be not divided and to be not one person and another, but the one and same person.

The Apostle distinguishes these two in him when he says: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

## IV

Yet while, through your profession of one nature, you try to remove the human nature from Christ, you nevertheless appear to confess what you deny. For you said:

“He himself is God, who was born in the flesh, who is the Word of God the Father; who became, without change, a perfect man, remaining the only-begotten Son of God; like God in power and like us in weakness.”

If he is like God in power and like us in weakness, and if likeness to deity in power is a property of the divine nature, then undoubtedly likeness to humanity in weakness is a property of human nature. For it is not the mark of a prudent person to confess unlike things in a similar matter.

Moreover, when you say, “who became without change a perfect man, remaining God,” you confirm our faith—indeed, the catholic faith against which you strive. For if he was not changed into flesh but became man while remaining God, then, since becoming man cannot be called a change, it must be called an assumption. Thus there will be a twofold reality: what existed and was not changed, and what did not exist and came to be or was assumed. For what existed was not changed into flesh, and yet it possesses flesh, as he himself says: “My flesh is truly food” (John 6:56); and Peter says: “Nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:31).

Since possessing and being possessed are not the same thing—for the Word possesses, while the flesh is possessed—it is plainly and clearly demonstrated that Christ is of both natures, but of one person.

## V

Therefore, whatever you wished to pursue at greater length and in greater detail in order to show that Christ is one, you should know that you spent your labor on unnecessary matters, wishing to demonstrate what we in no way deny.

In this, however, you subtly and impiously mock the Christian faith: because Christ is one, which cannot be denied, you turn the unity of person into a prejudice against both natures, since both natures are always called by one name.

For although “Jesus Christ” is properly the name not of the Word but of the flesh, and “God” is properly the designation of the Word, not of the flesh, nevertheless the Word, because of his flesh, is called the man Jesus Christ, and the flesh, because of the Word, is called God the Word.

The name “Christ” derives from what the Prophet says to him: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). The nature of the Word was not anointed, for it could not have companions according to itself. Hence it is clear that the anointing—and therefore the name “Christ”—belongs to that by which he became man.

But because, through recognition of both natures, there is one name for his divinity and humanity, the Apostle says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5–7).

Before the form of a servant was taken from him, he was not yet Christ but only the Word; that is, before he was man, he was not man but only God. Before he was found in the likeness of our condition, he was not yet Christ. And yet Christ is in the form of God; Christ is in the form of a servant; Christ is equal to the Father; Christ is less than the Father; the same one is God, and the same one is man.

Hence it is clear that divinity has the name of humanity and humanity has the name of divinity—that is, the Word is called flesh and the flesh is called the Word—not because either has been changed into the other in itself, but because both constitute one person, that is, one Christ.

Therefore we rightly believe and proclaim with the Apostle that God was crucified and died (1 Cor. 1:23), in the human nature which, through its union with the Word, possesses the name of deity.

Thus the one and same Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, died according to the form of a servant, and did not die according to the form of God. The same one is equal to the Father in the form of God, and less than the Father in the form of a servant.

## VI

Since these things are so, whatever you wished to argue concerning both forms according to the perversity of your understanding, you should know is nullified by this explanation.

We are not unaware of the ignorance—or rather, the madness—with which you wished to alter the Gospel wording. What is read there concerning Christ, that he was crucified between two thieves, on the testimony of the prophet who says, “He was numbered among the transgressors” (Isa. 53:12), you rendered: “He was numbered among the dead.”

These, finally, are your words:

“You say that the God who gives life and loves humanity in every way was numbered among the dead, although he was never overcome by corruption or death; indeed, he descended into hell as one subject to our nature, without sin.”

You see how much sacrilege is contained in the confession of one nature alone. You see into what precipices of impiety this novelty of doctrine drives you. Since you wish God to appear incarnate in such a way that he possesses nothing of human nature, making everything that he is belong to the divine nature, and since you know that the divine nature is immortal and cannot die, nor can the name of death properly apply to it, you have chosen to depart from the apostolic faith by saying that God was numbered among the dead, rather than confessing that he died according to his humanity.

The Apostle teaches that the Son of God died according to his humanity when he says to the Romans: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19).

That this obedience was an obedience unto death, which he undertook for us in the reality of our nature, the Apostle likewise teaches when he says of Christ: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). And again: “We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). And to the Corinthians: “I delivered to you what I also received: that Christ Jesus died according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3).

## VII

We are not unaware, therefore, of the fear that made you afraid to say that God died. Nevertheless, you should know that you act against your own profession when you say of Christ that he descended into hell “as one subject to our nature, without sin.”

If, then, he was subject to our nature, he certainly possessed our nature; or, if he did not possess it, show from where he was subject to it. No one ought to owe anything to one from whom he received nothing.

Moreover, when later, explaining the testimony of Jeremiah concerning Christ, you say, “And he lived among human beings” (Bar. 3:38), “according to the human form from Adam his servant,” you likewise contradict your own professions. For you plainly declared that God lived among human beings by assuming human nature.

Just as the form of God, in which the Son is equal to the Father, is nothing other than the nature of God, so the form of a servant is nothing other than human nature, in which he is less than the Father.

Consider, therefore, the force of your own statement, and believe yourself rather than us. You said that he possessed the form of a servant from Adam, although you did not wish to say that he received it, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7).

But what does it matter to us if you avoid the word whose meaning you could not escape? Whatever comes to him from another did not belong to him before he received it. For no one borrows from another what he is recognized as possessing in himself.

Hence it is clear that the Word of God became incarnate in such a way that he received from us what belongs to us, not by changing his nature into flesh. Thus there will be in him a twofold nature: that of the Word, which was not changed, and that of the flesh, which was received from Adam, his servant.

## VIII

But let us now see what the remaining things are like with which you criticize the catholic faith. Speaking to Leo and to the entire council, you insert their words as follows:

“You said,” you say, “adding also these words: ‘One and the same is truly the Son of God and truly the Son of man.’”

You accuse this statement in the following terms, attempting to weaken it with insolent abuse:

“Listen, I beg you, to the deceit of the poisonous tongue: introducing two sons, you placed ‘one and the same’ first, so that with bare words of truth you might obscure an impious distinction. It would have been enough to say: ‘There is one Son, who without change became man.’”

That is what they said. But you either do not understand, or—which is more true—you impiously slander them. For what you said, “he became man,” they said as “the same is the Son of man.” But if the name “Son of man” displeases you, erase the Gospel and contend that the Son himself spoke wrongly concerning himself. For he himself gave this rule of faith; he himself imposed both names upon himself.

To the blind man whom he had healed he says: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” (John 9:35). But that this Son of God is also the Son of man, he says elsewhere: “When the Son of man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke 18:8), and many other passages.

Are we then to believe that Christ himself divided himself, since he graciously confessed himself both the Son of God and the Son of man?

## IX

You also slander Leo as though he had said that some man was born from Mary, in whom the Word dwelt, on the basis of the testimony in which he says: “For each nature cooperates with the communion of the other in what is proper to it” (no. 4).

You will demonstrate that he never said “some man.” But that the Word dwelt in his flesh—that is, in the man whom he himself became—hear John saying: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), that is, in the flesh of our nature.

For he could have said “he dwelt with us” if he had wished to indicate his presence among human beings rather than his dwelling in his own flesh, which is from us. But because he became a man of our nature and inhabited a body of our nature, he is said to have dwelt in us.

The Apostle teaches us that he is now in heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father—in the very one who assumed a true body of our nature. For he says: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places, in Christ” (Eph. 2:6).

Where, then, do we sit, if we do not possess our nature there in Christ?

That Christ does not dwell as one person in another while dwelling in what properly belongs to him—that is, in his own flesh—hear the Apostle speaking of him: “In him,” he says, “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). And again: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). And again: “Destroying the hostility in his flesh” (Eph. 2:14).

We have already discussed above the proper operation of each nature, which you too are shown to confess with equal agreement. For you say:

“We confess and believe the Son of man from the seed of Abraham and David, an infant and a child, a Bethlehemite and from Nazareth, and whatever else belongs to his voluntary poverty.”

For what is his poverty except the weakness of our nature? When the Apostle says, “Although he was rich, he became poor” (2 Cor. 8:9), what else does this mean except that, although he was God, he became man?

Thus, without compromising the proper character of either nature, the one and same person is Christ. You yourself also confess this when you say: “We confess and believe the divine operations and the sufferings of the flesh.” For, by specifically ascribing the sufferings to the flesh, you plainly demonstrated the proper character of human nature.

## X

Let us examine also the other matters you criticize. You say to Leo:

“By this and that, do you divide the one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, into God and man: calling him God insofar as all things were made through him, but man insofar as he was made from a woman?”

If it is not permissible to say of Christ “by this and that”—that is, either according to divinity or according to flesh—how does the Apostle speak of him: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3)?

Yet how do you say in what follows: “Christ is divided in no respect, neither according to the incarnation, nor according to his co-eternal nature, nor according to voluntary sufferings, nor according to ineffable glory”?

If “by this and that” sounds to you like division, behold, you have divided Christ into four portions, although you said that he is indivisible as he truly is. Therefore, since you have dared to presume to do the same thing, you ought not to criticize it in another. It is foolishness to attempt to refute what you are equally shown not to deny.

## XI

Nor do I understand how you wished to criticize the following statement, which the same blessed Leo asserted:

“The birth of the flesh is a manifestation of human nature; the Virgin’s childbirth is an indication of divine power. The infancy of the child is displayed by the humility of the swaddling clothes; the greatness of the Most High is declared by the voices of angels. He is like human beginnings, whom Herod wickedly plots to kill; yet he is Lord of all, whom the Magi rejoice to worship in supplication” (no. 4).

According to the perversity of your understanding, you assert that in these words Leo wished to show two Christs, although the very one whom he said was an infant, wrapped in the humility of swaddling clothes as a manifestation of human nature, he likewise asserted to be the one declared by the voices of angels as an indication of divine nature.

If he had said, “One lay in swaddling clothes, another was proclaimed by the angels; Herod sought to kill one, while the Magi eagerly desired to worship another in supplication,” you would have had better grounds for charging him with erroneous doctrine.

But since he calls the one wrapped in swaddling clothes the same one whom thousands of angels proclaim, and the one attacked by Herod’s plots the same one whom the Magi’s watchful inquiry sought through the stars, why do you try to turn into the error of division what was said of one Christ to demonstrate both natures?

Why do you criticize what you yourself are shown to confess? For you address Leo in these culpable terms:

“Why,” you ask, “do you not confess that the true God was born an infant for our sake, while remaining likewise God, and that he assumed the wrappings of flesh of our nature for our sake? Thus he became like us in every respect without sin.”

Behold: what you everywhere accuse, everywhere reproach, and consider impious and sacrilegious, you are compelled to confess under the weight of truth. For if he assumed the wrappings of our nature, he certainly possessed the reality of our nature.

He could not have been nourished in God by the wrappings of cloth and the nourishment of his mother’s milk unless what belonged properly to our nature had been in him. Nor could he in any respect have become like us if he had not graciously received into himself what we ourselves are.

## XII

You nevertheless unwillingly confess what belongs to us—indeed, what belongs to the truth—when you say:

“Our nature, honored, glories as it sees him who is of one substance with the Father according to divinity, and of one substance with us according to the ineffable incarnation from the Virgin, sitting at the right hand of the majesty of his Father.”

For the weakness of our nature glories, since his divine flesh sits above every splendor of glory, shining with riches and ineffable light.

You have confessed that, through the riches of his divinity, the weakness of our nature has been glorified. You assert that the cause of this glorification is that this same nature, through union with the Word, glories in sitting at the right hand of God.

If these statements are understood simply, they are rightly and catholically expressed. You also said that, just as the Son is of one substance with the Father according to divinity, so he is of one substance with us according to the incarnation.

In this profession, to deal with you straightforwardly, you confess a twofold nature in Christ. For if, according to divinity, he is of one substance with the Father, and again, according to the incarnation, he is of one nature with us, then he is plainly of a twofold nature. But if I press you more closely and examine more rigorously what you think, you will see how many absurdities follow you.

## XIII

You said that Christ has unity of substance with the Father and likewise with us, yet you wish him to have one nature. Therefore there will be one nature both of God and of us. And what could be more impious than this profession?

Furthermore, according to both the authority of our Fathers and the common judgment of all wise people, communion in the same substance belongs not to one but to two. Thus you introduce two Christs: one who, according to divinity, is of one substance with the Father, and another who, according to the flesh, has unity of nature with us.

Since, as I said, our substance and the Father’s are not one, while you do not wish Christ to have a twofold nature, it will necessarily follow, according to you, that there is one Christ who has unity of substance with the Father and another who has it with us.

For if one person does not possess both, although there are two, and yet you have said that both are possessed, there must here be two persons, each possessing one. In this way, you rather introduce a quaternity into the Church, since you refuse to confess both natures in the one Christ.

Let me repeat the matter more fully, if I can. When the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea professed that the Father and the Son are of one substance, they most reverently taught that two persons are to be understood in the unity of one nature.

Therefore, when you say that the Word and the flesh are of one substance, you introduce two persons of Christ and two Christs. For, according to the authority of our Fathers—which established that unity of substance can be understood or spoken of only between two persons—reason requires that, if the Word and the flesh are of one substance according to your impious opinion, there must plainly be two persons, of the Word and of the flesh, sharing one nature.

## XIV

Next it will be necessary that the flesh also, like the Word, if it has the same nature as the Word, be uncreated, [Col. 0126B] invisible, intangible, and without beginning; for otherwise it cannot possess unity of nature with the Word. But since there is no doubt that the flesh is subject to these conditions, and since it is, as you say, of the same nature as the Word, then, according to the Arians, the Word will be creatable, tangible, visible, and existing from a beginning, because otherwise it could not possess unity of nature with the flesh.

Furthermore, if the Word and the flesh have one nature, how is it that, since the Word is everywhere, the flesh is not also found everywhere? For when he was on earth, he was certainly not in heaven. And now, because he is in heaven, he is certainly not on earth—and so far is he not there that, according to the flesh, we expect Christ himself to come from heaven, while according to the Word we believe him to be with us on earth [Col. 0126C]. Therefore, according to you, either the Word is confined to a place together with his flesh, or the flesh is everywhere together with the Word, since one nature does not admit within itself anything contrary or different.

But being confined to a place and being everywhere are different and utterly dissimilar things. Since the Word is everywhere, whereas his flesh is not everywhere, it is evident that one and the same Christ belongs to both natures: he is everywhere according to the nature of his divinity, and confined to a place according to the nature of his humanity; he is created and without beginning; he succumbs to death and cannot die. Of these, one belongs to him from the nature of the Word, by which he is God; the other from the nature of the flesh, by which the same one is God and man.

Therefore the one Son of God, who is also made the Son of man, has a beginning according to the nature of his flesh and has no [Col. 0126D] beginning according to the nature of his divinity; he is created according to the nature of his flesh and is not created according to the nature of his divinity; he is circumscribed by place according to the nature of his flesh and is not contained by place according to the nature of his divinity; he is lower than the angels according to the nature of his flesh and equal to the Father according to the nature of his divinity; he died according to the nature of his flesh and did not die according to the nature of his divinity.

## XV

This is the catholic faith and confession which the apostles handed down, the martyrs strengthened, and the faithful preserve to this day. How then, most impiously, and infected with the poison of the Eutychian heresy, do you dare to criticize Leo, when from the diversity of the actions of the one Lord Christ he teaches the truth of both his natures [Col. 0127A], and when you slander as a confession of two persons what he put forward to demonstrate both natures?

In the end, these are his words:

> “The birth of the flesh is the manifestation of human nature; the Virgin’s delivery is an indication of divine power” (No. 4).

And again:

> “For each nature performs, in communion with the other, what is proper to it: the Word, namely, performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh” (No. 4).

And again:

> “Although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and man, nevertheless there is one source of the common dishonor and another source of the common glory” (No. 4).

You attack these words with perverse interpretations in this manner:

> “Who,” you ask, “would dare to make one thing belonging to God and another belonging to man correspond to one [Col. 0127B] person, when two proposed articles and meanings are expressed under two different names? For in one person, one thing and another thing are never said collectively.”

Thus you plainly recalled one God the Word and another man who suffered dishonor, when you said: “There is one source of the common dishonor and another source of the common glory.” For no one understands, in one man, a communion of suffering flesh, although according to nature flesh is man.

How is one to believe or suppose that he meant one Word glorified and another man suffering dishonor, when in what follows he says:

> “The one whom the devil’s cunning tempts as man is served by angelic ministries as God” (No. 4)?

Did he say: “The devil’s cunning tempts one, and angelic ministries serve another as God”? And again:

> “The impassible God did not disdain to be a passible man.”

And again:

> “For the one who is true God is also true [Col. 0127C] man” (No. 4).

Did he say: “One is the impassible God and another is the passible man”; or, “One is true God and another is true man”? Rather, he says: “The one who is true God is also true man.”

Since this is so, you engage in a dishonorable practice and cunningly lie in wait for religious statements, removing what precedes and failing to add what follows, so that you select the middle passages and, stripping the words of their meaning, play with their nakedness at your pleasure. Restore everything, therefore, to its proper place, and return their proper clothing to the statements. Do not attach slanders through deceitful ambushes, so as to refer to a duality of persons what was said to demonstrate both natures.

## XVI

But because he said that in the one Christ one thing belongs properly to the Word and another to the flesh, yet in such a way that both are [Col. 0127D] common—that is, that death, which properly belongs to the flesh, pertains to the Word, and life, which properly belongs to the Word, pertains to the flesh—since Christ, subsisting from both, is one in both, you thought it appropriate to object that in one person one thing and another thing cannot be said collectively.

“For no one,” you say, “in one man accepts a communion of suffering flesh, although according to nature flesh is man.”

Let us inquire who agrees in this with the apostolic understanding: you or Leo, who follows the apostolic words just as he follows the rule of faith. The Apostle says to the Romans:

> “Just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function” (Rom. XII, 4).

Explaining this more fully to the Corinthians, he says:

> “For the [Col. 0128A] body is not one member but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If it were all hearing, where would the sense of smell be?” (I Cor. XII, 14).

And below:

> “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me’” (ibid. 21).

Here the Apostle says that in one man, in one person, there are different functions, greatly differing from one another; yet they are separated and proper to each member in such a way that they are nevertheless held in common with the other member. For because seeing with the eyes and hearing with the ears are different, it does [Col. 0128B] not follow that both do not belong to one man; nor, because walking belongs differently to the head and to the feet, does it follow that the activity is not common.

Therefore, just as the head and feet have different functions in one man, yet the man is one, and there is not one man in the head and another in the feet, so the functions of the Word and the flesh in Christ are different; yet there is not one in the Word and another in the flesh, but from both, and in both, Christ is one and the same.

## XVII

To die and not to die are certainly very different things, yet we ourselves are the ones who die, and we ourselves are the ones who cannot die. For the Savior says to his disciples:

> “Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you” (Matt. XXIV, 9).

But observe what he says again elsewhere:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 28).

He thus shows that in each of us there is one mortal and [Col. 0128C] another immortal thing. The flesh in us dies, but the soul does not die; hence in the Creed we confess the resurrection of the flesh, not of the soul, which we are commanded to believe immortal.

Therefore, because the Savior divided these two things in one man and assigned to each its own quality, he should not for that reason be thought to have divided one man into two men. Just as there is one man who dies in one respect and does not die in another, so there is one Christ who died in the flesh and did not die according to the Word. According to the nature that was mortal in him, he could die; according to that which could not die in him, he remained always immortal.

Therefore you who confess that he had or has only one nature, show us how the same one could die and how the same [Col. 0128D] one could not die. For one nature cannot both die and not die in the same respect. If it is immortal, then precisely because it is immortal it does not die; and if it is mortal, then by that same condition of mortality it dies. Both cannot exist in one nature.

Since Christ possessed both, he was plainly of both natures, from which both are found in him. But if he did not possess both—that is, both life and death in himself—but only life or only death, since the nature of death is one and the nature of life another, and since you say that Christ has one nature, then state more clearly which of these two natures was the one nature in him.

If it was the nature of life, that is, of the Word—for the Word is life—then the Word, that is, life, died in itself. [Col. 0129A] But since the Word, that is, life, cannot die, while Christ did die, nothing remains according to you except that Christ either did not die at all, possessing only the nature of the Word, that is, of life, which could not die; or, if he truly died, as cannot be denied, that he possessed only the nature of death, that is, of the flesh, which could die.

Recognize, therefore, wretched men, how great a perfidy and impiety it is to confess one nature in Christ: by this confession you are forced either to believe that he did not die or to form a false opinion about him, since you do not confess that he could die in the nature in which he was able to die.

## XVIII

Or perhaps this nature of yours was so formed and compacted from the Word and the flesh that, subsisting from both, it lost both in [Col. 0129B] both, and was neither one nor the other from both; that is, so that the Word retained neither its own nature, through its mingling with human flesh, nor the flesh the property of its own nature, through its mingling with the divine nature; and thus Christ was neither man nor God, deprived of both between the two. Consider, I ask, how great a sacrilege such a thought entails. For this is what the profession of one nature compels one to understand.

But if, as you yourselves also confess, the Word became flesh in such a way that it was nevertheless not changed or transformed into flesh, retaining and not losing the property of its nature in the communion with its flesh, which he brought about in a wondrous and ineffable manner in his mother’s womb; and if, in turn, his flesh did not lose or surrender the property of its nature and kind in its communion with the divine Word—who would not see that this union of the [Col. 0129C] Word and flesh advanced not toward the abolition of either nature but toward the union of a single person?

For since you also say—as indeed must truly be said—that he is perfect God and perfect man, the same true God and true man, from where will he be perfect and true in both unless through the truth and property of both natures?

But lest we seem to slander you by saying that you believe as perhaps you do not believe, let us set out your own words; if you possess any sense of shame, you ought not resist them. For in the book which you composed against the Council of Chalcedon with futile labor, this is expressly written:

> “For the Savior who was born from Mary, incarnate without change, while he was God became man, and was called the Son of man—the God the Word who existed before the ages—[Col. 0129D] remaining unchangeable in the nature of God. Therefore the one Son of God must rightly and devoutly be confessed in one person. For, separated from God the Word, the nature of the flesh does not subsist in the Virgin; and God the Word was united to the flesh in such an ineffable manner that, incarnate and having immutably become flesh, he truly and without confusion became perfect man. Therefore we confess him at once man and God: man, because there is from us a true incarnation; God, the same one, because his nature from God the Father remained unchangeable even after the incarnation.”

## XIX

You say that the Word was incarnate and made man without change; you say that the Word was united to the flesh; you say that he was made man without confusion; you say that the same one is both man and God: man [Col. 0130A] because there is from us a true incarnation, and the same one God because his nature from God the Father remained unchangeable even after the incarnation.

Who is so foolish and dull-witted as ever to fight against his own words? Who is so senseless as to slip so far that he accuses his own faith by the very defense with which he claims to vindicate it?

You say that there is one nature in Christ, and behold how many words by which you destroy that very assertion! For to confess that the Word was immutably made man and united to the flesh without confusion most plainly destroys the profession of one nature, since union ordinarily involves not one but two things, and since this very union, without change or confusion, indicates the integrity and property of both natures.

Likewise, when you say that the same one is both man and God, what else do you show except two things in one? No one properly says “at once” of any single thing.

Again, when you say that the Word is man because of his true incarnation from us, and that he is true God because of the unchangeable divine [Col. 0130B] nature from the Father even after the incarnation, you plainly confess that the two complete, unchanged, and unconfused natures of the Word and the flesh exist.

For if the nature of the Word was neither changed nor confused in the flesh, and again the nature of the flesh was neither changed nor confused in the Word, but each retains intact and incorrupt the property of its truth, the two cannot be called one. If they are called one, it immediately follows that they have suffered corruption of themselves and have been changed into something so one that both cannot exist.

Since you rightly flee this, because it is impious and detestable, why do you fall into it by one word, when you condemn it with many words? Why do you destroy by this one unspeakable profession the pious [Col. 0130C] and catholic understanding that you hold concerning the unchangeableness of the Word and the reality of his flesh?

Believe yourselves, therefore, and confess with the orthodox in the same profession that God the Word was united to his flesh in the Virgin’s womb and became flesh in such a way that he himself is one in both, possessing both in himself: the nature of the Word, by which he is God, and the nature of the flesh, by which the same one is God and man.

Otherwise what you believe with us cannot stand: that he was made what he was not without losing what he was. What he was and what he was not do not belong to one nature. Therefore the Son of God possesses both natures, without losing either. For just as the Son of God cannot be called such except from the truth of the nature of the Word, which he has from God the Father, so the same one cannot be called the Son of [Col. 0130D] man except from the truth of the nature of the flesh, which he has from his human mother.

## XX

What the great variety of your profession means—so that what you build with one hand you again destroy with the other—I do not understand, unless you evade the truth of religion with the disguises of lies, carrying one thing on your lips and another in your heart.

For you had just confessed that the Word of God was unchangeable, and now you wish to assert that it was changed by some sort of transformation. Thus you said of him:

> “Desiring to free the human race, as the creator of his own formation, the Word of God reshaped himself, incarnate from our substance.”

Who would fail to perceive the hidden deceit of so unspeakable an opinion—or rather, its openly displayed deceit? Did the Word of God then reshape himself, and not [Col. 0131A] create flesh for himself in his mother’s womb, to which he united himself in an ineffable manner, in accordance with Solomon’s words:

> “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1),

a house which could be destroyed by death, as he himself says in the Gospel:

> “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19).

The Evangelist adds: “He was speaking about the temple of his body.”

If, therefore, he reshaped himself, he had previously been shaped, not begotten. But we confess that the Son of God, before the ages, was begotten from the Father, not shaped. If, as you assert, he reshaped himself in the Virgin’s womb in the last times, then he was shaped, as I said—that is, made or created—not begotten.

Thus, according to this impious understanding, the Arian doctrine prevails, asserting that the Son of God is a created thing.

Furthermore, if he reshaped himself, then he destroyed himself—that is, what he previously was—and reshaped himself into what he [Col. 0131B] had not previously been. For reshaping cannot be understood without the destruction of the earlier form.

And hear Jeremiah:

> “The Lord said to me: ‘Go down to the potter’s house, and there you shall hear my words.’ And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making his work upon the wheel; and the vessel which he was making was spoiled in his hands. Then he turned and reshaped it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his eyes” (Jer. XVIII, 2).

You see, therefore, that the reshaping of the later work demonstrates the destruction of the earlier one. Thus the Word of God could not reshape himself in his mother’s womb without the abolition and destruction of his prior state.

But let us grant what the nature of this proposition does not permit: that he reshaped himself without abolishing himself. Then he is found to have taken nothing from the Virgin. And what was he seeking there to reshape, if he could receive nothing [Col. 0131C] from her?

But if he received something—for the Apostle says, “taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7)—then without doubt he formed by union with himself that which he was not.

The Father also speaks to him through Isaiah:

> “I formed you and gave you as a covenant to the nations” (Isa. XLIX, 8),

and he himself testifies in the same prophet in a corresponding voice:

> “And now the Lord says, he who forms me from the womb as a servant for himself” (ibid., verse 5).

Therefore, with astonishing shamelessness and the detestable error of depravity, you dare to assert that the Word of God was reshaped, although nowhere can you demonstrate this written in the divine Scriptures.

## XXI

Since it would be lengthy, if I wished to confine this impious understanding of yours with more subtle questions and to show how many unspeakable and absurd consequences follow from it, let us now examine what you [Col. 0131D] plainly said in the Arian sense: that nothing greater or lesser can be understood in Christ. By your customary cunning argumentation you wish to remove from him the human nature through which he can be found inferior.

These, in the end, are your words:

> “That nothing great and nothing least can be understood in Christ, even if he condescended to our measures through his will, is also shown by the divine deliberation of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, which contains the confession that we are to believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, whom they recognize as incarnate and of one substance with the Father; not dividing in Christ a humanity that is lesser and again a divinity equal to the Father.”

Would that you alone were known to err in this matter, and that you did not also, with sacrilegious presumption, call the [Col. 0132A] Fathers into the same charge of error!

For the Council of Nicaea said that the Lord Jesus Christ was of one substance with God the Father according to the fact that he was begotten from God the Father before the ages, because the Arians refuse to confess him according to this as being of one nature with the Father.

Of what nature, then, do you think they meant or mean when they say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was born, he was not”? Without doubt, they were speaking of the nature of the Word.
