Accordingly, concerning that nature they received the answer that he always existed, had no beginning, and did not come from nothing. For the Arians did not assert that Christ’s flesh was made from nothing; they certainly knew that it had been produced from the Virgin.

Finally, after the most religious Fathers had sufficiently discussed this divine nature of the Son of God, they subsequently also mentioned the nature of his [Col. 0132B] flesh, saying that he descended and became incarnate.

Therefore, as you wished to accuse them, they did not place the words in an inverted order by saying first that he was incarnate and afterward that he was of one substance with the Father. Rather, they first placed the expression “of one substance,” which pertains to the nature of the Word concerning which the controversy was being conducted, and afterward said “incarnate,” which pertains to the nature of his flesh, concerning which nothing had been mutilated.

Thus, because they preserved the time, order, and distinction between the *ousia* and the incarnation—calling the *ousia* coeternal with the Father but the incarnation something made in time—they clearly confessed two natures in one and the same Son of God: one by which he was begotten from the Father before the ages, and another by which he was made from a woman at the end of the [Col. 0132C] ages.

One by which he is coeternal with the Father, and another in which he is found later than the Father in time. One which shows him equal to the Father, and another which teaches that he is less than the Father.

Since this is so, by what authority do you dare to assert that nothing greater or lesser can be found in Christ, when he himself says:

> “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28);

and:

> “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30)?

And when the evangelist Luke reports concerning him:

> “The child grew and became strong” (Luke I, 80)?

You see these statements as contrary to the profession of one nature, because one nature—and especially the divine nature—cannot undergo loss and increase or be called greater and lesser at the same time.

With open shamelessness you have chosen to lie about Christ against the faith of the Scriptures rather than to confess catholically that he possesses two natures, through which the same [Col. 0132D] one cannot be denied to be both great and lesser.

## XXII

[Col. 0132D] I also wish to examine that passage in which the insanity of your entire unbridled fury has burst forth, as you strive to assert that the Word of God, through the nature of his divinity and not through the nature of his incarnation, deigned to make himself tangible and visible.

These are your words:

> “That he who was the Word in the beginning, who was announced through the prophets, became flesh, was seen upon earth, and lived among human beings, becoming visible and tangible, is eternal life and God by nature—this is attested by blessed John, who says: ‘What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we observed, and our hands touched [Col. 0133A] concerning the Word of life’” (I John I).

As far as I have been able to understand these words, you seem to wish to establish that the nature of the Trinity, since it is the nature of the Word, which always remains invisible and intangible, made the Word of God visible and tangible in itself, and not in the nature of the flesh which he united to himself in his mother’s womb.

If this is so, what could be more impious or sacrilegious than this profession? We who detest an error of such perfidy and presumption must therefore treat the words of the Apostle John—which you wickedly abuse in support of your depravity—in the Apostle’s own sense. First we must constrain and press your ignorance to answer this: if the Son of God was seen and touched in the nature of his divinity, why are only the apostles to be believed to have seen and touched him, when the soldiers who crucified him likewise [Col. 0133B] touched and saw him?

And through this they could also have seen the Father, because he himself says:

> “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

What could be more impious than this profession?

Furthermore, why was it necessary for the Apostle to say, “What we have seen we announce,” when all who were present at that time and believed in him had likewise seen him?

Since it is absurd and full of vanity to think in this way, let us understand spiritually the Apostle’s spiritual words, by which he testifies that he saw and touched the Word of God not with bodily eyes and hands but with the members of the inner man.

For with the very eyes, ears, and hands of the inner person by which his fragrance is drawn in through the nostrils and his sweetness is tasted with the mouth, he is touched.

Thus the Church says to him:

> “Your name is poured-out [Col. 0133C] perfume” (Song I, 2);

and:

> “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I, 3).

And Paul says:

> “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Cor. II, 15).

And David:

> “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

To believe in the Son of God, therefore, is to see him, to hear him, to smell him, to taste him, and to touch him.

In touch, moreover, the firmness of faith is signified, and this sense is trusted more than the other senses. For the eyes are often deceived by appearances, and the ears by falsehood.

With this sense, therefore, the Apostle had touched him—he had believed in him with such profound firmness that he could never afterward doubt him. Hence he says:

> “What we have seen with our eyes, and what our hands have touched” (I John I, 1).

Certainly even unbelievers saw and touched the Son of [Col. 0133D] God through the nature of his flesh; but the apostles alone recognized the nature of his divinity.

## XXIII

To make you understand that the Apostle John used “touch” and “vision” for the belief of the mind, [Col. 0134A] hear what he says later:

> “Little children, it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).

Certainly he had touched him; certainly he had seen him. Why, then, does he desire to see him as a great gift of blessedness, and place the whole reward of his labor in seeing him?

For he does not say, “We have seen him,” but, “We shall see him as he is”; nor does he say, “He appeared,” but, “When he appears.” This is because the Son did not appear as he is, but as he was made; and therefore in this world he was not seen as he is, but as he was made, while in the future he will be seen as he is.

Thus the Apostle says that he saw, through believing and not through physical sight, what existed from the beginning. He saw through the mirror of faith in an enigma, and he will see more clearly when the veil has been removed.

Concerning this manifestation of vision, which is reserved for the faithful, the Lord himself said in the Gospel:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will reveal myself [Col. 0134B] to him” (John XIV, 21).

If the apostles saw him, how could he promise that he would reveal himself to them in the future as a reward for their love, unless they both saw and did not see him? They saw him as he was made, and did not see him as he is. Yet they believed him as he is, and therefore they saw him as he is.

The manifestation of vision is the reward of faith.

But if you obstinately wish to resist this interpretation, asserting that the Word was touched by the apostles’ hands in his own nature, give us the complete continuity of the words according to this understanding. For the Apostle does not say, “Our hands touched the Word of life,” but says, “Our hands touched something concerning the Word of life” (I John I, 1).

Therefore they did not touch the Word itself, but something concerning the Word; and this is manifestly found to refer not to visible bodily touch but to the touch of the [Col. 0134C] mind.

Furthermore, were the apostles establishing the whole authority of the faith on this—that we should believe that they touched the Word of God with visible hands? The doubtful disciple who wished to test the Lord by such an experiment was rebuked for this. Or how can we share this grace with them, since we are unable to touch Christ as they touched him?

“What we have seen and heard,” he says, “we announce to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us” (I John I, 3).

Our fellowship with them will therefore consist in this: that we believe, as they did, in the Son of God, whom they understood through the faith of the heart according to his divinity and saw with bodily eyes according to his humanity.

And since, as I think, we have met with an adequate response [Col. 0134D] all the points which you raised against Leo’s letter, and have dispelled the clouds of empty questions with the radiant light of truth, let us now examine those things which you uttered against the Council of Chalcedon in insulting language. We shall begin their refutation from another starting point.

# BOOK FIVE  
## DEFENSE OF THE DECREE OF THE SYNOD OF CHALCEDON

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133D]

## I

The blessed Apostle Paul knew that the profane and harmful tenets of deadly doctrine can be shaded by the appearance of truth, and that the poison of a serpent’s attack can be concealed beneath the clever surface of words [Col. 0134D]. He also knew that a poisonous drink covered or mixed with the sweetness of honey is not easily perceived and distinguished at the first taste by one who merely sips it.

Therefore he gave us a great and singular means of investigating fraud, so that the soundness of a teacher’s doctrine might be tested from the quality of his character. In order that we might be able, with the easy and ready attention of discernment, to detect the tricks of criminal doctrine, he portrayed for us the vices of its authors as actions produced by disgraceful and unworthy desires. He says:

> “In the last times perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, blasphemous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, faithless, without affection, slanderers, not keeping peace” (II Tim. III, 1),

and so forth.

It is therefore not doubtful that disobedience to parents and attacking them with false arrows of accusation proceed from the impiety of heretical depravity [Col. 0135B]. For in this way the apostolic statement marked such people as treacherous and faithless: they are not only disobedient to their parents but also their most bitter accusers.

Since this is so, it will certainly be doubtful to no one that those who reject and despise the decrees of the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon are heretics, and that those who audaciously resist the religious constitutions of so many Fathers have departed from the catholic faith when, with sacrilegious speech, they accuse them of doing so.

## II

First, they accuse those persons now expelled from the council and afterward received again after an interval of time. As though it were not Christian and apostolic that someone who had perhaps been expelled from the council because of the fault of contentiousness should afterward be received again for the sake of peace and concord.

By this reasoning they could also accuse the Apostle Paul because, after rejecting John, who was called Mark, from his company—so that he would not even yield to Barnabas’ request and accept him again as his associate in the ministry of the word, on account of which such contention arose between two great and excellent men that they separated from one another—Paul afterward received the same Mark whom he had previously rejected, writing to Timothy:

> “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry” (II Tim. IV, 11).

Thus those Fathers whom they had perhaps earlier expelled from the council on account of some offense—for Solomon says, “Expel the contentious man from the council, and his contention goes with him” (Prov. XXII, 10)—received them again, now made more correct, in the grace of peace.

That is, if the matter is as these men assert with their insolent arrogance, or if it is even true.

Furthermore, they accuse the Council of Chalcedon of having decreed something new, different from what had been established by the Council of Nicaea. They do not know the rule and custom of catholic councils: later councils decree new matters as the necessity arising from new heretics demands, while the decisions previously promulgated by older councils against earlier heretics remain inviolable.

For if, after the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, it were permitted to receive nothing further, by what authority would we dare to assert that the Holy Spirit is of one substance with the Father, when it is entirely clear that this had been left unmentioned there?

Although in the books which we composed against Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius under the name of Athanasius—as though those who were present were dealing with those who were present, and in which even the person of a judge seems to have been introduced—we fully expressed our position concerning the various decrees of councils and the religious addition of new terms, nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, we shall now insert a very few points. From them it will become clear that these men are exceedingly ignorant and rash, since they do not know that, after the Council of Nicaea, bishops assembled in various places and issued many doctrinal constitutions against the insane outbreaks of new heretics.

## III

First, at Alexandria Athanasius, Eusebius, Lucifer through a legate, and several others who had recently been recalled from exile assembled. Although they were few in number, they were great in merit, and they composed a full rule of confession against Macedonius concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, demonstrating that he is of the same substance as the Father and the Son.

Macedonius relied against them, as these men do, on the authority of the Council of Nicaea, asserting that they had departed from the opinions of the Fathers by decreeing something new and, as he called it, impious concerning the Holy Spirit—something which, it is clear, had not been handed down there.

Apollinaris also employs this precedent of impiety against the Church in his wicked interpretation of the incarnate Word.

Finally, against the sacrilegious unity of the impious confession which had been composed at Sirmium by Hosius, Valens, Ursacius, Germinius, and others of similar depravity, all the bishops of the East assembled and issued other definitions—that is, twelve statements—which are not contained in the Council of Nicaea.

Likewise, at Sardica the bishops of all the provinces of the East assembled: Thebaid, Palestine, Phoenicia, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Arabia, Syria, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Paphlagonia, Galatia, Bithynia, the Hellespont, Asia, the two Phrygias, Pisidia; the Cycladic islands, Pamphylia, Caria, Lydia; and in Europe, Thrace, Haemimontus, Moesia, and the two Pannonias.

“We have set forth this faith,” they say.

In it they are found to have added seven chapters of definitions to the Nicene exposition—definitions directed against those for whom the council had been assembled and which they denied.

But who would be sufficient to comprehend the numerous doctrinal decrees of that catholic council assembled from the whole East at Sirmium against Photinus? Because no necessity of such a matter had arisen at the Council of Nicaea, those decrees had not been established there at all. Yet no believer dares reject them or hesitates to receive them, unless he wishes to be subject to the sentence of their anathema together with Photinus.

## IV

But now let us see what questions these men raise concerning the two natures, although they assert that the ancient teachers of the Church nowhere mentioned them, but that they were invented as a new doctrine by the bishops Diodore, Theodore, and Leo, through which the error of both Judaism and paganism was introduced, since it urges us to confess that something in Christ was created and made. O ignorant men, wholly unacquainted with every mystery of truth! Do the ancient Fathers nowhere, then, mention two natures in Christ?

Read, wretched men, what Athanasius, Hilary, John, and Ambrose, confessors of the faith, say about the two natures; what Theophilus, Gregory, Basil, Cyril, and Augustine teach. And finally cease from the error of Apollinaris and Eutyches, following those eminent and illustrious men, approved by the judgment of the whole world in the Catholic faith. When appropriate, we shall have to append their opinions.

Now it must be demonstrated by divine testimonies both that Christ was created according to the truth of his human nature, and that the same Christ was uncreated according to the particular character of his divine nature. But let us hasten to show one point which these men deny.

Peter therefore says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> Let the whole house of Israel know with certainty that God made both that Jesus whom you crucified Lord and Christ. (Acts 2:36)

Likewise Paul says to the Romans:

> Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh. (Romans 1:3)

And to the Galatians:

> But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman. (Galatians 4:4)

And to the Hebrews:

> Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him who made him. (Hebrews 3:1)

And there:

> Having been made so much better than the angels, as he has received a more excellent name than they. (Hebrews 1:4)

And the Son himself, through Isaiah:

> And now, says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as his servant. (Isaiah 49:5)

Through Solomon also he testifies in this way that he was created:

> The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways. (Proverbs 8:22)

He spoke this beforehand in anticipation of the human nature which he was to assume in the fullness of time.

Since it is therefore clear that Christ was created or made according to that by which he deigned to become human, either concede this to his human nature, or, if you do not wish to concede it, you will assert that the nature of his divinity was created. Thus you will be convicted, together with the Arians or with the pagans, of venerating and worshiping a creature.

## V

Likewise, in order to destroy the confession of both natures, they boast of this supposedly unavoidable syllogism: that there is no nature which does not have its own person, nor again any person which does not have its own nature.

They intend this because, since we confess that Christ has two natures, and each nature, according to them, plainly has its own person, it must follow, in accordance with the confession of two natures, that Christ has two persons.

Yet these men have not taken care to teach by any examples that each nature has its own person. They merely raised the question and then passed on, both to obscure the truth and to evade the danger of argument by silence. But observe, I beg you, how, while they weave snares, they themselves fall into inextricable knots of questions.

Let them answer the Arians: if each nature has its own person, and each person has its own nature, why are there not three natures in the Trinity, just as three persons are demonstrated to exist? Or, if there are three persons and one nature, then what they say—that each person has its own nature—is false.

Indeed, it is so false that, although in a human being the nature of the soul is one thing and that of the body another, there is nevertheless one and the same person of the human being.

For this reason I consider it necessary to extend the discussion here somewhat more broadly and not to employ excessive brevity, lest the matters requiring explanation be concealed by the very narrowness of brevity.

## VI

In the preceding books, as I think sufficiently, while disputing about the two natures of Christ, we showed how Nestorius and Eutyches, misusing the straight lines of the Catholic confession, had covered the entire East with the thickest darkness of error in service of their impious doctrine.

But because in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of the Word and the flesh, and two natures, they have attempted to introduce, through matters that cannot be denied, things that must be denied.

For Nestorius, taking occasion from the confession of two natures, attempted to demonstrate two persons in Christ. Eutyches, relying on the support of one person, deliriously declared that the nature of the Word and the flesh was one and the same.

Thus each of them drew the truth of the religious confession into the impiety of his error. If they had made use of divine teaching and followed the apostles who preceded them in their doctrines, they would certainly have recognized both that there can be two natures in one person and that one person can exist in two natures.

For, as I said above, it cannot be denied that a human being consists of two natures, namely, soul and flesh. Nevertheless, no one but a fool, utterly devoid of reason, would rightly say that a human being has two persons. Nor, conversely, because the human being has one person, would anyone rightly suppose that the flesh and soul have one nature.

But that body and soul are not of one nature, the Savior taught in the Gospel when he said:

> Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. (Matthew 10:28)

What, then, is unheard-of, what is foreign and alien to the canonical Scriptures, in believing—as we believe and experience—that a human being is one, consisting of a rational soul and flesh, and likewise that Christ is one, God and human, as the apostles taught and as apostolic men have handed down to us?

## VII

And because our present argument is directed chiefly against those who, following the error of one nature, resist the decree of the Council of Chalcedon with stubborn obstinacy, I think it useful to repeat a few points concerning the human nature of the Son of God, which they deny in him in every respect, so that the hammer of truth may crush their empty little objections and glass-like opinions, and so that I may demonstrate how entirely un-Christian they are and how wholly alienated from the hope of eternal salvation.

The rule of the Catholic faith is to confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ as truly God and truly human: one being from both, not two in both; the same one born timelessly from the Father, the same one born in time from the Virgin. Thus each birth embraces one Christ in such a way that he suffers no diminution of himself in either, retaining in himself what is proper to each kind: namely, that the nature of the Word was not changed into flesh, and that the nature of the flesh was not consumed in the Word.

Hence the Lord Jesus Christ is the same true God and the same true human being, existing from two natures ineffably united in one person within the Virgin’s womb. Since these natures were not abolished in him through that wondrous union, in order to demonstrate the existence of the proper characteristics of both, he spoke and acted in himself as the reality of both: he did not divide the words, partition the affections, or separate the deeds; rather, he himself, one and the same, was in himself their meeting-point, from both and in both, speaking and accomplishing what was proper to each.

And to make what we are saying clear, let us use an example. For example: I myself am the one who distinguishes white and black colors with bodily eyes, and I myself am again the one who judges the evil of iniquity and the good of justice with the gaze of the mind. Yet I am not therefore one person and another, because both come to me from different sources.

For I do not see colors with the same eyes with which I perceive speech, and yet I am the same one who acts from both. Both belong to me: it belongs to me not to see justice except with the eyes of the mind, and it belongs to me not to see colors except with the eyes of the flesh. It belongs to me not to see a voice with my eyes, and it belongs to me not to hear light with my ears. It belongs to me not to distinguish taste with my nostrils, and it belongs to my palate not to perceive scent.

Although everything is mine within myself—that is, seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting—nevertheless one thing in me is the source of sight, another of hearing, another of tasting and distinguishing odors. And although everything within me is diverse and divided in a certain private right, I myself nevertheless cannot be divided or separated.

Thus Christ himself, one and the same, is both created and uncreated; having a beginning and without a beginning; progressing in age and understanding, yet not receiving increase in understanding or age; suffering death, yet not subject to the laws of death; receiving honors on account of merit, yet needing no honor.

Although all these things are diverse in themselves, they nevertheless belong properly to him. Therefore he does not divide within himself the words, affections, and deeds appropriate to either reality, because both that he has belong to him. But one of these is his from the nature of the Word, which, remaining God, he did not lose, and the other is his from the nature of the flesh, which, having become human, he assumed. [lacuna]

## VIII

Let us speak still more plainly, for the sake of those who, through ignorance of the meaning of the expressions, do not understand how the properties and common possession of the natures are spoken of in Christ, and therefore reject and shun all these matters.

Not having a beginning and subsisting from a beginning are different and alien things; so are dying and being unable to die. Yet, just as both are proper to Christ himself, so both are common not to him but in him.

For if we say that something is common to him, we must necessarily be required to identify and show another with whom that same thing is common to him. Such a requirement in confession leads to the impious doctrine of Nestorius.

Therefore we say, better and in Catholic fashion, that the thing is common in him, not to him. And we say, better, that what is proper is proper to him, not in him.

Thus it is proper to him to die, because of the nature of the flesh, which is mortal; and it is proper to him not to die, because of the nature of the Word, which cannot die.

Likewise, because of the ineffable mystery of the union of both natures, the mortality of the flesh was common in him to the nature of the Word, which could not die; and the immortality of the Word was common in him to the nature of the flesh, which succumbed to death.

Therefore, just as dying and not dying are proper to him from both natures, so what is proper to either nature is common in him to both natures.

To give an example: it is proper to me, through the nature of my flesh, to bear on my body the recognizable mark of any bruise caused by a blow; and it is proper to me, through the nature of my soul, not to bear that same mark in my spirit.

Likewise, it is proper to me, through the nature of my soul, to bear in my mind the wound of a word—that is, a harsh statement; and it is proper to me, through the nature of my flesh, not to bear that same wound on my body.

Although both things are proper to me, and both are alien to body and soul individually—for the body does not understand a harsh or pleasant statement, nor does the soul become bruised by the wound of a whip—both are nevertheless common in me myself, both to my soul and to my body.

For neither does the soul experience outside the body what was proper for it to feel, nor does the body bear the marks of wounds apart from the fellowship of the soul.

What, then, is proper to me in each part and alien to each part individually is common in me myself to the individual parts. What is proper to each part is nevertheless common in me to each; yet I myself am one in both, one in what they share in me, and one in what is proper to each within myself.

## IX

Since this is so, we must traverse the sequence of the divine writings and gather numerous testimonies by which it may be demonstrated how impious and sacrilegious it is to refer what is proper to the flesh of Christ to the property of the nature of the Word, and to ascribe what is proper to the Word to the property of the nature of the flesh.

It is no less impious to alienate from the Word, by an exception based on property, what is proper to the flesh, and by the same law of exception to alienate from the flesh what is proper to the Word, since both are common to them in Christ, and Christ is both.

And since the professors of one nature flatter themselves with this confession, saying:

> What impossible or inappropriate thing was it for the condescension of the Son of God, in the nature of his divinity, to endure for the redemption of our salvation whatever indignities and humiliations he might choose, by which he might arouse in us an even greater affection of love for him, suffering for us in his own nature those things which are shown to be unworthy of him?

They must be asked why the one who was going to destroy death by his own death, as the prophet had foretold when he said, “I shall be your death, O death” (Hosea 13:14)—if it was possible for him to die in his own nature—needed to be born from a Virgin.

But surely this is where his goodness is to be admired, and this is where the greatness of his loving-kindness toward us is shown: because his death was necessary for us, while he could not die in his own nature, he deigned to assume our nature, in which he could die for us, as necessity required.

## X

But let us grant them, against the faith of all Scripture and Catholic truth, that he deigned to die for us in his own nature—which is utterly impossible—and that he endured all the sufferings of human frailty.

Did his nature also need to be raised to honors and increased by advances in dignity, so that by the merit of humility, obedience, and death he might hold the summit of exalted merits and deserve to receive power over heaven and earth, as though he had not possessed it before?

Or perhaps they will deny that all these things were bestowed upon the Lord Jesus Christ on account of the merit of his passion and death. Let them read the Apostle speaking of him:

> He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. (Philippians 2:8)

And David:

> He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head. (Psalm 109:7)

“From the torrent on the way,” that is, from the river of human death; “therefore he lifted up his head,” because he tasted death.

And he himself in the Gospel:

> Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life for my sheep. (John 10:17)

What, then, do you think? Was the nature of the Word an exile, empty of the honors of greatness and glory, or did it remain in eternity with an imperfect or diminished love from the Father? And did it therefore seek to undergo such things as would make it more acceptable, more honorable, and more distinguished by greater merits?

“He exalted him,” it says, “and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Did the Word, then, until that time not possess the name that is above every name, but earn through works what it did not possess by nature?

Likewise, to the Hebrews:

> Having been made so much better than the angels, as he received a more excellent name than they. (Hebrews 1:4)

Who could plunge into so great an abyss of impiety? Who could be so blinded by the cloud of madness as to fall into the belief that Christ was made better than the angels according to the nature of his divinity?

For the divine nature cannot be conferred upon or compared with the angels, so that it might be found more excellent and better by comparison with them, since it is incomparably superior to every nature.

But when he says, “Having been made better than the angels,” the later expression “better” must be understood as referring to what was made better by comparison with what preceded. What else can this be except his human nature?

He also describes him as having received a better name, which cannot at all be referred to his divine nature. For who could be found superior or better than the nature of the Trinity, so as to give or impose upon it a name better than that of the angels? It belongs to those who are better to bestow names upon inferiors.

Who, then, does not see that these things correspond in the Son of God to the nature of his flesh, according to which he was exalted, honored, and granted the dignity of a better name—he who, according to the nature of the Word, had never needed any of these things?

## XI

Let us therefore continue to pursue all the gifts of his blessedness, acquired through the merit of his passion. From them it will become clearer than light that these things cannot suit him according to the nature by which he is God, but only according to the nature by which he became human.

The prophet Isaiah says:

> If he makes his life an offering for sin, he shall see long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand, because his soul has labored. He shall see light and be satisfied with knowledge; he shall justify the righteous one who serves many, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. Therefore he himself shall possess many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he poured out his soul unto death, was numbered with the wicked, bore the sins of many, and prayed for transgressors. (Isaiah 53:10)

See how many things the prophetic word describes him as attaining on account of the merit of his passion. “He shall see long-lived offspring,” it says; “he shall see light and be satisfied with knowledge; he shall possess many and divide the spoils of the strong.”

I think none of these things is appropriate to him according to the nature of the Word. There is no need to demonstrate this, since the evidence of the matters themselves makes it clear.

Likewise, both he himself in the Gospels and the prophets speak of his receiving in time the power of heaven and earth, the inheritance of the nations, and the subjection of all things.

Would he, then, as the creator of all things, not possess power and dominion over his creation, so that in the last times he might receive all these things as gifts?

After his resurrection he says:

> All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. (Matthew 28:18)

The Father had formerly promised this power, saying:

> Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth. (Psalm 2:8)

The prophet Isaiah testifies that this petition of the Son and the Father’s gift were fulfilled at the time of the passion, announcing in the person of the Father:

> Thus says the Lord: In an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you; I formed you and gave you as a covenant to the nations, to establish the lands and possess the deserted inheritances, and to say to those who are in chains, “Come out,” and to those who are in darkness, “Be revealed.” (Isaiah 49:8)

Likewise, the Son himself in the same prophet:

> And now the Lord says, who formed me from the womb as his servant, that I might bring Jacob back to him; and I was glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and God became my strength. And he said: It is a great thing for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and gather the dispersed of Israel. Behold, I have placed you as a covenant of the people, as a light to the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth. (Isaiah 49:5–6)

Who could be so foolish and deranged in mind as not to see and understand that being formed from the womb, deserving to be made a servant, being heard at the proper time, awaiting the Father’s help, being strengthened in the Lord, and receiving possession of the lands in time properly belong to the nature of Christ’s flesh?

## XII

Moreover, if it is not tedious, let us offer a few more passages which cannot at all be referred to the nature of his divinity.

Thus the Father speaks of him through Isaiah:

> Behold my servant; I shall receive him. My chosen one, my soul has been pleased with him. I have put my spirit upon him, to bring judgment to the nations. (Isaiah 42:1)

He himself likewise speaks of himself:

> The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to preach the gospel to the poor. (Luke 4:18)

And David says to the same one:

> Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. (Psalm 44:8)

And in the person of the Father:

> I have placed help upon a mighty one and exalted the chosen one from my people. (Psalm 88:20)

And Peter concerning him:

> A stone rejected by human beings but chosen and precious in the sight of God. (1 Peter 2:4)

Could the Son of God be called chosen from that nature by which he is God, rather than from that by which he became human? If so, the nature of divinity would be chosen, although it is one and cannot be reckoned among many.

For the Church says in the Song of Songs:

> My beloved is chosen from among many. (Song of Songs 5:10)

And the Father says:

> I have exalted the chosen one from my people. (Psalm 88:20)

Tell us, then, you professors of one nature: since the nature of God is one, how or from where is it said to be chosen? Who could be superior to it and choose it from among many?

Or perhaps it chose itself from the midst of the people. Although no one chooses himself, and although this choice is openly said to have been made by God, suppose nevertheless that it chose itself in the last times: would it then, throughout all the preceding time, have been uncertain and unknown, mingled with the confusion of the people and its companions, from whose fellowship it deserved to be chosen and anointed with the Holy Spirit?

For David says:

> He has anointed you above your companions. (Psalm 44:8)

The divine nature is therefore chosen and anointed, and has the Holy Spirit above itself.

> I have put my Spirit upon him. (Isaiah 42:1)

And the Son himself says:

> The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. (Luke 4:18)

How, then, is the Holy Spirit equal to the Son, when he is described as being above him?

Isaiah says of him:

> The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, and the Spirit of wisdom shall fill him. (Isaiah 11:2)

And Luke in the Gospel:

> The child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom. (Luke 1:80; 2:52)

Thus it is clear that the Son of God is not chosen from among many, strengthened, or filled with wisdom according to the nature of the Word.

For it is not the nature of the Word to be strengthened, since it is itself power; nor to receive increase through growth, since it is perfect in itself; nor to be filled with wisdom, since it fills all things; nor to be chosen, since it rather chooses and has nothing from which it could be chosen.

Therefore, since these things do not suit the nature of the Word in Christ, they must correspond to his flesh, according to which he is rightly called a chosen servant, rightly strengthened, rightly filled with wisdom, rightly said to have grown, and rightly said to have the Holy Spirit above himself.

## XIII

To make this still more evident, let us add a few passages.

Isaiah says of him:

> Before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, before the child knows how to call his father or mother, he shall receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria. (Isaiah 8:4)

Would we dare subject the nature of the Word to such great ignorance, when nothing past or future is hidden from it?

And again Luke says:

> Jesus progressed in age, wisdom, and grace with God and human beings. (Luke 2:52)

If the nature of the Word progressed in him, then it became changeable through progress; for whatever progresses is changed for the better.

Let us also say briefly something about the power and glory of the kingdom and the authority of judgment which he received in time, on account of the merit of his passion, according to the nature of his flesh.

Gabriel says of him in the Gospel:

> The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob, and there will be no end of his kingdom. (Luke 1:32–33)

And the Father says these words concerning him to David:

> From the fruit of your womb I shall place one upon your throne. (Psalm 131:11)

Likewise:

> I shall establish his throne forever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven. (Psalm 88:30)

> I shall make him the firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. (Psalm 88:28)

Likewise:

> For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him. (Psalm 88:22)

> I shall place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. (Psalm 88:26)

> He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. (Psalm 71:8)

And David says of him to the Father:

> You crowned him with glory and honor and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet. (Psalm 8:6)

Likewise:

> You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone. He asked for life, and you gave him length of days forever and ever. (Psalm 20:4)

In accordance with what Isaiah says:

> If he gives his soul over to death, he shall see long-lived offspring. (Isaiah 53:10)

Likewise:

> For the sake of truth, gentleness, and justice, go forth and reign. (Psalm 44:5)

And Daniel:

> To him were given dominion, honor, and kingship. (Daniel 7:14)

The reason why he received all these things is not concealed. For, demonstrating the merit of the great dignity he received, he says:

> To the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end I will give authority over the nations; he shall rule them with an iron rod, just as I also received from my Father. (Revelation 2:26–28)

Likewise:

> The one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne. (Revelation 3:21)

To this victory the entire army of heaven bears witness, saying:

> Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive glory, honor, wisdom, strength, and power. (Revelation 5:12)

These things concerning the glory and power of the kingdom, which the Son of God received in time, on account of the merit of his passion, according to the nature of his flesh, we have stated briefly, since according to the nature of the Word he needed none of them.

Now let us speak much more briefly about the authority of judgment, although the authority of the Judge is demonstrated by his sitting upon the throne of the kingdom.

## XIV

The prophet therefore speaks of him to the Father:

> O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son. (Psalm 72:1)

And he himself says:

> When I receive the appointed time, I will judge with justice. (Psalm 75:3)

And in the Gospel:

> He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man. (John 5:27)

We find no better interpreter of these sacred utterances than the Lord himself, who is able to disclose to us the causes and merit of the great honors bestowed upon him.

Let all human cleverness in argument cease, and let unskilled expertise not dare to extend itself beyond the measure of divine exposition.

Let the Son of God himself teach with the sacred mouth of his divinity why, or according to what aspect, he was raised by the Father to such great honors—he who was so made human through incarnation that, while remaining unchangeably what he was, he lost none of the things he had previously possessed.

Let him say, then, why he received in time a power which he had always possessed.

> He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man. (ibid.)

What, then, Lord Jesus Christ, will you appear to us as one and another, when we confess you to be one and the same Son of God and Son of Man? Why, then, did you not say, “He gave him authority because he is the Son of God”?

“I am one and the same,” he says, “and cannot be divided. But I wished to demonstrate according to what aspect, and from where, I received what I have always possessed.

According to the nature by which I am God the Word, I needed and received nothing, because I am the Son of God, and for this I was born. But according to the nature of the flesh, by which I, God the Word, became incarnate and human, I both needed and received, because I am the Son of Man, and for this I was born.”

## XV

Although these things are sufficient, by the strength of their firmness, to demonstrate both natures in Christ, nevertheless, so that the clarity of truth may shine forth more and more, I am pleased also to discuss the Apostle’s statement that Christ was made mediator for us (1 Timothy 2:5).

He could not fulfill this office except from the truth of the nature of the flesh, which he received from us, because through it he appeared as mediator between God and human beings.

And because, as the Apostle says and the truth of the matter teaches, “a mediator is not of one” (Galatians 3:20), while according to you Christ has one nature, show from what source he is mediator between us and that nature.

For if, as you impiously think, his nature as mediator is one, then the mystery is frustrated in that which is the one and singular remedy of our salvation. From where will he be mediator if he does not possess both?

Unless you provide such a mediator between God and human beings that he is mediator in such a way that he is both from both—that is, both God because of the divine nature and the same person human because of the human nature—you do not show how human beings are reconciled to divine beings.

For because by the transgression of the commandment we had become enemies of God and were moving in opposite directions with discordant minds, turning away from the heights and tending toward the depths, it had been necessary, through the intervention of divine mercy, for enmity to be dissolved, opposites to be brought together, and what was below to be restored to what was above.

This could not happen in any other way unless there were such a mediator who, coming from heavenly things, was united to earthly things, retaining in himself what he was and assuming what he was not.

He would become one in both, and thus, through the communion of both natures in one and the same person, he would join human things to divine and divine things to human: first uniting both in himself without abolishing either, and then reconciling all the faithful to God the Father.

And because the mystery of reconciliation required an immaculate sacrifice, an offering had to be sought which would be so placed between God and human beings that it would both succumb to death through what it possessed as human and overcome death through what it retained in itself as divine.

## XVI

Hence the Apostle says:

> For although he was crucified through our weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. (2 Corinthians 13:4)

Therefore, through this offering of his death, which came to him from us, he fulfilled the office of mediator and reconciled us to God, as the Apostle says:

> For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son. (Romans 5:10)

And again:

> Abolishing enmity in his flesh. (Ephesians 2:14)

The same Apostle testifies to the Hebrews that this flesh was of our race and our nature, saying:

> For it was fitting that he, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the author of their salvation through suffering. For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. Therefore he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” (Hebrews 2:10–12)

“The one who sanctifies,” that is, Christ; “and those who are sanctified,” that is, the faithful: all, he says, are from one. From one, he says, they have their origin as brothers.

From what one, unless from the stock of our nature? For Christ’s faithful are not brothers from both natures, but from one—that is, the human nature.

> Therefore he is not ashamed to call them brothers.

He would be ashamed to call them brothers if he had one and the same divine nature only. But now, possessing both and subsisting in both kinds of nature, he calls them brothers from one and servants from the other.

Thus it is established that the Lord Jesus Christ was made mediator through the human nature ineffably united to the Word. Consequently, whoever strives to take this nature away from him, namely, the human nature, by confessing one nature, attempts to empty the entire mystery of our faith and salvation.

The Apostle continues, saying to the Hebrews:

> For he did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham, from which he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful priest in matters pertaining to God, to make expiation for the sins of the people. For because he himself suffered when tested, he is able to help those who are being tested. (Hebrews 2:16–18)

What he says is this: Christ assumed not the nature of angels but the nature of human beings from the seed of Abraham, so that through the reality of the nature he assumed he might be made like his brothers in every respect.

Thus he became a merciful and faithful priest because he assumed not the nature of angels but that of human beings, conscious of weakness and frailty. Through it and in it he experienced the weaknesses of suffering, and in mercy and faithfulness he might plead with the Father for sinners.

> For because he himself suffered when tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.

What is that in which he suffered and experienced weakness, except the human nature, concerning which during the time of his passion he said in the Gospel:

> The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. (Matthew 26:41)

Conscious of this weakness, he learned to help the weak.

Explaining the same meaning more fully, the Apostle says:

> For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tested in every respect and in all things, according to the likeness, without sin. (Hebrews 4:15)

Likewise:

> He himself was in the same way in those very sufferings. (Hebrews 2:18)

And again:

> Although he was the Son of God, through the things he suffered he learned. (Hebrews 5:8)

Hence he also sympathizes with our weaknesses.

I ask: from where did he learn the things that he suffered? From where does he sympathize? From where was he in those very sufferings? From where, having experienced weaknesses, did he learn to help the weak? From where did he offer a remedy to God on behalf of the weak, if he did not possess the nature of our weakness? For experiencing and learning what was previously unknown is ordinarily proper to human nature, not to divine nature.

XVII. I could still examine the matter of Christ’s humanity by assembling a manifold collection of testimonies, and by no means confine so extensive a subject within narrow limits, were not the discourse hastening to dispose of—or rather refute—the remaining points that have been written with impudent audacity against the Council of Chalcedon. Let us see what these are.

From the decree of the synod:

> This holy and salutary sacrament of divine grace would indeed be sufficient for a complete acknowledgment and confirmation of piety. For it teaches most fully concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and presents the incarnation of our Lord to those who faithfully receive it. (Council of Chalcedon, act 5)

[Col. 0147B] They reproach the council in this chapter on the grounds that, after confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it allegedly introduced some unknown fourth Lord as incarnate. Everyone with sound judgment can see how great a slander—or rather, a blunder—they have committed in making this charge.

For if the council had worded the passage as these hunters of words suppose, saying, “For it teaches most fully concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and his incarnation,” it would have been uncertain which person of the Trinity was incarnate. Indeed, the incarnation might have been taken to belong to the Holy Spirit, since the name of that person would immediately precede the mention of the mystery of the incarnation. Therefore, to distinguish the person of the Son and show that the mystery of the incarnation pertains to him, they preferred to repeat his name under the designation “Lord.”

The Apostle is also found to have done this at the beginning of the Epistle to the Romans. [Col. 0147C] There, lest anyone think that he was proclaiming the resurrection of the Holy Spirit, he was compelled to repeat the name of the Lord Christ so closely. For he says:

> Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord. (Romans 1:1–4)

What could he have named the Son of God more immediately and in almost the same breath? He could have said, “by his resurrection,” without repeating “Jesus Christ our Lord”—the one whom, as I have said, he had just called the predestined Son of God. But because he had inserted the name of the Holy Spirit, lest he appear to refer the resurrection to the Spirit by saying “by his resurrection,” he chose, by naming Christ a second time, to incur tautology, provided that he might demonstrate more pointedly that the mystery of the resurrection belonged to Christ.

Therefore, if the repetition of Christ’s name indicates two Christs, let them accuse the Apostle himself, who established this rule of expression.

Moreover, when he says, “concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David,” they can bring against him no small accusation on the ground that he left another to be understood—one who was not made from the seed of David but was begotten from the Father’s womb. To distinguish him from that one, born spiritually from the Father, he wished to show another, born according to the flesh from David’s seed, saying, “concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David.”

They will likewise mark with the same slander what he says, “who was predestined to be the Son of God,” arguing that since predestination properly belongs to one who had never existed, not to one who had always existed, he intended to indicate one temporal Son of God by the name of predestination and another eternal one. [Col. 0148A]

For how can the most blessed Fathers be thought to have introduced a fourth, when they say shortly afterward:

> Let us follow the judgments of our Fathers, so that, confessing one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, we may fittingly teach that the same one is perfect in divinity and the same one is perfect as a carnal human being, God. (Council of Chalcedon, act 5)

What could have been said more openly, more clearly, or more reverently concerning one and the same Lord Christ? Or what could be produced more powerfully to repel and utterly crush the rash accusations of his critics?

[Col. 0148B]

XVIII. Let us therefore pass to other chapters of the synodal decree.

> Against those who attacked the mystery of the substance, saying that a human being had been created without divinity from the venerable Virgin Mary, [the council cited] shamelessly and in vulgar fashion the letters of the venerable former bishop Cyril of the Church of Alexandria, appropriate to the whole East against the madness of Nestorius, in which the clear exposition of the certain and salutary creed was made known to those who desired it. It also cited the letter of Leo, archbishop of the first see, which had been sent and directed to the venerable Flavian of holy memory, to intercept the wickedness of Eutyches. (Council of Chalcedon, act 5)

The slanderers of this venerable council, in order to open for themselves some avenue of criticism, altered the beginning of the present chapter. What is there written as “against those who think that a human being was begotten without divinity,” they reported as “a mere human being.”

By this statement they accuse the council of having condemned not Nestorius, whom, they say, plainly held nothing of the sort, since these are allegedly his words against Paul of Samosata:

> So may Paul of Samosata perish, who deliriously proclaimed to us a naked humanity of the Lord.

And therefore, they say, it is evident that the council followed Nestorius, whose doctrine it refused to condemn in an explicit judgment.

But the Fathers, in order to convict Nestorius of error, most clearly wrote:

> Against those who attacked the mystery of the substance, saying that the one born from holy Mary was a mere human being.

Since Nestorius asserted that Christ had not always been merely human, but only that he was without divinity in the Virgin’s womb, the Fathers showed that they were marking those who thought the Lord Jesus Christ had always been merely human. Thus they did not contend that Nestorius had been struck down by the Fathers’ judgment. [Col. 0148D]

Accordingly, I see no need to refute here the deceit of men who are plainly shown to have lied. I believe that the exposure of their fraud is itself sufficient to refute so many deceptions. Let us now pass to other matters.

XIX. They also say, craftily, that the council mentioned the letters of Cyril and Leo so that, by this subtle trick, they might falsely claim that these letters agreed with them, although they know them to be opposed to one another. To make this appear, they insert two chapters from Cyril’s judgments and, comparing Leo’s statements with them, strive to show that the two are widely opposed.

First they set forth these words of Leo:

> For each nature performs what belongs to it in communion with the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles; the other succumbs to injuries. (Letter 10, no. 4)

Then, as though contrary to these, they append the following words of Cyril:

> If anyone divides between two persons or substances the expressions spoken of Christ in the evangelical and apostolic writings, assigning some of them, as appropriate to a human being considered separately from God the Father, namely the Word, and others, as worthy of God, only to him who is from the Father, God the Word, let him be anathema. (Cyril, chapter 4)

Likewise:

> If anyone does not confess that the flesh of the Lord is life-giving and properly belongs to him who is from God the Father, the Word, but to someone else joined to him according to dignity, as though possessing only a divine indwelling; and does not rather confess it to be life-giving, as I have said, because it became the proper flesh of the Word who gives life to all, let him be anathema. (Cyril, chapter 11)

In the preceding chapter Cyril most cautiously and catholically prescribed that this must be avoided: no one should dare to divide Christ into two separately subsisting persons, wishing to identify one as a human being to be known specifically and properly apart from God the Word, and the other as God understood to be from the Father, assigning to each, as though separated from the other, their respective experiences and expressions. He declares that whoever impiously presumes to do this will be subject to condemnation.

In the following chapter, he insists that we believe the Lord’s flesh to be properly the flesh of the Word who was born from God, and not that of someone else joined to him according to dignity, in whom divinity dwelt as though externally, as in any of the saints. For this reason, he says that we must confess the Lord’s flesh to be life-giving, since it became the proper flesh of the life-giving Word.

XX. The following words of Leo, therefore, correspond and agree with Cyril’s first chapter. They show that Leo did not divide Christ into two persons, as though he wished to indicate one as a human being subsisting in a proper person outside God the Word and another as God remaining in the person proper to him, assigning appropriate expressions to each as though they were separate. Rather, he taught that Christ, one and the same, remained substantially in one person; and, confessing the same one to be human and divine, he spoke not divisively but with greater significance, in order to demonstrate the truth of both natures in him.

He says:

> The same eternal Only-begotten of the eternal Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. (Leo, Letter 10)

Likewise:

> And to discharge the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, could both die by virtue of one nature and not die by virtue of the other. Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, the true God was born, wholly in what was his own and wholly in what was ours. (No. 2)

Likewise:

> The impassible God did not disdain to be a passible human being and to submit to the laws of death, though he was immortal. (No. 3)

Likewise:

> For one and the same is truly the Son of God and truly the son of a human being. (No. 4)

Likewise:

> So that it might be recognized that the proper character of the divine and human nature remained indivisible, let us confess one Son of God and Word, and the flesh. (No. 5)

Behold: he called the proper character of both natures indivisible. Behold: he confessed one Son of God, the Word and the flesh.

With Cyril’s second chapter, which defines the matter more prudently and catholically—namely, that the Lord’s flesh is to be believed to belong not to someone else but to the Word, and to have become proper to him—the following words of blessed Leo agree:

> For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he took our nature and made it his own—he whom neither sin could defile nor death could hold. (No. 2)

Likewise, speaking against Eutyches:

> For if he does not think the Lord’s cross was unreal, and does not doubt that the punishment undertaken for the world’s salvation was real, let him acknowledge the flesh of the one whose death he believes in. (No. 5)

There are very many similar passages, which I consider it both laborious and unnecessary to gather into a single heap. It is not necessary to cite what has been said repeatedly and at length; what has been said is sufficient.

XXI. In addition, these men, arguing against the venerable council concerning Leo’s person, say:

> Rejecting apostolic testimonies, you testified in favor of Leo as though he held correct beliefs, although against the divine Gospels and the apostolic Scriptures alike he taught the doctrine that one person wept over Lazarus, while another raised Lazarus by his voice; one was crucified, while another changed the elements into darkness at night; one was fastened with nails, while another opened the gates of paradise to the thief through faith; one said, “I and the Father are one,” while another said, “The Father is greater than I.”

Although it is familiar and characteristic of all heretics alike to alter, through zeal for falsehood and malice, the judgments of catholic men, they usually do this more subtly and through a lengthy circumlocution of words, so that what is obscured under the appearance of truth may seem plausible.

These men, however, used so open a lie, without any veil of embellished rhetoric, that they have left us no labor of conviction, since they have surpassed themselves by their own falsehood.

For the words of Leo which they attempted to violate with the criminal incest of their minds are these:

> As—to pass over many examples—it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend out of an emotion of compassion and, when the mound of the four-day tomb has been removed, to raise that same friend to life again at the command of one’s voice; nor to hang upon wood and make all the elements tremble when daylight has been turned into night; nor to be fastened with nails and open the gates of paradise to the thief through faith; so it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). In him, humanity is lesser than the Father because of what he has received from us; in him, divinity is equal with the Father because it is from the Father.

By these words he wished to demonstrate both natures in Christ: what he did or said that was loftier derives from the nature of his divinity; what he did that was lower or spoke more humbly derives from the nature of his flesh. Thus the diversity of this one Christ’s actions is known to proceed from the difference of his natures.

Cyril also speaks in this manner in his *Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*, chapter 13:

> One, therefore, is the true God before the incarnation, and the one who remained in humanity is what he was, is, and will be. We must not, then, distinguish the one Lord Jesus Christ into a human being separately and God separately; rather, we say that Jesus Christ is one and the same, not ignoring the differences of the natures but preserving them unconfused among themselves.

XXII. Since these men also slander the confession of both natures as something new, let us bring forward all the teachers of the Church. From their numerous statements we shall select a few brief passages and append them to this work, while referring those who are eager to learn to the longer and more extensive treatments of this confession which blessed Leo gathered with provident care into one great body of testimonies. And so that the production of so many and such great witnesses may yield us a double benefit, let us adapt their judgments to Leo’s meaning.

Leo said what these men consider especially deserving of reproach:

> Each nature performs what belongs to it in communion with the other. (Leo, Letter 10, no. 4)

Hilary the Confessor said the same in one book against the Arians:

> The only-begotten God, therefore, was born from a Virgin, a human being in the fullness of time, destined in himself to advance the human being into God. He maintained throughout the whole manner of evangelical speech that he might teach himself to be believed the Son of God and might instruct that he be proclaimed the son of a human being. As a human being, he spoke and performed everything that belongs to God; then, as God, he spoke and performed everything that belongs to a human being. Yet in that very speech concerning both kinds, he never spoke except with an indication that he was both human and God. (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX, near the beginning)

Behold: plainly teaching the communion of both natures, he said that the Word speaks and performs what belongs to the flesh, and the flesh what belongs to the Word.

Blessed Ambrose, likewise agreeing with this judgment, says:

> Sharing in both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of a human being, so that without distinction the one who suffered may be called both the Lord of majesty and, as it is written, the son of a human being who descended from heaven. (Ambrose, *On the Faith to Gratian*, book II, chapter 4, beginning)

He described with exceptional clarity both the communion of activity and the proper character of each nature. The divine utterances testify that the flesh descended from heaven because of the Word, and that the Word underwent death because of the flesh, although neither flesh descended from heaven nor the Word could die.

[Col. 0151D]

XXIII. Leo also said:

> To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is evidently human; and it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend out of compassionate feeling and to raise that same friend to life again at the command of one’s voice. (No. 4)

Blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, likewise affirmed this, saying:

> When God, therefore, had proceeded from the Virgin, the human nature that he had assumed—one thing composed of two mutually contrary elements, flesh and spirit—had one element taken up into God, while the other bestowed the grace of divinity. He was indeed sent, but as a human being, for his nature was twofold. Hence he also labored from the journey; hence he hungered, thirsted, was saddened, and wept according to the law of the human body. (Oration 38, *On the Nativity of Christ*, midway through)

Leo also said:

> An inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that one and the same mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ, could die by virtue of one and not die by virtue of the other; and it is not possible that the nature of the Word could have been fastened with nails. (No. 3)

Blessed Cyril said the same in the letter of the entire synod to Nestorius—the fourth among Cyril’s letters, preserved in the Council of Ephesus, act 1, and in the Council of Chalcedon, act 1:

> In the very womb and virginal uterus, the Word united himself with the flesh and endured a carnal generation, making the birth of his flesh his own birth. Thus we say that he suffered and rose again, not because God the Word suffered in his own nature wounds, the piercing of nails, or other such injuries—for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering—but because that body which became his own suffered. For this reason he himself is said to have suffered all these things for us.

> God, who could not suffer, was present in the body that suffered. In the same way we understand his death: the life-giving Word of God is naturally immortal and incorruptible; but because his own body, by God’s grace, according to Paul’s words, “tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9), he is therefore said to have suffered death for us—not because he himself experienced death, insofar as this concerns his nature, for it is madness to think or say this, but because, as we said above, his flesh tasted death.

> Likewise, when the flesh rose again, we speak of his resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, perish the thought, but because his body rose. Thus we worship Christ as a human being—whom we nevertheless confess to be God—not as a human being worshiped together with the Word, lest some appearance of division be introduced, but worshiping one and the same person.

Blessed Hilary explains this in a few words:

> Do you see how God and human being are proclaimed, so that death is attributed to the human being, while the raising of the flesh is attributed to God? Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of the human being in the death. Although both acts belong to both natures, remember nevertheless that the one who is both is one Jesus. (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX, not far from the beginning)

XXIV. Since, as I think, it has been made sufficiently and most clearly evident that the letter of blessed Leo agrees with Cyril’s synodical letters, let us briefly indicate what the other teachers of the Church also thought concerning the two natures of Christ.

Saint John Chrysostom says in a homily on the Ascension of the Lord:

> God was rightly angry with us, and we despised him in his anger, turning away from the merciful Lord. Christ placed himself between us, united both natures, and himself endured the punishment that threatened us. (John Chrysostom, Greek-Latin volume V, sermon 35)

Likewise:

> Let us therefore recognize which nature it is to which he said, “Sit at my right hand and share my throne.” It is surely the nature that had heard, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.”

Augustine, holding the same view, says:

> Human nature had cause for rejoicing, because it was so assumed by God the Word that it was established immortal in heaven; and thus earth was exalted, so that, made incorruptible, it might sit at the Father’s right hand. (Treatise 78 on John)

Likewise blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia:

> When, therefore, we see some things in Christ so human that they seem in no way different from the common frailty of mortals, and others so divine that they belong to no other nature but that ineffable nature of the Godhead, the narrowness of human understanding is arrested and, struck by the stupor of such great wonder, does not know where to turn, what to hold, or how to direct itself. Should it think him a human being or God, when it sees him, having conquered the kingdom of death, returning from the dead with its spoils?

> For this reason he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be demonstrated: neither should anything unworthy or unfitting be thought concerning that divine and ineffable substance, nor should the events that took place be judged deceptive images.

Where is there an escape from this? Where can one flee? By what inventions, by what tricks of argument, can the truth of such great authority be obscured?

Thus all the ecclesiastical teachers agree concerning the proper character of both natures, so that in one and the same Christ nothing unworthy and nothing false is believed.

Nothing unworthy: lest we believe that the Son of God, God and Lord Christ, according to the nature of his divinity, was subject to death.

Nothing false: so that we believe that the same one, according to the nature of his flesh, truly died.

Because he truly died, the dignity of the nature of the Word receives the honor of immortality, while the nature of the flesh is credited with the truth of death. Thus both belong to one and the same Christ: both to die and not to die—to die according to the nature of his flesh, and not to die according to the nature of his divinity.

XXV. But let us now examine the final chapter of the decree.

From the decree of the Council of Chalcedon:

> We are to recognize one and the same Christ, the Lord, the only-begotten, in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; nowhere has the difference of the two natures been abolished because of the union, but rather the proper character of each nature has been preserved, the two coming together into one person and one substance. He is not divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same only-begotten Son of God, the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ. (Act 5)

What displeases them in this chapter is that it says, “the proper character of both natures being preserved,” or “the difference of the natures not abolished.” To prove these statements weak, they employ their customary verbosity and empty assertions, inserting many testimonies from Cyril’s chapters, in which he does not deny that Christ has two natures but teaches that he is one person.

Therefore, lest we refute them merely by our own argument, let us also set forth Cyril’s words, so that, since they rely upon Cyril as their witness, they may be defeated by Cyril as their witness.

From Cyril’s synodical letter to Nestorius:

> For we do not say that the nature of God, having been changed or altered, became flesh, nor that it was transformed altogether into a human being—which consists of soul and body. Rather, we say that the Word united to himself flesh animated by a rational soul, and that he became a human being substantially, ineffably, and incomprehensibly, and was also called the son of a human being. This did not occur through a bare act of will, nor through the mere assumption of a person, but because natures different in a certain manner came together in one.

> Yet Christ and Son is one from both, and the difference of the natures was not abolished or removed by the conjunction. Since divinity and humanity together made for us one Lord, Christ, and Son through that mysterious and ineffable union, what could be demonstrated more clearly, what more plainly, to show the agreement of Cyril’s letter with the synodal decree of Chalcedon?

Behold: neither statements oppose statements nor judgments oppose judgments. Rather, just as they share one sense of faith, so they have used almost the same words.

The holy synod said: “Nowhere has the difference of the two natures been abolished.”

Blessed Cyril said: “The difference of the natures was not abolished or removed by the conjunction.”

The holy synod said: “The two natures coming together in one person.”

Blessed Cyril said: “Not through a bare act of will, nor through the mere assumption of a person, but because natures different in a certain manner came together in one.”

The holy synod said: “Not divided into two persons, but one and the same Christ.”

Blessed Cyril said: “Yet one Christ and Son proceeded from both”—that is, from the natures.

And again:

> Since divinity and humanity together made for us one Lord, Christ, and Son.

XXVI. Since, as I believe, the darkness of falsehood has been driven away by the clear and evident light of truth, and the ruinous structure of an evil doctrine—which was being erected against Leo’s letter and the Council of Chalcedon by the futile efforts of perfidy—has been violently shaken by the assault of catholic witnesses and has fallen beyond repair, let us give glory and honor to God, by whose favor and gift victory is granted and falsehood overcome.

If anything in these little works of defense has been said by us inadequately or otherwise than it ought to have been, we ask pardon. Either we lacked an abundance of words and were unable to express what we thought, or, because of the poverty of our intellect and the weakness of our mind, we were unable to think what ought to have been thought.

But if our work displeases, let our intention at least be pleasing. Let our willingness be accepted, if our inability is displeasing.

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155]

# VIGILIUS OF TAPSA, DIALOGUE AGAINST THE ARIANS, WITH ATHANASIUS, ARIUS, AND PROBUS AS THE SPEAKERS AND JUDGE (S)

[Col. 0155]

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0155A] 84

## I.

When at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia the faith of the Church was being confirmed by three hundred and eighteen bishops, through the spiritual power of evangelical and apostolic teaching, the perfidy of Arius was exposed in the presence of the Emperor Constantine. After his doctrine of perfidy had been refuted by the judgment of those same bishops, he was separated from the Church, lest such an impious teaching, long concealed within the Church, should insinuate itself into the minds of all.

But when the emperor learned that the integral faith of the Church, as handed down from the apostles, was being confirmed more sacredly by the Fathers, he ordered that Arius himself, as a rebel against the holy faith, be sent into exile.
