But just as the serpent ensnared Eve in paradise through deceitful persuasion, so Arius’s perfidy prevailed over Constantia, the sister of that prince, through one of his attendants. The poison of the devil lay hidden in her until it found the time to erupt, the time with which it had filled her.

When, therefore, on the final day of her life, she enjoyed a visit from her brother, a poisonous apple was immediately offered by her words to her innocent brother. At once, after the example of the first human being, he fell unknowingly along the path of transgression. Lending his ear to the viper’s requests, he recalled from exile Arius, whom he had formerly banished as a sacrilegious man, for the destruction of faithful souls.

Arius then laid open his faith to the prince through crafty arguments and falsely asserted that he had been condemned by the bishops. For this reason the same emperor ordered a synod to be assembled at Alexandria, so that, if his assertion were recognized as true, he might be restored to the Church after pardon had followed the judgment. He also wished that everyone, rejoicing in his correction, might proceed more peacefully from there to the dedication of the Church at Jerusalem.

Finally, while his case was being debated at length by the bishops, the same Emperor Constantine, having arranged a final judgment in a certain suburb called Nicomedia, ended his life in the thirty-first year of his reign.

## II.

He entrusted the disposition of his will to the aforementioned attendant of Arius, to be reserved for Constantius. When Constantius arrived after the death of his father and assumed the empire, he delivered the testament to Constantius as Constantine had directed.

Moreover, because of this service, the same presbyter Evangelus was held in such great intimacy by him that he was no longer called a presbyter but the father of the empire. The man who had been elevated to rule as emperor appeared to be subject to the rule of this presbyter.

At his request—or rather, at his command—Arius was recalled to the Church. The inexperienced prince, retaining Arius’s doctrine in his impious mind, rejected the catholic faith and, sacrilegiously departing from the traditions of his fathers, appears to have inflicted no small persecution upon the Church of God and its priests in his time.

At that time he also produced many martyrs and many confessors. Some he left half alive after having their eyes gouged out and their kneecaps cut through; others, seized by the madness of a raging fury, he condemned to exile from their own homes.

In them the Lord’s saying seems to have been fulfilled:

> If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. (John 15:20)

Before he deceitfully assembled the priests of the Lord from the whole world at Ariminum or Seleucia, therefore, wishing to make everything one, he ordered a certain judge named Probus, supported by his authority, to be present as arbiter between Arius and Athanasius.

He was a man whom the emperor had judged faithful in his kingdom and more learned than other men in all the worldly arts. Removing himself from every public duty, he preferred to fulfill the task imposed upon him with all speed, both to obey the imperial commands and to establish the truest faith by his own examination.

When, therefore, he had come to the city of Laodicea in Syria, in the second year of Constantius’s reign, he sat on the tribunal in the audience hall, while crowds stood on either side, and addressed Arius and Athanasius in these words:

## III.

“I have been instructed by the sacred command of the glorious and most devout Emperor Constantius, and I have ordered that the matter of faith between you be examined.”

Arius and Athanasius said:

“Who could be so foolish as to dare reject an imperial command?”

Judge Probus said:

“Then let the sacred command of the revered Augustus be read.”

And it was read as follows:

> Constantine Constantius, pious, perpetual, victorious, triumphant, always Augustus, sends greetings to the judge Probus.
>
> Having obtained the imperial power of my father by divine favor, I must first strive for this: that, with heretical conduct erased from the minds of the faithless, the whole world may rejoice in union with our holy faith. For whoever turns an impious person back from the way of error will save his soul and cover a multitude of his own sins.
>
> Since we now find many accomplices in this crime, cultivating this perfidy in sacrilegious fashion and asserting that they retain the integral rule of faith—men who not only deceive human beings through impious seduction but also inflict injury upon innate majesty by joining a created substance, that of the Son, to divinity—we admonish you, having received the authority of our clemency, to have the examination of this matter conducted between Arius, the venerable presbyter, and Athanasius, bishop of the same error.
>
> Above all, urge them, laying aside the perversity of their minds, to bow their necks to the true and approved faith. Otherwise, by despising the commands of our piety and clemency with their customary audacity, they will provoke us to severe anger.
>
> Although you have not yet received the laying on of hands of this faith, we nevertheless believe that, by the wisdom in which you excel all others, you will be able to decide everything faithfully, without favoring any person, seeking to please God rather than human beings.
>
> And in another hand:
>
> We wish you good health.
>
> Given at Constantinople, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

## IV.

When it had been read, Judge Probus said:

“Let the sacred command of the revered prince that has been read be entered into the record.”

And he added:

“Recognizing that no majesty of the true divinity exists in the worship of idols, I wish to submit myself to Christian doctrines, by which it is asserted that there is one true God who created by the power of his word all things that are seen and unseen.

“Since many are counted under the title of the Christian name but are said to wander far from the truth of that faith, thinking differently and following various systems of doctrine, I now greatly desire to know what the faith of correct doctrine is, so that, when every winding uncertainty has been removed, I may cling firmly to it.

“I do not wish, while hoping to be stripped of the blindness of error, to become entangled in greater errors of darkness by becoming indiscriminately and without any distinction of examination an imitator of whatever sect first happens to appear before me—a sect whose soundness or unsoundness, and whose support by truth, I do not know.

“Therefore, if it pleases you—or rather, since it ought to please you—let each of you set forth the judgment of his faith in our presence. Then, after an examination has been held, let us all rightly yield to whichever is found to be firmer and truer, and let us follow it without hesitation, rejecting the error of falsehood.”

Arius and Athanasius said:

“How can we entrust to you the secrets of so great a mystery and place the judgment of an unexamined matter in the hands of one who has not yet washed away the stains of paganism by receiving the true doctrine?”

Judge Probus said:

“This is precisely what I wish with all my strength to learn: what the correct and truthful doctrine is in which I ought to receive the sacred mysteries of the hidden mystery.

“I do not now desire the profound secrets of the mysteries to be disclosed to me. Rather, I demand that those matters which are found externally in your faith and publicly proclaimed be demonstrated now: namely, that there is one and the same true God, creator of visible and invisible things.

“I know that you both profess this with one voice. What, then, has caused you to be divided into such various sects that we cannot understand at all which is true and which false, before, through your contest conducted with due moderation of patience, we carefully learn what is fitting?”

## V

Athanasius said: Since you are versed in every branch of learning and highly educated in philosophical disciplines, you ought not to be surprised in the least that among us there have arisen numerous and varied doctrines of novelty, since among you too as many new opinions have emerged as there are almost names of their authors. For although there are three religions in the world—the religion of the Jews, of the pagans, and of the Christians—each religion, departing from itself through many and widely divergent differences of opinion, has been divided into various sects of its own institution; for each person, captivated by the attractiveness of a more recent opinion that prefers not the truth but a likeness of the truth, abandons the line handed down from ancient times by the Fathers. Thus he wanders irremediably through trackless ways, using novelty in place of antiquity, as though he were walking along the path of an ancient boundary-marker handed down by the Fathers. For either he thinks too much or believes too little, and therefore does not know how to walk the middle and right path. I have prefaced this so that I might show you the clearest indications for investigating the truth, so that you may easily recognize that the person is entangled in the error of perversity who, abandoning the ancient institutions of the apostolic faith, dreams up for himself, according to his own will, the faith he ought to follow.

[Col. 0158B] Arius said: Athanasius very properly declares that the error of faithlessness consists in things discarded and in recently invented novelties, agreeing in this with the apostolic testimony that says: “Avoid profane novelties of words” (1 Timothy 6:20). Therefore I beg you not to depart from this path of inquiry, but to investigate more carefully and attentively who uses the new sacrament of faith and who the ancient.

The judge Probus said: So that what you assert may become readily known and may come into the light of truth, every cloud of ambiguity having been removed, disclose the rule of the ancient faith and communicate it to our ears exactly as it was handed down by the apostles.

Arius and Athanasius said: We believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit. This is the rule of our faith, which the Lord handed down to the apostles by heavenly instruction, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

## VI

The judge Probus said: I remain stunned with profound amazement at this miracle, seeing that you proclaim three gods, from whom I had believed one must flee to the majesty of the singular power of the one God. Therefore, I beg you to explain briefly what the rationale of this faith is, or what the names of these three things and three terms signify.

Arius and Athanasius said: We do not confess three gods in the professions of our faith, but we faithfully profess that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The judge Probus said: Then explain your faith more fully and declare what kind of belief exists within that faith of yours.

Arius said: I confess that the unbegotten Father ineffably begot the Son before all ages, through whom and in whom he made visible and invisible creatures. In the last times, sent by the Father for the salvation of the human race, he bore a true human being in the world, whom he received from the Virgin Mary inviolate, without the mingling of human sexual intercourse. Although he is God and Lord of his own creation, he nevertheless cannot be compared or made equal in all things—or in anything—to his begetter, whom he confesses both as his God and as the author of his origin. Yet this does not mean that there are two gods, because he too is God; nor does it mean that he is not God because the Father alone is God. In the same way, he is not for that reason not good because the Father alone is good, since the Son too is not only good but the creator of good things. And just as it does not deprive him of being good that the Father alone, according to the Son’s own confession, is good, so it does not take away his being God that the Father alone is God. And just as the Son’s goodness does not prejudice the singularity of the Father’s goodness, so his divinity does not prevent the Father from being the one and singular God. In this way we confess one God—not, as I have said, by denying that the Son is God, but by assigning to the Father alone the authority of the one divinity.

Athanasius said: Arius has rightly defined in his profession that the Father ineffably begot the Son from himself before all ages; but in the statement he has just made he has kept silent about whether he wishes to assert that the Son was begotten from the very essence or nature of the Father, or from elsewhere. For I confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and of one nature. Thus I believe that the Son was begotten not from nothing, nor from something else, but from the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And although I profess that there are three persons subsisting in their own distinct properties, their nature is nevertheless one, and their divinity is shown to be one.

## VII

The judge Probus said: Although this varied and greatly dissimilar difference between your opinions casts a great darkness of confusion over our minds, nevertheless, so that we may quickly be freed from these ambiguities and learn what the profession of the true faith is, please strengthen your assertions with clearer testimonies from divine Scripture. And so that you may not wander far from the matter amid the confusion of an intermingled dispute through a lengthy circuit of speech, state your faith one by one, as I have said. But now let Arius continue, and let him not hesitate to support his faith with true testimonies.

Arius said: Since you have ordered me to engage first, let Athanasius answer whether God is of a simple nature.

Athanasius said: What impious person would deny this?

Arius said: Let him answer whether everything that is said about God is also to be understood according to essence.

Athanasius said: I would not rashly declare that everything said about God ought to be understood according to essence, except for certain relational uses of terms, expressed according to the customary language of human speech, which are applied not properly to God but to persons, times, or whatever kinds of things. That is, when he says that he does not know, or acknowledges that he has come to know again; or when he feels regret over things made by him and shows himself now angry, now appeased. If we wish to understand all these things according to essence, we undoubtedly profess the divine nature to be subject to suffering and lacking foresight, a nature into which either ignorance or knowledge arising at a particular time may enter; a nature which sorrow may wear down through repentance and joy may raise up through renewed vigor. What else would this be but enduring change and drifting here and there in instability? Therefore it is most clearly established that not everything said about God ought to be understood according to essence; rather, we most certainly confess that some things correspond to his dispensation and do not suit his nature.

The judge Probus said: Although you have answered sufficiently and learnedly, with praiseworthy brevity, that not everything said about God is said according to essence, I nevertheless wish to hear this from you at greater length when the time for the discussion of your position arrives. For now, as I already stated earlier, let Arius continue as he began.

## VIII

Arius said: If you carefully attend to what I set forth at the beginning, you will find there the whole of our faith and belief.

Athanasius said: Arius truly professes that the Son existed before the ages. But that he was born from the Father he grants only in the sound of the voice and in a feigned confession of words, not in the proper truth of the matter, since he separates him far from the substance of the paternal nature and asserts that he is subject to the Father by the condition of his nature, not by the rationale of the dispensation.

The judge Probus said: Give a very clear indication of your faith, and mark how you believe in a fresh statement, so that the matter of the discussion too may be fitted to the standard of the confession that has been proposed.

Athanasius said: So as not to burden your minds with an exceedingly long speech, I shall conclude my faith in brief. I confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in divinity, power, greatness, and nature. Nor do I assert that anything new or alien has been introduced into this Trinity, as though it had not existed before but were later added; rather, as I said, I believe it to be of one nature and one substance.

Arius said: Just as I confess three persons remaining distinct in their own properties, so I confess three substances: that of the Father, that of the Son, and that of the Holy Spirit. The substance of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. The nature of the unbegotten substance of the Father, the begotten substance of the Son, and the created substance of the Holy Spirit cannot in any way be compared. Therefore they are believed by our faithful confession to be neither equal in power, nor alike in greatness, nor participants in the same nature.

The judge Probus said: If this is the entire point on which you appear to disagree with one another—namely, that one of you says there are different substances, while the other says that the Trinity has one substance—then the logic of the discussion now requires that you support your assertions not with arguments deliberately arising from the subtlety of dialectical art, but more robustly with the simple and pure teachings of divine Scripture.

## IX

Arius said: I believe that the oblivion of memory has not at all removed Athanasius’s attack from your prudent recollection, by which he argued most elegantly that the person who pursues new and unusual inventions of words ought to be marked with the error of perversity, adding to apostolic doctrines what is known not to have been handed down by them.

The judge Probus said: I remember it well.

Arius said: Then let the decrees of the Council of Nicaea be brought forth by reading, and you will recognize that Athanasius, or his authors, corrupted the apostolic faith by the addition of new words, to such an extent that, using royal influence, they judged that those who clung to the ancient teachings of the Fathers should be banished by deadly edicts.

The judge Probus said: If the circumstances of the present matter require that the decree of the Council of Nicaea be brought forward for examination, let Athanasius also indicate this in his statement, so that, with the consent of both parties, whatever is being brought in from elsewhere may be recited.

Athanasius said: It is fitting to the case that the opportunity to read the record of what happened not be denied.

The judge Probus said: Then, as he wishes, let the reading of the aforementioned decree be aired for discussion.

And it was read as follows:

“We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father”—which the Greeks call *homoousion*, that is, “of the same substance”—“through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. He descended for our salvation, and was incarnate, was made human, suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into the heavens, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

“But those who say, ‘There was [a time] when he was not,’ and ‘Before he was born he was not,’ and that [he is] from things that do not exist, or from another substance or essence, calling God mutable or changeable—these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.”

## X

Arius said: You plainly see, excellent Probus, that the decrees of that council were written with reckless audacity to cast reproach upon the apostolic faith. For what need was there to insert this new term, *homoousion*, into the ancient rules of doctrine? Are we to say that the apostles, or their disciples, and all their successors in order who until that time lived in the confession of Christ, were ignorant of the term *homoousion* and followed sacrilegious impiety in the truth of the faith simply because, deprived of the meaning of this name and without the assertion of its proclamation, they proceeded to Christ? If, as these people wholly falsely claim, a new doctrine was being introduced by us against the ordinances of the apostles, surely it would have been appropriate for the new doctrine introduced by us to oppose the ancient doctrines of the apostles, and for antiquity to prescribe against novelty—not for novelty to overturn antiquity. Why does he impose on me the obligation to follow this term? Why does he drag me so violently toward such novelty? Why does he add this word to the apostolic faith, when neither the prophets nor the apostles make mention of it anywhere? What, I ask, is this term, without which the faith cannot be complete, without which Christians are deprived of the honor of the Christian religion? For in this matter one of two things must necessarily be followed. If the assertion of *homoousion* is true, then the preaching of the apostles, which flourished for long ages without this term, will be false. But if the apostolic faith is true without this term—as indeed it is—then without doubt this will be false, since it has added the novelty of a term to the ancient faith. Turn through all the books of the New and Old Testament: will you be able to find *homoousion* anywhere inscribed in the sacred pages?

## XI

The judge Probus said: What answer is made to this?

Athanasius said: Are you offended only by the novelty of the term, or do you also reject the power of the very reality that has received this name?

Arius said: I do not sufficiently understand what you are saying.

Athanasius said: Since an ancient reality has received a new name, and no new force has thereby been added to that reality by the new term, this is precisely what I am asking: whether you condemn the ancient reality itself together with the novelty of the name.

Arius said: You are speaking twisted things, worthy of every kind of foolish amazement. For if *homoousion* is a new name, there is no doubt that the reality it appears to signify is also new.

Athanasius said: Then you condemn the reality and the name alike?

Arius said: Precisely so.

Athanasius said: Therefore, if I demonstrate that a new name was assigned to an ancient reality handed down by the apostles, will you finally admit that you have been defeated? Or will you even then condemn the ancient reality together with the novelty of the name?

Arius said: You will not demonstrate this.

The judge Probus said: And what reason required that an ancient reality receive a new name? Before it acquired the designation of this name, did it remain without the distinctive character of a name? This seems to me to have no logical consistency.

Arius said: Very well.

Athanasius said: It has always been the practice of ecclesiastical discipline, whenever a new doctrine of heretics arises, to alter the words used as names against the insolent novelties of inquiries, while the realities themselves remain immutable, and to express the natures of things more meaningfully—terms which nevertheless accord with the force of existing realities and demonstrate more clearly that those realities existed from ancient times, rather than suggesting novelty in their origin. And to make what I am saying clearer, I shall use an example.

At the very beginning of the preaching of the Christian religion, all who believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were called not Christians but merely disciples. And because many authors of new doctrines arose who opposed apostolic teaching, and all called their followers disciples, there was no distinction of name between true and false disciples. For whether they were followers of Christ, of Dositheus, of Cephas, of Theodas, of some Judas, or even of John—those who claimed that they believed in Christ—everyone was designated by the single name “disciples.” Then the apostles gathered at Antioch, and, as the Acts indicate in Luke’s account, they called all the disciples by a new name, namely Christians, distinguishing them from the common designation of false disciples; so that the saying of the divine oracle through Isaiah might also be fulfilled, where it says: “Those who serve me shall be called by a new name” (Isaiah 65:15, according to the Septuagint).

## XII

Therefore, retaining this form handed down by the apostles—the practice of using new names in new circumstances—the Church, as the reasoning of sound faith required, issued various novelties of names against various heretics.

In the end, the Church imposed upon the Father the new name “unbegotten.” For when the Sabellian heresy wished to assert that the Father had been begotten from the Virgin, the Church, confessing the contrary, handed down that the Father is unbegotten. Yet nowhere in the divine Scriptures do we read that the Father is unbegotten. Sabellius may therefore turn his audacity toward this accusation and use a form of argument like yours, saying: “Why do you do violence to the divine Scriptures without any regard for shame by professing the Father to be unbegotten, when you cannot point to this in writing?”

Likewise, because that same Sabellius impiously professes that the Father was not only begotten but also suffered, you, agreeing with one another, said among the other decrees of faith that you promulgated that the Father is impassible—a position that we acknowledge you have established religiously and piously. But he makes the same proclamation. How far will you extend the audacity of your license by professing what you have not read written: that the Father is impassible, although neither the prophets handed this down nor the authority of the authentic creed, but it was presumed upon by your own rashness?

Again, you continue and establish this faith of religious confession concerning the Son, calling him “God from God, light from light.” Here, consider for yourself, I ask, how great an opportunity for accusation you have opened to Photinus, who attributes the beginning of the Son to the nature of human generation. Why should he not bring forward similar grounds for complaint? Why should he not also rave with a similar outcry, saying: “What are you saying? What are you establishing? What are you handing down to posterity, in your judgment, as something to be followed, when you confess the Son to be God from God, light from light? Show me whether you have read this written in that form of faith—that is, in the authentic creed handed down by the apostles. But I shall be content if it was not written there: at least let it be read to me from the prophets or shown from the writings of the apostles. Who could endure these novelties of words? Who could bear to admit to his own understanding what neither the prophets nor the apostles handed down?”

## XIII

Likewise, in many celebrated decrees of your councils you establish that the Son is like the Father. Let Eunomius now arise, confessing that he is unlike, and say: “Where did you read this? Where did you find it written? Did the Father or the Son use this expression about himself?”

Therefore, Arius, since today you bind me with this dilemma by requiring me to demonstrate that *homoousion* has been properly used, either admit that, against the insolent and furtive perversities of heretical interpretation, certain terms of confession were inserted into the authorities of the faith—not rashly presumed, but gathered by a consequent reasoning—so that, through the religious understanding of new words, there were as many refutations as occasions of faithlessness had been sought out or supplied; or, if you refuse to admit this, I shall deal with you through your own objections.

Show me not from conjectures, not from probabilities, not from things close to reason, not from what invites understanding, not from what the piety of faith persuades us to confess, but by the pure and bare propriety of the words, that “unbegotten” or “impassible Father,” or “Son, God from God, light from light,” or “like the Father,” is written. Do not tell me, “The reasoning of faith requires this; piety teaches this; the sequence of Scripture urges me to this profession of the term.” I do not want you, I say, to offer me such arguments, because you reject me when I put forward similar arguments for proving *homoousion*. Instead, carry in your hands the books of the divine volumes and read that the names of the terms mentioned above are inscribed in the same sound and with the same syllables.

Either show that “the Son is like the Father” is written, or admit that he is unlike. There is no way out for you from this position, nor any further escape. No ability is supplied for you to disentangle yourself from the knots of your own proposition. Either grant me the right to prove from consequences the doctrine of *homoousion*, that is, of one substance, or, if you refuse to grant this, you must deny everything that you yourself confess, because you will certainly nowhere be able to find those things set down in bare and exact terms.

## XIV

The judge Probus said: If it is the custom of ecclesiastical practice that certain terms are set down plainly in the authority of the faith to restrain the movements of heretics, though they are clothed in reasoning derived from the consequences of existing realities, while the truth from which they originate is found to be contained in the divine writings, what do you say, Arius? Do you grant that *homoousion*, as Athanasius says, is proved from the divine Scriptures through the corresponding qualities of the professions, or not?

[Col. 0164C] Arius said: By some trickery of syllogistic art he is trying to evade my objection. I want it demonstrated to me whether *homoousion* has been written with the authority of the Lord’s reading. Therefore, let him either read it as properly stated or withdraw from its confession.

The judge Probus said: But you see how he turns your question back upon you and binds you with the same points by which you bind him, requiring, as you yourself demand, a clearer document of your confession: show him from the canonical writings, plainly set down, an unbegotten or impassible Father, or God from God, or light from light, or that the Son is like the Father. If you are entirely unable to demonstrate all these things as expressly stated, the necessity of denying them will threaten you. Only one consideration, as I see it, can help you in this predicament: that you grant that the things plainly set down in your councils flowed from the sources of Scripture.

For it will be counted as a fault of contentiousness if you demand proof of a bare statement whose meaning you know to abound throughout the Scriptures. Seek, then, the meaning from which the nature of this term derived its origin; and when you have found the meaning, do not doubt that you have found the name as well.

## XV

Athanasius said: However many arguments he employs, he can in no way be removed from this intention. For he knows with absolute certainty that if the matter comes to this—that the one substance of the Father and the Son, which is *homoousion*, is taught from the consequences of the Scriptures—he can very easily be defeated. Therefore, driven by the danger of distrust and fear, he demands evidence of a bare statement.

But he must again be bound by his own professions. You demand that I show “one substance” of the Father and the Son—that is, *homoousion*—written. Yet you confess three *ousiai*, that is, three substances. Show me, then, where you have read of three *ousiai*. For if I must deny “one,” that is, *homoousion*, because I do not find it written plainly, how do you dare to confess three *ousiai*, when you will nowhere be able to demonstrate that this is written?

The judge Probus said: If there is any testimony from the divine authorities, expressly and specifically stated, by which it is approved that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three *ousiai* and, as you confess, three natures, let it be brought forward, so that Athanasius may withdraw from the confession of one substance, which is *homoousion*. For when you have shown that *triusion*—“three substances”—is expressly set down in the Scriptures, it will appear that Athanasius has persisted this long in the confession of *homoousion* through the reckless obstinacy of his determination, since he was unable to demonstrate that it was expressly stated. But if you yourself are unable to demonstrate three *ousiai*, you too will appear to me to be bound by the same necessity of circumstance.

Athanasius said: Let him teach that three *ousiai* are expressly stated, and I shall yield concerning one substance, which is *homoousion*.

Arius said: If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three, then necessarily there are also three substances in which each person is known to subsist separately and distinctly in its own proper way.

Athanasius said: Arguments are of no use here; here the truth is gathered by consequential reasoning, while the exact wording of the testimonies is demanded. Read *triusion* as specifically stated. Do not say by conjecture, “If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three, then necessarily there are also three substances.” For I too can form a more truthful opinion by a similar conjecture: “If the Father and the Son are one”—because he himself says, “I and the Father are one”—“how can there not be one substance?” But you entirely refused to enter this path of discussion when you demanded that I demonstrate a testimony in which *homoousion* was specifically stated.

Therefore, by the same reasoning, read *triusion* as specifically and properly stated. For if I must deny *homoousion* because I am unable to show it written plainly, then necessarily I must confess *triusion* if you demonstrate that it is expressly stated.

## XVI

Arius said: Does the Father subsist properly, or not?

Athanasius said: Unless you read of three *ousiai* expressly stated, I shall give no answer to your questions. For who does not see where your objection is aimed? You wish by an argument based on a crafty question to establish that the substances of the Father and the Son are different. But arguments are unnecessary here, where proof of three substances is demanded by a clearer testimony of exact wording.

But if you wish to pass from the exact wording of testimonies to the consequence of realities, let this become known to the public conscience itself: you have not been able to demonstrate three *ousiai* expressly stated. And when we have both been released from this point, I must satisfy your objections or questions.

The judge Probus said: As the aim of your discussion shows, neither can you demonstrate that *homoousion* nor can he demonstrate that *triusion* is expressly and specifically stated. Therefore, so that you may not linger longer in childish contention over superfluous matters, both of you must finally desist from this demand for a bare proof. Instead, gather from the authority of Scripture, by consequential reasoning, either *homoousion* or *triusion*. For it will not be permissible to doubt the designation of a name whose meaning can be more firmly strengthened by the abundant accumulation of testimonies.

Arius said: Since you have decided that we should gather the force of the aforementioned names through the persuasions of reasoning, from the causes that follow from the realities, so that Athanasius may not think that I demanded evidence of the bare propriety of the word because of the difficulty of demonstrating the truth, I shall do as your decision has decreed. I wanted rather to use brevity, so that the course of reasoning, wandering farther afield, might not obscure the truth with ambiguous meanings.

Athanasius said: Faith cannot be thrown into doubt when it is supported by the protection of truth and scatters the denser clouds of falsehood by the light of radiant clarity. For it cannot lack its own powers when it does not need to be aided by external supports.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0165]

## I

[Col. 0165D] The following day the judge Probus said: Since I do not doubt that you will preserve with unalterable resolve the terms of the agreement you initiated—by which you appear to have mutually granted one another that the profession of one substance or of three substances should be proved through a clear examination of the consequences of the divine writings—the question requiring proof of a pure term, expressly stated, having been set aside, the nature of the agreement now demands that, once every quibble of human argument has been removed, you teach from the sacred volumes of the divine authorities whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one substance or different substances.

For the proof of this matter has suspended not only my mind, as I suppose, but almost the minds of all mortals in such eager expectation that, if the importance of so great an affair allowed it, they would desire to reach the summit of truth and the final point of the clearest understanding without the adjournment of a single day or the interval of even a moment.

Therefore, so that the deeply religious intention of the faithful, eager for the truth, may not be frustrated, cast aside every seductive embellishment of luxuriant speech and discuss the matter, the case, the relevant points, and the necessary considerations. As I said, carefully avoid every circuitousness of words, every ornament of expression wandering far from the case, and every charm of language, so that the account of your discussion may be adorned more by truth than by the buskin of swelling eloquence.

Athanasius said: Although I have already discussed the unity of substance repeatedly and at length outside the formal proceedings, and have committed my discussions to writing—so that it would scarcely be possible for anything further to be added by me in this dispute—nevertheless, since these matters were spoken externally, with no opponent standing at a distance to challenge them, I must repeat the same things again and submit them to this public examination, so that they may be strengthened by the judgment of your court.

## II

The judge Probus said: If they are not weakened by Arius’s replies, then our judgment may be strengthened.

Arius said: Why are these traps of deception being set out? Why is the judgment of the judge being preferred in defense of a wicked assertion? Let us first do what the necessity of demonstrating the truth imposes upon us. Let our profession of faith be impressed upon human hearing. Let judgments perceive by what methods, by what arguments, and finally by what proofs our assertion is supported. Only then shall we ask the judge to pronounce a decision—a decision that certainly does not depend upon our will.

The judge Probus said: You ought to remember my preface, delivered recently at the beginning of this proceeding, and your pledge formerly inserted into the earlier proceedings, in which it was stated that, with superfluous matters omitted, one must descend to the stronghold of the case. You ought at last to do this.

Arius said: Let him teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, one power, one dignity, one glory, one majesty, one might, and one honor—something that he is accustomed to proclaim to the people in a profession sufficiently improvident and exceedingly incautious.

Athanasius said: Do you profess that the Son was truly born from the Father, or not?

Arius said: Do you yourself profess that the Father cannot be subject to any defect arising from derivation or division, or not?

Athanasius said: I most certainly profess it.

Arius said: I too profess that the Son was born from the Father.

Athanasius said: Do you consider “born from the Father” to be the same as “born of the Father”?

Arius said: It is enough for you that I have said he was born from the Father, which I can also readily demonstrate. Why do you employ crafty arguments? For the time being, however, I have nowhere happened upon the expression “born of the Father.” But I remember that “from the Father” is written, when the apostle John says: “Whoever loves the Father loves him who has been born from him.”

Athanasius said: Then do you think it makes no difference whether he is said to have been born from him or of him?

Arius said: If you are able to demonstrate to me that “the Son was born of the Father” is expressly stated, then I shall consider what I ought to think of it. But I am not unaware that in many copies the wording is variously given, so that in the same places where “of him” is read, “from him” is found in other manuscripts. Whether this has happened through the fraud of those who altered the text or because both expressions signify one thing—that is, that “from him” means the same as “of him”—this cannot sufficiently prejudice our faith in any way.

### III

Athanasius said: In this statement of yours I have observed a very definite point set forth with a carefully arranged argument. But I was sufficiently surprised that you said this could prejudice only our faith and did not indicate that it could prejudice the faith of both parties. I suppose that, hurrying to fortify your own faith, you worded it in this way, hoping that I would pass lightly over it without any proof.

In the Gospel, too, the Son said concerning the Father: “God is spirit” (John 4:24). And to show that he was born of the Father, he said: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). And: “I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:27). Behold, I have shown that the Son was born of the Father, by the testimony of the Son himself.

Arius said: You employ sufficiently crafty and suspicious arguments in order to say that I stated this for the defense of my faith. But so that every ambiguity of suspicion may be removed from your understanding, as I said above, whether he is said to have been born from him or of him, this can in no way prejudice the faith of either party.

Athanasius said: Did the Father, who begets from himself—that is, from his very self—the Son, beget what he himself is, or something else?

[Col. 0168C] Arius said: Certainly he begot what he himself is, because God begot God, light begot light, the perfect begot the perfect, and the almighty begot the almighty.

Athanasius said: Then he begot him not externally, nor from nothing, nor from any preceding or succeeding matter, but from himself. And he begot nothing other than what he himself is.

Arius said: One begot another.

Athanasius said: We too confess that one begot another—that is, the Father begot the Son. But if he begot him from himself, that is, from what he himself is, and begot what he himself is, then the Son cannot be of another substance or a different kind; and thus he will be of one and the same substance with the Father.

Arius said: If you knew into how many errors of faithlessness the profession of one substance tends, you would certainly never mention this term between the Father and the Son. Nor would you have concluded your discussion, divided into a series of questions, with such a point as to bring it to this end of impious profession.

Athanasius said: You should know, Arius, that I cannot be wholly ignorant that it is impious and sacrilegious to profess different substances of the Father and the Son, and that it is pious and religious to believe them to be of one substance. And I shall demonstrate that this has been handed down not through a conclusion drawn from human opinion, nor discovered by conjectures and arguments, but by the teaching of heavenly doctrine.

## IV

The judge Probus said: First explain to me the force and quality of the statement; only then will you be able to demonstrate whether it applies to the Father and the Son.

Athanasius said: Substance is distinguished by two kinds of designation. One kind is that quality which indicates the essence of an existing nature; another kind of substance is that by which the one who possesses something is distinguished from what he possesses. To make this clearer, I shall set forth what I mean by an evident explanation. For example, a human being is a substance of his own kind and nature. Again, whatever he possesses externally—that is, in the material of gold, silver, or other kinds of things—is called his substance. Although the same term appears to have a single designation, it nevertheless seems to signify two things. But we are discussing that kind of substance by which each nature, on account of the fact that it is or subsists, is called substance. And whatever it generates from itself—that is, from its very self—can be nothing other than what it itself is. Finally, a human father, begetting a son of his own kind—that is, of his own substance—begets a human being, because a human being begets a human being. And they are rightly said to be of one substance, because the truth of birth does not admit diversity of substances.

Diversity of substance, on the other hand, occurs, for example, if a human being were to beget an animal, or if an animal of any kind were to beget an animal of another kind—that is, if an ox were to beget a donkey, or a sheep a goat. Since this proceeds into diversity of kind, it would be a monstrous generation, preserving in no way the distinct property of its own nature.

Again, in the qualities of the elements, it is worthwhile to observe what constitutes the diversity or proper character of substances. For example, the nature of every fire or light seems to supply from itself that which it itself is: light supplies radiance, fire supplies burning. In this function of its activity, and subsisting in it, it appears to preserve inviolate the nature of its substance. But if light were to beget darkness from itself, it would be subject to alteration, imparting matter of a kind different from itself. It can preserve the integrity of its immutability only if it supplies from itself what it itself is. Otherwise, if—as I have said—that which it supplies from itself were something other than the very thing it supplies, it could be called of another substance. Yet the quality, order, or rational principle of all natures altogether refuses to admit this.

Come now, if it seems good, let us raise the eye of the mind from earthly and visible things to higher realities, and from things that have been made let us recognize the substance of the uncreated power, instructed by the teaching of apostolic authority, which says that the invisible power of divinity ought to be understood from the things that have been made (Rom. I, 20).

Arius therefore said that the Son was born from the Father, and that God begot God, light begot light. In this profession one of two alternatives must unquestionably be retained. Either the one who generates from himself begot what he himself is, and therefore the Son will be of one substance with the Father; or, if he begot a God of a kind different from himself, it cannot be called a true birth, since it could not preserve the proper character of the substance of the one generating. The reasoning of the argument is thus brought to the point that either he was not born at all, or he was degenerate; and it will appear utterly absurd and impious to confess either alternative.

[V, Col. 0170A] V. Probus the judge said: If Arius knows of anything that can be brought forward against this, let him not delay to state it.

Arius said: I do not think that Athanasius is unaware that God is of a simple and immutable nature. If, as he himself has asserted, God generated from his own substance, then he will unquestionably be mutable. For by generating from himself what he himself is, he must either have lost part of his substance through the process of derivational generation, or have been capable of undergoing the defect of division. I confess that the substance of God the Father neither brought forth anything from itself, nor was derived into qualities of parts, nor experienced—or could have experienced—division, subtraction, or anything of this kind that is subject to suffering.

Athanasius said: But neither do we believe that the divine nature is subject to these conditions of suffering. Rather, we faithfully confess that the impassible Father generated the Son impassibly from himself—that is, from what he himself is. Nor do any of the kinds of division, derivation, parts, or every other kind of thing and suffering that you wished to bring forward, driven by an empty anxiety, turn us away from the truth of our confession, so that we should deny that God could generate from himself lest he appear subject to these sufferings.

Consider, then, I beseech you hearers, on the equal scale of judgment what is more religious, more holy, and more in accordance with the divine laws. Raise the eyes of your minds, and, fearing the terrifying day of the future judgment, discern with devout attention of mind what better accords with catholic and apostolic truth: whether to confess that almighty God generated the Son impassibly from himself, or rather to suppose that, lest he be subject to suffering, he could not generate the Son from himself—that is, from his own substance.

For I assert and affirm with the clearest declaration of my voice that, just as God is impassible, so also he is omnipotent. I therefore believe that he could generate from his own substance and yet was not subject to any defect of suffering. For division and derivation, contraction, addition, flux, and whatever other kinds of suffering there may be, belong to corporeal and tangible things composed from diversity. But God, who is bounded by no signs of bodily form and distinguished by no outlines of limbs, cannot be subject to the defect of suffering. And rightly I confess generation in him, because he generated; and rightly, at the same time, I confess him impassible, because he was never passible.

[VI] VI. Arius said: Is it therefore to be acknowledged that, because omnipotence cannot be denied in God, he cannot suffer what the wholly incorrupt substance of his divinity does not admit? Hence it will seem most dishonorable and full of impiety to believe that, through the profession of one substance, neither the Father truly subsists nor the Son exists in his own proper character.

For the intention of this impious unbelief tends toward this: that, through the persons of the Father and the Son being mixed together, collected from diversity into one thing, congealed, and confused, they may in no way subsist in their own singularity of proper character, as I have said. This profession of yours also contains something exceedingly dreadful and far to be removed from the minds of the faithful: namely, that the inviolable Father, by generating from his own substance, was altogether unable to avoid the defect of corruption and division.

Athanasius said: Bound more tightly, as though by indissoluble knots, to the truth of divine generation, you seek an escape through I know not what devices of an impious intention—an escape from realities which it is certain the divine nature does not possess. You impute corruption to the incorruptible, suffering to the impassible, and inability to the omnipotent.

Yet, by repeating these charges again and again, no reverence for the divine majesty can restrain you from such impious objections. Rather, as I see, without the least regard for shame, you strive to oppose the venerable birth of the Son. But as you wander more recklessly, and drift with a kind of natural license like the swirling waters of a surging sea, the testimonies of divine authority will restrain you. They will confine you within the fixed limits of the divine confession and will not allow you to pass beyond the boundaries of the legal decrees.

The divine majesty is therefore impressed upon human minds by that sacred oracle of its own confession, in which it testifies that it ineffably generated the Son from the hidden secrets of its substance, saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3).

One thing, then, must be held in this divine testimony. Either he incorruptibly generated the Son from his own ineffable substance, or he did not generate him at all, lest he be corrupted. But I choose that part of the complete faith which more religiously persuades us to serve God as he testifies concerning himself. No obstacle of human suffering, descending from the sacrilege of unbelief, can in any way turn me back, so that I should rightly fail to believe that God could generate, lest he be subject to corruption in the manner of human custom. For I do not doubt that it is sufficient for me to confess that the one who is known to have proceeded from the Father’s womb was born from the substance of God.

[VII] VII. Arius said: As the purpose of your argument shows, you wish to introduce to us a God who is composite and subject to corruption; for you do not fear even to apply to him the bodily designation “womb.” It will therefore be necessary either that he be composed of limbs, if he has a womb, or, as I have said, that he be subject to corruption if he generated from his own substance.

Athanasius said: You would rightly accuse me of holding this view if I had asserted, through the presumption of my own rashness and without any testimony of the divine law, that God possesses a womb. But since God himself, to refute the madness of those unwilling to believe, deigned to pronounce this about himself, teaching more clearly through the designation “womb” that he generated the Son not externally, not from elsewhere, but from himself—that is, from his own substance—why do you brand me with the mark of defective belief? You could rather say this to God: “If you have a womb, you will be composite; if you have generated from yourself, you will be subject to corruption.”

For in God “womb” is understood without any composition of limbs, just as eyes, ears, hands, and feet are said to be present without any outlines of distinctions. Thus you must understand eyes because he sees all things, ears because he hears all things, hands because he performs all things, feet because he is everywhere, and womb because he ineffably generated from himself.

Nor should you unbelievingly suppose that, if he generated from himself, he could therefore be corrupted. It is fitting faithfully to confess that, as omnipotent and incorruptible, he could generate, and yet could not be corrupted by that very generation.

For if he is wondrously believed to have been born incorruptibly from a Virgin contrary to the nature of things, how much more must he be believed to have been generated incorruptibly from the Father? If the substantial nature of the Virgin, which by the condition of its corruptible nature could certainly be subject to suffering and corruption, generated a son with inviolate integrity of chastity and with the virginal barriers unbroken, in the wondrous integrity of incorruption, why should we not rather believe, as I have said, that the incorruptible God could not be corrupted when he incorruptibly generated the Son from himself?

O new and unspeakable, condemnable fear of a monstrous opinion: to confess that the Virgin could not be corrupted by childbirth, yet to fear that God might be subject to corruption and therefore could not generate from his own substance!

By the will of God, then, the Virgin of a corruptible nature generated a son without any loss to her chastity. And he who remains incomparably more incorruptible than all natures—could he not grant himself this, that he might generate the Son incorruptibly from his own substance?

Therefore, since both the words of the divine Scriptures testify that God generated the Son from himself, and Arius himself admitted this in his preceding argument, judge, excellent Probus, who accords more with the divine Scriptures: whether I, who confess that the Son is of one substance with the Father because it is known that he was born from him and not from elsewhere, and who again profess that he generated incorruptibly because the most excellent substance of the divine majesty could in no way be subject to corruption through its ineffable power; or this man, placed in such a crisis of divided understanding that he does not know where to turn the foot of his faith.

For, unwilling to confess that God incorruptibly generated from his own substance, he is drawn into the necessity of confessing that God did not generate him at all. But he will certainly never be able to deny this very thing, since prophetic and apostolic voices everywhere oppose him and cry out with clear proclamation.

[VIII] VIII. Probus the judge said: Whatever I have been able to recognize in the assertion of your arguments, the final judgment of our examination will retain. But now, if you think that anything further remains for you to bring forward from the divine Scriptures that accords with your faith, deign to produce it, so that by the easiest course of argument we may investigate what the truth contains.

Athanasius said: Since I perceive that your Excellence is devoting yourself to this matter with the utmost earnestness and fidelity, so that we may prove from the divine books that the Son was born from the substance of the Father, although the conclusion of all my arguments is shown to be this—that just as human beings, or animals of any kind, beget offspring like their own substance, so that neither a human being begets an ox nor an ox a human being, but each thing procreates according to its likeness, that is, according to its substance—I should not at all wonder that God could generate the Son from his own substance, since all power is subject to him.

But so that my speech may not wander without the testimony of the Scriptures, I shall undertake, fortified by their assistance, to prove from the divine oracles that the Son was ineffably born from the substance of the Father. When I have demonstrated this through a clear path of argument—not from an argument arising from philosophical technique, but, as I have said, from divine proofs—then at last Arius will fall silent, when he learns from the legal utterances, with me as his teacher, that the Son was generated from the substance of the Father.

The apostle Paul, writing about the Son to the Hebrews, says: “Since he is the image of the invisible God, and bears the form of his substance” (Heb. I, 3; Col. I, 15).

Jeremiah too, wisest of the prophets, proclaims concerning the person of God the Father and says: “If they had stood in my substance and heard my word, I would have turned them away from their evil pursuits” (Jer. XXIII, 22). And to prove that he had spoken of the Son, the same prophet adds and says: “Who stood in my substance and saw my word?” (Jer. XXIII, 18).

For that the Son is the Word, the prophet David testifies concerning the person of the Father, saying: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

The evangelist John too, knowing that the Word—that is, the Son—was with the Father in the beginning, and that the Word had never been separated from the Father, placed these words at the beginning of his Gospel, that is, of his proclamation: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

And again, elsewhere Scripture has handed down the saying: “The word is the beginning of the work” (Eccli. XXXVII, 20). This does not mean that, in the creation of the Word—that is, from the creation of the Son—he began to make the other creatures; rather, it means that all things are known to have been created through the Word of God, that is, through the Son.

Hence the prophet David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6). And to show that the Holy Spirit was a partner in this work, he says: “And by the spirit of his mouth all their power.”

There are many testimonies that the divine Scriptures bear concerning the Son, showing that he was begotten from the substance of the Father—that is, from what the Father himself is. Through this substance the Son is proved to be not merely like the Father, but equal to the Father.

This is the faith that Christ handed down to the apostles, and that has come down from the apostles even to us. We cannot alter it in anything, since we know that from the beginning we ought faithfully to preserve it as it was given.

[IX] IX. Arius said: In my preceding argument I began by saying that Athanasius’s unbelief would hurl him headlong into the abyss. For while he wishes to display the eloquence of his speech, he is unknowingly involved in a crime against divine Scripture when he says that the Son is made equal in the substance of God to his begetter, although the Son himself testifies concerning himself and says:

“The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28);

“And he who sent me gave me a commandment” (John XII, 19);

“I did not come of myself, but he sent me” (John VIII, 42);

“I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 38);

“As the Father said to me, so I speak” (John XII, 50);

“What he gave me, I have kept” (John XVII, 12);

“All that he gave me, no one takes away from me” (John VI, 39);

“I will ask him, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels” (Matt. XXVI, 53);

“If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (Matt. XXVI, 42);

“Let this cup pass from me. Not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39);

“I always do the things that please him” (John VIII, 29);

“To sit at my right or left is not mine to give you” (Matt. XX, 23);

“He gave him the name that is above every name, and exalted his servant” (Phil. II, 9);

“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. XLIV, 9);

“He raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand” (Eph. I, 20);

and many other passages like these, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

If, then, he has one greater than himself; if he was sent; if he did not come by his own will; if he did not do his own will; if he speaks what is said to him; if he keeps what was given to him; if he asks; if he prays concerning the cup; if he received his name from another; if he is exalted by another; if he does not grant the seats at his right and left to the disciples who request them by his own authority; if he does what pleases the Father; and if he is raised from the dead by the Father—is it reasonable that one who says so many and such great things about his own subjection should be made equal to the Father?

Probus the judge said: If Athanasius appears to have anything to say against the numerous testimonies of divine authority that Arius has brought forward concerning the Son’s subjection, let him not delay to state it. Let the superstructure of verbal argument be removed, and let the Son be shown from the divine books to be either like, unlike, or equal to the Father, so that, once the truth has been recognized, those things that accord with sound faith and reason may be strengthened.

[X] X. Athanasius said: However far Arius’s cunning may advance in the arrogance of speech, and however much he may applaud himself for the testimonies drawn from divine law that he has brought forward, by which he attempts to separate the Son from equality with the Father, all the passages that he is known to have inserted at length are easily nullified by us through those same testimonies.

Christ, the Son of God, in the form of a servant that he took from the Virgin, is said to be subject to the Father, as the apostle Paul affirms: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV, 4). He, therefore, is said to be subject who is known to have been generated from a woman under the law, and in that form he indicates that the Father is greater than he, which he voluntarily assumed from the Virgin.

In the form of God, the angelic choir is proved to have rendered him service. For it is written in the Gospel: “And the devil departed from him, and angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV, 11).

Arius objects that he did the will of the Father and not his own. In this saying of the Word he ought rather to be recognized as more praiseworthy, because he who equably did the will of the Father showed equality, as the Apostle confirms: “This is the will of God in Christ Jesus” (I Thess. V, 18).

And because he added, “As the Father said to me, so I speak” (John XII, 50), why should the human race, understanding what is right, be disturbed when it hears this word? If Christ were to speak otherwise than God the Father, he would then more properly be called unequal or unlike the Father. But if the Son speaks what the Father speaks, he is never found unequal or unlike the Father.

“He gave me,” he says, “I have kept,” and “All that he gave me, no one takes away from me.” Divine gifts must be understood as having been attributed to the Son in this way. For the Father gave power to the omnipotent Son, bestowed majesty on Majesty, gave strength to Strength, wisdom to Wisdom, foreknowledge to Foreknowledge, eternity to Eternity, divinity to Divinity, equality to the Equal, immortality to the Immortal, invisibility to the Invisible, kingship to the King, life to Life—and he did not give him anything different from what he has, but gave as much as he has, along with whatever else the Father is shown to have conferred upon the Son indivisibly and inseparably.

Yet he is shown to have given all these things to one who already possessed them rather than to one who lacked them, to whom the Son says: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (John XVII, 10).

[XI] XI. If all those things that the Father is said to have conferred upon the Son appear to be one thing in the Father and another in the Son, we unquestionably make the Son a liar, since he says that the things belonging to the Father are his own. But if the Son is found to be a liar in what he said, and the evangelist is likewise deceived in every respect when he says, “Making himself equal to God” (John V, 18), then it will follow that the Father is shown to have conferred nothing upon the Son fully or truthfully, and that the Son is not recognized as the true God.

But if the things that the Father inseparably and indistinguishably conferred upon the Son are true—as indeed they are—let the tongues of foolish people fall silent, those who strive to separate the Son from the substance of the Father.

The Son asks the Father in order to show that he bears true humanity. For, to make known the power of his divinity, he commanded the sea and the winds, and he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves. As a man in sorrow he accepted the cup of suffering; but as God he offered believers the fountain of living water springing up into eternal life.

He received a name so that in this name heavenly, earthly, and infernal things might bow down. He was exalted from the depths to the heights—that is, from the flesh of human weakness ascending to God—and he sits at the right hand of Majesty, so that human weakness may not hesitate to follow where it sees its Head glorified.

He was anointed so that by the anointing of his chrism we might be cleansed from the stain of the former man’s sin. He was raised from the dead so that by the example of his resurrection we might be freed from the sting of death.

He testifies that he cannot give the seats to the disciples who request them, lest division arise among them. For he who said, “It is not mine to give you” (Matt. XX, 23), also said, “I will that where I am, these also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

He did what pleased the Father because he does not know how to do anything contrary. For he who said, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 38), also said, “To do your will, my God, I have desired” (Ps. XXXIX, 9), and “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8).

He who said, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28), also said, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); “That they may be one in us, as you and I are one” (John XVII, 22); “All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine” (John XVII, 10); “Do you believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 10); “My Father works, and I work” (John V, 17); “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (John V, 21); “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9); “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (John XV, 23); “Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1); “I have glorified you upon the earth” (ibid., 4); and “I have manifested your name to the people” (ibid., 6).

And so that every intention of human quibbling may cease, I shall bring forward as a witness John the Evangelist, whose testimony I used earlier, who says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

If these many testimonies, so suitable to divinity, by which we have shown that the Father and the Son are one, are not sufficient for the unbelieving, we may, if it seems good, add others.

[XII] XII. Probus the judge said: If Arius attempts to oppose this argument, so strong and so certain, it is clear that he is not following reason but wandering recklessly through the fields of irrational words. Until now, he has been unable to demonstrate his assertion concerning the doctrine of three substances, as he admitted earlier, though Athanasius has shown at length the evidence for one substance.

Arius said: Is it because Athanasius, from the divine oracles and through I know not what arguments, has rashly dared to affirm that the Son is of one substance and equal to the Father, that he must therefore confer upon the Spirit, who is the minister of the Father and the Son, an equal confession? The Son himself says:

“He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine” (John XVI, 14);

“I will send you the Spirit of truth” (John XV, 26);

“The Spirit will proceed from me” (John XVI, 15);

“Whom the Father will send in my name” (John IV, 26);

and the Father says to the bones of the dead: “I will give my Spirit into you, and you shall live” (Ezek. XXXVII, 5).

Must the one who is sent or proceeds from the Father be made equal to the one from whom he proceeds? The prophet testifies concerning him and says: “Behold, the Lord who establishes thunder and creates the Spirit” (Amos IV, 13).

Surely a creature will never appear to me to be made equal to its Creator, or to be able to share the same power with him.

Athanasius said: If the clemency of the judge grants and permits it, I shall briefly demonstrate from divine authorities that the Holy Spirit is not a creature, but God and Creator with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0176D] Probus the judge said: As your profession declares, prove briefly what reason requires to be demonstrated. Show from the testimonies of the divine Scriptures—not from the argument of speech—that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father or the Son, or, as you yourself have confessed, that he is God or the Creator and partner in the common work. When you have proved these things through truthful testimonies, let Arius withdraw from his intention, convicted by the profession of the true faith.

[XIII] XIII. Athanasius said: Before I prove that the Holy Spirit is God, I shall establish through the words of the law that he is the Creator of all things. For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

And in Solomon: “He himself,” he says, “created her through his Spirit” (Eccli. I, 9).

And in the Psalm: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. CIII, 30).

And in the book of Job: “The divine Spirit,” he says, “who made me” (Job XXXIII, 4).

And Judith: “All your creation,” she says, “serves you, because you spoke, and they were made; you sent your Spirit, and he built” (Judith XVI, 17).

The Holy Spirit is shown to possess such great power, or power of creation, that, with his cooperation, the body of the Lord Jesus Christ—which has been given to us in the sacrament of faith—was formed in the Virgin’s womb, as the evangelist says: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife; for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20).

And again: “Before they came together,” he says, “she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 18). This does not mean that the Holy Spirit should be called the Father of our Savior, so that two Fathers might be believed; rather, it means that the same Holy Spirit is found to be a fellow worker with the Father and the Son, and their partner in one power, as the Lord declares: “Go,” he says to the disciples, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Therefore, if he is a minister, as your sacrilegious profession maintains, how is it that without him nothing is conferred upon believers in the sacrament of faith? For just as the Lord sent the apostles to preach, so the Holy Spirit is likewise declared to act.

Thus we find it written in the Acts of the Apostles: While Peter was pondering the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: “Behold, three men are seeking you. Rise, go with them, doubting nothing, because I sent them to you” (Acts X, 19–20).

And again: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have taken them” (Acts XIII, 2).

And again: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Acts XX, 28).

If he sends apostles, appoints bishops, and, as was shown above, created all things together with the Father and the Son, in what respect will such majesty possess the role of an inferior or a minister, as you do not fear to confess?

[XIV] XIV. And that he is also God, as I remember promising, I shall establish by these testimonies. The prophet David says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. LXXXIV, 9).

There is therefore no doubt that all the prophets announce or speak only through the Holy Spirit, as it is written in the Gospel: “When that Holy Spirit comes,” he says, “whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and announce future things to you” (John XIV, 26; XVI, 13).

And again the Lord says through the prophet: “They were unwilling to hear my words, which I commanded through my Spirit by the mouth of the former prophets, says the Lord” (Zech. VII, 12).

But lest, as we run through the testimony of the divine law like flowering meadows, we wander too far from our proposition, let us return to what we promised.

Paul, preacher to the Gentiles, also writes to the Hebrews and says: “The Holy Spirit also testifies to us; and this is the covenant that I will establish with them after those days, says the Lord” (Heb. VIII, 10).

In the Acts of the Apostles, we remember that Peter said to Ananias: “Why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3). And showing that he is the same as God, he says in what follows: “You have not lied to men, but to God” (ibid., 4).

And Paul says to the Corinthians: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4–6).

Behold: as the Apostle preaches, the Holy Spirit is declared to be the same God and the same Lord.

In the Gospel, as has already been said, the Lord himself says: “The Spirit is God” (John IV, 24).

Likewise, writing to the Corinthians, Paul says: “The Lord is the Spirit” (II Cor. III, 17).

And to the Ephesians: “Do not grieve,” he says, “the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you have been sealed” (Eph. IV, 30).

Likewise, to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?” And showing that he is God, he adds and says: “Glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 19–20).

And to demonstrate most clearly that the Holy Spirit is God and Lord, the angel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

[XV] XV. Behold by how many proofs from divine testimonies we have shown that the Holy Spirit is God and possesses one power or fellowship with the Father and the Son. I do not know what answer remains for the unbelieving. The apostle Paul most clearly demonstrated that the Holy Spirit has one fellowship with the Father and the Son, saying: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (II Cor. XIII, 13).

Probus the judge said: If Arius thinks that anything remains after the innumerable testimonies proclaimed by heavenly teaching, let him not hesitate to propose it. Although, as I judge, no answer remains for him by which he can drive Athanasius away from the doctrine of one substance—that is, homousion. But lest he later complain of having been oppressed, we take away no opportunity from him to respond.

Arius said: There is no doubt that Athanasius does not cease, by magical arts, to pervert the judge’s senses, so that he cannot hold to the path of right faith toward those who religiously follow and honor it. Therefore, what I am unable to explain in the examination before your Eminence, I shall reserve for the judgment of the emperor, where the investigation of truth prevails and where it must be believed that magical arts cannot prevail over observance of the true faith.

Athanasius said: Those who cannot support their assertions do not cease to find excuses for themselves through all kinds of deceptive arguments and quibbles, as your Eminence clearly sees Arius doing now. For my part, since I am defending the true faith, it is sufficient that I have answered everything he proposed in the presence of your Eminence.

[XVI] XVI. Probus the judge said: It is characteristic of the ignorant and of those who presume too little upon their own knowledge or teaching to devote themselves to perversity rather than to grant patience to the truth, when it is proper for defenders of the faith to follow the truth rather than be impeded by the fetter of error or falsehood.

It is the custom of such men, when they see the case for their unbelief reaching its conclusion, to fear that their unbelief will become known to all people and to turn to the presence of a more powerful person. They do not know that even there victory is granted to the truth where a generous judgment of power is proclaimed.
