Arius therefore appears to appeal in vain from our judgment to the person of the emperor, since in the conflict of the contest he has felt no injustice directed against him. It is clear that he has been completely unable to detach Athanasius from the defense of the homousion—which is one substance. But, as his superfluous intention has decreed, I shall in no way restrain him from doing so, lest, unable to endure the role of the defeated, he boast of the time taken away from him.

It will be the task of my diligence to make known to the ears of the glorious emperor everything that both parties have brought forward in our hearing, so that, once deceitful evasions have been removed, Athanasius, defender of the pure faith, may attain the palm of victory.

[Col. 0179A]

**A Dialogue of Vigilius of Tapsus against the Arians, etc., with Athanasius, Arius, Sabellius, Photinus, and Probus the Judge as speakers. (C, S)**

[Col. 0179]

**Preface of an Uncertain Author. (C)**
[Col. 0179B] 118 When this book, composed by the Catholic priest and most exemplary man, the blessed Athanasius, against the heretics Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius, comes into the hands of an energetic reader, most blessed Pope Maternus, he will immediately reply:

“How could Arius have engaged in controversy with the holy Athanasius, successor of the blessed bishop Alexander, when it is established that Arius, as one reads in ecclesiastical History, was poured out in the most shameful death—that is, after the example of Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ—so that what he had conceived in his foul mind he might bring to a foul end?”

But if he recalls what Sulpicius Severus of blessed memory wrote in his Chronicles, saying, “Two Ariuses, like two serpents, hissed from one mouth,” he will clearly discover that there were two Ariuses. Hence it is understood either that the holy Athanasius engaged in conflict with the surviving Arius, not with the one who was poured out, or with some Arian-minded man. Therefore these matters—an undertaking which, as we believe, was fulfilled by God—ought frequently to be reread by Catholics, so that they may learn how to avoid the poisons of heretics and, with God’s help, preserve their faith without any hesitation.

## PREFACE OF VIGILIUS

[Col. 0179C] 119 As I had long and earnestly been considering with myself the truth of the faith, and was searching the Scriptures to discover how I might refute the manifold and numerous questions of the heretics with brief replies, and overcome their sacrilegious statements, spread through various lengthy treatises, by a concise contest of argument—lest, by reporting lengthy matters at greater length, I should leave readers an interminable and excessively burdensome work—it appeared useful and most convenient to introduce each heretic’s person, together with his profession of doctrine, as though those present were debating with those present.

And lest the arguments of the several parties should come into doubt without anyone examining them, I arranged for a certain arbiter named Probus, exercising judicial authority, to be present. By discerning each matter reasonably, he would nullify the purpose of impious perversity. I therefore introduced Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius, and, on our side, Athanasius, so that the truth, refined through the supreme contest of the disputants, might come to everyone’s knowledge, and so that the varied arrangement of this work, diversified by the persons, answers, and exchanges, might remove weariness from its readers.

## BOOK ONE OF THE DIALOGUES

[Col. 0179D] **I. Probus the Judge said:** Observing that no majesty of the true deity exists in the worship of idols, I wish to submit myself to the doctrines of the Christians, by which it is affirmed that there is one true God, who by the power of his Word created all things that are seen and those that are not seen.

And since many are reckoned under the title of the Christian name, yet are said to wander far from the truth of that faith—holding different opinions, obviously, and following varied systems of doctrine—I now greatly desire to know what the faith of right doctrine is, so that, when all doubtful evasions have been removed, I may cling firmly to it. I do not wish, while seeking to be stripped of the blindness of error, to become entangled in greater errors of darkness by becoming indiscriminately and without any distinction of examination an imitator of whatever sect first presents itself, ignorant whether it is perverse or not, or whether it is supported by truth.

Therefore, if it pleases you—indeed, because it ought to please you—let each of you disclose before us the position of his faith, so that, after examination, we may all rightly yield to whichever is found firmer and truer, and follow it without hesitation, rejecting the error of falsehood.

**All said:** How can we entrust to you the secrets of so great a mystery, and place the judgment of a matter you have not experienced in your hands, when you have not yet washed away the stains of paganism by apprehending true doctrine?

**Probus the Judge said:** This is precisely what I desire with all my strength to learn: what the right and truthful doctrine is, in which I ought to receive the sacraments of the hidden mystery. For at present I do not seek to have the profound secrets of the mysteries disclosed to me; rather, I now demand that those things be demonstrated which are held externally in your faith and preached publicly—namely, that one and the same true God is the creator of visible and invisible things.

And because I know that you all profess this with one voice, what reason has arisen for your being divided into so many sects, so that we cannot understand at all which is true and which false, until, through a contest among you conducted with proper patience and restraint, we have carefully learned what is fitting?

**II. Athanasius said:** Since you are versed in every kind of literature and highly trained in philosophical disciplines, you ought not to be surprised in any way that many and varied novel doctrines have arisen among us, since among you also as many novel opinions have emerged as there are almost names of their authors.

For although there are three religions in the world—the religions of the Jews, the pagans, and the Christians—each religion, departing from itself through many and widely differing varieties of opinion, has been divided into various sects of its own institution. Each person, enticed by the attractiveness of a newer opinion, which presents not truth but a likeness of truth, abandons the line handed down from ancient times by the fathers. He then wanders irretrievably through trackless places, using novelty in place of antiquity, as though cutting a road through an ancient boundary and a path handed down by the fathers.

For either he thinks too much or believes too little, and therefore does not know how to walk along the middle and royal road. I have prefaced these remarks for this reason: to show you the clearest indications by which truth may be investigated, so that you may easily recognize that the person is entangled in the error of perversity who, abandoning the ancient institutions of the apostolic faith, dreams up for himself, according to his own will, the faith he ought to follow.

**Arius said:** Athanasius very well declares that the error of perfidy consists in additions and recently invented novelties of doctrine, agreeing in this with the apostolic testimony which says: “Avoid profane novelties of words” (1 Tim. 6:20). Therefore, I beg you not to depart from this path of inquiry, but to investigate more carefully and attentively who uses the ancient and who the new testimony of the faith (variant: “sacrament of the faith”).

**Probus the Judge said:** So that what you assert may become readily known, and may come into the light of truth after every darkness of ambiguity has been removed, disclose the rule of the ancient faith, and state it to our ears just as it was handed down by the apostles.

**III. All said:** We believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit. This is the rule of our faith, which the Lord handed down to the apostles by heavenly instruction, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

**Probus the Judge said:** I am held fast in great astonishment at this astounding matter, seeing that you proclaim three gods, from whom I had believed one must take refuge in the majesty of the singular power of one God. Therefore, I ask that you deign briefly to instruct us what the faith of this reasoning is, or what these names of three things and three designations signify.

**Sabellius said:** You certainly did not hear us proclaiming three gods; rather, we simply professed that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as it was handed down to us by the apostles.

For when we name the Father, we do not intend one to be understood as the Father and another as the Son; rather, we proclaim this same one to be both Father and Son. For God, by the ineffable power of his might, with which he fills all things, filled the womb of the Virgin Mary and, in order to expiate human sins, assumed from himself the substance of fleshly matter without any change in himself. He visibly displayed himself to human sight, and in that very man whom he assumed he is called the Son, although it is not one and another but the same Father who is understood.

For this reason we worship one God, understanding not one and another, as I have said, but professing this same one to be the one true God.

**IV. Photinus said:** Sabellius has impiously professed that God the Father was born through the Virgin, introducing into so great a majesty I know not what defect of extension, so that, by being extended in the Virgin, he himself is both Father and Son—something no Christian would grant him.

Therefore I say rather that God the Father has the Lord Jesus Christ as his Son, taking his beginning from the Virgin Mary. Through the most excellent and inimitable merit of his holy conduct and blessedness, he was adopted by God the Father as a son and endowed with the supreme honor of divinity.

But God, inviolable and immeasurable, neither begot another from himself nor was he ever begotten himself, so that he might rightly be believed either to have a Son from himself or to be his own Son. Rather, he is unique and singular: not subject to suffering by begetting, not increased by extending himself, and not subjected to division by transferring a portion of himself into the Virgin.

**Arius said:** I confess that the unbegotten Father ineffably begot the Son before all times, through whom and in whom he made visible and invisible creatures. Sent by the Father in the last times for the salvation of the human race, he bore a true human being in the world, whom he inviolate received from the Virgin Mary without the mingling of human intercourse.

Although he is God and Lord of his creation, he cannot nevertheless be compared with or made equal to his begetter in all things or in anything, since he professes both his God and the author of his origin. Yet there are not therefore two gods because this one also is God; nor is he therefore not God because the Father alone is God.

Just as he is not therefore not good because the Father alone is good according to the Son’s own profession, since the Son is not only good but also the creator of good things, so it is not taken away from him that he is good because the Father alone is good. In the same way, it is not taken away from him that he is God because the Father alone is God.

And just as the goodness of the Son does not prejudice the singularity of the Father’s goodness, so his divinity does not hinder the Father from being the one and singular God. In this way we profess one God—not denying, as I have said, that the Son is God, but assigning to the Father alone the authority of the one divinity.

**V. Athanasius said:** Arius has rightly defined in his profession that the Father ineffably begot the Son from himself before all times. But in this statement he has so far kept silent about whether he wishes to assert that the Son was begotten from the very essence or nature of the Father, or from elsewhere.

For I confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and of one nature, so that I believe that the Son was begotten from the Father, not from nothing nor from something else, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. And although I profess that there are three persons subsisting in their own distinct properties, nevertheless one nature and one divinity are established in them.

**Probus the Judge said:** Although this varied and widely divergent difference among your opinions casts a great darkness of confusion over our minds, nevertheless, so that we may quickly be freed from these evasions and learn what the profession of the true faith is, deign to support your positions with clearer testimonies from divine Scripture.

And lest you wander far afield through the diffuseness of a confused disputation and a lengthy circuit of speech, let each of you fight individually against the others. Thus, when all take up the weapons of their questions against one, support one another against the dissenter in those matters which you know to be common to you.

But if you have nothing in common in the faith, let each rely upon his own professions, so that it may readily become clear whether he himself does not entirely stumble over those things which he condemns in another.

If it pleases you, then, enter into conflict with Sabellius, and let him defend his side against you, so that, if you are able to overcome him, he may depart defeated. After him, Photinus must submit himself to the contest and defend his faith with truthful testimonies. Against him all of you must close the line of battle, so that, if he too yields after being overcome, he may leave room in the disputation for the others who follow.

In this way, I think, we can reach the investigation of truth as quickly as possible. Let Sabellius therefore, as I said, be permitted to prove his faith by heavenly proofs.

**VI. Sabellius said:** Since you have ordered me to engage with all of them, let them answer whether they confess that God is of a simple nature.

**Arius said:** What impious person would deny this?

**Sabellius said:** Let them also answer whether everything that is said about God is to be understood according to substance.

**Arius said:** These matters are recognized as proper to our faith.

**Photinus said:** I agree that everything about God is said according to substance.

**Athanasius said:** I should not rashly declare that everything said about God must be understood according to substance, because of certain relative uses of names, expressed according to the customary language of human speech, which are applied not properly to God but to persons, times, or whatever kinds of things.

This is the case when he says that he does not know, or when he admits that he has come to know again, or when he feels regret for things he has made, or shows himself now angry and now appeased. If we wish to understand all these things according to essence, we shall unquestionably profess the divine nature to be passible and without foreknowledge, a nature in which either ignorance or knowledge arising in time may occur, and which sorrow may exhaust through repentance while joy may invigorate.

What else will this be than to suffer change and to flow here and there with unstable motion? Hence it is most clearly established that not everything said about God ought to be understood according to substance; rather, some things correspond to his dispensation and do not accord with his nature—this we must profess with complete certainty.

**Probus the Judge said:** Although you have answered sufficiently and learnedly, with commendable brevity, that not everything about God is said according to substance, I nevertheless desire to hear these matters from you at greater length when the time for your part of the disputation arrives. For now, as I said before, let Sabellius continue as he had begun.

**VII. Sabellius said:** The profession of our faith, as I said above, proclaims this same one to be God both Father and Son, lest we be convicted of asserting two gods according to pagan error if we proclaim one as Father and another as Son.

Therefore, from those very statements which people who do not understand or understand less well think to be opposed to us, I shall demonstrate most clearly that the supreme and almighty God is one person.

For what else does “The Father who remains in me does the works” (John 14:10) mean than “I, remaining in myself, do the works”? And what else does “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9) mean than “I am myself the Father who am the Son”—so that, through contemplation of one divinity, you may understand there to be one person?

Likewise, when he says, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me,” or when Isaiah says to the same one, “In you is God, and there is no God besides you” (Isa. 45:14), he unquestionably wished to indicate more clearly that he remains ineffably in himself, without the intermixture of another person.

For if, as they too concede and as they acknowledged above, the divine nature is simple, it cannot be that, as though it were empty within itself, it contains within itself the person of another nature and is itself in turn contained by another. It is necessary either that it contract itself by diminishing itself, or empty itself by being evacuated, or spread itself out by expanding—because this is the condition of things contained and containing: either the receptacle must be enlarged by space in order to receive another, or what is to be received must be diminished by some contraction so that it can be contained within the nature emptied out to receive it.

Since these notions can in no way fit that simple and ineffable nature, it undoubtedly remains to understand that one and the same person, remaining in himself, appears to say of himself alone, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38), and “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9). Otherwise, if you wish to understand this as spoken of two, you will nevertheless be convicted of asserting two gods, separately distinguished.

Or, if you defend their remaining in one another in such a way that you say they have one nature, you will appear to profess some twofold form of persons, resembling a portent emerging from the beginning of a single thing, or dwelling in the substance of one nature in a confused and intermixed manner. In this way you will defend the simple and undefiled nature of divine power as composed of qualities unworthy of it.

Turn rather to those singular proclamations of the saints from heaven by which the divinity of the one who remains in one person is proclaimed, as Moses admonishes, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4).

And as God himself repeatedly testifies: “See, see, that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32:39). And again: “You are my witnesses, whether there is another God besides me” (Isa. 43:10).

We must not nullify, by confessing another God, a judgment drawn down to us from heaven with such authority, lest, to our destruction, we cancel the command of so great a proclamation and undergo the punishments due to worshipers of gods.

**VIII. Probus the Judge said:** If you think anything can be brought forward against this powerful argument, deign to plead your case.

**Arius said:** While Sabellius attempts to free himself from the error of a twofold divinity by a plausible and exceedingly useful confession of one God, he falls into the impiety of the Jewish understanding by sacrilegiously denying that the Son of God remains in his own substance and possesses a proper person.

I shall restrain the audacity of this most insane madness, using whatever brevity I can, by the authority of heavenly testimonies, in order to demonstrate the Son’s properly subsisting person—not adducing those testimonies which, as they quibble, apply to the man who was assumed, but bringing forward those which all alike acknowledge to pertain to his divinity without any uncertainty of interpretation.

In Genesis we read that the Lord said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Behold, he spoke in the plural: “Let us make,” clearly indicating another to whom the speech of the speaking God was addressed.

For it must not be understood so absurdly that he was speaking in such a way as to say to himself, “Let us make”—something proper only to those who have fallen into a state of madness. To show that one spoke to another, Scripture immediately added, saying: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (ibid., 27). If there were only one, it would have said that he made him in his own image. But now it more clearly describes one making him in the image of another.

Likewise, when the divinity had condemned the land of the Sodomites and its inhabitants to be burned by fiery rains because of their many deeds of unspeakable wickedness, the account says: “The Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24). Nothing could have been stated more clearly to reveal the Father and demonstrate the Son according to the Law: one hurled sulfurous flames from heaven from the other, not one from himself.

**IX.** The Son himself also speaks to Jacob, saying: “I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God” (Gen. 31:13). He could have said, “who appeared to you in my place,” if the person of the speaker were understood to be one.

Likewise: “Go up,” he says, “to Bethel and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you” (Gen. 35:1). This too can never apply to a single person, where one, so clearly distinguished from another, commands a shrine to be established. It would have been appropriate for a solitary person to say: “Make an altar to me, the God who appeared to you.”

Likewise God the Father speaks through the prophet Hosea about peoples to be saved in God the Son, saying: “I will save them in the Lord their God” (Hos. 1:7).

Likewise David, speaking to the Son of God, says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Ps. 44:7–8). What could have been said more clearly to remove the error of this confession, where God is recorded as having anointed God?

For now I have selected these few passages from the Old Testament. I have omitted many more and clearer passages for the sake of brevity; they establish more brightly than daylight that both the Father and the Son exist with distinct and separate properties of substance.

But as for Sabellius’s attempt, on the basis of the statement “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38), to demonstrate one nature or one person—namely, his argument that one thing cannot be within another without confusion and intermixture, apart from the other kinds of defects which, in the manner of sophistical questions, he wished to introduce—these words do not indicate one substance or one person any more than the nature of God and human beings can be one, although it is said that they are in God and God is in them.

Finally, the Son himself, speaking to the Father about believers, says: “That just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so they too may be in us” (John 17:21). And again: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). The Apostle also says concerning the uninstructed person: “Falling prostrate, he will confess that God is truly among you” (1 Cor. 14:25).

Therefore, just as when God is in us and we are in God there is no confusion of person, no unity of nature, no addition of increase, no subtraction of diminution, and no quality of a mutable substance, whether composite or ordered, but by the holiness of pure and simple faith we prepare a dwelling for the Lord in us, and he receives us into his dwelling as we remain in him by doing his will, so the Father and the Son are understood to remain in one another through an indissoluble bond of will.

**X. Probus the Judge said:** Since you have demonstrated by such clear proofs of testimony that the Father and the Son properly subsist—which Sabellius denied by casting clouds of questions over human minds—it is now asked of your side how, while separately and distinctly professing both God the Father and God the Son, you do not appear to introduce a plurality into the number of the divinity.

And although you have briefly touched upon a few points concerning this in your preceding argument, the proof of such a question must nevertheless be broad and specific. You will have to explain it more fully when the examination of the disputation between you and Athanasius begins.

And since, as I said, Sabellius’s perfidy has now been refuted by a truthful argument, let Photinus, if he can, come forward with certain testimonies in support of his faith.

**Photinus said:** I assign a beginning to our Lord Jesus Christ, and affirm that he was a mere human being who, through the supreme merit of a blessed life, attained the honor of divinity.

For who is carried in a woman’s womb and brought forth by birth? Who, having experienced the cradle of infancy and been nourished by milk, was carried in his mother’s arms? Who underwent growth in age? Who fulfilled all the conditions of bodily weakness—suffering hunger, being assaulted by the temptation of the most wicked spirit, being wearied by fatigue, sinking into sleep, being seized and bound in chains, being beaten with scourges and struck with blows, being mocked by the taunts of those who insulted him, being hung upon the gibbet of the cross and suffering the loss of life?

Whom the human condition subjected to parents; whose brotherly names of both sexes are designated; who is mistaken about knowledge of places; who asks about the name of the evil spirit; who confesses that he does not know the day of judgment; who testifies that he does not possess the power of assigning seats; who complains that he has been abandoned on the cross; who is shaken by fear of suffering and terror of death, and for this reason asks that the cup be taken from him; and who endures so many other things—too many to recount here—that pertain to humanity: who is so foolish as to think that these things are appropriate to God?

**XI.** For those miracles of power must be believed to have been performed not by his own power, but by God through him, just as he himself says: “The Father who remains in me does the works” (John 14:10). And again: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19).

Because he was greatly acceptable to God, he obtained by prayers whatever he wished. For if life was restored to the dead, light to the blind, strength to the weak, cleansing to lepers, if the sea and winds yielded, and if the creation of food experienced an increase through multiplied abundance, all these things are known to have been elicited only by the gift of prayer.

In a similar way, certain prophets accomplished works in God’s name. But because this man showed himself so worthy and so dear to God by persevering in his commandments—as he himself says, “I always do the things that please him” (John 8:29)—and because the Father also speaks to him through an angel, as it is written in Zechariah:

“The angel of the Lord stood and testified to Jesus: Thus says the Lord God of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you too shall judge my house” (Zech. 3:5),

and because he endured death calmly for the salvation of the world, for this reason, I say, because he showed himself so great and such a person, God gave him authority over all things and established him as God of the whole creation, as the Apostle teaches, saying:

“He humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:8).

Hence, after the Passion—which conferred such merit upon him—he himself also said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18).

But if he had been God before the ages, he would not have received authority in time, an authority which it was established that he had always possessed. Rather, as I have said, on account of the distinguished merit of his obedience and Passion, he was endowed with divine honor and exalted above all, as Peter also says:

“The God of our fathers raised up his servant Jesus” (Acts 3:13). And again: “Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God” (Acts 2:33). And again: “Let the whole house of Israel know with complete certainty that God made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 4:10).

This shows even more clearly that, because of the Passion of the cross, he was made God in time, not born God before the ages. Hence Paul also says: “He was made better than the angels, insofar as he received a name more excellent than theirs” (Heb. 1:4). For whatever is made or received takes its beginning from time.

Everywhere the divine utterances testify that he took the beginning of his origin from the seed of David, as God speaks to David, saying: “The son who will come forth from your loins, he shall build me a house” (1 Kings 8:19). And again: “From the fruit of your womb I shall place upon my throne” (Ps. 131:11). And Isaiah says: “Behold, the root of Jesse shall arise to rule the nations” (Isa. 11:10). And the Apostle says: “Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David” (Rom. 1:3). And again: “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, from the seed of David” (2 Tim. 2:8). And the angel says to Mary: “God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32).

From these and many other passages it is therefore demonstrated even more clearly that he was not God before the ages, but advanced into God through the merit of good action.

**XII. Probus the Judge said:** Let the responses coming from the opposing side answer the questions raised by Photinus.

**Athanasius said:** If you carefully observe what Arius argued against Sabellius, you will there also recognize that Photinus’s perfidy has likewise been excluded.

**Probus the Judge said:** How so?

**Athanasius said:** By confessing one person, Sabellius denied that the Son subsisted before the origin of all the ages. Photinus too undertakes to assert this with impious inventions, assigning to the Son a beginning from human birth and testifying that he did not exist at all before it. This sacrilegious opinion has been refuted, and more fully so, by Arius. For he clearly and plainly demonstrated that the Son of God, who is God, subsisted before the ages.

**Probus the Judge said:** I certainly remember that Arius dealt sufficiently with the Son’s distinct and subsisting person against Sabellius. But the order and logic of the disputation require that Photinus’s assertion also be removed by a proper barrier of refutation against those who oppose it, lest, by striving too much for brevity, you appear to omit necessary matters.

For he has introduced no small challenge to his faith by asserting with many proofs that the Son of God received his beginning from Mary and advanced into God through the merit of most distinguished action.

**Athanasius said:** Neither Arius nor I shall shrink from censuring Photinus’s madness by the authorities of divine Scripture. He has advanced to such insanity that, opposing prophetic and apostolic statements with the deranged mind of his fury, he has brought forward, as an insult to so great a majesty, certain most contemptible examples of diminution—things which God voluntarily endured for the sake of our redemption.

**XIII. Arius said:** The voices of the Jews insulting Christ, or the blasphemies of the thief who was crucified, are more tolerable to hear than the unspeakable perfidy of this Photinus can be endured.

For who could tolerate the proclamation that he was a mere human being, or that he took his beginning from Mary, when he himself testifies that he came from heaven and was begotten before the ages? Speaking of the Father and revealing the mystery of eternal birth, he says:

“Before the ages he established me, and before all the hills he begot me. When he prepared the heavens, I was with him” (Prov. 8:23).

The Father also speaks to the same one, saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). Since the stars were placed as signs of the times, God the Father testifies that the birth of his Son existed before the origin of the stars—that is, before the sequence of all times.

Or we may understand “before the morning star” spiritually, as meaning before the creation of the angels, since it is said concerning an angel: “Morning star, who used to rise in the morning” (Isa. 14:12).

**Photinus said:** This is understood to have been spoken according to the truth of predestination, as the Apostle testifies and says: “Who was predestined as the Son of God in power” (Rom. 1:4).

For “Before the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:25), or “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3), was spoken even though he was born in the last times, just as the Apostle asserts that the election of the saints took place before the beginning of the ages. “He chose us,” he says, “before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4).

Yet they were not chosen until the end of the world. Therefore, just as the apostles, who did not subsist before the ages, are nevertheless said to have been chosen in predestination, so, by the same mode of understanding, the statement that Christ was born before the ages is to be understood as spoken of him in predestination.

For it is customary in divine Scripture to narrate what will certainly happen as though it had already happened. Hence the prophet says: “He who made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint), that is, things made in predestination but not yet existing in reality.

In the same way, the Son’s birth, predestined before the ages, truly arose at the end of time.

**Probus the Judge said:** That birth of the Son which was predestined before the world is described as proceeding from the womb of God the Father; yet you testify that the Son received his beginning from Mary.

**XIV. Photinus said:** But it is not for that reason to be understood that Christ was born from God the Father, whether because he himself confesses that he was begotten from the Father or because the Father confesses that he begot him.

For God the Father is accustomed to say this concerning adopted or adoptive sons, as it is said through Isaiah: “I have begotten sons and exalted them” (Isa. 1:2). And again: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4:22).

And John says: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:18); and, he says, “he cannot sin, because the birth from God preserves him.”

Therefore, simply because faithful human beings are said to have been born from God, is the origin of their human birth thereby taken away? Or, before they were born from human beings, are they to be believed to have existed before the beginning of the world through the remembrance of divine birth?

Arius said: Since Photinus opposes the most manifest truth with the cunning art of disputation, he must be broken by the most evident authority of divine Scripture. For the apostle John—foreseeing, I believe, this madness long beforehand in the Holy Spirit—testifies that the Son substantially existed with God the Father before the beginning of the ages. Thus, by the proclamation of his most radiant voice, he awakens Photinus, sunk in the deep sleep of ignorance and buried in deadly slumber, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). Therefore, for him who was in the beginning with God, it is not left open to have received the beginning of his origin from a human being at the end of time. And lest anyone should think that this Word, which was in the beginning with God, was merely a sound passing through the divine utterance, he says: “And the Word was God” (ibid.). But if this Word was God, he was a continuing substance, not a passing sound. For the power of an established nature is shown, which is proclaimed to have existed and to exist substantially.

And since I now see Sabellius also standing here with us in this audience, I will brandish against both of them the weapons of this testimony, and from the same place where I kill Photinus I will destroy Sabellius. Let Sabellius hear that God was with God, and cease from his doctrine of a single person. Let Photinus hear that this Word existed as God in the beginning, and cease attributing his beginning to the virgin Mary. “He,” he says, “was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:2). “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (ibid., 10). Does the creator precede the making of his creation, or does he not?

### XV

Probus the judge said: It is established that the creator precedes the making of his work; for it cannot be admitted in any reasonable way that he began afterward who existed as the author of what was made.

Arius said: If, therefore, all things were made through the Son, and the world was made through him, it is evident that the Son existed before the world, or before all things that were made.

Probus the judge said: Nothing more evident than this proof could be demonstrated.

Arius said: But lest perhaps the proof of one apostle should seem insufficient to the unbelieving, if you command it, I will append in a brief statement further testimonies asserting that the Son subsisted before the ages.

Probus the judge said: Although, as I think, nothing is more useful or more powerful than this testimony, nevertheless, so that you may strengthen your assertion with testimonies of diverse proofs, pursue a few points, as you say, within the limits of brevity.

Arius said: It is the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Gospel, saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). And again: “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38). It is therefore evident that he already existed who had descended from heaven, so that Photinus may be put to shame; and that he is another from the Father, since he does not presume to do anything according to the choice of his own will, but in everything carries out the will of the Father who sent him, so that Sabellius and those like him may fall silent.

Likewise: “Father,” he says, “glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). Behold, he testifies that before the foundation of the world he had possessed glory and honor with the Father. Let Sabellius hear of one with another; let Photinus hear that he possessed glory before the beginning of the world.

Likewise, showing that he was in the proper form of divinity before he assumed the form of a servant, the Apostle says: “Who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6). He was therefore already God, since he is taught to have emptied himself of the form of God in order to become human.

Likewise Jeremiah more clearly reveals that he was God before he deigned to assume human form, saying: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him, who found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen one. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36). Let Photinus, if he can, dissolve by any argument these proofs, so firm and so exceedingly strong, drawn from divine authorities.

### XVI

Probus the judge said: If Photinus still desires to oppose documents so manifest and so complete, it is certain that he is driven by the vice of diseased contention, since he does not submit to so great a truth. But lest, from a desire to prolong the conflict, he introduce questions of murky falsehood and waste necessary time on superfluous matters, let him bring his arguments to a useful conclusion. Let Arius and Athanasius, however, who confess that the Son of God was begotten from the Father before the origins of the world—something which Sabellius and Photinus alike denied—not delay in stating how they create disagreement in one and the same confession of faith and fail to agree with one another.

Athanasius said: Arius truly professes that the Son subsisted before the ages. But that he was born from the Father he grants only in the sound of the words and in a feigned confession of language, not in the proper truth of the matter, since he separates him far from the substance of the Father’s nature and affirms that he is subject to the Father by a condition of nature, not by the reason of the dispensation.

Probus the judge said: Give a very clear indication of your faith, and mark out in a recent statement how you believe, so that the matter of the dispute also may be fitted to the standard of the confession proposed.

Athanasius said: Lest I burden your minds with an exceedingly long speech, I will sum up my faith in a brief statement. I confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in divinity, power, greatness, and nature. I do not assert that there is anything new or foreign in this Trinity, as though it had not previously existed but was afterward added; rather, as I have said, I believe it to be of one nature and one substance.

Arius said: Just as I confess three persons remaining in their individual proper identities, so I confess three substances of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The substance of God the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; nor can the nature of the unbegotten substance of the Father, the begotten nature of the Son, or the created nature of the Holy Spirit be in any way equated. Therefore, in our faithful confession we do not believe them equal in power, alike in greatness, or sharing the same nature.

### XVII

Probus the judge said: If this is the whole point on which you appear to disagree with one another—that one says the substance of the Trinity is diverse, while the other says it is one—then the order of the discussion now requires that you support your assertions more firmly, not with the subtle arguments deliberately produced by the dialectical art, but with the pure and simple proofs of divine Scripture.

Arius said: I believe that the memory of your prudent mind has by no means forgotten Athanasius’s argument, in which he concluded more elegantly that the person who pursues novel and unheard-of inventions of words ought to be branded with the error of perversity, adding to the apostolic teachings what is known not to have been handed down by them.

Probus the judge said: I remember it so.

Arius said: Therefore let the decrees of the Council of Nicaea be disclosed by being read, and you will recognize that Athanasius—or the authors of his position—corrupted the apostolic faith by adding new words to such an extent that, acting with royal arrogance, they judged those who clung to the ancient teachings of the Fathers worthy of being banished by deadly edicts.

Probus the judge said: If the circumstances of the present matter require that the decree of the Council of Nicaea be recited, let Athanasius also indicate this in his argument, so that, with the assent of both parties, whatever is to be offered may be recited from an external document.

Athanasius said: It is appropriate to the case that the opportunity to read the record of what was done not be denied.

### XVIII

Probus the judge said: Therefore, as you desire, let the reading of the aforesaid decree of the Nicene faith be brought forward.

And it was read as follows:

## Copy of the Nicene Faith

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the only-begotten, that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homousion*; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For our salvation he descended, was incarnate, was made human, suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten, he did not exist,” and who say that he came from things that did not exist, or from another substance or essence, and who declare God to be mutable and changeable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

### XIX

Arius said: You clearly perceive, excellent Probus, that the decrees of this council were written to cast reproach upon the apostolic faith through the audacious presumption of reckless boldness. For what need was there to insert this new term *homousion* into the ancient rules of doctrine? Shall we say that the apostles, or their disciples, and all their successors in order, who lived in the confession of Christ down to that time, followed sacrilegious impiety in the truth of faith because they were ignorant of the term *homousion*? Shall we say that, deprived of the meaning of this name, they proceeded to Christ without asserting this very doctrine?

For if, as these people wholly falsely claim, a new teaching contrary to the ordinances of the apostles was being introduced by us, it would surely have been appropriate for the ancient apostolic teachings to oppose the new teaching introduced by us, and for antiquity to proscribe novelty—not for novelty to corrupt antiquity. Why does he impose upon me the obligation to follow this term? Why does he drag me so forcefully toward such novelty? Why does he add to the apostolic faith this word, of which neither the prophets nor the apostles anywhere make mention? What, I ask, is this term, without which the faith cannot be complete? Without which Christians are deprived of the honor of the Christian religion?

One of two conclusions must necessarily be followed in this matter. If the assertion of *homousion* is true, then the preaching of the apostles, which flourished for so long without this term, is false. But if the apostolic faith, lacking this term, is true—as indeed it is—then this teaching is certainly false, since it added the novelty of a name to the ancient faith. Turn through all the volumes of the New and Old Testament: will you be able to find *homousion* inscribed anywhere in the sacred pages?

### XX

Probus the judge said: What is the reply to these points?

Athanasius said: Are you offended only by the novelty of the name, or do you also reject the power of the reality that has received this term?

Arius said: I do not sufficiently understand what you mean.

Athanasius said: Since an ancient reality has received a new name, and the power of a new reality was not thereby added by the new term, this is what I ask: do you condemn the ancient reality together with the novelty of the name?

Arius said: You are speaking of matters twisted and worthy of every marvel of stupidity. For if *homousion* is a new name, there is no doubt that the reality which it appears to signify is also new.

Athanasius said: Then you condemn the reality and the name alike?

Arius said: Precisely.

Athanasius said: Then, when I have shown that a new name was assigned to an ancient reality handed down by the apostles, will you at last admit that you have been defeated? Or will you even then condemn the ancient reality together with the novelty of the name?

Arius said: You certainly cannot demonstrate this. And what reason demanded that an ancient reality should receive a new name? Before it acquired the term bearing this name, did it remain without the proper designation of a name? This appears to me to have no logical consistency whatsoever.

Athanasius said: It has always been the practice of ecclesiastical discipline, whenever a new doctrine of heretics arises, to alter the names of things against the insolent novelties of their questions, while the realities themselves remain unchanged, and to express the natures of things more significantly. Yet these names correspond to the power of existing realities and demonstrate more clearly that those realities existed from ancient times; they do not suggest a novelty of origin.

To make what I am saying clearer, I will use an example. At the very beginning of the preaching of the Christian religion, all who believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were called not Christians but merely disciples. And because many authors of new doctrines had arisen, opposing apostolic teaching, and all called their followers disciples, there was no distinction of name between true and false disciples. Whether they were followers of Christ, Dositheus, Theodas, some Judas, or even John—those who professed to believe in Christ—they did not wish to be classified under the single name of disciples.

Then the apostles assembled at Antioch, as the Acts indicate in the account of Luke, and called all the disciples by a new name, that is, Christians, distinguishing them from the common designation of false disciples. Thus the word of the divine oracle spoken through Isaiah was also fulfilled: “The name of those who serve me shall be called by a new name” (Isaiah 65:15, according to the Septuagint).

### XXI

Therefore, retaining this practice handed down by the apostles, of using new names, the Church issued various new designations against different heretics, as the reason of sound faith required.

Finally, the Church gave the Father the new designation of “unbegottenness” (*innascibilitas*). When the Sabellian heresy wished to assert that the Father was begotten from the Virgin, the Church, by confessing the contrary against it, handed down that the Father was unbegotten. And certainly we never read “unbegotten” in the divine Scriptures as a designation of the Father.

Sabellius can therefore turn his audacity into a question of this sort of slander and use an argument like yours, saying: “Why do you do violence to the divine Scriptures without any sense of shame, professing the Father to be unbegotten, when you cannot show this written anywhere?”

Likewise, because that same Sabellius professes by impious doctrine that the Father was not only begotten but also suffered, the bishops who assembled together at Sirmium for three days [Latin *vel tridudum*, materially uncertain] declared, among the other rules of faith that they promulgated, that the Father is impassible. We rightly approve this as a religious and holy determination.

But he likewise cries out: “How far will you extend the audacity of your license, professing the Father to be impassible—a claim which you have not read written anywhere? Neither the prophets handed it down, nor did the authority of the authoritative creed hand it down; it has been presumed upon by your own recklessness.”

Again, these same men who had assembled at Sirmium proceed and establish this confession of piety concerning the Son: “God from God, light from light.”

Here, Photinus, who attributes the Son’s beginning to the nature of human generation, has a great opportunity for slander. You yourself, I ask, measure it. Why should he not raise similar grounds for complaint? Why should he not also rage with a similar outcry, saying: “What are you saying? What are you establishing? What are you handing down to posterity as binding according to your judgment, by confessing the Son to be God from God, light from light? Show me whether this is written in the same form of faith, that is, in the authoritative creed handed down by the apostles. But I will be content if, since it was not written there, it is at least read to me from the prophets or shown from the letters of the apostles. Who could tolerate these novelties of language? Who could allow his mind to accept what neither the prophets nor the apostles handed down?”

### XXII

Likewise, in many and very frequent decrees of your councils you have established that the Son is like the Father. Let Eunomius now arise, confessing that he is unlike, and say: “Where did you read this? Where did you find it written? Did the Father or the Son use this expression concerning himself?”

Therefore you, Arius, who today force me into the predicament of having to show that *homousion* is written explicitly, must either admit that certain terms of confession were inserted into the authorities of the faith—not rashly presumed, but gathered by necessary reasoning—against the insolent and underhanded perversities of heretical interpretation; so that there were as many religiously understood solutions in these new words as there had been occasions of unbelief, whether sought out or supplied.

Or, if you refuse to admit this, I will deal with you by your own objections. Show me—not from conjectures, not from probabilities, not from matters neighboring upon reason, not from considerations that invite understanding, not from what the piety of faith persuades us to confess—but in the pure and bare propriety of the words, show me written that the Father is unbegotten or impassible; that the Son is God from God, light from light; or that the Son is like the Father.

Do not say to me, “The reason of faith demands this; piety teaches it; the coherence of Scripture urges me to make this confession.” I do not want you to present such claims to me, because you reject me when I offer similar claims in proof of *homousion*.

Instead, bring the codices of the divine volumes in your hands and read the names of the terms mentioned above inscribed in the same sound and with the same syllables. Either show that the Son is written to be like the Father, or admit that he is unlike. There is no way for you to escape from this or find an exit. No ability is offered you to disentangle yourself from the bonds of your own proposition.

Either grant me the right to prove *homousion*, that is, the faith of one substance, from necessary consequences; or, if you refuse to grant this, you must deny everything that you yourself confess, because you will nowhere be able to find those things set down in bare and explicit terms.

### XXIII

Probus the judge said: If it is the custom of the Church to place certain terms of language plainly in the authority of the faith in order to restrain the movements of heretics, while those terms are clothed in reasoning derived from existing realities—and if the truth from which they take their origin is found to be contained in the divine writings—what do you say, Arius? Do you concede that *homousion*, as Athanasius says, is proved from the divine Scriptures by the corresponding qualities of the confession, or do you not?

Arius said: By some sophistical trick of syllogistic art, this man is trying to evade my objection. I want it demonstrated whether *homousion* is written on the authority of the Lord’s teaching. Therefore, let him read it as explicitly stated, or withdraw from confessing it.

Probus the judge said: But you see how he turns your question back upon you and binds you with the very arguments you use, demanding from you an even clearer proof of your confession: show him from the canonical writings, plainly set down, that the Father is unbegotten or impassible; that the Son is God from God or light from light; or that the Son is like the Father.

If you are wholly unable to demonstrate that all these things are explicitly stated, the necessity of denying them will threaten you. The only consideration that, as I see it, can rescue you from this difficulty is that you concede that the things set down plainly in your councils have flowed from the sources of Scripture.

For it will be counted a fault of contentiousness if you demand proof in bare wording of something whose meaning you know to overflow abundantly in the Scriptures. Therefore seek the meaning from which the nature of this term took its origin; and when you have found the meaning, do not doubt that you have likewise found the name.

### XXIV

Athanasius said: No matter how many arguments you use with him, he cannot in any way be called back from this position. He knows with complete certainty that, if the matter came to the point where it was shown from the consequences of Scripture that the substance of the Father and the Son is one—which is *homousion*—he could easily be defeated. Therefore, driven by the danger of distrust and fear, he demands proof in bare wording.

But he must again be bound by his own confessions. You demand that I show *homousion*, the one substance of the Father and the Son, written in Scripture; yet you confess three *ousiai*, that is, three substances. Show me, then, where you have read of three *ousiai*. For if I ought to deny one substance—that is, *homousion*—because I do not find it written plainly, how do you dare to profess three *ousiai*, when you will nowhere be able to demonstrate that this is written?

Probus the judge said: If there is some proof from the divine authorities, set down explicitly and specifically, by which it may be approved that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three *ousiai* and three natures—as you confess—let it be produced, so that Athanasius may withdraw from confessing one substance, which is *homousion*.

For when you have shown that *triusion* is explicitly set down in the Scriptures, it will appear that Athanasius has persisted in the confession of *homousion* through the rashness of his most stubborn obstinacy, since he has been unable to demonstrate that it is explicitly written. But if you yourself are unable to demonstrate three *ousiai*, you will appear to me to be bound by an equal necessity of condition.

### XXV

Athanasius said: Let him teach that three *ousiai* are explicitly set down, and I will yield concerning one substance, which is *homousion*.

Arius said: If there are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—then necessarily there are three substances in which each person is recognized to subsist separately and distinctly in his own proper identity.

Athanasius said: Here arguments are of no use; here the truth is gathered by necessary reasoning. The precise wording of the testimonies is demanded. Read *triusion* as specifically written, and do not say by conjecture, “If there are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—then necessarily there are also three substances.” For by a similar conjecture I can form an even truer opinion: “If the Father and the Son are one”—because he himself says, “I and the Father are one”—“how are they not one substance?”

But you have entirely refused to enter this path of discussion, since you demand that I demonstrate *homousion* as specifically written. Therefore, by the same reasoning, you too must read *triusion* as specifically and explicitly written. For if I must deny *homousion* because I cannot show it written plainly, then I must necessarily confess *triusion* when you demonstrate that it is explicitly written.

Arius said: Does the Father subsist in his own proper identity, or does he not?

Athanasius said: Unless you read to me three *ousiai* explicitly set down, I will give no answer to your questions. For who does not see where your objection is leading? By a crafty question you wish to establish that the substances of the Father and the Son are different. But arguments are not needed here, where proof of three substances is demanded by a clearer testimony of explicit wording.

Yet if you wish to pass from the precise wording of the testimonies to the necessary consequence concerning the realities, let this itself become known to the public conscience: you have been unable to demonstrate three *ousiai* explicitly set down. When both of us have been released from this particular demand, I must satisfy your objections or questions.

### XXVI

Probus the judge said: As the purpose of your dispute shows, neither you can demonstrate *homousion*, nor can he demonstrate *triusion*, as specifically and explicitly written. Therefore, lest you linger longer in a childish quarrel over superfluous matters, both of you must finally cease demanding this bare proof. By necessary reasoning, derive either *homousion* or *triusion* from the authority of Scripture. For it will not be permissible to doubt the designation of a term which a copious accumulation of testimonies can establish more firmly.

Arius said: Since this is your judgment—that we should gather the force of the terms mentioned above through persuasive reasoning and the causes of necessary consequence—and lest it seem to Athanasius that, because of the difficulty of demonstrating the truth, I had sought proof of the precise wording of a bare term, I will proceed as your judgment has decreed.

I wanted to use a shorter route, so that the purpose of the reasoning might not wander farther afield and obscure the truth beneath ambiguous meanings.

Athanasius said: Faith cannot be brought into doubt when it is supported by the protection of truth. The light of radiant truth disperses the denser clouds of falsehood. One who does not need the external support of aids cannot be deprived of his own strength.

## Book Two

### I

On another day Probus the judge said: Since I do not doubt that you will preserve, with an unalterable decision, the terms of the agreement you initially made—by which you appear to have mutually conceded that you would prove, through the necessary consequences of the divine writings and by a clear examination in debate, the confession either of one substance or of three substances—the reasoning of the agreement now requires that, setting aside every trick of human argument, you teach from the sacred volumes of the divine authorities that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have either one substance or diverse substances.

For the minds not only of myself, as I suppose, but of nearly all mortals are suspended in such eager expectation of this proof that, if the importance of so great a matter allowed it, they would desire to reach the summit of truth and the conclusion of the clearest understanding without the postponement of a single day or the interval of even a moment.

Therefore, lest so religious an intention, eager for the faithful and for truth, be frustrated, cast away every adornment of luxuriant speech and deal with the matter, the case, and the points that are relevant and necessary. As I have said, carefully avoid every circuitousness of words, every flourish and charm of language wandering far from the case, so that the account of your dispute may be adorned more by truth than by the buskin of swelling eloquence.

### II

Athanasius said: Although I have already disputed frequently and repeatedly, outside the formal proceedings, about the unity of substance, and have committed my arguments to writing—arguments to which nothing further could be added by me in this dispute—nevertheless, since these things were spoken externally, with no opponent standing at a distance to resist them, I must repeat the same points and bring them into this public examination, so that they may be strengthened by the sentence of your judgment.

Probus the judge said: If they are not weakened by Arius’s replies, then our judgment may be strengthened.

Arius said: Why are these traps of deception being set before us? Why is the judge’s sentence being preferred in support of a wicked assertion? Let us first do what the necessity of demonstrating the truth imposes upon us. Let our confession of faith be impressed upon human hearing. Let the judgments perceive by what methods and by what reasoning, and finally by what proofs, our assertion is supported; and only then will we ask the judge to pronounce a judgment that certainly does not depend upon our will.

Probus the judge said: You ought to remember my preface, delivered recently at the beginning of these proceedings, and the pledge of both of you inserted in the earlier record, in which it was concluded that, with superfluous matters omitted, you must descend to the heart of the case. This you must finally do.

Arius said: Let him teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance: of one power, one dignity, one glory, one majesty, one excellence, and one honor—the doctrine which he is accustomed to proclaim to the people in a sufficiently thoughtless and excessively heedless confession.

Athanasius said: Do you confess that the Son was truly born from the Father, or do you not?

Arius said: Do you yourself confess that the Father cannot be subject to any defect of derivation or division, or do you not?

Athanasius said: I most certainly confess it.

Arius said: And I too confess that the Son was born from the Father.

### III

Athanasius said: Do you consider “born from the Father” to be the same as “born of the Father”?

Arius said: It is enough for you that I have said “born from the Father,” which I can also very easily show to be written. Why do you employ crafty arguments? But as for “born of the Father,” I have not yet been able to find it written anywhere at present. I remember that “from the Father” is written, when the apostle John says: “Whoever loves the Father loves him who was born from him.”

Athanasius said: Therefore you think it makes no difference whether he is said to have been born from him or born of him?

Arius said: If you are able to demonstrate that the Son is explicitly said to have been born of the Father, then I will consider what I ought to think about it. But I am not unaware that in many copies the wording varies, so that in the same places where one reads “from him,” other manuscripts read “of him.” Whether this happened through the fraud of interpolators or because the two expressions signify one and the same thing—that is, whether “from him” means the same as “of him”—cannot sufficiently prejudice our faith.

Athanasius said: In this argument of yours I have noticed a very precise distinction based on the reasoning you have supplied. But I am sufficiently astonished that you said the words could prejudice only our faith and did not indicate that they could prejudice the faith of both parties. I think you proposed this while hastening to fortify your own faith, hoping that I would pass lightly over the matter without any proof.

In the Gospel, too, the Son says concerning the Father: “God is spirit” (John 4:24). And to show that he was born of the Father, he says: “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). And: “I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:27). Behold, I have shown that the Son was born of the Father, on the testimony of the Son himself.

### IV

Arius said: You employ sufficiently crafty and suspicious arguments, claiming that I said this to strengthen my faith. But so that every ambiguity of suspicion may be removed from your mind, as I admitted above, whether he is said to have been born from him or born of him can in no way whatsoever prejudice the faith of either party.

Athanasius said: Did the Father who generated the Son from himself generate what he himself is, or something else?

Arius said: He certainly generated what he himself is, because God generated God, light generated light, the perfect generated the perfect, and the almighty generated the almighty.

Athanasius said: Therefore he generated him neither externally, nor from nothing, nor from some preceding or subsequent matter, but from himself; and he generated nothing other than what he himself is.

Arius said: One generated another.

Athanasius said: We too confess that one generated another. But if he generated him from himself—that is, from what he himself is—the Son cannot be of another substance or of a different kind; and thus he will be of one and the same substance with the Father.

Arius said: If you knew into how many errors of unbelief the confession of one substance tends, you would certainly never mention this term between the Father and the Son, nor would you conclude your discussion, divided into successive stages of questions, with such a point as to bring it to this end of an impious confession.

Athanasius said: You must know that I cannot be ignorant that it is impious and sacrilegious to confess different substances of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that it is pious and religious to believe them to be of one substance. I will demonstrate that this has not been gathered from human opinion, nor discovered by conjectures and arguments, but handed down through the instruction of heavenly doctrine.

### V

Probus the judge said: First define for me the force and meaning of the term; only then can it be demonstrated whether it applies to the Father and the Son.

[Cols. 0200C–0211A; pp. 147–162]

Athanasius said: Substance, indeed, is distinguished by two kinds of designation. One kind is that quality which indicates the essence of an existing nature. Another kind of substance is that by which the one who possesses something is distinguished from the things he possesses. To make what I am saying clearer, I shall use a more evident explanation. For example: a human being is a substance of his own kind and nature. Again, whatever he possesses externally—that is, in material of gold or silver or of other kinds—is called his substance. Although there appears to be one designation with the same word, it nevertheless seems to signify two different things. But we are discussing that kind of substance by which each nature is called substance because it is what it is or subsists. And whatever a thing generates from itself—that is, from itself as such—can be nothing other than what it itself is. Thus a human father, generating a son, generates a human being of his own kind, that is, of his own substance, because a human being generates a human being; and they are rightly said to be of one substance, because the truth of birth does not admit diversity of substances.

Diversity of substance, however, exists—as I may give an example—if a human being should beget an animal, or if an animal of one kind should generate an animal of another kind; that is, if an ox should beget a donkey, or if a sheep should produce a goat. Since this proceeds into diversity of kind, it will be a monstrous generation, preserving not at all the property of its own nature.

Again, in the qualities of the elements, it is worthwhile to observe what constitutes the diversity or property of substances. For example: the nature of each fire or light seems to provide from itself that which it itself is—light, radiance; fire, burning. And, subsisting in this function of its own, it seems to preserve the unimpaired nature of its substance. But if light were to generate darkness from itself, it would be subject to change, supplying matter of a kind different from itself; for it will be able to preserve the substance of its immutability unspoiled in this respect if it supplies from itself what it itself is. But if, as I have said, what it supplies from itself is something other than the thing that supplies it, then it can be called of another substance; something that the quality, order, or rational principle of all natures wholly rejects.

Come now, if it seems appropriate, let us raise the eye of the mind from earthly and visible things to higher realities, and from things that have been made let us recognize the substance of the uncreated power, instructed by the teaching of apostolic authority, which says that the invisible power of the Godhead ought to be understood from the things that have been made (Romans 1:20).

Arius therefore says that the Son was born from the Father, and that God begot God, light begot light. In this profession one of two alternatives must certainly be retained. Either the one who generates from himself generated what he himself is, and therefore the Son will be of one substance with the Father; or, if he generated a God of a kind different from himself, it cannot be called a true birth, since it could not preserve the property of the substance of its kind. The reasoning of the argument is thereby brought to the conclusion that either he was not born at all, or that he was degenerate. Both alternatives will appear absurd and impious to confess.

### VI. Probus the judge said:

If Arius knows of anything that can be brought forward against these arguments, let him not delay in declaring it.

Arius said: I do not think Athanasius is unaware that God is of a simple and immutable nature. If, as he asserted, God generated from his own substance, he will unquestionably be mutable. For, by generating from himself what he himself is, he must either have lost part of his substance through the process of derivational generation, or have been capable of suffering the defect of division. For my part, I confess that the substance of God the Father neither brought forth anything from itself, nor was derived into the qualities of parts, nor experienced—or could have experienced—addition, subtraction, or anything of this kind subject to passion.

Athanasius said: But neither do we believe that the divine nature is subject to these conditions of passion. Rather, we faithfully confess that the impassible Father, impassibly, generated from himself—that is, from what he himself is—the Son. Nor do the kinds of passion belonging to divisions, derivations, parts, and all the other things that you wished to introduce, driven by an empty fear of anxiety, turn us away from the truth of our profession, so that we should deny that God could generate from himself lest he seem subject to these passions.

What, then, is more religious, what more holy, and what more fitting to the Divinity? I beg you, hearers, weigh it on the even scale of judgment. Raise the eyes of your minds, and, fearing the terrifying day of the future judgment, discern with religious attention what accords more fully with catholic and apostolic truth: whether to confess that almighty God impassibly generated the Son from himself, or rather to suppose that, lest he be subject to the defect of passion, he could not generate the Son from himself—that is, from his own substance.

For I assert and affirm with the clearest declaration that, just as God is impassible, so also he is omnipotent. I believe that he could generate from his own substance and yet not be subject to any defect of passion. For division, derivation, contraction, addition, flow, and any other such kinds of passion belong to corporeal and tangible things composed of diversity. But God, who is bounded by no corporeal signs of form and distinguished by no outlines of limbs, cannot be subject to the defect of passion. I rightly confess generation in him, because he generated; and I rightly confess him impassible nonetheless, because he was never passible.

### VII.

Arius said: Because omnipotence cannot be denied to God, must we therefore admit that he cannot undergo those things which the wholly incorrupt substance of his divinity does not admit? Hence it will appear highly dishonorable and full of impiety to believe that, through the profession of one substance, neither the Father properly subsists nor the Son remains in his own distinct property.

For the thrust of his perfidy proceeds toward this: that, through the mingling of the persons of the Father and the Son, composed of diverse elements gathered and confused into the coagulation of one thing, they are unable to subsist in the singularity of their own properties, as I have said. This is also contained in the perfidy of your profession, and is exceedingly dreadful and must be removed far from the minds of the faithful: that the inviolable Father, by generating from his own substance, was entirely unable to avoid the defect of corruption and division.

Athanasius said: Bound more tightly, as though by unbreakable knots, by the truth of the divine generation, you seek a refuge of escape through I know not what devices of wicked intent—devices which the divine nature certainly lacks—and bring against the incorruptible One corruption, against the impassible One passion, and against the omnipotent One impotence. Repeating this again and again, no reverence for the divine majesty, as far as I can see, can restrain you from such wicked objections. Without any regard for shame, you strive to rush headlong into an insult against the venerable birth of the Son.

But divine-authority testimonies will restrain you as you wander more recklessly and drift, by a kind of natural license, like a wave-tossed whirlpool of the sea. They will confine you within definite limits of the divine profession and will not permit you to cross the boundaries of the legal constitutions.

Divine majesty therefore impresses this upon human minds through that sacred oracle of its profession, in which it testifies and says that it ineffably generated the Son from the hidden mysteries of its substance:

> “From the womb, before the Morning Star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3).

One of two alternatives must therefore be retained in this divine declaration. Either he incorruptibly generated the Son from his ineffable substance, or he did not generate him at all lest he be corrupted. But I choose that part of the complete faith which urges us to serve God when he makes this religious declaration concerning himself. No obstacle of human passion, arising from the sacrilege of unbelief, will be able in any way to deter me, so that I should not believe that God could generate, lest, according to human custom, he might be subject to corruption. For I do not doubt that it is sufficient for me to confess that the one who plainly proceeded from the Father’s womb was born from the substance of God.

### VIII.

Arius said: As the direction of your argument shows, you wish to introduce to us a composite God subject to corruption, and you are not even afraid to give him the bodily designation of a womb. Therefore, if he has a womb, he must be composed of limbs; or, as I said, if he generated from his own substance, he must be subject to corruption.

Athanasius said: You would rightly accuse me of thinking this if, by my own rash presumption, without any testimony of divine law, I had asserted that God possesses a womb. But since God himself, in order to refute the madness of those unwilling to believe, deigned to declare this concerning himself, so that by the designation of a womb he might teach more clearly that he generated the Son not externally or from elsewhere, but from himself—that is, from his own substance—why do you brand me with the marks of defective belief, when you could rather say this to God:

“If you have a womb, you will be composite. If you generated from yourself, you will be subject to corruption.”

For in God “womb” is understood without any composition of limbs, just as eyes and ears, hands and feet, are said to be present without any outlines distinguishing them.
