Therefore, just as you should understand eyes because he sees everything, ears because he hears everything, hands because he accomplishes all things, and feet because he is everywhere, so you should understand “womb” because he ineffably generated from himself.

### IX.

Nor ought you to think unbelievingly that, if he generated from himself, he could certainly have been corrupted. Rather, it is fitting faithfully to confess that, since he is omnipotent, he could generate incorruptibly and could not be corrupted by that very generation.

For if he is wondrously believed to have been born incorruptibly from a Virgin, contrary to the nature of things, how much more must he be believed to have been generated incorruptibly from the Father? If the substantial nature of the Virgin—which, by the very condition of corruptible nature, could be subject to passion and corruption—generated a son with the unviolated integrity of modesty, with the virginal barriers unbroken, and with the marvelous integrity of incorruption, why should we not believe, as I have said, that incorruptible God could not be corrupted by generating the Son incorruptibly from himself?

O new and unspeakable fear, worthy of condemnation as a monstrous opinion: to confess that the Virgin could not be corrupted by childbirth, yet to fear that God might be subject to the defect of corruption if he could generate from his own substance! Therefore, by God’s will, the Virgin of corruptible nature generated without any defect of corruption. And could the one who, more incorruptible than all natures, granted the power to generate incorruptibly, not grant this to himself—that he could generate the Son incorruptibly from his own substance?

Therefore, since both the declarations of the divine Scriptures testify that God generated the Son from himself, and Arius himself acknowledged this in his preceding argument, judge, excellent Probus, who agrees more with the divine Scriptures: whether I do, who profess that the Son is of one substance with the Father because he is known to have been born from him and not from elsewhere, and who likewise profess that he generated incorruptibly because the supremely excellent substance of the divine majesty cannot, through its ineffable power, be subject to corruption; or this man, who is placed in so perilous a crisis of uncertain understanding that he does not know where to set the foot of his faith.

For, unwilling to confess that God incorruptibly generated from his own substance, he is drawn into the necessity of confessing that he did not generate at all. But he will never be able to deny this, since prophetic and apostolic voices everywhere oppose him and cry out with clear proclamation.

### X. Probus the judge said:

Whatever I have been able to discern in this assertion of your arguments, the final judgment of our examination will retain. But now, if you think that anything further remains from the divine Scriptures consistent with your faith, please bring it forward, so that by the easiest course of discussion we may investigate what the truth contains.

Arius said: The fact that I employed such brief and limited questions throughout the whole narrative of my argument was an expression of Christian modesty and reserve, so that the course of our discussion might begin with light beginnings. But because I see Athanasius shaking the strongest firmness of evident truth by the blows of certain battering questions, I think we must contend against him more sharply and more vigorously.

He says, then, that the Father and the Son are of one substance. But that inviolate and ineffable essence which is the Father has never overflowed from itself, so that it might rightly be said to have generated the Son, without harm to itself, through a kind of abundance or outpouring, since its essence is infinite, immense, and incorporeal with respect to all other things, and nothing can be an overflow of it. For it belongs to bounded things to overflow, as though to flow outside themselves.

But God, who embraces all things and has nothing outside himself, has neither anything into which he can flow out nor any infinity into which he might overflow; whereas flowing out belongs to things that receive increase. If he ever received increase, he must always receive it, and likewise must always generate through an equal overflow. But if he did not receive increase—as we too confess—then he neither flows nor overflows.

If, then, the Son is said to be such as the Father was when he generated him from himself, the Father necessarily divided his substance into the Son and called the Son only that portion of the paternal substance which had been separated and cut off from him in due proportion. The Father therefore took away from himself as much as he conferred upon the Son.

Consequently, either the Father now lacks whatever the Son is and is not perfect, or, if he does not need it, he possessed it superfluously in abundance. Neither alternative applies to God. Moreover, in this very circumstance the name of Father and Son could not exist, since there would not have been a birth but rather a division; and whatever can be divided must necessarily be capable of corruption.

If these things, as has been shown, cannot exist in God, why do we not rather confess that the Son belongs to will and love? Will is certainly no less free even in human beings, much less is it constrained by any law in God. But if he is not the Son of will, it remains that God seems to have produced the Son under compulsion, as though under some law of nature.

In this generation, if what was generated is what the Father was, a part of the Father is called the Son. It is uncertain what ought to be called Father and what Son, since the substance has been divided equally into two parts.

### XI.

But concerning the testimony of the paternal oracle which he brought forward as though to demonstrate the property of natural substance, so that we might rightly believe that the Father generated the Son from what he himself is, because he said, “From the womb, before the Morning Star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3), I shall demonstrate most clearly how absurd and inept this is.

For we read that not only some ordered structure existing among rational creatures, but also the subsistence of the sensible elements, proceeded from God’s womb. For he says:

> “Who is the father of rain, or from whose womb does the snow proceed?” (Job 38:28).

Does this mean that, because the quality of this chilling and inert element is read to proceed from the divine womb, it is therefore believed to be of one and the same substance with God?

Or because we read that human beings have likewise been begotten by God—as he himself says, “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isaiah 1:2), and again, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), and again, “Everyone who has been born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9)—shall we therefore more reasonably suppose that human beings are of one substance with God?

Or because the Apostle, embracing the entirety of creation in a general pronouncement, asserts that all things are from God, saying, “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36), shall we therefore more prudently conjecture that the entire universe of creation is what God is, or that it is of one substance with him, because it is read to have subsisted from him?

Thus, when we confess that the Son too proceeded from the womb of God the Father, we should appropriately understand this not as an indication of one nature, but as a statement concerning the mysteries of things that cannot be investigated.

### XII.

Athanasius said: In theatrical performances, those who change themselves through a variety of figures appear diverse and different to the eyes of the spectators. The very same person who once walked stiffly in the guise of an arranged image later, with his face adapted to the same role, playing with alternating movements of his limbs, relaxes into the softness of women.

Thus Arius now seems to me to be shaped by changing the images of his questions, making different conjectures as though by a variety of likenesses. For what he recently attempted through polished and concise objections, he repeats again and again under the pretext of another image, yet does not depart in any way from the property of the question he had raised.

Nor, because he now extends the sequence of his proposition more broadly and diffusely through a tangled maze of words, should he be thought to have done anything other than what he was previously convicted of doing. For he said that the Father and the Son cannot be of one substance because the same paternal substance could neither flow out through the most abundant overflow of derivation into an abundance of increase—for it has been bounded by no limits and could be confined by no final measures, since the abundance of overflow belongs, as we said, to what is enclosed by a definite end—nor, on the other hand, could it have undergone any complete and unimpaired loss of a portion.

But it is already evident that he has advanced all these kinds of passion, which are unsuitable to the divine nature, more maliciously than truthfully. It is clear that we have appropriately answered them through the understanding of religious faith.

### XIII.

For we do not call the Son an overflow of an overflowing substance, nor do we call him a small portion of a severed nature. Rather, we believe that the perfect Son was born from the perfect Father—not from those superfluous overflows that were overflowing in him, which it would be impious to say, but from himself, that is, from what he himself is: impassibly, indivisibly, incorporeally, without diminution, without division, without the overflow of an abundant outpouring, and without any kind of passion whatsoever.

For this reason we confess that he is of one substance, because we faithfully confess that he exists not from elsewhere, not from nothing, and not from underlying or preceding material qualities, but properly as God from God, light from light, power from power, wisdom from wisdom.

For if the Son were of another and different substance, as Arius believes, he would not say:

> “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

And again:

> “Just as the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John 10:15).

What, then, is meant by “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself,” except: “Just as the Father is, so also is the Son”? And if they have the same being, they are unquestionably of one substance.

For the being of the Father is not one thing and his living another; rather, living is the same as being. That is, the Father himself is not one thing and his life another; his life is essence, and his essence is life. Otherwise he would appear composite, subsisting through diversity, if he himself were signified as one thing and his life as another.

Since, therefore, it is evident that the life of the Father is what he himself is, just as he has life in himself, so he granted the Son to have life—that is, the being of the Son is as the being of the Father. There is no doubt, then, that the Father and the Son are of one essence and of one nature of being.

### XIV.

For when he said, “Just as the Father knows me, and I know the Father” (John 10:15), he unquestionably wished to indicate the unity of substance. For, according to the understanding of the preceding argument, the Father's knowing is not one thing and his being another. For he knows that very thing which he is, and what he knows, he is, because he does not know in one way and exist in another.

And because the Son knows the Father just as the Father knows him, while we have said that knowledge in God is essence, there is no doubt that just as the Father is, so also is the Son. Thus the matter admits no diversity of essence, since it subsists in one and the same manner.

Finally, so that we might understand more fully this unity of substance between the Father and the Son, the divine Scriptures set before us certain examples from visible things, by which they might more religiously summon us to an understanding of invisible realities. They presented the Son as the splendor of the Father’s light and the image of his goodness—not because examples drawn from bodily forms are sufficient to measure divine realities, but because that ineffable nature could not be expressed, and certain indications of likeness are therefore offered from visible things.

Thus, just as splendor and fire are not different substances, or just as an image cannot differ in any respect from the one whose image it is—for if it retained something different in itself, it could not be perfect and true—so the Father and the Son are to be believed not to be of different substance, but of one substance.

And because he brought forward several testimonies by way of example to establish that all things are from God, yet are not thereby believed to have proceeded from his substance, I ask whether he asserts that the Son came forth from the Father in the same way that all things are said to have come forth from him.

What, then, do you say? Are we to understand that the Son proceeded from the Father’s womb, or was begotten from the Father, in the same way as human beings are said to have been born from God, or as snow is read to proceed from his womb—or in a wholly different way? But I ask you to answer one of two alternatives: say either “in the same way” or “not in the same way.”

### XV.

Arius said: All things did not come into being or were begotten from God in the same way as the Son. The Son came into being in one way; creation came into being in another.

Athanasius said: If you confess that the Son came into being in a wholly different way from creation, why did you introduce examples of created things in discussing his birth and generation? Those who received the beginnings of their proper origin in dissimilar ways do not appear comparable according to an equal sense of understanding.

Since the direction of your argument tends toward this, it is evident that you are defending the sacrilegious error of the doctrine of Photinus, which you formerly rejected. For when Photinus himself denied that the Son of God was begotten from the Father, and was constrained by such proofs of testimony as demonstrate more clearly than daylight that the Son of God was truly and properly begotten as God from the substance of the Father, he turned the devices of his impiety toward this end: to assert that the Son was born from the Father in the same ways and according to the same order of reasoning as human beings are consecrated, through the grace of adoption, into the offspring of divine generation.

You too, although proceeding by other indications of the way, have nevertheless arrived at the same destination of unbelief, asserting that the Son should not be understood to have been born from that ineffable substance of the Father because he is read to have been begotten from God or to have proceeded from the Father’s womb, since, by similar reasoning, not only human beings born from God but even the qualities of insensible elements are read to have proceeded through the generation of the paternal womb.

And although you have already dissolved the entire narrative of your argument in one brief statement, when you said that the Son came into being divinely in a wholly different way from creation, nevertheless, because by the brevity of your obscure and perplexing statement you have veiled your intention from readers in certain gloomy clouds, I shall now bring into the light of the clearest understanding what is obscure and obscures the truth, stating it more clearly and plainly.

### XVI.

I shall therefore show that, so far as the property of divine generation is concerned, to be born from God is the same as to be generated from him. And, to use clearer testimonies from the divine Scriptures, I shall bring forward an evangelical proof.

The angel speaks to Mary as follows:

> “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

And again the Apostle says:

> “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4).

Does this mean that, because the angel addressed Mary in such a way as to say that the Son would be generated not de ipsa (“from herself”) but ex ipsa (“out of herself”), and because the Apostle asserted that the Son was born from a woman, we shall therefore not at all confess in Christ the birth of a true human being? Or shall we believe that he proceeded externally and not properly from the virginal womb?

You see, then, that you have introduced examples from visible creatures superfluously into the birth of divine generation, since the more evident proofs of the testimonies show that to be “from him” is also to be generated “from” him.

I therefore confess my astonishment that, while you avoid the name “creature” in the Son and believe that he was begotten from the Father—not made, but truly, as must be professed—you have in a certain sense imitated the impious doctrine of Photinus, though not with identical and complete statements, yet with arguments similar to his.

Arius said: Who follows the perfidy of Photinus more closely: I, who accept according to his divinity what the Son said to demonstrate a nature far inferior to the Father’s and not similar in all respects; or you, who attribute nearly all the examples of humanity to the assumed man, not in disguised words or through a simulated performance of deeds?

For, to show that he was not only another but also inferior to the Father, he said:

> “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

This profession declares more clearly that the Father and the Son are of different substances.

### XVII.

Athanasius said: Do you confess that the Son of God, who is God, assumed the servant-form of our race, or not?

Arius said: What impious person would deny that Christ, being God, must also be confessed as truly human?

Athanasius said: We must therefore ascribe some of the things Christ said to his divinity and some to his humanity, must we not? Or should we assign everything indiscriminately either to God or to man?

Arius said: It would be considered not only irreligious but the height of madness to suppose that he spoke everything either according to his divinity or according to his humanity.

Athanasius said: If, then, according to the judgment of your profession, some things are to be ascribed to his divinity and others to his humanity, why should we not attribute what he said—“The Father is greater than I” (same passage)—to his humanity, and what he said—“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—to his divinity?

And so that you may know that he said “The Father is greater than I” according to the fact that he was human, he says:

> “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

I ask, then: since the Son, according to the power of his divinity, fills all things, and no place is empty of that same divinity—for he fills heaven, earth, and the regions below with equal omnipotence—how did he say, “I am going to the Father,” with whom he was always and from whom he had never departed?

For going and coming belong to one who is bounded by certain limits of place, so that, leaving the place in which he was, he may come to another where he was not. He must therefore have been speaking of the man whom he had assumed, saying that he himself would go to the Father, from whom he will also come to judge the living and the dead.

Otherwise, where the divinity—which, as we have said, fills all things and is bounded by no spaces of place—is concerned, just as there is nowhere from which it can depart, so there is nowhere to which it can come.

### XVIII.

In this way it also appears that, according to what he is as man, he is lower not only than the Father but also than the angels. For if you wish to understand him as lower than the angels according to what he is as God, by the same necessity of the argument he will also appear to be lower than the angels according to his divine nature.

Finally, the Apostle says:

> “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:7).

If, therefore, there is no way to admit that he is regarded as lower than the angels according to what he is as God, it is evident that this act of being made lower must be attributed not to God the Word but to the man he assumed.

Probus the judge said: So that your assertion may everywhere be supported by truth, it is fitting that your side should prove, by the reading of divine testimonies, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance.

Athanasius said: Since I see that Your Excellence is most earnestly and faithfully intent upon this matter—that we demonstrate that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, and prove from the divine books that the Son was born from the substance of the Father—I shall undertake to establish from the divine oracles that the Son was ineffably born from the substance of the Father.

Although the whole substance of my arguments shows this to be the case, just as human beings or animals of any kind generate offspring like themselves in substance, and neither a human being generates an ox nor an ox a human being, but each thing reproduces according to its own likeness, that is, according to its own substance, I certainly ought not to be surprised that God was able to generate the Son from his own substance, since everything is subject to his power.

But so that my speech may not range beyond the testimony of the Scriptures, I shall proceed, fortified by their assistance, to prove from the divine oracles that the Son was ineffably born from the substance of the Father. Thus, when I have shown it through the clear path of argument—not from a philosophical argument, but, as I have said, from divine proofs—then Arius will fall silent when, through my instruction, he understands from the legal utterances that the Son was begotten from the paternal substance.

### XIX.

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews concerning the Son, says:

> “Since he is the image of the invisible God and bears the form of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15).

Jeremiah, also, the wisest of the prophets, speaks concerning the person of God the Father and says:

> “If they had stood in my substance and heard my word, they would have turned them away from their most wicked pursuits” (Jeremiah 23:22, according to the Septuagint).

And to prove that he spoke of the Son, the same prophet adds:

> “Who stood in my substance and saw my word?” (same passage, verse 18).

For that the Son is the Word, the prophet David declares concerning the person of the Father, saying:

> “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2).

The evangelist John, knowing that the Word—that is, the Son—was with the Father in the beginning, and that the Word had never been separated from the Father, placed this at the beginning of his Gospel, that is, of his proclamation, saying:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

And elsewhere Scripture has handed down the statement:

> “The Word is the beginning of the work” (Ecclesiasticus 37:20).

This does not mean that, in creating the Word—that is, from the creation of the Son—he began to make the remaining creatures; rather, all things are known to have been created through the Word of God, that is, through the Son.

Hence the prophet David sings and says:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32:6).

And to show that the Holy Spirit was a companion in this work, he continued:

> “And by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.”

There are, finally, many divine Scriptures bearing witness concerning the Son, by which it is demonstrated that he was generated from the substance of the Father—that is, from what the Father himself is. By this substance the Son is shown to be not merely like the Father.

This is the faith that Christ handed down to the apostles, and that has come from the apostles to us. We cannot alter it in any respect; it is established that we must faithfully preserve it from the beginning, just as it was given.

### XX. Probus the judge said:

Although the direction of your speech proceeds in a suitable order of argument through various byways of questions, and, deviating slightly and necessarily from the proposed straight line of correctness, advances along the winding curve of an oblique path, doing so in order to traverse every byway and leave nothing wholly unexplored or untouched, nevertheless, because the argument of Arius—which he recently bound with tighter knots of questioning—leaves this ambiguous sense of doubt to the hearers, while not all but only certain chapters of his objection appear to have been dissolved by Athanasius’ answers, it seems to me appropriate that Athanasius should turn the course of his speech toward resolving the remaining points on which the attention of the hearers is especially fixed.

For what causes us the greater scruple of hesitation is the statement made by Arius: that the Father did not naturally beget the Son, lest he appear subject to the necessities of natural conditions, but produced him through the voluntary affection of love, so that by this means an indication of free power might be demonstrated in God; and thus he should be understood to have generated more externally and from elsewhere than from himself.

The Son, therefore, is to be believed to be the result of the affection of the paternal will, and of love rather than of nature; for, as has been said, he is recognized to have been produced by will and not by natural law.

Since Athanasius clearly omitted this resolution of a question that is not knotty—whether through forgetfulness or difficulty, I do not know—let his answer now, if it seems appropriate, be directed against those matters that perhaps escaped his speech because of its length.

### XXI.

Arius said: With the exceptionally careful attention of your mind, as befits a most vigilant investigator, you use more cautious precautions. For this point of the question had almost slipped from my memory. Let Athanasius therefore declare how, if the Father naturally generated the Son, he is not bound by the necessities of nature, when it is not will but the force of nature that grants the power of generating.

For things carried out by natural impulses cannot be free, and the Father is less free in the affection of his will to the degree that the laws of his own nature exercise dominion.

Athanasius said: Of all the things Arius babbles as though they constituted an unassailable question, nothing more foolish, nothing more absurd, could ever be found; and for that reason I had thought it unworthy even to strike at them with a reply, since whoever prefers to refute extremely foolish statements sometimes incurs the mark of foolishness himself. Since, therefore, he is confident that this same question contains great assistance for his position, and since he thought it should be thrust upon me like an unavoidable snare of syllogistic art, with the arrogance of a petulant brow, let him answer whether he professes God to be mutable or immutable. [Col. 0211B]

Arius said: I profess him immutable.

Athanasius said: Then you confess him to be good, wise, just, almighty, and perfect.

Arius said: Yes.

Athanasius said: Does he remain unchangeable by will, or by nature?

Arius said: I do not understand sufficiently what you mean.

### XXII

Probus the judge said: What he is asking is perfectly clear, and is covered by no veil of obscurity. For he is asking whether you call God immutable by will or naturally. That is: is God believed to be good and wise by will, or does he possess these qualities of virtue by the privilege of his majesty and by a certain right of nature? [Col. 0211C]

Arius said: I do not rashly dare to pronounce any of these things.

Probus the judge said: Consider, then, what answer you ought to give. If you deny both alternatives, you hold neither; and thus you will be excluded from the piety of divine confession, if you retain no religious belief concerning God. Or, if you choose one of the two, so that you may not be judged empty of divine confession, say whether God is to be professed immutable by will or by nature.

Athanasius said: The listeners’ understanding plainly perceives by what waves of response and under what great constraints he is being driven. For, seeing himself entangled in the inextricable snares of my questioning, he refused to profess God immutable either by will or by nature; but deliberately remained silent concerning both, recognizing that he would be caught whichever alternative he chose. But let us see how the man who had arrogantly dictated terms to himself has protected his interests more prudently by keeping silent. 163 He said that the Father had begotten the Son not by nature but by will, lest he appear subject to certain necessities of nature. When I pressed him to say whether he called God immutable by will or by nature, he therefore remained silent about both. For if he had said that God is immutable by nature, he would have utterly overturned the whole question he had set before us; or certainly he would have fallen into it as into an abyss of a deeper precipice. It would have been necessary to turn our question-weapons back upon him at once and reply: If God is immutable by nature, then without doubt he must be professed neither good nor evil; for everything that, according to you, is borne along by natural impulses lacks the freedom of choice, being held enclosed within the limits of its condition by the final boundary of nature. He would then be like any one of the elements, like water or earth, which can be nothing other than what it is; for the laws of nature prevent it either from being increased by better developments or from falling into a worse condition. [Col. 0212A]

### XXIII

But since he asserts that God is to be professed by will rather than by nature, believing that the Son was begotten by the will, affection, and relation of the Father, rather than by natural power, let him hear what absurd reasoning follows from the meaning of this profession. It will therefore be necessary for God to be increased by progress toward a better choice, as he advances toward the highest things through the more favorable outcome of choosing good things and through the order of perfected virtues; and there will have to be someone superior to him, whom he strives to please by the effect of a good will. There would also be reason to fear that he might depart from him if perhaps the impulse of his good will abandoned him, since it is necessary that an affection of an evil will should sometimes assail one who enjoys no assistance from nature. [Col. 0212B]

The more irreligiously such things are said about God, the more wickedly they are conceived. You therefore perceive, excellent judge, that Arius, driven by an extreme impulse of impiety, has wished to compare the rights of divine nature and the substance of uncreated virtue with the natures of created things, namely, so that the Father begot the Son not by nature but by will, lest he appear subject, like creatures—whether rational or lacking reason—to natural 164 necessities. Let whoever thinks such things retain the freedom of his opinion, while he must expect a punitive judgment from the Majesty for judging matters so foolishly and sacrilegiously.

But we, instructed by the teaching of the divine Scriptures, retain this religious judgment concerning God: that we do not believe his will to be one thing and his nature another.

### XXIV

For when we confess him to be wise, good, almighty, and perfect, we do not assert that God subsists from a diversity of virtues or is composed of the quality of some distinct thing. He is not regarded as wise in one way except because he is almighty, or except because he is perfect. That is, his goodness is not one thing, his wisdom another, and his omnipotence something other than perfection; rather, all these qualities are possessed in God in one and the same manner, although they cannot be defined in a singular way. [Col. 0212D]

Take care, however, lest, because we have spoken of a “manner” in God, you understand this to mean a manner circumscribed by certain limits, since by the immensity of his power he surpasses all things. For just as, when we call him immense, we do not intend him to be understood as immoderate; or when we call him perfect, we do not introduce the notion of one who is progressing—that is, we do not assert that he reached the summit of perfection by advancing gradually through the effects of various virtues and by learning through experience—so you should understand this statement likewise.

But let us return to the matter at hand. Although God is undoubtedly simple, observe by how many names we call him: wise, good, almighty, provident, and perfect. These names refer to him in himself. In relation to us, we call him merciful, pious, just, and kind. Yet no one will dare to assert that he is composed of a multiplicity of qualities, since he subsists in the singular omnipotence of virtue and is believed to be of a pure and simple nature. But the human understanding, impeded by the natural obstacles of ignorance, could not explain this one and identical power of nature in a single expression. Therefore it uses varied and numerous names, so that from these it may more easily infer what and how great the nature of divine power is. Although it is one and equally simple, it cannot be fully explained by a single word.

For example, if we run through the various kinds of divine 165 activity and ask by what power he stretched out the vaulted heaven to such a height, founded the earth in immovable stability, and spread the seas through the flowing waters of their plains—whether by wisdom or by omnipotence—the answer is, plainly, by wisdom and by omnipotence. Will he therefore be composed of a diversity of powers? Certainly not. Rather, there are many forms of expression for one power, because wisdom does not do one thing in him, omnipotence another, and providence something else. [Col. 0213B]

### XXV

Finally, it is written: “God founded the earth by his wisdom, but established the heavens by prudence; by his understanding the abysses burst forth” (Proverbs 3:19). Shall we then become so foolish as to say that the heaven subsisted by one power, namely prudence; the earth by another, namely wisdom; and that by yet another power of God, namely his understanding, the abysses burst forth?

But see how divine Scripture, in order to reject the error of this absurd opinion, gathers together again into one what it had distributed among different forms of naming, and unites the power expressed by the names, saying: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24). And again: “My hand made all these things” (Acts 7:50). You see, therefore, that in God, whose nature is simple, whether we speak of hand, wisdom, prudence, or understanding, these do not indicate a diversity of things but one power.

Since this is so, no room remains for the question that was posed—whether God the Father begot the Son by will or by nature—since in God, as we have thoroughly demonstrated, will is nothing other than wisdom, nor is wisdom anything other than nature, which is also called power. And since Christ is all these things, as the Apostle says: “We proclaim Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), it is evident that he was begotten from the Father by the free omnipotence of natural power.

For nature in God is not, as Arius foolishly supposes, regarded as a condition of necessity—lest the Father himself, who subsists naturally, also appear to subsist by necessity. Rather, it is a power of free authority, bound by no necessities. Because it did not receive from elsewhere the fact that it exists, it is therefore called “nature,” as the source and origin of all things.

The Son is in this nature, and, subsisting in this source of origin, he proceeded as wisdom from the wise, 166 power from the strong, and radiance from the light. This profession—or birth, that is, the Son—shows that such power is present in him that he has always been in the Father and, once brought forth, never departed from the Father: just as wisdom does not abandon the wise, as the strength of the strong does not leave them, and as radiance does not separate itself from its own light. [Col. 0214A]

### XXVI

Arius said: You will never, as it seems to me, be able to untie the knot of the question I have posed. For, to repeat what I said earlier, I remember saying that God, who embraces all things and has nothing outside himself, cannot flow out anywhere through the increase of generation, nor, being infinite, overflow at all, nor divide his substance into the Son; or else that he named “Son” only that portion of the paternal substance which had previously been separated and cut off from him in due proportion, and that he seemed to have taken away from himself as much as he transferred to the Son. It is clear that you have given no answer to this. [Col. 0214B]

Athanasius said: See how far you fall into madness, thinking that the mystery of the divine birth—which is not known even to the heavenly powers—can be investigated more by philosophical arguments than be contemplated with the reverence of faith. You confine a matter known, in the dignity of its miracle, only to the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit within the limits of human understanding, and handle it with the bold hand of argument as though it were common and contained no secret.

Yet no account can be given even of creatures that are placed before the gaze of human sight, since they subsist through an order of miracles that cannot be investigated. And you scrutinize their Creator, who far surpasses them in wonder; you circumscribe him by argument and make him common through unworthy and profane reasoning. But while you refuse to serve faith, while you disdain to submit to marvelous and ineffable realities, while you are driven by the fever of impatience and measure immeasurable and infinite things, you carry the point of your argument to the conclusion that God either did not beget at all, or, if he begot, was subject to all the conditions of necessity that you have proposed. [Col. 0214C]

### XXVII

But you who babble such nonsense with a sacrilegious mouth and wish to introduce God as subsisting in bodily mass—for the things you 167 bring forward apply only to visible matters existing in tangible material—while you try to show that the Son was begotten externally and not from the substance of the Father, have abandoned the simplicity of faith for the questions of an empty philosophical art. Since the divine nature cannot fall away from its own infinity or overflow further through flowing abundance, you judge it to be like foolish and coarse matter, which cannot give anything from itself without loss.

Therefore, since a bodily thing receives increase and a thing subject to death experiences diminution, let us see whether God, who is none of these things, divided his substance proportionally by generating the Son from himself, as Arius supposes through empty fear and excessive apprehension; or whether he took something away from himself to transfer it to the Son, so that by this very act he either lacks it today and is not perfect, or, if he has no need of it, appears to possess an unnecessary excess.

Let us therefore first withdraw from every description of bodily affections and abandon all the conditions of visible natures. Let us speak spiritually about a spiritual birth, and let us presume nothing concerning it on the basis of our senses. Divine Scripture, then, in order to show the impassibility of the Father’s generation, declared the Son to be understanding, wisdom, power, Word, light, and Son.

Understanding: by it all things are conceived.

Wisdom: by it conceived things are ordered.

Power: by it ordered things are brought to completion.

Word: by it completed things are announced.

Light: by it announced things are illumined.

All these are forms of naming, not different powers, but one power. [Col. 0215A]

### XXVIII

Because his greatness could not be known through the expression of a single word, it is distinguished by a multiplicity of names, so that from the diversity or quality of the name we may recognize the measure of his power.

Since counsel is not separated from the one whose counsel it is; since power is not cut off from the strong; since wisdom is not distinguished from the wise; since understanding is not torn away from the one who understands; since the Word is not removed from the paternal mouth; and since radiance is not separated from its own light by any division, it is evident that the Father experienced neither increase 168 nor diminution through generating the Son. For these things are naturally present in God, and he himself is naturally present in them, as the Son himself declares more plainly when he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38; 14:10–11).

For “to be” and “to be in” are neither an overflowing abundance—that is, an overflow outside oneself—for Arius does not admit this very “being in,” namely being in the Father, but cavils that it means flowing outside—nor a loss through diminution, while the heart gives birth to wisdom, the understanding generates counsel, the mouth brings forth speech, and the light emits radiance.

For radiance is in the light and light is in the radiance; and each subsists naturally in the other in such a way that neither can exist without the other. Wherever there is light, there the radiance of the shining light also gleams with equal brilliance.

Therefore the Father is not an excess of superfluous overflow, as though flowing out beyond himself; rather, from himself and in himself, as the wise generated wisdom, he begot the Son, and for that reason he nowhere at all departed from the greatness of his infinity.

Nor did he separate from himself a small portion of his substance in due proportion, since light, in begetting radiance, is not subject to separation. And as you pursue each point in turn, you will find that in his generation the Father was neither increased by an abundance of overflowing mass, nor diminished by the loss of a divided portion, nor separated by a division of substance that had been detached. For the nature of things, to which that sacred and ineffable generation is compared, contains nothing of this kind that could be subject to overflow, diminution, or loss. [Col. 0215D]

### XXIX

Probus the judge said: It is certain that the nature of light, or of the Word and wisdom and the other powers you have mentioned, cannot be held by these conditions. But whether, as you say, the birth produced by the Father’s generation may be compared with such examples, it is appropriate for you to teach us by divine testimonies.

Arius said: In my preceding argument I began in this way: Athanasius is being hurled by the blindness of his faithlessness into the abyss. For while he wishes to display the eloquence of his speech, he is unknowingly involved in a charge, saying that the divine Scripture teaches that the Son is equal in substance to the Father, when the Son himself testifies concerning himself and says:

“The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28);

169 “And the one who sent me gave me a commandment” (John 12:49);

“I did not come of myself, but he sent me” (John 8:42);

“I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38);

“As the Father said to me, so I speak” (John 12:50);

“What he gave me, I have kept” (John 17:12);

“All that the Father has given me, no one takes away from me” (John 6:39);

“I will ask him, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels” (Matthew 26:53);

“If this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (Matthew 26:42);

“Let this cup pass from me. Not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39);

“I always do the things that please him” (John 8:29);

“To sit at my right or left is not mine to give you” (Matthew 20:23);

“He gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9);

“He exalted his servant”;

“And the Lord your God blessed you” (Psalm 44:8);

“He raised him from the dead and made him sit at his right hand” (Ephesians 1:20);

and many other passages like these, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

If, then, he has one greater than himself; if he was sent by him; if he did not come of his own spontaneous will; if he did not do his own will; if he speaks what is said to him; if he guards what was given to him; if he asks; if he prays concerning the cup; if he received a name from another; if he is exalted by another; if he does not by his own power grant the seats to disciples who ask for them; if he does what pleases the Father; and if he is raised from the dead by him, does it seem right that one who says so much and so plainly concerning his own subjection should be made equal to the Father? [Col. 0216C]

### XXX

Probus the judge said: If Athanasius thinks that anything can be said in response to these abundant testimonies of divine authority, which Arius has produced concerning the Son’s subjection, let him not delay in stating it, so that, once the superstructure of argument has been removed, the Son may be shown from the divine lights either to be unlike or equal to the Father. Thus, when the truth has been recognized, what agrees with sound faith and reason may be strengthened.

Athanasius said: However far Arius’s cunning may proceed in the arrogance of speech, and however much he may applaud himself for the testimonies drawn from the authority of divine law, by which he endeavors to separate the Son from equality with the Father, our response will without difficulty frustrate his intention through those same testimonies. [Col. 0216D]

Christ, therefore, the Son of God, is said to be subject to the Father in the form of a servant, which he assumed from the Virgin, as the Apostle Paul nevertheless affirms: “When the fullness 170 of time came,” he says, “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). He, then, is said to be subject who is known to have been born under the law from a woman; and in that form, which he voluntarily assumed from the Virgin, he indicates that the Father is greater than himself.

But in the form of God, the angelic choir is shown to have offered him ministry. For thus it is written in the Gospel: “And the devil departed from him, and angels came and ministered to him” (Matthew 4:11).

Arius objects that he did the Father’s will and not his own. In this statement of the Word he should rather be recognized as especially praiseworthy, because he who carried out the Father’s will with equanimity showed equality, as the Apostle confirms: “This is the will of God in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

For since he added, “As the Father said to me, so I speak” (John 12:50), why should the human race, understanding what is right, be disturbed when it hears this statement? If Christ spoke otherwise than God the Father, then he would be shown to be more unequal or unlike the Father. But if the Son speaks what the Father speaks, he is never found unequal or unlike the Father.

“He gave me,” he says, “I have kept” (John 17:12); and “All that he gave me, no one takes away from me” (John 6:39). These divine gifts must be understood as having been attributed to the Son in this way. [Col. 0217A]

### XXXI

For the almighty Father gave omnipotence to the Son; he granted majesty to Majesty; he gave power to Power, prudence to Prudence, foreknowledge to Foreknowledge, divinity to Divinity, eternity to Eternity, co-equality to Co-equality, immortality to Immortality, invisibility to Invisibility; to the King, a kingdom; to Life, life. He gave him not something different from what he has, but as much as he has, so much he gave. The same applies to any other qualities that the Father is shown to have conferred indivisibly and inseparably upon the Son.

Yet he is shown to have given these things to one who already possessed them rather than to one who needed them, to whom the Son says: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (John 17:10).

If all these things that the Father is said to have conferred upon the Son appear to be one thing in the Father and another in the Son, we undoubtedly make the Son a liar, since he says that the things belonging to the Father are his. But if the Son is found to be lying in what he said, and if the evangelist who says that he “made himself equal with God” (John 5:18) is entirely deceived, then it is shown that the Father did not confer anything upon the Son wholly and truthfully. 171

But if the things that the Father inseparably and indistinguishably conferred upon the Son are true—as they are—let the tongues of foolish men fall silent, for they strive to separate the Son from the substance of the Father. [Col. 0217C]

The Son asks the Father in order to demonstrate that he bears true humanity. Yet, to make known the power of his divinity, he commanded the sea and the winds, and he fed five thousand people with five loaves.

As a man in sorrow he received the cup of suffering; but as God he offered believers the fountain of living water springing up into eternal life. He received a name so that at this name heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings might bow in worship. He was exalted from the depths to the heights, that is, from the flesh of human frailty, ascending to God.

He sits at the right hand of Majesty so that human weakness may not hesitate to follow him where it sees its Head glorified. He was anointed so that through the anointing of his chrism we might be cleansed from the stain of the former man’s sin. He was raised from the dead so that, by the example of his resurrection, we might be freed from the sting of death.

He testifies that he cannot give the seats to the disciples who ask for them, lest division arise among them. For the one who said, “It is not mine to give you,” had already granted the disciples the power to judge over twelve thrones. He did what pleased the Father because he does not know how to do anything contrary.

Since he came not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him, he said: “I desired to do your will, my God” (Psalm 39:9); and “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Psalm 53:8).

The one who said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), also said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); “That they may be one in us, just as you and I are one” (John 17:21–22); “All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine” (John 17:10); “Do you believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:10–11); “My Father is working, and I am working” (John 5:17); “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” (John 5:21); “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9); “Whoever hates me hates my Father also” (John 15:23); “Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1); “I glorified you on earth” (John 17:4); and “I made your name known to the people” (John 17:6).

And so that every intention of human quibbling may fall silent, I shall bring forward as a witness John the Evangelist, whose testimony I used earlier. He says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

If these many 172 statements, so appropriate to divinity, by which we have shown the Father and the Son to be one, are not sufficient for the faithless, let us, if it seems appropriate, add others. [Col. 0218B]

### XXXII

Probus the judge said: If Arius attempts to oppose this argument, which is so strong and certain, it is clear that he is not following reason but wandering more wildly through the fields of irrational words. Until now he has been unable to demonstrate his assertion, although, as he admitted earlier, he has been circling through some sort of nebulous darkness concerning the theory of three substances, whereas Athanasius has shown the doctrine of one substance by very many proofs. [Col. 0218C]

Arius said: Because Athanasius, from the divine oracles, has dared—by I know not what arguments—to assert that the Son is of one substance and co-equal with the Father, must he also confer upon the Spirit, who is the minister of the Father and the Son, the same confession of equality? The Son himself says: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14); “I will send you the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26); “The Spirit will proceed from me”; and “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). And the Father says to the bones of the dead through the prophet: “I will give my Spirit into you, and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:5).

Must the one who is sent or proceeds from the Father be made equal to him, when the prophet testifies concerning him, saying: “Behold, the Lord who strengthens the thunder and creates the spirit” (Amos 4:13)? Surely it will never seem to me that a creature can be made equal to its Creator or share power with him. [Col. 0218D]

Athanasius said: I have already demonstrated above that wisdom and power are the Son of God, where I proved that the Apostle said: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). But now, if you consider it necessary, I shall repeat the testimonies concerning this same proof more fully and more accurately.

### XXXIII

Wisdom itself—that is, the Son—cries out through Solomon, saying: “I proceeded from the mouth of the Most High” (Sirach 24:5); and: “Before the hills, he begot me” (Proverbs 8:25).

That this same wisdom is the radiance of the Father’s light is likewise confirmed by the testimony of the aforementioned Solomon, David, and the Apostle. Solomon says: “She is the brightness of eternal light, a spotless mirror” (Wisdom 7:26), through which and in which, without doubt, the Father is seen, as the Son himself says in the Gospel: “Who 173 ever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

David also declares this more openly when he addresses the Father, saying: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10). Do you hear that light is seen in light—that is, that the Father is contemplated in the Son?

Paul likewise proclaims what accords with this, saying: “Since he is the radiance and image of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3).

He is also called the Word, as the Father declares in order to demonstrate the impassibility of his generation, saying: “My heart has poured forth a good Word” (Psalm 44:2); “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32:6); and “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

When he says, “The Word was God,” understand “Word” not as something merely uttered and passing away in the sound of the voice, but as remaining substantially in its own power.

That he is also counsel is testified by Isaiah, who says: “He shall be called the Angel of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:5), that is, the dispenser and author of the Father’s deliberations or consolations—or rather, the very consolation and deliberation itself.

The understanding of the Father’s heart is likewise shown, as Solomon says: “The Lord founded the earth by his wisdom; he established the heavens by prudence. By his understanding the abysses burst forth.” Concerning this understanding Isaiah and the Apostle say: “Who has known the understanding of the Lord?” (Isaiah 40:13; Romans 11:34), in accordance with the Gospel statement: “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matthew 11:27).

It has therefore become clear, as I think, that in begetting the Son from himself and possessing that same Son within himself, the Father was neither increased and expanded nor diminished in any way. For the one who begets is recognized as remaining in the substance of the perfect nature of the one begotten; nor are the two diffused outside themselves, since each is known to remain in the other.

Thus Isaiah does not declare the Son to be outside the infinity of the Father’s nature, as though flowing beyond it; rather, he declares the Father and the Son to dwell in one another through the unity of their common substance, when he addresses the Son and says: “God is in you, and there is no God besides you” (Isaiah 45:14). [Col. 0219D]

### XXXIV

Probus the judge said: To the fullest extent that the capacity of human understanding permits the perception of reason, I believe that Athanasius has completely cut away the knot of the preceding little question, with all the ambiguity of its perplexing and scrupulous opinion, in which our attention was entangled. If this has also become clear to Arius, 174 let him state it more openly; and from these matters let us finally pass to others—if indeed you think any remain—so that we may complete the business of this work more quickly.

Arius said: If you examine carefully, with an ever-watchful mind and the keenest understanding, both in general and in detail, the statements of the questions I proposed, you will certainly find that Athanasius has not answered everything.

Probus the judge said: What are those matters in which you think you have not been satisfied? Point them out more clearly.

Arius said: Why should we draw out the long thread of argument by repeating the same things, when you ought now to state your final judgment concerning the matter?

Probus the judge said: Your own prudence recognizes along with me that a judgment ought not to be pronounced while the matter remains only half complete. For this reason it is appropriate that you should also bring forward in debate some matters concerning the Holy Spirit.

Arius said: I confess that the Holy Spirit is not only less than the Father and the Son, but also their minister and servant of their will, as a creature offering the most reverent service to the Creator. Yet he is better than all creatures and is first after the Son. For if he were honored with the privilege of equality with the Father, as Athanasius professes, the Son would not say that he will not speak from himself but will speak whatever he hears. For one who speaks nothing by the authority of spontaneous power serves through the obedience of ministry under the command of the one who orders him. [Col. 0220B]

### XXXV

Athanasius said: If the clemency of the judge permits and grants it, I shall briefly demonstrate from the divine authorities that the Holy Spirit also is not a creature but God and Creator with the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0220C]

Probus the judge said: As your profession declares, briefly establish what reason requires to be demonstrated—not from the argument of speech but from the testimonies of the divine Scriptures—that the Holy Spirit is co-equal with the Father and the Son; or, as you yourself have confessed, show that he is God or Creator, the author of their common work. Thus, when you have proved these things by truthful testimonies, Arius may depart, convicted by the profession of the true faith, from the position he has maintained.

Athanasius said: 175 It is especially evident from this that the Holy Spirit is not alien to the substance of the Father and the Son: he does not act and speak from himself as someone alien and foreign, but as a companion of one and the same nature, carrying out and speaking the things that belong in common to the Father and the Son. [Col. 0220D]

For if he spoke from his own possessions, he would undoubtedly be regarded not only as alien to the Father but also as false and deceptive, since, as the Son says, “Everyone who speaks a lie speaks from his own possessions” (John 8:44). Therefore he speaks the truth because he does not speak from what is his own—that is, not from himself—but speaks the things of the Father and the Son that ought to be spoken.

“He will receive from what is mine,” he says, “and will announce it to you” (John 16:14). And to show that receiving from himself means also receiving from the Father, he said: “Therefore I said, He will receive from what is mine, because everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

You see, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is not separated from the Father and the Son, since he speaks the things that are known to belong to the Father and the Son.

The Son also makes a similar profession when he says: “I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10), but “the things I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

This statement shows the Son and the Holy Spirit to be equal to one another—even if, as you falsely suppose, the Son is less than the Father—which you impiously refuse to acknowledge. For if neither presumes to speak anything by his own authority, neither surpasses the other in any honor of dignity. [Col. 0221A]

### XXXVI

But hear still more clearly how they are held to be equal to the Father. The Son says: “The works that I do themselves testify about me” (John 10:25); and again: “I do nothing from myself, but the Father who remains in me himself does the works” (John 14:10).

How, then, does he now say that the works he does are his own, and shortly afterward say that they are not his own? He clearly wished to demonstrate the power of one nature and therefore referred the effectiveness of the works performed to the unity of the Father’s dignity.

Since the work is the Father’s and the Son’s, and the work of the Son is the Father’s—for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise—the communion of nature is recognized from the work they perform in common.

Therefore, just as he says that his works are not his own, although they are proved to be his, so he testifies that he does not speak words that are his own, although they are plainly known to be his.

And what you infer concerning the Son, infer also concerning the Holy Spirit. In order to demonstrate the 176 divinity of one nature, he does not speak from himself, yet what he speaks is to be believed to be his and not another’s.

“And they were speaking,” Luke says concerning the apostles, “in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). And in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

He therefore possesses his own authority to speak, since he freely grants the others the ability to speak. [Col. 0221C]

Arius said: By what scriptural authorities will you be able to teach that the Holy Spirit is God, whom I confess to be a creature?

Athanasius said: It is principally made clear that the Holy Spirit is God because he is everywhere and is contained by no place, as the prophet says to the Father: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Psalm 138:7). And Scripture declares: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7).

To be everywhere and, at one and the same moment, to fill the heavens, the earth, the seas, and the underworld—as David says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Psalm 138:8)—is proper not to a creature but to God alone. [Col. 0221D]

### XXXVII

Finally, because he too is uncompounded—that is, of a simple nature. For every creature, insofar as concerns the order of its nature, is composite. If, then, you are able to show that the Holy Spirit is composed from a diversity of forms, only then will it follow that no one will dare doubt that he is a creature. Then, if he is a creature, you will necessarily have to teach that he is common with the others, whether angels, archangels, powers, or principalities, and demonstrate that he is one among them and thus not unique and singular—which you certainly will not be able to demonstrate, since the prophets and apostles, prevailing and protesting on every side, [Col. 0222A] oppose it.

Solomon indeed says this: “The Holy Spirit is simple, unique,” and so forth (Wis. VII, 22). The Apostle also testifies: “One Spirit” (Eph. IV, 4). And again: “But all these things one and the same Spirit works” (I Cor. XII, 11). Again: “For through him,” he says, “we have access in one Spirit” (Eph. II, 18).

Do you see, then, that he who is of a unique and simple nature is God rather than a creature? Finally, if he is a creature and not God, by what benefit of usefulness is the regeneration of the living washing celebrated in his name? “Baptize,” says the Lord, “the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXIX, 19). For what benefit can he provide us if he is not God? What sort of creature, I ask, is this who possesses one name together with the Father? If you do not name him in baptism, the entire mystery will appear futile, and the sacrament will not be complete. For you will use the name of the Father and of the Son in vain if he is not named. It is therefore wholly beyond doubt that a creature cannot be creator.

### XXXVIII

The divine Scriptures everywhere declare that this Spirit is creator, as we read in the Book of Job: “The divine Spirit is he who made me” (Job XXXIII, 4). For the Holy Spirit is designated as having brought about creation in its entirety, as David more plainly declares, saying: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII, 4)—namely, of the Word and of the Holy Spirit.

The holy prophet sings with sacred voice that the Holy Spirit is the finger whose works are the fashioning of the heavens; the Lord plainly demonstrated this in the Gospel, saying: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke XI, 20). This is the finger by which the law of God is reported to have been written on two stone tablets, as we read in Exodus: “Moses received,” it says, “the two tablets written by the finger of God” (Exod. XXXI, 18).

From this it is shown that this Holy Spirit is the giver of the law, whose law frees human beings from sins, according to Paul’s proclaiming testimony: “The law of the Spirit of life has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. VIII, 2). The magicians of Pharaoh also wonderfully confess the power of this force, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII, 19).

Moreover, the prophet David more openly declares that the Holy Spirit is creator, saying: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6). And again: “Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Ps. CIII, 30).

No one doubts that the powers of heaven are angels. According to the Apostle’s testimony, they also reverently long to look into this Spirit as the author of their origin. For he says: “Those things that have been sent to you from heaven by the Holy Spirit, into which the angels long to look” (I Pet. I, 12).

### XXXIX

If he were not God, he would not possess the proper freedom of choosing and doing what he wills. But since, in the economy of the mystery, he exercises freedom of will and does not await the command of one who orders him, it is evident that he is not a creature but God.

For when the Apostle was speaking about the diversities of heavenly gifts, he concluded: “But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 11). And again: “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “distributes to all according to his own will” (Heb. II, 4). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III, 8).

If he is not God, how does he give life? The Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6). And again, concerning God: “He will give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. VIII, 11). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is the Spirit who gives life” (John VI, 64). Hence in Ezekiel he is also called the Spirit of life: “The Spirit of life,” he says, “was in the wheels” (Ezek. I, 20). Concerning this Spirit the Lord says in the same prophet to mortal bodies: “Behold, I will bring my Spirit into you, and you shall live” (Ezek. XXXVII, 5).

Therefore he who grants life is God. [Col. 0223B] For if he were not God, how is he proclaimed as coming to judge the world? The Lord says in the Gospel: “When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, he himself will convict the world concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment” (John XVI, 8).

### XL

Hear another argument by which it becomes clear that the Holy Spirit is God. The Father calls the faithful to his grace; the Son calls them; the Holy Spirit calls them. If he were a creature, he would not possess an equal and comparable authority to call.

For concerning the Father the Apostle says: “But when it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace” (Gal. I, 15). And writing to the Romans concerning Christ: “Among whom you also are,” he says, “called by Jesus Christ” (Rom. I, 6).

Concerning the Holy Spirit, Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “While they were fasting and ministering” —that is, the apostles—“the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts XIII, 2).

The same Scripture also testifies that the Holy Spirit reveals mysteries: “Agabus arose,” it says, “and signified through the Spirit that a great famine was about to come” (Acts XI, 28). And again: “While Peter was considering the vision, the Holy Spirit said: Behold, three men are seeking you. Rise, go down, and go with them without hesitation, because I have sent them” (Acts X, 19).

But lest, by piling many testimonies together, our discourse be extended at length, I briefly gather everything together. What, then, does it seem to you, excellent judge? Is the Holy Spirit not God—he who is not composite, who is unique and singular, who is creator and giver of life, who possesses one name with the Father and the Son, who forgives sins, who sanctifies, who distributes the gifts of grace according to his own will, who reveals mysteries, who gives the law, who by his own authority calls people to grace, who judges the world, who condemns those who tempt him, and in whom the impious blaspheme without remission?

If such a one is not God, let him show what more the one who is God could possibly possess.

### XLI

Arius said:

Although the whole argument is exposed to contradiction, and although, as though by some shield of reply, the weapons of objections are repelled and rendered ineffective, nevertheless, however subtly Athanasius may strive by the ingenuity of his mind to evade the question we are now pursuing, he will never be able to dissolve by rational arguments—not the whole of it, I do not say, but even any portion of it.

He says that the Holy Spirit is God, although nowhere has he been able to demonstrate this more clearly. Let it nevertheless be granted that, contrary to the truth of the matter, I concede to him that the Holy Spirit may appear or be God on the ground that he performs such works as are appropriate to God alone. Thus he confesses God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit; and thereby he appears, if not with open impiety, nevertheless by the very condition of his profession to introduce three gods. In this way he begins somehow to lead us back to the error of many gods, from which we had departed.

I should like, excellent judge—if indeed it is possible—to catch this remarkable master of his art, once the frauds of his illusions have been stripped away, deceiving the eyes of those who agree with him. For in order to escape the danger of confessing three gods, he suddenly fuses them by an incomprehensible phantom so that three may appear to be one, saying: “But these three are one God.”

Again, those whom by some sort of coagulation he had mixed and united into one God, he displays once more as separated and threefold, saying: “And this one God is a Trinity.” See, if you can—I beg you—investigate these unheard-of and unseen monstrosities of a most wicked imagination.

I cannot understand how God is now one, now divided into three; now confused from three into one, now distinguished from one into three; now formed by some composition from parts, now divided again from one into parts by I know not what derivation.

For he says: “There are three persons existing in their own substance, and they must not be mixed together, lest they lose their proper status.” According to my judgment—and even more according to the judgment of truth—he says: “If there is one person, let him simply confess this openly and pass over into the doctrine of Sabellius.”

For what need is there, in order to mock the truth, to vary things by different forms and images; and so to flee from Sabellius that he runs into me, and to flee from me in such a way that Sabellius catches him? For in order to strip himself of Sabellian impiety, he affirms that the one whom he calls one is three. But lest I hold him guilty concerning the three, by some artifice he fuses the three into one.

Now, if this faith has any plausible basis, it is for your equity to judge, excellent Probus.

### XLII

Probus the judge said:

To call the one whom you have called one three in turn, and to confess again as one God those whom you have believed to be three, appears, insofar as human reason is concerned, to be highly inconsistent—unless perhaps we are commanded to believe this by divine authority. Therefore let Athanasius not delay in answering these objections of Arius, so weighty and so invincible.

Athanasius said:

You seem to have woven, as you think, nets of words with insoluble knots, not understanding or foreseeing that you too may be entangled in these snares of objections. Since you bring an accusation against me concerning the three, I put to you a question concerning the two.

If you worship one God, and there is no other besides the one, how do you introduce two for worship and veneration? For by confessing the Father as God and the Son as God, you are shown either to confess a divided God or two distinct gods; and thus you offer impious service to a double divinity. The Lord says: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24).

But lest I too incur the charge of rashness if I press you with an equal question concerning your confession of God—for whose supreme veneration silence is more appropriate than crafty questions—I see that I must hasten to this point: I must prove, if not by the reasoning of a human being, at least by authority, that three are one and one is three.

Let us therefore hear the Trinity itself saying: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26). Those who determine that the human being should be made are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; but these three are one. Finally, it adds: “And God made the human being in the image and likeness of God” (ibid., 27).

Thus, so that you may recognize the Trinity, it says in the plural, “Let us make”; and so that you may not fail to know that this Trinity is one God, it adds in the singular, “And God made the human being.”

And again: “It is not good for the human being to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. II, 18). Here too it says in the plural, “Let us make.” In what follows, however, it states in the singular: “And God made the human being in the image of God; male and female he created them” (Gen. V, 1–2).

In the consultation, three are reported; in the work, one—so that it may be evident not that there is diversity of will, but unity of power.

### XLIII

And again: “God appeared to Abraham; he looked toward the oak of Mamre, and behold, three men stood before him. He fell down and worshiped, saying: If I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant” (Gen. XVIII, 1–3).

Behold, one is said to have appeared, and yet there were three; and although there were three, nevertheless there was one. For when he says, “If I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant,” he shows that there is one.

Again, when it is said, “Let water be brought, and wash your feet,” he shows that there are three. Again, when he says, “He set a table before them, and they ate, while he himself stood before them under the tree” (Gen. XVIII, 4), he shows that there are three. And when he adds, “But he said to him, Where is Sarah your wife?” (ibid., 8), he shows that there is one.

Likewise, when he says, “The men rose from there and went toward Sodom, while Abraham accompanied them” (ibid., 9), he shows that there are three. And when he repeats, “But the Lord said, Shall I hide from my servant Abraham what I am about to do in Sodom?” (ibid., 16), he shows that there is one.

Those sacred songs of the powers above likewise demonstrate that one is three and three are one. For they resound in this manner: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. VI, 3). By repeating “holy” three times, they signify the Trinity; by saying “Lord” once, they designate this same Trinity as one God.

This mystery also corresponds to that evangelical sacrament in which the Lord commanded the nations to be baptized “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Behold, you have three subsisting in one name of the Godhead. For the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is God.

Concerning this name, the Lord speaks to Moses in the Book of Numbers, saying: “As I live, and as my name lives” (Num. XIV, 21).

### XLIV

Nor should that seem insignificant to you which the same Son speaks under the great mystery of the Trinity: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Acts VII, 32).

In saying, “I am,” he shows one God; and in repeating three times, “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” he more plainly declares the mystery of the Trinity.

Hear and contemplate still more clearly the mystery of this secret. Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting on a throne,” and below: “And he said, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”—without doubt to preach to the Jewish people. “And I said, Behold, here am I; send me. And he said, Go, and you shall say to this people” (Isa. VI, 1, 8–9).

When, therefore, he says in the singular, “Whom shall I send?”, he indicates one God; and when he adds in the plural, “Who will go for us?”, he openly signifies the Trinity.

Receive still more manifestly, if you bear the ears of your mind open, the truth of this faith. That the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the creator of heaven and earth is more clearly declared by what we have already brought forward, when we showed that it was said in the plural, “Let us make the human being” (Gen. I, 26), where the whole Trinity is understood to have fashioned the human being, just as this same Trinity is believed to restore the human being in baptism.

Or consider also what the prophet says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6). And Solomon, speaking in the person of Wisdom, declares, saying: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things” (Prov. VIII, 27, 29–30).
