It is therefore established, as I have said, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the whole Trinity—is the creator of the world.

Let us therefore hear through the prophet Isaiah that the three are one God. For it is said there: “I am God, establishing the heavens alone and setting the earth firm; and there was none with me” (Isa. XLIV, 24).

Do you wish this utterance to belong to the Father or to the Son? If you do not believe the whole Trinity to be one God, this statement will not stand. For he says that he established the earth, and that there was none with him. Yet surely the Son was with the Father, who says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there; and when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him” (Prov. VIII, 27, 29–30).

Since it is therefore clear that the Father was not alone in the creation of the world—for the Holy Spirit and the Son were with him, as participants in one divinity and power—what does he mean by testifying that he was alone and that there was no other with him, unless you understand that he called himself, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God, with whom there was no other god foreign to or alien from his nature?

And Moses rightly spoke concerning the children of Israel, saying: “He alone led them, and there was no foreign god with him” (Deut. XXXII, 12). Arius certainly cannot deny that the Son and the Holy Spirit were with the people. But the Son and the Holy Spirit are not foreign, since with the Father they are one God.

### XLV

Let us also hear blessed Paul, who discusses this same mystery more openly and confirms that the three are one God, as is fully set forth in the book that we published against Maribadus, the deacon of your unspeakable heresy. Here we insert only a very small portion of it.

When he objected that union excludes the equality of the Trinity, and equality excludes union, among many other things I replied as follows. “Hear,” I said, “the Apostle proclaiming this union of the Trinity still more emphatically.”

He says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4–6).

Because there is a Trinity, he named three. And because this Trinity is one God, when he had numbered the three persons together, he did not say in the plural, “who work,” but in the singular, “who works.”

And lest you suppose, through a perverse interpretation, that he spoke only of the Father when he said “who works all things,” listen more carefully to what he says in what follows. After he had enumerated many works of divine grace, he said: “But all these things one and the same Spirit works” (ibid., 11).

You see the Father working, the Son working, and the Holy Spirit working; and although the three work together, it is not said of them, “those who work,” but “he who works,” so that one God in the Trinity may be shown.

Likewise, the same Apostle names the Son and the Father: “Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God the Father, who loved us” (II Thess. II, 15). When he had named two and shown them to be one, he did not say “who loved” in the plural, but “who loved” in the singular. Nor did he say “may they console,” but “may he console your hearts” (ibid., 16).

Likewise: “May God our Father himself, and the Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you” (I Thess. III, 11). Here too he did not say “may they direct,” but “may he direct.”

Thus far, borrowing very sparingly from that work, I have taught in apostolic fashion that the Trinity is one God. Let us hasten to what remains.

### XLVI

The Acts of the Apostles also teach that this mystery of the faith can be commended especially by natural examples, when Luke tells of the believers: “The multitude of those who believed had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32).

If grace, through the regeneration of baptism, bestowed this upon the faithful—that the many souls of believers should be one soul—why should it not be believed, with much greater appropriateness, concerning the Trinity that it is one God, so that what we possess through grace, that Trinity possesses by nature?

For if we examine more carefully, we also find in ourselves something of nature that resembles that most blessed and ineffable Trinity, though in a very different way. Nor was it without reason that it was written that God made the human being in his image and likeness (Gen. I, 17, and V, 1).

That the human being consists of three things—that is, body, soul, and spirit—the Apostle testifies, saying: “May the whole of you, body, soul, and spirit, be preserved blameless for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V, 23).

If in a corruptible and composite nature there is found so great a mystery of unity, so that one is three and three are one human being, how much more beautifully and properly is it understood of the Trinity that it is one God—not by a confused mixture, but by unity of nature?

Instructed, therefore, by these and very many other testimonies and examples of realities, we neither fall into Sabellius by confessing three to be one God, nor are we ensnared by the traps of your perfidy when we openly confess that this God is a Trinity.

### XLVII

Probus the judge said:

If anything remains for you to reply in opposition to what Athanasius has argued, take care to bring it forward.

Arius said:

There are indeed very many things that teach that the Son is of another nature and that the Son is inferior in power. But since our people have argued these matters more fully elsewhere against the errors of these men, why is it necessary to repeat the same things again and provide material for a drawn-out quarrel? If you please, therefore, deliver judgment concerning the matters debated between us.

Probus the judge said:

I have already stated above that a judgment should not be pronounced when the case is only half complete. It remains for you, if anything is left, to bring it to an end.

Arius said:

Deign to pronounce concerning what has been opened to your knowledge.

Athanasius said:

Of the remaining questions by which Arius thinks that the Son can be shown to be inferior to the Father, the principal one is that which the same Son says: “The Father is greater than I.” He has already been recognized as having raised this point, and all the limbs of the questions adhere to it as to their head.

For when he says, “I have not come to do my own will” (John VI, 38); “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John V, 19); “As the Father taught me, so I do” (John VIII, 28); “My teaching is not mine” (John VII, 16); “I must work the works of him who sent me” (John IX, 4); “I have not come from myself; he sent me” (John VIII, 42); “I am the vine, and my Father is the cultivator” (John XV, 1); “I live because of the Father” (John VI, 58); or when he confesses that he does not know the day (Matt. XXIV, 36; Mark XIII, 32), calls his Father God (John V, 18), prays that the cup might pass from him (Matt. XXVI, 39), complains that he has been abandoned on the cross (Matt. XXVII, 46), commends his spirit to the Father (Luke XXIII, 46), and whatever other statements of this kind there may be—they refer to this matter and are understood by us with all fear and reverence according to the administration of the flesh, by which he was made lower not only than the Father but also than angels and human beings.

### XLVIII

We believe ourselves indebted to him by so great a benefit precisely because we do not understand these things as unworthy of him: he loved us with such great love that he willed to lower himself to such lowly and injurious conditions.

Since he was made lower than the angels (Ps. VIII, 6), we have already, as I remember, taught this more fully above, where we set down the words of the Apostle who says (Heb. II, 7): “We see Jesus, because of the suffering of death, made for a little while lower than the angels.”

But hear Isaiah, who says that he was also made lower than human beings: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was despised and diminished before the children of men” (Isa. LIII, 2–3). The evangelist Luke also says of him: “And he was subject to his parents” (Luke II, 52).

If all these things are understood according to the form of his humanity, his divinity is found to be lower not only than the Father, but also than angels and human beings. But because he possessed both natures in himself—namely, that of God and that of a human being—he speaks and acts according to the reality of each nature.

For it is not the same nature that says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28), and says, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); that says, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John V, 19), and says, “Whatever things the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John V, 19); that says, “I have not come to do my own will” (John VI, 38), and says, “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John V, 21).

Accordingly, with the authority of free will he says to the leper: “I will; be cleansed” (Mark I, 41).

### XLIX

It is not, then, the same nature that is contained in the lap of a manger and is disclosed by the signs of the stars; that is subjected to human beings and ministered to by angels; that flees from place to place and displays its presence everywhere; that inhabits earthly things and does not abandon heavenly things; that is tempted by the devil and sends his legions into the abyss; that endures hunger and satisfies many thousands of people; that thirsts for water and changes streams of liquid into the nature of wine; that asks for the cup of a well for the quenching of thirst for a single moment and provides the perpetual channels of a flowing river; that crosses the waters in a boat and treads upon those same waters with wondrous movement on dry feet; that does not know the day and knows the Father; that refuses two seats to those who ask and freely promises twelve thrones at once; that fears death and mocks death; that fears being seized and leads captives back, completely plundering all the rights of hell; that complains of being deserted and soon admits the thief into the company of the patriarchs; that created all things from nothing and, having triumphed over death, receives authority over them.

You see, therefore, excellent Probus, most discerning examiner, that in this administration of the assumed flesh nothing at all was taken away from the divinity, while wherever the duty of the body’s humility is fulfilled, there the miracles of divine powers shine forth.

Therefore he is equal to the Father insofar as he is God, and he is lower than the Father insofar as he was made human.

### L

I have briefly gathered all these matters into a single mass of response because our blessed Ambrose has argued about all these headings of questions at greater length and more fully. Against him, Palladius, a bishop of Arian perfidy, believed that certain things ought to be written in refutation of his statements—when, I believe, that holy man had already been removed from human affairs.

If anything, then, can now be objected by you, he has already occupied the ground with his objections. Since I have already answered him in a single book, I think it better, if anything here perhaps appears to have been omitted, to explain it more fully there, with the help of divine grace, so that Arius may also recognize himself as defeated in that work.

Therefore deign, excellent Probus, to deliver the final judgment concerning what has been established.

Probus the judge said:

If, after innumerable testimonies promulgated under heavenly instruction, anything appears to remain for Arius, let him not hesitate to bring it forward. Although, as I think, nothing remains for him by which he could repel Athanasius concerning the doctrine of one substance—that is, the *homoousion*. But lest he later complain that he has been oppressed by us, let no opportunity for replying be taken away from him.

Arius said:

There is no doubt that Athanasius does not cease, by magical arts, to pervert the judgment of judges, so that they cannot maintain the path of right faith toward those who religiously follow and venerate it. Therefore, what I cannot explain before the judgment of your eminence, I shall reserve for the judgment of the emperor, where the investigation of truth prevails, and where it must be believed that magical arts cannot prevail over observance of the true faith.

Athanasius said:

Those who cannot support their assertions never cease finding excuses for themselves through whatever deceptive arguments or quibbles they can, as your eminence now sees Arius doing most plainly. For my part, since I am defending the true faith, it is enough that I have answered everything proposed by him in the presence of your eminence.

## BOOK THREE: THE JUDGMENT OF PROBUS THE JUDGE

### I

Probus the judge said:

For love of truth and faith, I sat as arbiter among the adherents of the Christian religion—that is, Athanasius, Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus. Since they are separated from one another by the diversity of their doctrines and the variation of their opinions, with a long interval of disagreement between them, I took special care to investigate whose faith was distinguished by true assertions.

So that I might learn this more easily, I required each of them individually to present his statement of faith and, through my questions, demanded that they strengthen it with credible proofs. Those who opposed one another were to meet and refute one another, so that, with some defending and others resisting, recognition of the clearest truth might be disclosed. That they did so is demonstrated by reading their arguments themselves.

### II

When, therefore, I first granted Sabellius permission to argue—not so much by formal authorization as by my inquiry—he put forward the following statement of faith concerning God: he said that the Father subsisted as solitary and unique, without any distinct person of the existing Son or of the Holy Spirit, in such a way that he himself was rather designated by the name of Son and of Spirit.

He asserted that God was three-named—that is, as though one species or person were called by three names, not through a distinction of kind but through a change of function—so that he was called Father not because he begot, but because he created. The same one, falling from the dignity of paternal honor through certain increases—or rather diminutions—of nature, passed into the name of Son through birth from a virgin.

But that these claims were foolish and impious, lacking all truth of faith, became entirely clear from the arguments of those who opposed him. For it was shown by many and abundant proofs from the divine readings that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each exist as distinct and proper persons: one is the begetter, another the begotten, and another the Holy Spirit of the begotten and the unbegotten.

Nevertheless, according to Athanasius’s credible statement of faith, they cannot be different in nature, although they can be believed—and certainly are—to be distinct from one another. For it is truly a form of extreme and profound folly to call him Father who has not begotten, and to believe him to be Son who has not been begotten; or, through empty inventions of false names devoid of reality, to divert the judgment of human minds and mock the Christian faith with the playful objections of opinions.

### III

After the tricks of this error had been exposed and laid bare, I ordered Photinus, through my questioning, to present his faith, if he were able. At the very beginning of his argument he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ was a mere human being and empty of the divinity of the Word. He said that Christ had advanced so conspicuously through certain stages of blessed life that he rightly passed into the designation of God and Lord—not by the natural privilege of dignity, but by the merit of an accidental, good, and most worthy action.

He called it impious to acknowledge the nature of divinity in one who had been carried in the womb of a mother, passed through the customary conditions of female modesty, experienced a cradle and cries, and undergone the increase of age; who had not escaped the common conditions of our frailty, since he had hungered and thirsted, lacked knowledge, been tempted, feared to die, and died.

As for those events in his deeds that are narrated as full of miracles, Photinus asserted that Christ had not performed them as God—for he was not God—but had obtained them from heaven through the favor of merits acting as advocates.

But this doctrine of disgraceful unbelief also appeared impious and empty through numerous and manifold proofs. It became especially clear that the one whom Photinus insisted was merely human was also God from the testimony that the evangelist John bore, saying:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1).

By this it was declared not only that God was with God before the ages, but also that he existed as the author of the whole creation.

Many other similar testimonies, as is contained in the body of the proceedings, were also brought forward. Through them it became clearly evident that this Word, God, begotten from the Father’s womb before the ages, assumed our nature at the end of time for love of the human race; and that, while preserving his own nature, he nevertheless underwent in one and the same person all the sufferings of human frailty.

### IV

Thus, after Photinus had also been excluded and his error rejected by my statements, the entire weight of the matter and the whole substance of the faith depended upon the conflict of the dispute between Arius and Athanasius.

When I granted them the opportunity to enter the contest, Athanasius disclosed the course of his faith by saying that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were of one essence and of one nature.

Arius, on the other hand, replied that they were so far from being of one substance that the Father greatly surpassed the Son in dignity, power, and honor; and he said that the Son subsisted beneath these things and far below them.

He also asserted that the term *homoousion* was foreign and alien to the divine Scriptures, had recently been discovered at Nicaea more by argument than by authority, and ought to be completely rejected; or at least he demanded that it be shown to be contained in the divine writings. Otherwise, he argued with the utmost insistence, the term itself must likewise be abandoned.

When Athanasius inquired whether Arius was offended by the novelty of the name or by the force of the word, Arius replied that both displeased him. From this it became clear that he did not refuse to accept *homoousion* because it was new, but because it destroyed the foundations of his faith.

But while he again and repeatedly demanded that the proper meaning of the term be found plainly and specifically in Scripture, Athanasius maintained that this belonged to ecclesiastical custom: when the insolent and reckless audacity of heretical fraud had overstepped the boundaries of apostolic faith, it would be bound inextricably by such interconnected propositions as it supposed would keep the very freedom of Catholic understanding entangled within the snares of its perfidy.

### V

And so, to fortify himself with the authority of the ancients, Athanasius brought forward examples of ancient usage of this kind—examples which Arius could not merely fail to deny, but would also defend with an equal regard for the faith. He proposed, therefore, in order to demonstrate the rule of ancient custom concerning the novelty of names, that against Sabellius, who asserted that the Father was begotten, Catholics had been required by the decree of earlier councils to profess him unbegotten and unborn, although this very point could not be shown more clearly by the authority of divine Scripture. Yet the matter had to be professed, because both the truth of the matter itself and the necessity of opposing the heretical profession demanded it.

Likewise, he said that the bishops who were followers of the religion handed down by Arius had professed at the Council of Sirmium that the Son must be confessed as “God from God, light from light”; yet this very expression could not be found set down simply and expressly in the divine Scriptures. He brought forward many more proofs similar to these, which are explicitly preserved in the sequence of the acts. By them it is shown that, in order to expose the insolence of heretics, terms expressing new names had been adopted; yet it must not be thought that they had acted contrary to the prohibition of the apostolic judgment, which commands that profane novelties of words be avoided. But it says “profane,” not “religious” ones.

For it is religious to call the Father “unbegotten,” and the Son “God from God, light from light”; and even the designation of true Christians as “Catholics” is taught to be a term involving a new name. In the same way, Athanasius said, the same thing had occurred at the Council of Nicaea. And when Arius introduced, contrary to the truth of the matter, *triousion*, that is, “three substances,” the bishops judged that *homousion*, that is, that the Son is of one substance with the Father, must be confessed. It necessarily followed that, if the profession of *homousion* was to be judged foreign to the law, the invention of *triousia* should likewise be rejected on the same grounds.

Or else Arius should demonstrate that *triousion* was expressly written in the law, just as he compelled Athanasius to prove the precise basis of *homousion*. But since he was wholly unable to demonstrate this, it became clear that he had demanded from Athanasius, without justification, what he himself could in no way prove.

### VI

When he recognized that he was constrained by an equal difficulty in the dispute, he finally turned his assent toward the position of the argument: leaving aside proof based on bare words, he agreed that it should be shown by facts and reasoning whether the Father and the Son possess one nature or different natures.

Athanasius therefore offered a clearer and more evident indication of one substance. He showed that the Father had begotten the Son from himself and not from outside himself; and that it was impossible for him to have produced anything other than what he himself is. The truth of divine generation, out of reverence for its own dignity, required this to be believed, and the authority of natural custom likewise invited the conclusion that parents cannot produce children of a nature unlike their own.

Accordingly, following the opinion of Arius, who asserted that the Son was of a substance different from that of the Father, Athanasius left it to human understanding to recognize that, if the Son truly belongs to a different nature, he appears to have been made rather than begotten. The designation “Son” and “Father” would then be empty and meaningless, since one would be said to have begotten and the other to have been born only in outward appearance and not in truth.

Or, if he is indeed asserted to have been born from the Father, yet is not believed to be of one and the same substance with him, it is appropriate to confess that he is degenerate and has been produced like some kind of monster, in a manner other than the paternal nature prescribed. Since this does not accord with that holy, most blessed, and ineffable majesty—and since nature has even freed living creatures from this most wretched form of monstrosity, so that they do not generate anything other than what they themselves are—it is clearly proved that the Son is of the same nature as his Father.

### VII

Against this Arius chiefly opposed the claim that the Father could not have begotten the Son from himself, lest by this he appear subject to some defect of division or corruption. For if he is believed, as Arius said, to have begotten the Son from himself—that is, from what he himself is—he will presumably be thought to have separated some portion of his substance from himself. Through this, without doubt, he would appear to have seriously departed from the fullness of his perfection, and to be divided and diminished.

Athanasius removed this objection by an argument grounded in truth. He said that it is impossible for God, who is incorporeal, invisible, and intangible, to receive or possess within himself anything subject to the defect of division or corruption, since division and diminution properly belong to tangible and bodily substances. But God, who possesses none of these characteristics, cannot suffer anything of the kind. For this reason it must be believed that he begat, because he testifies that he begot him. Yet it must by no means be acknowledged that he was corrupted by this generation, since he is always incorruptible.

This is especially so because many things are found among bodily substances subject to corruption which are imparted or born in such a way that they bring no loss to the materials from which they arise. Thus light taken from light, or communicated through addition and through a kind of progressive birth, can bring no diminution to the original matter. The divine birth from the most holy Virgin also demonstrates that something of this kind occurred within the wondrous and inexplicable mystery of the sacraments: a womb full of God was emptied without harm to its chastity.

And if virginal integrity—though belonging to a nature subject to corruption—is not corrupted by giving birth to God, how can it be believed that the incorruptible nature of the Father was corrupted by begetting that same God?

### VIII

Again Arius attempted to demonstrate from this that the nature of the Father and the Son was very unequal and unlike: the Son, he said, had declared himself to be less than the Father and to do, not his own will, but the Father’s in all things. He asserted that the Son had acknowledged many other statements compatible with this interpretation, but these seem to me very weak and wholly unsuitable as proof of a different nature.

For suppose that any human son does the will of his human father and acknowledges him as superior and greater than himself. Could he therefore be of a nature different from his father? Although the father may be preferred in honor, he is not thereby distinguished from his son in nature. I say this, of course, according to the law and condition of human nature.

Athanasius, however, opened for us a path to this understanding through a more evident argument, bringing forth the clear light of truth after all the darkness of hesitation had been dispelled. For what could be said or believed more clearly to drive away all the clouds of error than that, just as we believe there are two natures in the one Christ—namely, divine and human—we should likewise recognize that a twofold power is present in his words and deeds?

Thus, those things which he speaks in a loftier manner—“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and other statements of this kind—are to be referred to the nature of his deity; whereas those which he speaks more humbly are to be understood as spoken according to the human nature.

A suitable discussion was also held concerning the Holy Spirit. Arius thought that the Spirit was far removed and alien from participation in the nature of the Father and the Son, on the ground that he confessed the Spirit to be a creature. But Athanasius demonstrated above all that the Spirit is of one and the same substance with them by showing that he speaks and acts in ways which only God can perform or express, and that such things are attributed to him as befit no creature.

Therefore he cannot be foreign or divided from the unity of the deity of the Father and the Son, since the similar and identical power of his works demonstrates him to be equal. Indeed, he is thought to be alien from the fellowship of the Father and the Son only through the detestable error of depravity, even though he is shown to possess equal honor of name and power with them.

### IX

Athanasius also resolved that difficult and, as Arius maintained, insoluble question by which Arius had argued that “three” could be called one God and that the one could not be distinguished into three persons. Athanasius dissolved it by the authority of divine Scripture, so that the truth was disentangled with a more complete resolution than it had been entangled by the pliable syllogisms of crafty reasoning.

He taught more clearly that in the Trinity there is one God according to the unity of nature, not according to the distinction of persons. Thus the three are one God because the nature of the three is one. For when many souls are called one soul, and when all human beings are called one man, this is asserted according to the condition of nature, which is common to all, not according to the diversity of persons.

Therefore, he who is one God by nature is three in persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If you ask for the common name of these three, it is “God”; in this one and singular name the mystery of baptism is celebrated: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

In accordance with this commonality of name, the Father is called God, the Son is called God, and the Holy Spirit is called God. Although each of them is individually God, the unity of nature does not permit them to be called “gods” in the plural. For the name of the nature, which is “God,” is not private and peculiar to each individual but common. And what is common and one cannot be many.

Therefore the Trinity is called not “gods” in the plural but “one God.” Wherever, however, something peculiar exists—something which does not correspond reciprocally to another—there plurality and distinction can also exist. Since, therefore, the Father is properly called “Father,” the Son is properly called “Son,” and the Holy Spirit is distinguished by his proper designation, and since the Father cannot be understood as the Son, nor the Son as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit as either the Son or the Father, they are rightly named three according to the distinction of persons, although according to the unity of nature they cannot be counted as three.

Therefore there are three names in the persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one name in nature: God. For this reason the three are one God. Thus neither confusion among the three nor diversity in the one name is admitted. In this way the Trinity is one God according to the unity of nature, and the one God is the Trinity according to the distinction of persons.

Anyone can discuss this still more truly and fully according to Athanasius’s understanding. His confession of faith is supported by such authority of truth and by the testimony of so many probable considerations that, in a new and unusual kind of proceeding, it is confirmed more by the testimony of its own adversaries; and it stands firm through the very arguments by which it is thought capable of being destroyed.

### X

For Athanasius himself said that there are three persons and that their nature is one. This opinion is also confirmed by the testimony of Sabellius and Arius. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are so completely of one power and one nature that Sabellius, observing such force of truth, thought them to be one and a single person.

Yet they are not one person but three distinct persons to such an extent that Arius declares them unequal and different in nature. Thus Arius’s assertion of inequality indicates the distinction of persons, while Sabellius’s confusion more clearly displays the unity of nature.

Again, when Photinus, in support of his own opinion that Christ was merely a human being, repeats those testimonies in which Christ, conscious of his human nature, either spoke or acted—namely, when he says that the Father is greater than he and that he does not do his own will but the Father’s, together with other statements of this kind, which are set out more fully in the body of the discussion—he most clearly confirms Athanasius’s faith. Athanasius asserted that Christ spoke and did all these things not according to his deity but according to the human nature which he had assumed.

Arius likewise, when he wishes Christ to be understood as a creature on the basis of the weakness of his words or deeds—judging it unworthy for the nature of almighty God to be present in one whom he sees subject to such conditions of necessity—not only strengthens Athanasius’s opinion by these arguments, according to which everything Christ said or did in a human manner must be understood according to the dispensation of the flesh; he is also bound by a similar bond of impiety with Photinus, since he too, following the same opinion, dared to define the Son of God as a creature.

Although they differ in this respect—that Arius thought the Son of God a heavenly creature and better than the others, whereas Photinus thought him an earthly creature—both are nevertheless united by the name “creature.” Whether they call him heavenly or earthly, they do not depart from the confession that he is a creature. Thus they take away from the Son what belongs to him as one born from the Father, and by this very mode of assertion both are suitable witnesses for Athanasius.

Since they confess Christ to be a creature, they are also found equal in a similar error.

### XI

Athanasius’s faith therefore appeared probable and supported by every assertion of truth, strengthened as it was by apostolic traditions and proceeding from their rules. More clearly, according to the norm of the Catholic faith, it showed us one God—not divided into three parts, not singular, not confused, not divided, not composed from diversity, and not united by some composition—but such that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist and are distinguished in their own persons, while nevertheless there is one God according to the unity of their common nature.

The fabrications of old-womanish tales also collapsed, destroyed by the assertion of truth. Arius, Photinus, and likewise Sabellius had assigned ambiguous names to the Father and the Son: one foolishly proclaiming that he himself had become Son to himself, and the others that the Father had not so much begotten him as created him.

Although they proceeded along different paths, they nevertheless arrived at one crossroads. They all said that the Father had not begotten. Sabellius and Photinus attempted to establish this openly and impiously. Arius, at the beginning of his disputation, thought it should be evaded more subtly; but as the contest proceeded, he defended the same position with stubborn shamelessness, asserting that the Father had not begotten the Son from himself but had created him externally.

According to these wicked errors, therefore, the Father is called “Father” in vain if he did not beget; and the Son is called “Son” without purpose if heretical impiety has defined that he was not begotten. But Athanasius taught with the clearest truth that these arguments were the inventions of the most empty superstition, showing that the Father truly begat and that the Son was truly begotten by the very truth of the paternal name.

### XII

Falsehood therefore yielded to truth, and every disguise of adulterated doctrine finally vanished once the integrity of the faith had been revealed. The entire darkness of the clouded assertion, which had covered human minds with the dense veil of impiety, was so completely dispersed by the radiance of the shining faith that it could leave behind not even a trace of its error.

Therefore I exhort, and at the same time advise publicly, all who know themselves to be entangled in the errors of Sabellius, Arius, Photinus, or any other fabricated doctrine: if they care for their own salvation; if they do not prefer blindness to light; if they do not wish the fact that they have wandered for so long through the tangible darkness of empty opinions, far from the light of truth, to work against them; if they wish the fact that they are called Christians to benefit them—then, setting aside every shame of human modesty, let them abandon the harmful inventions of human error by which they deceived themselves into thinking that they had found the truth, and by which, under the pretext of the Christian name, they were held as exiles far from the confession of Christ.

Let them strive with all their strength and with every effort of faith to hasten toward retaining the true and straight path of the apostolic faith, of which Athanasius proved himself a competent and faithful defender, so that they may receive with unquestioned certainty the reward of a true and complete confession. Amen.

[Col. 0237A]

## THE TWELVE BOOKS OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSA ON THE TRINITY

Published under the name of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. (C, G, S)*

## BOOK ONE

On the Unity of the Trinity of the Godhead

[Col. 0237]

[Col. 0237B] **Question:** You are one God, Father; the only-begotten God, Son; God, the Holy Spirit, because you have declared to us one Godhead, revealed the undivided glory of the all-holy and unique divinity, and displayed the perfect glory and eternal fullness of your Trinity. Therefore I judged it best that your revealed truth should shine forth clearly and that the exposed blindness of heretics should become known.

For this reason my spirit was suddenly kindled with zeal and blazed like a shining fire in dense forests of trees. Since many have attempted to show the way of justice with the pen of light, and since it has pleased us to direct our journey through its narrow and winding paths, while first fleeing the broad and spacious way, who would not desire, once the ancient darkness has been wiped away, to be renewed through the water of life; after barren and empty pods, to eat the bread of life; abandoning the abyss of the poisonous cup, to receive the cup of salvation; overthrowing the profane worship of idols, to acknowledge God as the true Creator; and, despising the hissing of the ancient serpent, to sing a sweet hymn to God in unity?

Who would not finally desire, after rejecting the breasts of the scaly dragon, to drink milk and honey from the evangelical commandments, and then, having taken up immortality again, to judge the apostate angels, and after the earthly human being to be enrolled in the heavenly kingdoms and exalted Jerusalem?

I ask: what and how great is this love of humanity in God, who promises such rewards to believers? Who would not hasten with every eagerness to rise from heavy sleep and behold the brightest light with infinite wonder?

How I long not to display this before the pupils of my eyes, but to store it among religious brothers in the secret chamber of the heart. For this reason I have not piled up a mound of an ambitious volume, lest I offer more words than I communicate to those investigating the meaning. Rather, in brief and in part, according to the promise, I have comprehended the infinite, so that in humble speech I might indicate sublime things.

Thus everything is full there where nothing is lacking; indeed, the person who wishes to detract anything from this fullness of the divine Trinity seems entirely ignorant of the whole, since I have understood more about you than I have properly said anything from myself.

Did you permit yourself to be believed only in accordance with the profession of the rule of faith, and did you wish in no way to be defined by mental speech? Did you permit yourself to be believed through faith, and command us to narrate to one another the immeasurable Godhead of your divinity? Are you therefore understood properly by us and defined by our speech? Far from it: you alone are properly known as God by yourself.

For this reason I earnestly and suppliantly beseech the glory of your most tranquil Trinity to lead me to the perfect state of faith, as I bring forth the words of my confession. If heaven or the heavens are not sufficient to proclaim the praise of your sublime greatness; if the eye is not satisfied by seeing, nor the ear by hearing, the works of your magnificence, how can my smallness sufficiently render to you the great thanks that belong in my confession?

I ask forgiveness, lest, if I take up words of presumption, I appear to detract anything from your majesty. But I lie prostrate before the seat of the glory of your exaltedness, asking that you permit me to drink from the fountain of the law of your treasury’s fullness and draw the water of life from the four overflowing rivers.

From these sources, with confidence, let us prescribe the blasphemies of heretics by the authority of the rule of faith, and, from the eternal Spirit of life, as from a fountain of nectar, water the hearts of those who thirst among Catholics.

This, I say, is the formulation of the matter in the clash with heretics, and this is the victory of the title in the acquittal of Catholics, which the principal commandment of God signifies: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Hear in this admirable and royal decree how the whole sacrament is contained together in the Godhead of the Trinity. Since he said “in the name,” he clearly declared that one Godhead subsists in the Trinity. And by continuing, “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” he distinguished through the individual names that individual persons are present.

[Col. 0239A] **Heretic:** Certainly, I ask you first to explain to me, in summary, the many things that have been said in response to the questions concerning the unified name of the Godhead, and then to distinguish, in your continuation, the names of the persons.

**Question:** Why is the Godhead one?

**Answer:** Because there is no ambiguity in this fullness of the Trinity.

**Question:** Why is the Father one God, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

**Answer:** When you said “one,” you yourself referred the names which you distinguished among the persons to the unified name of the Godhead.

**Question:** Why is God alone?

**Answer:** Certainly, because the Godhead alone subsists in the Trinity; therefore, God alone.

**Question:** Why is God almighty?

**Answer:** Clearly, because the Godhead of the Trinity itself is almighty.

**Question:** Why is there one true God?

**Answer:** Without doubt, because the nature of the Trinity is one and true; therefore there is one true God.

**Question:** Why is God alone good?

**Answer:** Because there is no unequal diversity in the one substance of the divine Trinity; and for this reason God is one and good.

**Question:** Why is God supreme?

**Answer:** Because this same substance of the Trinity is supreme.

**Question:** Why is there one Lord?

[Col. 0239C] **Answer:** Remember that lordship is united in the nature of the eternal Trinity; therefore there is one Lord.

**Question:** Why is there one image of the invisible Trinity?

**Answer:** Because the same one Godhead is present in the image of truth.

**Question:** Why is the one God Spirit?

**Answer:** Is not the nature of the Godhead of the Holy Spirit one—the nature which subsists in the Father, in the Son, and in itself? Therefore there is one Spirit of the one Trinity, because the fullness of divinity in this Trinity itself is one and eternal.

**Question:** Why is the one Trinity equal?

**Answer:** Because the Godhead itself is eternal in the Trinity.

I ask: do you not observe that nearly all heresies, in this title, blaspheme the unified Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since they attribute to the one person of the Father alone the things which were said above together of the Trinity?

For this reason we must work energetically—or rather, we must fight fiercely, with boundless care, against the assaults of so many sects, so that, once the darkness of the heretics has been thoroughly dispersed, the light of evangelical knowledge may shine forth clearly and the exposed blindness of those who blaspheme may become known.

Therefore, for the sake of examination, we must briefly revisit what was said above, so that every scruple of unbelief may be removed completely from the secret recesses of the heart of those who read or seek the truth.

[Col. 0240A] Moreover, this concerns solely the most holy unified name of the Trinity.

Therefore, when I mentioned one God, I did not restrict this expression to the one person of the Father alone, since I did not deny that the Son is of the one fullness of the Father’s Godhead and that the Holy Spirit is likewise of it. And when I mentioned God alone, I did not indicate, to speak more accurately, the one person of the Father alone, because I did not deny that the Son and the Holy Spirit are of this same sole substance of the Father’s divinity.

Similarly, when I spoke shortly before of almighty God, true God, good God, supreme God, or one Holy Spirit, did I not declare that all these terms refer to the unified divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Thus, although many meanings have been expressed in this passage, they have nevertheless been more clearly affirmed as referring to the unified divinity of the Trinity.

For unity is not, as heretics often say, crushed beneath their blasphemies, a matter of will rather than of divinity. Far from it: unity is not merely in will but, indeed, in divinity. Accordingly, to make the point certain, this unity is not merely agreement but exists really—indeed, substantially—in the nature of divinity.

Therefore I ask you who read this profession of my Catholic faith in this writing: do not seek here superfluous or diffuse words; rather, consider the words, expressed concisely, comprehensively, and even spiritually, with the greatest care, in relation to the style of Sacred Scripture, and weigh them according to the equity of the rule, with justice as your guide.

Now accept not eloquent but powerful things; not earthly inventions but true heavenly teachings; not the wicked heretical fabrications of philosophers but the perfect apostolic mysteries; not grammar, which is a superfluous wisdom of instruction, but divine commandments from the evangelical Scriptures, sweeter and better than honey and the honeycomb.

Learn, therefore, that in this matter the foolish men of this world, the sophists, were made foolish or speechless, because they did not recognize true wisdom, and for that reason were rejected.

Accordingly, receive the role of the questioner and the respondent, which requires satisfaction to be given.

**Question:** Why is the Father called Spirit, the Son called Spirit, and the Holy Spirit called Spirit?

**Answer:** A complete answer is given to the questioner according to the place and context. Do you not know that the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Holy Spirit is one God? Is there not one God, since the name is unified in the nature of the *ousia*?

So also there is one Spirit, because his Godhead is unified. For if, through the individual names of the persons, you have designated the unified name “Spirit” three times, should you therefore say that there are three Spirits? Far from it. If this could be said, it would amount to this: that the confession should also introduce the expression “three gods” in the plural, so that there would no longer be one nature of divinity in these persons, but each would subsist in his own or different nature. Far be it from us.

Meanwhile I repeat the same point and compare it with your words, reporting to you the meaning of my understanding. The Father is one God, the only-begotten Son is God, and the Holy Spirit, united in the Father and the Son, is God.

Since I have designated the unified name—that is, the name of the Godhead—three times through the individual persons, can I therefore confess three gods? Far from it. Thus, although the expression is threefold, it nevertheless retains the indication of one name in the Godhead of the Trinity.

Meanwhile, observe even in this title the one who says: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). Did he designate three gods in this statement because he indicated the one name three times? Far from it.

Therefore we who hold the evangelical and apostolic faith of the Fathers neither hold nor receive in our hearts three gods, three lords, three Spirits, or other statements of this kind involving plurality, especially since we know that the unity of the Godhead subsists in the Trinity collectively, not plurally.

For this reason we must not profess three natures in these persons contrary to the authority of evangelical judgment, since the Father is one God, the only-begotten Son is God, and the unbegotten Holy Spirit is God. He is one God because the Godhead is unified, as it is written concerning the individual persons; and because there is no God except one.

For example: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4); or this: “I, the Lord God, stretched out the heavens alone and established the earth” (Isaiah 44:24). Also this: “For there is one God” (1 Timothy 2:5); or this: “Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one” (Galatians 3:20). And likewise: “Away with you, Satan!”—it is written—“You shall worship the Lord your God and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10).

There is also this: “What is born from the Spirit is spirit”; and elsewhere: “All these things the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills”; or this: “Maintaining the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit.” Also this: “We have all drunk of one Spirit.”

Remember that the name of the divinity is unified in the individual persons.

**Question:** I ask you to confirm these statements for me still further on the ground of authority.

**Answer:** Do you not know that it is written: “I speak to those who understand the law” (Romans 7:1)? Therefore, those who have ears to hear should hear what the Spirit testifies to the Churches through the historian Moses throughout almost the whole book of Genesis.

Let them understand that God spoke, that God acted, and that God was present or blessed those things. He also said there: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26); and he continued as follows:

[Col. 0241D] “God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them, and he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’” (ibid., 27–28).

**Question:** What, then, is the reason that one said “Let us make,” and one made, and one was present with the speaker and maker, and saw and blessed the things that had been made? For “Let us make” does not belong to the person of one solitary individual, but to the one who acts together with another; and “in the image of God” does not belong only to that one person, but also to the one who sees and blesses together with him.

The Response. Does it not seem to you that, through the names of the persons being left unspoken, however briefly, the one name of the Godhead operating has been indicated? Certainly, because he did not say, “The Father spoke, the Son made, and the Holy Spirit blessed”; rather, he briefly continued: “And God said, and God made, and God saw all the things that had been made, and blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’” (Gen. I, 28).

You see that no one says “Let it be made” to himself, but to the one who is making; and no one who makes speaks to his own person by saying “he made.” And who indicates of himself, “he saw” and “he blessed”? For, if there were one person, in the strict wording, of the speaker, the maker, and the blesser, he would have indicated that he had made his work in this way: “I spoke, I made, and I blessed.” Yet it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. XXXII, 6). Certainly, by “Word” he indicated the Son; by “Lord” he designated his Father; and by “the breath of his mouth” he called the Holy Spirit.

You see that in these persons the one name of the Trinity exists in nature? The psalmist also confirms this: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. XLIV, 8). Behold God and God; yet you will not find it said in the plural, “gods,” of these persons. Likewise hear the Lord from the Lord, and the Father bearing witness concerning the Son through the prophet Hosea: “I will save them in the Lord, their God” (Hos. I, 7).

This too is written concerning the one name of the Godhead: “And the Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. XIX, 24). Or take this example from Jacob speaking in the book of Genesis: “Rise and go up to the place of Bethel, and dwell there, and make there an altar to God, to him who appeared to you when you fled from the face of your brother” (Gen. XXXV, 1).

And in the book of Psalms we find it carefully stated: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). Holy Isaiah also indicates this: “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, whose right hand I have held, so that all the nations may obey him” (Isa. XLV, 1), and so forth.

Yet there is one God, because dominion is one in the eternal nature. Thus also, concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, the Chosen Vessel briefly concludes, saying: “The same Spirit is also Lord, and the same is also God, who works all things in all” (1 Cor. XII, 11). And elsewhere he repeats the same thing: “Because the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. III, 17).

Or take, in the person of the Father, what is said in the Gospel to the Samaritan woman: “For God is Spirit” (John IV, 24). Jeremiah, the most renowned of the prophets, also bears witness concerning the person of the Son: “The breath of our face, Christ the Lord” (Lam. IV, 20).

Or this: “Because God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6). Concerning the governing Spirit, the Son indicates: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know from where it comes or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of water and the Holy Spirit” (John III, 8).

Therefore, to gather briefly the sense of Scripture concerning the nature of the divine Trinity as speaking with one voice: “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and exalted is the God of my salvation” (Ps. XVII, 47). You see that through the individual expressions the one name of the Godhead is indicated three times: that is, God, God, and God; yet not “gods.”

Or take the same statement: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and repay your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of your trouble, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 14). Certainly, if in this example there were only one fixed person, he ought to have stated the matter without any distinction in its continuation, saying: “The Lord lives, who is blessed.” But when he says, “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God, and exalted is the God of my salvation” (Ps. XVII, 47), is the name of the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not thereby declared as one in these persons—in other words, God, and God, and God?

Likewise, elsewhere the one name of dominion is carefully stated: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring glory to his name” (Ps. XCV, 7). For, if there were only one person, he ought to have expressed it thus: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations; bring glory and honor to him; bring glory to his name.”

What more? Do we still need arguments to disclose the truth to us? Are the nations, for whom the entrance of the door is open to believers unto eternal life, baptized into only one person, the Father? Are they not baptized into three, whose names are distinguished in these persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who have one nature of divinity? As it is written: “Go, baptize all nations in the name,” and he continued: “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Therefore, in these persons the name is entirely one in the divinity of the Godhead, and through those names of the Trinity only the persons are distinct. The Apostle also bears witness to this: “To preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. IV, 3).

You see that the one Spirit is to be preserved in the one body of the Church, in the bond of peace, which consists in the confession of salvation? Or can the name “Spirit,” as the name of unity of nature, be said to belong to only one person of the same Spirit, while the name of the unity of nature grants life in baptism to believers in these three persons? In this hope we have all been called.

This is the hope of our faith: that in baptism you first confess the one name of the Godhead, so that you may be worthy to obtain forgiveness of sins in these persons. Therefore, although in the preceding examples from Scripture the names of the persons are left unspoken, the one name of the Godhead has been shown to you throughout in these passages. So also in this example of the truth, in which the names of the persons are plainly displayed and the one name of the Godhead is declared implicitly, the evangelist John says in his Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, and the Word, and the Spirit; and in Christ Jesus they are one” (1 John V, 7).

Yet he is not one, because in these there is not one person. For, when he said “one” concerning both, what else is understood than that God the Father is said to be the same in the nature of the Godhead and is also the same Lord, and is also the same Spirit; and that the Son is God, and likewise is Lord in divinity, and likewise is Spirit in the Godhead; and that the Spirit, the Paraclete, is God and likewise Lord in the nature of the Godhead, and is likewise Spirit?

You see that in divinity and in the substance of fullness they are entirely one, while in the names of the persons they are three. For, when he says that there are three, what else is understood than the true Father, one—or sole—who begot, who is not the same as the only-begotten who is from him; and the one Son, who did not beget, just as the one begotten from the Father is not the Father; and this Holy Spirit, who is neither Father nor Son?

Moreover, the one who neither begot nor was begotten, since one person is the one who begot, another person is the one who is the only-begotten from him, and another person likewise—as I have said according to divine Scripture—is neither Father nor Son: this is the Holy Spirit. Yet he is plainly of the united nature. Therefore, in the Godhead there is one united name of the divinity.

As the Son bears witness in the clarity of the Gospel concerning the Spirit, the Paraclete, saying: “He proceeds from the Father” (John XV, 26). And he continued: “And he will take from what is mine” (John XVI, 14). Therefore, where the persons are required, they are distinguished by their proper names; but where the Godhead is sought, the one name is indicated, since we are shown to be addressed in the plural according to the names of the persons. Accordingly, in the divinity of the Godhead they are one in unity, and in the names of the persons they are three. Hence the three are one, or the one is three.

Now, so that we may remove every scruple from our readers, I shall clarify this further and briefly, proving in many ways that this is truly the name of the unity of the Trinity. Yet this unity is related to the manifold wisdom of God, which exists as one in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. If you speak of the wisdom of the Godhead and the Godhead of wisdom, is this not itself the unity of wisdom, which is also the divinity of the Trinity?

Therefore, to summarize: whether it is called the glory of wisdom or the Godhead of glory, height, dominion, dignity, splendor, majesty, empire, power, or eternity, although these are expressed in many ways, are they not nevertheless declared as one in relation to the incomparable united Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

Or do you suppose that, as many expressions are spoken concerning the glory of the Godhead, so many forms of difference also exist? God forbid, since all these expressions are referred to the one substance. For if this is one and the same manifold, foreknowing wisdom of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one power, one form of greatness, one majesty, one splendor—which are found gathered here according to the rule of Scripture into this united fullness of the Godhead, can we, contrary to Scripture, speak in the plural within that same Godhead of the Trinity—three wisdoms, three powers, three images, three substances, three splendors, or three plenitudes of the Godhead, or anything of this kind—in the manner of the Ariomanites? God forbid.

So you, Osius, now advanced in years, who were not merely a beginner but were an authority of the Catholic Church at the Council of Sirmium, where, while serving royal power, you made void the faith that you had composed at Nicaea—moreover, when you were exceedingly near death, you fell into the snare of the abyss of hell, so that, as though dead in heart, you went beyond all bounds and said: “Who does not know that the Father is greater in honor, dignity, splendor, and majesty?”

As though there were two, or certainly three, splendors or majesties in each of these persons, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which God forbid. For if their blasphemy were as they assert, why do they not now name three gods in the plural and openly profess that they exist around their own distinct or diverse substances? God forbid, since the name of the Godhead, although expressed in many ways, remains perfectly one in the Trinity.

**Question.** But I ask you briefly to show me these very statements concerning authority, one and common, through each of the persons.

**Response.** Hear what is said as one in the Trinity: “God is wise, strong, and great, who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who enclosed the stars, and stretched out the heavens like a skin; who walks upon the sea as upon dry land, who does great things and things that cannot be investigated” (Job IX, 4, 7–8, 10).

And consider what he says in Solomon: “God founded the earth by his wisdom, but by his prudence he prepared the heavens” (Prov. III, 19). Or recognize the Apostle saying: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I, 24). And he himself says again: “So that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. XII, 9). It is also written in the psalmist: “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

Yet he did not signify in the plural that wisdoms or powers exist in these persons, just as he repeats: “The Lord God of powers is with us” (Ps. XLV, 8). And this too: “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Ps. CL, 1). And elsewhere: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10).

Solomon also says the same thing in Proverbs concerning the person of the Holy Spirit: “The lamp of the Lord is the spirit of human beings, searching the innermost parts of the heart” (Prov. XX, 27).

Or this: “So may the Father, God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation” (Eph. I, 17). And elsewhere we find it carefully stated: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts I, 8).

Or take this statement through the holy Micah, as the Lord the Father himself testifies: “Unless I fulfill power in my holy Spirit, and in judgment, and in power” (Micah III, 8). Remember from this that the Holy Spirit of wisdom and power is with the Father and the Son.

Or understand as one the holiness of the Trinity, which works all wonders in signs and miracles, as I said above: “Holiness and sanctity in his sanctification” (Ps. XCV, 6).

You see, then, that in both there is one wisdom, or power, or light, or holiness, or operation, as well as other things of this kind expressed in multiple ways. These have not been introduced into these examples, since it would be quite lengthy to recount the things said as one through the Trinity. Let it suffice that, although few, examples have been set forth as demonstrations for the knowledge of the light in place of many.

**Question.** Therefore, if the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in the divinity of the Godhead, I ask you to satisfy me further by the testimony of Scripture.

**Response.** You have already heard the evangelist John bearing such unequivocal witness in his Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and in Christ Jesus they are one” (John V, 7). Without any doubt, in the Trinity of the Godhead they are entirely one, and in the names of the persons they are three.

Thus, so that you may know concerning what I set forth above, I do not remember having made any division or distinction within the one Godhead, the substance of the fullness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

## BOOK TWO. Concerning the proper persons and the one name of the Trinity

[Col. 0245]

**Heretic.** Now I ask you to explain the name of the Godhead to me through the individual names of the persons.

**Athanasius.** Listen. If the Son comes in the name of the Father, is he himself the Father who says, “I have come in the name of my Father” (John V, 43), since the Father is God, in whose name the Son plainly comes?

Accordingly, in the united nature of the Godhead one name is confirmed, just as the Father himself testified to Moses the lawgiver, saying: “Pay attention to him, and do not disobey him, for my name is in him” (Exod. XXIII, 21).

The patriarch David also says: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 26). And if the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes in the name of the Son, as he himself says, “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV, 26), was he also called the Son, since without doubt the name of the Son is God in the one and likewise shared nature of the Godhead?

Therefore, in this name the Paraclete plainly comes. Thus, through the individual persons, according to the substance of the nature of the Trinity, the one name has been declared to you.

The holy Isaiah, confirming this, says: “The Spirit descended from God and led them out; so you led out your people to make for yourself a name of glory” (Isa. LXIII, 14). He himself also indicates the same thing: “And they provoked the Holy Spirit, and he was turned against them as an enemy. The Lord himself fought against them, and he remembered the days of old, the one who brought up from the earth the shepherd of the sheep.” And he added: “Where is the one who placed his spirit in them?” (ibid., 11).

You see, therefore, that this Lord, the Holy Spirit, who led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, is the glory of the Father and the Son within the one name of the divine nature, as the prophet says: “So you led out your people to make for yourself a name of glory,” and “who was turned against the children of Israel as an enemy” (Isa. LXIII, 14, 10).

**Question.** I ask: if the name is one in the glorious Godhead of the Trinity, why did each one not come in his own name? Moreover, since this united substantive name is referred as one to the Godhead, does this not already show that it is a proper name?

**Response.** Certainly it is proper in this respect, but it is also one. To make you certain: the names are proper in the persons, but they are not one. Yet you say to me: Why did he not come in his own proper name, which belongs to birth, but not in the Father’s, with respect to the undifferentiated Godhead, where it is stated: “In which the name of the unity of God will be found”?

Rather, in that very name which I set forth above, in which only the person of the begetter is distinguished, the Son himself did not come. Listen: if he had come only in this name, which is called “Son,” and not in the united substance of the Godhead, which is called “God,” you would have said to me: “There is no united name in the nature of the Son’s divinity with the Father, but only a proper name.” In this way you would not merely distinguish the proper names in the persons, but you would also separate the one name in the Godhead of the Trinity through those very persons: either dividing the united substance into three parts, or certainly indicating that the individual persons exist in individual substances.

But plainly, if the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are perfectly distinguished according to the individual names of the persons, is the united name in these persons likewise divided, according to the united divinity of the fullness, among the individual substances of the nature? God forbid.

For even though you, Arius, distinguish only the names in the persons where you ought to distinguish them, there you simultaneously distinguish natures with the names themselves, by separate degrees or different orders, so that you say there are three natures according to the names of the persons: a greater, a lower, and a very much lesser one. In this way you assign different substances through the names themselves.

Why are you ashamed, then, and do you not openly profess, like the nations, three lords in the plural—a greater, a lower, and a very much lesser—existing around their diverse or unequal substances? You are accustomed to professing one as true, eternal, without beginning, uncreated; another as having a beginning and proceeding from created things; and a third as coming from ministers, as though subordinate, so that you ascribe to the Father what is incomparable or indescribable, show the Son’s substance as proceeding from an ignoble work above the rest, and declare that the Holy Spirit likewise possesses a substance derived from ministering angels.

Let us therefore return to the matter that we were discussing above concerning the individual persons.

If the Spirit, the Paraclete, had come only in his own name, which is called “the Spirit, the Paraclete,” and not in the united substance of the Father and the Son, which is called “God,” his proper name would already seem to belong to his person, and not, according to the united nature of the Godhead, to both, so that each one would display only individual names in his own person and would not indicate the united name of the Godhead.

But in this united name of the Godhead the true Son of the Father comes, in which he is called “God,” in which he has the name of glory with the Father. In the name of this nature the Spirit, the Paraclete, also comes, because in this very most holy Trinity this name exists substantially, or as one, as I said above, with the Father indicating it concerning his Son: “My name is in him” (Exod. XXIII, 21).

And the Son confirms these words: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; but when another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John V, 43). The Holy Spirit himself also repeats: “Whom my Father will send in my name” (John XIV, 26). And thereafter hear him exhorting the disciples concerning his name: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI, 23).

Hear also the Apostle Paul bearing witness to the same thing: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. VI, 11).

Hear Isaiah also declaring the united name of the glory of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit descended from God and led them out; so you led out your people to make for yourself a name of glory” (Isa. LXIII, 14).

Learn now that the name is one in the nature of the divine Trinity.

**Question.** Explain to me, then, whether the Son is true or not.

**Response.** Did not the Father introduce this expression so that we might understand it, thereby indicating that the proper divinity of the birth of his Son was from himself, saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3)?

How so? Not because God the Father has a womb like a human being—for he is incomprehensible—but because, introducing these examples from our own experience, he made a comparison, through which he might indicate to us the true birth of his Son as proper to himself.

Consider, then, Arius, how it is said in this passage. Was he made who was ineffably born from the womb of the substance of the Father? Was he made who was announced to us by the evangelist as the only-begotten, who says: “Whoever does not believe in him has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III, 18)?

In his Epistle he likewise indicates the same thing: “And we are,” he says, “in the true Son of God, Jesus Christ, who is,” he says, “true, and eternal life, and our resurrection” (1 John V, 20).

Behold, you have him from the womb; behold him in the only-begotten of God; behold the true Son of God, Jesus Christ, who is, he says, true, and eternal life, and our resurrection, just as the Lord himself testified concerning himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

Isaiah likewise prophesied: “But for those who serve me a new name will be called, which will be blessed over the whole earth. And they will bless the true God; and those who are upon the earth will swear by the living God. They will forget their former trouble, and it will not ascend into their heart” (Isa. LXV, 15).

You see that the new name is that of Christians, which is blessed over the earth by the Lord. For they bless the true God, the Father and the Son, indeed also the Holy Spirit; and they will swear by the living God. “And they will swear,” he says, “by the true God”—which is the divinely united name.

I ask: what madness of the heretics is so great that they compare the true Son with the creator of his own work? Or what blindness is so great that they blaspheme such a great proof of the truth with false arguments, when a centurion, still a pagan, declared for your condemnation: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV)?

**Question.** And how is the name one in the nature of the Godhead, when one seems to have come in the name of another?

**Response.** Truly the dull hearts of the questioner and defender have been infected with a subtler poison and deceit. Without doubt, in this respect the Father is one person, who truly begot; and in this respect the Son is another person, begotten truly by the Father from whom he is.

In this respect also, the governing Spirit, the Paraclete, is another person, who was poured out upon the Apostles at Pentecost. Therefore remember that these things are said individually, so that the individual names may be distinct in the persons.

You see that one differs from another, or one person from another, only in person and not in the fullness of the divine substance (*usía*), just as the Lord himself says: “Another is he who bears witness concerning me, the Father who sent me” (John V, 32).

Elsewhere the same one indicates the person of the Holy Spirit: “I will ask my Father, and he will send you another Paraclete” (John XIV, 16).

Know that one differs from another, or one person from another, only in person and not in the united fullness of the divine substance. For, if according to the individual names of the persons one can undoubtedly be called “another” in relation to another, can God, in the united Godhead, likewise be pronounced to be another as Father, as though he were diverse in nature from the Son? And can another God be called the Son in relation to the Father, as though he were another in divinity? And can the Holy Spirit be openly professed as another God, as though he were different in substance from the Father and the Son?

God forbid, since the name is one in the one true nature, and therefore there is one true God.

**Question.** And how do you indicate, in the names of the persons, that one is from one, or another from another—that is, the Son from the Father?

**Response.** Do you not know that one Father begot the Son from himself? For no one is father to himself. And who is son to himself? The Father is not begotten, and the Son is not unbegotten; rather, the Father is the Father of the Son whom he begot, and the Son is the Son of the Father, who was truly begotten from him.

Therefore, not as certain blasphemers are accustomed to introduce two unbegotten principles into their confession, so that they altogether profess neither a true Father nor a true Son. For the Father cannot be said to exist without the Son at all, because one is from one—that is, the Son is from the Father—and one is in one: the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father.

For this reason, one person is the one who truly and ineffably begot, and another person is the one who was born from him. Yet, since their Godhead is united, this God cannot verbally be called another God from that other God, because the name is one both in the fullness of the Godhead, and therefore there is one God.

Therefore, if the Son came in the name of the Father, and the Spirit, the Paraclete, came in the name of the Son, as the Son bears witness concerning him: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV, 26), does it not seem to you that here also a twofold understanding is contained? That is, there is distinction only in the names of the persons, but no division in the Godhead?

**Question.** And why is no one found to have come in the name of the Holy Spirit?

**Response.** Blind guides, have you never heard this proverb in the holy or divine Scriptures: “Let not the hunchback boast as though he were straight”? In whose united natural name of the Godhead were the Apostles sent? “Go, baptize all nations in the name,” and he continued through the individual persons: “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

Did he not first silently and as one set forth the united name of the Godhead, and then declare it most openly in the names of the persons: “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”? Can the Holy Spirit, then, be excluded from this united name of the Godhead? Or can baptism be perfectly celebrated in the Church contrary to the rule of evangelical tradition and judgment, with the person of the Holy Spirit removed or left unspoken from this united name of the Trinity?

God forbid. Otherwise, how was this name of the Godhead—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—given in the faith of baptism to believers as one? Is this name not found to be honored as one among the nations? Thus the prophetic Holy Spirit bears witness through the prophet Malachi: “For my name is great among the nations, says the Lord God almighty” (Mal. I, 11).

John the Baptist also concludes: “I indeed baptize you in water of repentance, but after me will come the one who will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11).

**Question.** Explain to me whether the name of the Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit.
