**Response.** It has already frequently been shown to you from the authority of Scripture that God the Father testified through Moses the lawgiver: “I am the Lord God; this is my name, an everlasting memorial throughout generations and descendants” (Exod. III, 15).

Concerning the person of the Son he says: “My name is in him” (Exod. XXIII, 21). And elsewhere the same Father repeats: “I am the Lord God, who call your name, God of Israel” (Isa. XLV, 3). The Son himself confirmed this, saying: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me” (John V, 43).

David also says concerning this: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 26). The Son likewise testified concerning the person of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John XIV, 26).

You see that the Son came in this name, which is also shown to exist as one in the Father’s Godhead; and the Holy Spirit is indicated to have come in this name, and in that of the Son. The Apostles, however, were sent to baptize all nations in the united or common name of the Godhead, which belongs to the nature of the invisible Holy Spirit, as it is written: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption” (Eph. IV, 30).

Or take this: “And we all drank one Spirit” (1 Cor. XII, 13). Or receive the name of unity as effected in baptism, where he says: “And you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord almighty” (2 Cor. VI, 18).

Or take this: “They were born from God” (John I, 14). Also: “And let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts II, 38). And elsewhere: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. VI, 11).

John also bears witness that he was born from God: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John I, 11).

Learn, therefore, that this name is everlasting in the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as there is also one baptism of faith, which grants eternal life to believers. For, just as there is one name in the nature of the Trinity, so there is also one gift of the Godhead through baptism.

The Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). Therefore, just as the name of the Father is in the divinity, so this name is also the Son’s in the nature of the Godhead; likewise this name is also the Holy Spirit’s in the substance of glory.

Do you wish to know? When in the Father’s Godhead you name the name of God, or Lord, or Spirit, you indicate in this the united name of the Son and the Holy Spirit as well. Therefore, according to the fullness itself of the nature of the Godhead, when you refer to it as united, you show that the name exists entirely in these persons.

Here, according to the persons, the united name of the Godhead is briefly left unspoken. But when you proceed by naming the individual persons, you indicate that proper names are present. Therefore we must return again to the statements above, if anything can be added to or subtracted from the united name of the nature of the Godhead or Trinity.

Answer me. Here all the opinions of the heretics are confused. Moreover, where neither number nor any difference is found in the united fullness of the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one is distinctly contained in the divinity in the name of another, and yet they are contained as one.

**Question.** Explain to me, then, how the three are one, or the one is three.

**Response.** Remember that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three, who exist in the one nature of the Trinity. Therefore the three are one, or the one is three.

**Question.** Is this Trinity divided or undivided? Tell me.

**Response.** It is plainly divided only in the names of the persons, but undivided in the Godhead.

**Question.** Tell me how “unity” is interpreted.

**Response.** Do you not know that the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one?

**Question.** What is understood here by “nature”?

**Response.** That which is understood as truth and deity, or substance, concerning which the Greeks say *ousia* (οὐσία), which is plainly the united fullness of the Godhead.

**Question.** What is one Trinity?

**Response.** Certainly, because the fullness of the Godhead is one in that very Trinity. Thus the name of the unity of nature is declared to exist as one in the Trinity, and the Trinity itself is likewise perfectly demonstrated through the individual names of the persons.

Here it has already been stated briefly what above was gathered with great care according to the style of the rule of Catholic Scripture: just as you confess that the Father exists in the Godhead, so you should profess that the Son and the Holy Spirit exist.

## BOOK THREE. Concerning the assumption of humanity, against the heretic Marcellinus

[Col. 0251]

[Col. 0251B] **218 Heretic.** How do you confess that the Son has the same one equality with the Father in the one Godhead, when he himself bears witness concerning himself: “The one who sent me is greater than I” (John XIV, 28)?

Athanasius. Alas! If you understand the statement to have been made in this way, he is already seen to contradict himself before you, when elsewhere he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). What then? If he was inferior, ought he not to have compared himself with the Father even in that eternal nature? Or how, if he was unlike him and was not coequal with the Father in the very deity of divinity, does he say: “Who sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9)? Indeed, if there were not in them one invisible image of the nature of truth, he would never at all have presumed to declare: “Who sees me sees my Father also.”

But hear the Apostle also speaking of Christ: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found as a human being; obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2:6–8). Now he who is in the form of God cannot be inferior. I ask: how is the Father placed above the Son, and the Son made subject beneath the Father, when the form of God is one and perfect, and cannot be said to be equal in one part and unequal in another part of divinity? Surely, either he is wholly, in the whole, wholly equal [Note: The phrase is faulty and not easily corrected. The meaning seems to be the same as if it had been written: “Surely, either he is wholly in the whole,” and so forth. EDIT.], as is clear among us; or he is not wholly, in the whole, wholly so, but is at the same time unequal in the whole, as among you.

Therefore choose one of two alternatives for yourself: either there is one equality of the glory of divinity in them, or one inequality, since no one is greater or less than his own form. It is another matter if, contrary to the authority of the most blessed Apostle, the teacher of the nations, you deny that Christ is the form of God the Father. If, therefore, he is his form, then his form cannot be incomparably greater; otherwise the Father would be greater not than Christ but than himself, because his form is said by you to be greater. This can in no way happen, since no one is greater than himself.

But perhaps you will presume even this, Arian, by saying: “The Father, in the nature of divinity, has no equal comparison with the Son’s form; no one is worthy to be compared with him.” Why then do you reject the resounding eloquence of the Apostle Paul, who declares: “Christ, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:6)? Understand at least this: no one is compared as equal to his own form, since an equal form cannot be said to exist in one person, as Sabellius maintains, when a united equality subsists in both. And this united equality is not merely in the will of concord, but in the deity, since this equal form is in no way divided in part.

For where there is one equality, there is no diversity; or where there is one equality, one is not placed before the other, neither is one set above nor subjected beneath the other, since the united equality is undivided, and it is the fullness of divinity. Surely, because we say that the Father and the Son are equal in deity, according to evangelical and apostolic authority, have we, heretically, posited that some measurable comparison exists between them, when this united equality of divinity is incomparable? For I have stated with complete clarity what I think concerning you, God, since concerning you, God, one must believe, not define. I have been commanded to believe; I have not been permitted to investigate.

Therefore Christ is the form of God, or the true image of the invisible God the Father, because there is one form and an equality of glory in them. Is it not written: “All the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him” (Col. 2:9)? If something is lacking, where is all fullness? Or if something is absent, where is everything full?

Surely, in him in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily—that is, as one might say, divinely—what can be found lacking in him? Surely, O heretic, will you find Scripture speaking of “fullnesses,” “divinities,” “forms,” “images,” or “equalities” in the plural with respect to these persons, when their Deity is one? Surely, however many expressions are spoken concerning the glory of deity, are there equally many forms of diversity? Far from it. All these things are declared to have been spoken concerning the united deity of the substance of divinity, *ousia*.

This also bears upon the matter: where there is united fullness of divinity, is there some diverse part, or a severed and unequal part within it? Fullness admits no portion of diminution to be properly compared with it, since the form of God contains in itself the whole fullness of divinity, and the sacred undividedness of equality tolerates no difference of majesty, as he himself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

Isaiah also confirms this when he says: “For in you is God, and there is no God besides you; for you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior from God” (Isa. 45:14–15). Hear the Apostle also bearing witness to this: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

You see that all the fullness of the Father’s divinity is in the Son, and the whole Son is in the Father. Therefore there is eternal equality in these persons, because there is immeasurable deity, as the Evangelist said: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also because, by calling God his own Father, he was making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

Receive also this saying: “Although you are a human being, you make yourself God’s equal” (John 10:33). And this as well: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father; whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:23). Know that there is one and equal honor of deity in them.

Finally, hear him himself crying out to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John 17:10). And elsewhere he himself repeats: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). If you refer this to divinity, they are one; if you point to the works of creation, divine Scripture testifies that all these things were made in unity.

Understand also in this the statement of the Evangelist John: “We have all received from his fullness, grace upon grace” (John 1:16). The Lord himself explains this: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” (John 5:21). Or this: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). And elsewhere he himself declares: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19).

Learn that this is one united operation in the nature of divinity, which grants eternal life to believers. And: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44). And: “No one goes to the Father except through me” (John 13:6). Learn that through the Son one goes to the Father, and from the Father one comes to the Son.

Surely, as I have already said, did he designate “fullnesses” in the plural in this passage, O heretic, when the fullness of divinity is one and united, the fullness that works eternal life in believers? Certainly, all we believers have received from this same united fullness of the Father and the Son, indeed also of the Holy Spirit, and it is always full, because nothing of the undivided Trinity of deity is less.

Accordingly, there is one equality, which is indescribable and eternal brightness. Let us linger over these matters for a little longer, and by means of a carefully devised defense make our discourse so lengthy that, when presenting the question of Arius, we may not seem to have evaded it like quibblers.

Let them finally hear Isaiah pronounce this sentence against their wicked doctrines: “For the fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vain things, and he accomplishes iniquity, and speaks error against the Lord, to destroy hungry souls and leave thirsty souls empty. For he has wickedly devised the counsel of the wicked, to destroy the humble with wicked words and to pervert the words of the humble in judgment” (Isa. 32:6).

For the devout have conceived wisdom, and this counsel will endure. Therefore it is necessary for us, polishing or distinguishing all things according to the evangelical rule, to approach the issue of the contradictory claim stated above: “He who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Observe that this was said on account of the assumed human being, as it is written: “He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters” (Ps. 17:17). And: “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken” (Ps. 64:5). Also: “Yet the Lord took me” (Ps. 26:10).

Did a human being take up God, and not God take up a human being? Certainly God took up a human being, not a human being God. For although he took him from the Virgin Mary, he did not lose what he had always been with the Father before the assumption of the human being; nor did his deity undergo any increase or diminution in the human being. In the present human condition he was such as he is known always to have been in the bosom of the Father with the Father before the assumption of the human being.

But, on the contrary, you say to me: “How did God take up a human being?” You do not know that Isaiah prophesied: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14)?

The Apostle also confirms this when he says that the form of God took up the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7–8).

[Col. 0254D] Heretic. Why, then, “God with us”?

Athanasius. What else is understood than that the true God took up a true human being from the Virgin Mary for our salvation? Yet this Mary derived her lineage from the tribe of Judah, from the seed of David.

Heretic. How can he now be called neither a solitary human being without God nor a solitary God without the human being whom he took up, and therefore be called both the Son of God and the Son of Man?

Athanasius. As the evangelical judgment has carefully established: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Luke 18:38–39). The Vessel of Election briefly explains this: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). And: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead.”

Behold him according to the human being; behold him according to God. Yet he demonstrates that there is one person under a twofold designation, as he himself repeats elsewhere: “For there is one God.” And he did not distinguish these matters by speaking of another person: “There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

As it is written: “He is a human being, and who can recognize him?” (Jer. 17:9). You see that he is the mediator. He can no longer be called simply God without the human being whom he took up, nor a human being without God. Consider that there is a twofold designation in the one person of the mediator, God and human being: from God he is God, and according to the flesh he himself is the Son of Man.

Therefore this mediator is true God and true human being, just as he is the form of God and the form of a human being. Hence the most widely revered of the prophets, Jeremiah, says concerning this: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him. He discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

You see, therefore, O heretic, that God was recognized through his operation—that is, through the human being. But if you do not accept this single proof from the Scriptures, I shall question you concerning my mediator, indeed the mediator of us all.

Answer me: on whose account is it found written or distinguished—whether of God or of the human being who hungered, thirsted, wept, was placed in agony and sweated blood, and finally truly endured the passion of death? If you take God properly, saying that he suffered all these things, Isaiah meets you in contradiction.

Isaiah contradicts you, saying: “The eternal God, the God who made the ends of the earth, shall not hunger, nor shall he labor, and there is no searching out of his understanding; he gives food to those who rise and strength to those who labor” (Isa. 40:28–29).

Holy Jeremiah also declares: “Will you be like a sleeping human being, and like a man who cannot be saved?” (Jer. 14:9). You see that God will never hunger, since he established all things from nothing. Nor did his deity undergo any passion, since all things are governed and brought to life at his command.

Accordingly, all power of signs and wonders must be ascribed to God, who performs them, and every necessity of sorrow and passion must be attributed to the human being, as we read when the prophet says: “A human being placed in affliction, knowing how to bear infirmities; for his face was turned away and dishonored, and he was esteemed as nothing. He bears our sins and suffers for us” (Isa. 53:3–4).

And he continues: “The Lord handed him over for our sins; and because he was badly treated, he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth in humility.”

For what is more decisive than what the human being himself testifies concerning himself: “Why do you seek to kill me, a human being who has spoken the truth to you?” (John 8:40).

Does this statement pertain to deity: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38)? Is it on God’s account that this is written: “The Son of Man must suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day rise again” (Luke 9:22)?

Is this prayer offered on God’s account: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup from me” (Mark 14:36), if all these things are to be attributed to divinity? Far from it.

This human being truly suffered for us, possessing in himself a nature from the Virgin, drawn from our own weak stock. Therefore the mortal or passible human being truly bore our infirmities, and after the passion was again truly taken up by God.

The Lord himself explains this: “I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:17–18).

Understand, therefore, that this human being was first taken up at his birth from the Virgin Mary; in the passion he was handed over by the permission of his power; and after the passion he was again taken up or received by him, as it is written: “For although he was crucified through our weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

You see: according to our weakness he was truly crucified as a human being, and according to the power of God he lives.

Finally, consider that God spoke on account of his human being, whom he had taken up: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Did he not speak these words of the temple of his body, which he himself raised from the dead after three days?

Did the human being who prayed that the cup might pass from him speak against himself when he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18)? You see that where there is all power, there is no authority of death in the deity. But where there is weakness of the body, there is sorrow of the heart.

Did a solitary human being, Photinus, without God, change water into wine? Or did he walk upon the sea with confidence in himself? Is the human being who seemed to fear death found to have raised the dead without God? Did Simeon carry a phantom in his arms? Did the earth tremble through the power of a solitary human being? Did the rocks and stones split apart as they struck one another?

Did a human being without God rebuke demons or perform miracles? Did a human being without God command the winds and still the calm waves of the sea? Could a solitary human being rise from the dead by himself, or stand among the disciples behind closed doors and teach them about the kingdom of God?

Could a solitary human being ascend above all the heavens by himself, without God?

Since all these wonders were performed by God, on account of his human being whom he had taken up, every power of signs and wonders must therefore be ascribed to God who performs them, and every weakness of passion must be attributed to the human being.

Understand in this sense, according to the invisible nature of deity and not of the human being, the statement of him who says: “Who sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9).

And elsewhere he himself repeats: “No one has seen the Father except the Son. No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27). Or this: “No one has seen God and lived” (Exod. 33:20).

The Apostle also bears witness to this: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:15). The invisible Father himself explains it: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

You see that there is one image of the invisibility of the divine nature, belonging to the Father, the Son, and indeed purely also to the Holy Spirit, which no human being has ever seen and cannot see, as it is written: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

For if the human being truly taken up was seen, touched, scourged, wrapped in a cloak, crowned with thorns, given gall and vinegar to drink, fastened with nails to the wood of the cross, pierced in the side with a lance, and poured forth blood and water, and was finally handed over to burial and buried, did he not truly suffer all these things according to the nature of the human being, O Marcionite?

Finally, receive what is written concerning the very nature of the human being. And you too, Manichaean sun-worshiper, like the pagans: is this said of the nature of God? “See my hands and my feet, for I myself am he. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

Certainly, it was on account of the human being, and not of the deity, that after the resurrection he ate fish and honeycomb.

Was it so that the deity might be seen by Thomas that he asked him: “Put your finger here and see my hands, and put your hand into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John 20:27)? Far from it.

For he had first spoken concerning his deity: “No one has seen the Son except the Father.” And: “Who sees me sees my Father” (John 14:9).

Was there not complete absence of phantasy here, where the whole truth of the human being was declared after the passion, or after the resurrection?

I shall question you also, Photinus, who deny that Christ is true God and confess him to be merely a pure human being. Is this written on account of the human being: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3)?

Was the human being present in this beginning, O Homoousian, or was the Son of God not always with the Father before every beginning whatsoever? Certainly, he took up this human being recently from the Virgin Mary.

Were visible and invisible things made through the human being, as the teacher of the nations testifies: “All things were made through him, visible and invisible, whether those in heaven or those on earth, whether thrones, powers, or dominions” (Col. 1:16)?

Receive in this statement also, you who are like the synagogue of Satan—falsely named, O apostolic Jew—an answer to your claim that the Father spoke to the angels when he said: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). The image of the angelic creation is spirit or fire, and yet that creation was made by God the Son, as it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

Or this: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire” (Ps. 103:4).

Could the angel who was made for service himself make his own image? Far from it.

Clearly, God the Son made the human being according to the image of his united immortality and the likeness of his equality, so that the human being might remain in the righteousness in which he had been made and possess the likeness of the will by spiritually imitating the operation of his Maker.

Yet such a human being was not properly made as the pure image of the Creator’s divinity, since there is a sufficient distinction between being referred to an image and likeness and being said to be as great or as excellent as the one who made him.

Therefore, after the transgression, Adam lost the image of immortality in which he had been made, because he consented to the devil, as it is established: “For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:13).

Or this: “He indeed destroyed death, but brought life and immortality to light” (2 Tim. 1:10). Or this: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:54). Or this: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

And this also: “For God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4). It is also written: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:31).

And it is stated in the Gospel: “In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings” (John 1:4).

Therefore, what we lost in Adam we have received through Christ our Lord in baptism, as it is written: “The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47–49).

You see that the image of the first human being, made mortal or earthly through transgression, and the image of the second human being, made immortal or heavenly through righteousness and truth, are distinct: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22).

Learn now, Ebion and Photinus, that the Son of God was always with the Father—the one who established the human being and all things, who testifies in the clarity of evangelical judgment that he existed before Abraham, saying: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

Or this: “Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before this world existed.” Certainly, this is said by the one who recently took up this human being from the Virgin Mary.

Hence the human being who was taken up, the Son of David or the Son of Abraham, is proclaimed by the Evangelist, while God, who took up the human being, is God according to divinity, and the Son of David is the Son of Man according to the dispensation; while he is God from God, and according to the flesh a human being, the Son of Man; while he is both God and human being, and the human being is not without God, and God alone is not without the human being whom he took up.

Therefore let the whole confused forest of heretics know, where so many kinds of dragons and wild beasts lie hidden, that they blaspheme in this matter: some proclaim only a solitary God without the human being, while others confess only a pure human being without God.

By indiscriminately confusing the causes of the dispensation, they either attribute the human weakness of the mortal human being to immortal divinity, or compare impassible deity properly with the nature of a passible human being. In this they miserably labor: some to deny the true God, and others the true human being, as the Son of God.

Answer me, Manichaeans, sons of darkness, in whom so many kinds of serpents possess slippery coils: do you not confess the Son of God—that is, true God and true human being from the Virgin Mary—for our salvation, as it is written: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14)?

If it seems to you a phantasy that the angel Gabriel testified this to Mary, saying: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor before God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:30–31);

or if it seems a phantasy that the Evangelist testified to these things: “She gave birth to her firstborn son, wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and placed him in a manger” (Luke 2:7), then what did she conceive or bear, or what did she wrap in swaddling clothes and place in the manger?

Receive also this example, in which the angel testified to the shepherds: “And the angel said to them: Do not be afraid. For behold, I announce to you great joy, which shall be for all the people: today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke 2:10–14).

Did the angels rejoice in heaven on account of a phantasm? Was it a phantasy that the Magi came from the East and worshiped him? Was it a phantasy that, according to the law, he was touched by hands or circumcised on the eighth day? Were infants killed on account of a phantasy?

Was it a phantasy that John baptized him by touching him with his hands? Was it a phantasm over whom John saw the Holy Spirit coming in the form of a dove and remaining upon him? Was it a phantasy that he washed the disciples’ feet with his hands? Did a phantasm truly eat and drink?

Was it a phantasy that he made mud from spittle and anointed the eyes of the blind man, and he saw? Was it a phantasy that he raised Lazarus, stinking on the fourth day? Was it a phantasy that he gave life to the mother's only child? Was it a phantasy that he granted the centurion his boy-servant?

Was it a phantasy that he hung upon the cross, when the foundations of the world were shaken and the centurion, seeing this, gave testimony, saying: “Truly this is the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54)? Did Joseph wrap a phantasm in a linen cloth and place it in the tomb? Did a phantasm rise from the dead after three days, ascend into heaven, and sit at the right hand of the Father?

Far from it, O Manichaean, in whom the devil has produced all the phantasms of error—especially since all the things mentioned above, which are specifically spoken of as wonders performed on account of the human being, were performed by the true God in the human being, or on behalf of the human being, or through the true human being.

Therefore recognize in this passage also, O Arian, whom the devil dared to sow his weeds in the Lord’s field among the good wheat, with a view to uprooting the seed, as it is written:

“I know your works, that you have a name as though you were alive, and you are dead. Be watchful, therefore, and strengthen the things that remain, which are about to die. For I do not find your works complete before my God. Remember, therefore, how you received and heard; keep it and repent. But if not, I shall come to you like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I shall come to you” (Rev. 3:1–3).

You hear, O heretic, who have only the name of a Christian and speak with the mouth of the devil, that you do not understand that the statement “He who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28) was made on account of the dispensation of the human being.

Heretic. Tell me, orthodox teacher: if, as you maintain, “He who sent me is greater than I” was spoken on account of the dispensation of the human being, then at what time was he sent by the Father? Perhaps you will say that at that time his divinity is understood to have been absent from him.

[Col. 0260A] Athanasius. O exceedingly confused blindness of conscience, utterly infected with the serpent’s poison! Certainly, if he was absent from the Father, how is the nature undivided? And if he was divided, how is he one in the one? And if he was absent, when he was and is in the human being, why was he always announced to us by the fisherman John as one dwelling in the bosom of the Father, when he says: “No one has ever seen God except the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John 1:18)?

Finally, hear him himself speaking concerning this: “The words that I have spoken to you are not mine, but those of the Father who sent me” (John 14:24). And this also: “The works that I do are not mine, but the Father who sent me himself performs his works” (John 14:10). And: “If you do not believe me, believe the works, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38).

Behold: while the Son speaks, the Father speaks; while the Son works, the Father works together in unity; and while the Father remains in the Son, the Son remains in the Father.

You see that the nature of the divinity of the Father and the Son is undivided: what the nature of the Son speaks, the very same united nature of the Father also speaks; and what the nature of the Son works, that same united nature of the Father’s divinity also works. And while the Son naturally remains in the Father, the Father likewise remains substantially in the Son.

Therefore, so that you may be certain concerning the one who goes out and the one from whom he goes out, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and have come” (John 16:28), the names are shown in the persons; the united fullness of divinity, which is undivided, is not divided. For the one who was and is from the Father, as he himself testifies, says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11).

Moreover, this fullness of unity is present everywhere and fills everything within and without, from the summit of the heavens to the depth of the underworld, as it is written: “I am the Lord God who fills heaven and earth and all that is in them” (Jer. 23:24).

You see that this fullness is united and that the divinity is undivided.

Therefore consider that whatever is referred to deity signifies undivided unity; whatever indicates the cause of the human being displays the nature of weakness, as he himself says: “A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

Does he not show the human being in this statement? For according to God he continues thus: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is of no avail. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63).

You see that wherever he refers to authority, he shows that the divinity is undivided; wherever he refers to the human being, he designates the nature of weakness.

Accordingly, all power must be ascribed to God, and every weakness must be attributed to the human being, as he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

I ask: who is greater—the one who took up, or the one who was taken up? God, or the human being? That is, the form of God, or the form of the human servant? The one who glorifies, or the one who is glorified? As he himself says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 13:31).

Consider now that in these statements one person is declared under a twofold name, of God and of the human being, as the Apostle says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

Or this: “Now a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Gal. 3:20). You see that there is one God, and that the mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, is not another person.

But, on the contrary, you say to me, O heretic: “What can be distinguished in one person?” Therefore, if you do not distinguish these things, be certain that you also show the deity to have suffered at the same time.

And why do you distinguish the cause of the soul in one human being, O heretic, according to the Lord’s saying that one should not fear the human being who has power to kill the body but cannot kill the soul? If in this matter you distinguish the soul alone in one person, which is not killed by the human being, how much more do we distinguish in the one person of God and the human being—that is, of the Son of God—the cause of immortality, namely divinity, from the weak nature of the human being?

Finally, hear God speaking on this matter: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). Was the deity dissolved, O Marcellus of Ancyra, as you assert—whether the wisdom or power of God the Father—and not the human being?

Certainly, the human being truly suffered, the one who became the temple of God, the one who was raised by him, as divine Scripture testifies: “Pierce my flesh with nails, because of your fear” (Ps. 118:120). Or this: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

Did they fasten the deity with nails or pierce it with a lance? Far from it. Is it not one person, the Son of God, through whom such a distinction is made?

I ask: if he himself did not attribute the weakness of the human being whom he had taken up to his own immortality, do you attribute so great and immeasurable a deity, through which all things were made, to a passible human being?

As you too, Arian, are accustomed to propose that the Apostle said: “All things are subjected to him, except the one who subjected all things to him. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:27–28).

This statement plainly does not pertain to the deity of the Son of God, since all things were made through him and have always been subject to him, because no one fails always to rule over his own creation.

Therefore, all things were certainly not subject to the human being, who had only recently been born, before the passion, since that human being was still liable to death on our behalf. But after the passion, or ascension, or the future judgment, all things will be subjected to him, as this human being himself indicates, who had not yet been in heaven: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18).

Finally, receive this also: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27).

Or at least accept the statements of the Lord himself concerning the united goodness of nature: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

Did he write that he was alien to this same sole goodness of the Father when he added: “And Jesus Christ whom you have sent”? The Father himself also bears witness to the same thing: “My heart has uttered a good Word; I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 44:2).

You see that the Word of God is good, who exists substantially or naturally from the Father.

Therefore all such comparisons were spoken on account of the weakness of the human being: “He who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Or consider this statement, in which you are accustomed to argue: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19), although elsewhere he himself says: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:15). And also this: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:14).

We find the same carefully established concerning the person of the Holy Spirit: “Your good Spirit will lead me on a straight path” (Ps. 142:10).

Learn that goodness is one in the nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore now at least understand that every weakness must be attributed to the human being, and every power of goodness, signs, and wonders must be ascribed to the undivided deity of the Trinity.

**The Heretic.** I will therefore ask you whether the one nature of the Father and the Son is undivided—he who said, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” [Col. 0262B] (John 14:11)—and you assert that “He who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28) was said on account of the dispensation concerning humanity. What, then, will you say about the person of the Spirit Paraclete? Is he not lesser, since he was sent by the Son? For he himself says: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come; but if I go away, I will send him to you, and he will teach you all truth” (John 16:7)?

**Athanasius.** O utterly unheard-of written inquiry, so thoroughly pursued! Since the Holy Spirit himself now gives this testimony concerning himself, it is fitting that we offer one authoritative example in place of many. Remember that this is a reciprocal power of the nature of the sender and the one sent, since he who has now been sent is himself found long ago to have sent the one who sent him. Accordingly, through the holy Isaiah, hear the Lord, the Son of God, testifying:

“Draw near to me and hear these things. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when they came to be, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16).

Learn at last that the nature of the divinity of the sender and the one sent is united. For although in the Gospel he testified that he would send the Spirit Paraclete, nevertheless he himself confessed through the holy and illustrious Isaiah that he had previously been sent by him. The one who is sent by the sender is never divided from him, because the nature is undivided: persons are shown between the sender and the one sent, but there is no division in the divinity. Moreover, this united fullness is present everywhere and fills all things within and without, from the summit of the heavens to the depth of the underworld.

**The Heretic.** I ask you, since he is the Son of Man, please indicate this to me from the authority of the ancient Scriptures [Col. 0262D].

**Athanasius.** Hear the psalmist:

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the Son of Man whom you strengthened for yourself” (Ps. 79:18).

Likewise, holy Daniel testifies:

“I saw in a night vision: behold, one like a Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days, and sovereignty, honor, and kingship were given to him; and every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not cease, and his kingdom shall not perish” (Dan. 7:13).

Behold the man of the right hand; behold the Son of Man, as the Apostle says:

“He was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3).

But according to the Spirit of divinity he says:

“He was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Rom. 1:4) [Col. 0263A].

Thus he himself questions the Pharisees about his divinity:

“What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?”

They answered him, “David.”

And he said to them:

“How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’? If therefore David calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?”

And no one was able to answer him a word (Matt. 22:42).

Learn, then, that according to the flesh he is the Son of Man—that is, David’s son—and according to his divinity he is himself the Son of God in power, and he himself is David’s Lord.

Therefore, when Scripture calls him the Only-Begotten, it indicates his divinity, because in deity the Only-Begotten has no brothers at all from God the Father. But when it calls him the Firstborn, it reveals the nature of his humanity, as the Apostle declares:

“That he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29).

Or receive this example:

“And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead” (Rev. 1:5).

Is there not one person of the Son of God, with a twofold designation, God and man? Is there not one Son who according to the flesh is called the firstborn Son from the dead as man, as it is written:

“He is the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18) [Col. 0263B]?

Therefore believe me, you who read this written confession of my faith: many have discussed this matter, but they have gone astray because they did not understand it. By distinguishing the person instead of the cause, they introduced two sons into their confession. They ought to have distinguished the cause of the human passion from the divinity, and not the person, since there is one Son whose person it is.

There is, however, a twofold designation of nature: the Only-Begotten is God from God the Father, while the Firstborn from the dead is man; he is true God and true man, and, being God, he was assumed together with himself. Therefore the cause, not the person, is distinguished. Accordingly, when Scripture speaks in reference to deity, it designates the impassible divinity. But wherever it indicates the human cause, it demonstrates a passible nature.

You see that wherever Scripture speaks according to divine authority, it shows the divinity to be undivided from God the Father; wherever it speaks according to humanity, it declares the nature of weakness. Therefore all power must be ascribed to God, and all weakness of suffering must be attributed to man.

**BOOK FOUR. On the Individual Names, Against the Novel Heresy of a Certain Potentinus Urbicus.**

[Col. 0263]

**The Heretic.** Now, then, speak to me repeatedly about the individual names and persons.

**Athanasius.** It ought not to have been enough for you that I gave one example in place of many concerning the Lord’s faith:

“Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19),

about which I had already explained so fully in the first book, where I declared that the truth of the entire mystery consists in the united deity, and also distinguished that proper names exist in the individual persons.

Do you not know that there is one unbegotten Father, and that he himself is not the Son; that there is one Son truly begotten from him, who is not the Father; and that there is one Holy Spirit, who did not beget as the Father did, was not born as the Son was, and is not a created thing either? Clearly, as divine Scripture testifies, there is one true united deity. Accordingly, the names are truly proper to the persons, and are not empty designations.

**The Heretic.** I ask you to demonstrate these statements from authoritative testimony.

**Athanasius.** Concerning the man assumed in the glory of the Gospel, it is written:

“And when Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from the heavens said: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16).

Is not one person the one who was baptized, another the one who descended from heaven like a dove, and yet another the one whose voice was heard from heaven?

Elsewhere it is written:

“Everyone who loves the one who begot loves the one who was born from him” (1 John 5:1).

Surely the one who begot is not himself the one who was born. Far be it from us. Receive also this testimony:

“Whoever does not confess the Son does not have the Father; but whoever confesses the Son also has the Father” (1 John 2:23) [Col. 0264B].

Or this:

“He who hates me also hates my Father” (John 15:23).

But John indicates the matter in these words:

“Whoever denies the Father and the Son, this is the Antichrist” (1 John 2:22).

You see that the Antichrist is the one who denies the true Father and Son.

Finally, hear the Father’s voice from heaven saying:

“This is my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5) [Col. 0264C].

In every respect, the one who testifies from heaven is different from the one who likewise bears witness on earth.

Similarly, the Son cries out to the Father:

“Father, glorify your name.”

And a voice came from heaven:

“I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28).

Certainly, if the Son and the Father were one person, from whom was he asking for glory? And whose voice answered him, saying, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it”?

Also:

“Holy Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1).

You see that in these matters there is a mutual glorification according to the reciprocal relation of nature.

Or receive this:

“I came out from him, and I came” (John 16).

And elsewhere he repeats the same thing:

“I came out from the Father, and I came” (John 17) [Col. 0264D].

Certainly, if the Father and the Son were one person, he should have said: “I came out from myself into this world.” Without doubt, the one who came out is different from the one from whom he came out.

To this he added concerning the person of the Holy Spirit:

“When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will testify about me” (John 15:26).

Is the one who sends not different, the one from whom he proceeds likewise different in person, and the one who comes yet another?

Finally, if there were one person, by whom would he be sent, or from whom would he proceed?

The Apostle confirms these matters in his greeting to the Corinthians, saying:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God—that is, of the Father—and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. 13:13) [Col. 0265A].

Did he not clearly distinguish, through the individual names, as is also stated above, that individual persons are present?

Finally, receive the words of the Son himself:

“There is another who bears witness about me: the Father who sent me” (John 5:32; 8:18).

He says below that there is “another” in relation to himself. You see that the Father is another in person from the Son, but not another in divinity.

He also says concerning the Holy Spirit:

“I will ask my Father, and he will send you another Paraclete” (John 14:16).

Consider that the Spirit Paraclete is another in person, yet not another in divinity. Thus one differs from another in person only, and not in deity.

Accordingly, the Father who begot is one person; the Son begotten by him is another; and the Paraclete Spirit, who is from the united nature, is another.

But you ask me, heretic, how the Spirit exists from the united nature. Behold, the Son testified concerning him:

“He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26);

and he continued:

“He will take from what is mine” (John 16:14).

The Father confirmed this testimony, saying:

“The Spirit proceeds from me” (Isa. 57:16).

O man, if this Paraclete Spirit, as you say, is neither the Father nor the Son nor a created thing, what do you think he is? O true blindness! If Scripture is not sufficient for you, since it signifies these things concerning him, there is no longer anything for you to ask me about him.

Yet I must not conceal what I ought to disclose to you concerning my belief. But so that you may first know which snares to avoid, I will explain this to you.

There arose a novel and unheard-of heresy belonging to a certain **URBICUS POTENTINUS** [Col. 0265C], who presumes that this Holy Spirit should be confessed as either the Father, or the Son, or certainly a created thing. Thus, if some ignorant or inexperienced person in the divine Scriptures hears the notions he has brought forward amid the bitterness of his cunning and chooses anything from these blasphemous statements, he immediately falls into heresy.

Hear, then, how the twisted bonds of his wickedness must be undone.

O Potentinus, who alone, against the divine Scriptures and the whole world, dissent from the Catholics concerning this matter while following the teachings of philosophers, you think as follows: if the Holy Spirit, this Paraclete, as you say, were the Father, then without doubt there would no longer be one Father, but two fathers. Or if the Spirit, this Paraclete, were the Son, then without doubt there would no longer be one son, but two sons. Or if the Spirit Paraclete were a created thing, then plainly the one who was made would no longer be the true God—which is impossible [Col. 0265D].

Accordingly, I repeat these same points and, in clearer words, set forth these authoritative statements according to the rule of the faith.

If the Paraclete were another Father, why do we find the Apostle saying:

“For there is one God, the Father” (1 Tim. 2:5)?

Or this:

“For us there is nevertheless one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him” (1 Cor. 8:6).

Learn, then, that the Father is the one unbegotten God.

But if the Son were another, and this Spirit the Comforter, why is the Only-Begotten Son proclaimed by the evangelist John in these words:

“No one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1:18)?

Or this:

“And one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6) [Col. 0266A].

You see that there is one Son, who is the Only-Begotten God.

But if the Holy Spirit were a created thing and not the true God, why do we read that the Lord Christ indicated to Nicodemus:

“What is born from the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6),

since God is Spirit?

Or at least receive this example:

“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

Also receive these words:

“Unless someone is born from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

Remember that the Holy Spirit is God, who accomplishes all things in signs and wonders, as the chosen vessel briefly declares:

“All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11) [Col. 0266B].

If this one and the same Spirit were a created thing, how could he perform all these wonders?

Therefore, Potentinus, this Paraclete is not the Father, lest two Fathers be introduced into the confession contrary to the rule of authoritative teaching. He is not the Son, lest two sons appear contrary to the sacred Scriptures. He is not a created thing, lest he not be the true God.

Finally, so that you may learn from the divine creation itself that he is the true God, he exists from that true, united, and incomparable deity.

**The Heretic.** I ask: if the united deity is incomparable, are the names of the persons likewise incomparable?

**Athanasius.** Alas! If there are many fathers who were at some time not fathers, can any one of them rightly be compared with God the Father in eternal generation? Or because there are many sons who were recently born and were not previously sons, can any one of them be likened to the eternal divinity of the proper Son of God? Or because there are many spirits in heaven and on earth who were made, can any one of them be equal in eternal divinity to the Holy Spirit?

Far be it from us that a created thing should be compared with its creator, since a created thing has only recently begun, while its creator existed always, before every beginning whatsoever.

Remember that there is one Father, from whom are all things; one Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things, as it is written:

“All things are from him, through him, and in him” (Rom. 11:36) [Col. 0266D].

Consider, in relation to these arguments, that three significations are shown through the one united name of the one who acts: “from him,” “through him,” and “in him.” One is from another, or through another, because this statement pertains to the individual persons. For concerning the united name he says: “from him, through him, and in him,” which is itself one.

Therefore, when he says “from him,” he shows that all things were called forth to be from God the Father; “through him” indicates that these same things were made through God the Son; and “in him” declares that they were sanctified in God the Holy Spirit.

You see that “from whom” is spoken of the Father; “through whom” is accomplished through the Son; and “in whom” is consummated in unity through the Holy Spirit.

Thus, when he says “from him, through him, and in him,” because the divinity of the Father is itself also the divinity of the Son and likewise of the Holy Spirit, all things have been made from him, through him, and in him.

To the united and ineffable Trinity be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

Now receive why the names are distinguished only among the persons. Can the Father, who ineffably begot the Son, himself also be called the Son? Did the Father assume a human being from the Virgin Mary? Was the Father born, or incarnate, or subjected to suffering?

Far be it from us, heretic Sabellius, to admit this blasphemy. The true Son of God was truly and incomparably born from the Father, and for our salvation he graciously undertook once again to assume humanity from the Virgin Mary. Hence he is now called—and indeed is—true God and true man [Col. 0267B].

For this reason the names of the persons are distinguished in these matters, lest when you call someone the Father you should confusedly designate this same one as the Son; or lest you declare the Son to be the Father; or rashly testify that this immeasurable Holy Spirit is the Father or the Son, and thus be found to possess no firm position at all.

Through these very names of the persons you confuse the unity indiscriminately, saying that the same person is Father and Son, as though he had begotten himself, or were himself his own father and his own son—which is impossible. No one is his own father, and no one is his own son whom he has truly begotten. The father is father to the son, and the son is son to the father who truly begot him.

For this reason the names are perfectly distinguished among the persons.

**The Heretic.** Please confirm these statements for me from authoritative testimony [Col. 0267C].

**Athanasius.** Receive the Son testifying in the authority of the Gospel:

“When the Advocate comes, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will testify about me” (John 15:26).

Or immediately receive this:

“But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom my Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything I have said to you” (John 14:26).

Did he not distinguish the names in the individual persons with complete brevity, when he announced that this Advocate, the Paraclete Spirit, would come from the Father and would bear witness about himself in the world?

**The Heretic.** Why are the names designated?

**Athanasius.** Without doubt, because the Father truly begot; this is his proper name. The Son was truly born from him; this is his united name. And the governing Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, has the name of deity [Col. 0267D–0268A].

When the names are distinguished pluralistically by passing through the individual persons, proper names are shown. When they are referred to according to deity, the united name of *ousia*—that is, substance—is indicated in them.

**The Heretic.** What, then, do the persons designate as an indication of their individual properties—namely, the one Father, the Only-Begotten Son, and this one Holy Spirit? How, as you show here, is the united name substantive in the individual persons?

**Athanasius.** Hear that just as God the Father is substantive in divinity, so God the Son is substantive in the same nature and substance; and so God the Holy Spirit is substantive in the same nature and *ousia*. Or consider this statement: just as the Father is God, so the Son is God, and so the Holy Spirit is God [Col. 0268B].

You see that when you indicate the substantive name of divinity in these persons, you demonstrate the united name of deity.

Therefore there is a twofold understanding of this mystery: remember that their united name consists in the united substance, while the individual proper names are distinguished in the individual persons.

Or understand the truth through this argument:

“I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Certainly, “one” is the united name of nature; there are not multiple natures. But “we are” cannot refer to one person.

Thus, wherever he indicates the name of deity, he designates “one”; but wherever he turns to the names of the persons, he shows “we are.”

Accordingly, it is one thing to refer the united name of deity to the common authority of the Trinity in unity, and another to distinguish the individual names pluralistically among the individual persons. For wherever the nature of *ousia* is required, the united name is revealed; but wherever proper names are indicated, the individual persons are declared to be present.

As the chosen vessel—the Apostle—also briefly resolves in this argument:

“We speak from God, before God, in Christ” (2 Cor. 2:17).

Did he not, through these implicit names, declare that individual significations of the persons are present, namely: “from God,” evidently from God the Father; and when he continued, “before God”—that is, with God as witness—did he not indicate the Holy Spirit; and when he said, “we speak in Christ,” did he not mean that from God and before God we proclaim testimony in the Son of God [Col. 0268D]?

You see that it has been said to you in many ways that the individual names are manifested in the persons, since the individual names are perfectly shown only in the persons; and through these same names the indication of the united *ousia*—the deity—is also made in unity.

**BOOK FIVE. On the United and Eternal Substance of the Trinity. Here the speaker opposing the Ariomaniacs is introduced.**

[Col. 0267]

**The Heretic.** Why did you confess that the Son exists eternally with the Father, when birth in no way permits him to be admitted into eternity? If he was eternal together with the Father, he was not born; but if he was born, he cannot be eternal, since birth is later than eternity.

**Athanasius.** O empty contrivance, built of wood, hay, and straw upon the sand, whose collapse and burning are close at hand! Against your evil argument I must bring forward the prohibition of true wisdom.

Why should the Son not be eternal, whose birth is in no way excluded from eternity? Rather, he who had already been born before every beginning whatsoever possesses eternity together with the Father, since the eternal one was begotten from the eternal one [Col. 0269A].

But you say to me: “Birth is later than its begetter.” Indeed—as though he had first been conceived from seed, or coagulated in a womb, and his birth had advanced gradually until the final stage of development, so that at last he was born.

Far be it from us to compare anything with this birth, as it is written:

“Who shall declare his generation?” (Acts 8:33; Isa. 53:8).

Did the Father, who truly begot him, enter into any suffering, or suffer any loss in the very birth of his Son? Far be it from us. As I said above, this generation cannot be narrated at all.

Accordingly, if you can, err against divine Scripture, since it sometimes speaks of a hand, a Son, a right hand, and an arm; sometimes of the Word from the mouth of the Father; sometimes of one begotten from the womb before Lucifer (Ps. 109:3); sometimes of being in the Father; sometimes of having come forth and come from the Father; sometimes of being in the bosom of the Father; sometimes of being with the Father; sometimes of being and having been in the Father; and sometimes of the Father being in the Son and the Son being in the Father [Col. 0269B].

Consider whether any ordinary birth could be compared with or explained in relation to these many forms of speech concerning the generation of the Son of God.

How can the one who was incomparably born before the ages now be in the bosom of the Father? How can the one who came forth and came from the Father have always been in the Father and still be in him? Or the one who is signified as the hand, right hand, or arm—tell me, heretic, how was he begotten from the Father, when divine Scripture also calls or names him the wisdom and power of God the Father?

Or the one who was begotten from the womb—how did the Word also come forth and come from the mouth of the Father? Or how is the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father?

You see that this birth alone cannot be explained. It must rather be sought according to the confession of the Scriptures, not judged or scrutinized. Although it is ineffable, nevertheless, according to the confession of the Council of Ariminum, it is unknowable to a creature.

Why should he not truly have been born from the Father? Far be it from us, since I am certain that he was born. But in this matter I do not know how he was begotten from God the Father, because from the immeasurable Father the one truly begotten from him is immeasurable.

But you say to me: “The Son began, because he was born.” And in return hear this: “Then the Father also began, because he begot.” If the Son began, the Father also began.

To whom, then, do you ascribe this eternity, which you assert existed before the Son’s birth?

**The Heretic.** To the Father alone.

**Athanasius.** And why do you prejudice him in this way? Certainly, if he begot only recently, he cannot be eternal [Col. 0270A].

Choose one of two alternatives: either their eternity is one, or their posteriority is one.

Finally, why do you attribute so much to the Son, as though he had at some time not existed, when this ought rather to be charged against the Father, whom, according to your confession, you testify at some time not to have been the Father?

Indeed, if birth prevented the Son from being eternal, since you assert that he was born late or recently, it is necessary that the birth of his Son also brought an impediment to the begetter, so that he too is not eternal if he begot only recently.

Does it not appear that birth attacks both of them and excludes both from eternity? Why, then, is this not already the form of your confession: “A new Father, and a new Son”? “The Father begins, and the Son begins”?

And once you have excluded the Father and the Son from one eternity, I ask you: to which God do you ascribe this eternity? For you say that the Father begot late and recently, and that the Son was recently born. Therefore both appear to be excluded from eternity.

Consider, then, that the Father cannot be called eternal without the Son; rather, the Father is more truly eternal with his Son, because this Father cannot be called only the Father without his Son.

**The Heretic.** What you have said, you have drawn from your own reasoning, and you have satisfied me with nothing from the authority of sacred Scripture. Therefore I ask you to produce at least one example relevant to this matter in place of many, so that your preceding statements may be confirmed by legitimate authority [Col. 0270B].

**Athanasius.** Hear the holy psalmist David speaking—or rather, the Son of God speaking through David and referring to the person of the Father:

“And I am always with you; you have held my right hand” (Ps. 72:23), and so forth.

Or hear the Father himself speaking to the lawgiver Moses concerning the eternal united name of the Trinity:

“I am the Lord God; this is my name, an eternal memorial throughout generations and generations” (Exod. 3:15).

Elsewhere he shows that the same statement was spoken of his Son:

“My name is in him” (Exod. 23:21).

Or receive this statement:

“I am the Lord God, who calls your name, the God of Israel” (Isa. 45:3).

The Son himself also testified:

“I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John 5:43) [Col. 0270C].

David likewise cries out:

“Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117:29).

Finally, hear the Lord himself speaking over the body of Lazarus:

“Father, I knew that you always hear me” (John 11:14).

If he had not always been in the Father or with the Father, how could the Father always have heard him, if he had not always been united with God the Father? Therefore, since he had always been with the Father and had never been without him, the Father always heard him.

You see that the united name is eternal, consisting in the power of wisdom in unity, so that what is the Father’s name in the nature of divinity, wisdom, and power is itself also the name of the Son in nature.

Or hear the Apostle saying concerning this:

“And his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20).

This eternity—or divinity—is his Son’s.

Elsewhere he resolves the matter even more clearly by calling Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Was the Father ever without his power and wisdom, heretic, so that you may say that he existed without his Son? Far be it from us, since Scripture everywhere declares to you most openly that the Father has always existed with the Son, and the Son with the Father [Col. 0270D].

Why did you not consider that holy David drew Goliath’s sword in battle (1 Sam. 17:51)? Using the example of this truth, we have decided to triumph over you with your own sword, as he himself testified:

“Let their sword enter their own heart” (Ps. 36:15).

Do you not know that what you take away from the Son, you also take away from the Father?

Thus, when at the first confrontation they had been excluded from the one eternity of the Father and the Son, and were compelled by the very judgment of truth, it seemed to them that they should bring forward openly what they had previously blasphemed secretly, saying:

“There was once a time when the Father was without the Son.”

For if the Father had ever been without the Son, he would never have presumed to declare through the prophet:

“And I am always with you” (Ps. 72:23).

But to this the fisherman and evangelist John, beloved of God, bore witness:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1).

Consider that God the Son was always with God the Father, through whom every beginning whatsoever was made [Col. 0271A].

Therefore it was fitting for us to respond for a little while to foolish statements with foolishness, so that they might at least in this way be overcome and confounded by their own folly and blush with shame.

Certainly, if the Father existed before he begot the Son, then without doubt he was not the Father if he did not have a Son.

But lest blasphemers presume even this, “the Son existed before he was born.” If he had not been born, he evidently was not the Son.

Fool, what then must one say? Choose one of the two things that you are confusedly designating.

You declare that the Father existed before the Son. Either the Father existed before he begot the Son, or he was the Father who had already truly begotten the Son.

Or you mean this: “The Son existed before he was born.” Either the Son was already born, because he had truly been born from the Father, as it is written:

“He who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Rev. 1:4).

Or this:

“In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1).

You see that the Son always existed with the Father, who is, who was, and who is to come [Col. 0271C].

You fail to understand this, Arius, because you introduce everything falsely, calling someone Father who had not begotten, and naming someone Son who had not yet been born.

I ask you: if there was a Father, as you assert, who had not begotten, and a Son who had not been born from the Father, what were they then? Perhaps you will say that both were unbegotten—which is impossible.

Truly, in opposition to the doctrine of your wickedness, the governing Spirit, rightly denouncing it through holy Moses, made this comparison:

“But our enemies are senseless. Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is a cluster of bitterness. The wine of dragons is their wine, and the incurable fury of asps” (Deut. 32:31).

Since the true Son, eternal and born from him, declares the true Father eternal, and the true Father, eternal and having begotten him, demonstrates the true Son eternal, it follows—as I said—that just as the true Father, who begot the Son from himself, was always with him before all things and existed earlier than all things, so the true Son, who had already been ineffably born from the Father, was always with him before all things and existed earlier than all things [Col. 0271D].

This, I say, is the prior eternity in them, which existed and was before every beginning whatsoever.

Therefore the Father was never without the Son, because the Son always existed with the Father, and this Father can in no way be called Father without the Son.

In addition to this great proof of the truth, their wickedness added the following:

“Before he begot, he was not Father, but he was almighty God.”

O sacrilege! You dare to think such things about God the Father. Therefore, without doubt, as you say, if the honor of Fatherhood was recently added to almighty God, it is revealed that he was previously imperfect.

And if dignity grew for almighty God, as for a needy human being, according to a sequence of stages, it is recognized that previously he was not almighty. For when honor is added to someone, until he reaches the highest degree, he is seen still to be beneath that degree; and when he reaches it, he begins to be better at the end than he was at the beginning, advancing from lowliness to the summit of the highest rank [Col. 0272A].

But we report these things according to your statements so that you may blush with shame. Rather, the Father is found to be almighty precisely because that great judgment of omnipotence had first submitted itself to him, so that he might recently assume the honor through this rank of the paternal name.

It would take too long to rehearse at such length all their blind darkness as one whole. Let them therefore hear our true and immovable voice of confession.

The one whom you testified to be the almighty God in ignorance, we defend as the Father himself. We show why we proclaim him to be the almighty Father: because, being himself almighty God by nature, he begot a Son of the same nature, as we find affirmed in the Scriptures:

“He who is, and who was, and who is to come, the almighty God” (Rev. 1:4).

You see that the Son of God is almighty in nature, just as the Father is.

Therefore nothing recently accrued to the Father or the Son in the united divinity of eternal omnipotence.

Nor is anything understood to have accrued to the almighty Holy Spirit, since he is from the united substance of omnipotence; for this united nature suffers neither increase nor diminution [Col. 0272C].

Learn, then, how your error must be resolved.

The eternity of the Father is his Son, because the Son was ineffably born from him before every beginning whatsoever. The eternity of the Son is his Father, because the Father incomparably begot him before all ages of ages. Or the eternity of the Paraclete Spirit is his united deity with the Father and the Son, which was not made, as the Son testified concerning him:

“He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26),

and:

“He will take from what is mine” (John 16:14).

The Father also confirms these statements through the prophet, saying:

“The Spirit proceeds from me” (Isa. 57:16).

And elsewhere:

“I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28).

Divine Scripture testifies that this was accomplished at Pentecost upon the apostles [Col. 0272D].

For just as the Father declares his Son in his divinity, since he is true God, so the Son demonstrates the Father in his substance, since he is true God. Likewise, the Holy Spirit reveals the Father and the Son in his own united and eternal nature, since he is true God.

This, I say, is the united, almighty, eternal Trinity, to whose divinity no dignity has recently been added.

**The Heretic.** I ask you: then is this united substance of the Trinity not mutable or changeable?

### Athanasius

Listen, then. It is written: “I am God, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6). Or take the prophet speaking to this point: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the very same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101:28). Or accept this statement: “I am God, and I am not changed” (Malachi 3:6).

Truly, those who attempt to change in their confession this divinity of the eternal Trinity have themselves plainly been changed by the devil, as the Apostle declares: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is God, blessed forever” (Romans 1:25). Understand, therefore, that this unchangeable, united fullness of the Trinity’s substance can suffer neither increase nor diminution.

### Heretic

I ask whether the substance of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is united. Show me this from the authority of the Scriptures.

### [Col. 0273B] Athanasius

Listen to the Holy Spirit testifying through the prophet Jeremiah—or rather, rebuking heretics through these authoritative words:

“Upon the mountains take up lamentation, and upon the paths of the wilderness mourning, because they have failed, since there are no men; they have not heard the voice of substance, from the birds of the sky to the beasts” (Jeremiah 9:10).

And he continued in this way: “Who is the wise man and understands these things?” (ibid., 12).

Here, as may be understood, the mountains and hills raised up in pride are the powers of this world. The paths of the wilderness are the Jews, who, always wandering, did not recognize Christ as the true God, born from the substance of the Father before all ages. The birds of the sky are the heretics, who, carried here and there like birds by every wind of doctrine, do not confess that there is one united voice of command and one substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The beasts, likewise, are the Gentiles, who did not recognize God their Maker.
