Truly, no one among these who do not understand that the Trinity has one united *ousia*—that is, substance—should be considered wise.

Or understand the prophet crying out in this regard: “Who will stand in the substance of the Lord and see his Word?” (Jeremiah 23:18). Plainly, what human being could stand in the substance of the Lord and see the Word, that is, his Son? As he himself says: “No one has seen the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father” (Luke 10:22).

Or accept this statement: “Whoever sees me sees also my Father” (John 14:9).

Regarding the Person of the Paraclete, he himself likewise declared: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice but do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:8).

Consider that the Trinity has one invisible substance. Yet he added: “If they had stood in my substance, I would have turned them away from their evil pursuits” (Jeremiah 23:22). Or this: “My substance is my sweetness” (Wisdom 16:21). And also: “Who is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3).

But there is also this statement, which is rightly regarded as authoritative in the highest degree: “For she is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness”—God the Son (Wisdom 7:26).

You see that there is one invisible image of the substance of glory and goodness. Finally, hear the Apostle Paul speaking to rebuke heretics and declaring this image:

“But if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine upon them” (2 Corinthians 4:3).

### Heretic

What is the invisible image of God the Father and of the Son? Show me this from the authority of Scripture.

### Athanasius

I know that this is a difficult matter for the ignorant to resolve. But we must always look with attentive hearts toward the radiant eloquence of Paul, who says:

“We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Consider how, in one image, he designated one glory three times: “the glory of the Lord,” “from glory,” “into glory,” and “as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

Is not the image of God the Father in glory such that this very same image is likewise the glory of the Son? And is not the image of the Holy Spirit’s glory also this very same, equally great and of the same character?

### Heretic

Explain to me whether this one and the very same substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is divided or undivided, or whether it is extended within them in such a way.

### Athanasius

O human being’s lack of understanding, when he does not understand himself! When you indicated the fullness of unity, did you not demonstrate, in that very name, that the name of the substance is undivided? And again, by repeating what you distinguished, you demonstrated that the individual Persons possess their own particularity.

Remember that the things we say are indescribable and must be believed altogether. Yet no capacity has been granted us to examine these matters fully and precisely, since the sacred Trinity wished only to make itself known and did not permit its divinity to be defined in a proper manner.

Therefore, the divine substance is not divided, extended, stretched out in any way, or cut into parts. Nor is it comparable to the derivation of anything else, for there is plainly no liquid in this nature, nor any kind of outflow, since it suffers neither diminution nor increase—especially since this fullness of undivided substance is indescribable.

The Trinity is as the very God, the Son of God, indicates: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11).

The Holy Spirit also exists in the Father, in the Son, and in himself, as the evangelist John testifies so explicitly in his Epistle: “And the three are one” (1 John 5:7).

Why, then, is it called one if something belonging to it is divided into parts? And why is it called one if something different is believed concerning it? And how, O heretic, are the three one if the substance among them is divided or cut apart? Or how are they one if one is placed before another? Or how are the three one if the divinities among them are different? How are they one if there is not in them one united and eternal fullness of divinity?

Moreover, since one fullness has absolutely no division in any part, and since the united fullness of divinity cannot be called lesser or greater in any part, the Apostle likewise declares:

“For who among human beings knows the things that are in a person except the spirit of the person that is in him? So also no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of God. Now we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God; and these things we also speak” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Understand that this testimony establishes an indisputable proof of the proper truth concerning the human being and the spirit that is in him, and concerning God and the Spirit who is from him.

The same teacher of the Gentiles testified to us in faith and truth, saying: “For the Spirit of God searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

If the Holy Spirit were a nature different from God, how could he, while searching, penetrate or enter into the divinity of God’s depths? Or how could he be in that divinity and in himself, since the nature of God, being different from his own nature, could not be united to it, nor, as I have said, penetrate it by searching its depths? How could he be in it, be in himself, or be naturally united within himself—that is, exist mutually within one another in a divine manner—unless he is from that very united nature of divinity?

For the Apostle also said: “Whoever joins himself to God is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

You see that this fullness of the divine Trinity is undivided. You also see that this fullness of the divine Trinity is present everywhere, filling all things within and without, from the summit of the heavens to the depths of the underworld, as the Lord himself testifies through the prophet:

“I am the Lord God, who fills heaven and earth and all that is in them” (Isaiah 44:24).

Likewise, holy Jeremiah, together with the prophets, declares concerning him: “If a man hides himself in secret places, will I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:24).

Or understand this as spoken with one meaning concerning the Trinity:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into the underworld, you are present there. If I take up my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:7).

Thus, when he said, “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?”, the Psalmist clearly indicated the governing Spirit who proceeds from the Father. By “your presence,” he plainly demonstrated the Son, who is the Father’s presence.

Who can hide or flee from the united divinity of the Trinity in heaven or in the underworld? To it the whole globe of the earth is reckoned as a drop, or as a thin foam, or as dew that descends from heaven before daybreak, as it is written:

“He who holds the circle of the earth, and those who dwell in it, as locusts” (Isaiah 40:22).

And also: “He who measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with a span, and enclosed the whole earth in his closed hand” (ibid., 12).

And again: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66:1).

Consider the incomprehensible power of the united divinity: heaven, which is held within a span, is also his throne; and earth, which is enclosed within a fist, is again the footstool of his feet. The whole expanse of heaven is held within a span, and the whole earth is enclosed within a fist, yet it is both his throne and the footstool of his feet.

As it is also written: “The whole globe of the earth is reckoned as a grain on a balance” (Wisdom 11:23).

Accordingly, he fills the whole universe and holds all things within and without, so that this undivided and eternal Trinity is present everywhere, possessing an invisible fullness of divinity.

Therefore, lest an evil interpreter take material for slander from what was said above, I shall briefly make the matter clear. I have frequently spoken of one substance, or united divinity, the nature of one God, or the nature of unity; likewise, of one name of divinity, the name of one divinity, the name of one nature, and the name of the united substance of divinity.

All these expressions, so that you who read may be certain, refer to the united name of the fullness of divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; to the name of the one divine Trinity alone; to the sole united name of the omnipotent substance; and also to the one good name of divinity.

Do I not clearly see that all these statements made above refer to the declared divinity of the unity of the *ousia*—the substance—of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

I have set these things out so that you would not understand them otherwise than they were said, nor twist a simple meaning into ambiguity, since every statement must be examined according to the intention of the speaker and not according to the foolish will of some heretic.

## BOOK SIX  
### On the Blessedness of Faith and on the Proscription of the Most Evil Sect

### [Col. 0275] [Col. 0275C]

### Heretic

I ask you to repeat again, in many ways, what has been said about the united name of divinity, and, as you proceed, to distinguish the names of the Persons.

### Response

First learn that this second question of yours has been placed in ambiguity. Does unity in no way allow the idea of union to be introduced into the confession, since the name of the nature of unity exists in these three Persons, and these three Persons are distinguished only by their names?

Therefore, unity cannot be shown apart from the Persons, nor, as I have said, can these Persons exist without the unity of divinity.

Can you name God only in the confused manner of the Gentiles, who are ignorant even in this respect of which Person they ought to designate? He is the begetter: must we therefore suppose that only “God” is indicated here? No—unless in this you recognize that his united Person is distinguished as the Son who has been born.

Is it fitting to profess “God” only in such a confused manner, unless one first believes in him who is from the united nature and thereby distinguishes his Person, namely, this Holy Spirit, who is neither the Father nor the Son?

Therefore, the understanding of this mystery is twofold: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.

You see the sign of unity in three Persons, and that these three Persons are distinguished only by their names. Thus unity cannot be shown without the Persons, nor can these Persons exist without the united name of divinity.

Behold, you now have before your eyes the treasures of light and the treasures of darkness. Wherever you please, extend your hand.

It is therefore necessary for us now to establish an immovable boundary, according to the equity of the Gospel’s rule, against our enemies, and everywhere to guard the limit of justice with balanced wisdom against all the heresies that roam about, so that this truth, established from heaven, may immediately divide the way of light from the darkness.

This, I say, is the way of light, whose door of salvation is opened in confession. Therefore, those who enter upon this profession obtain its blessedness.

Blessed is the one who confesses one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses the one God alone, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses one omnipotent God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses one true God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses one supreme God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses one good God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to be eternal.

Blessed is the one who confesses that the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is undivided.

Blessed is the one who adds or subtracts nothing in the confession of the united nature of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that all good things were made by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that there is one equality in the eternal fullness of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Blessed is the one who confesses that, according to the individual names of the Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—their distinct Persons alone are proper to them.

Thus I repeat the same things, because I greatly fear that I may have placed some stumbling block before those who understand less. I therefore desire to explain these very statements briefly in clearer words.

When I mentioned “one God,” I declared the united divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, by “omnipotent God” I made known the omnipotent substance of the Trinity.

Likewise, by “the one God alone,” I indicated the sole nature of the Trinity described above.

Again, I referred the words “one true God” to the one true nature of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When I spoke of “the supreme God,” I referred it to the supreme greatness of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When I spoke of “one good God,” I indicated the one goodness of the Trinity’s nature.

And “one God” I revealed as referring to the united lordship of divinity.

When I spoke of the undivided Trinity, I referred these words to the united substance of their fullness.

All these things, which I indicated individually above, I made known as referring to the indivisible eternity of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, although the united name of divinity has been expressed in many ways with respect to the individual Persons, whatever you apply to the Father you must necessarily confess to exist in the Son also, in unity:

God from God, light from light, whole from whole, and whole in whole, perfect from perfect, fullness from fullness, complete from complete, eternal from eternal, wisdom from wisdom, power from power, one from one and one in one, true from true, the Son born from the Father, not made, of one substance with the Father.

And likewise the Holy Spirit, who exists from the united Trinity: true God, wholly perfect, wholly full, complete, eternal, existing in that very wisdom as the power and foreknowledge of the Father and the Son.

### [Col. 0278A]

Therefore, you who read, I call heaven and earth to witness to you today, through this profession of the Catholic faith contained in my writing: if you do not follow it with your whole heart, or if you suppose that it ought to be despised and rejected in the disgust of your mind, you yourself will be guilty on the day of judgment, when the written document of this work is read out as testimony against you before the tribunal of Christ.

Or, if—which I do not wish—you are found to have joined wholeheartedly in the way of the curse of the heretics, I ask you to beware of it. Therefore it will be recited below for you.

This, I say, is the way of darkness, to be fled and guarded against, in which so many kinds of serpents possess slippery winding paths. Against them we ought to raise the shield of faith, confessing the true names of the Persons, so that, according to that very authority, we may hurl divine weapons against them. Hence as many spiritual weapons must be brought forth as there are wounds to be cut away.

For this reason, the deadly cause could not be concealed, since it could not first be soothed with remedies and thus brought to the treatment of salvation unless their inward parts were healed and the serpentine cancer driven out.

If they were willing first to receive the instruments of severity, they could easily reach the remedy of salvation. But because the root of weeds has adhered to them, sprouting in the gall of bitterness, they distrust entering the way of saving confession, because this way of light is a stumbling block to them.

Therefore we must show them what fruits of the curse are eaten by all who believe wickedly, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not obey the words of this book, to carry them out in his heart” (Deuteronomy 27:26).

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the substance of the united and eternal divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exists. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that, according to the three Persons, there are three different substances among them. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that there are three principles in this eternal unity of their divinity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the one true God the Father, the one true and only-begotten Son, and the one true God the Holy Spirit. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that there is one united name according to the divinity of the Trinity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who professes the unchangeable divinity of the Son of God—that is, the Word of God—as transferred or changed into flesh in such a way that he thereby ceased to be or lost what he had previously been before the assumption of humanity, especially since in the humanity he now possesses he was and is such as he knew himself always to have been, together with the Father, before the assumption of humanity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the undivided divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who, because of the three names of the Persons, confesses three gods, three substances, or three spirits. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that, according to the individual Persons, the three names of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinguished only by name. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who, because of the three names of the Persons and the incomparable united fullness of divinity, compares the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to a triangle or even a quadrilateral; or to three heads joined together, as philosophers are accustomed to say; or who professes that there is one Person. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one Person. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who designates the one whom he calls the Son as that same Father in a confused manner. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the Father was born, or was incarnate, or suffered. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son was truly and ineffably begotten from the substance of the Father. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that this incomparable birth was made, created, or formed. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who, against this inestimable generation of divinity, believes that any comparison derived from its created work should properly be introduced into your confession. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who says that the true Son of God exists only by will and not rather by birth. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who says: “There was a time when the Son did not exist.” Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that this birth of God is a phantom from things that did not exist—what the Greeks call *ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων* (“from things that do not exist”). Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who says that the divinity of the Son of God has a beginning in time, an origin from nothing, or that a name resembling adoption recently came to him from another. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess one from one, the Son truly born from the Father. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son was born from the Father without suffering. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who says: “At some time the Father existed without the Son.” Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that, before every beginning and absolutely every origin, the Son always existed with the Father. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that these three names—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—belong to one Person only, the Father, and not that there are three according to these true names of the Persons. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the immortal divinity of the Son of God. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who says of the eternal Son of God: “He did not exist before he was born from Mary.” Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who professes that the united divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exists only through the love of concord, and not rather through this very united divinity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the united divinity exists in these three Persons. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the unity of the fullness of the divine Trinity is undivided. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess the incomparable, united, eternal divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who, against the force and authority of divine Scripture, presumes to confess that this true God, the Spirit Paraclete, ought to be the Father, or the Son, or indeed a created work. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the Son of God, true God, recently assumed a human being from the Virgin Mary for our salvation. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the Son of God is merely a solitary man or merely a pure man. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who assigns to the eternal God, the Son of God, the beginning of his existence to have arisen recently from the assumption of humanity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that his divinity suffered. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that the human being whom he assumed truly suffered. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who does not confess that this whole human being—that is, the soul and body which he assumed—was again assumed or liberated and rose from the dead on the third day. Let it be so, let it be so.

Cursed is the one who confesses that the incomparable divinity of the Trinity properly possesses the features of a human being, whereas we find it written: “There is no God like him in heaven above or on earth below” (1 Kings 8:23). Let it be so, let it be so.

### Likewise, there is discussion of various kinds of books

Woe to you who invalidate the first faith of baptism instituted from heaven and weaken, by repetition, the instruments of freedom once granted. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who do not believe that forgiveness ought to be granted to the fallen who repent. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who defend one Person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and not three, according to the very names of truth. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who profess that, within this united and incomparable fullness of the divine Trinity, there is some extension, cutting apart, or stretching out among them. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who defend that, from this united fullness of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, there is some derivation or outflow among them. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who deny that there is one foreknowledge in the united divinity of the Trinity. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who deny that the Son of God possesses that very foreknowledge which the Father possesses, so that you say that he was ignorant of the day and hour when the judgment would take place, although he himself had previously borne witness concerning himself to the Father, saying in the hundred and eighteenth Psalm:

“Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me, but they did not understand your testimonies; I have seen the consummation of all things, and the end.”

You see, therefore, that he knew not only his own day or the hour of judgment, but also the consummation of all the ages that were afterward to come.

Woe to you who believe that the Son of God assumed nothing from the Virgin Mary. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who do not confess the Son of God as mediator between God and human beings. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who accept false prophets or false apostles as authoritative.

Woe to you who commit grave sins and, against the authority of the Apostles, condemn second marriages. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who attribute sin or death to God as his work. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who maintain that this world has always been coeternal with God by itself, or deny that it was made by God. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who defend that the world was made from some underlying matter. Let it be so, let it be so.

Woe to you who do not believe that all things in heaven and on earth—that is, visible and invisible things—were made through God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the Maker of all.

Again, here we engage in combat against the various deadly poisons of dragons and asps.

### [Col. 0281A]

If anyone confesses that the apostate angel was not made by God in the nature in which he was made, but existed from himself, thereby giving him an eternal beginning alongside God, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the apostate angel was made by God with an evil nature, and does not say that he conceived evil from himself by his own will, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the angel of Satan made the world—which God forbid—and does not judge that every sin was devised through him, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that God made only the human soul and that Satan fashioned its body—which God forbid—let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that human souls return again through cycles in the world, whether in human beings, cattle, or serpents, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the human being will rise on the day of judgment in the soul alone and not with the body, just as God made him, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the Son of God appeared in a human being like a phantom, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the true human being whom he assumed did not truly eat or drink, weep, sweat blood, suffer, rise again, and sit at the right hand of the Father in heaven, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that the Son of God passed through Mary’s body like water through a pipe, or affirms that he assumed nothing from her, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that human souls are from God’s own substance—which God forbid—and does not affirm that they were made by God, and if anyone says that a person can make his own substance, let him be anathema.

If anyone confesses that human souls have always existed with God, thereby declaring them eternal, and says that they were neither made nor can be made, although it is written, “He who made what is outside made also what is within,” let him be anathema.

If anyone blasphemes the New and Old Testaments, let him be anathema.

If anyone blasphemes the holy patriarchs, prophets, apostles, or martyrs, let him be anathema.

If anyone worships the sun, the moon, or any such created thing, let him be anathema.

If anyone believes that, besides the one true God—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—there is another God to be worshiped, although there is absolutely no other God, let him be anathema.

If anyone says of the undivided and unchangeable fullness of eternal divinity, “The nature of the Son is changeable and transformable,” so that he thereby ceased to be what he had previously been, let him be anathema.

Although it is said to me that he was seen in many ways by the Fathers in visible matter, you do not understand that all these things were shown beforehand in him as a prefiguration of the work of the humanity he assumed or of the future judgment, and not as the pure invisible divinity itself, as it has been declared: “All these things happened in figure for us” (1 Corinthians 10:6).

If that is not so, answer me: because he was seen in an angel, is his divinity therefore properly angelic? Or because he was touched or seen as a human being in the struggle of one wrestling with him, is the nature of God therefore tangible or visible like human nature? Or because he was seen as fire in a bush, is his substance therefore of such a kind? Or because he was frequently seen in various forms, does he therefore contain within himself different, mixed, or compounded natures?

The united divinity is undivided, and its majesty invisible.

Therefore understand that when he was seen in angels, the messenger of the Father was shown beforehand. Or in a human being, because he was recently born from the Virgin Mary. Or in fire, because judgment is to come from him, since it is written that he is “the angel of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:5), that the mediator Emmanuel was born as a human being, and that in fire he is like a refiner of gold and silver, a tester of righteous hearts.

Although he was seen in these assumed forms as he wished, in his divinity he remains invisible, just as he always was and is with the Father.

Without doubt, God then worked all these things in the figure of a human being, because the work of the future was already shown beforehand in him; and he himself completed it when he said: “If you do not believe me, believe the works, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38).

Was God not present, performing miracles, and were his works not recognized as having been done through the human being? Yet his divinity was not seen in him, just as he said: “Whoever sees me sees also my Father.”

You see, O heretic, that no one has ever seen God as he is in his pure form.

Therefore, if there are any heresies unknown to us, as well as any that may arise in the future against the rule of faith and the Catholic Church, let them be held anathema.

If anyone wishes to place above the tradition of the canon or defend against it the apocryphal writings of heretics, which the Catholic Church wholly rejects, let him be anathema. Let it be so, let it be so.

## BOOK SEVEN  
### On the Profession of the Catholic Rule, with a Rebuke of Heretics

### [Col. 0281]

For this reason I earnestly beseech the glory of your greatness to drive far from our minds these seeds of weeds, which must be uprooted and burned. Let this adulterous confession of the heretics, prescribed by us in the preceding book, retreat from our hearts as far as the east is from the west.

Therefore, I think that no excuse of ignorance has now been left between the way of light and the way of darkness. So, wherever you please, whoever you are, depart.

Certainly, we are not rivals in concealing the divine mystery; rather, we urge that we be found entering together upon the way of blessing.

For this reason, our first and greatest concern was to teach concerning such an admirable and royal decree, in which the reward of eternal life is promised to all nations, when the Lord says:

“Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Truly, I am sufficiently amazed at this, and for a long time, absorbed in astonishment of mind, I praise the fact that so great a glory of the most sacred Trinity was briefly expounded in only twelve words or syllables of distinction.

Truly, in this decree the united name of the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is placed first.

Truly, in this most sacred Trinity the names are distinguished only among the Persons.

Truly, neither the Law nor the prophets revealed this hidden mystery so explicitly.

Truly, above every divinely established ordinance, this must be guarded above all.

Truly, nothing can be added to it, and nothing can be taken away from it.

Truly, in this matter it is blasphemous to add to or subtract from the commandment of the gift of baptism.

### Question

If these things are so, I earnestly beg you to show me this from the rule of the Scriptures.

**Response.** First understand that in this saying of Scripture an argument of faith is set forth, together with a rebuke of the nocturnal sower of weeds. O mind of heretics, full of deceptions and possessed by the devil! Why do you baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and blaspheme the one united Godhead? Why do you confess only the names of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and deny the one united name of divinity? Why is unity indicated if in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit there is not [Col. 0283B] one and the same equal fullness of divinity? Why does the Father signify to our understanding concerning his only-begotten Son, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3), if you testify that the divinity of the Son of God was created, made, or founded? Why is one in one, if the nature is divided? Why are I and the Father one (John 10:30), if there is not in them one power of wisdom and divinity? Why are “all things mine” and “yours are mine” (John 17:10), if there is not in them one divinity, or one operation of creation? Why do you blaspheme the true Father when you compare his true Son with his own creation? Why does he himself proclaim, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11), if their nature is different or severed? Why does he indicate, “Who sees me sees also my Father” (ibid., 9), if there is not in them one invisible [Col. 0283C] image of the true nature? Why do you read, “Maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3), if you do not accept that he is from the very united divinity of the Father and the Son? Why do you read that the chosen vessel said, “We all drank one Spirit” (1 Cor. 4:13), if you distinguish him from the united nature? Why does this Advocate, the Spirit of truth, proceed from God the Father and come, if you assert that he is of another substance? Why is this united name of divinity found celebrated and honored among the nations, if baptism is not celebrated in the name of the Trinity as one united divinity? Why do you read that John the Evangelist said, “The Three are one” (1 John 5:7), if you accept that the persons have different natures? Why do you say, according to the language of Scripture, that there is one gift of baptism, if you prescribe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy [Col. 0283D] Spirit have divergent natures? Why do you celebrate baptism according to tradition while blaspheming in your confession the one eternal name of the Trinity?

Hypocrites, how do you accept the statement, “What is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), if the Spirit the Paraclete is denied to be God? Hypocrites, how is it necessary to worship in the Spirit, if the Spirit is denied to be God? Hypocrites, how do you receive the statement, “All these things are worked by the one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11), if you separate him from the operation of the united Godhead? Hypocrites, how do you accept that it was said, “The same Spirit, the same Lord, and the same God” (ibid., 4–6), if you do not accept the true God, who works wonders in all things from the true united nature? Hypocrites, by whom is the [Col. 0284A] word of wisdom supplied, or the word of knowledge, or faith, or the grace of healings, or the working of miracles, or prophecy, or the discernment of spirits, except because they come from the united fullness?

Hypocrites, learn that there is one operation in the nature of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, since the works which the Father performs are themselves shown to be, in unity, the works of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Likewise, what the Son performs, those very works are referred to the Father and to the principal Spirit. In the same way, when the Spirit the Paraclete performs something, those very works are declared in unity to be the works of the Father and of the Son. Do you see that their operation is united in the one nature of the Godhead?

**Question.** I ask you to explain these statements to me still further on the authority of the Scriptures.

[Col. 0284B] **Response.** I ask you: how many times has it already been declared to you, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19)? Or, if you think this must be contradicted because the operations named in the one gift of baptism are not contained in unity in the Trinity, why, after removing this name of divinity, do you baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, saying, “I baptize you in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit,” and not in one name? In this way you would artfully fail silently to name—or deny—their united name in the Godhead, while assigning to them only their individual names according to their persons.

For if baptism were to be celebrated in this way, the assertion of the Arians would prevail. They think that wherever names are indicated according to the persons, there, together with those names, individual or different [Col. 0284C] substances must also be declared, so that unity is assigned merely to agreement in love and not rather to the united fullness of divinity. And what more would follow from this? They would profess that the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit had recently been added to the unity of God as something adoptive, so that this name would appear to have arisen from nothing, or from something else, or in time—which God forbid. For whenever they name the true name of divinity, they assign it only to the person of the Father, saying these things in order to divide the true unity of divinity. Where they ought merely to distinguish the names according to the persons, there they distinguish, together with the names, three different natures as well—which may this blasphemy be far from us. We accept instead that the one name of divinity has been spoken in unity in the Trinity, through which, as [Col. 0284D] baptism operates, we have received the remission of sins; while we perfectly distinguish only the individual names according to the persons.

I ask: where is the bond of faith found among them if the name of the unity of substance is not maintained in the Trinity? I ask: how do you assign individual or different fullnesses to the individual persons, when there is one nature in this very fullness of the divine Trinity? I ask: how are the Three one if the nature of divinity is different in the two—or in the several persons? I ask: how do those who do not confess that this sevenfold Spirit—of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord—consists in the united fullness of divinity, deserve to receive him through the laying on of hands in chrism? I ask: [Col. 0285A] have you not read that the apostle Peter, who holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven, said to Ananias, “Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” And he continued: “You have not lied to men, but to God,” if you deny that he is the true God?

I ask: if this Paraclete Spirit was not God, as you say, why did he presume such authority over the disciples, saying, “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas, whom I have chosen for the work of the ministry, for which I have taken them” (Acts 13:2)? You see that it is God who set them apart and chose them for the work of the ministry, in which he also took them. I ask: how is this united fullness of the divine Trinity divided by you, when they are shown to be one in one, or certainly one in both, existing with one another? I ask: where is one faith shown to exist if the eternal Trinity is not accepted by them as existing in unity? [Col. 0285B] Why do you read, “From him, and through him, and in him” (Rom. 11:35), if you divide the name of unity in the divinity of the Trinity and deny that their united operation is present in creation? I ask: have you not read that the Apostle said, “From God, before God, in Christ we speak” (2 Cor. 2:17)—that is, from God the Father, before God the Holy Spirit, we proclaim our testimony in Christ the Son of God? Why do you read that the historian Moses indicated, “And God said, and God made, and God blessed” (Gen. 1), if you do not accept that this was performed in unity by the united name of divinity?

**Question.** Since you have made the united name of the Trinity clear to me in so many ways, I therefore ask you to confirm these statements still further and rightly on the authority of the Scriptures, if indeed all these things were likewise done in unity.

[Col. 0285C] **Response.** Now hear one example among many that is pertinent. Remember that, after such a full satisfaction, this will be the end of the speaker’s discourse. Yet if [Col. 0286A] nothing further moves you concerning what I carefully explained above to you in accordance with the most upright line of Scripture, excellent Theophilus, so that you may recognize the truth of the words about which you have already been instructed, the psalmist—or rather, the prophetic Spirit through the psalmist—says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

In saying “the Word,” he certainly declared the Son; by “the Lord,” he indicated his Father; and by “the Spirit of his mouth,” he demonstrated that he is the principal Spirit. Do you see how briefly he distinguished their presence according to the individual significations of the persons—that is, the Word, the Lord, and the Spirit—and showed that their operation is united? For if ambiguity still holds you in some respect, I repeat the same point.

[Col. 0286B] When he says, “By the Word of the Lord,” do not understand an insubstantial sound of the voice, which, if someone strong were to utter it from the mountains, would ordinarily be echoed back by a reverberating echo—a mere auditory impression of something resounding, but with no thing made. Rather, this is the Word of our Lord and Father, who is our salvation, as the divine Scriptures everywhere testify: the Son of God is substantial God, through whom all things were made.

Therefore, since he said, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6), understand that this substantial Word was properly born from no one other than the Father. Likewise, by “the Spirit of his mouth” he meant the Spirit who proceeded from that same united substance, as we find it authoritatively established—not from another nature, but from that very one. Consequently, the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is united; the Greeks call this [Col. 0286C] **οὐσία** (*ousia*), “substance.” The operation of this same Trinity in creation is also united.

## BOOK EIGHT  
### On the Unity of the Faith. To Theophilus.

[Col. 0285]

[Col. 0285C] This is the faith in the one substance of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: without beginning of times, above every understanding, utterance, and spirit; one power, one God; but three names, one might. The Word of God is born from the Virgin Mary, receiving an animate body. Yet the Word of God himself is not a superior or exalted sense. The Word was not contained by the flesh, but was [Col. 0285D] in the flesh and above the flesh, as God who knows beforehand, the power of God, the truth of God.

He suffered human suffering, but the Word of God is impassible. In the passion, the body dies so that it may give life to the first-formed human being, who had fallen through disobedience.

O man, you seek the Godhead—I rebuke you; if you believe, you do well. You have been commanded to believe; you have not been permitted to investigate. But if you investigate and say, “How is he Father?” you have fallen away from the light. And if you say, “How is he Son?” the prophetic word will confront you, saying, “Who will recount his generation?” (Acts 8:33). See, then, that you do not likewise fall away from the light, for no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father.

Whoever introduces three powers confesses three gods. We, however, believe in [Col. 0286C] three persons and one divinity. When you name the Father, you glorify the Son; and when you name the Son, you adore the Father. If, on the other hand, we say that the Trinity is one person, we become like Jews, because the Jews speak of one person and confess one God. If we introduce three gods, we are like the nations. But we confess the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father, together with the Holy [Col. 0286D] Spirit.

Unity is not separated; divinity is not divided. God from God, not two gods; power from power, but one power; light from light, but one light; truth from truth, but one truth. Heaven is not witness, nor earth, nor sea, nor light, nor darkness, nor angels, nor archangels, nor cherubim, nor seraphim; rather, before the beginning the Son was with the Father. No one knows the Unbegotten except the one who was born from him: he knows from whom he was born. Nor does anyone know the Begotten except the one who begot him. The Father knows whom he begot; likewise, the begotten one knows his begetter—the Father’s counsel and wisdom, one power and one divinity.

Do you seek the birth of the Son of God? Read about his proper birth from the Virgin Mary. But the birth of the Son of God before the beginning is with the Father. [Col. 0287A] For I confess one Unbegotten and one Begotten. I confess the almighty Father, without beginning and without end, who holds all things and is held by none; who governs all things and is governed by none; who sees all things, while he himself is invisible.

I confess Jesus Christ, the Son of God, together with the whole counsel and power of the Father’s divinity. Whatever power the Father has, the Son has also. The one begotten is not diminished by him who is Unbegotten.

The Holy Spirit is neither born nor Unbegotten; he is neither made nor created. If I say that he is born, I establish two Sons from one Father, and not one from one, or the only one from the only one. Either there is one Father from whom all things are, or one Jesus Christ through whom all things are. And if I say that he is Unbegotten, then there is no longer one almighty Father who is Unbegotten; rather, I establish two gods.

And if I say that he is a created work, I inquire in a pagan manner, for the nations [Col. 0287B] worship the work of human hands and not the maker of heaven and earth. What, then, do you have to declare? A phantom? God forbid, since blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

How, then, when two pieces of wood are joined and placed in a furnace, and an inseparable flame proceeds from the two pieces of wood, so from the power of the Father and the Son does the Holy Spirit proceed, possessing that very power of divinity? As the most blessed Paul stated: “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). God is not the mediator of God, for there is one God even unto the Trinity; rather, receiving a body from the Virgin Mary and putting on the old human being, who had fallen through disobedience, he became the mediator of the flesh by [Col. 0288A] the power of the Father—that is, Jesus Christ.

When he took the apostles, as the Evangelist testifies, and ascended a high mountain and was transfigured before them, and behold, a bright cloud covered him, he did not display the bright power of the Father, as some teach through empty talk, saying: “Just as there are three persons in one power, so there are three names but one God—three names belonging to one voice, the names of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Again, dividing the power and divinity of the Trinity, they say: “As an emperor, a prefect, and a count.” God forbid! I do not hand on this doctrine or this explanation; rather, I anathematize it. For it is written in the divine precepts: “The visible things of this world are compared with the invisible things” (Rom. 1:20).

An earthly emperor consists of three elements, but there is one empire. [Col. 0288B] If he removes the diadem from his head, he is Caesar, not emperor. If he removes the purple, he is now a prefect, a solitary man. Those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit are not Christians but are like Jews. For the Jews worship one person, whereas we confess three persons.

As with the earthly emperor, so also with the heavenly: the man is in the purple, and the purple is in the man; but the crown on his head contains both the purple and the man and displays one empire of power. So the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father; while the Holy Spirit is the conjunction of the Godhead, the power and unity of the Trinity.

## BOOK NINE  
### A Little Book of Faith. To Theophilus.

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287C] I believe in God the almighty Father, and in his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ our Savior, and I confess that the Holy Spirit is one God. Not one in the sense of being solitary, nor the same person who is himself Father to himself and himself Son; rather, the true Father begot the true Son, as he is: God from God, light from light, life from life, perfect from perfect, wholly from whole, full from full; not created but begotten; not from nothing, but from the Father, of one substance with the Father.

And the Holy Spirit is true God: neither unbegotten nor begotten, neither created nor made, but proceeding from the Father and the Son, always coeternal with the Father and the Son. Yet we confess one God: the Son is from the one Father and is all that the Father is. The Son is God begotten, and the Father, all that he is, begot the Son wholly. [Col. 0287D] In begetting the Son, the Father neither diminished nor lost the divinity of his fullness.

Holding with complete certainty that the Son is all that God the Father is, we piously confess one God together with the Holy Spirit. We believe in Jesus Christ our Lord, his Son, through whom all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible; for our salvation he descended from heaven, although he had never ceased to be [Col. 0288C] in heaven.

He was born from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary. The Word became flesh; he did not lose what he had been, but began to be what he had not been. God was not changed, but remained God while also being born human—not imaginary, not airy, but possessing a bodily perception and a soul. We understand him to be so truly human that we confess him no less truly God; and so truly God that we in no way hesitate to confess him truly human.

We await this same Lord Jesus Christ to have fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, to have suffered under Pontius Pilate, to have been crucified, and according to the Scriptures to have died and been buried, and according to the Scriptures to have risen from the dead on the third day; to have been taken up into heaven and to sit at the right hand of the Father, and from there to come to judge the living and the dead. [Col. 0288D] In his death and blood we shall obtain the remission of sins. We shall be raised by him in these bodies and shall receive from him the soul together with the same flesh in which he was born, suffered, died, and rose again—either eternal life for good merits or eternal judgment for sins. This is what has been approved. Amen.

## BOOK TEN  
### An Exposition of the Catholic Faith. To Theophilus.

[Col. 0289] [Col. 0289A]

We are commanded to believe in the almighty power of God the Father, and of his Son Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit—the undivided and inseparable Trinity. For this the prophets sang, the Lord handed down, and the apostles held and taught. This is the redemption of the world; this is our faith and life: that we confess the one substance handed down to us, three subsisting persons, perfect, equal, and coeternal, and that we preserve the firm confession of faith unharmed to the very end.

This is what the Greeks call **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “of one substance”): that which subsists does not have its being from elsewhere, but is its own and exists from itself. Other things, however, possess whatever they have as something received. Therefore God speaks to Moses, saying, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14). And again: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me.’”

At that time there were certainly angels, [Col. 0289B] thrones, dominions, heaven, earth, and seas. But because that nature alone is uncreated, and the one divinity subsists in three persons, he therefore said, “I am who I am.” Whoever, however, speaks of three **ὑποστάσεις** (*hypostaseis*), that is, three substances, attempts under the name of piety to assert three natures.

And if this is so, why should we separate ourselves from the walls of Arius, joined to his unbelief? For he divides the divinity by degrees and confesses God from God—that is, the Son from the Father—in such a way that he was made from God and not born from God. If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not a true son. And if he is not a true son, neither is he true God. Or if he is true God and is not from the Father, there are two, each possessing a separate will and different authority.

But our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0289C] testifies in his Gospel that he is one with the Father and from the Father when he says, “I came forth from God” (John 16:27). And again, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). Likewise, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And, “Whoever sees me sees also the Father” (John 14:9). These things were indeed written so that his true divinity would not be denied.

But perhaps you claim for yourself those statements that were written because of his incarnation, such as, “The one who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28); and, “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30); and, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (ibid., 19); and, “It is not mine to give, but it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father” (Matt. 20:23); and other statements like these. None of these weakens or diminishes the Son; rather, they distinguish him from the Father and reveal his humility and incarnation.

Nor should those statements [Col. 0289D] scandalize the faithful soul in which the Lord is remembered to have hungered, slept, wept, and been sorrowful even unto death, as well as to have suffered and endured the cross. These things were written and done so that examples of endurance might also be offered and his true incarnation might be recognized.

When the Lord is said to have hungered, understand the assumption of a true body. But when he satisfies five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, recognize his true divinity. [Col. 0290A] Certainly, when he says, “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41), it does not enter our understanding that bread could be believed to hunger. The same must be understood concerning his sleep. For just as the truth of his body is recognized through sleep, so his true divinity is demonstrated by the fact that he immediately commands the winds and the waves.

Likewise, when he pours out tears over Lazarus, suspicion of a phantom is removed, for tears are fluids of a true body. But when he says, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43), and at once the man who had already begun to stink emerges alive as the earth opens, this is an indication of his great divinity.

The statement, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Mark 14:34), can also be understood from this very raising of Lazarus: it shows how it ought to be received. [Col. 0290B] The divinity was not afraid of death, since by a word it raised the dead; rather, he indicated human feeling through the sorrows of the soul.

The cross, suffering, and burial are likewise dispelled by one or another saying of the Lord, so that impotence or weakness may not be attributed to him. He says to the Jews, “Destroy this temple”—plainly referring to his body—“and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He also says, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

If he raises the temple of his body, if he has the power to lay down his life through suffering and to take it up through resurrection, let the opinion of weakness in Christ cease, since the sublimity of such great power is declared. Therefore all things must be understood piously; all things must be treated reverently. Both must be confessed in the Lord: the form of God, in which he always existed, and the form of a servant, which [Col. 0290C] he assumed for the sake of servants. His suffering according to the flesh and his impassibility according to divinity must both be believed.

## QUESTIONS OF HERETICS AND ANSWERS OF CATHOLICS

273 **Heretic.** Did God the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?

**Response.** Neither by will nor by necessity, because no necessity remains in God. But let me ask you in turn: Is God good or not?

Certainly he is good. Is he good by will or by necessity? If by will, then the will by which he is good is already greater and prior. If by necessity, then necessity is greater, and God is considered weaker. Therefore the Son was born from the Father not by will or by necessity, but from substance, [Col. 0290D] because that which is divinity is above will and necessity.

**Heretic.** I ask you again: What are the Father and the Son?

**Response.** God and the Word.

**Heretic.** Then he is not simple but composite, because he is himself and the Word.

**Response.** Does God act or not? And does he do what he does by will or not?

[Col. 0291A] **Heretic.** Certainly, by will.

**Response.** Then he is himself also will, and according to your question he is composite, not simple.

**Heretic.** But God, remaining in eternity, alone is eternal. For he who always is is all things [the wording is textually uncertain]; yet he is not many things, but one and simple—this which God always is.

**Response.** And for that reason it is impossible for one to be separated from one—that is, the Son from the Father or the Father from the Son. Because of the identity of divinity I say, “I and the Father are one,” while “I and the Father” is not understood as a solitary being, nor is “we are one” understood as implying difference.

We therefore say that the paternal divinity was never alien from its proper generation. For this reason the paternal divinity becomes intelligible to us in relation to time, but in itself it is [Col. 0291B] subject neither to time nor to novelty, lest the paternal divinity be found empty, superfluous, or in some way progressing. For it is free from every quality, every quantity, every beginning, and every composition.

But when he is called begotten, nothing other than the Father and the Son is shown to be signified. Nothing is more impious than to call him the Son of God and deny that he is true God; or to speak of the Father and confess him as Father without generation. For whatever has not come into existence in the manner in which God ought to exist ought not to be believed to be God.

“I am who I am,” but I have not been changed. Therefore what is divine cannot be changed, lest it cease to be what it always is. But it is changed from its simplicity if the Father is a new father, if from eternity the Son is with him and is not in him. And it is mutable if he begot the Son after nature [Col. 0291C] not by nature but by will.

**Heretic.** But only the Father should be believed to be wise and powerful.

**Response.** If, while venerating the Son together with the Father, you venerate one who is less wise together with him, you dishonor the Father. If, therefore, you determine that the Son is less wise, you ought not to assert him either as God or as the Son of God. But if you assert him to be fully wise, you rightly define him as God and as the Son.

**Heretic.** But it is clear that the Son is changed by the Father, whereas the Father cannot be changed by the Son.

**Response.** If this is so, I ask whether the Father begot an imperfect Son and dismissed him under suspicion, so that thereafter he might graciously impart to him the rudiments of wisdom, not so much in the role of a begetter as by the authority of a teacher.

[Col. 0291D] Is there, then, something that God the Father, perfectly wise, ought to teach, and something that God the Son, imperfectly wise, can learn? And how are all the things that the Father has the Son’s, if he is not perfectly wise or fully powerful? How are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge found in the Son? Or how is he named God above all?

**Heretic.** But only God the Father should be recognized as without beginning, without origin, simple, and indeterminate. His operation, however—that is, the Son—should not be understood as without end, especially since every work has a beginning and cannot be without an end.

**Athanasius.** We too confess this: [Col. 0292A] his nature is indeterminate and simple. Therefore what remains uncompounded and simple cannot be determined by any laws.

But answer me when I ask: Is God, whom you recall as having always existed without beginning and without end, so indeterminate? You establish that nothing can be added to him, not only according to nature but even according to the action of nature, so that he is declared to be neither a new father nor a begetter capable of beginning, and may thus be known as truly indeterminate and not progressing.

He will certainly progress if he hastens toward the act of a new generation, being thereby unable to know that he will at some time become a father. For us, however, let the one suffice who was in the beginning and was with God, since he was God with God.

But if the Son is not by nature, then Father and Son are not rightly proclaimed, [Col. 0292B] since neither begetter nor begotten is indicated. And if, according to Paul, the fullness of divinity is possessed in the Son, why is the God of fullness denied? And if all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him, why is he declared ignorant? And if the Word is in the beginning and is held to be God with God, why is he not believed to be natural God?

But let it be far from apostolic faith that, in the generation of the Son, what the Father is should either be increased in divinity or diminished so that he cease to be Father. Nor does the one born undergo advancement, nor does the begetter undergo diminution.

**Heretic.** How do you join birth to eternity, when birth is later than eternity?

**Athanasius.** Truly, you speak as though he were first conceived from seed or [Col. 0292C] coagulated in a womb, when Scripture says, “Who will recount his generation?” (Acts 8:33). You also bring an accusation against the begetter, as though something had accrued to him so that he could beget.

But if something accrued to him that he did not previously possess, he is found to be imperfect. If nothing accrued to him, he is found to have been eternal with the Eternal in eternity.

Hear of the Son’s eternity through David, with the Son speaking to the Father: “And I am always with you; you have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. 72:23). David says again: “The beginning is with you on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

**Heretic.** You call the Father Unbegotten and the Son Begotten. What will you say about the Holy Spirit, who is certainly [Col. 0292D] placed in the third rank? Do you confess in the Scriptures that he is begotten, or do you call him Unbegotten? If he is begotten, then the Son is no longer only-begotten, since another has also been born from the Father. If he is not born, then there is also another Unbegotten, and there is no longer one God the Father from whom all things are, but two fathers. And if the Spirit is neither born from the Father nor unbegotten, it remains that he must be called a creature.

**Athanasius.** If you believed the Lord’s Scriptures or the Lord when he speaks, you would never compare the Creator with creatures, since you read: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). David himself also says: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Ps. 103:30).

[Col. 0293A] I have heard the Father speaking as well: “The Spirit went forth from me” (Isa. 57:16). Likewise, through the prophet Joel he himself says: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28). And the Lord says to the apostles in the Gospel: “I will send you the Paraclete from my Father, the Spirit of truth; he proceeds from the Father and receives from what is mine” (John 15:26; 16:14).

It would indeed be enough for the faithful to believe this alone: the Son is begotten, but the Spirit proceeds from the Father. No one is permitted to know what or how great his procession is, just as it was said of the Son: “Who will recount his generation?” (Acts 8:33). But for the sake of unbelievers it must be examined more closely; answer me when I ask.

**Heretic.** I answer.

**Athanasius.** Certainly you confess that God is the Creator—that is, [Col. 0293B] the maker of all things—and that nothing is intermediate between him and what he created.

**Heretic.** Why should I confess what cannot be doubted?

**Athanasius.** Everything created is changeable, because it has a beginning and is not without an end. Do you confess that everything eternal is unchangeable and immutable, having neither a beginning nor an end?

**Heretic.** Certainly I say so, because that is how it is.

**Athanasius.** Is the Creator capable of being mixed with creatures, or not?

**Heretic.** He does communicate himself to the creature, but he is never mixed with it, lest he be found mutable and changeable and a participant in corruption.

Athanasius. You have answered correctly. And how do you read: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19)? If the Holy Spirit is a creature, how is he united with the Creator in name, [Col. 0293C] in power, in redemption, and in sanctification? And the one whom you think is named in the third place, the apostle Peter places in the first; he does not divide the Trinity by ranks, nor recognize a numerical order, but places the third first when he says to Ananias: “Why has Satan filled your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3). And shortly afterward: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (ibid., 4). Therefore, whoever lies to the Holy Spirit lies to God, because the Spirit is God.

Hear also the apostle Paul saying: “For no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him; so also no one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God who is in him” (I Cor. II, 11). If he were indeed a creature, as you endeavor to believe, he could not know what was in the Creator. Hence the same Paul says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI, 34).

If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, as we read; if he liberates, sanctifies, is the Consoler, and is good as God is, as it is written, “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land” (Ps. CXLII, 10); if he washes, justifies, and if whoever blasphemes him, as it is written, “has no forgiveness, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII, 32)—things that belong properly to no one except God—what more, then, is there to seek or doubt concerning him? Through the greatness of his works he reveals what he is: he is certainly not alien to the majesty of the Father and the Son, who is not alien to the power of their works. His divine name is denied in vain when his power cannot be denied.

There is also this: every creature is capable of divine powers and is in need of the glory of God. For the Spirit is capable of being received, not capable of receiving; and he lacks nothing, but generously pours himself into those in need. For concerning the Son it is written: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song I, 2). Likewise God speaks concerning the Holy Spirit: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28). Where have you ever read, “I will pour out my angel,” or any other of the heavenly creatures, as it is said of the Spirit?

We also read that the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit; and whatever part of the world each one was undertaking for the building up of the Church, the Spirit was wholly present with each of them. Among the angels, each is individually present with each person; and wherever one is sent, while he is there, he is necessarily absent elsewhere. The Spirit, wholly present with everyone everywhere, is something that belongs to God alone. Let us therefore adore the Father, let us adore the Son also, and let us adore the Holy Spirit, with one and the same veneration. If he grants us, together with the Father and the Son, forgiveness of sins, sanctification, and everlasting life, then together with the Father and the Son let us also render him glory. Or, if he is not to be worshiped with the Father and the Son, then he is not to be confessed in baptism either.

Heretic. A little earlier we both confessed God the Father to be invisible, incomprehensible, immutable, and everlasting without end.

Athanasius. That is so.

Heretic. And how do you confess the Son to be of his substance, when he was often seen by the Fathers to be changeable and mutable, and was frequently manifested to each of them in various forms? If he were of that very substance, then, even with the assumption of flesh, he would certainly not be seen; rather, he would have remained in the equality in which the Father exists, since he was of the Father’s substance. For what is from the Father must be believed incapable of being seen, changed, or transformed.

Athanasius. This is the cause of error; this is the origin of the Arian heresy: they do not understand the power of God, nor recognize the ordering of so great a mystery. They must first be answered that the Son of God was not seen as he was as God, but as a human being could apprehend him. Next, it belongs to the power of God that, when he graciously chose to reveal himself to individuals in whatever manner he willed, he changed his appearance without changing his substance; he did not lose the distinctiveness of his nature, but adapted his majesty according to the capacity of the one who saw him. Yet he himself, as he is always the same, remained in the distinctiveness of his substance, as it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. CI, 28).

For angels too have often been seen in the form of human beings, yet they are nothing other than what they know themselves to be; nor do they change their substance when they assume the form of a human body. How much more will the author of the angels not be changed, who in his generosity granted angels the ability to do this? You see, therefore, the arrangements of future things that were to be fulfilled in their proper times, prefigured for the Fathers through an image; yet God himself, as he properly is, was not seen.

[Col. 0295A] Heretic. I do not understand what you will say about the incarnation, or how you will excuse its changeability. For we read: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). At that point he certainly filled the Virgin’s womb; at that point something other than what had come was born. Thus the substance, having been mixed, changed its state and lost its order in the very act of changing: from God he became human, from spirit he became flesh. Every transformation, of course, is an interruption of the former state. Therefore, there is no doubt that the Son must be believed to be from another substance, one that can be changed, transformed, and seen; for it is not permissible to believe this of the Father’s substance, since he says: “I am; I am, and I will not be changed” (Mal. III, 6). And the Son says in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18).

Athanasius. The mingling, or concretion, [Col. 0295B] of natures is indeed a change; a change of nature produces a transformation; and transformation destroys what was and begins what was not. Christ’s birth does not involve this, as the angel Gabriel testifies. The evangelist reports that, when asked about the possibility of Mary’s conception, he answered: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 35). In both expressions he certainly named not a mingling, but the coming upon of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the Most High.

You read: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). But how this happened our mind does not reach, because what we believe exceeds our mind; yet we reach it by faith. In this way we hold wholly by faith what we believe, even though we do not comprehend it wholly with the mind. We must therefore know what and how much we have been granted to apprehend by understanding, and what we must receive by faith. For we read: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13). How was the Son of Man, who was speaking on earth, said to be in heaven? And how is he reported to have descended from there, when he had neither been made there nor yet ascended? For he had not yet suffered and risen. But because God the Word had descended in order to assume a human being, the human being, joined to divinity, ascended there from which flesh had not descended, but the Word.

We also read in the Apocalypse that the Lord spoke to John: “I am the first and the last, and I was alive and dead, and behold, I am living forever and ever” (Rev. I, 17). If he is the first, how is he the last? If he is living, since he himself is the life of all, how did he become dead, when life cannot die? And if he became dead, how is he to be called either God or life? No one will hold the perfect truth if he excludes any portion of the truth.

But you, who accuse the incarnation of your Creator and Redeemer, first investigate, if you can, the rationale of your own birth. Certainly you will confess that a human being subsists from two substances, soul and flesh; yet he is called not two, but one human being. And although his nature is united, the substances nevertheless remain unmixed. If, then, in a human being the substances bestowed by God remain unmixed, consider what you are compelled to think concerning the incarnation of your Creator, who is certainly joined to a human being by condescension, not mingled with him.

Thus the Word became flesh—that is, the only-begotten Son of God became the Son of Man—in such a way that neither was changed into the other, but with both remaining in their own substance, God in the human being suffered human things, while preserving the divine things intact in himself. He did not begin to be what he was not through any transformation or mutability; rather, by the power of the divine dispensation, the Word of the Father, never departing from the Father, graciously consented properly to become human, and the only-begotten Son was incarnated through that secret mystery which he alone knows. Our part is to believe; his is to know.

And so God the Word himself, taking wholly into himself what belongs to the human being, is human. And the assumed human being, receiving wholly what belongs to God, cannot be anything other than God. We must not, therefore, reason from visible things, as though we thought that God and the human being were mingled as creatures equal to one another, and as though some body had been produced by such a confusion of flesh and Word. Far be such a belief from us. Such a mingling is the corruption of both parts. God is capable of receiving, not himself capable of being received; penetrating, not penetrable; filling, not capable of being filled. He is wholly and simultaneously everywhere, and is everywhere diffused; through the gracious infusion of his power he has been joined to human nature; human nature, however, has not been mixed into divine nature.

The flesh, therefore, advanced into the Word; the Word did not advance into the flesh. Most truly, then, “the Word became flesh”; but, as we have said, this occurred properly and personally alone, not naturally with the Father or the Holy Spirit. For the only-begotten Son of God, true God, who is one in nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is distinct in person. We do not call the Father himself the Son; nor again do we call the same one the Son whom we call the Father. Nor do we call the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son. Rather, distinguishing the persons in their own properties, we properly call the Father “God the Father”; we properly call the Son “God the Son”; and we properly confess the Holy Spirit to be “God the Holy Spirit.”

Although we speak of God three times in number, we do not believe in three gods, but in one God perfect in the Trinity of his omnipotence. Therefore, one person of flesh and Word must be understood: one and the same God and human being, always inseparable, truly having performed all that belongs to the human being in his twofold substance, and truly always possessing what belongs to God. For although “he was crucified because of our weakness, he lives because of the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4).

Therefore, we do not hesitate to say that God was born according to the human being, and that the same God suffered and died according to the human being; but we glory in saying that God was born and that the same one suffered according to the human being. Although he existed in the form of God, not for his own sake but for ours he assumed the form of a servant and emptied himself.

How did he empty himself? When, being in the form of God, he took the form of a servant; when, as Lord in the principal sense, he graciously assumed the things that belong to a servant; and when, through his indulgence and compassion toward us, by bearing and performing things inferior to himself, the Word became flesh and was emptied in person of what he possessed in nature.
