And in the Word, having taken on the condition of humanity, he became obedient in the human being; through humility and obedience he restored in himself the condition of our nature that had perished through Adam’s disobedience.

And in the flesh he died, while always living in spirit; making all things alive with the Father, he will never again die. Raised by the Father in the flesh, he becomes for us the firstborn from the dead—he who is the only-begotten Son of the living God—and, for our sake, through various ages, poor in time and needy in the human being, he receives for us what he had always possessed abundantly for himself in the Father.

Heretic. You should know that what was said earlier has been established in my heart as reasonably and truthfully explained. But, for the fullness of faith, I ask you to explain why the persons and names are divided, when the substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one.

Athanasius. Do you not know that the Father is one God, the Son is one God, and the Holy Spirit is one God? Their name is united because their substance is one. Hence John also says in his Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and in Christ Jesus they are one” (I John V, 7). Yet he does not say that they are one person, because their person is not one.

Should anything else be understood than this: that the one true Father who begot is not the same as the one who was begotten by him; that the one Son who did not beget is not the Father; and that the Holy Spirit, who is neither Father nor Son, is distinct in person, since he is described as neither begetting nor being born?

[Col. 0298A] Heretic. Why do you name them with such precision?

Athanasius. Without doubt, the Father truly begot; this is his first name. The Son was born from him; this is his unique name. The Holy Spirit, who proceeded from the Father, has this as his natural name. Therefore, when the names are distinguished among the persons, their proper names are made evident; when the matter is referred to according to divinity, the united name is indicated in them, because the Father is substantive, the Son is substantive, and the Holy Spirit is also substantive.

Let our faith in the Trinity, therefore, be whole according to the confession of saving baptism; let there be one devotion of piety. Let us not, after the manner of the gentiles, suppose differences of powers, but rather, adoring and magnifying the perfect Trinity, let us hold in our conscience what we say with our mouth in the mysteries: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty” (Isa. VI, 3). By saying “holy” three times, you confess one omnipotence.

Or consider the Apostle’s words: “One Spirit” (Eph. IV, 4); “the Lord Jesus Christ in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 11). One Amen, because there is one religion and one glorification of the Trinity. And thereafter, pursuing peace and love, let us always abound in new works, so that we may hear from the Apostle: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen” (II Cor. XIII, 13).

# BOOK ELEVEN

## The Arian Profession and the Catholic Confession of Saint Athanasius

### To Theophilus

[Col. 0297]

[Col. 0297C] The Arians say that the Son of God was not begotten from the substance of God the Father, but created externally. I believe that the Son of God was born from the Father’s substance, not created, and likewise the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who belongs to the Son and proceeds from the Father. And therefore I say Homoousion, “of one substance,” with the Father saying to the Son: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). Likewise the Son bears witness: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7).

For when, at the time of his passion, Pilate asked him, in response to the accusations of the Jews, whether he was a king, the Lord answered: “For this I was born” (John XVIII, 37). The Lord also says concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Holy Spirit who proceeds from my Father” (John XV, 26). It is therefore established that, according to the one substance of divinity, the Son was begotten by the Father, not created, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and wholly belongs to the Son, just as a fountain is from a fountain and light is from light.

The Arians say that the Son, or the Holy Spirit, did not always exist with the Father or in the presence of the Father. I believe that the Son of God, according to the divine Scriptures, is the Word, power, and wisdom of the Father. And I confess in faith that the Father never lacked his Son, since he never lacked the name of fatherhood; thus the Father must never be believed to have existed without his own wisdom, Word, and power, according to the proclamation of the evangelist John, who says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (John I, 1). He says that all things were made through him, not that he himself was made. Likewise, neither the Father nor the Son ever existed without the Holy Spirit.

The Arians say that the Son has no power except insofar as he received something from the Father; and likewise concerning the Holy Spirit, except insofar as he received something from the Son. I believe that, according to the divine substance, just as the Son is the Word, power, wisdom, arm, and hand, so also he is the power of the Father.

For according to the Lord’s own statement: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John V, 19, 21). He cleansed the leper not by another’s command, but by his own power, saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII, 3). Likewise, when the Jews, ignorant that he was true God, said concerning the paralytic that no one could forgive sins except God alone, he most clearly revealed himself to be God and displayed his own power, saying: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Matt. IX, 6).

Likewise, he tested the faith of the blind, saying: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” (ibid., 28). When they confessed that this was within his power, he brought them the remedy of healing, saying: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (ibid., 29).

And, assigning the passion of his own body to his own power, he said: “No one takes my life from me; I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18). And there are countless other examples.

He himself also speaks of the power of the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III, 8)—that is, where he wills to breathe by his own will and divinity, not where he has been ordered. Likewise, the Apostle teaches concerning the gifts of grace: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 11). By his own power he fills the prophets, chooses and directs the apostles, and appoints bishops, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles.

There are innumerable other testimonies, which it would now take too long to explain. Therefore, just as I believe in one substance, so I believe in one power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But what the Son received, he received according to the human being—that is, according to the form of a servant, according to the nature of our condition—the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 27).

The Arians say that the Son cannot wholly receive or behold the Father, just as the Holy Spirit neither wholly sees nor receives the Son. I believe that, just as the Son is in the Father and is wholly seen by the Father, so the Father is wholly seen by the Son and is wholly in the Son, the Son himself saying: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11). And: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John X, 15).

Likewise concerning the Holy Spirit, the Apostle proclaims that the Spirit searches even the depths of God. And just as, according to the Apostle’s own statement, no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in the human being, so no one knows what is in God except the Spirit who is in him. For the Lord also says concerning the little ones in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII, 10). It is impious to believe that the Son and the Holy Spirit do not wholly behold or comprehend the Father.

Arians say that there is one perfect, omnipotent, incomprehensible, unbegotten, boundless, and immortal God alone: the Father. I believe, according to the divine Scriptures, in God and Lord the unbegotten Father; in God and Lord the Son, begotten from the Father; and in God and Lord the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and abiding in the Son.

As for the Son, just as I do not say that he is lesser in divinity, so I confess that he was made lesser in the form of a servant, which submitted to suffering, the Apostle saying: “But we see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II, 9). Therefore, in the three persons I do not understand three gods, but I adore and worship one God and Lord in substance, divinity, power, equality, and perpetuity, as it is commanded in the Law: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. VI, 13).

The Arians say that the Father alone is the invisible God, and greater, and therefore alone to be worshiped and adored. I believe, according to the divine substance and majesty, that the Son is spirit and that the Holy Spirit is also spirit, the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Spirit is God” (John IV, 21). Therefore, as I have said, according to the divine substance I confess the Father invisible, the Son invisible, and the Holy Spirit invisible; nor do I believe there is anything greater or lesser in the substance of divinity.

For this reason I render the same honor to the Son and to the Holy Spirit as to the Father, the Lord commanding: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father” (John V, 23). And concerning the Holy Spirit he himself says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII, 32). Therefore I believe in one God in the Trinity, as the divine Scripture teaches: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4).

The Arians say that the Son of God, according to the substance of divinity, is both visible and lesser. I believe that, in the form of God, as we established above, he is invisible, since he says to Moses: “No one has seen my face and lived” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). I believe him equal to the Father in all things, except that the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, as the Apostle proclaims concerning him: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. II, 6).

The Arians say that the Son or the Holy Spirit is so excluded from the Father’s secrets that he knows nothing of the hidden arrangements except what the Father chose to reveal to the Son, or what was manifested to the Spirit by the Son. I believe that the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son; and that the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father, belongs both to the Son and to the Father, because he also proceeds from the Son, as it is written in the Gospel that he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples by breathing upon them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 22).

Therefore I confess the Trinity to be inseparable. I do not say, as the heretics do, that the Son or the Holy Spirit is excluded from God the Father, since the Son, who is the wisdom of God the Father, is himself also the will of the Father, which was always in him; and he is himself the angel of the great counsel. Through him all things were created (Isa. IX, 5), as the apostle Paul proclaims, both the things in heaven and the things on earth, visible and invisible (Col. I, 16).

And the evangelist John teaches that all things were made through him, and that without him nothing was made (John I, 3). For just as the divine Scriptures say that all things were made through him, so the Son testifies that whatever he does, he does together with the Father, saying: “The Father who remains in me himself does the works” (John XIV, 10).

By these words he shows that the Father, who is wisdom, Word, will, and power, never arranged or did anything without the Son, nor did the Son do anything without the Father. Concerning the Holy Spirit, there is no doubt that he knows nothing by ignorance and is not excluded from the Father. For it would be the height of madness to say that the Father ever existed without his Spirit, since the Spirit searches, according to the Apostle, as has often been said, the depths and heights of God (I Cor. II, 10).

We have also proved through many testimonies of Scripture that this same Spirit belongs to the Son, and that he remains wholly in the Son; and just as he proceeds from God the Father, so he proceeds from the Son, so that the whole Trinity may be believed to be one God. Therefore the Father does nothing or arrange anything without his wisdom; nor does he know or arrange anything without his Holy Spirit, concerning whom the prophet says: “The Paraclete Spirit, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and power, the Spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isa. XI, 2)—all of which subsist in God, who is the Trinity.

The Arians say that the Son of God was not in heaven with the Father while he was living among human beings. I believe that God the Son of God, according to the power of his divinity, was in heaven and on earth during the time of his incarnation, and filled all things, never being absent, as he himself says to Nicodemus in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

The Arians say that the Son of God existed when he did not exist, that before he was born he did not exist, and that he was made from things that did not exist. I believe in one substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore I confess that the Son, who is the wisdom of the Father, was always in him and was begotten from him, because the faithful cannot believe that there was ever a time when the Father existed without his Word and wisdom, nor that the Son ever existed without his Father. The evangelist repeatedly says that in the beginning was the Word, and that he always was, and was God, and was with God; he was not made from things that did not exist, but was always God in the Father and with the Father, God with God.

The Holy Spirit also was, and is always, in the Father and proceeds from him. The Father was never without his wisdom, who is the Son, and never without his Holy Spirit.

The Arians say that the Son of God is passible and mortal in his substance. I believe that God the Word and the wisdom of the Father, because he is one with the Father, is impassible and immortal in his substance. But I confess that the human being Jesus Christ, assumed from the Virgin Mary, is passible and mortal, and that he was united to the Word of God, the same Lord saying: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 41). Again he says: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from Spirit is spirit” (John IV, 6).

Thus the Apostle also proclaims to the Corinthians, saying: “For although he was crucified because of our weakness, he lives because of the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4). He was therefore crucified because of the weakness of our flesh, but lives by his own power, because the Son of God is shown to be God and the power of the Father. For he himself is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

I also confess that the human being Christ Jesus, after his passion, was raised without corruption on the third day from the tomb by God the Word, by whom he had also been assumed, the same one saying to the Jews, according to the evangelist John, concerning the temple of his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19).

The Arians say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three different substances and unequal persons. I do not believe in different substances or unequal persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; rather, I confess three perfect, equal, and eternal persons, of one substance, one power, one might, and one majesty. [Col. 0302A] For what is different cannot be one, and what is ranked by degrees is not equal.

I believe that the Son of God, the Word of God, the power of God, and the wisdom of God, is always equal to the Father. The Son would not say that he is one with the Father, nor that the Father is in him and he in the Father, unless he knew himself to be equal. Nor would he do the same things similarly as the Father, or profess that he does whatever he wills, nor proclaim that he proceeded from the Father and came into the world, and would again leave the world and go to the Father, and that the Father remained in him, unless he knew himself to have been begotten from the substance of his Father.

In John’s Gospel, when the Jews sought to stone him, he asserts, saying: “Not only because he was breaking the Sabbath, but also because he was saying that God was his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John V, 18). Therefore what is equal cannot be unequal. The substance of the Father and the Son is one; their power is one, and their authority is one and undivided.

For, as he himself says in the Gospel, no one snatches his own sheep from the Son’s hand, nor can anyone snatch them from the Father’s hand. And what is one cannot be different. Again, after first asserting that his power and the Father’s power are one and the same, he assigns the unity of substance itself, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

The person of the Holy Spirit is likewise in no respect unequal, nor is his substance different from that of the Father and the Son, since the very same Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father also belongs to the Son. He was never absent from the Father, just as he was never absent from the Son. As he was always without beginning, and was with the Father and the Son in the creation of the world, so he himself also confirmed and enlightened all things.

Thus the sacrament of baptism is fulfilled only under his invocation and power, just as it is not fulfilled without the visitation of the Father and the Son. For no one becomes a member of Christ and a temple of God, according to the apostle Paul, unless the Holy Spirit both chooses and sanctifies him, and, as God with his own power, dwells in the one whom he has chosen.

The Arians say that, after the end of the world, the kingdom of the Son of God will come to an end. I believe the man from the Virgin Mary, united to God and taken up into heaven, to be God; I confess that he sits at the right hand of the Father, to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given. I also confess that he will judge the living and the dead, and that his kingdom will never end, as the prophet Daniel says:

“I was looking in a vision of the night; and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He reached the Ancient of Days, and they brought him before him. And he gave him authority, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His authority is eternal, and it shall not be taken away; and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. 7:15).

The prophet plainly speaks of the Son of Man as having received authority, honor, and a kingdom. But that these things were truly spoken of the Son of Man—that is, of the man who was assumed—the Lord himself makes clearer in the Gospel, saying: “You will see heaven opened, and the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God” (Matt. 26:64). And again: “You will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds, with great glory and majesty” (Mark 13:26). Likewise the angels said to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Therefore I believe that all authority in heaven and on earth was given to the Son of Man assumed from the Virgin Mary—authority which he did not possess before he was assumed by God the Word. For God the Word, and God the Son, who is the wisdom, power, authority, and will of the Father, always had and still has all the Father’s authority, as he himself says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). And: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19). And: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (ibid., 21).

I believe Christ to be God, the true Son of God, and therefore I am a Christian.

[Col. 0303B] 290

I confess the true God and the true man who was born of the Virgin Mary, as the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). I believe Jesus Christ to be perfect God and perfect man, the same one, as the Apostle proclaims: “According to Christ, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). And: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

I believe there is one image of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; in accordance with that one image of divinity we were created, for God said: “Let us make man—not according to images, but according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

I believe that there has always been and is one name of divinity in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because we are baptized and made Christians not in several names, but in the one name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, according to the Lord’s command.

This is the catholic, the true, the perfect faith. This is the one and complete baptism by which, as has been said, we are baptized according to the Lord’s command. There is one faith, without any diminution of a person; and one faith is professed in the Trinity.

Therefore a question must be put to those who oppose this unique faith, saying that the Son was not begotten from the substance of God the Father, but came later, alien to the substance of the divine Father, lesser and inferior in deity—and who also say that he is a creature. They say likewise that the Holy Spirit was created by a creature, namely by the Son, so that, in their view, the Father himself is altogether lesser when they blasphemously assert that his wisdom, Word, power, and Holy Spirit are creatures.

They must therefore be asked whether they believe that the Son of God advanced in age or increased in dignity over the course of time; and whether, just as he was begotten by the Father—or, as they themselves say, created—so he remains. If they say that this is so, and that he never has advanced and cannot advance, they must be asked about whom it is written in the Gospel: “But the child was growing and becoming strong, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon him” (Luke 2:40).

We most clearly confess that this was spoken of the man who was received by God the Word: nourished with milk, he grew, matured, and reached full age. Christ Jesus, the man who was assumed, was certainly filled with wisdom—the wisdom that is the Son of God the Father. For this same Wisdom built for herself a temple of human flesh in the Virgin Mary, as Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. 9:1).

Therefore, if that person answers, or confesses, that this was spoken of the man who was assumed, he has understood it in a catholic manner. For the one who builds the house is the Lord, whereas what is built and created is servile. Thus the house, which is the man, grows and is built; God, however, does not grow, for he is always perfect.

It remains, therefore, that he confess the Word, the Son of God, begotten perfect from the perfect Father, whole from the whole, and full from the full. For it is utterly contrary to the Christian faith to say that, because the man grew, God was always imperfect, never having advanced, and that he remains forever lesser, according to the blasphemy of perverse teachers.

[Col. 0304B]

Certainly, after so many years have passed, let them believe that he could at some point become equal to the Father, since it is written of him: “He was growing and advancing” (Luke 2:40, 52). Yet nowhere is it written of the Father that he advances, grows, or grows old. Therefore, since the Father neither grows nor grows old, but remains in the power proper to his deity, this one who is said to grow and advance ought by now to have reached equality with the Father.

But such human comparisons do not apply to the divine substance. The perfect God the Father begot a perfect Son, and we must never believe that God’s power and wisdom were imperfect or lesser. Whoever presumes to think in this way will do so at the cost of his salvation.

This, then, must be held and confessed as the truth: the man grew and advanced into God—that is, into the Son of God. The Evangelist says that “to those who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). And how did the Lord’s man, the servile form, not advance into God?

God the Word, however, the power and wisdom of the Father, was always perfect and equal to the one who begot him in the substance of divinity, as the Apostle says: “Though he was established in the form of God, he did not consider being equal to God to be robbery” (Phil. 2:6). Therefore, although he was equal to God the Father in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, as the same Apostle proclaims. That is, voluntarily and not under compulsion, he humbled himself to receive a servile form, so that the lowly or inferior form might grow and advance into a better substance through him who deigned to assume it—not so that the divine substance or power might be changed into a servile condition or reduced to it.

The Apostle speaks of the transformation of our form into a better condition: “When this mortal body has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:54). And: “As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22). And again: “We, brothers, have been called to freedom” (Gal. 5:13).

Therefore, if through Christ’s grace we have been called, as has been said, into a better condition—that is, into freedom through the faith that is in Christ—which Christian, or person of sound mind, would dare to say that his liberator was changed into a worse condition or state? Would he say that the divine substance, which is always unchangeable, was turned into a humble human substance; that God became flesh, the perfect became inferior, the equal became lesser, the Lord became a servant, the creator became a creature, and the Almighty suffered the injury of incapacity; and that he who was impassible in the substance of his divinity became passible, and the immortal succumbed to death?

All these things must be believed in faith as belonging to the one person of Christ, according to the Apostle’s preaching and Christian teaching. For he says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). And again: “In Christ dwells the whole fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9).

Therefore God assumed man, the Lord assumed a servant, the creator a creature, the maker what was made, the Almighty one who was inferior, the invisible one who was visible, the unfailing one who was weary, the immortal one who was mortal, the impassible one who was passible, and the immutable one who was mutable; but God was not changed into human flesh or substance.

He was impassible, yet in himself he glorified the nature that he assumed. Human flesh and nature, however—mortal and weak, as has been said—advanced into divine glory, the Lord himself saying in the Gospel concerning the Son of Man whom he had assumed: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 13:31). If God was glorified in him, and God glorified him in himself, then he immediately glorified him.

[Col. 0305B] 293

Receive, I ask, a few testimonies from the divine Scriptures, whoever you are who wish to be a perfect Christian and to follow the true and complete account, setting aside the empty talk and superfluous questions of those who have not only fallen away from the faith of Christ through their own error, but also, as the Apostle says, lead others into error.

For Christ’s being born in time at Bethlehem; his being laid in a manger; his being wrapped in swaddling clothes; his being nursed; his growing; his maturing; his being carried away in flight to Egypt; his being subject to his parents; his being tempted by the devil; his hunger; his thirst; his eating and drinking; his sleeping; his becoming weary; his weeping; his seeking, as though unaware, the tomb of Lazarus; his saying, as though ignorant, that he did not know the day of judgment; his being glorified by the Father’s testimony; his coming to his passion sad and trembling; his being struck with blows; his being judged by Pilate; his being scourged; his being crucified; his being given vinegar mixed with gall to drink; his side being pierced by a lance; his dying; his being taken down from the wood; his being buried; his rising alive from the dead on the third day; his receiving all authority after the resurrection; his asking the two men walking on the road, as though ignorant, what had happened in Jerusalem; and his asking Peter, as though unaware, whether he was loved by him more than by the other disciples—“Simon,” he said, “Peter, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15)—although the apostolic confession revealed him as knowing all things, even hidden things:

How can someone who calls himself a Christian fail to understand that these things belong to the human substance and servile form, not to divine majesty and power? For life never dies; a man dies.

Nor can God the Word be ignorant of anything, since all things are naked and open before his eyes, as the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight; rather, all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:12).

Therefore it is not God who is a creature, but man. It is not God, who is life, who is buried, but flesh. Nor does God, who is wholly everywhere and above all, rise from the depths; rather, man rises into God.

The one who is scourged and judged by Pilate is man. But when he comes to judge the world himself, he is God and man. It is clear that the one who is sad and trembling is man, not God, who is unchangeable and immutable.

But as for his not knowing the day or being unaware of the place: is it to be believed that the one who made days, hours, years, and seasons could be ignorant of anything? What man does not know, God nevertheless does not fail to know—God who existed before the ages, through whom all things were made. To think that God’s Wisdom could be ignorant of anything is a matter of the greatest danger.

He weeps and becomes weary as man, not as God the Word, who is the power of the Father; for it is impious to say that God’s power becomes weary.

Do you suppose that it is man who hungers and thirsts, or God, who gives life to the world—the bread that came down from heaven and also gives food to all flesh? But life does not hunger, nor can the fountain thirst.

He is tempted by the devil as man, but as God he is worshiped by angels, who also minister to him. Of him it is written: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4).

All these things, therefore, as has been said, must be referred to the servile, mortal, and passible nature that was assumed by God the Word. He accepted and endured all the things spoken of in humility for our sake, as the Apostle also teaches: “Though he was rich, he became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). And again: “Although he existed in the form of God, equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

Thus also his prophet, foretelling his passion in the flesh, says: “By his wound we have been healed” (Isa. 53:5).

Therefore, whoever you are—a human being—when you hear humble things spoken about Christ, do not judge them to have been spoken of his divine exalted nature. When you read things that involve indignity, believe them according to the humble form, not according to the divine lordship. When you read of things impossible, understand them as belonging to human frailty, not to divine power.

You must not bring the divine exalted nature down to a humble condition, nor strive to reduce divine power and majesty to lower things. Rather, raise what belongs to our weakness and fragile nature up to that power, as the Lord himself says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

Through the cross he himself raises our nature in himself by its union with him; he does not, by joining our nature to his, lower divine power. Thus he says elsewhere: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10)—not to lose what always existed, as the blessed evangelist John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” (John 1:1).

[Col. 0307A]

Therefore, according to the Lord’s own teaching and the Apostle’s preaching, while preserving the distinct property of each nature in the one person of Christ—that is, of God and man—we must believe, venerate, and worship the perfect God who glorifies in the perfect man who is glorified. He is also God, the Son of God, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and in whose fullness the Father is present.

For just as the Son is in the glory of the Father, according to the teaching of the blessed Apostle, so the Father is in the fullness of the Son, as he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). And again: “The Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (ibid.).

Therefore Christ the Son must be served, because he is both perfect God and the true Son. Whoever faithfully serves the Son serves the Father and the Holy Spirit who is in him. Whoever worships the Father worships the Son and the Holy Spirit in him, because the Son and the Holy Spirit who proceeds from God the Father are in the Father. The Lord himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid.).

Concerning the Holy Spirit he also says: “The Paraclete Spirit, who proceeds from my Father” (John 15:26). Whoever worships the Son worships the Father and the Holy Spirit in him, because the Father is in him, as he says: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9). And again: “The Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (John 14:10).

Concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14). And: “Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:15).

The Spirit of the Father is therefore the Spirit of the Son, as the Apostle says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4:6). And again: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). And again: “I know that this will result in my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 1:19).

In the Gospel the Lord himself also says: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). And in the Acts of the Apostles we read: “They passed through Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they came to Mesopotamia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:6).

Thus, by the clearest testimonies, it is proved that the Holy Spirit—the Paraclete Spirit, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father—is the Spirit of the Son, the Spirit of Christ, and the Spirit of Jesus.

For the whole Trinity must be worshiped, honored, proclaimed, and feared inseparably in one substance, divinity, and power.

All Christians must therefore flee and guard against being led astray according to the error of ignorant people—an error the Apostle notes—who wander concerning the faith. “Wandering and leading others into error,” he says (2 Tim. 3:13): that is, those who persuade others to believe that something created, or something inferior or later, exists within the holy and undivided Trinity.

For whatever is created cannot be God; what is inferior is not perfect; and what is later lacks perpetuity. Accordingly, nothing divine can exist in these degrees.

The blessed Apostle, the chosen vessel, condemns such teachers, and those who follow their teaching, when he writes to the Romans: “His eternal power and divinity also, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. 1:20–23).

And again he continues, saying: “They changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever and ever” (ibid., 25).

**BOOK TWELVE. On the Trinity and on the Holy Spirit. TO THEOPHILUS.**

[Col. 0307]

[Col. 0307C] 297 To those who profess that the Son of God was created, we shall by no means give a response concerning the Holy Spirit. For just as they dared to say that the Son, who was begotten impassibly from the substance of God, was created, so they certainly say similar things about the Holy Spirit—though they will eventually repent. But for the present we shall answer concerning the Holy Spirit those who hold a correct opinion about the Son. For it is to be hoped that those who have once begun to turn from irreligion toward religion will be brought to perfect profit.

We shall endeavor to set forth this argument from the divine Scriptures, and not from human interpretations. Tell us, then, admirable men: where in the divine Scriptures have you read that the Holy Spirit was created?

“We have heard John saying in the Gospel: ‘All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’” (John 1:3).

To this we reply: If, then, you also hear David in the one-hundred-eighteenth Psalm saying to God through the Holy Spirit, “All things serve you” (Psalm 118:91), will you consequently say that the Holy Spirit also is a servant? Yet he is not a servant, but free; and he has set creation free and advanced it to God in the adoption of sons.

Or have you not heard Paul writing to the Romans: “You did not receive a spirit of slavery again for fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:15)? And again: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (ibid., 2).

But if the Holy Spirit is not a servant, as the Scriptures have proved—and it is written, “All things serve you” (Psalm 118:91)—then the statement that all things were made through the Son does not show that the Holy Spirit was created. For it is not John who says, “All things were made through the Son, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). He was one of those who heard the Savior saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20). Likewise Peter, writing, says: “These things have now been announced to you through those who evangelized you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven.”

Therefore, if it is the Holy Spirit who says, “All things were made through the Son, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3), he ought indeed, if he himself had been created, to have said: “All things were made through him, and I was made through him, and without him nothing was made,” as is the practice of the saints. Thus Paul writes with the utmost care of himself and of all the saints: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

But because the Holy Spirit belongs not to the universe of created things but to the Trinity, the Holy Spirit said that all things that exist after the Trinity were created through the Son. My witness is the most blessed Paul in the Holy Spirit, who professes in his Epistle to the Colossians that all things were made through the Son: “For in him, the Son, all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things” (Colossians 1:16). He did not say, “whether the Holy Spirit.”

The Psalmist also, in the one-hundred-forty-eighth Psalm, again commanding the whole creation through the Holy Spirit to praise God, says: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:1), and so forth. He judged it unworthy to count the Holy Spirit twice among them and to say, “Let the Holy Spirit praise him,” [Col. 0309C] 299 because the Holy Spirit is one who is praised, not one who praises—as we shall prove shortly from the Scriptures—and one who gives life, not one who is to be given life, since he is life. Thus Paul says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5). To the Romans he says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Romans 8:10). And again: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid., 11).

The three holy martyrs, Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael, placed in the furnace of fire in the land of the Chaldeans, when God marvelously changed the heat of the fire into temperate coolness, exhorting the whole creation to praise God with them, begin as follows: “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord; praise and exalt him forever. Bless the Lord, heavens; sing a hymn and exalt him forever. Bless the Lord, angels; sing a hymn and exalt him forever. Bless the Lord, waters above the heavens; sing a hymn and exalt him forever. Bless the Lord, all the powers of the Lord; sing a hymn and exalt him forever. Bless the Lord, sun and moon; sing a hymn and exalt him forever” (Daniel 3:57–62). And later, urging themselves to this: “Bless the Lord, Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael; praise and exalt him forever” (ibid., 88).

While exhorting every creature to bless the Lord with them, they do not say, “Let the Holy Spirit also bless the Lord.” Moreover, the Seraphim were seen by Isaiah standing and praising, and the Cherubim by Ezekiel beneath the glory of the God of Israel.

Since, therefore, the saints most clearly and faithfully did not count the Holy Spirit among those things that were made through the Son, but everywhere the divine Scriptures profess him together with the Father and the Son, why do these men fearlessly remove him from the Father and the Son and count him among the universe of created things?

But Paul says to the churches of God: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7, and in the other Epistles of Saint Paul); he does not say, “and from the Holy Spirit.” And writing to the Thessalonians he says: “May God the Father himself and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you” (1 Thessalonians 3:11), without saying, “and the Holy Spirit.” Thus he makes clear that the Holy Spirit is pronounced not together with the Father and the Son, but together with the universe.

For God’s servant Moses also says: “The Lord rained sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Genesis 19:24), without mentioning the Holy Spirit. Having learned this from him, Paul likewise writes to Timothy concerning Onesiphorus: “May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day” (2 Timothy 1:18).

It is also written in Exodus: “Then the Lord said to Moses: ‘How long will you refuse to obey my commandments and my ordinances? Has not the Lord God given you this Sabbath day? Therefore he himself has given you bread for two days’” (Exodus 16:28). Here too, having mentioned the Father and the Son, he was silent about the Holy Spirit.

Finally, the prophet Zechariah says: “And the Lord said to the devil: ‘The Lord rebuke you, devil’” (Zechariah 3:2). Where is the Holy Spirit here, in their view?

Who would not be moved by the instruction of the mystery, as the Lord professes: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), when he had said nothing about the Spirit?

Likewise Paul, having learned the mystery of faith, handed it on in writing as follows: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

Therefore, whenever the divine Scriptures mention the Father and the Son, they do not also mention the Holy Spirit. To this we respond in the following way: If you hear Moses saying, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13); or if you hear God saying through Isaiah, “Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall not be” (Isaiah 43:10), where do you place the Son?

Or if you hear him again saying through Isaiah, “I am God, and there is no savior besides me” (Isaiah 43:11), then, as far as you are concerned, the Son of God is not confessed as God the Savior.

Or if you hear that same speaker again saying, “You are my witnesses: is there a God besides me?” (Isaiah 44:8), without testifying that the Son is God. And again: “I am God the first, and I am afterward, and besides me there is no God” (Isaiah 44:6). And again: “But you did not know me, because I am the Lord God, and there is no other besides me. I am the Lord, and there is no God besides me, and you did not know me, so that they may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is no one besides me. I am the Lord God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:4).

And if you hear God saying through Joel: “And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel. I am the Lord your God, and there is no other besides me” (Joel 2:27); and when you hear innumerable other professions of this kind in the divine Scriptures, you nevertheless do not hesitate to count the Son with God.

Will you now say that these statements contradict the Scriptures in which you previously agreed that the Father and the Son were mentioned? Or perhaps these are not words of Scripture? Do the divine Scriptures contradict one another in this way? Certainly not.

Although the saints speak individually, mentioning one name—whether that of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—they nevertheless understand that they proclaim the Trinity in one name, as we have most recently proved. For just as these professions do not exclude the Son from unity with the Father, but rather contain the Holy Spirit counted together with the Father and the Son, as we have shown from the holy Scriptures, so when the Scriptures name the Father and the Son, they do not count the Holy Spirit, as though he were created, among the universe.

Otherwise, how do you say, or have asserted, that the Scriptures mention the Father and the Son while supposing that the Holy Spirit is not counted with the Father and the Son? And if you hear the Scriptures mentioning God and the Spirit, what will you do?

The prophet Haggai says: “Therefore I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and my Spirit stands in the midst of you” (Haggai 2:5–6). Consider, then, where you place the Son: for here the Almighty and the Spirit are signified.

Or if you hear Isaiah saying: “Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord. You made a plan, but not through me, and a covenant, but not through my Spirit, adding sins upon sins” (Isaiah 30:1). And again: “The does met one another and saw their faces; they passed by in number, and not one of them perished. One did not seek another, because the Lord commanded them, and his Spirit gathered them” (Isaiah 34:15–16).

When you hear these things, where do you look for the Son?

Or if you hear the prophet Zechariah saying: “Where are your fathers and the prophets? says the Lord. Will they live forever? Yet receive my words and my ordinances, which I command through my Spirit to my servants the prophets, because they overtook your fathers” (Zechariah 1:5).

Or if you hear David saying to God: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm 138:7), what will you think about the Son?

And if the apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16), will you allow the Father and the Spirit to be counted together, but place the Son among those things that exist through the Spirit? By no means, I ask you. May such a thought never enter your minds, religious men.

But just as you said that Paul wrote, “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7), and suppose that he made no mention of the Spirit, so hear him again writing to the Corinthians in the Second Epistle: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

And just as here he said “the love of God,” so also to the Romans: “I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God for me” (Romans 15:30).

And while Paul had asserted that the fellowship of the Spirit was with you, John says: “Our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3). The apostle Paul, however, says: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:9).

In the First Epistle to the Corinthians we must again hear Paul preaching the Trinity. For he says: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of works, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4). Having said that God works all things in all, and having professed the gifts that are bestowed upon the Church through the Spirit, he added: “But all these things the one and same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid., 11).

By teaching that the operation of God is the operation of the Holy Spirit, did Paul cease to affirm the Trinity? Did he remove the Spirit from God and the Son, just as he wrote to the Thessalonians: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely” (1 Thessalonians 5:23)?

Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Do you see how everywhere in the Scriptures the Holy Spirit is counted with the Father and the Son?

The Son must plainly be heard in the prophet Isaiah, preaching himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. For he says:

“Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call: I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens. I shall call them all, and they shall stand together; they shall all be gathered, and they shall hear: who announced such things to them? Loving you, I did your will in Babylon, so that I might remove the seed of the Chaldeans. I spoke, I called, I brought him, and made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things—not from the beginning. In secret I spoke these things when they came to be; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:12).

And again:

“I am he who blots out iniquities. Say your iniquities first, so that you may be justified. Your former fathers and their rulers acted wickedly against me; they defiled my holy things, and I gave Jacob over to destruction and Israel to reproach” (Isaiah 43:25).

“But now hear, my servant Jacob and Israel whom I have chosen: for I shall give water to those who journeyed in thirst through a dry land; I shall place my Spirit upon your offspring and my blessings upon your children” (Isaiah 44:1).

Isaiah himself, preaching the Trinity, says:

“Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time, burning with anger, with the glory of his lips; his word is full of wrath and furious anger like fire. And his Spirit, like water drawing through a valley, will reach up to the neck” (Isaiah 30:27).

Hear also Zechariah preaching the Trinity. For he says:

“Thus says the Lord Almighty: Judge with just judgment; show mercy and compassion each to his brother. Do not use your power to harm the widow, the orphan, the resident alien, or the poor; and let none of you remember the evil of his brother in your hearts. But they refused to attend and turned their backs foolishly, and burdened their ears so as not to hear my law and the words which the Lord Almighty sent through his Spirit into the hands of the former prophets” (Zechariah 4:6).

The angel of the Lord said to Zechariah: “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: ‘Not by great power nor by strength, but by my Spirit,’ says the Lord Almighty” (Zechariah 4:6).

Let us also hear Micah proclaiming the Trinity. For he too says:

“Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray and bite with their teeth, who preach peace over him, but peace has not been given into their mouth, and they stirred up war against him. Therefore night shall be for you instead of vision, and darkness for you instead of divination. The sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day shall become dark over them. Those who see visions shall be confounded, and the diviners shall be mocked; all these will speak ill of them, because there is no one who hears them—unless I, in the fullness of power and in the Spirit of the Lord, announce to Jacob his iniquities and to Israel his sins” (Micah 3:5).

Let them therefore hear the saints consistently preaching the Trinity, and never counting the Holy Spirit among the universe that was made through the Son, but professing him together with the Father and the Son.

But if the Savior’s instruction moves them, as they claim, when he says, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), and he does not state that they should know the Holy Spirit, they will be satisfied when they hear the Lord himself, our Savior, also speaking about the Spirit:

“If you love me, keep my commandments, and I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may remain with you forever—the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you know him, because he remains with you and will be in you” (John 14:15).

Let them therefore observe that the apostles knew the Spirit, the Son, and the Father, but that the wretched world did not know the Father, the Son, or the Spirit, since the Lord says that “they did not know the Father, nor me” (John 16:3). And again, the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, is one whom the world cannot receive because it neither sees nor knows him.

Significantly, the Lord said that the Holy Spirit is “another Paraclete,” because he himself is also a Paraclete, as John says in his Epistle: “I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if we sin, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ, and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1).

Thus we are taught the equality of the Spirit with the Son.

Yet how does the Lord not terrify them when, handing on the mystery of faith to the apostles, he says: “Go now, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)?

There is also that great and blessed confession of faith—indeed, the very faith of the saints—and the testament that we have established with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as we come to the sacred washing of regeneration, confessing thus: “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, and in the Holy Spirit.”

Although the Lord said, “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1), and did not say, “Believe in the Holy Spirit,” nevertheless the apostles taught the churches of the whole world to believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Let them therefore say whether there is salvation for those who believe in the Father and the Son but do not believe in the Holy Spirit. But far be it from us. For those who do not believe in the Holy Spirit do not believe in God.

Finally, when Paul found certain disciples and asked them whether they had received the Holy Spirit when they believed, and they replied that they had not even heard that there was a Holy Spirit, he said: “Into what, then, were you baptized?” (Acts 19:3), proving that those who were not baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit had not been baptized in the name of the Father and the Son either.

Thus, plainly, we also recognize the Holy Spirit as Creator.

Otherwise, if the Spirit is not Creator, and we were created from the beginning without him, why are we not regenerated without him in regeneration? Or perhaps our regeneration restores us to that former condition which existed before Adam’s transgression? Since, as you say, we were created without the Holy Spirit, how was he taken up here without cause in our regeneration?

But to say this is irreligious. Or was man created greater and more cautious without him, and did he fall away, so that the Spirit is taken up in our regeneration for more certain protection? This too is exceedingly impious, or even unthinkable for anyone.

Let them therefore explain how the Spirit is taken up in our regeneration when he did not create us in the beginning—if indeed he did not create us.

Perhaps you say that he sanctifies those who approach the washing of regeneration? For the Holy Spirit is one who sanctifies the holy, but not the Creator; all things were created from God through the Son, according to Paul, who says: “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Here, however, he said nothing about the Holy Spirit.

To this we reply: Was the creature created through the Son holy, or was it not holy? Certainly it is unlawful to say that the Lord created it unholy. But if the Son created it holy, then the sanctification given to it through the Spirit is superfluous, very weak, and empty—like the splendor of a lamp being superfluous, weak, and vain when the sun is illuminating the world beneath the sky in the middle of the day.

“But,” they say, “the creature did not deserve to be sanctified through the Son; therefore God assigned the ministry to the Spirit, so that it might be sanctified through him.”

Then the creature deserved to be created through the Son but did not deserve to be sanctified. What, therefore, is greater: to be created or to be sanctified?

Weigh this, then, on the scale of your mind, so that you may at least in this way consider what you yourselves unwillingly confess concerning the dignity of the Spirit. The creature deserved to be created through the Son, but to be sanctified through the Spirit, because the Son would not have created it unworthy of his sanctification.

“But,” they say, “it had to be sanctified first through the Holy Spirit, so that it might thereby become worthy to receive sanctification through the Son and the Father.”

To this we reply: Will you then say that the Son created it unholy? But far be it from us. For the Spirit does not sanctify without the Son, nor the Son without the Spirit or the Father, just as you yourselves have said—and it is true what Paul writes to the Thessalonians: “May he himself, God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ, sanctify you completely” (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

In the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Do you see the unity of sanctification—how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit sanctify the creature?

If, therefore, the holy creation was created, but was not sanctified without the Holy Spirit, it is necessary that we all confess the Holy Spirit also to be Creator.

Otherwise, if you do not wish to confess this, what will you do when you say that creation was not holy and was afterward sanctified through the Spirit? You fear the stigma of irreligion. Yet by fully confessing that the created order is holy, while also confessing that it was not sanctified at all without the Spirit, you will necessarily confess the Spirit to be Creator as well.

[Col. 0315C] 307 If you know that the Word of God is his Son, hear David saying in the Psalm: “By the word of God the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6). He teaches us that creation was not made without the Holy Spirit—the Word breathed him into the face of the apostles with his bodily mouth, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

Nor did he have a mouth, since he is the incorporeal Word, nor did his Father have one. Otherwise, if we were created from the beginning without the Holy Spirit, how will the resurrection of the dead be accomplished through him?

Paul says to the Romans: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11).

David, singing to God in harmony with this, says concerning creation: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 103:29).

It is incongruous that creation should be constituted one way at the beginning and created another way at the end. Therefore, even if you do not wish it, the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete and Creator who is sent by God, is proclaimed by the saints: “You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.”

And just as the Father and the Son are said in Scripture to have acted, so the Holy Spirit will also be found to have acted.

For God says in Jeremiah that he led Israel through the desert, saying to the people: “And you did not say, ‘Where is the Lord, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, who led us into the desert?’” (Jeremiah 2:6).

Isaiah also says—and he must be heard—that the Holy Spirit led Israel through the desert, as follows: “He led them through the abyss like a horse through the desert, and they did not grow weary like beasts across the plain. The Spirit came down from the Lord and led them” (Isaiah 63:13).

The law of God is also called the law of the Spirit. Concerning each of the saints, it was said in the thirty-sixth Psalm: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 36:31). Paul says of himself: “To those without the law I became as one without the law—not being without the law of God, but being within the law of Christ—so that I might win those who are without the law” (1 Corinthians 9:21). And again he writes to the Romans: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Romans 8:2).

Thus the unity of the Trinity is found in the holy Scriptures: [Col. 0316B] for in them we find things that belong to God, to Christ, and to the Holy Spirit. The Lord says to the Jews: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20:25). Paul also writes to the Philippians: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21). And again to the Corinthians: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

Our fathers are called men of God by the name of God; the Christian disciples are named by the name of Christ; and spiritual people are called by the name of the Holy Spirit.

We must hear that widow of Sarepta in Sidon speaking to Elijah the Tishbite: “What have I to do with you, man of God?” (1 Kings 17:18). And again: “Now I know that you are a man of God” (ibid., 24). The Shunammite woman likewise said to her husband concerning Elisha: “Behold, a great man of God has come to us” (2 Kings 4:9). Scripture itself, in the Books of Kings, says: “And a man of God came from Judah and prophesied over the altar at Bethel” (2 Kings 23:17). The title of the eighty-ninth Psalm also reads: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God” (Psalm 89:1).

Luke, however, says in the Acts of the Apostles: “It happened that for a whole year they met in the Church, and that the disciples were first called Christians in the Church” (Acts 11:26).

And Paul writes to the Corinthians: “Concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were gentiles, you were led astray, however you were led, toward mute idols. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:1).

And again: “The natural person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually judged. But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. For ‘who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?’ But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

The Apostle professed the mind of Christ in his own substance to be the Holy Spirit: “For who knows the things of God except the Spirit of God? Just as our spirit knows what is ours. Thus Paul himself writes to the Corinthians: ‘God has revealed them to us through his Holy Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God’” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

And again: “For I seem also to have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:40).

Paul also says that he was called by God, writing to the Galatians: “But when it pleased the Lord, who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son to me, so that I might preach him among the gentiles” (Galatians 1:15).

He says that the Romans were called by Christ, writing to them: “Among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:6).

And the Holy Spirit said that Paul and Barnabas had been called by him to announce Christ to the gentiles.

It is truly remarkable that, when the Savior said to Paul in the temple, “Go, for I shall send you far away to the gentiles” (Acts 22:21), and Paul wrote to the Galatians, “Paul, an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Galatians 1:1), nevertheless the Holy Spirit sent Paul and Barnabas, having approved them, to preach Jesus Christ to the gentiles.

For Scripture says as follows: “There were in Antioch, in the Church, prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas and Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, who was the foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. As they were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then, after fasting and praying, they laid hands on them and sent them away. So, being sent by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus” (Acts 13:1–4).

And thereafter the preaching carried out by Paul among the gentiles is set forth.

There is also a time when the prophets speak in the person of the Father. Thus David says in the Psalms: “Once I swore by my holy one: if I should lie to David, his offspring shall remain forever, and his throne like the sun before me” (Psalm 88:36). And again: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set upon my throne” (Psalm 131:11). As Peter says: “Since he was a prophet, David knew that God had sworn an oath to him that he would set the Christ according to the flesh upon his throne, from the fruit of his loins” (Acts 2:30).

When do they speak in the person of the Son? When Isaiah says: “Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the gentiles. Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am he—the very one who was speaking; I am present” (Isaiah 52:5).

When do they speak in the person of the Holy Spirit? When the prophet Agabus says: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews will bind the man to whom this belt belongs in this way in Jerusalem and deliver him into the hands of the gentiles” (Acts 21:11).

Paul writes to Timothy: “But the Spirit clearly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving attention to deceitful spirits” (1 Timothy 4:1), and to the doctrines of demons, and similarly in the other passages through the prophets.

There is a time when the Father speaks, a time when the Son speaks, and a time when the Holy Spirit speaks.

Thus the Father himself says concerning the Savior: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Before the Son lived among human beings, he spoke to each of the saints; and after his ascension into heaven, the Holy Spirit also said to the disciples: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

The prophet Ezekiel, however, crying out against the former people, says: “And you grieved me in all these things, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 16:43). Paul, on the other hand, writes to the new people: “Do not grieve the Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30).

David likewise says against the Jews: “And they provoked the Lord in the desert” (Psalm 77:40). Isaiah also says concerning the same people: “But they acted rebelliously and grieved his Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10).

And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “Are you seeking a test of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

And again: “A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my judgment; for I seem also to have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:39).

And to the Romans he says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 9:1).

And in Isaiah the Lord says: “I begot sons and exalted them, but they rejected me” (Isaiah 1:2).

In the Gospel: “What is born from the flesh is flesh; and what is born from the Spirit is holy, because God is Spirit” (John 3:6). And again: “The Spirit blows where he wishes, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes. So is everyone who is born from the Holy Spirit” (ibid., 8).

Therefore, when comparing these things with the beginning of the Gospel, does he diminish the dignity of the Holy Spirit?

For at the beginning of the Gospel John says concerning the Savior and those who believed: “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:12).

And the Lord, also explaining the regeneration of the faithful, and …
afterward, instructing Nicodemus, he said that those who believe in him—that is, who receive him—must be regenerated by the Holy Spirit, as follows: “Do not be amazed that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Holy Spirit” (John III, 7). And earlier, recalling this, he says: “What is born of the Spirit is spirit” (ibid., 6): “What is born of the flesh is flesh; and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.”

If, then, those who are generated by heavenly regeneration are generated from the Holy Spirit and are generated from God, why should we not think that whatever is great, divine, and worthy of the Trinity must be thought about the Spirit, insofar as human possibility permits? What, moreover, shall we think when we again hear Paul writing to the Corinthians about the Spirit: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you received from God? And you are not your own, for you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your hearts” (I Corinthians VI, 19)? Are such things properly said of any creature, and would they write such things about the Holy Spirit as they do about God, if he were a creature?

What, moreover, shall we do when we hear Peter saying to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit and withhold part of the price of the land? You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (Acts V, 3). But perhaps they will say that those who lie to the Spirit of God and lie to God are like those who insult a servant and thereby dishonor the king. [Col. 0319A]

To them we reply: Then, when those men lied to the apostles, did they not lie to God? Or, when people receive the apostles, do they not receive God, just as the Lord said to the apostles: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Matthew X, 40)?

Peter, therefore, when he said, “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings, but to God,” ought either to have said, “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to the Holy Spirit, but to God”; or else, “Why has Satan tempted you to lie to us? You have not lied to human beings, but to God,” so that the subsequent reasoning would have coherence. For God entrusted to his saints both understanding and confession of this truth, just as when Israel requested a king, rejecting that great Samuel, and God, when Samuel was grieved, said to him: “They have not rejected you, but me” (I Samuel VIII, 7).

Peter did not, indeed, use such words; but when Ananias and his wife Sapphira thought that they were deceiving human beings, Peter—one of those whom they thought they were deceiving—said: “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings, but to God.” And so, when Sapphira entered immediately afterward, he said to her: “Why have you agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?”

The sacred writings teach us to live in holiness for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, just as Paul writes to the Romans: “For the one who died died to sin once; but the one who lives lives to God” (Romans VI, 10). And again: “So that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again” (II Corinthians V, 15). And again, rebuking the Galatians, he writes: “If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians V, 25).

And when Paul said: “For us there is one Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (I Corinthians VIII, 6)—and what is greater in the whole creation, namely, the Lord’s body, is believed to be from the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist Matthew handed down:

“The generation of Christ was as follows. When Mary his mother had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly. While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said to him: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not fear to receive Mary your wife; for what is born from her is from the Holy Spirit’” (Matthew I, 18).

Although the Wisdom of Solomon, in Proverbs, speaking about the Savior’s body, said, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs IX, 1), and here he declares the Only-begotten to be the creator of his own body, this angel nevertheless said that it was from the Holy Spirit; and thus every Christian believes when instructed. For Scripture does not disagree concerning the Trinity, teaching everywhere that one and the same operation has been performed by it.

Finally, when the blessed Virgin Mary was about to give birth to God and heard Gabriel say, “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke I, 31), and when she asked, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (ibid., 34), she was immediately instructed by him, who said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (ibid., 35).

And if the power of the Most High is the Only-begotten, according to Paul’s statement, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Corinthians I, 24)—while the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth—and if, when these overshadowed Mary who was about to give birth to him, the Lord’s temple was created, and the angel said that he had been created from the Holy Spirit, why should we not be taught that the Trinity has one operation?

For the Lord also said to Nicodemus that all the faithful are from the Holy Spirit, declaring: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
