Do not be amazed that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Holy Spirit” (John III, 6–8).

When, therefore, we hear, “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Corinthians VIII, 6), and we have what is greater and more glorious than the whole creation—that is, the Lord’s body—and when all the saints are also made holy by the Holy Spirit, why should we not understand from the Scriptures that the same things must be believed about the Holy Spirit as about the Father and the Son?

If this seems harsh or impious to the impious, then, just as they believe in the Father and the Son, let them not likewise believe in the Holy Spirit; and just as they baptize in the name of the Father and the Son, let them not likewise baptize in the name of the Holy Spirit. But let us see whether those who think in this way either believe in God or baptize at all, since they do not perceive in the sacred Scriptures the unity of the Trinity.

For the most blessed Paul wrote to the Ephesians: “Therefore take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day; and when you have accomplished everything, stand, having girded your loins with truth and having put on your feet the preparation of the gospel of peace. Above all these, taking up the shield of faith, and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI, 13).

Behold the whole armor, and the Son’s helmet—for he himself is salvation, as the prophet Isaiah said: “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Isaiah XL, 5). But the sword of the Holy Spirit—has it ceased to belong to the Trinity? Does it not teach unity?

What, then, does anyone say about the Holy Spirit, when he hears such declarations about him in the Scriptures, and also hears the saints praying to the Lord: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” (Psalm VI, 2)? And in the psalm: “I will rebuke you and set your sins before your face” (Psalm XLIX, 21). And he hears the Savior speaking about the Holy Spirit: “But if I go, I will send the Paraclete to you; and when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John XVI, 7).

And in Isaiah we hear about the conduct of the Only-begotten among human beings: “A shoot will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root; and the Spirit of God will rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him. He will not judge according to appearance, nor reprove according to speech, but he will judge with humble judgment, reprove the proud, rescue the humble of the earth, strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and by the spirit of his lips put the wicked to death” (Isaiah XI, 1–4).

We therefore see that he lived among human beings, and that the Spirit of God—that is, the Holy Spirit, who is also called the seven spirits—rested upon him. We have not yet seen him as judge, but we await seeing him at his second coming. Thus, hearing these things also about the Holy Spirit, we consider them: he himself is the Son of God who said, “When the Paraclete comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John XVI, 8).

For the Lord will not come in the flesh without the Holy Spirit, but, together with his divinity, he will contain him who fills the universe, since he is an anointing upon his flesh. Thus also we heard David singing and saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 7). Was he not uttering these declarations as one awaiting the Spirit as judge?

For every work of God, of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit is properly theirs.

Or have we not heard him say in the ninety-fourth psalm concerning God: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me” (Psalm XCIV, 8)? And concerning himself: “They tested me and saw my works. For forty years I was near this generation, and I said: ‘They always go astray in their heart.’ But they did not know my ways, so I swore in my anger: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’” (ibid., 9–11).

If they say that the one who says, “Therefore I hated that generation,” and all the preceding words, is God and not the Spirit, let them hear Paul writing to the Hebrews about the words spoken in that same psalm: “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts’” (Hebrews III, 7).

Let them come to the prophet Isaiah and hear him say: “Not an envoy or an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them; he himself received them and exalted them all the days of the age. But they acted rebelliously and provoked the Holy Spirit, and he turned against them as an enemy” (Isaiah LXIII, 9).

Let them also listen to Stephen, the firstfruits of the martyrs, rebuking the rulers of the Jews for the benefits God bestowed upon their fathers when he led them out of the land of Egypt, after performing signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years; and for the impious things they did, making a calf and worshiping idols; and for all the wicked schemes they devised. He said to them:

“Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute and kill? They announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become. You received the law by the ordinance of angels, and you did not keep it” (Acts VII, 51–53).

Who, then, will not marvel at the divinity of the Holy Spirit, when such things have been said about him? Who will not venerate the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, when he sees him convicting the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment? When he sees him raising the dead, giving life, and doing what the Father and the Son do?

For it is written in the Gospel: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” (John V, 21). And the apostle Paul says to the Romans: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans VIII, 11).

And David says in the one hundred third psalm: “You will take away their Spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm CIII, 29).

Can anyone refuse to confess that the Paraclete, who is sent and creates bodies dissolved from the beginning of the world and reduced to their dust, is the creator, and renews the face of the earth? This accords with what is written in the prophet Isaiah: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isaiah LXV, 17). Without him neither the Father nor the Son does anything in creation, as we demonstrated earlier from the sacred Scriptures.

And again Paul writes to the Romans: “I have confidence in Christ Jesus before God, but I do not dare to speak about everything that Christ has not worked through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit” (Romans XV, 17). He teaches that Christ performed signs and wonders through the Holy Spirit.

And to the Ephesians: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians III, 14).

Paul writes these things individually about the Father and the Son. Thus, as we have often recalled, he says to the Thessalonians: “May the God and Father himself sanctify you completely” (I Thessalonians V, 23). He does not say “may they sanctify you” in the plural, but “may he sanctify you” in the singular.

But when he speaks to the Corinthians about the Son and the Spirit, he says: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Corinthians VI, 11). And concerning the Father and the Spirit: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (I Corinthians III, 16).

David also speaks of the Father and the Spirit: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 7). He did not say “you are there” in the plural, although he had spoken of the Spirit and the Father. For where God is, there the Son and the Spirit are also shown to be; and God is worshiped in the Son and in the Holy Spirit.

When the Samaritan woman was still thinking carnally about God, supposing that God was to be worshiped in a particular place, she said: “Lord, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship” (John IV, 19). But the Lord, excluding the worship of God as confined to a place, said to her:

“Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. But the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such people; and those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth” (ibid., 21).

If they worship in spirit and truth, then God is worshiped in the Son, for the Son is the truth, who said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). Why, then, should the Spirit not be worshiped by us together with the Father? For it is unacceptable that, while venerating God bodily, they should not worship in the Spirit and in the Son.

Otherwise, if they worship God in the Spirit, the Spirit is worshiped together with him. Since they hear that the Father is glorified in the Church in Christ, what will they claim that they themselves should do? For Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says: “To him who is able to do abundantly beyond all that we ask or think, to him be glory in the Church, in Christ Jesus, throughout all generations, forever and ever” (Ephesians III, 20).

And again Paul says: “For through Christ the Amen is spoken to God’s glory” (II Corinthians I, 20). Through us glorifying the Father and the Son, and in the Son the Father—not, indeed, with the Son himself glorifying together with us.

Thus, worshiping God in the Spirit and in the Son—that is, worshiping through the Spirit and through the Son—we worship together the Lord, the Son, and the Spirit. Finally, Paul writes: “So that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II, 10).

If those who bow their knees at the name of Jesus Christ glorify the Son with the Father, why should those who worship the Father and the Son in the Spirit not worship him together with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

If, therefore, we have heard Moses say, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy VI, 13), we know that the Son and the Spirit are proclaimed together with God. And lest we seem to be recalling unwritten things and speaking from our own ideas, the worship of the heavenly powers must be demonstrated, just as we have learned it from the holy Scriptures. Perhaps, becoming emulous of them, they will learn both to venerate and to pray in this way.

Whom do they wish to have been seen by Isaiah being praised, worshiped, and glorified in the temple by the seraphim—the Father or the Son? Perhaps they will close their ears if they hear that it was also the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah says:

“It happened in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and his house was full of his glory. Seraphim stood around him; each had six wings, and the other also had six. With two they covered their face, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. They cried out to one another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.’ The threshold was lifted by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke.

“And I said: ‘Woe is me, for I am pierced through! Because I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord Sabaoth, with my eyes.’

“And one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he held a coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs. He touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse your sins.’

“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?’ And I said: ‘Behold, here am I; send me.’ And he said to me: ‘Go to this people and say to them: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; and seeing, you will see, but will not perceive. For the heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.’ And I said: ‘How long, Lord?’” (Isaiah VI, 1–11).

Whom, then, do they wish this to be? Let them state it; perhaps they will say that it is the Son. For in the Gospel according to John—κατὰ Ἰωάννην, “according to John”—it is written:

“And for this reason they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (John XII, 39).

Isaiah said these things when he had seen his glory, and he spoke about him. What, then, will they do with Paul, who says that it was the Spirit who was seen in that glory of Isaiah and who spoke to him when he sent him to say the things mentioned above?

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“When the Jews had conferred with one another, they departed after Paul had spoken one word: ‘The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers, saying: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; and seeing, you will see, but will not perceive. For the heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (Acts XXVIII, 25–27).

Behold: John says that it was the Son, while Paul says that it was the Holy Spirit who was seen by Isaiah, sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and who is worshiped, praised, and glorified by the seraphim.

All the Churches of Christ, from East to West, however, unanimously profess in the report of their ministries that the Father is praised by the seraphim. Let those, therefore, who deny veneration to the Holy Spirit tell us which of these speaks the truth and which is deceived—John, or Paul, or all the Churches of Christ? For all the Churches confess that the one worshiped by the seraphim is the Father; John says that it is the Son; and Paul says that it is the Holy Spirit.

But if none of them is deceived and all speak the truth, it has plainly been proved that even when the name of the Father is spoken, the Son and the Holy Spirit are nevertheless proclaimed with him.

Otherwise, what will they do when they hear the Savior saying to the disciples: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII, 19), when Scripture would name not the Trinity but a unity?

For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning those who believed in Samaria and were baptized by Philip: “They had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts VIII, 16). And concerning those who were baptized by Paul at Ephesus: “When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 12; Acts XIX, 5).

Peter also addressed the Jews: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts II, 38). “When they heard and approved his words, they were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day” (ibid., 41).

Did they become transgressors of the Savior’s command? Did they baptize so great a multitude contrary to the Savior’s tradition? For it is not written that they baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but only in the name of the Lord Jesus. Did they therefore transgress? Far from it. Although only the name of the Son is mentioned, the Father and the Spirit are nevertheless proclaimed with him, as we have proved from the sacred Scriptures.

Thus the Holy Spirit is also called Sabaoth, and together with God and the Son is worshiped by the seraphim. For this reason they say three times, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah VI, 3), so that they might proclaim the Trinity.

Therefore Paul does not deny that the Lord is called Spirit, saying to the Corinthians: “The Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Corinthians III, 17). And to the Romans he says: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Romans VIII, 2).

How, then, did you dare to call the Holy Spirit a servant, when he freed the creature? If all things were made through him, does this show that the Holy Spirit was created? Surely the statement written in the one hundred eighteenth psalm, “All things serve you” (Psalm CXVIII, 91), also shows that the Holy Spirit is a servant?

But neither does the statement that all things were made through the Son assign the Holy Spirit to servitude, for he himself is the one who speaks; nor does the statement “all things serve you” show that he is a servant.

Otherwise, how should Paul be heard when he says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans VIII, 15)? Thus the Holy Spirit is taught to be neither a servant nor a creature.

Yet you slander him by saying that he is carnal and a servant, although he is not only free but also grants freedom to the creature, as we proved above.

And again Paul writes: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (I Corinthians XII, 4). And: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid., 11). And Jesus says: “The Spirit breathes where it wills.” If he does what he wills, he is no longer a servant but free.

With what death, then, will those end who profess that the Lord of the heavenly host is a servant? For “Lord of powers” is the interpretation of “Lord Sabaoth.” Certainly he does not grant freedom to the creature unless he is Lord of creation.

For the Holy Spirit is also in the name of Jesus, as the Lord says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you” (John XIV, 26)—the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—remaining in his own life and substance, since he himself is life.

Otherwise, what will you do when you hear Solomon saying in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out perfume; therefore the young women loved you” (Song of Songs I, 2)? Isaiah, moreover, says: “The Lord Sabaoth will make this for the nations on this mountain: they will drink in gladness, they will drink wine, they will be anointed with perfume, and they will hand all these things over to the nations” (Isaiah XXV, 6).

Did the prophet not call the Holy Spirit, with whom we have been anointed, perfume? David also calls him the oil of gladness in the forty-fourth psalm, saying about the Savior’s human life: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Psalm XLIV, 8).

Taking this up, Peter says: “Jesus who was from Nazareth—God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts X, 38).

Therefore, when the Holy Spirit is called both oil and perfume, he is the name of God and of the Son, remaining in his own life and substance, since, as we said above according to the prophet, he is “your name, poured-out perfume.”

It is clear that the Lord poured out the Holy Spirit abundantly upon those among the Gentiles who believed, as Paul writes. And since we have an anointing and a seal, and again the same Paul writes in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

“He who establishes us with you in Christ and anoints us is God, who also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (II Corinthians I, 21).

And again he says to the Ephesians: “In him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians I, 13).

The saints prepare us to understand great things about the Holy Spirit. For when David said in the fifteenth psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Psalm XV, 5); and Moses wrote: “There will be no portion or inheritance for the Levites in the land; the Lord himself is their portion”; and Jeremiah cried out: “The one who formed all things is himself the inheritance of Jacob; the Lord is his name”; and when the Scriptures called the Lord the inheritance of the saints, Paul said that the Holy Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance of the saints:

“In whom, he says, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Ephesians I, 13),

teaching that the Holy Spirit is inherited, not that he inherits.

Consider the declarations of the saints. Isaiah says to those who did not have the Holy Spirit, and who therefore did not know the inheritance prepared for the saints after the departure from this age, instructing them at the same time:

“There is an inheritance for those who worship God, and you will be righteous, says the Lord” (Isaiah LIV, 17). “You who thirst, go to the water” (Isaiah LV, 1),

calling the Holy Spirit water, as we shall show later. Since he is the pledge of the saints’ inheritance, David too, when he possessed this Holy Spirit, called him the seal and pledge of the inheritance.

But he says that those who do not believe that there is an inheritance for the saints after the end of this life are wretched. Speaking confidently about himself and those like him, he says in the fourth psalm: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’ The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV, 6). He calls the marking a seal, declaring that it is the light of the Lord’s countenance.

Let them therefore believe Paul, who says that believers have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise. And let them know that David, who possessed the same spirit of faith, sang: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm CXV, 10).

Let them know that he also calls the seal he received the light of the Lord’s countenance—that is, the Holy Spirit—so that, knowing the Son also to be the light of God, he might sing to God in the thirty-fifth psalm: “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm XXXV, 10), that is, “in your Son we shall see the Holy Spirit.”

Thus Isaiah knows that the Spirit who sanctifies is called not only light but also fire, saying: “And he will be the light of Israel, and he will sanctify him with burning fire” (Isaiah X, 17). And behold, in the light—which is fire—God sanctifies this Israel; and our Lord is a consuming fire, as Moses says: “Your God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy IV, 24).

Paul also says: “So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit” (Romans XV, 16). The Gentiles are not sanctified by God in one way and Israel in another, but in the Holy Spirit, who exists as light and fire.

The wisdom of Solomon also says in Proverbs: “The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings, searching the inner parts of the belly” (Proverbs XX, 27). It is clear that the Spirit searches all things, as Paul writes.

And when Adam was formed in the beginning, God breathed the Holy Spirit into his face, as Moses says: “And God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Genesis II, 7).

What was breathed by the Lord is not the soul, as the Jewish fabulists claim. Otherwise, how would God condemn to eternal fire what he himself breathed? Rather, it is the life-giving Spirit, about whom Paul also says: “The Spirit gives life” (II Corinthians III, 6). “And God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.”

Therefore the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of life. Some, falling away from him, though living, have become dead, as Paul writes: “She who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (I Timothy V, 6).

Otherwise, how should Solomon be heard when he says, “The light of the Lord is the breath of human beings, which searches the inner parts of the belly” (Proverbs XX, 27), if you say that the souls of human beings are the light of God, unless you confess the Holy Spirit to be the light of God?

But you may believe that he is the inspiration of the Son, since Moses says: “God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life” (Genesis II, 7), and the Son of God says: “I am life” (John XIV, 6).

The wisdom of Solomon also, introducing the Savior, says: “Behold, I will bring forth for you the declaration of my inspiration” (Proverbs I, 23). For thus he says in Proverbs:

“Wisdom sings aloud in the open places, and in the streets she speaks boldly. At the gates she stands with greater strength; at the walls of the city she confidently says: ‘How long will the simple possess righteousness without being ashamed? But the foolish, being desirous of insult, have become impious and have hated understanding, and have become liable to rebukes. Behold, I will bring forth for you the declaration of my breath; I will teach you my word’” (Proverbs I, 20–23).

And Isaiah, proclaiming the promise of the Holy Spirit, says:

“Thus says the Lord who made heaven and fixed it, who established the earth and the things in it, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isaiah XLII, 5).

Tell us: what people received the breath? Will you say here also that breath is the soul? Or will you grant that a people was established upon the earth without a soul? But it is not so. The prophet says these things while proclaiming the promise of the Holy Spirit.

Finally, Luke wrote that the promise was fulfilled for the faithful who were present at that time:

“When the days of Pentecost had been fulfilled, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there was a sound from heaven as of a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and one rested upon each of them; and they began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts II, 1).

In a similar way, that great Job, speaking against his friends when they were deprived of the Holy Spirit, said that they spoke nothing true and did not consider that they were speaking before God: “Do you speak before the Lord?” (Job XIII, 7). And again: “To whom have you announced words? And whose breath is this that proceeds from you?” (Job XXVI, 4).

One of them, speaking grandly, said: “It is the Spirit who intercedes for mortals, but the breath of the Almighty is what teaches me” (Job XXXIII, 4).

The Almighty is the Son of God, concerning whom Zechariah says: “Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: ‘After the glory he sent me against the nations that plundered you’” (Zechariah II, 8).

We also heard Solomon say: “The light of the Lord is the breath of human beings” (Proverbs XX, 27). And we have been instructed by Moses that “the Lord breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Genesis II, 7).

We also hear the Savior saying: “I am life” (John XIV, 6); and Paul writing: “For the law of the Spirit of life” (Romans VIII, 2); and again: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Galatians IV, 6).

We also see the Only-begotten breathe upon the faces of the apostles and say: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22).

Let us therefore be taught that the Spirit is the Son’s inspiration, remaining in his own life and substance. Let us not believe that he was begotten or created by the Son, lest we believe that the Only-begotten Son is the Spirit, and that he is not the Son’s Word. The Word was begotten by God, his own Word remaining in his own life and substance, since he himself is life.

The Spirit is not begotten by him because he is not his Word. But it is impious to say that the Holy Spirit was created. Nevertheless, we have been taught by the sacred Scriptures that he is the inspiration of the Son of God.

We say that the Son of God is the fountain of the Holy Spirit, with the Son himself saying in Jeremiah: “For this people has committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that could not hold water” (Jeremiah II, 13).

The living water is the Holy Spirit, as John taught when he recorded that the Savior said to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John IV, 10). And again: “Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst forever” (ibid., 13).

For he also cries out in the midst of the temple: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 37).

And he interpreted it as follows: “Now he said this about the Holy Spirit,”
whom those who were going to believe in him were to receive (ibid., 39). Thus Isaiah too says that the Lord declared: “For I shall give water to those who have walked in a dry place, and I shall place my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessings upon your children; and he shall spring up like grass in water, like a willow among streams of water” (Isa. XLIV, 3). Therefore, since the holy Scriptures plainly proclaim it, we have recognized that the Holy Spirit is living water.

**325** The Lord declared that he is the fountain of the Spirit in this way: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II, 13). Thus David too sings in the thirty-fifth Psalm, saying to the Lord: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10). Therefore, show another fountain of life besides the Lord, which is with him. For he did not say, “Because you are the fountain of life,” but, “Because with you is the fountain of life.” It is indeed with God, and the Son is the fountain, the Spirit existing [there]. Concerning this Paul writes to the Romans: “But the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. VIII, 10). Thus he declares that the Spirit is not alien but the Father’s own. For after confessing, “With you is the fountain of life,” he added, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10)—that is, “In your Son we shall see the Spirit.”

Moreover, the Spirit is also called by the name of God’s power, and is shown to be power and wisdom. For we heard the Savior in the Gospel promising his disciples that he would send the Holy Spirit, saying: “And behold, I shall send the promise of my Father upon you. But you, remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49). In the Acts of the Apostles the same Lord says: “But you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you” (Acts I, 8). We find that this too was fulfilled when the day of Pentecost was completed.

Therefore, either confess that the Holy Spirit is the power of God, or, like Sabellius, since he is the power of God, proclaim that the Paraclete Spirit is the same person as the Son. And hear Paul saying: “The Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. VIII, 10). Again we are taught that the Son is the fountain of the Spirit. Hear Jeremiah crying out against the Jews: “For they have abandoned me, the Lord, the fountain of life” (Jer. XVII, 13).

But another, knowing that the Spirit is wisdom—according to Isaiah, who says, “And the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isa. XI, 2), and according to Paul, who writes, “I do not cease giving thanks to God for you, so that he may give you the Spirit of wisdom and revelation” (Eph. I, 16)—declared that the Spirit is the fountain, saying above: “You have abandoned the fountain of wisdom” (Baruch III, 13).

That he has here called the Spirit “wisdom” is clear from what follows. When the people were in the land of the Chaldeans and living among the Chaldeans—people who did not possess the Holy Spirit, but lived carnally in sin, while they were **326** dead with respect to righteousness and deprived of the Holy Spirit—he lamented with tears, saying: “What is this, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies and have grown old in a foreign land? You have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted among those who are in the underworld. You have abandoned the fountain of wisdom. If you had walked in the way of the Lord, you would surely have dwelt in peace forever” (Baruch III, 10).

Let them consider the way that the children of Israel abandoned. The one who says, “I am the way,” is God; he is called the fountain of life in the prophet, and the Jews abandoned him, defiling themselves with the Babylonians, who were dead with respect to righteousness. For since they did not have within themselves the Paraclete Spirit—the Spirit of truth, who is life and gives life—they were dead while living.

Hence Paul also writes concerning such people: “But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. V, 6). And Solomon cries out: “He who lives in pleasure from childhood shall be a slave; at the end he shall grieve within himself” (Prov. XXIX, 21). For those who live in the pleasures of sin do not hear Paul writing: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII, 15). Since they are sons of sin, they are dead with respect to righteousness.

But those who have received the gift of the Holy Spirit should say: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. VIII, 2). Moses therefore rightly took care to say: “Then the Lord breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Gen. II, 7). Those who do not have the Holy Spirit are dead while living.

Thus, to Israel that had abandoned the Lord, who is the life-giving fountain of life, he says: “You have abandoned the fountain of wisdom. If you had walked in the way of the Lord, you would surely have dwelt in peace forever” (Baruch III, 13).

Therefore, hearing him say, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6), and also taught by the holy Scriptures that the fountain is the Spirit, namely God who says, “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II, 13), let us by no means suppose that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Rather, we have again proved from another Scripture that he is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, just as above we learned from the prophet Isaiah.

**327** But that great evangelist John writes in the Apocalypse, saying: “And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, flowing through the middle of the street” (Rev. XXII, 1). He was speaking of the Jerusalem above, concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “The rushing of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5).

But if they say, “Why, then, is it written ‘water’?” let them listen. At the throne of God and of the Lamb there is the water of life. When some become capable of receiving its waters, they are called rivers, and the Spirit is said to be fulfilled in each individual, just as the Son is fulfilled in each individual, according to Paul’s writing: “His fullness, because he is fulfilled in all things in all” (Eph. I, 23).

There are times when those who are filled with this living water are called rivers, as David says in the ninety-second Psalm: “The rivers lifted up their voice, at the voice of many waters” (Ps. XCII, 3–4). There are also times when the word of teaching and each operation of the Spirit are called rivers, according to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture said, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

Therefore he did not say, “It has been filled with waters”—for the water is the living Spirit—but, “The river of God has been filled with waters.” And the Lord says: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II, 13).

Therefore the water of life—that is, the Holy Spirit—belongs to the same throne as God and the Lamb, as John said together with Isaiah; and he is neither a servant nor a minister, as you say.

But if they persist in saying that the Spirit is created and produce what is written in the prophet Amos: “Prepare yourself to invoke your God, O Israel, because I am the one who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces his Christ among human beings” (Amos IV, 12), let them hear that the Son of God did not say this concerning the Holy Spirit, but concerning the spirit of the wind that follows thunder.

For thunder does not precede the Holy Spirit; rather, it precedes the spirit of the wind, which the Lord said he created after the thunder. Otherwise let them say whether he created thunder before the Holy Spirit. But if it is impious to say this, let those who say that the Holy Spirit was created be utterly rejected, since Scripture was not silent even concerning the first creation, which was created by the Son of God.

For example, the one who speaks to Job says: “But behold, the beasts are with you; they eat grass like oxen, and their strength is in their loins, while their power is in the navel of their belly. He set his tail like a cypress; his sinews are intertwined like ropes. His sides are like sides of bronze, and his back like molten iron. This is the beginning of the Lord’s work, made to be mocked by the angels” (Job XL, 10).

Thus the devil is written to be the first creation, made to be mocked by the angels. For it is written: “This is the beginning of the Lord’s work, made to be mocked by the angels” (Job XL, 14).

**328** But we have learned from the holy Scriptures that the mind of Christ is the Holy Spirit, just as Paul wrote: “But taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are judged spiritually. But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. II, 13–16).

Therefore, since this Holy Spirit is the mind of the Lord, existing in the proper substance of life, as we have frequently said, he knows all the things of God, just as our spirit knows what belongs to us.

Finally, Paul also says: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit, for the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God; and these things we also speak, taught not by words of human wisdom, but taught by the Spirit” (1 Cor. II, 10).

The Lord also taught that this Holy Spirit is the finger of God. According to Matthew he says: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Matt. XII, 28). According to Luke: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Luke XI, 20).

“For this reason I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven them. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. XII, 31–32).

Through this Holy Spirit, since he is the finger of God, the stone tablets given to Moses were written—written by the finger of God, as Moses himself explained.

Otherwise, if they do not say that the Holy Spirit is the finger of God, they will openly declare that the stone tablets are more glorious than the hearts of the saints, upon which the letter of Christ was written through the Holy Spirit, as Paul says: “You are a letter of Christ, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the **329** living God; not on stone tablets but on tablets of the heart” (2 Cor. III, 3).

We believe that this Holy Spirit is also the light of God’s countenance, according to David, who says in the fourth Psalm: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV, 7). In the thirty-fifth Psalm: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). And according to Solomon, who writes in Proverbs: “The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings, which searches the inner parts of the belly” (Prov. XX, 27). And Isaiah says: “And he shall be a light to this Israel in the fire, and he shall sanctify him with burning fire” (Isa. X, 17).

The divine Scriptures have also taught us that this is the inspiration of the Son of God. Solomon says: “The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings” (Prov. XX, 27). Moses says: “And God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Gen. II, 7).

And when Adam was subsequently created, receiving the spirit of life and becoming a living soul, and possessing the Holy Spirit, he was spiritual, so much so that he prophesied that for this reason “a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (ibid., 24).

Likewise, he called the woman taken from his rib “Eve,” prophetically saying: “This is the mother of all the living” (Gen. III, 20).

In the same way, all the saints, after being baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, having received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the hands of God’s priests, are restored to the ancient state, to what they were before Adam’s transgression; and it is by this Spirit that the law is given in the churches of the Gentiles.

We neither circumcise the flesh nor observe the law of Moses carnally. For when Paul and those who preached God’s word with him to the Gentiles, together with those who had been faithful from the circumcision, said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and command them to observe the law of Moses” (Acts XV, 5), the Holy Spirit ordered that believers from the Gentiles should not be circumcised and should not follow carnally the rite that Moses handed down to the Jews.

Therefore the apostles wrote the following to those who were from the Gentiles:

“The apostles and presbyters, brothers, to the brothers who are among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings. Since we have heard that certain people from among us have disturbed you with words that we did not authorize, it has seemed good to us, **330** having assembled together, to send to you, with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, men who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Judas and Silas, who themselves will also announce these same things by word.

“For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you except these necessary things: that you abstain from sacrifices offered to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Farewell” (Acts XV, 23–29).

And when the Holy Spirit had promulgated this, all the churches of Christ observed it.

Let them consider that no one of the things that have been created has been permitted to give a law to the whole world. Therefore, seeing the Holy Spirit giving a law, let them not blaspheme by saying that he is created. For the Lord speaks especially against those who blaspheme him: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven human beings; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. XII, 31).

The Lord would not have said such things about him if he were a creature.

Furthermore, in the Book of Kings it is written: “If a man sins against a man, the priest shall pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who shall pray for him?” (1 Kings II, 25). The Lord also said similar things about the Holy Spirit, as we proved above: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Therefore, fearing this sentence and hearing what the Scriptures have said about the Holy Spirit, let us hold the same beliefs about the Holy Spirit as about the Father and the Son. For just as we believe in God the Father and in his only-begotten Son, so also we believe in the Holy Spirit; and just as we were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son, so also we were baptized in the Holy Spirit.

In this name—in which we believe and in which we have been baptized—if we hold such beliefs concerning the Trinity and imitate the worship of the seraphim, we shall be able to become heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

[Col. 0333A]

**Vigilius of Tapsus, Against Felicianus and an Arian, on the Unity of the Trinity, a Book Addressed to Optatus.** (C, S)

[Col. 0333]

## Chapter One

You have pressed me, dearest son, to write something about the unity of the Trinity, who is perfect and supreme God forever, as one mindful of my priestly office. Although I repeatedly excused myself on account of my awareness of my own weakness, you demanded this of me in many ways, asserting that the exposition of the common faith is something religious people receive and priests ought not to deny the faithful: otherwise, while they do not receive it, they may easily begin to be deceived by unbelievers; or, when those who possess the heavenly treasure do not provide what is desired to Christ’s members, they may seem somehow to have hidden it in the earth through barren learning.

Thus I confess that I have been overcome by persuasive reasons, lest I appear to hand over the unarmed to hostile evils, while they are not equipped with the defense of truth against unbelievers. But because in questions of this kind a certain obscurity frequently arises during continuous discourse, I therefore thought it appropriate to encompass in the brevity of this little book the conversation recently held between Felicianus and me, prefacing it with the initial letters of the principal names for the sake of distinguishing the speakers.

## Chapter Two

For when we were sitting together a few days ago, he said:

“Among the other things that frequently offend me in your debates, I consider nothing worse than the way you transmit the precepts of faith to the uneducated, prescribing that they converse not about the rational understanding of matters, but rather about a kind of display of testimonies. To say nothing for the moment of how crafty this is, everyone knows how rustic it is. First, if the person being instructed has already come to believe through the books, he obeys and does not resist; otherwise, he must contradict you no more than he must contradict those same testimonies which are brought forward as proof. And therefore this method seems better to me for teaching: first, the reasoning of the faith should be presented without testimonies; after the person has been convinced by reasoning, that path should be polished with the answering testimony of Scripture. And not without reason. For if these testimonies are approved because they are not devoid of reason, then that reasoning which appears to establish even these testimonies by itself ought to be sufficient on its own. But if the opposite is true, who can submit the neck of rational faith to irrational testimonies, even if those testimonies are falsely represented as divine?

“I would indeed tolerate that manner of debate in others whom the necessity of ignorance compels to flee to borrowed resources, because they cannot stand by themselves. But in you I endure this in no way whatsoever, because I see that you do not lack eloquence along with knowledge of the faith.”

Then I said:

“Do you think that I can be led so far by praise of myself that I would do an injury to the holy men who preceded us, and that I would ever presume upon the wisdom of speech, ‘lest the cross of Christ be emptied’ (1 Cor. 1:17)? Rather, content with the authority of Scripture, I strive to obey simplicity rather than self-importance.

“But you say that a person is taught better by reasoning than by testimonies. What reasoning, then, can you bring forward if you proclaim the birth from a virgin, if you do not deny that eyes were restored to the blind, if you show that the buried returned from the dead? If, therefore, the rational explanation of these things is incomprehensible while their truth is evident, then in matters of faith it is easier to believe testimonies than to investigate the reasoning. Yet because you distinguish these two things not altogether inconsistently—since, after reasoning has been put forward, you also do not omit the testimonies—I confess that in this discussion I shall follow what you yourself have approved.”

## Chapter Three

[Col. 0334C]

**Felicianus said:** “Since we are at leisure, then, let us come to the question of your *homoousion*—the ‘consubstantiality’—about which discussion has often taken place not only between us but also among our elders. And so that the speech may not wander too far, assume yourself, as you usually do, the role of the proposer, and, when we ask you to give an account of our faith, ask in turn so that you may provide the answer.”

Then I said:

“Tell me: is it true that, as I hear you say, the Son is not altogether *homoousios* with the Father?”

**Felicianus said:** “It is true. I cannot be persuaded that what is begotten is unbegotten, lest I seem to proclaim the same person as Father and Son.”

**Augustine said:** “That is not so. For I too do not intend that the same be unbegotten which is begotten, but rather that what is begotten be of the same substance as what is unbegotten.”

**Felicianus said:** “And how do you not say that the unbegotten and the begotten are the same, if you regard both as one and not as two?”

**Augustine said:** “I perceive that you have not attended closely enough to the force of the words. For when I say that both are one, I do not separate at all the substance of the true Father and the true Son. And when I do not proclaim the Father to be the same as the Son, I distinguish the person of each while preserving the property of each. Therefore, if you ask about substance, the Trinity itself is one God; if about person, the Son is another.”

[Col. 0335A]

**Felicianus:** “How can you say both that he is the same and that the Son is another?”

**Augustine:** “The same by communion of substance; another by the property of person.”

**Felicianus:** “I do not know how one substance can be believed when one person is not spoken of.”

**Augustine:** “It is not one person, because one is said to have begotten and another to have been begotten. Yet the substance of the one born and the one begetting is not different, because what has proceeded is taught to be not unlike the one who begets.”

**Felicianus:** “Please clarify what you have said for me by an easier example.”

**Augustine:** “In matters that are incomprehensible, examples are not readily available to one conducting an argument; nevertheless, insofar as possible, I shall not fail even in this respect. Consider, then: a human father has a human son. It is common to both that each is human; yet it appears proper to one that he is a son and to the other that he is a father. For in both the persons are distinguished in such a way that their common humanity is not denied: one begets, the other is begotten. Yet both the one who begot and the one who was begotten are equally called human.”

## Chapter Four

**Felicianus:** “I should like you to say whether the begotten is separated from the unbegotten by a beginning, or not.”

**Augustine:** “The truth of spiritual understanding does not even admit that the Father is separated from the Son by an interval—not merely of time, which is measured by days and nights, but of any age or period whatsoever.”

**Felicianus:** “If this is so, you admit two unbegotten beings. And how is one person regarded as the Father and the other as the Son, when, through the common signification of ‘unbegotten,’ both seem to be confused?”

**Augustine:** “In this matter a considerable sophistical slander is woven by your elders; nevertheless, with the help of the Trinity itself, it must be preserved by Catholic simplicity. I call the Father unbegotten and the Son begotten, yet I do not thereby deny that the begotten is coeternal with the unbegotten. I call the Father unbegotten only because he did not proceed from another; I call the Son begotten because he did not come into existence from himself. For being born is not common to both, nor is not being begotten common to both; yet it is common to them that one is not separated from the other by the intervention of an intermediate time.

“Therefore, if we seek what is proper to the Father, it is sufficient that he alone has no father; if what is proper to the Son, it is enough that he has no offspring. But we say that the divinity of the Father and the Son is one and coeternal.”

**Felicianus:** “As far as I am concerned, I do not see what you are now establishing. For although you contend with me with Aristotelian subtlety, it is nevertheless impossible for you to distinguish the one who was begotten from the one who begot by no antiquity of an intervening age.”

**Augustine:** “I certainly know, as he says, how difficult the argument is in this place. Yet we have nothing to fear, since through the assistance of the Holy Spirit we bear witness to God. What, then, shall we say? Is there something in the Father that is denied to be unbegotten, or not? If there is, let him be called unbegotten not in his entirety but rather in part; otherwise the Son did not begin to exist in time. For if the fatherhood of the Father did not begin, no beginning can be found for the offspring. If a beginning is assigned to the offspring, the Father’s fatherhood will not be shown to be eternal. And how will it stand that you teach everything in the Father to be unbegotten, when you suppose that the very name of fatherhood had a beginning, while you say that the Son began in time—although he could not be called the Son while the Father did not yet exist?”

**Felicianus:** “I am not so foolish as to place time before the Son, but it is certain that a beginning is assigned to the begotten.”

**Augustine:** “What, then? Do you say that there was nothing intermediate between the Father and the Son?”

**Felicianus:** “Precisely so.”

## Chapter Five

**Augustine:** “How, then, do you deny that the Son is coeternal with the Father, when you admit that there is nothing intermediate between the Father and the Son—lest that very thing prove to be not merely an intermediate but a third?”

**Felicianus:** “Since you have trapped me by your skill in argument, I shall briefly explain what was said by our elders. Whenever the beginning of the Son and the eternity of the Father are under discussion, they say: ‘There was when he was not, and before he was born he was not.’”

**Augustine:** “As I understand it, while the error of evil belief remains, only the words have been changed. You said: ‘There was when he was not.’ Do you want this ‘was’ to refer to an age, or to the Son? If to an age—that is, to something like a period of eternity before the Son’s birth—then, compelled by necessity, you fall into the blasphemy mentioned above, since you insert a third thing, time, between the Father and the Son. You say that before the Son there were God the Father and time; after these two came the Son; after those three, the Spirit as a fourth.

“If we admit that the Son could not have been begotten without time, see how widely the things we are saying extend. For if the Son did not exist without time, then certainly he must also be said to have been begotten only in a place. Once this is admitted, before the Son and the Spirit, time and place are somehow shown to be coeval with the Father. If this is so, and the Son could not be born without place and time, in what place or in what time do you say that place and time themselves were made? If in none, then place and time could have been made without time and place. If in something, that something itself appears to be time and place, at whose origin place and time are likewise required. And if something could be made without time and place to such an extent that you do not teach place to have been made in a place or time to have been made in time, I do not know with what rashness you insist that the Son could not have been born without these things, when, according to sound faith, he is taught to have made both place and time. But enough of this.

“Now let us examine what you claim was said by your elders: ‘There was when he was not.’ If you refer ‘was’ to time, then time existed before the Son. If to the Son, then the Son was never absent—for the Son already existed when there was no time, by which time is said to have been made. But you say: ‘Before he was born, he was not.’ Who, I ask, was not before he was born? If the Son, then by that very understanding time is said to have existed before the Son. But if there was no time before the Son was born, it follows that the Son is coeternal with the Father, between whom and the Father no time is said to have existed—especially since, among other things, with the Evangelists bearing witness, the Son is also said to have made time.

“Perhaps someone might think that the statement ‘There was when the Son was not’ was spoken about the Father. But the following words do not agree with that interpretation, for they say: ‘And before he was born, he was not.’ The Father, existing always in himself, cannot even by you be said to have been born. He is not taught to have arisen from a beginning, and the statement cannot apply to the Father: ‘There was when he was not begotten.’”

## Chapter Six

**Felicianus:** “Since you are tiring me considerably by battling with words of, as I think, unexpected subtlety, I ask you, if it can be done, to show by the example of some thing that what you are trying to teach is possible. For I cannot otherwise believe that the begotten is coeternal with the Father, although overcome by the force of your argument, unless you say either that both were begotten or that both are mutually fathers.”

**Augustine:** “Since you compel me to give examples of incomparable things, let us consider the power of fire, from which splendor and vapor always proceed. Both are born from it, yet fire is not found without either of them. These three do not beget one another, because splendor and vapor do not arise from the splendor of fire, nor fire and splendor from vapor; rather, splendor and vapor are always begotten from fire.

“Since this is so, do you see that even among created things something can be born, while nevertheless it is not shown that the thing from which it was born could ever be found without the begotten? If, then, we perceive these things through visible examples, why should we not say similar things of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, insofar as concerns only their common and undifferentiated eternity? For it is not necessary on that account to say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are equally unbegotten, because we say that none is separated from another by an intervening age, since even among other things certain beings are begotten and yet are not therefore equally begetting or shown to exist without one another.

“But what benefit is there in collecting many such examples, when the rest may also be assessed from the testimony of a few?”

**Felicianus:** “Since you disturb by a new method of argument the opinion of mine founded upon the authority of the Fathers who preceded us, I should like you to tell me what you think about the nature of the Son of God—that is, about the substance itself. For if, as you are accustomed to say, he is *homoousios* with the Father, he is in some way the Father himself; otherwise he cannot be consubstantial with the one who begot him. One of our number used to mock the opinion of the *homoousion* in this way: ‘If the Son was brought forth not from outside but from the very same substance, then one has somehow been divided into two, since the one who begets is said to be no other than the one who is begotten.’”

## Chapter Seven

**Augustine:** “Although you say that we contend with Aristotelian skill, you yourself appear to have fled to the snares of the dialecticians. But these things cannot terrify us, who trust in the truth of the faith. What, then, do you say? I believe that the Son could not be born from the substance of the Father, lest we seem to divide the unbegotten Father through the generation of the Son. If this is so, then the Son is wrongly believed to have been made outside the Father—that is, not begotten from the Father himself.

“To make this easier to understand, I shall explain it as far as I can. Among sons, some are adopted and others natural. Those who are begotten are sons always and properly from the beginning; the others are first strangers and afterward sons, when they are seen to be received into the family through adoption. To which, then, should the Son of God be compared? If to adopted sons, he will be like us before the Father. If to natural sons, he must be said to have subsisted from the substance of the one who begot him.

“But you say that the fatherly substance is divided into two if the Son is substantially begotten from the Father alone. How foolish this is, even visible things teach us. For which of the earthly fathers was ever divided by begetting? And if division itself does not fall even within the condition of the body, and no one begot a son in such a way as to lose himself in the process, do you say that the Son could not have been born while the integrity of the Father remained?

“But why say more? To those investigating the birth and origin of the Son of God, these possibilities present themselves, unless I am mistaken: either he is from the Father, or from nothing, or from another, or from himself. Let us examine the consequence of these alternatives. If he is from himself, he is not rightly called Son, since he is proclaimed not begotten but unbegotten. If from nothing, he is shown to be a creature along with the rest, not the author of creatures. If from another, he is proclaimed the son not of the one in whom we believe, but of some unknown father. And if no fifth possibility can be found beyond these four, while three of these cannot at all be proclaimed because of their evident blasphemy, it remains that he was substantially begotten from the Father. For, as we have said, no fifth possibility can be found, nor can any mode among these be taught except the first: he is neither a creature, nor the son of another father, nor unbegotten in the manner of the Father.”

## Chapter Eight

**Felicianus:** “But if I have proclaimed either a fifth possibility beyond these or one of the three, then I do so by saying that the Son did not come into existence from the substance of the Father, while nevertheless I do not deny that he was begotten by the Father’s will.”

**Augustine:** “The consequence of the matter itself thrusts you into one of the alternatives mentioned above. For when we inquire about the Son’s substance, and you do not admit that he was substantially begotten from the Father, you undoubtedly maintain that he was made from nothing, since we say that even corruptible creatures came into existence only because God both willed to bring them forth through his ineffable dispensation and was able to do so through his singular power—since we know both that he had the will by which it pleased God to act and the power by which the Lord is able to act.”

**Felicianus:** “Then the Father’s power is not sufficient for the Son’s existence?”

**Augustine:** “As though I were arguing about the Father’s power rather than about the truth of fatherhood itself! Did he prefer to be called the Father of one whom he wished to be like creatures rather than like himself? Therefore you must confess that the Son came into existence from the Father’s substance if he is both begotten and God; or else deny both that he is Son and that he is God, if he was created not from the Father’s substance but from nothing, by the Father’s will and power alone operating, just as in the case of the other creatures.”

**Felicianus:** “Since you compel me by necessity to make such a confession, I shall not conceal what is customarily said by our elders. They say that the Son is a creature, but a perfect one, able to rule over all creatures.”

**Augustine:** “I rejoice that you have exposed by an open confession the innermost poison of your irreligious doctrine. Yet you offer nothing that appears worthy of belief. A creature is the substance of any corruptible thing, made, insofar as it depends upon itself, by the will of almighty God from that which either does not yet exist or at some time did not exist. Let us see whether this definition applies to the Son of God.

“The Son, in what he is, proceeded through the truth of an undifferentiated nature, because he was born from one who is—that is, from the begetter—without being unlike him. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, the first distinction between the Son and a creature is this: the Son is substantially begotten from the Father, whereas a creature is brought to completion not from the substance of its maker but by will and power alone.

“The creature is corruptible by nature unless preserved by grace. The Son is incorruptible, appearing by his birth to possess substance from the incorruptible Father. The Son is entirely like the Father; the creature is unlike its maker. The Son did not come from what is not into what is, and therefore from what is he never returns to what is not. The creature comes from what is not into what is and therefore, insofar as it depends upon itself, returns by the condition of its origin from what is into what is not.”

## Chapter Nine

**Felicianus:** “I do not see what you are wrapping in the secret recesses of this obscurity. Therefore you will do well to explain more intelligibly what, as I think, you have stated incomprehensibly.”

**Augustine:** “I spoke about the Son when I distinguished him from the definition of a creature: ‘If he did not come from what is not into what is’—which is equivalent to saying that he was not made from nothing. ‘And therefore he will never return from what is into what is not’—that is, he will never be dissolved from what he is into nothingness by the property of his nature.

“But the creature comes from what is not into what is. This shows that it was brought forth from nothing. And therefore, insofar as it depends upon itself, it must be changed from what is into what is not—that is, into nothingness—by the quality of its nature, unless perpetual grace preserves it.

“Therefore the Son will never not exist, since he is taught to be substantially perpetual; and for this reason, as something proper to him, he is rightly understood to be separated from the condition of all creatures, which were made through him.”

**Felicianus:** “Although you strike at my understanding with this new subtlety about things, I nevertheless do not know how you can say that the Son is coeternal with the Father, since both common usage and the law of nature appear to make the begetter prior to the begotten.”

## Chapter Ten

**Augustine:** “If we judge the author of nature according to the laws of creatures, and proclaim the Father to be prior to the Son, why should we not by the same law of nature say that the Son becomes stronger than the Father through the addition of time, since the one being born is not without increase, while old age inflicts the injury of weakness upon the Father?

“But if reason itself does not accept this, let us set aside in God the law of bodily understanding, lest we say that the maker is like his works. Especially since, from what is evident among us, we can also demonstrate what is hidden. Just as a mother gave birth, without an example to follow, to her own creator, so the Father must be believed ineffably to have begotten the Son who is coeternal with him.

“He who already existed was born from a mother; he who was never absent was born from the Father. Let faith believe this; let understanding not demand an explanation, lest, on the one hand, it consider unbelievable what it has not discovered, or, on the other, refuse to believe what it has discovered because it is unique.

“For Christ was born from a mother, yet the mother’s modesty was not diminished by the touch of a man. A virgin gave birth because a virgin conceived; and without preserving the ordinary order of things, Christ assumed an integral body from the mother’s integral body. If, therefore, according to a new custom and without precedent, he is taught to have been born bodily according to the flesh, what wonder is it if he proceeded from the Father not according to the ordinary manner of human birth?

“The son begotten from the mother alone did not diminish her substance, and we know that the body of the son was born without harm to the body of the one giving birth. Is it then believed that the incorporeal substance of the Father was diminished when the Son is said to have proceeded substantially and incorporeally from the Father himself and to have been begotten?

“Therefore, if we weigh the nature of things under the guidance of understanding, let us grant a beginning if we do not deny an end. Otherwise, let us say that the Son has no beginning for this reason: because we confess him to be perpetual not by grace but by nature.

“In summary, ‘greater’ and ‘lesser’ can be said in three ways: by age, by form, or by power, when one is stronger than the weak. Let us see whether any of these applies to the Son. He is not lesser in age, since it is established that he existed as the beginning from the Father who is the beginning; nor in form, since it is not lawful to proclaim him anything other than God; nor in power, since we know that all things have been perfected through him.”

## Chapter Eleven

[Col. 0340D]

**Felicianus:** “I want to know how the Father’s dignity passes to the Son but the lowliness of the offspring does not return to the Father.”

**Augustine:** “Everyday examples of things teach us that these matters are not now being spoken of according to nature. Let us suppose that a king and the king’s son put aside the insignia of royal majesty, assume the clothing of a subordinate soldier, and, for a definite purpose of the father and for the safety of their companions, endure the insults of rebels. Since it is certain that participation in royal power passes by birth to the son, does injury to the son therefore certainly reach the one who begot him—not through compassionate feeling for the son, but through the very property of suffering?

“It is not so, because the son is certainly born from the father, not the father from the son. Therefore we say that everything between them which concerns communion of nature is similar, while that which is known to have happened accidentally to one person is proper to that person.

“Thus, by being born, the Son has everything with the Father that the Father is, but the Father does not have it from the Son. Whatever the Son himself suffered in a particular way is not common to both. That he was born human from a human being is a special accident—something that, generally speaking, neither is taught to possess in the other without prejudice to their common nature.

“There is one substance of the Father and one person. When this substance begot, what proceeded from it is certainly known not to have been different but another: it is taught to be nothing other than the first, since it is both common and proper. Common, I say, through unity of substance; proper through distinction of person.

“Since the one who was born exists in himself, whatever has happened to him does not necessarily pass to the begetter, just as whatever is proper and substantial to the begetter evidently passes to the one being born. For just as the Father’s divinity was conferred upon the Son by generation itself, so illness, poverty, death, and the lowliness of the Son are not referred back to the Father.

“This does not happen because, although the Son was born similar from one substance—that is, from the Father’s substance—he already exists in himself; therefore whatever is imposed upon him inwardly is not called common but proper to him.

“If this is the condition of the human race, when the substance of sons has never been changed so completely from the one who begot them into something else that it could not remain the same yet another, while the common nature nevertheless remains despite many accidental qualities in the son, what should we believe worthy of God and his Son? What ought we to proclaim?

“Although their nature is not different according to the simple glory of undivided majesty, a body was specially assumed by the Son so that he might be humbled in the weakness of our flesh—he who could suffer nothing in the common substance of divinity. A human being, the son of a human being, did not assume another nature. And although he suffers in the same nature that he shares with the Father, he does not transmit the injury to the Father.

“Nor is God the Father believed to have been passibly humbled in the Son, since the Son is believed to have endured the faithlessness of the Jews not in the very nature common to both, but rather in our nature, which he alone assumed.

“In summary, what, I ask, was hanging on the cross? What was pierced by the spear? Was it susceptible flesh, or the substance of divinity? If you as an impious preacher attribute this to the majesty of the incorporeal one, you appear to believe in a corruptible God. If it was susceptible flesh, then this flesh is not common with the Father, so that the cross could affect him through it.”

## Chapter Twelve

**Felicianus:** “Since you sweep away everything we have said as though in a torrent, you proclaim two Christs rather than one. And rightly so: for if the divinity suffered nothing whatsoever in him, Christ according to the human being was another; otherwise, through the participation of the common divinity, the suffering itself also reached the Father.”

**Augustine:** “It is not so. I neither confuse nor divide our Savior. I do not confuse him, lest I proclaim either an incorporeal and imaginary flesh or a carnal and mortal divinity. I do not separate him, lest I seem to introduce one offspring of God the Father according to the flesh and another according to majesty. For the same Son of God proceeded without beginning from the Father and deigned to be born in time from the Virgin.

“He is impassible in what is his own and suffered in what is ours, when he deigned to clothe his incomprehensible majesty as though in a garment of flesh. From both there is one person of the mediator, not one substance. One person, I say, lest Christ not be one; not one substance, lest, once the mediator’s dispensation had been removed, he be called either God alone or the Son of man.

“I therefore do not extend the assumed flesh in Christ through the perpetuity of the divine generation, nor do I confine the immeasurable divinity within the age of bodily birth. For the same one is the author of creation in divinity who is the Redeemer of human beings in the flesh; the same one is impassible in himself who suffered in the body.

“Thus, while truly expressing the property of each nature, he was born like the begetter from both, so that it is established both that he assumed true flesh from his mother and that he possesses undifferentiated divinity from the Father.

“When these were joined into one person through the incomprehensible dispensation of the mediator, he preserved what was proper to each while joining to each what belonged to the other. He preserved what was proper, since he did not lose the immensity of divinity and did not reject the weakness of flesh. He joined to what was proper what belonged to the other, since the same and inseparable Christ is killed by what is proper to flesh and is not held in the underworld by what is proper to divinity.

“By what is proper to flesh, life tasted death; by what is proper to divinity, he restored flesh to perpetual life. Therefore it is not rightly said that the Father suffered in the Son, since the Son suffered in flesh that is not common to him and the Father.

“Thus the flesh was glorified by majesty, while majesty is taught to have been humbled in the flesh. Yet both things are proclaimed not of two Christs, as you think, but of one and the same Christ, whom we know after the Virgin’s childbirth to be God and man.”

## Chapter Thirteen

**Felicianus:** “If Christ was born from a virgin, how is he said to be coeternal with God the Father?”

**Augustine:** “On this matter we also have a different dispute with others; therefore, so that the explanation of the truth may not be more difficult, let us first set forth the cause of the error. For, beginning from one principle of evil belief, two, so to speak, ravings of divergent understanding arise.

“The two groups have this in common: they proclaim one birth of Christ, not two. But some accept as the defining doctrine of their sect that principal birth by which God was born God from God before all things; others accept only this birth by which the Lord proceeded from the Virgin, and through the consequence of a badly sown seed they have fallen into an abyss of similar blasphemy.
