“For behold: those who do not believe that he was born from the Virgin overturn, as though blinded by Jewish unbelief, the entire faith of the Gospels, the entire benefit of baptism, the entire preaching of the apostles, and, in short, the entire authority of the New Testament. Therefore they must not even be thought to have recognized the majesty of the Son of God, because they rejected the mystery of the mediator by which the Father willed him to be made known to the nations.

“But those who contend that he was born not from the Father before every beginning but in time from the Virgin’s childbirth have not learned that he is creator of all things, nor that he is Lord, like the Father in omnipotence and majesty.

“For how will he be thought to have made all things before whose birth it is certain that the universe already existed? Or how is his divinity to be professed if individual things were made before he was born? Or how is his divinity believed to be perpetual when it is proclaimed to have come into being not always, as the Father’s did, but in time?

“Thus these people too, in a certain sense, deny the mystery of the mediator by the necessity of the consequences of their position. They proclaim Christ not as God and man; not as from eternity but from time; not as from power but from weakness; not as the Son like the Father, born from the Father before all things, but as a son of man from his mother among all things—not a true but an imaginary son of man, born manifestly rather than through likenesses of truth.

“Consequently, they must not even be thought to know God in the flesh, since they do not think that he was begotten from the Father before assuming flesh.”

## Chapter Fourteen

You see, then, how among these people, although their intervening positions differ, the same beginning and the same outcome of error are nevertheless taught. We, on the contrary, defend both births in such a way that neither is destroyed by the affirmation of the other.

“We neither condemn the temporal birth by the perpetuity of the former, nor confine the eternal birth by the brevity of the temporal latter. We know the inseparable offspring of the true God and, afterward, the utterly real flesh of this true offspring.

“We do not say that Christ’s divinity began when the Virgin conceived; nor that the flesh began when that *monas* (‘unit’), by an ineffable birth and without an intervening interval of time, begot a *monas* differing in nothing except that it is taught to be a *monas*.

“His omnipotent majesty did not shrink from Christ’s voluntary weakness, nor did bodily weakness extinguish his omnipotence. I know that the divinity of the Son of God descended to the underworld through the property of flesh; I know that flesh ascended to heaven through the merit of divinity.

“It is not proper to God that he felt hunger; but it is proper to God that he satisfied so many thousands of people with a few loaves. It is not proper to flesh that he walked on dry feet over raging waves; but it is proper to flesh that he endured spittle, blows, and scourges.

“Yet the Christ who endured insults so many times and did not sink his limbs into the depths is one and the same. In this way, in the mediator of God and human beings, I confess that the divinity was affected by the injury inflicted upon his body, just as we know that the flesh was glorified by the majesty of divinity.

“Therefore Christ died—the one who also rose again; yet the two things did not arise from one nature, but each from its own. In both, however, the same perfect Christ completed everything, when the one and inseparable Christ completed such different things: by one nature he tasted death; by the other he raised the dead.

“Thus the true mediator, God and man, showed himself to be both without a doubled person and without a confused substance. The Son of God entered the Virgin’s womb so that he might be born again, though he had already been born; and he assumed the whole human being, though he already possessed from the Father complete divinity.

“He was not unlike his begetter when, eternal in his own nature, he was born; he was not unlike human beings when, born from his mother, he was destined to die. Yet he is the same, eternal in what is his own and destined to die in what is ours, since he contains both from himself and loses neither through the other.

“Thus Christ was born from God and man, not imperfect but utterly complete in the distinct properties of each, just as every human being is taught to be one perfect being from soul and body.

“One person is not a body and another a soul, although the soul is one thing and the body another; nevertheless the same one human being is taught to consist of both body and soul. Again, body and soul are not one and the same thing, since one human being is made from both.

“For these things neither confuse substance in the truth of the person nor double the person through diversity of substance, since one human being is known to have come into existence from them. They do not lose what is proper to each; but because they came together into one and inseparable whole, what is common appears to have been made from what is proper to each.

“The mind is affected in the body by bodily pains, and the body is wearied by the thoughts of the mind; yet one of these is proper to the body and the other to the mind. When this occurs in one human being, it appears common both to the body and to the mind.

“Thus after the Virgin’s childbirth there was not one Christ who was God and another who was man; rather, the same Christ was Son of God and son of man. And just as in one human being the soul is one thing and the body another, so in the mediator of God and human beings the Son of God was one thing and the son of man another; yet the Lord Christ was one from both.

“Different, I say, in the distinction of substance; not another, because of the unity of person.”

## Chapter Fifteen
[Col. 0344C] Felix. In the preceding discussion you compelled me to believe in Christ’s birth from his mother while preserving his eternity. But since, contrary to reason, things that arise through the force of an operation cannot be continuous within us, when I now look attentively into my proposition, I still do not seem to have found in what you have said the answer I seek. For I do not know how you can teach that one was born in time whom you say had already been coeternal with the Father. To be born is, as it were, a movement of something that did not exist before it was born, by which, through the benefit of birth, it comes to be. From this it follows that Christ, who existed, could not have been born; and if he could be born, he did not exist.

Augustine. You compel us to investigate incomprehensible matters with the novel curiosity of your questions. Therefore what you ask can be explained only through certain outlines of examples [Col. 0344D]. Permit me, then, to introduce, as an established premise, a matter belonging to another question. Since I am now presenting it not for its own truth but to illustrate another matter, do not suppose that I am explaining in it what I believe; rather, for the present, assume that I believe it, so that you may more easily understand what I shall say.

Let us suppose, as many wish, that there is in the world a universal soul which, by an ineffable movement, gives life to all seeds, so that it is not physically compounded with the things it brings forth, but itself gives life to those that are to be generated. Certainly, when this soul enters the womb in order to shape the passible material according to its purposes, it makes the thing whose substance is admittedly not identical with its own into one person with itself. Thus, while the soul acts and matter suffers, one human being arises from two substances [Col. 0345A], since the soul is one thing and the flesh another. In this way we confess that the soul is born from the womb, although we say that, coming to the womb, it bestowed life upon the conceived child.

It is said to be born from its mother because from her it fashioned for itself a body in which it could be born—not because, before it was born, it had in itself utterly not existed. Here, if you attend carefully to the force of the words and to ordinary speech, we propose contradictory things and proclaim things that oppose one another; yet in these very statements the truth of what we say is evident. We know that the soul is born from the mother’s womb together with the body, but we also see that the soul is declared to have preceded the mother. In the son, the mother gives birth to a mind, yet even in the mother herself nothing but a soul lives; without that soul, she herself could not exist who gave birth.

Therefore, if we inquire into the origin of the power that gives life, the soul precedes the mother, and yet appears to have been born again from her together with her offspring. The soul, I say, is prior, through which the mother is animated; the mother is prior, through whom the soul too appears to have been born in the son. But the mother did not turn the soul into flesh, nor did she change flesh into soul. Rather, the Creator of the same flesh and soul, and of the whole human being, brought forth from the mother’s womb flesh endowed with life—flesh, soul, and the whole human being—who, through the ordered joining of diverse things, united both in one and the same human being by an indissoluble bond, without confusing either with the participation of the other.

## CHAPTER XVI

Thus, or rather in a manner far more incomprehensible and sublime, the Son of God was born through the assumption from his mother of a perfect human being. Through his unique omnipotence he is, for all things that are begotten, not merely the capacity but also the cause of birth [Col. 0345C]. God, I say, was born from the Virgin according to the human being, in the same way in which the soul is taught to be born together with the body—not because the substance of both is one, but because one person is formed from both. The body is not one human being and the soul another; rather, body and soul are one human being.

Thus, after the Virgin’s giving birth, there was not one Son of God and another son of man, but the same Christ, Son of God and of man. And just as, in one human being, the body is one thing and the soul another, so, in one Mediator, the Son of God is one thing and the son of man another. Yet he is the same Son, and not one Son of God and another son of man, although he is Son of God for one reason and son of man for another.

We do not say that the Son of God began with the flesh, lest anyone believe the deity to be temporal. Nor do we understand the flesh of the Son of God as existing from eternity, lest we think that he assumed not the reality of a human body but some semblance of one [Col. 0345D]. For the reality of the flesh does not consume the majesty of the Son of God, nor does the immensity of the deity consume the reality of the flesh, while one is manifested by its own powers and the other is taught through our weaknesses.

Christ, one and inseparable, is humbled in what he assumed and glorified in what properly belongs to him. He does not disdain to be affected by insults, yet he preserves equality with his Begetter.

Mary therefore gave birth to the Son of God and did not give birth to the Son of God. She gave birth when Christ was born from her according to the flesh; she did not give birth when the Son existed without beginning from the Father. She gave birth when the Word proceeded from her as flesh in order to dwell among us; she did not give birth when, in the beginning, the Word was God, the one who gave origin to all things.

Do not, then, determine the origin of God the Word by the Virgin’s childbirth [Col. 0346A]. Do not call the body born from the Virgin coeternal with the deity, because the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), is coeternal with the Father in his first birth and, in his second, a participant in our time. In the first, he is the author of time; in the second, he shares our age.

## CHAPTER XVII

Felix. Since you have treated the mystery of the Mediator with clear reasoning, and sufficiently for anyone to believe, I therefore ask you to explain what we ought also to think about Christ’s soul. Our elders have always handed down the teaching that Christ’s body was animated in place of an ordinary soul by the indwelling of the Son of God himself, and that he did not need the addition of a life-giving spirit, since the fountain of life dwelling within him could grant that it lived.

[Col. 0346B] Augustine. We could indeed instruct you, through testimonies from the divine books, in what the definition of catholic authority prescribes concerning this question. But since for the present it has pleased us to examine everything by reason alone, rather than by the testimony of books, reserving the evidence of Scripture for another time—as was done above—we shall likewise investigate the soul [349]. To make this easier, let us briefly inquire, using only one passage from the Apostle, what the reason was that our Savior assumed a human being. Once this has been established, we shall pass without difficulty to the consequences that follow from this preceding matter.

From the beginning, then, God made the human being from body and soul. After transgressing the commandments of the law and taking possession of the forbidden tree, the human being incurred, in a certain sense, the sentence of capital punishment [Col. 0346C]. He could return to the condition from which he had fallen only after being restored by the grace of his Creator, as though by a right of return. Someone who has deliberately thrown himself headlong from a height had the power to do what he did, but what falls is no longer subject to his own decision.

Thus the one who fell by his own act rises through another’s benefit. Yet he is not for that reason to be said not to have fallen by his own act because he is known to rise through another; nor is he for that reason to be said to have risen by his own act because it is certain that he did not fall through another. But this belongs elsewhere; let us now return to the subject.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The venerable Paul says, then, that Christ was born according to the flesh for this reason:

> “Just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

And shortly afterward:

> “But the gift is not like the trespass. For if the many died through the trespass of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ, abound for the many. And the gift is not like what came through one sin: for judgment came from one trespass to condemnation, but grace came from many trespasses to justification. For if death reigned through one person because of one person’s trespass, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification unto life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous” [Col. 0347A].

Christ therefore came to save what had perished (Luke 19:10). Let us first see, then, what it was that perished through the transgression of the first human being [350]; then we shall easily know what the Lord was able to save by coming.

We must therefore ask who received the Creator’s law. That person undoubtedly sinned, because he despised the commandments; and he despised the commandments who did what had been forbidden. Scripture says:

> “The Lord commanded Adam, saying: ‘You shall eat from every tree that is in paradise; but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. On the day on which you eat from it, you shall die by death’” (Gen. 2:16).

Let us ask, then, whether the whole human being received this law [Col. 0347B]. For if, as the book of Genesis records, the human being already perfected from body and soul received it, the whole human being sinned by transgressing; and if the whole human being sinned by transgressing, the whole human being then perished through the fault of sin. But if the whole human being perished, the whole human being needed the Savior’s benefit. And if the whole human being needed the Savior’s benefit, Christ saved the whole human being by coming. If he saved the whole human being by coming, he assumed not a body without a soul, but body and soul, from which the whole human being consists and through which he had previously sinned.

For if, when the whole human being sinned, Christ assumed only the person’s flesh, the soul would remain even now condemned to the punishment of that first transgression, without any hope. If this is so, I do not know what the person of the Mediator has brought us: instead of redeeming us wholly, he would have assumed brute flesh by itself, flesh that, without a soul, could not even experience his benefit [Col. 0347C].

## CHAPTER XIX

I should nevertheless like to ask such preachers why, after assuming flesh, the Mediator’s dispensation omitted the soul. Perhaps, knowing it to be innocent, he did not believe it needed medicine; or, thinking it alien to himself, he did not grant it the benefit of redemption; or, judging it altogether incurable, he was unable to heal it; or, rejecting it as worthless and apparently fit for no purpose, he cast it aside.

Two of these alternatives, through the incredulity of a blasphemous spirit, lead to madness against the Creator of the whole human being. In the first case they believed him incapable; in the second, not God of all. For how is he taught to be omnipotent if he could not heal what was considered beyond hope? Or how is he God of all if he himself did not make our soul? [Col. 0347D]

In the other two alternatives, the cause of the soul is unknown in one case, and its worth is denied in the other. Should we think that someone understands the soul’s purpose who strives to separate from sin by voluntary transgression the soul that, in order to receive the law, was endowed with the form of implanted reason? Or how can someone know its nobility who says that it was despised because of the defect of ignobility, while preferring flesh, which is admittedly formed not by God’s breath like the soul but from the clay of the earth?

Since none of these views about the soul is correct, let us believe that our Redeemer assumed the whole human being, lest the everlasting benefit of our soul seem in some way to perish.

Alas! they say: “Christ assumed flesh alone; he did not seek the soul.” If you, a thoughtful observer acquainted with the origin of both, consider the matter, the substance of the soul is more precious; if you consider the guilt of transgression, its condition is worse because of its understanding.

I know Christ to be perfect in wisdom, and I do not doubt that he is most compassionate. By the first quality he did not despise what was better and capable of understanding; by the second he assumed what had been more deeply wounded. For it is not consistent with wisdom to love more what is most foolish among two things equally one’s own, nor with perfect compassion not to help what is more in need.

## CHAPTER XX

Felix. I admit that I have understood everything you have said previously—not only rationally but also truthfully—and I do not deny that I have approved it. But I do not know in what manner Christ’s divinity is said to have experienced death [Col. 0348B]. Whether you have spoken obscurely about this, or whether, because of the slowness of my understanding, I have been unable to grasp what was sufficiently expressed, I do not know.

For I would not dare to believe that the fountain of life, from which all things have what enables them to live, during the three days in which the body lay in the tomb fell so far from the property of its nature that—if it is lawful to say so—having buried its senses, it lost all movement of its life-giving substance; and that, for the redemption of the human race, it abandoned not only the Father but also all the ornaments of spiritual glory.

Augustine. Far be such a suspicion from the faithful—far be it—that Christ experienced our death in such a way as to lose life, insofar as that depended on him. For if this were so, how can we say that anything could have lived during those three days, if we believe that the fountain of life had dried up?

Christ’s divinity therefore experienced death through participation in the human feeling that he had voluntarily assumed; it did not lose the power of its own nature, through which it gives life to all things. In the tomb he did not abandon his flesh while dying with it, just as in the Virgin’s womb he formed it by being born with it [Col. 0348C]. In both cases the Lord willed to be born and to die, not compelled by another but voluntarily, so that it may be clear that he endured what he himself accomplished: not therefore not suffering because he himself was acting, nor therefore not acting because someone else was not enduring it.

For if you consider the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation while preserving the cooperation of the undivided Trinity, the same person is both author and work in this humility. He is the author because he is born voluntarily and suffers voluntarily; he is the work because, although no other compels either event, he alone endures both.

He made the flesh in his mother’s womb: you have the author of the work. He himself deigned to be born in that flesh: you have the work of the author. Yet there is one person, while the distinct property of each substance—the author and the work—is preserved.

Thus he died without life departing, just as he suffered without power perishing. “No one takes his soul from him, because he has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up” (John 10:18). Here you have the author of the work. “He lays down his soul for his friends”: you have the work of the author.

To summarize this by a general definition: whenever Christ suffers anything in the flesh, it is the work of the author. But because he endures that very thing by his own power, without another compelling him, he himself is the author of the work.

## CHAPTER XXI

The deity therefore did not come to Mary by a movement through space [Col. 0349A], but, by the manifestation of his ineffable power, filled the womb in which he was to be born and did not deprive the whole of the fullness of his substance. He did not leave the Father when he came to the Virgin.

He was wholly everywhere and perfect everywhere, because incorporeal simplicity admits no division, and fullness knows no parts. Thus, at one and the same time, he was wholly in the underworld and wholly in heaven: there suffering injury in the flesh, here not abandoning the glory of the deity. In the realm below he was the resurrection of the dead; above the heavens, the life of the living.

Truly dead and truly alive: in him the assumption of mortality underwent death, while the preserved deity did not lose life [353]. Therefore, whenever you consider the things Christ humbly endured, recognize him as the author of his voluntary passion. In this way, while humility is attributed to the one who suffers and power to the one who acts, the same Christ is shown to be weak when he suffers and omnipotent when he acts, at one and the same time [Col. 0349B].

But lest you still think that we attribute any insensibility to the death of the Son of God, it is not irrelevant to investigate what is meant by death. In death, without doubt, our life abandons the body but does not perish. When the soul departs, it does not lose its power; it merely leaves what it had made alive. Insofar as it depends on the soul, it itself causes the death of another; it does not receive death.

It causes death, I say, not by giving life to what it abandons, but by not losing what lives. Thus human death is nothing other than the setting of the flesh. When the power of the life-giving force has departed from it, the flesh returns to the earth from which it was taken, having lost those senses that it did not possess by itself.

## CHAPTER XXII

“But,” you say, “death is contrary to life.” I admit it, but it is not among those contraries that destroy one another through the opposition of existing substances. Rather, it belongs to those things that, when they affect something, cannot exist together, but arise through the possession and privation of one substance.

For example, we teach that night and day are contraries. They are said to be contraries of the same kind, although the substance appears to belong not to both but only to one. We say that it is day when the sun is above the earth; and it is certain that the sun is a substance. When, after completing the course of the day, the sun withdraws from human sight, by departing it immediately makes night. It makes night, I say, by withdrawing the supply of light, not by receiving the substance of night into itself [Col. 0349D].

Thus one substance of light appears to make both night and day, but not in the same way. When it comes, it makes day; when it departs, it makes night.

For this reason we often refute the Manichaeans’ not merely irreligious but also foolish division, by which they strive to separate good and evil as equally existing substances. We point out to them the greater luminary by which we know day to be made and compel them likewise to explain what, if it is lawful to say so, the greater darkness might be by which they would believe night to be substantially made.

But this belongs elsewhere: they appear, through the folly of their blasphemous doctrine, to affirm either non-existent things in place of existing ones, consequences in place of principles, or common things in place of contraries. Anyone who examines these matters with the eyes of faith, without being deprived of them, easily overturns all their devices [Col. 0350A].

Therefore, as we began to say, the soul gives life to the flesh in the same way as the sun: when it comes, it gives life; when it departs, it causes death. But lest anyone think that the soul is consumed by the body’s death, let him hear how the Lord defines this matter with general authority in the Gospels:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

Thus, while the soul survives, the body is nevertheless shown to be killed; and consequently it is neither necessary nor inevitable that souls be consumed by the destruction of bodies. If this is so, minds live even after the body’s death. If this is correctly believed of each of us, how can it be asserted that the fountain of life lost its power to give life through participation in a human mind?

“But,” you say, “the soul and body can be killed in the fire of Gehenna.” This does not first work against us because that death appears to belong not to nature but to guilt. Once guilt has been removed, we are commanded not to fear human beings who, although they can kill the body, are nevertheless said to be unable to kill the soul.

Furthermore, since this is said to be possible only for God, we do not believe that the one whom we believe to be his only-begotten Son, sharing his nature and equal in power, deserved such a fate. The Savior therefore assumed the condition of our death, but not in such a way as to make it worse when, as its Lord and contrary to custom, he allowed it to affect the soul. Rather, he did so to demonstrate that it could in no way harm either the soul or the life of all the righteous.

## CHAPTER XXIII

But let us suppose—although the Gospels protest the contrary—that souls perish. Does not our Savior possess, even though he did not repel death in these matters, a third and unique majesty that human death could not affect?

Let us consider, above all, what he promised while hanging on the cross:

> “Today,” he said, “you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

“Today,” he said—not after three days, when I shall raise my flesh from the rest of the tomb; not when I shall display in myself the first fruits of the future resurrection [355].

Whose voice do we think this is: the voice of the majesty, the mind, or the body? No one is unaware that the body was in the grave. It remains, then, that this voice belongs either to the deity or to the mind.

But someone says: “We believe this to be the voice of the deity, not of Christ’s soul.” What, then, do we understand the one to whom the promise was made to receive? “Today,” he says to the thief, “you will be with me in paradise”—although common death enclosed the thief’s body until the future resurrection.

It is therefore the soul to which the Lord made and fulfilled this promise. If, then, after the body’s death the soul is immediately called to paradise, can we still believe anyone so impious as to dare say that our Savior’s soul, during those three days of bodily death, was confined in the underworld under guard?

“And who else,” you ask, “was it who, as Christ’s passion approached, groaned, saying: ‘My soul is sorrowful unto death’” (Matt. 26:38)? It was sorrowful unto death because of the feeling of the flesh he had assumed, not after death, when the fellowship of the deity promised blessedness. This death is not the beginning of grief but its end. Nor do the scourges of the righteous begin after it; rather, they cease, when they both set aside the impediments of fluctuating matter [Col. 0351A] and already grasp their author through the contemplation of fuller understanding.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Then,” you ask, “did the Son of God endure death neither in the soul nor experience it in his majesty?” What, then, did you say he endured?

He certainly experienced and endured it, but through participation in an alien disease, not through the property of his own wound. He experienced it as do all who live in mind while the flesh dies, not as the impious do, who, as the same person says, are destroyed by the fires of Gehenna in both respects.

Some define common death in this way also: they say that it is nothing other than a separation, as though by some dissension, of things that had formed life through the agreement of diverse elements. If this is human death—that it does not consume joined things but divides them, while restoring each to its origin—what shall we now say about the Savior’s soul, which, not to mention the indwelling deity and his unique righteousness, certainly by reason of the common lot of dying could leave the body during those three days without itself being utterly destroyed?

“Then,” you ask, “were neither Christ’s soul nor his divinity in the underworld?”

They were, I say. For I cannot otherwise see how he could have raised his flesh if I were to assert that, in the underworld, there was no power of the absent God. Yet let no one therefore think that we teach a spatial presence of God. We say these things because of the manifestation of a definite work: he was somewhere, just as one who was absent nowhere [Col. 0351C–0352A].

As far as the flesh was concerned, he lay dead in the tomb; in the underworld he raised the dead; in heaven he gave life to all. He did not leave the world when he ascended to heaven, nor did he abandon heaven when he came to earth. Rather, at one and the same time he filled everything wholly, being wholly present. In one place, through the manifestation of his works, he appeared more clearly, and he withheld recognition of his presence from the unworthy; he did not thereby produce an absence of his immeasurable deity.

## CHAPTER XXV

“Do you wish to know,” you ask, “what I think about this death of the Mediator?”

This is the complete position that follows from all the questions scattered through the preceding discussion by necessity: I believe that the Son of God died, not according to the punishment of injustice, which he did not possess at all, but according to the law of nature, which he assumed for the redemption of the human race.

It was the death of which it is said:

> “Who is the human being who shall live and shall not see death?” (Ps. 88:49 [89:48])

—not the death of which Isaiah says:

> “But the dead shall not see life” (Isa. 26:14).

It was the death that is common to all according to nature, not the death that is peculiar to the wicked.

Let us suppose, then, that this is, in a certain sense, the force and power of the seed: through it the soul restores souls, and through the flesh of all of us, when judgment is imminent, he raises our flesh. While giving life to all things through the operation of his own deity, from the single grain of the human being he assumed he will return an innumerable harvest to the Father. Then he will separate the crop from the weeds (Matt. 13:30), when he begins to repay the righteous with their reward.

[Col. 0351C]

## THREE BOOKS OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSUS AGAINST MARIVADUS THE ARIAN DEACON, UNDER THE NAME OF IDACIUS CLARUS, AGAINST VARIMADUS. (G,S)*

[Col. 0351]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0351C] 357 Previously, beloved brothers, while I was staying in Naples, a city of Campania, I composed in a single work some brief treatises on the unity of the Trinity, responding in rustic speech to the propositions of a certain Varimadus, a deacon of the Arian sect, which had been brought to me by a certain zealous and most religious man [Col. 0351D].

But since we have now learned that they do not wish their propositions to be opposed by private words alone, but rather desire their propositions to be attacked by the force of testimonies, we have adapted our response, with the help of the Holy Spirit, to all their objections by means of testimonies, taking into account those of modest ability and slower understanding. Thus the reader may refute them not with bare words, as they customarily object, but with authoritative scriptural proofs.

In this way they may be convicted and confounded on every side, and reduced to nothing—those who strive to construct such fabrications upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles. Since this building is compared not with gold and silver or precious stones, but with wood, hay, and straw, when it is consumed by fire on the last day, according to the Apostle’s statement (1 Cor. 3:13), it must suffer loss in its own work [358]. For people of this kind can scarcely be turned away from the course of a depraved doctrine and made to pursue better things, because they have increased the audacity of their presumptuous spirit to such an extent that they will never reach the truth of faith at all.

They could attain brotherly love and hold perfect faith with Catholics if they boasted of the power of God alone, and not of the pride of unbelieving kings. Therefore, when defenders of the catholic faith begin rightly to constrain them and they see that no place of escape is available to them, they do not cease, with their customary recklessness, to weave together certain artifices of empty words with clever subtlety.

They say that what our Lord and Savior spoke in the Gospels about his deity should be understood by abandoning the path of the divine Scriptures. Through various interpretations they refer everything to the substance of the flesh, even though they themselves, in the very words he spoke—“The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); “He himself sent me”; and “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38); “Let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will” (Luke 22:42)—assert that he cannot be equal to the Father, not in the form of a servant, in which he is human, but in the nature in which he is God; they judge him to be of an inferior substance [Col. 0353A].

They would certainly not say this if they had believed in catholic fashion that the same Son is true God, begotten from true God.

The nature of God, therefore, is neither increased by remaining singular in unity nor diminished by generating the Son from itself. The perfect deity remains continually within itself, and it will also forever be the same as it was in the beginning, before we read that heaven and earth and all the elements received their beginning.

Now, therefore, leaving aside the superfluous and disorderly words that they produce to overthrow the faithful, let us proceed to refute those things that we recognize as having been placed, through the ingenuity of their unbelief, for the destruction of innocent souls [Col. 0353B].

Their statements, then, which they have boldly and recklessly set forth against the unity of the Trinity, must be presented, so that, by adding testimonies to testimonies in due succession, the pride of the faithless may at last be restrained [Col. 0354A].

The ineffable Trinity is powerful enough to provide its worshipers with testimonies concerning the worship owed to it, not only from the Old Testament but also from the New, by which the truth of the catholic faith may be confirmed and the falsity of the Arians destroyed.

I also urge you, reader, to examine with a discerning mind all the proofs gathered from the divine Scriptures against this heresy. Examine especially those placed at the end of this work concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in a threefold conjunction, soberly and attentively. Through them you will undoubtedly be taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one and the same inseparable and everlasting substance [Col. 0354B].

# BOOK ONE. THAT THE SON IS ONE GOD WITH THE FATHER

[Col. 0353]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Trinity

[Col. 0353B]

If they say: “What unity of the Trinity can be taught from the divine readings, when neither three can properly be affirmed to be one, nor one to be in three?”

**Response.** Listen, then, and recognize the unity of the Trinity from these testimonies, and cease following the perversity of the Arians, so that through it you may be able to merit forgiveness of sins, as the prophet Isaiah says:

“I saw the Lord Sabaoth seated upon a lofty throne, and Seraphim stood around him: six wings for one and six wings for the other; with two they veiled their face, with two they veiled their feet, and with two they flew, and they cried out to one another, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Sabaoth’” (Isa. VI).

If there is no Trinity, why did they say “holy” three times? Or if there is no unity, why, under a threefold repetition, did they declare one God and Lord?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Genesis: “God said, God made, God blessed” (Gen. I)? If there is no unity, why did God speak three times, and why did it not commend “gods” in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said three times in Exodus, “Lord, Lord, merciful and compassionate God” (Exod. XXXIV, 6)? If there is no unity, why, while saying “Lord” three times, does it afterwards say “merciful” in the singular, and not “merciful ones,” thereby indicating several?

If there is no Trinity, why did Abraham, openly encountering three seated at the oak of Mamre, address one as “Lord,” and not render the service of greeting to the three whom he had seen (Gen. XVIII)?

If there is no unity, why, when “God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob” was said three times to Moses, did he, indicating unity, say, “This is my name” (Exod. III, 45), and not designate these as names?

If there is no Trinity, why did David say three times, “May God bless us, our God, may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI, 8)? If there is no unity, why, after naming God three times, did he say “may he bless,” and not add “may they bless”?

If there is no Trinity, why did Isaiah say again, “Lord God Sabaoth, God of Israel, who sit upon the cherubim” (Isa. XXXVII, 16)? If there is no unity, why did he say “who sit,” and not assert “you who sit” in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in the Books of Kings, “Lord God almighty, God of Israel, your words are faithful”? If there is no unity, why is “your” said, and not rather “your [plural]”?

If there is no Trinity, why is it sung in the fifty-eighth psalm (verse 6), “Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, attend to visit all the nations”? If there is no unity, why did it say “attend,” and not “attend [plural],” as a prayer?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said three times in the Apocalypse, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is, and who was” (Apoc. IV, 8)? If there is no unity, why are “those who are” and “those who were” not designated in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Deuteronomy, “The Lord your God is merciful; he will hear your voice” (Deut. IV, 31)? If there is no unity, why did it say “he will hear,” and not indicate “they will hear”?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in the book of Joshua, “The Lord God is God of gods” (Jos. II, 11)? If there is no unity, why did it say “is,” and not, according to the manner of speech, “they are”?

If there is no Trinity, why did Elijah say in prayer, “Lord, Lord God of Israel, show that you are my God” (III Kings XVIII, 36)? If there is no unity, why did he say “show,” and not “show [plural]”?

If there is no Trinity, why did Mordecai say in prayer, “Lord, Lord almighty God, everything is in your power” (Esther XIII, 9)? If there is no unity, why did he say “in your” power, and not designate it as “in your [plural]” power?

If there is no Trinity, why did Judith also say in prayer, “Lord, Lord God of all powers, look upon my prayer” (Judith IX, 17)? If there is no unity, why did she say “look,” and not indicate “look [plural]”?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Jeremiah, “The Lord your God is the true God” (Jer. X, 10)? If there is no unity, why does it say “the true one is,” and not rather indicate “the true ones”?

If there is no Trinity, why is it written in the Apocalypse, “The Lord God and the Spirit of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place” (Apoc. XXII, 6)? If there is no unity, why, after naming the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, does it say “he sent,” and not, under the wording of three persons, “they sent”?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in Deuteronomy, “The Lord your God, he is God” (Deut. X, 17)? If there is no unity, why did it say “he is,” and not designate “these are” in the plural?

If there is no Trinity, why is it said in the same book, “The Lord your God is a great and powerful God” (ibid.)? If there is no unity, why is it said “great and powerful,” and not named “great and powerful ones” in the plural?

Why is Tobias, when sending his son with the archangel Raphael to the city of Rages, taught to have blessed him in these words: “May the God of Abraham, and the God of Jacob, and the God of Isaac himself fulfill his blessing in you” (Tob. VII, 15)? If there is no unity, why did he say “may he himself fulfill,” and not indicate “may they themselves fulfill”?

Finally, if there is no Trinity, why did the Lord teach his disciples to baptize all nations “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19)? If there is no unity, why did he say “in the name,” and not teach that it was to be understood “in the names”?

If there is no Trinity, why did the apostle Paul say, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36)? If there is no unity, why did he say “from him,” and not establish “from them”?

If you wish with complete certainty to recognize the unity of the Trinity, you can learn everything from the apostle, the often-mentioned teacher of the nations, and follow the catholic faith while rejecting the perversity of the Arians. He says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (II Cor. XIII, 13). For if grace, love, and communion are of the Holy Spirit himself, and of the Father and the Son, how are they not one in the Trinity, since by nature and substance they cannot be separated from one another?

## CHAPTER II. On the Unity of the Father and the Son

If they say to you: How are the Father and the Son one God, since besides the Father there is no other God who is called invisible and unbegotten?

**Response.** As for your unwillingness to confess the Father and the Son as one God, we too show that they were preached by the prophets and apostles as one true God; and from them we also believe that the Holy Spirit is not separate. The prophet Isaiah says:

“I am God, and there is no other besides me. By myself I swear: truth has gone forth from my mouth, and my word will not be withdrawn, because every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will swear by the Lord, saying: ‘Righteousness and glory will come to him’” (Isa. XLV, 22).

And so that you may recognize that the Father and the Son were together in this testimony, listen to the apostle Paul, who says that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the almighty Father” (Phil. II, 10).

But if, according to you, the Son is lesser than his Father, then the Father’s glory in the Son has also been diminished. And where is what Scripture says in Solomon:

“For just as he appeared in their sight, he says, among us, so you will appear in our sight among them, so that they may know you as we have known you, because there is no other God besides you, Lord” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 4)?

Pay careful attention, and recognize that it is the Son who will appear in judgment, when he comes to judge the living and the dead.

Isaiah likewise says:

“Hear, house of Jacob and remnant of Israel, you who come forth from the womb and are instructed from childhood to old age: From the beginning I am, and until you grow old I am. I made, I sustain, I will forgive, I will receive,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVI, 3).

And again:

“I am the Lord God, and there is no other God besides me, declaring the last things before they come to pass, and immediately they were accomplished” (ibid., 9).

Again there:

“Hear me, Jacob and Israel, whom I made: I am the Lord your God, and there is no other besides me.”

Again there:

“I am the Lord God, the first, and I am the last; and in the things that are to come, at the end, I am” (Isa. XLVIII, 12).

Again there:

“I am God, who created you, helped you, and strengthened you with my right hand.”

And Isaiah, assigning the unity of the Father and the Son, says:

“I am your witness, says the Lord God, and my servant whom I chose, so that you may know and believe that I am he. Before me there was no other, and after me there will not be” (Isa. XLIII, 10).

Choose one of two alternatives, O heretic: either confess that the Father and the Son are one God, or, if you insist that the Father alone is God, then for you the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, will not be God, because it is written, “Before me there was no other, and after me there will not be.”

If this is so according to you, why does the Apostle (Rom. IX, 5) proclaim such things and indicate that the same Son is “God over all, blessed forever”? He says: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

Isaiah likewise says:

“The Lord God of Israel, who delivered them from Egypt: I am the first, and I am after these things; and besides me there is no God like me, who will stand and call and prepare for me from the time when I made humankind in the age” (Isa. XLIV, 6).

Again there:

“This is God, and we did not know it, and there is no other God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior” (Isa. XLV, 15).

If the Father and the Son are not one God, who is this God in whom God is said to exist, concerning whom the prophet declares under the number that there is no other God besides him? I ask you, answer.

And Jeremiah says:

“This is our God, and no other will be compared with him, who discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen upon the earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 37).

And in Solomon:

“Have mercy on us, God of all, and show us the light of your mercy; send your fear upon the nations that have not sought you, so that they may know that there is no other God except you” (Ecclus. XXXVI, 1).

Again there:

“Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above or on earth below.”

And in the seventeenth psalm (verse 32):

“For who is God besides the Lord? Or who is God besides our God?”

And in Genesis:

“The Lord rained fire and sulfur from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah, and he overthrew those cities” (Gen. XIX, 24).

If the Father alone is God, who rained fire and sulfur from the Lord in order to overthrow the cities mentioned above? I ask you, answer.

And in Deuteronomy:

“The Lord alone led them, and there was no foreign god with them” (Deut. XXXII, 12).

And the apostle Paul:

“One God, he says, who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. III, 30).

And to the Corinthians:

“God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19).

And again:

“There is no God except one.”

And to the Galatians:

“Now a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (Gal. III, 20).

And, demonstrating the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he confirms it in writing to the Ephesians:

“Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Eph. IV, 3–6).

For if, O heretic, you wish to receive the unity of faith with a simple heart, from this testimony you can learn together the unity of the Father and the Son in the one Spirit.

You have therefore previously placed the Father as properly unbegotten in the divine writings; yet you can neither read this at all nor prove it. But because Christian faith itself demands this, he is believed, without any doubt, to be unbegotten; nevertheless, according to the sequence of the Scriptures, he is shown to have been seen in the Son begotten from him.

## CHAPTER III. On the Statement: “I Did Not Come from Myself, but He Sent Me”

If they say to you that the Son said, “I did not come from myself, but he sent me” (John VIII, 42).

**Response.** The apostle Paul, foreseeing from far earlier the sending of the Son of God in the Holy Spirit, also testified to this when writing to the Roman church:

“For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God did: he sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and, because of sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled” (Rom. VIII, 3–4).

Do you see that the Son was not sent by the Father according to his deity, but according to the flesh, which in his mercy and piety he did not disdain to assume for us?

For, in that he briefly emptied himself of the power of his majesty, the same Son sent the apostle, who testifies and says:

“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. II, 7).

And Isaiah:

“It was not an ambassador or an angel, but the Lord himself who came and saved them” (Isa. XXXV, 4).

Again there:

“I appeared openly to those who were not seeking me” (Isa. LXV, 5).

And Jeremiah:

“I abandoned my house, I left my inheritance, and I came and became a reproach to them” (Jer. XII, 7).

And in Micah:

“Behold, the Lord will come, and the mountains will be shaken beneath him” (Mic. I, 3).

And in Zechariah:

“Rejoice and exult, daughter of Zion, because behold, I am coming and I will dwell in your midst,” says the Lord (Zech. II, 10).

And the Apostle to Timothy:

“This saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (I Tim. I, 15).

And Malachi:

“Behold, suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III, 1).

And in the Gospel:

“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke V, 32).

Again there:

“What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Luke IV, 34).

“The Son of Man came to save and seek what had been lost” (Luke XIX, 10).

Again there:

“I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (John X, 10).

Again there:

“I came in the name of my Father” (John V, 43).

Again there:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

Can you possibly say, in the face of so many and such great testimonies by which the Son testified that he was God from himself, that he came from another and not from himself? It is manifest that he who graciously assumed our flesh came by his own will, and was not sent by another.

For he who, remaining in the Father, abides through the power of his might had no need to be sent by the Father at all, since no part of the ages or of the earth is excluded from the Father’s sight, to which, according to you, the Son would be sent by the Father.

## CHAPTER IV. Where It Is Said, “The Lord Created Me”

If they cite to you that testimony of Solomon, “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22).

**Response.** The apostle Paul does not indicate that Christ was created according to the nature of his deity, but affirms that the same one was created according to the substance of human nature. He himself writes to the Ephesians:

“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new person, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23).

And to the Hebrews:

“For in that which he suffered, having himself been tempted, he is able to assist those who are tempted” (Heb. II, 18).

Therefore, holy brothers, participants in the heavenly calling, “consider the Apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, faithful to him who created him” (Heb. III, 1–2).

And to the Colossians:

“But now you too must put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy. Let no obscene speech proceed from your mouth. Do not lie to one another; strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new one, who is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him” (Col. III, 8–10).

Could the one who, by the power of his own authority, created and made all things—visible and invisible—from nothing have created himself either beforehand or afterward, which it is impious to say? Or could he have done so?

## CHAPTER V. How the Statement “The Father Is Greater Than I” Is to Be Understood

If they cite what the Son said in the Gospel, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

[Col. 0359A] **Response.** The Son is less than the Father in the form of the human being he assumed, but he is equal to the Father in the substance of the nature of deity, as he himself testifies:

“I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

And again:

“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John XIV, 9).

And again:

“So that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John V, 23).

And again:

“Let them be one in us, just as we are one: you in me and I in them” (John XVII, 22).

And again:

“All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (John XVII, 10).

And again:

“All that the Father has is mine” (John XVI, 15).

And again:

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10).

And again:

“The Father, remaining in me, does these works” (ibid.).

And the evangelist John says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

The same apostle says to the Parthians:

“There are three that bear witness on earth: water, blood, and flesh, and these three are in us. And there are three that bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one” (I John V, 7–8).

Therefore, in the nature of deity, in which they are one, we believe in the Father and the Son. We believe neither that the Father preceded the Son at some time, so that he might be greater than the Son, nor that the Son was born later, so that the Father’s deity might be diminished in the Son.

## CHAPTER VI. Where They Say That the Son Is Not Equal to the Father

If they say to you, “The Son is not equal to the Father.”

**Response.** If the Son is not equal to the Father, why did the evangelist John testify concerning him as follows?

“For this reason, he says, the Jews were persecuting Jesus and seeking to kill him: not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John V, 18).

And the apostle Paul:

“Have this mind among yourselves, he says, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he existed in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5).

And in Solomon:

“He who begot me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. XXIV, 12).

And in Isaiah:

“As he was from the beginning, so he is unto the age. Nothing has been added to him, nor will anything be diminished from him. For he is the Lord of his creation, who needed nothing from anyone.”

And in the seventy-second psalm (verse 25):

“For what do I lack in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?”

All these things do not demonstrate a lower nature in the Son, but proclaim equality of deity, since the one who spoke both statements spoke the truth, because truth could not lie.

## CHAPTER VII. Those Who Deny That the Son Has the Father’s Will

If they say to you, “The Son is not the will of the Father.”

**Response.** If you examine the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures with a pure intention of mind, you will undoubtedly find that the Son is coeternal with the Father by nature, everlasting with him in substance, and not separate from him in will, which is one in both. The prophet Isaiah says:

“My salvation will burn like a torch, and all the nations will see your righteousness, and all the kings of the earth your honor; and you will be called by a new name, which the Lord will name” (Isa. LXII, 1).

And below:

“For you will be called ‘My will’” (ibid., 4).

And the Apostle:

“This is the will of God in Christ Jesus” (I Thess. V, 18).

And again:

“In him the entire fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9).

And again:

“For in him all the fullness of deity was pleased to dwell” (Col. I, 19).

And the voice of the Father from the cloud to the disciples:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

If the Son had not been the will of God the Father, how could the Father have been pleased in him? Or how could the fullness of his deity dwell in him, in whom, according to you, the will of God the Father is not held to be present?

## CHAPTER VIII. “I Did Not Come to Do My Own Will, but the Will of Him Who Sent Me”

[Col. 0360B] If they cite what the Lord said in the Gospel: “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John V, 30).

**Response.** This proposition does not require a response in human words, but rather divine testimonies should establish the Son’s own will. The prophet sings in the thirty-ninth psalm (verse 8):

“Then I said: ‘Behold, I come to do your will; my God, I have desired it.’”

And in the twenty-seventh psalm (verse 7):

“In him my heart hoped, and I was helped; my flesh blossomed again, and by my will I will confess to him.”

And again:

“I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8).

And in Deuteronomy:

“Loving you, I have done your will.”

And in the Apocalypse:

“You are worthy, Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, because you created all things, and because of your will they came to be” (Apoc. IV, 11).

And in the Catholic Epistles:

“Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first beginning of his creation” (James I, 18).

From what has been said above, you must therefore recognize that the one who says he willingly did the Father’s will cannot be inferior to him.

## CHAPTER IX. When They Say That God Made Him Lord and Christ

If they set against you what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “God made him Lord and Christ” (Acts II, 36).

**Response.** The Son is not said to have been made according to the nature of his deity, but according to the form of the human being he assumed. The divine utterances testify to this concerning him, as the apostle Paul confirms:

“He had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 2).

The same apostle says to the Galatians:

“When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV, 4).

And to the Philippians:

“Made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II, 7).

And in the thirtieth psalm (verse 11):

“My strength was weakened in poverty, my bones were troubled, and I became a reproach to my enemies.”

Again there (verse 13):

“I was handed over to oblivion like one dead from the heart, and I became like a ruined vessel.”

And in the psalm (LXX, 7):

“I became like a portent to many, but you are my strong helper.”

And in the seventy-second psalm (verse 23):

“I became like a beast before you, yet I am always with you.”

And in the eighty-sixth psalm (verse 5):

“Mother Zion will say: ‘A human being, and a human being was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her.’”

And in the eighty-seventh psalm (verse 7):

“I became like a human being without help, free among the dead.”

And in the one hundred eighth psalm (verse 25):

“I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.”

And in the one hundred first psalm (verse 8):

“I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on a roof.”

And in the Gospel:

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

The Son, therefore, is said to have been made according to the flesh; for according to his divinity he is never read to have been made by the Father, but to have been begotten.

## CHAPTER X. “The Things I Speak, I Speak Just as the Father Told Me”

If they say to you that the Son said, “The things I speak, just as the Father told me, so I speak” (John XII, 50).

**Response.** When the Father speaks, the Son speaks; and when the Son speaks, the Father speaks. That the Father speaks in him is proved by heavenly testimonies, as the apostle Paul attests:

“God, who in many parts and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. I, 1).

And, to show that the same Son spoke apart from a command of the Father, we bring forward a testimony from the book of the prophet Isaiah:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘On that day my people will know that I am the one who spoke through my servants the prophets; and, proclaiming the gospel, you will hear distinctly: Behold, I am he.’”

Again there:

“I am the Lord, who speak righteousness and announce truth” (Isa. XLV, 19).

Again there:

“I have planned and spoken; I have brought about, created, and made.”

And the Apostle:

“Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

And in the one hundred nineteenth psalm (verse 46):

“I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame.”

And the Lord himself says in the Gospel to the blind man whom he had enlightened:

“You have seen him, and the one who speaks with you is he” (John IX, 37).

And he says to the Samaritan woman:

“I am the one who speaks with you” (John IV, 26).

And to the disciples:

“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 64).

And to the Father:

“I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world” (John XVII, 13).

And again he says to the Jews:

“I speak to you and you do not listen; but if another comes, you will listen to him” (John V, 43).

And again:

“Jesus spoke these things in the treasury while teaching in the temple, and no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come” (John VIII, 20).

Behold, in all these things stated above, you are not taught that the Son spoke at the Father’s command, but rather that he exercised authority in speaking.

## CHAPTER XI. How the Son Made What Was Made by the Father’s Command

If they say to you that the Son made what was made by the Father’s command.

**Response.** The Son did not make what was made by the Father’s command, as you assert, but created all things by the authority and will of his own power, which in his providence he foresaw would have to be created. The prophet Isaiah says:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘I made the earth by my word, and the human being upon it; I established the heavens with my hand; I commanded all the stars to shine in heaven’” (Isa. XLV, 12).

Again there:

“All my counsel will stand, and everything I have planned, I have done” (Isa. XLVI, 10).

Again there:

“Thus says the Lord, who established heaven and earth and made it; he determined it” (Isa. XLV, 18).

Again there:

“I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens” (Isa. XLVIII, 13).

Again there:

“I made the earth by my great strength and by my exalted arm.”

And in Jeremiah:

“The Lord, who made the earth by his great power, established the inhabited world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heavens and placed the sound of water in the heavens” (Jer. LI, 15).

Again there:

“O Lord, who made heaven and earth by your great power and your exalted arm, who repays the sins of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them” (Jer. XXXII, 17).

And in Solomon:

“For your hand, which created the universe from invisible matter, was not powerless” (Wis. XI, 18).

And in the one hundred thirty-fourth psalm (verse 6):

“All that the Lord willed he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses.”

And in the one hundred thirteenth psalm (verse 11):

“But our God is in heaven.”

And again:

“In heaven and on earth he did everything that he willed.”

And in the sixty-fourth psalm (verse 7):

“Preparing the mountains by his strength, girded with power.”

Since he is described as having done all these things not by the Father’s command but by his own power, how can he be judged by you to be inferior to the Father?

## CHAPTER XII. That the Son Is the Beginning

But if they say, “There was a time before the Son was born from the Father,” because he said to the Jews, “The beginning that I speak to you.”

**Response.** Recognize that the Son was born neither from time nor after time, but was ineffably generated from the Father’s womb before all times. God the Father himself says through the prophet in the one hundred ninth psalm (verse 3):

“In the splendors of the holy ones, from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

The prophet Isaiah also clearly expressed this statement to the doubtful and unbelieving, showing that the Son was born ineffably no differently from the Father:

“In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; but who will declare his birth?” (Isa. LIII, 8).

And in the book of Job:

“Where will you find the wisdom of God the Father? For it is hidden from human eyes and concealed from the birds” (Job XXVIII, 21).

Awaken a little, and if you possess even a small amount of the light of knowledge within yourself, pay attention and you will find that the one whose birth the prophet could not declare was not able to have been generated in time, as you yourself attempt to assert.

“In the beginning,” says the evangelist John, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1).

And again:

“There was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9).

If you wish to seek a time in this word, “was,” you will not find one, because from the time when the Father is, the Son also is; and what the Father is, the Son also is. Solomon says:

“I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature. I caused unfailing light to rise in heaven, and I covered the whole earth with mist. I dwelt in the heights, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud. I alone traversed the circuit of heaven, penetrated the depth of the abyss, stood upon every earth, and held primacy among every nation and people” (Ecclus. XXIV, 5–9).

Again there:

“When he prepared heaven, I was with him; and when he marked out his throne, when above the mighty winds he made the clouds on high; when he fixed the springs beneath heaven; when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging them; and I was the one in whom he rejoiced when he delighted in the completed world” (Prov. VIII, 7).

And in the one hundred first psalm (verse 28):

“You, Lord, founded the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment, and you will change them like a covering, and they will be changed. But you are yourself unchanged.”

There was not, as you claim, some period of time before the Son was born from the Father. For the one who established all times by his own power could not have been born from time or after time.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Father Gave Judgment to the Son

[Col. 0363C] But if they say that the Father gave the Son power to carry out judgment.

**Response.** Let the prudent recognize from these testimonies that the Son of God will carry out judgment by his own power. Let them offer a just judgment in this matter and show whose statements agree more closely with reason and whose faith they attack. The prophet Isaiah says:

“Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who was his counselor? Or who advised and instructed him? Who showed him judgment?” (Isa. XL, 13).

Again there:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘Woe to the powerful in Israel, because my anger against them has not ceased; I will execute judgment upon the enemies and burn them completely with fire’” (Isa. I, 24).

Again there:

“The Lord will establish his people in judgment, and the Lord himself will come to judgment with the elders of his people and his rulers” (Isa. III, 13).

Again there:

“He put on righteousness and glory; he placed the helmet of salvation upon his head and covered himself with the garment of vengeance, to repay his adversaries with recompense” (Isa. LIX, 17).

Again there:

“For behold, the Lord will come like fire, and his course like a storm, to repay vengeance in anger and retribution in a flame of fire” (Isa. LXVI, 15).

And in the ninth psalm (verse 9):

“He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness.”

And in the one hundred second psalm (verse 19):

“The Lord prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all.”

And in the ninety-third psalm (verse 1):

“God of vengeance, the Lord; God of vengeance acted freely.”

And in the epistle of the apostle Jude:

“Behold, the Lord will come with thousands to execute judgment, to destroy all the ungodly, and to convict all flesh concerning all their ungodly works” (Jude XIV).

And in the Gospel:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats; and he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matt. XXV, 31).

Therefore, according to what he is as God, we read that the Son received nothing from the Father; we believe that, remaining inseparably in the Father’s heart, he possessed all things. But the one who received power to carry out judgment is the one who, emptying himself, deigned to assume the form of a servant.

## CHAPTER XIV. When They Say That the Son Did Not Have the Power to Grant the Two Disciples Seats at His Right or Left

[Col. 0364B] But if they say to you that the Son said to two disciples:

“You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you” (Matt. XX, 23).

Response. We have already taught in the preceding discussion that the Son possesses authority in his own right, and now, with his assistance, we shall teach it again, as the Gospel testifies: “When he had called his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity among the people” (Matt. X, 1). And again: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit with him upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). And again: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy; and if you drink any poison, it will not harm you” (Luke X, 19). And again: “But to all who received him, he gave authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12). And in the Apocalypse: “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Apoc. III, 21). Likewise there: “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Apoc. II, 7). He who gave all the disciples authority to judge the twelve tribes and permitted them to sit with him—did he not have the power to grant only two disciples permission to sit at his right or at his left?

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the statement: “The Son can do nothing of himself”

376. But if they object to you that the Son said: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, 19).

Response. If you held the right faith and were not attacking the Catholic faith through the perversity of a false doctrine, you would recognize that the Son acted by his own authority in doing those things which we do not read that the Father accomplished except through the Son. Did the Father turn water into wine? Did the Father board a ship or command the winds and waves to become still? Did the Father feed five thousand people in the desert with five loaves and two fish? Did the Father walk upon the sea with his feet? Did the Father open the eyes of one born blind? Did the Father restore a paralytic to his former health in the presence of the Jewish rulers? Did the Father heal, before all who were standing there in the temple, the man who had a withered hand? Did the Father, while the crowds were unaware, heal by the power of his divinity the woman suffering from a flow of blood? And we believe that our Lord Jesus did many other things even more marvelous than these; by believing, we recognize and confess that the one who carries out the Father’s work is not believed to be alien to the Father’s works.

## CHAPTER XVI. Where they say that the Father and the Son are not one God

[Col. 0365B] If they say: “There is not one God, because by saying, ‘We are one,’ you show two, not one” (John X, 30).

Response. Apart from the incarnation of the Son, which he assumed for our redemption, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called one God, not divided among three—as you attempt to assert with sacrilegious mind—but one substance of divinity is demonstrated in three persons and names. The prophet Zechariah says: “The Lord will be king over the whole earth, and on that day the Lord will be one, and his name one” (Zech. XIV, 9). No one is unaware that the day designated by the prophet is the day of the future judgment. I therefore ask you to explain yourself what the prophet’s statement means. Who, then, will be king? Who will be the one Lord? Or which one of the three bears the name of divinity?

If it is the Father, then he alone is called the one God. Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit are shown to have been alien—God forbid—to the name of divinity, because it is written: “On that day the Lord will be one, and his name one.” But if, as is the case, there is one name of the Trinity, why do you persuade me to believe what I do not see the prophets and apostles proclaiming? For Malachi also speaks only of the Son, whom he designates in prophetic proclamation as the one God, creator of the human race, saying: “Did not one God create you? Is not one Father of you all?” (Mal. II, 10). And in Deuteronomy: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4). And the Apostle: “There is no God except one” (I Cor. VIII, 4). And again: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Eph. IV, 5).

Now observe that the one God is not divided. He is called one God in three persons and names, as the Apostle testifies: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4).

What, then, is the reason you did not hesitate to disparage the Son? When he said, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), you nevertheless attempt to introduce two gods, different from one another in nature and divinity, and are not afraid to assert this. You do not understand that, when he says “we are,” he distinguishes the persons, not separates the substance of the divinity, so that he might both destroy Sabellius, who followed a doctrine of union, and in every way refute you Arians, who deny that there is one God in the Trinity.

## CHAPTER XVII. The statement “Father, glorify your Son” explained

378. But if they say that the Son is therefore lesser because the Father glorified him, as it is written: “Father, glorify your Son” (John XVII, 1).

Response. Just as the Father is taught to have glorified the Son, so also the Son is declared to have glorified the Father, as the evangelist says: “Jesus answered and said: I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me” (John VIII, 49). And the Son himself says to the Father: “Glorify your Son, so that your Son may also glorify you” (John XVII, 1). And again: “I glorified you upon the earth” (ibid., 4). And to the disciples: “If you ask anything in my name, I will do it, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son” (John XIV, 13). And again: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John XIII, 31). And Isaiah: “The Lord of hosts will be exalted in judgment, and the holy Lord will be glorified in it” (Isa. V, 16).

Recognize at last, faithless one, that where there is one glorification of power, there is no distinction of authority.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Where they say that the Son did not truly see the Father

But if they say that the Son cannot truly see the Father, because it is written: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18).

Response. Let us now return to the source itself, from which we shall teach through clearer testimonies from the books of the Old and New Testament that the Son has always been able, and is able, to see the Father.
