Solomon says: “And with you is Wisdom, which knows your works, which was present with you when you made the world, and knows what is pleasing to your eyes” (Wis. IX, 9). And the Lord in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X, 22). And likewise: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John I, 18).

And again he says to the Jews: “You do not know him, but I know him; and if I were to say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar” (John VIII, 55). Likewise there: “The one who is from God knows him” (ibid., 47). And again: “I know him, because I am from him.” Behold, we have shown that the Son always sees the Father. How, then, do you maintain that he cannot see the Father?

## CHAPTER XIX. What it means that the Father bears witness to the Son

If they say that the Son is therefore lesser than the Father because the Father bears witness to him.

Response. If you examine the divine Scriptures with a clear understanding, you will find not only the Father bearing witness to the Son, but the whole inseparable Trinity bearing witness together. The Lord himself declares: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John VIII, 18). And again: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I come from and where I am going” (John VIII, 14). And concerning the Holy Spirit: “When that holy Paraclete comes, the Spirit of truth, he will bear witness concerning me” (John XV, 26).

Pay attention, I ask you, pay attention: where one power of testimony is displayed, no one is judged either more powerful or lesser than another.

## CHAPTER XX. What it means that the Father is invisible but the Son visible

If they say to you that the Father is greater because he is called invisible, whereas the Son is proclaimed visible.

Response. We have already said this many times: the Son is called visible according to the form of a human being, but according to the substance of his divinity he is proclaimed invisible. The Apostle Paul declares: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33). And in Isaiah: “Whom do you consider like the Lord, or to whom do you compare him, since he himself is invisible?” (Isa. XI, 18).

The Apostle says: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to proclaim among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden for ages in Christ, who created all things” (Eph. III, 8). The same apostle says: “He is the image of the invisible God.” And to the Colossians: “I, Paul, am a minister, because now I rejoice in my sufferings and complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for his body, which is the Church. I became its minister according to the dispensation of God, the mystery of Christ, which was hidden for ages and generations” (Col. I, 15).

Likewise there: “That their hearts may be comforted in love, unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II, 2).

And in Psalm 76 (verse 20): “Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known.” And in Solomon: “Who has investigated the wisdom of God, which precedes all things?” (Sir. I, 3). Likewise there: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed, and who has known its subtleties?” (ibid., 6). Likewise there: “To whom has the discipline of wisdom been revealed, and who has understood the multitude of its paths?” (ibid., 7). Likewise there: “For the works of the Lord alone are marvelous, glorious and hidden, and his works are unseen by all” (Sir. XI, 4).

Behold: just as the Father is invisible, so also the Son is found to be invisible. How, then, do you judge him inferior to the Father because he graciously allowed himself to be seen bodily for our sake?

## CHAPTER XXI. How the statement “I always do what pleases him” is to be explained

If they object that the Son said of the Father: “I always do what pleases him” (John VIII, 29).

381. Response. If you wish to reduce this to the Son’s obedience, so that you may say that he is subject to the Father, you nevertheless make a similar judgment about the Father, who is likewise taught in the holy Scriptures to have offered obedience to the Son. The prophet Isaiah says: “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, my Lord, whose right hand I have held, and I will cause all the nations to obey him” (Isa. XLV, 1). Likewise there: “I will go before him, and I will make the mountains level, and I will open doors before him, and cities will not be closed” (ibid., 2). Likewise there: “I called him and led him, and I made his way prosperous” (Isa. XLVIII, 15, 17).

And in Psalm 131: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with shame.” And in the Gospel: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Mark I, 2). And in Habakkuk: “The Lord went forth for the salvation of his people, with his Christ” (Hab. III, 13).

In all these passages, does it not seem to you that the Father offered obedience to the Son? Yet it is impious to say that the Father could be subject to the Son, because the Father’s divinity neither diminished itself by giving the Son what belongs to it, nor did the Son, by receiving what belongs to the Father, change his nature into something better than it had been or into something previously nonexistent. The Son therefore does what pleases the Father because he does not know how to do anything contrary.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Apostle’s statement that only the Father is immortal

If they say to you: “The Son cannot be equal to the Father in this respect, because the Apostle asserts that only the Father is immortal.”

Response. The divine utterances everywhere testify that the Son, according to his divinity, has always been and is immortal. Solomon makes this especially clear: “Immortality is in the thought of wisdom, and the enjoyment of her friendship is a good thing” (Wis. VIII, 17). Likewise there: “In the works of the hands of wisdom there is unfailing nobility; in the contest of her words there is immortality, and in the sharing of her words there is perpetual clarity of eternal life” (ibid., 18).

And the Apostle: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “We announce to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them” (Acts XIV, 14). And in Deuteronomy: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘because I raise my hand to heaven, I will swear by my right hand and say: As I live forever, I sharpen my sword like lightning; my hand will hold judgment, and I will repay those who hate me’” (Deut. XXXII, 40).

But he who is proclaimed eternal and immortal by the divine Scriptures is judged lesser in substance than the Father only by the perfidy of the Arians.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Psalmist’s passage explained: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing”

If they say to you that the prophet spoke in the person of Christ: “The Lord will shepherd me,” and that he is therefore lesser than the Father (Ps. XXII, 1).

Response. That the Son is shepherded by himself and not by another—hear the prophet Micah, through whom God the Father deigned to proclaim the power of his only-begotten Son in these words: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah,” he says, “are by no means least among the thousands of Judah; for from you will come forth a King who will shepherd my people Israel” (Mic. V, 2).

And in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life” (Apoc. VII, 17). And in the book of Maccabees: “He himself is our Father, he himself is our King, he himself will shepherd us forever. For he scourged us because of our iniquities, but again he will have mercy on us” (II Macc. VII, 32). And in Psalm 47 (verse 15): “This is our God forever and ever, and he himself will shepherd us forever.” And in Psalm 27 (verse 9): “Shepherd them and lift them up forever.”

For if the Son, as you yourselves imagine, is not shepherded by himself, he is called King, or the King’s Son, in vain, since the name of King and of dignity is established only by shepherding others.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the Arians say that the Father is lesser than the Son from the fact that Christ alone was tempted by the devil in the desert

383. If they say to you: “The Son is not equal to the Father because he alone was tempted by the devil in the desert.”

Response. The Son’s divinity was not subjected to the devil’s temptation; he was tempted only in the flesh, which he graciously assumed from the Virgin’s womb, as the Apostle testifies: “Because he himself suffered and was made obedient, he was tempted; for he is able to assist those who are tempted” (Heb. II, 18).

When the tempter, the devil, said to him, “Throw yourself down,” he restrained him once and again by the scourge of his response, saying: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” and, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV, 7). Hence I do not doubt that the Apostle James also said: “God is not a tempter of evils” (Jas. I, 13).

And in the Gospel: “Then the Pharisees came to Jesus with the Herodians and said: ‘Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth; you do not accept anyone’s person, nor are you concerned with anyone. Is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?’ They said this to tempt him, so that they might accuse him” (Mark XII, 14), and so forth. Do you see, unbeliever, that he was subjected to temptation because he did not refuse to be scourged by the Jews?

## CHAPTER XXV. The Arians deny that the Son called himself God in his own right

But if they say: “Where did the Son of God call himself God in his own right?”

Response. Even people of slower understanding perceive and refute how foolish this proposition of yours is and how far it wanders from the reason of truth—namely, those who confess the Son of God to be true God and true man. For he did not cease to be God because he put on flesh; rather, true God appeared in a true man, as the Apostle John testifies: “This is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20).

But if you wish to know where the Son called himself God in his own right, learn from the Gospel’s account: “The man from whom the demons had gone out was asking to be with him. But Jesus dismissed him, saying: ‘Return to your house and tell how great things God has done for you.’ And he went throughout the whole city proclaiming how great things Jesus had done for him” (Luke VIII, 39).

And again: “The devil led him out and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. And he said to him: ‘I will give you all this authority and their glory, because it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you worship before me, all these things will be yours.’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Matt. IV, 10).

And again, concerning the lepers who had been cleansed, he says: “One of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned, glorifying God with a loud voice; and he fell at his feet, giving thanks. And he was a Samaritan. Jesus answered and said: ‘Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?’” (Luke XVII, 15). Behold where the Son of God called himself God: the one who had been cleansed returned and gave thanks to him as God.

And again: “There was a certain judge in a certain city who did not fear God or respect man . . . There was a widow in that city, and she came to him daily, saying: ‘Vindicate me against my adversary.’ For a long time he was unwilling. But afterward he said to himself: ‘Although I do not fear God or respect man, nevertheless, because this widow is troublesome to me, I will vindicate her, lest she finally come and weary me.’ Then Jesus said: ‘Have you heard what the unjust judge says? And will God not vindicate his servants who cry out to him day and night, and will he be patient with them? Amen, I say to you, he will vindicate them quickly’” (Luke XVIII, 2).

We have set down the whole text of this parable so that we might show where the Son called himself God in his own right. For this statement cannot apply to the Father, since the Son will come for judgment to avenge the wrongs done to his servants.

And again the Evangelist says: “When he had reclined again, he said to his disciples: ‘Do you know what I have done for you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am’” (John XIII, 12). And in Mark Jesus answered and said: “Because of the hardness of your heart he wrote this commandment for you. But from the beginning of creation God made them male and female” (Mark X, 5).

And again the Jews answered and said: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because although you are a man, you make yourself God” (John X, 33). Since, therefore, he calls himself God and Lord, why do you maintain that he is lesser and sacrilegiously deny his divinity?

## CHAPTER XXVI. Where they say that the Father revealed the Son

If they say to you: “The Son is therefore lesser because the Father revealed him to human beings.”

Response. In the mystery of this revelation the Father and the Son are one. For just as the Father revealed the Son, so the Son, with the same divine nature, is likewise taught to have revealed the Father to the world and to human beings. The Lord himself testifies in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke X, 22). And again: “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known” (John XVII, 26).

And to teach that he himself had revealed himself to human beings, he testified through Isaiah, saying: “I appeared openly to those who did not seek me; I was found by those who did not ask about me” (Isa. LXV, 1). And in the Apocalypse: “If anyone opens the door to me, I will enter in to him, dine with him, and reveal myself to him” (Apoc. III, 20). And again: “This was now the third time that Jesus revealed himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, after he had risen from the dead” (John XXI, 14). He who revealed the Father and testified in many ways that he had revealed himself cannot be called lesser.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How it is to be understood that the Father handed over the Son

386. If they say to you that the Father handed over the Son.

Response. The Son, voluntarily fulfilling the dispensation of the flesh he had assumed, deigned through the Apostle to teach his faithful in a clear declaration that he had handed himself over for us. The Apostle himself testifies: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins” (Gal. I, 3). And again: “The life I now live in the flesh I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. II, 20). And to the Ephesians: “Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us” (Eph. V, 1). Likewise there: “Love your wives as Christ loved his Church and handed himself over for her” (ibid., 25).

And to Timothy: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for many” (I Tim. II, 5). And to the Hebrews: “For if the blood of goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse us?” (Heb. IX, 13). Likewise there: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, who dedicated for us a new way, and a way through the veil—that is, through his flesh—offering himself for us” (Heb. X, 19).

And in the Epistle of John: “By this we have known his love, because he laid down his life for us” (I John III, 16). And in Isaiah: “Sanctify him who handed over his life for us” (Isa. LIII, 12). Likewise there: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (ibid., 7). And in Jeremiah: “I have given my beloved soul into the hands of his enemies” (Jer. XII, 7).

The Apostle likewise says: “He did this once, offering himself” (Heb. VII, 27). And again: “We know that the Son of God came, put on flesh, and suffered.” And the Apostle Peter: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21). And in Solomon: “I will penetrate the lower regions of the earth, inspect those who sleep, and enlighten those who hope in him” (Sir. XXIV, 25).

And the Lord himself in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John X, 18). He who handed himself over and by his own authority laid down and took up his life cannot be called lesser.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the Son’s saying to the Father: “Let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will”

[Col. 0372A]

If they object that the Son said to the Father: “Let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you.”

Response. To teach that the Son voluntarily drank the cup of his passion, learn, if you are not reluctant, from these testimonies. He himself sings in the Psalms: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 12, 16).

This statement cannot be applied to a prophet or to anyone else, since in the following verse he called himself both a servant and the son of a handmaid: “O Lord,” he says, “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.” And in the Gospel he says to the disciples: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke XXII, 15).

Likewise he said to the two sons of Zebedee, John and James: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark X, 38). Pay close attention: he said, “I am going to drink,” so that it would not be said that he did this at another’s command and not by his own will.

And he said to the Apostle Peter: “You do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings. The cup that the Father has given me, do you not want me to drink it?” (John XVIII, 11). If the Lord had not drunk this cup voluntarily, he would certainly not have desired that it should come to him; but because he drank it willingly, he neither trembled nor refused it.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Where the Son is said to have asked the Father

388. If they say to you: “The Son is therefore lesser because he is said to have asked the Father.”

Response. If the one who asks is lesser than the one whom he asks, then God, who is prescribed through the prophet as asking his people, is proved inferior to the people. The prophet Micah says: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and freed you from the house of slavery, and sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you on your journey. My people, remember, I ask you, what Balak king of Moab plotted against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him from Shittim” (Mic. VI, 3).

But to make clear for whom the Lord had so often pleaded with the Father, he confirms it in the Gospel, saying: “Holy Father, I ask not only for these”—that is, for the disciples—“but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John XVII, 20). And again: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name” (ibid., 11).

When that leper said to him, “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me,” the Son did not wait to ask the Father that the sick man be healed. Rather, freely imparting his own medicine, he healed him by a single touch, finding in him only faith for healing, and saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII, 3).

Likewise, when the blind had pleaded with him because of the darkness of their sight, asking to recover their vision, he did not defer the cure to the authority of the more powerful Father. In accordance with the merit of their faith, he brought eyes extinguished and long covered by destructive darkness into the light of his knowledge by his spontaneous will, saying to them: “Let it be done for you according to your faith” (Matt. IX, 29).

He also expelled the demon whose name was Legion because of the multitude of demons associated with it. He drove it away by commanding with his own authority, without asking the Father, and when asked by them, he permitted it to enter the pigs (Mark V, 9).

Likewise, with an imperial voice he commanded the mute and deaf spirit, and as soon as it heard, it departed. He did not say, “I ask the Father that you go out,” but, “I command you to depart”: “Deaf and mute spirit,” he said, “I command you: come out of him and do not enter him again” (Mark IX, 24).

Listen further to the one who said, “I ask,” and observe how, as one commanding the Father, he says elsewhere in the Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, these also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

The Son, then, who, for those who believed in him, and in the human nature he had assumed—as has already been said—asked the Father: would he ask the Father for himself? Certainly not, because there was in him no weak or infirm person who might merit receiving healing through supplication.

For if the Son had been lesser than the Father, as you maintain, he would certainly not have said such things, since one who says “I will” to the more powerful cannot be inferior.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Father is said to have exalted the Son and given him a name above every name

But if they say that the Father exalted his Son and gave him the name that is above every name.

Response. He who is taught according to the sequence of Holy Scripture to have exalted himself is judged inferior to the Father in no respect, as we have already said many times. The prophet sings in Psalm 109 (verse 7): “He will drink from the stream on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.” And in Psalm 9 (verse 33), the Church says of the same one: “Arise, O Lord; let your hand be exalted.” And in Psalm 45 (verse 11), the same Lord proclaims through the prophet: “I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted on the earth.”

Isaiah likewise bears witness to the same things, saying: “The eyes of the lofty will be humbled and will fall, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day” (Isa. II, 11).

The Son, therefore, is not read to have been exalted by the Father in the nature of his divinity. Rather, the one who was exalted and received a name above every name is he who, having assumed flesh from the Virgin’s womb, appeared born as God and man.

## CHAPTER XXXI. When they say that the Son was raised from the dead by the Father

390. But if they add that the Father raised his Son from the dead.

Response. Just as in the preceding discussion we taught that the Son was exalted by himself, so now also we shall teach that he was raised from the dead by himself. David confirms this in Psalm 3 (verse 6): “I slept and took sleep, because the Lord received me.” Pay close attention: he said, “I arose,” and did not say, “I slept and appeared after being raised by another.”

And in Jeremiah: “I will intoxicate the hungry soul, and I will fill the hungry soul; therefore I arose, and my sleep became sweet to me” (Jer. XXXI, 25). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “On the day when he chose the apostles through the Holy Spirit to preach the Gospel, he also presented himself alive to them after his passion, appearing to them with many proofs and teaching them about the kingdom of God” (Acts I, 3).

And the prophet Amos says: “He establishes his ascent above the heavens and confirms his promise on the earth” (Amos IX, 6). And the Apostle: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. VI, 9). Likewise he says: “For I delivered to you first of all that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (I Cor. XV, 3). And to Timothy: “Remember that Jesus Christ rose from the dead, from the seed of David” (II Tim. II, 8).

And in Psalm 138 (verse 18): “I arose, and I am still with you.” And in the Gospel: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to them” (Luke XXIV, 34). And the angels to the women: “He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (Matt. XXVIII, 6). And the Lord himself: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinful men; they will hand him over to the nations to be mocked and crucified, and on the third day he will rise” (Matt. XX, 18). And again: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John XI, 25).

He who raised a human being from the dead and taught that he himself is the resurrection of life is not without the power of divinity.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Where they say that the Son went forth not *de Deo* (“from God”) but *ex Deo* (“out of/from God”)

391. If they say to you that the Son is therefore lesser because he proved himself to have gone forth not *de Deo* (“from God”) but *ex Deo* (“out of/from God”).

Response. Whether the Son is said to have gone forth *ex Deo* or *de Deo*, no diminution can come to his ineffable divinity. He himself testifies in the Gospel: “I came forth from God the Father and came” (John XVI, 27). And in the Epistle of the Apostle John: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (I John III, 9).

And in the Gospel the Pharisees, questioning him, said: “Rabbi, we know that you came from God as a teacher; no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him” (John III, 2).

Recognize that the one who confessed that he had gone forth *de Deo*, and not *ex Deo*, as you slanderously claim, was neither judged inferior nor separated from the equality of the Father’s power.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That there is none good except God alone

If they object that the Son himself said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, God.”

Response. Who could judge him evil when he declares himself the good shepherd? Or who could affirm him unequal to the Father when he shows himself to be one with the Father? “I am,” he says, “the good shepherd.”

And David, revealing the Son in the person of the Father, says in Psalm 44: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” And Jeremiah: “The Lord is good to those who wait for him, and in the day of tribulation he will recognize those who fear him” (Lam. III, 25). And the Lord himself: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. XX, 15).

And in Psalm 118 (verse 68): “You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your statutes.” And the Apostle: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (II Cor. II, 15).

You see that he is not without goodness, who contains in himself the whole fullness of divinity.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Apostle’s statement explained: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent”

If they say what the same Son said: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

Response. We prove by prophetic and evangelical testimonies that the Son is true, as the Father is. [Col. 0375B] Isaiah says: “For those who serve me a new name shall be called, which shall be blessed upon the earth; and they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God” (Isa. LXV, 15). And in Solomon: “They will fear those whom they suppose to be gods, from whom they will be destroyed; seeing him whom formerly they denied, they acknowledged the true God” (Wis. XII, 27). And in the Psalm: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). And there he says to the Father: “Your word is truth” (John XVII, 17). And in the Epistle of the apostle John: “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding so that we may know what is true, and that we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. [Col. 0375C] This is the true God and eternal life” (I John V, 20). From this, therefore, you ought to recognize the unity of the Father and the Son, since divine Scripture does not cease to proclaim the Son to be true God, just as it proclaims the Father.

### CHAPTER XXXV. Where it says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

If they bring against you what is said in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II, 8).

393 **Response.** Since all things visible and invisible—whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers—came forth from the Son before they existed, show what inheritance you say the Son received from the Father by asking for it, when he himself says in the Gospel: “All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John XVII, 10). [Col. 0375D] We also find it written in the book containing the history of Esther: “I heard,” she says, “in my books, Lord, that you took Israel for yourself as an eternal inheritance from among all the nations” (Esth. XIV, 5). Is it not said in the eighty-eighth Psalm (v. 12): “The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness”? Is it not said of him in the thirty-second Psalm (v. 12): “The people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance”? Did he not himself say in the forty-ninth Psalm (v. 10): “All the beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen; I know all the birds of the air; the beauty of the field is with me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine”? [Col. 0376A] Is it not said of him in the seventy-first Psalm (v. 8): “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth”? Since the Son has declared by prophetic proclamation that all these things are his, show now what other inheritance the Son could have received from the Father by asking for it.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Where it says that the Father sanctified the Son.

If they object to you that the Son said of himself in the Gospel: “Whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world” (John X, 36).

**Response.** In the sanctification of deity the Father and the Son are one, as is also confirmed by the testimony of the Apostle: [Col. 0376B] “He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Heb. II, 11). To show that the Son was sanctified by himself, let us bring forward his own testimony from the Gospel. He says: “I sent them into this world, and for their sake I sanctified myself” (John XVII, 18). And again, in the forty-fifth Psalm (v. 5), he sings and says concerning the sanctification of the temple of his body: “The Most High will sanctify his tabernacle; God is in its midst; it shall not be moved.” And to demonstrate fully that this sanctification is the common work of the Trinity, I produce the Apostle’s statement in defense of this position: “But these things you were,” he says, “but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Cor. VI, 11). Consider finally, you who assert these things, [Col. 0376C] that he who sanctified himself had no need of another’s sanctification.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. Where it says: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.”

But if they object to you that saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1), or that of the Apostle: “Establishing him at his right hand” (Eph. I, 20).

**Response.** Recognize from these testimonies, founded upon divine authority, that the Son sat at the right hand of the Father not at another’s command but by his own power. The apostle Paul proclaims: “Who, bearing all things by the word of his power, having himself made purification for sins, sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Heb. I, 3). [Col. 0376D] And again: “For Jesus did not enter into a holy place made by hands, which is an allegory of words, but appeared in heaven itself at the right hand of God” (Heb. IX, 24). And again: “Let us run toward the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame, and sat at the right hand of the throne” (Heb. XII, 1). And in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will grant that he sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. III, 21). And in the ninth Psalm (v. 5): “For you have carried out my judgment and my cause; you have sat upon the throne judging righteousness.” [Col. 0377A] Consider carefully what was said above by the Apostle: “Having made purification, he sat at the right hand of God” (Heb. I, 3). [Note: [Col. 0377D] Some material is missing here.] Again. [Note: [Col. 0377D] Some material is missing here.]

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. Where they say that the Son was mocked by the Jews and suspended on the cross.

395 If they say to you: “He is therefore lesser, because the Son himself was suspended and mocked by the Jews.”

**Response.** [Note: [Col. 0378D] Something is also missing here.] [Fragmentary:] would be inseparable from the Son, and would neither suffer insult nor be subject to passion; rather, only the flesh he assumed was suspended on the cross, for that flesh could be seized and bound by the Jews. Therefore, as man, the Son of God was suspended and mocked on the cross; but as God, seated in heaven, he will mock the impious, as the Psalmist says: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Ps. II, 4).

As man, he feared death; but as God, he will raise the dead, as he himself says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” (John V, 21). [Col. 0377B]

As man, he was spat upon; but as God, he deigned to illumine the blind man with his own spittle, as the Evangelist says: “He spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and spread it over his eyes” (John IX, 6), and so forth.

As man, he was crowned with thorns; but as God, he was called the crown of beauty, as the prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will be a crown of beauty, which surrounds the remnant of his people” (Isa. XXVIII, 5).

As man, he was scourged; but as God, he suffered none of these things, as the prophet says: “Evil shall not approach you, and the scourge shall not come near your dwelling” (Ps. XC, 10).

As man, he was struck with blows; but as God, he grasped the waters in his fist and measured the whole expanse of heaven with his palm, as Isaiah says: “Who has measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with his palm?” (Isa. XL, 12). [Col. 0377C]

As man, he endured sorrow; but as God, he will grant consolation to the sorrowful and to all who are worn down by affliction, as the apostle Paul says: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds” (II Cor. I, 5).

As man, he was given gall and vinegar to drink; but as God, he deigned to give his people a land flowing with milk and honey, as the book of Deuteronomy declares: “When the Lord your God has brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey, beware lest, when you have eaten and been filled, you forget the name of the Lord your God” (Deut. VI). 396

As man, he came to be baptized by John in the Jordan; but as God, he baptized his disciples in the Holy Spirit, saying: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit, which you will also receive” (Acts I, 5). [Col. 0377D] And John the Baptist says: “One stronger than I will come, who will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke III, 16).

As man, he was tempted by the devil in the desert; but as God, he rebuked that same devil, saying: “Get behind me, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. IV, 10).

As man, he was hungry; but as God, he satisfied five thousand people with five loaves.

As man, while thirsty, he asked the Samaritan woman for a little water to drink; but as God, he offered believers the fountain of eternal living water, saying: “Whoever drinks from this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst” (John IV, 13). [Col. 0378A]

As man, he wept for his friend Lazarus; but as God, he will wipe away with the brush of mercy the tears of those who suffer for his sake, as the Apocalypse declares: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Rev. XXI, 4).

As man, his garments were divided by lot; but as God, he deigned to give his people the promised land as their allotted inheritance, as the Psalmist says: “He drove the nations out before them and distributed the land to them by lot, by the measuring line of their inheritance” (Ps. LXXVII, 54).

As man, he slept; but as God, he was never subject to bodily sleep, as the prophet says: “Behold, he shall neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel” (Ps. CXX, 4).

Finally, to pass over many things, as man, he died and was placed in the tomb and rested; but as God, rising from the dead on the third day, he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day and, after the interval of ten days, sent the promise of the Holy Spirit to his disciples. [Col. 0378B]

Recognize at last, heretic, who it was that endured the insult of the cross, and who, dwelling in the man he had assumed, could not suffer it.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. Where they say that the Father was changed into flesh and was born from the Virgin with the Son.

397 If they say to you: “If the Father and the Son are one, then the Father too was changed into flesh, came to the Virgin, and appeared born together with the Son.”

**Response.** We say that the Word of the Father became flesh, not that the Father was changed into flesh or, as you claim, transformed into something else, as the Evangelist says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 24). [Col. 0378C] The Father sent that very Word, and he healed us. That very Word poured forth from the heart. By that Word the heavens were established, whose power remains perpetually founded upon the breath of his mouth. He himself assumed the form of a servant, in which he obeyed the Father and endured the insults of the Jews. For God is impassible, because he is not corporeal; only the flesh he assumed endured passion. That flesh, announced by the angel, grew within the Virgin, as the angel Gabriel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

For he who is the Son is certainly not the Father, since no one can be called both his own Father and his own Son. And when the prophet, speaking in the person of the Father, says: “He will call upon me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation, and I will rescue him” (Ps. XC, 15), [Col. 0378D] he shows the dispensation of unity. For the divinity of the Father and of the Son, which is one, could not be subjected to the defect of passion.

### CHAPTER XL. Where they say that the Son did not possess foreknowledge of future things.

If they say: “The Son of God did not possess foreknowledge of future things,” because he said to the unclean spirit: “What is your name?” and, “How long has this happened to him?”

398 **Response.** Recognize from divine authority that the Son of God cannot be ignorant of future events, as the prophet Jeremiah says: [Col. 0379A] “I am the Lord, searching hearts and testing the kidneys, to give each one according to his ways and according to the fruit of his endeavors” (Jer. XVII, 10). And Isaiah says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, for they are vain” (Isa. LV, 8; Ps. XCIII, 11).

The apostle Paul says the same to the Hebrews: “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every sharp sword, penetrating even to the division of soul and spirit, and of thoughts and of all marrow, and a judge of the thoughts of the heart; and no created thing in the world is hidden from his sight” (Heb. IV, 4–5). [Col. 0379B]

He himself also says: “When the Lord comes, he will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts; then each one will receive praise from God” (I Cor. IV, 5).

And in Solomon: “But if you say, ‘I do not know him,’ know that the Lord knows the hearts of all” (Sir. XXIII, 27). And there: “The eyes of the Lord are many times brighter than the sun; they survey all the ways of human beings, the depth of the abyss, and they look upon the hearts of human beings and their hidden parts” (ibid., 28).

And in the book of Kings: “Let old things depart from your mouth, for the Lord is the God of knowledge” (I Kings II, 3).

And in Maccabees: “God, creator of the world and fashioner of humankind, who searches every deed and origin, will himself restore spirit and life to you again in his mercy” (II Macc. VII, 23).

And the Evangelist says: “Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning a person; for he himself knew what was in a person” (John II, 24). [Col. 0379C]

And Jeremiah says: “The Lord, who made heaven and earth, can have nothing hidden from me, for I show mercy to thousands and repay the sins of fathers upon their children after them” (Jer. XXXII, 18). And there: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘I am the Lord God of all flesh; can anything be hidden from me?’” (ibid., 27).

And in Daniel: “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, who knows all things before they come to be, you know that these men bear false witness against me” (Dan. XIII, 42).

And the Apostle says to the Romans: “On the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ” (Rom. II, 16). 399 [Col. 0379D]

He who searches the hearts and deeds of human beings and will bring them to light cannot be ignorant of future events.

### CHAPTER XLI. Where they say that the Son is subject to the Father.

If they should object that the Son is subject to the Father, because it is written: “Then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him” (I Cor. XV, 28).

**Response.** To make you recognize that the Son of God subjected all things to himself by his own power, listen to the apostle Peter proclaiming this more fully. “At one time,” he says, “in the days of Noah, while the patience of God was waiting, when the ark was being built, into which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water—which also now saves you in a similar form of baptism, not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God—he went into heaven and subjected angels, authorities, and powers to himself” (I Pet. III, 20–22). [Col. 0380A]

And the apostle Paul says: “When he has abolished every principality, every authority, every power, and every dominion, he must reign until he places all his enemies beneath his feet” (I Cor. XV, 24).

And to the Philippians: “Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to his power by which he is able to subject all things to himself” (Phil. III, 20).

On this same subject recognize David speaking in the sixty-seventh Psalm (v. 19): “He ascended into heaven, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings.”

And in the Epistle of the apostle Jude: “The angels who abandoned their own principality he has kept bound with fiery chains and shut away in dark prisons, reserved for punishment at the judgment to come” (Jude 6). [Col. 0380B]

From these things, therefore, recognize the Lord: the subjection of the Son does not concern his deity but his flesh. When, at the end of the age, all the vices of the human race have been subjected and death has been swallowed up in victory, then the Son of Man too is said to be subject to the Father—not in the nature of his deity, but in the substance of the human nature he assumed. 400

### CHAPTER XLII. Where they say that the Son could not know the day of judgment.

But if they object that the Son said in the Gospel: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. XXIV, 36).

[Col. 0380C] **Response.** The Son, therefore, cannot be ignorant of the day of judgment, since he appears previously to have instructed his disciples with a paternal admonition: “When you see battles and reports of battles,” he says, “see that you are not troubled; for these things must happen, but the end is not yet” (Matt. XXIV, 6). And there: “For just as lightning goes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (ibid., 27).

And Zechariah says: “Behold, my Lord will come, and all the saints with him; and on that day there will be neither light, but cold and frost; and that day is known to the Lord” (Zech. XIV, 5).

And in Solomon: “What is richer than wisdom, which produces all things? And if understanding produces them, who among these appears to be their maker? But if someone loves righteousness, her labors possess great virtues: for she teaches sobriety and prudence, gives righteousness and virtue to those who believe in her, things more useful to human beings in life than anything else. But if someone desires an abundance of knowledge, she makes it known; she knows past things and is prescient of future things; she knows the subtleties of speech and the solutions of arguments; she knows signs and wonders before they occur, and she does not ignore the end of times and ages” (Wis. VIII, 5–8). [Col. 0380D]

And the Evangelist Luke says: “The Pharisees asked him, saying, ‘When will the kingdom of God come?’ He answered them and said: ‘The kingdom of God does not come with observation, nor will they say, “Behold, here!” or “Behold, there!” For behold, the kingdom of God is within you.’ And he said to his disciples: ‘The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, “Behold, here!” or “Behold, there!” Do not go out, nor follow them. For just as lightning flashing from heaven shines upon the things beneath heaven, so will be the coming of the Son of Man on his day’” (Luke XVII, 20–24). 401 [Col. 0381A]

If this is his day, how can you say that he could not or cannot know what belongs to him?

### CHAPTER XLIII. Where they call the Son the abbreviated Word, or say that he was made so.

But if they say that the Son is lesser because the prophet said of him: “The Lord will make a shortened word upon the whole earth” (Rom. IX, 28).

**Response.** The shortened word that the Lord will make upon the earth does not signify a diminution of the deity in the Son of God, but announces the dispensation of the flesh assumed. In that dispensation we read that the Son of Man was made lower not only than the Father but also than the angels, as the apostle Paul declares: “We see Jesus, who was made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II, 9). [Col. 0381B] And below: “For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you’” (ibid., 11).

And in the eighth Psalm (v. 6): “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor.”

And to show that the Word of God the Father was not shortened in the Son, we confirm this judgment from the book of the prophet Isaiah: “Has my speech been shortened, or made small, so that I cannot redeem? Or is there no power in me to deliver?” says the almighty Lord (Isa. L, 2). And again: “Thus says the almighty Lord God: Has my hand been shortened, so that it cannot save?” (Isa. LIX, 1). Or is he unable to give life to the heart of the humble and to the spirit of the contrite? [Col. 0381C]

And to show that the Son is the arm of the Father, which is his hand, he adds: “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see his salvation” (Isa. LII, 10).

For even in the last age this meaning can appropriately be applied—not without reason—when the Lord came for our redemption by assuming flesh, so that by his death he might destroy the one who held the power of death and, by the power of his might, free within that brief and limited span of time those whom he had subjected as captives in darkness and the shadow of death. 402 [Col. 0381D]

He was also instructing his disciples concerning this brief time when he urged them to walk in the light while they still had time. “Children,” he says, “it is the last hour; while you have the light, walk in the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII, 35). And in the Catholic Epistles: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). And how do we know that it is the last hour? Because many false prophets have gone out into this world.

And the apostle Paul says: “For the time is short” (I Cor. VII, 29). And again: “For the form of this world is passing away” (ibid., 31). And again: “All these things happened for our correction, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (I Cor. X, 11).

Moreover, in the Lord’s Prayer itself the Lord abbreviated the whole discourse, since, forbidding us excessive speech, he taught everything that pertains to salvation: “When you pray,” he says, “do not speak at length” (Matt. VI, 7). And below: “When you pray, say: ‘Our Father, who are in heaven’” (ibid., 9), and so forth. [Col. 0382A]

For the prophet did not designate the Son of God as diminished in the Word in this passage, since in former times he spoke in this manner through the prophets, and even now he speaks through the apostles and apostolic men at the last time: “I am the one,” he says, “who spoke to my servant-prophets; behold, I am present” (Jer. VII, 25).

And another prophet says: “As it was from the beginning, so it will remain forever; nothing has been added to him, nor will anything be diminished from him, for he is the Lord of his creation.”

Behold what kind of shortened word the Lord made throughout the world: not one that, as you suppose, declared the Son inferior to the Father, but one that announced his final coming.

### CHAPTER XLIV. Where they say that the Son was not born from the substance of the Father.

But if they say: “The Son was not born from the paternal substance, but was generated from another substance.”

403 **Response.** We too, who confess the Father and the Son to be of one substance, have taught by divine authority that the Son is from the substance of God the Father, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Take up lamentation over the mountains, and mourning over the paths of the wilderness, because they have failed, because there are no people, because they refused to hear the voice of my substance; from the birds of heaven to the beasts, they have slipped from understanding” (Jer. IX, 10). [Col. 0382B]

And there: “Who stood in the substance of the Lord and saw the word of God? Who gave ear and heard?” (Jer. XXIII, 18). And there: “If they had stood in my substance, and if they had heard my words, and if they had taught my people, I would have turned them away from their most evil pursuits” (Jer. XXIII, 22). [Col. 0382C]

And the Apostle says: “Since he is the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. I, 3). Again he says: “For we have become partakers of God; let us hold firmly to the beginning of his substance” (Heb. III, 14).

And in Solomon: “My substance is my sweetness” (Wis. XVI, 21).

From this, then, recognize that he who is called the substance of God the Father is not believed to be alien from that same substance.

### CHAPTER XLV. Where they say that the Son is lesser because through him thanks are rendered to the Father.

If they say to you: “The Son is therefore lesser because through him thanks are rendered to God the Father.”

[Col. 0382D] **Response.** From the very apostolic passage from which you appear to derive this testimony, we prove from that same passage—and without the name of the Son—that he himself very often rendered thanks to God the Father. He writes to the Roman Church: “But thanks be to God,” he says, “that you were servants of sin” (Rom. VI, 17). And below: “But having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness.”

And to the Corinthians: “But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV, 57). And there: “But thanks be to God” (II Cor. II, 14).

And to the Ephesians: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. III, 14). 404 [Col. 0383A]

And to the Colossians: “Strengthened according to the might of his glory for all endurance and patience, with joy giving thanks to God and the Father” (Col. I, 11).

And to Timothy: “I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers in faith” (II Tim. I, 3).

Recognize that, just as there is one faith and confession in the Father and the Son by which we are called and are Christians, so also thanksgiving is one in them, whether we ask to deserve something or render thanks for benefits bestowed.

### CHAPTER XLVI. Where the Son says: “The Father has appointed a kingdom for me.”

If they say that the Son himself said to his disciples: “I appoint for you, just as my Father appointed a kingdom for me” (Luke XXII, 29).

**Response.** Just as the Father is said to have appointed a kingdom for his Son, so the Son is taught to have handed over the kingdom to the Father, as the Apostle confirms: “Each one in his own order,” he says: “Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming. Then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every principality, every authority, and every power” (I Cor. XV, 23). [Col. 0383B]

And in the Apocalypse: “You redeemed us for God by your blood, from every tribe, language, and nation, and you made us a kingdom for God” (Rev. V, 9).

But that the Father and the Son possess one common kingdom, the Apostle proves in writing to the Ephesians: “For know this, understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 5). [Col. 0383C]

Since, then, you see that the kingdom of the Father and of the Son is one, why do you attempt, in your impious doctrine, to assert such things about him?

### CHAPTER XLVII. Where they say that the Son, not the Father, appeared to the prophets.

405 If they say to you: “By this the Son is recognized as lesser in power than the Father, because he alone is read to have appeared to the prophets.”

**Response.** Just as it is proved by divine authority that the Son appeared to the apostles and prophets, so the same writings teach that the Father also appeared to them, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and he said to me: ‘Rise, go out into the plain, and there I will speak to you.’ And I rose and went out, and behold, the majesty of the Lord stood there, like the majesty of the one whom I had seen by the river Chebar” (Ezek. III, 22). [Col. 0383D]

And in Daniel: “I was watching, and behold, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat; his garments were white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool” (Dan. VII, 9).

And to show that it was the Father whom he had seen, he continued: “I was watching in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven, and he reached the Ancient of Days” (ibid., 13).

And in the Acts of the Apostles, this is reported concerning the first martyr Stephen: “But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, gazing into heaven, saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts VII, 55).

And the Lord in the Gospel bore witness that the prophet Isaiah had seen the glory of God the Father with his own eyes, saying: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke about him” (John XII, 41). [Col. 0384A]

And in Genesis the same Lord said to Jacob: “I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God, where you anointed the stone for me and vowed a vow to me” (Gen. XXXI, 15).

And in the book of Judges: “While Gideon was still in Copher, of the father of the son of Hesdri [names uncertain], the Lord spoke that night, saying: ‘Go and overthrow the altar of Baal, which your father built, and cut down the place that is above it; and you shall build an altar to your God who appeared to you on the summit of Mount Macoth according to the ordinance’” (Judg. VI, 24).

Likewise in Genesis to Jacob: “God said to Jacob: ‘Rise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you on the way when you fled from the face of Esau your brother’” (Gen. XXXV, 1). 406 [Col. 0384B]

Choose whichever of the two alternatives you wish: either say that the Father appeared to Jacob as he went and the Son as he returned, or the Son as he fled and the Father likewise as he came back. Whichever way you turn, you will have no opportunity to escape.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Where they make an issue of the syllable “and,” because it was said to the disciples: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

But if they say that the syllable “and,” because the Son said to his disciples, “Baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” divides the Son and the Holy Spirit from the Father (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

**Response.** If this syllable—which is used especially as a conjunction both of words and of names—separates the Son and the Holy Spirit from the Father, as you say, then the name of God the Father, which in Genesis we read repeated three times under the names of the three patriarchs, namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, must appear to be divided within itself; or, what it is impious to say, he must be divided under the name of one God. [Col. 0384C]

Far be it from us: what is shown to be one in the substance of deity is not divided, as the Lord himself says: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III, 6). Again he says to Moses: “If they ask you, saying, ‘What is his name?’ you shall say to them: ‘The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you’; this is my name forever” (ibid., 15).

You see that by the syllable “and” what is known to be one is not divided. Therefore the Son and the Holy Spirit are not separated from the Father by this syllable, for they are taught to be joined to one another by nature, deity, and power.

### CHAPTER XLIX. Where they say: “The Father is named first, and afterward the Son.”

407 If they say to you: “For this reason the Son is not equal to the Father, because in the divine Scriptures the Father is named first and the Son afterward.”

**Response.** The apostle Paul, teacher and instructor of the nations, did not, by naming the Father first, detract from the Son or show him inferior to the Father. For he had previously named the Son and the Holy Spirit again before the Father, and certainly neither did he wrong the Father nor demonstrate that the Son and the Holy Spirit were inferior. He confirms this when writing to the Roman Church: “Therefore I have glory in Christ Jesus before God” (Rom. XV, 17). [Col. 0385A]

And to the Thessalonians: “Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold to the traditions that you have learned, whether by word or by our letter: our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us…” (II Thess. II, 11).

And in the Apocalypse: “And I saw, and behold, the Lamb was standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father” (Rev. XIV, 1).

And in the Epistle of John: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father” (I John II, 23). And there: “If you remain in the word, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father” (ibid., 24).

The Apostle likewise says: “Know this, understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 5).

Behold, we have shown that the Son is named before the Father. Listen also to the Holy Spirit designated before the Father and the Son. The same Apostle says to the Ephesians: “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. IV, 4). [Col. 0385B]

Because the apostles said, “We are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him” (Acts V, 32), are the apostles therefore to be said to be prior to the Holy Spirit? Or because, when the Lord disclosed the mystery of baptism to Nicodemus, the ruler of the Jews, he first named water before the Holy Spirit, is he for that reason understood to have placed water before the Holy Spirit? “Unless someone,” he says, “is born of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5). [Col. 0385C]

Yet no one among human things can place water before the Holy Spirit or judge it equal to the Spirit, since we know with complete certainty that it is not the Holy Spirit who is purified by water, but water that is purified by the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER L. Where they say: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

If they say that the Lord said in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6).

**Response.** In the grace of faith, the calling of the Father and the Son is one, since just as we are brought to the Father through the Son, so through the Father we are drawn to the recognition of the Son, as the Lord himself declares in the Gospel: “Do not murmur among yourselves: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him to me” (John 6:44).

And Paul says to the Thessalonians: “But we [Col. 0385D] ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers chosen by God, because he called us from the beginning of the age into salvation, in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth, in which he called us through our Gospel into the adoption of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thess. 2:12).

Likewise there: “We always pray for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose and work of faith in power, and that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him” (2 Thess. 1:11).

And again: “That you may walk worthily of God, who called you into his kingdom and glory” (1 Thess. 2:12).

And to Timothy: “For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God, who wills all human beings to be saved and [Col. 0386A] to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:3).

Likewise there: “God is faithful, who called us into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 5:2).

Likewise there: “Strengthened according to the power of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering, with joy giving thanks [409] to God and the Father, who called us into the fellowship of the inheritance of the saints” (Col. 1:11).

If through the Father we are called into the grace of his Son and into the adoption of children, so that we may truly be sons, and if we reach the Father through the Son, what distinction between them can be established? For no one except an unbeliever denies or rejects that those whom the Father calls the Son will receive, and that those whom the Son calls may likewise receive the Father.

## CHAPTER LI. [Col. 0386B] Where they say that sacrifice is offered to the Father alone

But if they say that the Father is shown to be greater than the Son because sacrifice is offered to him alone,

**Response.** To give an appropriate and fitting answer to your empty proposition, without any subtle manipulation or contrivance of words: we prove that sacrifice was offered to the Son as well as to the Father—not only in Christian times, but also by many and various priests of ancient times—the prophet Daniel saying: “There is no place,” the three youths say, “for sacrificing to your name and finding mercy; but may we be received with a humble soul and spirit, as with the holocausts of rams and bulls and with the multitude of fat lambs. So may our sacrifice be today in your sight, [Col. 0386C] that it may please you” (Dan. 3:38).

And so that you may recognize that the Son was the one to whom these three youths confessed that they had offered sacrifice, learn this from the confession of the very king and tyrant who had ordered them to be thrown into the furnace of fire. He disclosed that he had seen a fourth person joined with them amid the flames of the blazing furnace: “Did we not,” he said, “throw three men bound into the furnace?” And they answered him, “Truly, O king.” And he said, “Behold, I see four men loosed and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (ibid., 91–92).

Likewise the Son of God speaks through the prophet, saying: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, sacrifice is offered to my name, and a pure offering, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord” (Mal. 1:11).

And David says in the Psalms [Col. 0386D] [410]: “In your temple at Jerusalem kings offer gifts to you” (Ps. 67:30).

And to show that he had spoken these things about the Son of God, he says in another psalm: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents, and all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71:10).

And to show that all the things designated above had been offered by the Father to the Son of God, we prove that they were fulfilled at the birth of that same Son of God, which took place according to the flesh, as the Gospel confirms: “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying, ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’” (Matt. 2:1).

And below: “Entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, [Col. 0387A] and falling down they worshiped him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts” (Matt. 2:11).

Therefore the sacrifice brought to the holy altars by Christians is offered, with a common devotion, not only to God the Father but also to the Son, since it can neither be offered to the Father without the Son [Note: [Col. 0387D] Add “can” here.], nor be consecrated by the Son without the Father.

## CHAPTER LII. Where they say that the Son had no work in common with the Father

If they say that the Son had no work in common with the Father,

**Response.** That the Father and the Son do have a common work is taught to us in this way. It is reported that God fashioned the first human being in the image of God through the power of a common operation, Scripture saying: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness [Col. 0387B]” (Gen. 1:26).

Likewise there: “Let us make for him a helper like him” (Gen. 2:18).

Likewise there: “Let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11:7).

And: “The Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven upon Sodom” (Gen. 19:24).

And in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

Likewise there: “The Father dwelling in me does these works.”

And: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does in the same way” (ibid., 19), and so forth.

“The things that I do are not my own, but those of the Father who sent me” (John 8:28).

And: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

All these statements do not display a distinct power of the Father and the Son, but announce one operation of the Godhead; and the one who carries out the Father’s work is not believed to be alien to the Father’s works.

## CHAPTER LIII. [Col. 0387C] Where they say that only the Father is called the Most High

For if they bring forward against you that prophetic testimony concerning the Father alone, in which it is said: “Let the nations know that your name is Lord; you alone are the Most High over all the earth” (Ps. 82:19),

**Response.** If from the Gospel you knew that the Son of God is called the Most High, you would never, by disparaging the Son, present this testimony as spoken of the Father alone, since it is written: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1:76).

But so that the Son may be believed to have dwelt with the Father without distinction in the highest places, this is confirmed by Solomon’s testimony: “I, Wisdom,” he says, “dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in [Col. 0387D] a pillar of cloud” (Sir. 24:7).

And in the ninety-second psalm: “But you are the Most High forever, O Lord, for behold, your enemies shall perish” (Ps. 92:9).

For when the devil wished to set his throne against the throne of his Creator in the highest places, lifted up by pride, he seems to have uttered these words with his wicked mouth: “I will set my seat toward the north; I will ascend above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the lofty mountains, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

Likewise in Solomon: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is a patient requiter” (Sir. 5:4).

If you do not wish to lend the hearing of your heart to the divine Scriptures, which teach that the Son is called the Most High, then [Col. 0388A] at least believe the devil, who wished to establish a seat for himself against the throne of his Maker.

## CHAPTER LIV. Where they say that the Son called himself the Beginning

But if they say that the Son had his beginning from the Father, because, when the Jews asked him, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25),

**Response.** The apostle Paul, writing that the Son of God can have neither a beginning of days nor an end of life, explains this in the Letter entitled to the Hebrews, saying: “This Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom Abraham also divided a tenth of everything—first, by interpretation, is king of righteousness, [Col. 0388B] then king of Salem, without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God” (Heb. 7:1).

And in Isaiah: “In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; for his life will be taken from the earth. But who will declare his birth?” (Isa. 53:8).

And in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Thus, in the word *was*, he shows the Son always remaining in the Father, whose beginning no mortal can investigate, nor his end.

## CHAPTER LV. Where it is said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

If they say to you that the Son is therefore lesser because, hanging on the cross, he himself said: “My God, my God, why have you [Col. 0388C] forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46),

**Response.** So that you may recognize that the Son was not utterly abandoned by the Father, as you foolishly suppose, he gave this testimony about himself in the Gospel: “My Father is with me; he will not leave me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8:29).

And again: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (ibid., 16).

And again: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:10).

And the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19).

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him” (Acts 10:38).

And Habakkuk: “You went forth, O Lord God, for the salvation of your people, with your Christ” (Hab. [Col. 0388D] 3:13).

And the prophet: “He who begot me rested in my tabernacle” (Sir. 24:12).

From this, unhappy men, recognize that he who, while still dwelling in our mortal flesh, never departed from the Father cannot be called lesser than the Father.

## CHAPTER LVI. Where they say that the Apostle testifies that he did not know Christ according to the flesh

If they object to you that the Apostle says about Christ: “Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Cor. 5:16),

**Response.** Do you not see, wretched men, that by proposing such things you are altogether following the error of the Manichaeans? Like them, you too are attempting to empty the mystery of the flesh [Col. 0389A] assumed by him, so that after his resurrection from the dead you believe that no sign of humanity remained in him.

You do not consider that after that venerable passion he rebuked his disciples with these words: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

And again: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’ And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (John 20:19).

And again: “After eight days the disciples were inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, although the doors were closed, [Col. 0389B] and stood among them and said, ‘Peace be with you.’ Then he said to Thomas, ‘Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put your hand into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing’” (ibid., 26).

And again: “When morning came, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them, ‘Children, do you have any food?’ But they offered him a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he ate before them, taking the remaining portions he gave them to them” (John 21:4).

And in the Apocalypse: “All nations will see him, who crucified him, and will lament themselves over him” (Rev. 1:7).

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going [Col. 0389C] into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

Likewise there: “He granted that he be made manifest to us, witnesses who were appointed beforehand by God, who ate and lived together with him for forty days after he had risen from the dead” (Acts 10:40).

You see that he who for forty days lived with his disciples, going in and out among them, ate and, taking the remaining portions, handed them to those same disciples with his blessing, and showing the scars and wounds in a true body freed his disciple from the vice of unbelief. It is only the sect of the Manichaeans—and yours—that refuses to accept that he truly rose in the flesh.

## CHAPTER LVII. [Col. 0389D] Where they say that the Son will descend from heaven at the command and voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God

If they object to you what the Apostle said: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with the command of the archangel and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4:15),

**Response.** Does it seem right to you that the one to whom, while he was still present in the flesh before his passion, angels rendered service should, when coming from heaven for judgment, be summoned by the command of angels? Far from it. He will come by his own power, to grant a reward to the just and eternal punishment to the unjust, together with the devil whom they followed, as he himself declares in the Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then he will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals and those who practice iniquity, and he will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:41).

And [Col. 0390A] again: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and glory. Then he will send his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest part of the earth to the highest part of heaven” (Matt. 24:30).

And again: “When the Son of Man comes, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his majesty, and all nations will be gathered before him. He will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, and he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left” (Matt. 25:31).

And the Apostle: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15:52).

And Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord himself will come for judgment with the elders and princes, to render vengeance in anger and in a flame [Col. 0390B] of fire” (Isa. 3:14).

From these things you must finally recognize that he who directs the angels to gather the nations for judgment cannot come at the command of archangels.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Where they say that only the Father is worshiped by the faithful

But if they say: The Son is not equal to the Father in this respect, because only the Father is worshiped by the faithful,

**Response.** If the assault of unbelief had not robbed your minds of their eyes, you would undoubtedly recognize that just as the Son is worshiped in the Father, so the Father is worshiped in the Son, the prophet Isaiah saying: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Egypt has labored, and the commerce of Ethiopia; the Sabeans, men of stature, will cross over to you and will be yours as servants. They will follow you, bound in chains, and they will worship and plead with you [Col. 0390C]” (Isa. 45:14).

And in the Apocalypse: “The twenty-four elders fell down before the throne and worshiped the one who lives forever and ever” (Rev. 4:14).

Likewise there: “And I saw another angel flying in midheaven, carrying an eternal Gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth, saying with a loud voice: ‘Fear God and give him honor, because the hour of his judgment has come; worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the fountains of waters’” (Rev. 14:6).

And in the seventy-first psalm: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 72:11).

And in the sixty-fifth: “Let all the earth worship you and sing psalms to you” (Ps. 66:4).

And in the Gospel: “They found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him” (Matt. 2:11).
