And Ezra: [Col. 0390D] “You alone are the Lord God, who made heaven and the heaven of heavens and all their host, the earth and everything in it, the sea and everything in it; you give life to all, and the hosts of heaven worship you” (2 Esdr. 9:6).

For he who is worshiped as the Father and honored with divine worship—who says that he cannot be equal to the Father?

## CHAPTER LIX. Where they say that the Son gave thanks to the Father

But if they say to you that the Son is therefore lesser because he is reported to have given thanks to the Father, through whom the disciples gave thanks,

**Response.** Just as the Son gave thanks for us in the form of the human being he assumed, so the Father made the fragrance of his Son and of the knowledge of him known everywhere through the apostles [Col. 0391A], Paul saying: “We give thanks to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Cor. 2:14).

For that the grace of the Father and the Son is one and the same, through which the Apostle likewise teaches that we have been liberated, he indicates in this way, saying: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 3:23).

And again: “For if, because of one offense, many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for many” (Rom. 5:15).

And again: “The wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 6:23).

And again: “Wretched man that I am! Who will [Col. 0391B] free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

Moreover, apart from the name of the Son, the disciples frequently gave thanks to the Father as well. If you wish to consider the argument we presented earlier on this matter, you will recognize it without any ambiguity.

## CHAPTER LX. Where they say that the Son was appointed king by the Father on Mount Zion

If they object that the Son said through the prophet: “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6),

**Response.** Insofar as the Son is the Word of the Father and remains God in God, he naturally possesses with the Father [Col. 0391C] dominion over the kingdom.

But insofar as the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, we read that he was appointed king and made a little lower than the angels, the Psalmist saying: “What is a human being that you remember him, or the son of man that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and you set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8:5, 7).

For if you search the Scriptures of the Gospel with a sound understanding, you will find that the Son was not appointed king by the Father but was born king, as the Evangelist says: “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the city of David, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying, ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?’” (Matt. 2:1–2).

And when Pilate said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” he answered him: [Col. 0391D] “For this I was born.”

And: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would fight for me, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews” (John 18:36–37).

For, as you yourselves concede, the Son then acquired the power of the kingdom through death. Therefore, before the Son had been appointed king by the Father, he had no dignity of shared kingship in the Father’s bosom.

If this is so, how does the prophet signify that he had been king before the ages, whom he declares, in prophetic foreknowledge, to be destined to work at least in the midst of the earth: “But God our King,” he says, “has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 74:12)?

He was appointed king by God the Father—the one who, although he was God, deigned to be born for us as a human being from the Virgin. For he who stood everywhere with the Father [Col. 0392A]: in what parts of the earth could he be appointed king, when he is naturally known to rule heaven, earth, and the abysses?

## CHAPTER LXI. Where they say that the Son is inferior to the Father in power and nature

But if they say of the Son that, just as he is inferior in nature, so also he is inferior in power,

**Response.** The Son is not inferior in nature to the Father, because the Son was born God from God, perfect from perfect, whole from whole. He did not proceed as an unequal being begotten by the Begetter, but came forth fully equal, born from the Father’s womb, so that he might possess the fullness of the Father’s equality and nevertheless receive omnipotence from the Almighty.

The apostle Paul declares: [Col. 0392B] “Although he was constituted in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6).

We also affirm that he is omnipotent, as the Father is, not by words of human wisdom but by divine testimonies, the prophet Zechariah saying: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: After the honor he sent me to the nations that plundered you, for whoever touches you touches the apple of his eye. For behold, I will raise my hand against those who plundered you, and they shall become plunder for those who plundered you; and they shall know that the Lord God Almighty sent me” (Zech. 2:8).

Behold: the Almighty is sent by the Almighty. What inequality is proved to exist between the sender and the one sent?

But if these things still seem small to your foolishness, learn from what follows the omnipotence of the one who was sent, which now you appear to ignore. The Apocalypse says: “I am α and ω [Alpha and Omega],” says the Lord, “who was and who is and who is [Col. 0392C] to come, the Almighty” (Rev. 1:8).

And David says in the Psalms: “I have placed help upon one who is mighty” (Ps. 89:20).

And again: “You are mighty, O Lord, and your truth surrounds you” (ibid., 9).

It is therefore now fitting that, like a perverse teacher, you demonstrate what distinction there can be in the omnipotence of the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER LXII. [Col. 0392D] Where they say: “The power of the one who commands and the one who acts cannot be one”

But if in their customary vanity they say to you that the Father and the Son cannot be one, because the power of the one who commands and the one who acts cannot be one,

**Response.** We have certainly never read anywhere in divine Scripture that the Father said to the Son, “Do what I command or order you,” as though he were displaying the authority of one who commands; nor that the Son replied, “I do it,” as though he were thereby demonstrating the role of one who obeys or acts.

But since by proposing these things so often we recognize that you have little shame, we are now compelled to impress upon your foolish minds once again what we remember having said above at some length about the common work of the Father and the Son—things which, as though speaking to a wise person, we had believed could suffice once stated.

Listen, therefore, and you will recognize that the work of the Father is the work of the Son, because we read that neither the Father without the Son nor the Son without the Father has done [Col. 0393A] anything, as the Lord himself declares in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

And: “The Father dwelling in me does the works” (John 14:10).

And: “If you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, so that you may recognize that I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 10:38).

And: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

And: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

And: “Let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11:7).

Since from these things you know that the work of the Father and the Son is one, why do you assert that the Father commands the Son and present the Son as acting or obeying?

## CHAPTER LXIII. Where they say that the Son is not coeternal with the Father

[Col. 0393B] [420] If they say to you that the Son is not called eternal, as the Father is called eternal,

**Response.** But that the Son is eternal, as the Father is, is declared more clearly in the hundred and nineteenth psalm: “Forever, O Lord,” he says, “your word remains in heaven” (Ps. 119:89).

And in Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all the glory of human beings is like the flower of grass; the grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6).

Likewise there: “I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven” (Isa. 48:12).

Therefore the Son is found neither unlike the Father in eternity nor inferior in power, since those who are one in divinity and power cannot be distinguished by eternity. Nor is the Son without the eternity of nature, for he is taught to possess in himself the whole [Col. 0393C] fullness of the Godhead.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Where they say that the Father made the Son, but the Son made everything

If they say that the Father made the Son, but the Son made everything,

**Response.** In the nature of the Godhead, in which the Father and the Son are one, we never read that the Son was made by the Father, but that he was begotten.

For if you assert that the Son was made insofar as he is the Word of the Father, then God the Father will by no means possess the perfection of his substance in himself, since he could not have the perfect and abiding Word within himself before the birth of his Son.

But we, who believe that the Son was ineffably and without beginning born from the Father, neither yield to your impiety, resisting in defense of the unity of faith, nor are overcome by your cunning, so as to deny the truth [421] of the Father’s begetting [Col. 0393D] in the Son. His birth was concealed neither by the Father himself who begot him nor by the Son himself who was born from the Father, for he himself says: “For God so loved this world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it” (John 3:16).

And again: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1:18).

And the Lord himself says to the Jews: “Are you angry with me because I said to you, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 7:23).

And again: “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John 16:28).

And David sings in the Psalms in the person of God the Father, saying: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 45:2).

Likewise he himself: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you in the splendors of the holy ones” (Ps. 110:3).

Likewise he himself concerning the Son: [Col. 0394A] “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. 2:7).

And in the Gospel, when that same Son was baptized in the Jordan, the voice of the Father thundered, saying: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22).

And on the mountain to the three disciples: “This is my most beloved Son; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5).

Hear the Father testifying with his own voice that he begot him from himself; hear the Son demonstrating the origin of his birth, from where and from what source he came forth in an indescribable begetting. Cease calling him a creature—the creator of the heavens, the world, and all creatures.

## CHAPTER LXV. Where they say: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself”

If they object that the Son said: “Just as the [Col. 0394B] Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26),

**Response.** If the Son, abiding in the Father before the beginning of the world, did not have life, how is he called the author of life and proved to be eternal life?

“You asked,” says the apostle Peter, “that a murderous man be granted to you, but you killed the author of life by hanging him on a tree” (Acts 3:14).

And the apostle John: “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

And the Lord himself says to Martha: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).

Likewise there: “I am the bread of life, which came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

And to the Father: “As you loved me, so I loved them” (John 15:9).

And: “I give them eternal life” (John 10:28).

And again: “I came so that they may have life.”

For just as, in the designation of this [Col. 0394C] name, life cannot be divided from life, so the Son cannot be separated from the Father in the substance of divinity. The Father did not give the Son a different life from the one he has abiding in himself; rather, he gave him the very life that he has. As much as there is in the Father, so much he gave; and by giving life to the Son, he himself did not lose it.

## CHAPTER LXVI. Where they say that only the Father dwells in inaccessible light

If they object that this was said of the Father alone: “He alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16),

**Response.** The Father does not dwell in inaccessible light without the Son alone, because wherever the Father is, there too the Son must be believed to be, with unshakable faith.

For if the Father alone, without the Son—which is impious to say—dwells [Col. 0394D] in inaccessible light, the Father must have a dwelling separated from the Son. But if this is so, how could the Son, standing at the right hand of the Father, be seen by the blessed martyr Stephen (Acts 7:56), if, according to you, the Father is confined to other abodes?

Let this be far from the understanding of the faithful who cling to Christ in the unity of faith. For just as it is not true that the Son is absent when the Father alone is said to dwell in inaccessible light, so it is not enough for the Father when Wisdom, who is the Son, is said alone to traverse the circuit of heaven (Sir. 24:8).

Thus, although he is invisible and unbegotten, his being seen in the Son is confirmed by the testimony of the Apostle. And it is shown that he remained and rested in the Son whom he ineffably begot from himself, when the Son himself says through the prophet: “He who begot me rested in my tabernacle [Col. 0395A]” (Sir. 24:12).

And in the Gospel: “The Father dwelling in me does these works” (John 14:10).

And: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18).

The Son was in the bosom of the Father from the beginning, and from the Father’s heart a good word was uttered. How could he not be believed to have dwelt in inaccessible light, abiding together with the Father in the Father’s heart?

Could the Father have remained in the Son without any light, or have rested in the Son’s tabernacle without that same light, when the Son is the radiance of eternal light and the spotless mirror of the Godhead (Wis. 7:26)?

Solomon said that he loved her above his own well-being and always longed to delight in her appearance: “Above well-being and beauty [Col. 0395B] I loved her, and I chose to have her instead of light, because her light is unquenchable” (ibid., 10).

Desiring this light, the prophet David cries out anxiously, saying: “Send forth your light and your truth” (Ps. 43:3).

And again: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 36:10).

In the splendor of this light, therefore, the Son displayed himself beforehand on the mountain to the three disciples; and, terrified by the fear of death, they fell on their faces, sensing that the end of their life had come.

I say that the Son showed this light in himself when he proclaimed and warned his disciples to walk in it: “While you have the light,” he says, “walk in the light” (John 12:35).

And again: “I am the light of this world. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have [Col. 0395C] the light of eternal life” (John 8:12).

And the Evangelist says: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

If this light, which is promised to believers, is proved to be in the Son and is said to be eternal together with the Eternal, how can you separate the Son from the inaccessible light of the Father?

For if the Son is the true God and eternal life, without a doubt he must be believed to dwell together with the Father in this light, which no one presently established in this mortal body can in any way behold. But when he appears, then truly the one who is deemed worthy to be brought into his presence will see it as it is—not as Moses and the other prophets saw it through riddles and figures, but, according to the Apostle, he will truly behold in the Son the substance of the Godhead.

For if [Col. 0395D] you wish to investigate this same testimony of the prophet with a calm gaze of the mind, you will find that the Son did not say that he was completely separated from the Father’s light, since, although he said that the Son alone had dwelt on earth among human beings, he did not make the Father alien from him.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Where they say that the Son is not perfect as the Father is

If they say that the prophet could have spoken of the Son: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book they will all be written” (Ps. 139:15),

**Response.** If, as the Apostle said, you used the law of Christ lawfully, you would certainly recognize that the Son is affirmed in the divine Scriptures to be both prince and perfect, the apostle Paul bearing witness: [Col. 0396A] “In the days of his flesh,” he says, “he offered prayers and supplications to God, who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears. He was heard because of his reverence. Although he was a Son, he learned obedience from the things he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him, and was proclaimed by God a high priest” (Heb. 5:7).

Likewise there: “The word of the oath, which came after the law, [makes] the Son perfect forever” (Heb. 7:28).

Likewise there: “Since, then, we have a chief priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Heb. 4:14).

Likewise there: “Let us run toward the prize of the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter” (Heb. 12:2).

And again: “Until we all attain [Col. 0396B] to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

Review, I ask, what was set forth above concerning the perfection and principality of the Son, and do not deceitfully devise another’s falsehood to your own destruction.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Where they say: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father”

But if they say that the Son is lesser than the Father in this respect, because he himself said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,”

### 425. Response

This statement does not indicate inequality in the Son, but demonstrates the fullness of divinity in him, since the Son does not subsist from himself, nor from nothing, but from the Father. This is the supreme and singular indication of unity. For what else is the Father’s living than his being? And what else is the Son’s living because of the Father than his subsisting in the Father?

“Therefore,” he says, “just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father” (John 6:57). He could certainly have said, “And I live through the Father,” if he had wished to show some difference of inferior power in himself, since one who lives through another plainly cannot live through himself. But one who lives because of another exists rather as the cause of the other’s living.

Just as the Son was made known to the world through the mission of the living Father, so the Father’s name was made known to the world and to humanity through the living Son, when he demonstrated that he did not live for the Father’s sake by himself, saying: “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known,” and “I have revealed your name to humanity” (John 17:6). For those who are equal in revealing one another cannot be unequal in power.

## CHAPTER LXIX  
### Where they say that the Father was compounded in the Son

If they say to you: “If God is in God—that is, the Father is within the Son—then one was compounded in the other.”

### Response

For this very reason we too believe in the Son: because the Father is in him, since he himself says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10:38). For the same reason we believe the apostle Paul when he proclaims, because he himself said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

[Col. 0397A] For this reason we lend a Christian ear to the prophet Isaiah, because he began to proclaim the mystery of their inseparable unity, asserting that the Father had always been one God in the Son and declaring that there was no other besides him: “God is in you,” he says, “and we did not know it; for you are God, the Savior of the ages” (Isaiah 45:14).

We believe the prophecy of Solomon without hesitation for this reason also: through his announcement we learn that the unbegotten God rested in the tabernacle of the only-begotten Son: “The one who begot me,” he says, “rested in my tabernacle” (Sirach 24:12).

God, therefore, who is of simple nature, was not compounded in another, because according to the substance of the divine nature there is one God in the Son. Even if two persons and names are designated in them, there is nevertheless one power of the divine name in them; for those who are one by nature cannot be diverse in divinity.

## CHAPTER LXX  
### Where they say: “The Father is the one from whom all things are, and the Son the one through whom all things are”

But if they say: “If the Father and the Son are one, how is the Father one, from whom all things are, and the Son another, through whom all things are?”

### Response

At last drive from your understanding those notions that the Arian heresy has impressed upon you while you wander from the path of truth, and recognize that Scripture records the same thing concerning the Father as concerning the Son: just as all things are through the Son, so too all things are believed to have been perfected through the Father.

But if you judge the Son inferior to the Father because the Apostle said, “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6), you must carefully attend to everything said by the Apostle. You will find that the Father too is not excluded from the designation associated with this work, since the same Apostle affirms: “Brothers, one God, through whom you were called in the one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4:4). And again: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36).

Of whom do you think this was said? Please answer. If the Apostle says this of the Father, consider that “from him and through him and in him are all things.” But if he says it of the Son, you must likewise observe that “from him and through him and in him are all things.” By whatever argument you wish to attack the unity of the Father and the Son, you will appear to be subject to the conclusions of your own words.

## CHAPTER LXXI  
### Where they say: “If the Father and the Son are one God, then the Word came first and God afterward”

### 427

If they say to you: “If the Father and the Son are one, then the Word was named first and God afterward, because it is written: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’” (John 1:1).

### Response

If the Father and the Son are not called one God according to the distinction of their common nature, then two gods of unlike nature and unequal power are worshiped by you in the manner of the Gentiles, contrary to what was said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

We, then, confess in our profession of faith neither the Word before God nor God before the Word, but both together as one God, because no intervals of time separate the Father and the Son from one another. Where neither time nor any moment of time is found, neither an earlier nor a later can be found—something which it is impious to say.

We call the one Son of God not only the Word but also the splendor and power of the Father, and Wisdom, according to the declarations of the divine Scriptures. It is sacrilege to say that the Father was ever light without splendor, or powerful without power, or Wisdom without his Wisdom. His perfect divinity acquired nothing for its perfection from accidental things; the rational universe recognizes through faith that he contains within himself all that belongs to him.

[Col. 0398B] The fact that the Evangelist first chose to use the designation “Word” more clearly declared the unity of the divinity. In naming the Son before the Father, he was assigning no relation of time or honor, since where the Word is said to have been with God, and God to have been the Word, neither God is placed before the Word nor the Word before God.

## CHAPTER LXXII  
### Where they say: “If the Father and the Son are one God, then God was named first and Father afterward”

### 428

If they say to you: “If the Father and the Son are one God, then he was God beforehand and was afterward called Father by begetting the Son.”

### Response

If, according to you, he first subsisted as God alone and was afterward called Father by begetting the Son, then the name “Father” will by no means be eternal, since it began in time as the designation of his title.

If this is so, according to you he is mutable and will progress, and therefore he will be mutable because he passed from the name “God” to the designation “Father.” He progressed, then, because, seeing himself placed under the name “God” as less perfect, he added the name “Father” to himself, as though in the manner of one completing his perfection.

Who would not see that you used the testimony of the Apostle in this passage for the purpose of showing that, because he said, “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows” (2 Corinthians 2:31), the dignity of God precedes the affection of Father? And although we remember that much has already been said above concerning what you have now wished to repeat, it seems superfluous to repeat again what, once said, may serve to instruct readers.

But lest you accuse us of evading the matter proposed, you should know that the same Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, first named the Son and the Father and afterward applied to him the designation of divinity: “Always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ, to the Father and God” (Ephesians 5:20).

When, therefore, you see the Apostle sometimes using “God” and sometimes “Father” first as a designation, he teaches most clearly that the name of God and Father was eternal, that the Son is coeternal with the eternal Father, and that he remains perpetually with him.

## CHAPTER LXXIII  
### Where they say: “The Son and the Father are not called one God, since the Son was born from the Father before the ages and afterward from the Virgin”

### 429

If they say to you: “How will the one who was born from the Father before the ages and afterward brought forth from the Virgin be one God with the eternal and unbegotten Father?”

### Response

One is the nature of the Word, who, remaining impassible, is shaken by no fear of sorrow; and another is the soul of our race, by which the Son graciously deigned to assume humanity from us—that is, from his mother—in order to show himself a complete human being. Concerning this soul he also said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew 26:38).

Therefore the twofold birth—that is, the divine and the human—did not prove the Son different from the Father. In the former, he remained as great as he is in the substance of the Father’s nature; and in the latter, in which he was afterward brought forth from the Virgin, he did not change. He himself testifies in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and: “Let them be one in us, just as we are: you in me, and I in you” (John 17:21).

For what he said—“I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18)—is altogether fitting to his divinity, since apart from his divinity no place can be found where it should be laid down by him or from which it could be taken up again.

We do not confess the Son to be unbegotten as the Father is, because if the Son were called unbegotten just as the Father is unbegotten, then they could even less be one: each, existing in his own nature, would have no communion of substance with the other.

# BOOK TWO  
## THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT IS ONE GOD WITH THE FATHER

[Col. 0399]

## CHAPTER I  
### Where they say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one God because they are distinguished by their proper names

### 430

If they say to you: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one because they are distinguished by their proper names.”

### Response

If they cannot be one because the Father is called God, the Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, then neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit will be allowed to be called by the designation “divinity.”

If this is so, where is what the Apostle said concerning the Son? “Their fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5). Or why did Jeremiah offer him such testimony as to call him God dwelling on earth with human beings? “This is our God,” he says, “and no other shall be accounted beside him” (Baruch 3:36). And shortly afterward he said: “After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (ibid., 3:38).

Again the Apostle says: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13).

If, therefore, the Father is called God and the Son is called by the same name, how are the Father and Son not one name, since they are not divided from one another even in this designation of divinity?

The Holy Spirit is shown not to be excluded from this designation of divinity, since the Apostle calls that same Holy Spirit God and Lord: “God is Spirit,” he says (John 4:24). The Son said in the Gospel: “What is born of flesh is flesh, because it is born of flesh; and what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit” (John 3:6).

You have therefore wished in vain to divide common names among each person by some special distribution, since even the praises of the heavenly powers appropriately testify to the inseparable mode of designation belonging to the sacred Trinity.

## CHAPTER II  
### Where it is said: “When I depart, I will send you the Paraclete”

[Col. 0400B]

If they say to you concerning the person of the Holy Spirit what the Lord, the Son of God, said: “When I depart, I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, and he will teach you all truth” (John 15:26; John 16:13).

### Response

The divine order of the words themselves ought to have taught you that, blinded by the error of faithlessness, you are not permitted to look with a clear intention of mind. For what support could the divinity have provided to the human race so pious and so appropriate as this: that the one who declared himself to be the truth should also indicate by his preaching that the Holy Spirit is the truth?

If, according to you, he were not the truth, or possessed a substance inferior to the Son, then on coming he certainly would not teach the disciples all truth. But because the divinity and power of both are one, what the Son teaches, the Spirit too is known to teach us. In this respect the Holy Spirit cannot be called or said to be inferior to the Son, since just as the Son himself sent the Spirit to the disciples, so he beforehand announced prophetically that he himself had been sent by the Holy Spirit, with Isaiah himself speaking:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me. He has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind” (Isaiah 61:1), and so forth.

And the Evangelist announces concerning him: “But Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee” (Luke 4:14). He who returned in the Spirit and performed works of power cannot announce that the Holy Spirit was inferior to him.

## CHAPTER III  
### Where it is said: “I am the Lord, strengthening the thunder and creating the spirit”

### 432

If they bring against you the prophetic testimony in which it is said: “I am the Lord, strengthening the thunder and creating the spirit” (Amos 4:13).

[Col. 0401A] **Response.** In saying this, the prophet does not show the Holy Spirit to be a creature, but means the wind, which frequently arises through the agitation of the air and which is also shown to be preceded by flashes of lightning and thunder. Jeremiah says:

“The spirit blows in every region among the clouds; when it is commanded to traverse the whole world, it accomplishes what was commanded. The flashes sent from above, which burn mountains and forests, likewise do what was commanded” (Baruch 6:60).

These things resemble that one Spirit neither in form nor in power. Therefore they must neither be considered nor called gods, since they can neither pronounce judgment nor benefit human beings, because they are not gods.

And in Ezekiel: “Thus says the Lord: I will bring a spirit raising itself up with my anger; at the consummation you shall perish, and the one whom you anointed. Its foundations shall be revealed, and they shall fall” (Ezekiel 13:13).

And the prophet Jonah: “The Lord stirred up a spirit in the sea, and there arose a great storm in the sea, so that the ship was covered by the waves” (Jonah 1:4). Again there: “On the following day, at sunrise, God commanded a spirit of burning, and the sun struck Jonah’s head, and he was faint” (Jonah 4:8).

Again in the Psalms: “With a violent spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47:8). Again there: “He will rain upon sinners snares of fire; and the spirit of the storm is the portion of their cup” (Psalm 10:7). Again there: “He established the spirit of the storm, and its waves were lifted up” (Psalm 106:25). Again there: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, and the spirit of the storm, which do his word” (Psalm 148:8).

But because the Holy Spirit is creator and not a creature, as you say, this is taught in the following way, as the prophet David says: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail; you will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created” (Psalm 103:29).

Again he himself: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6). And in the Book of Job’s sayings: “It is the divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4).

And in the Song of Judith: “Let every creature of yours serve you, because you commanded, and they were created; you sent forth your Spirit, and they were built” (Judith 16:17).

And in Solomon: “He saw, counted, and measured all things, and he himself created them through the Holy Spirit, who is creator and maker of his work” (Sirach 1:9). That is, a creature made by him cannot be compared with him or even judged to be like him.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit was subject to the prophets

If they say to you what is written: “The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets” (1 Corinthians 14:32).

### Response

The spirit of the prophets is subject to the Holy Spirit, not the Holy Spirit itself, through whose outpouring the spirit of the prophets spoke. David sings in the Psalms: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me” (Psalm 34:9).

Would the one who is called God and Lord by a prophet, and even by an apostle, be subjected to the prophets after the power of his own lordship had been removed? Far be it! The one who, by his own power, bestowed the gifts of grace upon apostles and prophets cannot be subjected to another’s power. The apostle Peter affirms:

“Prophecy was never brought forth by human will; rather, human beings, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke” (2 Peter 1:21).

And in Solomon: “The spirit is not in a human being’s power, so that it can be restrained; nor is it subject to him, because he is mortal” (Sirach 8:8).

And in Maccabees: “Heliodorus was carrying out what he had decided, present at the treasury in that place with his attendants; but the almighty Spirit made a great manifestation of his coming” (2 Maccabees 3:23).

For if your inner mind were illumined by the inward light, you would never produce such statements concerning the power of the Holy Spirit. The one who filled the prophets with his own power so that they might proclaim future events could certainly not have been subject to the prophets.

## CHAPTER V  
### Where they say that, in searching, the Holy Spirit does not know what belongs to God

### 434

If they say to you: “The Holy Spirit searches out the hidden things because he does not know what is certain; rather, he desires to know through searching what he knows less fully.”

### Response

The Holy Spirit is not shown to be inferior to the Father or the Son in searching out the things that belong to God, since even the divinity itself, when it searches the things belonging to its Spirit, is judged by no Christian to be inferior to the Holy Spirit. The Prophet says: “I meditated at night with my heart; I exercised and searched my spirit” (Psalm 76:7).

And the Apostle: “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him. So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Hear, heretic: the Holy Spirit is not ignorant of the things of God; rather, he reveals to those who believe in him the knowledge of God that he himself knows spiritually.

## CHAPTER VI  
### Where it is said: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine”

If they say to you what the Son said concerning the Holy Spirit: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14).

### Response

If you wish to recognize what kind and how great the power of the Holy Spirit is, you can learn everything from the teaching of the apostle Paul, who says:

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, workings of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:7).

“One and the same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing his own gifts to each as he wills” (ibid., 11).

And the Lord in the Gospel: “Do not be astonished that I said to you, ‘You must be born again,’ because the Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice but do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3:7).

And the Apostle: “If the word spoken through angels became firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” (Hebrews 2:2). “Since it first began to be proclaimed through the Lord, it was confirmed among us by those who heard, God bearing witness through signs and wonders, various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

Since you know that the Holy Spirit has distributed to each person, by his own will, the gifts listed above, how can you assert that, as though he possessed nothing, he received all these things from the Son—the one who also sent the Lord himself and filled the prophets and apostles with his own power?

## CHAPTER VII  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit did not speak from himself before the ages

If they say concerning the Holy Spirit that he did not speak from himself but uttered what he heard from the Son (John 16:13).

[Col. 0403B] **Response.** We therefore, who confess the Holy Spirit to be God and Lord, demonstrate that he spoke not at another’s command but by his own power, with the apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, bearing witness:

“Strive for spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God; no one hears him, for the spirit speaks mysteries” (1 Corinthians 14:1).

And the Lord said to the disciples: “When they hand you over, do not worry about what you will say, for it will be given to you in that hour what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19).

And the evangelist Mark: “When they lead you away and hand you over, do not worry beforehand about what you will say; but whatever is given to you in that hour, say it. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13:11).

From this, therefore, you should infer that the Son and the Holy Spirit are not diverse from one another in the nature of their divinity, since they appear to be joined to one another in the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit came not from himself but through the Son’s breathing upon the disciples

But if they say that the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples not of his own accord but through the Son’s breathing.

### Response

You cannot establish any difference between the Son and the Holy Spirit on this basis, since you see that the same Lord and our Savior filled the hearts of the disciples not with a spirit belonging to another but with his own. He bestowed upon them a spirit not inferior but equal to himself, so that one Spirit might breathe in those who clung to him in faith and to him himself.

“The one who clings to a prostitute,” says the apostle Paul, “is one body; but the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:16).

We therefore demonstrate that the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples by his own will and filled them with his own power, and we learn this from the book that contains the Acts of the Apostles:

“When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in one place. Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole place where they were sitting. Divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, which also rested upon each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:1).

Again: “But Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit and fixing his gaze upon him, said: ‘O man full of deceit and trickery, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, why do you seek to pervert the ways of the Lord, which are straight?’” (Acts 13:10).

And the angel to Zechariah: “Do not fear, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Behold, your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you will call his name John. He will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:13).

Again there: “And Zechariah, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied” (ibid., 1:41). Again there: “Elizabeth, his mother, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke, blessing God.”

From these testimonies, then, recognize at last that the spirit which the disciples received from the Savior’s breath is not shown to possess a substance inferior to the Son. For we know of no one who remains in his own nature and has a spirit inferior to himself or coming from another substance, by which he might serve the needs of his other members. But no one doubts that he can fill or govern other members from his own spirit, from which he himself subsists, as we have said.

## CHAPTER IX  
### Where it is said that the Holy Spirit is compared with breath

But if they say what is written: “The spirit proceeds from me, and I have made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16).

### Response

We do not believe that the breath which the Lord recalls having made was the Holy Spirit; rather, we confess it to be the spirit of a creature, which creatures received so that they might subsist.

For we do not read that the Holy Spirit was made by the Son, whom we know to have been, with the Son, the maker of all things. If, in making the things that had to be made, the Holy Spirit did not use his own power as the Son did, how did he establish by his own will those things which, in his foreseeing majesty, he perceived had to be established?

The patriarch Job proves this very point in his book of sayings: “By the Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “ice is given upon the earth; he directs the water as it pleases him and waters the grain in the clouds. He scatters his light through the cloud, and it itself turns about under his guidance to accomplish everything he has commanded it, because these things have been established by God upon the earth” (Job 37:10).

And the Apostle: “The one who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:6).

And in Acts: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us,” the apostles say, “to impose no greater burden upon you” (Acts 15:28).

That he sent these same apostles where he wished and forbade them to go where he wished is also taught from the same book: “When they had fasted and prayed, they laid hands upon them and dismissed them” (Acts 13:3). They, therefore, being sent forth by the Holy Spirit, came to Seleucia.

And again: “As Peter was pondering the vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: ‘Rise and go with them, doubting nothing, because I sent them’” (Acts 10:19).

That he also forbade them is taught as follows: “They came to Phrygia and the region of Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia” (Acts 16:6).

For the Holy Spirit is shown to possess such exceedingly great power that the angels and archangels, who daily dwell and stand in the presence of God the Father and his only Son, also desire, according to the teaching of the Apostle, to look into him with a gentle inclination and, so to speak, furtive glances. The apostle Peter confirms this:

“Concerning this salvation the prophets who prophesied of the grace destined for you searched and examined, searching into what person or what time the Spirit of Jesus Christ within them was signifying” (1 Peter 1:10). And below: “Into these things the angels desire to look” (ibid., 12).

You, therefore, show him reverence and honor him as God, and do not compare him with the breath of a human being or of any kind of creature. By the coming of his inspiration we believe that our bodies will at the last be raised from the grave.

For if—God forbid—he were a creature, Paul would certainly have named him among the heavenly and invisible creatures when he listed the thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers in their order.

## CHAPTER X  
### Where they compare the Son of God and the Lord with the Holy Spirit

If they say to you: “Just as God the Father is Lord of his Son, so the Son is Lord and God of the Holy Spirit.”

### Response

We remember that we have already set forth many testimonies showing that the Holy Spirit is called God and Lord, so that we ought not to add anything further. But lest you attribute this to laziness, or think that we are evading the burdensome weight of your proposition, we teach doubtful minds—through the divine oracles themselves, which he has graciously provided for his own defense—that divinity and lordship are naturally inherent in him, not by our words but by those oracles.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Jacob did not hear the Lord, who redeemed him, received him, and exalted him” (Isaiah 63:9). And below: “But they provoked the Holy Spirit, and he turned against them as an offense” (ibid., 10).

And Jeremiah: “The Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord, was captured in their destruction; under his shadow we live among the nations” (Lamentations 4:20).

And the apostle Peter said to Ananias: “Was it not yours while it remained, and when it was sold, was it not in your power? Why did you wish to test the Holy Spirit, so that you might hold back part of the price of the property?” (Acts 5:4). And below: “You have not lied to human beings but to God.”

And the Apostle: “But when he turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed; now the Lord is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:16).

From this, faithless one, you should recognize that the one who is called God and Lord is equal to the Father and the Son in the very designation of divinity.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit is named third after the Father and the Son

If they say to you that the Holy Spirit is inferior because he is named third after the Father and the Son.

### Response

The Holy Spirit will not be inferior to the Father and the Son merely because he is named third. For when, as we said above, the Lord named water before the Holy Spirit, he certainly did not show water, which he placed first, to be superior to the Holy Spirit.

For it is the custom of the divine Scriptures to name last things first and to list first things last, as it is written in Genesis: “I am the God of Isaac and Abraham, your fathers” (Leviticus 26:42).

The evangelist Luke too, in tracing the ancestry of our Lord and Savior—that is, of Joseph and his mother Mary—began from Joseph and proceeded upward as far as Adam, the first human being, who was made by God. Yet certainly there is no Joseph in the human race who, according to the flesh, was called the father of Christ and could be placed before Adam, the first human being.

But to satisfy your crude objections, we also show that the Holy Spirit was named first, before the Father and the Son, as the Apostle bears witness: “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one God, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4).

The Holy Spirit is certainly not inferior to the Father and the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son; and because of the Spirit who dwells in them, they cannot be said to be perfect in one respect and called to imperfection in another.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten

If they say to you: “Show from where the Holy Spirit derives his origin, since you confess him to be neither unbegotten like the Father nor begotten like the Son.”

### Response

The origin of the Holy Spirit is certain and manifest: the Father and the Son. The faithful do not believe him to be unbegotten with the Unbegotten or begotten with the Only-Begotten, but the declarations of the sacred Scriptures prove that he is the Spirit of the Father.

King Nebuchadnezzar says through the prophet Daniel: “Daniel, whose name is Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, has the Holy Spirit of God in himself” (Daniel 4:5).

Again he himself: “None of all the wise men of my kingdom could make the interpretation of my dream known to me; but you, Daniel, can, because the Holy Spirit of God is in you.” Again there: “Behold, a man in your kingdom in whom is the Spirit of God.”

And in Zechariah: “Nevertheless, receive my ordinances and my words that I command in my Spirit to my servants the prophets” (Zechariah 1:6). Again there: “Not by great strength nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord” (Zechariah 4:6).

And the Apostle to the Romans: “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9).

And to the Galatians: “Because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

And to the Ephesians: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Ephesians 4:30).

And to the Philippians: “For I know that this will result in my salvation through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:19).

And the apostle Peter: “Concerning this salvation the prophets searched and examined, who prophesied of the grace destined for you, searching into what person or what time the Spirit of Jesus Christ within them was signifying” (1 Peter 1:10).

And in the Book of Judges: “They came and encamped in the valley of Jezreel, and the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon” (Judges 6:33).

Consider, wretched men, that the one who was named first before the Father and the Son, and who in many passages of divine Scripture is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is not shown to be inferior to the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### Where they say that the Holy Spirit did not receive life from the Father as the Son did

If they say to you: “We read that the Son received life from the Father so that he might give it to believers in this way; concerning the Holy Spirit we read nothing of the kind, and we judge him inferior to the Son in this respect.”

### Response

Since he is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the divine readings undoubtedly prove him to be the Spirit of life, just as they prove the Father and the Son to be so. The prophet Ezekiel says:

“When the living creatures rose from the earth, the wheels sprang up; wherever the clouds went, and wherever the spirit of the wheels was beside them, it was lifted up with them, because the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezekiel 1:19).

And the Apostle to the Romans: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:2). Again there: “The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (ibid., 6). Again there: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (ibid., 10).

And to the Corinthians: “The first Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving Spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Again in the second letter: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

And in the Apocalypse: “After three and a half days, the spirit of life from the Lord entered them, and they stood upon their feet” (Revelation 11:11). Ezekiel, with the same words and syllables, likewise bears witness concerning the dry bones of the dead (Ezekiel 37:10).

Pay attention, I ask you—pay attention! For he did not speak idly of the “spirit of life,” and the one who, according to the testimonies cited above, grants life to the living and the dead is in no way shown to be inferior to the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Where they say: “Show that the Holy Spirit can proceed from the Father”

If they say to you: “Show that the Holy Spirit could proceed from the Father or the Son.”

## Response

If you wished to lead your hearts, already hardened by the fault of unbelief, toward the tenderness of our faith, you would very readily acknowledge that the Spirit can proceed from God the Father. For the Father is God, and the Spirit of God proceeds from him; he is omnipotent, and the omnipotence of the Spirit proceeds from him; he is light, and the Spirit of light proceeds from him; he is power, and the Spirit of power proceeds from him; he is wise, and the Spirit of wisdom proceeds from him; he is prudence, and the Spirit of prudence proceeds from him; he is counsel, and the Spirit of counsel proceeds from him; he is strength, and the Spirit of strength proceeds from him; he is peace, and the Spirit of peace proceeds from him; he is love, and the Spirit of love proceeds from him; he is knowledge, and the Spirit of knowledge proceeds from him; he is life, and the Spirit of life proceeds from him; he is upright, and the Spirit of uprightness proceeds from him; he is good, and the Spirit of goodness proceeds from him; he is piety, and the Spirit of piety proceeds from him; he is gentle, and the Spirit of gentleness proceeds from him; he is a sword, and the sword of the Spirit proceeds from him.

And there are many other things that we have omitted for the sake of brevity, knowing that for the wise, much is contained in a few words; but however much is said to fools, it does not satisfy them at all. Yet, lest you disturb simple minds with your customary slanders and quibbles by demanding more exact proof from the divine Scriptures concerning the matters stated above, with the Lord’s help we shall fit divine testimonies to each point, so that readers may recognize how they answer your perversity.

That the Spirit is God, the Son taught in the Gospel when he said: “The Spirit is God” (John 4:24). That he is omnipotent is shown in Solomon, where he is described as “the Spirit, all-powerful and all-seeing” (Wis. 7:23). That the Spirit is light, Ezekiel bears witness, when he describes the Spirit of the Lord coming from the north like a brilliant light in a cloud (Ezek. 1:4). That he is power, the Apostle teaches when he says: “In the demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1 Cor. 2:4). That he is called wisdom, Isaiah bears witness, when he says that the Lord’s Son was filled with the spirit of wisdom (Isa. 11:2). That he is called prudence is shown in the same prophet. That he is called the Spirit of counsel and strength is declared in the same book. That he is peace, the Acts of the Apostles testify (Acts 9:31). That he is called love, an apostolic pronouncement confirms. That he is called the Spirit of wisdom is taught by Isaiah’s proclamation. That he is the Spirit of life, the Apostle instructs us when he declared that the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace (Rom. 8:6). That he is called upright is shown by David’s utterances, when he prays that a right spirit may be renewed within him (Ps. 50:12). That he is called good, the same prophet shows, when he sings his desire to be led by the Holy Spirit on a straight path (Ps. 26:11). That he is called the Spirit of gentleness, the Apostle bears witness, when he says that he will come not with a rod, but in the love and gentleness of the Spirit (1 Cor. 4:21). That he is called perfect, the same Apostle teaches, when he presents him as the judge of all and the spirit of the righteous and perfect (Heb. 12:23). That he is called a sword, the same Apostle proves when he declares him to be the word of God (Eph. 6:17). For if they read all these things with minds that were not blind, they would neither doubt the Son of God nor question the power of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XV. Where they say that the Holy Spirit is not diffused everywhere

If they say to you that the Holy Spirit is not everywhere, as the Father and the Son are, but fulfills the office assigned to him locally,

### Response

To show that the Holy Spirit is diffused everywhere, we shall investigate David’s testimony. From his prophecy the Holy Spirit is shown—not to be confined to places, as you are while held fast in deep sleep, but to be diffused everywhere by his power, like the Father and the Son. Finally, in Psalm 138 (verse 7) he sings and says:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings toward the east and dwell at the end of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.

And in Solomon:

> The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world (Wis. 1:7).

Again there:

> Do not say, “I am hidden from the Spirit of God”; and, “Who will remember me from the Most High?” I am not recognized among a great people. For what is my soul amid so great a creation? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens, the abyss and the whole earth, and the things that are in them, are before his sight. At his presence the mountains and hills, the foundations of the earth, will be moved; and when he shakes them, they will be shaken with trembling (Sir. 16:16).

And in the Apocalypse:

> I saw seven golden lampstands, and seven lamps at the head of the seven golden lampstands, and I said: “What are these, Lord?” And he said to me: “The seven lamps are the seven spirits, sent throughout the whole world” (Rev. 1:12).

Behold, we have shown that the Holy Spirit is not held within places and is not bounded by any region. How, then, do you assert that he is not diffused everywhere? Anyone can nevertheless hear his voice, according to the Lord’s saying; but no mortal has been granted to know whence he comes or whither he goes.

## CHAPTER XVI. Where they say that the Holy Spirit is specifically compared with Lucifer

If they say to you that the Holy Spirit is compared with Lucifer, before whom the Father testified that he had begotten the Son, saying:

> In the splendors of the holy ones, from the womb, before Lucifer, I begot you (Ps. 109:3);

or with that which the Apostle Peter said:

> Until the day dawn and Lucifer arise in your hearts (2 Pet. 1:19),

### Response

When the Apostle Peter placed these words in his Epistle for the instruction of believers, he neither called nor taught nor commanded that the Holy Spirit should properly be named Lucifer. But we who believe that there is one God in the Trinity also show that our Lord and Savior himself was proclaimed under the figure of this star, not only by the prophets but also by the Apostles.

In the Book of Numbers, when the most impious and sacrilegious king Balak had induced the false prophet Balaam, by the promise of payment, to curse God’s people, Balaam is shown to have spoken not by his own will but by divine command:

> A star shall arise from Jacob, and a scepter shall rise from Israel, and it shall strike all the kingdoms of the earth (Num. 24:17).

And in another place:

> The pillars of heaven trembled before the Lord, and the stars of heaven feared him (Job 26:11).

For this is his peace and power: that his star should shine in heaven, to enlighten all who believe in him. In the Gospel they say:

> We saw his star in the east, and we came to worship him (Matt. 2:2).

And in the Apocalypse of the Apostle John:

> I am the first and the last (Rev. 22:13). I am the root and offspring of David; I am the bright morning star (ibid., 16).

If, on account of the name of this star and because it was called Lucifer, you insist that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son, will you not also show that the Son—whom we have already taught to have been proclaimed under the type of this same star—is less than the Holy Spirit? Far be it from us; for just as the Son, announced in the image of this star, cannot be said to be inferior to the Holy Spirit, so the Holy Spirit, if he had properly been compared with Lucifer, could not appear inferior to the Son.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where they denounce Catholics because they are said to ask the Holy Spirit for forgiveness of sins

If they attack you, saying that Catholics blaspheme with sacrilegious lips because they are known to ask the Holy Spirit, after the Father and the Son, for forgiveness of sins,

### Response

That the Holy Spirit is judge and can convict the whole world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, the Lord taught in the Gospel, saying:

> When the Holy Spirit comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8).

And Isaiah:

> The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment (Isa. 4:4).

And in Solomon:

> The Spirit of the Lord will stand against them and, like a whirlwind, will divide them (Wis. 5:24).

Again Isaiah:

> Behold, I make judgment in my spirit, says the Lord (Isa. 26:9).

Why, then, do you refuse to allow each person to ask forgiveness of sins from his own judge, so that he may become cleaner and more purified from sins, when by asking he can escape? If, perhaps through some deed or through an unwary utterance, someone had incurred the guilt of wrongdoing, forgiveness was rightly and fittingly sought from the Holy Spirit, that he might grant remission and pardon for sins—the one who intercedes for us with the Father through inexpressible groanings.

But because you call us sacrilegious for asserting, according to the confession of the Trinity, that the Holy Spirit is God and Lord, beware lest you yourself be more deserving of being called by that name, since you refuse to confess the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord willed to be proclaimed to all nations, inseparable from the Father and the Son, through the Apostles:

> Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19).

For if the Holy Spirit is not equal to the Father and the Son in the substance of the Godhead, why is nothing completed without him in the sacrament of holy baptism?

## CHAPTER XVIII. Where they say that the Holy Spirit does not know the Father as the only-begotten Son does

If they say to you: “The Holy Spirit is inferior because the Son alone says of himself that he knows the Father and makes no mention of the Holy Spirit [the text reads: ‘made no mention’],”

### Response

Just as the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ, so the depths of the Godhead are manifest in the Holy Spirit. Since the Apostle affirms this more fully and abundantly, why does your unbelief challenge the truth of the divine majesty? For he says:

> No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him; so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:11).

Behold, the Son is no longer the only one who knows, since the Holy Spirit also knows. This does not introduce any difference between the two persons, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in their knowledge of the things that are God’s; rather, it faithfully makes known to believers the communion of unity.

In another place the same Apostle continues, saying:

> The Spirit searches even the depths of God (1 Cor. 2:10).

And again:

> We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God (ibid., 12).

And in the Gospel the Son says of himself to the Jews:

> You do not know him, but I know him, because I am from him (John 8:55).

If the Holy Spirit is from God, just as the Son is from God, how will he be inferior, since he himself knows what the Son knows in the Father? We have further taught that the Holy Spirit proceeds ineffably from God the Father, as does the Son, because the united Trinity possesses inseparable unity within itself.

## CHAPTER XIX. Where they say that they did not baptize in the name of the Holy Spirit as in the name of the Son

If they say to you: “The Holy Spirit is therefore inferior because the disciples did not baptize in his name, but in the name of the Son,”

### Response

There is no diversity in the Trinity, in which there is not only undivided love of power and will, but also equality of Godhead and majesty. For what is expected from the Father is found in the Son, and what is found in the Son is also bestowed by the Holy Spirit.

But if you wish to inquire with curious mind into the distributions of the Holy Spirit, you will hear the Apostle proclaiming:

> To each of us the illumination of the Spirit is given for our benefit. To one, through the Spirit, is given the spirit of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, charismatic gifts in one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretations of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one his own gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12:7–11).

That one is baptized in the name of the Holy Spirit, as in the name of the Father and the Son, the Lord himself bears witness in the Gospel, and Paul makes the same declaration. The Lord says:

> Baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19).

The Apostle, moreover, indicates and confirms that we have all been baptized in the Spirit:

> For we were all baptized in one Spirit, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit (1 Cor. 12:13).

And again:

> In him, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of adoption (Eph. 1:13).

And again:

> May he grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through the Holy Spirit in the inner person, for Christ to dwell in your hearts (Eph. 3:16).

And again:

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all your fathers were under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink (1 Cor. 10:1).

In these testimonies, therefore, only this is lacking to the divinity of the Holy Spirit which is lacking to your unbelief.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE UNITY OF THE FATHER, THE SON, AND THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 0411]

In these testimonies the unity of the Trinity is shown: whatever the Father is called or does, the Son and the Holy Spirit are likewise called or do the same.

## CHAPTER I. On the common designation of the Godhead

God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit.

Of the Father, the Apostle says:

> One God the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6).

And again:

> There is no God but one (ibid., 4).

Of the Son, in Psalm 99 (verse 3):

> Know that the Lord himself is God; he himself made us, and not we ourselves.

Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says:

> The Spirit is God (2 Cor. 3:17).

And in the Gospel:

> Because he himself is God (John 4:24).

## CHAPTER II. Where the whole Trinity is called Lord

The Father is called Lord, the Son is called Lord, and the Holy Spirit is called Lord.

Of the Father, in Leviticus:

> I am the Lord your God, who freed you from the land of Egypt (Lev. 19:36).

Of the Son, in Psalm 95 (verse 10):

> Say among the nations, “The Lord has reigned from the wood.”

Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says:

> There are divisions of ministries, but it is the same Lord (1 Cor. 12:5).

Again there:

> The Lord is the Spirit.

## CHAPTER III. On the common omnipotence of the Trinity

The Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, and the Holy Spirit is omnipotent (2 Cor. 3:17).

Of the Father, in Solomon:

> Your omnipotent word, leaping from the royal thrones, came (Wis. 18:15).

Of the Son, in the passage cited above:

> For the one Most High is the omnipotent Creator, a powerful king and exceedingly fearsome (Sir. 1:8).

Of the Holy Spirit, in the passage cited above:

> For in wisdom there is a holy, unique spirit of understanding (Wis. 7:22);

and below:

> all-powerful (ibid., 27).

## CHAPTER IV. On the common power of the Trinity

The Father is powerful, the Son is powerful, and the Holy Spirit is powerful.

Of the Father, the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> God is able to make all grace abound toward you (2 Cor. 9:8).

Again there:

> So that your faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God (1 Cor. 2:5).

Of the Son, in the passage cited above:

> When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 5:4).

Again, in the Second Epistle:

> Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ, who is not weak toward you but is powerful (2 Cor. 13:3)?

Of the Holy Spirit, in the passage cited above:

> For I will not dare to speak of any of those things that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, through the power of the Spirit (Rom. 15:18).

And again:

> May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit (ibid., 13).

## CHAPTER V. On the common designation of fatherhood

God the Father, the Father the Son, the Father the Holy Spirit.

Of the Father, the Apostle says:

> One God the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6).

And again:

> The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ knows—he who is blessed forever (2 Cor. 11:31).

Of the Son, in the song of Deuteronomy:

> Is he not your father, who possessed you, made you, and established you (Deut. 32:6)?

And Isaiah:

> A child is born to us, a son is given to us (Isa. 9:6).

And below:

> Mighty God, father of the age to come, prince of peace.

Of the Holy Spirit, in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> We had human fathers of our flesh as correctors, and we respected them; how much more shall we submit to the Father of spirits and obey him, so that we may live? They disciplined us for a few days according to their will, as seemed good to them; but the Spirit [gives discipline] for the benefit of receiving his sanctification (Heb. 12:9).

## CHAPTER VI. Where the whole Trinity is called holy

The Father is holy, the Son is holy, and the Holy Spirit is holy.

Of the Father, in Ezra:

> For holy God is truth.

And in Leviticus:

> Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy (Lev. 11:44).

Of the Son, in the Gospel:

> I know who you are: the Holy One of God (Mark 1:24).

Again there:

> The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35).

Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon:

> For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding (Wis. 1:5).

## CHAPTER VII. On the common sovereignty of the Trinity

The Father is sovereign, the Son is sovereign, and the Holy Spirit is sovereign.

Of the Father, in Judges:

> Gideon said to them: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son; God is ruler among you” (Judg. 8:23).

And in Numbers:

> There is no labor in Jacob, nor is toil seen in Israel, because the Lord their God is with him, and the illustrious prince is with him (Num. 23:21).

Of the Son, in the Epistle of the Apostle Peter:

> Tend the flock of God that is among you, not as compelled but willingly and wholeheartedly, so that when the chief Shepherd appears you may receive the unfading crown (1 Pet. 5:2–3).

Of the Holy Spirit, in Psalm 50 (verse 14):

> Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the whole Trinity is called by the name “King”

The Father is king, the Son is king, and the Holy Spirit is king.

Of the Father, in Isaiah:

> The Lord is the great king, and rich in his works (Isa. 33:22).

And in the Psalm:

> But God our king, before the ages, has worked salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73:12).

Of the Son, in the Apocalypse:

> The heavenly army followed him on white horses, clothed in clean linen (Rev. 19:14).

And below:

> On his garment and on his thigh he has a name written: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (ibid., 16).

Of the Holy Spirit, in Isaiah:

> I saw the Lord, the King of Sabaoth, with my eyes (Isa. 6:5).

And I heard a voice saying to me:

> Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?

And I said:

> Here I am; send me.

And he said to me:

> Go, and say to this people: “With your ears you will hear and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not perceive” (ibid., 8).

To understand that this was the Holy Spirit, hear Paul rebuking the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles:

> Well did the Holy Spirit speak to your fathers: “With your ears you will hear and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not perceive” (Acts 28:26).

## CHAPTER IX. Where the whole Trinity is called by the name “Judge”

The Father is judge, the Son is judge, and the Holy Spirit is judge.

Of the Father, in Psalm 49 (verse 6):

> The heavens will proclaim his righteousness, because God is judge.

And in Psalm 7 (verse 12):

> God is a righteous judge, strong and patient.

Of the Son, in the Canonical Epistles:

> Behold, the judge stands before the door (James 5:9).

Of the Holy Spirit:

> And now the man of sin, the son of perdition, will be revealed, whom the Lord will destroy with the spirit of his mouth (2 Thess. 2:3, 8).

And in Isaiah:

> Behold, I make judgment in my spirit, says the Lord God.

## CHAPTER X. On the common perfection

The Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, and the Holy Spirit is perfect.

Of the Father, in the Gospel:

> Therefore be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matt. 5:48).

Of the Son, in the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> From what he suffered he learned to become obedient; and, having been made perfect, he was made perfect for all who obey him (Heb. 5:8).

Of the Holy Spirit, in the passage cited above:

> But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living Jerusalem (Heb. 12:22).

And below:

> And the spirit of the righteous who have been perfected (ibid., 23).

## CHAPTER XI. On the common truth

The Father is true, the Son is true, and the Holy Spirit is true.

Of the Father, in Solomon:

> Our God is gracious and true; and to know you is the fullness of righteousness (Wis. 15:1, 3).

Of the Son, in John:

> So that we may be in his true Son, Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life (1 John 5:20).

Of the Holy Spirit, in the Gospel:

> When the Paraclete comes, that Spirit of truth, he will teach you all truth (John 16:13).

## CHAPTER XII. On the designation “righteous”

The Father is righteous, the Son is righteous, and the Holy Spirit is righteous.

Of the Father, in Exodus:

> Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: “I have sinned now, for the Lord is righteous, but I and my people are impious” (Exod. 9:27).

Of the Son, in Zephaniah:

> The Lord is righteous in your midst; he will do no injustice (Zeph. 3:5).

And in the Epistle of John:

> As he taught you, remain in him (1 John 2:27).

And below:

> If you know that he is righteous, know also that everyone who practices righteousness is from him (ibid., 29).

Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says:

> The great mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh and justified in the Spirit (1 Tim. 3:16).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the common strength

The Father is strong, the Son is strong, and the Holy Spirit is strong.

Of the Father, in Isaiah:

> Strong and powerful God, of great name, Lord (Isa. 28:2).

Of the Son, in Psalm 117 (verse 14):

> The Lord is my strength and my praise.

Of the Holy Spirit, in Solomon:

> In the fear of God there is a spirit of strength, and in his ways, peace and eternal life (Prov. 14:26).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the common judgment

The Father judges, the Son judges, and the Holy Spirit judges.

Of the Father, in Psalm 42 (verse 1):

> Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause.

Of the Son, in Psalm 9 (verse 9):

> He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness.

Of the Holy Spirit, in Isaiah:

> The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse their blood from their midst by the Spirit of judgment (Isa. 4:4).

## CHAPTER XV. On the common work of the Trinity

The Father works, the Son works, and the Holy Spirit works.

Of the Father, the Apostle says to the Philippians:

> It is God who works in you both to will and to act (Phil. 2:13).

Of the Son, in the Gospel:

> I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day (John 9:4).

Of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says:

> One and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each one his own gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11).

## CHAPTER XVI. That the whole Trinity bears the name “Most High”

The Father is Most High, the Son is Most High, and the Holy Spirit is Most High.

Of the Father, in Daniel:

> The signs and wonders that the Most High God performed with me (Dan. 3:99).

And in Psalm 77 (verse 35):

> The Most High God is their redeemer.
