Bishop Ambrose said: “Today we are proving that you falsify the divine Scriptures. For it is written this way: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. Let not your heart be troubled. I do not give to you as this world gives. If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I said, “I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I”’ [Col. 0442B] (John 14:27–28). He did not say, ‘The one who sent me is greater than I.’”

Palladius said: “The Father is greater.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Anathema to him who adds anything to or subtracts anything from the divine Scriptures.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “According to the flesh, the Son is lesser than the Father; according to divinity, he is equal to the Father. I have therefore read that the Son of God is equal to the Father, as the copies now produced also testify. According to the flesh, however, why are you surprised that he is lesser, since he said that he was a servant, since he called himself a stone, since he said that he was lower than the angels, because it is written, ‘You made him a little lower than the angels’ (Ps. 8:6)?”

Palladius said: “I see you making impious assertions; we do not answer you without hearers.”

[Col. 0442C] Bishop Sabinus said: “Let no one ask the judgment of one who has blasphemed in so many innumerable judgments.”

Palladius said: “We do not answer you.”

Bishop Sabinus said: “Palladius has now been condemned by everyone. The blasphemies of Aetius are far less serious than those of Palladius.” And when Palladius rose and wished to go outside, he said: “Palladius has risen for this reason: he sees that he is to be convicted by the clear testimonies of the Scriptures, just as he has already been convicted. For it has been read that, according to divinity, the Son is equal to the Father. Let him accept that, according to divinity, the Son of God has no one greater. It is written: ‘When God made the promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself’ (Heb. 6:13). You see, therefore, from the Scripture that he has no one greater by whom he might swear. But it is the Son of whom it is said that he appeared to Abraham. Hence he also says: ‘Abraham saw my day and rejoiced’ (John 8:56).”

Palladius said: “‘The Father is greater.’”

Bishop Eusebius said: “When he spoke as God, he had no one greater; when he spoke as man, he had one greater.”

Palladius said: “The Father begot the Son; the Father sent the Son.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Anathema to him who denies that the Son is equal to the Father according to divinity.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

[Col. 0443A] Palladius said: “The Son is subject to the Father; the Son keeps the Father’s commands.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Subject according to the condition of the flesh. Moreover, you yourself remember that you read: ‘No one comes to me unless the Father draws him’ (John 6:44).”

Bishop Sabinus said: “Let him say whether he is subject to the Father according to divinity or according to the incarnation.”

Palladius said: “Then the Father is greater.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “And elsewhere it is written: ‘God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son’ (1 Cor. 1:9). I say that the Father is greater according to the assumption of the flesh, which the Son of God assumed, not according to divinity.”

[Col. 0443B] Palladius said: “For what comparison is there with the Son of God? The flesh too can say, ‘God is greater than I.’ Was it the flesh that spoke, or divinity, since the flesh was there?”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Flesh does not speak without a soul.”

Bishop Eusebius said: “God was speaking in the flesh according to the flesh when he said: ‘Why are you persecuting me, a man?’ (John 8:40). Who said this?”

Palladius said: “The Son of God.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Then the Son of God is God according to divinity and man according to the flesh.”

Palladius said: “He assumed flesh.”

Bishop Eusebius said: “Then he used human words?”

Palladius said: “He assumed human flesh.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Let him say that the Apostle did not call him subject according to divinity, but according to the flesh. For it is written: ‘He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death’ (Phil. 2:8). In what, then, did he taste death?”

Palladius said: “Because he humbled himself.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “It was not the divinity but the flesh that was humbled and subjected.” And he added: “Did Arius rightly or wrongly call him a perfect creature?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you, since you have no authority.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Profess whatever you wish.”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you.”

[Col. 0443D] Sabinus the bishop said: “You do not answer on behalf of Arius? You do not answer the questions put to you?”

Palladius said: “I did not answer on behalf of Arius.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “You have answered to such an extent that you denied the Son of God to be powerful; you denied him to be the true God.”

Palladius said: “I do not accept you as judge, since I accuse you of impiety.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “You yourself compelled us to sit.”

Palladius said: “I ordered you to sit so that I might accuse you. Why did you deceive the emperor? You surreptitiously prevented there being a full council.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “When the impieties of Arius were being read, your impiety too was condemned, since it consented to the Arian impiety. In the middle of the reading of the letter you chose to put forward what you wanted. You were answered concerning the way in which the Son of God called the Father greater: he called the Father greater according to the assumption of the flesh. You also proposed that the Son of God was subject, and you were answered on this point: the Son of God is subject according to the flesh, not according to the divinity. You have our profession; now listen to the rest. Since you have been answered, respond to what is being read.”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you, because none of the things I said are written down. Only your words are written down. I do not answer you.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “You see everything being written down. Indeed, the things that have been written provide abundant evidence of your impiety.” And he added: “Do you call Christ a creature, or do you deny it?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “A short while ago, during the proceedings, when it was read that Arius called Christ a creature, you denied it. You were given the opportunity to condemn the false faith, but you refused. Say now, at least, whether Christ was born from the Father or created.”

Palladius said: “If you wish, let our notaries come, and let the whole matter be recorded in this way.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “Let him bring his own notaries.”

Palladius said: “We shall answer you in a full council.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Attalus signed the statement of the Council of Nicaea. Let him deny that he came to the council. Let him say today whether or not he signed the statement of the Council of Nicaea.”

When Attalus remained silent, Ambrose the bishop said: “Attalus the presbyter, although he is among the Arians, nevertheless has authority to speak. Let him freely profess whether or not he signed the statement of the Council of Nicaea under his bishop Agrippinus.”

Attalus said: “You have already said several times that I have been condemned; I do not answer you.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Did you sign the statement of the Council of Nicaea or not?”

Attalus said: “I do not answer you.”

Palladius said: “Do you now want the full statement to be produced, or not?”

Chromatius the presbyter said: “You did not deny that he was a creature; you denied his power. You denied everything that the Catholic faith professes.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “We are witnesses that Attalus signed at the Council of Nicaea and now refuses to answer. What does everyone think?”

When Attalus remained silent, Ambrose the bishop said: “Let him say whether or not he signed the statement of the Council of Nicaea.”

Palladius said: “Let your notary and ours stand together and write everything down.”

Valerian the bishop said: “Everything you have said and denied has already been written down.”

Palladius said: “Say whatever you wish.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Since Palladius, who has already been condemned many times, now wishes to be condemned yet again, I shall read the letter of Arius, which he refused to condemn. Profess what seems right to you.”

All the bishops said: “Let it be read.”

And it was read: “BUT BORN, NOT IN PRETENSE,” and the rest.

Ambrose the bishop said: “I answered you concerning the greater one; I answered you also concerning subjection. Now answer yourself.”

Palladius said: “I shall not answer unless the authorities come after Sunday.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “You came to conduct the proceedings, but after I confronted you, you saw the letter of Arius, which you refused to condemn, though you cannot affirm it. Therefore you now withdraw and quibble. Read it out in full: speak to each point. Does Christ appear to have been created? Was there a time when Christ did not exist? Or was he always the only-begotten Son of God? Once you have heard the letter of Arius, either condemn it or approve it.”

Palladius said: “Since I accuse you of impiety, I do not use you as judge. You are a transgressor.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “What impieties do you charge against our brother and fellow priest Ambrose? State them.”

Palladius said: “I have already told you: I shall answer in a full council and in the presence of the authorities.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “I desire to be refuted and disproved in the assembly of my brothers. Therefore state what I have said impiously. But do I seem impious to you because I uphold piety?”

Sabinus the bishop said: “So he seems impious to you because he rebukes the blasphemies of Arius?”

Palladius said: “I did not deny that the Son of God is good.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Then you say that Christ is the good God?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you.”

Valerian the bishop said: “Do not press Palladius too much; he cannot simply confess our truth. His conscience is confused by a twofold blasphemy. For he was ordained by the Photinians and condemned together with them; and now he will be condemned even more fully.”

Palladius said: “Prove this.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “He could not deny Christ to be true except by following his own authorities.” [The printed text reads *non liter poterat*; the wording is uncertain.]

Ambrose the bishop said: “You accused me of being impious; prove it.”

Palladius said: “We shall bring forward our exposition. When we have brought it, the disputation will take place.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Condemn the impiety of Arius.”

When Palladius remained silent, Eusebius the bishop said: “We are lingering over what is superfluous. Palladius refused to condemn so many impieties of Arius; indeed, by affirming them, he confessed them. Whoever does not condemn this man is like him and must rightly be called a heretic.”

All the bishops said: “Let Palladius be anathema from us all.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Palladius, do you consent to the rest being read?”

Palladius said: “Provide hearers; let notaries from both sides come. You cannot be judges if we do not have hearers, and unless people come from both sides to listen, we will not answer you.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “What hearers are you seeking?”

Palladius said: “There are many distinguished men here.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “After so many blasphemies, you ask for hearers?”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Priests ought to judge laymen, not laymen priests; nevertheless, state whom you seek as judges.”

Palladius said: “Let hearers come.”

Chromatius the presbyter said: “Without prejudice to the priestly condemnation, let the statements of Palladius’s own people also be read in full.”

[Col. 0446B] Palladius said: “Let the hearers not be permitted to speak; let notaries from both sides come, and these men will answer you in a general council.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Although he has been caught in many impieties, we nevertheless are ashamed that one who claims the priesthood should appear to have been condemned by laymen. Accordingly, since the man who awaits the judgment of laymen must himself also be condemned on this very point—whereas priests ought rather to judge laymen—in accordance with what we have heard Palladius profess today, and in accordance with what he refused to condemn, I declare him unworthy of the priesthood and order that a Catholic be ordained in his place.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema to Palladius.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “The most merciful and Christian emperor [Col. 0446C] entrusted the case to the judgment of the priests [Note: [Col. 0446D] The words meaning ‘permitted us’ are missing.], and had established that they themselves should be arbiters of the dispute. Since, then, it appears that judgment has been entrusted to us, Scripture is our interpreter: let us condemn Palladius, who refused to condemn the judgment of the impious Arius. And since he himself denied that the Son of God is eternal, along with the other matters attached to the proceedings, let him therefore be held anathema.”

All the bishops said: “Let us all condemn him; let him be held anathema.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Since all present are Christian men, brothers approved by God, and our fellow priests, let each one state what seems right to him.”

Valerian the bishop said: “It seems to me that whoever defends Arius is an Arian; whoever does not condemn his blasphemies is himself a blasphemer. Therefore I judge that such a man must be excluded from the fellowship of priests.”

Palladius said: “Have you begun to play games? Then play: we will not answer you without an Eastern council.”

Anemius, bishop of Sirmium, said: “Whoever does not condemn the Arian heresies must necessarily be an Arian. Therefore we judge that this man too must be excluded from our communion and from the priestly assembly, and must again be deprived of them.”

Constantius, bishop of Arausio, said: “Palladius, a disciple of Arius, whose impieties were long ago condemned by our fathers at the Council of Nicaea, and which have now been brought forward today—when each of them was recited to Palladius, he was not confounded, while confessing that the Son of God is alien from God the Father and belongs among creatures, and while calling him temporal—therefore I judge that he must be condemned forever for denying the true Lord.”

Justus the bishop said: “I judge that Palladius, who refused to condemn the blasphemies of Arius and even appears rather to confess them, can no longer be called a priest or counted among the bishops.”

Eventius, bishop of Ticinum, said: “I believe that Palladius, who refused to condemn the impiety of Arius, must be permanently removed from the priestly fellowship.”

Abundantius, bishop of Tridentum, said: “Since Palladius defends manifest blasphemies, let him recognize that he has been condemned by the Council of Aquileia.”

[Col. 0447B] Eusebius, bishop of Bononia, said: “Because Palladius not only refused to condemn the impieties of Arius, written in a diabolical style and not even fit to be admitted to the ears, but also became their defender by denying that the Son of God is the true Son, the good Lord, the wise Lord, and the eternal Lord, I judge that he has rightly been condemned—by my judgment and by the judgment of all Catholics—and must be removed from the priestly assembly.”

Sabinus, bishop of Placentia, said: “Since it has been made clear to everyone that Palladius is an author of Arian false faith and holds its impiety, which is contrary to the evangelical and apostolic ordinances, the sentence brought against him by the entire council is just. By my sentence—although perhaps through the judgment of my own smallness [F. *parvitatis*, ‘smallness’, for *pravitatis*, ‘depravity’]—he must rightly be expelled from this most holy assembly and again deprived of the priesthood.”

[Col. 0447C] Felix and Numidius, envoys of the Africans, said: “Anathema to the sect of the Arian heresy, in which Palladius was declared at the Synod of Aquileia. We also condemn those who resist the truth of the Synod of Nicaea.”

Limenius, bishop of Vercellae, said: “It is evident that Arian doctrine has often been condemned. Therefore Palladius, summoned before this holy Synod of Aquileia, where he refused to correct or amend it but rather approved it, has defiled himself with a detectable false faith, which he publicly professed to hold. By my sentence, I too declare him deprived of the priestly fellowship.”

Maximinus, bishop of Emona, said: “God knows, and the conscience of the faithful has condemned, that Palladius, who refused to condemn the blasphemies of Arius but rather confessed them himself, has been justly and deservedly condemned.”

Exsuperantius, bishop of Dertona, said: “Palladius refused to condemn the sect or doctrine of Arius and instead defended it. As my other colleagues have condemned him, so do I condemn him.”

Bassianus, bishop of Lauda, said: “I heard, as did my other fellow priests, the impieties of Arius, which Palladius not only did not condemn but confirmed. Let him be anathema, and let him be deprived of the priesthood.”

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, said: “Together with all the others, I condemn the blasphemies and wickedness of Palladius, who follows and defends Arian doctrine.”

Constantius, bishop of Siscia, said: “I, together with my other fellow priests, judge that Palladius, who did not condemn the blasphemies and impieties of Arius, must be condemned.”

[Col. 0448A] Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum, said: “Together with my fellow priests, I condemn the false faith of Arius and of all the heretics whose associate Palladius is—this foolish man whose heart did not confess the truth.”

Felix, bishop of Jadera, said: “Together with all the others, I condemn Palladius, who blasphemed the Son as Arius did.”

Theodorus, bishop of Octodurum, said: “We judge Palladius, who denied Christ to be the true God, coeternal with the Father, to be neither a Christian nor a priest in any way.”

[Col. 0448B] Domninus, bishop of Gratianopolis, said: “I too judge Palladius, who remains in the false faith of Arius, to be condemned forever, as the brothers have condemned him.”

Proculus, bishop of Marseille, said: “Palladius defended the blasphemies of Arius by refusing to condemn them under a certain impious inheritance. Since the sentence of many already venerable priests has designated him a blasphemer and judged him alien from the priesthood, my sentence likewise designates him as condemned forever.”

Diogenes, bishop of Geneva, said: “I judge that Palladius, who denied Christ the Lord, the true God, by refusing to confess him similar and equal to the Father, must share condemnation with my other brothers and fellow priests.”

Amantius, bishop of Nice, said: “I too condemn Palladius, who did not destroy the sect of Arius, in accordance with the judgment of my fellow priests.”

Januarius the bishop said: “As all my fellow priests have condemned Palladius, so I too, by the same judgment, judge that he must be condemned.”

And when Secundianus had interjected, Ambrose the bishop said: “You have heard, Secundianus, the kind of judgment Palladius, the impious man condemned by the priestly council, received. Although we were displeased that you did not recoil from his madness—that is, Palladius’s madness—I nevertheless ask you specifically whether you say that God’s Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is or is not the true God.”

[Col. 0448D] Secundianus said: “Whoever denies that the Father of our Lord and God Jesus Christ is the true Lord is not a Christian; nor is he a Christian who denies that the Son is the true Lord.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Do you confess the Son of God to be the true God?”

Secundianus said: “I call the true Son of God, the only-begotten true Son of God.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Do you call him the true God?”

Secundianus said: “Who denies that the true only-begotten Son is the true Son of God?”

Eusebius the bishop said: “It is not enough that you confess the Son of God to be the only-begotten, for everyone confesses this. What is at issue is that Arius called the Father alone Lord, alone true, and denied the Son of God to be the true Lord. Do you simply confess the Son of God to be the true God?”

Secundianus said: “I do not know who Arius was, nor do I know what he said. You are speaking with me, a living man, face to face. I say what Christ said: he asserts himself to be the only-begotten Son of the Father, the only-begotten Son; the true Son of God is God.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “The Son of God is true God, true God; the Son is God.” And he added: “It is written in the divine Scriptures: ‘Those who swear upon the earth will swear by the true God’ (Isaiah 65:16).” There can be no doubt that this concerns Christ. Therefore we profess the true God, and this is our faith and profession: the only-begotten Son of the Father is the true God. You too must speak of the true God; say that the Son of God is the true God.

Secundianus said: “Of the true God.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Is the Son of God the true God?”

Secundianus said: “Then he is a liar.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “You are committing fraud in this, by refusing to call him the true God and instead calling him the only-begotten God. Therefore say simply: ‘The only-begotten Son of God is the true God.’”

Secundianus said: “I said ‘the only-begotten Son of God.’”

Eusebius the bishop said: “Photinus does not deny this; Sabellius confesses it.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “And whoever does not confess this is rightly condemned. Accordingly, I question you again, although you deny the truth by quibbling. I am not asking you merely to call him the only-begotten Son of God, but also the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I profess myself a servant of the truth. The things I say are not written down, while the things you say are written down. I call Christ the true Son of God. Who denies that the Son of God is true?”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Whoever denies the only-begotten Son of God, let him be anathema.”

Secundianus said: “The true God, the only-begotten Son of God? Why are you making me profess something that is not written down?”

Ambrose the bishop said: “It is manifest sacrilege when Arius denied Christ the Son of God to be the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I call Jesus Christ the Son of God, God; I call him the true Son who is called Christ, the Son of God.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “You have not yet come to your senses.” And he added: “So that it may not appear that anything has been slipped past him, let him confirm his own statement. Let him say that the only-begotten Christ, the Son of God, is the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I have already said it. What more do you wish to force from me?”

Ambrose the bishop said: “What did you say? Certainly, if you had said something so glorious, it ought often to be repeated.”

Secundianus said: “It has been said: ‘Let your speech be yes, yes; no, no’ (Matthew 5:37).”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Whoever says that the Father himself is the Son is sacrilegious. What I ask of you is that you say, concerning the true God, that the true Son of God was born from the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I confess the Son begotten from God—since he himself says, ‘I have begotten you’ (Psalm 109:3)—and I say that the Son confesses himself to have been begotten.”

[Col. 0450B] Ambrose the bishop said: “Is he the true God from the true God?”

Secundianus said: “When you add ‘true’ even to the name, you hear what sort of faith you have and whether you are a Christian.”

Eusebius the bishop said: “Who denied him to be the true God? Arius and Palladius denied it. If you believe him to be the true God, you ought to identify him simply.”

Ambrose the bishop said: “If you do not say that the true God was born from the true God, you have denied Christ.”

Secundianus said: “When questioned about the Son, I gave my answer; I answered as I ought to profess. We have your exposition; we shall bring it forward. Let it be read.”

Ambrose said: “You ought to have brought it today; instead, you are trying to evade the matter. Demand a profession from me, and I demand a profession from you. Is the Son of God the true God?”

Secundianus said: “He is the only-begotten God, the Son of God. And I ask you: is he the only-begotten?”

Ambrose the bishop said: “Your impiety and foolishness ought to move us to reason. When you say ‘the true only-begotten God,’ you do not say ‘the true God,’ but ‘the true only-begotten one.’ Therefore, to remove this ambiguity, answer as follows: Is the true God from the true God?”

Secundianus said: “Then did God not beget God? The true God, who is what he is, begot what he is: he begot one true, only-begotten Son.”

Ambrose said: “You do not confess the true God; you wish to say ‘the true only-begotten one.’ I too say ‘only-begotten,’ but I also say ‘the true God.’”

Secundianus said: “I say that he was begotten true, begotten from the Father; I say this to everyone.”

# BOOK TWO. ON THE FAITH, IN THE PERSON OF AMBROSE

[Col. 0449]

[Note: [Col. 0449] Although in the Divion manuscript the text runs continuously, we have nevertheless retained the division into eight chapters found in the printed editions.]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0449D]

Ambrose the bishop said: “We know many serious heresies to bubble up from many sources and, like poison, to pour the virus of their cancer into the innermost heart (2 Timothy 2:17). But those whose entire purpose is revealed in their first proposition can either easily be overcome or easily avoided. Yet those who agree with us in many respects can easily strike minds that are innocent and devoted solely to God through a deceptive association, defending their own evils by means of our goods.

“For nothing can be more dangerous than these heretics, who, although they proceed wholly and completely in every respect, nevertheless infect, with a single word—as though with a drop of poison—that pure and simple faith of the Lord’s tradition and thereafter of the apostolic tradition. Therefore we must be exceedingly careful lest something of this kind secretly insinuate itself into our understanding or ears, since nothing drives a person so effectively to death as violating the integrity of the faith under the pretext of faith itself.

“For just as gypsum mixed with water imitates milk in color, so here an alien tradition is introduced under the appearance of a plausible confession. Consequently, it is not the similarity of the confession but the meaning of the mind by which the confession itself is made firm that must be weighed.

“Indeed, if you attend more carefully and precisely, you will undoubtedly see why they wanted the name ‘of one substance’ removed from the evangelical and apostolic faith and from the tradition of the Fathers: by this subtle and abbreviated expedient, once the name had been removed, they introduced the Arian heresy. Nor do I assert this as something gathered merely from suspicion or opinion; nor do I appear—as they think—as an Academic disputant, twisting simple meanings through subtlety. Rather, I bring into the light of knowledge meanings that have been twisted and corrupted and composed through a thin argument, so that the iniquity, once known and established, may more easily be avoided by all.

“For what cause, what reason, existed for them to labor—not without great effort—to remove what had been handed down for teaching and belief to all the churches, and what our fathers, apostolic men, filled with the Holy Spirit, had established by Catholic reasoning against all heresies, especially the Arian heresy, as a kind of barrier of truth by which all entrances to pestilential doctrine might be blocked? Surely it was so that they might fabricate the Son of God as mutable and changeable, as one who did not subsist from the Father’s own substance; so that they might now freely, securely, and without hesitation deliver and insinuate to the churches what they had always taught—and for which they had often been condemned—namely, that he had a beginning in time, an origin from nothing, and a name derived from another.”

## CHAPTER TWO

“You see, therefore, that in their statement they have placed everything not according to the evangelical faith but through deceitful wickedness, in order to seduce the simple. It should no longer be merely suspected but manifest to everyone that they posited God from God in the manner Arius used to teach: that he was made from God, not born from God.

“If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not the true Son; and if he is not the true Son, he is not the true God. Or, if he is the true God but is not from the Father, there are two beings, each possessing its own will and differing authority. Or, if they are one only through agreement and fellowship, but not also in substance, then, as I have already said, he is not the true God. In that case he will be God in the way Moses was God to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1): by power, not by kind.

“The Son, too, will have to be believed to be such as was said to the people through Isaiah: ‘I have begotten and exalted sons’ (Isaiah 1:2), and as it says elsewhere: ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’ (Psalm 81:6). He will also be regarded as firstborn in the way Israel was called by God his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), and as the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15), as though he were firstborn in the order of created things, so that from him they might assign a certain sequence to the things of the world that were to be created.

“Finally, after removing ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), that is, the term ‘of one substance,’ they substituted ὁμοιούσιον (*homoiousion*), that is, ‘similar to his maker,’ although similarity is one thing and truth another. For man too was made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), and yet he is not God; nor should it be believed that man came into existence as what God is.

“In the same way they want the Son of God to be similar, so that they may say that he is similar from another source, not from that one holy and blessed substance of the Father. If he is not from the Father’s substance, he is ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, that is, ‘from things that do not exist,’ as Arius himself taught. Once that by which he is Father has been removed, wherever the Son may have come from, he must necessarily have both a beginning from nothing and an origin in time. Nothing is without a beginning except God alone.

“Therefore the Son, as the Lord himself says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). He said this in order to display the names of two persons in the majesty of one divinity, just as the prophet also says in the voice of God: ‘My heart has poured forth the good Word; I speak my works to the king’ (Psalm 44:2).

“You see, therefore, that this good Word is the Son of God, whom we believe to have been born from nowhere other than the Father’s breast and—as I might put it—from the womb of God’s heart. For this reason he calls him king, because he is the King of kings; the Lord God, before whom all divine works bow; the one who said: ‘Everything that the Father has is mine’ (John 16:15).

“Of him the Evangelist also says: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’ (John 1:1). Therefore what was in the beginning must be believed always to have existed. Nor should he be believed to be from anywhere other than from him who has no beginning—that is, from the Father’s heart—for, as he says, ‘my heart has poured forth the good Word.’

“For he did not say, ‘In the beginning the Word was made,’ but, ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ Whatever beginning you wish to assign to the Word, you will find yourself refuted, because he says, ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ We are not saying that there are two beginnings because of a difference among things; rather, the Word, the Son, is always with the Father and was born from the Father.

“Therefore, since his origin has no beginning, he must be believed eternal. For the Father can never be named without the Son, nor the Son called without the Father; and thus the Son is always the Son because the Father is always the Father.

“And ‘the Word was God.’ What is God always is; for if he has not always been, he cannot be the true God—just as with the name ‘wisdom,’ since according to the Apostle he himself is the wisdom of the Father (1 Corinthians 1:24). ‘I came forth,’ he says, ‘from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclesiasticus 24:5). Therefore he is from nowhere other than the Father, because he is always with the Father.

“For this reason he is called the Wisdom of God, so that the Father may never be believed to have existed without wisdom, that is, without his Son. This is that ineffable wisdom which Solomon describes as either founded, born, or created as the beginning of God’s works (Proverbs 8). Yet he describes it as founded in such a way as to show that it had always been with God.

“What beginning will you assign to God so that you can designate a beginning for his wisdom? God did not establish his wisdom in such a way that he once existed without wisdom. Rather, when he calls it the beginning of his ways, he indicates the beginning of the movement of some work, so that the beginning of God’s wisdom is that it proceeded from God in order to establish all things, heavenly as well as earthly—not that it began to exist in God.

“Therefore wisdom was created—or rather, born—not for itself, which always existed, but for those things that had to be made by it. Since its greatness and nature could not be known, its power and strength might be recognized from the effect of its works, so that, when we estimate the creator from created things, we may fear all the more as we marvel at what has been made.

“But if you call wisdom created in such a way that you understand the Son of God to be a creature, the Apostle confronts you, condemning those who worship the creature, saying: ‘Therefore God handed them over to the desire of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever, God’ (Romans 1:24–25).

“This, I say, is that Wisdom of God which says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclesiasticus 24:5), the founder and maker of the universe—that is, the Son of God, through whom and in whom all things exist. For, as the Apostle said: ‘In him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or powers or principalities or authorities; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him’ (Colossians 1:16–17).

“Solomon also says: ‘Although she is one, she can do all things; remaining in herself, she renews all things, and through the nations she passes into holy souls’ (Wisdom 7:27). Confirming this, the Apostle says that Christ dwells in the inner person, so that through him by whom all things were made in the beginning, all things may also be saved at the end (Ephesians 3:16).”

## CHAPTER THREE

“But you say that the name ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), ‘of one substance,’ ought not to be used because it is not contained in the divine Scriptures. I ask you, then, you who forbid this, whether it ought not to be named because it is not written, or because it is not permitted to be believed in this way. If it ought to be believed in this way, why should it not also be professed in this way? For the Apostle says: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Romans 10:10).

“Or, if it ought not to be named because it ought not to be believed in this way, the assertion of the Arian corruption has prevailed. It denied that the Father and the Son are of one substance because it introduces the Son of God as made—sometimes from nothing, sometimes from the Father but from another substance—whenever, however, and from wherever it wishes, provided that it fabricates him as having existed from elsewhere and not from what the Father is.

“Although it says that he was born, it says so only in words, because it again understands everything born to have been made, since we too are called begotten by God, although it is clear that we are made.

“Or, if you are not an Arian and acknowledge the true Son born, not made, from the true Father, why do you not say that he is one substance with the Father? You are foolishly afraid to profess what you believe—or foolishly believe if you do not believe in this way—and rightly you are marked out as a heretic.

“And although you have not changed the statement by which you thought to have forbidden the Son of God to be called a creature, yet when you add, ‘Like one of these things that has been made,’ you plainly show that you did not refuse to call him a creature in order that he should not be understood as made. Rather, you do not want him made in the same way as one of those things that has been made, but nevertheless made. For you say that he was made in another way—as a perfect creature, through whom all things were made—provided that you still understand him to have been made, although not in the same way as the rest.

“But to return to what you say, that the term ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), ‘of one substance,’ is not found in the divine Scriptures: suppose for the moment that this is so, because wherever ‘substance’ is read, it is understood to mean a thing belonging to God and not God himself. What of the other expression that you likewise profess even though it is not written—namely, ‘God from God’ and ‘light from light’? What do you say to this? Either hold everything with me, or abandon everything.

“For if you are afraid to say ‘of one substance’ because it is not written, you must likewise be afraid to profess ‘God from God’ and ‘light from light.’ But I prove that ‘God from God,’ ‘light from light,’ and the term ‘of one substance’ are contained in the divine Scriptures.

“When the Son of God himself, who is God, says in his Gospel, ‘I came forth from the Father’ (John 16:28), we rightly and deservedly profess God from God, because we recognize the Son of God, the true God, to have been born from God the Father, the true God. This is not in the way that we are called gods (Psalm 81:6), or in the way Moses was called the god of Pharaoh (Exodus 8:1), but because the true Son, born from the true Father, was not made, he must truly and confidently be called God from God.

“Likewise, you say ‘light from light’—which is not written—but you do not share my understanding. For it is written of the Father: ‘God is light’ (1 John 1:5); and of the Son: ‘He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world’ (John 1:9); and: ‘The light shines in the darkness,’ that is, Christ in the world, ‘and the darkness did not overcome it’ (John 1:5).

“These are the people whose hearts have been blinded by the darkness of ignorance; they did not recognize Christ as the true God and the true Son of God. But the Lord himself says: ‘I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life’ (John 8:12).

“Therefore, since the Father is light and the Son is light, it is rightly said, ‘light from light.’ But you assert ‘light from light’ as though another light were made from the Father, who is the true light, and were not from the very substance of the Father; as though it were like any other light, which, although made by God, is nevertheless entirely different from the one who made it. For this reason you say ‘light from light,’ not ‘light from the light.’

“Since I have prefaced these points, although you do not understand them with me, nevertheless you pronounce the very expressions in some fashion, even though they are not written. Do you not therefore also profess with me the term ‘of one substance,’ which you think is not contained in the Scriptures? Or is it because there you found a way, by hidden fraud, to conceal your malicious meanings in both cases, so that you might express this very thing with me in the sound of your voice while nevertheless separating the meaning of the statement far from mine?

“It is like those heretics who deny the resurrection of the flesh. To deceive the minds of the simple, they say ‘Woe to those who do not rise in the flesh.’ But if you investigate why they said this, although you know that they altogether deny the resurrection of the flesh, they will say to you: ‘Woe, indeed, will befall the person who has not been baptized in the flesh, so that, while the soul is in the body, it may rise in that same flesh through baptism from the death of its sins, as from the tomb of its crimes.’

“They defend only the resurrection of the soul in the flesh through the grace of the life-giving washing, and they exclude the salvation of the flesh itself. By a plausible confession these people too deceive innocent minds through hidden fraud.

“And just as a deadly drink, tempered with the sweetness of honey, kills through a deceptive pleasantness, so this evil too, by caressing the ears, contaminates the understanding of its hearers with a certain stain and infects it with the contagion of an adhering vice.”

## CHAPTER FOUR
[Col. 0455B] Finally, even now they could name ὁμοούσιον (“consubstantial”), just as they do the other terms, merely in words, if they had a way to twist it by a perverse interpretation into another meaning. But when they saw themselves trapped by this word, they absolutely refused to mention it, lest by professing it they should appear to believe it, or by believing it should appear that they professed it. With subtle ingenuity they offered the excuse that either it was not written, or that God ought not to be called “substance,” lest He be thought corporeal. “God,” they say, “causes something to be substance, but this does not mean that God Himself is to be reckoned as substance.” For, they say, since every substance admits contraries, whereas God can admit nothing diverse, He ought not to be called substance.

I would forgive you if you said this simply, if you wished to know the truth of the matter, if you approached this question as an uninstructed person, [Col. 0455C] if you were not yourself the one who had always asserted that the Son of God was either of another substance or from things that did not exist. But since you are the very same person who has often been convicted and often confessed on this point, and who has often been condemned for denying it and then changing your position, and who even now, by force, ambition, and power, are agitating and throwing everything into confusion—how do you suppose that I can forgive you when you repeatedly retract the same claim?

Yet, lest this perversity seem to be condemned as prejudged rather than examined, I shall answer you briefly concerning this objection. You therefore forbid the word “substance” to be used of God, as though everything called “substance” were considered a thing of one and the same kind. Do you not know that heavenly things exist in one way and earthly things in another, and that even among heavenly and worldly things there is great difference? For angels received the substances of their constitutions in one way, and each of the powers in another, just as the Apostle says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (I Cor. XV, 41). So also in this world, just as there are different kinds of things, so there are different bodies of living creatures, and each has the substance proper to its kind, as the Apostle says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh” (ibid., 39).

If, then, the things made by God possess different qualities of substance, do you suppose that the substance in God is such as that possessed by something among these created things, so that it can admit contraries? Far from it. For what is the substance of God except that very reality which God is—simple, singular, pure, unmixed with any combination, clear, good, perfect, blessed, whole, [Col. 0456A] entirely holy? Do you suppose that what God is is something empty and void? It is blasphemy to think that He through whom all things were established is empty—He who brought forth all things by His word, ordered them by His reason, perfected them by His power, by whose will and command the universe is governed, and to whom all things are subject.

And rightly you read that it is written concerning God: “I am who I am”; and, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. III, 14). The Savior and Lord Himself also says: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3). God therefore exists in His substance, and the knowledge of Him is eternal life; and He is as great as cannot be expressed. He is rightly regarded when He is called inestimable—whether you wish it or not.

Therefore, that which is—that is the substance of the thing whose existence is asserted. Yet, as has already been said, what it is in quantity and quality cannot be conceived by the mind, estimated by the senses, or defined in the soul. Provided only that what is believed to exist is established as existing: from that very reality which God is, the Son must proceed, so that He is the true Son, and the true Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father. This is ὁμοούσιον, that is, “of one substance” with the Father. As the Lord Himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11); “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); and, “I came forth from the Father” (John XVI, 28); and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

Not without reason, since the Son of God was born from God the Father: therefore, through unity of substance and through the majesty of divinity, they are one, just as Jeremiah also prophesied: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen the word of the Lord?” (Jer. XXIII, 18). And again: “If they had stood in my substance, and if they had heard my words, I would have turned them away from their evil pursuits” (ibid., 22). And in Solomon: “My substance is sweetness” (Wis. XVI, 31).

## CHAPTER V

[515] Since, then, you recognize this unity of substance in the Father and the Son not only by prophetic authority but also by evangelical authority, how can you say that ὁμοούσιον is not found in the divine Scriptures—as though ὁμοούσιον were something other than what is expressed by “I came forth from God the Father” (John XVI, 28), and “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), or other than what the prophets openly declared concerning the substance of God?

This is the meaning of the term: that you believe in unity of substance in the Father and the Son, even though you cannot define the reality itself, which is ineffable; so that whether you say “light from light,” “word from word,” “spirit from spirit,” or “Lord from Lord,” whatever you say of Him, you nevertheless believe the Father and the Son to be of one essence, and understand the Son from that very reality which the Father is.

For if you make some comparison between Him and those things that are visible, by the very dissimilarity of the things you will not demonstrate an argument but introduce contentious disputation. And since it is written in the voice of God, “To whom will you compare me?” (Isa. XLVI, 5), and since God cannot be likened to anything, it is enough to believe what He is perceived to be, because He wished Himself to be believed, not displayed.

Finally, if, concerning this very matter that you profess with me, you wished to establish some likeness in God, I do not know whether you could define more precisely what you compared with Him. For example, when you say “light from light,” if you were compelled to explain it through a painstaking account, I ask how you believe light to be from light. Is it like a lamp from a lamp, or like a sun from a sun, so that under this example you introduce either two lamps or two suns, as though they were two gods? Or do you designate as “light from light” the radiance of the same lamp or the brightness of the sun shining forth from that same sun, likening the Father to the source of light and displaying the Son as the radiance of its brightness? This is what the prophet said: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). Or perhaps this is what Solomon meant when he said: “She is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. VII, 26). Or perhaps the Apostle proclaimed here that our Savior is “the image of the invisible God” (Col. I, 15), because the light of the sun is the image of the sun itself, proceeding from that same sun.

[Col. 0457A] But it would take too long to state how many answers might be given to these matters, which generate disputes—as the Apostle forbids (II Tim. II, 14); especially since it is established that that light which God is cannot be estimated, comprehended, or defined. Nor, in truth, can anything among the things that exist in this world be compared with the divine majesty, because none of all those things that are seen or spoken of can be judged by a likeness worthy of God according to what God is; for He is greater than our very intellects and senses.

Therefore I warned you to believe in the divinity of His substance and to recognize the true Son from the true Father; but you ought not to inquire into the quality of the reality, since you cannot know what its quality or magnitude is. This is what the prophets and the Apostles proclaimed.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0457C]

Finally, according to our capacity, our strength, and our faith, let us contemplate what God is and see whether anything can be compared with Him. Certainly, this is He of whom, when He is spoken of, nothing can be said; when He is estimated, He cannot be estimated; when He is compared, He cannot be compared; when He is defined, He increases by the very act of definition. He covers the heaven with His hand and encloses the entire compass of the world in His fist. All things do not know Him in His fullness, yet they know Him with awe. This world serves His name and power, and even the momentary succession of the elements bears witness to Him.

See, then, whether anything can exist with which the Father and the Son can be compared, since the Son is such as the Father is. He would not say that He and the Father are one unless He knew Himself to be such as the Father is.

There is a certain reason, called Λόγος (“Word” or “Reason”) among the Greeks, which distinguishes the persons or names of the Father and the Son, because the Son Himself is also called Reason. Yet this Reason is designated by many names: now Word, now Power, now Wisdom, now Right Hand, now Arm, now Pearl, now Treasure, now Net, now Plough, now Fountain, now Rock, now Cornerstone, now Lamb, now Man, now Calf, now Eagle, now Lion, now Way, now Truth, and Life.

He is God, all in all, so that through these names the mysteries of the divine dispensations may be recognized, not so that the majesty of the Son of God might be properly defined and displayed. For what is the Son in relation to that which the Father is? Another, yet the same.

He is called Word because He proceeded from the Father’s own divine mouth, and the Father neither commanded nor did anything without Him. He is called Power because He is truly from God and always with God, and all the Father’s power subsists in Him. He is called Wisdom because, coming from the Father’s heart, He opened the heavenly secrets to believers. He is called Right Hand because through Him all divine works have been perfected. He is called Arm because all things are held together by Him. He is called Pearl so that nothing may be regarded as more precious than He. He is called Treasure so that it may be understood that in Him all the riches and wealth of the heavenly kingdoms are stored.

He is called Net because through Him and in Him the diverse multitude of the nations, like fish from the sea of this age, is gathered into the Church through the water of baptism, where the distinction between the good and the wicked is recognized. He is called Plough because, by the sign of His cross, hard hearts are subjected so that they may be prepared for the necessary seed. He is called the Fountain of living water because from Him thirsty hearts are watered by the grace of heavenly water. He is called Rock because He grants strength to believers and hardness to unbelievers. He is called Cornerstone because, as the one Mediator, He joined together within Himself both walls—the New and the Old Testament—holding them together.

He is called Lamb so that Christ’s innocence and passion might be shown. He is called Man because, according to the flesh, He deigned to be born for us human beings. He is called Calf because He endured suffering for our salvation. He is called Eagle because, after His venerable resurrection, He flies back to the Father’s seat like the king of birds. He is called Lion because He is the King of kings, who by the power of His strength crushed death and the devil. He is the Way because through Him there is ascent. He is the Truth because He knows no falsehood. He is the Life because He gives life to all things.

You see, therefore, that through these names the meanings of the divine dispensations and works are prefigured, but God Himself is not thereby properly defined. The Father, then, is God, immeasurable, eternal, incomprehensible, inestimable. His Son also is God and our Lord, as great as the Father is, but from no other source than the Father; for He says, “I came forth from the Father”—that is, “light from light” (John XVI, 28).

## CHAPTER VII

But lest the heretic seize upon this as an occasion to claim that, when I establish two names or two persons—that is, of the Father and the Son—I am speaking of two gods, as they fabricate two gods from their distinction, we name the Father and the Son in such a way that we affirm one God in these persons and names.

Let the philosophers look to it; let the heretics, their disciples, look to it—those who vary according to a diversity of powers. For us, however, there is one God, the Father, as the Apostle said: “from whom are all things, and we are from him”; and one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Son of God, “through whom are all things, and we are through him.”

For what else is meant by “two” than a substance divided into parts, and a nature separated along with the names themselves, with both the will and the commands for action and governance divided? The Father and the Son, although believed to be two persons, are nevertheless one in reason and substance.

For in the society of equals, an offense is committed against the better; and against the one who is true God, no other true one is compared as though equal. Whoever unjustly compares God violates Him. But when I establish the Father and the Son, I assign unity of kind. And although I distinguish it in the persons, the distinction of the persons again marks the same names as one through the natural law of their bond.

Thus the Son is as great as the Father appears to be: wholly from the Whole, complete from the Complete, perfect from Perfect and consummate Power, just as the Apostle says: “In him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9).

Jeremiah too, the most widely accepted of the prophets, knowing this unity of divinity in the Father and the Son, says: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. He found the whole way of prudence and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 36–38).

Isaiah also proclaims this very thing, saying: “Thus says the Lord God: Egypt has labored, and the commerce of the Ethiopians, and the tall men of the Sabeans shall pass over to you; they shall be your servants, and they shall walk behind you, bound in fetters, and they shall pray to you; for God is in you, and there is no other God besides you; for you are God” (Isa. XLV, 14).

But do not suppose that I have said this with the presumption attributed to Sabellius, who professes that the Father Himself is the Son Himself. We do not compress everything into one single meaning in such a way that we are caught by the deceit of other heretics. Rather, because the authority of the persons is recognized as distinct in the very names, and the Son is named from the Father personally, not generically, we accordingly ascribe to the Father the whole of what the Son is, and to the Son the whole of what the Father is.

Nothing that is judged to belong to the Son will fail to appear as the Father’s; nor will anything defended as the Father’s fail to be the Son’s, because the unity of majesty does not permit them to be called gods by a plural designation, since it is established that the Father and the Son are of one substance. Hence both are called one God.

Above all, we fear lest, if the Father and the Son are not one, an adulterated birth should redound to the reproach of its author. For this pleased the heretics: that the omnipotent, invisible, immeasurable God should degenerate in the Son, changed not only in power but also in condition—as though the Father could not have a Son from Himself who was such as He Himself is.

Therefore we defend the true Son from the true Father, who always was and is of one substance with the Father. This is what the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον, that is, “one thing itself with one” [literally, “with one, the same thing”], so that the persons might be distinguished by the hearing of the names, not so that the terms should separate the substance.

## CHAPTER VIII

But in order to expose the whole mystery of the Arian heresy, I shall briefly explain why they refuse to believe that the Son is from the Father’s substance. They say: Since God the Father is omnipotent, invisible, unchangeable, immutable, perfect, always the same, and eternal, whereas the Son is visible—for He was often seen by the patriarchs—and changeable and mutable, because He manifested Himself in various forms to different individuals, then, they say, if He were of the Father’s substance, it could never happen that He should be seen as visible or mutable before the assumption of flesh. Rather, He would have remained in the equality in which the Father exists, [Col. 0460A] since He was from the Father’s substance. For what is from the Father, they believe, must be neither visible, nor changeable, nor capable of alteration.

They add this to their argument: when He descended into Mary and filled the Virgin’s womb, something other than what had come forth was certainly born from her. Thus, they say, the substance was already corrupted, its state changed, its order lost, being immediately transformed from God into man and from spirit into flesh. Every transformation, they say, is the destruction of the former state. Consequently, if the Son were from the Father’s substance, the Father too would already appear diminished, either through the surrender or through the ending of His substance. They therefore preferred to believe that the Son was of another substance, so that He could be changed, altered, and seen, since this could not be believed of the Father’s substance.

This is the cause of their error, this the origin of the Arian heresy: they do not understand the power of God, nor recognize the ordering of so great a mystery, and they compare God with human conditions.

They must first be answered that the Son of God was not seen as He was as God, but as human beings were capable of receiving Him from God. In the various forms, moreover, it was not He Himself who was changeable and mutable; rather, this manifested the power of God: when He deigned to reveal Himself to individuals as He willed, He changed His appearance, not His substance. He did not lose the proper character of His nature, but, according to the worth of the one who saw Him, He moderated His majesty. He Himself nevertheless remained the same, as He always is, abiding in the proper character of His substance.

As it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. CI, 28).

For although many things among those seen in this world are transformed from one thing into another, so that they cease to be what they were and become what they previously were not—as clay ceases to be clay when it is formed into a human being; as fish or birds, when they emerge from water, are no longer water, because they are something else; as the potter’s mud becomes pottery when it hardens; as stone, when it is burned, is dissolved into lime; as sand is changed into glass; and other examples that would take too long to enumerate—there is a great difference, foolish heretic, between things that have been made and the One who made all things as He willed.

Created things serve the condition assigned to them; but He who made them belongs to His own will and to His own right. He cannot be compelled to change into anything other than what He is, but reveals Himself as He wills and to whom He wills. If angels have often been seen in the form of human beings and yet are nothing other than what they know themselves to be, and if they do not change their substance when they assume the form of a human body, how much more is this true of our Lord Himself, who made all things and who by His own ordering granted even to the angels the ability to do this?

Furthermore, if we approve, as has already been said, that the Son of God was seen by the patriarchs in such a way that not all that He is as God was visible in Him, but that the arrangements of future events, which were to be fulfilled in their appointed times, were perceived in Him through images—for who could see the Son of God before He assumed, as He willed, visible matter, or before He deigned to put on humanity?

He was indeed seen by Abraham (Gen. XVIII), but He was seen in the form of a human body, so that it might be shown that in the last times He would come as a human being. Jacob likewise is seen in one place as an angel and elsewhere also as a human being (Gen. XXVIII). He therefore revealed Himself as an angel in order to indicate that He was the messenger of the great counsel. In human form, however, when He is described as having wrestled with Jacob, He clearly indicated the image of the future struggle that He would have with Israel (Gen. XXXII, 30), when He came as a human being.

But so that Israel might believe in the Lord with whom he wrestled in such a great struggle under the figure of a human being, he received the name Israel, that is, “a man seeing God.” For he says: “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Exod. III, 2). Certainly he had seen the human form that the Son of God had assumed.

To Moses He appeared in the bush in a flame of fire, in order to show light to believers and judgment to unbelievers, because Christ is salvation to believers and punishment to unbelievers, as the Apostle says: “To some an odor of life unto life, and to others an odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16).

By day He went before the people of Israel in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire, as their guide on the journey (Exod. XIII, 21), in order to show through the cloud the grace of baptism and through the fire the gift of the Holy Spirit, because the Apostle Paul writes that the patriarchs were baptized in the cloud (I Cor. X, 2). The Acts of the Apostles also declare that the Spirit is like fire (Acts II, 3).

[522] You see, therefore, heretic, that throughout these events the marks of the divine dispensations were prefigured for the honor of God before the patriarchs; yet God Himself was not revealed as He is in His proper being.

Finally, when Moses prayed that he might see God’s face clearly, what did God immediately say to him? “You cannot,” He said, “see my face. For no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20). By this very denial of sight, the radiance is indicated—radiance so great as that which must be believed when it is declared invisible.

Although Moses had arranged, indicated, and described the structure of heaven, the orders of the world, the changes of the elements, and finally the adornments of the whole universe—and although the Lord Himself bore witness to him, saying, “There shall be no prophet like my servant Moses, with whom I spoke face to face, mouth to mouth” (Num. XII, 7)—he nevertheless could not see God clearly.

He was rightly worthy of every prophetic distinction, but not to such an extent that he could behold God, since he was merely a human being. And certainly we defend here all the words of the Son, whom we know to have spoken with Moses on Mount Sinai. He had come from the Father to conduct and unfold events, because it was fitting that from the beginning all things should be ordered, explained, and maintained through Him, so that this might especially establish the purpose for which the Son exists.

Yet He is understood to have been seen in such a way that He appeared after assuming, as I said, the arrangement of some visible matter, while His invisibility remained intact; His majesty, diffused beyond the sight of all, had withdrawn Him from view. He was not revealed to human eyes in such a way that the whole of His divinity appeared in Him, but, as in a mirror, when He gathers the features conceived within His own light into the complete likeness of a human being, then, with the radiance of His majesty preceding it, what was seen within that form displayed the image of the truth, not God Himself in His proper being.

So also, when He deigned to put on humanity, He did not inflict injury upon eternity by changing spirit into flesh, but, by assuming humanity, granted immortality and the eternity of heavenly life to the human being He had assumed.

For although the Apostle says that He “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7), we do not understand this emptying as meaning that the same Spirit became something other than what He had been. Rather, having temporarily set aside the honor of His majesty, He put on a human body, and, by assuming it, became the salvation of the nations.

Just as the sun, when covered by a cloud, has its brightness restrained but not extinguished, and that light which is spread throughout the whole world and bathes everything in its clear radiance is enclosed by the very small obstruction of a cloud but is not removed, so the human being whom our Lord and Savior—God and the Son of God—put on did not cut off the divinity within Him but concealed it.

Finally, when on the mountain He raised Himself for a short time above that humanity, the apostles were almost blinded by the radiance of His light (Matt. XVII)—for the human beings fell to the ground—and would have lost their lives had the Lord, in His mercy, not helped them by again restraining the honor of His majesty, according to the saying: “No one has seen God and lived” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

Thus, just as the sun’s radiance remains intact even when it does not shine all the way to our eyes—for what is not seen is due to our weakness, since the obscurity of clouds covers our eyes—so that divine majesty, which, as I have said, had put on a body, shows that it concealed its own brilliance not through any loss, but through the benefit of the flesh. For this reason the Son of God endured being the Son of Man.

For certainly the Virgin conceived from the Spirit of God, and what she conceived she bore: namely, God joined to His human being, as I have already said. As He Himself said: “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit, and he was born from God” (John III, 6).

The angel likewise says to the virgin Mary: “The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

You see, then, that the Spirit Himself—that is, the Son of God—came to the Virgin, and that from her proceeded the Son of God and Man. Yet the Son of God was not changed by that garment of flesh; rather, He remained the same in the human being as He had been before the world with the Father, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, as the Evangelist says: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I, 10).

Otherwise, it would be the belief of a madman that one could be freed by the one who was lost in order to free us, crushed in order to be born, and passed over into death in order to restore immortality. Far be it, far be it, heretic, that the sense of your wickedness should be admitted by Catholics.

We believe that the Word and Spirit—that is, the Son of God—are unchangeable and immutable. When He put on humanity, He did not change His state, lose His order, or alter His substance; rather, He illuminated the impurities of that same body with the eternal light of His glory, so that through the passage of His body the light of the Holy Spirit and the grace of eternal life might flow abundantly to us.

Although we believe that He suffered and was buried, it was that human being whom the Son of God assumed, whom He put on, whom He carried, who suffered. But because everything that that human being suffered was referred to its author, the death and suffering of the Lord are therefore proclaimed. For it is established that what belongs to God is immortal, while what belongs to the human being is perishable.

On the third day He also rose again—not God into a human being, but rather the human being into God. He ascended into heaven and offered that most pleasing human being to His Father as a gift. He sat at the Father’s right hand, according to what is written: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

He sent us the Holy Spirit from His own substance, which is itself one substance, as protector, sanctifier, and guide into eternal life, just as it is written in the voice of God: “I will pour out from my Spirit upon my male and female servants” (Joel II, 29). And again: “The Spirit will go forth from me” (Isa. LVII, 16). The Lord and our Savior Himself also says: “He will take from what is mine” (John XVI, 14)—namely, from that which the Son is, because the Son is from that which the Father is.

[Col. 0463B] Thereafter, at the predetermined time, He will come to judge the living and the dead, to render rewards to believers and punishments to unbelievers. His kingdom is eternal and immortal; it has neither beginning nor end. To Him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## LETTER OF THE COUNCIL OF AQUILEIA TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

The Council that assembled at Aquileia to the beloved brothers, the bishops of the province of Vienne and of the first and second provinces of Narbonne.

We give thanks to your holy unanimity because, in our lords and brothers Constantius and Proculus, you have granted us the presence of all of you; and, following the precedent established by our predecessors, you have added no small weight to our decisions, since the profession of your holiness, beloved brother-lords, also agrees with them.

Therefore, just as we gladly welcomed the holy men mentioned above into the fellowship that you share with us, so also we dismiss them with an abundant giving of thanks. How necessary this assembly has been is made clear by the facts themselves: when the adversaries and enemies of God, the interpreters and defenders of the Arian sect, Palladius and Secundianus—the only two who dared to come to the council—were present, they received the sentence due to them, having been convicted of impiety.

May our almighty God protect you in safety and in flourishing prosperity, beloved brother-lords.

## LETTER OF THE SAME COUNCIL TO THE EMPERORS GRATIAN, VALENTINIAN, AND THEODOSIUS

To the most merciful emperors and most blessed Christian princes, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, the holy Council that assembled at Aquileia.

Blessed is God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has given you the Roman Empire; and blessed is our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who in his goodness preserves your kingdom. Through him we give thanks to you, most merciful princes, because you have also demonstrated your zeal for the faith: you resolved to convene a council of priests to remove disputes, and in your graciousness reserved honor for the bishops, so that no one might be absent who wished to attend, and no one might be compelled against his will.

Accordingly, in accordance with the ordinances of your gentleness, we assembled without envy toward the multitude and with a readiness for debate. No bishops from among the heretics were found except Palladius and Secundianus, men of ancient treachery, on whose account they had demanded that a council be convened from the farthest region of the Roman world [Col. 0464A].

Behold, no man burdened by the years of old age, whose venerable gray hair alone might have commanded respect, was forced to come from the uttermost shore of the Ocean, and the council lacked nothing. No one dragging along a feeble body, weighed down by the burdens of fasting, was compelled by the hardship of the journey to lament the losses of his diminished strength. Finally, no one lamented that, though poverty is glorious in priests, he lacked the means to come.

Thus, most merciful of princes, Gratian, what divine Scripture praised has been fulfilled in you: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL). How serious a matter it would have been if, because of two men rotten in their perfidy, the churches throughout the whole world had been deprived of their priests! Even those who could not come because of the length of the journey were nevertheless represented by delegates sent from nearly all the Western provinces. Through clear statements in the debates they showed that they held what we assert and indicated that they agreed with the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, as the following documents make clear.

Therefore, everywhere the prayers of the peoples now resound in support of your empire. Nor did defenders of the faith fail to appear at your command. Although the precedents of our forefathers had been clearly prescribed, from which it would be impious and sacrilegious to depart, we nevertheless offered them the opportunity for debate. First, we examined the very beginning of the question that had arisen and thought that the letter of Arius, who is recognized as the author of the Arian heresy, ought to be read aloud.

The heresy received its name from him for this reason: since the Arians had been accustomed to deny that they were Arians, they might either condemn the blasphemies of Arius by denouncing them, defend them by affirming them, or at least refuse to reject the name of the man whose impiety and perfidy they followed. But because they could neither condemn nor approve their author, although three days earlier they themselves had challenged us to debate and a place and time had been appointed, they had appeared without waiting for the assembly. Suddenly, those who had said that, because they were Christians, they would easily prove their case—which we gladly accepted and desired them to prove—immediately avoided the encounter and began to evade the debate.

Nevertheless, we had much discussion with them. The divine Scriptures were set before us, and from the first hour of the day until the seventh an opportunity for debate was granted, with patience extended throughout. Would that they had said little—or at least that we could erase what we heard! For through sacrilegious statements—since Arius, by saying that the Father alone is eternal, alone good, alone the true God, alone possessing immortality, alone wise, and alone powerful, wished the Son to be understood as lacking these attributes—they preferred to follow Arius rather than confess the Son of the eternal God as true God, good God, wise, powerful, and possessing immortality [Col. 0464D].

We wasted many hours. Their impiety was increasing, and it could not be corrected in any way. Finally, when they saw that they were being pressed by the sacrileges of Arius’s letter—which we therefore appended, so that your Clemency too might recoil from it—they withdrew from the middle of the reading of the letter and asked us to answer their propositions, although it was neither orderly nor reasonable to interrupt what had been placed first. We replied that they should condemn the impieties of Arius, and that, with order and place preserved, we would answer whatever points they wished to raise. Nevertheless, we yielded to their disorderly desire.

They then falsified the written Gospel and claimed that the Lord had said, “He who sent me is greater than I,” although the sequence of Scripture teaches otherwise [Col. 0465A]. They were convicted of falsification and admitted it, yet they were not corrected by reason. For when we said that the Son is called less than his Father according to the assumption of flesh, but according to divinity is proved by the testimonies of Scripture to be equal and coequal; and that there can be no gradation of rank or greatness where there is unity of power, they not only refused to correct their error but began to increase their madness, saying that the Son was subject even according to divinity—as though any subjection of God could exist according to divinity.

Finally, they refer death not to the mystery of our salvation but to some weakness of divinity. We shudder, most merciful princes, at such dreadful sacrileges. We judged that these wicked teachers, lest they deceive further the peoples whom they held, ought to be deprived of the priesthood [Col. 0465B]. For it is not fitting that they should claim for themselves the priesthood of one whom they have denied.

We beseech your faith and your glory to show reverence for the author of your empire, and to decree that the defenders of impiety and adulterers of the truth, by letters issued through your Clemency to the appropriate judges, be barred from the thresholds of the Church, so that, in place of the condemned, holy priests may be appointed through the delegates of our insignificance.

Let the same sentence also include the presbyter Attalus, who confessed his treachery and openly clings to sacrileges. For what shall we say about his teacher Valens? Although he was nearby, he avoided the council of priests, lest he be compelled to give an account to the priests for the overthrow of his homeland and the destruction of his fellow citizens [Col. 0465C]. He is also said to have been profaned by a Gothic torque and armlet and, wearing the dress of pagans, to have dared to appear before the Roman army.

This is undoubtedly sacrilegious not only in a priest but in any Christian. It is abhorrent to Roman custom—unless perhaps the priests of idolaters customarily appear in this fashion among the Goths.
