May the name of the priesthood, which that sacrilegious man disgraces, move your piety. He is also accused of unspeakable crime by the voices of his own people, at least those who may still survive.

Certainly, let him return to his own home and not pollute the flourishing cities of Italy—he who now associates with himself men like himself through unlawful ordinations and seeks, through every kind of reprobate, to leave behind a seedbed of his impiety and perfidy, although he has not even begun to be a bishop. For at first he had been placed over the holy man Mark, a priest of admirable memory, at Poetovio [Col. 0465D]. After he had been disgracefully expelled by the people and could no longer remain at Poetovio, he has now, after the overthrow of his homeland—not to say its betrayal—ridden into Milan.

Therefore, may your piety deign to console us in all these matters, lest, because we obeyed the ordinances of your tranquility, we appear to have assembled in vain. For we must take care not only that our decrees but also yours are not mocked.

We therefore ask that your Clemency deign equally to hear the holy men who are delegates of the council and order them to return promptly, with the requests we make having been effectively fulfilled, so that you may receive your reward from the Lord God Christ, whose churches you have cleansed from every stain of sacrilege.

We also ask this concerning the Photinians, whom you decreed by an earlier law should hold no assemblies and whom you excluded by the measure issued for convening a council of priests. Since we have learned that they are still attempting to hold an assembly in the town of Sirmium, we ask that your Clemency, now also prohibiting their gathering, order that reverence first be shown to the Catholic Church and then to your own laws [Col. 0466A], so that, with God as your guide, you may triumph, since you provide for the peace and tranquility of the churches.

## NAMES OF THE BISHOPS WHO SIGNED

Valerian, Ambrose, Constantius, Justus, Abundantius, Eventius, Limenius, Eusebius [Col. 0466B], Savinus, Exsuperantius, Macedonius, Bassianus, Anemius, Constantius, Maximus, Almachius, Januarius, Theodorus, Domninus, Diogenes, Proculus, Heliodorus, Philaster, Jovinus, Felix, Maximus, Amatus, Felix, Viator, Maximinus, Ephesius, Numidius, Artemius, Felix: bishops, signed.

[Col. 0466B]

## TREATISE OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSA, BISHOP, ON THE NICENE FAITH AGAINST THE ARIANS, ATTRIBUTED BY SOME TO GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS: WHICH IS ANOTHER EDITION OF BOOK II AGAINST PALLADIUS, WITH A NEW PREFACE. (C,G,S)*

### The Faith Written at Nicaea by the Three Hundred and Eighteen Bishops Who Believed Correctly

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the only-begotten, born from the Father, that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμούσιον); through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth.

For us human beings and for our salvation he came down, was incarnate, and became man; he suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead [Col. 0466D].

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was born he was not,” and who say that the Son of God is mutable or changeable—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them. Amen.

Moved by love for the Catholic faith, I had some time ago published a little work against the Arians. When I gave it to a friend to read, because he approved it, he believed that it should be copied. I earnestly asked him meanwhile to conceal the author’s name and to read it to learned and prudent men, so that, if anything in it seemed to have been stated too much or too little, it might be corrected by the advice of many.

For no one is so arrogantly confident as to assume for himself the whole of heavenly knowledge and think that he possesses all the mysteries with complete clarity, since the apostle Paul says, “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. VIII, 2), and, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

But if everyone should judge that all the things written there stood in accordance with the true faith, then I myself would not refuse the requests that it be circulated. When it became clear that this had been done, and since the work was judged worthy both of the Catholic confession and of a response to heresy, many wished either to read or to copy it.

Yet there was someone who, either from zeal for learning or from a duty of charity, subjected what I had said to a more scrupulous reconsideration. He declared that certain points were either superfluous or ambiguous and might be understood by some in a way different from what I had intended. Therefore, I have again arranged those same matters in this little work in clearer language [Col. 0467B], so that I might both demonstrate the simplicity of my meaning and remove any scruple from readers.

For this is what they say can be criticized: where we have placed the Word of God as referring to the person of the Son, they think that we understand “word” in the sense taught by grammarians—as something produced by the breath of the mouth, a sound perceptible to hearing. But we know not the wisdom of this world, which is being destroyed, but the wisdom that is from God. This wisdom indicates that the Word of God is God when it says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3).

Therefore, I confess that I am astonished that this could have been understood as though we denied the distinct person of the Word, who is the Son. No one merely names in words someone whom he repeatedly professes truly to exist in his own person [Col. 0467C]. For how could we have confessed a true Son or a true Father if we had not truly preserved the distinct properties of the persons, both of the Father and of the Son?

But because we said that there is one God, we are thought to have denied the persons. From this it seemed plausible that we had set forth the following position: We name the Father and the Son in such a way that we designate one God in these persons and names. Moreover, although the Father and the Son are called by two names, they are nevertheless one in reason and substance. When I establish the Father and the Son, I designate the unity of kind.

All this was thought capable of being understood as though these terms had been placed between the Father and the Son as name and surname, belonging nevertheless to one person, although the preceding or following statements could have prevented such a suspicion.

For since I had said that the Son of God was born from no one other than the Father himself—whole from whole, complete from complete, perfect from perfect, and consummate power—how could I have made the Father himself his own Son and in this way called one person by two names? Especially since, in the same little work, I had condemned this sect, namely Sabellianism, and had written about the distinction of persons according to their names.

No one can say of one person, “They are one,” or assign a unity of kind except to persons. Who among Catholics, moreover, is unaware that the Father is truly Father, the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit truly the Holy Spirit? As the Lord himself says to his apostles:

“Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

This is the perfect Trinity, existing in unity, which we confess to be of one substance. We do not make a division in God according to the condition of bodies; rather, according to the power of the divine nature, which is not in matter, we believe that the persons truly exist in their names and testify that there is unity of divinity.

Nor do we say that the Son of God is an extension of some portion of the Father, as certain people have thought. Nor do we understand the Word as something without a reality, like a sound of the voice. Rather, we believe that the three names and three persons are of one essence, one majesty, and one power [Col. 0468A].

And therefore we confess one God, because the unity of majesty prevents the plural designation “gods,” despite the plurality of names. We call the Father and the Son Catholicly by their proper names; but we neither can nor ought to say that there are two gods [Col. 0468B]. This is not because the Son of God is not God—indeed, he is true God from true God—but because we know the Son of God to be from no other source than that one Father himself, and therefore we call them one God.

The prophets handed this down, the apostles handed it down, and the Lord himself taught it when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). “One” refers, as I said, to the unity of divinity; “are,” however, assigns the statement to the persons.

The Apostle also says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him. But not everyone possesses knowledge” (1 Cor. VIII, 6).

Since I have explained these words, which caused scruple not in me, who know what I said, but in others, I think that an opportunity for false interpretation has been removed. For the confession of faith is clear, the person is established together with the names, and one divinity is designated.

Or, if something in the words still seems ambiguous to readers, the words should be referred to their meaning. For it is not the simplicity of the words but the obstinacy of a wicked understanding that gives off the odor of guilt. When our meaning agrees with the truth, the words too must agree with the most sincere reason. Therefore, let the Academic disputant withdraw from Christian simplicity.

“Many indeed and serious heresies, etc.” (as found above, beginning on page 506). After the words, “Whose kingdom is eternal and immortal, which has neither beginning nor end; to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen,” Vigilius added the following in this second edition of the same little work:

> I beseech you by God, whoever reads this, do not twist the simplicity of the meaning into ambiguity or interpret it otherwise than it was said. For we confess the Father to be truly the Father, and the Son of God to be truly the Son of God, and we believe the Holy Spirit to be truly the Holy Spirit, confessing three persons of one substance and one divinity. We condemn the sect of Sabellius and Photinus, as well as that of Arius, and any others that depart from the rule of truth. We embrace the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, preserving them with all the effort of our soul and from the whole of the faith; for we know that these proceedings have been set against all heresies with unconquerable truth.

## As an Appendix to the Works of Vigilius of Tapsa

Here, finally, are several objections of the Arians and their solutions, which were appended in the Cluniac, Paris, Pictavian [Col. 0469A], and Pontiniac manuscripts to the dialogue against the Arians, with Athanasius and Arius alone as interlocutors and Probus as judge. It is easy to suppose that Vigilius added them to his first dialogue under the name of Athanasius, against the Arians, before undertaking its second edition, in which he also refuted the Photinians and Sabellians together with the Arians.

## THE SOLUTIONS OF THE ARIANS’ OBJECTIONS BEGIN

Their first objection is that it is impossible for God the Father, who is incorporeal and invisible, to beget from his own substance.

First, they should be asked whether the Father was unable to beget because his will restrained him. If he did not beget by his will, then he had it in his nature to be able to beget, but his will restrained him from the act of generation. Thus their superfluous objection is defeated and dismissed: they say that it was impossible for the Lord to beget from his own substance, although it is certain that the divine nature is free from the defect of impossibility [Col. 0469B].

But if they say that he cannot beget because of an impossibility in his nature, they fall into the open abyss of blasphemy, asserting that he who is omnipotent is incapable. In addition, they will accuse God of falsehood, as though he deceived human beings by his proclamation when he said, “I have begotten,” although, according to them, he was incapable of begetting.

For in order to show that he had begotten from himself his proper Son, from the ineffable substance of his nature, and to blunt the madness of unbelievers, he drew the vocabulary of earthly birth into the example of divine generation, saying, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3).

What could divinity have spoken more clearly or brilliantly? By what indications, by what examples drawn from existing things, could it have made known the property of generation more plainly than by comparing itself even to a womb? This is not because he is composed of bodily limbs or divided according to the outlines of bodily members, but because we could not otherwise perceive the truth of divine generation with the hearing of the mind unless we were prompted by the example of a human womb. Thus there could no longer be doubt that he was born from the substance of God, since it is established that he proceeded from the Father’s womb [Col. 0469C].

These men, as far as I can see, wish to give great economy to the matter. For if they admit that God did not beget, there is no reason why they should not confess that the Son was born. Thus our entire dispute will have been brought to an end.

While they openly deny, while they pretend to confess, they raise the objection again: “When he existed, was he born, or when he did not exist?”

They would be right to raise this objection if they did not entirely deny the Son’s birth. The only question would then concern times: whether he was born before time or in time, while it would nevertheless be established that he was born. But since they entirely remove the truth of paternal generation, why do they ask when the birth began for one whom they wholly deny to have been born?

Nevertheless, lest we seem to evade this by lack of an answer, let us solve the question at the beginning of our argument by proposing a similar question in return: When the Father was God, did he beget the Son, or when the Father was not?

If he begot him when the Father was God, then he begot the Son when the Son existed as Son. But if he did so when the Father was not, then he received an advancement in honor [Col. 0470A]. Thus he was not perfect in himself, since, in order to enjoy perfection, he later added the name “Father” to himself by begetting the Son. On this account he would be mutable in his substance, since he passed from the dignity of divinity to the exercise of paternal honor.

Why, I ask, do you delight in these tortures of questions? Why are you not ashamed to be bound by the knots of insoluble objections, while you yourself set the snare and do not perceive that you are caught in it?

You say, then, “When he existed, he was born.” And where, you ask, was he? In the heart of the Father, in the womb of the Father, in the bosom of the Father—that is, in the hidden mysteries of nature. In being born he proceeded from there; he did not depart by withdrawing.

“I,” he says, “came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV, 5). “I,” he says, “came forth from the Father” (John XVI, 28). Behold, you have the procession of birth; now hear that he remained where he had proceeded from, without departing:

“I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11).

Again, they say, “The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten. It cannot be that the substance of the begotten and the unbegotten is one.”

If, just as the Father is unbegotten, the Son were also unbegotten, then their substance could more readily be different, because, with each existing from himself, neither would share substance with the other. But since the unbegotten Father begot the Son from himself—that is, from what he himself is, whatever that may be—it is evident that the nature of the begetter and the begotten is one [Col. 0470B].

In brief, I have answered what he said. Let him dissolve my proposition by whatever art he can, if he is able.

He says, “The Father is unbegotten,” in order by this very assertion to establish that the Father is unbegotten. But he will nowhere be able to show this written. I, however, wish to call God the Father the begetter, and I shall very easily demonstrate that this is written [Col. 0470C].

Let him answer me, then, whether the unbegotten and the begotten can have different natures—a distinction he will not be able to demonstrate even in Adam, who was not begotten, and in the one who was born from him.

If he wishes to admit this, I wonder whether he will not collapse under the testimony of all nature, which cries out against him. For nature generates nothing other than what it itself is.

Nor should they accuse us of wanting to use an earthly example. Let us return to the teaching of divine authority, although he himself measures the ineffable birth of almighty God by the custom of human generation, objecting to the Son that, if he was born, he did not exist before he was born.

Therefore, as I said, it must be demonstrated by divine testimonies that the Father and the Son are of one nature.

Concerning God the Father, we read, as the apostle John bears witness: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him” (1 John I, 5). The Son, however, says of himself, “I am light” (John VIII, 12).

If, then, the Father is light and the Son is light, it is evident that they are of one substance, since the nature of light and light cannot be different—namely, the nature of that which generates from itself and that which exists from the begetter.

Finally, lest anyone introduce through rash presumption a difference of natural light between the Father and the Son, Scripture has declared the Son to be the splendor of the Father’s light, saying: “He is the splendor of eternal light and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty and the image of his goodness” (Wis. VII, 26).

In this passage he is taught even more clearly to be coeternal with the Father, inseparable from the Father, and of one nature with him. For the whole confession of the Catholic faith is contained in this brief verse: splendor is always coeternal with light; splendor is never separated from light; and splendor can never differ from light in nature and substance [Col. 0471A].

This is what we confess, by the straight path of faith: the Son is indivisible from the Father and of one substance with him.

They say, “The Son alone appeared to the prophets, and he who appeared to no one must be called lesser.”

But if we demonstrate that the Father too appeared to human beings, let them either confess as equal those who were seen in the same way, or let them seek someone to whom they can make the Father lesser, if appearing makes the one who appears lesser.

And lest I delay proving that the Father appeared to human beings, I shall set forth the testimonies themselves. In Genesis, it is clearly stated concerning Jacob that, while he was going to Mesopotamia of Syria, fleeing from his brother Esau [Col. 0471B], he saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him:

“I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; do not be afraid” (Gen. XXVIII, 13).

Again, after a long period of time, when he had returned to his father, God appeared to him and said:

“Rise and go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you were fleeing from the face of Esau your brother” (Gen. XXXV, 1).

Let these men choose whichever alternative they wish: either the Father appeared to Jacob while he was fleeing and the Son when he was returning, or the Son appeared while he was fleeing and the Father nevertheless appeared when he returned [Col. 0472A]. They cannot escape from this, because divine Scripture testifies that both appeared.

Again, the prophet Daniel describes himself as having seen God the Father in human form:

“I watched until thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days sat down. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head was like clean wool. His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were burning fire. A river of fire flowed forth from before him. A thousand thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII, 9).

To make this still clearer, he shows in the following passage that it was God the Father who appeared to Daniel in the form of the Ancient One. Concerning the Son he says:

“Behold, the Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven and came even to the Ancient of Days” (ibid., 13).

Therefore, according to the truth of this present testimony, both the Father and the Son appeared to the prophet Daniel [Col. 0472B].

Again, they object: “I live because of the Father,” as though he should therefore appear inferior because he lives not for himself but for another.

But let them reread the preceding passage: “As the living Father sent me, so I live because of the Father” (John VI, 58). It is similar to what he says elsewhere: “As the Father has life in himself” (John V, 26).

This does not indicate inequality but demonstrates unity of substance, and shows that the Son subsists not from himself but from the Father.

## APPENDIX

[Note: In the Chifflet edition, the first twenty-five pages of this appendix belong to the works of Victor of Vita, which the learned man had published in one and the same edition with the work of Vigilius. EDITOR.]

### To the Works of Vigilius of Tapsa, Containing Two Little Works Prepared by Peter Chifflet

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0471B]

## FIRST LITTLE WORK, OR THE VINDICATION OF THE WORKS OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSA. (S)*

### PREFACE OF CHIFFLET

[Col. 0471C] 26

The little crow in the poet provokes laughter when stripped of its stolen colors. By contrast, the bishop Vigilius, hitherto unknown to the public and stripped of all his possessions and ornaments, now arouses admiration, having been restored by right of return to his own seat and to his proper wealth, which we have vindicated for him with arguments that are far from empty.

Some years ago, our Sirmond had Theodulf of Orléans under the press. In Theodulf’s *Collectanea* he saw Vigilius described as an African bishop, but he did not know his see. I showed him a Jurensian manuscript, of excellent quality and great antiquity, in which the work of Vigilius against Eutyches, praised by Theodulf, was attributed to Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus.

That exceptionally perceptive man, overcome by this illustrious monument of antiquity, did not doubt that the author of these books against Eutyches had been bishop of Tapsus, an episcopal town in the province of Byzacena; nor did he doubt that this was the same Vigilius of Tapsus who is regarded as the last bishop of that province among those ordered, by royal command, to come together at Carthage to give an account of their faith on the Kalends of February in the eighth year of King Huneric.

I then disclosed to that most learned man, with whom I had already been connected for a long time by correspondence, my plan for collecting, vindicating, revising, and publishing the works of this most eloquent writer. My reader, learn briefly how I carried this out; at the same time, understand why the writings of so great a man remained unknown to the public for so long and were not sufficiently recognized even by those in whose hands they circulated.

When the Vandals, barbarous in their savagery and Arian in their sect, occupied Africa, and after Rome had been captured and—as Prosper says in his *Chronicle*—emptied of all its wealth during fourteen days of unrestricted and secure plunder, they filled the islands and all the shores of the Mediterranean Sea with terror of their name. Burning no less with zeal to spread their heresy widely than to extend their empire, they tortured orthodox people of every condition, but especially clergy and bishops, with unheard-of torments.

It was therefore of the greatest importance for the Christian cause that there should be men who could support the wavering spirits of the faithful, both by other duties and especially through that kind of discourse which is confined by neither the limitations of time nor those of place—writers, I mean, who, by publishing various books in defense of the Catholic faith against the Arians, would refute the triumphant and raging heresy in every street and in every recess of private houses [Col. 0473A].

But the authors had to be careful lest, if they were discovered, they should be put to death under the severest punishments as criminals against divine and human majesty. In this way, when the sheepfolds had been thrown into confusion by the destruction of their shepherds, they might perhaps harm the cause more by their misfortune than they had helped it by their courage.

Among these writers, Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus or Tapsitanus, devised the plan of clothing the works he composed to refute the Arians in the names of great men—namely Athanasius, Idacius, Ambrose, and Augustine—and of skillfully adapting his style to their character, so that those who handled the books would think that they were reading the works of those very men.

This plan was intended to prevent the disclosure of his identity to powerful enemies driven mad with rage. Yet by the time he wrote the dialogue in which, speaking in the person of Athanasius, with Probus as judge, he defeated not only Arius but also Sabellius and Photinus, he had already escaped the hands of the Vandals.

For, having laid aside his mask, he openly declares in the preface to the entire dialogue that, for the sake of method and brevity, he introduces Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius on one side, and Athanasius on the other, disputing about the faith before Probus as judge. Then, near the end of the second part, he does not conceal that he refuted Maribadus, a deacon of the Arian heresy, in one particular book, and Palladius, an Arian bishop and calumniator of Ambrose, in another.

When our Vigilius came to Constantinople, however, he set aside the Arians and took up arms against the Eutychian heresy that was spreading throughout the East. He published five books against Eutyches, which have been falsely attributed to Vigilius, bishop of Trent, just as the earlier works were falsely attributed to Athanasius, Ambrose or Gregory of Nazianzus, Idacius, and Augustine.

Thus, through the malice of the times, Vigilius of Tapsus was robbed of the well-earned glory of his immense labors undertaken for the Church of God. Yet he did not lack that glory which, with God as the rewarder, is repaid in heaven to the merits of the just.

Nevertheless, I grieved for this eloquent writer, who had set himself as a wall before the house of God and had raised monuments more enduring than bronze—monuments that neither devouring time, nor violent north wind, nor the countless succession of years could destroy—and yet had suffered this injury: that he should be read only in scattered and mutilated form and under another man’s name.

Therefore, we have revised, supplemented, corrected, and restored each of his works to its author from many ancient manuscripts, so that Vigilius of Tapsus might now emerge for us as a new member of the company of the ancient Fathers, as though from the ruins of Africa. What works of his have been vindicated by us, and by what arguments, must now be disclosed.

## THE FIRST LITTLE WORK BEGINS

[Col. 0473]

[Col. 0473B]

### I. The Five Books Against Eutyches

29 Five books against Eutyches have been published several times under the name of Vigilius, bishop and martyr of Trent. Learned men, however, observed that these books could not be attributed to Vigilius, bishop of Trent, a contemporary of the bishops Ambrose and Simplician of Milan, who suffered martyrdom during the first consulship of Stilicho—that is, in the four-hundredth year of the Christian era—long before Saint Leo the pope and the Council of Chalcedon, both of whom are frequently mentioned in these books, and indeed before the time of Eutyches himself.

Therefore, they suspected either that there had been two Vigiliuses of Trent, one younger than the other, or that this Vigilius had been bishop of a city other than Trent; and the conjecture was not without foundation.

For I read in a manuscript from the Thuane library, a work against the Greeks by Aeneas, bishop of Paris, where the following appears in chapter 74:

> Vigilius, an African bishop, demonstrates in the books he wrote at Constantinople, in defense of Pope Leo’s *Tome* against the Eutychianists, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Similarly, let them raise against us some question concerning the Trinity: since there are certain attributes proper to the Father that do not belong to the Holy Spirit; certain attributes proper to the Son that belong neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit; and also certain attributes proper to the Holy Spirit that are shown to belong neither to the Father nor to the Son, let them accuse Catholics of worshiping three gods separated from one another. But, lest perhaps you be disturbed by an unexpected question, consider each point separately. The assumption of human nature belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, but only to the Son; for it was the Son specifically, not the Father, who was born of a Virgin. Again, the voice heard above him—“This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17)—belongs neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, but only to the Father. Likewise, the form of a dove that appeared in the Jordan, and the distribution of the divided tongues of fire, are shown to belong specifically to the person of the Holy Spirit. But, lest you still doubt these distinctions, hear more plainly: it is proper to the Father to beget; it is proper to the Son to have been born; and it is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son. What is specially proper to each person is in no way transferred to another person. If, then, these three persons, each possessing properties of its own by which they are more distinctly differentiated, not separated, are one God, how is the Son, while preserving the property of both natures, not one Christ?

A little earlier Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, had related these very matters to Aeneas in almost the same words in his *Collectanea on the Holy Spirit*, near the end; and it is taken from book 1 of Vigilius *Against Eutyches*, chapter 10. Which city in Africa this Vigilius was bishop of, moreover, is revealed—as I said—by a very old manuscript of the monastery of Saint Augendus, or Saint Claudius of the Jura, of excellent quality. It gives the following title to Vigilius’s books *Against Eutyches*: “Here begins the book of Vigilius, bishop of the Church of Tapsus, against Eutyches.” Then, at the end of book 2 and the beginning of book 3: “Book 2 ends. Here begins book 3 of the same holy Vigilius, bishop, on the Catholic faith against Eutyches.” You see that in this manuscript, of venerable antiquity, Vigilius is described as both bishop of Tapsus and holy.

Since there is a Tapsus both in Africa and in Sicily, the authority of Aeneas and Theodulf, who call him an African bishop, inclines me to think that he was bishop of African Tapsus; so too does the fact that, so far as I know, no records attest a bishopric of Tapsus in Sicily. In Africa, however, Tapsus is a coastal city and an episcopal see of the province of Byzacena.

Nor is it an objection that Victor of Vita, in the *Notitia of Byzacena*, listed Vigilius not as a bishop *Tapsensis* but as *Tapsitanus*, and that Aulus Hirtius, in his book *On the African War*, repeatedly called the inhabitants of this Tapsus *Tapsitani*, never *Tapsenses*. Antiquity used both forms of these adjectival names almost interchangeably, as it did *Beneventensis* and *Beneventanus*, *Tigavensis* and *Tigavitanus*, and other such forms. The first form was derived from the name of the city itself; the second from a Greek gentilic ending in *-της*, as Priscian noted in book 2, and was subsequently extended. Thus, just as Tapsus produced *Tapsitanus*, Greek *Ταψίτης* (*Tapsitēs*), so it also produced *Tapsensis*. These two forms are virtually synonymous, with this distinction: *Tapsitanus* is properly the gentilic and designates someone born at Tapsus, whereas *Tapsensis* designates a person or other thing that in some way belongs to Tapsus. Thus one would properly say a *Tapsensis* prefect, or *Tapsenses* towers, but a citizen would be *Tapsitanus*. To call the bishop by either name makes no difference: although he may not be a citizen by birth, by rank and office he possesses the rights of the city over which he presides.

## II. A Disputation under the Name of Athanasius, against Arius, Sabellius, and Photinus

From this, a great light also shines upon the task of distinguishing the other works of our Vigilius. For in book 5 of his work *Against Eutyches*, chapter 2, he says:

“And although we expressed fully, in those books that we wrote against Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius under the name of Athanasius—as though those present were dealing with those present, and in which the person of a judge also seems to have been introduced—what concerns the various decrees of the councils and the names religiously added in their headings, nevertheless even now, for the sake of brevity, we insert a very few passages from which it may become clear that these men are excessively ignorant and rash, since they do not know that, after the Council of Nicaea, bishops assembled in different places and issued many definitions of the faith against the insane outbreaks of new heretics.”

From this passage Georgius Cassander long ago recognized that this dialogue, consisting of three books, was readily attributable to the same author. He was the first to join it to the books *Against Eutyches* in the Cologne edition of 1555. But why does the style of this dialogue, which was published by Vigilius— as I noted above—when he apparently had nothing to fear from the Vandals, appear considerably different from that in which the books *Against Eutyches* were composed? The reason is as follows.

## III. Two Forms of This Disputation

Ancient manuscripts present two editions of the disputation between Athanasius and Arius before the judge Probus. The first has only three interlocutors—Athanasius, Arius, and Probus; the second introduces Sabellius and Photinus as speakers as well.

The preface of the first begins, “When at Nicaea,” and is followed by the fictitious imperial letter of Constantius. A single Thuane manuscript supplied the previously unpublished preface of the second, beginning “When you and I were discussing the truth of the faith.” After this preface has been omitted, together with the preface “When at Nicaea” and the letter of the emperor Constantius, the Thuane manuscript begins with these words: “The judge Probus said, observing the worship of idols…”

The first consists of two proceedings, or two books, and concludes with Arius’s appeal to the tribunal of the emperor. The second, in addition to the two proceedings, has at the end, in the manner of a third book, the judgment of the judge Probus, which summarizes what was said by Athanasius, Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus.

The first is much shorter than the second, in which a large part of the former is contained, though not absolutely all of it. Vigilius wrote the first while he was still oppressed under the yoke of the Vandals and therefore did not want its authorship to be recognized; the second he wrote when he was outside their power. For in the latter he openly acknowledges both that he had falsely assumed the person of Athanasius and that he had refuted the Arians Maribadus and Palladius in written works.

Since, then, the first edition was deliberately adjusted to resemble the style of Athanasius and was later, with a few exceptions, incorporated into the second, it is not surprising that the second edition, although composed at a time when there was no need to imitate someone else’s style, nevertheless does not bear the character of the books *Against Eutyches*.

I considered it worthwhile to publish these two editions in full. Although the second contains most of the first, it does not contain all of it. In addition, they differ in beginning, ending, and method, and could not be compiled into one without injury to the author, as Cassander combined them. We have collated both editions chiefly from four manuscript codices: one from the Jura, the second and third from the Thuane collection, and the fourth from Saint Mary of Reims.

We prefixed to the second the commonly transmitted preface beginning, “When it came into the hands of the energetic reader, most blessed Pope Maternus,” and so forth. This preface is also found in ancient manuscript copies and is not inconsistent with Vigilius’s purpose and character. Let us now proceed further in investigating his other works.

## IV. Vigilius’s Book against Palladius, the First Part of Which Was Until Recently Taken for the Acts of the Council of Aquileia

In book 2, chapter 50, of the second dialogue, he makes Athanasius speak as follows, with little concern for whether these statements corresponded to the age of Athanasius himself, so long as he represented some orthodox person in Athanasius’s character:

“For this reason I have briefly gathered everything into one mass of response, because our blessed Ambrose discussed all these questions more broadly and fully. Against him Palladius, a bishop of Arian perfidy, believed that he ought to compose certain writings in refutation of his statements, when, I suppose, that holy man had already been taken from human affairs. Therefore, if anything can now be brought forward by you, he has already anticipated it in his objections. Since I have already answered him in one little book, I think it better, if anything here appears perhaps to have been omitted, to explain it more fully there, with God’s grace assisting, so that in that work Arius too may acknowledge himself defeated.”

Vigilius teaches us many things here:

1. That blessed Ambrose had argued at length against the Arians. Everyone knows that he did so, both in various places and especially in the books *On the Faith* to Gratian and *On the Holy Spirit*.

2. That Palladius was an Arian bishop during that period; we shall say more about him shortly.

3. That Palladius composed a book to refute Ambrose’s statements after Ambrose had died, as Vigilius believed.

4. That Palladius had anticipated in his objections whatever could be objected by Arius—that is, by an Arian.

5. That Vigilius answered Palladius’s arguments in a single little book.

6. That Vigilius thought it better, if he had perhaps not then collected certain arguments against the Arians, to explain them more fully in his treatise against Palladius—that is, in my opinion, to direct his readers to that other work of his—so that Arius, or any Arian, might acknowledge himself convicted by Palladius’s defeat.

This Palladius, I think, was a bishop, one of the heads of the Arian hydra or Scylla. Ambrose says of him in book 1 of *On the Faith* to Gratian, chapter 4, where he is speaking about the Arians:

“Thus they have now divided themselves into several forms. Some follow Eunomius or Aetius; others Palladius or Demophilus, and Auxentius, as heirs of his—that is, Arius’s—perfidy; others follow different leaders. Is Christ divided? But those who divide him from the Father tear themselves apart. And therefore, since they have conspired together against the Church of God, although they do not agree among themselves, I shall call them by the common name of heretics, to whom a response must be given. For heresy, like some hydra of the fables, has grown through its wounds; and although it is often cut down, it has sprouted again, destined for fire and doomed to perish in flames. Or, like the monstrous Scylla of some prodigious tale, divided into various forms of perfidy, it falsely assumes the empty name of a Christian sect; but those whom, amid the shipwrecks of faith, it finds miserably wavering in that strait of its impiety, it tears apart with the savage tooth of a foul doctrine, girded about with beastly portents.”

This is how the passage of Ambrose stands in our very old manuscript of excellent quality.

Nor is any other bishop Palladius designated in the letter of the pseudo-synod of the Arians of Singidunum, transmitted through the presbyter Secundianus during the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus—that is, in the year of Christ 366—or in the response of the semi-Arian Germinius preserved by Hilary in the fragments.

Up to now I have not discovered the see of which this Palladius was bishop. It is certain that he was different from Palladius, a Galatian by nationality and bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia, formerly a monk, a disciple of Evagrius Ponticus, an Origenist, and, as Jerome says in the preface to his *Dialogues against the Pelagians*, a Pelagian of servile wickedness. Our Rosweyd has written much about him, especially in the *Preliminaries* to book 8 of the *Lives of the Fathers*, which contains this Palladius’s *Lausiac History*.

With these points established, it seems entirely to me that this work of Vigilius against Palladius is none other than the work that conciliar collectors have recently presented to us as the genuine acts of the Council of Aquileia, together with the two synodical letters included in the commonly printed editions, and with the book appended at the end that is found among the works of Ambrose under the title *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son, against the Arians*. I am led to this conclusion by the following arguments.

1. These acts of the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia, together with the two synodical letters—one to the bishops of the province of Vienne and of both Narbonnenses, and the other to the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, beginning “Blessed be God”—do not appear in the Merlin editions of the councils of 1523 and 1535, nor in the Crabb edition of 1538. They appeared only afterward, from manuscript codices in which they are joined to various short works of Ambrose. They are not found in the ancient manuscript collections of councils. It is therefore evident that in antiquity they were not regarded as the genuine acts of the synod, but were rejected among the works of Ambrose, whose name they bore—just as several short works of Vigilius appeared among the works of Athanasius because Vigilius made Athanasius speak in them.

2. Although in these acts Ambrose opens the synod, as is usually the prerogative of the more eminent bishop, nevertheless at the beginning of the acts, and again at the end of the synodical letter to the emperors, Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, is named before Ambrose, contrary to right and contrary to the custom of that age.

This disturbance of order greatly perplexed more recent scholars, who were deceived by this invention of Vigilius. I do not know what he intended by it, unless he imagined Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, either to be subject to no one in his own Church or to be an apostolic legate at that council. The latter is incredible, since it could hardly have happened without offending the bishop of Milan; the former is plainly contradicted by Athanasius, who in his letter to the Solitaries calls Milan “the metropolis of Italy” (*μητρόπολιν τῆς Ἰταλίας*).

It is also contradicted by the *Notitia of the Empire*, which assigns Milan as the seat of the vicar of Italy just as it assigns Rome as the seat of the vicar of the City. This means Italy in the strict sense, which consisted of seven civil provinces: Venetia with Istria, Raetia Prima, Raetia Secunda, the Cottian Alps, Aemilia, Flaminia with Picenum Annonarium, and Liguria.

That distinction between Italy properly so called and Italy in the broader sense was first introduced by Constantine the Great and remained in force during the time of Ambrose, even in ecclesiastical administration, so that the bishop of Milan presided over all Italy, whether as primate or merely as metropolitan—I do not discuss that question here. This is shown by other evidence, but especially by the subscriptions of the bishops at the First Council of Arles and at the Council of Sardica. It is also shown by the two synodical letters of the council of Italy, addressed “To the most blessed emperor and most clement prince Theodosius, Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy,” which Sirmond published after the appendix to the Theodosian Code.

Therefore Ambrose, bishop of Milan, ought everywhere to have preceded Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, who belonged to Venetia and Istria, as a bishop subject to him, and ought to have been named before him.

Perhaps, however, Vigilius, who was writing not long before the year 500, took account of the conditions of his own time. At that time I would not deny that Aquileia was not merely a metropolis but also exempt from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Milan, since it was later elevated to patriarchal status.

3. The ardor of the disputing bishops has the flavor of a school exercise, although in councils bishops ordinarily sit not as schoolmen for the purpose of disputing, but as judges for the purpose of delivering a sentence.

4. The many statements of the bishops, linked together with one another, smell of the lamp; by their very variety and their appropriate connection they reveal themselves as the product of one and the same mind.

5. Whose spirit is that—and how theatrical!—in the statement:

“Anemius the bishop said: ‘The head of Illyricum is none other than the city of Sirmium. I, therefore, am the bishop of that city.’”

Certainly Anemius could not have made this boast modestly in that assembly of so many bishops; nor could he have made it truthfully, if one considers the date of the Council of Aquileia and the age of Anemius, bishop of Sirmium. It must therefore be attributed to the age of Vigilius of Tapsus and to his declamatory license.

The emperor Justinian, or his chancellor, may have taken the statement from Vigilius. In *Novella* 11, concerning First Justiniana, he says:

“When the prefecture of Firmum had been established, and there was in that place all the preeminence of Illyricum, both in civil and in episcopal matters; but afterward, when those regions had been devastated in the time of Attila, Appennius, the praetorian prefect, had fled from the city of Firmiana to Thessalonica, then both the prefecture itself and sacerdotal honor followed him, and the bishop of Thessalonica, not by his own authority but under the shadow of the prefecture, obtained a certain prerogative.”

No one doubts that Sirmium is meant here by the name Firmum, just as in Jordanes’s *On the Gothic Affairs*, where he says:

“Alaric, having been made king, took an army and entered Italy through Pannonia and through Firmum, with his right flank, as it were, passing through a country empty of living inhabitants. Since no one offered any resistance whatever, he reached the bridge of Condinianus, which was three miles from the royal city of Ravenna.”

In these passages everyone understands Sirmium by Firmum or Firmium, whether this was the usage of the language in the time of Justinian and Jordanes, or—as is more likely—a scribal error caused by a copyist’s carelessness.

Let us therefore first examine when Sirmium was destroyed; afterward we shall inquire whether, while the city of Sirmium still stood, it had been the head of Illyricum both ecclesiastically and civilly.

From Ammianus, book 30, under the consulship of Gratian for the third time and of Aequit(i)us—that is, in the year of Christ 374—we learn that a report of the prefect Probus was submitted to Gratian, describing the disasters of Illyricum. Likewise, from the *Fasti* of Idatius, in the years 377 and 378, the year in which Valens died, the Goths spread through Thrace and Illyricum, laying waste to them.

Saint Ambrose speaks of these devastations in book 2 of *On the Faith*, chapter 4, near the end:

“Have we not heard that from the regions of Thrace, through Riparian Dacia and Moesia, and through all Valeria of the Pannonias, that entire frontier was resounding alike with sacrilegious cries and barbarian movements?”

And in book 2 of *On Duties*, chapter 15:

“These things are all too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace: everywhere throughout the entire world captives were being offered for sale in such numbers.”

The Goths were then subdued by Theodosius in the years 379 and 380. Sirmium was still standing in the year 379, under the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius, when Theodosius Augustus was raised up at the city of Sirmium by Gratian, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, according to Idatius in the *Fasti* and Marcellinus’s *Chronicle*.

Justinian therefore correctly assigned the destruction of Sirmium to the time of Attila. There is no more certain date for this event than the year 442 of the Dionysian era, under the consulship of Diodorus and Eudoxius. Prosper records for that year:

“When the Huns were devastating Thrace and Illyricum with savage plundering, the army that had been stationed in Sicily returned to defend the eastern provinces.”

Marcellinus likewise says:

“Bleda and Attila, brothers and kings of many nations, devastated Illyricum and Thrace.”

We must now inquire whether, before the year 442, Sirmium was still standing and had been the head of Illyricum both in civil matters, as Justinian says, and in episcopal matters.

There is no complete agreement about what is meant here by the name Illyricum. Rufus says in his *Breviary*:

“Illyricum has seventeen provinces: two Noric provinces, two Pannonias, Valeria, Savia, Dalmatia, Moesia, and two Dacias. In the diocese of Macedonia there are seven: Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaia, the two Epires, Praevalitana, and Crete.”

Rufus wrote this to Valentinian, the successor of Jovian, in the leap year 364.

Jordanes, writing almost two hundred years later, says in book 1 of *On the Succession of Kingdoms and Times*:

“Illyricum, although conquered in its parts and members, has nevertheless been fitted together into one body. It contains within itself eighteen provinces. These are: the two Noric provinces, the two Pannonias, the two Valerias, Savia—for this is how it should be read, not Suevia as in the commonly printed editions—Dalmatia, Upper Moesia, Dardania, the two Dacias, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaia, Epirus, Praevalitana, and Crete: eighteen in all.”

I do not concern myself here with this division of Illyricum, nor with another division not greatly different from it that is presented by the *Notitia of the Empire*, since these arrangements arose after the division of Illyricum into Eastern and Western.

I compare only Rufus’s seventeen Illyrian provinces with the diocese of the praetorian prefect of Illyricum established by Constantine. It is clear that this diocese was smaller than the Illyricum of Rufus by three provinces: Valeria and both Noric provinces—unless Zosimus is misleading in book 2, where he says:

“To the other [division] he assigned the Macedonians, the Thessalians, the Cretans, Greece and the islands surrounding it, both Epires, the Illyrians, the Dacians, the Triballi, καὶ τοὺς ἄχρι τῆς Βαλερίας Παίωνας—that is, the Pannonians as far as Valeria—and, in addition, Upper Moesia.”

Sirmium belonged to both of these Illyrica: to the diocese of the praetorian prefect of Illyricum established by Constantine, and also to the Illyricum of Rufus. The question is whether, and in what manner, Sirmium was ever the head of this latter Illyricum.

I shall here restrain my style and condense into a few words matters that could be treated at length.

It is certain, first, that Sirmium was the metropolis of the second, or Lower, Pannonia; for this reason it was called Sirmian Pannonia by Cassiodorus in book 4 of the *Variæ*, chapter 13. Ammianus also proves this in book 15, designating Sirmium as the seat of the governor of Second Pannonia in these words:

“At a banquet of Africanus, governor of Second Pannonia, at Sirmium, certain men, made reckless by excessive drinking and supposing that no judge was present, freely criticized the present government as most burdensome.”

Likewise, according to Herodian in his account of Maximinus, Sirmium was the largest city of all Pannonia, and thus the chief city not only of Second or Lower Pannonia but also of First or Upper Pannonia.

Furthermore, according to Ammianus, book 21, when Constantius was still alive, the people of Sirmium brought Julian, who had traveled from Gaul into Illyricum, into the palace. Ammianus says:

“There, rejoicing at the outcome and the omen, and with his hope for the future strengthened, so that, after the example of a populous and celebrated mother-city, he might also be received as a saving star by the other cities, he gave a chariot race on the following day, to the delight of the people, and so forth.”

In this passage Ammianus seems to assert that Sirmium was the mother of many cities—that is, the metropolis of both Pannonias, as we have already related from Herodian. But no one can infer from these words of his that Sirmium was the head of all Illyricum.

Nevertheless, I think that under the emperor Constantius Sirmium was both the civil and ecclesiastical head of all Illyricum, but only intermittently and accidentally, because the emperor was residing in that city.

My uncle Claudius Chifflet, a highly learned man, says in his short work *On the State of the Roman Republic under Constantine*, speaking of the praetorian prefects:

“One always seems to have been in the retinue of the Augustus or Caesar, according to the place in which the emperor was staying; I have detected this from Ammianus in more than one passage.”

I infer the same from Severus, book 2 of his *History*, where he mentions the prefect Evodius, who was staying at Trier with the tyrant Maximus. The reason seems to have been that, since the praetorian prefects presided over the administration of justice on behalf of the emperor, to whose tribunal the most serious cases were brought, it was fitting—and indeed necessary—that wherever the emperor was stationed, one of his praetorian prefects should be there to administer justice in his name.

Certainly, I read in Ammianus, book 20, near the beginning:

“The prefect ought nowhere to be separated from the emperor amid the fury of terrible affairs.”

Throughout the whole course of his history one may observe that a prefect was scarcely ever absent from the side of the Caesar or emperor in whose diocese he was staying.

Ammianus shows us in several passages that Sirmium was Constantius’s imperial residence. In book 16 he says:

“In the ninth consulship of Constantius and the second of Julian—that is, in the year of the Christian era 357—after celebrating a triumph at Rome with great pomp, Constantius received news of the invasion of the Roman provinces by the Suebi, Quadi, and Sarmatians. Thirty days after he had entered the city, he departed from Rome on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, hastened through Tridentum into Illyricum, and came to Sirmium, where he weighed plans either for peace with the Persians or for war against the Quadi and Sarmatians.”

In book 17, under the consulship of Dacianus and Cerealis, in the year of Christ 358, Ammianus says:

“While the emperor was resting through the winter at Sirmium, serious and frequent messengers reported that the Sarmatians and Quadi, united by proximity and similarity of customs and arms, were making various incursions in wedge-shaped formations into Pannonia and one of the Moesias.”

In books 18 and 19, under the consulship of the brothers Eusebius and Hypatius, in the year of Christ 359, he says:

“Amid these uncertain circumstances, Constantius, still spending the winter in repose at Sirmium, was disturbed by alarming and serious reports of repeated invasions by the Sarmatians.”

From book 20 we learn that in the following year, 360, under the consulship of Constantius for the tenth time and Julian for the third, Constantius spent the winter at Constantinople. Thus his residence at Sirmium lasted for three years, 357, 358, and 359, while Anatolius was praetorian prefect of Illyricum, as Ammianus mentions in book 19.

During these three years, I think, “all the preeminence of Illyricum, both in civil and episcopal matters,” was at Sirmium, as Justinian says in *Novella* 11. The praetorian prefect of Illyricum, who was not to be separated from the emperor amid that fury of terrible affairs, had his tribunal there and administered justice from it. At that time Constantius feared Julian Caesar, who was usurping imperial power in Gaul, and was being attacked on every side by the Persians, Quadi, Sarmatians, and other barbarians.

Under the shadow of the prefecture, to use Justinian’s words, many ecclesiastical cases were brought before it. Since Constantius was then favorable to the Arians, I would not deny that the bishop of Sirmium sometimes sat with the praetorian prefect to deliberate on such cases—but only as an assessor, not as an ordinary judge or as the true ecclesiastical primate of all Illyricum. For ancient history clearly declares that this jurisdiction belonged, long before the disaster of Attila and already from the time of Pope Damasus, to the bishops of Thessalonica.

Socrates, in book 2 of his *History*, chapter 12, calls Thessalonica the metropolis of Macedonia. To prevent anyone from understanding this as Macedonia in the strict sense, but rather as Macedonia in the broader sense, consisting according to Rufus’s *Breviary* of seven provinces—Macedonia proper, Thessaly, Achaia, both Epires, Praevalitana, and Crete—Theodoret makes the point clear in book 5, chapter 17:

“Thessalonica is a very large city, populous in its inhabitants. It is assigned to the Macedonians, but it is set over Thessaly, Achaia, and very many other peoples governed by the praetorian prefect of Illyricum.”

Saint Leo, in letter 84, or 82, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, says:

“Just as my predecessors entrusted their authority to your predecessors, so I too, following the example of those earlier men, have entrusted to your affection the functions of my administration, so that, having become an imitator of our gentleness, you might assist in the care that by divine institution we principally owe to all the Churches, and might in a manner extend the presence of our visitation to provinces distant from the apostolic see.”

Saint Leo began to hold the Roman see in the year of Christ 440, two years before Attila devastated Sirmium and Illyricum.

Which of Leo’s predecessors entrusted their functions to the bishop of Thessalonica, and in which provinces, is explained by Pope Nicholas I in letter 2 to Michael, emperor of the Greeks. There he teaches that the bishop of Thessalonica exercised the functions of the Roman pontiff throughout Old Epirus, New Epirus, Illyricum, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaia, Riparian Dacia, Mediterranean Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalitana. This occurred in the time of his predecessors Damasus, Siricius, Innocent, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, and Hormisdas. Of these, Leo was the seventh and witnessed the devastation of Illyricum and Sirmium by Attila; the preceding six lived before it.

Before that disaster, therefore, the bishops of Thessalonica were primates not only in the Illyricum later called Eastern, after the beginning of the reign of Honorius, but also in other provinces of the Illyricum later called Western—namely, in Moesia, in both Dacias, and in Illyricum strictly so called, which at that time seems to have included the Pannonias and therefore Sirmium.

Since, then, Pope Damasus appointed the bishop of Thessalonica primate also in Illyricum, in Moesia, and in both Dacias, as Pope Nicholas asserts; and since, according to the Greek author of the synodical account, in the time of Damasus Acholius, bishop of Thessalonica, presided with Ambrose of Milan over the Council of Aquileia in the year of Christ 381, it already appears that at that time the bishop of Thessalonica was primate in Illyricum.

This primacy, or apostolic vicariate, of the bishop of Thessalonica is much more clearly established by several letters of Roman pontiffs recently published at Rome in 1662 in the posthumous collection of Lucas Holstenius.

There, on page 43, Damasus entrusts his functions to Acholius, so that at the ecumenical synod of Constantinople he might ensure that Maximus the Cynic, ordained by certain Egyptian bishops, was deposed. This was also done there, in canon 4 of that synod.

On the same page, 43, Pope Siricius wrote to Anysius, the successor of Acholius, saying that no one should presume to ordain bishops in Illyricum without his consent.

On page 49, Pope Innocent entrusts his functions to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, throughout the Churches of Achaia, Thessaly, Old Epirus, New Epirus and Crete, Mediterranean Dacia, Riparian Dacia, Moesia, Dardania, and Praevalitana, so that he might be first among their primates. “We imitate,” he says, “our apostolic predecessors, who wished these responsibilities to be entrusted, in accordance with their merits, to the most blessed Acholius and Anysius.”

On page 51, Pope Boniface writes to the same Rufus:

“Frequent letters, as the records of our archives make clear, have flowed from that source”—that is, from the blessed Peter—“to your charity. Through them it is certain that the care of the Churches situated throughout Macedonia and Achaia has been entrusted to your fraternity.”

On page 68, the same Boniface writes to the bishops of Thessaly:

“Let no one presume to ordain bishops throughout Illyricum without the knowledge of our fellow bishop Rufus.”

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, under the consulship of Honorius for the thirteenth time and Theodosius for the tenth.

On page 89, Pope Sixtus writes to Perigenes, bishop of Corinth:

“Now, therefore, dearest brother, preserve toward our holy brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, bishop of the city of Thessalonica, the reverence which the other pontiffs appointed throughout Illyricum likewise do not refuse to preserve toward the dignity of the aforesaid man.”

On page 99, the same Sixtus writes to all the bishops of Illyricum:

“All the Churches of Illyricum, as we received from our predecessors and have ourselves continued to do, now belong to the care of the bishop of Thessalonica.”

On page 145, Pope Leo writes to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica:

“Let no negligence arise concerning the governance of the Churches located throughout Illyricum, which we entrust to your affection in our place, following the example of Siricius of blessed memory, who entrusted them to Anysius, your predecessor of holy memory.”

On page 154, the same Leo writes to the metropolitans of Illyricum:

“We have therefore entrusted our function to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, following the example of those whose memory we rightly venerate.”

The same Leo writes to the metropolitans of Achaia:

“We desire that the priests of the Lord preserve what the authority of the apostolic see has frequently established: namely, that the Churches established throughout Illyricum should belong to the care of our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, bishop of the city of Thessalonica.”

From these passages Holstenius rightly concludes that Blondel, a minister of the Calvinist sect, was far from the truth when, in his book *Against the Primacy*, page 393, he denied that any trace of the vicariate of the bishop of Thessalonica under the Roman pontiff existed in ancient records.

As for what Holstenius says in several places—that the vicariate of the Holy See throughout Illyricum was granted not to the place or see of Thessalonica but to individuals, that is, to the personal merits of the bishops of Thessalonica—I do not see how this agrees with the letters of the pontiffs just cited.

I return to Acholius, also called Ascholius by Basil the Great in letters 337, 338, and 339, by Theodoret in book 5 of his *History*, chapter 9, and elsewhere. Since he attended the ecumenical Council of Constantinople in May of the year 381, as is clear from the letter of Damasus cited above and is affirmed by Socrates in book 5, chapter 8, and Sozomen in book 7, chapter 4, he could quite properly have attended the Council of Aquileia in September of that same year, 381.

“For he traveled everywhere with frequent journeys,” Ambrose says in letter 25 to Anysius, his successor, “to Constantinople, Achaia, Epirus, and Italy, so that the younger men could not keep up with him.”

Just as he attended the Council of Constantinople outside his own diocese only as legate of Pope Damasus, so he also seems to have attended Aquileia—which likewise belonged to Italy, not to Illyricum—as the legate of that same pontiff.

But since it is certain, especially from the letter of Pope Innocent cited above to Rufus of Thessalonica, that Acholius—by privilege granted by Damasus—was first among the primates throughout all Illyricum, and since he does not appear to have been sent as a papal legate to Constantinople or Aquileia unless he was already primate of Illyricum, so that his authority in those places might be greater by virtue of that dignity, with what assurance could Anemius, the bishop of Sirmium, boast at the Council of Aquileia:

“The head of Illyricum is none other than the city of Sirmium. I, therefore, am the bishop of that city”?

I would say instead that these words were declamatorily invented by Vigilius of Tapsus, since they do not correspond to the time of the Council of Aquileia or to historical truth.

Nor should anyone suppose that Acholius had not yet been constituted primate of all Illyricum by Damasus when the Council of Aquileia was held, namely in September of the year 381. For unless Acholius had already attained that dignity by then, he scarcely ever obtained it, since his death fell at the end of 382, or certainly at the beginning of 383, as we establish by the following reasoning.

Acholius attended the ecumenical Council of Constantinople in May 381 as legate of Pope Damasus, and then the Council of Aquileia in September of the same year. In the following year, 382, he was present at the Roman council, as is proved by the synodical letter of the Constantinopolitans in Theodoret, book V, chapter 9. In that same year, when Antonius and Syagrius were consuls, the entire Gothic nation, with its king, surrendered itself to the Roman Empire on 3 October [Col. 0482B], as Idatius records in his *Fasti*. Marcellinus Comes agrees with him, writing under the same consuls: “The entire Gothic nation, after the death of its king Athanaric, surrendered itself to the Roman Empire in the month of October.”

Now hear Ambrose, in Letter 22 to the Thessalonians, speaking as follows of Acholius, recently taken from the living:

> Like Elisha, he lived amid arms and battle-lines, arranging the conflicts by his merits. Finally, when security had been restored to those dwelling together—which was harder for him than war itself—he breathed forth his holy spirit, and, like Elijah, was lifted up even to heaven.

He had prefaced this in the same letter:

> I have learned that the holy man Acholius is now resting in the heavenly places, whom we were seeking on earth. You ask who announced this, since the letters of your Holiness had not yet arrived. I do not know the author of the message; and indeed it often happens that we are reluctant to retain a message of sorrow. Yet although the sea was then closed and the lands were occupied by barbarian invasion, so that no one who could arrive was available, there was nevertheless someone to announce it; [Col. 0482C] so that it seems to me that the holy man himself announced himself to us.

Acholius therefore had died during the winter, while the sea was closed, and thus toward the end of 382 or not far from the beginning of the following year, 383. Who can believe that Damasus reserved for this final period of his life the dignity of primate in Illyricum [46], rather than that it had been conferred upon him several years earlier, when, like Elisha, he was driving back the Goths by his prayers and fulfilling all the duties of a most holy bishop?

From this chronology of Acholius’s death, meanwhile, learn how to refute Theodoret’s calumny. In the *Ecclesiastical Annals* it is noted that the title of Damasus’s synodical letter to Paulinus, bishop of Thessalonica, issued from the Roman council in the very year 382, was false—although Acholius, bishop of Thessalonica, attended that council, and, as Theodoret observes in book V, chapter 11, the emperor Gratian was still alive at that time. But this difficulty is resolved by the Greek-Latin edition of Theodoret’s works published at Paris in 1642, where the letter of Damasus bears this title [Col. 0482D]:

> **Confession of the Catholic faith, which Pope Damasus sent into Macedonia to Paulinus the bishop who was then staying at Thessalonica.**

Here is the stumbling-block into which Theodoret’s interpreters fell long ago: failing to understand his meaning, they supposed that Paulinus was the bishop of Thessalonica who was Antiochene, and who happened at that time to be staying at Thessalonica on business.

Before Acholius, or Aschol(i)us, in the episcopate of Thessalonica were Alexander, who attended the Council of Nicaea in 325; Aetius, who attended the Council of Sardica in 347; and Eremius (Ἡρέμιος), who, after the Council of Ariminum in 359, endured great violence and serious insults in order to be torn away from communion with Athanasius, as Athanasius himself testifies in his *Apology to the Emperor Constantius*. Acholius followed him; and after Acholius died, as we have said, in 382 or 383, Anisius succeeded him. Anisius is recorded in Letter 22 of Pope Innocent, chapter 5, as having attended the Council of Capua in 389 [Col. 0483A].

**6.** Who would not laugh at Palladius’s evasions? They make him appear not so much a heretical man as a dolt and a fool, and they suit a comic drama better than a genuine council.

**7.** By what reasoning, then, is Ambrose introduced as becoming enraged [47] at the statement, “The Father who sent me is greater than I,” and adding, “Anathema to him who adds anything to the divine Scriptures or takes anything away”? And all the bishops of that council report the matter in their synodical letter to the emperors:

> There, falsifying the written words of the Gospel, they proposed that the Lord had said, “He who sent me is greater than I,” although the sequence of the Scriptures teaches that it was written otherwise.

How can men of such judgment and learning condemn what Athanasius, Cyril of Alexandria, and Epiphanius—men of the greatest critical discernment, κριτικώτατοι—approved? Or how cleverly and foolishly does Palladius fall silent at this criticism, as though struck from heaven?

Certainly Epiphanius, speaking of the Arians in *Against Heresies* 69, section 53 of Petavius’s edition [Col. 0483B], says:

> They first of all produce from the Gospel this statement, corrupted by their own interpretation: “The Father who sent me is greater than I.”

He does not refute the quotation, but the interpretation. Indeed Cyril of Alexandria, in the *Thesaurus*, proposition 11, and Athanasius, at the end of his book *On the Human Nature Assumed by the Only-Begotten Word*, as well as repeatedly in the disputation against Arius held at the Council of Nicaea, affirm that Christ said in the Gospel:

> Ὁ Πατὴρ ὁ πέμψας με, μείζων μου ἐστί — “The Father who sent me is greater than I.”

Thus at least some doubt remains whether among them there were Greek copies of the Gospel of Saint John that represented this entire statement as spoken by Christ together in chapter 14, verse 28.

But let it be granted that the proposition was formed from two passages of Scripture, however separated from one another. It is nevertheless entirely true and must be accepted by all Catholics in its correct sense. Therefore, although Vigilius may have attacked it with declamatory license in that imitation of a contest, no prudent person can persuade himself that this was done by the eloquent Ambrose, and by the other Fathers seriously engaged in that most solemn Council of Aquileia [Col. 0483C].

**8.** Anyone who examines this dispute more closely will recognize that it is almost of the same method, and certainly of the same character, as the one in which Vigilius made Athanasius dispute either with Arius alone or with Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. In both, an imperial rescript is read aloud. Objections and replies follow, in order to refute the entire heresy of the adversaries. The only difference [48] is that in the first, which takes the form of a dialogue, there are few interlocutors; whereas this one assumes the appearance of a council assembled at Aquileia from more than thirty bishops.

In the former, Athanasius begins against Arius: “Although I have already often and repeatedly discussed the unity of substance outside the official proceedings …” In this one Ambrose begins against Palladius: “We have long discussed the matter outside the official proceedings …” Finally, a graceful speech under the name of Ambrose responds to Probus’s judgment in this fictitious council and brings the entire dispute to a close [Col. 0483D]; more will be said below about that speech.

**9.** Palladius and Secundianus are tacitly identified as Westerners in the two genuine synodical letters, specifically from Ripensian Dacia and Moesia. There can be no doubt that Upper Moesia is intended, since, together with all Illyricum—of which it was a part—it belonged to the Western Empire. Lower Moesia, on the testimony of Zosimus in book II, was in the diocese of the prefect of the praetorian prefecture of the East.

It is known from Zosimus and other writers that, although there had previously been only two praetorian prefects throughout the Roman Empire, Constantine the Great established four: one for the East, another for Illyricum, a third for Italy, and a fourth for Gaul. The same authors report how extensive their jurisdictions were.

That two praetorian prefectures were sometimes entrusted to one man is shown by Ammianus in book XXVI, where he records an event that occurred during the first consulship of Valentinian and Valens Augustus, in the year of Christ 365:

> And after this, when both brothers had entered Sirmium, the palace having been divided as seemed preferable to the more powerful ruler, Valentinian departed for Milan and Valens for Constantinople. The East was governed by Sallustius with the authority of prefect; Italy, together with Africa and Illyricum, by Mamertinus; and the provinces of Gaul by Germanianus.

From this it follows that, since only one of the four prefectures was called Eastern, the remaining three belonged to the Western Empire. This remained so from the time of Constantine the Great until Honorius, or even later, when Illyricum was divided into Eastern and Western Illyricum. From that time both Upper Moesia and Ripensian Dacia were in Eastern Illyricum, as is clear from the *Notitia* of both empires.

[49] Certainly, in Athanasius’s time Thessalonica was in the West. Thus he writes in his *Apology to Constantius*:

> For everywhere it was being reported that Vincentius at Capua, Fortunatianus at Aquileia, and Eremius (Ἡρέμιος) at Thessalonica, together with the other bishops in the West, had suffered no ordinary violence and grave insults until they promised that they would abstain from communion with us.

Now observe that in that *Altercation*, which until now has commonly passed under the name of the acts of the Council of Aquileia, Palladius calls the Eastern bishops his colleagues and fellow priests, and thus declares himself an Easterner. Hence its compiler is plainly found to be considerably later than the actual Council of Aquileia held in 381, and his date falls conveniently within the age of Vigilius of Thapsus [Col. 0484B].

**10.** A consideration of the chronology likewise refutes the inscription of the synodical letter to the bishops of the provinces of Viennensis and First and Second Narbonensis. For Sextus Rufus, in the *Breviarium* that he wrote for Valentinian I, the successor of Jovian, and Ammianus Marcellinus in book XV, writing before Honorius, recognize only one province of Narbonensis. The *Notitia* of the seventeen provinces of Gaul and the *Notitia Dignitatum*, which mention the province of Second Narbonensis, are later than Honorius, as the most learned Sirmond and other scholars testify.

Vigilius plainly spoke according to the circumstances of his own age [Col. 0484C], whereas none of the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia could have spoken in that manner. Indeed, Vigilius seems either not to have noticed these chronological anachronisms at all or, if he noticed them, to have considered them insignificant and to have aimed solely at refuting his African—or rather Vandal-Arian—opponents in the person of Palladius.

**11.** Why, I ask, does that synodical letter to the Gauls not contain even a single word about the most serious matters dealt with at the Council of Aquileia—for example, the plans adopted to restrain the audacity of Ursinus, who was aiming at the Roman see, and to protect the orthodox Easterners who were being oppressed by the troubles caused by heretics and impious men—but speak only of Palladius and Secundianus being convicted and condemned?

**12.** Since the two genuine synodical letters addressed to Gratian and Theodosius [50] mentioned those two bishops of the Arian sect from Ripensian Dacia and Moesia, whom the council, after convicting them of error, had expelled from their sees, what need was there for that third letter to the same emperors, in which Palladius and Secundianus were mentioned as rotten in their perfidy; the great courage of the Fathers who had assembled for the council was praised; the wickedness of the two Arians was exaggerated; and the entire artifice of a seven-hour disputation was reconstructed with unmistakable rhetorical purpose?

What are we to make of those lengthy complaints about Valens, the bishop of Poetovio, a new soldier who, after being profaned by Gothic impiety—even with a torque and armlet—and dressed in the manner of pagans, had dared to appear before the Roman army? Was it not enough that the genuine synodical letter had indicated to the princes that Valens was stirring up disturbances together with Ursinus, so that they might understand that both were to be punished by the same sentence?

Yet, if conjecture is permitted, Vigilius seems here to have taken a shot at the Arian deacon Marivadus through the person of Valens: a man who had influence with a barbarian king and perhaps from time to time appeared in his entourage in Gothic or Vandal dress and ornament.
