This is all the more likely because Valens the Arian bishop does not seem to have survived to the year of the Council of Aquileia, 381.

For Ursacius of Singidunum in Moesia and Valens of Mursa in Pannonia—then younger in age and character, as Athanasius says in his second *Apology*, but already bishops—had attended the false Council of Tyre, convened against Athanasius in 335. It is therefore improbable that the same Valens was still alive forty-six years later, namely in 381. After the Council of Ariminum in 359, scarcely any trace of him appears in history.

Thus what Vigilius gathered about Valens in his synodical letter belongs to the same license by which, in another of his works, he made Athanasius converse before the judge Probus with Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius.

What I have said thus far about the published acts of the Council of Aquileia is confirmed by the synodical book translated from Greek into Latin by Johannes Pappus. It was first published at Strasbourg by Rietsch in 1601, again there by Christoph ab Heyden in 1611, and most recently in volume II of the *Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris*, at Paris in 1661 [Col. 0485B].

The anonymous Greek author of this book, who summarized all the councils from the time of the apostles to the eighth council, held concerning the union between Pope John VIII and Photius of Constantinople, thereby indicated that he had written approximately eight hundred years earlier, toward the end of the ninth century after Christ. In chapter 74 he has the following account of the Council of Aquileia:

> When Gratian had taken the field against the Goths and appointed Theodosius—the husband of his sister—as commander, the enemies made peace, and the general returned in triumph to the emperor. Therefore Gratian, honoring the great Theodosius with a fitting reward, ordered him to govern the realm of his paternal uncle, which Constantius and Valens, favoring the Arians, had ruined; and he appointed him emperor of the Eastern Romans. He also ordered Pope Damasus to convene a council at Aquileia, presided over by Ambrose of Milan and Ascholius of Thessalonica. This holy council, having drawn up a volume full of exhortation, sent it, together with trustworthy men, to the most pious emperor Theodosius, as though it were an ecumenical council. For the Romans, as well as those of Spanish Gaul, were free from the plague of heresy: from Spanish Gaul, Italy, Campania, Dalmatia, Sardinia, Achaia, and all those of the West who were subject to the rule of Gratian.

We render this as follows:

> When Gratian had undertaken a war against the Goths and had appointed Theodosius, who was the husband of his sister, commander of the army, the enemies became quiet, and the general himself returned to the emperor bearing a trophy. Therefore Gratian, wishing to repay the great Theodosius with an honor worthy of him, ordered him to govern the empire of his paternal uncle, which Constantius and Valens had corrupted by favoring the Arians; and he appointed him emperor of the Eastern Romans. He also commanded Pope Damasus to convene a council at Aquileia, which was presided over by Ambrose of Milan [Col. 0485D] and Ascholius of Thessalonica. This holy council, composing a volume full of exhortation—as though it too were an ecumenical council—sent it with suitable men to the most pious emperor Theodosius. For among the Romans, including those from Spanish Gaul, persons were found free from the plague of heresy: from Spanish Gaul, Italy, Campania, Dalmatia, Sardinia, Achaia, and all the Western peoples who were subject to Gratian’s rule.

John Pappus’s Latin translation inserts Calabria between Dalmatia and Sardinia. Hence one may suppose that the word Καλαβρίας was present in the Greek text but omitted through the printer’s negligence.

From this account it is first understood that the Council of Aquileia was presided over, together with Ambrose, bishop of Milan, by Ascholius or Acholius, bishop of Thessalonica. Yet in the published acts he is not even said to have attended that council; instead, the first place is assigned to Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, as though he were the chief bishop [Col. 0486A].

Second, no synodical letter to the bishops of Gaul is mentioned here; only a volume sent to the emperor Theodosius. It is natural to interpret this as the two synodical letters mentioned above, which contain an account of what was genuinely done at the Council of Aquileia. And although, according to custom, they are addressed to the three Augusti—Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius—each is directed to the individual emperor as though he alone ruled. There is no doubt that each was intended for its respective recipient. Yet the more solemn embassy was the one sent from Aquileia to Constantinople, where Theodosius had established his residence, and which a Greek writer in particular could hardly have omitted.

As for this author’s apparent description of the Council of Aquileia as ecumenical [53], the difficulty should be softened by a twofold interpretation. First, he did not explicitly call it an ecumenical council; he merely said that it sent a volume with envoys to the emperor, ὡς ἂν οἰκουμενικὴ γένοιτο σύνοδος, “as though it were an ecumenical council.” He was claiming for it the right that seemed almost peculiar to ecumenical councils, although the council itself was not ranked in that order.

The second interpretation is that the Council of Aquileia is called ecumenical here because it had assembled from almost the whole empire of Gratian. For, as Bellarmine observed in book I of *On Councils*, chapter 4, general or universal councils were often so called when they had assembled from all or most of the provinces of some kingdom. Thus, in the Fourth Council of Carthage, held in the year of Christ 398 under the consuls Honorius IV and Eutychianus, Aurelius is said to have sat in a universal council together with other African bishops. Likewise, in the Third Council of Toledo of 589, chapter 18 of the first edition, the holy and universal council is said to have decreed, and so forth.

**13.** The prudent reader will observe that the two genuine synodical letters of the Council of Aquileia are not found—so far as I know—in the ancient manuscript codices joined to that disputation [Col. 0486C] which has been substituted as the legitimate acts of the council, nor to the two other synodical letters that are always appended to those acts. Yet it would have been very important for all these materials to be published together if they belonged to the same council.

Therefore, just as certainly as those genuine synodical letters are held to have proceeded from the genuine Council of Aquileia, so justly it is concluded that the disputation, or dialogical speech, dressed in the form of a council, together with the two letters attached to it, has nothing to do with the actual Council of Aquileia.

My opinion, which I willingly submit to the judgment of scholars, is therefore that the true and legitimate acts or decrees of the Council of Aquileia have perished, or at least have not yet come down to us. Vigilius, for his part, composed the fictitious material, designed to refute the Arians of his own age, out of his own imagination. Nevertheless, he preserved the date of that council and the names of the Fathers who were present, although in some places they are corrupted and are given neither in the proper order nor in the proper number [54]. For in many respects the sequence of names prefixed to the acts differs from that subscribed to the synodical letter to the emperors [Col. 0486D]. In both sources, moreover, Ascholius, bishop of Thessalonica, is absent, although, after the testimony of the ancient Greek writer cited above, there can be no doubt that he presided over the council together with Ambrose of Milan.

I would also add Tenax, bishop of Celeia, or Cel(e)ia, in Upper Pannonia, if Charles of Saint Paul had truly reported from Lazius that he too had attended the Council of Aquileia in Western Illyricum. No mention of Bishop Tenax appears in the published acts. But Lazius does not say this. He has only the following in book XII, chapter 6, of his *Commentaries on the Roman Republic*:

> That the seat of the bishop of Celeia existed is confirmed by the decrees of Pope Fabian; and in the council of the Church held under the emperor Decius, Tenax, bishop of Celeia, is recorded as having attended, in the year of the Lord 203.

I think that what we have proposed has been sufficiently established by the other arguments. The occasion for Vigilius’s writing, therefore, was—as may be inferred from his words quoted above—that a certain pamphlet by Palladius the bishop was circulating against Ambrose. Vigilius decided to strike down this babbler, and in his person all the Arians, through a disputation presented as though it had been held in the midst of the Council of Aquileia [Col. 0487A].

## V. The Later Part of Vigilius of Thapsus’s Books against Palladius, Attributed by Most to Ambrose and by Some to Gregory of Nazianzus

Since the disputation that has hitherto commonly passed for the acts of the Council of Aquileia ends abruptly, concluding with the words, “Secundianus said: I say that he was truly begotten by the Father; I say that he was begotten for all,” Baronius, and after him Severinus Binius, thought that these acts were mutilated and that something was missing at the end.

But in a very ancient manuscript from Dijon—and the same is found in the Elno manuscript, mentioned by Sanderus in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, page 36, no. 67, letter A [55]—the book of Ambrose *On the Faith* immediately follows those words of Secundianus. In both manuscripts it now bears the title [Col. 0487B] that it has in volume IV of Ambrose’s works: *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son against the Arians*. Its opening is: “We know that many serious heresies …”

I therefore think that nothing at all is missing from the end of this debate. Just as, in the dialogue under the name of Athanasius, Vigilius brought the abrupt objections and replies of the disputants to an end with the lengthy judgment of the judge Probus, so here he concluded his refutation of Palladius and Secundianus with this somewhat extended speech, presented as the words of Ambrose.

The connection between this little work and the preceding disputation is indeed remarkable. Vigilius, speaking in the person of Ambrose, had pressed Palladius and Secundianus with almost scholastic fervor, so that they would say that the Son of God was not merely God and Lord, or even the Only-Begotten, or God from God, but God born from God and not made, and thus acknowledge that he possessed the same divine nature as the Father. Immediately afterward, he makes Ambrose excuse himself on the ground that he was not, as they thought, acting as an academic disputant [Col. 0487C]. He also exposes all the cunning devices of the Arians, by which they were accustomed to conceal their errors and deceive the unwary, lest they should confess the Son to be ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantial,” with the Father.

After warning that those heretics must especially be avoided who boast that they are Christians and differ from Catholics by only one word—not to say one letter—he addresses the heretic, sometimes in the singular and sometimes in the plural, and adds:

> Yet when you are the very same person who has often been convicted here, often confessed, often denied, and more often condemned after changing your position in another way; who even now, through force, ambition, and power, are causing disturbances and throwing everything into confusion—how do you suppose that I can forgive you, when you repeatedly retract the same things?

He is plainly alluding to the disputation that he had just presented against Palladius and his followers.

There are also other indications that suggest that this treatise is by Vigilius of Thapsus. Compare the opening words:

> We know that many serious heresies bubble up from many sources and, like poison, pour the venom of their cancer into the innermost heart …

with the opening of Vigilius’s books against Eutyches:

> We have discovered that a great and serious danger to the faith, which cannot easily be perceived or easily avoided by most people because it is hidden beneath the appearance of piety, is spreading through many churches of the East by domestic strife …

Consider also that passage from Solomon, “My substance is my sweetness,” which occurs at the end of chapter 4. It is read in exactly the same words in the books on the Trinity that we shall also claim for Vigilius, in book V, approximately halfway through, and in another work of his—of which I shall speak shortly—that appeared under the name of Idacius against Varimadus, book I, chapter 44.

That passage nowhere appears in this form in the divine Scriptures; it is derived only from Wisdom of Solomon 16:21. Ambrose likewise did not use it in book I of *On the Faith to Gratian*, chapter 7, where he proved even more fully the same point—namely, that the word “substance” is very frequent in Scripture—than it is proved in this treatise *On the Divinity of the Son*, which is before us. No Father, so far as I know [Col. 0488A], ever expressed that passage in this form. It therefore seems, not without reason, to be peculiar to Vigilius of Thapsus, a kind of characteristic mark of his works.

Consider also the passage from Baruch, chapter 3, verse 36: “This is our God,” and so forth. In chapter 7 of this treatise its author praises Jeremiah as “the most widely acknowledged of the prophets.” The same passage, with the same praise of Jeremiah, is quoted in book III of Vigilius’s *On the Trinity*, approximately halfway through. Jeremiah is called not merely “the most widely acknowledged,” but also “the wisest of the prophets,” in Vigilius’s dialogue against Arius, book II, chapter 8. I do not see on what basis this amplification rests. Certainly Ambrose, although he frequently mentions Jeremiah, nowhere calls him either “the wisest” or “the most widely acknowledged of the prophets.”

This entire little book *On the Divinity of the Son*, when examined more closely, was indeed composed by Vigilius to imitate Ambrose’s style; yet it has less vigor and substance than Ambrose himself, whose natural elegance, arising from his choice and apt arrangement of words [Col. 0488B], possesses greater grace and majesty.

We therefore believe that the book which Vigilius claims to have written against Palladius consists of two parts: the first, which has hitherto been substituted for the acts of the Council of Aquileia [57]; and the second, which appeared under Ambrose’s name with the title *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son against the Arians*. We present both parts after collating them with an ancient manuscript, in a form much more correct than that of the editions generally circulated.

The question debated among critics concerning the author of this second little work must not be passed over. Although most attribute it to Ambrose, some assign it to Gregory of Nazianzus. It appeared long ago among Gregory’s works, with a preface stating that a second edition of the treatise had been issued by its author for certain reasons. From this preface two lessons of the third nocturn are found in the Roman Breviary, on the feast of the Holy Trinity, under the title: “Homily of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, in the treatise *On the Faith*.”

It was published at Strasbourg as early as 1508 and afterward at Leipzig in 1522, with this title: *A Treatise of Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, Bishop of Nazianzus, on the Faith, translated by Rufinus*. In the time of Josias Simler, as he himself reports in the *Epitome of the Library of Conrad Gesner*, some people said that it existed in Greek in the Vatican Library.

John Costerus and several others thought that it should be claimed for Nazianzus on the basis of Letter 111 of Saint Augustine to Fortunatianus, where Augustine writes:

> The holy Gregory, also a bishop of the East, most clearly says that God, invisible by nature, could be seen by the Fathers—such as Moses, with whom he spoke face to face—when he had assumed the arrangement of some visible material, while preserving his invisibility.

Yet this treatise, sought in Greek both in the Vatican Library and elsewhere, has nowhere so far been found. Federicus Morellus therefore wrote perceptively in volume I of the Paris edition of Nazianzus’s works of 1609, in his notes on Oration 49—which is this very treatise on the Nicene faith:

> This oration does not seem to be a genuine work of Gregory, nor of any Greek author, but of a Latin author, although an ancient one. For it cites Scripture, and especially the prophet Isaiah, not using the words of the Latin Vulgate but of the old Itala, which was translated from the Greek of the Septuagint.

Rufinus’s prologue, however, is prefixed not to this treatise but only to the *Apologeticus*. To make this clearer, here is the prologue from the very ancient Dijon manuscript of the library of the illustrious senator John Bouhier, in a more corrected form than has previously appeared [58].

## THE PROLOGUE OF RUFINUS TO THE APOLOGETICUS OF SAINT GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS, TO APRONIANUS

When I was departing from the City, you earnestly charged me, dearest son, to devote some work to you even while absent, and not to allow the necessity of my departure to restrain us from our accustomed studies. You therefore asked me to translate Gregory of Nazianzus into Latin: a man in every respect incomparable, who, renowned in word and deed, offered the churches of Christ the most splendid light of knowledge, teaching what he practiced and never condemning himself by doing the opposite of what he taught.

He was born in Cappadocia, of a bishop for his father and a sufficiently devout mother. He was educated and trained at Athens, as few have been. Yet he did not surrender his chastity amid student life or yield to the allurements of his companions. Rather, as though it were a treasure entrusted to him by God, he brought home to his chaste household the seal of chastity intact.

Finally, while he was flourishing at Athens in the study of philosophy, he saw in sleep, as he sat and read, two exceedingly beautiful women seated beside him, one on his right and the other on his left. Looking at them with a stern gaze, prompted by his instinct for chastity, he asked who they were and what they wanted from him. But they embraced him more familiarly and eagerly and said:

> Do not be displeased, young man. We are well known and familiar to you. One of us is called Wisdom, the other Chastity. We have been sent by the Lord to dwell with you, because you have prepared for us a pleasant and sufficiently pure dwelling in your heart.

Later, when he was being compelled, because of his outstanding progress in literary studies, to teach rhetoric at Athens, he secretly boarded a ship and departed. After entrusting himself to an uncharted sea, he was troubled by a storm during which he vowed that he would serve God. When he fulfilled this vow, he was suddenly appointed to the priesthood by his bishop-father. Distressed by this, he withdrew for a time.

Afterward he returned and delivered this *Apologeticus* in the church, explaining the reasons for his departure and also for his return [59]. Later, after his father’s death, he succeeded him in the episcopate at Nazianzus, a small town. From there, when the Catholics had recovered their churches because of the times of the Arian Valens, he was persuaded to go to Constantinople to establish or instruct the church.

There, while he was carrying out a magnificent work in the word of God and converting almost countless crowds every day from the heretics to the true faith, rivalry followed glory, as usually happens. But he was so perfected in the fear of God that, when he perceived that a dispute among the bishops had arisen on his account [Col. 0489C], he immediately departed voluntarily, saying only that prophetic saying:

> “If this storm is because of me, take me up and cast me into the sea, and the disturbance among you will cease” (Jonah 1:12).

No one more admirable and holy in life, clearer and more distinguished in eloquence, purer and more upright in faith, or fuller and more perfect in knowledge can be found. He alone is a man concerning whose faith not even opposing parties and factions—though they usually do so—have been able to dispute among themselves. Rather, he has obtained such merit before God and the churches of God that whoever dares to contradict his teaching in any respect is thereby proved to be the more heretical, precisely because he has opposed Gregory.

For it is a manifest indication that anyone who does not agree with Gregory in matters of faith does not possess the right faith.

Read him, therefore, without any hesitation at all; but know that the brilliant light of his eloquence in Greek is considerably dimmed by the necessity of translation. Whether this is caused by the poverty of our language or by the very nature of translation, you, who possess knowledge of both languages, are better able to judge. Thus far Rufinus [Col. 0489D].

You see this prologue inscribed “to Apronianus,” just as it is in the codex of Nicolaus Fabri mentioned by Morellus. I also read it in both codices as “when, because of the times of Valens the Arian, the Catholics had recovered the churches”; the common editions instead have “after Valens,” and so forth, which appears more correct. Nevertheless, I would not think that one should depart even here from those two ancient and reputable copies. For the use of the adverb *propter* in Lucretius, Cicero, and other masters of early Latin is well known, to denote proximity either of place or of time; thus “in the times of Valens” (*propter Valentis tempora*) means the same as what someone might say, “not long after the reign of Valens had ended.” After Valens was certainly removed during the month of August in the year 378 of the Dionysian era, two years later, namely in the year 380, the Catholic churches were restored by the edicts of Theodosius, after the Arians had held them for about forty years.

Which works of Nazianzen Rufinus translated into Latin can scarcely be determined from this prologue, which mentions only the *Apologeticus*; nor can it readily be determined from the Dijon codex, in which Rufinus the translator is prefixed as the translator of the *Apologeticus* alone. Nevertheless, since both the codex of Nicolaus Fabri and the Dijon codex contain eight books of Nazianzen, orations of the same style and genius, I agree with Morellus in thinking that all of them belong to Rufinus the translator. The following titles are found in the Dijon manuscript, differing somewhat from those in the printed editions:

1. Book I: *The Apologeticus*, translated from Greek into Latin by Rufinus.
2. Book II: *On the Epiphanies*, or *On the Nativity of the Lord*.
3. Book III: *On the Lights*, that is, *On the Second Epiphany*.
4. Book IV: *On Pentecost and the Holy Spirit*, delivered in the church at Constantinople.
5. Book V: *On the Words of Jeremiah*, in the presence of the emperor, before whom he also intercedes for a certain man in danger.
6. Book VI: *On the Reconciliation and Unity of the Monks*.
7. Book VII: *On the Devastation by Hail*, when his father, who was a bishop, remained silent.
8. Book VIII: *On Himself, Returning from the Field*.

In the 1609 edition of Federicus Morellus, these books are eight orations in the following order: 1, 38, 39, 44, 17, 12, 15, and 28.

As for the claim made by some more recent writers that Rufinus also translated from Nazianzen’s Greek text a short work *On the Nicene Faith*, this rests neither on rational judgment nor on the authority of ancient codices. Nor can it be inferred from the letter of Augustine to Fortunatianus that they cite. So that the prudent reader may understand this, let him, I beg, read through Nazianzen’s thirty-fourth oration in Morellus’s edition, which is the second *On Theology*. He will see that the theologian proves that neither Moses—although he had been a god to Pharaoh—nor Paul, although he was caught up to the third heaven—nor Abraham, Jacob, Elijah, Isaiah, Ezekiel, or any other of the Fathers saw God in this mortal life except “through a mirror and in an enigma,” and through things subject to the senses.[^c0048-61]

Augustine, compressing this teaching into a summary, reported it in that letter from Gregory, bishop of the East:

> God, invisible by nature, when he appeared to the Fathers—as to Moses, with whom he spoke face to face—could have become visible by assuming the arrangement of some perceptible material, while remaining in his own invisibility.

Vigilius inserted these few and carefully selected words of Augustine into his own work, while borrowing more on the same subject from that thirty-fourth oration of Nazianzen. The preface attached to this treatise among Nazianzen’s works is evidence that it was issued in a second edition by Vigilius. We shall restore it in its proper place, so that the diligent reader may not complain that we have omitted anything relating to Vigilius.

Yet considerable difficulty remains concerning the acts of the Council of Aquileia and its two commonly circulated synodal letters. For if we decide that these were fabricated by Vigilius of Tapsus, what will remain for us by which to determine the council’s date, its proceedings, and the number, names, and order of the Fathers who took part in it? I add that these commonly received acts have been approved by men of the greatest authority and learning: Sirmondus, who inserted in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul* the synodal letter of this council to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and of First and Second Narbonensis, and appended to it the opinions delivered at that synod by the bishops of Gaul; Petavius, in his notes on Epiphanius, heresy 72, concerning the Marcellians, where he writes:

> For in the Council of Aquileia also, at which, with Ambrose urging the matter on, the bishops Palladius and Secundianus were condemned, Ambrose pursued it so zealously that he attempted to elicit from them some indication of Arian profession and therefore pressed them with various questions. He made no mention at all of “consubstantial,” but asked only these common questions: whether the Son was immortal, good, and true, and other matters of the same kind.

And, concerning heresy 69, the Arians, he says:

> See the acts of the Council of Aquileia, where through the efforts of Ambrose the Arian bishops Palladius and Secundianus were condemned. Although compelled, among other things, to confess that the Son of God is true God, they evade the matter by astonishing evasions.

I add Cardinal Baronius, who illuminated these very acts with a learned commentary in his *Annals*; and Cardinal Perronius, who defended the same acts against the cavils of Calvin and other innovators in a repeated reply to the king of Great Britain.[^c0048-62] Not to mention the many editions of the Councils that reproduce these acts together with the two synodal letters I have mentioned.

To this I reply that, since the dispute against Palladius and the two synodal letters attached to it were written by the pious and learned hand of Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus, and contain sound doctrine especially well suited to refuting the Arians, and since they had long been published as the acts of the Council of Aquileia, it is not surprising that learned men accepted them as the council’s genuine acts. Thus Aeneas of Paris, Theodulf of Orléans, Hincmar of Reims, and other men distinguished in their age for learning and wisdom regarded as legitimate works of Athanasius his dialogue with Arius and several books *On the Trinity*, which a later age discovered to be by this Vigilius. As Aristotle says, it is characteristic of the great-hearted to be easily led into error; nor should inventions or discoveries of younger men cast a stain of ignorance or idleness upon venerable antiquity.

To the objection proposed at the outset, then, I reply first that it is established by the synodal letter of the second Council of Constantinople under Damasus—held in the year of Christ 382—that a certain synod had been held at Aquileia in the preceding year, 381, in accordance with which Pope Damasus sent a letter to the emperor Theodosius. Theodoret reports this synodal letter in book V, chapter 9 of his *History*, and it is reproduced in the common editions of the Councils.

Anyone wishing to know something certain about what took place at the Council of Aquileia should consult the two synodal letters issued from it. They were published long ago among the letters of Ambrose, but Sirmondus printed them in a more accurate form after the appendix to the Theodosian Code.

In the first of these, which begins *Provision has indeed been made*, we read:

> As far as the regions of the West are concerned, only two have been found who dared to oppose the council with profane and impious words, accustomed to cause disturbance near the border of Ripensis Dacia. There is another matter that troubles us even more. Since we have assembled concerning it, it had to be properly dealt with, lest the whole body of the Church spread throughout the world should be disturbed by it.

The Fathers of the synod continue by making many complaints about Ursinus, who, having been passed over in favor of Damasus fourteen years earlier, still had not acquiesced. Finally, they ask the emperor Gratian to grant security at last to the Roman people and clergy by removing this most troublesome man.

In the other letter, addressed to Theodosius, they likewise state that scarcely two heretics had been found in the Western regions who could oppose the holy council. Then, after a few lines:

> Indeed, they say, throughout the Western regions the faith seemed to be opposed only in two corners—that is, on the borders of Ripensis Dacia and Moesia. Yet now, after the council’s judgment, we think that, through the favor of your clemency, provision should immediately be made for them. Throughout all districts and regions, and in the enclosures of the villages—for this is how I read the 1614 edition of Ambrose’s works, rather than *the enclosures of the pagans* with Sirmondus—right to the Ocean, the undefiled and single communion of the faithful remains.

From this point to the end they ask the emperor to order a council to be held at Alexandria for the pacification of the Eastern churches, especially those of Alexandria and Antioch:

> This, they say, both the African and Gallican churches beg of you through their legates; that is, that you make the bishops throughout the world your debtors.

From these passages it can be understood that the synod was chiefly concerned with restraining Ursinus, the disturber of the Roman Church, and also with restoring peace to the Eastern churches. I would not deny that the two heretics accustomed to oppose the faith on the borders of Ripensis Dacia and Moesia, and who had opposed the council, were the bishops Palladius and Secundianus. Nor would I reject the commonly transmitted list of the Fathers of this synod, since it represents the legates of Africa and Gaul who are mentioned in the second of the genuine synodal letters. I also accept the date on which the council began, the fifth of September—or, as the Dijon manuscript reads, the third of the Nones.[^c0048-63]

I think that Vigilius gathered all this from the genuine acts, which had perished through the injury of time; but that he composed from his own ingenuity and industry the dispute against Palladius, Secundianus, and Attalus, together with the two synodal letters responding to it, for the purpose of restraining the Arian Vandals.

## VI. The Book of Vigilius, Bishop of Tapsus, against Marivadus, hitherto published under the name of Idacius Clarus, against Varimadus

Antiquity counted two Idaciuses—or Itaciuses or Hydatiuses—among ecclesiastical writers: Idacius Clarus, a contemporary of Priscillian, and Idacius of Gallaecia, bishop of Lemica, considerably later than the former.

Of the first, Isidore writes in chapter 2:

> Itacius, a bishop of Spain, surnamed “Clarus” both in name and eloquence, wrote a book in the form of an *Apologeticus*, in which he exposes the detestable doctrines of Priscillian, his magical arts, and the shamefulness of his lusts. He shows that a certain Marcus of Memphis, highly skilled in magic, was a disciple of Mani and the teacher of Priscillian. This man, having been deprived of communion with the Church together with Bishop Ursacius because of the death of Priscillian himself—whose accusers they had been—was condemned to exile. There he died, while Theodosius the Elder and Valentinian were reigning.

Of the second, the author of the appendix *On Twelve Writers*, published after Isidore and Ildefonsus, writes:

> Idacius, bishop of the province of Gallaecia, following the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea—or of Jerome the presbyter—which is declared to have been published down to the reign of Valens Augustus, then continues the history appended from the first year of Theodosius Augustus to the eighth year of the reign of Emperor Leo. In it he narrates chiefly the cruel wars of barbarian peoples that were oppressing Spain. He died under the emperor Leo, at an almost extreme old age, as the beginning of his own preface also shows.

Sigebertus identifies this man as the Lemican in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 18. Trithemius, however, wrongly fused these two Idaciuses into one in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

But concerning the author of the book against Varimadus—about whom the ancients are entirely silent—Sirmondus writes in his preface to the *Dogmatic Opuscula of Five Ancient Writers*:

> We cannot agree with those who assign Idacius to the times of Theodosius and identify him with the other Idacius, the accuser of Priscillian. The preface of the book makes clear that this man was younger than the other, for it tells us that kings were then in power who favored the Arians. This does not at all suit the times of Theodosius, but it does suit those of the Vandals. Finally, it is evident that this Varimadus was a deacon of the Arian sect, supported by the favor of his king, and that he was the very man who, through a transposition of letters, is called Marivadus at the end of book I of Victor of Utica, and who is likewise remembered as an Arian deacon honored by King Huneric.

Vigilius of Tapsus mentions the book he wrote against Maribadus, a deacon of the Arian sect, in book II, chapter 45 of his *Dialogue against Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius*:

> Let us hear, he says, blessed Paul discussing this same mystery more openly and confirming that the three are one God, just as is fully demonstrated in the book we published against Maribadus, the deacon of your abominable heresy. We shall now insert a few passages from it here.
>
> When he objected that unity excludes equality in the Trinity, and equality repels unity, among many other things I replied as follows: “Hear,” I said, “the Apostle proclaiming this unity of the Trinity even more emphatically. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians he says: ‘There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all’ (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). Because there is a Trinity, he named three. And because the Trinity itself is one God, after he had counted the three persons he did not say in the plural, ‘who work,’ but in the singular, ‘who works.’
>
> “And lest you suppose, through a perverse understanding, that he spoke only of the Father when he said ‘who works all things,’ and not also of the Son and the Holy Spirit together, listen more carefully to what he says in what follows. For after enumerating many works of divine grace, he says: ‘But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit’ (ibid., 11). You see the Father working, the Son working, and the Holy Spirit working; and although the three work together, Scripture does not say of them ‘who work,’ but ‘who works,’ so that one God in the Trinity may be shown.
>
> “Again, naming the Son and the Father, the same apostle says: ‘Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God the Father, who loved us’ (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Although he had named two and shown them to be one, he did not say ‘who loved,’ in the plural, but ‘who loved,’ in the singular. Nor does he say ‘may they console,’ but ‘may he console your hearts.’
>
> “Again: ‘But may our God and Father himself, and the Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you’ (1 Thessalonians 3:11). Here too he does not say ‘may they direct,’ but ‘may he direct.’
>
> “Thus, drawing extensively from that work, I have taught by apostolic reasoning that the Trinity is one God. Let us hasten to what remains.”

There seems, therefore, to be scarcely any doubt that our Vigilius, just as in some of his other compositions he assumed now the name of Athanasius, now that of Ambrose, and now even that of Augustine, wished in this work against Marivadus to conceal himself under the name of Idacius Clarus. I think that he deliberately altered the name of his adversary by transposing two letters, writing *Varimadus* instead of *Maribadus* or *Marivadus*, lest he be convicted of attacking a man powerful through the favor of kings, while in the meantime refuting Marivadus completely under the name of Varimadus.

Add to this that Vigilius also indicates that he disputed against Maribadus by means of questions and answers, which is precisely the method of Idacius’s book. Add also that, in question 44, Idacius used the passage from Wisdom 16:21, “My substance is my sweetness,” which is a kind of distinctive mark characteristic of Vigilius and his works, as I noted above. It would therefore be futile for anyone to confuse this disguised Idacius with Idacius of Lemica in Gallaecia, nearly his contemporary, the author of the *Consular Fasti* and of a *Chronicle* carried from the first year of Theodosius the Great down to the reign of Anthemius.

We must, however, consider how the four passages of the Apostle Paul, which Vigilius of Tapsus claims to have used against Maribadus, the deacon of the Arian sect, are found in Idacius. The author of the book against Varimadus, bearing the name of Idacius Clarus, states in his preface that long ago he had arranged in a single body a group of short works on the unity of the Trinity for the purpose of refuting that same man. Accordingly, the books *On the Trinity* that are found among the works of Athanasius are also discovered to have been written against the same Varimadus. We shall soon show, on the basis both of the presumption of learned men and of other arguments, that these too belong to Vigilius of Tapsus.

In these books written against Varimadus—whether they bear the title of Idacius Clarus or that of Athanasius—it is evident that the four passages of the Apostle Paul are found, not all together or in precisely the same verbal form, but with the same meaning and the same essential features.

The first two passages, from chapter 12 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, are found in book XII *On the Trinity*, above, on page 302, and again on page 320; and in another book bearing the title of Idacius Clarus, on pages 377, 434, 437, and 448.

The third passage of the Apostle, from 2 Thessalonians 2:15, is found in Idacius Clarus, book II, chapter 27.

The fourth passage, from 1 Thessalonians 3:11, is found in book XII *On the Trinity*, page 300.

In both places one observes that Varimadus, or Marivadus, a deacon of the Arian sect, is being refuted; in both places the reader is ordered to hear the Apostle Paul proclaiming the unity of the Trinity. Thus it is clear that these are precisely the passages which Vigilius said he had previously introduced against Marivadus in the *Dialogue* or *Altercation against Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius*.

## VII. The Twelve Books of Vigilius, Bishop of Tapsus, on the Trinity against Marivadus

That the books *On the Trinity* circulated in Latin among the works of Athanasius are not legitimate offspring of Athanasius but belong to Vigilius—rather, to the man who fabricated the dispute between Athanasius and Arius—was long ago conjectured by Sirmondus in his notes on Theodulfus *On the Holy Spirit*, and by Philippus Labbeus in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers Mentioned by Bellarmine*. Labbeus writes:

> The eleven books *On the Trinity* are likewise by this same Vigilius. They concern various controversies with heretics about the Trinity and were published in the Latin language, separately and under the name of Athanasius, and counted among his works, as though they belonged to Athanasius himself.

This conjecture will not appear groundless to anyone who first considers that they nowhere appear in the Greek copies of Athanasius’s works.[^c0048-68] Next, their very style shows that they were not translated into Latin from Greek but composed in Latin by their original author. Moreover, they are found joined to the *Dialogue of Athanasius and Arius before the judge Probus* in the manuscripts of Fleury, Paris, and Pontigny. More explicitly, in a very ancient manuscript from Cluny, after the final book *On the Trinity*, entitled *On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*, the following is written:

> The book of Saint Athanasius *On the Trinity* ends. Here begins the *Altercation of the same author against the heretics Arius, Sabellius, or Photinus*.

Since Athanasius is asserted to be the author both of the books *On the Trinity* and of the *Altercation against Arius*, and since the latter work, under the name of the pseudonymous Athanasius, is unquestionably by Vigilius of Tapsus, it follows that the preceding work also should be assigned to Vigilius.

All this is confirmed by Idacius Clarus—that is, by Vigilius himself—at the beginning of the preface to his book against Marivadus, where he says:

> Some time ago, dearest brothers, while I was staying in the city of Naples in Campania, I composed together in one body a collection of short works on the Unity of the Trinity, responding in rustic speech to the propositions of a certain Varimadus, a deacon of the Arian sect, which had been brought to me by a certain studious and most religious man. But since we now learn that they do not wish their propositions to be opposed by private words, but rather desire their own statements to be attacked by the force of testimonies, we have taken thought for those of moderate ability and slower understanding. With the assistance of the Holy Spirit, we have therefore adapted our response to all their objections by means of testimony, so that whoever reads it may refute them not with bare words—as they are accustomed to object—but with authoritative proofs, and so that those who endeavor to build such fabrications upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles may be confounded and reduced to nothing in every respect.

Certainly these short works *On the Trinity* are composed in a style far from polished, whether to conceal the author’s more distinguished genius or to counterfeit the dignity of Athanasian expression as though it had been rendered from Greek. Although they are occasionally sprinkled with scriptural testimonies, they are not entirely woven from them, as is the book bearing the name of Idacius Clarus.

Nor need one be deterred by Theodulfus of Orléans, Aeneas of Paris, and Hincmar of Reims, who, in *Collections on the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, in his work *Against the Greeks*, and in his book *On the One and Not Threefold Deity against Gottschalk*, respectively, repeatedly reproduce long passages from these books *On the Trinity*, attributing them to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. For what is surprising if, eight hundred years ago, these books were thought to be by Athanasius, when, during the lifetime of Vigilius of Tapsus himself, almost twelve hundred years ago, they bore the name of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria?

Concerning the number and order of these books, the following must be observed. The Paris edition of Athanasius presents only eleven books *On the Trinity*, because the eleventh and final book is made up of two books that are distinguished in the manuscript copies.

The first, very brief, begins, “I believe in God the Father almighty,” and in the Cluny and Pontigny codices is entitled *A Short Book of Faith*.

The second, much longer, begins, “To those who profess that the Son of God is a creature,” and bears the title *On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*.

Thus, by dividing this one book into two, there are twelve books.

When, therefore, Hincmar, in his book *On the One and Not Threefold Deity against Gottschalk*, page 423, says that Athanasius composed eight books against the Arians, this seems to indicate only that Vigilius published eight books together against the Arian heresy under the name of Athanasius. It does not prove that no other books on the same subject were later added or even composed before those eight. Hincmar himself, in the same book, page 535, cites another book *On the Trinity* from Athanasius, which on page 497 he calls the tenth book.

All twelve books I have mentioned exist in manuscript copies, although not all are found in each manuscript, nor are all distinguished from one another by numbers. The diligent reader who undertakes to compare this edition with all the earlier ones will understand that I have restored these books, which were mutilated in large part and corrupted in six hundred places, to their integrity with the aid of ancient codices.

## VIII. The Book of Vigilius against Felicianus, under the Name of Augustine

Concerning the *Altercation between Augustine and Felicianus*, which is found in volume VI of the works of blessed Augustine, I conjectured long ago that this too was by Vigilius of Tapsus, both from the word *altercation* and from other traces of Vigilius’s style and intellect.

My inclination was already moving in that direction because of the very ancient Jura codex, in which this *Altercation* was joined both to the *Dialogue of Athanasius with Arius before the judge Probus* and to the first three books of Vigilius against Eutyches.

Then, while examining the Frobenian Basel edition of Augustine from the year 1528, I read the following brief preface by Erasmus attached to this little work:

> It is not probable that this dialogue is by Augustine, since he does not mention it in his books of *Retractions*. For a passage is usually added to ecclesiastical acts; sometimes also an account of what the proposer or respondent did. Moreover, Arians do not usually concede points so readily in debate as Felicianus does here. Augustine is also more profuse than this work in citing Scripture. I say nothing of the difference in phrasing. Some learned person fabricated the dialogue as an exercise of ingenuity; we see that Jerome did the same.

But, Erasmus, could this learned person not have been Augustine, who did not record a decisive controversy but composed a dialogue in which, under the name of Felicianus, he refuted an Arian by reasoning alone, omitting testimonies from sacred Scripture? This criticism is therefore worthless except insofar as it appeals to the absence of the work from Augustine’s *Retractions* and to the difference of style.

Certainly, the books of Vigilius against Eutyches are perceptible in this work: certain expressions familiar to him, the long sweep of the periods, and frequent homoioptota and homoioteleuta that leap along almost rhythmically. These features are alien to Augustine’s style.

Our conjecture was confirmed above all by the ancient and reputable Dijon codex, in which the little book against Felicianus bears the name of Vigilius as its author.

Nor should you object that Lanfranc, in his work against Berengar; the Master of the Sentences, in book III, distinction 21, chapter *Sicut*, and distinction 22, chapter *Et utique*; and, indeed, the still earlier Bede, in his commentary on the first chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, cite this work as Augustine’s.[^c0048-71] It is not surprising that this book was believed to be Augustine’s, since even in very ancient codices it is prefixed with Augustine’s name—and it was assigned to Augustine by the deliberate plan of Vigilius, who did not wish to reveal himself.

I know that Bellarmine says in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that this book is considered to be listed in the *Catalogue of Possidius*. It certainly appears in that catalogue in the Paris edition of 1571. But the more accurate Paris edition of 1586 omitted it. Nor does it appear in the ancient and excellent codices of Jura and Thuane, which I have examined. From this alone one may reasonably suppose that it was inserted into Possidius by the boldness of some later person.

We have collated this little work against the Dijon and Jura codices, the Geneva codex, and the manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes, so that it might see the light not only vindicated for its true author but also corrected in many places and restored, as we trust, to its original purity.

These remarks may suffice concerning the known books of Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus, that still survive. Cassiodorus adds in book I, chapter 9 of his *Divine Readings*:

> Vigilius too, an African bishop, discussed with the fullest and most careful account the interpretation of the thousand years contained in the Apocalypse mentioned above, from which a major question arises for some.

But I would not dare to attribute this book—which is known to me solely from this testimony of the senator—to Vigilius of Tapsus, since there is nothing to prevent several bishops named Vigilius from having existed in Africa. Nevertheless, I would not wish to deprive him of it, since I know of no other Vigilius, African bishop and writer, besides the one of Tapsus.

## IX. The Order of the Books of Vigilius of Tapsus

Enough has now been said about the works of Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus, whose earlier works, as is clear, we have identified from the later ones. Therefore, if they are to be arranged according to chronological order, his books against the Eutychians will occupy the last place of all.[^c0048-72]

Among those in which he attacked the Arian heresy, the following order should be observed:

First will come the twelve books *On the Trinity*, since he mentions them in the preface to the Idacian book against Maribadus.

They will be followed by the earlier form of the *Altercation between Athanasius and Arius before the judge Probus*.

Next will come the book against Felicianus, which appears to be one of the short works that Idacius Clarus declares in his preface to have composed against Varimadus *On the Trinity*, using private words rather than, as he says, “the force of testimonies.” I would therefore not reject the opinion that Vigilius attacked Marivadus under the fabricated name of Felicianus, since that man too enjoyed the king’s favor and was conspicuous at his court, having, in the popular estimation, attained the summit of human felicity.

This work will next be followed by the book published under the name of Idacius Clarus against Varimadus.

Then come the two short works against Palladius. The first has been substituted in the collections of the Councils for the acts of the Council of Aquileia and its two synodal letters; the second has wrongly been attributed to Ambrose or Gregory Nazianzen. Vigilius mentions this work in the passage we cited, after mentioning his book against Maribadus, or perhaps he silently indicates that he composed it earlier than that work.

Next comes the later form of the *Altercation*, in which he presents not only Arius but also Photinus and Sabellius as vanquished by the hand of Athanasius.

In publishing these books, however, we have followed another order, which we shall set out shortly.

Thus far we have vindicated for Vigilius of Tapsus his works—at least those that have come to our knowledge. Not all, however, with equal certainty. For we wish to warn you, candid reader, that our purpose has not been to enrich Vigilius of Tapsus with the spoils of others. We have established two orders for the works we have assigned to him.

The first is the order of his indubitable works. These are:

- Five books *Against Eutyches*, the fourth of which contains a defense of the letter of Saint Leo, pope, to Flavianus of Constantinople; the fifth, a defense of the decree of the Council of Chalcedon.

- The earlier form of the *Altercation between Athanasius and Arius*.[^c0048-73]

- The later form of the same *Altercation*, which represents not only Arius but also Photinus and Sabellius as convicted by Athanasius and condemned by the judgment of the judge Probus.

The second order consists of Vigilius’s doubtful works, which we have attributed to him on the basis of substantial conjectures—yet still conjectures that do not demonstrate the matter so decisively that they cannot nevertheless incline the reader’s judgment in their favor.

These are:

- The twelve books *On the Trinity* inserted among the Latin works of Athanasius.

- The book against Felicianus the Arian, commonly attributed to Augustine.

- The work published under the name of Idacius Clarus against Varimadus, the Arian deacon.

- The book against Palladius the Arian, consisting of two parts. The first was presented in the collections of the Councils that began to appear after the year 1550 as the acts of the Council of Aquileia; the second, *On the Faith*, or *On the Consubstantiality of the Son with the Father*, has hitherto been attributed by many either to Gregory Nazianzen or to Ambrose.

We have presented our conjectures concerning these books in such a way as to leave everyone free to form his own judgment. If anyone encounters a more probable explanation, we shall readily accept his view.

Having therefore vindicated, as far as we could, the works of Vigilius of Tapsus, we must now inquire whether Vigilius himself has also been vindicated—that is, whether he has been received into the catalogue of the saints, and consequently whether he ought to be honored as a saint by public worship.

## X. Whether Vigilius Should Be Regarded as a Saint
The question is certainly difficult because of the poverty of the historical evidence. By an edict of King Huneric, the bishops were ordered to assemble at Carthage: 54 from the province of Proconsularis, 123 from the province of Numidia, 111 from Byzacena—of whom the last, and therefore the last in episcopal rank, was Vigilius of Tapsus—120 from Caesariensis Mauretania, 42 from Sitifensis Mauretania, 5 from the province of Tripolitania, and 8 from the island of Sardinia: 463 in all.

Of these, 88 are reported to have perished [Col. 0497B], namely 4 from Proconsularis, 34 from Numidia, 10 from Byzacena, 32 from Caesariensis Mauretania, and 8 from Sitifensis. Of the remaining 375, twenty-eight fled, one endured suffering, one was a confessor, and the rest were banished, some to Corsica and some to Constantinople. All this is established from Victor’s own work *On the African Persecution*. But, apart from eight or ten of so large a number of bishops, it is unknown what each of the others endured or what end he met.

Aeneas of Paris and Theodulf of Orléans affirm that Vigilius wrote against Eutyches at Constantinople. Vigilius himself indicates this at the end of the first book, when he says:

> Meanwhile, I ask the reader not to despise the poverty of our style altogether, since perhaps the discourse could have been made more eloquent and polished. But we have tempered our style in such a way that we might commend the subject rather than the words to our readers. Above all, this work ought not to be inflated with the buskin of swelling eloquence, lest there should be any need to translate it into Greek; for it is more difficult to preserve the integrity of meanings with equal verbal fidelity in another language.

By these words he indicates that he wrote both in Latin and among the Greeks. But who knows whether he was one of the twenty-eight who secured their safety by flight, either with permission or at the urging of the Gospel? And although it were established that Vigilius belonged to those sixty distinguished for learning—of whom both the Greek *Menologion* and *Menaea* make mention—who did not cease speaking even after their tongues had been cut out, who can guarantee that he was not one of those two whom Nicephorus Callistus, in book XVII, chapter 11, reports from Procopius to have miraculously lost the power of speech without the organ of the voice after they had been defiled by sexual sin?

Certainly the Greek Church collectively commemorates these confessors or martyrs, who were punished by Huneric with various torments, on 7 December, and the Latin Church on 12 October. But it has reserved their individual designation for the day of the Lord, who, as the Apostle says, “will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. 4:5) “and will make manifest the counsels of hearts”; and then each person will receive praise from God. 75

Nor is this contradicted by the fact that ancient copies of the books against Eutyches append the title “saint” to Vigilius as author, including that very ancient Jurensian manuscript which revealed to us that he was bishop of Tapsus. Otherwise Eusebius of Caesarea also would be a saint for us, although—as many believe—he was branded with the stain of the Arian heresy, because we read that some writers likewise preface his name with the title “saint.”

Certainly, during several of the early centuries after Christ, this designation was applied to everyone, especially to the faithful who professed the sacred religion. In this sense the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Philippians, “All the saints greet you” (Phil. 4:22); and in Ephesians, chapter 3, verse 8, he calls himself “the least of all the saints.” But a later age called or regarded as “saints” in the substantive sense only those to whom honors had been decreed by the public authority of the Church.

Although, therefore, Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus, by so many books written against the Arians, Eutychians, and other heretics during the most turbulent times, won for himself a great reputation for steadfast faith and learning, and although he deservedly ought to be numbered among distinguished ecclesiastical writers, he cannot in the same way be numbered among the saints, because we have received from no trustworthy records that public worship was decreed for him by the Church by name.

## OPUSCULUM II, OR NOTES ON THE WORKS OF VIGILIUS OF TAPSUS

### [ON VIGILIUS OF TAPSUS.]

Vigilius.

76 Some unknown rogue played a trick in the name of our Vigilius, insultingly calling him *Dormilius*—plainly imitating Jerome, who fastened the name *Dormitantius* upon the heretic Vigilantius. As though he ought to be regarded in the same way as that infamous apostate from the faith, when he was a doctor crowned with so many laurels and a confessor crowned with so many palms!

See how this sarcasm stirred even the bile of the non-Catholic Josias Simler, in the Zurich edition of 1571, containing several Latin writers against Nestorius and Eutyches, including Vigilius. After praising him, as was fitting, Simler says:

> It is therefore astonishing that in our own age someone should, by his own judgment, call this excellent Father and most learned theologian, the leader of theologians, by the disgracefully altered name *Dormilius*. While he thinks that by this device he is attacking him, he meanwhile exposes his own shameless presumption and arrogance to the ridicule—or rather the pity—of decent men.

### Tapsus

There are two places called Tapsus: one in Africa and the other in Sicily; they are similar not only in name but also in situation and form. For Tapsus in Sicily is truly a peninsula, called by Thucydides, book VI, a *chersonesos* (χερσόνησος), “peninsula,” although Servius, in his commentary on Virgil, and the *Itinerary of the Islands* call it an island; hence it is commonly called *l’isola delli Manghisi*.

Tapsus in Africa is likewise similar to a peninsula, as I shall shortly show from Dio. Our Vigilius was bishop of Tapsus in Byzacena. Tapsus lies midway between Leptis Minor and the Tower of Hannibal.

It was considered improper to aspirate this name, since the ancient Jurensian manuscript from which we took it does not aspirate it, and the itinerary map, section 4, gives *Tapsus*, not *Thapsus*. But Tapsus in Sicily is also read without aspiration in Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 689, in two manuscripts that we consulted, in the *Itinerary of the Islands*, and in Silius Italicus, book XIV. The Greeks, however, wrote Θάψον (*Thapson*) in both senses.

Thucydides, book VI, Stephen the Epitomator, and Plutarch in his *Life of Nicias* speak of Thapsus in Sicily. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 3, Strabo, book XVII, Dio Cassius, book XLIII, and Plutarch in his *Life of Caesar* speak of Thapsus in Africa. In Plutarch, the copyists’ negligence introduced *Thapsacus* for *Thapsus*.

Hortensius says that the name of Thapsus in Sicily was derived from ἀπὸ τοῦ θάπτειν, “from burying,” because it appears in some sense to be buried in the sea and is almost level with the waves, as Servius says in commenting on Virgil’s words, “and fallen Tapsus.”

Tapsus in Africa—which is now called Caps by the Arabs, if the maps do not mislead us—is mentioned by Livy, book IX, third decade. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, and book VI, chapter 34, counts it among the free towns—opposed to the towns of the Romans—in Byzacena, or Libyphoenicia. In table 2 of Africa, Ptolemy assigns it 37 degrees and 30 minutes of longitude, and 32 degrees and 30 minutes of latitude.

Strabo, book XVII, writes that Scipio, defeated by Caesar, was first defeated near Ruspinum, then near Uzitta, and third near Thapsus and the lake adjoining it. Plutarch, in his *Life of Caesar*, records the outcome of the war, reporting that fifty thousand soldiers on Scipio’s side were killed, while scarcely fifty men were lost from Caesar’s army. Aulus Hirtius is more moderate in his book *On the African War*, where he says that only ten thousand of the enemy were killed; he adds that the victorious Caesar fined the people of Thapsus 20 million sesterces.

Dio Cassius, book XLIII, also discusses this battle and describes the city’s position as follows:

> Thapsus is situated, in a manner of speaking, on a peninsula (ἐν χερρονήσῳ); on one side it is washed by the sea and on the other by a marsh. Between the sea and the marsh there is a very narrow isthmus belonging to the city, and on it there is a lake, so that on either side of the lake, because of the shore itself, there is only a very narrow passage open.

Hirtius calls this marsh the Salt Lake. “Between it and the sea,” he says, “there was a narrow space of no more than fifteen hundred paces.” It appears to be the lake of the isthmus of Tapsus, the very lake into which, as Leo Africanus reports in book V, a hot spring of sulphurous odor flows. It is commonly called the Lake of Lepers, because lepers and the wounded are easily cured there.

## ON THE BOOKS AGAINST EUTYCHES

### Book I, page 1: “By the severe enactments of religious rulers”

He is speaking of the emperors Marcian and Leo. He also refers to Zeno, who acted more prudently after he had begun to reign again through the favor of the martyr Thecla, as Evagrius reports in book III, chapters 8 and 9. Likewise he refers to the elder Justin and his successor Justinian, if Vigilius lived into their reigns—as is probable, since in the year of Christ 484 he was the last of all the bishops of Byzacena and perhaps no more than thirty years old. Sacred history teaches that all these rulers issued enactments against the Eutychian heresy.

### Page 12: “Of the city of Constantinople”

79 All the copies that we have seen read this way, except the Jurensian copy, which has “of the city of Constantina.” I would think this reading preferable to the other unless, while avoiding the appearance of tautology, it fell into ambiguity. For the city of Constantina is properly Cirta, the metropolis of Numidia. Victor of Schott, *On the Caesars*, under Constantine, says:

> Then throughout Africa a priesthood was decreed for the Flavian family; and when the town of Cirta, which had fallen during the siege by Alexander, had been restored and adorned, it was given the name Constantina.

### Page 12: “We offer from outside”

Vigilius indicates that he appended to this work statements of the Fathers concerning the distinction between the two natures in Christ: Greek statements, discussed here, and also Latin statements, which he mentions at the end of book II. From these sayings of the Fathers he transcribed a few brief passages—as he says—in book V, beginning at chapter 22.

### Page 13: “To translate into Greek”

For he was writing among the Greeks, and indeed at Constantinople. Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in his work *Against the Greeks*, chapter 74, drawing almost entirely from Theodulf’s *Collectanea*, says:

> Vigilius, an African bishop, demonstrates by these words, in the books that he wrote at Constantinople in defense of Pope Leo’s *Tome* against the Eutychianists, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

He then adds a passage from Vigilius, book I, chapter 10, which we transcribed in the *Vindications*, page 29.

### Book II, page 17: “Without God”

In this passage, concerning Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, verse 9, where the Vulgate edition reads, “that by the grace of God” (χάριτι Θεοῦ, *by the grace of God*) “he might taste death for everyone,” Theodoret reads χωρὶς Θεοῦ, “without God.” He explains it in such a way that Christ is said to have died for everyone except God alone, and therefore even for the angels: “For the divine nature alone,” he says, “does not need this remedy.”

Theophylact, together with Oecumenius, adds that the corruption of this passage originated with the Nestorians, who, because they acknowledged two persons in Christ, asserted that the human person had undergone death without God—that is, without the divine person.

But the orthodox Theodoretus reported χωρὶς Θεοῦ, “without God,” not as the reading of the Nestorians but as his own. Ambrose, who was earlier than Nestorius himself, also uses it, explaining “without God” more appropriately of Christ suffering according to his human nature, not according to his divine nature. Thus he says in book II of *On the Faith*, addressed to Gratian, chapter 4:

> How well the Apostle put it: “That he might taste death for all without God,” lest we should think that the passion belonged to the divinity and not to the flesh.

And in book V, chapter 3:

> “That he might taste death for all without God,” that is, so that every creature, without any suffering of the divinity, might be redeemed by the price of the Lord’s blood.

Therefore, in this respect our Vigilius followed not the Nestorians but Ambrose and other Catholic Fathers; in these very books he is a most vigorous opponent of Nestorianism.

### Page 22: “While it is trampled when brought forth by the voice”

This is how the very ancient and excellent Jurensian manuscript reads, whereas the printed editions have *palpatur*, “is felt,” which gives an obscure—or rather no—meaning. But *calcatur*, “is trampled,” has the same meaning as “is neglected.”

### Page 23: “Eusebius”

You see that Vigilius counts Eusebius among the apostolic men of the Latin language, together with Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome; you should not suspect that he means Eusebius of Emesa, or a Greek Eusebius.

Nor do certain homilies of his demonstrate merely that he was Latin, but also that he was Gallic and Lugdunensian. These are among the fifty first published by Joannes Gaigneius under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, and later issued under the title of Eusebius Gallicanus from the recension of Andreas Schott in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*. It is otherwise certain that some of these homilies belong to Faustus, bishop of Riez and abbot of Lérins. 81

The ancient author of the *Life of Saint Hilary*, bishop of Arles, also mentions a written work of the Latin Eusebius—whether the author was Hilary’s successor Reverentius or Ravennius, or Honoratus of Marseilles.

The book *The Sparkles* by Defensor also mentions him, quoting seven sayings from his work in chapters 15, 30, 35, 71, 73, 77, and 78.

According to the records of Lyon, in the year of Christ 1287, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, at Lyon in the old basilica of Saint Just, the body of the blessed confessor Eusebius was discovered or identified together with many other bodies of saints. A stone placed above it bore his name.

A manuscript ritual book of that same church of Saint Just notes that his feast was celebrated on 14 August, with the prayer for a confessor who was not a bishop: “O God, who annually [grant us] the [memory] of your blessed confessor Eusebius,” and so forth. If the feast fell on a Sunday, the morning Mass was read at the high altar from the Sunday liturgy; but the Sunday, or solemn, Mass was celebrated for Saint Eusebius.

It is easy to think that this was Eusebius of Lyon, a most eloquent writer, whose cited homilies contain outstanding testimonies concerning the two natures and the one person of Christ, together with severe condemnation of Eastern error—especially homilies 1 and 2 on the Nativity of the Lord, and several on Easter.

In one of these, we noted the following notable passage in two manuscript copies, in one of which it is the fifth homily on Easter:

> The fact that Scripture tells us that we ought to eat the head of this lamb together with its feet means that we should venerate God and man with an equal confession. The head, therefore, is the divine substance; the feet are the human substance. Let us understand the head from what blessed John says: “In the beginning was the Word”; and the feet from what the Apostle Paul writes: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man”; and, “Born of a woman, born under the law.”

### Book III, page 24: “An exile from the Father’s divinity”

The manuscripts read this way, not—as in the printed editions—*exortem*. Vigilius likewise says in book XI of *On the Trinity*, “an exile from the Father’s secrets,” and shortly afterward, “nor let him be an exile from the Father.” *Extorris*, by its etymology, means something like “outside the land,” just as *exsul* means one who is outside his native soil.

Here *extorris* is used by Vigilius in the sense of alienated, separated, or foreign. In the usage of the ancient Christians, *extorres* were distinct from professors and confessors, and indeed also from exiles and deportees.

A *professor* was one who voluntarily professed the faith of Christ without being questioned. A *confessor* was one who did so only after being questioned; if he happened to suffer something for the faith, even if not unto death, he was called a martyr—although a later age restricted that designation to those tormented unto death.

An *extorris* was one who had voluntarily departed from his native land, whether through fear of torture or for some other reason. An *exsul* was one who had been expelled from his homeland. A *relegatus* was one who had been sent away to a specified place. Baronius, 2 January, letter II, and Ludovicus de la Cerda, *Sacred Adversaria*, chapter 72, no. 6, discuss this matter more fully.

### Page 25: “According to which, because of the union of person, although he is God, he was made the Father’s servant”

All the manuscript copies that we have seen read this way. The printed editions appear to have the corrupt reading:

> And according to the truth of its nature, the divinity was united to the same person; because of this union of person, although he is God, he was made the Father’s servant.

### Book IV, page 34: “Defense of Saint Leo’s epistle”

This is the Epistle of blessed Pope Leo I to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. It is counted as the twelfth among his decretal letters in the Roman edition published in 1591, and as the tenth in most other editions. In this fourth book our Vigilius expressly defends it against an unnamed Eutychian, who had produced a book against this letter of Saint Leo and against the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. Vigilius calls him “most impious” in chapter 15 and says that he was infected with the poison of the Eutychian heresy.

Anyone who remembers in what words the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon commended this letter, and with what consensus and applause it was received by the orthodox throughout all the Churches, will understand how excellent a cause Vigilius is defending. Concerning its text, someone—Gelasius, or Hormisdas, in the *Decree on the Scriptures*—says:

> If anyone disputes against it down to a single iota and does not receive it in every respect with veneration, let him be anathema.

The ancient author of the *Life of Saint Amatus*, first a monk of Agaune, then of Luxeuil, and abbot of Habend, says:

> When he had nearly reached the end, he ordered a certain brother: “Bring,” he said, “the letter of Pope Leo addressed to Saint Flavian; let it be read before me, because it contains the fullest exposition of the Catholic faith.”

When the letter had been brought, it was read before him. As it was being examined, the holy man said:

> Thus I believe, O ineffable Trinity; thus I confess, almighty God; thus I think of you, Son of God, Jesus Christ, who for our salvation deigned to come into this world; thus I understand you, Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, the Father and the Son. I confess one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity. Thus, most merciful Christ, instructed by you, I understand your Incarnation.

What more need be said? Throughout all the statements he always adapted his confession, so that the holy man might prove himself orthodox in every respect.

This is how the manuscripts of Romaric and Saint Maximin of Trier read, and Surius has nearly the same text under 13 September. Baronius also reports that this letter was once customarily read in the Western Churches during Advent, in the year of Christ 449, no. 42, from a manuscript of Saint Mary of the Martyrs. We ourselves saw it transcribed in a very ancient manuscript of Saint Benignus at Dijon, among the readings customarily recited during the week immediately preceding Christmas.

I do not mention the story reported by John Moschus, or Sophronius, in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 147, which he says he received from the mouth of Gregory the Great: namely, that after Saint Leo had written this very letter, he placed it upon the tomb of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and that blessed Peter’s own hand corrected it.

For this reason, the dispute concerning the author of this letter seems to me superfluous. Some object on the basis of Marcellinus Comes, who, while speaking of Prosper under the consulship of Vivian and Felix, says:

> The letters of Pope Leo, written against Eutyches concerning the true Incarnation of Christ, are also believed to have been dictated by him.

Gennadius repeats this in the same words in his account of Prosper, although in his account of Leo he expressly attributes those very letters to Leo.

Certainly, a secretary who serves an emperor or pontiff as his correspondent or secretary is, in a sense, the ruler’s hand. For once he has understood his master’s mind with regard to the substance of the matter, he ordinarily gives the reply its form and commits it to writing in his own style. Thus the same document may be attributed both to the ruler and to the secretary, as can be seen in the edicts of Theodoric the Visigoth, which are also attributed to Cassiodorus.

The particular question is whether this letter to Flavian, written against the Eutychian heresy, arose from the genius of Prosper or of Pope Leo, since it is certain that both were highly eloquent and thoroughly skilled in matters of the doctrines of the faith. It is difficult to determine anything certain about this.

If conjecture is permitted, I would think that it was the work of both Leo and Prosper, who, after conferring with each other and with God, completed it in every respect. It is certainly not unlike the other undoubted works of the great Leo. And even if Prosper contributed something to it, it should nevertheless be attributed chiefly to Leo, since he revised it, submitted it to the Apostle Peter for correction, confirmed it by his authority, and disseminated it throughout all the Churches of East and West. Thus it drew from him, as from the supreme head of the Catholic Church, its force for establishing the faith.

Moreover, the great care taken from the first edition of this sacred little work onward to preserve it intact and inviolate exactly as it had proceeded from its author, without changing even a letter, is demonstrated not only by the decree of Gelasius mentioned above, but also by the bishops of Gaul—Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus—when they wrote to Leo concerning this very letter:

> Furthermore, we increase in a certain great and ineffable joy peculiar to us because of you, since that special page of your teaching is celebrated in the assemblies of all the Churches, so that the harmonious judgment of all truly declares that the primacy of the apostolic see was rightly established there, from which the oracles of the apostolic Spirit are still disclosed.

> Therefore, if you graciously permit it, we beg your Holiness to read through and, if anything is missing because of a copyist’s error, to correct this work, which we have committed to leaves for preservation and for the benefit of both the present and future generations.

> Or, if you should enrich the salutary page for all its readers with some addition arising from your own study, may you command, with careful piety, that this very addition be appended to the little book, so that not only many holy bishops, our brothers throughout Gaul, but also many of your lay sons, who greatly desire this letter for the manifestation of the truth, may deserve to transcribe, read, and possess it once it has been sent back to us and corrected by your holy hand.

Nevertheless, we grieve that a page of such importance has not appeared in Italian, Gallic, or German type in a form so unblemished as to be entirely free from every error. This led us to undertake its purification, using the Greek version attached to the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, as well as three manuscripts of sound quality and venerable antiquity.

The first is a manuscript of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, compiled by the deacon Rusticus, from the library of Joannes Bouhier of Dijon, a senator. The second is from the book of sacred readings of Saint Benignus. The third is our own; it contains excerpts on the doctrines of the faith from Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, and various decrees of popes and councils.

We therefore present this letter after revising it from these witnesses. We shall also append scholia to it, in which the first manuscript will be designated by the letter A, the second by B, and the third by C.

## [LETTER OF SAINT LEO, POPE I]

## [Col. 0503]

### LETTER OF SAINT LEO, POPE I, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE
