Against the Eutychian heresy, now more accurately corrected from ancient manuscripts than it has previously appeared. (S)

## [Col. 0503A]

86 To his most beloved brother Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, Leo, bishop.

Having read the letter of Your Affection—which we are surprised was so long delayed—and having reviewed the sequence of the episcopal proceedings, we have at last learned what scandal had arisen among you against the integrity of the faith. What previously seemed hidden has now been laid open and made clear to us. In these matters Eutyches, who appeared honorable under the title of presbyter, is shown to be extremely imprudent and exceedingly unlearned, so that even of him it may be said by the prophet: “He was unwilling to understand how to do good; he devised iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. 35:4). For what is more wicked than to hold impious opinions and refuse to yield to those wiser and more learned?

But those who, when some obscure difficulty prevents them from recognizing the truth, turn not to the prophetic utterances, not to the apostolic writings, nor to the authority of the Gospels, but to themselves, fall into this folly. Thus they become teachers of error because they were not disciples of the truth. What learning from the sacred [Col. 0503B] pages of the New and Old Testament did he acquire who has not grasped even the beginnings of the Creed itself? And what is proclaimed by the voice of all those throughout the world who are to be regenerated is still not comprehended in this old man’s heart.

[87]

Since, then, he did not know what he ought to believe concerning the incarnation of the Word, and since he was unwilling to labor through the breadth of the holy Scriptures in order to merit the light of understanding, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common and undifferentiated confession by which the whole community of the faithful professes that it believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

By these three statements almost all the engines of the heretics are destroyed. For when God is believed to be both almighty and Father, the Son is shown to be coeternal with him: differing in nothing from the Father, because he is God from God, almighty from almighty, born eternal from the eternal; not later in time, not inferior in power, not unlike in glory, [Col. 0503C] not divided in essence.

This same only-begotten, eternal Son of the eternal Begetter was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. That temporal birth diminished nothing and contributed nothing to his divine and eternal birth; rather, it wholly devoted itself to restoring the deceived human being, so that he might conquer death and by his power destroy the devil, who held the authority of death. We could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he assumed our nature and made it his own—a nature which neither sin could defile nor death retain.

He was conceived of the Holy Spirit within the womb of the Virgin Mother, who brought him forth with her virginity preserved, just as she had conceived him with her virginity preserved.

But if he could not draw a sound understanding from this most pure source of the Christian faith, because through his own blindness he had darkened the splendor of the evident truth, he should at least have submitted himself to evangelical teaching, Matthew saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1).

He should also have sought instruction from the apostolic preaching, [Col. 0503D] and, reading in the Epistle to the Romans, “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:1), he should likewise have directed pious attention to the prophetic pages.

There he would have found God’s promise to Abraham: [88] “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). And, so that he might not doubt the particular identity of this seed, he should have followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham [Col. 0504A] and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

He should also have grasped Isaiah’s preaching with inward hearing, where he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a Son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23). He should likewise have read faithfully the words of the same prophet:

“A child is born for us, and a Son is given to us, whose power is upon his shoulder; and they shall call his name Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isa. 9:6).

Nor should he have spoken deceitfully by saying that the Word became flesh in such a way that Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, possessed the form of a human being but did not possess the reality of a body derived from his mother.

Or did he perhaps think that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature because, when the angel was sent to blessed Mary, he said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)? Did he therefore suppose that, because [Col. 0504B] the Virgin’s conception was the work of God, the flesh conceived was not from the nature of the one who conceived?

But that generation, singularly wondrous and wondrously singular, must not be understood in such a way that, through the novelty of creation, the particularity of its kind is removed. The Holy Spirit gave fecundity to the Virgin, but the reality of the body was taken from a body; and, while Wisdom was building a house for itself, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:11)—that is, in the flesh which he assumed from a human being and which the spirit of rational life animated.

Therefore, with the proper character of both natures preserved and the two brought together in one person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity. And, in order to cancel the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that—as was fitting for our healing—the one and same mediator between God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus, might be capable of dying by virtue of one nature and incapable of dying by virtue of the other.

Thus, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, [Col. 0504C] true God was born: wholly in what belonged to him, wholly in what belonged to us.

[89]

By “ours,” however, we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore. Those things which the deceiver introduced and the deceived human being admitted left no trace in the Savior. Nor, because he entered into communion with human weaknesses, was he therefore a participant in our sins.

He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, enlarging what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that emptying by which he who was invisible made himself visible, and by which the Creator and Lord of all things chose to be one among mortals, was an inclination of mercy, not a loss of power. Therefore, he who, remaining in the form of God, made the human being, himself became human in the form of a servant.

Each nature retains its proper character without defect. Just as the form of God did not lose the form of a servant, so the form of a servant did not diminish the form of God. For, because the devil gloried that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and stripped of the gift of immortality had undergone the harsh sentence of death—and because he found a certain consolation in his evils [Col. 0504D] through the fellowship of the transgressor—and because he thought that God, compelled by the demands of justice, had changed his own judgment toward the human being whom he had created in such great honor, it was necessary that, through the hidden dispensation of his plan, the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness—should complete his original dispensation of mercy toward us by a more mysterious sacrament, so that the human being, driven into guilt by the cunning of the devil’s wickedness, might not perish contrary to God’s purpose.

Therefore the Son of God enters these lowest regions of the world, descending from his [Col. 0505A] heavenly seat but not departing from the glory of the Father, generated in a new order and by a new birth.

In a new order, because he who was invisible in what belonged to him was made visible in what belonged to us; he who was incomprehensible chose to be comprehended; remaining before the ages, he began to exist in time; the Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, his majesty’s immensity being veiled; God impassible did not disdain to become a passible human being and to submit to the laws of death.

He was generated by a new birth because inviolate virginity, knowing no lust, supplied the material of the flesh. The nature, not the guilt, was taken from the Lord’s mother. Nor is the nature of the Lord [90] Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin’s womb, unlike ours simply because his birth is wondrous.

For he who is true God is the same true human being. There is no falsehood in this unity, since in him are mutually present both the humility of the human being and the exaltation of the deity. Just as God is not changed by mercy, so the human being is not consumed by dignity.

Each form acts, in communion with the other, according to what is proper to it: the Word [Col. 0505B] doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines with miracles; the other submits to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the glory of the Father, so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.

For one and the same person is truly the Son of God and truly the Son of man: God, in that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; human, in that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” God, in that “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1); human, in that he “was made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

The birth of the flesh is the manifestation of human nature; the Virgin’s delivery is evidence of divine power. The infancy of the little one is displayed in the lowliness of the cradle; the greatness of the Most High is proclaimed by the voices of angels. He whom Herod impiously attempts to kill is like human beings in the beginnings of life, but he whom the Magi gladly adore in humble worship is Lord of all.

[Col. 0505C] When he came to the baptism of his forerunner John, lest it remain hidden that divinity was concealed beneath the covering of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). Thus the one whom diabolical cunning tempts as a human being is served by angelic ministries as God.

To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is unquestionably human; but to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves, to give the Samaritan woman living water whose drinking prevents her from thirsting again, to walk with feet that did not sink upon the surface of the sea, and to rebuke the waves and subdue the surging waters by calming the storm is unmistakably divine.

Therefore, to pass over much else, it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend in compassionate affection and, by a command of the voice, to raise that same person alive after the removal of the [91] four-day burial; nor is it of the same nature to hang upon wood and, when daylight is turned into night, make all the elements tremble; nor is it of the same nature to be pierced with nails and to open the gates of paradise to the faith of a thief.

Likewise, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father [Col. 0505D] are one” (John 10:30), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). For although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and of the human being, there is nevertheless one source of what is common to both in dishonor and another source of what is common to both in glory. From us comes his humanity, in which he is less than the Father; from the Father comes his divinity, in which he is equal with the Father.

Because of this unity of person, which must be understood in both natures, the Son of man is read to have descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from the Virgin from whom he was born. Again, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in divinity itself—in which the only-begotten is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father—but in the weakness of human nature.

Hence, in the Creed also, we all confess that the only-begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

When our Lord and Savior was instructing the faith of his disciples by his questions, [Col. 0506A] he said: “Who do people say that the Son of man is?” (Matt. 16:13). And when they had recounted the various opinions of others, he said: “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15)—that is, “I who am the Son of man, whom you behold in the form of a servant and in the reality of flesh: who do you say that I am?”

Then blessed Peter, divinely inspired and destined by his confession to benefit all nations, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). He was rightly declared blessed by the Lord, and from the principal rock he drew both firmness of virtue and of name, because by the Father’s revelation he confessed him to be both the Son of God and the Christ. For accepting one of these without the other did not contribute to salvation; and it was equally dangerous to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be God alone without the human being, or a human being alone without God.

After the Lord’s resurrection—which was certainly a resurrection of the true body, since someone other than he who had been crucified and died was not raised—what else was accomplished during the [92] forty-day interval except [Col. 0506B] that the integrity of our faith might be cleansed of every darkness?

For he conversed with his disciples, lived with them, and ate with them; and he allowed himself to be handled by those whom doubt had touched, with careful and searching contact. Therefore he entered to the disciples through closed doors, gave them the Holy Spirit by his breath, and, granting the light of understanding, disclosed the hidden meanings of the holy Scriptures.

Again, he displayed the wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the freshest signs of his passion, saying: “See my hands and my feet, for I am he. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39). Thus it was to be recognized that the proper character of the divine and human nature remained indivisible in him, and that we should know the Word not to be identical with the flesh, so that we might confess one Son of God, both Word and flesh.

Eutyches must be judged exceedingly empty of this sacrament of faith, since he recognized neither our nature in the only-begotten Son of God through the humility of mortality nor through the glory of resurrection. [Col. 0506C] Nor was he alarmed by the judgment of blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist, who says: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:2).

For what does it mean to dissolve Jesus except to separate the human nature from him and to empty, by the most shameless inventions, the sacrament through which alone we have been saved?

If he is confused concerning the nature of Christ’s body, he must also rave, under the same blindness, concerning Christ’s passion. If he does not think the Lord’s cross false and does not doubt that the punishment undertaken for the world’s salvation was real, let him recognize whose death he believes in, and let him acknowledge the flesh. Let him not deny the man of our body, whom he knows to have been capable of suffering. For denial of true flesh is also denial of bodily suffering.

If, then, he accepts the Christian faith and does not turn his hearing away from the Gospel’s preaching, let him see what nature was pierced by nails and hung upon the wood of the cross. When the side of the crucified one was opened by the soldier’s lance, let him understand from where blood and [Col. 0506D] water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the bath and by the cup.

Let him also hear blessed Peter the Apostle proclaiming that [93] the sanctification of the Spirit takes place through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. Nor should he read casually the same Apostle’s words: “Knowing that you were redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers, not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18).

Nor should he resist the testimony of blessed John the Apostle, who says: “The blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7). And again:

“This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Who is the one who conquers the world, except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is truth. For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and the three are one” (1 John 5:1).

The Spirit, certainly, of sanctification; [Col. 0507A] the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism. These three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others. For the Catholic Church lives and advances by this faith: that humanity is not believed without true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity.

When Eutyches, in response to the questioning of your examination, replied by saying, “I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature,” I marvel that so absurd and perverse a profession was not restrained by any rebuke from the judges, and that a statement so foolish and so blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard.

For it is no less impious to say that the only-begotten Son of God existed in two natures before the incarnation than it is wicked to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there was in him a single nature.

To prevent Eutyches from judging that this was either correctly or tolerably said merely because it was not refuted by your sentence, we urge Your Affection, dearest brother, that, [Col. 0507B] if by the inspiration of God’s mercy the case is brought to satisfaction, the ignorance of this unlearned man may also be cleansed of this plague in his thinking.

As the order of the proceedings revealed, he had begun well to withdraw from his persuasion when, compelled by your decision, he professed that he was saying what he had not said before [94] and to acquiesce in the faith from which he had previously been alien.

[Col. 0508A] But when he refused to consent to the condemnation of the impious doctrine, your fraternity understood that he remained in his own perfidy and was worthy to receive the sentence of condemnation.

If he grieves over this faithfully and beneficially, and recognizes—even if late—how rightly episcopal authority acted; if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns by living voice and present signature everything that he has wrongly thought, then no amount of mercy toward one who has been corrected will be blameworthy.

For our Lord, the true and good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save human souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his goodness: justice should restrain sinners, but mercy should not reject those who have turned back. True faith is defended most fruitfully when false opinion is condemned even by its own adherents.

To carry out the entire matter piously and faithfully, we have sent our brother Julian, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter, as well as my son Hilarus, deacon, as representatives of our See. We have joined to them [Col. 0508B] our notary Dulcitius, whose fidelity has been tested by us. We trust that divine assistance will be present, so that the one who had gone astray may be saved after condemning the perversity of his thinking.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious Asterius and Protogenes.

Tiburtius the notary, at the command of my lord, the venerable Pope Leo, published this.

---

[Col. 0507B]

# SCHOLIA ON THE FOREGOING LETTER OF SAINT LEO

[Col. 0507]

### 1. “What scandal has arisen among you.”

In the common editions: “What scandal has occurred among you, and what [has arisen] against …” We have removed the two words *contigerit* (“has occurred”) and *atque* (“and”), because they seemed superfluous, were absent from the three manuscript codices, and had no corresponding words in the Greek text.

[95] ### 2. “Imprudent.”

Thus all the copies, corresponding to the Greek version’s ἀσύνετος (*asynetos*), “without understanding.” Nowhere is *impudens* (“shameless”), [Col. 0507C] as the 1551 Cologne edition notes in the margin.

### 3. “It may be said by the prophet.”

Thus in the printed editions and in B and C. A has it incorrectly as *praedictum* (“foretold”), since the Greek has εἰρηάσθαι, “to have been said”; and this is an accommodative sense, as it is called, not a prophecy.

### 4. “Yield.”

Thus C, corresponding to the Greek εἴκειν, “to yield.” A, B, and the common editions have *credere*, “to believe.”

### 5. “Obscure.”

Thus A, B, and C. The Greek paraphrases it as ἐμπόδιον ἀσαφείας, “an impediment of obscurity.” But if one reads simply “an obstacle,” one does not express the author’s meaning.

### 6. “Not even the beginnings of it.”

Thus A, B, and C; more gracefully than the printed editions, which have “not even the beginning of it.”

### 7. “Those who are to be regenerated.”

That is, catechumens or candidates for baptism, who were commanded to recite the Creed from memory when they were about to receive baptism, as Augustine frequently testifies, as does Ferrandus, and Fulgentius in the *Letter on Two Questions*.

A, B, and C have this reading, appropriately [Col. 0507D] exposing Eutyches’ ignorance, whereas the printed editions incorrectly have *regeneratorum*, “of those who have been regenerated.” The Greek interpreter used neither a future- nor a past-tense term, but rendered ἀναγεννωμένων, “of those who are being regenerated,” thereby designating the candidates for baptism, who were initiated only after being taught the Creed.

### 8. “He should have received.”

Thus A, B, and C, whereas the common editions read “he should have grasped.” The Greek rendering does not reproduce the words here, but the sense can be adapted to either reading.

### 9. “Of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

Thus A, B, and C, not—as in the common editions—“from the Virgin Mary.” The Greek version supports this: ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, καὶ Μαρίας τῆς παρθένου, “of the Holy Spirit and Mary the Virgin.”

We read the same in ancient Greek and Latin copies of the Constantinopolitan Creed. When, therefore, the sacred Virgin and the influx of the Holy Spirit coming upon her for the ἐνανθρώπησις, or incarnation, of the divine Word are joined under the single preposition *de* or *ex* (“of” or “from”), the opinion of Bonaventure, Scotus, and other theologians is strengthened: [Col. 0508B] they acknowledge effective concurrence not only on the part of the Holy Spirit but also on the part of the Virgin Mother in the formation of Christ’s body within her womb. [96] Otherwise, as they suppose on the basis of Galen’s principles, she would hardly have become a mother.

### 10. “God is believed to be both almighty and Father.”

The common editions have: “God is believed to be both almighty and eternal Father.” But the word *aeternus* (“eternal”) is found neither in A, B, nor C, nor in the Greek text, [Col. 0508C] where we see only ἀΐδιος (“everlasting”) added in the margin. Its superfluity is shown by Saint Leo’s words: “God is believed to be both almighty and Father.” He then takes up only what he had stated earlier: that one believes in God the almighty Father, without mentioning “eternal.”

### 11. “Instruction.”

Thus all the manuscripts. The Greek has εἰσήγησιν, “instruction” or “introduction.”

### 12. “And there he would have found.”

Thus the three manuscripts, corresponding to εὑρίσκων, “finding.” The common edition has “and he would have found.”

### 13. “And they shall call.”

ΚΑΛΈΣΣΟΥΙ (“they shall call”). Thus A, B, and C, not—as in the common editions—“and he shall be called.”

### 14. “It must not be understood.”

In most printed editions: “It must not therefore be understood by us.” The addition is unnecessary.

### 15. “Of the transgressor.”

Thus A, together with most printed editions, corresponding to προσδότου, “of the betrayer” or “traitor.” In B and C, however, I read *praevaricationis*, “of transgression.”

### 16. “These lowest regions of the world.”

The Greek has τὸ ταπεινόν, “the lowly” or “the humble.” Thus C, A, and most copies of the common edition. Some have it incorrectly as *infirma*, “the weak.”

### 17. “The nature was taken from the mother.”

The common editions have: “The nature, therefore, [Col. 0508D] was taken from the mother.” This is needlessly fuller, since the word *igitur* (“therefore”) is neither rendered in the Greek nor found in the manuscripts.

### 18. “Therefore the nature is unlike ours” (*Ideo nostri est natura dissimilis*).

Thus the three manuscripts, and correctly: the Greek has ἡμῖν, “to us,” and the sense is coherent.

The passage is likewise found in Fulgentius’s response to the second of Ferrandus’s five questions, in most copies. Some codices there have *nostrae est naturae dissimilis*, “is unlike our nature”; others, *nostrae est natura dissimilis*, “the nature is unlike ours.” We followed the latter in our edition of this letter of Fulgentius with Ferrandus’s works; it is also found in the common editions of this letter of Saint Leo. [The quoted lemma is governed by the preceding *nec*, “nor,” in the letter: Leo denies a difference of human nature.]

### 19. “Does not depart.”

The Greek has ἔστιν ἀχώριστος, “is inseparable.” Thus the three manuscripts. The common editions incorrectly have “did not depart.”

### 20. “For one and the same person is truly.”

The printed editions, together with [97] B and C, have: “For one and the same person is—which must often be said—truly …” But this parenthesis appears neither in the Greek nor in A, nor in Vigilius, [Col. 0509A] who cites this passage in Book V *Against Eutyches*. We therefore reject it as an interpolation.

### 21. “Diabolical cunning tempts.”

Thus all the codices except A, which has only “the devil,” in agreement with the Greek version: ἡ τοῦ διαβόλου πανουργία, “the devil’s cunning.” Whichever reading one chooses, the meaning is the same.

### 22. “But with five loaves.”

Thus the Greek, with C and A. Others superfluously read *sed et de quinque panibus*, “but also concerning the five loaves,” instead of *sed quinque panibus*, “but with five loaves.”

### 23. “Whose drinking prevents her from thirsting again.”

Thus C and A. The Greek has ὑπῆρχε, “was” or “existed.” B has “he provided”; most others have “he provides,” incorrectly.

### 24. “With feet that did not sink.”

Thus A and C. The common copies have “with feet that did not sink down.” The interpreter has τῶν ποδῶν οὐ βαπτιζομένων, “with the feet not being submerged.”

### 25. “The faith of the disciples by his questions.”

Thus the Greek, together with the three manuscripts. Some add pointlessly: “the faith of his disciples by his own questions.”

### 26. “Which was certainly a resurrection of the true body.”

Thus the three manuscripts, as in the Greek, σώματος, “of the body.” Most of the common editions incorrectly have “of a true human being.”

[Col. 0509B]

### 27. “Not another” (*Non alter*).

Οὐκ ἄλλος, “not another”; thus in the three manuscripts. Some have it incorrectly as “not otherwise.”

### 28. “Flesh, so that [he is] one” (*Carnem, ut unum*).

Thus the three manuscripts. The common editions read *carnem, et ut unum*, “flesh, and so that [he is] one.” The Greek inserts *ἀλλά*, “but”: “flesh, but one.” The sense is clearer in the manuscripts.

### 29. “And the sacrament through which.”

The common editions have: “and the sacrament of faith through which.” The word *faith* is superfluous, since it occurs neither in the Greek nor in the three manuscripts.

### 30. “From where blood and water flowed.”

The Greek has ἐρρύη, “flowed.” Thus the three manuscripts. The common editions have “from where blood and water flowed forth” in the plural.

### 31. “Because the Spirit is truth.”

Saint Leo cites this passage from 1 John 5:6 in this form in the very ancient codices A and C and in the Greek interpreter, who has it thus in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon: ἐπειδὴ τὸ Πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια, “because the Spirit is truth.”

Since the common Latin biblical version renders this passage “because Christ is truth,” certain printed and manuscript copies of Saint Leo’s letter, written by hands that were not very ancient, reproduced the passage in that form. They added [Col. 0509C] *Spiritus* (“Spirit”) in the margin because they had found it in [98] more ancient copies.

Certainly, the Greek text of John’s Epistle reads ὅτι τὸ Πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια, “because the Spirit is truth.” This reading agrees with the Syriac interpreter, Fulgentius in Book X *Against Fabianus*, and several other Fathers. There can therefore be no doubt that Saint Leo also read it in this way.

I do not dispute here about the Apostle’s intention, since either reading yields a sound and orthodox sense.

### 32. “And the three are one.”

Thus the three manuscripts. The Greek likewise has the phrase without a pronoun: καὶ οἱ τρεῖς τὸ ἕν εἰσι, “and the three are the one,” unless one says that the article here has the force of a pronoun, which is less likely. For Idatius also reads, “and the three are one.”

The common editions have: “and these three are one.”

### 33. “In response to the questioning.”

The Greek has διαλαλίαν, “conversation” or “interlocution.” Nearly all the codices have the same. The Roman and Paris editions, however, read *interrogationem*, “questioning,” less appropriately.

### 34. “When Eutyches replied.”

I read this form only in A. All the others, whether printed or manuscript, have *responderit*, “when he has replied.” The former reading is preferable, indicating that Eutyches, even while advancing his most absurd confession, ought to have been refuted [Col. 0509D] by the judges. The Greek can be adapted to either reading.

### 35. “His perverse profession.”

In A and in the Greek, *ejus*, “his,” is absent.

### 36. “Was restrained by rebuke.”

Thus A. The others have “was reproved,” not without the blemish of tautology. The Greek can be understood in either way.

### 37. “The diligence of Your Affection.”

Thus A and the 1551 Cologne edition. The Greek interpreter likewise has τὴν τῆς σῆς ἀγάπης ἀκρίβειαν, “the exactness of your affection.” Other copies have “the diligence of your solicitude.”

### 38. “May be cleansed even of this plague in his thinking.”

Thus the three manuscripts. The common editions have: “may be cleansed by you even of this stain in his thinking.” The Greek has καὶ ἀπὸ ταύτης τῆς φθορᾶς κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν καθαρθῇ, which may be rendered: “may be cleansed even of this corruption in his own thinking.”

### 39. “Recognizes, even if late.”

Thus all the copies. The 1551 Cologne edition has it incorrectly as “recognizes himself to be guilty.”

[Col. 0510A]

### 40. “Julian, bishop.”

A alone has *Julium*, “Julius.”

### 41. “Renatus, presbyter.”

B, C, and all the common editions add *tituli Sancti Clementis*, “of the title of Saint Clement.” This note seems suspicious to me because [99] it appears neither in A nor in the Greek, and because it does not seem to have been customary for Roman presbyters to be designated in writing by their titles before the time of Pope Symmachus. Under Symmachus, however, at the first Roman synod, three presbyters of the title of Saint Clement subscribed among the others.

Nevertheless, I think that this Renatus really was a presbyter of the title of Saint Clement, since this is noted in most copies of the letter, including ancient ones, and since, having first been written in the margin, it may have entered the text from there.

In any case, this appears to be the same Renatus the presbyter to whom Theodoret’s Letter 116 is addressed.

### 42. “Whose fidelity has been tested by us.”

The common editions have: “whose fidelity has often been tested by us.” But *often* occurs neither in the Greek nor in the three manuscripts.

### 43. “In the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes.”

This is the year 449 of the common era. Adding 38 to it gives the year [Col. 0510B] 487 of the Spanish era. The codices must therefore be corrected when they assign the letter to the years 483 or 486. We have deliberately omitted this chronological notation as an interpolation.

### 44. “Tiburtius the notary … published this.”

We owe this subscription to Rusticus the deacon and to codex A. Tiburtius the notary testifies here that he published this letter at the command of Pope Leo. It thereby appears that the letter was not transmitted only to Flavian, to whom it is addressed, but was dispersed throughout all the Churches of the Christian world and was therefore encyclical. Its purpose was, as happened, that it might serve the orthodox as a rule of faith, like the Creed.

---

# Book V, p. 56: Defense of the Decree of the Synod of Chalcedon

What is commonly entitled *The Definition of the Faith of the Council of Chalcedon*, Vigilius repeatedly calls *Decrees* in Books IV and V, and, [100] in the singular, *the Decree*, in chapters 17 and 18 of this fifth book, which contains [Col. 0510C] its special defense.

This decree of faith is found in Action 5 of the Council of Chalcedon. There Severinus Binius rightly noted that the ancient Latin editions incorrectly present at this point two definitions of that council under the following titles:

“Definition of the Council of Chalcedon in fourfold edition: Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, etc.”

Then, on the following page:

“Another Definition of the Council of Chalcedon, likewise in fourfold edition: It would be sufficient, etc.”

For in both the common Greek editions and the Latin manuscript copies there is only one Definition of the faith of the Chalcedonian Fathers, bearing one inscription and running continuously in one composition. It was first published and promulgated in the fifth action and then read again in the sixth action before Augustus Marcian.

Since it has hitherto appeared with no small number of errors, and since it is the subject of this fifth book, we decided to present two versions of it from very ancient and excellent manuscripts: one by an anonymous author, from our own codex; the other from the already mentioned codex of the most illustrious Joannes Bouhier, by an author identified as Rusticus, by the grace of [Col. 0510D] God deacon of the holy Church of Rome.

Rusticus frequently warns that he compared, distinguished, and corrected his text against Greek and Latin copies, especially those of the monastery of the Sleepless Ones. He also records the ferial days and dates of the months on which he completed the revision of each section.

The copyists have corrupted most of these notes, except for one, which appears at the end of the eighth action as follows:

“I completed it on Friday, the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.”

At that time the Sunday letter was B, and the year was 550 of the Christian era. In that year Rusticus the deacon was staying in Constantinople with Pope Vigilius. Later, having defected through schism, he was deposed from the rank of deacon together with Sebastian, likewise a deacon of the Roman Church, by a sentence of Pope Vigilius issued against the schismatics in that same year, 550, in the thirteenth indiction. This may be seen, if desired, among the letters of the Roman pontiffs or in Baronius under that same year.

In the two versions of the Chalcedonian decree mentioned above, [Col. 0511A] we have combined the Nicene and Constantinopolitan formulas of faith into one, [101] because in the autograph copies they differed from one another only in a very few and insignificant details.

The Greek expression inserted into the anonymous translation, μαχομένους, “contending” or “opposing,” so confused the copyist that, in the Cologne edition of the Councils [Col. 0512A] of 1551, p. 883, column 4, he wrote *Macedonians* in its place. This agrees neither with the original text nor with the other versions.

He failed to notice that this Greek word had been retained by the ancient interpreter emphatically, ἐμφατικῶς, to indicate that it had not been adequately expressed by a Latin word.

---

[Col. 0511A]

# DEFINITION OF THE FAITH OF THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON, OF THE SIX HUNDRED AND THIRTY FATHERS

Published and promulgated in the fifth action, and again read in the sixth action before Augustus Marcian.

[Col. 0511]

[Note: Col. 0511. The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0511A]

## From the Version of Rusticus the Deacon
Holy, great, and universal synod, which was assembled by the grace of God and by the commands of our most pious and most Christian emperors, Valentinian and Marcian Augustus, in Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the church of the holy and victorious martyr Euphemia, has defined the following.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, confirming the knowledge of the faith to his disciples, said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27), so that no one might disagree with his neighbor concerning the doctrines of piety, but that they might jointly proclaim the preaching of truth. But since the devil does not cease, through his weeds, to rise up against the seeds of piety and always to devise something new against the truth, for this reason the Lord, as is his custom, taking thought for the human race, raised up this most pious and faithful emperor for emulation. He summoned to himself from every quarter the leaders of the priesthood, so that, by the grace of our Lord working in all of us through Christ, he might remove every plague of falsehood from Christ’s sheep and cause them to grow rich in the flowers of truth.

This we have also accomplished, banishing the doctrines of error by common judgment; and we have renewed the unerring faith of the Fathers, proclaiming to all the creed of the three hundred and eighteen. We also acknowledge as our own Fathers those who afterward assembled in great Constantinople, one hundred and fifty in number, and who likewise confirmed the same faith.

We therefore define, preserving the order and all the formulas of the faith, that the holy synod formerly held at Ephesus is also to be maintained—whose presidents were the bishop of the city of Rome, Celestine of holy memory, and Cyril of the Church of Alexandria. The exposition of the right and undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy and most blessed Fathers assembled at Nicaea under the pious Emperor Constantine is indeed to shine forth. There is also to prevail the definition of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers at Constantinople, formulated for the destruction of the heresies that had then arisen, but for the confirmation of this same catholic and apostolic faith of ours.

## From another manuscript codex of Dijon

Holy, great, and universal synod, which, according to God’s grace and the decrees of our most pious and most Christian emperors, Valentinian and Marcian Augustus, was assembled at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, in the shrine of the holy and venerable martyr Euphemia, defined the following.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, confirming the knowledge of the faith to his disciples, said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace,” so that no one might disagree with his neighbor in the doctrine of piety, but that they might equally proclaim the preaching of truth. Since, however, the most wicked one does not cease to scatter his weeds among the sowings of piety, always devising something new against the truth, for this reason our Lord, taking thought for the human race as usual, raised up this most pious and faithful ruler to zeal for the faith. He summoned the leaders of the priesthood from every quarter, so that, by the grace of our Lord working in all of us through Christ, he might remove every plague of falsehood from Christ’s sheep and make them rich in the shoots of truth.

This indeed we have done, driving out the doctrines of error by common decree; and we renew the whole faith of the Fathers, proclaiming to all the creed of the three hundred and eighteen. We also reckon as household members those Fathers who afterward assembled at Constantinople, one hundred and fifty in number, and who themselves likewise subscribed to the same faith.

We have therefore defined the order and all the forms of the faith, preserving also the holy synod formerly held at Ephesus, whose presidents were Celestine, the bishop of the city of Rome, of holy memory, and Cyril of the Church of Alexandria. The exposition of the right and undefiled faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy and most blessed Fathers assembled at Nicaea under the pious Emperor Constantine is to shine forth; and the definition of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers at Constantinople is also to prevail, for the destruction of the heresies that had then arisen, but for the confirmation of this same catholic and apostolic faith of ours.

## Creed of the 318 Holy Fathers at Nicaea

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten from the Father before all ages: light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made. For us human beings and for our salvation he came down, was incarnate and became human, suffered, and rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead.

And in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and “Before he was begotten he did not exist,” and that he was made from things that did not exist, or from another substance or subsistence, and who say that the Son of God is either subject to alteration or change—these the catholic and apostolic Church of God anathematizes.

## Creed of the 150 Holy Fathers assembled at Constantinople

We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of heaven and earth and of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten from the Father before all ages: light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made. For us human beings and for our salvation he came down; he was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and became human; he was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate and was buried; he rose again on the third day; he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; he will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets.

In one catholic and apostolic Church.

We confess one baptism for the remission of sins. We await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

This wise and salutary creed, by the grace of God, would indeed suffice for full knowledge and confirmation of piety. For it teaches perfection concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and faithfully presents the Lord’s becoming human to those who receive it.

But since those who attempt to reject the preaching of truth have generated new expressions through their own heresies—some of them daring to corrupt the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation, which took place for our sake, and denying of the Virgin the term θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”; others introducing confusion and mixture, foolishly fabricating one nature of flesh and divinity, and monstrously saying, through confusion, that the divine nature of the Only-begotten is passible—for this reason the present holy, great, and universal synod, wishing to close every device of theirs against the truth, and teaching this proclamation as immovable from the beginning, has decreed above all that the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers remain inviolable.

It also confirms the teaching handed down concerning the substance of the Holy Spirit by the one hundred and fifty Fathers who later assembled in the imperial city, on account of those who opposed the Holy Spirit. They made this known to all, not introducing anything lacking into what had preceded, but explaining by testimonies from Scripture their understanding concerning the Holy Spirit against those who attempted to reject his dominion.

But because of those who endeavor to corrupt the mystery of the dispensation and shamelessly rave that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was merely a human being, it received the synodical letters of blessed Cyril, formerly bishop of the Church of Alexandria, addressed to Nestorius and to others throughout the East, as appropriate for refuting the madness of Nestorius and for interpreting the meaning of the saving creed to those who desire to know it with pious zeal.

Together with these it most suitably joined the letter of the bishop of the greatest and most ancient city of Rome, the most blessed and holy archbishop Leo, written to the archbishop Flavian of holy memory, to destroy Eutyches’ evil understanding, as corresponding to the confession of that great Peter and serving us as a kind of common pillar against perverse doctrines, for the confirmation of right doctrines.

For it resists those who attempt to divide the mystery of the divine dispensation into two Sons; it expels from the sacred assembly those who have dared to call the divinity of the Only-begotten passible; it resists those who seek mixture or confusion in the two natures of Christ; and it drives away as madmen those who say that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance. It anathematizes those who claim that the Lord had two natures before the union but fabricate one after the union.

Following, therefore, the holy Fathers, we all unanimously teach the confession of one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity; truly God and truly human, the same consisting of a rational soul and a body; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us, the same, according to humanity, like us in every respect except sin; begotten before the ages from the Father according to divinity, and in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same born from the Virgin Mary, the God-bearer, according to humanity.

One and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten, is to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The distinction of the natures is nowhere removed because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together into one person and one subsistence. He is not divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same Son, the Only-begotten, true God, the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets taught beforehand concerning him, and as Jesus Christ himself instructed us and delivered the creed of the Fathers to us.

Having thus arranged all things with the utmost exactness and diligence, the holy and universal synod decreed that no one may produce, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith in any other manner.

Those who dare to compose another faith, or to produce, teach, or hand down another creed to those wishing to convert—whether from paganism to knowledge of the truth, from Judaism, or from any heresy—if they are bishops or clerics, are to be deprived of their episcopate and the clerics of their clergy; if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.

## [Col. 0513A]

This creed, wise and salutary through the grace of God, would indeed suffice for full knowledge and confirmation of piety. For it teaches the fullness concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and presents the Lord’s becoming human to those who faithfully receive it.

But since those attempting to injure the preaching of truth put forward new expressions through their own heresies, some daring to corrupt the mystery of the Lord’s divine dispensation made for our sake and refusing the Virgin the title “Mother of God,” while others introduce confusion and mixture and foolishly fabricate one nature of flesh and divinity, saying with monstrous confusion that the divine nature of the Only-begotten is passible, for this reason the present holy, great, and universal synod, wishing to close every device against the faith, and teaching this proclamation as unshaken from the beginning, established that, above all, the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers remain unharmed.

And because of those who fight against the Holy Spirit, the discipline concerning the essence of the Spirit handed down by the one hundred and fifty Fathers later assembled at Constantinople is strengthened—μαχομένους, “those who oppose” or “fight against” the Spirit. They made this known to all, not implying that anything was lacking in what preceded, but proclaiming their judgment concerning the Holy Spirit and strengthening it by testimonies from Scripture against those who attempted to injure his truth.

But because of those who endeavor to violate the mystery of the dispensation, raving even more shamelessly that the one born from the holy Virgin Mary was merely human, it received the synodical letters of blessed Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, addressed to Nestorius and to others throughout the East, as most favorably received, for refuting Nestorius’s blasphemies and for interpreting the saving creed for those who desire to know it.

Together with these it most suitably adapted the letter of the bishop of the great and ancient City, the most blessed and holy archbishop Leo, written to the archbishop Flavian of holy memory, to remove the most wicked opinions of Eutyches. It corresponds to the confession of that great Peter and constitutes for us a kind of pillar against perverse doctrines, for the confirmation of right doctrine.

For it resists those who attempt to divide the mystery of the divine dispensation into two Sons; it expels from the sacred assembly those who have dared to call the divinity of the Only-begotten passible; it resists those who seek mixture or confusion in Christ’s two natures; it drives away as madmen those who say that the form of a servant which he assumed from us is heavenly or of some other substance; and it anathematizes those who claim that the Lord had two natures before the union but fabricate one after the union.

Following, therefore, the holy Fathers, we all teach with one voice the confession of one and the same Son and Lord, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity; truly God and truly human, the same consisting of a rational soul and a body; the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, like us in every respect except sin; begotten from the Father before the ages according to divinity, and in the last days, for us and for our salvation, the same born from Mary the Virgin, the Theotocos, according to humanity.

One and the same Christ, Son, Lord, Only-begotten, is to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The essence of the natures is nowhere removed because of the union; rather, the property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together into one person and one subsistence. He is not divided, separated, or disjoined into two persons, but is one and the same Son, the Only-begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, just as the prophets taught beforehand concerning him, and as Jesus Christ himself instructed us and delivered the creed of the Fathers to us.

Having defined these matters with complete truth, diligence, and care, the holy and universal synod established that no one may produce, write, compose, hold, or teach another faith in any other manner.

Those who dare to compose another faith, or to produce, teach, or hand down another creed to anyone wishing to convert—whether coming from the nations to knowledge of the truth, from Judaism, or from any heresy—if they are bishops or clerics, are to be deprived of their episcopate and clergy; if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized.

## Page 58. Lucifer through a legate

That Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, did not attend the Synod of Alexandria (held under the emperor Julian in the year of Christ 362, with Athanasius presiding), but sent his deacon there as his legate, is attested by Rufinus, book I, chapter 27, and Socrates, book III, chapter 4. Nor does the synodical letter—Athanasius’s letter to the Antiochenes, subscribed by the two deacons Herennius and Agapetus, legates of Lucifer—contradict this. For it is likely that there was an order of precedence between those two: Herennius, who is named first, performed the more important part in that embassy, while Agapetus attended rather as the legate’s companion than as a legate.

## Page 58. Few, but great in merits

No one will wonder that Vigilius here counts Lucifer of Caralis among bishops great in merits if he has read Saint Athanasius’s letter to him, which is full of his praises. Since we found this letter joined to the Dialogue of Vigilius of Tapsus, under Athanasius’s name and Against Arius, in the ancient Cluniac, Parisian, Poitevin, and Pontigny manuscripts, and since it is considerably more correct than its published editions, we reproduce it here, as something that will be neither unwelcome nor, I think, useless to the learned reader.

## Letter of Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, to Lucifer, Bishop of Caralis

Athanasius to the most blessed lord and holy bishop Lucifer, deservedly most glorious. Although I believe that word has reached your holiness also concerning the persecution which the enemies of Christ have even now attempted to inflict upon our brotherhood, seeking our blood, yet our beloved friends can also report it to your religious devotion. For they have dared to extend their fury so far through the soldiers that they not only drove out the clergy of the city, but also went out to the hermits and laid their deadly hands upon the monks. Therefore I too withdrew farther away, lest those who received us should suffer trouble from the same men. For whom would the Arians spare, who have not spared even their own souls? And when will they be able to desist from their wicked deeds, while they persist in denying Christ, the Lord, the only Son of God? This is the root of their perversity; upon this sandy foundation they build their crooked ways, as we find written in the thirteenth Psalm [Psalm 14:1]: “The fool has said in his heart, There is no God.” And immediately it follows: “They have become corrupt and abominable in their works.” Thus the Jews, denying the Son of God, deserved to hear: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people full of transgressions, an evil seed, lawless children” (Isaiah 1:4). How lawless? Clearly because “you have forsaken the Lord.”

Thus blessed Paul, when he began not only to believe in the Son of God but also to preach his divinity, said: “I am conscious of no evil in myself” (1 Corinthians 4:4). So, in accordance with your confession, we also desire, by holding apostolic tradition, to live according to the divine law, so that we may be found with you in that choir in which the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs now rejoice. Although Arian madness, joined with foreign power, raged so fiercely that the brethren were not even permitted freely to visit the wilderness, yet, with God’s favor according to your prayers, although with labor and danger, I was able to see the brother who customarily conveys matters of necessity as well as letters from your holiness and from others.

We therefore received the letters and books of your most devout and most wise soul, in which we discerned the apostolic image, prophetic confidence, instruction in truth, teaching of the true faith, the heavenly way, the glory of martyrdom, triumphs over the Arian heresy, and, together with the integral tradition of our Fathers, the straight rule of ecclesiastical order. O truly Lucifer, who, bearing the light of truth, have set it upon the lampstand that it may shine upon all! For who, except Arians, does not clearly see from your teaching that you have admirably and most effectively separated the true faith from the stain of the Arians, as light from darkness; that you have distinguished truth from trickery and defended the catholic Church from the perversity of heretics; and that you have proved that Arian words are nothing but a phantom? You have taught that devilish rulers are to be trampled underfoot. How good are your exhortations to martyrdom! How earnestly you have shown that one must die for Christ, the Son of God! How you have made manifest love for the age to come and for heavenly life!

You appear truly to be a temple of the Savior, who dwells in you and himself speaks these things through you; he himself has granted such grace to your words. For although you were formerly beloved by all, such great love for your affection has now been placed in the minds of all that they call you Elijah in our times. Nor is this surprising: if those who appear pleasing to God are called sons of God, how much more fitting is it that confessors who share in the prophets—and especially you—should be so called? We believe that you have not spoken these things alone, but that the Holy Spirit is with you. Whence comes such remembrance of the Scriptures? Whence their sound sense and understanding? Whence such an ordered composition of speech? Whence such exhortations to the heavenly way? Whence confidence against the devil and proofs against heretics, unless the Holy Spirit has been placed in you and is in you?

Rejoice, therefore, that through faith you are already in that place where your predecessors, the martyrs, now are: namely, in the choir of angels. We too rejoice in having you as an example of virtue, patience, and freedom. As for what you wrote concerning my name, I blush to say anything, lest I seem a flatterer; but I know and believe that the Lord himself, who revealed all knowledge to your holy and devout soul, will also render you a reward in the kingdom of heaven for this labor. Since, therefore, you are such a man, we ask you to be an intercessor for us with the Lord in your prayers, that he may now deign, being merciful, to look upon the catholic Church and deliver all his servants from the hands of persecutors. Thus all those who fell through temporal fear may at last rise again and return to the way of righteousness, from which, deceived, they wander, not knowing in what pit those wretches are.

I especially ask that, if anything has been said less adequately by me, you may deign to forgive it. For my ignorance has scarcely been able to draw what it could from so great a fountain. Concerning our brethren also, if I was unable to see them, I ask you again to forgive me. Truth itself is witness that I wished and longed to obtain this, and that I felt such grief because I could not. For neither tears ceased from my eyes nor groans from my heart, because we are not allowed even to see the brethren. The Lord is witness that I have not been able to see even the relatives whom I have, since they began persecuting us. For what do the Arians not do? They watch the roads; they keep watch over those entering and leaving the city; they search ships; they scour the wilderness for hermits; they disturb houses; they harass the brethren; they contrive troubles for each individual. But thanks be to God: while they do these things, they are all the more and increasingly detested by everyone, and are truly recognized, as your holiness said, as slaves of Antichrist. These wretches, while they are hated, persist in their malice, until they too are condemned by the death of their grandfather Pharaoh.

Those who are with me greet your religious devotion. Deign to greet those who are with you. May the divine grace of God preserve you safe, ever mindful of us, blessed man of God by merit, servant of Christ, companion of the apostles, consolation of the brotherhood, teacher of truth, and most dearly desired in all things.

## Commentary

So far the letter. Marcellinus and Faustinus, Luciferians priests, mention in their petition to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius these exceptionally elaborate praises heaped upon Lucifer of Caralis by Athanasius. They further accumulate other encomia of the same Lucifer, saying that he was grievously afflicted in four exiles over ten years and performed divine and apostolic works of power in them. They say, moreover, that his books were so highly valued by the great Athanasius that Athanasius translated them into Greek prose, lest the Greek language lack so great a good. They consequently complain that, although Lucifer believed, taught, and lived according to the divine Scriptures and performed miracles in Christ’s name, the defenders of the true faith called those Luciferians who followed Lucifer by that name as an insult, in order to oppress them.

Yet one must attend to when and by whom these praises of Lucifer of Caralis were uttered. Lucifer was praised by the praiseworthy Athanasius while still alive, when until then he had done or written nothing unworthy of praise. Likewise Hilary of Poitiers, at the beginning of his book Against Constantius, after Lucifer’s death counted him among the holy men exiled for the catholic faith. He was praised by the schismatics Marcellinus and Faustinus when long dead, after he had stained the life he had conducted piously and holily with the foulest blot of schism.

Lucifer, distinguished by contempt for the world, knowledge of Holy Scripture, steadfastness in faith, integrity of conduct, and even miracles, had displayed in himself an example of every sanctity. But after the Synod of Alexandria was dissolved in the year of Christ 362, he seems to have become more agitated against Eusebius of Vercelli because Eusebius did not approve the ordination of Paulinus as bishop of Antioch, which Lucifer had performed. At the same time, taking badly that bishops who had fallen at the Councils of Rimini and Seleucia should be restored not only to catholic communion but also to their former honors, he voluntarily withdrew himself from communion with the greater part of the orthodox. He became the head of many schismatics, who were called Luciferians after him.

Severus, History, book II, says: “Lucifer condemned those who had been at Rimini so thoroughly that he even withdrew himself from communion with those who had received them upon satisfaction or penitence.” Whether he decided rightly or wrongly, I would not dare to say. This was certainly a controversy full of obscurity and danger, as its outcome showed; nevertheless, most catholics disapproved of Lucifer’s action. The ancient author of the book On Heresies, to which Sirmond gave the title Predestined, says as follows in heresy 81: “We do not charge the eighty-first heresy against Lucifer, but we accuse him of schism. He was catholic in every respect; but by making peoples Luciferians and separating himself from the Church, he excluded charity from his faith.”

Prosper, in the Chronicle under the third consulship of Valentinian and the third of Valens, which concerns the year of Christ 370, says: “Lucifer, bishop of Caralis, dies. He, together with Gregory, bishop of Spain, and Philo of Libya, never involved himself in Arian perversity; but, because he did not relax the rigor of justice toward the correction of those who had yielded, he himself fell away from communion with his own.” Ambrose, in the Funeral Oration for Satyrus, says: “For Lucifer had then separated himself from our communion; and although he had been exiled for the faith and had left heirs to his faith, Satyrus nevertheless did not think that faith could exist in schism. For even if they maintained faith toward God, they did not maintain it toward the Church of God, whose limbs they allowed, as it were, to be divided and whose members to be torn apart.”

Augustine, On Christian Combat, chapter 30, from whom Isidore also drew in Origins, book VIII, chapter 5, says: “Who would not recognize as detestable the fact that the Luciferians also wished to be cut off from the very root? And this especially because what displeased them in the catholic Church is truly characteristic of catholic holiness. For nowhere ought the bowels of mercy to flourish as strongly as in the catholic Church, so that, like a true mother, she may neither proudly insult her sinful children nor be difficult in forgiving those who have been corrected.” And shortly afterward: “Accordingly, after the persecution inflicted by the Arian heretics, after peace—the peace which the catholic Church possesses in the Lord—had also been restored by the rulers of this world, many bishops who had assented to the perfidy of the Arians during that persecution chose, having been corrected, to return to the catholic Church, condemning either what they had believed or what they had pretended to believe. The catholic Church receives them in a motherly embrace, like Peter after the tears of denial, admonished by the cock’s crow, or like that same Peter after his perverse dissimulation, corrected by Paul’s voice. Those men, arrogantly receiving and impiously reproaching this maternal love, because they did not rejoice at Peter rising after the cock’s crow, deserved to fall with Lucifer, who was rising in the morning.”

Rufinus, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret agree in the same judgment. From them it is clear that Lucifer ought not now to be praised without qualification. He did many things excellently; by this single fault—if it is permitted to say so—whether obstinacy or severity, he obscured the glory of his earlier good deeds. This, indeed, was the line lacking to him from the prototype after whose likeness all saints must be formed, since this is the voice of that prototype in the Gospel: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice; for I came not to call the righteous but sinners” (Matthew 9:13).

Jerome seems to excuse his deed in the Dialogue Against the Luciferians, chapter 7, speaking thus of him: “We have come to a most difficult point, at which, against my will and purpose, I am compelled to judge something concerning blessed Lucifer other than what both his merit and my humanity demand. But what am I to do? Truth opens my mouth, and my conscious heart impels my reluctant tongue to speak. At such a crisis for the Church, amid such raging of wolves, he separated a few sheep and abandoned the rest of the flock; himself indeed a good shepherd, but leaving much prey to the beasts. I pass over what some malicious persons, as though defending it firmly enough, allege: that he did this from love of glory and of passing his name down to posterity, and also out of hostility which he had conceived against Eusebius because of the Antiochene dispute. I believe none of these things about such a man. One thing I will state firmly even now: he differs from us in words, not in deeds, since he receives those who received baptism from the Arians.”

What then follows? Jerome adorned Lucifer with the title “blessed”; did he thereby also teach us that Lucifer was entered in the registers of the saints? The Sardinians indeed honor him publicly as a saint; indeed, so do the people of Vercelli, although under the guidance of their Eusebius they were strongly opposed to the Luciferians. The ancient tradition of the Churches just mentioned carries great weight in Lucifer’s defense; Jerome’s encomium prepares the way for it, although, examined more closely, it is sufficiently qualified. For Jerome only removes from Lucifer the charge made by Hilary the deacon, a new—as he calls him—Deucalion, who thought Arian baptism invalid. But he openly censures Lucifer because, though a good shepherd, he left much prey to the beasts. Throughout that whole work he argues against the Luciferians that fallen bishops or priests are wrongly excluded from their honors if they have satisfied the Church by their repentance. Lest anyone perhaps interpret this as applying only to their adherents, at the end he strikes at the leader himself in these words: “The Synod of Nicaea preserves the rank of presbyter for a bishop of the Novatians if he converts; this judgment also attacks Lucifer and Hilary, since the same man is both a cleric and baptized.”

Jerome’s statement that Lucifer differed from the rest of the body of the Church rather in words than in deeds should therefore be understood roughly in the way stated by Socrates, book III, chapter 7, and Sozomen, book V, chapter 12. A little after the Synod of Alexandria, to which he had assented through a legate, Lucifer himself, agreeing also with the catholic Church, withdrew to his Sardinia; yet afterward he nevertheless became the author of the Luciferian schism. The apparently contrary statements are to be reconciled thus: in accordance with the decree of the Council of Alexandria, he held that fallen bishops should be received in their offices, provided it was evident that they had repented not falsely but sincerely and wholeheartedly withdrawn from the Arians. To that end he thought more ought to be demanded of them than a bare profession of the Nicene faith, by which Arians, not once, had deceived the orthodox through pretence: namely, that they should be kept among the laity for a longer time and, in proportion to the gravity of their defection, satisfy the offended peoples before being restored to their sees. But when in this matter he saw that his view was being treated more leniently, he then became indignant and separated himself from communion both with the fallen bishops and with those who had received them with open arms.

Finally, it is to be lamented that, although very weighty and eminent writers mention Lucifer’s schism, they nowhere mention his repentance—unless someone considers it implicitly indicated by the designation “blessed,” uttered from Jerome’s otherwise severe mouth. He certainly did not lack time for repentance, since he outlived the Synod of Alexandria, which had been an occasion of stumbling for him, by eight years, and did not die until the seventh year of Valentinian, A.D. 370, as Jerome, Prosper, and others have observed.

## Page 58, line 19. He relied upon the authority of the Nicene Council

[Col. 0519C]

Similar things are said about Macedonius by Athanasius in his *Epistle to the Antiochenes*. For those who hypocritically boast of their confession of the Nicene faith, while meanwhile daring to utter blasphemies against the Holy Spirit, do nothing other than deny the Arian heresy with their words while retaining it in mind and judgment. Therefore Rufinus too, in book I, chapter 25, asserts that the Macedonians arose from the Arians. “Thus,” he says, “that pestilential beast which, through Arius, had first raised its head as though from the underworld, suddenly appeared three-formed: through the Eunomians, who say that the Son is in every respect unlike the Father, because a creature cannot in any way be like its creator; through the Arians, who say that the Son may indeed be called like the Father, but by the generosity of grace, not by the propriety of nature—insofar, that is, as a creature can be compared with the Creator; and through the Macedonians, who say that the Son is indeed like the Father in every respect, but that the Holy Spirit has nothing in common with the Father and the Son.” Augustine likewise reports in his *Book on Heresies*, chapter 52, that the Macedonians were designated by the name “Semi-Arians” for the same reason.

**Page 58. At Sirmium.**

Three formulas of faith from Sirmium are known, either from Hilary or from Athanasius’s *On the Synods*. But Socrates, Sozomen, and Nicephorus departed far from the truth when they stated that all three had been proposed in one and the same council at Sirmium, assembled against Photinus. For our Petavius proved, both in his *Annotations on Epiphanius* concerning the heresy of the Semi-Arians, heresy 73, and in his *Dissertation on Photinus the Heretic*, which he appended to the third edition of his *Chronological Calculations*, that only the first of the three formulas was composed at that council, in the year of Christ 351, during the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus.

The second was composed six years later, namely in 357, at an assembly of a few bishops, which Phoebadius of Agen improperly called a synod. The third was composed finally in 359, during the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, again on the authority of a few bishops, and especially of Marcus of Arethusa; this formula was immediately brought to the Council of Ariminum. Vigilius speaks of the second, which in Hilary is entitled “A Copy of the Blasphemy Written at Sirmium by Hosius and Potamius”; near its beginning, it is said to have been examined by the bishops Valens, Ursacius, and Germinius.

**Page 58. All the Eastern bishops.**

The Eastern bishops assembled at Ancyra in Galatia in 358, under the presidency of Basil of Ancyra, to rescind that Sirmian formula—the second in number and chronological order—which Hosius, bishop of Cordova, already more than a hundred years old, as Severus says in book II, had signed under force and torture.

Not all of them, however, assembled there, but only twelve, whose signatures to the Ancyrene synodical letter are found in Epiphanius, heresy 73, “On the Semi-Arians.” Nor does Hilary’s *On the Synods* say anything more than that the Eastern bishops, gathered together, condemned that formula. Vigilius wrongly interpreted this indefinite statement as referring to all the Eastern bishops.

**Page 58, line 28. The definitions of twelve opinions.**

He took this from Hilary’s *On the Synods*, which contains only twelve anathemas of the Ancyrene bishops. In the Ancyrene synodical letter preserved by Epiphanius in the place cited, however, nearly nineteen are found.

**Page 58, line 30. At Sardica, the bishops assembled from all the provinces of the East.**

We have restored the word *East* from the ancient manuscripts—the Regius, Trecensis, and Corbeiensis—just as we have restored the provinces of the bishops of the false synod of Sardica, or rather of Philippopolis, which Vigilius copied from Hilary’s *On the Synods*.

That bishops from other provinces as well, especially from the provinces of the West, were present at the legitimate Council of Sardica is demonstrated by the headings and subscriptions of three Sardican synodical letters: one to Pope Julius, one to the Alexandrians, and one to all Catholic bishops. These are preserved in Hilary’s *Fragments*, in Athanasius’s *Apology II*, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 6, in Epiphanius Scholasticus’s *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 24.

Perhaps those who first printed these books of Vigilius inserted at this point Rome, Spain, Gaul, Sardinia, Africa, and the other provinces of the West. But they could have noticed that the reference here is not to the true synod of Sardica, but only to the council at Philippopolis, which the heretics proclaimed to be Sardica. Its synodical letter is preserved in Hilary’s *Fragments*, subscribed by seventy-three heretical bishops; from it Hilary transferred the formula of faith into his book *On the Synods*.

Meanwhile, one cannot help wondering why Hilary of Poitiers, a thoroughly Catholic man, inserted into his treatise *On the Synods* without qualification not only the formula of faith of this false Sardican synod, but also the canons of the councils of Ancyra and Sirmium, which had been held by the Semi-Arians.

Unless his purpose was the following. When he wrote to his Gallic bishops—who perhaps were to be summoned in pairs, or at least singly, as he says, to the East for the synods convoked by the emperor Constantine—almost the whole East had fallen away from the Catholic faith, divided among many and varied heresies. The bishops of each heresy were more effective at refuting the doctrines of others than at establishing their own. Hilary therefore wished the bishops of Gaul to be forewarned, so that they might know how to refute one group by means of another: for example, the blasphemous Sirmian formula attributed to Hosius by means of the Semi-Arian decrees of Ancyra; the Photinian heresy by means of the Sirmian council of those same Semi-Arians; and so with the others.

They were not to appear in the assemblies of the Easterners as judges of all things—for that would have been extremely offensive—but rather as admirers, indeed even as adherents, of whatever had by then been rightly established in the East.

**Page 58. Lydia, Europe, Thrace.**

This is how I read and punctuate the passage, not as the Regius manuscript has it, *Libya*, nor as the Corbeiensis, *Lydia of Europe*. Lydia is a province of Asia; Libya, on the other hand, belongs either to Africa or even to Asia, if by Libya one understands Marmarica or Pentapolis, which belonged to the Alexandrian patriarchate and, in the broader sense, to Egypt, and therefore to Asia.

I have written, however, “Lydia, Europe, Thrace, etc.” because Lydia and nearly all the provinces previously named by Vigilius must be assigned to Asia, whereas those that follow—Thrace, Haemimontus, Moesia, and the Pannonias—belonged to Europe.

**Page 59. The chapters of seven definitions.**

From the words Vigilius prefixed, after Hilary’s *On the Synods*, “We have set forth this faith,” it is evident that the seven chapters referred to here are none other than those with which, in the same Hilary, the formula of faith of the Pseudo-Sardican council concludes. We have distinguished them by numbers as follows:
