1. “Likewise, the holy and Catholic Church anathematizes those who say that there are three gods.

2. Or that Christ is not God.

3. Or that Christ did not exist before the ages.

4. Or that he is not the Son of God.

5. Or that he himself is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

6. Or that the Son is unbegotten.

7. Or that the Father begot the Son neither by deliberation nor by will.”

Baronius, therefore, in the year 347, number 38, and Binius in his notes on the Council of Sardica, wrongly rebuke Vigilius on the basis of these words of Athanasius in his *Epistle to the Antiochenes*:

“Do not even allow the tablets which some people boast of as having been composed concerning the faith at the Sardican synod to be read once or brought forward. For that council defined nothing of the kind. Although certain men wished to add certain things, as though something were lacking from the Nicene Council, and pressed the matter vigorously, the holy synod assembled at Sardica nevertheless took this very badly and decreed that nothing further should be written concerning the faith. They declared themselves content with the Nicene faith, since nothing was lacking from it and it contained piety in its integrity and solidity. Nor was another confession of faith to be issued, lest the one written at Nicaea appear not to possess its proper completeness, and lest those who are always eager to establish something new be given an opportunity to define the faith again and again.”

These words, I say, may perhaps serve to reject the formula of faith which is appended, in the manner of an appendix, to the Sardican synodical letter addressed to all the bishops, in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 6, and in Cassiodorus, or Epiphanius Scholasticus, *Tripartite History*, book IV, chapter 24.

But they cannot be used to refute Vigilius, who, following Hilary, mentions seven chapters added to the Nicene formula—not by the legitimate Council of Sardica, but by the pseudo-synod at Philippopolis, which falsely assumed the name of Sardica. Hilary himself gives the complete formula of faith of that false synod in the same place, from its synodical letter.

**Page 59. At Sirmium against Photinus.**

Our Petavius learnedly observed in his *Dissertation on Photinus the Heretic* that Photinus was condemned in five synods.

First, according to Severus, book II of his *History*, by heretics in a synod that appears to have been held at Constantinople in the year of Christ 336.

Second, by Catholics at Sardica in 347.

Third, likewise by Catholics at the synod of Milan in the same year, 347.

Fourth, also by Catholics at Sirmium in 349. Until now this synod, generally unknown, has been revealed by Hilary’s *Fragments*.

Fifth and finally, at the second council of Sirmium, in the year 351, during the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus, as Socrates noted in book II, chapter 24. This council was held by heretical Semi-Arians, with Basil of Ancyra playing the leading role.

Therefore Vigilius could not have called this council Catholic, unless perhaps he did so in view of what occurred there: a Catholic sentence against Photinus was issued, and the Semi-Arian heretics were more powerful than the Catholics themselves in overthrowing him. For at this second synod at Sirmium Photinus was not only convicted and condemned, but also—something that had never previously happened—deposed from the episcopate by an edict of the emperor Constantius.

Henricus Valesius rightly observed in his notes on Ammianus, page 7, that Baronius incorrectly assigns that final synod at Sirmium to the year 357. For Thalassus, or Thalassius, the praetorian prefect whom Epiphanius, heresy 71, says was present at that synod and at the Sirmian disputation between Photinus and Basil of Ancyra, had already died in 353, according to Ammianus, while the emperor Constantius was in Gaul. Ammianus says in book XIV, shortly after the middle:

“When Constantius later heard these things, and learned certain matters from Thalassius, whom he had already discovered to have died according to the common law, and so forth.”

That Sirmian synod, therefore, must have taken place before the year 353.

**Page 59. To Diodore and Theodore.**

The Eutychians, following Apollinaris and Eutyches, their authorities, burned with hatred against Diodore—Diodore, the presbyter of Antioch who became bishop of Tarsus—and against his disciple Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia.

Domnus of Antioch, in his letter to the emperor Theodosius, says:

“He dares to anathematize Diodore and Theodore, men who were pillars of the truth and champions of piety, and who displayed their strength openly against every heresy”—that is, Eutyches; “and in this he resembles Apollinaris in his folly.”

Both men were distinguished among ecclesiastical writers. Facundus of Hermiane devotes much space to their defense and praise in the books he composed for the emperor Justinian concerning the Three Chapters.

He especially adorns Diodore with the praises of Athanasius, Peter of Alexandria, Timothy of Alexandria, Basil of Caesarea, John Chrysostom, and Epiphanius. Suidas, enumerating a great many of his books from Theodore the Reader, mentions among others his *Chronicle*, in which he corrected the error of Eusebius Pamphilus concerning chronology.

**Page 78. “There is therefore one,” etc.**

This very passage of Cyril is cited in Saint Leo the pope’s letter 97, or 95, to Leo Augustus, from a book said to be called *Golia*, with so persistent an error that it has spread through many editions of that letter. It should be read “in the book called *Scholia*.” Cyril’s *Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten* are well known; this passage was copied from chapter 13 of that work.

**Page 79. “Which the most blessed Leo gathered together into one, etc.”**

These testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the two natures of Christ are found in Saint Leo’s letter 97, or 95, to Leo Augustus, and again after his letter 10, or 12, to Flavian, in the Greek-Latin acts of the Council of Chalcedon, part 2, action 2; but not quite all of them, nor in the same order.

**Page 79. “When therefore he had proceeded.”**

This passage of Gregory Nazianzen is quoted from Rufinus’s translation. It is cited by Saint Leo in letter 97, or 5, from the homily *On the Epiphany*, although it is found in the oration commonly entitled *On the Nativity of Christ*.

The reason is that, in an old manuscript of Nicolaus Faber and in another from Dijon, this oration is entitled *On the Epiphanies*, or *On the Nativity of the Lord*. In the Dijon manuscript it is followed by another, *On the Lights*, that is, on the Second Epiphany; this is the very oration that in printed editions bears the title *On the Epiphany*.

Thus these ancient writers called the Lord’s Nativity an Epiphany, or *Epiphaneia* in the neuter gender. Certainly, when Ammianus Marcellinus says in book XXI that Julius Caesar proceeded solemnly into the church on a festival day which Christians, celebrating it in January, called the Epiphany, this very event is reported by Zonaras as occurring on “the birthday of the Savior” (*τῆς γενεθλίου τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμέρας*).

Valesius further notes on this passage of Ammianus that, following Baronius in the *Martyrology* under 6 January, he long believed that the Easterners held that Christ was born on the same day—8 January—and baptized in his thirtieth year. Zonaras seems to have held this opinion, if what was the Epiphany in Ammianus, in the month of January, was for him the Nativity of the Lord.

Unless perhaps he confused the First Epiphany, customarily celebrated on 25 December, with the Second, and failed to notice that Ammianus refers to the Epiphany occurring not in December but in January.

# INTO THE DIALOGUE AGAINST THE ARIANS

**Page 84. “Constantia, the sister of that same prince.”**

Concerning Constantia the Arian, sister of Constantine the Great and widow of Licinius, who, as she was dying, infected her brother Constantine with the poison of her error, see Rufinus, book I of his *History*, chapter 11; Socrates, book I, chapter 19; Theodoret, book II, chapter 3; and Sozomen, book II, chapter 26.

Jerome had this in mind in his *Against the Pelagians*, addressed to Ctesiphon, near the middle, when he says:

“Arius, in order to deceive the world, first deceived the sister of the prince.”

There, with a lengthy argument, he also proves that almost all heresies were spread throughout the Church through the intervention of women.

**Page 85, line 2. Alexandria.**

Vigilius has not preserved the chronological order here. For, as is clear from all those who recorded the life and deeds of Athanasius in their writings, and indeed from Athanasius himself, the dedication of the church of Jerusalem was celebrated before Arius was sent back by the emperor to Alexandria for judgment.

**Page 85. The dedication of the Jerusalem church.**

This basilica, built beside the Savior’s tomb, was called simply the *Martyrium*, or, as Eusebius puts it, the *Martyrium of the Savior*. In Athanasius’s *On the Synods*, in the synodical letter of the council at Jerusalem, it is called *μαρτύριον τοῦ Σωτηρίου*, “the martyrion of the Savior.”

Jerome notes in his *Chronicle* that this church was built at Jerusalem through the efforts of Eustathius, presbyter of Constantinople. Eusebius describes its elaborate construction and solemn dedication magnificently and in greater detail than any other writer, in book III of the *Life of Constantine*, chapters 24–40, and in book IV, chapter 43 and several chapters following, adding in chapter 47 that this Council of Jerusalem was held in the thirtieth year of Constantine’s reign, just as Nicaea was held in the twentieth.

Eusebius also mentions this building and the other churches that Constantine erected in honor of Christ in his *Oration in Praise of Constantine*, delivered at Constantine’s thirtieth anniversary celebration.

**Page 85. In a certain suburb called Nicomedia.**

Vigilius expressed this passage badly, although he generally follows Rufinus in this preface. Rufinus says in book I, chapter 11, that Constantine died in a suburban villa of Nicomedia. Jerome calls that villa Acyron in his *Chronicle*. Vigilius received Rufinus’s words as though Rufinus had said that the suburb itself was called Nicomedia.

**Page 85. In the thirty-first year of his reign.**

Rufinus likewise says this in book I, chapter 11. It is not easy to explain this form of expression except as referring to the passing part of the thirty-first year of his reign.

Paulus Orosius, however, says in book VII, chapter 26:

“Constantine, the thirty-fourth emperor after Augustus, received the reins of empire from his father Constantius, and held them successfully for thirty-one years.”

Socrates too, in the final chapter of book I, and Sozomen at the end of book II, say that Constantine reigned thirty-one years. Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Constantine, the thirty-fourth of the Romans, reigned thirty years and ten months.” Prosper likewise fixes his reign at the same number of years and months in his *Chronicle*.

Eusebius, moreover, says in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 53:

“He was in power for thirty-two years”—apart from a few months and days.

Victor of Schott likewise records in his book *On the Caesars* that Constantine died at Acyron, in the countryside near Nicomedia, in the thirtieth year of his reign and the second year thereafter. Theophanes agrees, saying that he died in the thirty-second year of his reign, or, as he adds, after reigning thirty-one years and ten months.

Victor too, in the *Epitome*—whether he is the same author as the former or a different one—assigns Constantine ten years of reign, then twelve, and then another ten, which together make thirty-two. “A mocker rather than a flatterer,” he says; hence, according to the common saying, he was called “excellent for ten years, a robber for the following twelve, and a ward for the final ten,” because of his extravagant expenditures. There is therefore an error in what the same *Epitome* states earlier, namely that he reigned only thirty years.

The day and year of Constantine’s death were certainly marked by ancient writers with so many chronological indications that no doubt remains on this point. It is agreed that he died on Pentecost Sunday itself, 22 May, during the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, and therefore in the year of the Christian era 337. So say Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 64; Socrates at the end of book I; Prosper in his *Chronicle*; Idatius in his *Fasti*; the Alexandrian *Chronicle*; and nearly all the others who follow them.

As for the day that was Constantine’s anniversary of accession to the empire, scholars agree that it was 25 July, on the basis of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, Idatius’s *Fasti*, and the very ancient calendar published by Bucherius together with the cycle of Victorius. Socrates, book I, chapter 1, assigns that very day to the death of Constantius Chlorus, apparently indicating that it was both the final day of life for the emperor Constantius, his father, and the first day of imperial rule for Constantine, his son.

This day, falling within the twentieth anniversary of Constantine’s reign, fixes the epoch of the Council of Nicaea in the year of Christ 305. Thus, after nine months and twenty-seven days, Constantine reigned a complete thirty-one years: for that many years are counted from 25 July 305 to 22 May 337.

That the Council of Nicaea was held during the summer months, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus—that is, in the year of Christ 325—is the constant assertion of the more learned authorities. So say Socrates, book I, chapter 9; the Alexandrian *Chronicle*; the Council of Chalcedon, action 2; and the ancient inscriptions of the canons, both Greek and Latin. Baronius, in the year 325, Binius in his notes on the Council of Nicaa, and Petavius in book XI of *On the Doctrine of Time*, chapter 41, and in his *Chronological Calculations*, draw upon these sources.

The Nicene synod lasted, according to these same authorities, from 19 June to 25 August. Eusebius, who attended the synod, says in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 47, that it was held in the twentieth year of Constantine (*ἐν εἰκοσαετηρίδι τῆς βασιλείας*).

But in book III, chapter 21, Eusebius says that Constantine honored the festival of his twentieth anniversary (*τὴν ἑορτὴν τῆς εἰκοσαετοῦς βασιλείας*) both with his own largesses and with letters sent to those who were absent. No one should therefore think that this twentieth-anniversary festival was customarily celebrated on the first day of the twentieth year of his reign. Attention should be paid to what Eusebius had stated earlier, in chapter 14 of the same book III: at the time of the Council of Nicaea, Constantine had completed his twentieth year of imperial rule.

One should also remember the origin of these festivals. Dio says in book XIII, in his account of Caesar Augustus:

“When his first ten-year period had ended, another five years were decreed; when that had elapsed, again another five years; then ten years; and when that had ended, yet another ten years, and another ten years up to five times. Thus, through successive decades, he ruled throughout his entire life. For this reason later emperors too, although their authority was granted to them not for a fixed period but for their entire lives, nevertheless celebrated a festival every ten years for its renewal; this is still done today.”

You see that the decennalia—frequently mentioned in the *Historia Augusta* and on the coins of the emperors—arose from Augustus’s real or affected modesty. At the completion of each ten-year period he would discuss, rather than seriously contemplate, laying down the empire and restoring it to the state.

From this we should note the distinction between the tenth year of a reign and the decennial festivals. The tenth year of imperial rule was the year immediately following the completion of the ninth; the decennalia, on the other hand, were festivals customarily celebrated after the decade had been completed, and therefore on the first day of the eleventh year, which also coincided with the anniversary of the emperor’s accession.

This solemnity was celebrated with almost the same ritual as the emperor’s original elevation. It was distinguished by panegyrical speeches, banquets, games, contests, gifts, acclamations, and every other kind of pageantry.

The first Constantine, as Eusebius testifies in book I of his *Life*, chapter 41, book III, chapter 14, and book IV, chapter 46, removed from these festivals anything that smacked of pagan superstition, and celebrated his decennalia, vicennalia, and tricennalia in a thoroughly Christian manner.

Now to the matter at hand. The Council of Nicaea began toward the end of Constantine’s twentieth year, on 19 June. Then, on 25 July—the anniversary of his accession—his vicennalia were celebrated, both with the royal banquet at which he received all 318 bishops without exception and with other acts of generosity toward those present and absent. The synod continued from then for a full month into the twenty-first year of his reign.

If, therefore, Constantine’s vicennalia fell on 25 July 325, we must conclude that his tricennalia fell in 335, his decennalia in 315, and that this same day in 305 was the anniversary of his accession. In short, as we have said, he reigned thirty-one complete years, nine months, and twenty-seven days.

With these points established—that Constantine’s anniversary of accession was 25 July 305—the remaining question is whether the beginning of his reign should be reckoned from the death of his father Chlorus, or from the imperial dignity of Caesar, which was conferred upon him at least one year before his father’s death. Anyone who wishes to compare Petavius’s books *On the Doctrine of Time* with his *Chronological Calculations* on this subject will understand how greatly this difficulty exercised his remarkable intellect.

That the death of Constantius Chlorus occurred in the year 305 is suggested above all by Victor of Schott, who writes that Chlorus held the empire for one year. For since Idatius, Prosper, and others report that Diocletian and Maximian laid down the purple—that is, abdicated the empire—on the Kalends of April in 304, Chlorus, who succeeded them, if he was Augustus for only one year, cannot have lived or ruled beyond the following year, 305.

Eusebius and Prosper in their *Chronicles* suggest the same thing, for they place the beginning of Constantine the Great’s reign after his father under the fourth year of the persecution. Since the persecution began around Easter of 302, its fourth year must necessarily have begun at Easter of 305, during which Chlorus died.

The Socrates cited above also supports this view, assigning the very same day, 25 July, to the death of Chlorus that is known to have been the anniversary of imperial rule for Constantine his son.

The consular *Fasti*, however, stand against these arguments. They record Constantius Chlorus as still alive and consul with Galerius Maximianus for the sixth time in the following year, 306. Prosper writes in his *Chronicle* under that consulship:

“Constantius died in Britain at Eboracum in the sixteenth year of his reign. After him his son Constantine, born from his concubine Helena, seized the kingdom; at the beginning of his reign the fourth year of the ninth persecution was already in progress. Constantine, the thirty-sixth emperor, reigned thirty years and ten months.”

The Alexandrian *Chronicle*, under the same consuls, says:

“Constantius, father of Constantine the Great, died after he had reigned twelve years.”

Idatius writes in the *Fasti*:

“During these consulships Constantius died; afterward Constantius was elevated on 25 July.”

The same conclusion is confirmed by the years of Maxentius’s tyranny. As soon as he heard that Constantine had succeeded his father Chlorus and that Constantine’s images had been brought to Rome, Maxentius, with the Praetorian soldiers favoring him, seized the imperial power for himself. The panegyrics addressed to Constantine repeatedly say that he governed for a full six years, so that he died on the last day of his sixth year, lest he violate the sacred and religious number seven even by beginning it, as an unknown speaker says in a panegyric.

Nazarius indicates the season in which Maxentius’s head was carried to Africa by referring to a winter sea that was not yet sufficiently favorable. It is certain, moreover, from the *Fasti* of Idatius, under the consulship of Constantine II and Licinius II—the year in which Maxentius alone was consul—that Maxentius was defeated and drowned at Rome at the Milvian Bridge in the Tiber. This was the year of Christ 312. If six years are subtracted from it, the remainder is 306, the year marked by the death of Constantius and by the beginning of Constantine’s rule after him.

This is essentially Petavius’s argument in his *Chronological Calculations*. His reasoning, however, assumes that Maxentius was defeated during the part of winter preceding the Kalends of January. For if he had taken office in January or February and then died after a full six years, this calculation would place the death of Chlorus in the summer of 305.

But Constantine did not send Maxentius’s head to Africa immediately after Maxentius’s death. After entering Rome, Constantine ordered divers to search for Maxentius’s body among the great heaps of corpses carried along by the Tiber. Then, after preparing a triumph, he ordered the head to be cut from the body and carried about on a spear throughout the city. It is uncertain how long afterward it remained at Rome before being transported to Africa.

Indeed, Nazarius’s words, “the sea not yet sufficiently favorable,” are more naturally referred to February, as spring was approaching. At the beginning of spring the sea is usually opened for the reception of ships, in accordance with the words of the Roman lyric poet:

> The harsh winter loosens, in welcome exchange for spring and the west wind;  
> the engines draw the dry keels.

Panvinius marks the day of Maxentius’s defeat as 25 September, without any testimony from antiquity. I believe it should instead be taken from the very ancient Roman calendar published by our Bucherius together with the Easter canon of Victorius. It was written in the time of the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine the Great.

In that calendar Constantine the Great’s birth into this light is marked on 27 February, the anniversary of his imperial accession on 25 July, and certain of his victories on other days. Finally, on 28 October appears the entry:

> EVICTION OF THE TYRANT

No fuller designation was necessary for the victory over Maxentius, whom that age called “the tyrant” without further qualification.

The triumphal arch erected for the victor, in Baronius, year 312, number 60, bore this inscription:

> TO THE EMPEROR CAESAR FLAVIUS CONSTANTINE, THE GREATEST, PIOUS AND FORTUNATE AUGUSTUS,  
> THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME,  
> BECAUSE, THROUGH THE INSPIRATION OF DIVINITY AND THE GREATNESS OF HIS MIND,  
> HE AVENGED THE REPUBLIC WITH HIS ARMY  
> BOTH FROM THE TYRANT AND FROM HIS ENTIRE FACTION AT ONCE  
> WITH JUST ARMS,  
> DEDICATED THIS ARCH, DISTINGUISHED BY TRIUMPHS.

The inscription that Constantine himself attached to his statue, which bore the Labarum atop its spear, points in the same direction. Eusebius reports it in book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 33:

> BY THIS SAVING SIGN, THE TRUE INDICATION OF COURAGE,  
> I FREED YOUR CITY FROM THE YOKE OF TYRANNY,  
> AND, VINDICATING THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME IN LIBERTY,  
> I RESTORED THEM TO THEIR FORMER MAGNITUDE AND SPLENDOR.

Maxentius is likewise repeatedly called “the tyrant” in Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 8, book VIII, chapter 26, and *Life of Constantine*, book I, chapters 29–32; in Nazarius’s panegyric of Constantine; and in Socrates, book I, chapter 1.

Nor was he undeserving of the name. His cruelty and barbarity toward the Romans were so atrocious—whether one considers the indiscriminate slaughter of senators and other people, the violation of married women, or the disemboweling of boys and pregnant women so that their entrails might be examined by magical arts; whether one considers that he not only loosened the reins for his soldiers but also added incentives to every kind of lust and wickedness—that his unhappy end, which ought not to have been omitted from that ancient Roman calendar, could not have been more aptly designated than by the words “the eviction of the tyrant.”

From all this we learn that Maxentius was elevated as emperor by the Praetorian soldiers at Rome on 29 October, about three months after Constantine’s accession to rule following his father, in the year 306; and that he perished at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October, the day before his accession anniversary, in the year 312, after completing six years in his tyranny. This was, as Socrates says in book I, chapter 1, the seventh year of Constantine’s reign, counting from the time when he assumed power after his father’s death.

You may object as follows. If Constantine was first elevated only after the death of his father Constantius, who died in 306, he did not complete thirty-one years in the empire, but only thirty, as Victor in the *Epitome* and Eusebius and Prosper in their *Chronicles* assign to him. Nor would his vicennalia, as we said above, have fallen at the time of the Council of Nicaea.

To untie this knot, and to reconcile these authors both with one another and with themselves, three beginnings of Constantine’s reign, so to speak, must be distinguished.

The first is the one most familiar: the beginning reckoned from his father’s death, as all have noted—Eusebius in book I of his *Life*, chapter 16; the authors of the panegyrics; Zosimus in book II; Aurelius Victor; and others. As we have seen, this falls in the year 306 with the death of Chlorus.

The second, and chronologically latest, was introduced by Constantine’s modesty. The anonymous author of the panegyric delivered to Maximian and Constantine as Augusti says:

“So great was your maturity that, although your father had left you the empire, you were content with the title of Caesar and preferred to wait until the same man who had declared him would declare you Augustus. For you judged that the empire itself would be more glorious if you did not receive it as hereditary by succession, but earned it from the supreme emperor as something owed to your virtues.

“For there was no doubt that he would soon raise you to that sacred summit of divine power, the man who had long before freely chosen you as his son-in-law, even before you could ask for it.”

The ancient plan of Maximian is then proved by a picture placed in the palace at Aquileia, where it could be seen during the banquet. In it a girl, already venerable with divine beauty but still unequal to her burden, holds out to you—that is, to Constantine, still a boy—a helmet shining with gold and jewels and rising above the feathers of a beautiful bird, so that a bridal gift may make you more beautiful in a way that scarcely any adornments of dress could achieve.

From this same panegyric it is clear that Constantine was made Augustus from Caesar by order of Maximian and that he married Fausta, Maximian’s daughter. I assign this event to 25 July 307 on grounds that are not without substance.

No historian or chronologist, so far as I know, has extended the beginning of Constantine’s reign to this final kind of beginning, especially since this proclamation as Augustus by a man who had already abdicated three years earlier could seem to be of no importance. It was clear that, in having this honor conferred upon him, Constantine had no other aim than to win the marriage of Fausta, Maximian’s daughter.

It remains, therefore, either to trace the beginning of his reign from his father’s death, or from the dignity of Caesar conferred upon him in the year 305.

Eusebius, *Book I of the Life of Constantine*, chapter 13, says that he daily lived among those who shared imperial power with his father; and when, passing from boyhood into youthful strength, he was deemed worthy of the foremost honor among them (*τιμῆς τῆς πρώτοις παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἠξιοῦτο*: “he was deemed worthy of the foremost honor among them”). At that age and in that position we saw him when he traversed the region of Palestine together with the emperor who surpassed the others in age.

Victor, in the *Epitome*: “Constantius, Constantine’s father, and Armentarius, being Caesars, were called Augusti; after Caesars had been created—Severus for Italy, and Maximinus, the son of Galerius’s sister, for the East. At the same time Constantine was made Caesar.”

The *Alexandrian Chronicle* indicates the date. For after it had assigned the first day of Constantine’s reign to the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth consulship of Constantius and Maximianus Jovius, that is, in the year 305, it immediately attributes Constantius’s death to the following year, 306, when the same Constantius and Maximianus were consuls for the sixth time, having previously recorded that his son Constantine was heir to the empire and to the dignity of Augustus.

I had suspected at another time that Constantius Chlorus had created Constantine Caesar in Britain, and that this was what Eumenius had in mind when he exclaimed in his panegyric: “O fortunate Britain, now happier than all lands, which first saw Constantine as Caesar.” For I seemed to discern in ancient writers two visits of Constantine to his father, already Augustus and, as Eusebius asserts in Book I of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 12, the first of the four Augusti then living.

The first was at Bononia, or Gesoriacum, the Port of the Gauls, from which he crossed over to Britain with his father; the second was at Eboracum, when he unexpectedly came to his father as he lay dying. Here, springing from his couch, he rushed into the embrace of his beloved son; and shortly afterward, having transferred the empire to him and arranged his other affairs, he departed this life amid a kind of chorus of his sons and daughters, as Eusebius says in chapter 15.

An anonymous author mentions the first visit in a treatise on Constantius Chlorus and his descendants, which Valesius published from a manuscript of our Sirmond, together with his notes on Ammianus. “Therefore,” he says, “Galerius Maximianus Armentarius sent Constantine to his father, who had requested him. To avoid Severus while passing through Italy, he crossed the Alps with the greatest haste, having hamstrung the post-horses behind him, and came to his father at Bononia, which the Gauls formerly called Gesoriacum.”

Eumenius speaks even more explicitly in Constantine’s panegyric: “For even then you were being summoned by heavenly favor to the salvation of the commonwealth, when, at the very time your father was crossing over to Britain, your sudden arrival illuminated the fleet already spreading its sails; so that you seemed to have flown to him by some divine vehicle, not to have been conveyed by the ordinary public route.”

Thus, on this first arrival of Constantine to his father, Augustus and the first of the Augusti, in Britain, it would seem that his father made him Caesar on the eighth day before the Kalends of August in the year 305 of Christ. Eumenius would therefore have spoken accurately in saying that Britain was the first of all lands to see Constantine as Caesar.

On this assumption, one would have to say that Constantine was sent back from Britain by his father to Galerius Maximianus; that, after avoiding Galerius’s plots, he returned to his father in the following year and was present at his death. But after considering the matter more carefully, and since Eusebius in the *Life of Constantine* and the other writers mention only one journey of Constantine to his father after the abdication of Diocletian and Herculius, it does not seem to me that the journey should be doubled on the basis of Eumenius. If his words are examined more closely, they convey precisely what Eusebius and the others do: namely, that Constantine hurried to Bononia to see his father, but that, while the fleet was already setting sail and Chlorus was crossing over in it, Constantine himself shortly afterward followed his father’s footsteps and finally met him at Eboracum as he lay dying. Nothing else can be inferred from the anonymous author cited above.

We therefore think that Constantine was made Caesar by Galerius Maximianus on the eighth day before the Kalends of August in the year 305 of Christ, while he was being held in Galerius’s court as a hostage given by his father. Nor can Eumenius’s statement that Constantine was first seen as Caesar in Britain mean anything other than that there, succeeding to his father’s kingdom, he began to exercise power.

There were two kinds of Caesars among the Romans. Some were designated heirs to the majesty of Augustus merely by virtue of being Caesars, as Spartianus says of Aelius Verus; others were also partners in the empire and ruled the provinces entrusted to them with full authority. Constantine was admitted to the first class of Caesars on the eighth day before the Kalends of August in the year 305; into the second class in the following year, at Eboracum in Britain, after the death of his father Constantius.

It remains, then, to derive Constantine’s reign from these two beginnings. If it is reckoned from the dignity of Caesar that he received, he reigned thirty-one years, nine months, and twenty-seven days; if from his father’s death, he ruled one year less. The decennalia and vicennalia are reckoned from the earlier date, and Eusebius followed that calculation in his *Life*. Prosper, Bede in *The Six Ages*, and others after Eusebius in the *Chronicle* used the later calculation; in that work, only the years of the Augusti, not those of the Caesars, are extended.

The coins that survive bearing the inscription “Constantine, NOB. CAESAR,” while he was not yet Augustus, must be assigned to that two-year period which elapsed from the first time the title of Caesar was conferred upon him until his marriage to Fausta and the dignity of Augustus bestowed upon him by Herculius.

Nor should it seem surprising that Constantine’s quinquennalia and decennalia were reckoned from the dignity of Caesar that he received before becoming Augustus. For although the earlier emperors, from Augustus almost down to Diocletian, are found to have reckoned those anniversaries from the very day on which they were proclaimed Augusti, from that time onward the Caesars also began to celebrate them. They did so with such regularity that, when Caesars were subsequently named Augusti, they inaugurated those festivals not from the day on which they assumed the dignity of Augustus, but from the day on which they received the purple of the Caesars.

This is evident from the coins of Constantius Chlorus, Galerius Maximianus, Crispus, Constantine, and the sons of Constantine the Great—Constantius and Constans—as well as from those of Julian. Ammianus, Book XXI, reports that Julian celebrated his quinquennalia at Vienna after he had already become Augustus and had recently been elevated to the rank of the new Augustus at Paris in the same year, 360. Yet five years earlier he had been made Caesar and had assumed the purple, on the eighth day before the Ides of November in the year 355, in the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus, according to Idatius in the *Fasti*, Socrates, Book II, chapter 27, and Ammianus, Book XV.

We do not agree with Socrates concerning the day of Constantine’s death. He says that it occurred on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. That day, however, was the anniversary of Constantine’s imperial accession, reckoned from the dignity of Caesar that he acquired in 305. Although it was more solemn on account of the quinquennial and decennial celebrations, it was nevertheless observed as a festival every year.

Even though Constantine was covered with his father’s purple while still mourning over his father, who had only recently died, and even though, clothed in that purple, he presided over the solemn procession of his father’s apotheosis, while the people rejoiced and acclaimed—as the authors of the panegyrics relate with Eusebius—because he thus displayed his father as though restored to life in himself, the postponement—although Constantius had died some days earlier—of the festival of the administration of his father’s kingdom to the eighth day before the Kalends of August, the anniversary of the dignity of Caesar that he had acquired, is indicated by Idatius under the sixth consulship of Constantius Chlorus and Galerius Maximianus. He says: “Constantius died during the consulship; afterward Constantine was elevated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.” Thus he separates the day on which Constantine was elevated from the day of his father’s death. Otherwise he would have said that Constantine died on the eighth day before the Kalends of August and that Constantine, his son, was elevated on the same day.

The fourth year of the persecution, which Eusebius and Prosper assign to the beginning of Constantine’s reign after his father, should be understood as a completed year, not as a year in progress.

The one-year reign that Victor attributes to Chlorus should not be reckoned from the emperors who abdicated on the Kalends of April in the year 304, but from the division of the empire agreed upon between Chlorus and Galerius: that is, from the time when Chlorus relinquished Africa together with Italy to Galerius, retaining only Gaul, Spain, and Britain, as Eutropius testifies in Book X. For it can scarcely have been possible for this division of the empire to have been agreed upon between the new Augusti before the year 305.

Perhaps Chlorus’s reign was also reckoned as one year because, after Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had stripped themselves of the purple and administered Italy and Africa for only a single year, those territories afterward passed to Galerius’s advantage.

**Page 85, line 13. “As it had been delegated by Constantine.”**

Concerning the testament of Constantine the Great, Photius writes differently in the *Life of Athanasius*: “He left a testament,” he says, “to a certain Arian presbyter, ordering it to be delivered to Constantine, his namesake (*τῷ ὁμωνύμῳ*: ‘to his namesake’). By this testament, in place of the West, the paternal rule of the East was transferred to him. But that fraudulent man, when many asked whether the emperor had made a testament, denied that he had done so, having eunuchs as accomplices in his wicked deception. Shortly afterward Constantius came to him. The presbyter secretly displayed his father’s testament to him, asking only this favor: that Constantius should agree with Arius.”

Photius took this account from a book entitled *The Life and Contest of Our Holy Father Athanasius, Great Bishop of Alexandria*. Simeon Metaphrastes and another anonymous Greek author in the published *Life of Saint Athanasius* agree with him.

**Page 85. “The same presbyter Evangelus.”**

Baronius, under the year 337, section IX, says that no one had ever committed to writing the name of that Arian presbyter who first wielded such influence with Constantia, the wife of Licinius; then with Constantine the Great; and finally with his son Constantius. With no slight plausibility, he suspects that the man was Acacius Luscus, who became bishop of Caesarea after Eusebius Pamphili.

Vigilius certainly calls him Evangelus in the Thuane manuscript, while leaving it uncertain whether this was truly his name or whether it was an appellative, because he had carried good news to Constantius by delivering his father’s testament and placing him in charge of the Eastern empire.

**Page 85, line 20. “Arius has been recalled to the Church.”**

Whatever the etymology may be among the Greeks, I think that the Latin forms *Arrius* and *Arrianus* should be written with double *r*. First, this is supported by the authority of ancient writers and good manuscripts, which represent them in that form. Second, it is supported by the Arria family, very well known among the ancient Romans, from which came M. Arrius Secundus, found on an ancient silver coin in the collection of Fulvius Ursinus and in the work of his editor and enlarger Charles Patin, who also publishes coins of Q. Arrius and L. Arrius, previously unknown to the public.

Vigilius asserts that Arius the heresiarch survived Constantine the Great and was highly favored by his son Constantius. In this he follows Rufinus, Book I of the *History*, chapter 11, and Paul Orosius, whose words in Book VII, chapter 29, under the year 1092 from the founding of the City, are these: “Thus a ready access and easy path to the familiarity of the emperor Constantius was opened to Arius, the author of the new error, and to his other disciples.”

Indeed, the same thing is reported by all the ancient authors who wrote expressly about the life and deeds of Saint Athanasius: Photius, drawing on an older anonymous author; Metaphrastes; and the other uncertain author of the life published with Athanasius’s works.

Yet Socrates, Book I, chapter 25; Theodoretus, Book I, chapter 14; Sozomenus, Book II, chapters 28 and following; the presbyters Marcellinus and Faustinus in their petition addressed to the emperors around the year 385, midway between the beginning of Arcadius’s reign and the death of Valentinian the Younger; and Athanasius himself, in his First Oration against the Arians and in his *Letter to Serapion on the Death of Arius*, explicitly assert that Arius died while Constantine of blessed memory was still alive.

Constantine had threatened him with divine vengeance if he made a false profession of the Nicene faith. After Arius was removed, Constantine, Socrates says, declared that the faith of the Council of Nicaea had truly been confirmed by divine authority and will, and for that reason rejoiced greatly at Arius’s death.

I think that these weighty writers, who appear to have spoken contradictorily, can be reconciled if, following Hilary, Epiphanius, Sulpicius Severus, and others whom we shall cite below on this matter, one recognizes two Ariuses—namesakes, contemporaries, and adherents of the same error. One of them, the first craftsman of his wicked sect, breathed out his miserable soul while Constantine was still alive, with his entrails poured out; the other survived Constantine and enjoyed great favor with Constantius.

**Page 85. “At Ariminum or Seleucia.”**

Socrates, Book II, chapters 29–32, asserts that these two councils—one of Western bishops and the other of Eastern bishops—were convened by Constantius on behalf of the Arians in the same year, 359, during the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius. Theodoretus, Book II, beginning with chapter 18, should also be consulted concerning them; as should Sozomenus, Book IV, beginning with chapter 15, and especially Athanasius in his book *On the Synods*.

**Page 86. “Constantine Constantius.”**

This is how nearly all the manuscripts read. In one Jurensian manuscript the order is “Constantius Constantine,” so that there can scarcely be any doubt that in this fictitious letter Vigilius attached to Constantius either the praenomen or the cognomen of Constantine’s father. Whichever it was, it was certainly contrary to custom. For neither on ancient coins nor in edicts or other inscriptions is this emperor called anything other than Flavius Julius Constantius.

**Page 86. “Athanasius, a bishop of the same error.”**

Thus read the Jurensian, Remensian, and Thuane manuscripts, although in some other copies *deacon* is read instead of *bishop*. But it would be excessively absurd to introduce Athanasius as a deacon in the second year of Constantius, since it is established that at least ten years before the death of Constantine the Great he had succeeded Alexander in the episcopate of Alexandria.

**Page 108. “To investigate.”**

After this word, the commonly printed edition inserts nearly six columns, which are absent from the Jurensian, Thuane, and Arvernian manuscripts. In those manuscripts, after *to investigate*, the text immediately continues: “Athanasius said: Since your Excellence,” and so forth.

Therefore, on the authority of these manuscripts, we have omitted those very columns here and relegated them to a fuller edition of this disputation, consisting of three books, which we have placed after the other edition. In that work not only the Arians but also the Photinians and Sabellians are refuted for their errors.

**Page 109, line 19. “The same prophet adds.”**

Rather, he introduces it four verses earlier. In this passage, therefore, when Vigilius says *adds*, he means “he further says” or “asserts jointly.”

**Page 112, line 10. “He will be deceived in every virtue.”**

All the manuscript copies read this way. Cassander’s annotation of *in every truth* here is therefore pointless. “He will be deceived in every virtue” means the same as saying, “However great he may be, he will err from the truth.” Whatever truth the Evangelist may possess in judgment, or whatever reliability he may have in narration, he is nevertheless mistaken if Christ also is mistaken.

**Page 113, line 31. “Establishing thunder.”**

Thus reads the Jurensian manuscript; other copies incorrectly read “forming thunder.” In this passage Amos 4:13 has, in the Septuagint, *στερεῶν βροντήν*—“establishing thunder.” The Vulgate version, taken from the Hebrew, has something different: “forming mountains.”

# Against the Arians, Sabellians, and Others

**Page 118. Preface by an uncertain author to the following Dialogue**

Someone might think that Vigilius was the author of this preface, since he would thereby persuade readers that the disputation belonged to Athanasius himself and not to some later writer who had appropriated his name. But this cannot be said, since the preface completely overturns Vigilius’s position.

First, Vigilius introduces Athanasius disputing with that very Arius the heresiarch who had been condemned at the Council of Nicaea and sent into exile by the emperor. The author of this prologue therefore needlessly brings into conflict with Athanasius another Arius of the same sect and name.

Moreover, Vigilius, following Rufinus and the authors of the *Life of Saint Athanasius*, assumes that Arius the heresiarch survived Constantine the Great, and consequently makes him dispute with Athanasius about the faith in the presence of the judge Probus at Laodicea in the second year of Constantius.

The author of this preface, however, seems to have thought that Arius died before the Council of Nicaea. Some believe that this is what Epiphanius asserted in Heresy 69, concerning the Arians. He also seems to have thought that Arius was removed by divine action through the prayers not of Alexander of Constantinople but of Alexander of Alexandria, Athanasius’s predecessor.

Finally, since the author of this preface was concerned to place Athanasius and Arius in the same period in the *Disputation of Athanasius against the heretics Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius*, it is surprising that he did not also consider the chronology of Sabellius, who had advanced his heresy nearly eighty years before the beginning of the reign of Flavius Julius Constantius.

Add to this that Vigilius published the *Dialogue against Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus*, as we have demonstrated in our vindication, after he had laid aside his assumed persona and openly professed that he had imagined Athanasius disputing with those three heretics before the judge Probus. It would therefore have been entirely superfluous to preface the work with anything concerning Arius and Athanasius surviving at the same time.

Nevertheless, the author of this little preface to Pope Maternus is ancient. Cassander was the first to publish it from a manuscript copy, and we saw it in an old manuscript of Saint Mary of Rheims, written in the hand of Hincmar himself, archbishop of Rheims. On nearly every gathering he had written: “Hincmarus the archbishop gave this to Saint Mary of Rheims.”

We established with certainty that these characters were Hincmar’s from an original privilege of the monastery of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, issued at the assembly of Pistres in the year 864 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the twenty-fourth year of King Charles the Bald, in the twelfth indiction. Hincmarus subscribed that document together with twenty other bishops, immediately after Uvanilo, bishop of Sens, in the following form: “Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims in name, not by merit, and servant of the people of God, have subscribed.”

Since all twenty-one bishops subscribed with their own hands—a very rare practice in ancient documents—rather than in the common hand of a notary, it is evident that Hincmar’s handwriting differs markedly from the other twenty and is so nearly identical in the form of its individual letters to the inscription in the Remensian manuscript that, as the saying goes, “a drop is not more like a drop, nor an egg more like an egg.”

**Page 118. “Two Ariuses.”**

Hilary’s fragments in the Paris edition of 1598, page 29: “When our Fathers had learned that there had been two Ariuses, preachers of the most profane faith, and so forth.”

In Epiphanius, Heresy 69 concerning the Arians, section 8, the letter of Arius the heresiarch to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, is subscribed, among others, by “Arrius, Ethales, Carpones, Sarmates, Arrius, presbyters.”

Likewise, in the encyclical letter of that same Alexander, preserved by Socrates, Book I, chapter 3, I read: “Those who have withdrawn from the Church are Arrius, Achillas, Aeithales, Carpones, the other Arrius, Sarmates, and so forth.” Sozomenus, Book I, chapter 15, has nearly the same account.

Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the *History*: “For even the emperor was corrupted by the two Ariuses, the most vehement authors of this treachery.”

But the words attributed here to Severus by this author—“Two Ariuses, like two serpents, hissed from one mouth”—I nowhere find in him. This gives rise to the suspicion either that the *Chronicles* of Sulpicius, from which this passage is taken, had not yet been published, or that, if they are the same work as his sacred *History*, the work has not yet come down to us in a sufficiently complete form.

**Page 130. “Upon my seat.”**

Thus read all our manuscripts, as well as some copies of Vigilius, Book III against Eutyches, chapter 8. Lorinus also notes that Hilary read this way in verse 11 of Psalm 131. It is likewise found in Cyprian and Ambrose, at least in some manuscripts, whereas the commonly printed edition reads “upon your seat.”

# On the Twelve Books on the Trinity

**Page 198. Book I: On the Unity of the Trinity of the Godhead**

There is some reason to doubt whether this is truly Vigilius’s or Athanasius’s first book on the Trinity. For the Floriacensian manuscript places first a book entitled *The Faith of Saint Athanasius against the Heretics*, whose opening is: “We are commanded to believe in the omnipotence of God the Father.” This is the ninth among the printed books.

Second, under the title *The Arian Profession and the Catholic Confession of Saint Athanasius*, it places the work beginning: “The Arians say that the Son of God was not begotten from the substance of God the Father.” This is the eighth in the printed editions.

Third, it places the work that is first in our edition. In the manuscripts of Aeneas and Theodulf, however, the first place seems to have been occupied by the work that is eighth in the printed editions.

In Hincmar, and in the Cluniacensian, Parisian, and Pontiniacensian copies, the work that we likewise regard as first is placed first. The author Vigilius himself settles the question: in Book IV he cites something from the first treatise that is genuinely found in our first book, which is also first in the printed editions of Commelinus and the Parisian printers.

We have discussed the number and order of the following books in the preface. The title that we have placed at the beginning of this book is found in the Floriacensian manuscript, though the other copies differ somewhat from it.

In the Pictavian and Cluniacensian manuscripts, and in Aeneas of Paris, the title is *On the Unity of the Trinity*. In Theodulf it is *Book against the Arians*. In Hincmar it is sometimes *First Book on the Faith* or *First Book on the Trinity*. In the commonly printed editions it is *On the United Deity of the Trinity, to Theophilus*.

But no mention of Theophilus occurs in the manuscripts, nor in Aeneas, Hincmar, or Theodulf. Nor does it sufficiently accord with reason that these books should be addressed to Theophilus, since in them some Arian—Marivadus, namely, a deacon who was regarded in Africa as the leader of Arian impiety—is introduced and refuted. Vigilius indicates in the preface to his work on Idatius that he refuted Marivadus in these books.

**Page 198. “For this reason the mind suddenly…”**

The Floriacensian manuscript reads: “For those reasons,” namely, the heretics. In the Pontiniacensian manuscript the whole sentence is expressed somewhat differently, as follows: “For this reason the mind suddenly undertook these things in rivalry and was inflamed,” and so forth.

**Book III, page 200, line 24. “Question. Answer.”**

These words generally distinguish questions and answers throughout these books, in Hincmar and in the manuscripts. In their place, the commonly printed editions have “Athanasius” and “The Heretic.”

**Page 218. “Against Marcellinus the heretic.”**

This is how the title of the third book reads. The Floriacensian manuscript has *Mascellionem* in place of *Marcellinum*. There is a letter of Athanasius, *On the Interpretation of the Psalms*, addressed to Marcellinus—but he was a pious man, not a heretic, unlike the Marcellinus whom Vigilius here makes converse with Athanasius.

It seems pointless to inquire who this Marcellinus, or Mascellion, was, since Vigilius had only one purpose in these books: to refute Marivadus the deacon by making him assume one person or another, as though speaking through the mouth of Athanasius.

**Page 225. “Homousionista.”**

Thus reads the Pontiniacensian manuscript, whereas the printed editions have *Homuncionita*. An ancient author on heresies, whom Sirmond entitled *Praedestinatus*, mentions the Homuncionites in Book I, Heresy 76. They say that the image of God is in the human body, not in the soul.

Vigilius clearly shows that he understands something entirely different here when he says: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. “Was man in this beginning, Homousionista? And was not God the Son of God always with the Father before every beginning whatsoever? Certainly he recently assumed this man from the Virgin Mary. Were visible and invisible things made through man?”

From this it may be inferred that just as the Arians insultingly called Catholics *Homousians*, because they said that the Son of God was *homousios* with the Father—that is, consubstantial with him—so the orthodox called those people *Homousionists* who falsely claimed that Christ was of one substance or nature only, and consequently made Christ, even as man, *homousios* with the Father.

Vigilius attacks them when he says: “Is the man recently born from the Virgin Mary, according to his human nature, coeternal with God the Father, or did he create all things together with him?”

**Page 231. “Marcellio the Montensian (*Montensis*).”**

Thus reads the Floriacensian manuscript, whereas the commonly printed edition has “Marcellinus, heretic.” The man who in this same book had incidentally attacked Sabellius, Photinus, Ebion, the Marcionites, the Manichaeans, the Homousionists, the Jews, and the Arians here also attacks Marcellion of Mons—that is, a Donatist.

The Theodosian Code, Book XLIII, *On Heretics*: “Those decrees which were enacted against the Donatists, who are also called Montenses,” and so forth.

Augustine, *To Quodvultdeus on Heresies*, chapter 69, speaking of the Donatists: “These heretics,” he says, “are called Montenses in the city of Rome.”

*Praedestinatus*, Book I on Heresies, chapter 69: “These heretics are called Montenses in the regions of Italy, Parmeniani in inner Africa, and Donatists in the Carthaginian region. In the parts of both Numidias they have people resembling monks, whom we call Circumcellions,” and so forth.

Philaster of Brescia also called these same people Montanists. Optatus, Book II against Parmenianus, speaking of the Donatists who had established a seat for themselves at Rome, says: “They enclosed a kind of cave outside the city with steps, where at that time they could hold their assembly; hence they were called Montenses.”

Jerome also mentions them in Letter 133, speaking of Rheticius, bishop of Autun, who was sent to Rome by the emperor Constantine under Pope Sylvester on account of the Montenses; he also brings the Donatists back to the Novatians. Epiphanius, at the end of Heresy 59, asserts in the *Ancoratus*, chapter 13, that the Novatians were likewise called Montenses at Rome.

Baronius, under the years 254, sections 35 and 38, and 321, section 8, states that the Novatians were called Montenses after the heretic Felicissimus, who in the time of Saint Cyprian gathered his followers on a certain mountain.

Who this Marcellion of Mons was, and what error Vigilius attaches to him here, was, I suppose, known to Vigilius from some little work that has not survived to us. Certainly Augustine and *Praedestinatus*, in the passages cited, report that the Donatists held the same view as Arius concerning the divine persons.

**Book IV, page 234. “Potentinus Urbicus.”**

In Book IV, entitled *On the Individual Names*, Vigilius refutes a certain novel heresy of this man. Bellarmine says in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Athanasius, that this man was a disciple of Eunomius. From this he also concludes that these books could not have been written against him by Athanasius, since Basil, who was younger than Athanasius, disputed against Eunomius, the teacher of this Urbicus, as though he were his contemporary.

But since Bellarmine found no other indication that Urbicus Potentinus was an Eunomian than the similarity of his error concerning the Holy Spirit, he could have noticed that in this book Potentinus is marked as the author of a novel and hitherto unheard-of heresy.

These are Vigilius’s words: “There arose a novel and unheard-of heresy belonging to a certain Urbicus Potentinus, who claims that this Holy Spirit ought to be confessed as the Father, or the Son, or certainly a created thing.” Against him he concludes that either there would be two Fathers and two Sons in God, or God would not be the Holy Spirit.

This is not Eunomius’s own heresy, but another akin to it, whose author was not Eunomius but Urbicus Potentinus. My conjecture, therefore, is that the name Urbicus Potentinus signifies the deacon Marivadus, or Vatimadus, against whom Vigilius composed these books on the Trinity, as I have already shown in the first treatise from Vigilius’s own words in the book published under the name of Idatius.

For when that man was at Carthage, enjoying complete power under King Huneric and through him, he could scarcely have been more appropriately disguised under the names Potentinus and Urbicus.

I add that pronouns are not ordinarily placed before proper names unless perhaps the person’s condition is added, when he is less well known—for example, “a certain Alexandrian presbyter named Arius.” Nor is it customary to alter the order of proper names when several are pronounced together. Who would say “a certain Marcus Tullius,” and then shortly afterward “a certain Tullius Marcus,” or “a certain Aurelius Augustine,” and a little later “a certain Augustine Aurelius”?

Yet Vigilius, in the title of this book, mentions “the heresy of a certain Potentinus Urbicus,” while in the body of the text he has “the heresy of a certain Urbicus Potentinus.” By this he sufficiently indicates to more perceptive minds that these words are appellatives, not proper names, by which he points to Marivadus as though he were pointing with a finger to a proper name.

**Book VI, page 253. “This, I say, is the way of light.”**

From this point onward, the blessings and curses found in this sixth book are repeated in almost the same words in the second sermon of Saint Augustine for the Nativity of the Lord, which is Sermon 6 *De tempore*. That they belong to Vigilius and not to Augustine is demonstrated either by their style or by their connection with what is prefixed or appended in this little book of Vigilius.

**Page 256. “Three heads joined together in themselves, as philosophers are accustomed to say.”**

The heretics whom Vigilius attacks here seem to have been the Triscilidae, mentioned by the ancient author on heresies whom Sirmond entitled *Praedestinatus*, chapter 74.

Philaster, in Book 45 of his *On Heresies*, and Augustine, *To Quodvultdeus on Heresies*, chapter 74, also discuss them in these very words: “There is another heresy,” he says, “which asserts God to be threefold in such a way that one part of him is the Father, another part the Son, and another part the Holy Spirit. That is, the parts of the one God constitute this Trinity; God is completed from these parts, and neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Spirit is perfect in himself.”

That Tritheist Gobarus seems to have belonged to this group. Photius reports some excerpts from his ravings in the *Bibliotheca*, volume 232.

What Vigilius adds—“as philosophers are accustomed to say”—is confirmed by Petavius in volume II of the *Theological Dogmas*, Book I on the Trinity, chapter 1. He shows that the armed impiety of the Arians, Anomoeans, and other Tritheists was drawn from Plato, Philo the Jew, and other Platonists, and that the source of these heresies was the Platonic notion of three gods.

The first was the parent and creator of the others; the second was created by the first but was the craftsman and origin of all other things; the third was the work of the second and likewise the soul of the world. Proclus, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, calls these three gods the grandfather, the son, and the grandson.

As for Vigilius’s statement that they were “three heads joined together in themselves,” I seem to have found it expressed on an old Gothic gold coin, which the following table displays first. In the table, the middle circles, together with the mark indicating the metal, show the size of the coins.

On its reverse side it has three heads arranged in a triangle. One is placed above and represents the supreme god of Plato and the Tritheists; the two lower heads, on the right and the left, suitably represent the two other gods derived from that first one.

I therefore conjecture that the other side of the coin displays the face of some Arian prince, one of those who, about twelve hundred years ago, seized Gaul, Spain, and Africa after taking them from the Romans, and who wished this public monument of his sect to survive.

Concerning the other two bronze coins, which have the same meaning, we have a different conjecture: namely, that they were struck at Rheims during the baptism of Clovis, king of the Franks, under the direction of Saint Remigius.

Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 31, writes the following about this event: “Accordingly, the king—Clovis—confessing the omnipotent God in the Trinity, was baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and, anointed with sacred chrism, with the sign of the cross of Christ.”

Since the three heads on these coins are plainly equal and none rises above the others, the Trinity of the divine persons, equal among themselves in one deity, is rightly depicted in this emblem.

The word *REMO*, I conjecture, designates Clovis himself, to whom these coins were dedicated, now that he had become Remensian, or of Rheims. For when the city of Rheims, in which he had been reborn through baptism together with his people, had been adopted as his homeland, he renounced the polytheism of the pagans and began, according to the Catholic rite, to acknowledge and profess the one true Deity in the Trinity.

**Page 261. “The apocrypha of the heretics.”**
Quite rightly. For there were apocrypha of two kinds: some belonging to the orthodox, others to heretics. Ἀπόκρυφον (*apocryphon*) means “hidden” or “concealed” by etymology; from this meaning a twofold usage of the word arose.

The first usage designates a writing that is noncanonical, though not condemned. [Col. 0536A] In this sense Origen appears to have spoken near the end of chapter 13 of Matthew:

“For they also have cut this off,” he says, “and it refers to Isaiah; just as the statement ‘they died by the slaughter of the sword’ refers to Zechariah, who was killed between the temple and the altar, as the Savior taught; and, as I think, he supports this with his testimony from a Scripture which, although it is not found among the common and published books, is nevertheless probably extant among the apocrypha—that is, among writings which are read in secret.”

Do you see how Origen defines apocryphal books as those read in secret, and contrasts them with the common and published books? Indeed, the canon appears in Ferrandus’s *Breviary*, no. 228, and in Cresconius, no. 300:

“Let nothing be read in the Church apart from the canonical Scriptures.”

This was taken from the final canon of Laodicea and from one transferred from Hippo, and subsequently incorporated into the Councils of Carthage of the years 397 and 418. Yet this decree is not formulated in exactly the same way in all these synods. In Laodicea it is absolute and without exception; but in Hippo, or Carthage, since the following canon is added—“Let the Passions of the Martyrs be read on their anniversaries”—the preceding canon is restricted as follows:

“Let nothing be read in the church under the name of divine Scripture apart from the canonical Scriptures.”

It is evident, then, that in Origen’s age nothing was ordinarily read publicly in the churches except the canonical Scriptures. Hence he called apocryphal, or noncanonical, those writings that were read only in secret, and not also in the churches and publicly.

Jerome clearly calls apocryphal, in Letter 106, which is also the *Prologue Galeatus*, all writings that are not in the canon of the divine Scriptures. Some of these he nevertheless recommends for reading in the churches, in Letter 115 to Chromatius and Heliodorus, for the edification of the people, but not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines.

The later usage of the word is narrower. Of noncanonical Scriptures it counts as apocryphal only those that conflict with the faith and with sound morals, and that have consequently been condemned either in their entirety or in some part—whether they claim to have a certain author or no author at all. Otherwise, quite a few books highly useful to the Church circulate under an unknown author; indeed, some canonical books do so as well, namely Judges, Ruth, Job, and others, as Bellarmine correctly noted in book I, chapter 20, *On the Word of God*.

It is true, however, that most apocrypha of this kind, especially the older ones, did not bear the name of their true author. This is all Jerome intended in Letter 7 to Laeta, concerning the education of her daughter:

“Let her beware of all apocrypha; and if she should ever wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but out of reverence for their signs, let her know that they are not by those whose names appear as their titles; that many corrupt things have been mixed into them; and that it is a mark of great prudence to search for gold in mud.”

Accordingly, Jerome himself, in his commentary on Psalm 132, professes to report certain things from an apocryphal book—not as authoritative, but as a matter of recollection.

Speaking of these same apocrypha, Augustine says in book XV, chapter 23, of *The City of God*:

“Many things are brought forth by heretics under the names of other prophets, and more recent things under the names of the apostles. All of these, under the name of apocrypha, have been removed from canonical authority after careful examination.”

In this sense Gelasius also condemned the apocrypha in his decree on the Scriptures—if it was Gelasius and not Hormisdas, of whom I shall speak shortly. First, however, I note that apocrypha of the later kind seem to have been so called either because they contained the hidden poison of corrupt teaching beneath attractive titles, or because, on account of their harmfulness, they ought not to be brought into the light but rather concealed and condemned to darkness.

**Page 261. Against the tradition of the canon.**

It might seem that the canon of Pope Gelasius I concerning canonical and apocryphal Scriptures is meant here. Since it is reported to have been issued at the Roman Council during the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius—that is, in the year of Christ 494—it agrees well with the age of Vigilius of Thapsus. But this is contradicted by the very ancient Jurensis manuscript, in which this same decree concerning the Scriptures is attributed to Pope Hormisdas. Since it is neither very long nor unrelated to the present subject, and since it is found in that manuscript both more orderly and more accurately, I think it will not be unwelcome if I set it out here.

[Col. 0537]

**HERE BEGINS THE DECRETAL ISSUED IN THE CITY OF ROME BY POPE HORMISDAS.**

What the universal Catholic Church receives concerning the divine Scriptures, and what it ought thereafter to avoid. (C, S)

[Col. 0537]

**HEADINGS**

[Col. 0537A]

I. On the order of the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments.  
II. On the number of the apostolic sees.  
III. On the constitutions of the holy councils.  
IV. On the works of the holy Fathers that are to be received.  
V. On the works of the apocrypha that are not to be received.

## I

150 The order of the Old Testament that the holy and Catholic Roman Church receives and honors is as follows.

One book of Genesis. One book of Exodus. One book of Leviticus. One book of Numbers. One book of Deuteronomy. One book of Jesus son of Nave. One book of Judges. One book of Ruth. Four books of Kings. Two books of Chronicles. One book of the 150 Psalms. Three books of Solomon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Also one book of Wisdom. One book of Ecclesiasticus.

Also, the order of the prophets: one book of Isaiah. One book of Jeremiah, with his *Cinoth* and Lamentations. One book of Ezekiel. One book of Daniel. One book of Hosea. One book of Amos. One book of Micah. One book of Joel. One book of Obadiah. One book of Jonah. One book of Nahum. One book of Habakkuk. One book of Zephaniah. One book of Haggai. One book of Zechariah. One book of Malachi.

Also, the order of the histories: one book of Job. One book of Tobit. Two books of Ezra. One book of Esther. One book of Judith. Two books of Maccabees.

Also, the order of the Scriptures of the New and eternal Testament.

Four books of the Gospels: one according to Matthew, one according to Mark, one according to Luke, and one according to John. Also one book of the Acts of the Apostles. Fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul: one Epistle to the Romans; two Epistles to the Corinthians; one Epistle to the Ephesians; two Epistles to the Thessalonians; one Epistle to the Galatians; one Epistle to the Philippians; one Epistle to the Colossians; two Epistles to Timothy; one Epistle to Titus; one Epistle to Philemon; one Epistle to the Hebrews. Also one book of the Apocalypse of John. Also seven canonical Epistles: two Epistles of the apostle Peter; one Epistle of the apostle James; three Epistles of the apostle John; one Epistle of the apostle Jude, the Zealot and apostle.

## II

After all the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures that we have listed above, through which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we also thought it necessary to make this known: although all the Catholic churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church was not placed above the other churches by synodal decrees, but obtained primacy through the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior:

“You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

There was also added the fellowship of the blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election, who—not at a different time, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on the same day—was crowned by a glorious death while suffering martyrdom with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero. Together they consecrated the holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and placed it above all other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

The first see, therefore, is that of the apostle Peter, the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind. The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter, Mark preached the word of truth in Egypt and completed a glorious martyrdom there. The third see is honorably held at Antioch by the same most blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before coming to Rome, and there the first name of the Christian people arose.

## III

Although no one can lay any other foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus, nevertheless, for our edification, the same Roman Church does not prohibit the reception of the following Scriptures in addition to those of the Old and New Testaments that we have regularly enumerated above.

That is: the holy Council of Nicaea, held under the authority of the 318 Fathers and under the leadership of the most powerful Augustus Constantine, in which the heretic Arius was condemned. The holy Council of Constantinople, held under the authority of the elder Augustus Theodosius, in which the heretic Macedonius received his deserved condemnation. The holy Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Celestine, under the leadership of Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and of the bishop Arcadius, sent from Italy. The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the authority of Augustus Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus and his associates.

We also decree that any councils subsequently established by the holy Fathers are to be both preserved and received after the authority of these four.

## IV

What follows now concerns the works of the holy Fathers that are received in the Catholic Church.

The works of blessed Caecilius Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage, are to be received in their entirety. Likewise, the works of blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop. Likewise, the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia. Likewise, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Likewise, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople. Likewise, the works of blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Likewise, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. Likewise, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. Likewise, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Likewise, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius. Likewise, the works of blessed Jerome, presbyter. Likewise, the works of blessed Prosper, a most religious man.

Also the letter of blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople: if anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

We decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in its communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read.

Also the decretal letters that the most blessed popes issued at different times from the city of Rome in response to consultations concerning various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Also the Acts of the holy martyrs, which shine with manifold torments and with the marvelous triumphs of their confessions. What Catholic would doubt that they endured even greater sufferings in their contests, and that they bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and assistance of God? Yet, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought by unbelievers and ignorant people to contain material that is superfluous or less suitable than the order of events requires. Such are the Passions of a certain Quiricus and Julitta, and of George and others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics.

Therefore, as has been said, so that no slight opportunity for mockery might arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church. Nevertheless, together with the aforementioned Roman Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious contests, who are known to God more than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with every honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed man Jerome nevertheless wrote.

Likewise, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown, we know that the Acts of the most blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome; and, because of ancient usage, many churches imitate this practice.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross, and the other writing concerning the discovery of the head of blessed John the Baptist, are indeed recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these writings come into the hands of Catholics, the statement of the blessed apostle Paul should precede them:

“Test everything, and retain what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20).

Likewise, the most religious man Rufinus published many books of ecclesiastical writing and also interpreted several Scriptures. But since the venerable Jerome criticized him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we accept the views that we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held—not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that often-mentioned man criticized out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

We receive for reading some works of Origen that the most blessed Jerome does not reject; but we declare that all the rest, together with their author, are to be rejected.
