Likewise, although Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Chronicle* and his books of *Ecclesiastical History* grew lukewarm in the first book of his narrative and later wrote a book in praise and defense of Origen the schismatic, we nevertheless do not declare them wholly to be rejected, because of their knowledge of particular matters useful for instruction.

Likewise, we praise Orosius, a most learned man, who arranged for us a history highly necessary against the accusations of the pagans and composed it with remarkable brevity.

We place before others, with distinguished praise, the *Paschal Work* of the venerable Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verse. Nor do we despise the laborious work of Juvencus; rather, we admire it.

The Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives the remaining works written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics. Of these, we have thought it appropriate to append a few that have come to mind and that Catholics ought to avoid.

## V

First, we confess that the Council of Ariminum, convened by Caesar Constantius, son of Constantine, under the authority of the prefect Taurus, was then, is now, and will be condemned forever.

We also know that the *Itinerary in the Name of the Apostle Peter*, which is called the nine books of Saint Clement, is apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.  
The Acts in the name of the apostle Thomas, ten books: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of the apostle Peter: apocryphal.  
The Gospels in the name of the apostle Thomas, which the Manichaeans use: apocryphal.  
The Gospels in the name of the apostle Bartholomew: apocryphal.  
The Gospels in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

These works, and others like them, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus and Bonosus—who fell away through a similar error—Montanus together with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus, or Manichaeus, Faustus, Africanus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Conomius, Novatian, Sabbatius, Callistus, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinian, Pelagius, Julian of Eclanum, Celestine, Maximian, Priscillian of Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic, Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and another Peter—one of whom brought disgrace upon Alexandria and the other upon Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople together with his associates, and all the heresiarchs and their disciples who taught or wrote schismatic doctrines, whose names we have not retained—these works, I say, the Roman, Catholic, and apostolic Church has not merely rejected but expelled altogether. Together with their authors and the followers of their authors, we confess that they have been condemned forever under the anathema and an indissoluble bond.

**The Decretal issued by Pope Hormisdas of the city of Rome ends here.**

You see that this Decretal is suitably divided into five headings and restored in many places where it had been corrupted, especially in title 1, where the sequence of the canonical books reads two books of Ezra and likewise two of Maccabees. Thus there is no need to say with some others that the pontiff had conflated two books into one in each case.

I once seriously doubted whether Gratian, in distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*, truly attributed this decree to Gelasius, since I saw it attributed to Hormisdas in ancient copies. My doubt was increased by the fact that I found no trace of this decree concerning the Scriptures either in the book on the Roman pontiffs or in Dionysius’s collection among the decrees of Gelasius. But Pope Nicholas I strengthened my wavering mind in Letter 42, addressed around the year 865 to all the bishops of Gaul. He says:

“Holy and eloquent Pope Gelasius agrees with this most blessed Pope Leo in his decrees, saying: ‘We decree that the decretal letters which the most blessed popes issued at various times from the city of Rome in response to consultations concerning various Fathers are to be received with reverence.’”

These words occur in title 4 of this Decretal.

Ancient codices also confirmed the matter. In them this decree is noted as having been issued by Gelasius at a Roman synod of seventy bishops, during the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, which was the year of Christ 494, the third year of Pope Gelasius and twenty years before the beginning of Hormisdas’s pontificate.

My opinion, therefore, is that this decree was first enacted at the Roman Council of 494, over which Gelasius presided, but in such a way that it appeared not as a papal decree but as a canon of the entire council. It was subsequently issued by Hormisdas in the form of a papal Decretal, divided for the sake of method into five headings, and perhaps restored in certain places—especially in the mention of the two books of Ezra and the two books of Maccabees, which had been handled less carefully at the council of 494.

But whatever the truth of this question—whether this decree belongs to Gelasius alone, to Hormisdas alone, or to both—I deny that Vigilius had this decree concerning the apocrypha in mind here. Nor do I think that he had in mind the older decisions that survive, whether of councils or of pontiffs—for example, the cited canons of Laodicea, Hippo, or Carthage, or Letter 3 of Pope Innocent I to Exuperius of Toulouse, title 7.

For Vigilius says:

“If anyone wishes to place above or defend against the tradition of the canon the apocrypha of the heretics, which the Catholic Church in no way receives, let him be anathema.”

Shortly before this he had said:

“If anyone blasphemes the New and Old Testament, let him be anathema.”

It would have been rather imprudent for Vigilius, while impersonating Athanasius and speaking in his person, to praise synodal or papal canons later than Athanasius. By “the tradition of the canon,” therefore, he means not a particular sanction of any synod or pontiff, but the very sequence of the canonical books handed down by the ancestors, to place the apocrypha of heretics above it or to compare them with it being sacrilegious.

**Book VIII, page 266. The Eighth Book on the Unity of the Faith.**

This is the tenth book in the commonly circulated editions; yet Aeneas of Paris calls it the eighth, and it is reckoned as the eighth in the Cluniac, Paris, and Pontigny manuscripts. We have made the *Booklet of Faith*, which is earlier and the smaller part of the eleventh printed book, the ninth. To it we have appended the tenth, which is the ninth in the commonly circulated editions, since it is the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, whose formula he had prefaced.

Our eleventh book is the *Arian Profession* and the *Catholic Confession of Saint Athanasius*, which is the eighth printed book; for in the Florus manuscript it immediately follows the exposition of the faith, which for us is book ten. Our twelfth and final book is *On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit*, which is the latter and by far the greater part of the eleventh book in the common editions. This book closes the series also in the Paris, Florus, and Cluny manuscripts.

**Page 268. “Made the mediator of flesh, by the Father’s power.”**

Thus the Paris manuscript reads better than the common editions: “Made the mediator in flesh, equal in power”; or than the Pontigny manuscript: “Made the mediator in flesh, by the Father’s power.”

**Book XII, page 323. “Believe that the inspiration belongs to the Son.”**

Thus I read from the Florus manuscript, whereas the common editions, and even Aeneas and Theodulf, corruptly read: “Believe that the breathing, the light of God, belongs ...”

[Col. 0541B]

# AGAINST FELICIAN

[Col. 0541]

**Page 331. “To Optatus.”**

[Col. 0541C]

159 I did not find this name in our manuscripts; nevertheless, I retained it from the printed editions, into which I have no doubt it was transmitted from some ancient handwritten exemplar.

**Page 342. “A profane preacher of the incorporeal.”**

Thus the Jurensis, Benignian, Portas Charterhouse, and Geneva codices read, whereas it had previously been read incorrectly as “in his body.” Vigilius is attacking those heresies that attributed to Christ not true flesh but an assumed appearance of flesh. Such were the heresies of the Apollinarians, Manichaeans, and Eutychians, and also of Marcion, concerning whom Hilary says in his book *On the Synods*:

“Let the Epistle written to the Philippians also perish, either by fire or by the sponge, lest Marcion read in it, ‘and being found in appearance as a man,’ confessing a phantasm of a body, not a body.”

**Page 349. “He will have sent down.”**

The Portas and Geneva codices read “he will have sown.” In the Jurensis and Benignian manuscripts: “he will have sent back.”

**Page 350. “Impossible.”**

Thus all the manuscripts read. Moreover, although ancient and pure Latin used this word in no such sense, Vigilius also employed it actively; the common people use *impotent*. The expression “penetrable cold” is well known from Virgil.

[Col. 0541C]

# IN THE BOOK AGAINST PALLADIUS

[Col. 0541]

**Page 485. “The third day before the Nones of September.”**

[Col. 0541D]

160 Thus reads the very ancient manuscript of Dijon. Nor do I approve the reading in the common editions, “on the Nones of September.” For in the year of this council, 381, the Nones of September fell on a Sunday; and from time immemorial that day, by prescription, was devoted to more solemn divine services and kept free from business.

Accordingly, if one reviews the opening days of the ancient synods, indeed all their sessions, one will scarcely find that the Fathers abstained from business, even ecclesiastical business, on a Sunday, because their proceedings generally differed little from the noise of the schools and the forum. At most—and even this rarely—a council began on Sunday with a common supplication and some exhortation by the presiding officer to prepare their minds, followed by the announcement of the subsequent sessions.

How absurd, then, would it have been for Vigilius to prolong this lengthy dispute of the Fathers of Aquileia with the heretics concerning the first rising of the day, as he calls it in his synodical letter to the emperors, until the seventh hour, when the custom of every age had assigned the morning of Sunday to divine sacrifices and more sacred services?

**Page 486. “The letter of Arius was read.”**

The letter of Arius examined in this dispute is not the one that Theodoret reports in book I, chapter 4, written in Greek to Eusebius of Nicomedia. Rather, it is the letter that Arius sent to Alexander, bishop, and that Epiphanius describes in *Heresy* 69.

**Page 529. “The names of the bishops who subscribed.”**

[Col. 0543A]

These names, which are missing from the common editions, followed the synodical letter to the emperors in the Dijon manuscript. Since they seem to have been largely transferred by Vigilius from the genuine acts themselves into his dispute against Palladius, they must be examined more closely by us and compared with one another.

For the bishops are named in this work in three places: first at the very beginning, then in the course of the dispute, and finally near the end of the synodical letter to the emperors; yet not everywhere are they all present, nor are the same men always listed.

We have already noted that Acholius, or Ascholius, of Thessalonica is absent, although in the synodical letter of Pappus he is said not only to have attended the genuine Council of Aquileia but also to have presided over it.

What moved Vigilius to insert Valerian, bishop of Aquileia, as president of the council in place of Acholius may perhaps be inferred from the rescript of Gratian ordering the synod to be convened. Since this was addressed to someone honored by the emperor with the title of “excellence,” it is conjectured that he was Valerian the prefect. The Theodosian Code reports six imperial rescripts addressed to him during the very consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius, and therefore in the Christian year 381, when the Council of Aquileia was also held. Vigilius, whether prudently or imprudently, may therefore have placed the homonymous bishop of Aquileia at the head of his fictitious council.

Among the bishops, the following sees are known: Ambrose of Milan; Valerian of Aquileia; Anemius of Sirmium; Eusebius of Bologna; Sabinus of Piacenza; Constantius of Siscia; Maximinus of Emona in the manuscript, where the common editions read Maximus. Emona is a city of Upper Pannonia according to Ptolemy, as is Siscia.

Eventius of Ticinum; Abundantius of Tridentum; Philaster of Brescia; Heliodorus of Altinum; Felix of Jadera. Jadera is in Dalmatia.

Theodorus of Octodurum; Proculus of Massilia; Constantius of Arausio, a legate of the Gauls; Limenius of Vercellae; Domninus of Gratianopolis; Diogenes of Geneva; Bassianus of Laus Pompeia, both in the text and in the subscriptions, though perhaps corruptly Basilianus at the beginning. Laus Pompeia is in Liguria.

Exuperantius of Dertona. Amantius is called bishop of Nice in the common editions, but in the manuscript he is called bishop of the Jovians. Could this be Jovavia in Noricum, which is now Salzburg? The *Itinerary* places Joviacum and Jovavim in Noricum. But Ptolemy, in the fourth map of Africa, counts Jovis Parva and Jovis Magna among its cities, Diospolis; from Africa, Felix and Numidius are found in this assembly as legates of the Africans.

Justus, a legate of the Gauls, is believed to have been bishop of Lyon and is listed among the saints. In his Life, as printed by Surius, it is said that, having been summoned to a certain council in Italy, he never returned to Lyon. Instead, after stopping at Turnus in his homeland and saying farewell to his friends and acquaintances, he went from there to Massilia, then boarded a ship and withdrew to Egypt, where he spent his life among the anchorites with his assistant Viator.

His attendant Viator, who was only a lector by office, seems to have been distinct from the Viator who is listed among the bishops as a subscriber to the synodical letter of Aquileia.

Unless Vigilius confused the matter: for in his work Artemius, Cassianus, Marcellus, and Eustathius—Eustosius in the manuscript—are also listed at the beginning, yet they are found neither in the text of the dispute nor among the subscribers to the synodical letter. The order of those who subscribed is also different from that of those listed at the beginning.

**In the year of the Lord 520. Rusticus Helpidius, Illustrious Man, former quaestor.**

[Col. 0543B]

## NOTICE

*(From the Library of the Fathers at Lyon)*

Rusticus Helpidius lived during the time of Symmachus and Boethius, under the emperor Anastasius. He was the physician of Theodoric, king of the Goths, a man of noble birth and a former quaestor. He wrote a consolation for his own grief, which he mentions:

“From this too a figure was playfully devised for our grief,” etc.

That book is no longer extant.

[Col. 0543C]

# THE POEMS OF RUSTICUS HELPIDIUS ON THE HISTORY OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS (C, G, S)*

## EVE DECEIVED BY THE DEVIL

“The envious serpent contrives by his art that Eve pluck  
the forbidden fruit; unaware of so great a deceit,  
the unhappy woman believed her husband, her companion, though she was to perish with him.”

[Col. 0543D]

## THE ANGEL’S ARRIVAL TO MARY

“The angel, through dreams, urges Joseph  
to preserve his marriage with Mary unstained. Here, with her dowry fulfilled,  
the Spirit—[the text is uncertain]—burning with this, is saved in honor.”

the servants of punishment leave the blessed realms;  
the court, ever friendly to the pious, rejects sinners.”

## THE THIEF IS BROUGHT INTO PARADISE

“Through the pleasant green places of the sacred grove,  
the blessed thief, with the Lord as his guide, wins a life-giving dwelling;

[Col. 0544D]

## NOAH TAKES EVERYTHING INTO THE ARK AT THE LORD’S COMMAND

“Here Noah gathers birds, cattle, men, and every kind of wild beast,  
so that the violence of the Flood might destroy nothing;  
and he confines within one ark all that had been created.”

## A VISION FROM HEAVEN IS SHOWN TO PETER

“A disk contains the kinds of reptiles and cattle, and all the birds,  
which the Father commands Peter to eat,  
judging nothing common that the Creator had made clean.”

[Col. 0545A]

## THE TOWER OF CONFUSION IS DESTROYED

“Madness builds a tower with immense resources,  
but God, the supreme ruler of discord, confounds their speech,  
so that foolish hands might undertake nothing beyond their rights.”

## PETER AND THE APOSTLES SPEAK IN VARIOUS LANGUAGES

“One harmonious account pours forth diverse languages;  
each foreign nation recognizes its own voice,  
which the sacred Spirit utters through a human mouth.”

## JOSEPH IS SOLD BY HIS BROTHERS

“Here gnawing envy compels the conspiring brothers  
to sell their brother. Adversity benefits the just;  
this is a divine work, so that the one who now sells may later worship.”

## CHRIST IS SOLD BY JUDA

[Col. 0545B]

“The dreadful hunger for money compels Judas to sell  
the royal head. The wicked mind completes traffic  
in such great blood for a small profit.”

## ABRAHAM LEADS HIS SON TO BE SACRIFICED

“The victim himself bears the wood for the cost of the slaughter;  
the father, Abraham, prepared to slaughter his dear pledge,  
leads him onward: it is the merit of faith not to spare one’s son.”

## CHRIST IS LED TO BE CRUCIFIED

“The hands of the illustrious man eagerly bear the wood  
to be honored by all, on which the holy victim of the world  
allows himself to be hung! He is lifted up so that one death  
may restore salvation to the wretched.”

## QUAILS AND MANNA ARE GIVEN TO THE JEWS

“Here the quail sent down restores the eager people with flesh,  
and heavenly abundance fills those who did not deserve it with bread;  
for to each deserving person manna gives whatever taste he wishes.”

## CHRIST FEEDS FOUR THOUSAND PEOPLE WITH SEVEN LOAVES

“Here he feeds thousands of peoples with seven loaves,  
and a few fish satisfy the feast;  
for twice six baskets were filled with fragments of bread.”

## MOSES ASCENDS THE MOUNTAIN

“Moses reveals the inner chambers of the truthful law,  
which teaches that there is one supreme ruler over all, the same throughout,  
and that the world is not governed by divided powers but by a single authority.”

[Col. 0546A]

## CHRIST TEACHES ON THE MOUNTAIN

“Seated in the valley of the mountain, he proclaims  
a solemn and immutable word and pious commands of justice to the people;  
wherever wisdom goes and wherever it proceeds, it reveals itself.”

## MARTHA AND MARY

“Martha reproaches her companion with undeserved complaints  
because she is free from her duties. The truthful judge says  
that care for God is the better household, and more useful for her.”

## THE CENTURION TO CHRIST

“Alas for me, Savior: the servant longs to be saved.  
I am not worthy that you should enter beneath my roof,  
but you can heal by a word, for you are sufficient even when absent.”

## CHRIST MAKES WINE FROM WATER

[Col. 0546B]

“Once tasteless fluids, mere elements, took on the flavor  
of fiery wine, for the provident Creator made  
gifts of joy the beginning of miracles.”

## A WOMAN IS HEALED BY CHRIST

“He gives his right hand to the wretched, and in compassion  
he kindly raises up ...”
... whom the prolonged pangs of her disease had bent.
Faith rises upright, and the believer’s mind is clean.

## THE WOMAN IS HEALED OF HER FLOW OF BLOOD

This woman stole healing by touching his garment,
And faith dried her veins and the shameful flow:
Beautiful faith, whose power to constrain the Thunderer is great!

## CHRIST RAISES THE WIDOW’S SON

The mother, unknowing in mind, mourned a lifeless body;
When the salvation of the world and of humankind met her
At the threshold of the gate, he changed mourning into joy. [Col. 0546C]

## CHRIST SEES ZACCHAEUS IN THE TREE

The Lord’s sweet favor shone upon his friend Zacchaeus,
Speaking with majesty: “Today you advance to be my host;
Leave the branches now, and descend to greater things.”

## LAZARUS CALLED BACK FROM DEATH

Here Lazarus rises again, casting death aside;
The law is changed, and tombs give birth to souls.
He who knows how to restore life to the dead by a word is Life.

[Col. 0545C]

## RUSTICIUS HELPIDIUS’S POEM ON THE BENEFITS OF CHRIST JESUS (C,G)*

[Col. 0545D]

Almighty creator of all things, sole mind of the highest
God and his eternal offspring: for you are the Father’s glory
And the fruitful honor of the Word, through whom he spread
The blue expanses of the sea, made earth firm, and suspended heaven.
The elements hold their appointed places; even in their discord
They preserve faithful alternations. Day obeys when it receives
The sun; the days allow the moon to return
To its risings and settings; nor do the stars refuse
To yield to daylight. They permit their appointed courses to blaze,
And the swift moon’s horns are content to wane.
By this Word the Creator prepared such great kingdoms for himself;
He also acknowledged you as partner in his kingdoms and as his Son.
All things bound together tremble alike before you;
Our praise thrice celebrates the ever-ready faith, for, free of time,
You sit with the Father. What have you ever lacked? [Col. 0546D]
Or can you be more than the Father, when one paternal majesty
Always rules in you both, and your names reign?
For the Spirit too is always held worthy of celebration
In shared worship; bearing rule, one power flourishes,
Without beginning as without end; the honor is the same
Throughout and rightfully shared. Amid earth’s sorrows
You bore heavenly glory, deigning to display
Both conditions: no greater than your mother in body,
No less than your Father in power; never absent from heaven,
Never abandoning the limbs once assumed for our sake.

Always mighty everywhere, be present, I pray, and as guide
Direct my heart; give my soul and mind the joy
Of vanquishing the plague of vices and conquering at last
Whatever perverse love or savage passion commands:
Whatever is shameful to say or cruel to commit, [Col. 0547A]
Whatever harms me or anyone, obstructs good conduct,
And takes hearts captive, bound in perpetual punishment.
Grant pardon to our falls—you, the first and provident author
Of the laws of salvation and of life [the phrase *in omnem*, “into all ...,” is incomplete as printed]—
And lighten them by a merciful judgment, that I may suffer less.
May I repent of sinning against you, and be corrected as your pledged servant.
You whose vengeance is to spare the guilty, receive, I pray,
The needy offerings of my mouth, which sings nothing worthy of praise.
Approve my vows rather than my gifts; do not reckon among poets
These arts of speech trained in error,
Which the Permessian dweller beside Aganippe’s water
Stirs up by drinking from the spring, and holds as food
For a mind captured by empty sweetness; he delights himself
With an idle murmur, to be mighty in the utterance of pleasing song.
From this source poetic form has also trifled with my sorrow, [Col. 0547B]
Fashioning chattering satires with erring Muses,
So that the singing page might beguile anxious complaints.
But to you my confessing mind lies open; to you my earnest
Tongue pours out panting prayers and labors at sober words.

You are Lord, true honor and everlasting glory,
The maker of things; you are the manifest hope
And ample pattern of the restored soul; you conquer and inherit
The fallen body, afterward the same, surviving even [the death of] its limbs,
God after the underworld, alive after mortality.
You, divine salvation, taking pity on bitter cries
And grieving over diseases, madness, and the faults of afflicted blood,
Consented to descend into our sight
And to unite man with God. Soon faith, conscious of the truth,
Displayed its proofs; the subject world marveled
At miracles foretold in ancient times. [Col. 0547C]
Before him earth lies low, the sea falls silent,
And heaven, less than he, scarcely suffices to serve with flashing obedience;
The swift vault of heaven ministers beneath his feet upon the clouds.
Him fruitful virginity bore, made pregnant by God,
Unacquainted with mortal conception; in a chaste birth
The work of mercy was accomplished. Ordinary nature could not
Bring forth a new birth, nor could the height of majesty appear openly,
Unless it gave earth something wonderful and unknown.
Nor did the tokens of so great an offspring shine out together
[The printed *nec*, “nor,” leaves this transition uncertain]: for the world,
Radiant with a bright star, recognized the honor of glowing light,
That its Creator “had perished” [*perisse*, apparently corrupt in this account of his birth]—
He who, bearing the beginnings of a noble age, came forth into frail limbs,
At once enduring the allotted times in the body he assumed.
Before him nothing existed; for there is no origin of a created
Beginning [in him; the construction is unclear here]: God could be born after all
The things he begot with the Father and with the mighty Spirit.
He flourishes, threefold in praise, and always shall flourish.

The Chaldaean nation honored the divine, holy cradle with devotion,
Seeing him shining above the stars, whom earth had lifted up:
God. Endowed with the light of the holy flame,
And following the radiance revealed in heaven,
It first deserved to know you; in consecrated offerings
It brought tokens of things to come through their outward form.
It gives gifts to a king—*Divinitas* (“divinity,” apparently corrupt for *divitias*, “riches”)—
Incense to God, and myrrh for the tomb.
There the glory of the all-begetting Word increased:
Joyful wine was restored to the couches, and dishes to the tables.
The company of guests marveled at the heaped platters,
Conducting a wedding feast with abundant food.

With a gentle touch you commanded the empty hollows
Of a darkened brow to shine; [Col. 0548A] breaking their hiding places,
You commanded them to rejoice in the daylight received;
Driving night from a disfigured face, you made eyes for a blind man.
Through you, highest Father, the sick man with dislocated joints,
His soul scarcely remaining, returns; indeed, carrying dead bones
Like a corpse, he sprang up whole by the Word’s power,
His strength restored. Since his fallen limbs could no longer remain down,
He put his neck beneath the hard pallet.
You have power to restrain diseases and, driving away the tomb’s
Sorrows, to recall a corpse to the breaths of life,
And to trample the shattered bars of grim death,
So that, when the face of one man returned, the world might grasp
What your right hand had prepared to bestow on all its own.

You were not content, for us, to found the earth, make the tilled fields fruitful,
Pour foliage over the woods and grass over the meadows, [Col. 0548B]
Subject the beasts, renew the various waters,
Open the air to birds and the waves to fish,
Endow our race with discerning reason and a strong hand,
And raise its head erect toward the stars.
Moved, you come to the aid of those long “flowing” [*manantibus*, whose sense is uncertain here];
Healing the stain of the first guilt, you bring back
Extinguished souls and lifeless bodies to heaven
And to merciful laws. You redeem your offspring and your stock
Not with pleasant plants and the produce of a ripened harvest,
Nor with the splendor of soft clothing
Stained by the brilliant wave of Sidonian dye,
Nor with Libyan skins or Indian merchandise;
Instead, with sacred blood and at a great price, you endow them.
Teaching good conduct amid frail limbs, that you might restore life,
You overcame the guilt that flesh had earned through its sin, [Col. 0548C]
Bringing praise to flesh, pure amid so many contaminations.
Rejoicing on man’s behalf, you endured man’s sorrows,
Suffered death for death, and paid the token
Of heaven’s height for the death that came from our tree.
From that tree the earlier punishment bit into the rights of nature,
When nature broke the warnings and reverend commands of its parent
And maker. His hands, stretched out in death, showed the one deserving punishment
That the maker must always be entreated with outstretched hands, so that enduring glory might bear witness on earth,
And no one refuse willingly to bear the torments of the cross
For the Lord, with hesitant arms,
Which the Lord bore for his people.

Nor may our limited understanding declare
With how great an honor grace is celebrated:
Opening the innermost places of the sacred font,
It calls everyone to pardon, grants a better rebirth, [Col. 0548D]
And opens the upper doors and thresholds
To the path toward a better world and the everlasting kingdom
Of the heavenly homeland. There will be no parching fever there,
No thirst, no violent hunger, no flame of fear;
There will be neither war nor disease; unjust power
Will not rage, nor will anyone wield a stolen sword
To exercise a criminal right, nor any guilty robber rule
In the holy dwelling. Pious conduct will bear its rewards,
And faithful love and flourishing youth will shine.
Infancy will not crawl through silent years,
Nor bowed old age be furrowed in a withered face.
Joyful rest alone will rejoice in an “unstable” age
[the printed *instabili* is retained as a genuine corruption; the expected sense would require *in stabili*, “in a stable/enduring age”].
We believe, and shall enjoy the Lord’s gentle mercy
Here too, hoping also for the gifts of righteousness and life.

## DATE DISPUTED. EUGYPPIUS, AFRICAN ABBOT

[Col. 0549]

## PRELIMINARIES

[Col. 0549]

### NOTICE

(From Abbot Trithemius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.)

Eugyppius, priest and abbot [Note: [Col. 0549] Feller’s *Biography* says that Eugyppius was abbot of the Lucullan monastery near Naples. EDITOR.], was learned in the Holy Scriptures, exceptionally devoted to reading Saint Augustine’s books, and sufficiently instructed in secular learning. His life and conduct also distinguished him in monastic discipline. Several letters of Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe addressed to him are reported. He wrote certain useful short works, of which I have found only those listed below. He gathered from the books of the blessed bishop Augustine a large volume containing three hundred chapters, addressed to Proba. Its prologue begins, Letter I: “To the lady deservedly venerable”; the book itself begins, Book I: “What I wrote to you, honored one.” He also wrote the *Life of Saint Severinus the Monk* and his *Rule for Monks* [Note: [Col. 0549] This rule is not extant. Also attributed to Eugyppius are: 1. the *Life of Saint Augustine of Flaviana*, to be read in Bollandus; 2. the *Life of Saint Severinus*, found among the works of Marcus Welser; 3. a letter to the deacon Paschasius. EDITOR.]. According to the priest Honorius, he flourished under Emperor Anastasius; according to Sigebert, however, he flourished under Tiberius Constantine, in the time of Pope Pelagius II, in the year of the Lord 580.

[Col. 0549]

# Dedicatory Letter

**To the most reverend father in Christ and most illustrious prince, Lord J. Rudolf Stoer, most devout abbot of the monasteries of Murbach and Lure, most generous patron of letters, his honored patron: John Herold Acropolita wishes well-being.**

[Col. 0549]

It is now almost three years, most illustrious prince, since, besides suffering the greatest loss to my household affairs and my income—which consists solely in the vigils of study—I have expended much weariness and labor. For while I have been compiling the *Chiliads of Stratagems* for Emperor Charles, the maker of peace; the *Austriads* for Ferdinand, most merciful Roman Caesar; and the *Deisidaimonia*, on the rites and worship once offered to idols by all pagan peoples, for you, our most generous Maecenas, whatever the kindness of good men supplies me and whatever is scraped together by lamplight is spent on acquiring and preparing good authors. The result is that, in my poverty, if books and children are excepted, nothing has been added to our cottage besides these three volumes. This could draw even the strongest man away from these delights—the Muses—let alone a young man such as myself, if anything apart from God Most Good and Most Great and letters offered him consolation.

For these studies require a free man—and some maintain that this is why they are called “liberal.” I think no one can fail to know the constraints that press upon the head of a household and the variety of business he is forced to serve. Yet those same studies make me subscribe without reluctance to Cicero’s judgment: that good letters are the one refuge of an entire life, the delight of prosperity, and salvation in adversity. They teach me both to digest present hardships and at last to hope for greater and sounder things; at every moment they bring forward and investigate whatever they show to be pleasant to good people or useful to the commonwealth; and everywhere they win for us devout, learned, and good friends. Since nothing in this life can be more pleasant than a good person, I have therefore been well rewarded for the two years now completed.

Indeed, with the assistance of the consuls Jerome Fabri and George Wickram, we have brought within our reach the treasures from the works of Saint Augustine, collected by Eugyppius, the African abbot, which the Senate and People of Colmar preserved through many centuries; and the college named for Saint Dominic generously offered them for common use. To these benefactions was added the support of John Hoffmeister, a man highly praised for keenness of mind and celebrated for the vigilance with which he governs the Augustinian community in that city.

[Col. 0551]

Through these men’s generosity, students of sacred letters will doubtless acknowledge that they have now been enriched. I, however, am forced to lament my limited powers, because I lack the ability to raise with worthy praises so distinguished a city and our fellow members of the Holy Roman Empire. Some maintain that Alexander the Great gained more glory from Homer’s poem, which he carried in the most precious casket of the Persian king, than advantage from defeating either Darius or Porus. What fair-minded judge of sacred teaching, then, will give less applause to so great a commonwealth, from whose repositories treasures emerge protected from the injuries of so many ages—treasures which, I believe, no one would wish to place on a level with the poems even of the oldest and never sufficiently praised poet, unless he preferred humane learning to remedies for the soul?

As candid sincerity satisfies generous minds more quickly than any expenditure of labor or wealth, I trust that I have repaid the most generous city with the greatest possible gratitude by inscribing this worthy volume to the worthiest recipient. I think I have observed this duty excellently and opportunely by publishing under the auspices of your name, most illustrious prince, these treasures that I now dedicate, consecrate, and offer to you. If ever I have followed the footsteps of the ancients, it is both praiseworthy and unmistakable here: they customarily appointed as patrons of their nightly labors men whom they knew to be good and celebrated and, finally, preeminent in authority and favor; nor did they burden anyone indiscriminately or with studies foreign to him.

I shall therefore set out my reasons, most illustrious prince, and show that I could never, without doing wrong, have ascribed this volume to any person other than you. I think no one fails to know that you occupy no low place among the princes of the Roman Empire. Since you have recently been inaugurated in your principality, with what customary gifts could I congratulate you more suitably than with the very works by which every devout prince who is no enemy of true religion may prepare himself as the most approved example for his subjects, and may recall those whom he governs to the sweetness of peace, concord, love, and tranquility? Anyone who does not wish to be ungrateful to God Most Good and Most Great will candidly admit that these things can be imbibed and learned only from the divine oracles—and all the more readily when devout men have piously interpreted and illuminated what seems somewhat obscure in divine Scripture.

Add that one would never properly dedicate to a mighty emperor, except in his leisure, a discipline foreign to him, such as the art of painting, when military instruction ought to be offered him. But who could ever call it absurd to dedicate the studies of a devout abbot to a good abbot? The *Life* that we have written as a preface to the second volume of this work shows how Eugyppius, in an age not unlike our own, labored over these very studies.

[Note: [Col. 0551] In the Basel edition this *Life* was placed before the later volume of the *Treasury of Eugyppius*. We have brought it back here because the order seemed to require it. —Editor.]

Indeed, if one weighs carefully the tragedies that then brought the Church into the greatest danger, one sees them vigorously reenacted in this most unhappy age. Who, then, can deny that aid must generally be given through the same remedies that we saw Saints Augustine and Eugyppius employ? Yet a patient afflicted by a grave disease will hardly be cured if his physician possesses no authority; distinguished birth and ancestry customarily confer very great authority upon approved men.

I therefore acted wisely in commending these vigils to you, most illustrious prince, for among the people of the Sequani you stand out greatly through the dignity of your most noble family and lineage. The most serene princes of Austria are well aware how long your ancestors held the lordship of Saint-Amarin and how, in that Armagnac war [printed *bello illo Armeniaco*], they were aided in their most difficult affairs by the service of your great-grandfather. Finally, everyone knows how the most celebrated Stoer family adorns the town of Guebwiller with liberal public spirit and most kindly relieves the poverty of its citizens.

You may count it no small gift of fortune to have been born of such parents. Yet I think this deserves the highest praise: from your cradle they wished you to learn those arts by which even people of low birth become cultivated, and than which nothing can be more splendid in an eminent man—namely, good letters. For who does not know that you have advanced so far in literary study that, if you are compared with the others who preside over colleges here and there—let the expression give no offense—you leave most of them looking wholly ignorant of letters? Hence your ardor and your ready love for students; hence your insatiable mind, eager for the volumes of learned men, by whose labors you wish to enrich the exceedingly ample library you are establishing; hence the prayers of all who desire that you, their Maecenas and the patron of letters, may long survive, and who already stand ready to commend your most illustrious name to eternity. All know you to be endowed with so many virtues that few writers can hope to celebrate you in a manner equal to your rank.

A kinsman of yours, himself as devoted to good letters as any man, long ago recognized this disposition in you and took great care that you should succeed him in this degree of dignity. In my judgment, by Hercules, he was inferior neither to Trajan nor to the emperor Antoninus: when he perceived in you refinement of character and strength of mind, he easily foresaw what further qualities more mature age would add; and from life with you he learned your moderation. This quality alone—although many virtues bring honor to the name of princes—could have made you more renowned, for moderation comes close to a wonder when it binds to itself a man greater than others.

Since princes bear a certain image of God, they can never express it [printed *exprimi*, “be expressed”; perhaps *exprimere*, “express”] more fully than through justice itself, which cleaves to moderation as its highest member. Among Christian men, however, that justice does not properly mean something perfect in every respect, for perfection must be attributed to God alone. It is rather a disposition of mind by which natural affections are made more conformable to divine and human laws.

The injustice of our age has, among other things, introduced this plague: no one’s religion can be approved or disapproved without offending many people and arousing the hostile suspicions of many more.

[Col. 0553]

I therefore pass over the magnificence with which you have thus far enriched the worship of the divine majesty at the most lavish expense, and will say only this candidly: you are not ungrateful to God Most Good and Most Great. For I hear that you continue diligently to promote and assist whatever you judge to pertain to Christ’s glory.

As for your devotion to your parents and kinsmen, would that certain people preferred to experience it rather than watch for ways to provoke your patience! Anyone who knows that from boyhood you yielded to your parents’ will in every plan of life and were so obedient to your other relatives can surely expect the highest clemency from you now that you are a man and have laid aside youthful fierceness. A person cruel to his parents appears inhuman to everyone; reverence toward one’s elders must therefore promise humanity and no small measure of kindness.

Your citizens sufficiently declare your devotion to your native land when they look up to you almost as a divine power. Their universal love, as they are governed under your auspices without any servile fear, and the many prodigious buildings restored or built almost from their foundations show what a useful prince you are. In emulation of Augustus, you desire to make marble everything you found built of brick; and thus, adorning the Sparta allotted to you, you excellently claim the role of a good and prudent prince.

Fortitude, another part of moderation, possesses a very broad dominion in you and shines far more in greatness of spirit than in bloodthirsty boasting. Although the burdens of war conflict with your religious profession, the snares of a most hostile enemy stir up fresh disturbances for you day by day. At one time you must keep favorable success underfoot [printed *prosperum*; perhaps *prosper*, “favorable”]; next you must endure the hatred of many with patience; finally—and in this they say you stoutly discharge the duty both of a commander and of a vigorous soldier—how many passions of the mind must you put to death in order to be an example to those upright men over whom you preside! Those acquainted with your character proclaim how unbroken your spirit otherwise remains; indeed, they acknowledge that through nature’s kindness you have obtained the highest constancy.

I come to prudence, without which a person can scarcely be called moderate and upright. Canon law—to use the customary terms—commands prelates to embrace this single virtue above all others, so that they may be equally capable in the judgment of letters and skillful in governing affairs. Christ himself commands us to join it to simplicity and adapt it to ourselves. Who is more keen-sighted than you in administering private or public business? Who attends more carefully to times, places, persons, things, and transactions? What word has ever escaped you that was not mature and had not been considered long and thoroughly? I say nothing for the moment of the insight you display in those habits by which a distinguished name is customarily earned. If the circumstances of the time put your liberality to the test, who considers more carefully to whom, what, or how much ought to be given? If they test your magnificence, how solicitous you are for public utility and adornment!

But where have your virtues, so lovable and delightful, led me, most illustrious prince? I fear that, wishing to avoid Scylla, I may fall into Charybdis. For while I contend that I have not inappropriately inscribed this work to you, I come close to seeming, in the judgment of many who estimate others by their own character, to seek your favor through petty flattery—a fault from which nothing is more foreign to my nature.

For your part, in accordance with your clemency and authority, protect and defend this volume, and receive kindly this most respectful disposition of mine toward you. Although this author is most worthy to be rescued under your auspices from long and lamentable darkness, I want you to be persuaded that we have spent no little labor upon him. Anyone who wishes to emend old copies is cleansing the stable of Augeas; I can affirm this with certainty. Besides many passages that require a Delian swimmer, passages gnawed by beetles and moths, and passages corrupted by scribes’ carelessness or ignorance, this further annoyance is added: sometimes one is forced, like a schoolboy learning his letters, to master the shapes of an unfamiliar script; indeed, like a schoolmaster, one must often patiently endure and correct the obstinacy of the compositors, troublesome as they are.

The man who proclaims your clemency and the inclination of your kindness toward me is that John Huber, adorned with every title of virtue: a true physician both in the loveliness of his character and in his profession, inferior to no one—and preferable to many—in the art by which divine mercy has so well provided for the necessities of the human race. One might say of him, no less aptly than Nestor said of the whole company of physicians:

> Ἰατρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἀλλῶν.
>
> “For one physician is worth many other men.”

Who does not know how powerful he is in medicine? You yourself, most illustrious prince, are a witness; the high-hearted lords William and George of Rappoltstein can also bear witness, as can all who are counted among the more distinguished people of the Sequani and Triboci. Almost every one of them entrusts the whole ordering of his health to Huber’s judgment, asks help from him, and expects well-being from him. Without him every day passes less pleasantly for you; in his presence it passes most pleasantly.

Nor is this surprising. Through admirable learning he stands as an ornament to his family; in this illustrious city he appears, especially for his age, worthy of everyone’s respect; he is courteous to all and honored and loved by every good person. Thus that most judicious man in this commonwealth, the distinguished senator Jacob Ruede, rejected many suitors and chose Huber alone as his son-in-law. To him he joined a daughter who, among the women of this age—and this is no small gift of heavenly grace, as Solomon himself testifies—was a singular model of chastity, grace, and loveliness. This Huber alone, your most respectful client and our excellent patron, was judged worthy of her.

I therefore congratulate you most warmly in this matter too: you have taken into your patronage a man whose work, loyalty, and aid you may employ. For myself, I rejoice that I have gained so distinguished a guide, through whose counsel I know that you have become our patron and the most generous Maecenas of our studies.

I would think I had acted less than candidly if my silence suppressed anyone’s goodwill toward you. Know, therefore, that John Hoffmeister, head of the Augustinian college at Colmar, also urged me in a most friendly letter, with a most honorable mention of your name, to dedicate these labors to you.

[Col. 0555]

He proclaims you so devoted to good letters that you always have this saying of Pindar upon your lips:

> Ὅσσα δὲ μὴ πεφίληκε  
> Ζεὺς, ἀτύζονται βοὰν  
> Πιερίδων, ἀνιόντα  
> Γᾶν τε καὶ πόντον κατ` ἀμαιμάξησων.
>
> “Whatever Zeus has not loved is terrified at the voice of the Pierian Muses, hearing it—[creatures upon] earth and the untamable sea.”

[Translation note: the printed *ἀνιόντα* is apparently corrupt for *ἀΐοντα*, “hearing.” The final phrase, *κατ` ἀμαιμάξησων*, is also corrupt; “untamable sea” is a conjectural rendering of its recoverable sense. The supplied Greek is retained above.]

Proceed, then, nobly in virtue; show yourself an open-handed Maecenas of studies. There will never be lacking people who refuse to make your name immortal [the printed *recusent*, “refuse,” contradicts the surrounding praise; “who do not refuse” may be intended]. Excellent minds make virtue—the most precious thing of all—far more illustrious; and, to use Pindar’s words myself:

> Τὸ δὲ παθεῖν εὖ, πρῶτον ἀέθλων,  
> Εὖ δ` ἀκούειν δευτέρα μοῖ-  
> Ρ`, ἀμφοτέροισι δ` ἀνὴρ  
> Ὅς ἂν ἐγκύρσῃ καὶ ἕλῃ,  
> Στἑφανον ὕψιστον δέδεκται.
>
> “To fare well is the first of prizes; to be well spoken of is the second portion. The man who meets with and wins both has received the highest crown.”

May Christ Jesus preserve you long in safety, most devout abbot and most illustrious prince, for us and for all good people.

Basel of the Rauraci, the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the year 1542 from the birth of Christ.

[Col. 0555]

## LIFE OF EUGYPPIUS, BY JOHN HEROLD ACROPOLITA

[Col. 0555]

[Col. 0555A] Although we knew well that, besides Gennadius and Honorius, whom we ourselves saw, Trithemius too, along with other authors by no means to be despised, had mentioned our Eugyppius—especially Sabellicus and Platina, who, deceived by the error of Philip of Bergamo, otherwise a man of remarkable discernment in historical knowledge, falsely name him “Egesippus”—the older authors whom we have named nevertheless affirm that Eugyppius composed the Life of Severinus the abbot and a Rule for a stricter and solitary life. Furthermore, all who have written the life of St. Fulgentius remember the letter written to Eugyppius, which we have arranged to append at the end of this volume [Note: [Col. 0555] We have refrained from including it, since it may be read in Migne, *Patrologia*, vol. LXV, col. 344. EDITOR]. Besides those whom we mention in honor, there are Vincent of Beauvais, Antoninus of Florence, and many others.

We have therefore thought, most illustrious prince, that we should perform a worthwhile service if we brought forward a few observations concerning the author’s life, Proba, to whom he wrote, and the general character of the whole work—although we are not unaware how difficult it is to give a fuller account of a matter which, as we see, all learned men up to now have merely sampled superficially. For we have never yet seen anyone who gives an account of this author’s homeland, parents, or life, whenever mention is made of him. Yet all, like Fulgentius himself, commend him as a man of the highest reputation, calling him a most valiant, most illustrious, most learned man and a worthy laborer in Christ’s vineyard. His refined judgment in that divine philosophy readily proves that from childhood he had been steeped in the best studies.

He was born at Carthage, after Rome had already been captured by Genseric. As soon as he had completed his elementary studies, his parents sent him to Rome when he was already twelve years old. There, while the two rival cities, stripped of all imperial power and splendor, were living, as it were, under common laws, he joined himself to learned men and was instructed under Boethius as his teacher. He completed his **κυκλοπαίδεια**—his “encyclopaedia”—with distinction. Then, because of the brilliance of his natural abilities, he was received into the patronage of the Anician family, a consular house, through whose influence he was later raised to the highest dignity.

But when the Vandals favored the Arian doctrine and referred everything to this one heresy, so that many who resisted only weakly underwent the danger of their lives, and when, moreover, King Huneric, who had succeeded his father in an extensive kingdom, was eager to surpass his father also in impiety, he proscribed many, deported not a few, and sent great numbers into exile. Every prison was filled with innocent people; threats were everywhere, terror on every side, and the most mournful image of death. Yet when the tyrant, by the just judgment of God, had been gnawed by worms and finally consumed by the rotting of his flesh—for physicians call this disease *phthiriasis*—all hoped that Gundabund, the king’s nephew through his brother, would prove more merciful.

In this upheaval of affairs Eugyppius was therefore recalled to his homeland. After his return, his concerned parents urged him to choose a way of life by which he could live honorably and devote himself zealously to the service of the Catholic Church. At that time, or certainly not many years earlier, the institution of the solitary life had taken root in Egypt; and in Africa, after the tyrant of the Arian faction had died, it had begun to increase wonderfully in many places. For Gundabund was taking care to reopen the Catholic churches closed by his uncle, restore the priests of God, and recall those who had been sent into exile or transported elsewhere.

This form of life therefore appealed to him above all. At that time Marinus was the head of a community which Severinus had governed, having been adopted as its leader by his predecessor because of his exceptional holiness of life. More thoughtful men, having embraced truth, piety, innocence, and gentleness, had hidden themselves within it so that they would not be separated from such companions. Having withdrawn from worldly affairs and clinging to divine things, they chose fellow members whom they educated in good morals and letters and instructed in a simpler way of life. So that there might not be a shortage of those who, when the Church’s condition was disturbed, could come to its aid if necessary, whether by teaching or by example, they supported them with resources collected in common or donated through the generosity of others. They practiced the worship of God with a devotion somewhat greater than that of others, but entirely free of superstition; their food was plain and their clothing clean.

Attracted by these virtues, our Eugyppius joined himself as a companion to their community. In a short time he became so dear to all the members that, after Marinus alone, they all honored, revered, and loved him as an example. They credited him with so much ability that they did not doubt there was any task so weighty or laborious that he alone could not undertake or complete.

Eugyppius did not wish to disappoint the hope of his brothers. At that time, by the divine and hidden judgment of God, various turbulent heresies were being approved by some within the Church and, most perniciously, were occupying and agitating people’s minds. Many showed the greatest favor toward the Arians, Manichaeans, and Priscillianists, whose poisons they had imbibed. The holy men both recoiled from these sects and diligently warned others not to be infected by them.

Although the Lords Augustine, Eugenius, Fulgentius, Maximus, and countless others—pious men as well as learned—had strained every resource in Africa to refute their beliefs, nevertheless, since Satan did not rest, certain men arose who were more changeable than Proteus and who transformed themselves into every shape, so that, if not everyone, at least some might be retained in their heresy. Reflecting sadly on this, St. Eugyppius thought that no other kind of weapon should be set against those enemies than Augustine’s writings and his most holy thoughts.

When Guthamund had died, his brother Thrasimund succeeded him in the kingdom, and persecution of the Catholics again broke out. Good men were proscribed; among them were 220 highly learned bishops, especially Fulgentius. There is no doubt that all of these had been Eugyppius’s acquaintances. For while they were exiles in Sardinia, sustained in food and clothing by the generosity of Symmachus, they had no consolation except Eugyppius’s writings, which they used to examine and read through with the greatest eagerness. Finally, through the mouth of Fulgentius, as they were accustomed to do in other matters as well, they wrote to him by common agreement concerning charity.

After these men had been driven into exile, the fury of the populace began to grow more savage, following the example of the ruler. Those who had come under suspicion because they were thought to agree less readily with wicked Christians were miserably torn apart. With steaming tears, tenderest childhood mourns the funerals of its parents; the anxious father worries over the feeble hearts of adolescence and wavering youth; each person firm in faith strengthens unstable minds, lest they reject the true faith and the belief of their ancestors in Christ, lest they place confidence in promises or deceptive persuasion, and lest, by avoiding a few torments, they become unwilling to attain eternal life. Many are taken to the slaughterhouse; most are dragged away to punishment.

The venerable old man Marinus encouraged his companions to be strong in the Lord. He said that, insofar as the injustice of the times had permitted and insofar as the strength of body and mind had allowed, he had kept watch and faced many dangers for the benefit of all; that only a little labor remained for him; and that at last he must seek rest through his own blood. Taking Eugyppius by the hand, he earnestly entreated and implored him thereafter to lead the companions by his teaching, diligence, and watchfulness, and to care assiduously for their common affairs. His final day, he said, was approaching, and he would have no successor except him. If Eugyppius vigorously completed the journey he had begun, he would finally gain Christ for himself and very many people for Christ, together with the honorable renown of his name.

Burning with the ardor of love and extraordinarily inflamed by so honorable a request, Eugyppius applied himself even more intensely to letters than before. He continued preparing antidotes against the approaching poison and fashioning remedies for the disease then present. He passed over none of the good authors without examining them with the greatest exactness.

Now the day foretold by Marinus was approaching; the crown had been prepared, and the venerable old man was being summoned to take possession of the throne. As the Arians raged, Catholics were either thrown to wild beasts to be torn apart or killed by smoke and fire; but those who defected from the Catholic faith were treated with the highest honor.

Marinus, inflamed by zeal for God, pressed forward and ran to the scene. “What madness is this, brothers?” he exclaimed. “Why, after rejecting the true and sound rule, does a king driven mad by the persuasion of an insane man tear innocent people apart like wild beasts? What frenzy is this? Why, adhering to the same footsteps and devoted to a heretic, do you regard the commands of a perverse and ruined man as superior to the true precepts of God? What evil steals away the merits of so many years by means of threats of torments and martyrdom against the saints? I confess that I was regenerated by ritual water in the name of the undivided Trinity. No torturer, no sword, no execution will ever strip me of the garments of true salvation.”

Immediately a band of executioners appeared; the holy man was seized and finally torn apart miserably. When news of his death spread through the city, the entire community at once rushed together and burst into Eugyppius’s study.

“We have lost our father, Eugyppius!” they cried. “The glory of martyrdom has taken from us our sweetest brother. From now on, be our champion and faithful guardian. Cruel torments await us unless we adapt ourselves to the will of one tyrant—which would be the immediate destruction of the soul—or, aided by divine power, refute the arguments of the enemy through the keenness of your intellect.”

Compelled by the necessity arising from the dejection of his brothers, Eugyppius took up the burden of his predecessor and, until peace returned to the Church, assumed the rank of leadership. The more he felt himself raised in dignity and honor, the more conscious he was that he ought to serve Christ’s servants, and he sought every opportunity by which he might provide for the godly.

At last, Thrasimund’s son, Hilderic, born of Valentiniana, a Roman mother, had assumed responsibility for the kingdom. Eugyppius was very close to him and gained easy access to him. He approached the prince and urged him to recall the pious company exiled in Sardinia. He declared that God was deeply concerned with the condition of kingdoms and rulers, but meanwhile he recounted many examples showing how God himself raises the pious and miserably casts down the persecutors of truth.

Persuaded by the counsel of this most pious man, Hilderic—although bound by a most solemn oath, having promised his furious father that provision would at some time be made for the Catholics in his kingdom—nevertheless annulled the tyrant’s edicts and restored the exiles. Then, through the efforts of pious men, he expelled throughout Africa the most pestilential sect which had grown savage over forty-seven years, doing so within eight years.

Now that he had leisure, Eugyppius arranged the treasures which he had once compiled from the works of St. Augustine and, under the auspices of your name, most illustrious prince, brought to light and organized them into the order you see.

Thus the good fragrance of Eugyppius had also spread through Europe, and at Rome his reputation was held in high regard among good men. The Anician family in particular, delighted by the distinction of its foster son, strove with all its strength to glorify the name of so great a man; nor did Eugyppius, ungratefully, think it right not to inscribe his labors to this family.

There was a woman named Proba, advanced in years and venerable in character, the wife of Anitius Paulinus Ruffus—the great-grandson of the man who had held the consulship with Publilius Optatus, a man of distinguished rank and a poet of great talent, in the year 1080 from the founding of the City. After her husband’s death, she lived in widowhood and solitude with the greatest reverence toward Christ.

She had a granddaughter of the same name, born of her daughter Juliana, herself the wife of a consul. A virgin dedicated to Christ, she rivaled Cornelia of the Gracchi and the most celebrated women of antiquity chiefly in her devotion to study. She placed corrupt morals beneath holy disciplines and did not yearn for pearls, gems, or other worthless possessions; instead, she had furnished a library with innumerable volumes.

Just as she showed the most ardent Christian love toward good and pious people, so she was esteemed by all who were learned and pious. For when St. Augustine wrote to her grandmother and mother, he poured out all the resources of his eloquence in praising this virgin. Fulgentius too did not neglect her; writing to her sister Galla, with what praises did he exalt her! Nor can I restrain myself, although I am hastening toward another matter, from quoting his own words exactly:

“For we have resolved, if the Lord wills and if we live, to write something on fasting and prayer to your sister, the holy virgin Proba of Christ, whom the Lord has now deigned to give to the city of Rome as an outstanding example of virginity and humility, as my promise contained in the letter which I recently sent her declares. Her holy way of life is especially to be imitated by you in all things.

“Although she is known through grandfathers and great-grandfathers who were consuls and was raised amid royal luxuries, such great humility has been infused into her by the gift of heavenly grace that, through her love of submission and her practice of service, she no longer knows that she was once a mistress, since she delights to have all people as her masters through the holy service of submission.

“For she knows that the Lord—whom she vowed her virginity of heart and body—accepted the humility of a servant’s form for our liberation. For this reason she delights to please her Bridegroom in the humility of this service, so that, numbered among the company of the five wise virgins, she may be able to reign with her Bridegroom in eternal glory.

“You can learn more fully by seeing for yourself with what strength she has despised the pleasures of the body and how she makes her hunger serve the satisfying of the poor; and how, for that reason, she is clothed in shabby garments for no other purpose than to fulfill her purpose of humility and to devote continual care, in holy piety, to clothing the poor. You wish to hear this from me, but I can explain it less fully in words than you can learn it by observing her.

“Set her before you, therefore, as a mirror, and by considering her learn what you already possess and what you still lack in holy studies and works.”

Thus far Fulgentius concerning Proba, to whom Eugyppius dedicated what he had excerpted.

In the first volume he inserted the matters that had raised the greatest controversies in his own time, along with explanations of very many obscure passages of Scripture: concerning charity, the soul, the senses of man, the sacrament of the Mediator, the Christian religion, the Sabbath, divine judgment, the resurrection, eternal life, and eternal death—in short, whatever Augustine had published that was more learned.

In the second volume he teaches by what arguments that bishop of Hippo defeated the Arians, Manichaeans, Donatists, and Pelagians. To put it briefly, most illustrious prince, you have here not Augustine’s body but his mind, enclosed in this book from his innumerable volumes.

After publishing his labors, the pious man did not live much longer. Following Fulgentius after an interval of a year and a half, he departed amid universal mourning, returning to his heavenly homeland.

These are the matters concerning this author’s life which I thought useful to set forth briefly in advance and pleasant for the reader to hear. Farewell, most illustrious prince, my most revered patron.

Basel of the Rauraci, 29 August, in the year of Christ’s birth 1542.

[Col. 0559C]

**TO THE LADY PROBA, RIGHTLY VENERABLE, AND ALWAYS ILLUSTRIOUS IN THE GRACE OF CHRIST THROUGH THE FRUIT OF SACRED VIRGINITY AND IN ALL THINGS APPROVED, EUGYPPIUS, SERVANT OF ALL THE SERVANTS OF GOD, SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD.** (C)

[Col. 0559]

[Col. 0559D] You wished the codex of excerpts which I had assembled in some fashion from several works of St. Augustine, at the urging of my lord Marinus, the abbot, and the other holy brothers, to be transcribed immediately for you, in accordance with the holy zeal by which you are distinguished. Although your library contains a rich and complete abundance of works, from which I have selected a few, you nevertheless approved of having excerpts.

But, foreseeing that perhaps readers might accuse me of rashness, I deemed it necessary to confess in a preface the reason for what I had done. It is as follows.

Who does not know that blessed Augustine was and is an illustrious figure among the great and outstanding doctors of the Catholic Church, and also a bishop? Since all orthodox people throughout the world venerate him as remarkable in divine and human learning, the bishops of the apostolic see in particular have always embraced his writings with the greater zeal, the more broadly they testify that they have used them as a source of consolation. For, instructed by his teaching—or rather, illumined by the same grace—while fighting against many enemies of the Church, and especially against the crafty enemies of God’s grace, they have always emerged victorious. By God’s gift, the rewards of this victory benefit posterity so greatly that they both feed the hungry more abundantly and equip the strong with spiritual weapons.

For the Catholic exposition of the divine law becomes not only food for those who hunger but also armor for those who fight. [Col. 0561A] Nor without reason did the vicars of him to whom the Lord, with his own mouth, entrusted the feeding of the sheep love even more greatly the companion of their pastoral office, who supplied abundant nourishment to the Lord’s flock from the meadows of Scripture. They truly considered as their own good what they rejoiced to have discovered through fraternal knowledge.

Knowing that this intelligible salt would be useful for seasoning souls, even the most insignificant sheep, I—who am altogether more insignificant than all of them—selected, by somehow chewing and tasting, a very few passages from the distinguished works of that blessed man, works which I had read in full while friends were present. For who could possess or find all his works?

Since I had no means of obtaining certain works which I was reading and desired to possess, I therefore collected some passages from the books whose abundance was available to me, as from a vast meadow scattered with heavenly flowers. I was poor in resources, that is, in learning; sick because of offense; eager either to be instructed by such great teaching or to be healed.

I experienced the truth of Solomon’s saying—“The words of the wise are a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the bones”—in the sweetest and most health-giving teaching of the man mentioned above.

I therefore trust that the few things I have gathered will benefit not only me, who am poor in understanding and possessions, but also those who possess both gifts. For when these same excerpts come into their hands, whether they are stirred by the fervor of a beggar or moved by the disorderly accumulation customary in such matters, they will take pains either to acquire more diligently a larger number of passages or to select the more suitable ones from these and, having reduced them to a single body, to read them repeatedly.

Thus perhaps the desire of the unlearned may serve the learned through a shortcut. For what is often grasped awkwardly by the small is more aptly completed by the great.

Certainly, if none of the great deigns either to undertake or possess this work, at least those who lack the complete work of so great an author may perhaps take pleasure in these excerpts, since anyone can more easily acquire a single codex than many.

At the beginning of each chapter, the various matters, questions, and opinions are identified, together with the work or book to which they belong, so that anyone who does not know where to find them in full may learn where they can be found.

It seemed, however, that the complete book should be the beginning of the Excerpts. The book which first occurred to me as most suitable for this position was the one which that blessed bishop is known to have written to the holy presbyter Jerome, after his first letter concerning the question of the soul. In it he resolves the question from the Epistle of the Apostle James, which I noted at the beginning of the first chapter. In the same book he wonderfully referred the four virtues—that is, prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—to the broad commandment of the twofold love of God and neighbor, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

For this reason I thought it fitting and appropriate that charity, through whose wholeness scattered things are ordinarily brought together, should give these Excerpts their beginning. Charity is both the perfection of all the virtues and the fullness of the heavenly law. It also gives the work its end, since it has no end.

The penultimate numbered title contains the order for nourishing charity; the final one contains praise of charity once nourished.

By this charity I adjure those who read to grant pardon graciously to me, though unworthy, and mercifully to offer me the support of their prayers.

If anyone, in transcribing this work, should wish to add other material to what has been gathered, let him add it in the appropriate places, so that the two aforementioned titles concerning charity may always remain at the end of the Excerpts.

[Col. 0561C]

**THE TREASURY OF ST. EUGYPPIUS, AFRICAN ABBOT, FROM THE WORKS OF ST. AUGUSTINE.** (C)

[Col. 0561]

**FIRST VOLUME**

**CHAPTER ONE.** [Col. 0561D] Concerning the saying of the Apostle James: “If anyone keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all,” while he says the same thing elsewhere: “We all stumble in many ways.” Also concerning charity and the four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The complete book addressed to the presbyter Jerome.

What I wrote to you, my honored brother in Christ, Jerome, inquiring about the human soul—whether, as each person is born, individual new souls are made even now, and where they contract the bond of sin, which we do not doubt must be loosed even in newly born infants through the sacrament of Christ’s grace—was becoming a work of no small length. I did not wish to burden you with any other question; but what presses more urgently must even less be neglected. Therefore I ask, and beseech you by the Lord, to explain to me something which I think will benefit many; or, if you already have an explanation of it, whether given by yourself or by someone else, send it [Col. 0562C] to us: how are we to understand what is written in the [Col. 0562D] Epistle of the apostle James: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all”?

The matter is so weighty and important that I greatly regret what I wrote to you about it not long ago. For this question concerns the conduct of the present life, how we may attain eternal life—not the investigation of the past, which oblivion has completely submerged, as was the case with what I thought should be asked about the soul. An apt and elegant saying is reported that suits this matter well. When someone had fallen into a well in which there was enough water to receive him so that he would not die, rather than to suffocate him so that he could not speak, another person approached and, seeing him, said compassionately, “How did you fall in here?” But the man replied, “Please consider how you may get me out of here; do not ask how I fell in.” Thus, since we confess and hold by the catholic faith [Col. 0563A] that even the soul of a little infant must be freed from the guilt of sin as from a well by the grace of Christ, it is enough for him that we know the manner in which he is saved, even if we never know how he came into that evil condition.

But I thought this ought to be asked, lest perhaps we unwisely hold one of those opinions about the soul’s incarnation which altogether contradicts the liberation of the little one’s soul by denying that it is in this evil condition. Holding this firmly, then—that the soul of the infant must be freed from the guilt of sin, and that it can be freed in no other way than by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord—if we can also know the cause and origin of this evil, we shall be more ready and better equipped to resist not disputers but vain talkers and quarrelers. If we cannot, however, the fact that [Col. 0563B] the beginning of misery is hidden must not make the work of mercy sluggish. Against those who seem to themselves to know what they do not know, we are the safer because we are not unaware of our own ignorance. For one thing is evil not to know; another is something that either cannot be known, or need not be known, or is irrelevant to the life we seek.

But the matter I am now asking about from the apostolic letter of James concerns precisely this life in which we live and in which we strive to please God so that we may live forever. How, then, I beg you, is this to be understood: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all”? Does this mean that someone who has committed theft—or rather, someone who has said to the rich man, “Sit here,” but to the poor man, “Stand there”—is guilty also of murder, adultery, and sacrilege? If not, [Col. 0563C] how has the person who offends in one point become guilty of all? Or does what he said about the rich and poor not pertain to these matters, although anyone who offends in one of them becomes guilty of all?

We must recall from where this statement came, and what preceding words produced it, upon which it depends in connection. “My brothers,” he says, “do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. For if a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also enters, and you pay attention to the one wearing the splendid clothing and say, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ but to the poor man say, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit below my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?”

[Col. 0563D] “Listen, my beloved brothers: has not God chosen the poor in this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which God promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor”—that is, the one to whom it was said, “You stand there,” while the man with the gold ring was told, “You sit here in a good place.”

Then he continues, expanding and explaining the same statement at greater length: “Do not the rich oppress you by their power, and do they not themselves drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you? If indeed you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.”

Observe how he calls [Col. 0564A] those who say to the rich, “Sit here,” and to the poor, “Stand there,” transgressors of the law. Therefore, lest they think that transgressing the law in this one matter was an insignificant sin, he went on to add: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all. For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ If you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law,” because of what he had said: “being convicted by the law as transgressors.”

If this is so, then, unless it is shown that it must be understood in another way, it seems to follow that whoever says to the rich, “Sit here,” and to the poor, “Stand there,” giving the former greater honor than the latter, must be judged guilty both of idolatry and blasphemy, adultery and murder—and, not to enumerate everything at length, of every crime. For by offending in one point, he has become guilty of all.

Yet it is said [Col. 0564B] that whoever has one virtue has them all, and whoever lacks one has none—“Cicero.” If this is true, the statement is confirmed. But I wish it to be explained, not confirmed, since among us it is already more firmly established than all the authority of the philosophers. Even if that statement about virtues and vices is made truthfully, it does not follow that all sins are equal.

As for the inseparability of the virtues, although I may be mistaken, nevertheless, if I remember correctly—though I scarcely remember it—all the philosophers agreed that the same virtues are necessary for the conduct of life. But only the Stoics dared to argue for the equality of sins, against the entire judgment of the human race. You most clearly refuted their folly from the Holy Scriptures in the case of that Jovinian [Col. 0564C], who was a Stoic in this opinion but an Epicurean in pursuing and defending pleasures. In that most charming and brilliant work of yours, it became sufficiently evident that our authorities—or rather, the Truth that spoke through them—did not approve the claim that all sins are equal.
