I shall try, with the Lord’s help, to explain as well as I can how it may be that, even if this is true of the virtues, we are nevertheless not compelled to admit the equality of all sins. If I succeed, you will approve; where I fall short, you will supply what is lacking.

Those who say that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all, [Col. 0564D] and that all are absent from anyone who lacks one, certainly establish this from the fact that prudence cannot be lazy, unjust, or intemperate; for if any of these is absent, it is not prudence. Moreover, if prudence exists only when it is also courageous, just, and temperate, then wherever it exists it certainly possesses the others with it. Likewise, courage cannot be imprudent, intemperate, or unjust; temperance must be prudent, courageous, and just; and justice is not justice unless it is prudent, courageous, and temperate. Thus, wherever one of them is true, the others are likewise present; but where the others are absent, that one is not true, even if it appears in some manner to resemble it.

There are, as you know, certain vices that are plainly and distinctly contrary to the virtues, such as imprudence to prudence. But some things are contrary merely because they are vices, while nevertheless resembling the virtue in a deceptive appearance—for example, not imprudence but cunning in relation to prudence.

By “cunning” I now mean [Col. 0565A] what is more commonly understood and called cunning among malicious people, not what our Scripture commonly means by the term, since Scripture often uses “cunning” in a good sense, as in, “Be cunning as serpents,” and, “To give cunning to the innocent.” Even the most eloquent writer of the Roman tongue said, “Yet he did not lack deceit or cunning for taking precautions,” using “cunning” in a good sense. But this is exceedingly rare among them and very common among our writers.

Similarly, in the sphere of temperance, extravagance is plainly opposed to frugality; but what is commonly called stinginess is indeed a vice, yet it resembles frugality—not by its nature, but by a most deceptive appearance. In the same way, injustice is manifestly contrary to justice; yet the desire for vengeance sometimes attempts to imitate justice, though it is a vice. Laziness is clearly contrary to courage, while hardness of endurance differs from it by nature but deceives by resemblance.

Steadfastness is a part of virtue. [Col. 0565B] Inconstancy is far removed from it and unquestionably stands opposed to it; but obstinacy pretends to be called steadfastness, though it is not, because the one is a virtue and the other a vice.

To avoid having to repeat the same things, let us give an example from which the others may be understood. Catiline, as those who were able to know him wrote about him, could endure cold, thirst, and hunger; he was extraordinarily capable of tolerating fasting, cold, and sleeplessness, beyond what anyone would believe. For this reason he seemed to possess great courage both for himself and for his followers.

But this was not prudent courage, [Col. 0565C] for he chose evil things instead of good; it was not temperate, for he was defiled by the most shameful corruptions; it was not just, for he had conspired against his country. Therefore it was not courage at all, but hardness of endurance which, to deceive fools, assumed the name of courage. For if it had been courage, it would have been a virtue and not a vice. And if it had been a virtue, it would never have been abandoned by the other virtues as inseparable companions.

When we inquire similarly about vices—whether, as with the virtues, all are present wherever one is present, or none are present wherever one is absent—it is difficult to demonstrate the matter, because two vices are usually opposed to a single virtue: one that is openly contrary to it, and another that is shaded by a resemblance of appearance.

Thus it was easier to see what Catiline’s condition was, since what he possessed was not courage and he did not have the other virtues with it. But that he was lazy, when he possessed an ability to exercise and endure any of the most grievous hardships beyond what anyone could believe, is difficult to persuade people of. Yet to those who look more keenly, that very hardness may appear to be laziness, because he had neglected the labor of good pursuits by which true courage is acquired.

Nevertheless, [Col. 0565D] since some people are bold without being timid, while others are timid and lack boldness, although both are vices—for one who is strong with true virtue neither acts rashly nor fears thoughtlessly—we are compelled to admit that vices are more numerous than virtues.

Thus at times one vice is removed by another, as the love of money by the love of praise; at times one gives way so that several may follow, as when someone who was a drunkard learns to live somewhat more freely through stinginess and ambition. Vices, then, can give way to vices that replace them, not to virtues; and for that reason they are more numerous.

But wherever a virtue enters, [Col. 0566A] since it brings the others with it, all the vices that were present will certainly give way. For they were not all present: at one time an equal number replaced a smaller number, at another more replaced fewer, or fewer replaced more. Whether matters are truly so must be investigated more carefully. For this too is not a divine pronouncement—that whoever has one virtue has them all, and that no virtue belongs to anyone who lacks one—but merely the opinion of human beings: highly gifted and diligent, indeed, but still human beings.

I do not know how to say that not merely a man, from whom virtue is said to derive its name, but even a woman who preserves fidelity to her husband’s marriage-bed, if she does so because of God’s command and promise and is first of all faithful to him, does not possess chastity, or that chastity is no virtue or only a small one. The same applies to a husband who preserves this fidelity toward his wife.

And yet there are many such people, [Col. 0566B] although I would not say that any one of them is without some sin. Surely whatever that sin may be comes from some vice. Therefore conjugal chastity in religious men and women, although it is undoubtedly a virtue—for it is neither nothing nor a vice—does not nevertheless possess all the virtues with it. For if all were present, there would be no vice; if there were no vice, there would be no sin at all.

But who is without some sin? Who, then, is without some vice—that is, without some kind of tinder or, as it were, root of sin—when the one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast cries out: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”?

Nor is it necessary to dwell on this longer with you; [Col. 0566C] I say it for the sake of others who may perhaps read these words. For you, in that very splendid work against Jovinian, carefully established this also from the Holy Scriptures, where you quoted from this same Epistle, whose words we are now seeking to understand: “For we all offend in many things.”

He did not say, “You offend,” but “We offend,” when Christ’s apostle was speaking. And here he says, “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all”; there he says that we offend not in one thing but in many, and not that some offend but that all offend.

Far be it from any believer to think that the many thousands of servants of Christ who truthfully say that they have sin—lest they deceive themselves and the truth be absent from them—possess no virtue, since wisdom itself is a great virtue. Wisdom said to humanity: “Behold, piety is wisdom.”

Far be it, then, from us to say [Col. 0566D] that so many and such great faithful and devout people of God do not possess piety, which the Greeks call either εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*) or, more explicitly and fully, θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*). And what is piety except the worship of God? [3] And from where is he worshiped except through love?

Love, therefore, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith is a great and true virtue, because it is itself the end of the commandment. [Col. 0567A] It is rightly said to be “strong as death,” either because no one conquers it, just as no one conquers death; or because in this life the measure of love extends to death, as the Lord says: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends”; or rather because, just as death tears the soul away from the senses of the flesh, so love tears it away from carnal desires.

Knowledge serves love when it is useful, for without love it “puffs up”; but what love has fulfilled by building up finds nothing empty there with which knowledge may puff itself up. He showed what useful knowledge is by defining it in this way: after saying, “Behold, piety is wisdom,” he immediately added, “To abstain from evil is knowledge.”

Why, then, do we not say that whoever possesses this virtue possesses all of them, since love is the fullness of the law? Or is it rather that the more love there is in a person, the more virtue he possesses; and the less there is, the less virtue is present, because love itself is virtue, and the less virtue is present, the more vice there is? Wherever love is full and perfect, nothing of vice will remain.

Therefore the Stoics seem to me to be mistaken because they refuse to allow a person who is progressing in wisdom to possess wisdom at all, granting that he possesses it only when he has become entirely perfect in it. They do not deny that he has advanced; but unless, emerging suddenly from some deep place, he bursts into the free air of wisdom, they say that he is wise in no respect.

Just as [Col. 0567B] it makes no difference to suffocate a person whether the water above him is many stades deep or only one palm or one finger, so they say that those who strive toward wisdom do indeed make progress, as though rising from the bottom of a whirlpool into the air; but unless, by progressing and emerging, they escape all the foolishness that presses upon them like water, they do not possess virtue and are not wise. Once they have escaped, however, they immediately possess it all, and no foolishness remains from which any sin could arise.

This comparison, [Col. 0567C] in which foolishness is represented as water and wisdom as air, so that the mind, emerging into wisdom as from the suffocation of foolishness, suddenly breathes again, does not seem sufficiently suited to the authority of our Scriptures. The more suitable comparison is that vice or foolishness be likened to darkness, and virtue or wisdom to light, insofar as such bodily likenesses can be transferred to intelligible realities.

A person does not therefore rise from water into air and, once he has passed above the surface, suddenly draw in as much breath as is sufficient. Rather, he proceeds from darkness into light and is gradually illuminated as he advances. Before this is fully accomplished, we nevertheless say that he is like someone emerging from a most hidden cave, touched by the nearness of the light: the nearer he comes to the exit, the more he is affected by it. What shines in him comes from the light toward which he advances; what remains dark comes from the darkness out of which he is emerging.

Thus, [Col. 0567D] “No living person shall be justified in your sight,” and yet “the righteous lives by faith.” The saints are clothed with righteousness, one more and another less; and no one here lives without sin, one more and another less. The best person, however, is the one who has the least.

But what am I doing? I have become like a teacher, as though forgetting whom I am addressing, when I had proposed to learn from you what I wish to know. Yet because the question of the equality of sins was the point from which the present discussion arose, I had decided to set forth my opinion for you to examine, and I shall finally bring it to a conclusion.

Even if it is true that whoever possesses one virtue possesses all, and whoever lacks one possesses none, sins are nevertheless not equal. For where there is no virtue at all, nothing is right; yet it does not follow that what is crooked is not more crooked, or what is distorted more distorted.

But if—as I think [Col. 0568A] more true and more consonant with the Holy Scriptures—the dispositions of the soul are like the members of the body, not in that they occupy visible places but in that they are perceived through their affections, and if one is illuminated more, another less, and another is altogether without light and overshadowed by a dark obstruction, then, according as someone is affected by the illumination of holy love—more in one action, less in another, and not at all in a third—he may be said to possess one virtue and not another, or to possess one more and another less.

We may rightly say, “There is greater love in this person than in that one,” and, insofar as love is concerned—for love is piety—“There is some love in this person and none in that one.” We may likewise say of one and the same person that he has greater chastity than patience, greater chastity today than yesterday if he is progressing, and that he does not yet possess continence but does possess no small measure of mercy.

To summarize [Col. 0568B] briefly and generally my understanding of virtue: insofar as it pertains to right living, virtue is love, by which what ought to be loved is loved. In some people it is greater, in others less, and in others absent. But the fullest love, which can no longer increase, is found in no one so long as that person lives here. And so long as it can increase, whatever is less than it ought to be comes from vice.

Because of this vice, there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin; because of this vice, no living person will be justified in God’s sight; because of this vice, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us. For this reason, no matter how far we may have progressed, it is necessary for us to say, “Forgive us our debts,” even though all that has been said, done, and thought has already been forgiven in baptism.

Anyone who sees rightly therefore sees [Col. 0568C] where, when, and from whom that perfection is to be hoped for which can have nothing added to it. If there were no commandments, there would be no sure place where a person could examine himself and see what he should turn away from, toward what he should strive, for what he should rejoice, and for what he should pray. The commandments are therefore greatly useful, provided that free will is granted only so far as to honor the grace of God more fully.

If this is so, how does one become guilty of all by offending in one point, when one has kept the whole law? Is it perhaps because the fullness of the law is love, by which God and neighbor are loved, and upon which commandments the whole law and the prophets depend? It is therefore rightly said that whoever acts against love becomes guilty of all, since everything depends upon it.

No one sins except by acting against love. [Col. 0568D] For “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,” and whatever other commandment there may be, is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love does no evil to one’s neighbor; therefore love is the fullness of the law.

No one loves his neighbor without loving God, so that he may do for his neighbor, whom he loves as himself, as much as he can to lead him also to love God. If he does not love God, he loves neither himself nor his neighbor. Accordingly, whoever has kept the whole law but offends in one point becomes guilty of all, because he acts against love, upon which the whole law depends; he therefore becomes guilty of all by acting against the commandment upon which everything depends.

Why, then, [Col. 0569A] are sins not said to be equal? Is it perhaps because the person who sins more grievously acts more strongly against love, while the one who sins less grievously acts less strongly against it? By the very act he commits, each becomes guilty of all, but the one who sins more grievously—or sins in more matters—is more guilty, while the one who sins more lightly—or in fewer matters—is less guilty. The guilt is therefore greater in proportion as the sin is greater, and lesser in proportion as it is lesser; yet even if a person offends in one point, he is guilty of all because he acts against the love upon which all depend.

If these things are true, they also explain the statement of the man who belonged to the apostolic grace: “We all offend in many things.” We all offend, but one more grievously and another more lightly. Each is more or less guilty in committing sin according as he has sinned more or less; and each is more guilty in sinning insofar as he is less in loving God and neighbor. Conversely, each is less guilty in committing sin insofar as he is greater in the love of God and neighbor.

A person is therefore fuller of iniquity insofar as he is emptier of love; and he is most perfect in love when nothing remains of infirmity.

Nor, as I think, [Col. 0569B] should it be considered a light sin to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality, if we refer that distinction between sitting and standing to ecclesiastical honors. Who could tolerate a rich man being chosen for a seat of honor in the Church while a poorer man, more learned and more holy, was disregarded?

But if he is speaking of ordinary places at the table, who does not sin in this matter—if indeed he sins—unless he judges inwardly within himself in such a way that the richer person seems to him better precisely because he is richer? This is what he appears to have signified by saying: “Are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?”

The law of freedom, then, is the law of love, [Col. 0569C] of which he says: “If indeed you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.”

After that most difficult statement, about which I have said sufficiently what I thought should be said, he recalls the same law of freedom for the sake of understanding it: “So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of freedom.”

And because he knows what he said shortly before—“For we all offend in many things”—he offers the Lord’s medicine, as though a daily remedy for daily wounds, even if they are lighter. “For judgment,” he says, “is without mercy for the one who has shown no mercy.”

For this reason the Lord also says: [Col. 0569D] “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.” “Mercy triumphs over judgment.” It does not say that judgment defeats mercy—for mercy is not opposed to judgment—but that mercy triumphs, because many are gathered through mercy, namely, those who have shown mercy. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy from God.”

It is just that they should be forgiven because they have forgiven, and that it should be given to them because they have given. For mercy belongs to God when he judges, and judgment belongs to him when he shows mercy. Hence it is said to him: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

Whoever, as though excessively righteous, confidently awaits judgment without mercy provokes the most righteous anger, fearing which the Psalmist says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.” Hence it is said to a rebellious people: “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment?”

When [Col. 0570A] the just King sits upon his throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin? What hope is there, then, unless mercy triumphs over judgment—but toward those who have truly shown mercy, saying, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” and giving without complaint? “God loves a cheerful giver.”

Finally, holy James now speaks from this point about works of mercy, so that he may console those whom that severe statement had greatly frightened. He reminds them how even daily sins, without which no one lives here, may be expiated by daily remedies, lest a person who, by offending in one point, becomes guilty of all, and who offends in many things—for “we all offend in many things”—carry to the [Col. 0570B] tribunal of so great a judge the great mound of his guilt, collected little by little, and fail to find the mercy he did not show. Rather, by forgiving and giving, he may deserve that his debts be forgiven and that what has been promised be restored to him.

I have said much, perhaps causing you weariness, although you do not expect to learn these things from me, since you are accustomed to teach what you so thoroughly approve. But if there is anything in them that concerns the matters themselves—for I do not care greatly about the eloquence with which they have been expressed—if there is anything that offends your learning, I ask you to admonish me by writing back, and do not hesitate to correct me.

For he is unhappy [Col. 0570C] who neither honors worthily the great and holy labors of your studies nor gives thanks for them to our Lord God, by whose gift you are such a man. Since I ought more willingly to learn from anyone what I ignorantly fail to know than eagerly to teach anyone what I do know, how much more justly do I demand this debt of love from you, whose teaching, in the name and with the help of the Lord, has aided ecclesiastical literature in the Latin language to a degree that had never before been possible!

Above all, however, I ask concerning this statement: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all.” If your affection knows of any other way in which it may be better explained, I beseech you by the Lord to be willing to share it with us.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the four virtues mentioned above, which he distinguished in the preceding book. In his book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, while discussing them, he referred them all to a single commandment: love.

There is therefore nothing else that is the highest good of a human being, to which it is supremely blessed to cling, except God. We cannot rightly cling to him [Col. 0570D] except through love. For that virtue which is said to be fourfold is named from certain varied dispositions of love itself: temperance is love offering itself wholly to what is loved; courage is love readily enduring all things for the sake of what is loved; justice is love serving the beloved alone and therefore ruling rightly; prudence is love wisely choosing those things by which it is helped over those by which it is hindered.

But we have said that this love is not love of just anything, but love of God—that is, of the highest good, the highest wisdom, and the highest harmony.

It is therefore also possible to define the virtues in this way: temperance is love preserving itself whole and undefiled for God; courage is love readily enduring all things for God; justice is love serving God alone and therefore ruling well over the other things subject to human beings; prudence is love rightly discerning those things by which it may be helped toward God from those by which it may be hindered.

Why should I discuss morals further? [Col. 0571A] If God is the highest good of humanity, which cannot be denied, it follows that, since to desire the highest good is to live well, living well is nothing other than loving with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind the God from whom one exists, so that love may be preserved incorrupt and whole in him—which is the work of temperance; that it may not be broken by any adversities—which is the work of courage; that it may serve no other—which is the work of justice; and that it may remain watchful in discerning things, lest deception or cunning gradually creep in—which is the work of prudence.

This is the one perfection of a human being, [Col. 0571B] which alone obtains the enjoyment of the truth’s sincerity. This is sung to us throughout both Testaments; this is urged upon us from both sides. Let us therefore love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, whoever has resolved to attain eternal life.

“This,” says the Savior, “is eternal life: that they know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” Eternal life, then, is the knowledge of truth itself. How perverse and backward, therefore, are those who suppose that they transmit the knowledge of God in order to be most perfect, when that knowledge itself is the reward of the perfect!

What, then, must be done except that we first love with sincere charity the very one whom we wish to know?

## CHAPTER III

Whether the virtues by which one strives toward eternity will cease when they have led us to eternal things; from Book XIV of *On the Trinity*, among other passages.

Whether the virtues by which one lives well in this [Col. 0571C] mortality—since they too begin to exist in the soul, although the soul existed before it possessed them—will cease when they have led us to eternal things is a matter of some question.

Some have thought that they will cease, and that good souls will be blessed solely by knowledge and understanding, that is, by contemplation of the nature than which nothing is better or more lovable: the nature that created and established all the others. To be subject to this nature as ruler is justice; justice is therefore entirely immortal and will not cease to exist in that blessedness. Rather, it will be such and so great that it cannot become more perfect or greater.

Perhaps the other three virtues will also exist [Col. 0571D] in that happiness: prudence, without any danger of error; courage, without the hardship of enduring evils; and temperance, without resistance from desires. Prudence will consist in preferring or equating no good with God; courage, in clinging to him most firmly; temperance, in taking pleasure in no harmful deficiency.

But what justice now does in helping the miserable, what prudence does in guarding against ambushes, what courage does in enduring hardships, and what temperance does in restraining perverse pleasures will not exist there, where there will be no evil at all.

Accordingly, these works of the virtues that are necessary for this mortal life, like faith, will be regarded as belonging to the past; and they now form one trinity when we hold them as present, love them, and behold them, but then they will form another, when we discover that they do not exist but once existed, through certain traces of them which, as they pass away, they will leave behind in the memory.

For there will also then be a trinity [Col. 0572A] when that trace, whatever it may be, is retained in the memory, truly recognized, and these two are joined together by a third element, the will.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the four affections, which Cicero called disturbances and others called passions, and which Virgil said arise in human beings because of the flesh; from Book XIV of *The City of God*.

We are weighed down, then, by a corruptible body. Knowing that the cause of this burden is not the nature and substance of the body but its corruption, we do not wish to be stripped of the body but to be clothed with its immortality. Then too the body will exist, but because it will not be corruptible, it will not weigh us down.

Now the corruptible body burdens the soul, [Col. 0572B] and an earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks about many things. Nevertheless, those who think that all the evils of the soul have arisen from the body are in error.

Although Virgil seems to explain the Platonic opinion in splendid verses, saying:

> Their vigor is fiery, and their origin heavenly,
>
> So far as harmful bodies do not hinder the seeds,
>
> And earthly limbs and dying members do not dull them;

and although, intending us to understand that all those four familiar disturbances of the soul—desire, fear, joy, and sorrow—arise from the body as the origins of all sins and vices, he adds:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, nor do they—

[The supplied passage ends here.]

They receive [or: look back], shut in by darkness and in a blind prison; [Col. 0572C] nevertheless, our faith has it otherwise: for the corruption of the body, which weighs down the soul, is not the cause but the punishment of the first sin. Nor did corruptible flesh make the sinful soul sinful; rather, the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible. Although certain incentives to vice, and the vicious desires themselves, arise from this corruption of the flesh, not all the vices of an unrighteous life are nevertheless to be attributed to the flesh, lest we thereby absolve the devil from all responsibility, since he has no flesh.

Although the devil [who has no flesh [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from St. Augustine’s Benedictine edition. EDITOR]], cannot be called a fornicator or drunkard, or anything of that sort which belongs to the pleasures of the flesh, since he is also the hidden persuader and instigator of such sins, he is nevertheless supremely proud and envious. This viciousness so possessed him that, because of it, he was destined to eternal punishment in the prisons [Col. 0572D] of this darkened air.

Yet the Apostle attributes to the flesh those vices that hold primacy in the devil, although it is certain that the devil does not have flesh. For he says that enmities, quarrels, rivalries, resentments, envies, are works of the flesh. The head and source of all these evils is pride, which reigns in the devil without flesh. Who, indeed, is more hostile to the saints than he? Who is found to be more quarrelsome, more resentful, more rivalrous, and more envious against them? Since he possesses all these qualities without flesh, how are they works of the flesh unless they are works of the human being whom, as I have said, he calls “flesh”?

For it was not by possessing flesh—which the devil does not possess—but by living according to himself, that is, according to humanity, that the human being became like the devil. The devil, too, wished to live according to himself when he did not stand in the truth, so that he might speak falsehood not from God but from himself; and he is not merely a liar but also the father of falsehood. He was the first to lie, and from the one from whom sin began, falsehood also began.

Therefore, when a human being lives according to humanity and not according to God, he is like the devil. The soul is moved not only by the flesh, so that it desires, fears, rejoices, or grieves; it can also be stirred by these movements from within itself. What matters is the quality of a person’s will: if it is perverse, these movements will be perverse; but if it is upright, they will be not only blameless but praiseworthy. For the will is present in all of them; indeed, all of them are nothing other than wills.

For what are desire and joy except the will consenting to what we want? And what are fear and sorrow except the will dissenting from what we do not want? When we consent by seeking what we want, this is called desire; when we consent by enjoying what we want, it is called joy. Likewise, when we dissent from what we do not want to happen, such a will is fear; but when we dissent from what happens against our will, such a will is sorrow. In general, according to the variety of things that are sought or avoided, just as the human will is attracted or offended, so it changes and turns toward one or another of these affections.

Therefore, a person who lives according to God and not according to humanity ought to be a lover of the good; consequently, he must hate evil. And since no one is evil by nature—for whoever is evil is evil by vice—the person who lives according to God ought to hate evil completely: he must neither hate the human being because of the vice nor love the vice because of the human being, but hate the vice and love the human being. Once the vice has been healed, everything that ought to be loved will remain, and nothing that ought to be hated.

For the one whose purpose is to love God, and to love his neighbor—not according to humanity but according to God—as he loves himself, is undoubtedly said to possess a good will. In the Holy Scriptures this is more commonly called *charity* (*caritas*), though according to those same sacred writings it is also called love (*amor*).

Some people think that *dilectio*, or *charitas*, is one thing and *amor* another. They say that *dilectio* should be understood in a good sense, and *amor* in a bad one. Yet it is quite certain that even the authors of secular literature did not speak in that way. An upright will, therefore, is good love, and a perverse will is evil love.

6. Love that longs to possess what it loves is desire; when it possesses and enjoys that object, it is joy; when it flees what opposes it, it is fear; and when it senses that opposition has occurred, it is sorrow. These affections are therefore evil if the love is evil, and good if the love is good.

As for the philosophers, however, insofar as this question concerning the soul’s disturbances is concerned, we have already answered them in the ninth book of this work, showing that they are more eager for contention about words than about realities, and more desirous of dispute than of truth.

Among us, however, in accordance with the Holy Scriptures [Col. 0574A] and sound doctrine, the citizens of the holy City of God, while journeying as pilgrims through this life and living according to God, fear and desire, grieve and rejoice. Because their love is rightly ordered, all these affections are rightly ordered in them.

They fear eternal punishment; they desire eternal life; they grieve in actuality, because they still groan within themselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of their body; they rejoice in hope, because the saying that is written will be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” Likewise, they fear sinning, desire perseverance, grieve over sins, and rejoice in good works.

To make them fear sinning, they hear: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold.” To make them desire perseverance, they hear what is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” To make them grieve over sins, they hear: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” To make them rejoice in good works, they hear: “God loves a cheerful giver.”

Likewise, according to the measure of their weakness and strength, they fear temptation, desire temptation, grieve in temptations, and rejoice in temptations. To make them fear temptation, they hear: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself lest you also be tempted.” But to make them desire temptation, they hear a certain strong man of the City of God saying: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart.” To make them grieve in temptations, they see Peter weeping; to make them rejoice in temptations, they hear James saying: [Col. 0574C] “Consider it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various temptations.”

They are moved by these affections not only on their own behalf, but also on behalf of those whom they desire to be liberated: they fear that they may perish, grieve if they perish, and rejoice if they are liberated.

Let us recall especially that excellent and most courageous man who glories in his weaknesses: the one through whom we Gentiles came into the Church of Christ, the Teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. He worked harder than all his fellow apostles, and through many Epistles instructed the people of God—not only those whom he seemed to see present, but also those whom he foresaw would exist in the future.

This man, I say—the athlete of Christ, taught by him, anointed by him, crucified with him, glorified in him—was made a spectacle to angels and human beings in the theater [Col. 0574D] of this world. They behold him with the eyes of faith gladly engaging in a lawful and mighty contest, and pressing forward toward the prize of the heavenly calling. They see him rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep; outwardly facing struggles, inwardly fears; desiring to depart and be with Christ; longing to see the Romans, so that he might have some fruit among them as among the other Gentiles; being jealous for the Corinthians and, in that very jealousy, fearing lest their minds be led astray from the chastity that is in Christ; experiencing great sorrow and unceasing pain in his heart for the Israelites, because, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to God’s righteousness; and declaring not only his sorrow but also his mourning over certain people who had sinned previously and had not repented of their uncleanness and fornications.

If these movements, these affections, arising from love of the good and holy charity, are to be called vices, then let us allow what are truly vices to be called virtues. But since these affections follow right reason and are employed when and where they ought to be, who would dare call them diseased or vicious passions?

For this reason the Lord himself, though he deigned to live a human life in the form of God and possessed absolutely no sin, adopted these affections whenever he judged that they should be adopted. For where there was a true human body and a true human soul, the human affection was not false. Thus, when the Gospel records that he was angered and grieved over the hardness of the Jews’ hearts; that he said, “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe”; that, when he was about to raise Lazarus, he even shed tears; that he desired to eat the Passover with his disciples; and that, as his Passion drew near, his soul was sorrowful—all these things are certainly reported truthfully.

Yet he assumed these movements in his human soul for the sake of a certain dispensation, just as, when he willed, he became human. Therefore, it must be acknowledged that even when we possess these affections rightly and according to God, they belong to this life, not to the life that we hope will come, and that often we yield to them even against our will. Thus, although we may be moved not by blameworthy desire but by praiseworthy charity, we sometimes weep even when we do not want to.

We have these affections, then, because of the weakness of the human condition. The Lord Jesus did not possess them in the same way, for his weakness too arose from power. Yet while we bear the weakness of this life, if we have none of these affections at all, then we are not living rightly. For the Apostle condemned and detested certain people (Rom. 1), whom he also said were “without affection.” The sacred Psalm likewise censured those of whom it says: “I looked for one who would grieve together with me, and there was none.”

To feel no sorrow at all while we are in this place of misery does not, as one of the learned men of this age perceived and said, occur without a price: it is purchased by brutality of soul and insensibility of body.

Accordingly, that condition which in Greek is called *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια), and which in Latin could be called *impassibilitas*—“impassibility”—if it is to be understood as a state in which one lives without those affections that arise contrary to reason and disturb the mind (for it is understood of the soul, not of the body), is plainly good and greatly to be desired. But it does not belong to this life either. For the following is not the voice of just any people, but especially of the pious, the deeply righteous, and the saints: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

That *apatheia*, then, will exist when there is no sin at all in a human being. But now one lives well enough if one lives without crime; anyone who thinks that he lives without sin is not acting so as to have no sin, but so as not to receive forgiveness.

# CHAPTER V. On the Five Senses of the Body, from Book X of the *Confessions*

Lord, I love you. You struck my heart with your word, [Col. 0576A] and I loved you. Yet heaven and earth, and everything in them, behold, say to me from every side that I should love you; nor do they cease saying this to everyone, so that they may be without excuse.

But you will have greater mercy on whomever you have mercy, and you will show compassion to whomever you are compassionate; otherwise heaven and earth speak your praises to the deaf.

What, then, do I love when I love you? Not a bodily form, not the beauty of temporal things, not the brightness of light—so dear to these eyes—not sweet melodies of every kind of song, not the fragrance of flowers, ointments, and spices, not manna and honey, not limbs pleasing to the embrace of the flesh. None of these things do I love when I love my God.

7. And yet I do love a certain light, a certain voice, a certain fragrance, a certain food, and a certain embrace when I love my God: the light, voice, fragrance, food, and embrace of my inner self. There shines for my soul what no place contains; there sounds what no time carries away; there is fragrance that no wind disperses; there is taste that eating does not diminish; there clings what satiety does not tear apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

And what is this? I questioned the earth, and it answered: “I am not he”; and everything in it confessed the same. I questioned the sea and the abysses, and the creeping creatures of living souls, and they answered: “We are not your God; seek above us.” I questioned the blowing winds, and the whole air with its inhabitants said: “Anaximenes is mistaken; I am not God.” I questioned heaven, the sun, the moon, and the stars: “Nor are we the God whom you seek,” they said.

And I said to all these things that surround the doors of my flesh: “Tell me about my God—since you are not he; tell me something about him.” And they cried out in a loud voice: “He made us.”

My questioning was my attention, and their answer was their appearance. Then I turned toward myself and said to myself: “Who are you?” And I answered: “A human being.” And behold, body and soul were present within me, one external and the other internal. From which of these should I have sought my God, whom I had already sought through the body, from earth to heaven, as far as I could send the messengers, the rays of my eyes?

Better, surely, was the inner self, since all the bodily messengers reported to it, which presided over and judged the answers of heaven and earth and all that is in them, saying: [Col. 0576D] “We are not God, but he made us.”

The inner human being knew these things through the service of the outer; I, the inner self, knew them—I, I, the mind—through the sense of my body. I questioned the mass of the world about my God, and it answered me: “I am not he, but he made me.”

Does not this appearance present itself to everyone whose senses are sound? Why does it not speak the same thing to everyone? Small and great animals see it, but they cannot question it, for rational judgment has not been placed over the senses that serve as messengers in them. Human beings, however, can question it, so that “the invisible things of God may be understood and perceived through the things that have been made.”

But they become subject to these things through love, and once subjected to them they cannot judge. Nor do these things answer those who question them unless the questioners are capable of judgment. They do not alter their voice—that is, their appearance—if one person merely sees them while another sees and questions them, so that they appear one way to the former and another way to the latter. Appearing in the same way to both, they are mute to one and speak to the other. Indeed, they speak to everyone, but only those understand who compare the voice received outwardly with the truth within.

For the Truth says to me: “Your God is not earth and heaven.”

# CHAPTER VI. A Beautiful and Lengthy Prayer on the Same Five Senses of the Body, from Book X of the *Confessions*
Behold how far I have ranged through my memory, seeking you, Lord, and I did not find you outside it; for I found nothing concerning you that I had not remembered from the time I learned to know you. For from the time I learned to know you, I have not forgotten you. For where I found truth, there I found my God, truth itself—which, from the time I learned it, I have not forgotten. And so, from the time I learned to know you, you remain in my memory, and there I find you whenever I remember you and delight in you. These are my holy delights, which you have granted me in your mercy, looking upon my poverty.

But where do you remain in my memory, Lord? Where in it do you remain? What kind of chamber have you made there for yourself? What sanctuary have you built for yourself? You granted this dignity to my memory, that you should remain in it; but in what part of it you remain is what I am considering. I passed beyond the parts of it that the beasts also possess when I remembered you, because I did not find you there among the images of bodily things. And I came to the parts where I had entrusted the affections of my soul, but I did not find you there either. And I entered [Col. 0577C] into the seat of my soul itself, which it possesses in my memory—for the soul also remembers itself—and there you were not: because just as you are neither a bodily image nor the affection of a living being, such as exists when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, forget, and whatever else is of this kind, so neither are you the soul itself, since you, Lord God, are the Lord of the soul. All these things change, but you remain unchangeable above all things, and you have deigned to dwell in my memory from the time I learned to know you.

And what am I asking, in what place of it you dwell, as though places existed there? Certainly you dwell in it, since I remember you from the time I learned to know you, and I find you in it when I remember you. Where, then, did I find you, so as to learn to know you? For you were not yet in my memory before I learned to know you. Where, then, did I find you, so as to learn to know you, if not in you, above me? And there is no place; we withdraw and draw near, and there is no place.

You preside everywhere as truth over all who consult you, and at the same time you answer all, even those who consult you about different things. You answer clearly, but not all hear clearly. All consult you about whatever they wish, but they do not always hear what they wish. Your best servant is the one who does not pay greater attention to hearing from you what he himself wants, but rather wants what he has heard from you.

Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new; late have I loved you! And behold, you were within, while I was outside, and there I sought you; and in the beautiful things you made I rushed about, myself deformed. You were with me, but I was not with you. Those things kept me far from you which would not exist if they did not exist in you.

You called, you cried aloud, and you broke through my deafness; you flashed, you shone, and you drove away [Col. 0578A] my blindness; you burned, and I drew breath, and now I pant for you; I tasted you, and I hunger and thirst; you touched me, and I was set on fire for your peace.

When I shall cleave to you with my whole self, nowhere will there be pain or labor for me, and my life, wholly full of you, will be alive. But now, because you lift up the one whom you fill, and because I am not full of you, I am a burden to myself. My joys, which ought to be wept over, contend with my sorrows, which ought to be rejoiced over, and I do not know on which side victory stands. My evil sorrows contend with my good joys, and I do not know on which side victory stands.

Alas for me! Lord, have mercy on me. Alas for me! Behold, I do not hide my wounds: you are the physician, I am the sick man; you are merciful, I am wretched.

Is not human life upon earth a trial? Who would want troubles and difficulties? You command that they be endured, not loved. No one loves what he endures, even though he loves to endure it; for although he rejoices that he is enduring, he would nevertheless prefer that there were nothing for him to endure.

Amid adversities I desire prosperity; amid prosperities I fear adversity. What middle ground is there between these, where human life is not a trial? Woe, woe, and again woe to the prosperity of the world, because of fear of adversity and the corruption of joy! Woe, woe, and a third time woe to the adversity of the world, because of the desire for prosperity—and because adversity itself is harsh, lest it break endurance.

Is not human life upon earth a trial without any interval? And my entire hope lies only in your exceedingly great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will.

You command us to practise continence. “And when I knew,” someone said, “that no one can be continent unless God grants it, this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was.” For through continence we are gathered and brought back into unity, from which we had flowed out into many things: for he loves you less who loves something with you that he does not love for your sake.

O love that always burns and is never extinguished, love, my God, kindle me. You command continence: give what you command, and command what you will.

Certainly you command that I abstain from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition. You commanded abstinence from sexual intercourse and, concerning marriage itself, you advised something better than what you permitted. And because you granted it, it came to pass, even before I became a minister of your sacrament. Yet the images of such things still live in my memory, about which I have said much, images that my habit has fixed there. They confront me while I am awake, without force; but in dreams they confront me not only to the point of pleasure, [Col. 0578D] but even to the point of consent and something very like the act itself. So powerful is the illusion of the image in my soul and in my flesh that, when I am asleep, false appearances persuade me of what true appearances cannot persuade me when I am awake.

Am I not then, Lord my God? And yet how great is the difference between myself and myself within the moment in which I pass from waking into sleep, or pass back from sleep into waking! Where then is prayer [variant: “reason”], by which one resists such suggestions while awake? And if the things themselves are introduced, I remain unshaken? Is reason shut up when the eyes are closed? Does it fall asleep together with the bodily senses? And why is it that often even in dreams we resist, remembering our resolve and remaining most chastely faithful to it, giving no assent to such allurements? And yet the difference is so great that when the opposite happens, upon waking we return to the rest of conscience, and in the very difference we discover that we did not do what nevertheless we grieve to have somehow taken place in us.

Is not your hand powerful, almighty God, to heal all the sicknesses of my soul and, by your more abundant grace, to extinguish even the wanton movements of my body? You will increase your gifts in me more and more, Lord, so that my soul may follow me to you, freed from the sticky snare of desire; so that it may not be rebellious against itself; and so that even in sleep it may not merely refrain from committing these disgraceful acts of corruption through animal images, even to the emission of the flesh, but may not even consent to them. For that no such thing, however slight, should give pleasure—so slight that it could be restrained by a mere act of the will—even in the chaste affection of one who sleeps, is not difficult for the Almighty, who can do more than we ask and understand.

Yet for now I have told my good Lord what I still am in this form of my evil, rejoicing with trembling in what you have granted me, and mourning over what in me remains unfinished, hoping that you will complete your mercies in me, until there is full peace, which my inward and outward parts will possess with you when death has been swallowed up in victory.

There is another evil of the day—would that it were enough for the day! We restore the daily ruin of the body by eating and drinking, before you destroy food and stomach, when you kill my need by wondrous satisfaction and clothe this corruptible nature with everlasting incorruption.

But for now necessity is pleasant to me, and against this pleasantness I struggle, lest I be captured by it. I wage a daily battle, more often in fasts, bringing my body into subjection; and my pains are driven away by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are certain pains: they burn and, like fever, kill unless the medicine of nourishment comes to their aid. Since that medicine is at hand, through the consolation of your gifts, in which earth, water, and heaven serve our weakness, calamities are called delights.

You have taught me to approach food as I would medicines. But while I pass from the distress of need to the repose of satisfaction, in that very passage the snare of desire lies in wait for me. For the passage itself is pleasurable, and there is no other way by which one may pass to what necessity compels one to seek. And although health is the reason for eating and drinking, a dangerous pleasure joins itself to it like a handmaid, and very often tries to go first, so that what I say or wish to do for the sake of health may instead be done for its sake.

The measure of the two is not the same. What is sufficient for health is too little for pleasure; and often it becomes uncertain whether the body’s necessary care is still asking for support, or whether the deceit of luxurious desire is supplying its service. At this uncertainty the unhappy soul smiles, and prepares in it a defense of excuse, rejoicing that what is enough for the moderation of health does not appear, so that under the pretext of health it may conceal the business of pleasure.

I try daily to resist these temptations, and I call upon your right hand for my salvation, and I bring my agitations concerning this matter back to you, because I have not yet reached a settled judgment about it. I hear the voice of my commanding God: “Let not your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness.” Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, so that it may not approach me. But gluttony sometimes steals upon your servant; you will have mercy, so that it may be far from me.

No one can be continent unless you grant it. You grant many things to us when we pray, and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from you. And we received this from you also, so that later we might recognize it.

I was never a drunkard, but I know drunkards whom you have made sober. Therefore it was your doing that those who had never been drunk were not drunk; it was your doing that those who had been drunk were not always drunk; and it was also your doing that both groups might know from whom it was done.

I heard another word of yours: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your will.” I also heard, by your gift—a saying I have loved greatly—“Neither shall we abound if we eat, nor shall we lack if we do not eat.” This means: “Neither will the one thing make me wealthy, nor the other wretched.”

I heard another saying: “I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am; I know how to abound and how to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” Behold the soldier of the heavenly camp—not dust, as we are. Yet remember, Lord, that we are dust; from dust you made the human being, and he had perished and was found.

Nor could that man do anything by his own strength, since he too was dust—the man whose words, spoken under the breath of your inspiration, I loved: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” Strengthen me, so that I may be able; give what you command, and command what you will. He confesses that he received, and “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

I heard another person asking to receive: “Take away from me,” he said, “the desires of the belly.” From this it is clear, my holy God, that you grant what you command to be done when it is done.

You taught me, good Father: “To the pure all things are pure,” but that it is evil for a person to eat through giving offense; and that every creature of yours is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving. And because food does not commend us to God; and so that no one may judge us in food or drink; and so that the one who eats may not despise the one who does not eat, nor the one who does not eat judge the one who eats.

I have learned these things. Thanks be to you; praise be to you, my God, my teacher, my awakener of the ears, my illuminator of the heart. Deliver me from every temptation.

I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh suitable for food; that Elijah was restored by food of flesh; and that John, endowed with marvelous abstinence, was not polluted by animals—namely, locusts—being made his food.

And I know that Esau was deceived by his desire for lentils; that David reproved himself because of his desire for water; and that our King was tempted not by meat but by bread. Therefore the people in the wilderness deserved condemnation not because they desired meat, but because, through desire for food, they murmured against the Lord.

Placed amid these temptations, I fight daily against the desire to eat and drink. For I cannot decide once and for all to cut it off and never again approach it, as I was able to do concerning sexual intercourse. Therefore the reins of the throat must be held through a measured loosening and tightening. And who, Lord, is not carried somewhat beyond the limits of necessity? Whoever that person is, he is great; let him magnify your name. But I am not that person, because I am a sinful human being. Nevertheless, I too magnify your name; and the one who conquered the world intercedes with you for my sins, counting me among the weak members of his body, because your eyes saw its unfinished state, and in your book all will be written.

I am not excessively concerned about the allure of scents. When they are absent, I do not seek them; when they are present, I do not reject them, and I am always prepared to do without them. So I seem to myself—perhaps I am deceived. For these too are darknesses that ought to be mourned, in which my capacity, which is in me, is hidden from me. Thus my soul, questioning itself about its own strength, thinks that it should not easily trust itself, because what is present in it is often hidden unless experience reveals it. No one ought to be secure in this life, which is wholly called a trial, as to whether one who could become better from worse might not also become worse from better.

One hope, one confidence, one firm promise: your mercy.

The pleasures of the ears had ensnared and subjected me more tenaciously, but you loosened and freed me. In the sounds now animated by your words, when they are sung with a sweet and artful voice, I confess that I rest somewhat—not indeed so as to cling to them, but so as to rise when I wish. Yet together with the very meanings by which they live, when they seek admission to me, they ask for a place of some dignity in my heart, and I scarcely grant them one that is fitting.

Sometimes I seem to myself to give them more honor than is proper, when I feel that our souls are moved more religiously and more ardently into the flame of devotion by those holy words when they are sung in this way than when they are not sung in this way; and that all the affections of our spirit, according to their diversity, have their own modes in voice and song, by some hidden familiarity with which they are aroused.

But the pleasure of my flesh, which must not be allowed to weaken the mind, often deceives me, when reason does not follow the sense in such a way that the sense patiently remains behind, but, merely because it has deserved admission on account of reason, also tries to run ahead and lead. Thus I sin in these matters without realizing it, and only afterward realize it.

Sometimes, however, in guarding against this very deception too immoderately, I err through excessive severity. At times I even wish that all the melody of sweet songs with which the Psalter of David is frequently sung might be removed from my ears and from those of the Church. And safer seems to me what I remember having often been told about Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: he made the reader sound the Psalm with so slight a modulation of the voice that it was closer to speaking than to singing.

Nevertheless, when I remember the tears I shed at the songs of your Church during the early days of the recovery of my faith, and when now I myself am moved—not by the singing, but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and entirely appropriate modulation—I again acknowledge the great usefulness of this practice. Thus I fluctuate between the danger of pleasure and the experience of its beneficial effect, and I am inclined—though I do not pronounce an irrevocable judgment—to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the delight of the ears the weaker spirit may rise into an affection of devotion.

Yet whenever it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I sin in a manner deserving punishment, and then I would rather not hear the singer.

Behold where I am. Weep with me, and weep for me, you who are inwardly engaged with me in some good work, from which actions proceed. For those who are not so engaged are not moved by these things. But you, Lord my God, hear me, look upon me, see me, have mercy, and heal me—in whose eyes I have become a question to myself, and that question is my sickness.

There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, concerning which I shall speak confessions for the ears of your temple, fraternal and devout ears, so that we may conclude the temptations of the lust of the flesh, which still assail me as I groan and desire to put on over my dwelling the habitation that is from heaven.

The eyes love beautiful and varied forms, bright and pleasing colors. Let these things not possess my soul; let God possess it, he who made them. They are indeed very good, but he himself is my good, not they. They touch me while I am awake throughout the days, and I am given no rest from them, as I am sometimes given rest from melodious voices—from all of them, in silence.

For this light itself, queen of colors, flooding all that we see, wherever I may be during the day, caresses me with manifold approach while I am occupied with something else and do not attend to it. Yet it insinuates itself so powerfully that, if it is suddenly withdrawn, it is sought with longing; and if it is absent for a long time, it saddens the mind.

O light, which Tobias saw when, with his eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life and went before him with the foot of charity, never straying; or which Isaac saw when, his bodily eyes weighed down and covered by old age, he merited to bless his sons by not recognizing them, and to recognize them by blessing them; or which Jacob saw when, himself blinded by great age, he radiated in his luminous heart the kinds of the future people marked out in his sons, and placed his hands mystically crossed upon the sons of Joseph—not as their father corrected them outwardly, but as Jacob himself discerned inwardly.

That is the light; it is one, and all who see and love it are one.

But this bodily light of which I was speaking, with its alluring and dangerous sweetness, seasons the life of the world for blind lovers. Yet those who know how to praise you even for it, God, creator of all things, take it up in your hymn; they are not taken up by it into its sleep, as I desire to be. I resist the seductions of the eyes, lest they entangle the feet with which I walk along your way, and I raise invisible eyes to you, so that you may draw my feet out of the snare.

You continually draw them out, for they are continually ensnared. You do not cease drawing them out, while I frequently become caught in the snares scattered everywhere, because you neither slumber nor sleep, you who guard Israel.

How innumerable are the things human beings have added, through various arts and crafts, in garments, shoes, vessels, and manufactures of this kind; also in paintings and different objects fashioned beyond what is necessary and moderate for use and beyond pious symbolism—all for the allurements of the eyes. They pursue outwardly what they make, while inwardly abandoning the one by whom they were made, and destroying what they were made to be.

But I, my God and my glory, sing a hymn to you even concerning this, and offer a sacrifice of praise to my Sacrificer. How beautiful are the things that, conveyed through souls into the hands of craftsmen, come from that beauty which is above souls, to which my soul sighs day and night. Yet the makers and pursuers of outward beauties draw from that source the standard by which they are approved, but do not draw from it the proper manner of using them. It is there, and they do not see it, so that they may not go farther, but preserve their strength for you and not scatter it into pleasurable exhaustion.

But while I speak and discern these things, I too entangle my steps among these beautiful things. Yet you draw me out, Lord; you draw me out, because your mercy is before my eyes.

## CHAPTER VII. [10] On the sacrament of the mediator for the purification of souls; from the same Book X of the *Confessions*, among other passages and at this point

You are the truth presiding over all things; but through my avarice I did not want to lose you, and I wanted to possess falsehood together with you—as no one wants to tell a falsehood in such a way that he himself does not know what the truth is.

And so I lost you, because you do not deign to be possessed together with falsehood. Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Should I have sought the angels? With what prayer, with what sacraments? Many who tried to return to you but were unable to do so by themselves, as I hear, attempted these things and fell into a desire for curious visions, and were judged worthy of illusions.

For, lifted up by the pride of learning, they sought you, thrusting out their breasts rather than striking them; and they brought upon themselves, through the likeness of their heart, powers of this air that conspired with them and shared their pride, so that by magical powers they might be deceived by them. They were seeking a mediator through whom they might be purified, but there was none. For it was the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light, and he greatly enticed proud flesh by the fact that he himself was not clothed in fleshly body. For they were mortal and sinful. But you, Lord, with whom they proudly sought reconciliation, are immortal and without sin.

The mediator between God and human beings had to possess something like God and something like human beings, lest, if he were like human beings in both respects, he should be far from God, or, if like God in both respects, he should be far from human beings, and thus not be a mediator.

That deceitful mediator, through whom, by your hidden judgments, pride deserved to be mocked, has one thing in common with human beings: sin. He wishes to appear to have another thing in common with God, so that, because he is not covered by the mortality of flesh, he may display himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, he shares this with human beings, so that together he may be condemned to death.

But the true mediator, whom your hidden mercy revealed to the humble and whom you sent so that, by his example, they might also learn humility itself—that mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ—appeared among mortal sinners and the immortal righteous: mortal with human beings, righteous with God. Thus, since the wages of righteousness are life and peace, through the righteousness joined to God he might abolish the death of those justified from ungodliness, a death which he chose to share with them.

He was revealed to the holy people of ancient times, so that they might be saved by faith in his future passion, just as we are saved by faith in his past passion. Insofar as he was human, he was a mediator; but insofar as he was the Word, he was not a mediator, because he was equal to God, God with God, and at the same time one God.

How you loved us, good Father, who did not spare your only Son, but delivered him up for us ungodly people! How you loved us, for whose sake he, although equal to you, did not regard equality with you as something to be grasped, but became subject even to death on a cross!

He alone among the dead was free, having authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again; for us both victor and victim, and therefore victor because victim; for us priest and sacrifice to you, and therefore priest because sacrifice; making us from slaves into sons, by being born from you and serving us.

With good reason my hope in him is firm: that you will heal all my sicknesses through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us. Otherwise I would despair. For my sicknesses are many and great, many and great indeed; but your medicine is greater.

We might have thought that your Word was removed from union with humanity and despaired of ourselves, unless he had become flesh and dwelt among us.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the same sacrament; from Book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 15

All human beings, so long as they are mortal, must also necessarily be wretched. A mediator must be sought who is not only human but also God, so that the blessed mortality of this mediator, intervening, may lead human beings from mortal wretchedness to blessed immortality.

He had to become mortal, but he ought not to remain mortal. He became mortal not through the weakening of the Word’s divinity, but by assuming the weakness of flesh. He did not remain mortal in that flesh, however, for he raised it from the dead. This is the fruit of his mediation: that those for whose liberation he became mediator might not themselves remain forever in the death of the flesh.

Therefore the mediator between us and God had to possess both a mortality that passes away and a blessedness that remains, so that through what passes away he might correspond to those who are dying, and transfer them from the dead to what remains.

Accordingly, the good angels cannot be mediators between wretched mortals and blessed immortals, because they too are both blessed and immortal. The evil angels, however, can be intermediaries, because they are immortal with the former but wretched with the latter.

Opposed to them is the good mediator, who, against their immortality and wretchedness, both willed for a time to be mortal and was able to remain blessed for eternity. Thus, by the humility of his death and the beneficence of his blessedness, he destroyed those proud immortals and harmful wretches in the persons whose hearts he cleansed through faith in himself, freeing them from those evil powers’ utterly unclean domination; thus they might not, by their boast of immortality, seduce them into wretchedness.

A mortal and wretched human being, therefore, separated by a great distance from immortals and the blessed: what mediator should he choose, through whom he might be joined to immortality and blessedness? That which can give delight in the demons’ immortality is wretchedness; that which could give offense in Christ’s mortality no longer exists. There, therefore, everlasting wretchedness must be avoided; here, death is not to be feared, since it could not be everlasting; and everlasting blessedness is to be loved.

For an immortal and wretched mediator places himself between us and the goal in order to prevent us from passing to blessed immortality, since what hinders us—the wretchedness itself—continues to exist. But a mortal and blessed mediator placed himself between us and the goal so that, once mortality had passed away, he might make immortals from the dead, as he demonstrated by rising again, and make the wretched blessed, from which state he himself never departed.

Thus there is one evil mediator, who separates friends, and another good one, who reconciles enemies. There are therefore many mediators who separate, because the multitude that is blessed becomes blessed through participation in the one God; and through deprivation of that participation, the wretched multitude of evil angels—which opposes itself as an impediment rather than interposes itself as an aid to blessedness—also somehow obstructs the multitude, preventing it from reaching that one who makes blessed.

To bring us to this one, we needed not many mediators but one. And this one is himself the one through participation in whom we are blessed: the Word of God, not made, through whom all things were made. Yet he is not a mediator for this reason—for he is the Word. The Word, supremely blessed, is far from wretched mortals; but he is mediator insofar as he is human, thereby showing that no other mediators should be sought through whom we might imagine that stages of approach must be constructed for us. The blessed and beatifying God, having become a participant in our humanity, provided a short path by which we might participate in his divinity.

[11] For, in liberating us from mortality and wretchedness, he does not lead us to immortal and blessed angels in such a way that, by participating in them, we too become immortal and blessed, but to that Trinity in whose participation the angels also are blessed. Therefore, when he wished to be below the angels in the form of a servant, so that he might be a mediator, he remained above the angels in the form of God.

The same one is the way of life in what is below, and life itself in what is above.

For it is not true that, as that Platonist says Plato said, “No god mingles with a human being,” and that the chief sign of their loftiness is that they are not contaminated by any contact with human beings. Thus he admits that demons are contaminated, and for that reason they cannot cleanse those by whom they are contaminated; and all become unclean together—demons through contact with human beings, and human beings through the worship of demons.

## CHAPTER IX. On miracles performed by magical arts; from Book III of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7
Here I see what might occur to a weak mind: namely, why these miracles are also performed by magical arts. For the magicians of Pharaoh likewise made serpents and other similar things. But this too is even more astonishing: how the power of the magicians, which was able to make serpents, failed completely when it came to the tiniest flies. For *sciniphes* are very small gnats, by which the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague. There, certainly, when they failed, the magicians said: “This is the finger of God.” From this it may also be understood that not even the transgressing angels themselves, and the aerial powers—who were thrust down from the habitation of that lofty ethereal purity into manifest darkness [Ed. Ben.: “into this lowest darkness”], as into a prison of their own kind—can accomplish anything through magical arts, whatever they can do, unless power has been granted from above.

This power is granted either for deceiving the deceitful, as it was granted to the Egyptians and even to the magicians themselves, so that they might appear wondrous through the seduction of wicked spirits—wondrous to those by whom these things were performed, but condemned by the truth of God; or for admonishing the faithful not to desire to do anything of that sort as a great achievement, which is why these things too have been handed down to us by the authority of Scripture; or for exercising, testing, and displaying the patience of the righteous. For the power of visible miracles is not small. Job lost everything he possessed, his children, and even the health of his body.

Yet it must not for that reason be thought that this material of visible things serves those transgressing angels at their command, but rather that it serves God, by whom this power is granted to the extent that he judges unchangeably from his lofty and spiritual seat. For even water, fire, and earth serve condemned wicked men, so that they may make from them whatever they wish—but only insofar as they are permitted. Nor, surely, should those wicked angels be called creators, because through them the magicians resisting God’s servant made frogs and serpents; for they themselves did not create them.

Indeed, hidden seeds of all things that are born bodily and visibly lie concealed in the bodily elements of this world. Some are already conspicuous to our eyes, arising from fruits and living creatures; others are the hidden seeds of those seeds. Thus, when the Creator commanded, water first brought forth swimming creatures and flying creatures, while earth first brought forth sprouts of its own kind and animals of its own kind.

For these offspring were not then produced in such a way that the power by which they were produced was exhausted in them. Rather, suitable opportunities for combinations and conditions are often lacking, by which they burst forth and complete their forms. Consider: a very small shoot is a seed, for when suitably entrusted to the earth it produces a tree. But the subtler seed of this shoot is a grain of the same kind—and up to this point it is visible to us. The seed of this grain, however, although we cannot see it with our eyes, we can nevertheless infer by reason; for unless there were some such power in these elements, things not sown there would not often grow from the earth.

Nor would so many animals be born, without the prior union of males and females, whether on land or in water—animals that nevertheless grow and, by coupling, produce others, although they themselves arose from parents that had not coupled. Certainly bees do not conceive the seeds of their offspring by coupling; rather, they gather them with their mouths as though they had been scattered across the earth.

The creator of invisible seeds is himself the creator of all things. For whatever emerges into our eyes by being born receives from hidden seeds the beginnings of its development, the increases appropriate to its size, and the distinctions of its forms from its original patterns, as though from rules.
