Thus, just as we do not call parents the creators of human beings, nor farmers the creators of crops—although God’s power works inwardly to create these things through the outward movements they apply—so it is not lawful to think that either wicked or good angels are creators, if, on account of the subtlety of their senses and bodies, they know seeds of these things that are more hidden from us, and secretly scatter them through suitable combinations of the elements, thereby providing opportunities for things to be generated and for their growth to be accelerated.

Neither do the good angels do these things except insofar as God commands; nor do the wicked do them unjustly except insofar as he justly permits them. For the wicked possess an unjust will through their wickedness, but they receive power only justly—whether for their own punishment, or for the punishment of others who are wicked, or for the praise of those who are good.

Accordingly, the Apostle distinguishes between God, who creates and forms inwardly, and the works of the creature that are applied outwardly. Taking an example from agriculture, he says: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth.”

Thus, just as in our own life God alone can form the mind by justifying it, while people can preach the Gospel outwardly—not only the good through truth, but also the wicked through opportunity—so God works inwardly in the creation of visible things. He employs the external operations of good or wicked angels, human beings, or even any animals, according to his command and the distributions of powers and desires for useful things that he has granted, applying them to the nature of things in which he creates everything, just as one applies agriculture to the earth.

Therefore I cannot say that wicked angels, called forth by magical arts, were the creators of the frogs and serpents, any more than I can say that wicked human beings are the creators of the crops which I see springing up through their labor. Nor was Jacob the creator of the colors in the flocks because, while the mothers were drinking at the time of conception, he placed before them variegated rods for them to look at.

Nor were the sheep themselves creators of the variation in their offspring, because a differently colored mental image had been impressed upon their souls through their eyes by the sight of the varied rods. This image could affect only the body that was animated by a spirit disposed in that way, through the sympathetic interaction of the union, so that the tender beginnings of the offspring were sprinkled with color.

For the appropriate principles by which soul is affected by body, or body by soul, so that they are affected in this way from themselves, live unchangeably in the very highest Wisdom of God. No spatial distances contain that Wisdom; and although it is itself unchangeable, it abandons none of the things that are changeable, because nothing of them was created except through it.

Thus, for sheep—not rods—to be born from sheep, the unchangeable and invisible principle of God’s Wisdom accomplished this, through which all things were created. But for the color of the sheep conceived from the varied rods to derive something from that variation, this was accomplished by the soul of the pregnant sheep, outwardly affected through the eyes and inwardly drawing, according to its capacity, the formative pattern that it had received from the innermost power of its Creator.

But how great is the power of the soul to affect and alter bodily matter, although it cannot be called the creator of the body—for every cause of changeable and perceptible substance, and every measure, number, and weight by which it comes to be and is of one nature or another, proceeds from the intelligible and unchangeable life that is above all things and reaches down to the lowest and earthly things—is a lengthy subject and not necessary here.

I have mentioned what happened with Jacob’s sheep for this reason: so that it might be understood that if the man who placed those rods in that manner cannot be called the creator of the colors in the lambs and kids, and if not even the souls of the mothers can be called creators—souls that, insofar as nature allowed, sprinkled the bodily seeds conceived with flesh with the variation imagined through the eyes of the body—then wicked angels can much less be called the creators of frogs and serpents, through whom the magicians of Pharaoh at that time performed those things.

## CHAPTER X. On the original causes of natural creatures that the Creator implanted in the world, from Book III of *On the Trinity*, title 8

But with regard to animals, as though a different principle were involved because they possess the spirit of life, together with the sensation of desiring what is natural and avoiding what is contrary to nature, one may also observe how many people know from which herbs, meats, or juices and fluids of whatever kind—placed in this way, buried in that way, crushed in another way, or mixed in yet another way—certain animals usually arise. Who would be so insane as to dare call himself their author?

What wonder is it, then, if, just as any utterly wicked human being can know from what substances particular worms and flies arise, so wicked angels, on account of the subtlety of their senses, know in the more hidden seeds of the elements from what sources frogs and serpents arise, and, by applying these through hidden movements at definite and recognized opportunities for combining them, cause them to be created rather than creating them?

People are not astonished by those things that people commonly produce. If someone happens to be astonished at the speed of their growth, because those animals were made so quickly, let him consider how even these things are brought about by human beings, according to the measure of human ability. Why do the same bodies become worm-infested more quickly in summer than in winter, and more quickly in warmer places than in colder ones?

These processes are applied by human beings with greater difficulty precisely because they lack subtle senses and mobility of body in their earthly and sluggish limbs. It is therefore easier for whatever angels there may be to draw proximate causes from the elements; consequently, their speed in such operations appears all the more astonishing. Yet the creator is no one except the one who forms these things originally. No one can do this except the one with whom, in the first place, are the measures, numbers, and weights of all that exists.

He alone is the one Creator, God, through whose ineffable power it also happens that, although these angels could do something if they were permitted, they cannot do it because they are not permitted. For no other explanation presents itself for why those who made frogs and serpents could not make the tiniest flies, except that the greater dominion of God, who prohibited them, was present through the Holy Spirit. The magicians themselves also confessed this when they said: “This is the finger of God.”

But what they can do by nature, yet cannot do because of prohibition, and what they are prevented from doing by the very condition of their nature, is difficult—indeed impossible—for a human being to investigate except through that gift of God which the Apostle mentions when he says: “To another, the discernment of spirits.”

We know that a human being can walk, yet cannot do even that if he is not permitted; but he cannot fly, even if he is permitted. So too those angels can do certain things if they are permitted by more powerful angels, acting under God’s command. But there are other things they cannot do even if they are permitted by those angels, because the one from whom they received the limits of their nature does not permit them. Through his angels he often does not permit even those things that he has granted them power to do.

## CHAPTER XI. On the single death of our Savior, which corresponds and harmonizes with our twofold death, from Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3

But what is presently required must be explained, insofar as God grants the ability: how the single death of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ corresponds and, in a certain way, harmonizes with our twofold death for salvation.

We are certainly—something no Christian doubts—dead both in soul and in body: in soul because of sin, in body because of the punishment of sin, and thus also in body because of sin. Both aspects of our condition, therefore—that is, both soul and body—required healing and resurrection, so that what had been changed for the worse might be renewed for the better.

The death of the soul is impiety, while the death of the body is corruptibility, through which the soul’s departure from the body also takes place. For just as the body dies when the soul abandons it, so the soul dies when God abandons it. The latter then becomes senseless, the former lifeless.

The soul is therefore raised through repentance, and while the body is still mortal the renewal of life begins through faith, by which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly. It is increased and strengthened by good conduct from day to day, as the inward person is renewed more and more.

But the body, as the outward person, becomes increasingly corrupt the longer this life lasts, whether through age, disease, or various afflictions, until it reaches the final state that human beings call death. Its resurrection is deferred until the end, when our own justification will also be completed ineffably.

Then we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. But now, as long as the body that is subject to corruption weighs down the soul, and human life upon the earth is entirely a time of testing, “no living person shall be justified in his sight” when compared with the righteousness by which we shall be made equal to the angels, and with the glory that will be revealed in us.

Why should I say more about the death of the soul, which must be distinguished from the death of the body, when the Lord, in an evangelical saying, set forth both deaths in a way that anyone can easily distinguish? He said: “Let the dead bury their own dead.” The dead body had to be buried; but he wanted those who buried it to be understood as dead in soul through the unbelief of impiety. Such people are raised when it is said: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

The Apostle also condemns a certain kind of death when he says of a widow: “But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.”

Thus the soul that was once impious but has now become devout is said, because of the righteousness of faith, to have risen from death and to be alive. The body, however, is not only destined to die through the departure of the soul that will occur, but, because of the great weakness of flesh and blood, is also called “dead” in a certain passage of Scripture, where the Apostle says: “The body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

This life has been brought about through faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith.” But what follows? “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.”¹³

Our Savior therefore applied his single death to our twofold death, and, in order to bring about our twofold resurrection, set forth and presented his one resurrection both sacramentally and as an example.

For he was neither a sinner nor impious, so that, like one dead in spirit, he would need to be renewed in the inner person and recalled to the life of righteousness as though by repentance. Rather, clothed in mortal flesh—which alone died and alone rose again—through that flesh alone he corresponded with both aspects of our condition: in it he became the sacrament of the inner person and the example of the outer person.

For the sacrament of our inner person was given in the words signifying the death of our soul, not only in the psalm but also on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” To this saying the Apostle’s words correspond: “Knowing that our old person was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin.”

The crucifixion of the inner person signifies the pains of repentance and a certain healthy anguish of self-restraint, through which the death of impiety is put to death—the death in which God did not abandon us. Therefore, through such a cross, the body of sin is destroyed, so that we no longer present our members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin.

For the inner person, if indeed it is renewed from day to day, was certainly old before it was renewed. Within us takes place what the same Apostle says: “Strip off the old person and put on the new,” which he then explains as follows: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth.”

Where is falsehood put away except within, so that one may dwell in the holy mountain of God, speaking truth in one’s heart?

The Lord’s bodily resurrection is shown to pertain to the sacrament of our inner resurrection when, after rising, he said to the woman: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” This mystery corresponds to the Apostle’s words: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above.”

Not to touch Christ until he has ascended to the Father means not to understand Christ in a carnal manner.

The death of the Lord’s flesh, however, pertains to the example of the death of our outward person. Through such suffering he especially encouraged his servants not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Hence the Apostle says: “That I may complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ.”

The Lord’s bodily resurrection is also found to pertain to the example of the resurrection of our outward person, for he said to his disciples: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see me have.” One of the disciples, moreover, touched his scars and exclaimed: “My Lord and my God!” Since the whole integrity of that flesh was visible, there was demonstrated in it what he had said when encouraging his own: “Not a hair of your head will perish.”

Why, then, did he say first, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father”? And why, before he ascended to the Father, was he touched by the disciples? Because in the former case the sacrament of the inner person was being indicated, while in the latter the example of the outer person was being provided.

Would anyone be so absurd and so turned away from the truth as to dare say that men touched him before he ascended, but women touched him after he had ascended?

Because the example of our future bodily resurrection preceded us in the Lord, the Apostle says: “Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who belong to Christ.” That passage concerned the resurrection of the body, for which reason he also says: “He will transform the body of our humiliation to conform to the body of his glory.”

Thus, the one death of our Savior served the salvation of our two deaths, and his one resurrection provided us with two resurrections, since his body, both in death and in resurrection, was given to us through a medicinal correspondence both as the sacrament of our inner person and as the example of our outer person.

## CHAPTER XII. On the devil as mediator to death and Christ Jesus as mediator to life, from the same Book IV

Next he indicates in this way that he himself is the mediator through whom we are reconciled to God: “I in them, and you in me, so that they may be perfected in unity.”

This is true peace and our firm connection with our Creator, once purified and reconciled through the mediator of life, just as, stained and alienated from him, we had departed through the mediator of death.

For just as the proud devil led the proud human being to death, so the humble Christ brought the obedient human being back to life. Just as the devil, exalted, fell and cast down the one who consented to him, so Christ, humbled, rose and raised up the one who believed.

Because the devil had not reached the place to which he had led humanity—for he bore the death of the spirit in impiety but had not undergone the death of the flesh, since he had not assumed flesh—he appeared to human beings as a great prince among the legions of demons through whom he exercises a kingdom of deceit.

By inflating humanity through the arrogance of pride, making it more desirous of power than of justice, or by puffing it up through false philosophy, or by ensnaring it through sacrilegious rites—within which he casts curious and proud souls into the deception and mockery of magical illusions—he keeps humanity subject to himself.

He even promises purification of the soul through those rites which they call *τελεταί* (*teletai*, initiatory rites), transforming himself into an angel of light through his manifold contrivance in signs and lying wonders.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the ease with which unclean spirits deceive human beings through their illusions, from the same Book IV, chapter 11

For wicked spirits can easily accomplish many things through aerial bodies that souls weighed down by earthly bodies—even souls of better disposition—marvel at.

If earthly bodies themselves, modified by certain arts and exercises, display such astonishing feats to human beings in theatrical spectacles that those who have never seen such things can scarcely believe them when they are recounted, what great thing is it for the devil and his angels to accomplish through aerial bodies things at which flesh marvels, using corporeal elements? Or, even through hidden inspirations, to devise images and phantasms in order to mock human senses—phantasms by which they deceive people awake or asleep, or drive them into frenzy?

But if it can happen that a person superior in life and conduct watches utterly wicked people walking on a rope or performing many incredible feats through movements of their bodies, without in any way desiring to do anything of the kind or thinking that such people should therefore be preferred to him, so too a faithful and devout soul—even if it sees, or, because of the weakness of the flesh, shudders at the miracles of demons—will not for that reason either grieve that it cannot perform such things or judge those demons to be better.

This is especially so since, within the fellowship of the saints, there have been human beings and good angels who, through the power of God to whom all things are subject, have performed deeds both free from deception and far greater.

## CHAPTER XIV.¹⁴ On false and deceptive purifications, from the same Book IV

The soul is therefore by no means purified and reconciled to God through sacrilegious imitations, impious curiosities, and magical consecrations. The false mediator does not carry it upward; rather, by occupying the way, he blocks it through the desires that he inspires in his fellowship—desires all the more malign because they are all the more proud.

These desires cannot nourish wings for flying upward through virtues; instead, they increase the weights of vices for sinking downward. The soul will fall more heavily the higher it imagines itself to have been raised.

## CHAPTER XV.¹⁵ On those who promise themselves purification through their own virtue, from the same Book IV

There are those who think that by their own virtue they can be purified so as to contemplate God and cling to God. It is pride itself that chiefly stains them.

No vice is more strongly resisted by divine law, and into none does that most proud spirit—the mediator to the depths and the blocker of the way to the heights—receive a greater right of domination, unless he is overcome by the cross of the Lord, prefigured by Moses with his hands extended, whether he is secretly avoided while lying in ambush by another way, or openly rages through the failing people (which is interpreted Amalek), resisting and denying passage to the promised land.

These people promise themselves purification through their own virtue because some of them have been able to send the edge of their minds beyond every creature and to touch, however slightly, the light of unchangeable truth. They ridicule the many Christians who, meanwhile, live by faith alone and have not yet been able to do this.

But what does it profit the proud person, who for this reason is ashamed to climb the wood, to view from afar the homeland across the sea? Or what harm does it do the humble person not to see it from such a great distance on that wood, while coming toward it on the one by which the proud person disdains to be carried?

## CHAPTER XVI. On the sacrament of the Mediator, on the faith by which we believe events accomplished in time, and on the truth that renders eternal, from Book IV of *On the Trinity*, title 18

Since, therefore, we were not capable of attaining eternal things, and since the filth of sins contracted through love of temporal things weighed us down—sins that had grown into us as though naturally through the propagation of mortality—we had to be purified.

But in order to be purified and brought into harmony with eternal things, we could be purified only through temporal things, since we were already held in conformity with such things. Health is very far removed from illness; but an intermediate treatment does not lead to health unless it corresponds to the illness.

Useless temporal things deceive the sick; useful temporal things are received by those who are to be healed and carry the healed onward to eternal things. Just as the rational mind, once purified, owes contemplation to eternal things, so, while it is being purified, it owes faith to temporal things.

Someone—one of those who were once regarded as wise among the Greeks—said: “As eternity relates to what has come into being, so truth relates to faith.” This is certainly a true statement. For what we call “temporal,” he called “what has come into being”; and we too belong to this class, not only according to the body but also according to the mutability of the soul.

Strictly speaking, what changes in any respect is not called eternal. To the extent that we are mutable, therefore, we are distant from eternity.

Eternal life is promised to us through the truth, from whose clarity our faith is likewise as far removed as mortality is from eternity. Now, therefore, we apply faith to events accomplished temporally for our sake, and through that faith we are cleansed, so that when we come to the vision itself, eternity may succeed mortality just as truth succeeds faith.

Therefore, since our faith will become truth when we arrive at what is promised to us who believe—and eternal life is promised to us—the Truth spoke, not as something that will come to be, as our future faith will, but as the Truth that always is, because eternity is there. The Truth said: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

When our faith becomes truth through seeing, eternity will take possession of our changed mortality.

Until this happens—because we attach the faith of belief to things that have come into being, just as in eternal things we hope for the truth of contemplation—in order that the faith of mortal life might not be discordant with the truth of eternal life, the very Truth, coeternal with the Father, arose from the earth. The Son of God came in such a way that he became the Son of Man, and in himself received our faith, by which he would lead us to his truth. He assumed our mortality without losing his eternity.

As eternity relates to what has come into being, so truth relates to faith.

We therefore had to be purified in such a way that the one who would arise for us, yet remain eternal, might come to be; otherwise one person would be ours in faith and another in truth. Nor could we pass from the fact that we had come into being to eternal things unless, through his becoming in accordance with our condition, the Eternal were joined to us and we were carried over into his eternity.

Thus our faith has in a certain sense followed there where the one in whom we believe ascended after being born, dying, rising again, and being taken up.

Of these four things, we knew the first two in ourselves, for we know that human beings are born and die. We rightly hope that the other two—being raised and being taken up—will also occur in us, because we have believed that they occurred in him.

Therefore, because in him what had come into being passed over into eternity, so too what is ours will pass over when faith reaches truth.

Already, to those who believe, so that they might remain in the word of faith and from there be led to truth and thus to eternity and freed from death, he says: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” And as though they asked what benefit this would bring, he continued: “And you will know the truth.”

Then, as though they said, “What benefit is truth to mortals?” the Truth replied: “And the truth will set you free.” From what, if not from death, corruption, and mutability?

For the immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable Truth remains. True immortality, true incorruptibility, and true unchangeability are themselves eternity.

## CHAPTER XVII. That some testimonies foretold Christ’s coming, while others testified that he had come, from Book IV of *On the Trinity*, title 19

Behold for what purpose the Son of God was sent—or rather, behold what it means for the Son of God to have been sent.

Whatever was accomplished temporally, in order to produce the faith by which we would be cleansed and to contemplate the truth brought forth from eternity in things that came into being and restored to eternity, was either a testimony to this mission or was itself the mission of the Son of God.

But some testimonies foretold that he would come, while others testified that he had come.

It was necessary that the one who became a creature—the one through whom all creatures were made—should have every creature as a witness. For unless the One were proclaimed by many who were sent, the One would not be held to by many who were dismissed; and unless the testimonies were such that great things appeared to the small, people would not believe that the Great One, who was sent to the small, became small in order to make them great.

For the deeds of the Son of God—the heaven, the earth, and everything in them, since all things were made through him—are incomparably greater than the signs and wonders that burst forth as testimonies to him.¹⁵

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the same sacrament of the Mediator, from Book I of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

Since Christ himself is the Wisdom of God through whom all things were created, and since no rational minds, whether of angels or human beings, become wise except through participation in him—and since through the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts, we cling to him, and this Trinity is one God—it was provided by divine providence for mortals whose temporal life was occupied with things that arise and perish that this same Wisdom of God, by assuming a human being into the unity of his person, might be born, live, die, and rise again in time.

Through words and deeds, suffering and endurance appropriate to our salvation, he became below an example for human beings of returning to the one who is above, and to the angels who are above an example of remaining there.

For unless something temporal arose in the nature of the rational soul—that is, unless something began to exist which had not existed—no one would ever pass from a life that was utterly bad and foolish to one that was wise and excellent.

Accordingly, since the truth of those who contemplate is enjoyed in eternal things, while the faith of those who believe is owed to things that have come into being, a human being is purified through faith in temporal things so that he may receive the truth of eternal things.

For Plato, one of their most distinguished philosophers, says in the book they call the *Timaeus*: “As eternity relates to what has come into being, so truth relates to faith.”

Those two things are above: eternity and truth. These two are below: what has come into being and faith. Thus, in order that we may be recalled from the lowest things to the highest, and that what has come into being may receive eternity, we must come to truth through faith.

And because everything that moves toward an opposite is restored through some intermediary, temporal iniquity alienated us from eternal justice. There was therefore need of a temporal mediating justice: temporal in its position among the lowest things, just in its relation to the highest, and thus neither severing itself from the highest nor failing to accommodate the lowest. In this way it would restore the lowest things to the highest.

For this reason Christ is called the Mediator of God and human beings: between the immortal God and mortal humanity, God and human, reconciling humanity to God, remaining what he was and becoming what he was not.

He is our faith in things that have come into being, and he is the truth in eternal things.

This great and unspeakable sacrament, this kingship and priesthood, was revealed to the ancients through prophecy and proclaimed to their descendants through the Gospel. For what had long been promised through one nation had eventually to be bestowed upon all nations.

Therefore the one who sent prophets before his descent also sent apostles after his ascension.

## CHAPTER XVIII bis. The kinds of apostleship and the meaning of the name “apostle”; and how we can know who has been sent by God, from the book *Responses to Orosius*

“An apostle” means “one who has been sent.”

There are four kinds of apostles: sent by God not through a human being; sent by God through a human being; sent through a human being alone; and sent by himself.

Moses was sent by God, not through a human being. Jesus son of Nun was sent by God and through a human being. Those sent through a human being alone are like the many who in our own times have been appointed to the priesthood through popular favor. Those sent by themselves are like the false prophets themselves.

Recognize as sent by God the person whom the praise—or rather the flattery—of a few people does not choose, but whom both an excellent life and character, as well as the conduct of apostolic priests, commend; or even the person who is approved by the judgment of all the peoples, who does not desire to preside, and who does not give money to obtain the honor of the episcopate.

For one of the Fathers aptly described the person who hastens to preside, saying: “Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside rather than to be of benefit.”

## CHAPTER XIX. What Plato might have answered about the Christian religion if he had been questioned while alive, from the book *On True Religion*
I would say with the greatest confidence, while respecting all those who obstinately cherish their books, that there ought to be no doubt which religion is especially to be held in Christian times, and which is the way to truth and blessedness. For if Plato himself were alive and did not disdain to answer me when I questioned him—or rather, if one of his disciples, at the very time when Plato was alive, were to ask him, having been persuaded by him that truth is seen not with bodily eyes but with a pure mind, and that whatever soul had cleaved to it would become blessed and perfect; that nothing impedes its apprehension more than a life given over to lust and the false images of sensible things, which, impressed upon us through the body by this sensible world, generate various opinions and errors; and that the soul must therefore be healed, so that it may behold the unchangeable form of things and the beauty that always remains the same and is everywhere like itself, neither extended through places nor altered by time, but preserving unity and sameness in every respect—a beauty which, although it truly and supremely exists, human beings would not believe to exist, while other things are born, die, flow, and slip away, yet, insofar as they exist through that eternal God, remain established because they were fashioned by his truth—

[Col. 0596A] and in which only the rational and intellectual soul has been granted the capacity to enjoy the contemplation of his eternity, to be affected and adorned by it, and to merit eternal life; but while it is wounded by love and grief for things that are born and pass away, and, devoted to the habits of this life and to the senses of the body, fades away amid vain images (vanescit; variant: evanescit, “vanishes”)., it mocks those who say that something exists which is perceived neither by these eyes nor conceived through any phantasm, but can be seen by mind and understanding alone: if, then, that disciple were persuaded of these things by his teacher and asked him whether, if there were some great and divine man who persuaded peoples to believe such things—at least if they were unable to comprehend them, or if those who could comprehend them, entangled in the multitude’s corrupt opinions, were overwhelmed by popular errors—he would judge that man worthy of divine honors,

[Col. 0596C] he would, I believe, answer that this could not be accomplished by a human being, unless perhaps the very power and wisdom of God had set him apart from the ordinary nature of things and, not through human instruction but through inward illumination, enlightened him from his cradle; unless it had ennobled him with such grace, strengthened him with such steadfastness, and finally raised him up with such majesty that, by despising everything wicked people desire, enduring everything they dread, and doing everything they admire, he would turn the human race toward so salutary a faith with the greatest love and authority. As for his honors, it would be pointless to consult him, since it can easily be judged how great are the honors owed to the Wisdom of God, under whose guidance and governance that man would merit something great and uniquely his own, something surpassing humanity, for the true salvation of the human race.

[Col. 0596D] If these things have indeed been done; if they are celebrated in writings and monuments; if, from one region of the earth where alone one God was worshiped, and where such a man ought to have been born, chosen men were sent throughout the whole world and, by their virtues and words, kindled fires of divine love; if, having established a most salutary discipline, they left the lands illuminated for those who came after; and—to say nothing of the past, which anyone may refuse to believe—if today it is proclaimed among nations and peoples:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

If, for the apprehension, love, and enjoyment of this, so that the soul may be healed and the mind’s vision strengthened to drink in so great a light (lucis; variant: luci),

[Col. 0597A] the following is said to the greedy:

> Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and rust (rubigo; variant: aerugo, “verdigris”) destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also.

It is said to the lustful:

> Whoever sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit.

It is said to the proud:

> Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

It is said to the angry:

> You have received a blow; prepare the other cheek as well.

It is said to the quarrelsome:

> Love your enemies.

It is said to the superstitious:

> The kingdom of God is within you.

It is said to the curious:

> Do not seek what is seen, but what is not seen; for what is seen is temporal, but what is not seen is eternal.

Finally, it is said to everyone:

> Do not love the world, because what is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.

If these things are now read to peoples throughout the whole world and heard with veneration and the greatest delight; if, after so much blood, so many fires, so many crosses of martyrs, the Churches have spread with such greater fertility and abundance even among barbarian nations; if no one is now astonished at the thousands of young men and virgins who despise marriage and live chastely; whereas when Plato did this, he feared the perverse opinion of his age so greatly that he is said to have sacrificed to Nature, as though he had cursed nature, so that that sin might be abolished;

[Col. 0597C] if these things are received in such a way that it would now be as monstrous to argue against them as it once was to argue for them; if Christian sacred observance is handed down throughout all the regions of the earth inhabited by human beings with such a promise and pledge; if these things are read daily in the churches and expounded by the priests; if those who strive to fulfill them beat their breasts; if so countless a number undertake this way that the solitude of once-deserted islands and of many lands is filled with people from every class who, having abandoned the riches and honors of this world, wish to dedicate their whole life to the one supreme God; if, finally, in cities and towns, fortified places, villages, fields, and even private estates, turning away from earthly things and turning toward the one true God is openly urged and desired to such an extent that daily throughout the whole world the human race almost with one voice answers that it has its heart raised upward to God (Deum; variant: Dominum, “the Lord”);

[Col. 0597D] why do we still yawn from yesterday’s debauch and search out divine utterances in dead animals? Yet whenever the time comes for disputation, do we desire to have mouths rattling with the name of Plato rather than a heart filled with truth (vero; variant: vero Deo, “the true God”)?

Those, therefore, who think it foolish or evil to despise this sensible world and to subject the soul, purified by virtue, to the supreme God and join it to him (subjungere; variant: subjugare, “subjugate”) must be refuted in another manner—if, indeed, it is worth disputing with them. But those who confess that this is good and desirable should come to know God and yield (cedant; variant: credant, “believe”) to God, through whom all peoples have now been persuaded that these things ought to be believed. They themselves would have done this, if they had possessed such power; or, if it had not happened, they could not have avoided the charge of envy.

[Col. 0598A] Let them therefore yield to him by whom this has been accomplished (ei a quo; variant: ei et a quo), and let them not be hindered by curiosity or empty vaunting from recognizing the difference between the timid conjectures (timidas; variant: tumidas, “swollen, arrogant”) of a few and the manifest salvation and correction of peoples. For if those men in whom these people glory among human beings were to come back to life and find churches filled, temples deserted, and the human race being summoned and hastening away from desire for temporal and transitory goods toward hope of eternal life and spiritual and intelligible goods, they might say—if they were such as they are reported to have been:

> These are the things we did not dare to persuade peoples to accept; instead, we yielded to their customs rather than bringing them over to our faith and will.

[Col. 0598B] Therefore, if those men [or: “these men”] could live this life again with us, they would certainly see by whose authority it would be easier to provide for human beings, and, with only a few words and opinions changed, they would become Christians, as many Platonists of our own more recent times have done. Or, if they neither confessed nor did this, remaining in pride and envy, I do not know whether, with such filth and sticky mire, they could fly back to those very things which they had said ought to be desired and sought.

As for the third vice, curiosity in consulting demons, by which those pagans with whom we are now dealing are chiefly recalled from Christian salvation—for this is exceedingly childish—I do not know whether such men would be hindered by it. But however the vaunting of the philosophers may stand, this is easy to understand (transmitted cuius; variant: cuivis, “for anyone”): religion is not to be sought from those who accepted the same sacred rites as the peoples, while in their schools, with the same multitude as witness, they loudly proclaimed divergent and contrary opinions about the nature of their gods and the supreme good.

[Col. 0598C] Even if we saw only this one vice healed by Christian discipline, no one ought to deny that it should be proclaimed with ineffable praise. For the countless heresies turned away from the rule of Christianity bear witness that those who think differently about God the Father, his Wisdom, and the divine gift, and try to persuade human beings of views contrary to what truth requires, are not admitted to share the sacraments.

For this is believed and taught—and it is the foundation of human salvation—that there is not one φιλοσοφία, that is, a pursuit of wisdom, and another religion, since those whose teaching we do not approve do not share the sacraments with us. This is less surprising in those who also wished to differ from us in the rite of those sacraments themselves, such as certain people called Serpentines, the Manichaeans, and some others. But it must be observed and proclaimed more emphatically in those who celebrate the same sacraments yet, because they differ in doctrine, preferred to defend their errors more boldly than to correct them more cautiously.

[Col. 0598D] Excluded from catholic communion and participation, they nevertheless deserved, on account of their identical sacraments, to have their own proper names and their own assemblies, not merely in speech but also in superstition—as did the Photinians and the Arians, and many others besides (printed munique, apparently multique). For those who created schisms are a separate question: the Lord’s threshing floor might have sustained them like chaff until the time of the final winnowing, unless they had yielded to the wind of pride with excessive levity and voluntarily separated themselves from us.

The Jews, however, although they pray to the one omnipotent God, nevertheless expect from him only temporal and visible goods. With excessive confidence they refused to recognize, in their own Scriptures, the beginnings of the new people arising from humility, and thus remained in the old man.

[Col. 0599A] Since these things are so, religion is not to be sought either amid the confusion of the pagans, the refuse of the heretics, the weakness of the schismatics, or the blindness of the Jews, but only among those who are called Christian Catholics, or orthodox—that is, guardians of integrity and followers of what is right.

For this Catholic Church, spread powerfully and extensively throughout the whole world, uses all who are in error for its own advancement and for their correction when they wish to awaken. It uses the Gentiles as material for its work, heretics as a test of its doctrine, schismatics as a demonstration of its stability, and Jews as a comparison for its beauty.

[Col. 0599B] It therefore invites some, excludes others, leaves others behind, and surpasses others; yet it grants all the power to share in the grace of God, whether they still need to be formed, reformed, gathered again, or admitted. But its own carnal members—that is, those who live or think carnally—it tolerates like chaff, by which the grain on the threshing floor is kept safer until it is stripped of such coverings.

## CHAPTER XX. How appropriately the Wisdom of God, Christ, came to the aid of human beings through his humanity; likewise from the same book, *On True Religion*

[Col. 0599C] In no way did he provide more benevolently for the human race than when the very Wisdom of God—that is, the only-begotten Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father—deigned to assume the whole human being: “and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Thus he demonstrated to carnal people, who were unable to behold the truth with the mind and were devoted to bodily senses, how exalted a place human nature holds among creatures. He appeared not merely visibly—for that could also have been accomplished in some ethereal body adjusted to the endurance of our sight—but to human beings in a true human being.

[Col. 0599D] For the very nature that was to be liberated had to be assumed. And so that no one of either sex might think that he had been despised by his Creator, he assumed a man, born of a woman.

He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition, although he did drive sellers and buyers from the temple with a whip. Yet what is this, or how much does it amount to, even though he also drove demons unwillingly out of human beings—not by persuasive speech but by the force of his authority?

The old servitude had been brought to an end, and the time of freedom had dawned. It was therefore opportune and salutary to persuade human beings of how they had been created with free choice. He won faith in the God whom he was by his miracles, and in the man whom he bore by his suffering.

[Col. 0600A] Thus, speaking to the crowds as God, he denied that the mother announced to him was his mother; and yet, as the Gospel says, the Child was subject to his parents. In teaching he appeared as God, but in age as a human being.

Likewise, when he was about to change water into wine as God, he said:

> Withdraw from me, woman; what is there between you and me? My hour has not yet come.

But when the hour had come in which, as a human being, he was to die, from the cross he entrusted his acknowledged mother to the disciple whom he loved above the others.

Those who served pleasure greedily desired riches among the people; he chose to be poor. They longed for honors and commands; he refused to become king. Carnal people thought children a great good; he rejected such marriage and offspring. They dreaded insults with the greatest pride; he endured every kind of insult. They considered injuries intolerable; what injury is greater than the condemnation of one who is just and innocent? They cursed bodily pains; he was scourged and tortured. They feared death; he was punished with death. They thought the most disgraceful kind of death was crucifixion; he was crucified.

[Col. 0600B] By abstaining from everything we wrongly desired to possess, he made it worthless. By enduring everything we avoided while pursuing truth, he overthrew it. For no sin can be committed except either while we pursue what he despised or while we flee what he endured.

Thus his entire life on earth, in the human being whom he deigned to assume, was a discipline of morals.

His resurrection from the dead sufficiently showed that nothing of human nature perishes, since all things are safe with God. It also showed how everything serves its Creator, whether for the punishment of sins or for human liberation, and how readily the body serves the soul when the soul itself is subject to God.

When these things have been perfected, not only is no substance evil—for that can never happen—but nothing is afflicted by evil, although through sin and punishment this could happen.

[Col. 0600C] This is the natural discipline: to those Christians who understand little, it is wholly worthy of faith; to those who understand, it is cleansed of every error.

Moreover, the entire method of teaching—partly most explicit, partly expressed through likenesses in words, deeds, and sacraments, and adapted to the instruction and exercise of every soul—what else did it accomplish than the rule of rational discipline?

For the exposition of the mysteries is directed toward those things that have been stated most openly; and if Scripture contained only what is easily understood, truth would neither be sought with diligence nor found with delight. Nor, if there were sacraments in Scripture but no seals of truth in the sacraments, would action sufficiently correspond with knowledge.

[Col. 0600D] But now, since piety begins with fear and is perfected by love, the people, restrained by fear during the time of servitude under the old law, were burdened with many sacraments. This was useful for such people, so that they might desire the grace of God, which the prophets sang would come.

When that grace came through the very Wisdom of God, who assumed humanity and by whom we have been called into freedom, a few most salutary sacraments were established to preserve the fellowship of the Christian people—that is, of the free multitude under one God.

But many practices imposed upon the Hebrew people—that is, upon the fettered multitude under that same one God—were removed from action and remained in faith and interpretation. Thus now they no longer bind the soul in servitude, but exercise the mind freely.

## CHAPTER XXI. He reproves the pleasure-loving, the curious, and the proud; from the same book, *On True Religion*

[Col. 0601A]

I deny that there is anyone among those who think that nothing ought to be worshiped who is not either subject to bodily pleasures, fostering empty power, or driven mad by delight in some spectacle.

They love temporal things so ignorantly that they seek blessedness from them. Yet everyone must serve the things by which he wishes to become blessed, willingly or unwillingly. Wherever they lead, he follows; and whoever seems able to take them away is feared.

But these things can be taken away—even by a spark of fire or some tiny creature. Finally, to omit countless adversities, time itself must take away everything transitory.

[Col. 0601B] Since this world contains all temporal things, therefore those who think that nothing ought to be worshiped lest they become servants serve every part of the world.

Nevertheless, although they lie wretched at the lowest extremity of these affairs, permitting their vices to rule them—condemned by lust, pride, or curiosity, or by two of these, or by all three—as long as they are in this arena of human life, they may struggle and conquer, if they first believe what they are not yet able to understand and do not love the world.

For everything that is in the world, as has been divinely said, is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.

In this way those three things have been marked out. The desire of the flesh signifies lovers of the lowest pleasure; the desire of the eyes, the curious; the ambition of the age, the proud.

[Col. 0601C] A threefold temptation was also shown to be guarded against in the human being whom Truth itself assumed.

“Tell these stones,” says the tempter, “to become loaves.” The one and only Teacher says to him [variant: “but he says to him”]:

> Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.

Thus he taught that the appetite for pleasure must be subdued, so that one must not yield even to hunger.

But perhaps he who could not be overcome by bodily pleasure could be deceived by the arrogance of temporal dominion. Therefore all the kingdoms of the world were shown to him, and it was said:

> I will give you all these things if you fall down and worship me.

He answered:

> You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.

[Col. 0601D] Thus pride was trampled down.

The final enticement of curiosity was also subjected. For the tempter urged him to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple solely to make a trial of something. Yet here too he was not defeated, and he answered in such a way that we might understand that, in order to know God, there is no need to investigate the divine visibly by attempts made through temptations:

> You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

Therefore, whoever is inwardly nourished by the word of God does not seek pleasure in this wilderness. Whoever is subject to the one God alone does not seek vaunting on the mountain—that is, in earthly exaltation. Whoever clings to the eternal spectacle of unchangeable truth is not hurled down through the pinnacle of this body—that is, through these eyes—in order to know temporal and inferior things.

## CHAPTER XXII. That it is better to be overcome by a human being than by a vice; from the same book, *On True Religion*

[Col. 0602A]

We labor on earth, and with great disgrace we are overcome by everything capable of moving and disturbing us. Thus we do not wish to be overcome by human beings, yet we cannot overcome anger. What could be said to be more detestable than this disgrace?

We admit that another human being is what we are, though even if he has vices, he himself is not a vice. How much more honorably, then, does a human being overcome us than envy—or than any vice?

Who could doubt that envy is a monstrous vice? The person who does not wish to be overcome in temporal matters must be tortured and subjected by it.

It is therefore better for a human being to overcome us than for envy, or for any other vice. Yet the person who has overcome his vices cannot be overcome even by a human being. For no one is overcome unless his adversary takes away what he loves.

[Col. 0602B] Whoever therefore loves only what cannot be taken away from one who loves it is unquestionably invincible, and no envy torments him. He loves what ought to be loved and apprehended; the more people come to possess it, the more abundantly he rejoices with them.

For he loves God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind; and he loves his neighbor as himself. He therefore does not envy his neighbor, so that the neighbor may be what he himself is; indeed, he helps him as much as he can.

Nor can he lose the neighbor whom he loves as himself, because he does not love in himself those things that are subject to the eyes or to any other bodily senses. Therefore he possesses within himself the one whom he loves as himself.

The rule of love is that whatever one wishes to come to oneself as good, one should wish to come to the other; and whatever evil one does not wish to happen to oneself, one should not wish to happen to the other.

[Col. 0602C] He preserves this will toward all human beings, for no evil ought to be done to anyone, and love of neighbor does no evil.

Let us therefore love even our enemies, as we have been commanded, if we truly wish to be invincible. No human being is invincible through himself, but through that unchangeable law. Those who serve it alone are free; for what they love cannot be taken away from them. This one thing makes men invincible and perfect.

But if one human being loves another not as himself but as he loves a beast of burden, a bathhouse, or a painted or chattering little bird—that is, in order to obtain from him some temporal pleasure or advantage—he must serve not the human being but, what is more disgraceful, that foul and detestable vice by which he does not love a human being as a human being ought to be loved. While that vice rules him, he is led on to the extreme limit of life, or rather to death.

[Col. 0602D] Yet even in this way a human being must not be loved as carnal brothers, children, spouses, relatives, connections, or fellow citizens are loved, for this love too is temporal.

Therefore Truth itself, calling us back to our original and perfect nature, commands us to resist carnal custom. It teaches that no one is suited for the kingdom of God who does not hate these carnal relationships.

Nor should this seem inhuman to anyone. It is rather inhuman not to love in a human being what is human, but to love what is a son. For this is not to love in him what belongs to God, but to love what belongs to oneself.

Why, then, is it surprising that one does not reach the kingdom who loves not what is common but what is private? “Both,” someone might say. “Rather, the one,” God says.

For Truth says most truly:

> No one can serve two masters.

No one can perfectly love the destination to which we are called unless he hates the place from which we are recalled.

[Col. 0603A] We are called to the perfect human nature that God made before our sin; we are recalled from the love that we earned through sinning. Therefore we must hate that from which we desire to be freed.

Let us therefore hate temporal relationships if we burn with the love of eternity.

Let a human being love his neighbor as himself. Certainly no one is his own father, son, relative, or anything of that kind; he is simply a human being. Whoever therefore loves someone as himself must love in that person what he himself is.

Bodies, however, are not what we are. Therefore the body is not to be sought or desired in a human being.

The command also applies here:

> You shall not covet your neighbor’s possession.

Therefore whoever loves in his neighbor something other than what his neighbor himself is does not love him as himself. Human nature itself, without its carnal condition, is therefore to be loved, whether it is still to be perfected or already perfect.

[Col. 0603B] All who love the one God and do his will are related under the one God as Father. They are fathers to one another when they care for one another, and children when they obey one another, and above all they are brothers, because one Father calls them by his testament to one inheritance.

Why, then, should this person not be invincible through loving a human being, since he loves in that person nothing except the human being—that is, God’s creature, made in his image—and since the perfect nature that he loves cannot be lacking to him when he himself is perfect?

For example, if someone loves a person who sings well—not this or that particular singer, but anyone who sings well—while he himself is a perfect singer (cantator; variant: cantor), he wants everyone to be such, yet what he loves is not lacking to him (diligit; variant: diligat), because he himself sings well.

[Col. 0603C] If he envies someone who sings well, then he no longer loves good singing, but either praise or something else which he hopes to attain by singing well, and which could be diminished or taken away from him if another also sang well.

Whoever therefore envies one who sings well does not love good singing. Yet, conversely, whoever needs another’s good singing does not sing well himself.

This can be applied much more suitably to one who lives well, because he can envy no one. The goal to which those who live well attain is the same for all, and it is not diminished when there are more who possess it.

There can be a time when a good singer is unable to sing becomingly and needs another’s voice to provide him with what he loves—just as he might be a guest somewhere where it would be shameful for him to sing but proper for him to listen to a singer. But it is always proper to live well.

[Col. 0603D] Therefore whoever loves and does this not only does not envy those who imitate him, but most willingly and humanely offers himself to them as much as he can, while he does not need them. For everything that he loves in them he possesses wholly and perfectly in himself.

Thus, when he loves his neighbor as himself, he does not envy him, because he does not envy himself; he gives him what he can, because he gives it to himself; he does not need him (non; variant: nec), because he does not need himself. He needs only God, by cleaving to whom he is blessed.

No one takes God away from him. Therefore the truly and most certainly invincible human being is the one who cleaves to God, not so that he may earn some external good from him, but because nothing other than cleaving to God himself is good for him.

[Col. 0604A] As long as this man remains in the present life, he uses a friend to repay kindness, an enemy to exercise patience, those whom he can to practice benevolence, and everyone to practice goodwill.

Although he himself does not love temporal things, he uses temporal things rightly and, according to their condition, provides for human beings when he cannot provide equally for everyone.

Therefore, if he addresses one of his intimates more readily than someone else, he does not love him more, but has greater confidence in him and a more open door of time toward him.

He treats those devoted to temporal things better in proportion as he himself is less bound by time.

Since he cannot benefit all whom he loves equally unless he prefers to benefit those closer to him, he would be unjust.

The union of souls is greater than that of places or times, by which we are joined in this body; but the greatest union is that which surpasses all others.

[Col. 0604B] This man therefore is not afflicted by anyone’s death, because the person who loves God with his whole soul knows that one who is not lost to God is not lost to him either. God is Lord of the living and of the dead.

He is not made wretched by anyone’s misery, because no one’s injustice makes him unjust. And just as no one takes justice or God (Deum; variant: deitatem, “divinity”) away from him, so no one takes blessedness away from him.

If he is ever moved by someone’s danger, error, or pain, he permits this movement to extend as far as that person’s aid, correction, or consolation, but not as far as his own overthrow.

In all his labors of service he is not broken, because he awaits future rest with certainty.

[Col. 0604C] For what can harm the person who can make good use even of an enemy? He does not fear enmity under the protection and defense of the one whose command and gift enable him to love his enemies.

For this man, in tribulations it is not enough not to grieve; he also rejoices, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; hope, however, does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

Who will harm him? Who will subjugate him?

The person who prospers in favorable circumstances will learn (discet; variant: discit, “learns”) in adversity what progress he has made. When an abundance of changeable goods is present, he does not trust in them; but when they are taken away, it is recognized (agnoscitur; variant: agnoscit, “he recognizes”) whether they have not captured him. For often, when they are present to us, we think that we do not love them; but when they begin to be absent, we discover who we are.

[Col. 0604D] What was present without our love will depart (discedet; variant: discedit, “departs”) without our grief.

Therefore the person who, by conquering, reaches what he will lose with grief seems to conquer when he is conquered; and whoever, by yielding, reaches what he will not unwillingly lose conquers when he seems to be conquered.

Let the person who delights in freedom therefore desire to be free from love of changeable things. Let the person who delights in ruling cleave in submission to God, the one ruler of all, loving him more than himself.

This is perfect justice: we love the greater things more and the lesser things less. Let him love a wise and perfect soul as such as he beholds it (videat; variant: videt, “sees”); let him love a foolish soul not as such, but because that soul can become perfect and wise. For one ought not to love oneself as foolish.

[Col. 0605A] No one will progress toward wisdom who loves himself as foolish, nor will anyone become what he wishes to be unless he hates what he is.

But until wisdom and perfection are attained, let each person bear the foolishness of his neighbor with the disposition with which he would bear his own foolishness if he were foolish and loved wisdom.

Therefore, if pride itself is also a shadow of true freedom and true kingship, divine providence reminds us through it what our vice signifies and where we ought to return once corrected.

Moreover, all spectacles and everything called curiosity seek nothing else than joy from knowledge of things. What, then, is more marvelous, what more beautiful than Truth itself, toward which every spectator confesses that he desires to arrive, since he watches attentively lest he be deceived?

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the law of God is a certain lofty discipline; from Book II of *On Order*, and elsewhere, and concerning the passage

[Col. 0605B]

As I saw everyone seeking God with the utmost zeal and each according to his ability, but not following the very order under discussion, by which one reaches an understanding of that ineffable majesty, I beg you, I said, since, as I see, you love order greatly, do not allow us to be backward and disordered. For although the most hidden reason promises that it will show that nothing happens apart from the divine order, nevertheless, if we were to hear some schoolmaster attempting to teach syllables to a boy whom no one had first taught letters, we would think him not merely ridiculous as a fool but deserving to be bound as a madman—not, I think, for any other reason than that he was not observing the order of teaching. Yet no one doubts that many such things are done by the unskilled, things which the learned criticize and deride, and that demented people do things which do not escape even the judgment of fools; nevertheless, even all these things which we admit to be perverse are not outside the divine order. [Col. 0605C]

A certain profound discipline, far removed from the multitude and even from its suspicion, promises that it will reveal itself to minds devoted to study and loving only God and souls, so that nothing may be more certain to us than the highest truths of number. This discipline itself is the law of God. Fixed and unshaken in him forever, it is, as it were, transcribed into wise souls, so that they may know that they live better and more sublimely in proportion as they contemplate it more perfectly through understanding and observe it more diligently in their lives. [Col. 0605D]

This discipline, therefore, commands those who desire to know it to follow two orders simultaneously, one of which concerns life and the other learning. Young men devoted to study must so live that they abstain from sexual matters; from the enticements of the belly and throat; from immoderate care and adornment of the body; from the empty business of games; from the sluggishness of sleep and laziness; from rivalry, detraction, and envy; from ambition for honors and offices; and even from an excessive desire for praise. Let them regard love of money as the surest poison of all their hopes. Let them do nothing feebly and nothing rashly. In the sins of their own people, let them either completely drive away anger or restrain it so that it resembles anger already driven away. Let them hate no one, and let them be unwilling to neglect any vices. Let them be especially watchful, when they punish, that there be not too much, and, when they forgive, that there be not too little. Let them punish nothing that does not contribute to improvement; let them indulge nothing that turns toward worsening. Let them consider all those over whom authority has been given to them their own. Let them serve in such a way that they would be ashamed to rule them; let them rule in such a way that they take pleasure in serving them. In the sins of others, let them not be troublesome against their will. Let them avoid enmities with the greatest care, endure them with the greatest equanimity, and end them with the greatest speed. [Col. 0606A]

In every transaction and association with human beings, it is enough to observe this one common proverb: “Let them do to no one what they do not wish to suffer themselves.” Let them refuse to administer the commonwealth unless they are perfected. Those who are perfected should hasten either before reaching senatorial age or, at any rate, within youth. But whoever turns to these pursuits late should not think that nothing has been prescribed for him; for, with age ripened, he will certainly observe these things more easily. [Col. 0606B]

Throughout life, in every place and time, let them either have friends or strive to have them. Let them obey those who are worthy, even when the latter do not expect it; let them pay less attention to the proud; let them be least of all proud themselves; let them live suitably and harmoniously. Let them worship, contemplate, and seek God, supported by faith, hope, and charity. Let them desire tranquility and a secure course for their studies and those of all their companions, and for themselves, insofar as they can, a good mind and a peaceful life. [Col. 0606C]

It follows that I should say how those devoted to study ought to be educated, since, as has been said, they have undertaken to live in order to learn. We are necessarily led in two ways, by authority and by reason. In time, authority comes first; in the matter itself, reason does. For one thing is placed first in action, and another is esteemed more highly in desire.

Thus, although the authority of the good may seem more beneficial to the unskilled multitude, while reason may seem more suitable to the learned—since no one becomes learned except from having been unskilled, and no unskilled person knows what sort of attitude he ought to present to teachers, or by what sort of life he can become teachable—it follows that, for all who desire to learn great and hidden things, authority alone opens the door. Once someone has entered through it, he follows, without any doubt, the precepts of the best life. When he has become teachable, he will then learn both how much reason supports the very things he followed before reason and what reason itself is—the reason which, after the cradle of authority, he now follows and grasps, firm and fit for the task. [Col. 0606D]

And what is understanding, in which all things exist—or rather, which itself is all things? And what is the principle of all things beyond all things? Few in this life have attained to that knowledge [Latin variant: *pervenere*, “have attained”]; beyond it, no one can advance even after this life.

Those who are content with authority alone and steadily devote themselves only to good morals and upright desires, either despising or being unable to receive a liberal and excellent education—I do not know quite what name to give them when they live among human beings—yet I firmly believe that, as soon as they have left this body, those who have lived well will be freed, more or less easily according to the degree of their life.

Authority, however, is partly divine and partly human. But true, firm, and supreme authority is that which is called divine. In regard to it, one must fear the extraordinary deception of aerial beings. Through certain divinations and powers concerning things belonging to these bodily senses, they are accustomed very easily to deceive souls—whether souls curious about perishable fortunes, desirous of fragile powers, or fearful of empty miracles. [Col. 0607A]

Therefore that authority is to be called divine which not only surpasses every human capacity in sensible signs, but, acting through the human being himself, shows him how far it has humbled itself for his sake, and commands him not to remain attached to the senses through which those marvelous things are seen, but to fly upward to understanding. At the same time it demonstrates how much power is present here, why it does these things, and how little it values them.

For it must teach its power by deeds, its mercy by humility, and its nature by command. All these things are conveyed more secretly and more firmly in the sacred rites into which we are initiated. In them, the life of the good is purified most easily, not through the winding paths of disputation but through the authority of the mysteries. [Col. 0607B]

Human authority, on the other hand, is usually deceptive. Nevertheless, it rightly seems to excel among those who, insofar as the understanding of the unskilled permits, give many indications of their teachings and do not live otherwise than they command others to live. If gifts of fortune have also accrued to them—gifts whose use makes them appear great and whose contempt makes them greater still—it is altogether most difficult for anyone to be rightly blamed for trusting them when they give precepts for living.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the serpent’s speech to Eve, and on the incantations of the Marsi, from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

From him, therefore, whose supreme power extends over all that he created, through the holy angels [“his,” *suos*], by whom the devil is mocked when the Church of God also consults them concerning his own malevolence, the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent, nor the man except through the woman. In the serpent he himself spoke, using it as an instrument and moving its nature in the manner in which he could move it and it could be moved [variant: *quomodo vere ille movere*, “in the manner in which he truly could move it”], so as to produce the sounds of words and bodily signs through which the woman might understand the will of the tempter.

In the woman herself, however, since she was a rational creature capable of using her own movement to produce words, he did not speak himself. Rather, it was his activity and persuasion—although, by a hidden impulse, it inwardly assisted what he had outwardly done through the serpent. If he had acted more secretly by impulse alone, as he acted in Judas when he induced him to betray Christ, he could have brought this about in a soul driven by proud love of its own power. But, as I have already said, the devil has the will to tempt; he does not have the power either to carry it out or to determine how he carries it out. Because he was permitted, therefore, he tempted; and he tempted in the manner in which he was permitted. [Col. 0607C]

He neither knew nor wished that what he was doing would benefit the human race; and precisely in this he was mocked by the angels. The serpent, therefore, did not understand the sounds of the words that came from it to the woman, for its soul must not be thought to have been transformed into a rational nature. Indeed, even human beings themselves, whose nature is rational, do not know what they are saying when a demon speaks through them, under the affliction in which such utterances are elicited from their mouths. How much less, then, would the serpent have understood the sounds of the words that the devil produced through it and from it in that manner, when it would not have understood a speaking human being if it had heard him free from demonic affliction. [Col. 0607D–0608A]

For even in the case of what serpents are thought to hear and understand—the words of the Marsi, so that when those people chant their incantations the serpents usually leap out of their hiding places—it is likewise demonic power that is at work. This serves to make known everywhere the providence by which God subjects each thing to its natural order and, in his supremely wise power, permits certain things even to evil wills. The fact that serpents are more moved by human songs than any other kind of animal is itself no small testimony that the first human nature was seduced by conversation with the serpent.

For demons rejoice that this power is granted to them: that, in response to human incantations, they may move serpents and deceive those whom they can by whatever means. They are permitted this so that the memory of the first deed may be preserved—namely, that they have a certain familiarity with this species. Moreover, the first deed itself was permitted so that, through the serpent’s nature, there might be signified to the human race, for whose instruction these events had to be written, a likeness of every demonic temptation. This will become clear when the divine sentence begins to be pronounced against the serpent. [Col. 0608B]

Accordingly, the serpent is called the wisest of all the beasts—that is, the most cunning—because of the devil’s cunning, which was working deceit in it and through it. In the same way, a tongue is called prudent or cunning because a prudent or cunning person moves it to persuade someone prudently or cunningly—not because this power or virtue belongs to the bodily member called the tongue, but because it belongs to the mind that uses it. So, too, the “lying pen of the scribes” is called lying. For being a liar belongs only to a living and sensing creature; but the pen is called lying because through it a liar works deceitfully. In the same way, the serpent would be called lying if it were said to be lying because the devil used it as a pen for lying. [Col. 0608C]

I have thought this worth emphasizing so that no one, supposing that animals without reason possess human understanding or are suddenly changed into rational animals, may be led into that ridiculous and harmful belief that souls are transmigrated—human beings into beasts or beasts into human beings.

Thus the serpent spoke to the human being just as the she-ass on which Balaam sat spoke to a human being, except that the former work was demonic and the latter angelic. Good and evil angels have certain works in common, as Moses and Pharaoh’s magicians did; yet in such matters the good angels are also more powerful. Nor can evil angels do anything even of this kind except what God permits through the good angels, so that each person may be repaid according to his heart or according to God’s grace—both justly and mercifully, through the depth of God’s riches, wisdom, and knowledge. [Col. 0608D]

## CHAPTER XXV. How God fortified the way of authority sevenfold for those who follow him in love, from the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*

Let us ask how a human being ought to live. Certainly, we all wish to live happily. Yet no one can be called happy who does not possess what he loves, whatever that may be; nor the person who possesses what he loves if it is harmful; nor the person who does not love what he possesses, even if it is excellent. For the person who desires what he cannot attain is tortured; the person who has attained what ought not to have been desired is deceived; and the person who does not desire what ought to be attained is sick. None of these conditions occurs in the soul without misery; therefore none of them is happy. [Col. 0609A]

What remains, then, in which the happy life can be found, except that what is best for a human being is both loved and possessed? For what else do we mean by “to enjoy” than to have present what you love? If we intend to live happily, therefore, our highest good must be present to us. For whoever follows what is worse than himself becomes worse himself.

Every human being ought to follow what is best. But this must be something that he cannot lose unwillingly, since no one can trust in such a good if he feels that it can be taken from him, even if he wishes to retain and embrace it.
