Whoever does not feel secure about the good he enjoys—how can he be happy amid such fear of losing it?

Who could doubt that, if we thought it sufficient to follow a wise human being, he could be taken away from us, even when we refused and resisted? [Variant: *cunctandum putet hominem sapientem, si eum sequi putaverimus, auferri a nobis, non modo recusantibus, sed…*—“let anyone think that a wise human being can be taken away from us, if we suppose that we should follow him, even when we not only refuse but…”] God, therefore, remains. If we follow him, we live well; if we attain him, we live not only well but happily. Following God is the desire for happiness; attaining him is happiness itself. [Col. 0609B]

But how do we follow one whom we do not see? Or how will we see him, when we are not only human beings but foolish human beings? We must therefore take refuge in the precepts of those whom it is reasonable to believe were wise, so that authority may lead our wavering sight, as though shaded by the branches of humanity, into the light of truth. God has fortified this way for us by the separation of the patriarchs, by the bond of the law, by the prediction of the prophets, by the sacrament of the assumed human being, by the testimony of the apostles, by the blood of the martyrs, and by the occupation of the nations. Therefore let us submit our little reasonings to divine dispositions.

Let us hear, then, what end of good things you prescribe for us, O Christ, toward which you command us to strive with supreme love. “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.” What more do you want? And Paul says: “For those who love God, all things work together for good.” He also states the measure of love: “Who, then, shall separate us from the love of Christ?” and so forth. A little later: “For I am convinced that neither death nor life,” and the rest. [Col. 0609C–D]

If, then, nothing separates us from his love, what can be not only better but also more certain than this good? No one separates us from it by threatening death, for God himself, whom we love, cannot die; rather, for the person who does not love God, death itself is not to love God, which is nothing other than preferring something to him in love and pursuit. No one separates us from it by promising life, for no one separates water from its very source by promising it.

An angel does not separate us from it; for, when we cling to God, no angel is more powerful than our mind. Nor does power separate us, if by “power” is meant a power that holds some authority in this world: the mind that clings to God is altogether higher than the whole world. But if “power” means the perfectly right disposition of our own mind, then, if that power is in another, it favors our union with God; if it is in us, it itself unites us. [Col. 0610A]

Present troubles do not separate us, for we feel them lighter in proportion as we cling more fiercely to the one from whom they strive to separate us. Nor does the promise of future things separate us, for God promises whatever good is to come more certainly, and nothing is better than God himself, who is already present to those who cling to him well.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the beginning of Genesis, initiated by Moses with great mystery, and on how a plurality of interpretations is not contrary to faith, from Book XII of the *Confessions*

Let no one now trouble me by saying: “Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say.” For if he said to me, “How do you know that Moses meant what you declare concerning these words of his?” I ought to bear it calmly and perhaps reply as I replied above, or at somewhat greater length, if he were more insistent. But when he says, “He did not mean what you say, but what I say,” while not denying that what each of us says is true—O life of the poor, my God, in whose bosom there is no contradiction—rain consolations into my heart, that I may bear such people patiently. They do not say this to me because they are divine and have seen in the heart of your servant what they say, but because they are proud: they do not know Moses’ meaning, but love their own—not because it is true, but because it is their own. Otherwise they would equally love another true interpretation, just as I love what they say when they advance what is true, not because it is theirs, but because it is true.

And therefore it is no longer theirs, because it is true. But if they love it because it is true, it is both theirs and mine, because it is held in common by all lovers of truth. But their contention that Moses did not mean what I say, but what they say, I neither want nor love; for even if it is so, such rashness arises not from knowledge but from audacity, and it was produced not by sight but by blindness. Therefore, Lord, your judgments are terrible: for your truth is neither mine nor that man’s nor another’s, but belongs to us all, whom you publicly call to share in it, solemnly warning us not to wish to possess it privately, lest we be deprived of it. For whoever claims for himself as his private possession what you set before all for their enjoyment, and wishes what belongs to all to be his own, is driven from what is common to what is private—that is, from truth to falsehood. For whoever speaks a lie speaks from what is his own. [Col. 0610B–D]

Attend, O God, most excellent judge, Truth itself; attend to what I say to this opponent; attend, for I speak before you and before my brothers who use the law lawfully, unto the end of charity. Attend and see what I say to him, if it pleases you; for I return to him this brotherly and peaceful answer. If we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true, where, I ask, do we see it? Certainly neither I in you nor you in me, but both of us in that immutable truth which is above our minds. Since, then, we do not contend about the light of the Lord our God himself, why do we contend about our neighbor’s thought, which we cannot see as we see immutable truth? Even if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, “This is what I thought,” we would not thereby see it, but would believe it. [Col. 0611A]

Therefore let no one, beyond what is written, be puffed up on behalf of one against another. Let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. Unless we believe that Moses understood whatever he understood in those books in accordance with these two commandments of charity, we make the Lord a liar when we form an opinion about the mind of our fellow servant other than that which he taught. See now how foolish it is, amid such an abundance of completely true meanings that may be drawn from those words, rashly to assert which of them Moses chiefly intended, and by destructive contentions to offend against charity itself, for the sake of which he said all that he said, and whose utterances we endeavor to expound.

For as a spring, richer in a small place, supplies its flow through several streams into wider spaces than any one of those streams which is led from the same spring through many regions, so the narrative of your steward, intended to benefit many speakers, gushes forth, within the narrow compass of its words, streams of clear truth. From these one person may draw this true meaning, another that, by the longer windings of their discourse, each drawing what he can concerning these matters. [Col. 0611B]

For when some read or hear these words, they imagine God as though he were a human being, or some vast mass endowed with immense power, who by a new and sudden decision made heaven and earth outside himself, as though distant from himself in places: two great bodies, one above and one below, containing all things. And when they hear, “God said, Let this be,” and “it was so,” they imagine words beginning and ending, sounding in time and passing away, after whose passing that which was commanded immediately comes into existence. Or they form some other such opinion from familiarity with the flesh. In such still-childlike creatures, while their weakness is borne in the maternal bosom, as it were, of this most lowly kind of speech, faith is beneficially built up: they may hold firmly and certainly that God made all the natures which their senses behold in wonderful variety.

If one of them, scorning these expressions as mean, should in proud weakness stretch himself beyond the nursing cradle, alas, he will fall miserably; and, Lord God, have mercy, lest those who pass along the road trample the unfledged chick. Send your angel to put it back in the nest, that it may live until it can fly. [Col. 0611C–D]

But others, for whom these words are no longer a nest but shady thickets, see hidden fruits in them. They fly about joyfully, chirping as they search and plucking the fruits. For, when they read or hear these words, they see that all past and future times are surpassed by your eternal and stable abiding, O God; yet they also see that there is no temporal creature which you did not make. Since your will is identical with yourself and has in no way changed, you made all things not by a will that had arisen in you when it did not previously exist, nor from yourself did you form your likeness, the form of all things, but from nothing you made an unformed dissimilarity, to be formed through your likeness by returning to you, the One, according to the ordered capacity bestowed upon each thing in its kind. Thus all things became very good, whether they remain near you or, at a gradually more distant remove through times and places, make or undergo beautiful changes. [Col. 0612A]

They see these things and rejoice in the light of your truth, insofar as they can here. One of them attends to the words, “In the beginning God made,” and understands “beginning” as Wisdom, because Wisdom itself speaks to us. Another likewise attends to the same words and understands “beginning” as the commencement of created things, taking “In the beginning he made” as though it said, “First he made.” In those words they understand: “In the beginning,” that is, in Wisdom, you made heaven and earth. Another believes that “heaven and earth” are names given to the creatable matter of heaven and earth. Another understands already formed and differentiated natures; another, one formed spiritual nature under the name of heaven and another unformed bodily matter under the name of earth.

Those who understand by “heaven and earth” matter still unformed, from which heaven and earth were to be made, do not all understand it in one way. One understands it as that from which the intelligible and sensible creature would be completed; another only as that from which this sensible bodily mass, containing in its vast bosom manifest and readily perceptible natures, would be completed. Nor do those all understand it in one way who believe that the already ordered and arranged creatures are here called heaven and earth: one understands the invisible and the visible creation, another the visible creation alone, in which we discern the bright heaven, the dark earth, and all things in them. [Col. 0612B]

But one who takes “In the beginning he made” only as though it said, “First he made,” cannot truthfully understand heaven and earth unless he understands the matter of heaven and earth—namely, that of the whole creation, intelligible and bodily. For if he wishes to understand the whole creation as already formed, he may rightly be asked: if God made this first, what did he make next? After the universe he will find nothing, and will therefore hear, against his will, “How was that first, if nothing followed?” But when he says that what was unformed came first and what was formed afterward, he is not absurd, provided that he can distinguish what is prior in eternity, in time, in choice, and in origin: in eternity, as God is prior to all things; in time, as the flower is prior to the fruit; in choice, as the fruit is prior to the flower; in origin, as sound is prior to song.

Of these four, the first and the last that I mentioned are understood with the greatest difficulty; the middle two most easily. For it is a rare and exceedingly arduous vision to behold, Lord, your eternity, which makes mutable things without change and is therefore prior to them. And who, again, sees with a mind so keen as to discern without great labor how sound is prior to song? Song is formed sound; something unformed can certainly exist, but what does not exist cannot be formed. Thus matter is prior to that which is made from it. It is not prior because it makes the thing, since it is itself rather made; nor is it prior by an interval of time. For we do not first produce unformed sounds without song and later fit or shape them into the form of a song, as wood precedes a chest or silver a small vessel: materials of that kind also precede in time the forms of things made from them. [Col. 0612C–D]

But it is not so in song. When a song is sung, its sound is heard; it does not first sound in an unformed fashion and then acquire the form of song. Whatever first sounds in any manner passes away, and you find nothing in it which you may take up again and compose artistically. Therefore song takes place in its sound; that sound is its matter, and the same sound is formed in order to become song. Accordingly, as I said, the matter of sounding is prior to the form of singing—not prior in the power to effect it, for sound is not the craftsman of singing but is subject, from the body, to the soul that sings and makes of it what it will; not prior in time, for it is uttered simultaneously with the song; nor prior in choice, for sound is not better than song, since song is not merely sound but beautiful sound [the supplied text repeats *sonus*, “sound,” in the phrase “not merely sound but sound most beautiful”]; it is prior in origin, because song is not formed in order to be sound, but sound is formed in order to be song. [Col. 0613A–B]

By this example let whoever can understand the matter of things to have been made first and called heaven and earth, because heaven and earth were made from it; not made first in time, because the forms of things bring forth times. That matter was unformed, and yet it is observed already along with times. Nevertheless, nothing can be narrated of it except as if it were prior in time, because it is judged inferior; for formed things are certainly better than unformed ones. It is preceded in eternity by the Creator, so that there might be, from nothing, that from which something could be made.

May Truth itself bring forth harmony from this diversity of true interpretations, and may our God have mercy on us, that we may use the law lawfully, with the end of the commandment being pure charity. Therefore, if anyone asks me which of these meanings your servant Moses intended, these words of mine are not confessions unless I confess to you that I do not know. Yet I do know that these are true interpretations, except for the carnal ones, about which I have spoken as much as I judged necessary. These words of your book do not terrify those little ones of good hope: they are lofty in humility and abundant in brevity. [Col. 0613C]

But let us all love one another—all whom I acknowledge to see and speak truth in these words—and let us together love you, our God, the fountain of truth, if we thirst not for vain things but for truth itself. Let us honor your servant, the steward of this Scripture, as filled with your Spirit, so that, through your revelation, we may believe that when he wrote these words he attended above all to that meaning which excels in them both in the light of truth and in the fruit of usefulness.

Thus, when one person says, “He meant what I say,” and another says, “No, what I say,” I judge it more religious to say: Why not rather both, if both are true? And if a third, a fourth, or anything else whatever is true is seen in these words by anyone, why should Moses not be believed to have seen all those meanings—he through whom the one God adapted the sacred writings to the many understandings of those who would see true yet diverse meanings? Certainly, to declare fearlessly what is in my own heart, if I were writing anything at the summit of authority, I would prefer to write so that my words might express whatever truth each person could grasp from these matters, rather than to state one true meaning so openly as to exclude the others, whose falsity could not offend me. [Col. 0613D–0614A]

Therefore, my God, I do not wish to be so rash as not to believe that that man deserved this from you. He unquestionably understood and thought, when writing these words, whatever truth we have been able to discover here, and whatever we have not been able, or are not yet able, to discover but can nevertheless be discovered in them. Finally, Lord, you are God and not flesh and blood. If a human being sees less, could anything which you yourself intended to reveal in those words to later readers have been hidden even from your good Spirit, who will lead me into the right land, even if the man through whom they were spoken perhaps thought of one meaning among many? And if this is so, then let the meaning he thought be higher than the rest. But for us, Lord, either show us that meaning itself, or another true meaning which pleases you, so that whether you disclose to us what you disclosed to that your servant or something else on the occasion of the same words, you may nevertheless feed us and error may not mock us. [Col. 0614B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. Beginning of the book *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

[Source columns: 0614C–0623D.]

All divine Scripture is divided into two parts, in accordance with what the Lord signified when he said that a learned scribe in the kingdom of God is like a householder bringing forth from his treasure new things and old—namely, the two Testaments. In all the holy books, however, one ought to discern what is intimated as eternal, what is narrated as having happened, what is foretold as future, and what is commanded or urged as something to be done.

In the narrative, therefore, of things that happened, the question arises whether everything is to be understood only according to the meaning of figures, or whether it must also be affirmed and defended according to the truth of the events themselves. For no Christian, attentive to the Apostle’s statement, “All these things happened to them figuratively,” and to what is written in Genesis, “And the two shall be one flesh,” commending a great mystery in Christ and in the Church, would dare say that they are not to be understood figuratively.

If, then, that Scripture is to be examined in both ways, how is the statement “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” to be understood apart from its allegorical meaning? Does “in the beginning” mean at the beginning of time? Or because they were made before all other things? Or does it mean “in the Beginning,” who is the Word of God, the only-begotten Son?

And how can it be shown that God, without any change in himself, works things that are changeable and temporal? What is signified by the names “heaven” and “earth”? Did a spiritual and a bodily creature receive the names “heaven” and “earth”? Or only a bodily creature, so that in this book the spiritual creature is understood to have been passed over in silence, and “heaven and earth” is said in order to signify every bodily creature, higher and lower?

Or was the formless matter of both meant by “heaven and earth”—namely, spiritual life, insofar as it can exist without having turned toward its Creator? For by such turning it is formed and perfected; but if it does not turn, it is formless. And was bodily matter to be understood through the deprivation of every bodily quality that appears in formed matter, when the forms of bodies have already become perceptible either by sight or by any other bodily sense?

Or is “heaven” to be understood as the spiritual creature, perfect and always blessed from the beginning at which it was made, while “earth” is bodily matter still imperfect? For, Scripture says, “the earth was invisible and unformed,” and “darkness was over the abyss.” These words seem to signify the formlessness of bodily substance. Or is the formlessness of both signified by these later words as well? That of the bodily creature, in the statement, “The earth was invisible and unformed”; that of the spiritual creature, in the statement, “Darkness was over the abyss”—so that, by transferring the term, we understand the dark abyss as the formless nature of life, unless it turns toward the Creator, who alone can form it so that it is no longer an abyss, and enlighten it so that it is no longer dark.

And how is the statement “Darkness was over the abyss” to be understood? Was it because there was no light—which, if it had been present, would necessarily have been above it and, as it were, poured over it? This is what occurs in the spiritual creature when it turns toward the unchangeable and incorporeal light that is God.

And how did God say, “Let there be light”? Did he say it temporally, or in the eternity of the Word? If temporally, then certainly mutably. How, then, can God be understood to have said this except through a creature? He himself is unchangeable. And if God said through a creature, “Let there be light,” how, then, is light the first creature? Was there already a creature through which God could say, “Let there be light”? Or is light not the first creature, because it had already been said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and a voice could have been produced temporally and mutably through a heavenly creature by which it was said, “Let there be light”?

If this is so, the bodily light that we see with bodily eyes was made when God said through the spiritual creature—which God had already made when, “in the beginning,” he made heaven and earth—“Let there be light.” This could have occurred through the inner and hidden movement of such a creature, by divine command, whereby it could be said, “Let there be light.”

Or did the voice of God saying “Let there be light” also sound bodily, just as the voice of God saying “You are my beloved Son” sounded bodily—and did this occur through a bodily creature that God had made when, “in the beginning,” he made heaven and earth, before the light came to be, which was made in that sounding voice?

If so, in what language did that voice sound when God said, “Let there be light”? For there was not yet the diversity of languages that later arose in the building of the tower after the Flood. What was the one and only language in which God spoke, “Let there be light”? And who was there to hear and understand the person to whom such a voice would be addressed?

Or is this an absurd and carnal thought and suspicion? What, then, shall we say? Is what is understood in the sound of the voice when “Let there be light” is said—but not the bodily sound itself—properly understood as the voice of God? And does this very thing pertain to the nature of his Word, of whom it is said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?

For when it is said of him, “All things were made through him,” it is sufficiently shown that the light too was made through him when God said, “Let there be light.” If this is so, what God said, “Let there be light,” is eternal, because the Word of God, God with God, the only Son, is coeternal with God the Father. Yet through God’s speaking this in the eternal Word, a temporal creature was made.

Although words are temporal when we say “when” and “at some time,” it is nevertheless eternal in the Word of God when something ought to come into being; and it comes into being at the time at which, in that Word, it is established that it ought to have come into being. In that Word there is no “when” or “at some time,” because the whole Word is eternal.

And what is the light itself that was made? Is it something spiritual or bodily? For if it is spiritual, it can itself be the first creature, perfected as soon as this was said. It was first called “heaven” when it was said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Thus, when God said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be, this may be understood as the conversion of that creature toward its Creator—its Creator turning it back toward himself—and as its being made and illuminated.

Why, then, is it said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” rather than, “In the beginning God said, ‘Let heaven and earth be,’ and heaven and earth came to be,” as the account of the light says, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and light came to be”?

Was it necessary first to comprehend and commend universally, under the name of heaven and earth, what God made, and then to explain in parts how he made it, when it is said of each thing, “God said”—that is, because he made whatever he made through his Word?

Or, when the formlessness of matter was first being made, whether spiritual or bodily, was it not appropriate to say, “God said, ‘Let it be’”? For the imperfect creature, as it tends toward nothingness in a certain formlessness, being unlike him who supremely and primarily exists, does not imitate the form of the Word—which is always united to the Father, through whom God eternally speaks all things—not by a sound of the voice or by a thought unfolding temporal sounds, but by the coeternal light of the wisdom begotten from him.

Rather, it imitates the form of the Word when, according to the conversion proper to its kind, it receives form from that which truly and always exists—that is, from the Creator of its substance—and becomes a perfect creature. Thus, in what Scripture narrates as “God said, ‘Let there be,’” are we to understand God’s incorporeal utterance in the nature of his coeternal Word, calling the creature’s imperfection back to himself so that it may not remain formless, but may be formed according to the several things that the account proceeds to describe?

In this conversion and formation, by which the creature in its own manner imitates God the Word—that is, the Son of God, always united to the Father, in full likeness and equal essence, whereby he and the Father are one—it does not imitate this form of the Word if, turned away from the Creator, it remains formless and imperfect.

For this reason the Son is mentioned not insofar as he is the Word, but only insofar as he is the Beginning, when it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” The beginning of the creature is thereby indicated as still lying in the formlessness of imperfection.

But the Son is mentioned as also being the Word in the statement, “God said, ‘Let there be.’” Through the fact that he is the Beginning, the beginning of the creature’s existence is indicated, while it is still imperfect through him; through the fact that he is the Word, the perfection of the creature is indicated, when it is called back to him to be formed by cleaving to the Creator and, according to its kind, imitating the form eternally and unchangeably united to the Father, from whom it is at once what he is.

For the Word, the Son, does not possess a formless life. In him, being is not merely the same as living; living is also the same as living wisely and blessedly. But the creature, although spiritual, intellectual, or rational, and seemingly nearer to that Word, can possess a formless life. For it is not the case with it that being is the same as living, nor that living is the same as living wisely and blessedly.

When turned away from unchangeable wisdom, it lives foolishly and miserably; this is its formlessness. But it is formed when it turns toward the unchangeable light of the wisdom of God’s Word. From him it has come into existence, so that it exists in some fashion and lives; toward him it turns so that it may live wisely and blessedly.

The beginning of the intellectual creature is the eternal Wisdom. Remaining unchangeably in itself, that Beginning would in no way cease, by a hidden inspiration of calling, to speak to the creature for which it is the Beginning, so that it might turn toward that from which it exists—for otherwise it cannot be formed and perfected.

Therefore, when asked who he was, the Lord answered, “The Beginning, who speaks to you.” What the Son speaks, the Father speaks, because when the Father speaks, the Word that is the Son is uttered according to an eternal manner—if it is proper to speak of a manner when God utters his coeternal Word.

For in God there is supreme, holy, and just goodness, and love for his works that comes not from need but from beneficence. Therefore, before it was written, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’” Scripture first said, “And the Spirit of God was hovering over the water.”

Whether by the name “water” he wished to designate all bodily matter, thereby indicating from what all things that we can now discern in their several kinds were made and formed—calling it water because we see all things on earth formed and brought together in various shapes from a moist nature—or whether he meant a certain spiritual life, as it were floating before its conversion into form, the Spirit of God was nevertheless hovering over it.

For whatever that substance was which had begun to be formed and perfected plainly lay subject to the Creator’s good will. Thus, when God said through his Word, “Let there be light,” what had been made remained, in good will—that is, in his good pleasure—according to the measure of its kind. Therefore it is said that it pleased God, Scripture stating, “And light came to be. And God saw that the light was good.”

Thus, just as at the very beginning of the nascent creature, which was mentioned under the name of heaven and earth because of what was to be perfected from it, the Trinity of the Creator is intimated—for when Scripture says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” we understand the Father under the name “God” and the Son under the name “Beginning,” who is the Beginning not of the Father but of the spiritual creature created first and above all through himself, and consequently of the whole creation—so, when Scripture says, “And the Spirit of God was hovering over the water,” we recognize the complete mention of the Trinity.

Likewise, in the conversion and perfection of the creature, by which the forms of things are ordered, the same Trinity is intimated: God’s Word, and the Begetter of the Word, when it is said, “God said,” and holy goodness, in which whatever is perfected according to the measure of its nature pleases God, when it is said, “God saw that it was good.”

But why, after the imperfect creature had been mentioned, is the Spirit of God mentioned later, Scripture first saying, “The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,” and then adding, “And the Spirit of God was hovering over the water”?

Was it because needy and indigent love loves in such a way that it subjects itself to the things it loves? For this reason, when the Spirit of God is mentioned—in whom his holy benevolence and love are understood—he is said to hover over them, lest God be thought to love his works from the necessity of need rather than from the abundance of beneficence.

Remembering this, the Apostle, when he is about to speak of charity, says that he will show “a way surpassing all others”; and elsewhere he says, “the charity of Christ surpassing knowledge.” Since, then, it was necessary to indicate the Spirit of God in such a way that he would be said to hover over the works, it was fitting that something begun should first be indicated, over which he might be said to hover—not spatially, but by a power surpassing and excelling all things.

Likewise, when the things that had arisen from that beginning had been perfected and formed, “God saw that it was good,” for what had been made pleased him in the goodness by which he had been pleased that it should be made.

There are two reasons why God loves his creature: that it should exist, and that it should remain. Therefore, that there might be something which would remain, the Spirit of God was hovering over the water; and that it might remain, God saw that it was good. What is said of the light is also said of all things.

For some things remain, having risen above all temporal change, in the fullest holiness under God. Others remain according to the measure of their own time, while the beauty of the ages is woven together through the departure and succession of things.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Against Those Who Say, “Was Moses There When God Made Heaven and Earth, That He Should Be Believed?” From Book XI of *The City of God* [Col. 0618C].

## CHAPTER XXIX. That Those Who Cavil About the Time of the World Can Be Refuted by the Place of the World. From the Same Book XI

The visible world is the greatest of all visible things, and God is the greatest of all invisible things. We see that the world exists; we believe that God exists. But that God made the world, we trust no one more safely than God himself.

Where have we heard him? For the present, nowhere better than in the holy Scriptures, where his prophet said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Was that prophet there when God made heaven and earth? No. But there was the Wisdom of God, through which all things were made, which also transfers itself into holy souls, making them friends of God and prophets, and silently recounting his works to them within.

The angels of God also speak to them—those who always behold the face of the Father and announce his will to those to whom it is fitting. This prophet was one of them: he spoke and wrote, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He is such a reliable witness through whom we should believe God that, by the same Spirit of God through whom he recognized that these things had been revealed to him, he also foretold, so long beforehand, our future faith itself.

But what pleased the eternal God to make heaven and earth at that time, when he had not made them previously? Those who say this—if they wish the world to be eternal, without any beginning, and therefore not to have been made by God—are exceedingly estranged from the truth and rave with the deadly disease of impiety.

For, apart from the prophetic voices, the world itself, by its exquisitely ordered mutability and motion and by the most beautiful appearance of all visible things, proclaims, as it were silently, both that it was made and that it could have been made only by the ineffable and invisible God, great and ineffably and invisibly beautiful.

## CHAPTER XXX. That Angels Too May Be Understood to Have Been Signified and Created under the Name of “Light.” From the Same Book XI

Since, then, they say that there is one world, indeed immense in bodily size but finite, determined by its own place, and made by the working of God, let them answer this concerning the infinite places outside the world: why does God cease from his work in them? Let them answer the same concerning the infinite times before the world: why did God cease from his work in them?

Just as it does not follow that God established the world in this place rather than another by chance instead of by divine reason—for, although infinite places lay open everywhere and no superior merit could have made this place preferable, no human nature could comprehend the divine reason by which it was done—so it does not follow that we should think something happened to God by chance because he created the world at that time rather than at an earlier one. For earlier times would equally have passed away through an infinite stretch backward, and there would have been no difference by which one time could be preferred to another for selection.

If they say that human thoughts are empty when they imagine infinite places, since no place exists beyond the world, they may be answered in the same way: it is empty for human beings to think of past times in which God was inactive, since no time existed before the world.

For if eternity and time are rightly distinguished—time does not exist without some mutability, whereas in eternity there is no change—who does not see that there would have been no times unless a creature had been made that changed something by some movement? When, through the intervals of shorter or longer pauses, one thing gives way to and succeeds another, things that cannot exist simultaneously, time follows upon that motion and change.

Since God, in whose eternity there is absolutely no change, is the Creator and Ordainer of times, I do not see how he can be said to have created the world after spans of time—unless one says that some creature existed before the world, through whose movements time flowed.

But if the sacred and supremely truthful writings say that God made heaven and earth “in the beginning,” so that he is understood to have made nothing previously—for this would rather be said to have been made “in the beginning” if he had made something before all the other things he made—then clearly the world was not made in time but with time.

For what is made in time is made after some time and before some time: after what is past and before what is future. But there could have been nothing past, because there was no creature whose mutable movements could produce it.

The world was made with time if, in its creation, mutable movement was made—as seems also to be indicated by that order of the first six or seven days in which morning and evening are named, until everything God made on those days was completed on the sixth day and God’s rest on the seventh was commended in a great mystery.

What kind of days these were is either exceedingly difficult for us to conceive or even impossible—how much more difficult, then, to express! We see that these familiar days have no evening except from the setting of the sun, and no morning except from its rising. But the first three of those days passed without the sun, which is reported to have been made on the fourth day.

At first, light was made by the word of God, and God is said to have separated it from the darkness and to have called the light “day,” but the darkness “night.” Yet what sort of light it was, by what alternating movement it operated, and what kind of evening and morning it produced, is remote from our senses. Nor can it be understood by us as it truly is, although it must be believed without any hesitation.

For either it is some bodily light, whether in the upper regions of the world, far from our sight, or the source from which the sun was afterward kindled; or the name “light” signifies the holy city, in the holy angels and blessed spirits, of which the Apostle says, “Jerusalem above is our eternal mother in the heavens.”

He also says elsewhere, “For you are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of the night or of darkness.” Nevertheless, if we can understand the evening and morning of this day in some reasonably fitting way, it may be because the knowledge of the creature, compared with the knowledge of the Creator, grows dark in a certain sense. It becomes light again and becomes morning when that knowledge is referred to the praise and love of the Creator, and does not turn into night, where the Creator is abandoned for love of the creature.

Finally, when Scripture counted those days in order, it nowhere inserted the word “night.” It does not say anywhere, “Night came to be,” but, “Evening came to be, and morning came to be—one day”; then, “the second day,” and the others.

The knowledge of the creature in itself is, so to speak, more discolored than when it is known in the wisdom of God, as in the art by which it was made. For this reason it can more appropriately be called “evening” than “night.” Yet, as I have said, when it is referred to the praise and love of the Creator, it returns to morning.

When this occurs in the knowledge of the creature itself, it is one day; in the knowledge of the firmament, which was called heaven and placed between the lower and upper waters, it is the second day; in the knowledge of the earth and sea and of all things that grow, fixed by their roots in the earth, it is the third day; in the knowledge of the greater and lesser lights and of all the stars, it is the fourth day; in the knowledge of all the swimming and flying animals made from the waters, it is the fifth day; in the knowledge of all terrestrial animals and of humanity itself, it is the sixth day.

But when, on the seventh day, God rests from all his works and sanctifies it, this must not be understood childishly, as though God had grown weary through working. He who spoke and they came to be did so by an intelligible and eternal word, not by a sounding and temporal one.

The rest of God signifies the rest of those who rest in God, just as the joy of a house signifies the joy of those who rejoice in the house, even when it is not the house itself but something else that makes some people joyful. How much more is this so if the very beauty of the house makes its inhabitants joyful—not merely in the manner of speech by which we signify the container through what it contains, as when we say “the theaters applaud” and “the meadows low,” although people applaud in the theaters and cattle low in the meadows, but also in that manner by which the efficient cause is signified through its effect, as when a letter is called joyful because it signifies the joy of those whom it makes joyful when they read it.

Accordingly, when prophetic authority narrates that God rested, it most appropriately signifies the rest of those who rest in him and whom he himself makes to rest. The same is promised by prophecy to the human beings to whom it speaks and for whose sake it was certainly written: after the good works that God performs in them and through them, if in this life they first approach him, so to speak, through faith, they will have eternal rest in him.

This was prefigured among the ancient people of God by the Sabbath rest and the commandment of the law.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Against Those Who Say That the World Was Made for the Purpose of Enclosing in It Souls That Had Previously Sinned; Here He Proves Origen to Have Erred from His Books Called *περὶ Ἀρχῶν* [*Peri Archon*], That Is, *On Principles*. From Book XI of *The City of God*

Where the sacred Scriptures speak of the creation of the world, they do not clearly say whether, or in what order, the angels were created. But if they were not passed over, they were either signified under the name of heaven, where it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” or rather under the name of this light of which I am speaking.

I do not think they were passed over because it is written that God rested on the seventh day from all the works he had made, while the book itself begins in such a way—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth”—that he seems to have made nothing before heaven and earth.

Since, then, he began with heaven and earth, and since the earth itself, which he first made, was, as Scripture subsequently states, invisible and unformed, with the light not yet made, there must certainly have been darkness over the abyss—that is, over a certain undifferentiated mixture of earth and water. For where there is no light, darkness must exist.

Afterward, all things were created and ordered, and these are narrated as having been completed over six days. How, then, could the angels have been passed over as though they were not among God’s works, from which he rested on the seventh day?

That the angels are God’s work is not passed over here, but neither is it clearly expressed. Elsewhere, however, Holy Scripture bears clear witness to it. In the hymn of the three youths in the furnace, after the words “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord,” the angels are also named in the enumeration of those works.

And in the Psalm it is sung: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.”

Here too it is most plainly declared by divine authority that the angels were made by God. For, after they have been mentioned among the other heavenly things, the statement is applied to all: “He spoke, and they came to be.”

Who, then, would dare suppose that the angels were made after all those things that are enumerated over six days? And if anyone is so foolish, Scripture of equal authority refutes this vanity where God says, “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me with a loud voice.” The angels therefore already existed when the stars were made, and the stars were made on the fourth day.

Shall we say, then, that the angels were made on the third day? Far from it. It is obvious what was made on that day: the earth was separated from the waters, the two elements received distinct species proper to their kinds, and the earth brought forth whatever is rooted in it.

Were they made on the second day? Not that either. On that day the firmament was made over the waters above and was called heaven; on the fourth day the stars were made in that firmament.

Therefore, if the angels belong among the works of God made on those days, they are that light which received the name “day.” To commend its unity, the text does not say “the first day,” but “one day.” Nor is there another second, third, or subsequent day; the same one day is repeated in order to complete the number six or seven—because of the sixfold [or sixfold and sevenfold] knowledge: the sixfold knowledge of the works God made, and the seventh of God’s rest.

When God said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be, if the creation of the angels is rightly understood in this light, then surely they were made participants in the eternal light, which is the unchangeable wisdom of God, through whom all things were made. This is the one-begotten Son of God.

Illuminated by that light in which they were created, they would become light and be called “day,” through participation in the unchangeable light and day that is the Word of God, through whom both they and all things were made.

For the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world also enlightens every pure angel, so that the angel is light not in himself but in God. If an angel turns away from him, it becomes impure, as are all those who are called impure spirits.

Then there is no longer light in the Lord but darkness in themselves, deprived of participation in the eternal light. For evil is not a nature; rather, the loss of good has received the name “evil.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Same Error and on Eternal Fire. From the Book of the *Response to the Questions of the Presbyter Orosius*.

But it is much more astonishing that certain people, who believe with us that all things have one Beginning and that no nature which is not what God is can exist except from that Creator, nevertheless refused to believe properly and simply that the reason for making the world was so good and simple: that the good God created good things, and that after God there should be things which were not what God is, yet were good things that only a good God could make.

They say that souls—not indeed parts of God, but made by God—sinned by withdrawing from God their Creator, and that, according to the differing degrees and variety of their sins, they deserved different bodies as bonds, from heaven down to earth. They say that this is the world and that this was the reason the world was made—not so that good things might be created, but so that evils might be restrained.

For this reason Origen is rightly censured. In the books that he calls *περὶ Ἀρχῶν*, that is, *On Principles*, he held and wrote this view.

I am amazed beyond what can be expressed that a man so learned and practiced in ecclesiastical writings did not first observe how contrary this was to the intention of that Scripture of such great authority. Throughout its account of God’s works, it adds, “And God saw that it was good”; and, when all things have been completed, it concludes, “And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” Thus it wished no other reason for the making of the world to be understood than that good things should be made by a good God.

If no one had sinned, the world would have been adorned and filled only with good natures. And because sin exists, it does not follow that everything has been filled with sins, since the number of good things in the heavens is far greater and preserves the order of its nature. Nor did the evil will, because it refused to preserve the order of nature, thereby escape the laws of the just God who orders all things well.

For just as a painting is beautiful when black is placed in its proper position, so the universe, if anyone could behold it, is beautiful even with sinners in it, although, considered in themselves, they are disfigured by their own deformity.

Next, Origen—and anyone who thinks in this way—should have seen that, if this opinion were true, and the world had been made so that souls might receive bodies as prisons in which they would be enclosed and punished according to the merits of their sins, then the higher and lighter bodies should have belonged to those who had sinned less, while the lower and heavier bodies should have belonged to those who had sinned more.

Demons, therefore, since nothing is worse than they are, should have received earthly bodies, since nothing is lower or heavier than these, rather than good human beings.

But, so that we might understand that the merits of souls are not to be weighed by the qualities of their bodies, the worst demon received an airy body, while the human being—even now, though evil, is far less and more mildly evil, and certainly before sin—received an earthen body.

What could be more foolish than to say that, in order that there might be one sun in one world, God the Craftsman provided not for the beauty of its appearance or even for the welfare of bodily things, but that this happened because one soul had sinned in such a way that it deserved to be enclosed in such a body?

Consequently, if it had happened that not one but two—or not two but ten or a hundred—had sinned in the same and equal way, this world would have had a hundred suns. If that did not happen, it was not because of the Craftsman’s wondrous provision for the welfare and beauty of bodily things; rather, it would have happened because the sinful progress of one soul had been so great that it alone deserved such a body.

It is not the progress of souls—about which they do not know what they are saying—that must plainly be restrained, but the progress of those who think such things, who are far removed from the truth and deserving of restraint.

Textual variants preserved in the source: *haec* [*hoc*, “this”]; *aeternum tamen est Verbo Dei* [*in*, “in”]; *eam revocantem ad se Creatorem* [*revocante Creatore*, “with the Creator calling it back”]; *tempora sonorum volventem* [*volvente*, “unfolding”]; *imperfectio* [*imperfecto*, “the imperfect creature”]; *qua* [*quia*, “because”]; *a quo statu* [*statim*, “immediately”]; *ita hoc vivere* [*nec*, “nor”]; *adversa* [*aversa*, “turned away”]; *exstitit* [*existit*, “exists”]; *cessaret* [*cessabit*, “will cease”]; *interrogatus* [*Dominus*, “the Lord”]; *superferebatur* [*ferebatur*, “was borne”]; *pro modo* [*modulo*, “measure”]; *an quia* [*quoniam*, “because”]; *indigus* [*indigens*, “needy”]; *angeli* [*sancti angeli*, “holy angels”]; *septenariam* [*senariam vel septenariam*, “sixfold or sevenfold”]; *profecti sunt* [*profecto*, “surely”]; *ullamque* [*nullamque*, “and no”]; *a conditore* [*a Deo conditore*, “from God the Creator”]; *hoc scribit* [*scripsit*, “wrote”]; and *colore nigro loco suo posito* [*posita*, “placed”].

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Same Error and on Eternal Fire. From the Book of the *Response to the Questions of the Presbyter Orosius*.

Thus, in what he made from nothing, the will is said to be not nothing to such an extent that it is especially commended. For to one who is told, “Power is at your command when you will,” whether there is something available from which the deed may be done or not, will is sufficient where supreme power exists. How, then, in what is created from nothing, can the will of the creator be declared to be nothing, when something can be created from nothing precisely because the creator’s will, even without matter, is sufficient unto itself?

But if perhaps they wish to maintain that not only the soul, but no creature whatsoever, was made from nothing, on the grounds that whatever God made, he made by his will—which will is certainly not nothing—let them consider from what man was made according to the body. Certainly, as Scripture testifies, God made him from clay or from the dust of the earth, and unquestionably he made him by his will. [Col. 0624A] Yet God’s will is neither dust nor clay. Therefore, just as in what was made from clay, although it was made by the will, the will is not clay, so in what was made from nothing, although it was made by the will, the will is not nothing.

Now, as for what you added with grief—that men among you had fallen from the Priscillianist heresy into the error of Origen, and could not be healed from that plague unless the medicine itself had also introduced something diseased—your grief is not blameworthy. For truth, not falsehood, ought to have driven out falsehood; for this is to change evil, not to avoid it.

Nevertheless [Col. 0624B], since you mention that those who brought Origen’s books to you transmitted from them what is true concerning God himself, the creator of all creatures—that is, concerning the coeternal and immutable Trinity—against which truth Priscillian restored the ancient Sabellian doctrine, in which the very Father is said to be the Son and also the Holy Spirit, he is worse in this respect also: he thinks the soul likewise does not possess a nature of its own, but flows down from God himself like a particle, and dares to affirm with the Manichaeans that it is so shamefully polluted and changed for the worse. Your province has nevertheless received no small benefit from those books, especially in the matter concerning which the gravest error is committed: such false and impious opinions are held about the Creator, not the creature.

Whether, then [Col. 0624C], those who had deviated were restored to this faith, or those who had not yet known it learned it by reading those discussions, let them rejoice that they have learned what is sound. But although I already see that you have recognized what in those works is erroneous, you will be able to learn better there how to argue against such things—there where the error itself arose long ago and was exposed not long ago.

Yet, as far as I can, I also warn you not to dare to hold opinions about the correction and restoration of the devil and his angels to their former state—not because we begrudge the devil and the demons, or in that way repay their malevolence, since they attempt to disturb the paths by which we strive toward God for no other reason than that they are driven by the goads of envy, but because we ought not, through our presumption, add anything to the final sentence [Col. 0624D] of the supreme and most truthful Judge.

For he himself foretold that he would say to those like them: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” Nor should what is written elsewhere—“for ever” and “for ever and ever”—move us to take “eternal” in this passage as meaning merely long-lasting. The Latin translator did not wish to say *in aeternum et in aeternum aeterni*—“for ever and for ever of eternity.” Rather, because what is called αἰών (*aiōn*) in Greek can be translated both as “age” and as “eternity,” other translators more suitably rendered it “for the age” and “for the age of the age.” But this was not said where it says, “Go into the eternal fire.”

For it does not say αἰῶνα (*aiōna*), but αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*). If the latter were derived from *saeculum* (“age”), it would be called *saeculare* in Latin, not *aeternum* (“eternal”), a term which no translator has ever dared to use in that way. [Col. 0625A] Therefore, although in Latin *saeculum* may be understood as having some end, whereas *aeternum* is ordinarily applied only to what is without end; and although αἰών in Greek is understood sometimes to mean “eternal” and sometimes “age,” what is derived from this noun and called αἰώνιον, as I understand it, is not ordinarily taken by the Greeks to mean anything except what has no end.

We, however, customarily use neither αἰῶνα nor αἰώνιον except for “eternal.” We use αἰῶνα also for “age,” but αἰώνιον only for “eternal.” Although some occasionally also dare to say *aeternale* (“eternal”), so that the Latin language may not seem to lack a derivative from the same noun, perhaps such people may find, according to the usage of Scripture, something called αἰώνιον that is not without end.

Thus God repeatedly says in the books of the Old Testament [Col. 0625B]: “This shall be your perpetual ordinance,” where the Greek has αἰώνιον, although he often gave commands concerning such rites as were destined to have an end. If these words are understood more carefully, perhaps the things signified by those rites were not destined to have an end. For, not to go farther afield, we call God eternal—not, of course, these two very brief syllables, but what they signify.

The Apostle also spoke of “eternal times,” meaning former and ancient times; in Greek this is written instead of *χρόνων αἰωνίων* (*chronōn aiōniōn*). Writing to Titus, he says: “The hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before eternal times.” But since times appear to have begun backward from the foundation of the world, how are they eternal, unless he called those things eternal which have no time preceding them?

But whoever carefully [Col. 0625C] attends to what was said—“Go into the eternal fire”—proves by the contrary that the expression means what has no end, from that very Gospel passage concerning eternal life, which the righteous are to receive. For it too does not have an end. The passage concludes: “So these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” In both places the Greek has αἰώνιον.

If mercy urges us to believe that the punishment of the wicked will not be without end, what are we to believe about the reward of the righteous, when in both cases, in the same passage, in the same sentence, and with the same word, eternity is proclaimed? Are we again to say that the righteous will fall from that sanctification and eternal life into the uncleanness of sins and into death? Far be this from the soundness of Christian faith.

Both, therefore, are said to be eternal, that is, αἰώνιον, without end [Col. 0625D], lest, while grieving over the devil’s punishments, we doubt Christ’s kingdom. Finally, if “eternal” and *aeternale*—that is, αἰών and αἰώνιον—are customarily used in Scripture with both meanings, sometimes without end and sometimes with an end, what shall we answer concerning the words of the prophet where it is written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished”? Whatever punishment is signified by the names “worm” and “fire,” certainly, if it will not die and will not be extinguished, it has been foretold as without end.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How “Every creature groans and labors in birth until now” is to be understood. From the same book, the *Response to the Presbyter Orosius*.

We see that the sun, moon, and other stars are heavenly bodies [Col. 0626A]; we do not see that they are animate. Let this be read in the divine books, and we shall believe it. For the testimony from the Apostle’s Epistle which you said they are accustomed to cite can also be understood of human beings alone, since in each human being there is every kind of creature—not universally, as heaven and earth and everything in them exist, but in a certain generic way.

For in him there is the rational element, which angels are either proved to possess or are believed to possess; and, so to speak, the sensory element, which even beasts do not lack—for they use their senses and sensory movements to seek what is useful and avoid what is harmful; and there is also the vital element deprived of sensation, such as can be observed in trees. For bodily growth takes place in us without our sensation: hair feels nothing even when it is cut, and yet it grows.

Now [Col. 0626B] the bodily creature itself is more clearly apparent in us. Although it was made and formed from earth, there are nevertheless within it particles from all the elements of this corporeal world, contributing to the balance of health. For the limbs are invigorated by heat, which comes from fire, whose light also flashes forth through the eyes; the circulation of the veins, which are called arteries, and the passages of the lungs are filled with air; and if there were no moisture, no saliva would collect, and dryness would consume life. The blood itself, flowing moistly and filling other veins like streams and rivers, is diffused throughout everything.

Thus there is no kind of creature that cannot be recognized in man. And so every creature groans and suffers in him, awaiting the revelation of the children of God. Through the resurrection of the body, every creature will be freed from slavery to corruption, though not in all [Col. 0626C] human beings, because everything is present in each individual. The same passage of the apostolic writings may perhaps be understood in some other and better way.

It does not, however, follow from the same words that we should believe the sun, moon, and stars to groan together until, at the end of the age, they are freed from slavery to corruption.

Since I said, “Let this be read in the divine books, and we shall believe it,” take care lest what they habitually bring forward from the Book of holy Job mislead you—those who assert these things. There it is written:

“How then can man be righteous before the Lord?  
Or how can one born of a woman be clean?  
If he commands the moon, and it does not shine,  
and the stars are not clean before him,  
how much less man, who is rottenness,  
and the son of man, a worm!”

From this they wish to infer that the stars possess a rational spirit and are not free from sin, but that they are in heaven because a lesser fault earned a higher or better place.

I do not think this opinion should be accepted as divinely authoritative. [Col. 0626D] For it was not Job himself who uttered it; Job is given, in a certain sense, the singular testimony from God that he did not sin with his lips before the Lord. Rather, it was one of his friends who said it—those who are called the comforters of evils and who were all rejected by the divine judgment.

Just as in the Gospel, although it is entirely true that certain things were said, not everything that is reported as having been said is believed to be true—for the truthful Gospel narrative testifies that many false and impious statements were made by the Jews—so in this book, where many persons are reported to have spoken, we must consider not only what is said [Col. 0627A] but also who says it. Otherwise, by indiscriminately accepting whatever is written in any holy book, we would be compelled to confess—God forbid—that what the foolish wife suggested to her holy husband was true and just: that he should say something against God and thereby be freed by dying from that intolerable punishment.

I do not say this because those friends, who were rejected by the Lord and rightly censured by the holy servant of God, were unable to speak anything true, but because not everything they said should be considered true. Although they said nothing true against Job, someone who knows how to distinguish wisely what is said may nevertheless take a sound statement from their words as a testimony to the truth.

But when, in seeking to establish something for us by the testimony of the holy utterances, we wish to rely on them, we must not be told [Col. 0627B] that we should also believe whatever is written in the Gospel if the evangelist happens to report that it was said by someone who should not be believed.

For there the Jews said to the Lord Christ: “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” We detest this statement all the more because Christ is dearer to us. Yet we cannot doubt that it was uttered by the Jews, since we believe the Gospel narrative to be entirely true. Thus we neither deny the credibility of the evangelist who records it, nor fail to shudder at the blasphemous voice of the Jews.

We do not accord the authority of the canon either to impious and wicked persons, or to those who are still little ones in faith—immature and unlearned—who may happen to be mentioned there as speaking. For when the man whose eyes the Lord had opened—he had been born blind—said, “We know [Col. 0627C] that God does not hear sinners,” we must not therefore accept this statement as having Gospel authority in such a way that we resist the very words of the Lord in the Gospel. The Lord’s own voice affirmed that the man who said, “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner,” went down from the temple more justified than the Pharisee who recalled and boasted of his own righteousness.

Nor should this man, recently enlightened in the flesh, take offense that we said he uttered the statement “God does not hear sinners” less cautiously during the infancy of his faith, when he still did not know who had healed him. For even the Apostles, chosen above others, clinging to the Lord’s side and hanging upon his words, are found to have said many things deserving rejection—too many to recount at length [Col. 0627D]. Indeed, blessed Peter deserved not only to be rebuked for some of his words but even to be called “Satan.”

Nevertheless, in comparison with the righteousness of God, it does not seem an inappropriate opinion to say that even the holy angels in heaven are not righteous. This is not because they fell away from righteousness in order to become what they are, but because they were made and are not God, and therefore cannot possess as much spiritual light as he possesses by whom they were made.

For where there is supreme righteousness, there is supreme wisdom, and this is God, of whom it is said: “To the only wise God.” But another question is how much of his righteousness the angels comprehend and how much they do not comprehend. By participation in him they are righteous; in comparison with him they are not righteous.

But this, as I have said, is one question; another concerns the stars [Col. 0628A], the sun, and the moon—whether they possess rational spirits within these visible and luminous bodies. Anyone who doubts that these are bodies does not know at all what a body is.

Nor is this matter of much concern to us, so that we should investigate with the utmost zeal things remote from our senses and from the understanding of human weakness, and not so placed in Scripture that knowledge of them has been entrusted to us. Indeed, lest through rash suspicion we rush into sacrilegious fables, divine Scripture cries out: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not scrutinize what is too strong for you. But always consider what the Lord has commanded you.” Thus reckless presumption appears more deserving of blame in these matters than cautious ignorance.

Certainly the Apostle says: “Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers.” I therefore firmly believe that thrones, dominions [Col. 0628B], principalities, and powers exist in the heavenly realms, and I hold with unquestioning faith that they differ from one another in some way. But, so that you may not despise me, whom you consider a great teacher, I do not know what these beings are or how they differ from one another. Nor do I think that this ignorance places me in danger, as I would be endangered in obedience if I neglected the Lord’s commandments.

For this reason I think that the Spirit of God, through the authors of our sacred writers, did not explain these matters fully, but touched upon and briefly indicated them, so that if something of this kind should perhaps be revealed through a higher revelation to someone such as we are, he would not think that those through whom the holy proclamations of the canonical Scriptures were delivered to us were inferior.

For the more anyone progresses in knowledge, the more he will find himself beneath those writings [Col. 0628C] which God established as a firmament above all human hearts.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Likewise, from the book *On Heresies*, concerning the error of Origen.

Epiphanius, then, immediately introducing other Origenists, says:

“The Origenists are another group, also followers of Adamantius the interpreter, who likewise reject the resurrection of the dead, while introducing Christ as a creature and the Holy Spirit as a creature [or: ‘who also deny the resurrection of the dead, but say that Christ and the Holy Spirit are creatures’], and allegorizing paradise, the heavens, and everything else.”

This is what Epiphanius says about Origen. But those who defend him say that he taught the Father [Col. 0628D], the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one and the same substance, and that he did not reject the resurrection of the dead—although those who have read more of his works also strive to convict him on these points.

But this Origen has other doctrines which the Catholic Church entirely rejects. In these matters it neither falsely accuses him nor can it be deceived by his defenders, especially concerning the purification and liberation of the entire rational creation, and its return again, after a long period, to the same evils.

For what Catholic Christian, whether learned or unlearned, would not recoil vehemently from the purification of the wicked that he asserts—that even those who ended this life in the greatest possible crimes, offenses, sacrileges, and impieties, and finally the devil himself and his angels [Col. 0629A], are, after exceedingly long periods, purified and liberated and restored to the kingdom and light of God; and that again, after exceedingly long periods, all who have been liberated fall back and return once more to these evils; and that these alternating cycles of blessedness and misery of the rational creation have always existed and will always exist?

Against this utterly vain impiety, and against the philosophers from whom Origen learned it, I argued at great length in the books *On the City of God*, especially in the twelfth.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Against those who introduced cycles of recurrence, from Book XII of *The City of God*.

Therefore, what we are now asking after five thousand and more years [Col. 0629B], our descendants could also ask after six hundred thousand years, with the same curiosity, if this mortality of human beings continued to arise and perish and human weakness continued in ignorance.

Those who lived before us could have raised this question in the earliest times after the creation of man. Indeed, the first man himself could have asked, either on the day after he was made or on that same day, why he had not been made earlier. And whenever he might have been made earlier, this same dispute about temporal things would have found another reason why his powers were different then, different now, or different later.

The philosophers of this world thought that they could or ought to resolve this question in no other way than by introducing cycles of time. They asserted that the same events in nature had always been renewed and repeated [Col. 0629C], and that thereafter the cycles of coming and passing ages would continue without interruption—whether these cycles occurred while the world remained in existence, or whether, at fixed intervals, the world arose and perished and always displayed the same things, as though new, which had already passed or were yet to come.

They cannot by this deception free the immortal soul, even after it has acquired wisdom. It goes without cessation toward a false blessedness and without cessation returns to true misery. For how can that blessedness be true whose eternity is never secure, while the soul either ignorantly fails to know the misery that is to come or unhappily fears it while in blessedness?

Or, if it will never again return to misery but proceeds from misery to blessedness, then something new occurs in time that has no end in time. [Col. 0629D] Why, then, should the world not also have been made, and why should man, who was made in the world, not also have been made, so that those supposed cycles, discovered by false sages through false reasoning, might be avoided in sound doctrine by the path of the straight way?

Some wish to understand the following passage [Col. 0630A] from the book of Solomon called *Ecclesiastes* as referring to these cycles:

“What is that which has been? The same that shall be;  
and what is that which has been done? The same that shall be done;  
and there is nothing new under the sun.  
Who can say, ‘Behold, this is new’?  
It has already existed in the ages that were before us.”

They wish this to be understood as referring to the cycles that return to the same things and recall everything to the same condition. But Solomon either spoke of the matters about which he had been speaking above—that is, of generations passing away and others coming, of the courses of the sun, and of the flows of streams—or certainly of all classes of things that arise and perish.

There were human beings before us; there are human beings with us; there will be human beings after us. Thus animals and plants, and even the monsters that are born as unusual occurrences, although they differ from one another and some are reported to have been created only once, nevertheless, insofar as they are generally marvels and monsters, certainly have existed and will exist. It is not new or recent that a monster is born under the sun.

Although they have understood these words in this way, they also wished the wise man to mean that everything had already been made in God’s predestination, and therefore that nothing is new under the sun.

But far be it from right faith to believe that Solomon’s words signify those cycles by which they think that the cycles of times and temporal things [Col. 0630B] are repeated in such a way that, for example, just as in this age the philosopher Plato taught his disciples in the city of Athens, in the school called the Academy, so throughout innumerable previous ages—at very long but nevertheless fixed intervals—the same Plato, the same city, the same school, and the same disciples were repeated, and thereafter will be repeated through innumerable ages.

Far be it, I say, from us to believe such things. Christ died once for our sins; having risen, he dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him. After the resurrection we shall always be with the Lord. To him we now say what the sacred psalm admonishes: “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation for ever.”

I think what follows fits these people well: “The wicked walk in a circle”—not because their life will return through the circles they imagine, but because their way is now such an error, that is, false doctrine.

What wonder is it if, wandering in these circles, they find neither entrance nor exit [Col. 0630C]? The human race and this mortality of ours neither know by what beginning they began nor by what end they are enclosed, since they cannot penetrate the height of God. For although he himself is eternal and without beginning, he nevertheless originated time from some beginning, and in time made man [Col. 0630D], whom he had never made before—not through a new and sudden plan, but through an immutable and eternal purpose.

Who can investigate this unsearchable height and scrutinize what cannot be fathomed? According to it, God created temporal man in time by an unchanging will, before whom no human being had ever existed, and multiplied the human race from one man.

For the psalm itself, after first saying, “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation for ever,” then struck down those in whose foolish and impious doctrine no eternity of the soul’s liberation and blessedness is preserved, immediately adding: “The wicked walk in a circle.” It is as though someone were saying to him: “What, then, do you believe, think, and understand? Is it to be supposed that God suddenly decided to make man, whom he had never made throughout the infinite eternity of the past—that God, to whom nothing new can happen and in whom there is nothing mutable?”

He immediately replied, speaking to God himself: “According to your height you have multiplied the children of men.” Let human beings think [Col. 0631A] what they think, he says; let them suppose and debate what pleases them. According to your height, which no human being can know, you have multiplied the children of men.

For it is exceedingly profound that God should always have existed, and that he should have first willed at some point to make the man whom he had never made, without changing his purpose or will.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Against the claim: “From where did the devil first acquire an evil will, since he was created good by God?” Likewise, from Book XII of *The City of God*.

God, who is the Supreme Being—and for this reason every essence that is not supreme was made by him, since what was made from nothing ought not to be equal to him, nor could it exist in any way if it had not been made by him—[Col. 0631B] is not to be blamed for any offense of vices but is to be praised in consideration of all natures. Accordingly, the truest explanation for the blessedness of the good angels is found in this: they cleave to him who is supreme.

But when the cause of the misery of the evil angels is sought, the fitting answer presents itself: they turned away from him who is supreme and turned toward themselves, who are not supreme. And what else is this vice called but pride? “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” They therefore did not wish to preserve their strength for him; and although they would have been greater if they had cleaved to him who is supreme, by preferring themselves to him they preferred what is lesser.

This was the first defect and the first impoverishment, the first vice of a nature created so that it would not be supreme, yet could attain blessedness by enjoying him who is supreme. [Col. 0631C] When it turned away from him, it was not indeed nothing, but it was less than it otherwise would have been, and for this reason it became miserable.

Now, if the efficient cause of this evil will is sought, none is found. For what is it that makes the will evil, when the will itself makes the evil deed? Thus an evil will is the efficient cause of an evil deed. But there is no efficient cause of an evil will. For if there is some thing, it either has a will or does not have one. If it has one, it certainly has either a good or an evil will. If it has a good will, who could be so foolish as to say that a good will makes an evil will?
