If that were so, the good will would be the cause of sin—nothing more absurd can be imagined. But if this thing that is thought to make the evil will itself has an evil will, I ask in turn about the thing that made that will.

[Col. 0631D]

And, so that there may be some limit to the inquiry, I am asking for the cause of the first evil will. The first evil will is not one made by an evil will, but the first one is that which nothing made. For if there preceded something by which it was made, that earlier will made the other. If it is answered that no thing made it and that therefore it always existed, I ask whether it existed in some nature. If it existed in none, it did not exist at all. But if it existed in some nature, it would have corrupted and ruined that nature, would have been harmful to it, and thereby would have deprived it of good. Therefore an evil will could not have existed in an evil nature, but in a good, though mutable, nature, one that could be harmed by this vice; for if it did no harm, it was certainly not a vice.

Consequently, it cannot even be called an evil will. But if it did harm by taking away or diminishing the good, then it certainly did harm. Therefore an eternal evil will could not have existed in a thing in which a natural good had preceded, a good that the evil will could remove by harming it. If, then, it was not eternal, I ask who made it.

It remains to say that the thing in which there was no will made the evil will. I ask whether this thing is superior, inferior, or equal. If superior, it is certainly better. How, then, could it be the cause of another’s will rather than a good will? The same applies, plainly, to an equal thing: for as long as two beings are equally of good will, one does not make an evil will in the other.

It remains that an inferior thing, which has no will, made the evil will of the angelic nature that first sinned. But whatever this inferior thing may be, down to the lowest earth, since it is nature and essence, it is undoubtedly good, possessing its own measure and form within its kind and order. How, then, can a good thing be the efficient cause of an evil will? How, I ask, can good be the cause of evil?

For when the will, abandoning what is higher, turns toward lower things, it becomes evil—not because the thing toward which it turns is evil, but because the turning itself is perverse. Therefore the inferior thing does not make the will evil; rather, the will itself, having been made, perversely and disorderly desired the inferior thing.

Suppose that two people, equally disposed in mind and body, see the beauty of one body. When they have seen it, one is moved to enjoy it unlawfully, while the other remains steadfast in chaste willing. What do we suppose to be the cause that an evil will arises in one but not in the other? [The printed continuation, “quae illam res [rem] fecit in quo facta est,” is corrupt and uncertain.] It is not that bodily beauty, for it did not produce this in both, since it presented itself equally to the sight of both. Is it the flesh of the one who looked? Why not also of the other? Or is it the mind? Why not the mind of both? We have already stated that both were equally disposed in mind and body.

Should we say that one of them was tempted by the hidden suggestion of an evil spirit, as though he had not consented by his own will to that same suggestion and to whatever persuasion it involved? We are asking what thing produced this consent, this evil will that he applied to the one who wickedly persuaded him.

Let this obstacle also be removed from the question. Suppose both are tempted by the same temptation, and one yields and consents to it, while the other remains as he had been. What else is evident except that one did not wish to depart from chastity, while the other did? From where, unless from his own will, when the same disposition of body and mind existed in both, the same beauty was equally seen by the eyes of both, and the same hidden temptation pressed upon both?

Therefore, for those who wish to know what thing made the evil will in one of them, if they look carefully, nothing presents itself. For if we say that he himself made it, what was he before the evil will except a good nature, whose author is God, who is the immutable [unchangeable] good?

Thus, when someone who consents to the tempter and persuader, while another does not consent, turns to enjoy unlawfully the beautiful body that was equally present to both through sight—although before that sight and temptation both had been alike in mind and body—says that he himself made his own evil will, then let him ask whether he made it because he is a nature or because he is made from nothing. He will find that the evil will begins not from the fact that he is a nature, but from the fact that the nature was made from nothing.

For if nature is the cause of the evil will, what else are we forced to say except that evil is made by the good and that good is the cause of evil? For if an evil will is made by a good nature, how can a good nature, although mutable, make something evil before it has an evil will—that is, how can it make the evil will itself?

Let no one, therefore, seek an efficient cause of the evil will. It is not efficient but deficient, because its production is not an effecting but a defecting. To defect from what is supreme toward what is lesser—that is to begin to have an evil will.

To seek the causes of these defections, since they are not efficient but deficient, as I have said, is like wanting to see darkness or hear silence, although both are known to us: the one only through the eyes, the other only through the ears—not in a form, certainly, but in the privation of form. Let no one, then, ask me to know what I know that I do not know, unless perhaps he wishes to learn not to know what must be understood to be unknowable.

For things known not in their form but in the privation of their form—if it may be said or understood—are known in a certain way by not knowing, so that they are known by being un-known. When even the sharpness of bodily sight passes through bodily forms, it sees darkness nowhere except where it has begun not to see. Similarly, the inability to hear silence pertains not to any other sense but solely to the ears; yet silence is perceived in no way except by not hearing.

Thus our mind beholds intelligible forms by understanding, but where they fail it learns by not knowing. “For who understands his transgressions?”

This I know: the nature of God can never, nowhere, and in no part defect. Those things can defect that were made from nothing. Yet when they are more fully existent and do good, then they do something, for they have efficient causes; insofar as they defect and thereby do evil—for what do they then do except futile things?—they have deficient causes.

I also know that where the evil will arises, it arises in something that, if it did not will it, would not arise. Therefore just punishment follows defects that are not necessary but voluntary. One does not defect toward evils, but evilly—that is, not toward evil natures, but evilly because one turns against the order of natures from what is supreme toward what is lesser.

Avarice [or covetousness] is not a vice of gold, but of a person who perversely loves gold, abandoning justice, which ought to have been preferred incomparably to gold. Lust is not a vice of beautiful and pleasing bodies, but of a soul that perversely loves bodily pleasures, neglecting temperance, by which we are joined to things spiritually more beautiful and incorruptibly more pleasing. Boasting is not a vice of human praise, but of a soul that perversely loves to be praised by human beings, scorning the testimony of conscience. Pride is not a vice of the one who grants power, nor even of power itself, but of a soul that perversely loves its own power, despising the more just justice of one more powerful.

Thus whoever perversely loves the good of any nature, even if he obtains it, becomes evil in relation to that good and miserable because deprived of what is better.

Since, then, there is no natural or, if one may say so, essential efficient cause of the evil will—for evil begins from the mutable spirits themselves, by which the good of their nature is diminished and corrupted, and no such will is made except by a defection in which God is abandoned, while the cause of that defection itself likewise defects—if we say that there is no efficient cause even of a good will, we must take care lest the good will of the good angels be believed to be unmade and coeternal with God.

Since they themselves were made, how can that will be said not to have been made? And since it was made, was it made with them, or did they first exist without it?

But if it was made with them, there is no doubt that it was made by the one by whom they too were made. At the same time as they were made, they cleaved to the one by whom they were made, through the love with which they were made [or: with which they were made to cleave]. They were distinguished from the company of the others by this: the former remained in that same good will, while the latter were changed by defecting from it—by an evil will, namely, in the very fact that they defected from the good will, from which they would not have defected unless they had willed to do so.

But if the good angels first existed without a good will and made that will within themselves without God’s action, were they made better by themselves than by him? Far be it! For what were they without a good will except evil? Or, if they were not evil for the reason that no evil will was present in them—for they had not defected from a will that they had not yet begun to possess—at least they were not yet such, not yet as good as they became when they began to possess a good will.

Or, if they could not make themselves better than the one who had made them—for no one makes anything better than he does—then plainly they could not have a good will, by which they would be better, unless the Creator’s assistance were at work.

And when their good will brought it about that they turned not toward themselves, who were lesser, but toward him who is supreme, cleaving to him so that they might be more truly existent and live wisely and blessedly through participation in him, what else is shown except that the good will, however good, was helpless and would have remained only a desire, unless he who had made the good nature from nothing capable of receiving him had himself made that will—first making it better by filling it, and then making it more eager by awakening it?

For this too must be examined: if the good angels made the good will in themselves, did they make it from something, or from no will at all? If from none, then they did not make it. If from something, was that something evil or good? If evil, how could an evil will have been the maker of a good will? If good, then they already had it; and who had made that will except the one who created them with a good will—that is, with the chaste love by which they would cleave to him—at once creating nature in them and bestowing grace?

Therefore, unless they had a good will—that is, the love of God—we must never believe that the holy angels existed.

But those who, although created good, nevertheless became evil through their own evil will—a will that good nature did not make except when it voluntarily defected from the good—either received a lesser grace of divine love than those who remained in it, or, if both were created equally good, then, when these fell through evil will, the others were given greater assistance and reached that fullness of blessedness from which they became utterly certain that they would never fall. We have already discussed this in the book that follows the present one.

We must therefore confess, with due praise of the Creator, that it can be said not only of holy human beings but also of the holy angels that “the love of God has been poured out in them through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them.” And not only of human beings but first and especially of angels is the statement true: “But for me it is good to adhere to God.”

Those who share this good possess, together with the one to whom they cleave, a holy fellowship among themselves. They are one City of God, and likewise his living sacrifice and his living temple. One part of it is gathered from mortal human beings to be joined to the immortal angels; it now journeys mutably on earth, or rests among those who have died, in the hidden receptacles and dwelling places of souls. [Col. 0635B]

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### That the Devil Apostatized from His Creator through Pride from the Very Beginning of Creation, from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

When pride cast down the devil, so that he perverted his good nature through an evil will, Scripture does not say. Yet reason clearly shows that this happened first, and that from this he became envious of the human being.

It is evident to all who consider the matter that pride does not arise from envy; rather, envy arises from pride. Nor can it be thought without reason that the devil fell through pride at the beginning of time, and that there was never a time before this when he lived peacefully and happily with the holy angels. Instead, he apostatized from his Creator from the very beginning of creation, so that we may understand both parts of what the Lord says—“He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth”—as referring to the beginning: not only that he was a murderer, but also that he did not stand in the truth.

He was a murderer from that beginning at which a human being could be killed; for a human being could not be killed before there was someone to be killed. The devil was therefore a murderer from the beginning, because he himself killed the first human being, before whom there had been no human beings.

But he did not stand in the truth—and this also from the beginning, from the moment he himself was created. He would have stood if he had wished to stand. [Col. 0635D]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### How the Statement of Isaiah Is to Be Understood: “How You Have Fallen from Heaven, Lucifer,” etc., also from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

When, therefore, it is thought that the devil never stood in the truth, never led a blessed life with the angels, but fell from the very beginning of his creation, this must not be understood in such a way that he is thought to have been created evil by the good God rather than corrupted through his own will. Otherwise he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning; for he did not fall if he was made such.

Rather, as soon as he was made, swollen with pride and corrupted by delight in his own power, he turned away from the light of truth. Thus he did not taste the sweetness of the blessed and angelic life: he did not disdain it after receiving it, but by refusing to receive it he abandoned and lost it.

Accordingly, he could not have foreknowledge of his own fall, since wisdom is the fruit of piety. But having immediately become impious, he consequently became blind in mind. He did not fall from what he had received, but from what he would have received if he had wished to submit to God. Because he did not wish to do so, he fell from what he was about to receive, yet he did not escape the power of the one under whom he refused to exist. The weight of his merits was therefore established in him, so that he could neither delight in the light of justice nor be freed from its judgment.

Thus, what is said of him through the prophet Isaiah—“How Lucifer has fallen from heaven, he who rose at dawn; he has been crushed to the earth, who sent forth to all the nations”—and what follows, spoken figuratively of the king, as though of Babylon but understood as referring to the devil:

“You said in your heart: I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne. I will sit on the lofty mountain, above the lofty mountains that are toward the north. I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High. But now you will descend to the underworld,”

and the rest, is understood as having been said against the devil.

Many of these statements apply to his body as well, which he also gathers from the human race, and especially to those who cleave to him through pride by apostatizing from the commandments of God. For just as the one who was the devil is called a human being—“An enemy has done this,” as it says in the Gospel—so the one who was a human being is called the devil: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?”

And just as Christ’s body, which is the Church, is called Christ—as in the statement, “You are Abraham’s seed,” after it had shortly before said, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed”; it does not say “to seeds,” as though referring to many, but “as though to one, and to your seed, which is Christ”—and again, “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ”—in the same way the body of the devil, whose head is the devil, namely, the multitude of the impious, and especially those who fall from Christ or from the Church as from heaven, is called the devil. Many things are figuratively said of this body that apply not so much to the head as to the body and its members.

Therefore Lucifer, who rose at dawn and fell, may be understood as the race of apostates, whether from Christ or from the Church, which turns to darkness after losing the light it bore. In the same way, those who turn to God pass from darkness to light—that is, those who were darkness become light.

Likewise, in the figure of the prince of Tyre, what is said through the prophet Ezekiel is understood as referring to the devil:

“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty. You were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were adorned with every precious stone,”

and so forth.

These words apply not so much to the spirit of wickedness himself, the prince, as to his body. For the Church is called paradise, as it is read in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a sealed spring, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruit of apple trees.”

From there all heretics fell through open and bodily separation, or all who have turned back to their vomit through a hidden and spiritual separation, although they appear to be bodily within the Church. After they had walked for a little while in the way of justice following the remission of sins, their latter condition became worse than the former. Of them it was fitting not to know the way of justice rather than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.

The Lord describes this most wicked generation when he says that an unclean spirit goes out from a person and then returns with seven other spirits, entering the house that it had already found cleansed, so that the final condition of that person becomes worse than the first.

To such a generation of human beings, which has now become the body of the devil, these words could apply:

“From the day on which you were created, you were with the Cherub”—that is, with the seat of God, which is interpreted as “abundant knowledge”—“I placed you on God’s holy mountain”—that is, in the Church. Hence the statement, “And he heard me from his holy mountain.” “You were in the midst of fiery stones”—that is, of fervent holy spirits, living stones. “You walked without blemish in your days from the day on which you were created, until iniquities were found in you.” [Col. 0637B]

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### Against Those Who Ask Why God Created the Human Being Whom He Foreknew Would Sin, from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*
If, then, it is asked why God permitted a human being to be tempted whom he knew beforehand would consent to the tempter, I cannot penetrate the depth of his plan, and I confess that this lies far beyond my powers. Perhaps, then, there is some more hidden reason, referred [variant: reserved] to better and holier persons, by his grace rather than on account of their merits. Nevertheless, insofar as he grants me understanding or permits me to speak, it does not seem to me that the human being would have merited great praise if he could live rightly for the reason that no one persuaded him to live wrongly—since, both by nature and by his power, he had [or: has] the ability to will not to consent to the persuader, though assisted by him who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. [Col. 0637C]

Why, then, would he not permit the one whom he himself knew beforehand would consent to be tempted? Why would he do this so that the human being, by his own will, would commit the fault, and by God’s justice would be ordered through punishment, in order that even in this way he might show the proud soul, for the instruction of future saints, how rightly he himself makes use even of the wills of evil souls, when they use good natures perversely? Nor should it be thought that this tempter would have overthrown the human being unless there had first arisen in the human soul some pride that needed to be restrained, so that through the humiliation of sin he might learn what he had falsely presumed about himself. [Col. 0637D]

For it was most truly said: “The heart is exalted before ruin, and it is humbled before glory.” Perhaps this is also the voice of that human being in the Psalm: “I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever [or: eternally].” Then, having learned by experience what evil there is in the proud presumption of one’s own power, and what good there is in the help of God’s grace, he says: “Lord, by your will you furnished strength to my beauty, but you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled.” But whether this was said of that human being or of another, it nevertheless had to be demonstrated to a soul that exalted itself and trusted excessively, as though in its own virtue, by the experience of punishment, how badly a created nature fares if it withdraws from its maker. [Col. 0638A]

For from this, too, the goodness of God is especially commended: no one who departs from him can fare well. Even those who rejoice in deadly pleasures cannot be without fear of pain. Those, moreover, who do not perceive the evil of their abandonment at all, through an even greater stupor of pride, appear utterly more miserable [to others who know how to discern these things], so that, if they are unwilling to receive the medicine by which such things are avoided, they may at least serve as an example by which such things can be avoided.

For, as the Apostle James says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire; then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin, and sin, when it has been completed, produces death.” [Col. 0638B] Hence, once the swelling of pride has been healed, one rises again if the will that was absent before the experience—so that one might remain with God—is present at least after the experience, so that one may return to God.

If, however, some are troubled by the temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, as though they did not now see the entire human race being tempted without ceasing by the devil’s snares, why does God permit this also? Is it because virtue is tested and exercised, and because it is a more glorious crown not to have consented when tempted than not to have been able to be tempted? Even those who, having abandoned the Creator, follow the tempter increasingly tempt those who remain in the word of God, providing them with an example of avoiding desire and instilling in them, against pride, a pious fear. [Col. 0638C] Hence the Apostle says: “Pay attention to yourself, lest you also be tempted.”

It is astonishing how greatly this humility—[the transmitted text has *istum*; variant: *cur tamen ista*, “why nevertheless this”]—by which we submit to the Creator lest, as though we did not need his help, we presume upon our own powers, is commended throughout all the divine Scriptures by continuous care. Since, therefore, the righteous make progress even through the unjust, and the pious through the impious, it is said in vain: “God should not have created those whom he knew would become evil.” For he would not have created those whom he knew would benefit the good, so that both useless [variant: useful] people might arise to exercise and admonish the good will of others, and they might justly be punished for their own evil will.

“Such a human being,” they say, “he should have made who would not wish to sin at all.” We grant that the nature which does not wish to sin at all is better. Let them also grant that the nature which was made so that it could refrain from sinning if it wished is not evil, and that the judgment by which the one who sinned by will, not by necessity, was punished is just. [Col. 0638D]

Therefore, just as true reason teaches that the creature whom nothing illicit delights at all is better, so true reason likewise teaches that the creature is also good which has it in its power, if illicit pleasure arises, to restrain it in such a way that it rejoices not only in other lawful and rightly performed acts, but also in the restraint of that very perverse pleasure.

Since, then, this nature is good and that one better, why would God make only the one and not both? Accordingly, those who had prepared [or: had been prepared] to praise God for that one alone ought to praise him more abundantly for both. The one exists in the holy angels, the other in holy human beings. [Col. 0639A]

Those, however, who chose the portions of iniquity and corrupted a praiseworthy nature by a culpable will should not, merely because they were foreknown, have been left uncreated. They too have their proper place, which they fill among created things for the benefit of the saints. For God does not need the justice of any righteous person—how much less the iniquity of anyone perverse?

Who, with sober consideration, would say that it would have been better not to create one whom God knew could be corrected through another’s iniquity than to create one whom he knew would have to be condemned for his own iniquity? For this is to say: “It would be better that there should not be one who, by mercifully making good use of another’s evil, would be crowned, than that there should even be one who would be evil and would be justly punished according to his deserts.” [Col. 0639B]

When certain reasoning clearly demonstrates two goods that are not equal, one higher and the other lower, dull-hearted people who say that both must be of the same kind do not understand that they are saying nothing other than that only the higher one should exist. Thus, when they wish to equalize the kinds, they reduce the number of goods; and by excessively enlarging one kind, they abolish the other.

Who would listen to them if they said that, because the sense of sight is more excellent than that of hearing, there should be four eyes and no ears? Likewise, if that rational creature is more excellent which submits to God without any comparison to punishment and without any pride, while another kind among human beings was created in such a way that it cannot recognize God’s beneficence in itself except by seeing another’s punishment, so that it does not become high-minded but fears, and does not presume upon itself but trusts in God—who, rightly understanding, would say that this creature is of the same kind as the former and would not see that he was saying nothing other than that this one should not exist, but only the other? [Col. 0639C]

If, then, it is said foolishly and without instruction, “Why, therefore, did God not also create those whom he knew would become evil, wishing to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, and for this reason enduring with much patience the vessels of wrath that are prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory?”—then indeed the one who glories glories only in the Lord, when he recognizes that it is not his own but God’s, not only that he exists, but also that it is well with him only through the one from whom he has received existence.

It is therefore said most improperly: “There would be no persons to whom God could show such great kindness of his mercy if they could not exist otherwise than with those in whom he would demonstrate the justice of his vengeance.” Why, rather, should both not exist, since in both God’s goodness and his equity are rightly proclaimed? [Col. 0639D]

“But,” they say, “if God had wished it, these people too would have been good.” How much better, then, did God will that they should be what they themselves willed to be: good people not without fruit, and evil people not without punishment, while even in that respect they would be useful to others.

“But he knew that their future will would be evil.” Certainly he knew this; and because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is not his but theirs. Why, then, did he create those whom he knew would become such? Because, just as he foresaw what evil they would do, so he also foresaw what good he himself would bring about from their evil deeds.

For he made them in such a way as to leave them the capacity to do something themselves, so that, whatever they might choose culpably, they would find him working in them laudably. From themselves they have an evil will; from him, however, they have a good nature, a just punishment, a place due to them, and for others an instrument of exercise and an example of fear. [Col. 0640A]

“But,” they say, “he could also have converted their will to good, since he is omnipotent.” Why, then, did he not do so? Because he did not wish to. Why he did not wish to is his concern; for we must not be wiser than we ought to be.

Nevertheless, I think we have shown shortly before that this rational creature too is no small good—even that kind which, by comparison with evil people, avoids evil. That kind of good creature would certainly not exist if God had converted everyone’s evil will to good and inflicted due punishment on no iniquity. In that case there would be only the one kind that made no progress through any comparison with the sin or punishment of evil people; and, as though the number of the more excellent kind had been increased, the number of kinds of good would actually be diminished. [Col. 0640B]

“Then,” they say, “is there something in God’s works that needs another’s evil in order to progress toward good?”

Have human beings become so deaf and blind, I do not know through what passion for argument, that they do not hear or see that, when some are punished, very many are corrected? What pagan, what Jew, what heretic would not prove this every day in his own household?

Yet when they come to the discussion and investigation of truth, people do not wish to direct their attention to their own perceptions: they do not see that, through the work of divine providence, the commotion of discipline that must be imposed upon them arises for their benefit, so that, even if those who are punished are not corrected, the others may nevertheless fear by their example, and the just destruction of some may contribute to the salvation of others. [Col. 0640C]

Is God, then, the author of the malice or wickedness of those whose just punishment he takes into account and for whose benefit he has determined that this should be done? Certainly not. But although he knew beforehand that they would become evil through their own vices, he did not therefore cease to create them, assigning them to the usefulness of those whom he created in such a way that they could not progress toward good except by comparison with evil people.

For if they did not exist, they would certainly benefit nothing. Is it a small good that there should be those who are certainly useful to that kind? Whoever does not want that kind to exist does nothing other than ensure that he himself will not belong to it.

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in accordance with all his wills.” He foreknows who will be good, and creates them; he foreknows who will be evil, and creates them, offering himself to the good for their enjoyment, bestowing many gifts of his own, mercifully forgiving the evil, justly punishing them, and likewise mercifully punishing and justly forgiving; fearing nothing from anyone’s evil, needing nothing from anyone’s justice, and seeking nothing for himself even from the punishments of the wicked. [Col. 0640D]

Why, then, would he not permit the human being to be tempted by that temptation through which he would be exposed, convicted, and punished, when the proud desire for his own power gave birth to what it had conceived and was confounded by its own offspring, and when, by a just punishment, it would deter future generations from the evil of pride and disobedience, for whom these things were being prepared to be written and proclaimed?

If, however, it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt specifically through a serpent, what person would not be reminded that this was done for the sake of signification, when Scripture acts in prophecy through testimonies of such authority and divinity, confirmed by such effects that the world is already filled with them? [Col. 0641A]

This is not because the devil wished to signify something for our instruction. Rather, when he approached in order to tempt, he could not do so except by permission. Could he have approached through anything other than that by which he was permitted to approach?

Whatever, therefore, that serpent signified must be attributed to the providence under which the devil himself has a desire to harm, but no power except what is granted for the overthrow and destruction of the vessels of wrath, and for the humbling or testing of the vessels of mercy.

We know, then, from where the serpent’s nature comes. At God’s word, the earth produced all cattle, beasts, and serpents. This entire creation, possessing a living but irrational soul, is subject, by the law of the divine order, to every rational creature, whether of good or evil will. What wonder is it, then, if the devil was permitted to do something through a serpent, when Christ himself permitted demons to enter pigs? [Col. 0641B]

More careful inquiry is usually directed toward the very nature of the devil. The heretics, offended by the distress caused by his evil will, try to alienate that nature entirely from the creation of the supreme and true God and to assign it another origin opposed to God. They cannot understand that everything that exists, insofar as it is some substance, is good, and that it cannot exist except from that true God from whom all good comes.

An evil will, however, moves disorderly, preferring lower goods to higher ones. Thus it happened that the spirit of a rational creature, delighting in its own power because of its excellence, swelled with pride before it fell from the blessedness of the spiritual paradise and withered away through envy.

Yet even in this there is something good: the fact that it lives and gives life to a body, whether an aerial body, as in the spirit of the devil himself or of demons, or an earthly body, as in the soul of any human being, even one malignant and perverse. [Col. 0641C]

Thus, while they do not wish [variant: wish] anything made by God to sin by its own will, they say that God’s own substance was first corrupted by necessity and afterward, inexpiably, by will. But we have already said much elsewhere about the utterly insane error of these people.

In the present work, however, we must ask, according to Holy Scripture, what should be said about the devil. First, whether from the beginning of the world he, delighted by his own power, withdrew from that fellowship and love in which the angels who enjoy God are blessed, or whether at some time he too belonged to the holy assembly of the angels, righteous and blessed along with them.

Some say that his fall from the heavenly abodes occurred because he envied the human being made in the image of God. But envy follows pride; it does not precede it. For envy is not the cause of pride; pride is the cause of envy. [Col. 0641D]

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is sufficiently clear what arises from what. For, by loving his own excellence, each person envies equals because they are made equal to him; inferiors, lest they become equal to him; or superiors, because he is not made equal to them.

Thus, by becoming proud, one becomes envious; one does not become proud by becoming envious. The Scripture rightly defined pride as the beginning of every sin when it said: “The beginning of every sin is pride.” [Col. 0642A]

To this testimony can also be suitably applied what the Apostle says: “The love of money is the root of all evils,” if we understand avarice in a general sense: the desire by which each person seeks something more than is proper, out of a desire for his own excellence and a certain love of what belongs to him.

The Latin language wisely gave this desire its name when it called it *private* (*privata*), a term that clearly derives more from loss than from increase. For every privation diminishes. Therefore, pride is driven into narrowness and poverty by the very thing from which it wishes to rise, when it is reduced from what is common to what is private through a destructive love.

There is also a particular avarice, more commonly called love of money. The Apostle, using the species to signify the genus through this name, wished universal avarice to be understood when he said: “The love of money is the root of all evils.” For the devil too fell through this avarice—not because he loved money, but because he loved his own power. [Col. 0642B]

Accordingly, a perverse love of self deprives the swollen spirit of holy fellowship and confines it in misery, though it already longs to be satisfied through iniquity. Hence, after saying in another place, “People will be lovers of themselves,” he immediately added, “lovers of money,” descending from that general avarice, whose head is pride, to this particular form, which is proper to human beings.

For human beings would not be lovers of money unless they thought themselves more excellent in proportion as they were richer. The charity opposed to this disease does not seek what is its own; that is, it does not rejoice in private excellence. Therefore, it is rightly said that it is not inflated.

These two loves—one holy, the other impure; one social, the other private; one concerned with the common good for the sake of the heavenly fellowship, the other reducing even what is common to private power for the sake of arrogant domination; one submissive, the other rivaling God; one tranquil, the other turbulent; one peaceful, the other seditious; one preferring truth to the praises of those who err, the other eager for praise by any means; one friendly, the other envious; one wishing for one’s neighbor what one wishes for oneself, the other wishing to subject one’s neighbor to oneself; one ruling one’s neighbor for the neighbor’s benefit, the other for its own benefit—these two orders preceded in the angels: one among the good, the other among the evil. [Col. 0642C]

They distinguished the two cities established among the human race, under the admirable and ineffable providence of God, who administers everything that he creates [or: everything created]: one the city of the righteous, the other the city of the wicked. Through a certain temporal intermingling of these, the age proceeds until the final judgment separates them. The one, joined to the good angels, will attain eternal life in the kingdom [or: with its king]; the other, joined to the evil angels, will be sent into eternal fire with its king.

## CHAPTER XL

### On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from Book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

Next, let us consider the tree of the knowledge—that is, the discernment—of good and evil. This tree too was plainly visible and bodily, like the other trees. There is no doubt what kind of tree it was; what must be sought is why it received this name. [Col. 0643A]

As I consider the matter again and again, I cannot express how pleasing that interpretation is according to which the tree was not harmful as food. For he who had made all things very good would not have placed anything evil in paradise. Rather, the evil was the human being’s transgression of the command.

It was necessary, however, that the human being, placed under the Lord God, should be prohibited from something, so that obedience itself might be the virtue by which he pleased his Lord. I can say with complete truth that this alone is the virtue of every rational creature acting under God’s authority. The first and greatest vice is the swelling of pride: the desire to use one’s own power for one’s ruin. The name of this vice is disobedience.

There would therefore have been no means for the human being to think and perceive that he had a Lord unless something had been commanded him. That tree, then, was not evil, but it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, if the human being ate from it after the prohibition, the transgression of the command would take place in connection with it. Through the experience of punishment, the human being would learn what difference there was between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. [Col. 0643B]

Accordingly, this too should be understood not as something said figuratively, but as an actual tree. Its name was imposed not because of the fruit or apple that would grow from it, but from the event itself that would follow when it was touched contrary to the prohibition.

## CHAPTER XLI

### Further discussion of the same tree, from Book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

If that tree had been evil, the tree from which God prohibited the human being, it would appear to have been poisoned by the nature of that evil, producing death. But since the one who made all things very good had planted all the trees in paradise as good, and since there was no nature of evil there—for nowhere is there any nature of evil—we shall discuss this more carefully, if the Lord wills, when we begin to speak about that serpent. [Col. 0643C]

The human being was prohibited from a tree that was not evil, so that the preservation of the command itself would be good for him in its own right, and transgression would be evil in its own right. Nothing could have demonstrated [or: commended] more clearly how great an evil disobedience alone is: the human being became guilty of iniquity because he touched something contrary to the prohibition, although he would certainly not have sinned if he had touched it without being prohibited. [Col. 0643D]

For, if someone says, for example, “Do not touch this plant,” because it happens to be poisonous and foretells death if touched, death does indeed follow the one who despises the command. But even if no one had prohibited it and he had touched it, he would nevertheless have died. That thing would be contrary to his health and life, whether he were forbidden to touch it or not.

Likewise, someone may prohibit another from touching something that would not harm the person touching it, but would harm the one who issued the prohibition—for example, if someone put his hand into another’s money after being forbidden to do so by the owner. The sin would consist in the fact that the action could harm the person who issued the prohibition.

But when something is touched that would not harm the one touching it if it were not prohibited, nor harm anyone else whenever it might be touched, why was it prohibited except to demonstrate that obedience is good in itself and disobedience evil in itself? [Col. 0644A]

Finally, the sinner desired nothing other than not to be under domination. The thing that was lost was precisely that in which, so that it might not be lost, the command of the ruler alone ought to have been heeded. If that alone had been heeded, what else would have been heeded but the will of God? What else would have been loved but the will of God? What else would have been preferred to the human will but the will of God?

Let the Lord see to the reason why he commanded. The servant must do what he commanded, and perhaps afterward the one who seeks to please him may consider why he commanded it.

Nevertheless, so that we need not pursue the reason for this command any longer: if it is itself a great benefit to the human being to serve God, then by commanding God makes beneficial whatever he wishes to command. There is no need to fear that he could command something useless. [Col. 0644B]

Nor can it happen that a person’s own will does not fall upon him with the weight of a great ruin if, by exalting it, he places it above the will of the one who is superior. The human being experienced this when he despised God’s command, and through this experience learned the difference between good and evil: the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience, that is, of pride, defiance, perverse imitation of God, and harmful liberty.

This happened in connection with the tree, which, as has already been said, received its name from the event itself. We would not perceive evil except by experience, because there would be no evil if we had not committed it. There is no nature of evil; rather, the loss of good has received this name.

God is the unchangeable good. The human being, insofar as his nature is concerned—the nature in which God created him—is indeed good, but he is not unchangeable as God is. A changeable good that comes after the unchangeable good becomes a better good when it adheres to the unchangeable good, loving and serving it through reason and its own will. [Col. 0644C]

This nature is therefore also a great good, because it has received the capacity to adhere to the nature of the supreme good. If it is unwilling to do so, it deprives itself of good, and this is evil for it; hence, through God’s justice, punishment also follows.

For what is as unjust as for the deserter of the good to fare well? This cannot happen in any way. Yet sometimes the evil of having lost a higher good is not perceived when one possesses the lower good that one has loved.

But divine justice requires that the one who voluntarily lost what he ought to have loved should lose with pain what he did love, while the creator of all natures is praised everywhere. For what is lost is still a good: unless some good had remained in the nature, there would be no pain over lost good in the punishment.

The one who, without the experience of evil, loves good—that is, who chooses to retain good before experiencing its loss, so as not to lose it—must be proclaimed above all human beings. But unless this were a matter of singular praise, it would not have been attributed to that child who, born from the race of Israel as Emmanuel, “God with us,” reconciled us to God: the human being who is mediator between human beings and God; the Word with God, but flesh among us; the Word made flesh between God and us.

Of him the prophet says: “Before the child knows good or evil, he rejects evil in order to choose good.” [Col. 0645A]

How can one reject or choose what one does not know? Because these two things are known in different ways: good through prudence, evil through experience. Evil is known through the prudence of good, even if it is not felt. Good is held fast so that its loss will not be experienced as evil.

Likewise, good is known through the experience of evil, because the person who suffers from the loss of good feels what he has lost. Before, therefore, the child knew through experience either the good of which he would be deprived or the evil he would feel through the loss of good, he rejected evil in order to choose good. That is, he did not wish to lose what he possessed, nor, by losing it, to experience the loss of what he ought not to lose [variant: ought not to have lost; *Ed. Ben.*: “so that he would not experience losing what he ought not to have lost”].

He is the singular example of obedience: he came not to do his own will but the will of the one by whom he was sent, unlike the one who chose to do his own will rather than the will of the one by whom he was made. Therefore, just as through the disobedience of one many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous. For just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ. [Col. 0645B]

Some people are perversely sharp-witted and dull when they ask how the tree could have been called the tree of the discernment of good and evil before the human being had transgressed the command through it, and before that very experience had revealed the difference between the good he lost and the evil he committed.

The tree received such a name so that, if it were not touched contrary to the prohibition, people would guard against what they would experience if it were touched contrary to the prohibition. For it was not made the tree of the discernment of good and evil because they ate from it contrary to the command. Even if they had obeyed and had taken nothing from it contrary to the command, it would rightly have been called what would have happened to them if they had taken from it. [Col. 0645C]

For example, suppose it were called the tree of satiety because human beings could be satisfied by eating from it. If no one approached it, would the name thereby be inappropriate? Certainly not, since, when they approached it and were satisfied, they would then discover how rightly that tree was called so.

“And how,” they ask, “would the human being have understood what was meant by the tree of the discernment of good and evil, when he had no knowledge at all of what evil was?”

Those who think this way pay too little attention to how many unknown things are understood through their opposites. Even words referring to things that do not exist cause no confusion when they are introduced into speech. For what does not exist at all is called “nothing,” and everyone who hears and speaks Latin understands these two syllables. This occurs because the mind attends to what exists and recognizes, through its privation, what does not exist. [Col. 0645D]

Likewise, when we say “empty,” we look at the fullness of a body and understand, through its privation as an opposite, what “empty” means. In the same way, through the sense of hearing, we judge not only voices but also silence.

Thus, from the life that was present in the human being, he could guard against its contrary, namely the privation of life called death. He could also understand the cause by which he would lose what he loved—that is, any action of his by which he would bring it about that he lost his life—whatever syllables might be used to name it. In Latin, when “sin” or “evil” is said, he could understand it as a sign of what he would distinguish in his mind.

How do we understand what is meant by “resurrection,” which we have never experienced? Is it not because we sense what it is to live, call the privation of that condition “death,” and call the return to what we sense “resurrection,” whatever other name may be given to the same thing in any language? [Col. 0646A]

A sign is conveyed to the mind through the voice of those speaking, and when it sounds, the mind recognizes what it could also think of without the sign. It is astonishing how even an inexperienced nature avoids the loss of things it possesses. Who taught animals to avoid death except the sense of life? Who taught a little child to cling to the person carrying him when that person threatened to throw him down from a height? This response begins at a certain age, but it does so before the child has experienced anything of the kind. [Col. 0646B]

Thus life was as sweet to those first human beings as it certainly was something they avoided losing. They could understand God signifying this very thing by whatever forms or sounds he used. Nor could sin have been persuaded to them in any other way unless they had first been persuaded that, as a result of that action, they would not die—that is, that they would not lose what they possessed and rejoiced to possess.

This will be discussed in its proper place. Let those who are troubled by how human beings could understand God naming or threatening things they had not experienced pay attention and see that we recognize the names of all things unfamiliar to us only through opposites that we already know, when they concern privations, or through similarities, when they concern forms, without any disturbance of doubt.

## CHAPTER XLII

### On the twofold work of God’s providence, and on the same twofold operation of divine governance in the human being, from Book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

From this point the eye of thought is raised to the world itself, as though to a great tree of things, and in the world too a twofold operation of providence is found: partly natural, partly voluntary. [Col. 0646C]

The natural operation occurs through God’s hidden administration, by which he also gives growth to trees and grasses. The voluntary operation occurs through the works of angels and human beings.

According to the first, the heavenly bodies are ordered above and the earthly bodies and lights and stars shine below; the alternations of day and night take place; the earth, founded upon the waters, is washed by them and surrounded by them; the air is spread broadly over all; plants and animals are conceived, born, grow old, and die; and whatever else occurs in things through an inner and natural movement. [Col. 0646D]

According to the second, signs are given, people are taught and learn [or: teach and learn], fields are cultivated, societies are governed, arts are practiced [or: are exercised], and whatever else is done either in the heavenly fellowship or in this earthly and mortal one, so that the good may be helped, even through those who do not know what they are doing.

The same twofold power of providence is active in the human being. First, it operates naturally with respect to the body, namely through the movement by which the body comes into being, grows, and grows old. It operates voluntarily with respect to the body by providing for its food, clothing, and care.

Likewise, with respect to the soul, it acts naturally so that the soul may live and perceive; voluntarily, so that it may learn and consent. [Col. 0647A]

Just as agriculture works externally upon a tree so that what takes place internally may flourish, so, with respect to the body, nature serves what acts within, while medicine serves it externally. Likewise, with respect to the soul, doctrine is supplied externally so that nature may be made blessed internally.

What negligence in cultivation is to a tree, carelessness in treatment is to the body, and sluggishness in learning is to the soul; and what useless moisture is to a tree, destructive nourishment is to the body, and persuasion to iniquity is to the soul.

God, therefore, who is above all things, who created all things and governs all things, being good creates all natures [variant: creates all natures good], and orders all wills justly.

What, then, is contrary to truth if we believe that the human being was placed in paradise so that he might cultivate it, not with servile labor but with the honorable pleasure of the soul? What work is more innocent for those who are at leisure, and what is fuller for those who are prudent and deeply reflective?

## CHAPTER XLIII

### That the eternal Divinity, moved neither by times nor by place, moves the creature, from Book VII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*
We therefore say that the supreme, true, one and only God is the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, God, his Word, and the Spirit of both—the Trinity itself, neither confused nor divided: the God who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see. He is contained neither by a finite nor by an infinite spatial extent, nor does he vary through the finite or infinite succession of time [Col. 0647C]. For in his substance, insofar as he is God, there is nothing that is shorter in one part than in the whole, as must be the case with things that exist in places; nor was there in his substance something that now no longer is, or will be something that is not yet, as occurs in natures capable of undergoing temporal change.

Living, then, in immutable eternity, he created all things simultaneously. From them times would proceed, places would be filled, and the ages would revolve through the temporal and spatial movements of things. Among these things he made some spiritual and some corporeal, forming matter which no other being, nor any being at all, but absolutely he himself established as unformed yet formable, so that it would precede its formation not in time but in origin. He placed spiritual creation above corporeal creation, because the spiritual can be changed only through time, whereas the corporeal can be changed through both time and place [Col. 0647D].

For example, the mind is moved through time, whether by remembering what it had forgotten, learning what it did not know, or willing what it did not will; but the body is moved through place, whether from earth to heaven, from heaven to earth, from east to [or: in] west, or in some other similar manner. Everything that is moved through place must also be moved simultaneously through time. But not everything that is moved through time must also be moved through place.

Just as, therefore, a substance that is moved through time and place is preceded by a substance that is moved only through time, so the latter is preceded by that which is moved neither through place nor through time. Accordingly, just as the created spirit, which is moved only through time, moves the body through time and place, so the creator Spirit, who is moved neither through time nor through place, moves the created spirit through time [Col. 0648A]. The created spirit moves itself through time, and through time moves the body toward a place; but the creator Spirit moves himself without time or place, moves the created spirit through time without place, and moves the body through time and place.

Therefore, whoever attempts to understand how the eternal, truly immortal, and immutable God himself—moved neither through place nor through time—moves his creature temporally and locally, cannot, I think, attain this understanding unless he has first understood how the soul, that is, the created spirit, moved not through place but only through time, moves the body through time and place [Col. 0648B].

For if he cannot yet grasp what occurs within himself, how much less can he grasp what is above himself? The soul, affected as it is by the habit of bodily senses, even supposes that it itself is moved through place together with the body, when it moves the body through place. But if it could carefully inspect, as it were, the hinges of its bodily limbs and observe how they are arranged joint by joint, and from which the beginnings of movement arise, it would discover that things moved through spatial intervals are moved only from those things that are fixed in place.

A finger, for example, does not move by itself unless the hand is fixed, so that it may be moved from the hand’s joint as from an immovable hinge. Likewise, the entire palm is moved from the elbow joint; the elbow from the shoulder joint; and the shoulder from the scapula. The hinges on which the movement depends remain fixed, while what is moved passes through spatial extent [Col. 0648C]. Similarly, the foot has a joint at the ankle, and, when that joint remains fixed, the foot is moved; likewise the leg at the knee, and the entire foot at the hip.

No movement of any limb is produced by the will unless it proceeds from some joint or hinge [variant: articular joint] which the impulse of that same will first fixes, so that what is moved may be set in motion by that which is not moved through spatial extent. Indeed, even when one is already walking, one foot is not lifted unless the other remains fixed and carries the whole body, until the foot that has been moved from the place where it stood reaches the place toward which it is carried and rests upon the lowermost joint of its hinge [variant: “unmoved”].

If, then, in the body the will moves no limb through place except from the joint of that limb which it does not move—and both the part of the body that is moved and the part by which it is fixed in order to be moved possess their own corporeal dimensions, by which they occupy their respective spatial regions [Col. 0648D]—how much more does the impulse of the soul itself, to which the limbs are subject so that what is pleasing may be fixed and from it what is to be moved may take its support, move the limbs? For the soul is not a corporeal nature and does not fill a spatial region as water fills a bottle or sponge; rather, in wondrous ways it is joined to the body it vivifies by that incorporeal impulse, by which [variant: which] it also commands the body through a certain intention, not by bulk.

How much more, I say, is the impulse of its will itself not moved through place when it moves the body through place—when it moves the whole body through its parts, yet moves no parts through place except through those parts which it does not move through place?

If this is difficult to understand, let both propositions be believed: that spiritual creation, moved not through place, moves the body through place; and that God, moved not through time, moves spiritual creation through time [Col. 0649A].

If someone does not wish to believe this concerning the soul—a matter which he would undoubtedly not only believe but also understand if he could conceive of it as it truly is, incorporeal—he should consider: who would not readily see that what is not extended through spatial regions is not moved through place? Whatever is extended through spatial regions is a body; consequently, if the soul is not believed to be a body, it follows that it should not be thought to move through place.

But, as I had begun to say, if someone does not wish to believe this concerning the soul, he is not to be compelled. Concerning the substance of God, however, unless he believes that it is moved neither through time nor through place, he does not yet believe perfectly in its immutability.

Since the nature of the Trinity is wholly immutable, and therefore so eternal that nothing can be coeternal with it, it nevertheless moves, within itself and in itself, the creature subject to it through time and place, without any time or place [Col. 0649B]. It creates natures by goodness and orders wills by power, so that among natures there is none that does not come from it [printed marker: “from him” with reference 38], while among wills there is no good will to which it is not beneficial (*prosit*) [variant: over which it does not preside, *praesit*], and no evil will that it cannot use well. But since he has not given all natures freedom of will, those to which he has given it are more powerful and superior; consequently, natures without will must be subject to the nature endowed with will. This too occurs by the ordering of the Creator, who never punishes an evil will in such a way as to destroy the dignity of its nature.

Since, therefore, no body and no irrational soul possesses freedom of will, these are subject to those natures endowed with freedom of will—not all things to all things, but in the manner distributed by the justice of the Creator [Col. 0649C].

Thus God’s providence, governing and administering the whole of creation—natures so that they may exist, and wills so that good wills may not be fruitless and evil wills may not remain unpunished—first subjects all things to himself; then corporeal creation to spiritual creation, irrational creation to rational creation, earthly creation to heavenly creation, the feminine to the masculine, the weaker to the stronger, and the more needy to the more abundant.

Among wills, it subjects the good to himself and the others to those that serve him, so that an evil will may suffer what a good will has done at God’s command—whether through the good will itself or through an evil will, but only in matters that are naturally subject even to evil wills, namely, bodies. For evil wills possess their own inward punishment within themselves: their very iniquity [Col. 0649D]. Consequently, all corporeal nature, all irrational life, and every will, whether weak or perverse, are subject to the holy angels who enjoy subjection to God and serve God blessedly, so that with or among those subject to them they may do what the order of nature requires, under the command in all things of him to whom all things are subject.

Accordingly, the angels see immutable truth in him and direct their wills according to it. They thus become participants in his eternity, truth, and will, always doing his will without time or place—[variant: “always fulfilling his will”]. Yet they are moved by his command temporally, although he himself is not moved temporally—not in such a way that they recoil or fall away from contemplating him, but so that simultaneously they contemplate him without place or time and fulfill his commands in the lower realms [Col. 0650A], moving themselves through time and the body through time and place, insofar as this accords with their activity.

## CHAPTER XLIV

### That God’s speech to Adam and his walking in paradise must be understood without hesitation as occurring not through God’s own substance but through a creature subject to him; likewise from Book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

As for the action of the angelic creature, through which God’s providence chiefly cares for every kind of thing, and especially for the human race, it assists from outside both through appearances resembling bodily things and through the bodies themselves that are subject to angelic power [Col. 0650B].

Since this is so, almighty and all-sustaining God, who in immutable eternity, truth, and will is always the same and is moved neither through time nor through place, moves spiritual creation through time and also moves corporeal creation through time and place. By this movement he administers externally the natures that he established inwardly, through wills subject to him, which he moves through time, and through bodies subject both to him and to those wills, which he moves through time and place. This occurs at that time and place, the rationale of which in God himself is life without time or place.

When God does something of this kind, we must not suppose that the substance by which he is God is changed by times and places or moved through times and places. Rather, we must recognize these things in the work of divine providence, not in the work by which he creates natures, but in the work by which he also administers externally the natures he has created inwardly.

He himself exists in no place, interval, or spatial extent, by immutable and transcendent power; he is interior to everything, because all things are in him, and exterior to everything, because he is above all things [Col. 0650C]. Likewise, by immutable eternity he exists in no temporal interval or extent; he is older than all things, because he is before all things, and newer than all things, because he himself is after all things.

Therefore, when we hear Scripture say:

> “And the Lord God commanded Adam, saying: ‘You shall eat for food from every tree that is in paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it. For on the day on which you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”

if we seek to know how God spoke these words, the precise manner cannot properly be comprehended by us. Nevertheless, we must hold with complete certainty that God speaks either through his own substance or through a creature subject to him [Col. 0650D]. He speaks through his own substance only for the creation of all natures; but to spiritual and intellectual beings he speaks not only in order to create them but also in order to illuminate them, once they are capable of receiving his speech—such speech as is in his Word, which “in the beginning was with God, and God was the Word,” through whom all things were made.

When God speaks to those who cannot receive such speech, he speaks only through a creature: either through a spiritual creature alone, whether in dreams or in ecstasy, by means of a likeness of bodily things; or even through the bodily creature itself (*per seipsam corporalem*) [variant: *per ipsam corporalem*, “through that bodily creature”], when some appearance is presented to the bodily senses or voices resound.

If Adam was such that he could receive that speech of God which God offers to angelic minds through his own substance, we must not doubt that God moved Adam’s mind through time in a wondrous and ineffable manner—although God himself was not moved through time—and impressed upon him this wholesome [variant: useful and wholesome] command of truth, while ineffably showing him, by that same truth, what punishment was owed to the transgressor [Col. 0651A]. In the same way, all good commands are heard or seen in that immutable Wisdom which, at some point in time, transfers itself into holy souls, although it itself undergoes no movement in time.

But if Adam was in such a condition of righteousness that for this task he required the authority of another, holier and wiser creature, through whom he might learn God’s will and command—as we learn through the prophets, and as the angels themselves learn through one another—why should we hesitate to believe that God spoke to him through some such creature, by means of vocal signs that he could understand? [Col. 0651B]

As for the passage written later, that after they had sinned they heard “the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise” [variant: “the voice of the Lord God who was walking in paradise”]: since this occurred not through God’s own substance but through a creature subject to him, no one who understands the Catholic faith can doubt it.

I have discussed this matter at somewhat greater length because certain heretics think that the substance of the Son of God was visible in itself, without his assuming a body, and therefore suppose that he himself was seen by the patriarchs before receiving a body from the Virgin. They reason as though the statement, “No human being has seen or can see him,” were spoken only of God the Father, because the Son was seen before assuming the form of a servant, even through his own substance [Col. 0651C]. This impiety must be driven far from Catholic minds.

## CHAPTER XLV

### On the question of Methuselah’s years, from the *Book of Questions on Genesis*

It is commonly asked how Methuselah could have lived, according to the reckoning of his years, after the Flood, when everyone except those who entered the ark is said to have perished. But this question arose from the corruption of numerous manuscripts. Not only is the matter found differently in the Hebrew text, but even in the Septuagint translation Methuselah is found, in the fewer but more reliable manuscripts, to have died six years before the Flood.

## CHAPTER XLVI

### On the statement that the angels of God had intercourse with the daughters of men, from the same *Book of Questions on Genesis*

It is also asked how angels could have had intercourse with the daughters of men, from whom giants are said to have been born. Some Latin and Greek manuscripts, however, do not read “angels” but “sons of God.” To resolve this question, some have believed that these were righteous men who could also have been called by the name “angels.” For it is written concerning the man John:

> “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way.”

But the question remains: how could giants have been born from human intercourse, or how could angels have united with women, if they were not human beings but angels? [Col. 0651D]

As for the giants—that is, people of extraordinary size and strength—I think there is nothing surprising in their having been born from human beings. Even after the Flood, some such people are found to have existed, and in our own times too certain human bodies have appeared of incredibly great size—not only those of men but also those of women [Col. 0652A].

It is therefore more credible that righteous men, called either angels or sons of God, fell through desire and sinned with women than that angels without flesh could have descended into such a sin. Nevertheless, many people say so much about certain demons who are wicked toward women that it is not easy to formulate a settled judgment concerning the matter [variant: “to define the matter”].

## CHAPTER XLVII

### On Noah’s ark: whether it could have carried all the animals with their food, from the same *Book of Questions on Genesis*

Concerning Noah’s ark it is commonly asked whether, given the capacity with which it is described, it could have carried all the animals said to have entered it, together with their food [Col. 0652B].

Origen resolves this question by means of the geometrical cubit, asserting that Scripture did not say without reason that Moses had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who valued geometry. He says that the geometrical cubit was worth as much as six of our cubits. If, therefore, cubits so large are understood, there is no question that the ark had sufficient capacity to contain all those things.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### That God’s reconsideration of changing things is an immutable rationale, and concerning the dimensions of the ark, in which the human body is plausibly measured on account of Christ’s body, from Book XV of *The City of God*

“And God reconsidered and said: ‘I will destroy the human being whom I have made from the face of the earth, from human being to cattle, and from creeping things to the birds of the heavens, because I am angry that I made them.’” [Col. 0652C]

God’s anger is not a disturbance of his mind, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted for sin. His thought concerning changing things is an absence of reconsideration (*irrecogitatio*) [variant: “reconsideration as well,” *et recogitatio*], an immutable rationale. For God does not repent of any deed of his as a human being does; his judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain.

But if Scripture did not use such expressions, it would not in a certain way draw itself more familiarly into the understanding of every kind of person whom it wishes to help. It would not pass by the proud [editorial variant: “and terrify them”], rouse the negligent, exercise the seekers, and nourish those who understand. It would not do this if it did not first bend down and, in a certain manner, descend to those who lie below [Col. 0652D].

When it also announces the destruction of all terrestrial animals and flying creatures, it expresses the magnitude of the coming disaster; it is not threatening creatures without reason to destruction as though they themselves had sinned.

Now, when God commands Noah—a righteous man, and, as truthful Scripture speaks of him, perfect in his generation—not, of course, as the citizens of the City of God are to be perfected in that immortality in which they will be equal to the angels of God, but as he could be [variant: as they can be] perfect in this pilgrimage—to make an ark in which he, his wife, his sons, and his daughters-in-law, together with the animals that entered the ark at God’s command, would be saved from the devastation of the Flood, this is undoubtedly a figure of the City of God journeying as a stranger in this world [source reading uncertain: “in this age”], that is, of the Church, which is saved through the wood on which the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, hung [Col. 0653A].

The measurements themselves—its length, height, and width—signify the human body, in the truth of which he was foretold and came to human beings. The length of the human body from the crown of the head to the feet is six times its width, which extends from one side to the other, and ten times its height, measured from the back to the belly.

If you measure a man lying on his back or stomach, he is six times as long from head to foot as he is broad from right to left or from left to right, and ten times as long as he is high from the ground. Hence the ark was made three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. Its receiving a door in its side clearly signifies the wound made when the side of the Crucified One was pierced by a lance [Col. 0653B].

Those who come to him enter through this opening, because from it flowed the sacraments by which believers are initiated. The command that it be made of squared timbers signifies the stable life of the saints on every side: however you turn a square, it stands firm. The other details that are mentioned in the construction of the same ark are likewise signs of ecclesiastical realities.

It would take too long to pursue them now, and we have already done so in the work we wrote against Faustus the Manichaean, who denied that anything concerning Christ had been prophesied in the books of the Hebrews [Col. 0653C].

It is possible for one person to explain these things more suitably in one way and another person in another way, provided that everything said is referred to the City of God of which we are speaking, journeying as a stranger in this wicked age as in a flood. If the interpreter does not wish to depart far from the intention of the person who wrote these things, he may say, for example, that the passage written here, “You shall make the lower parts [of the ark] double-chambered and triple-chambered,” does not mean what I said or understood in that work [Ed. Ben.: “wishes it to be understood”]: namely, that because the Church is gathered from all nations, it is called double-chambered on account of the two classes of human beings—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision, which the Apostle expresses in another way as Jews and Greeks [Col. 0653D].

It may instead be said that it is called triple-chambered because all nations were restored after the Flood from the three sons of Noah. Or someone may say something else that is not foreign to the rule of faith.

Since Noah was commanded to make the ark not only with lower chambers but also with upper ones, and since he called the lower ones double-chambered and the upper ones triple-chambered, so that a third habitation might rise from the bottom upward, the three things commended by the Apostle may be understood here: faith, hope, and love.

The three evangelical yields may also be understood more appropriately: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold. In the lowest level, conjugal chastity may dwell; above it, widowhood; and above that, virginity. Other interpretations may also be given, if they can be understood and stated more suitably according to the faith of this city.
