I would say the same about the other matters that must be explained here: although they are discussed in more than one way, they must nevertheless all be brought back to the single harmony of the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### How the statement “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” is to be understood, from Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

“And God said: ‘Behold, Adam has become like one of us in knowing good and evil.’” [Col. 0654]

However and by whatever means this was said, since God nevertheless said it, the statement “one of us” must be understood only as a plural number referring to the Trinity, just as it had been said, “Let us make man,” and as the Lord also said of himself and the Father, “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Thus what the proud man desired is requited upon his own head with its outcome: “You will be like gods.” “Behold,” he says, “Adam has become like one of us in knowing good and evil” [Col. 0654B].

What else should be understood here except that an example intended to inspire fear is being set forth? He not only failed to become what he could [variant: wished] to become, but he did not even preserve what he had become.

“And now,” God says, “lest he stretch out his hand at some time and take from the tree of life, eat, and live forever”—and the Lord God sent him out of the paradise of delight to work the ground from which he had been taken.

The preceding words are God’s words; the act that followed occurred because of those words. Since Adam had been alienated from the life that he would have received with the angels had he kept the command, and also from the life that he had been leading in paradise in a blessed condition of body, he had to be separated from the tree of life—whether that blessed bodily condition subsisted from the tree itself through an invisible power proceeding from a visible thing, or whether in them [variant: in it] there was a visible sacrament of invisible Wisdom [Col. 0654C].

He had to be excluded from it, either because he was already going to die or even as one excommunicated, just as in this paradise also—that is, the Church—people are customarily removed by ecclesiastical discipline from the visible sacraments of the altar.

“And he drove Adam out, and stationed him opposite the paradise of delight.” This too was done for the sake of signification, but it was nevertheless actually done: the sinner was made to dwell opposite the paradise in which blessed life was also signified spiritually, and therefore in misery.

“And he stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns, to guard the way to the tree of life.” This must certainly be believed to have occurred in the visible paradise through heavenly powers, so that a fiery guard was there through angelic ministry. Yet it must also be beyond doubt that this was not done without signifying something concerning the spiritual paradise [Col. 0654D].

## CHAPTER L

### How Adam was not deceived, as the Apostle says, although the same Apostle calls him a transgressor, from the same Book XI

What is more perplexing is this: if Adam was already spiritual, although in mind and not in body, how could he have believed what was said through the serpent—namely, that God had forbidden them to eat the fruit of that tree because he knew that, if they did so, they would become like gods through their discernment of good and evil—as though the Creator had begrudged this one great good to his creature? [Col. 0655A]

It is astonishing if a man endowed with a spiritual mind could have believed this. Or was the woman added because Adam himself could not believe it, while she possessed little understanding and perhaps was still living according to the sense of the flesh rather than according to the spirit of the mind? Is this why the Apostle does not attribute the image of God to her?

For he says:

> “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man.”

This does not mean that the female mind cannot receive that same image, since he says that in this grace there is neither male nor female. Rather, perhaps she had not yet grasped what comes about through knowledge of God and would gradually have grasped it under the man’s direction and administration [Col. 0655B].

The Apostle also did not say without reason:

> “Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, became a transgressor,”

that is, so that through her the man too might transgress.

He also calls Adam himself a transgressor when he says:

> “In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the form of the one to come.”

Yet he denies that Adam was deceived. When questioned, Adam did not say, “The woman whom you gave me deceived me, and I ate,” but rather, “She gave me from the tree, and I ate.” The woman, however, said, “The serpent deceived me.”

Take Solomon, a man of such great wisdom. Are we to believe that he thought there was some benefit in the worship of idols? Yet he was unable to resist the love of women, which drew him toward this evil. He did what he knew should not be done lest he sadden his deadly delights, for which he was pining and wasting away [variant: “perishing”] [Col. 0655C].

So too Adam, after the deceived woman had eaten from the forbidden tree and given some to him to eat with her, did not wish to grieve her. He believed that, if he were alienated from her affection, she might waste away without his consolation and might altogether perish through that discord.

He was not overcome by the desire of the flesh, which he had not yet experienced in the law of his members resisting the law of his mind, but by a certain friendly benevolence—the kind of benevolence that often causes God to be offended lest a human being become an enemy from being a friend. The just outcome of the divine judgment showed that he did not do this [variant: that he ought not to have done this].

Adam, then, was deceived in another way, but I do not think that he could in any way have been deceived by the serpent’s particular trick by which the woman was deceived [Col. 0655D].

The Apostle properly called this “deception,” because what was suggested was false but was believed to be true: namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods—as though he begrudged them divinity, although he had made them human beings.

Even if some desire to experiment troubled the man because of a certain elevation of mind—an impulse that could not escape God, the examiner of inward things—and even if Adam saw that the woman had eaten the food without dying, nevertheless, according to what we discussed above, I do not think that, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, he could in any way have believed that God had forbidden them the food of that tree out of envy.

## CHAPTER LI

### On the creation of the first human being, on causal principles, and on how fifteen years were added to the life of King Hezekiah, whom God had foretold would not live, from Book VI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*

[Col. 0656]

[The supplied source ends here.]

In that first creation of the world, when God created all things, man too was made simultaneously [when God created all things simultaneously, man was made], who was to be. The rationale for creating man is not the act of his creation, but these matters exist differently in the Word of God, where they are not made but eternal; differently in the elements of the world, where all things were made simultaneously and are destined to be; differently in things that, according to causes created simultaneously, are no longer created simultaneously but each in its own time [variant: *quoque*, “also”]—in these Adam, already formed from clay and animated by God’s breath, is like grass that has sprung up; and differently in seeds, in which the primordial causes are again, as it were, repeated [Col. 0656B], derived from things that came into being according to the causes that God first established—just as grass comes from earth and seed from grass. In all these things, what had already been made received the modes and acts proper to its time, and came forth from hidden and visible rational principles, which lie causally hidden in creation, into manifest forms and natures: thus grass sprang up upon the earth, and man was made into a living soul, and other things of this sort—whether thickets or living creatures—belong to that operation of God by which he continues to work even now.

Yet these things also carry within themselves, as it were, the capacity to become invisibly once again what they are, through a certain hidden power of generation which they drew from those beginnings of their causes. In those beginnings, when the world was created and day was made, they had been inserted before they emerged into the manifest form of their own kind [Col. 0656C].

For if those first works of God, when he created all things simultaneously, had not been perfected in their own mode, then doubtless those things would have been added later which were lacking for their perfection, so that a certain perfection of the universe would have consisted of both sets of things, each being like a half—as though they were parts of some whole, which would be completed by the joining of the parts into the whole of which they were parts.

Again, if those things had been perfected in the same way that they are perfected when each is brought forth in its own time into manifest forms and acts, then either nothing would subsequently arise from them over the course of time, or what would arise would be precisely what God does not cease to work from those things that each emerge in their own time.

But now, because the very things that were to be unfolded in subsequent times are both completed and, in a certain manner, begun, God first created all things simultaneously when he made the world [Col. 0656D]. They were completed, because in their proper natures—in which they proceed through the courses of their times—they possess nothing that had not already been made causally in those first things. They were begun, however, because some of them were like seeds of future things, to be brought forth over the course of the ages from hiddenness into manifestation at the appropriate places [variant: “because some were like seeds of future things, to be brought forth over the course of the ages from hiddenness into manifestation at appropriate places”]. The words of Scripture itself are remarkably effective in urging this upon us, if one awakens to their meaning [variant: “the words of Scripture itself”].

For Scripture speaks of them both as completed and as begun. If they had not been completed, it would not have been written: “And the heaven and the earth were completed, and all their completion” [variant: “composition”], nor: “God completed on the sixth day his works which he had made,” and: “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” [Col. 0657A]. Again, if they had not been begun, what follows would not have been said: “On that day he rested from all his works which God began to make.”

If, then, someone asks how he completed them and how he began them—for he did not complete some things and begin others, but the very same things—it is clear from what we have said above. We understand that God completed these things when he created all things simultaneously, so perfectly that nothing remained to be created by him later in the order of time which had not already been created by him in the order of causes. He began them, however, so that what he had established in the causes might subsequently be fulfilled in effects.

Therefore God formed man, dust of the earth, or clay of the earth—that is, from the dust [variant: “or clay”] of the earth—and breathed, or blew [variant: *insufflavit*, “breathed into”], into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul. He was not then predestined, for this had occurred before the ages in the foreknowledge of the Creator; nor was he then causally, or incompletely, begun, or begun in such a way as to be completed, for this had occurred from the beginning in the primordial rational principles, when all things were created simultaneously. Rather, he was created in his own time: visibly in body, invisibly in soul, consisting of soul and body [Col. 0657B].

Let us now see how God made him. First we shall consider his body from the earth; afterward, if we are able, we shall consider his soul. To suppose that God formed man from clay with bodily hands is an exceedingly childish notion, so much so that, even if Scripture had said this, we ought rather to believe that the writer was using a metaphorical expression than that God was limited by the sorts of bodily features we see in our own bodies [Col. 0657C].

For it is written: “Your hand destroyed the nations, and by your strong hand and exalted arm you led out your people.” But who could be so foolish as not to understand that the name of this bodily member is used for God’s power and strength?

Nor should we accept what some people think: that man is God’s pre-eminent work because God spoke of the other things and they were made, whereas he himself made man. Rather, man is pre-eminent because God made him in his own image. For those things that God spoke and that came to be are described in this way because they were made through his Word, just as human beings can speak to other human beings through words that are conceived in time and uttered by the voice. God does not speak in this way except when he speaks through a bodily creature, as to Abraham, to Moses, or through the cloud concerning his Son [Col. 0657D].

Before every creature, however, so that the creature itself might exist, it was said through that Word “which was God in the beginning with God.” And because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, man too was certainly made through him.

Indeed, God made heaven by his Word, because “he spoke and it came to be,” yet it is written: “The heavens are the work of your hands.” And concerning what is, as it were, the lowest foundation of the world it is written: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.”

Let this therefore not be counted as an honor bestowed upon man, as though God spoke the other things and they came to be, but made this one himself; or as though he made the other things by his Word but this one with his hands. What is pre-eminent in man is that God made man in his own image, because he gave him an intellectual mind by which he surpasses cattle; concerning this we have already spoken above [Col. 0658A].

If, placed in this honor, he does not understand how to act well, he will be compared with the very cattle over which he was set. For it is written: “Man, placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless cattle and became like them.”

God also made cattle, but not in his own image. Nor should one say: “He himself made man, but commanded the cattle and they were made.” He made both man and the cattle through his Word, through which all things were made. But because that same Word is also his wisdom and power, it is called his hand—not a visible bodily member, but the power of bringing things into being. [Editorial supplement: *non*, “not,” before “a visible bodily member.”]

For the same Scripture that says that God formed man from the clay of the earth also says that he formed the <sup>42</sup> beasts of the field from the earth, when he brought them, together with the birds of the sky, to Adam so that he might see what he would call them. For it is written: “And God formed from the earth all the beasts” [Col. 0658B].

If, then, he himself formed both man from the earth and the beasts from the earth, what does man possess that is superior in this respect, except that he was created in the image of God? Yet this is not according to the body, but according to the understanding of the mind, about which we shall speak later.

Although the body itself also possesses a certain characteristic that points to this: it was made upright in stature, so that by this very fact man might be reminded not to pursue earthly things like cattle, whose every pleasure is from the earth, and therefore all their members are inclined and prostrate toward the belly.

Thus his body also corresponds to his rational soul—not according to the lines and shapes of the limbs, but rather according to the fact that it is raised toward heaven to contemplate the higher things in the body of the world itself, just as the rational soul ought to raise itself toward the things that excel most in spiritual nature, so that it may seek the things above, not the things upon the earth [Col. 0658C].

But how did God make him from the clay of the earth? Was it with a sudden [variant: *repente*, “at once”] fully developed age—that is, in manhood and youth—or as he continues even now to form human beings in their mothers’ wombs? For it was no other than he who said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.” Perhaps Adam had only this distinctive feature: he was not born from parents but made from the earth, yet in such a way that, by progressing and increasing through the ages, the numbers of time might be completed which we see assigned by nature [variant: *naturae*, “of nature”; the transmitted text has *naturale*] to the human race.

Or rather, is this question not to be asked? Whichever way he made him, he made what it was fitting for the omnipotent and wise God to be able to make and to make. For he assigned definite laws of time to the kinds and qualities of things that were to be brought forth from what was hidden into what was manifest, in such a way that his will is above all [Col. 0658D].

By his power he gave numbers to creation; he did not bind his power to those numbers. His Spirit, in making the world, was borne above it, and after it was made he remained above it—not in bodily places, but in the superiority of his power.

Who does not know that water condensed in the earth, when it reaches the roots of a vine, is drawn into the nourishment of the wood, and there takes on the quality by which it gradually emerges into a grape; as the grape grows, it becomes wine, ripens, and grows sweet; when pressed out it still ferments, and, strengthened by a kind of aging, reaches the use of drinking in a more useful and pleasant form [Col. 0659A]?

Did the Lord therefore need wood, or earth, or these delays of time when, with marvelous swiftness, he changed water into wine—and wine such as even a drunken guest would praise? Did the Creator of times need the assistance of time?

Does not every nature of creeping creatures grow, take shape, come to birth, and gain strength according to definite numbers of days suited to each kind? Were those days awaited so that the rod might be changed into a dragon from the hand of Moses and Aaron? Such things are contrary to nature only for us, who know one customary course of nature; not for God, for whom what he has made is nature.

It may rightly be asked how those causal principles which he implanted in the world when he first created all things simultaneously were established. Were they established so that, as we see all things being born—whether plants or living creatures [variant: *animalium*, “of animals”]—proceeding through their forms and growth, they would pass through periods of time differing according to the diversity of their kinds? Or were they established so that, as it is believed Adam was made without any gradual increase, they would immediately be formed in mature manhood?

But why should we not believe that they possessed both capacities, so that what would arise from them would be whatever pleased their Maker? If we say that they were established only in the first way, then not only the transformation of water into wine but all miracles performed contrary to the customary course of nature would appear to have been made against those principles. If we say that they were established only in the second way, it would be much more absurd for the ordinary forms and kinds of nature to pass through their appointed periods contrary to the primordial causal principles of all things that are born [Col. 0659B–C].

It remains, therefore, that they were created capable of both modes: both the mode by which temporal things most ordinarily run their course, and the mode by which rare and miraculous things occur, as God willed to do whatever was fitting for the time.

Nevertheless, man was made in accordance with what those first causes had established for the making of the first man—one who was not to be born from parents, since no parents preceded him, but was to be formed from clay, according to the causal principle in which he had first been made.

For if he was made otherwise, God had not made him among the works of those six days. When he is said to have been made among them, God had made the cause itself by which man was to come into being in his own time, and according to which he was to be made by the one who had both completed what had been begun, for the perfection of the causal principles, and begun what was to be completed, for the order of times [Col. 0659D].

If, then, in those first causes of things which the Creator initially implanted in the world, he placed not only the fact that he would form man from clay but also the manner in which he would form him—whether as in his mother’s womb or in youthful form—then he undoubtedly made him in the way he had established there, for he would not act contrary to his own disposition.

But if he placed there only a power of possibility, so that man might come to be by whatever manner he came to be, so that he could be made in either way—that is, so that this possibility too was present there because he could be made in either way—while reserving the one particular manner in which he would make him in his own will, then he did not weave that manner into the constitution of the world [variant: “when he wove the constitution of the world together”] [Col. 0660A].

For it is clear that man was not made contrary to what existed in that first condition of the causes [variant: “contrary to what existed in that first condition”], since the possibility of being made in this way was present there, although the necessity of being made in precisely this way was not there. This necessity did not belong to the condition of creation, but to the pleasure of the Creator, whose will is the necessity of things.

Even we, insofar as human weakness permits, can know, in things that have already appeared in time, what exists in each thing’s nature insofar as we have learned it by experience; but we do not know whether it will also occur in the future. For in the nature of a young man there is, for example, the possibility that he will grow old; but we do not know whether this is also in God’s will. Yet it would not be in nature either, unless it had first been in the will of God, who created all things.

There is certainly a hidden principle of old age in a youthful body, and of youth in a child’s body. It is not seen by the eyes, as childhood itself is seen in a child and youth in a young man, but by another kind of knowledge it is understood that there is hidden in nature something by which hidden numbers are brought forth into the open—those of youth from childhood, or of old age from youth [Col. 0660B].

This principle by which it is possible for something to be is hidden, then, but it is not hidden from the mind. Whether it is also necessary, however, we do not know at all.

And we know that the principle by which something can be is present in the nature of the body itself. But it is clear that the principle by which it must be is not present there. Perhaps, however, it is in the world, so that this man must grow old; but if it is not in the world, it is in God. For what he wills will necessarily happen, and those things are truly future which he has foreknown.

Many things will occur according to lower causes; but if they are also so in God’s foreknowledge, they are truly future. If they are otherwise there, they will occur rather as they are there, where the one who foreknows cannot be deceived.

Old age is said to be future in a young man, yet it is not future if he is destined to die beforehand. This, however, will happen according to the condition of the other causes, whether they are woven into the world or reserved in God’s foreknowledge.

According to certain causes of future events, <sup>43</sup> Hezekiah was destined to die, but God added fifteen years to his life. In doing this he was doing what he had foreknown before the foundation of the world that he would do, and had preserved in his will. He was therefore not doing what was not future; rather, that was more truly future which he had foreknown he would do.

Yet those years would not rightly be called “added” unless something was added that had stood otherwise in other causes. According to some lower causes, therefore, Hezekiah’s life had already reached its end; but according to those causes that exist in the will and foreknowledge of God, who from eternity knew that he would act at that time, the extension was truly future.

He was destined to finish his life when he did finish it. Even if this was granted in response to his prayer, God certainly foreknew that he would pray in such a way that such a prayer ought to be granted [variant: *quia et sic*, “because he would also pray in this way”]. His foreknowledge could not be deceived, and therefore what he foreknew necessarily came to pass [Col. 0660C–D].

Consequently, if the causes of all future things were implanted in the world when the day was made, at the time when God created all things simultaneously, Adam was made in no other way when he was formed from the clay of the earth—most probably already in fully developed manhood—than he had been in those causes in which God made man in the works of the six days.

For in those causes it was established not merely that he could be made in this way, but that he had to be made in this way. God does not act against a cause which he unquestionably established willingly, any more than he acts against his own will [Col. 0661A].

But if he did not establish all causes in the creation first made, and reserved some in his own will, then those causes which he reserved in his will do indeed not depend by necessity upon those he created. Nevertheless, they cannot be contrary to those which he established by his will, because God’s will cannot be contrary to itself.

He created these causes in such a way that the thing whose causes they are could arise from them, but would not necessarily do so. He concealed the other causes in such a way that what he made from them must necessarily exist, so that it may be able to exist [Col. 0661B].

## CHAPTER LII

### The star followed by the Magi: Christ’s servant, not subject to fate, from Book II *Against Faustus*

We do not place any human race under the fate of the stars. Because God’s judgment is just, we vindicate the free choice of the will, by which one lives well or badly, from every bond of necessity. How much less, then, do we believe that the temporal birth of the one who is the eternal Creator and Lord of all was made subject to the condition of the stars!

Therefore, the star which the Magi saw when Christ was born according to the flesh did not rule by decree; it served as a testimony. It did not subject him to its authority, but indicated him by its service.

Accordingly, it was not one of those stars which, from the beginning of creation, maintain the order of their courses under the law of the Creator. Rather, at the new birth of the Virgin, a new star appeared. It performed its ministry even for the Magi who were seeking Christ, going before them until it led them to the very place where the Word of God lay as an infant [Col. 0661C].

What astrologers, then, have ever established the fates of human beings born under the stars in such a way that they would assert that one of the stars, when some person was born, had abandoned the order of its course and proceeded toward the one who had been born? They think that the lot of the person being born is bound to the order of the stars [variant: *ordini*, “to the order of the stars”], not that the order of the stars can be changed for the day on which a human being is born.

Therefore, if that star was one of those that perform their courses in heaven, how could it decree what Christ, once born, would do, when it was commanded, after Christ’s birth, to abandon what it had been doing? But if, as is more plausibly believed, it arose because it was not previously present in order to point out Christ, then Christ was not born because the star appeared; rather, the star appeared because Christ was born.

Thus, if the expression were required, we should say not that the star was made for Christ, but that Christ was made for the star. He, not the star, brought the cause of its appearance; not the star the cause of his birth.

If events are called *fata* because they are derived from *fari*, “to speak,” then, since Christ is the Word of God in whom all things were spoken before they existed, the fate of Christ is not the fellowship of the stars. Rather, Christ is also the fate of the stars, since he assumed the very flesh created under heaven by the will with which he created heaven, and laid it aside and took it up again by the power with which he also commanded the stars [Col. 0661D–0662A].

## CHAPTER LIII

### The commandments concerning the life that is to be lived and the commandments concerning the life that is to be signified, from Book VI *Against Faustus*

We have already explained above how and why the Old Testament is received by the heirs of the New Testament. But because Faustus recently discussed its promises and now wished to discuss its commandments, I reply that these people have no understanding at all of the difference between commandments concerning the life that is to be lived and commandments concerning the life that is to be signified.

For example, “You shall not covet” is a commandment concerning the life that is to be lived. “You shall circumcise every male on the eighth day” is a commandment concerning the life that is to be signified.

Through this ignorance the Manichaeans, and all who dislike the writings of the Old Testament, criticize according to the custom of the present time whatever God commanded his former people, failing to understand that whatever God commanded his own [variant: former] people was given for the celebration of the shadow of future things. Those commands were appropriate to the time in which the things now made manifest were to be signified as future.

But what will they say against the Apostle, who says: “All these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come”?

He himself has made clear why those writings are received by us and why it is no longer necessary for us to observe those signs of things. When he says, “They were written for us,” he undoubtedly demonstrates how carefully they must be read and understood by us, and how greatly they must be held in authority, since they were written for us.

When, however, he says, “They were figures of us,” and “These things happened to them in figure,” he shows that, now that we are carrying out the realities themselves in their manifest form, it is no longer necessary for us to serve the celebration of the figures that foretold them.

Hence elsewhere he says: “Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in respect of a feast, or of a new moon, or of sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things” [variant: *quae sunt*, “which are,” rather than *quod est*, “which is”]. Here too, when he says, “Let no one judge you in these matters” [variant: *hinc*, “from this”], he declares that it is not necessary for such things to be observed now. When he says, “Which are a shadow of future things,” he shows why it was appropriate for them to be observed at the time when the things now manifested and shining upon us were foretold as future through such shadows of figures [Col. 0662B–C].

Accordingly, if the Manichaeans were justified by the resurrection of the Lord—whose resurrection day was, counting from the day of his passion, the third, but after the Sabbath, that is, after the seventh day, the eighth—then they would surely be stripped of the carnal veil of mortal desires. Rejoicing in the circumcision of the heart, they would not mock that circumcision which was shadowed and figured in the flesh during the time of the Old Testament, even though in the time of the New Testament they are not compelled [variant: *cogerentur*, “would be compelled”] to perform and observe it.

In what member could the stripping away of carnal and mortal desire be more appropriately figured than in the member from which carnal and mortal offspring arises? Yet, as the Apostle says, “All things are clean to the clean.”

44. ## CHAPTER LIV

### Why certain foods of animal flesh are forbidden in the Old Testament, signifying either unclean souls or doctrines, from the same book *Against Faustus*

In the Old Testament, where certain foods of animal flesh are forbidden, let them understand, if they can, why this judgment is not contrary to the Apostle’s statement, “All things are clean to the clean,” and “Every creation of God is good.” The Apostle was speaking of the natures themselves; those writings, because of certain prefigurations appropriate to their time, called certain animals unclean not by nature but by their significance.

Thus, for example, if the pig and the lamb are considered, both are clean by nature, because every creation of God is good. By a certain significance, however, the lamb is clean and the pig unclean.

It is as if one were to speak of a foolish person and a wise person: each of these two words is certainly clean by the nature of the sound, letters, and syllables of which it consists; but by its significance one of these words—the word “foolish”—can be called unclean, not by its own nature but because it signifies something unclean. Perhaps what the pig represents among things is what “foolish” represents among kinds of things, and both that animal and those two syllables forming the word “foolish” signify one and the same thing [Col. 0663A–B].

That animal was declared unclean in the Law because it does not chew the cud, although this is not a fault of the animal but its nature. There are people who are signified by this animal and who are unclean by their own fault, not by nature: they gladly hear the words of wisdom, but afterward give them no thought at all.

For when you recall what you have heard that was useful, bringing it back, as it were, from the stomach of memory to the mouth of thought through the sweetness of recollection, what is this other than to chew the cud, in a spiritual sense? Those who do not do this are represented by the kind of animals from which such abstinence from flesh warned us to avoid such a fault.

Since wisdom itself is a desirable treasure, Scripture speaks elsewhere of this purity of chewing the cud: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it.” These likenesses of things, in speech or in figurative observances, beneficially and pleasantly move [variant: *monent*, “admonish,” rather than *movent*, “move”] rational minds through the exercise of seeking and comparing. But in the case of the earlier people, many such things were commanded not only to be heard but also to be observed [Col. 0663C–D].

For it was a time when what was later to be revealed had to be prophesied not only in words but also in deeds. When these things were to be revealed through Christ and in Christ, the burdens of observances were not imposed upon the faith of the nations, but the authority of prophecy was commended.

## CHAPTER LV

### Unleavened bread, the Feast of Booths, and other matters, from Book VI *Against Faustus*

In the time of the Old Testament, not eating unleavened bread during the prescribed seven days was a sin; in the time of the New Testament it is not a sin. Rather, we have in Christ the hope of the future age: Christ, clothing our soul with righteousness and our body with immortality, renews us wholly.

To believe that, because of the necessity and weakness of the old corruption, we will always suffer or do something belonging to it is always a sin, so long as these seven days through which time proceeds are still turning.

This was understood by certain holy people in the time of the Old Testament, when it was hidden in figure; in the time of the New Testament it is preached to the peoples as having been revealed in manifestation. Hence Scripture itself was then a commandment, but now it is a testimony.

At one time it was a sin not to celebrate the Feast of Booths; now it is not a sin. But not being joined to the tabernacle of God, which is the Church, is always a sin. At that time this was enacted under a figurative commandment; now it is read in a revealed testimony.

For what was then made would not have been called “the tabernacle of testimony” unless it bore witness, by an appropriate correspondence of significance, to some truth that was to be declared in its own time [Col. 0664A–B].

At one time it was a sin to mix purple with linen garments and to wear a garment of linen and wool; now it is not a sin. But to live disorderly and to wish to mix professions of different kinds—so that either a consecrated woman has the adornments of married women, or a woman who did not remain continent and married assumes the appearance of a virgin—is altogether a sin. So too is anything woven incongruously from different kinds into the life of any person.

What was then figured in garments is now declared in conduct. That was the time of signifying; this is the time of manifesting.

Therefore, the very Scripture that was then an exactor of works that signified things is now a witness to the things signified. What was then observed for the sake of foretelling is now recited for the sake of confirmation.

At that time it was not permitted to yoke an ox and a donkey together for work; now it is permitted. The Apostle made this clear when, recalling the Scripture’s statement that an ox treading grain should not be muzzled, he said: “Is God concerned about oxen?”

Why, then, is this now read, when what it prohibited is now permitted? Because the same Apostle, continuing there, says: “For our sake Scripture says this.” It is certainly impious for us not to read what was written for us—indeed, it was written more for us, for whom it is made manifest, than for those in whom it was figured [Col. 0664C].

If necessary, anyone may yoke an ox and a donkey without detriment to the work. But no one should make a wise person and a foolish person companions, with equal authority and together announcing the word of God—not so that one commands and the other obeys—for this would not be without scandal.

Thus we retain the same Scripture: then, with the power of a commandment, ordering that what is now to be disclosed be covered by shadows; and now, with the authority of a testimony, bearing witness in the open light to what was then concealed [Col. 0664D].

## CHAPTER LVI

### Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in this way, from Book XI *Against Faustus*
Source/review notes: The final edit is a null replacement and should be disregarded; all substantive corrections are represented in the preceding edits.

Although we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him. The very context of the passage of Scripture sufficiently shows what the Apostle is saying. For, in his customary manner, he contemplates our future life—which has already been completed in the mediator himself, Christ Jesus, our head, when he rose again—with such certain hope as though it were already present and possessed. That life, of course, will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s life is now no longer according to the flesh.

For in this passage he does not mean by “flesh” the very substance of our body, which the Lord also calls flesh after his resurrection, saying, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have”; rather, he wants the corruption and mortality of the flesh to be understood—something that will not then be in us, just as it is no longer in Christ. For he was also specifically calling this “flesh” when he spoke quite clearly about the resurrection itself and said what I mentioned above: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

When, therefore, what he next says there has come to pass—“Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed, in an atom, that is, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality”—then, according to the sense in which he calls “flesh” not the substance of the body itself but the corruption of mortality, there will certainly no longer be flesh, because the changed flesh will no longer have the corruption of mortality. According to the origin of the substance and body itself, however, it will be the same flesh, because it will itself rise and itself be changed. For this too is true which the Lord said after he had risen: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have”; and this also is true which the Apostle said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

The former statement was made according to the substance itself, which will exist even then, because it will be changed. The latter was made according to the fleshly quality of corruption, which will then no longer exist, because the changed flesh will not be corrupted.

We therefore knew Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of the flesh—before he rose again; but now we no longer know him, because, as the same Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him.”

For if you hold strictly to the propriety of the words, he was lying when he said, “We knew Christ according to the flesh,” if Christ was never according to the flesh; for no one knew what did not exist. Yet he did not say, “We thought Christ according to the flesh,” but “we knew him.” Nevertheless, not to press the word, lest someone assert that the Apostle spoke by misuse of language, saying “we knew” instead of “we thought,” I am astonished that blind people—or rather, I am not astonished that blind people do not see—that if Christ did not have flesh for the reason that the Apostle said he now no longer knew Christ according to the flesh, then neither did those have flesh of whom he says in the same passage: “Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh.” For if he had wished this to be understood of Christ alone, he could not have said, “We know no one according to the flesh,” [but because he contemplated the future life of those who would rise and be changed as though it were present, he said: “From now on we know no one according to the flesh,” that is, we hold so certain a hope of our future incorruption and immortality that from now on we already rejoice in that very joy].

Hence elsewhere he says: “If, therefore, you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.” Certainly we have not yet risen as Christ has, but nevertheless, according to the hope that is ours in him, he testified that we have already risen with him. Hence he also says: “According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration.”

Who, however, does not understand that in the washing of regeneration the hope of future salvation was given to us, not the salvation itself that is promised? Yet because the hope is certain, he says as though that salvation had already been given: “He saved us.” [Col. 0666B]

For elsewhere he says most plainly: “We groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body; for by hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.”

Therefore, just as here he did not say, “We shall be saved,” but, “We have already been saved,” though not in reality but in hope—“For by hope,” he says, “we have been saved”—so also what is said there, “From now on we know no one according to the flesh,” is understood not yet in reality but in hope, because our hope is in Christ, because in him has already been completed what we hope will be granted to us.

For he has already risen, and death will no longer rule over him. Although we knew him according to the flesh when he was still destined to die—for that mortality which the Apostle specifically calls “flesh” was present in his body—now we no longer know him according to the flesh. His mortal nature has already put on immortality, and therefore he can no longer be called “flesh” according to that former mortality.

Let us therefore consider the sequence of the passage itself, in which this statement occurs and for which these people bring accusations, so that what I am saying may become clearer.

“Christ’s love,” he says, “presses upon us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even though we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him.”

Certainly it is now clear to anyone that the Apostle said this on account of Christ’s resurrection, since these words were preceded by the statement that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. For what else does it mean to live not for oneself but for him, except not to live according to the flesh in the hope of earthly and corruptible goods, but according to the spirit in the hope of the resurrection that has already taken place in Christ?

Thus, among those for whom Christ died and rose again, and who now live not for themselves but for him, the Apostle knew no one according to the flesh, because of their hope of future immortality, in expectation of which they lived—an immortality that in Christ was already not hope but reality.

Although he knew Christ according to the flesh when he was still destined to die, he nevertheless no longer knew him, because he knew that Christ had risen, that death would no longer rule over him, and that in him we all, though not yet in reality, are already so in hope.

He continues and says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new”—[“all things” supplied in the text]—“and all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ.”

Every new creation, therefore—that is, the people renewed through faith, so that for the present they may have in hope what will later be perfected in reality—already possesses in Christ what it hopes for in itself. Thus the old things have now passed away according to hope, because it is no longer the time of the Old Testament in which a temporal and fleshly kingdom is expected from God; and all things have become new according to that same hope, so that we may hold fast the promised kingdom of heaven, where there will be neither death nor corruption.

But in the resurrection of the dead the old things will pass away not according to hope but according to reality, when death, the last enemy, is destroyed; and all things will become new when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality.

This has already happened in Christ, whom Paul, according to reality, no longer knew according to the flesh. But among those for whom he died and rose again, he knew no one according to the flesh, not yet according to reality but according to hope, because, as the same Apostle says to the Ephesians, we have been saved by his grace.

For that passage also bears witness to this interpretation: “But God,” he says, “who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ”—[Col. 0667C] “by whose grace we have been saved.”

What he says here—“he made us alive together with Christ”—he said to the Corinthians in the words that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. And when he says here, “by whose grace we have been saved,” he speaks of what he holds in hope as though it were already perfected.

For, as I mentioned shortly before, he says most openly elsewhere: “By hope we have been saved.” 46 Therefore here too he continues and counts as perfected what is still future.

“And he raised us up together,” he says, “and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.”

Certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we do not yet. Yet because with certain hope we already possess what is to come, he said that we sit together in the heavenly places—not yet in ourselves, but already in him.

And lest you think that what is said in hope as though it were perfected is already perfected now, and so that you may understand that it is still future, he continues and says: “So that in the ages to come he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace, in truth [variant: ‘kindness’] toward us in Christ Jesus.”

This is also the meaning of the statement: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins that are through the law were at work in our members, so that they bore fruit for death.”

For he said, “when we were in the flesh,” as though we were no longer in the flesh. This is understood as follows: “When we were in hope of fleshly things,” at the time when the law—which cannot be fulfilled except through spiritual love—was imposed upon them for transgression, so that sin might abound, and so that later, when the New Testament had been revealed, grace might abound more greatly through forgiveness.

Similarly, elsewhere he says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” And lest anyone think that he meant those who had not yet died, he immediately adds: “But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit”—that is, those who are in hope of fleshly goods cannot please God; but you are not in hope of fleshly things, but in hope of spiritual things, that is, of the kingdom of heaven, where the body itself also, through that change, will be spiritual in its own manner, although now it is animal.

“For an animal body is sown,” as the same Apostle says to the Corinthians, “a spiritual body will rise.”

Therefore, if the Apostle already knew none of those according to the flesh who were for that reason said not to be in the flesh, because they were not in hope of fleshly things, although they still carried corruptible and mortal flesh, how much more explicitly would he say of Christ that he no longer knew him according to the flesh, in whose body what they held promised to them in hope had already been completed in reality?

## CHAPTER LVII  
### On the six days in Genesis and the six ages, and on the wife made from the side of the sleeping man; from Book XII Against Faustus

In six days God completed all his works in Genesis, and on the seventh he rested. Through six ages the human race in this world marks out God’s works by the succession of times.

The first of these is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity [“to Babylon”: variant reading]; the fifth thereafter until the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now taking place, until the Most High comes for judgment.

The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints, not in this life but in another, where that rich man saw the poor man at rest while he himself was being tormented in the underworld. There is no evening there, because there is no decline of anything there.

On the sixth day in Genesis the human being is formed in the image of God; in the sixth age of the world our reformation is manifested, in the renewal of the mind according to the image of him who created us, as the Apostle says.

While the man is sleeping, a wife is made from his side; while Christ is dying, the Church is made from the sacrament of the blood that flowed from the side of the dead man.

Eve is called “life,” the mother of the living, because she was made from the side of her husband. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, he will not have life in himself.”

Everything that is understood there, treated and unfolded in detail, speaks beforehand of Christ and the Church, whether in good Christians or in bad ones.

For the Apostle did not say without reason, “Adam, who is a form of the one to come,” so that the words, “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” might be understood. “This mystery is great,” he says; “but I am speaking of Christ and the Church.”

For who does not recognize that Christ left the Father in this manner: although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant? He also left his mother, the synagogue of the Jews, which was carnally attached to the Old Testament, and clung to his holy wife, the Church, so that the two might be one flesh in the peace of the New Testament.

For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh a sharer in our condition, so that we might be the body of that head.

## CHAPTER LVIII  
### How Cain and Abel prefigured two peoples, and whoever killed Cain would pay sevenfold vengeance; or, concerning the sign that God placed upon Cain; from the same Book XII Against Faustus

Thus Abel, the younger by birth, is killed by his elder brother; Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the elder. The former was killed in a field, the latter at the place of Calvary.

God asks Cain—not as one ignorant from whom he must learn, but as a judge questioning the guilty whom he is to punish—where his brother is.

He replied that he did not know, and that he was not his brother’s keeper.

What do the Jews still answer us when, by the voice of God—that is, by the voice of the holy Scriptures—we ask them about Christ, except that they do not know the Christ of whom we speak?

For Cain’s pretended ignorance is the Jews’ false denial. They would in some way be Christ’s keepers if they had been willing to accept and preserve the Christian faith. For whoever keeps Christ in his heart does not say what Cain said: “Am I my brother’s keeper?”

God says to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth.”

Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the holy Scriptures. The blood of Christ has a great voice on earth, when, received by all nations, it is answered with “Amen.” This is the clear voice of the blood, which the blood itself expresses from the mouths of the faithful redeemed by that same blood.

God says to Cain: “And now you are cursed by the earth that opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand, because you will work the earth, and it will no longer add its strength to give to you; groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth.”

He did not say, “Cursed is the earth,” but, “Cursed are you by the earth that opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.”

The unbelieving Jewish people is cursed by the earth—that is, by the Church—which opened its mouth in the confession of sins to receive the blood of Christ, poured out for the remission of sins from the hand of the persecutor, who did not wish to be under grace but under the law, so that he might be cursed by the Church—that is, so that the Church might understand and show him to be accursed. The Apostle says: “For all who are of the works of the law are under the curse of the law.”

Then, after he had said, “You are cursed by the earth that opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand,” he did not say, “Because you will work it,” but, “Because you will work the earth, and it will not add its strength to give to you.” 47

Hence it is not necessary to understand that Cain works the same earth that opened its mouth to receive his brother’s blood from his hand. Rather, he is understood to be cursed by this earth because he works the earth that will not add its strength to give to him.

That is, the Church recognizes and displays the Jewish people as accursed because, after Christ was killed, it still practices an earthly circumcision, an earthly Sabbath, an earthly unleavened bread, and an earthly Passover. Every such earthly practice contains a hidden power—the grace of Christ, which must be understood—but this grace is not given to Jews who persist in impiety and unbelief, because it has been revealed in the New Testament and they have not passed over to the Lord.

The veil that remains when the Old Testament is read is not removed from them, because it is taken away only in Christ—not the reading of the Old Testament itself, which contains hidden power, but the veil by which it is concealed.

Therefore, when Christ had suffered on the cross, the veil of the temple was torn, so that through Christ’s passion the secrets of the mysteries might be revealed to the faithful who pass over to drink his blood with an open mouth in confession.

For this reason that people, like Cain, still works the earth and still practices the work of the law carnally. It does not receive its strength from it, because it does not understand in it the grace of Christ.

For this reason also, in the very earth that Christ carried—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins. Yet that same earth did not give them its strength, because they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, who rose for our justification.

For although he was crucified in weakness, he lives in the power of God, as the Apostle says. This, then, is the power of that earth which he does not reveal to the impious and unbelieving. Hence, after rising, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, just as the earth did not show its fruit of power to Cain while he worked the earth, so that the grain might be sown.

“For you will work the earth,” he says, “and it will not add its strength to give to you; groaning and trembling you shall be upon the earth.”

Now who does not see, who does not recognize, throughout the whole earth wherever that people has been scattered, how it groans in grief over the loss of its kingdom and trembles in fear beneath innumerable Christian peoples?

Therefore Cain answered and said: “My punishment is greater; if today you cast me away from the face of the earth and I am hidden from your face, I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth, and it shall come to pass that everyone who finds me will kill me.”

Indeed, he groans and trembles lest, after losing even his earthly kingdom, he be killed by this visible death. He calls this the greater punishment, greater than the fact that the earth does not give him its strength, lest he die spiritually.

For he thinks carnally and does not regard being hidden from the face of God—that is, having God angry with him—as a serious matter, except insofar as he might be found and killed. He thinks carnally, like one working the earth whose strength he does not receive.

To think according to the flesh, however, is death. Not understanding this, he groans over the loss of his kingdom and trembles at bodily death.

But what did God answer him? “Not so,” he said. “Whoever kills Cain will pay sevenfold vengeance.” That is, it will not happen as you say: the impious race of carnal Jews will not perish by bodily death. For whoever destroys them in this way will pay sevenfold vengeance—that is, he will remove from them the sevenfold vengeance to which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s murder.

Thus, throughout this whole period that revolves in the number of seven days, it becomes especially clear to Christian believers, because the Jewish nation does not perish, what subjection those deserved who killed the Lord in their proud kingdom.

And God placed a sign upon Cain, so that no one who found him would kill him.

This is truly a great wonder: how all the nations that were subjected by the Romans passed over into the Roman rite of religious observances and accepted those sacrileges to be observed and celebrated, while the Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or under Christian ones, did not lose the sign of its law by which it is distinguished from the other nations and peoples.

Every emperor or king who finds them in his kingdom finds them with that sign and does not kill them—that is, he does not make them cease to be Jews. They remain separated from the fellowship of the other nations by a certain distinctive sign of their own observance, except for any of them who passes over to Christ, so that he is no longer found as Cain, no longer goes out from the face of God, and no longer dwells in the land of Naim, which is said to be interpreted as “commotion.” Against this evil God is entreated in the Psalm: “Do not let my feet be moved, and do not let the hands of sinners move me.”

## CHAPTER LIX  
### How the words “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” may be understood in different ways; from Book XV of The City of God

When God spoke to Cain in the manner in which he had spoken to the first human beings—through a subordinate creature, as though he were their companion, in a form suited to them—what benefit did this bring him? Did he not, even after the divine warning, carry out the crime he had conceived of killing his brother?

For when God distinguished between the sacrifices of the two brothers, looking favorably upon one and with disfavor upon the other—as must be understood to have been made known by some visible confirming sign—and did this because Cain’s works were evil but his brother’s good, Cain became very sorrowful and his face fell.

For it is written: “And God said to Cain: Why have you become sad, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be quiet; for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.”

In this warning or admonition that God gave to Cain, the statement, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” has produced many interpretations because its obscurity does not make clear why or from what cause it was said. Each interpreter of the divine Scriptures attempts to explain it according to the rule of faith.

A sacrifice is rightly offered when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice must be offered. But it is not rightly divided when the places, times, the things themselves that are offered, the one who offers, the one to whom it is offered, or those to whom what has been offered is distributed for eating are not properly distinguished.

Thus, “division” here may be understood as discernment: whether one offers where one ought not, or what ought to be offered elsewhere; whether one offers when one ought not, or what ought to be offered at another time; whether one offers something that ought never and nowhere to have been offered; whether a person keeps for himself the better things of the same kind rather than those he offers to God; or whether an outsider, or anyone who ought not to become a participant, becomes a participant in the thing that has been offered.

Which of these displeased God in Cain cannot easily be discovered. But since the Apostle John, speaking about these brothers, says, “Not as Cain, who was from the evil one and killed his brother—and for what reason did he kill him? Because his works were evil but his brother’s righteous,” it may be understood that God did not look favorably upon his gift because by this very act he divided wrongly: he gave something of his to God but gave himself to himself.

All who follow not God’s will but their own do this; that is, they live not with an upright but with a perverse heart. Yet they offer God a gift by which they think he can be bought off, so that he may not assist in healing their depraved desires but in gratifying them.

And this is characteristic of the earthly city: to worship God or the gods so that, with their help, one may rule in earthly victories and peace—not from the love of helping others, but from the desire to dominate.

The good use the world in order to enjoy God; the wicked, by contrast, wish to use God in order to enjoy the world, although they at least believe that he exists or cares for human affairs. Those who do not even believe this are much worse.

When Cain therefore learned that God had looked favorably upon his good brother’s sacrifice, but not upon his own, he ought to have changed and imitated his brother, not proudly rivaled him. But he became angry, and his face fell.

God chiefly reproves this sin: grief over another’s goodness, especially that of a brother. In reproving it, he asked: “Why have you become sad, and why has your face fallen?”

Because Cain envied his brother, God saw this and reproved it. For people, to whom another’s heart is hidden, might have been uncertain and entirely unable to determine whether his sadness expressed his own wickedness, in which he had learned that he had displeased God, or whether he grieved over his brother’s goodness, which had pleased God when God looked favorably upon his sacrifice.

But in explaining why he had refused to accept Cain’s offering—so that it might be clear that Cain himself deservedly displeased God rather than his brother undeservedly—God showed that Cain, being unjust because he did not divide rightly, that is, because he did not live rightly, and unworthy of having his offering approved, was still more unjust because he had killed [variant: “hated”] his righteous brother without cause.

Yet God did not leave him without a holy, just, and good command: “Be quiet,” he said; “for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.”

Was this about his brother? Certainly not. About what, then, if not sin?

For he had said, “You have sinned,” and then added, “Be quiet; for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.”

This may indeed be understood as meaning that the turning of sin ought to be toward the man himself, so that he may know that he should attribute to no one but himself the fact that he sins.

This is the healing medicine of repentance and the appropriate request for forgiveness: when he says, “Its turning is toward you,” the verb “will be” should not be supplied, but the statement should be understood as a command rather than merely a prediction.

A person will then rule over sin if, instead of defending it by placing it above himself, he subjugates it through repentance. Otherwise he will serve the sin that rules him if he offers protection to what has happened.

But if sin is understood as that very carnal desire of which the Apostle says, “The flesh desires against the spirit,” and if among the fruits of the flesh he mentions envy—the envy by which Cain was goaded and inflamed toward his brother’s destruction—then it is rightly understood [or: “rightly supplied”] as: “Its turning will be toward you, and you shall rule over it.”

For when that carnal part itself has been stirred—which the Apostle calls sin when he says, “It is not I who do it, but sin that dwells in me”—that part of the soul which even philosophers call vicious, not one that ought to drag the mind along but one over which the mind ought to rule and which reason ought to restrain from illicit acts, then, when it has been stirred toward committing some wrongdoing, if one remains quiet and obeys the command of the Apostle, “Do not present your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin,” it is turned toward the mind, subdued and conquered, so that reason rules over it once it has been subjected.

God gave this command to the man who was inflamed by the torches of envy against his brother and wanted to take away the one whom he ought to have imitated: “Be quiet,” he said. “Keep your hands from crime. Do not let sin reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires; do not present your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin. Its turning is toward you,” since it is restrained not by being aided through relaxation but by remaining quiet, “and you shall rule over it,” so that, when it is not permitted to act outwardly, it may become accustomed, under the power of a governing and benevolent mind, not to be stirred inwardly either.

Something similar was said in the same divine book about the woman, when, after the sin, God questioned and judged them and they received the sentence of condemnation—through the serpent, the devil, and through themselves, the woman and her husband.

For after he had said to her, “Multiplying I will multiply your sorrows and your groaning, and in sorrow you shall bear children,” he then added: “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

What was said to Cain about sin or about the vicious desire of the flesh is said in this passage about the sinful woman. Here the husband must be understood as being suited to rule the wife in the same way that the mind rules the flesh. For this reason the Apostle says: “He who loves his wife loves himself; for no one has ever hated his own flesh.”

These things must be healed as our own, not condemned as another’s.

But Cain received God’s command as a transgressor. For, as the vice of envy grew strong, he lay in wait for his brother and killed him.

Such was the founder of the earthly city.

How he also signified the Jews, by whom Christ, the shepherd of all human beings, was killed, while Abel, the shepherd of sheep and cattle, prefigured him—for this is an allegorical prophetic matter—I shall refrain from saying now. I remember having said some things about it against Faustus the Manichaean (Against Faustus, Book XII), namely:

That the flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark, because we are baptized in the hope of future rest, which was signified by the seventh day;

that every living creature which the earth supported was destroyed in the flood outside the ark, because outside the fellowship of the Church the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction;

that it rained for forty days and forty nights, because every guilt of sins committed against the ten commandments of the law is washed away throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts. For ten multiplied by four makes forty.

Whether that guilt was contracted in relation to the days through prosperity in worldly affairs, or in relation to the nights through adversity in worldly affairs, it is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism.

## CHAPTER LX  
### On the number seven as rest and eight as resurrection, and on the sending out of the raven and the dove; also from Book XII Against Faustus

The fact that the twenty-seventh day of the month is mentioned also pertains to the significance of the same square number, which has already been explained from the square-shaped pieces of wood.

Here, however, the meaning is clearer: the Trinity perfects us, prepared for every good work—that is, in a certain sense made square—through memory, by which we remember God; understanding, by which we know him; and will, by which we love him.

For three times three, and that again three times, make twenty-seven, which is the square of the number three.

The fact that the ark settled, that is, rested, in the seventh month refers back to that seventh rest. And because the perfected rest, the number of that square is repeated there as well.

For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this sacrament was commended; and again, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, the same commendation was confirmed when the ark came to rest.

What is promised in hope is exhibited in reality.

Moreover, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection—for the rest that receives the saints after this life does not end when the body is restored; rather, the whole human being, no longer in hope but already in reality, renewed in every respect with the perfect immortal salvation of both spirit and body, is received into the gift of eternal life—because, therefore, the seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, and because this too is a deep and profound mystery in the sacrament of our regeneration, that is, in baptism, the water rose fifteen cubits above the mountains.

That is, this sacrament transcends all the wisdom of the proud. Seven and eight together make fifteen. And because seventy is named from seven and eighty from eight, the water rose for one hundred and fifty days, commending and confirming to us that same height of baptism in the consecration of the new human being, so that we might hold fast the faith of rest and resurrection.

The raven, sent out after forty days, did not return, either because it was intercepted by the waters or because it was enticed by some floating corpse. This signifies people made exceedingly filthy by the uncleanness of desire and, for that reason, excessively intent upon the things outside in this world; or those rebaptized; or those seduced and held by the people whom baptism outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—has killed.

The dove, sent out, returned because it found no rest. This shows that through the New Testament rest was not promised to the saints in this world.

For it was sent out after forty days, a number that signifies the life conducted in this world. Finally, after seven days it was released and brought back a fruitful olive branch, signifying that some who have also been baptized outside the Church, if they have not lacked the richness of love, may at a later time, as though in the evening, in the mouth of the dove—as in a kiss of peace—be led into the fellowship of unity.

When it was released after another seven days and did not return, this signified the end of the world, when there will be rest for the saints—not still in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is joined together in this age, so long as what flowed from Christ’s side is being drunk, but already in the perfection of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in the manifest contemplation of unchangeable truth we may no longer need bodily mysteries.

## CHAPTER LXI  
### On God’s commandments to Noah after the flood; from the same Book XII Against Faustus

Why, although both clean and unclean animals were in the ark, are only the clean animals offered to God in sacrifice after leaving the ark?

What, moreover, is intended when God speaks to Noah and, as though beginning again from the start, commends the figure of the Church—which had to be signified in many ways—by declaring that his descendants are blessed so that they may fill the earth, and that all animals are given to them for food, just as it is said to Peter on the dish: “Kill and eat”?

## CHAPTER LXII  
### That flesh must not be eaten with blood
When they are commanded to eat after the blood has been poured out, this signifies that their former life should not be retained in the conscience as though suffocated, but should have something like an outpouring through confession. The covenant that God established between himself and human beings—and with every living creature, so that he would not destroy it by a flood—is the bow that appears in the clouds, which never shines except from the sun. Those who, separated from the Church, do not perish in the flood are the ones who, in the Prophets and all the divine Scriptures, as though in God’s clouds, recognize Christ’s glory and do not seek their own. But lest the worshipers of this sun become still more puffed up, let them know that Christ is sometimes signified by the sun, just as by the lion, the lamb, and the stone: this is because of a certain resemblance, not because of an identity of substance.

Now, in the case of the vineyard that Noah planted, when he became drunk and was exposed in his house, who would fail to see Christ suffering among his own people? For then the mortality of his flesh was exposed—“a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles”—but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, he is “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” because “what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.”

Accordingly, in the two sons, the elder and the younger, two peoples were represented. Carrying one garment behind them—that is, the mystery of the Lord’s passion, already past and completed—they neither look upon their father’s nakedness, because they do not consent to Christ’s death, nor do they fail to honor him with a covering, as though knowing from whom they were born. The middle son, that is, the Jewish people, is called “middle” because it held neither the primacy of the apostles nor, among the Gentiles, the last place in believing. He saw his father’s nakedness because he consented to Christ’s death, and he reported it outside to his brothers. Through him, what had been secret in prophecy was made manifest and, in a sense, public; therefore he becomes the servant of his brothers.

For what else is that nation even today except a kind of archivist for Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s affirmation, so that we honor through the sacrament what that nation announces through the written letter? Who would not be stirred by this? Who would not be instructed or strengthened in faith? Thus those two are blessed who honored their father’s nakedness, although they turned away from it, as though displeased by what had been done to the criminal vineyard. “Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Shem.” Although he is the God of all nations, he is nevertheless called, in a certain sense and by a proper name, even among the nations themselves, “the God of Israel.” And how did this come about, except through Japheth’s blessing? For in the people of the Gentiles the Church occupied the whole world. This was plainly foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. On Abraham’s departure from his land, and on Joseph sold and honored; and on Israel’s departure from Egypt. From Book XII Against Faustus.

You say that Christ was not foretold by the Israelite prophets, although all those books are intent upon proclaiming him—if only you would examine them with reverence rather than attack them with frivolity.
