Who else, in the person of Abraham, departed from his land and his kindred in order to become rich and prosperous among foreigners, except the one who, having left the land and kindred of the Jews, from whom he was born according to the flesh, so prevails and excels among the Gentiles that we see it plainly?

Who else was Isaac carrying [variant: carried; Latin: portaret/portabat] wood for himself to the sacrifice, except the one who himself carried the cross for his passion? Who else was the ram to be sacrificed caught by its horns in the thicket, except the one who was to be fastened to the cross’s gibbet and offered for us? Who else wrestled with Jacob in the angel, when the weaker and defeated one, as though the stronger, prevailed against the one who was stronger and victorious, blessing him in part and in part making the breadth of his thigh lame, except the one who allowed the people of Israel to prevail against him, blessed among them those who believed, while Jacob’s broad thigh limped in the multitude of the carnal people?

Who else was the stone placed beneath Jacob’s head and, as though expressly naming him, also anointed, except Christ, the head of the man? For who does not know that Christ is named from anointing? While recalling this very event in the Gospel and openly testifying that it had been prefigured in him, the Lord said that Nathanael was truly an Israelite in whom there was no deceit. When Nathanael, as though having that stone beneath his head, confessed that he was [editorial correction: “would be,” Latin: esset] the Son of God and the King of Israel—anointing the stone, in a sense, by this confession, that is, confessing him to be the Christ—the Lord appropriately recalled there also what Jacob had seen, Jacob who through the blessing was called Israel: “Amen, I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

[Col. 0677A] This is what Israel had seen when he had that stone beneath his head: a ladder from earth to heaven, upon which the angels of God ascended and descended. In these angels the evangelists, the preachers of Christ, were signified. They ascend when, in order to understand Christ’s supremely exalted divinity, they rise above the whole of creation and find him “in the beginning God with God,” through whom all things were made. They descend when they find him made of a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law. In him there is a ladder from earth up to [variant: to; Latin: usque in/ad] heaven, from flesh [variant: up; Latin: carne/usque] to spirit, because in him carnal people, by making progress as though ascending, become spiritual.

The spiritual likewise descend in a certain sense to nourish him in his little members with milk when they cannot speak to them as to spiritual people but only as to carnal people [variant: so that his little ones may be nourished in his members]. Thus one ascends and descends upon the Son of Man. For the Son of Man is above in our Head, who is the Savior himself, and the Son of Man is below in his body, which is the Church.

We understand him also to be the ladder, because he said: “I am the way.” One therefore ascends to him in order to understand him in the heights, and one descends to him in order to nourish him in his little members. Through him one ascends and descends: following his example, his preachers not only raise themselves up so as to contemplate [variant: await; Latin: spectent/exspectent] him sublimely, but also humble themselves so as to proclaim him with moderation.

Observe the Apostle ascending: “Whether,” he says, “we have been carried beyond ourselves, it is for God.” And observe him descending: “Whether,” he says, “we are moderate, it is for you.” Let him say through what he ascended and descended. “The love of Christ,” he says, “compels us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again.”

Whoever does not delight in these holy spectacles in the sacred Scriptures, and does not uphold [variant: not upholding; Latin: non sustinet/sustinens] sound doctrine, turns to fables; and those fables, with various forms of delight, entice minds—or, according to the variant, souls—that are childish at any age of the body. But we now recognize [variant: let us recognize; Latin: agnoscimus/agnoscamus] the body of Christ and our voice in the Psalm, so that we may say to him: “The unjust have told me of their delights, but not as of your law, O Lord.”

Christ meets me everywhere as I traverse and pant through those books and all those Scriptures in the sweat of that human condemnation, whether openly or secretly, and he refreshes me. He also inflames my desire through a certain difficulty in finding him, so that whatever [variant: so that that which; Latin: quod/quo id quod] I find I may eagerly swallow and, stored away in my marrow, retain it for my health.

He points himself out to me [variant: is pointed out] in Joseph, who, after his brothers had persecuted and sold him, was honored in Egypt after his labors. For we have learned of Christ’s labors in the world of the Gentiles, which Egypt signified, through the various sufferings of the martyrs; and now we see Christ’s honor in that same world, distributing his grain and subjecting all things to himself.

He points himself out to me [variant: is pointed out] in Moses’ staff, which, having become a serpent on the ground, signified his death arising from the serpent; but when it is seized by the tail, this signifies that afterward, when all the actions [variant: action] have been completed at the end, it returns by rising again to what it had been. There, through the restoration of life, death having been consumed, nothing of the serpent appears.

We too are rolled about in the same mortality as his body through the slippery course of the ages; but at the final end, as though the tail of the age were seized by the hand—that is, by the power of judgment, so that it may no longer slip away—we shall be restored. And when the last enemy, death, has been destroyed, we shall rise again and be the staff of the kingdom in the right hand [variant: in God’s right hand; Latin: dextra/dextera Dei].

Now concerning Israel’s departure from Egypt, it is not I but the Apostle who speaks: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that [variant: because; Latin: quia/quoniam] our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed [variant: accompanied; Latin: sequente/consequente] them, and the rock was Christ.”

By explaining one point, he introduced understanding of the others. For if the rock was Christ because of its firmness, why was the manna not also Christ, as the living bread that came down from heaven? Those who truly eat it live spiritually; for those people, receiving the ancient figure carnally, died. But when the Apostle says that they ate the same spiritual food, he shows that this too is to be understood spiritually in Christ. He likewise explained why he had called the drink spiritual when he added: “The rock was Christ.” Once this was disclosed, everything shone forth.

Why, then, were not also the cloud and the pillar Christ, because he is upright, firm, and supports our weakness—shining by night and not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind?

The Red Sea is red [editorial alternative: “the cloud”; Latin: Rubet/Nubes]: surely it is baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood. The enemies pursuing from behind die: they are past sins. The people are led through the desert. All who have been baptized, not yet enjoying the promised homeland but hoping for what they do not see and awaiting it with patience, are as though in the desert. There they laboriously and dangerously endure temptations lest they return in their hearts to Egypt. Yet Christ does not abandon them there, for the pillar also does not depart.

The bitter waters are sweetened by wood, because the enemies of the people are softened when the sign of Christ’s cross has been honored. And the twelve springs watering the seventy palm trees prefigure apostolic grace watering peoples through the number seven multiplied by ten, so that through the gift of the sevenfold Spirit the Decalogue of the Law may be fulfilled.

And the enemy who attempted to block the way is overcome when Moses’ hands are extended, through the sign of the Lord’s cross. The deadly bite of the serpents is healed [variant: the deadly bites are healed; Latin: sanatur/sanantur] when the bronze serpent is raised up and looked upon. This is declared by the Lord’s words: “As Moses raised up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be raised up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

Do these things not cry out as well? Is the deafness so great? The Passover is celebrated in the slaughter of the sheep; Christ is slain, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Those who celebrate the Passover are forbidden to break the bones; the Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross. The evangelist testifies that this is why it was said: “You shall not break a bone of his.”

The doorposts are smeared with blood so that destruction may be driven away; the people’s foreheads are marked with the sign of the Lord’s passion for the protection of salvation. The Law is given there fifty days after the Passover has been completed; the Holy Spirit comes fifty days after the Lord’s passion. There the Law is said to have been written by the finger of God; the Lord says of the Holy Spirit: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God.”

And Faustus cries out, with his eyes closed, that he has found nothing in those writings relating to the foretelling of Christ! But what wonder if he has eyes for reading and no heart for understanding—if, placed before the closed door of the divine mystery, he does not knock with the faith of reverence but assails it with the pride of irreverence?

Let it plainly be so; let it happen so. For it is just that the door of salvation be closed to the proud. Let the gentle one come, the one whom the Lord teaches his ways. Let him see in those books these things and the others—either all of them or some of them, of whatever kind he believes them to be in all the books. Let him see the one who led the people into the promised land. For this man was not called by that name rashly from the beginning; rather, after the name had been changed according to the very working of salvation, he was called Jesus.

Let him see the cluster of grapes hanging from wood in the promised land. Let him see in Jericho, as in this mortal age, a prostitute—one of those concerning whom the Lord says that they precede the proud into the kingdom of heaven—sending scarlet from the window of her house, as through the mouth of her body. This is plainly a sign of blood, because confession for salvation takes place through the remission of sins.

Let him see the walls of that city, as though they were the fortifications of the mortal age, fall when the ark of the Testament has gone around them seven times. So now, through the ages that pass in the succession of seven-day cycles, the Testament of God circles the whole world, so that at the end of the ages the last enemy, death, may be destroyed, and one house, as though one Church, may be delivered from the destruction of the impious—cleansed from the disgrace of fornication through the window of confession in the blood of remission.

Let him see the times first of the Judges and afterward of the Kings, just as there will first be judgment and afterward a kingdom; and within those times of the Judges and the kingdom, let him see Christ and the Church prefigured again and again in many different ways.

Who was the one killing the lion that came against Samson as he went toward foreigners to seek a wife, except the one who, intending to call the Church from the Gentiles, said: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world”?

What does the honeycomb constructed in the mouth of that slain lion signify, except that we now see the laws of the earthly kingdom—which had previously roared against Christ—having their former fierceness destroyed and now supplying even defenses for the sweetness of evangelical preaching?

What [variant: Who; Latin: Quid/Quae] is that confident woman piercing the enemy’s temple with wood, except the faith of the Church, destroying the kingdoms of the devil through Christ’s cross?

What is the fleece drenched with rain while the threshing floor is dry, and afterward the threshing floor drenched while the fleece is dry, except that at first one nation, the Hebrew nation, possessed secretly in its holy mysteries the mystery of God, which is Christ, while the whole world was empty of that mystery? But now, in its manifestation, the whole world possesses it, while that nation has been emptied.

And what of the times of the kings, to mention only a few examples? From the very beginning, when the priesthood was changed to Samuel after Eli was rejected, and the kingdom was changed to David after Saul was rejected, does this not cry out that a new priesthood and a new kingdom are foretold [variant: “are to be foretold”; Latin: praenuntiatori/praenuntiari] as coming in our Lord Jesus Christ, once the old—an image of what was to come—has been rejected [variant: approved; Latin: reprobato/probato]?

When David himself ate the bread of the Presence, which only priests were permitted to eat, did he not prefigure, in one person, what was to come—that is, in the one Christ Jesus, both kingdom and priesthood?

When the ten tribes were separated from the Temple and two were left behind, does this not sufficiently indicate what the Apostle says concerning that entire nation: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace”?

Elijah is fed in a time of famine by ravens, which bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and the Manichaeans do not understand Christ in those books. To him, as it were, hungry for our salvation, sinners confess the faith whose first fruits of the spirit they now possess, while at the end, as though in the evening of the age, they will possess also the resurrection of the flesh.

Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow who wished to gather two pieces of wood before she died. Here the sign of the cross is expressed not only by the name of the wood but also by the number of the pieces of wood. Her flour and oil are blessed: the fruit and joy of love, which is given out and does not fail. For “God loves a cheerful giver.”

When the boys insulted Elisha and shouted, “Baldhead, baldhead!”, they were eaten by beasts. Those who ridicule Christ with childish folly, crucified at the place of Calvary, perish when attacked by demons.

Elisha sends a staff through his servant over a dead man, but the man does not revive. He comes himself, joins and adapts himself to that man’s death, and the man revives. The Word of God sent the Law through his servant, and it did not benefit the human race, dead in sins; yet it was not sent without reason. The one who sent it knew that it had first to be sent. He himself came, conformed himself to us, became a participant in our death, and we were given life.

When wood was being cut with axes, the iron flew off and sank into the depths of the river; then, when Elisha threw a piece of wood upon it, it returned to the wood above. Thus, when Christ’s presence, working through his body, was cutting down the impious Jews as unfruitful trees—because John had said of Christ, “Behold, the axe is laid at the roots of the trees”—the body itself departed from them through the intervening passion, descending into the depths of hell. When it had been placed above in the tomb, it rose again, as though the spirit had returned to its handle.

How many things am I passing over, constrained by the necessity of brevity? Those who read know.

Now, the very migration into Babylon—where the Spirit of God, through the prophet Jeremiah, also commands them to go and pray for those in whose kingdom they are living as foreigners, because their peace would also be their peace, and to build houses, cultivate vineyards, and plant gardens—who would fail to recognize what this prefigured, if he considered the true Israelites, those in whom there is no deceit, having migrated through the apostolic dispensation, together with the evangelical sacrament, into the kingdom of the Gentiles?

Therefore the Apostle, as though repeating Jeremiah, says to us: “I urge, then, first of all [variant: first; Latin: primum/primo], that supplications and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and love. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

For through this, dwellings of peace have also been built for those who believe: the basilicas of Christian congregations; the cultivated vineyards of the faithful people; and the planted garden where, among all the vegetables, that grain of mustard also reigns. Beneath its far-stretching shade, the lofty pride of the nations, taking refuge as though among the birds of heaven, also finds rest.

And because, after seventy years, according to the prophecy of that same Jeremiah, there is a return from captivity and the Temple is renewed, what faithful Christian would not understand that, after the ages have passed—ages that run their course through the repeated cycle of the number seven—we too, that is, the Church of God, must return from our pilgrimage in this age to that heavenly Jerusalem?

Through whom, except through Jesus Christ, the true great Priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus who was the great priest of that time when the Temple was built after the captivity? The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing; the devil, who stood to accuse him, was defeated; his filthy garment was removed from him, and a garment of honor and glory was given him. So the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, when its adversary has been overcome through judgment at the end of the ages, is taken up from the grief of pilgrimage into the glory of eternal salvation. This is also sung most clearly in the psalm of the dedication of the House: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. That certain manifest sins are shown to proceed as punishment from certain hidden sins. From Book XIII Against Faustus.

What, then, did the Jews do wrong, if God blinded them so that they would not recognize Christ? As far as we could, by instructing an inexperienced person, we would show that the just punishment of this blindness arose from other hidden sins known to God. We would show not only that the Apostle said of certain people, “For this reason God handed them over to the desires of their heart,” or “to an undiscerning mind, so that they might do what is improper,” intending to show that certain manifest sins arise as punishment from certain hidden ones, but also that the prophets themselves did not keep this silent.

For, not to go farther, in that very passage where Jeremiah says, “And he is a human being, and who will recognize him?”—lest the Jews should seem to be excused on the grounds that they did not know him, since, as the Apostle says, “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory”—he continues: “And he showed that it was because of their hidden merits that they would not recognize him.” For he says: “I am the Lord, who examines hearts and tests the kidneys, to give to each according to his way and according to the fruit of his endeavors.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. On what is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Against Faustus.

Let us see, prompted by the opportunity provided by heretical calumniators, how that mystery is to be explained to the faithful.

Human death is the punishment of sin; hence death itself is also called sin. This does not mean that a person sins while dying, but that death came about because of sin. Similarly, in one sense “tongue” properly means the flesh that moves inside the teeth beneath the palate; in another sense, “tongue” means what is done through the tongue. In this latter sense one language is called Greek and another Latin.

Likewise, in one sense “hand” means the bodily member itself that we move in order to work; in another sense “hand” means [variant: is said to mean; Latin: dicit/dicitur] the writing produced by the hand. For we say, “His hand has been proved,” “His hand has been read against him,” “I have your hand,” and “Take back your hand.” Properly speaking, the hand is a human bodily member. I do not suppose, however, that the writing is a human bodily member; yet it is called a “hand” because it was made by the hand.

So it is with sin. Sin means not only the evil deed itself, which deserves punishment, but also death itself, which came about because of sin and is therefore called sin.

Christ did not commit that sin by which he would have been liable to death. But he took upon himself for us the other sin—that is, death, which had been inflicted because of sin upon human nature. He hung this upon the tree. This is what was cursed through Moses, where death was condemned so that it would not reign, and cursed so that it would perish.

Therefore, through Christ’s sin of this kind, our sin was condemned, so that we might be freed and not remain condemned under sin’s reign.

Why, then, does Faustus wonder that sin is cursed, that death is cursed, that the mortality of the flesh without Christ’s sin is cursed, although it came about in Christ from human sin? For he took a body from Adam, because the Virgin Mary, who bore Christ, came from Adam.

God had said in paradise: “On the day when you touch it, you shall die by death.” This is the curse that hung upon the tree.

Let him deny that Christ was cursed who also denies that he died. But whoever confesses that he died cannot deny that death comes from sin and that for this reason death itself is also called sin.

Let him hear the Apostle saying, “Our old person was crucified together with him,” and let him understand whom Moses called cursed. Therefore the Apostle goes on to say of Christ: “He was made a curse for us,” just as he was not afraid to say, “He died for all.”

For “he died” is the same as “he was cursed,” because death itself comes from a curse, and every sin is cursed—whether the sin itself that is committed so that punishment follows, or the punishment itself, which is called sin in another way because it comes from sin.

Christ took upon himself our punishment without guilt, so that from it he might release us from our guilt and bring our punishment also to an end. I would have said these things on my own authority if the Apostle did not repeat them so often that he both awakens those who sleep and silences those who calumniate.

“God,” he says, “sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and, because of sin, condemned sin in the flesh.” That flesh, therefore, was not sinful flesh, because it had not come into Mary through the transmission of mortality by a male. Yet because death comes from sin, that flesh, although it came from a virgin, was mortal. Precisely because it was mortal, it had the likeness of sinful flesh.

He calls this also “sin” when he immediately says: “So that, because of sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh.”

Again, in another passage: “The one who knew no sin,” he says, “he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.”

Why, then, should Moses have been afraid to call cursed what Paul was not afraid to call sin? Clearly, the Prophet had both to foresee and to proclaim this, prepared to be reproached by heretics together with the Apostle. For whoever reproaches the Prophet for saying “cursed” is compelled to reproach the Apostle for saying “sin.”

The curse is surely sin’s companion. Nor is the accusation against God thereby greater because he added the words “by God,” saying: “Cursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Unless God hated sin and our death, he would not have sent his Son to take them upon himself and destroy them.

What, then, is surprising if something is called cursed by God that God hates? For the more mercifully he hates our death, which hung upon the tree when Christ died, the more willingly he grants us immortality, which will come when Christ returns.

As for the addition of “everyone,” so that it was said, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” Moses certainly did not fail to foresee that the righteous would also be on the cross. Rather, he wisely foresaw that heretics would deny the Lord’s true death and would therefore wish to separate Christ from this curse so as to separate him also from the reality of death.

If that death was not real, no curse hung upon Christ crucified on the tree, because he was not truly crucified. But Moses cries out from afar against the heretics who would come long afterward: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” You evade this without cause because you dislike the truth of Christ’s death. It does not say “this one” or “that one,” but “everyone”—absolutely everyone!

Even the Son of God? Yes, absolutely. For this is what you do not want; this is what you strive against and from which you lead people astray. You dislike that he was cursed for us because you dislike that he died for us.

He is outside the curse of that Adam only if he is outside that Adam’s death. But when, from a human being and for human beings, he accepted death from him and for him, he did not disdain to accept even the curse that accompanies death—yes, he accepted it, even he, the Son of God, always living in his righteousness but dead because of our offenses, in the flesh assumed from our punishment.

For this reason “everyone” was added, so that Christ would not be said not to belong to the true death if he were separated, through foolish honor, from the curse joined to death.

A person faithful to evangelical truth understands that Moses’ words, when he called Christ cursed, are no more an insult to Christ—who was not cursed in the divinity of his majesty but in the condition of our punishment, because of which he was suspended on the tree—than the Manichaeans’ denial [variant: denial; Latin: negarent/negant] that he possessed mortal flesh, in which he would suffer a true death, is praise of Christ.

From that prophetic curse, the praise of humility is understood; from that heretical semblance of honor, a charge of falsehood is brought against them.

If, then, you deny that he was cursed, deny that he died. If you deny that he died, you are no longer fighting Moses but the Apostles. But if you confess that he died, confess that he took upon himself the punishment of our sin without our sin.

Now, when you hear “the punishment of sin,” believe either that it comes from blessing or that it comes from cursing. If the punishment of sin comes from blessing, wish always to remain in the punishment of sin. But if you wish to be freed from it, believe that, by the justice of the divine sentence, it came from a curse.

Confess, therefore, that the one whom you confess to have died for us accepted the curse for us also; and do not suppose that Moses intended anything else when he said: “Cursed is everyone who hung [variant: hangs; Latin: pependit/pependerit] upon a tree.”

He could have said, “Cursed is every mortal,” or “Cursed is everyone who dies.” But this is what the prophecy asserts: it knew that Christ’s death would take place on a cross, and that heretics would arise who would say, “He did hang upon a tree, but only in some appearance, not so as truly to die.”

By crying out, therefore, “Cursed,” Moses cried out nothing other than that Christ truly died. He knew that the death of a sinful human being—which Christ himself assumed without sin—came from the curse expressed in the words: “If you touch it, you shall die by death.”

The serpent suspended upon the tree also pertains to this. It signified that Christ did not fabricate a false death but suspended upon the tree of his passion the true death into which the serpent had cast humanity by giving evil counsel.

These people do not wish to behold that true death, and therefore they are not healed from the serpent’s poison, just as everyone in the wilderness who looked upon it was healed.

Thus we admit that some unlearned people say that being fastened to a tree is one thing and hanging upon a tree another. Some think that this is how the question should be resolved: they say that Moses’ curse referred to Judas, who hanged himself with a noose, as though they knew first [variant: firstly; Latin: primo/primum] whether he hanged himself from wood or from stone.

But what Faustus also recalled is true: the Apostle does not permit us to understand otherwise than that this was foretold concerning Christ. Yet the ignorance of certain Catholics is the hunting ground of the Manichaeans. They customarily attack such people, entangle such people in their deceptions; we too once fell among such people and remained entangled with them, but we were freed—not by our own strength, but by God’s mercy.

## CHAPTER LXV. On what Moses says: “You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life.” From Book XVI Against Faustus.

As though anything worse could occur among the curses that befell the Jews as the deserved punishment of their proud irreverence than to see their life—that is, the Son of God—hanging, and not to believe in their life!

For when curses are spoken prophetically, they do not arise from the evil wish of one pronouncing them, but from the spirit foretelling what is to come. Those that arise from an evil wish are forbidden when it is said: “Bless, and do not curse.”

Yet such words are often found in the speech of the saints, as when the Apostle Paul says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works.” And in another passage, as though irritated and indignant, the Apostle even seems to have wished evil upon them: “Would that those who trouble you would cut themselves off!”

If you consider the person of the writer, however, you will understand that through a most elegant ambiguity he wished them well. For there are eunuchs who have cut themselves off for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

Faustus would also have understood this in those words if he had brought a reverent palate to the Lord’s food. For what was said—“You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life”—may perhaps have sounded to the Jews as though, seeing their life hanging in uncertainty amid the threats and deceptions of their enemies, they would not believe themselves victorious.

But the son of the Gospel, when he hears, “For he wrote about me,” sees in this very ambiguity of the sentence what the prophets throw before swine and what they intimate to human beings. Christ, the life of humanity, immediately comes to his mind, hanging before them; and the Jews do not believe in him precisely because they see him hanging.

Someone else might quickly say, among the other curses that do not pertain to understanding something about Christ in the reading, that the only passage there concerning Christ is this: “You will see your life hanging, and you will not believe your life.” For it certainly could have happened that, among the various curses prophetically foretold against the impious people, this too was included.

But I, and those who reflect with me somewhat more attentively upon that evangelical and lordly statement—which does not say, “For he also wrote about me,” as though we should believe that he wrote other things that do not pertain to Christ, but says, “He wrote about me,” so that by searching we might consult the entire intention of that Scripture only for understanding Christ’s grace—we recognize that the other curses in this reading were also foretold because of Christ.

## CHAPTER LXVI. Why the Sabbath’s rest may also be understood in the Lord’s burial, and why the circumcision of the eighth day signifies the stripping away of mortality. From the same Book XVI Against Faustus.

That Sabbath which you ineptly and impiously ridicule—unless it too possessed an interpretation among the prophecies written about Christ—Christ would not have borne witness to it in this way: although he suffered by his own will, as you yourself stated in praising him, and therefore had the times of his passion and resurrection under his control, he arranged that his flesh should rest in the tomb on the Sabbath from all its works, so that, rising on the third day—the day we call the Lord’s Day, which is counted after the Sabbath—he might also declare that the circumcision of the eighth day pertained to the prophecy concerning him.

For what does the circumcision of the flesh signify, except the stripping away of the mortality that we bear from carnal generation? For this reason the Apostle says: “Having stripped off the flesh, he made a spectacle of principalities and powers, triumphing over them confidently in himself.” When he says “having stripped off the flesh,” in that passage we understand “flesh” to mean the mortality of the flesh, according to which it is properly called flesh, since it will not exist in that immortality of the resurrection. Therefore it is written: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God”—words with which you are accustomed to slander our faith, by which we believe that this body will rise, a resurrection that has already preceded us in the Lord himself. You conceal what follows, however, in which the Apostle plainly explains what he meant there by “flesh.” For, wishing to show what he had meant by “flesh” in that passage, he immediately added: “Nor shall corruption possess incorruption.” He says that this body—which, because of its mortality, is properly called flesh—will be changed in the resurrection, so that it will no longer be corruptible and mortal.

And lest this be thought to be said merely on our own interpretation, attend to his own following words: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed, in an indivisible moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed; for this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality.” Thus, in order that it may be clothed with immortality, it is stripped of mortality. This is the mystery of circumcision, which was commanded to take place on the eighth day; and on the eighth day—that is, the Lord’s Day after the Sabbath—it was already fulfilled in reality by the Lord. Hence it is said that, “stripping off the flesh, he made a spectacle of principalities and powers.”

For through this mortality the devilish powers, envious of us, held dominion over us. He is said to have made a spectacle of them because, in himself, our Head, he provided an example of what will be completed in his whole body—that is, the Church—when it is finally liberated from the power of the devil in the last resurrection. This is our faith.

And since, as Paul recalls as a prophetic testimony, “the righteous person lives by faith,” this is our justification. The pagans too believe that Christ died, but that Christ rose again is the distinctive faith of Christians. “For if,” says the Apostle, “you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” Since, therefore, we are justified by this faith in the resurrection, that apostolic statement also concerns Christ: “He died for our sins and rose again for our justification.”

And because this resurrection, which is believed and justifies us, was prefigured by the circumcision of the eighth day, the Apostle says of Abraham, to whom circumcision was first given: “And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith.” Thus Moses also wrote this circumcision among the other prophetic figures concerning Christ, of whom Christ himself says: “He wrote about me.”

## CHAPTER LXVII  
That the pagans gave the names of their gods not only to days but also to months, from Book XVIII Against Faustus

The nations gave the names of their gods to these days, whose number seven returns in a cycle. Of them the Apostle says that they “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.” In this respect you imitate them as well, except that you do not worship with them the two brighter lights and the remaining stars.

They also gave the names of their gods to the months. Out of respect for Romulus—for they believed him to be the son of Mars—they dedicated the first month to Mars and called it March. They then called April not by the name of any god of theirs, but from the thing itself, as though from *aperilem*, because at that time the abundance of new growth first opens into blossom. The third month they called May, because they worship Maia, the mother of Mercury, as a goddess; the fourth, June, from Juno. The remaining months, up to December, they named from the numbers. Yet Quintilis and Sextilis were called July and August, after men to whom they had decreed divine honors. September, the seventh month, and the remaining months, as I have said, up to December, are designated by names derived in numerical order. January, moreover, was named from Janus, and February from the sacred rites of the Luperci.

Do you therefore wish it to be said that you worship Mars in the month of March? For in that month you celebrate your Bema with great festivity. But if you think that in March you may consider something else—not Mars—why do you try to introduce Saturn into the divine Scriptures on the basis of the seventh day, which was named Sabbath from rest, because the nations called that day Saturn’s day? Surely you now see with what piety you rave.

As for animal sacrifices, who among us does not know that they were imposed more appropriately upon a perverse people than offered to a God who desired them? Yet even in these there were figures of our realities, because neither our cleansing nor God’s reconciliation with us is possible without blood; but the reality of those figures is Christ, by whose blood we have been redeemed and cleansed. For in the figures of the divine utterances, he was also called a bull because of the power of the cross, with whose horns he scattered the ungodly; a ram because of the primacy of innocence; and a goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin through sin. If you mention any other kind of sacrifice expressed more distinctly, I will show you that Christ was likewise prophesied in it.

Accordingly, whether circumcision, or the Sabbath, or the distinction of foods, or the offering of sacrifices, all these were our figures and prophecies. Christ came not to abolish them but to fulfill them, when he brought to completion the things they foretold.

## CHAPTER LXVIII  
That “an eye for an eye” is not contrary to “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek …,” from Book XIX Against Faustus

Now how is the ancient statement, “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” contrary to what the Lord says: “But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also”? The ancient commandment too was given to restrain the flames of hatred and to curb the uncontrolled passions of those who rage.

For who is easily content to return only as much vengeance as he has received injury? Do we not see people who have been lightly harmed plotting murder, thirsting for blood, and scarcely finding anything in their enemy’s misfortunes with which to satisfy themselves? When struck with a fist, who does not either set the courts in motion to secure the condemnation of the one who struck him, or, if he wishes to strike back himself, batter the whole man with fists and kicks, if not even after seizing some weapon?

Against this immoderate—and therefore unjust—revenge, the law established a just measure by instituting the penalty of retaliation: namely, that each person should suffer punishment corresponding to the injury he inflicted. Therefore “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” is not fuel but a boundary for fury. It was imposed not so that what had been quiet might be kindled from it, but so that what was already burning might not spread further.

There is indeed a certain just vengeance, and it is justly owed to the person who has suffered injury. Thus, when we forgive, we in a certain sense give away something that belongs to us. For this reason the things we are instructed to forgive humanly in the Lord’s Prayer are also called debts, so that our debts may likewise be forgiven us divinely.

What is owed, even if it is generously remitted, is not unjustly demanded. Thus, just as even the person who swears truthfully approaches perjury, the person who does not swear at all is far removed from it. Although the one who swears truthfully does not sin, the one who does not swear is farther removed from sin. The Lord preferred that, by not swearing, we should not depart from the truth, rather than, by swearing truthfully, approach perjury. Therefore, just as the warning not to swear preserves us from the sin of perjury, so, although the person who seeks vengeance unjustly through immoderation sins, and the person who seeks just vengeance with restraint does not sin, the person who does not wish to be avenged at all is farther removed from the sin of unjust vengeance.

The person who exacts more than is owed sins; the person who exacts what is owed does not sin. But much safer from the sin of an unjust exactor is the person who does not exact what is owed at all—especially lest he himself be compelled to repay a debt to one who owes no debt.

## CHAPTER LXIX  
How the Apostle’s statement is to be understood: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers,” from Book XXI Against Faustus

The Apostle says: “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.” Many of us distinguish this sentence in such a way that they say the true God blinded the minds of unbelievers. When they read “in whom God,” they pause there, and then continue: “has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.” Even if they do not distinguish it this way, but, for the sake of explanation, alter the word order and say, “in whom God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age,” the same meaning emerges as in that division.

For an operation by which the minds of unbelievers are blinded can also, in a certain sense, pertain to the true God—not because of malice but because of justice. Thus the same Paul says elsewhere: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” And elsewhere: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? By no means.” For Moses says: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

After prefacing what must be held without hesitation—namely, that there is no injustice with God—observe what he says shortly afterward: “But if God, wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, endured with great patience vessels of wrath that have been prepared for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy that he prepared for glory,” and so forth.

Here it cannot in any way be said that one God displays wrath and demonstrates his power in vessels prepared for destruction, while another displays his riches in vessels of mercy. Apostolic teaching testifies that one and the same God does both.

Hence there is also the statement: “For this reason God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves.” Shortly afterward: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions.” And again shortly afterward: “And because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind.”

Behold how the true and just God blinds the minds of unbelievers. For in all the words of the Apostle that I have cited, no other God has ever been understood than the one who sent his Son, who said: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

Here too it is sufficiently evident to the minds of the faithful how God blinds the minds of unbelievers. For something hidden precedes in the hidden places, where God carries out the most just examination of his judgment, so that the minds of some are blinded and those of others enlightened. To him it is most truly said: “Your judgments are a great abyss.” Astonished at the inscrutable depth of this, the Apostle exclaims: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments,” and so forth.

But you are unable to discern what God does by mercy and what by judgment, because our psalmody is far from both your heart and your mouth—the psalmody in which it is said: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”

## CHAPTER LXX  
On the Apostle’s statement, “God fitted the body,” from the same Book XXI Against Faustus

The Apostle says: “God fitted the body,” whereas Faustus says *hylē* (ὕλη), “matter,” not God. What could be more appropriate to these hostilities, which ought to be condemned before they are refuted?

When the Apostle said “God,” did he also add “of this age”? Even if someone understands the devil to blind the minds of unbelievers, we do not deny that this occurs through evil suggestions, by which those who consent to them lose the light of justice, while God repays what is just.

We read all these things in the holy Scriptures. For concerning a seduction coming from outside it is said: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that is in Christ.” Similar is the statement: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals.” And there is also the statement that each person may be his own seducer: “Whoever thinks that he is something when he is nothing deceives himself.” There is likewise the statement about God’s vengeance that he cited above: “God gave them over to a debased mind, to do things that are not fitting.”

So too in the older books, after it had been said, “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living,” it is added shortly afterward: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world.” And again, concerning that very death, lest human beings exempt themselves from blame: “The ungodly,” it says, “summoned it with their hands and words, and, considering it a friend, they wasted away.” Elsewhere, however, it says: “Good and evil, life and death, riches and poverty are from the Lord God.”

Here confused people do not understand that, in one and the same evil deed, what follows afterward is not something manifestly different, but that through a certain continuous accompanying vengeance one thing comes from the cunning of the tempter, another from the wickedness of the one who wills, and another from the justice of the one who punishes. When the devil suggests, the human being consents, and God abandons him.

Accordingly, in an evil deed—that is, the blinding of unbelievers—if the devil is understood to be involved because of the malignity of his persuasion, so that “the god of this age” is distinguished in this way, it does not seem absurd to me. For the expression “god” is not used without an addition when “of this age” is attached—that is, of ungodly people who wish to flourish only in this age, according to the statement that Christ came “to rescue us from the present evil age.”

The same applies to the statement: “Whose god is the belly.” Unless “whose” were present, one could not say “the belly is god.” Nor could demons be called gods in the Psalm unless “of the nations” were added. For it is written: “For all the gods of the nations are demons.”

Here, however, neither “the god of this age,” nor “whose god is the belly,” nor “the gods of the nations” is written. Rather, it is simply stated: “God fitted the body.” This can mean only the true God, the Creator of all things. Those other expressions are spoken reproachfully; this one is spoken in praise.

Unless, perhaps, Faustus understands “God fitted the body” to mean not the ordering of its members—that is, not its fashioning and construction—but a mingling with his light, so that someone else placed these members, distinguished and arranged in their proper positions, who fashioned them, while God, by mingling his goodness with them, tempered the malice of this construction.

With such fables they dull childish souls. But even this, with God coming to the aid of little ones through the mouths of the saints, he did not allow them to claim. For a little earlier you have: “God placed each one of the members in the body as he willed.”

Who, then, would not understand that, according to this statement, God is the one who fitted the body together, since he fashioned the body from many members, preserving the functions of diverse works within the unity of its structure?

## CHAPTER LXXI
By Abraham’s example in concealing his wife, he teaches that, when a person has something to do, he should not put God to the test; from Book XXII Against Faustus

Someone may say: Why did Abraham not rather place such confidence in his God that he was unafraid to acknowledge his wife? For surely God could have averted from him the death that he feared, and kept him and his wife safe from every danger in that journeying, so that neither should his wife, however beautiful she was, be desired by anyone, nor should he himself be killed on her account. God certainly could have done this. Who is so mad as to deny it?

But if, when questioned, Abraham had identified that woman as his wife, he would have entrusted two things to God’s protection: his own life and his wife’s chastity. Sound teaching requires, however, that when a human being has something he can do, he should not put the Lord his God to the test. The Savior himself could indeed have protected his disciples; yet he said to them: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” He himself first provided the example of this.

For although he had power to lay down his life and would not lay it down except when he willed, yet as an infant he fled into Egypt, carried by his parents. He went up to the feast not openly but secretly, although on other occasions he spoke openly to Jews who were angry and listened with the most hostile disposition, yet could not lay hands on him because his hour had not yet come—not an hour by whose necessity he would be compelled to die, but one at whose fitting opportunity he would deign to be slain.

Therefore, while by teaching and rebuking openly, yet not allowing the rage of his enemies to have any power over him, he displayed God’s power, by fleeing and hiding he instructed human weakness, lest a person dare to put God to the test when he has something he can do, so as to escape what ought to be avoided. Nor had the apostle Paul despaired of divine help and protection, or lost faith, when he was lowered in a basket through the wall in order to escape the hands of his enemies. Thus he fled not because he did not believe in God, but because he feared that he would be putting God to the test if, though he could flee in this way, he had refused to flee.

## CHAPTER LXXII
What realities Jacob’s four wives prefigured, from the same Book Against Faustus

Having refuted the charge brought by a wicked error, let us, as we are able, search out the hidden meanings of the book of mysteries, and knock with the devotion of faith, that the Lord may open to us what these four wives of Jacob prefigured—two free women and two female slaves.

For we see that the Apostle understands the free woman and the slave woman whom Abraham had to signify the two covenants. There, with one of each, the point is easier to see; here, however, there are two and two. Moreover, there the slave woman’s son is disinherited, whereas here the sons of the slave women, together with the sons of the free women, receive the promised land. Thus something different is undoubtedly signified here.

Although I judge that Jacob’s two free wives belong to the New Testament, by which we have been called into freedom, they are not two without reason. Perhaps this is because, as can be observed and found in the Scriptures, two lives are proclaimed to us in Christ’s body: one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the delight of God. The Lord disclosed the former by his passion, the latter by his resurrection.

The names of these women themselves direct us to this understanding. They say that Leah is interpreted “Laboring,” while Rachel is “the beginning seen,” or “the word by which the beginning is seen.” Thus the activity of human and mortal life, in which we live by faith while doing many laborious works, uncertain with what result they may prove useful to those whom we wish to help, is Leah, Jacob’s first wife; and for this reason she is also recalled as having weak eyes. For the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight uncertain.

But Rachel is the hope of the eternal contemplation of God, possessing a sure and delightful understanding of truth. Hence she too is said to be beautiful in face and lovely in appearance. Every devout student loves her; and for her sake he serves the grace of God, by which our sins, even if they are like scarlet, shall be made white as snow. For Laban is interpreted “whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel. No one turns, under the grace of forgiveness of sins, to serve righteousness except in order to live at rest in the Word by which the Beginning, which is God, is seen. Therefore one serves for Rachel, not for Leah.

For who has ever loved, in works of righteousness, the labor of actions and sufferings? Who has sought that life for its own sake? Jacob did not seek Leah for her own sake either; yet, placed under him at night, he embraced her for the purpose of begetting children and experienced her fruitfulness. Since she could not be loved for her own sake, the Lord made her first to be endured in order that Rachel might be attained; afterward he commended her on account of her children.

So every useful servant of God, established under the grace that whitens his sins, what else has he considered in his conversion? What else has he borne in his heart? What else has he loved except the teaching of wisdom? Many suppose that they will attain and grasp it as soon as they have exercised themselves in the seven precepts of the law concerning love of neighbor, that no harm be done to any human being: “Honor your father and mother; You shall not commit adultery; You shall not kill; You shall not steal; You shall not bear false witness; You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

After observing these as far as they are able, when, for the desired and hoped-for beautiful delight of teaching, endurance of labor has clung to a person through various temptations, as though through this world’s night—when Leah has unexpectedly been joined to him in place of Rachel—and he endures her so that he may reach Rachel, if he loves steadfastly, he receives another seven precepts. It is as though he were told: “Serve another seven years for Rachel,” so that he may be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and a peacemaker.

For a person would wish, if it were possible without any endurance of labor—which must be embraced in acting and suffering—to arrive at once at the delights of beautiful and perfect wisdom. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying. This seems to be signified in what was said to Jacob: “It is not our custom in our country for the younger to be married before the elder,” because she who is earlier in time is not unreasonably called the elder. In the right instruction of a human being, the labor of doing what is just comes first; the delight of understanding what is true comes afterward.

This is the force of what is written: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide her for you.” The commandments, of course, concern righteousness; and righteousness is from faith, which moves amid the uncertainties of temptations, so that by devoutly believing what it does not yet understand, it may also attain the merit of understanding. For the force of the text just cited—“Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide her for you”—is, I think, equal to that of: “Unless you believe, you will not understand,” so that righteousness is shown to belong to faith, and understanding to wisdom.

Accordingly, in those who burn with a great love of evident truth, their zeal is not to be condemned but recalled to order: it must begin from faith and strive through good morals to arrive where it aims. In that in which virtue is exercised there is labor; in that which it seeks there is radiant wisdom.

“What need is there,” he says, “to believe what is not shown to me? Produce some manifest word by which I may see the beginning of all things.” This is what a rational mind, if it is a student of truth, chiefly and first burns to know. To such a person the reply should be: “What you desire is indeed beautiful and most worthy of love; but Leah is married first, and Rachel afterward.” This ardor therefore serves so that one does not reject the order but rather endures it, without which one cannot arrive at that which is loved with so great an ardor.

When one has arrived, however, one will possess in this world both beautiful understanding and laborious righteousness. For however keenly and sincerely mortals discern the unchangeable good, the body that is corrupted still weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things. One must therefore tend toward the one thing, but for its sake many things must be endured.

Thus Jacob had two free wives; for both were daughters of the forgiveness of sins, that is, of the whitening which is Laban. Yet one is loved and the other endured; but the one endured is first and more abundantly fruitful, so that, if not for her own sake, she may at least be loved for her children’s sake. For the labor of the righteous has its greatest fruit in those whom they beget for God’s kingdom by preaching the Gospel amid many temptations and tribulations. Those for whom they are more abundant in labors, excessive in beatings, more frequent in deaths, and for whom they have conflicts without and fears within, they call their joy and crown.

They are born to them more easily and abundantly from that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified, and whatever of his humanity is more readily apprehended by human thought and does not disturb even Leah’s weak eyes. But Rachel, clear in appearance, passes beyond the mind to God, sees the Word with God in the Beginning, and wishes to bear children but cannot, because “who shall declare his generation?”

Accordingly, the life suited to the pursuit of contemplation, so that it may behold with the eyes of the mind—not weakly—through the things that have been made, the invisible realities of God’s nature, and may ineffably discern his eternal power and divinity, wishes to be free from every business and is therefore barren. For, in seeking the leisure in which the pursuits of contemplation grow warm, it does not accommodate itself to the weakness of people who in various troubles desire help. Yet it too burns with the love of begetting: it wishes to teach what it knows and not to waste away in envious inactivity. It sees its sister abundant in children through the labor of acting and suffering, and grieves that people run rather to that virtue by which provision is made for their weaknesses and necessities than to that by which something divine and unchangeable is learned. This grief seems to be figured in what is written: “Rachel was jealous of her sister.”

Accordingly, because a clear and pure understanding of that substance which is not body, and therefore does not pertain to bodily sense, cannot be expressed in words uttered by flesh, the teaching of wisdom chooses to suggest divine things for thought, in whatever way it can, through bodily images and likenesses rather than cease from the office of teaching such things. So Rachel chose to receive children from her husband and her slave woman rather than remain altogether without children.

Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman, is said to mean “grown old.” For from the old life, devoted to bodily senses, bodily images are conceived even when one hears something about the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity. Leah also receives children from her slave woman, inflamed by a desire for more numerous offspring. We find that Zilpah, her slave woman, is interpreted “gaping mouth.” Therefore, when in the preaching of evangelical faith we observe people whose mouth gapes but whose heart does not gape in the Scriptures, this is understood as Leah’s slave woman.

For it is written of some: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” And to such persons the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?” Yet, in order that even through this slave woman Leah, that free wife of Jacob who labors, may receive children as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.” Hence the apostolic life is one of the labor of chains. “Whether,” he says, “in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, yes, and I shall rejoice”—as though glad at the more numerous offspring borne by a slave woman.

## CHAPTER LXXIII
On Judah’s deed in lying with his daughter-in-law, from the same Book XXII Against Faustus
Considering the deed of Judah, who had intercourse with his daughter-in-law, let us examine what it signified concerning things to come. But first it must be stated, lest anyone of limited understanding be offended that certain deeds of human beings which are evil are represented in the holy Scriptures as signifying certain future things that are not evil but good. [Col. 0694C] For divine providence everywhere preserves the power of its goodness. Just as from the intercourse of adulterers a human being is formed and born through a sinful human act, yet as a good work of God—as we have already said in the preceding discussion, through the fecundity of the seed, not through the shamefulness of the vice—so in the prophetic Scriptures, which narrate not only people’s good deeds but also their evil deeds, because the narrative itself is prophetic, something concerning future good things is signified through evil human deeds—not by the work of the sinner, but by that of the writer.

For when Judah entered Tamar, overcome by desire, he did not entertain the intention that something relevant to human salvation should be signified through his lust; just as neither did that Judas who betrayed the Lord intend that anything should come from his deed which would contribute to the same human salvation. [Col. 0694D] Yet if the Lord made so great a good work from the very evil deed of that Judas, that by the blood of his own Passion he might redeem us, what wonder if his prophet—of whom he himself says, “For he wrote about me”—signified something good through the evil deed of that Judas, so that by its mystery he might instruct us?

For the prophet-narrator, under the arrangement and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, gathered together those human deeds whose insertion was not without the foreshadowing of the things he intended to prophesy. For the purpose of signifying certain good things, it makes no difference whether the deeds through which they are signified are good or evil. What difference does it make to me, when I wish to learn something by reading, whether I find black Ethiopians written in red pigment and white Gauls in ink? [Col. 0695A] Yet if I were looking at such a thing not as writing but as a painting, I would certainly criticize it. Thus, in human deeds that are set before us for imitation or avoidance, it matters greatly whether they are good or evil. But in deeds that are written or spoken for the purpose of signifying something, it makes no difference, as regards the character of those who perform them, what praise or blame they deserve, provided only that they possess some necessary correspondence for prefiguring the matter under discussion.

Thus, in the Gospel, as far as Caiaphas’s harmful and destructive intention was concerned—and finally as far as the words themselves were concerned, if one attends to the speaker’s will, by which he sought to have a just man unjustly killed—they were certainly evil. Yet, without his knowing it, they signified a great good when he said, “It is expedient that one man should die, and that the whole nation should not perish.” [Col. 0695B] And it was said of him: “He did not say this from himself, but, because he was high priest, he prophesied, because Jesus was destined to die for the nation.”

So Judah’s deed was evil according to his lust, but, without his knowing it, it signified a great good. He did the evil from himself, but he did not signify the good from himself. What I have thought necessary to say in advance applies not only to Judah’s deed but also to any other evil deeds of human beings that may arise, through which the narrator prophetically signified something good.

In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the people of the kingdom of the Jews are understood, and kings from the tribe of Judah were appointed over them as husbands. Her name is rightly interpreted as “bitterness,” for she gave the Lord a cup of gall. [Col. 0695C] Two kinds of rulers who did not act rightly among the people are represented [the text varies: *significatur*, “is represented,” or *significabantur*, “were represented”] in Judah’s two sons: one kind consisted of those who did harm, the other of those who did no good. One of the sons was evil, or savage, before the Lord; the other poured out his seed upon the ground so that he would not give seed for the fertilization of Tamar.

There are no more than two kinds of useless people for the human race: one consists of those who do harm, the other of those who are unwilling to provide benefit—and who, if they possess any good in this earthly life, lose it by pouring it out upon the ground. Since the one who harms is worse than the one who does not benefit, the first is called “evil,” while the one who poured out his seed upon the ground is called the second [the text varies here, reading *saeviens*, “savage,” in place of the expected form].

The name of the elder, who was called Er, is interpreted as “leathery,” referring to the leather tunics in which the first human beings were clothed when, as punishment for their condemnation, they were sent out of paradise. [Col. 0695D] The name of the younger, who was called Aunam [elsewhere Onan], is interpreted as “their grief.” Whose grief, if not that of those who benefit no one although they possess the means to do so, and lose that means by pouring it out upon the ground? The greater evil is the taking away of life, signified by “leathery,” than the failure to provide help, signified by “their grief.” Yet God is said to have killed both of them; this signifies that he took the kingdom away from people of such a kind.

Judah’s third son, because he was not joined to that woman, signifies the period beginning when kings of the Jewish people ceased to come from the tribe of Judah. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not receive him as her husband, because the tribe was still the tribe of Judah, yet no one from it was any longer ruling the people. Hence his name, namely Shelah, is interpreted [Col. 0696A] as “his dismissal.”

Holy and just men do not belong to this interpretation. Although they lived in that period, they belong to the New Testament, for which they were knowingly useful through prophecy; David was such a man. Nor should Herod the Great be counted among the kings of Judah in the period when Judaea had begun to have no kings from the tribe of Judah, as though he were Tamar’s husband, for he was a foreigner. He was not joined to that people by the sacramental bond of mystical anointing as by a marriage covenant; rather, he ruled as an outsider.

He had received that authority from the Romans and from Caesar, as did his sons, the tetrarchs. One of them was Herod, called by his father’s name, who agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 0696B] These foreigners were so far from being counted as belonging to that mystical kingdom of the Jews that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ, “We have no king but Caesar.”

This was not true except in the sense of that universal domination: Caesar of the Romans was king—not properly of the Jews, but of the Romans. Yet in order to deny Christ and flatter Caesar, they condemned themselves by using such a cry.

When the kingdom had already failed from the tribe of Judah, the true Savior, our Lord Christ, had to come—one who would not harm but would greatly benefit. For it had been prophesied:

> “The prince shall not fail from Judah,  
> nor the ruler from his thighs,  
> until he comes to whom it has been reserved;  
> and he is the expectation of the nations.”

By this time every form of Jewish teaching, as well as the mystical anointing from which they were called “Christs,” had also failed, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel. [Col. 0696C] Then he came to whom it had been reserved, the expectation of the nations, and the Holy of Holies was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

He was born during the time of Herod the Great, but suffered under Herod the Lesser, the tetrarch. Judah himself therefore bore the figure of this coming one to the sheep that had perished, the sheep of the house of Israel, when he went to shear his sheep at Timnah, which is interpreted as “failing.” For the prince had already failed from Judah, and so had all Jewish teaching and anointing, so that he might come to whom it had been reserved.

He came with his Odollamite shepherd, whose name was Hiras. “Odollamite” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” [Col. 0696D] The Lord plainly came with this testimony. He had a testimony greater than John’s, yet he used this testimony in water for the sake of the weak sheep. Hiras, the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.”

John certainly saw his brother: his brother according to the seed of Abraham, according to kinship through his mother Mary and John’s mother Elizabeth, and the same one who was his Lord and God [the text also reads “his Lord and his God”], because, as John himself says, “he received from his fullness.” He certainly saw him, and therefore no one born of women arose greater than he. Since, among all those who foretold Christ, John himself saw what many righteous people and prophets desired to see and did not see, he greeted him from the womb [variant: “he leapt in the womb”], recognized him more perfectly through the dove, and therefore, like an Odollamite, truly bore testimony in water.

The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to unload them from their burdensome loads—so that the teeth of the churches praised in the Song of Songs might be like a flock of shorn sheep. [Col. 0697A]

Now let Tamar change her appearance, for Tamar is also interpreted as “one who changes.” Yet let the name “bitterness” remain in her—not the bitterness in which she gave the Lord gall, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. For Judah in Latin means “confession.” Let bitterness therefore be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be foreshadowed.

By this repentance the Church, established among all the nations, is made fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. [Col. 0697B]

Even the harlot’s attire signifies confession of sins. Tamar already bears the figure of the Church, called from the nations, sitting in this attire at the gate of Enan or Enaim, which is interpreted as “fountains.” For like a deer she ran to reach the fountains of water, to come to the seed of Abraham. There she conceives from one who does not know her, because it was foretold concerning her: “The people whom I did not know served me.”

She secretly received the ring, necklace [the text reads *monife*, probably *monile*, “necklace”], and staff. Calling is signified by the ring, justification is adorned by the necklace, and glorification is exalted by the staff. For “those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

But, as I said, these things are still hidden, where the conception of holy fruitfulness also takes place. The promised kid is sent to her as though she were a harlot: a kid, signifying the reproach of sin, sent through the same Odollamite, as one rebuking and saying, “Brood of vipers.” [Col. 0697C] Yet the reproach of sin did not find her, because the bitterness of confession had transformed her.

After the signs of the ring, necklace, and staff had been made public [the text varies: “after the ring, necklace, and staff had already been published”], she overcame those who judged rashly—those whose person Judah himself already represented. Even today they say that we are not the people of Christ and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are produced, they will undoubtedly be confounded and will confess that we have been justified more than they.

I would examine and explain these matters more fully, almost piece by piece and clause by clause, as far as the Lord might assist my intention, were I not prevented from such more laborious diligence by the need to bring this work to an end—a work that has already become longer than I wished.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

### On David’s sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite; from the same book XXII

[Col. 0697D] I shall now touch upon what David’s sin signified in prophecy, as briefly as I can. The interpretations of the names themselves sufficiently show what this deed also prefigured.

David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” or “desirable.” And who is stronger than that lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world? And who is more desirable than the one of whom the prophet says, “The desired one will come to all the nations”?

Bathsheba is interpreted as “well of satiety,” or “seventh well.” Whichever of these interpretations of her name we adopt for the point we intend to make, it agrees sufficiently. [Col. 0698A] For in the Song of Songs the bride is the Church, which is called a well of living water. The name of the number seven is joined to this well in reference to the Holy Spirit, also because of the reason for Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit came, sent from heaven.

The Scripture of Tobit also testifies that this same feast consists of weeks. To forty-nine, which is seven times seven, one is added, commending unity. In this arrangement lives that apostolic saying: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

By the spiritual gift—that is, the sevenfold gift—the Church became a well of satiety, because in her there was made a spring of water leaping up into eternal life; whoever possesses it will never thirst.

But what else does Uriah, who had been her husband, signify by the interpretation of his name than the devil? [Col. 0698B] All those whom God’s grace liberates were bound to him in that most evil marriage, so that the Church might be joined to her own Savior without stain or wrinkle.

For Uriah is interpreted as “my light is God.” Cethite is interpreted as “cut off”—either because he did not stand in the truth but, through the fault of pride, was cut off from the heavenly light he had from God, or because, having fallen and lost his true strength, he nevertheless transforms himself into an angel of light and still dares to say, “My light is God.”

Therefore this David did indeed sin gravely and wickedly; God also rebuked his crime through the prophet, and David cleansed it by repentance. Nevertheless, that desirable one of all the nations loved the Church as she washed herself upon the roof—that is, cleansed herself from the impurities of the world and, through spiritual contemplation, transcended and trod underfoot the house of clay. Having begun with her an initial knowledge of the covenant, after the devil had been wholly separated from her he killed him and joined her to himself in an everlasting marriage. [Col. 0698C]

Let us therefore hate the sin, but not extinguish the prophecies. Let us love that David insofar as he must be loved—the one who in mercy liberated us from the devil. Let us also love this David, who healed so grave a wound of iniquity in himself through the humility of repentance.

## CHAPTER LXXV

### On Solomon’s earlier good deeds and later evil deeds; from the same book XXII

What shall I say now about Solomon, whom Holy Scripture severely reproves and condemns, and concerning whose repentance or God’s mercy toward him it mentions absolutely nothing? [Col. 0698D] I cannot at all think of what good this lamentable downfall of his might signify in allegory, unless someone should say that the foreign women whose love inflamed him signify the elect churches from the nations.

This could perhaps be understood without absurdity if, on Solomon’s account, they had abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But since he offended his own God on their account and worshiped their gods, I cannot conjecture what good could be signified by it. Yet I do not think that it signifies nothing; rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters.

In the person of Solomon there appears a remarkable excellence and a remarkable downfall. What therefore existed in him at different times—first good and afterward evil—is displayed in the Church in this present age at one and the same time. [Col. 0699A] I think that by his goodness the good people of the Church are signified, and by his evil the wicked people of the Church, as in the unity of a single threshing floor: in that one man, the good are represented by the grain and the wicked by the chaff; in the unity of a single crop, the good by the wheat and the wicked by the weeds.

If, upon more careful examination of what has been written about him, something else more plausible should become clear either to me or to more learned and better teachers, so be it.
