For now, however, we have not left the matter in such a way that it would obstruct the chain of our discussion, as our intention hastens toward other subjects.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

### On the calf’s head being burned, scattered into water, and given to the people to drink; from the same book XXII, Against Faustus

[Col. 0699B] We must also inquire what prophetic significance lay in the fact that Moses ordered many of those who, while he was absent, had fashioned an idol to be killed without distinction according to any relationship.

It is easy to understand the killing of those men as signifying the destruction of the vices into which they had fallen through the same idolatry. For the Psalm commands us to rage against such vices when it says, “Be angry and do not sin.” The Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says, “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.”

But what does it mean that he first burned the calf itself with fire, cut it into pieces, scattered it upon the water, and gave it to the people to drink? [Col. 0699C] This calls for a more attentive investigation of its significance. If he broke the tablets that he had received written by the finger of God—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit—because he judged them unworthy to read them; and if, finally, he burned that calf so that it might be completely destroyed by them, crushed it, scattered it in water, and submerged it, why did he also give this drink to the people? Who would not be roused by this deed to inquire into and understand its prophetic meaning?

Let us therefore see, with minds already attentive, the devil’s body in the calf—that is, the human beings among all the nations for whom the devil is the head, meaning the author, of these sacrileges. It was golden because the rites of idolatry appeared to have been instituted by wise men. [Col. 0699D]

The Apostle speaks of them:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed animals and serpents.”

From this supposed wisdom came the golden calf, resembling the images that even the leading and supposedly learned men of the Egyptians used to worship.

This calf therefore signified the whole body—that is, the whole society—of the nations devoted to idolatry. The Lord Christ burns this sacrilegious society with the fire of which he says in the Gospel, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” [Col. 0700A] Since no one can hide from its heat, while the nations believe in him the devil’s form in them is dissolved by the fire of his power.

Then that whole body is crushed: that is, it is torn away from the fusion of its evil conspiracy and humbled by the word of truth. Once crushed, it is thrown into water, so that the Israelites—that is, the preachers of the Gospel—may transfer them through baptism into their own members, that is, into the Lord’s body. Concerning these Israelites, Peter was told regarding the nations themselves, “Kill and eat.” If “kill and eat,” why not also “cut up and drink”?

Thus, through the fire of zeal, the edge of the Word, and the water of baptism, that calf was itself swallowed up by those whom it had tried to swallow.

If, then, these passages of Scripture—which heretics slander on the basis of those same Scriptures—are carefully examined and, in a sense, questioned, [Col. 0700B] they answer that the more obscure they appear, the more wonderful are the treasures of mysteries hidden within them. The blasphemous mouths of the impious ought all the more to be silenced when they are closed by the clearest truth. They find nothing to mutter against it with choked breath, yet in their misery they prefer to have their throats obstructed by its manifestation rather than their hearts filled by its sweetness.

All these things therefore proclaim Christ: that head which has already ascended into heaven, and his body, which labors on earth until the end. The entire intention of those who wrote the truly sacred Scriptures gave birth to this. Nothing narrated through the sequence of the prophetic books should be believed to have been included without signifying something concerning future events, except those things that were inserted so that through them, in a certain way, the matters that foretold that king and his people—whether through proper or figurative expressions or through actual events—might be linked together. [Col. 0700C]

For just as in harps and similar musical instruments not everything that is touched produces a musical sound, yet the strings—and all the other parts of the harp—are fashioned so that there may be a place where the strings are fastened and from which and toward which they are stretched, while the craftsman tunes and strikes them for the sweetness of the song, so in these prophetic narratives, which are selected from human events by the prophetic Spirit, some things already sound through their signification of future events. If some signify nothing of that kind, they are inserted so that there may be a point from which the significant things, as though sounding, can be joined together.

If heretics refuse to accept these allegorical narratives of historical events as we explain them, or insist that they signify nothing except what they literally express, [Col. 0700D] there is no need to quarrel with people who say, “What you say does not appeal to my palate as you say it does to yours.” Provided, however, that what is divinely commanded is believed or understood either to form morals and piety, or to signify something figuratively, or preferably both rather than neither—and provided that even those things understood as figuratively spoken or done are referred back to the same good morals and piety.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

### On raising up seed for a deceased brother; from book XXXII, Against Faustus

[Col. 0701A] If we are asked why we hold to the authority of that Testament whose ritual we do not observe, we answer from the apostolic writings. The Apostle says:

> “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come.”

In this way he also shows why those things ought to be read and accepted: namely, so that we do not extinguish the prophecy, because they were done as a shadow of future things. He also shows why we should not be concerned about those who wish to judge us on this account, because we no longer observe them bodily, just as elsewhere he said something similar:

> “These things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the end of the ages has come.”

When something is read in the document of the Old Testament that we either do not observe, or are not commanded to observe in the New Testament, or are even forbidden to observe, we must ask what it signifies rather than criticize it. [Col. 0701B] For by the very fact that it is no longer observed, it is shown to have been not condemned but fulfilled.

Thus we have often already said many things, including this matter itself: Faustus, failing to understand it, charged the commands of the Old Testament as a crime because a brother was ordered to take his brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring not for himself but for his brother, and the child born from that union was to be called by the brother’s name.

What else does this prefigure than that every preacher of the Gospel ought to labor in the Church in such a way that he raises up seed for his deceased brother—that is, for Christ, who died for us—and that the seed he raises up should bear Christ’s name?

The Apostle fulfills this—not carnally in the preliminary signification, but spiritually in the completed truth. He says that he has begotten people in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, [Col. 0701C] and he rebukes and corrects those who wish to be called Paul’s:

> “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

As though he were saying: “I have begotten you for your deceased brother; you are called Christians, not Paulians.”

But whoever, after being chosen by the Church, refuses the ministry of evangelization is rightly and deservedly despised by the Church herself. This is what is meant by the command that she spit in his face—not without a sign of this disgrace, namely, that he should be stripped of one shoe. He is not to belong to the lot of those of whom the Apostle says, “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace,” and concerning whom the prophet says, “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things.” [Col. 0701D]

For whoever holds the evangelical faith in such a way that it benefits himself and does not refuse to benefit the Church is rightly understood to be shod on both feet. But whoever thinks that, because he has believed, he has taken sufficient care for himself, while avoiding the effort of winning others, will not merely signify the disgrace of that barefoot man figuratively, but will bear it fulfilled in himself.

What is more, Faustus also reproached us for celebrating Passover, nor does he taunt us on the ground that we celebrate it as the Jews do. Yet we possess the reality of the present Gospel, not the shadow of what was to come. We do not prefigure Christ’s future slaughter, both daily and especially in the annual solemnity; we commemorate it as something accomplished.

For this reason the day of our Passover solemnity does not coincide with the day of the Jews’ shadowy celebration, so that we might also include the Lord’s Day on which Christ rose. [Col. 0702A] Unleavened bread signifies Christians of right faith, who keep it not in the leaven of the old life—that is, wickedness—but in the truth and sincerity of that faith; they keep it not for seven days but every day, the seven-day number signifying the daily cycle by which every day turns.

Although this is somewhat laborious in the present age, because narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, a certain reward is nevertheless preserved. For that labor itself is signified by those bitter herbs, which are somewhat bitter.

We also celebrate Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day from the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, when he sent us the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete whom he had promised. This future event was also signified through the Jewish Passover, when, on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the sheep had been celebrated, Moses received on the mountain the law written by the finger of God. [Col. 0702B]

Read the Gospel and observe that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God. The events that were remarkably great and took place on definite days are celebrated annually in the Church, so that the necessary and salutary memory of them may be preserved through the solemnity observed together.

If you wish to know why we celebrate Passover, it is because Christ was sacrificed for us at that time. [60] If you wish to know why we do not celebrate it according to the Jewish rite, it is because the Jewish rite was a prefiguration of the true one to come, whereas ours is a commemoration of the one already fulfilled.

What is future and what is past are not expressed in the same way even in our own words. We have already discussed this sufficiently in the present work.

But if you also ask why, among all the foods from which that people was forbidden in the shadow of future things, we do not eat an animal that has died of itself or one sacrificed to idols, hear this as well, and at last prefer truth to the slanders of vanity. [Col. 0702C]

Why it is not appropriate for a Christian to eat meat sacrificed to idols the Apostle says:

> “I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

He does not condemn the sacrifice itself that the fathers performed while prefiguring the blood of the sacrifice by which Christ redeemed us, but the sacrifices that the nations offer:

> “They sacrifice to demons and not to God.”

Then he added what I have quoted: “I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

For if the nature of meat sacrificed to idols were itself unclean, it would contaminate even one who was unaware. It would be no less unclean because it was received unknowingly rather than knowingly. The concern is instead that someone might appear to have shared in fellowship with demons.

As for an animal that has died of itself, I think it was excluded from human use as food because the flesh of animals that have died, rather than being killed, is diseased and unsuitable for bodily health, for whose sake we take nourishment. [Col. 0702D]

As for the ancient command concerning the pouring out of blood, which was given figuratively—first to Noah after the Flood, as we have already shown what it signified—many understand that this command was also given by the apostles in the Acts of the Apostles: that the nations should abstain from fornication, from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood. That is, they were not to eat any flesh whose blood had not been poured out [the text also reads, “were in no way to eat flesh”].

Others do not understand it in this way, but think that the command to abstain from blood means that no one should defile himself by homicide. It would take too long to discuss this now, and it is unnecessary. For even if the apostles then commanded Christians to abstain from the blood of animals, so that they would not eat the flesh of strangled animals, they seem to me to have chosen, for the time being, an easy matter that was by no means burdensome to those who observed it. [Col. 0703A]

In this way, together with the Israelites, the nations too observed something in common for the sake of that cornerstone which makes the two into one. At the same time they were reminded that in Noah’s ark, when God gave this command, the Church of all nations had been prefigured, and that the prophecy of this event was beginning to be fulfilled as the nations came to faith.

After the time had passed during which those two walls—one coming from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision—although agreeing in the cornerstone, still stood out as distinct through their particular characteristics, and once the Church of the nations had become such that no carnal Israelite appeared in her, [Col. 0703B] what Christian now observes this rule by not touching thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been poured out, or by refusing to eat a hare if it has been killed by striking it by hand at the neck without a bloody wound?

Those few who perhaps still fear touching such foods are mocked by the others. Thus that saying of truth has held all minds in its power:

> “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out.”

No kind of food is rejected by human fellowship; rather, sin is condemned, which iniquity commits.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

### On the statement that clean and unclean birds entered the ark; from the book of Questions on Genesis, among other matters concerning the passage

[Col. 0703C] It is written that clean birds and unclean birds, clean cattle and unclean cattle, and all the serpents of the earth entered. In the latter case “clean and unclean” is understood even though it is not added. Then it is said that two by two entered the ark with Noah, male and female.

The question is how the earlier passage distinguished “two by two” from the unclean animals, whereas here it says that two by two entered, whether clean or unclean. But this does not refer to the number of clean or unclean animals. It refers to male and female, because in every kind there are two: male and female.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

### What the Lord means when he says, “I will not again curse the earth”; from the same book of Questions on Genesis

[Col. 0703D] What does the Lord mean when he says, “I will not again curse the earth because of human deeds, because the mind of man is inclined to evil from his youth. I will not again strike every living creature as I have done”?

He then adds the gifts that, according to the abundance of his goodness, he grants to unworthy human beings. Is the indulgence of the New Testament represented here, while the punishment of the past belongs to the Old Testament—that is, is the latter related to the severity of the law and the former to the goodness of grace?

## CHAPTER LXXX

### What is meant by, “From the hand of a brother I will require the life of a man”; from the same book of Questions on Genesis

[Col. 0704A] What is meant by, “From the hand of a man’s brother I will require the life of a man”? Did he intend every human being to be understood as the brother of every other human being, according to the kinship derived from one ancestor?

## CHAPTER LXXXI

### Ham sins, but is cursed not in himself but in his son; from the same book

The question is why Ham, who sinned in the offense against his father, is cursed not in himself but in his son Canaan. Is it not because it was in a certain way prophesied that, after the Canaanites had been expelled from the land and defeated, the sons of Israel, who would come from the seed of Shem, would receive the land of Canaan?

## CHAPTER LXXXII

### “The whole earth had one language,” said by way of recapitulation; from the same book

[Col. 0704B] How can it be understood that “the whole earth had one language,” when it was said above that the sons of Noah, or the sons of his sons, were distributed throughout the earth according to their tribes, nations, and languages?

It can only be because the text later recalls by way of recapitulation what had existed earlier. Yet the obscurity is caused by the fact that it joins these matters together in such a form of expression as though the narrative concerning what happened later followed directly afterward.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

### How Sarah, after spending several days with the king of Egypt, is not believed to have been defiled by intercourse with him

[Col. 0704C] “It will therefore be, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife.’” It happened that, as soon as Abraham entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful.

How should we understand the fact that, when Abraham came into Egypt, he wished to conceal that Sarah was his wife, according to everything written about this matter? Was this fitting for so holy a man, or should it be understood as a failure of his faith, as some have thought?

I have already discussed this matter against Faustus, and the presbyter Jerome has explained it more carefully: it does not follow that, because Sarah spent several days with the king of Egypt, she should be believed to have been defiled by intercourse with him.

For it was the royal custom to admit women to himself in turn, and no woman entered the king’s presence until her body had first been carefully treated for a long time with lotions [or fomentations] and perfumes. [Col. 0704D] While this was happening, Pharaoh was afflicted by the hand of God, so that he might return untouched to her husband the woman whom her husband had entrusted to God. Abraham remained silent about her being his wife, but did not lie in saying that she was his sister. He took precautions as far as he could—as far as a human being could—and entrusted to God what he could not guard.

Otherwise, if he had entrusted even to God alone what he could guard himself, he would be found not to have believed in God but rather to have tempted God.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

### How “I will give you the land as an eternal possession” is to be understood; from the same book

[Col. 0705A] “I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you dwell, the whole cultivated land, as an eternal possession.”

The question is how he could have called it eternal, since it was given to the Israelites for a limited time. Was it called eternal in relation to this present age, so that it was named *aeternum* from the Greek word αἰών, which also signifies “age,” and αἰώνιον means something like what could be called *saeculare* in Latin, “belonging to an age”?

Or are we compelled here to understand something according to a spiritual promise, so that it was called eternal because something eternal is signified through it? Or is it rather a usage of the Scriptures to call something eternal when no end has been assigned to it?

Or is it not understood in such a way that it will not thereafter be done, insofar as it belongs to the care or authority of the one doing it, as Horace says:

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

He will serve forever who does not know how to use what is small. For he cannot serve forever whose very life, which serves, cannot be eternal. I would not have brought forward this testimony unless it concerned a manner of expression; for they are authorities for us in matters of words, not of things or meanings. But if the Scriptures are defended according to their proper modes of expression, which are called idioms, how much more according to those that they share with other languages?

## CHAPTER LXXXV. “I knew,” he says, “that he would command his sons after him to keep the ways of the Lord”; from the book of *Questions on Genesis*

[Col. 0705B]

“For I knew that he would command his sons and his household after him to keep the ways of the Lord, to practice righteousness and judgment, so that the Lord might bring upon Abraham everything that he had spoken to him.” Behold, here the Lord promises Abraham not only rewards but also the obedience of his sons in righteousness, so that the promised rewards might likewise be fulfilled with regard to them.

[Col. 0705C]

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. “Going down, I shall see whether they are being destroyed according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I shall know”; from the same book

“Going down, therefore, I shall see whether they are being destroyed according to the outcry of them that has come to me; and if not, I shall know.” If we take these words not as those of one uncertain which of two outcomes is more likely to occur, but as the words of one who is angry and threatening, there is no difficulty. For in the Scriptures God speaks to human beings in a human manner, and those who know how to understand his anger know it without attributing disturbance to him.

We also customarily speak in a threatening way: “Let us see whether I do not do this to you,” or, “Let us see whether I do not do it to him”; and, “If I cannot do this to you, I shall know”—that is, “I shall test whether I cannot.” When this is said in threatening rather than ignorant fashion, it displays the attitude of anger, but disturbance does not befall God.

[Col. 0705D]

The custom of human speech is also ordinary and conforms to human weakness, to which God adapts his speech [*congruit*; the variant reads *congruat*, “may conform”].

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. “I shall not destroy it if I find ten righteous men”; from the same book

[Col. 0706A]

It is commonly asked whether what God said concerning Sodom—that he would not destroy the place if ten righteous men were found there—was a special pronouncement concerning that city, or whether it should be understood generally of all places: that God would spare any place wherever ten righteous men might be found.

In this question, it is not necessary that we be compelled to take the statement as applying to every place. Nevertheless, it could also have been said concerning Sodom because God knew that there were not even ten righteous men there. Thus he answered Abraham in order to indicate that not even that number could be found there, thereby intensifying the enormity of their wickedness.

For God was not obliged to spare such wicked people, nor to destroy the righteous together with them, since, after rescuing the righteous from that place, he could inflict upon the wicked the punishments they deserved. But, as I have said, to display the depravity of that multitude he said: “If I find ten there, I shall spare the whole city”—as though he were saying: “Certainly I can neither destroy the godly together with the ungodly, nor for that reason spare the ungodly, since, after rescuing and separating the godly from them, I can repay the ungodly what they deserve; and yet, if they are found there, I spare the city”—that is, because not even that number could be found there.

[Col. 0706B]

Something similar occurs in Jeremiah, where he says: “Go around the streets of Jerusalem, and see and search in its squares, and learn whether you will find a man practicing righteousness and seeking faithfulness; then I shall be merciful toward their sins”—that is: “Find even one, and I shall spare the others,” to intensify and demonstrate that not even one could be found there.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Concerning Lot offering his daughters to the citizens in a disturbed state of mind; from the same book

[Col. 0706C]

When Lot said to the Sodomites: “I have two daughters who have not yet known men. I shall bring them out to you; use them as you please. Only do not do this wicked thing to these men,” he apparently wished to prostitute his daughters as compensation, so that his male guests would suffer nothing of the kind from the Sodomites.

It is rightly asked whether a compensation of crimes or of any sins should be admitted—whether we may do something evil so that another may not do something more grievously evil—or whether this should rather be attributed to Lot’s disturbance, not to deliberate counsel, since he spoke in this way. Certainly, this compensation is lost at the greatest peril. If, however, it is attributed to human disturbance and to a mind shaken by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. What God said to Abimelech: “I spared you, so that you would not sin against me”; from the same book

[Col. 0706D]

When God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah, “I spared you, so that you would not sin against me,” as he warned him that she was Abraham’s wife, whom he had thought to be his sister, this should be observed and noted: sin is committed against God when people do things that human beings think should be regarded lightly, as though they were merely sins committed in the flesh.

When he also said to him, “Behold, you are about to die,” this too should be noted: God speaks as though he were predicting without doubt what would happen, although by giving the warning he is urging the man to guard himself by refraining from sin.

## CHAPTER XC. How “God tested Abraham” is not contrary to James’s statement, “God tests no one”; from the same book

[Col. 0707A]

“And God tested Abraham.” It is commonly asked how this can be true, since James says in his Epistle that God tests no one. The explanation is that, in the language of the Scriptures, *tests* is customarily said for *proves*.

The temptation of which James speaks is understood only as the entanglement of a person in sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps the tempter should have tempted you.” Elsewhere also it is written: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.” Here too, “to know” is said according to this mode of expression, as though it were said, “to make you know,” since the strength of a person’s love is hidden from him unless it is also made known to him by a divine trial.

## CHAPTER XCI. 62. Concerning the similar expression, “I have known that you fear God”; from the same book

[Col. 0707B]

The angel’s voice from heaven to Abraham said: “Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him; for now I have known that you fear God.” This question too is resolved by a similar mode of expression. For this is what is meant: “Now I have known that you fear God,” which signifies, “Now I have made you know.”

The same kind of expression appears more clearly in what follows, where it is said: “And Abraham called the name of that place ‘The Lord saw,’ so that it is said to this day, ‘On the mountain the Lord appeared.’” “Saw” is used for “appeared”—that is, “saw” for “caused himself to be seen”—signifying through the efficient cause what is effected, just as “sluggish cold” means cold that makes people sluggish.

[Col. 0707C]

## CHAPTER XCII. Concerning Abraham’s servant’s oath over his thigh; from the same book

What Abraham commands his servant—to place his hand upon his thigh and then makes him swear by the Lord God of heaven and the Lord of earth—often troubles the uninstructed, because they do not attend to the fact that this was a great prophecy concerning Christ: that the Lord God of heaven and the Lord of earth himself would come in that flesh which was propagated from that thigh.

## CHAPTER XCIII. How unlawful auguries differ from the servant of Abraham’s request for a sign; from the same book

[Col. 0707D]

It must be asked how unlawful auguries differ from the request for a sign by which Abraham’s servant asked God to show him that the woman would be his master Isaac’s future wife: when he asked her for a drink, she was to say to him, “Drink, and I shall also water your camels until they cease drinking” [*desinerent*; variant *desinent*, “until they cease”].

For it is one thing to ask for something marvelous that, by the very miracle, may serve as a sign; it is another to observe things that happen without being marvelous, but are interpreted by diviners with superstitious vanity.

[Col. 0708A]

Yet even when something marvelous is requested in order to signify what a person wishes to know, whether this should be heeded is not a minor question. For this is related to the statement that those who do this improperly are tempting the Lord. When the Lord himself was tempted by the devil, he brought forward testimony from the Scriptures: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” The suggestion was made to him as though he were merely human, that he should test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much power he possessed with God. This is done wickedly when it is done.

What Gideon did when the danger of battle was imminent is distinguished from this; that inquiry was more consultation than temptation of God. Hence Ahaz in Isaiah is afraid to ask for a sign, lest he appear to tempt the Lord [variant: “the Lord God”], although the Lord urges him through the prophet to do so. I think Ahaz believed that the prophet was testing whether he remembered the commandment by which we are forbidden to tempt the Lord [variant: “we are forbidden to tempt God”].

## CHAPTER XCIV. Concerning Jacob’s statement, “There is nothing here but the house of God”; from the same book

[Col. 0708B]

“And Jacob awoke from his sleep and said: ‘Because the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.’ And he was afraid and said: ‘How terrible is this place! This is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.’”

These words pertain to prophecy, because the tabernacle that God [variant: “the Lord”] established among human beings in his first people was destined to be there. We should understand the gate of heaven as the entrance by which believers gain access to possess the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XCV. That Jacob did not do anything resembling idolatry when he set up the stone and poured oil over it; from the same book

[Col. 0708C]

When Jacob set up the stone that he had placed at his head, made it into a memorial stone, and poured oil over it, he did nothing resembling idolatry. For neither then nor afterward did he regularly worship the stone or sacrifice to it [variant: “or worship it”]. Rather, it was established as a sign in an exceedingly clear prophecy pertaining to anointing; hence the name “Christ” derives from *chrism*.

## CHAPTER XCVI. Concerning Jacob’s wrestling and his lameness; from the same book

The fact that Jacob desired to be blessed by the angel whom he overcame in wrestling is a great prophecy concerning Christ.

[Col. 0708D]

For this very fact admonishes us to understand something mystical, because every human being wishes to be blessed by one who is greater. How, then, did this man wish to be blessed by one whom he overcame in wrestling?

Jacob prevailed over Christ—or rather appeared to prevail—through those Israelites by whom Christ was crucified. Yet he is blessed by him in those Israelites who believed in Christ, among whom was the one who said: “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

Thus one and the same Jacob is both lame and blessed. He is lame in the breadth of his thigh, as in the multitude of his descendants, concerning whom it was said: “And they have limped from their paths.” But he is blessed in those concerning whom it was said: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.”

## CHAPTER XCVII. Whether Jacob poured oil over the stone a second time, or whether the second passage merely recalls the earlier event; from the same book

[Col. 0709A]

“God went up from the place where he had spoken with him, and Jacob set up a memorial stone in the place where he had spoken with him, a stone memorial, and he poured out a libation over it and poured oil over it [variant: “over him,” *eum*], and Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him there ‘Bethel.’”

Did what had happened before occur again at this place, or is it merely recalled again? Whichever is the case, Jacob poured a libation over the stone, not to the stone. Therefore he did not act as idolaters customarily do when they set up altars before stones and pour libations to stones as though they were gods.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. The question of how Jacob’s twelve sons are counted although Benjamin had not yet been born, resolved by the trope *synecdoche* (συνεκδοχή); from the book of *Questions on Genesis*

[Col. 0709B]

The question concerns the fact that Israel’s twelve sons are counted and it is said, “These are the sons of Israel who were born in Mesopotamia,” although Benjamin was born much later, after Jacob had already passed through Bethel and was approaching Bethlehem.

There is no easier solution to this question than to understand it through *synecdoche* (συνεκδοχή). For when one part is greater or more important, it is customary for what does not belong properly to that name to be included under the name of the more important part.

Thus Judas no longer belonged among the twelve Apostles; indeed, he was already dead when the Lord rose from the dead. Yet the Apostle retained the name of that number, saying in his Epistle that the Lord appeared to “the twelve.” The Greek codices have the article, so that the phrase cannot be understood as referring to any twelve individuals, but to those distinguished within that number.

[Col. 0709C]

I think that the statement made by the Lord is expressed in the same way: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” Thus even Judas does not appear to belong to the election. For the name “the elect” is not readily found in an evil sense, except when evil people are chosen by evil people.

If we should think that Judas too was chosen so that, through his betrayal, the Lord’s Passion might be fulfilled—that is, that his wickedness was chosen for some purpose, since God makes good use even of the wicked—let us attend to another passage where he says: “I do not speak concerning all of you; I know whom I have chosen.” Here he declares that only the good belong to the election.

[Col. 0709D]

Consequently, the statement, “I chose you twelve,” is spoken by *synecdoche*, so that what does not properly belong to that name is included under the name of the greater and better part.

The same mode of expression occurs in this same book [variant: “passage”]. Hamor, on behalf of his son Shechem, went out to speak with Jacob so that Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, might be given to Shechem; Jacob’s sons, who had been absent, also came. Hamor said to all of them: “Shechem my son has set his heart upon your daughter; therefore give her to him as a wife.” Because the father’s person was the more important, in saying “your daughter” he included by *synecdoche* the brothers, who were not his daughter [variant: “sons”].

The same applies to the statement: “Run to the sheep and take two young goats from there for me.” The sheep and the goats were being pastured together, and because the sheep are the more important, the flock of goats too was included under the name of the sheep.

[Col. 0710A]

So, because the eleven sons of Jacob who had been born in Mesopotamia were the more important number, Scripture included Benjamin in its mention of them, although he had not been born there, and said: “These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria.”

## CHAPTER XCIX. Whether only the wicked, or also the righteous dead, customarily descend into hell; from the same book

“And he refused to be comforted, saying: ‘For I shall go down mourning to my son in hell.’”

It is often a major question how “hell” should be understood: whether only the wicked, or also the righteous dead, customarily descend there. If only the wicked are there in some sense, how does this man say that he wishes to descend mourning to his son? For he does not believe that his son is in the punishments of hell. Or are these the words of a disturbed and grieving man, exaggerating his own misfortune?

—Concerning the same matter.—

“And they descended alive, they and all that belonged to them, into hell.” Here “hell” should be understood according to the location of the earth, that is, as the lower regions of the earth. For the name “hell” is used variously in the Scriptures and with different meanings, as the sense of the matters under discussion requires; most often it is understood in connection with the dead.

But since these people are said to have descended alive into hell, and the narrative itself sufficiently shows what happened, it is clear, as I have said, that the lower regions of the earth are here called hell, in comparison with this upper earth upon whose surface human beings live.

[Col. 0710B]

Likewise, in comparison with the higher heaven, where the holy angels dwell, Scripture says that the angels who sinned were thrust into the darkness of this air and kept in reserve for punishment as though in the prisons of hell.

“For if,” he says, “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of the darkness of hell and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment,” since the Apostle Paul calls the devil the ruler of the power of the air, who works in the sons of disobedience.

—Concerning the same matter.—

[Col. 0710C]

“And you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.”

What shall we say, brothers? If I do not explain this to you as something certain, do not be angry with me. I am a human being, and I dare to say only as much as is granted to me from the holy Scriptures; I say nothing on my own authority. I have not yet experienced hell, nor have you, and perhaps there will be another way, and it will not be through hell. These matters are uncertain.

But because Scripture says something that cannot be contradicted—“You have rescued my soul from the lower hell”—we understand that there are, as it were, two hells, an upper and a lower. For why would one speak of a lower hell unless there were an upper hell? It would not be called “hell” in comparison with any other than that upper region.

It appears, then, brothers, that there is a certain heavenly dwelling of the angels: there is the life of ineffable joys, immortality, incorruption, and all things that endure according to God’s gift and grace. That is the upper region of reality.

[Col. 0710D]

If that region is above, then this earthly region—where there are flesh and blood, corruption, birth and mortality, departure and succession, mutability and instability, fears, desires, terrors, uncertain joys, fragile hope, and perishable substance—cannot be compared with that heaven of which I spoke a little earlier.

[Col. 0711A]

If this region cannot be compared with that region, then that is the upper region and this is the underworld; and after death, where does one go from here except to a hell lower than this hell in which we are in the flesh and in this mortality?

“For the body,” the Apostle says, “is dead because of sin.” Therefore there are dead people here too, so that you should not be surprised that it is called hell when it abounds in the dead. He does not say, “The body will be dead,” but, “The body is dead.” Our body still has life, certainly; yet when compared with that body which is to come—such as the bodies of the angels are—the human body is found to be dead, although it still possesses a soul.

But from this hell—that is, from this region of hell—there is another, lower one, where the dead will be, from which God wished to rescue our souls by sending his Son there as well.

[Col. 0711B]

Indeed, brothers, the Son of God was sent because of these two hells, liberating us from every side: he was sent to this hell by being born, and to that one by dying.

Therefore his voice occurs in that psalm—not through anyone’s conjecture, but as the Apostle explains it—where he says: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell.” Thus either this is also his voice: “You have rescued my soul from the lower hell”; or it is our voice through Christ our Lord, because he reached hell for this reason: so that we would not remain in hell.

I shall mention another opinion as well. Perhaps among those in hell there is a lower region to which the ungodly who have sinned greatly are thrust. For we cannot determine with sufficient certainty whether Abraham was already in certain regions among those in hell.

[Col. 0711C]

The Lord had not yet come to hell to rescue from there the souls of all the preceding saints, and yet Abraham was there in a place of rest.

A certain rich man, moreover, was being tormented among those in hell. When he saw Abraham, he lifted up his eyes. He could not see him with his eyes lifted unless one were above and the other below. And what did Abraham reply to him when he said: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus so that he may dip his finger and let it drip upon my tongue, because I am being tormented in this flame”? He said: “Son, remember that you received good things during your life, while Lazarus received evil things; but now he is resting here, whereas you are being tormented.”

[Col. 0711D]

And in addition to this he said: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that neither can we cross over to you, nor can anyone cross over from there to us.”

Therefore, perhaps between these two hells—one in which the souls of the righteous rested, and the other in which the souls of the wicked are tormented—a certain person, praying here and already placed here in the body of Christ, prayed in the voice of Christ and said that the Lord had rescued his soul from the lower hell. He meant that he had been freed from such sins as could have led him to the torments of the lower hell.

It is as when a physician sees that an illness is threatening you, perhaps as a result of some exertion, and says: “Spare yourself; take care of yourself in this way; rest; use these foods, for if you do not, you will become ill.” If you follow his advice and are saved, you rightly say to the physician: “You have rescued me from illness”—not from an illness in which you already were, but from one in which you were going to be.

[Col. 0712A]

Someone who had a troublesome case was about to be sent to prison. Another person came and defended him. What does the one who gives thanks say? “You have rescued my soul from prison.” A debtor was about to be hanged; payment was made on his behalf, and he is said to have been rescued from hanging.

In all these cases they were not yet in those places, but they were being led toward such outcomes by their merits, so that, unless help had come, they would have been there. Thus they are rightly said to have been rescued from the place to which their rescuers did not permit them to be taken.

Therefore, brothers, whether this interpretation or that one is correct, regard me here as an investigator of the word of God, not as a rash assertor: “And you have rescued my soul from the lower hell.”

## CHAPTER C. 64. That the Holy Spirit is intimated for the third time in Genesis; from the same book of *Questions on Genesis*

[Col. 0712B]

“Shall we find a man such as this, who has the spirit of God in him?” Behold, unless I am mistaken, the Holy Spirit—that is, the Spirit of God—is intimated to us for the third time in this book.

First, where it was said, “The Spirit of God was over the waters”; second, where God said, “My spirit will not remain in these people, because they are flesh”; and third, here, when Pharaoh says of Joseph that the Spirit of God is in him. Yet we have not read the words “the Holy Spirit” up to this point.

## CHAPTER CI. How the statement that so many souls came forth from Jacob’s thighs is to be understood; and concerning Levi’s tithing; from the same book

When Scripture says that Leah bore so many souls, or that so many souls came forth from Jacob’s thighs, we must consider what answer should be given to those who attempt to confirm by this testimony that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies.

[Col. 0712C]

No one doubts that “souls” is used for “human beings,” in an expression in which the part signifies the whole. But how are we to understand that the very part by which the whole has been mentioned—that is, the soul, by whose name the whole human being is signified—is said to come forth from his thighs, so that we should understand only flesh to have been born from him, even though only souls are named? We must examine the modes of expression found in the Scriptures.

Although no human being’s soul is in his father’s loins according to the flesh, Levi was in Abraham’s loins and was tithed there; Christ too was in them according to the flesh, but was not tithed there.

[Col. 0712D]

For Levi was there according to that seminal principle by which he was destined to enter his mother through intercourse. According to that principle, Christ’s flesh was not there, although Mary’s flesh was there according to that same principle.

Therefore neither Levi nor Christ was in Abraham’s loins according to the soul, but both Levi and Christ were there according to the flesh. Levi was there according to carnal desire, whereas Christ was there only according to bodily substance.

Since in the seed there are both visible corporeal bulk and an invisible seminal principle, both proceeded from Abraham—or even from Adam himself—down to Mary’s body, because Mary’s body too was conceived and brought forth in that manner. Christ, however, took the visible substance of his flesh from the flesh of the virgin, while the principle of his conception came not from male seed but in a very different manner, from above.

[Col. 0713A]

Accordingly, insofar as he received something from his mother, he too was in Abraham’s loins. The one who was tithed in Abraham is therefore the one who, although only according to the flesh, was nevertheless in his loins just as Abraham himself was in the loins of his own father—that is, the one born from father Abraham in the same manner as Abraham had been born from his own father: through the law resisting the law of the mind and through invisible desire, which is, as it were, transmitted through the seminal principle in all flesh propagated from it, although chaste and good marital rights do not allow it to prevail except insofar as they can use it to provide for the continuation of the race.

But the one whose flesh drew from there not the heat of the wound but the material of the remedy was not tithed there. For since the tithe pertained to the prefiguration of healing, what was tithed in Abraham’s flesh was what was being healed.

[Col. 0713B]

That same flesh—not only Abraham’s but also that of the first earthly human being—simultaneously possessed both the wound of transgression and the remedy for the wound. The wound of transgression was in the law of the members resisting the law of the mind, which is, through the seminal principle, transmitted as if copied into all flesh propagated from it. The remedy for the wound was in what, without the activity of desire, was assumed from the virgin solely in bodily substance, and formed through the divine principle of conception and formation, for the sharing of death without sin and the example of resurrection without falsehood.

Therefore, I think that even those who defend the propagation of souls agree that Christ’s soul did not arise by transmission from the soul of that first transgressor.

[Col. 0713C]

For they wish the seed of the soul to be transmitted through the seed of the father who engages in intercourse, and Christ is alien to that manner of conception.

Moreover, if Christ had been in Abraham according to the soul, he too would have been tithed. But Scripture testifies that he was not tithed, and by this too it distinguishes his priesthood from the Levitical priesthood. Perhaps they will say: just as he could be there according to the flesh without being tithed, why could he not also have been there according to the soul without being tithed?

The answer is that even those who think the soul is a body have certainly not believed that the simple substance of the soul is increased by bodily growth. Most especially among them are those who think that the soul is created from parents.

[Col. 0713D]

Accordingly, in the seed of the body there can be an invisible power that operates in a noncorporeal manner through numbers. It must be distinguished by the intellect, not by the eyes, from that corporeal bulk which is perceived by sight and touch [variant: “by sight and touch together”]. The very size of the human body—which incomparably exceeds the small measure of the seed—plainly shows that something can be taken from it that does not possess that seminal power but only bodily substance. This substance was divinely assumed and formed into Christ’s flesh, not from the propagation of those who engage in intercourse.

But who could affirm this concerning the soul: that it possesses both the manifest material of seed and the hidden principle of seed? Yet why should I labor over a matter that perhaps cannot be persuaded by words to anyone, unless the person has such great and powerful intelligence that he can outstrip the speaker’s effort and not wait for the whole matter to be unfolded in speech?

[Col. 0714A]

I shall summarize it briefly. If something could also happen with respect to the soul analogous to what we perhaps understood when we spoke of the flesh, then Christ’s soul could likewise have been transmitted and could have drawn the stain of transgression along with it. But if it could not be from there without that guilt, then it is not from there.

As for the origin of other souls—whether they come from parents or from above—let those who can prevail decide. I remain uncertain and troubled between the two positions, sometimes inclined one way and sometimes the other. I am certain of this alone: with God’s help I trust that my mind will not believe the soul to be a body, or some corporeal quality or arrangement—if it should be called that—which the Greeks call *harmonia* (ἁρμονία), nor anyone babbling about these matters in whatever fashion.

## CHAPTER CII. What Jacob said to Joseph: “Place your hand under my thigh, and you will show me mercy”; from the same book of Genesis

[Col. 0714B]

As he was dying, Jacob said to his son Joseph: “If I have found favor in your sight, place your hand under my thigh, and you will show me mercy and truth.”

By this oath he binds his son in the same way as Abraham had bound his servant: Abraham was commanding his servant concerning the wife to be brought for his son; Jacob was entrusting the burial of his body.

[Col. 0714C]

In both cases, however, two things are named that are to be highly valued and esteemed throughout all the Scriptures, wherever they are found separately: mercy and justice, or mercy and judgment, or mercy and truth. For in one passage it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” These two qualities, therefore, are greatly commended and greatly to be considered.

Abraham’s servant had said: “If you show mercy and justice toward my master,” just as Jacob says to his son: “that you may show me mercy and truth.”

Why such a great man was so concerned to entrust his body to be buried not in Egypt but in the land of Canaan, beside his fathers, appears strange and almost absurd, and inconsistent with the excellence of his prophetic mind, if it is measured according to human custom. But if sacramental meanings are sought in all these matters, the joy of the greater wonder will arise in the one who discovers them.

[Col. 0714D]

There is no doubt that the corpses of the dead signify sins in the law, since people are commanded, after handling or in any way touching them, to be purified as though from uncleanness. From this comes the saying: “He who is baptized from a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit?” So too: “The one who fasts over his sins and then goes out and commits the same things again.”

The burial of the dead therefore signifies the remission of sins, corresponding to the statement: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered.” Where, then, were the corpses signifying these things to be buried if not in the land where the one was crucified whose blood brought about the remission of sins? For the sins of human beings were represented by the deaths of the patriarchs.

[Col. 0715A]

It is said that the place called *Abramium* [variant: *Abraemium*], where these bodies are located, is about thirty thousand paces from the place where the Lord was crucified. Thus that number too may be understood as signifying the one who appeared in baptism at approximately thirty years of age, along with anything else that may be understood concerning so great a matter, either in this way or in a more sublime manner.

Let us nevertheless not suppose that such and so great men of God took such care for the burial of their bodies without reason. The security of the faithful is, and ought to be, that wherever their bodies are buried—or even if, through the fury of enemies, they are left unburied or torn apart and consumed according to the enemies’ will—their resurrection will not on that account be either less whole or less glorious.

## CHAPTER CIII. What is meant by the statement, “He was gathered to his fathers”; from the same book of *Questions on Genesis*

[Col. 0715B]

We must consider how the Scriptures repeatedly say of the dead: “He was gathered to his fathers,” or, “He was gathered to his people.”

For example, this is said of Jacob, who was already dead but not yet buried, and it is not readily apparent to what people he was gathered. From him arose the later people called the people of Israel, while those who preceded him were so few righteous people that we hesitate to call them a people.

If it had been said, “He was gathered to his fathers,” there would be no question. Or perhaps a people includes not only the people of holy human beings but also the people of the angels of that city of which it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of God, Jerusalem, and thousands of rejoicing angels.”

[Col. 0715C]

Those who finish this life pleasing to God are gathered to this people. They are said to be gathered then, when no anxiety from temptations and no danger from sins remains. Observing this, Scripture says: “Before death, praise no one.”

## CHAPTER CIV. Concerning the mourning Joseph conducted for his father for seven days; from the same book

“And he mourned for his father for seven days.”

I do not know whether the Scriptures record that the mourning of any saint lasted nine days, which the Latins call *novendialia*. Therefore it seems to me that Christians who observe this number in mourning for their dead should be prohibited from doing so, since it belongs more properly to the custom of the pagans.

The seventh day, however, has authority in the Scriptures. Thus it is written elsewhere: [Col. 0715D]

“The mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but for the fool all the days of his life.” The number seven, because of the mystery of the Sabbath, principally signifies rest. Therefore it is rightly observed for the dead as for those who are resting.

Nevertheless, the Egyptians multiplied this number tenfold in Jacob’s mourning, for they mourned him for seventy days.

## CHAPTER CV. Concerning what is written in Exodus: “The angel met him and wanted to kill him”; from the book of *Questions on Exodus*

[The supplied source ends here, with the chapter heading incomplete.]

In the passage where it is written: “And it came to pass on the way at the lodging-place that an angel encountered him and sought to kill him; and Sephora took a flint and circumcised [Col. 0716A] the foreskin of her son, and fell at his feet and said: ‘The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped,’ and he departed from him; for this reason she said: ‘A bridegroom of blood by circumcision.’” First it is asked whom the angel wanted to kill: Moses, because it is said, “An angel encountered him and sought to kill him”? For whom could he be thought to have encountered except the one who presided over his entire company and by whom the others were being led? Or was he seeking to kill the boy, whom his mother assisted by circumcising him, so that it may be understood that he wanted to kill the infant because he was not circumcised, and thus to establish the commandment of circumcision by the severity of its punishment?

If this is so, it is uncertain of whom he had first said, “He sought to kill him,” since it is unknown who was meant, unless the answer is discovered from what follows. It is indeed a remarkable and unusual manner of expression to say first, “He encountered him and sought to kill him,” without having previously said anything about the person concerned. Yet there is a similar case in the Psalm: “His foundations are in the holy mountains; God [variant: ‘the Lord’] loves the gates of Zion.” For the Psalm begins with these words, and he had said nothing either about a male or a female whose foundations he intended by saying, “His foundations are in the holy mountains.” But because it follows, “The Lord loves the gates of Zion,” the foundations must be understood as either the Lord’s or Zion’s; and for easier understanding, Zion is more suitably taken as the city whose foundations are meant.

But because the pronoun *eius* (“his”) is grammatically ambiguous—for this pronoun can be masculine, feminine, or neuter—while in Greek the feminine is written αὐτῆς (*autēs*), and the masculine and neuter αὐτοῦ (*autou*), and the Greek manuscript has αὐτοῦ, this compels us to understand not “the foundations of Zion,” [Col. 0716C] but “the foundations of the Lord,” that is, the foundations which the Lord established; of him it is said: “The Lord builds Jerusalem.” Yet neither Zion nor the Lord had previously been named when he said, “His foundations are in the holy mountains.” So also here, although the infant had not yet been named, it is said, “He encountered him and sought to kill him,” so that from what follows we may recognize whom he meant.

Nevertheless, if someone wishes to understand the passage as referring to Moses, there is no need to resist strongly. Rather, if possible, we should understand the point of what follows: namely, that the angel withdrew from killing either of them because the woman said, “The blood of the circumcision of the child has stopped.” For she did not say that he withdrew because she circumcised the child, but because the blood of the circumcision had stopped—not because it flowed, but because it stopped; this, unless I am mistaken, has a profound sacramental significance.

### CHAPTER CVI. On the fact that God repeatedly says, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart”; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

God repeatedly says: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” and he seems to offer a reason why he does this: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” he says, “and I will also fulfill my signs [variant, uncertain: ‘may do. And I will fulfill my signs’] and my wonders in Egypt,” as though the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart had been necessary in order that God’s signs might be multiplied or fulfilled in Egypt.

God therefore makes good use of evil hearts for what he wishes to show to the good, or to those whom he intends to make good [variant: ‘what he will do for the good’]. Although the quality of each person’s heart in evil—that is, the kind of heart one has toward evil—is produced by that person’s own fault, having grown out of the freedom of the will, nevertheless, when that evil quality moves the heart in one direction or another, and when it moves it wrongly in either direction, this occurs through the causes by which the mind is driven.

Whether these causes arise or do not arise is not within human power. Rather, they come from the hidden providence—which is plainly most just and most wise—of God, who orders and governs the whole universe that he created. Thus, the fact that Pharaoh had such a heart that God’s patience did not move him toward piety but rather toward impiety was due to his own vice. But the fact that circumstances occurred through which his heart, already so malignant by its own fault, resisted God’s commands—for this is what is meant by being hardened, since it did not consent flexibly but resisted inflexibly—was part of the divine dispensation. By this dispensation, a punishment was being prepared for such a heart, a punishment not unjust but manifestly just, by which those who feared God would be corrected.

For example, when the prospect of profit is placed before someone as the reason for committing murder, the miser is moved in one way and the person who despises money in another: the former is moved toward carrying out the crime, the latter toward avoiding it. Yet the prospect of that profit was not within the power of either of them. Thus causes come to evil people that are not indeed within their power, but these causes reveal them as the people they had already become through their own vices arising from past acts of will.

It should certainly be considered whether the words “I will harden” may also be understood in this way, as though he were saying: “I will demonstrate how hard he is.”

### CHAPTER CVII. That Aaron’s staff swallowed the staffs of the magicians; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

“And Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.” If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their staffs,” it would be understood that Aaron’s true dragon had not swallowed those imaginary forms, but staffs. For it could swallow what they were, not what they appeared to be but were not.

But since it says, “Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs,” the dragon could indeed swallow the staffs—not as a staff, but the object was called by the name of what it had been transformed from, not by the name of what it had been transformed into. Since it was also changed back into its former state, it ought to be called by the name of what it principally was.

What, then, should be said about the magicians’ staffs? Had they too truly been turned into dragons, but were called staffs for the same reason that Aaron’s was? Or did they appear to be what they were not, through magical deception? Why, then, are both staffs and dragons spoken of on either side, so that the manner of speaking makes no distinction concerning those apparitions?

It is difficult to demonstrate how, even if true dragons were made from the magicians’ staffs, neither the magicians nor the evil angels through whose agency these things were performed were nevertheless the creators of the dragons. For throughout all the elements of the world there exist in corporeal things certain hidden seminal principles. When a temporal and causal opportunity is provided, these principles burst forth into the forms appropriate to them, according to their proper modes and limits.

Thus the angels who bring these things about are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or anything else that grows from the earth, even though they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes by which such things are born. What these farmers do visibly, the angels do invisibly. But God alone is the true Creator, for he implanted the causes themselves and their seminal principles in things.

The point has been stated briefly. If it were explained by examples and a lengthy argument so that it might be more easily understood, it would require a long discussion, from which the demands of our haste excuse us.

### CHAPTER CVIII. How the magicians could turn water into blood if it had already been done everywhere; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

“But the magicians of the Egyptians also acted similarly by their magic arts, and they brought frogs up over the land [Col. 0718B] of Egypt.” It is asked how they could do this if everything had already been affected everywhere. A similar question arises concerning how they could turn water into blood if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood.

Accordingly, we must understand that the region where the children of Israel lived had not been struck by such plagues. From there the magicians could either draw water which they then turned into blood, or bring forth some frogs merely to display magical power. They may also have been able to do this after those things had been restrained, but Scripture, in its rapid narration, joined together what could also have happened later.

### CHAPTER CIX. Likewise, on the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart.

“And Pharaoh saw that there had been relief, and his heart was burdened [Col. 0718C], and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.” Here it becomes clear that the causes of the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart were not only the fact that his magicians performed similar acts, but also God’s own patience, by which he spared him.

God’s patience, in relation to human hearts, is useful to some for repentance, but useless to others for resisting God and persevering in evil. Yet it is not useless in itself, but according to the evil heart, as we have already said. The Apostle also says this: “Do you not know that the patience of God has led you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each one according to his works.”

Elsewhere, too, when he said, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place,” he added, “both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” He did not say that he was a good fragrance of Christ to those who are being saved but a bad one to those who are perishing; he simply said that he was a good fragrance. Yet they are such that they perish even through the good fragrance, according to the quality of their hearts—as has often been said—which must be changed by a good will through the grace of God, so that the judgments of God, which harm evil hearts, may begin to benefit them.

Therefore, after his heart had been changed for the better, one man sang: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” He did not say “your gifts” or “your rewards,” but “your judgments.” It is a great thing to be able to say with sincere confidence: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart.” And lest he seem to have attributed anything to his own strength, he immediately added: “For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have pleased in your truth.” He recalls the mercy shown toward him, so that he might be able to please in the truth, since “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

—On the same matter.—

“And for this very reason you have been preserved, so that I might show my power in you and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” The Apostle also quoted these words of Scripture when he was dealing with the same very difficult passage. There he says this as well: “But if God, wishing to show wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath,” sparing those whom he had foreknown would become evil, “which vessels,” he says, “he calls perfected for destruction.”

“And in order,” he says, “to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy.” Hence the voice concerning the vessels of mercy in the Psalms: “My God, his mercy shall go before me; my God has shown me among my enemies.”

The Lord therefore knows how to make good use of the wicked. Yet he does not create an evil nature for evil; rather, he bears with them patiently for as long as he knows is necessary—not uselessly, but using them for the admonition or training of the good. For behold, the fact that the name of the Lord should be proclaimed throughout all the earth is certainly beneficial to the vessels of mercy. Pharaoh was preserved for their benefit, as Scripture itself testifies and the outcome demonstrates.

—On the same matter.—

“The Lord said to Moses: Enter in to Pharaoh, for I have burdened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in succession.” This should not be understood as though God had need of anyone’s wickedness. It should be understood as if he were saying: “I was patient toward him and toward his servants, so that I would not remove them, in order that my signs might come upon them in succession.”

Because the evil mind became more obstinate through God’s patience, what is in fact “I was patient toward him” is expressed as “I burdened his heart.”

—On the same matter.—

“And not one locust was left in the whole land of Egypt. And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart.” Scripture certainly recalled God’s benefaction, by which he removed the locusts, and then followed by saying that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart—by his benefaction, plainly, and by his patience, through which Pharaoh became more obstinate while he was being spared. In the same way, all evil human hearts become hardened when they misuse God’s patience.

### CHAPTER CX. That in taking gold and other things from the Egyptians they did not commit theft; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

“God said to Moses: Speak secretly into the ears of the people, and let each person ask his neighbor, and the woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold [gold and silver] and clothing.”

No one should think that he may take an example from this for stripping his neighbor in such a manner. God commanded this, for he knew what each person ought to suffer; and the Israelites did not commit theft, but carried out a service at God’s command. It is like a judge’s attendant killing someone whom the judge ordered killed: if he did this on his own initiative, he would certainly be a murderer, even if he killed someone whom he knew ought to be killed by the judge.

### CHAPTER CXI. Pharaoh will not listen, so that the signs may be multiplied; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

[Col. 0720A]

“Then the Lord said to Moses: Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt.” This is as though his disobedience had been necessary for those signs to be multiplied [multiplied], signs that were beneficially performed to terrify the people of God and, through that very discernment, to form them toward piety. But this was God’s doing: he made good use of the malice of Pharaoh’s heart, rather than Pharaoh’s doing, since Pharaoh misused God’s patience.

### CHAPTER CXII. How the phrase “an everlasting appointed day” should be understood; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

Concerning what is written: “And you shall make this day an appointed observance for your generations, everlasting or eternal,” which in Greek is called αἰώνιον (*aiōnion*), it should not be understood as though any day belonging to these passing things could itself be everlasting. Rather, that is everlasting which this day signifies. It is like saying that God himself is everlasting: we do not mean that these two syllables are everlasting, but what they signify.

Nevertheless, it must be carefully investigated how Scripture is accustomed to call something everlasting, lest perhaps it used the word “everlasting” in a solemn sense for something which they were not permitted to omit or to alter on their own initiative. For one thing is commanded only until it has been carried out—for example, when the ark was commanded to circle the walls of Jericho seven times. Another thing is commanded to be observed in such a way that no limit is prescribed for its observance, whether it is solemnly observed daily, monthly, yearly, or at fixed intervals of many years or of some number of years.

Either, then, Scripture called it everlasting because they were not permitted on their own initiative to cease celebrating it, or else, as I have said, the signs themselves are not to be understood as everlasting, but the realities signified by those signs.

“And the children of Israel set out from Rameses for Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, apart from the equipment or the census.”

### CHAPTER CXIII. That the four hundred years should be referred not to servitude but to the sojourning of Abraham’s seed; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

When God said to Abraham, “Know with certainty that your seed will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own, and they will reduce them to servitude and harm them for four hundred years,” this should not be understood as though the people of God had been in that most severe servitude for four hundred years.

Rather, since it is written, “In Isaac shall your seed be called,” from the year of Isaac’s birth until the year of the exodus from Egypt, four hundred and five years are reckoned. When the twenty-five years between the promise and Isaac’s birth are subtracted from the four hundred and thirty, it is not surprising if Scripture chose to call the solid total of four hundred and five years simply four hundred. Scripture is accustomed to name periods in such a way that what slightly exceeds or falls short of the total of a more complete number is not counted.

Therefore, what he says—“They will reduce them to servitude and harm them”—is not to be referred to the four hundred years, as though they had kept them in servitude [Latin variant: *in servitutem* / *in servitute*] for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years are to be referred to what was said: “Your seed will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own.” For whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that seed was sojourning before they received the land as an inheritance according to God’s promise, which happened afterward, once they had been liberated from Egypt.

Thus, a transposition (*hyperbaton*) is to be understood here, and the order of the words is: “Know with certainty that your seed will be a sojourner in a land that is not its own for four hundred years.” The intervening words—“And they will reduce them to servitude, and they will harm them”—are to be understood as an insertion, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For it was toward the end of this total period, that is, after Joseph’s death, that the people of God came to endure harsh servitude in Egypt.

### CHAPTER CXIV. By what division the Ten Commandments of the Law are to be counted; from the same book of Questions on Exodus.

It is asked how the Ten Commandments of the Law should be divided: whether there are four commandments up to the commandment concerning the Sabbath, which pertain to God, and six remaining commandments, the first of which is “Honor your father and your mother,” which pertain to human beings; or whether there are rather three commandments of the first kind and seven of the second.

Those who say that there are four separate what is said, “You shall have no other gods besides me,” so that “You shall not make for yourself an idol,” and the rest, where the worship of images is prohibited, constitutes another commandment. They wish “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house,” together with everything that follows to the end, to constitute one commandment.

Those, however, who say that there are three of the first kind and seven of the second wish everything commanded concerning the worship of the one God to constitute a single commandment, so that nothing else may be worshiped as God besides him. They divide the final commandments into two, so that “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” is one, and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” another.

Neither group doubts that there are ten commandments, since Scripture testifies to this. Yet it seems to me more fitting to understand the division as three and seven, because, for those who examine the matter carefully, the three commandments pertaining to God seem also to indicate the Trinity more explicitly.

Indeed, the statement “You shall have no other gods besides me” is fully explained by the prohibition against worshiping images. Moreover, the coveting of another man’s wife and the coveting of another man’s house differ so much in the act of sinning that to the statement “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” Scripture adds other things, saying: “Nor his field, nor his male slave, nor his female slave, nor his ox [Latin *bovem*; variant *boves*, ‘oxen’], nor his beast of burden [Latin *subjugale*; variant *subjugalem*], nor any of his cattle, nor anything belonging to your neighbor [Latin variants *proximi sui* / *proximi tui*, ‘of his/your neighbor’].”

The desire for another man’s wife appears to have been distinguished from the desire for any other possession belonging to another, since both statements begin in this way: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; you shall not covet your neighbor’s house,” and to the latter Scripture begins adding the other things.

But after saying, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” it did not continue by saying, “nor his house, nor his field, nor his male slave,” and so forth. Rather, these things clearly belong together and appear to be contained in one commandment [Latin variants *uno* / *in uno*], distinct from the commandment in which the wife is named.

The statement “You shall have no other gods besides me” appears to receive a more detailed exposition in the things appended [Latin variants *subjuncta* / *subjecta*]. For what else does “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of whatever is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not worship them [Latin variants *eis* / *ea*, ‘them’] or serve them” refer to, except to the statement “You shall have no other gods besides me”?

But again it is asked how “You shall not steal” differs from the commandment given shortly afterward concerning not coveting the possessions of one’s neighbor.
