Not everyone who covets his neighbor’s property steals; but if everyone who steals covets his neighbor’s property, then the commandment prohibiting coveting another’s property might also have included what concerns theft.

Similarly, it is asked how “You shall not commit adultery” differs from what is said shortly afterward, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” For in the statement “You shall not commit adultery,” the latter might have been understood, unless perhaps in the two sins of adultery and theft—or, in the variant reading, “in the commandments not to commit adultery and not to steal”—the acts themselves are marked, while in these final commandments the desire itself is marked. The difference is such that someone may sometimes commit adultery without coveting his neighbor’s wife, when another cause is involved; at other times he may covet her but refrain from adultery because he fears punishment. Perhaps the Law wished to show that both are sins.

It is also customary to ask whether fornication is included under the term adultery. For this is a Greek word which Scripture already uses in place of the Latin term; yet in Greek *moichos* means only “adulterers.”

But this Law was certainly given not only to the men of the people, but also to the women. A woman should not think that, because it says “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife,” no commandment here applies to her, as though she might licitly covet the husband of her female neighbor.

If, then, what was said to the man is understood to apply also to the woman, although it was not stated in a form that explicitly includes her, how much more are both sexes bound by what was said, “You shall not commit adultery,” since this commandment itself can be referred to both sexes, just as “You shall not kill,” “You shall not steal,” and other commandments that, without explicitly naming one sex, appear to speak commonly to both.

Nevertheless, where one sex is explicitly named, the more honored sex is named, that is, the male, so that from this the woman may also understand what is commanded to her. Accordingly, if a married woman commits adultery by having intercourse with a man who is not her husband, even if that man has no wife, she is an adulteress; and a married man is an adulterer if he has intercourse with a woman who is not his wife, even if she has no husband.

But whether both persons are held guilty of transgressing that commandment if an unmarried man has intercourse with an unmarried woman is rightly questioned. For if they are not held guilty, then fornication is not prohibited in the Decalogue, but only μοιχεία (*moicheia*), that is, adultery—although every μοιχεία is understood to be fornication, as Scripture speaks.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, causes her to commit adultery.” Here he certainly called it fornication if a woman who has a husband sins with another man; that is adultery, μοιχεία (*moicheia*).

Thus every μοιχεία is also called fornication in Scripture. But whether every fornication can likewise be called μοιχεία in those same Scriptures, I do not presently recall an example of such usage. If not every fornication can also be called μοιχεία, I do not know whether it can be found where the fornication committed by men who have no wives with women who have no husbands is prohibited in the Decalogue.

But if, under the name of theft, every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood—for the one who prohibited theft did not permit robbery, but certainly wished the whole to be understood from the part, namely, everything unlawfully taken from another’s possessions—then surely, under the name of adultery, every unlawful intercourse and every illegitimate use of those bodily members must likewise be understood as prohibited.

And when it is said, “You shall not kill,” it should not be thought that the commandment is violated when the Law kills someone or when God commands someone to be killed. The person who commands does this, since it is not permissible for the minister to refuse his service.

Likewise, concerning the statement “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” it is customary to ask whether every lie is prohibited. Perhaps this commandment is not directed against those who say that one must lie when the lie benefits someone and harms no one to whom one lies; for such a lie is not against one’s neighbor. This may be why Scripture added these words, since it could have said briefly, “You shall not bear false witness,” just as it said, “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not steal.”

But this is a major question and cannot suitably be explained by those in haste: how are we to understand, “You will destroy all who speak lies,” and “Do not wish to lie—any lie,” and other statements of this kind?

### CHAPTER CXV. An exposition of the Ten Commandments and the Ten Plagues, while preserving their essential meaning; from the Exposition of the Decalogue for the People.

First, with the firmness of the historical events laid down as a foundation, we must seek their significance, lest, after removing the foundation, we seem to wish to build in the air.

The first event does not belong among the ten plagues: it was performed as a sign, namely, that the staff should be changed into a serpent. For this was the very means of access to Pharaoh by which Moses was commended, since he was to lead the people of God out of Egypt. The rebellious were not yet being struck; they were already being terrified by a divine sign.

The staff signifies the kingdom of God, and likewise the people of God, since they are the kingdom of God. The serpent, however, signifies this period of mortality, for death was offered through the serpent. Thus, as though falling from the hand of the Lord onto the earth, they became mortal; hence, when the staff was thrown from the hand, it became a serpent. Pharaoh’s magicians did the same: when their staffs were thrown down, they became serpents. But Moses’ serpent—that is, Moses’ staff—first devoured all the magicians’ serpents. Then, when its tail was seized, it again became a staff, and the kingdom returned to the hand.

Thus the magicians’ staffs signify the peoples of the ungodly, conquered in the name of Christ when they are transferred into his body; as though they are devoured by Moses’ serpent, until the kingdom of God returns to the hand of God. But at the end of the mortal age, signified by the serpent’s tail, a great sign will take place.

You have heard what you ought to desire. Hear what you ought to avoid.

The first commandment in the Law concerns worshiping the one God: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” The first plague of the Egyptians was water changed into blood. Compare [69] the first commandment with the first plague. Understand the one God, from whom all things are, in the likeness of water, from which all things are generated. But to what does blood pertain except to mortal flesh? What, then, is the changing of water into blood except this: “Their foolish heart was darkened”; for, “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man.”

The glory of the incorruptible God is like water; the likeness of the image of corruptible man is like blood. This takes place, indeed, in the heart of the ungodly. God, however, remains unchangeable; for, although the Apostle said, “They exchanged,” God was not thereby changed.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” Whoever takes the name of the Lord his God in vain “shall not be cleansed.” The name of our Lord God, Jesus Christ, is truth; for he himself said, “I am the truth.” Truth therefore cleanses, while vanity defiles. Since whoever speaks the truth speaks about God—for whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own source—to speak truth is to speak rationally; to speak vanity, however, is rather to make a din than to speak. It is rightly so, because the second commandment concerns the love of truth, to which the love of vanity is opposed.

Truth speaks; vanity makes a din.

Observe the plague contrary to this second commandment. What is the second plague? An abundance of frogs. You have an explicit representation of vanity if you attend to the frogs’ croaking. Consider the lovers of truth, who do not take the name of the Lord their God in vain: they speak wisdom among the perfect, and even among the imperfect. They do not speak what the imperfect cannot grasp, but neither do they depart from the truth and proceed into vanity.

For although the imperfect do not grasp something if a somewhat loftier discourse has been given concerning the Word of God, who was God with God, through whom all things were made, they can nevertheless grasp what Paul speaks among them as among the little ones of Christ: “Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” Yet the former is truth and the latter is not vanity. It would be vanity if we said that Christ had not truly undergone death but had merely pretended to do so; if those wounds had existed only in an apparition; if real blood had not flowed from the wounds but merely simulated blood; if he had displayed false scars as though following false wounds.

But when we say that all these things were true, when we say that they happened, when we believe and proclaim them as certain, manifest, and fulfilled, although we do not speak of that lofty and unchangeable truth of his, we are not thereby proceeding into vanity.

Those who say that all these things in Christ were false and simulated are frogs croaking in a swamp. They may possess the noise of a voice, but they cannot impart the doctrine of wisdom.

Finally, in the Church those who cling to the truth speak of the truth through which all things were made: the Truth, the Word made flesh and dwelling among us; the truth that Christ was born from God, one from one, the only-begotten and coeternal; the truth that, having taken the form of a servant, he was born from the Virgin Mary, suffered, was crucified, rose again, and ascended.

Everywhere there is truth: truth which the perfect grasp and truth which the little one cannot grasp; truth both in bread and in milk—in the bread of the mature and in the milk of the little ones. For the same bread is conveyed through the flesh so that it becomes milk.

Those who contradict this truth, deceived in their own vanity and deceiving others, are frogs, inflicting weariness on the ears rather than nourishment on the minds.

Hear, finally, human beings speaking rationally: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard,” but their voices are not empty, “for their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” If, on the other hand, you wish to understand frogs in the opposite sense, recall that verse of the Psalm: “Each has spoken vanity to his neighbor.”

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day.” In this third commandment a certain summons to rest is intimated—the tranquility of the heart and mind, which a good conscience produces. There is sanctification there, because there is the Spirit of God.

Finally, observe the rest—that is, the quiet: “Upon whom,” the Lord says, “shall my Spirit rest?” Upon “the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words.”

The restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit: those who love quarrels, sow slanders, and desire contention more than truth. Through their restlessness they do not admit into themselves the spiritual rest of the sabbath.

Against their restlessness it is said, as though so that they may possess the sanctification of the Spirit of God as their sabbath: “Be gentle,” he says, “in hearing the word, so that you may understand.” What am I to understand? God saying: “Cease from your restlessness; let there be no kind of tumult in your heart, with phantasms flying about through corruption and pricking you. Let there be none.”

For in this way you will understand God saying to you: “Be still, and know that I am the Lord.” But because of your restlessness you do not wish to be still; blinded by the corruption of your contentions, you demand to see what you cannot see.

Observe, then, the third plague contrary to this third commandment. Gnats were born in the land of Egypt from the mud. They are certain very tiny flies, exceedingly restless, flying about disorderly, rushing into the eyes, and not allowing a person to rest while they are driven away and rush back, while, after being driven away, they return again [or: “while, after being expelled, they return again”], just like the empty phantasms of contentious hearts.

Hold fast to the commandment; beware of the plague.

The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother.” The fourth plague of the Egyptians, contrary to this, is the *kynómyia* (κυνόμυια). What is *kynómyia*? A dog-fly; it is a Greek word. It is characteristic of a dog not to acknowledge its parents. Nothing is so doglike as for those who were its parents not to be recognized. Therefore, appropriately, the puppies of dogs are also born blind.

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery.” The fifth plague is the death of the Egyptian livestock.

Let us compare them. Consider a man contemplating adultery, not content with his own marriage, unwilling to subdue within himself a certain appetite of the flesh, which we share with animals. For to have intercourse and to beget children belongs also to animals; to reason and understand is human.

Therefore reason, which presides in the mind as a ruling and governing power, ought to restrain the lower movements of the flesh, not to release them indiscriminately, immoderately, unlawfully, and at random. For this reason nature, under the direction of the Creator, has given even animals the condition that they are not moved toward females and intercourse except at appointed times. The animal does not restrain itself by reason at other times; rather, when the movement itself grows cold, it becomes entirely torpid.

A human being, however, can therefore be moved at all times because he can also restrain the movement. The Creator has given you the dominion of reason; he has granted you the commands of continence as reins for the lower beasts. You possess what the animal cannot, and therefore you hope for what the animal cannot attain. You labor for a while in restraint; the animal does not labor. But you will rejoice forever in eternity, to which the animal does not attain.

If the task causes weariness, let the reward console you. For patience itself consists in restraining the inner movement and not releasing into everything, like an animal, what you share with the animal.

But if you have despised yourself within yourself and neglected the image of God in which he made you, overcome by the desire for insinuating things, you will be an animal, as though you had lost your humanity—not as though you had been changed into the nature of an animal, but as one bearing, in human form, the likeness of an animal. You do not heed the saying: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, without understanding.”

But perhaps you choose to be an animal for yourself [70], and to roam freely in lust, restraining the appetite of the flesh toward continence by no law. Observe the plague: if you are not afraid to be an animal, at least be afraid to die.

The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill.” The sixth plague is pustules upon the body, with blisters boiling and bursting forth, and the inflammation of wounds from the soot of the furnace.

Such are murderous souls. They burn with anger, because through anger the brotherhood involved in murder has perished. People burn with anger, and they also burn with grace; but one is the heat of health, another the heat of an ulcer. Blazing pustules, conceived murders, burst forth all over, and it is not healthy. It is hot, but not from the Spirit of God.

For the person who wishes to help also burns, and the person who wishes to kill burns: the former burns through obedience to a commandment, the latter through disease; the former through good works, the latter through festering ulcers.

If we could see the souls of murderers, we would grieve more than over the decaying bodies of those covered with sores.

Next follows: “You shall not steal,” the seventh commandment; and the seventh plague is hail upon the crops. What you withdraw by theft, contrary to the commandment [or: “what you withdraw through theft, contrary to God’s commandment”], you lose from heaven.

No one has unjust gain without just loss. For example, the person who steals acquires a garment but loses faith through heavenly judgment. Where there is gain, there is loss: visible gain, invisible loss; gain from his own blindness, loss from the Lord’s cloud.

For nothing occurs without Providence, beloved. Or do you think that the things human beings suffer happen while God sleeps? These things seem to happen randomly: clouds gather, rains pour down, hail is hurled, the earth is shaken by thunder, people are terrified by flashes of lightning; they are thought to happen randomly and, as it were, not to pertain to divine Providence.

Against such thoughts that Psalm keeps watch: “Praise the Lord from the earth,” after praises had been uttered from heaven—“dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which fulfill his word.”

Therefore those who steal outwardly through their evil desire are inwardly pelted with hail by God’s judgment.

O, if they could inspect the field of their own heart, they would surely mourn when they found there nothing to put into the mouth of the mind. And if, through their theft, they found something to put into the appetite of the belly, the inner human being would have greater hunger—greater hunger, a more dangerous plague, and a heavier death.

Many dead people walk about, and many criminals exult in empty riches.

Finally, Scripture calls the servant of God rich within: “The hidden person of your heart,” it says, “who is rich before God.” Not rich before human beings, but rich before God; where God sees, there he is rich.

What benefit is it to you, then, if you steal where a human being does not see, but where God sees you are pelted with hail?

The eighth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness.” The eighth plague is the locust, an animal harmful through its teeth.

What does a false witness desire except to injure by biting and consume by lying? Finally, when the Apostle of God warns people not to attack one another with false accusations [or: “lest we attack one another with false accusations”], he says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.”

The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” The ninth plague is dense darkness.

For there is a kind of adultery contrary to the commandment given above, even in the matter of not desiring another man’s wife. An adulterer is one who does not go to another man’s wife merely because he is not content with his own.

But to sin not only after having possessed one’s own wife, but also to attempt another’s, is truly dense darkness. Nothing wounds the heart of the one who suffers in this way so deeply; and the person who does this to another wishes to suffer nothing so much himself.

Every person is more ready to approach another’s wife; but whether anyone can bear this tolerably, I do not know. O dense darkness of those who do such things and covet such things! They are truly blinded by a horrible frenzy. For it is an untamed frenzy to trample upon another man’s wife.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor: not his livestock, not his property, not his beast of burden; you shall covet nothing at all belonging to your neighbor.”

The tenth plague, contrary to this evil [or: “commandment”], is the death of the firstborn. When I seek some comparison in this plague, nothing occurs to me for the moment—perhaps something better will occur to those who inquire more carefully—except the case of one who keeps all the possessions he has for his heirs and is condemned for it.

But here the person who covets his neighbor’s property cries out, and the person who takes it by theft—who steals something belonging to his neighbor—cannot help but steal his neighbor’s property. But theft was already commanded against above; here understand robbery as well. For Scripture would not command against theft and remain silent about robbery unless it wished you to understand that, if secretly taking something away is punishable, violently snatching it away is punishable much more severely.

Taking something from someone unwilling, whether secretly or openly, has its own commandment.

But coveting what belongs to one’s neighbor—which God observes in the heart—is not permitted, even if you seek there a rightful inheritance.

Finally, those who wish to possess another’s property as though by right seek to become heirs of the dying. For what seems so just as possessing what has been left to oneself, having it by common right? “What is this doing with you, man?” “It was left to me. I obtained an inheritance. I am reading the will.” Nothing seems more just than this voice of avarice.

You praise the person who possesses it as though by right; God condemns the person who unjustly covets it. See what kind of person you are when you wish to become someone’s heir. You do not wish him to have heirs.

Among heirs, however, nothing is dearer than the firstborn. Therefore you will be punished in your firstborn, because, by coveting another’s possessions, you seek something that was not owed to you by right, as though seeking the shadow of a legal claim.

It is easy, indeed, brothers, to lose one’s firstborn bodily. People die, whether before their parents or after their parents; those who are destined to die do die. But what is grievous is that, through this hidden and unjust covetousness, you should lose the firstborn of your heart.

For the firstborn in us bears the image of God’s grace: newly born, first born among all those born, the firstborn of our heart is faith. No one performs a good work unless faith has preceded it. All your good works are your spiritual children, but among them faith is your firstborn.

Whoever secretly covets another’s property loses faith inwardly. For without doubt you will first become a pretender, showing obedience not out of love but through deceit. You will seem to love the person from whom you desire to become heir, while, by loving him, you seek his death; and, so that you may see yourself as possessing his property, you begrudge him an heir.

Come, brothers. Having gone through the ten commandments and the ten plagues, comparing the despisers of the commandments with the obstinacy of the Egyptians, we have made you cautious, so that you may possess your possessions securely in the commandments of God—your possessions, I say, the possessions of your inner chest, your inner treasure: possessions which neither thief, nor robber, nor powerful [or: “wicked”] neighbor can take from you; possessions in which neither moth nor rust need be feared, and with which even a shipwrecked person emerges rich.

Thus you will be the people of God among the iniquitous Egyptians: while they suffer these things in their hearts, you will remain unharmed in those inner human beings of yours, until the people are led out of Egypt by its own kind of Exodus. The former happened once; this continues to happen.

No sanctification is divine and true except that which comes from the Holy Spirit. For he is not called the Holy Spirit without reason in a proper sense. Although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, the Spirit received this as his proper name, so that the Holy Spirit might be called the third person in the Trinity.

He himself rests upon the humble and quiet person, as though in his sabbath. For this reason the number seven is also assigned to the Holy Spirit [71]; our Scriptures indicate this sufficiently. Let better people see better things, and greater people see greater things, and let them say and explain something more subtly and divinely about this number seven.

For my part, I see at present what is sufficient, and I remind you of it so that you may see it: this sevenfold structure is found assigned properly to the Holy Spirit because sanctification sounds forth on the seventh day.

And how do we prove that the sevenfold structure of the number is assigned to the Holy Spirit? Isaiah says that the Spirit of God comes upon the faithful, upon the Christian, upon a member of Christ: “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God.”

If you followed this, you have traversed seven things, as though the Spirit of God were descending to us from wisdom down to fear, so that we may ascend from fear to wisdom; “the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom.”

Thus there is a sevenfold Spirit and one Spirit: one Spirit in a sevenfold operation. Or do you desire something more evident?

Holy Scripture records that the feast of Pentecost was made from the weeks. You have it in the Scripture of Tobit, where it is clearly said that this day was made from the weeks. Seven times seven produces forty-nine in all. But, as though to return to the beginning:

For by the Holy Spirit we are gathered into unity, not scattered away from unity. Therefore one is added to the forty-nine, the one of unity, and they become fifty.

It was therefore not without reason that the Holy Spirit came on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s ascension. The Lord rose again and ascended from the dead, though not yet into heaven. From that resurrection, from that taking up from the dead, fifty days are counted, and the Holy Spirit came in the number fifty, as though celebrating his birthday among us.

For the Lord remained here with his disciples for forty days; on the fortieth day he ascended into heaven; and when ten days had been completed there, as though corresponding to the tenth sign of the commandments, the Holy Spirit came, because no one fulfills the Law except through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, brothers, it is manifest that this number seven pertains to the Holy Spirit.

Whoever does not adhere to the unity of Christ and barks against the unity of Christ must be understood not to possess the Holy Spirit. For only natural (animal) people produce contentions and dissensions. Of them the Apostle says: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.”

It is also written in the Epistle of the apostle Jude: “These are the ones who separate themselves.” He spoke reprovingly: “These are the ones who separate themselves, animal, not having the Spirit.”

What could be clearer? What more evident? Let them come, even if they believe the same things we do; nevertheless, they will receive the Holy Spirit, whom they cannot possess so long as they are enemies of unity.

The Apostle compares these people especially with Pharaoh’s magicians: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power,” he says. They failed at the third sign.

Now see why they failed at the third sign. Remember that those who oppose unity do not possess the Holy Spirit.

The first three commandments in the Decalogue are understood to pertain to the love of God, while the remaining seven are understood to pertain to the love of one’s neighbor. Thus, in the two tablets of the Law and the ten commandments, those two commandments are held as summaries:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength,” and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

Let us therefore refer the first three commandments to the love of God. Which three first commandments?

First: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” The plague contrary to this is water changed into blood, because the supreme principle of the Creator was brought down into the likeness of human flesh.

The second commandment—“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”—pertains, as I think, to the kingdom of God, which is the Son of God. For “there is one God and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things are.”

Against the Word are the frogs. Observe: against the Word, frogs; against reason, noise; against truth, vanity.

The third commandment, concerning the sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit because of sanctification, which first sounded forth in the sabbath. We commended this to you somewhat earlier with all the force we could.

The restlessness born from corruption in the flies, rushing into the eyes, is contrary to this commandment. For this reason those who were enemies of unity failed at the third sign and did not possess the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit does this as punishment.

For grace does one thing, punishment another; one acts by filling, the other by abandoning.

Finally, so that we may now recognize more clearly, with Pharaoh’s magicians themselves confessing it, how the Spirit of God is named in the Gospel, let us consider what name he received.

The Jews insulted the Lord by saying, “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.” He replied: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you.” Another Evangelist recounts this as follows: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God.”

What one Evangelist called the Spirit of God, another called the finger of God. Therefore the finger of God is the Spirit of God. For this reason the Law, given on Mount Sinai, was written by the finger of God. That Law was given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb, when the Passover had been celebrated by the Jewish people.

Fifty days were completed after the slaughter of the lamb, and the Law written by the finger of God was given. Fifty days were completed after the slaughter of Christ, and the Holy Spirit came.

Thanks be to the Lord, who conceals providently and reveals graciously.

Now observe this also, brothers: Pharaoh’s magicians most clearly confessed it. When they failed at the third sign, they said: “This is the finger of God.”

## CHAPTER CXVI. Further exposition of the Decalogue to the people; from the discourse on the Ten Strings of the Psalter

The whole Law is contained in two commandments: in the love of God and in the love of one’s neighbor. Therefore the Decalogue pertains to the two commandments, that is, to the love of God and of one’s neighbor.

Three strings pertain to the first commandment, because God is a Trinity. To the other commandment, that is, to the love of one’s neighbor, seven strings pertain: how one should live among human beings.

For the number seven itself, like seven strings, begins with honoring one’s parents: “Honor your father and your mother.” A person opens his eyes to his parents, and this life begins from friendship with them.

Whoever, however, does not show honor to his parents—whom will he be able to spare? The Apostle says: “Honor your father and your mother,” which is the first commandment.

How is it the first, when it is the fourth commandment? It is first in the number seven. In relation to the love of one’s neighbor, it is first on the other tablet.

For this reason two tablets of the Law were given. God gave his servant Moses two tablets on the mountain. On those two stone tablets the ten commandments of the Law had been written. This is the ten-stringed psalter: three on one tablet, pertaining to God, and seven on the other, pertaining to one’s neighbor.

The first is: “Honor your father and your mother.”

The second: “You shall not commit adultery.”

The third: “You shall not kill.”

The fourth: “You shall not steal.”

The fifth: “You shall not bear false witness.”

The sixth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” [72]

The seventh: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.”

Let us join these to the three commandments pertaining to the love of God, if we wish to sing the new song on the ten-stringed psalter.

Now do not look at me, but at the word of God. Do not grow angry with your medicine; I found no other way by which to pass through this subject.

I have come to the fifth string, the person who strikes the ten-stringed psalter. Surely I was not going to pass over the fifth? Rather, I must strike it continually. For in it I see almost the whole human race lying; in it I see people laboring most of all.

What do I say by striking it? Do not commit adultery after your wives, because you do not want your wives to commit adultery after you.

Do not go where you do not want them to follow. You try to excuse yourselves without cause when you say: “Surely I am not going to another man’s wife; I am going to my maidservant.” Do you want her to say to you: “Surely I am not going to another man; I am going to my male servant?”

You say, “She is not another man’s wife, the woman to whom I am going.” Do you want it said to you: “He is not another man, the man to whom I am going”? God forbid that she should say this. It is better that she suffer because of you than imitate you.

For that chaste and holy woman, a true Christian, who grieves over her husband’s fornication does not grieve on account of the flesh but on account of love. She does not refrain from doing it merely because she herself does not do it, but because it is not good for you.

For if she refrains so that you will not do it, then, if you do it, she will do it too. But if she owes that to God, if she owes it to Christ, which you demand, and therefore returns it because he commands it, then, even if the husband commits fornication, she offers her chastity to God.

For Christ speaks in the hearts of good women. He speaks inwardly, where he is not heard, because one who is such is not even worthy to hear him. He speaks within and says, comforting his daughter with words such as these:

“You are tortured by the injuries inflicted by your husband. Whatever he has done to you, grieve over it, but do not imitate him by doing evil; let him imitate you in doing good.

For in the evil he does, do not consider him your head, but me [or, according to the alternative reading: “but fear me, your God”]. For if he is also your head in the evil he does, the body will follow its head, and both will go headlong into destruction.

But so that you may not follow an evil head, hold fast to Christ, the head of the Church. To him you owe your chastity; to him you render your honor. Let your husband be absent or present: she does not sin, because the one to whom she owes her refusal to sin is never absent.”

## CHAPTER CXVII. Testimony from the law of the Emperor Antoninus against the excuse of adulterous husbands; from the book *On Adulterous Marriages*, to Pollentius

Christians hear, “The head of a woman is her husband,” and recognize themselves as leaders, while understanding that women ought to be their companions. Therefore a man must take care not to live in such a way that he fears his wife may follow him by imitation.

But those who dislike equal standards of chastity being maintained between husband and wife, and who choose—especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to those of Christ, because forensic laws do not seem to bind men by the same obligations of chastity by which they bind women, should read what the Emperor Antoninus, certainly not a Christian, established concerning this matter.

He ruled that a husband is not permitted to accuse his wife of adultery if, by his own conduct, he had not provided an example of chastity, so that both are condemned if the very proceedings prove both equally unchaste.

For these are the words of the aforementioned emperor, as they are read in Gregorianus:

“Certainly,” he says, “my letter will in no respect prejudice the case. For if the fault was yours, so that the marriage was dissolved and, under the Julian law, your wife Eupasia married another, she will not on that account be condemned for adultery by my rescript unless it is established that the offense was committed.

They must first inquire into this: whether, while you were living chastely, you also encouraged her to cultivate good morals. For it seems utterly unjust to me that a husband should demand chastity from a wife whom he himself does not display.

This circumstance can also condemn the husband; it does not settle the matter between the two by balancing reciprocal offenses or remove the basis of the case.”

If such standards must be observed for the honor of an earthly state, how much more chastely does the heavenly homeland and the society of angels require us to live?

## CHAPTER CXVIII. Completion of the foregoing exposition to the people: against the shameful liberty of men who wish to excuse themselves for fornication; likewise from the same discourse on the Ten Strings
Therefore, my brothers, do this, so that you may be able to agree with your adversary. What I say is not bitter—or, if it is bitter, it heals. If this potion is bitter, let it be taken, because the inner organs are in danger. It is bitter; let it be drunk. A little bitterness in the throat is better than eternal torment in the inner organs.

Change yourselves, then, all of you who were not practicing this good of chastity; practice it now. Do not say, “It cannot be done.” It is shameful, my brothers, disgraceful for a man to say, “What a woman does cannot be done.” It is criminal for a man to say, “I cannot do what a woman can do. Can a man not do what a woman can?”

For does she not carry flesh? She was the first to be deceived by the serpent. Your chaste wives show you that what you do not want to do can be done, and you say that it cannot be done!

But perhaps you say that she can do it more easily because she is subject to many forms of supervision: the commandment of the law, marital vigilance, and even the terror of the public laws. She also has the great protection of modesty and shame. The many forms of supervision make a woman more chaste; let manliness itself make a man chaste. For this reason the woman has greater supervision: because she has greater weakness.

She is ashamed before her husband; are you not ashamed before Christ? You are freer because you are stronger, because you conquer easily; for that reason you have been entrusted to yourself. Over her there are her husband’s vigilance, the terror of the laws, the custom of moral conduct, and greater modesty; over you there is God—God alone.

You easily find men like yourselves, before whom you are not afraid to be ashamed, because many of them do the same thing. And so great is the perversity of the human race that sometimes one must fear that a chaste man will be ashamed among the shameless. For this reason I do not cease to strike this fifth string, because of that perverse custom and the corruption of the whole human race, as I have said.

[Col. 0732D]

If one of you commits murder—which may God avert—you want to drive him from the homeland and, if possible, exclude him immediately. If someone commits theft, you hate him and do not want to see him. If someone gives false testimony, you detest him, and he does not seem human to you. If someone covets another’s property, he is judged a robber and an unjust man.

[Col. 0733A]

But if someone has rolled about with his slave-girls, he is loved and received with affection; wounds are turned into jokes. If, however, there is someone who says that he is chaste and does not commit adultery, and it is known that he does not do so, he is ashamed to approach those unlike himself, lest they insult him, mock him, or say that he is not a man.

[Col. 0733B]

Human perversity has sunk to this point: that a man is considered defeated by lust, while a man who has conquered lust is not considered a man. Those who triumph exult, and they are not men. Those who lie prostrate are men!

If you were watching, that man would seem stronger to you who lay beneath a beast than the man who killed the beast. But because you turn away from the inner battle and take pleasure in outward battles, you do not want to belong to the new song, where it is said: “He trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war.”

There is indeed a war that a person wages against himself: fighting against evil desires, restraining greed, striking down pride, suffocating ambition, and slaughtering lust. You fight these battles in secret, and you are not defeated in public. For this your hands are trained for battle and your fingers for war.

[Col. 0733C]

This is not what occurs in your spectacles. In those spectacles the hunter is not the same as the harpist: the hunter does one thing, the harpist another. In God’s spectacle there is one activity. Strike these same ten strings, and you will kill the beasts; you do both at once.

You strike the first string, by which the one God is worshiped, and the beast of superstition falls. You strike the second, by which you do not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, and the beast of the wicked heresies that thought this falls. You strike the third string, on which you do whatever you do for the hope of future rest, and the love of this present age—the most savage of all the beasts—is killed.

[Col. 0733D]

For it is because of their love of this present age that people labor in all their affairs. You, however, should labor in all your good works not for love of this present age, but for the eternal rest that God promises.

See how you do both things at once: you strike the strings and kill the beasts; that is, you are both harpist and hunter.

[Col. 0734A]

Such spectacles do not delight you [us], in which they may win [we may win] the eyes not of the producer but of the redeemer.

“Honor your father and your mother.” You strike the fourth string, so that you may show honor to your parents, and the beast of impiety falls.

“You shall not commit adultery.” You strike the fifth string, and the beast of lust falls.

“You shall not kill.” You strike the sixth string, and the beast of cruelty falls.

“You shall not steal.” You strike the seventh string, and the beast of rapacity falls.

“You shall not bear false witness.” You strike the eighth string, and the beast of falsehood falls.

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” You strike the ninth string, and the beast of adulterous thought falls.

For it is one thing not to do anything of this kind with a woman other than one’s wife, and another thing not to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” You strike the tenth string, and the beast of covetousness falls.

When all the beasts have thus fallen, you live secure and innocent in the love of God and in human society. By striking ten strings, how many beasts do you kill? There are many heads beneath these headings. On each individual string you kill not individual beasts but herds of beasts.

[Col. 0734B]

Thus you will sing the new song with love, not with fear.

Do not say to yourself, when perhaps you want to do something lustful, “I do not yet have a wife; I will do what I want. For I am not sinning after taking a wife.” You already know your price; you already know where you are approaching, what you eat, what you drink—indeed, whom you eat and whom you drink.

Abstain from fornication, lest you say to me, “I am going to the brothel; I am going to the prostitute; I am going to the courtesan. I am not violating the commandment that says, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ because I do not yet have a wife, and I am doing nothing with another man’s wife. Nor am I violating the commandment that says, ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.’ When I go to a public woman, which commandment am I violating? Do we not find a string to strike? Do we not find a cord with which to bind this fugitive?”

[Col. 0734C]

Do not let him flee. There is something by which he can be bound. But let him love, and it will not be a fetter but an ornament. For in those ten strings we find not a fetter but an ornament.

The ten commandments are referred to those two commandments, as we have heard, that we should love God and our neighbor; and those two are referred to that one commandment: “What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.” The ten are contained there; the two are contained there.

But you will say: “If I commit theft, I do what I do not want to suffer. If I kill, I do what I do not want to suffer at another’s hands. If I do not show honor to my parents, although I want honor shown to me by my children, I do what I do not want to suffer. If I am adulterous and plan something of this kind, I do what I do not want to suffer.

[Col. 0734D]

“For if someone is questioned, he says, ‘I do not want my wife to do anything of this kind.’ If I covet my neighbor’s wife, I do not want anyone to covet mine; I do what I do not want to suffer. If I covet my neighbor’s property, I do not want mine to be taken away; I do what I do not want to suffer.

“But when I go to a prostitute, to whom am I doing what I do not want to suffer?”

What is more serious, you are doing it to God himself. Let your holiness understand.

“What you do not want done to you, do not do to another” pertains to the two commandments. How does it pertain to the two commandments? If you do not do to a human being what you do not want to suffer from a human being, it pertains to the commandment concerning your neighbor, to love of your neighbor, and to the seven strings. But if you want to do to God himself what you do not want to suffer from a human being, what is this? You do not do to another what you do not want to suffer, and yet a human being has become dearer to you than God?

[Col. 0735A]

“Then how,” you ask, “do I do an injury to God?”

You corrupt yourself.

“And how do I do an injury to God because I corrupt myself?”

How does someone do an injury to you if he should perhaps want to stone your painted panel, in which your image is depicted—a panel pointlessly placed in your house for your empty honor, neither feeling, speaking, nor seeing? If someone stones it, does not the insult reach you?

But when you corrupt within yourself the image of God—which is what you are—through fornications and the outpourings of lust, you take notice that you have not approached anyone’s wife; you take notice that you have done nothing after your wife, because you do not have a wife; and you do not take notice of whose image you have violated through lusts and illicit fornications.

Finally, God, who knows what is useful for you, who truly governs his servants for their benefit and not for his own—for he does not need servants as though for assistance, but you need the Lord’s assistance—this Lord, then, who knows what is useful for you, granted you a wife and nothing more.

[Col. 0735B]

He commanded this; he prescribed this, so that through illicit pleasures his temple, which you have begun to be, might not collapse.

Am I saying this? Listen to the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” He says this to Christians; he says this to the faithful: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” “If anyone corrupts God’s temple, God will corrupt him.”

Do you see how he threatens? You do not want your own house to be corrupted; why do you corrupt God’s house? Certainly you are doing to someone what you do not want to suffer.

[Col. 0735C]

There is therefore no way to escape. The man who did not think that he could be held is caught.

For all human sins either belong to the corruption of disgraceful acts or to crimes that inflict harm. Since you cannot harm God through crimes, you offend him through disgraceful acts; you offend him through corruptions; against him you do an injury to yourself. For you do an injury to his grace, to his gift.

If you had a slave, you would want your slave to serve you. You, then, serve the better Lord, God. You did not make your slave, and he made both you and your slave. You want the one with whom you were made to serve you, and you do not want to serve the one by whom you were made.

Therefore, when you want your human slave to serve you, but you do not want to serve the Lord your God, you are doing to God what you do not want to suffer.

Thus that one commandment contains two; those two contain ten; those ten contain everything.

## CHAPTER 119. What is meant by “And all the people saw the voices”; from the Book of Questions on Exodus

[Col. 0735D]

“And all the people saw the voice, and the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain.”

It is usually asked how the people saw the voice, since a voice seems to belong not to sight but rather to hearing. But just as I have now said, “Let it be understood concerning all the things that have been said by me,” so “to see” is customarily used in a general sense, not only of the body but also of the soul. Thus we have the statement: “When Jacob saw that there was food in Egypt,” although he was certainly absent from Egypt.

Some, however, have thought that “to see the voice” means nothing other than “to understand,” which is a sight of the mind.

But if it had been necessary to say briefly here that the people saw the voice, the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain, a greater question would arise: how did they hear the lamps and the smoking mountain, which belong to the sense of sight? Unless someone says that it should not have been stated so briefly, but that the whole should have been said:

“They heard the voice, saw the lamps, heard the voice of the trumpet, and saw the smoking mountain.”

[Col. 0736A]

There were, in fact, two kinds of voice: one from the clouds, like thunder, and one from the trumpet—if indeed he called “voice” the sound that came from the clouds.

Accordingly, in these matters that pertained to the sense of hearing, the general sense has been expressed—that is, seeing—because Scripture wished to include everything briefly, rather than having hearing understood in matters that pertain to the sense of sight. We ourselves customarily speak in this way.

For we are accustomed to say, “See what it sounds like,” but not, “Hear what it shines like.”

## CHAPTER 120. How “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk” is to be understood; from the same Book of Questions on Exodus

[Col. 0736B]

“You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

How this is to be understood according to the literal propriety of the words, I do not know whether it can be discovered. If we take the prohibition against boiling a lamb in milk as having some symbolic meaning, there is no customary practice of boiling it in this way.

But if the reference is to the days during which it is nursing, which Jew ever observed this, so as not to boil a lamb until it had stopped suckling?

What, moreover, does “in its mother’s milk” mean? Even if this were understood, it could be boiled without violating the commandment if, after it was born, its mother had died and it were suckled by another ewe. Yet no one doubts that the commandment was given to signify some particular thing.

Moreover, even those things that can be carried out as observances have not been commanded without a reason; they signify something. But how this commandment is to be observed according to the propriety of the words either cannot be determined or is not clear.

Nevertheless, I approve the interpretation that it was understood concerning Christ, who was foretold by this prophecy not to be killed as an infant by the Jews. When Herod sought him in order to kill him, he did not find him. Thus “you shall boil” refers to the fire of the Passion, that is, to tribulation.

Hence it is said: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous people through tribulation.” Therefore, because the child did not suffer at that time, when, as Herod sought him, such danger seemed imminent, it was foretold in these words: “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

—Here what follows has now been added from another work of Saint Augustine.—

[Col. 0736C]

You shall not kill Christ. For this seems to be a prophecy warning good Israelites not to join themselves to the wicked Jews, by whom Christ suffered. The tribulation of the Passion is like fire. Hence it is written: “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a burnt offering he accepted them.”

[Col. 0736D]

The Lord also bears witness to this interpretation, saying: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, which you do not know.” He said this after saying, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” For John says: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.” This is understood both as the purification of sanctification and as the testing of tribulation.

He himself also signified this fire when he was led to his Passion, where he said to those who were mourning him that they ought rather to mourn for themselves. For he ended by saying:

[Col. 0737A]

“If they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?”

Good people are therefore warned not to consent with the wicked to crucify Christ. For he was called “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.”

Therefore, “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.” Do not impose the fire of the Passion on Christ on that day on which he was conceived, when he is also handed over to suffering—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. From that day until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on which his birth is commemorated, nine months are counted, with the tenth beginning.

Women’s breasts are said to begin gathering milk from the day of conception.

There is another, easier interpretation:

[Col. 0737B]

“You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk”—that is, one still small and nursing, such as those to whom the Apostle says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

Do not send him into a premature Passion, as though this had been said concerning Christ, who spared such disciples as these. Offering himself, he said: “If you seek me, let these go away.”

And so that it might be understood that they were still weak and less suited to suffering, like lambs in their mother’s milk, the Evangelist continued: “So that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke: ‘Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none.’”

From this it is clear that, if they had suffered at that time, they would have perished. For they did not yet suffer what they suffered later: they were no longer lambs in milk but rams in the flock.

## CHAPTER 121. Why he said that the mercy seat was to be placed above the ark; from the same Book of Questions on Exodus

[Col. 0737C]

It is usually asked upon what he says the mercy seat is to be placed—above the ark. But since he commands that it be made of gold, and states its length and breadth to be as great as those of the ark itself, he clearly commanded that a golden panel of such dimensions be made to cover the ark.

On the mercy seat itself there were to be two Cherubim, one on each side, looking toward one another, so that their faces were toward the mercy seat and they shaded the mercy seat with their wings. This is a great sacrament.

Gold signifies wisdom; the ark signifies the secret of God. The law, the manna, and Aaron’s staff were commanded to be placed in the ark. In the Law there are commandments; the staff signifies power [signifies authority]; the manna signifies grace, because without grace there is no power to carry out the commandments.

Nevertheless, because the law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone who is making progress, the mercy seat is above it. For this purpose God must be merciful; and therefore it is placed above, because mercy exults over judgment.

[Col. 0737D]

The two Cherubim shade the mercy seat with their wings—that is, they honor it by veiling it—for these are ministries [mysteries] there, and they look toward one another because they agree.

The two Testaments are represented there, and their faces are toward the mercy seat because they strongly commend the mercy of God [the Lord], in which alone there is hope.

Finally, God promised that he would speak with Moses from between the Cherubim, above the mercy seat.

Moreover, if rational creation is signified by those two animals in the multitude of knowledge—for this is the interpretation assigned to “Cherubim”—they are two so that they may commend the fellowship of love.

[Col. 0738A]

They shade the mercy seat with their wings because they attribute their wings to God, not to themselves: that is, they honor the Lord [God] with the virtues by which they excel.

Their faces are directed only toward the mercy seat because, for anyone making progress toward the multitude of knowledge, there is no hope except in God’s mercy.

75

## CHAPTER 122. Concerning the Lord’s reply to Moses, who said, “Show me your glory”: “I will pass before you,” and so forth; from the same Book of Questions on Exodus

[Col. 0738B]

When Moses had said to the Lord, “Show me your glory,” the Lord answered him: “I will pass before you in my glory, and I will call the name of the Lord in your presence [I will call the name of the Lord, or I will be called in the name of the Lord, in your presence], and I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

Shortly before, he had said, “I myself will go before you and give you rest.” Moses seems to have understood this as meaning that he would go before him but would not be present with the people on the journey. Therefore he said: “If you yourself do not come with us, do not lead us out from here,” and so forth.

God did not deny him this either, saying: “I will also do this thing that you have said.”

How, then, after Moses had said to him, “Show me your glory,” does he again seem to say, as though he were going ahead and would not be with them, “I will pass before you,” unless this means something else?

The one understood to be speaking is he of whom the Gospel says: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father.” This passing is also reportedly the meaning of the word “Passover.”

[Col. 0738C]

This, therefore, is an entirely great prophecy. For he passed before all the saints from this world to the Father in order to prepare for them the dwellings of the kingdom of heaven, which he will give them at the resurrection of the dead, because, in passing before all, he became the firstborn from the dead.

He strongly commends his grace in this very statement when he says: “And I will call the name of the Lord in your presence,” as though in the presence of the people of Israel, whose type Moses bore when he heard these things.

For in the presence of that nation, dispersed everywhere, Christ the Lord is called among all nations.

[Col. 0738D]

He said, “I will call,” not “I will be called,” placing an active verb for a passive one in an unusual form of expression, in which a profound meaning is concealed. For perhaps he wished to signify that he himself would bring this about: that is, that by his grace the Lord would be called among all nations.

But when he added, “And I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” he clearly and more explicitly showed that the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and glory was not on account of our merits but on account of his mercy.

[Col. 0739A]

For because he promised that he would bring the Gentiles in, saying, “I will call the name of the Lord in your presence,” he commended this as something he would do mercifully, just as the Apostle says: “For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, but that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy.”

This, then, was foretold: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

By these words he prevented a human being from glorying as though in the merits of his own virtues, so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord.” For he did not say, “I will have mercy on such and such people,” but “on whom I am merciful,” showing that no one had earned the mercy of so great a calling through good works that preceded it [or, in the variant *se demonstraret*, “that he might show himself”].

[Col. 0739B]

For Christ died for the ungodly.

But whether he wished to repeat this same idea when he added, “I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” or whether, as others have interpreted it, “To whom I am merciful,” I do not know whether there is a difference.

What is said in Greek with the two words ἐλεήσω, “I will have mercy,” and οἰκτειρήσω, “I will have compassion,” which seem to signify one and the same thing, could not be expressed by the Latin translator with different words; therefore he repeated the same mercy in different forms.

If it were said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,” or “I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy,” it would not seem to be expressed very appropriately.

And yet the very meaning there is more forceful: either God showed the firmness of his mercy through this repetition, as in “Amen, amen,” and “Let it be, let it be,” and in Pharaoh’s repeated dream and many similar examples; or in this way God foretold that he would show mercy to both peoples, namely the Gentiles and the Hebrews.

[Col. 0739C]

The Apostle says this as follows: “For just as you once did not believe God, but now have received mercy through their unbelief, so they also now have not believed in your mercy [*vestram misericordiam*; variant *vestra misericordia*], so that they too may receive mercy. For God has shut up all in unbelief [*incredibilitate*; variant *incredulitate*], so that he may have mercy on all.”

Then, after this commendation of his mercy, he answers what had been said to him: “Show me your glory,” or what Moses had earlier asked: “Show me yourself [your very self] clearly, so that I may see you.”

“You cannot,” he says, “see my face, for no human being shall see my face and live.” He thereby shows that, for this present life conducted through the senses of mortal flesh, God cannot appear as he is—that is, he cannot be seen as he is in that life in which, in order to live, one must die to this life.

[Col. 0739D]

Then, after an intervening clause in which Scripture says, “And the Lord said,” it continues and speaks: “Behold, there is a place with me.”

For what place is not with God, who is nowhere absent? But by saying, “Behold, there is a place with me,” he signifies the Church, as though commending his temple.

“And you shall stand,” he says, “upon the rock,” because, as the Lord says, “upon this rock I will build my Church.”

“As soon as my glory passes by”—that is, “as soon as my glory passes by, you shall stand upon the rock.” For after Christ’s passing, that is, after Christ’s Passion and resurrection, the faithful people stood upon the rock.

“And I will place you,” he says, “in a cleft of the rock.” He signifies the firmest protection.

Others, however, have translated it “in a lookout [*specula*; variant cave, *spelunca*] of the rock.” But the Greek has ὀπήν. We more correctly interpret this as an opening or cavern. “And I will cover you with my hand [my hand over you] until I pass by, and I will take away my hand [my hand from you], and then you will see my back; but my face shall not be seen by you.”

[Col. 0740A]

Since he had already said, “You shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by,” where he is understood to have promised stability upon the rock after his passing, how should we understand what he says: “I will place you in a cleft [the cavern] of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand [my hand over you] until I pass by, and I will take away my hand [my hand from you], and then you will see my back”?

It is as though, once Moses had been established on the rock, God covered him with his hand and then passed by, although he could not be upon the rock except after God’s passing.

But a recapitulation of an omitted matter is to be understood here, such as Scripture often uses in many places. For afterward it said what occurred earlier in temporal order.

[Col. 0740B]

The order is therefore as follows:

“I will cover you with my hand [my hand over you] until I pass by, and then you will see my back, for my face shall not be seen by you. And you shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by, and I will place you in a cleft of the rock.”

This occurred in those whom the person of Moses then signified, that is, the Israelites, who later believed in the Lord Jesus, as the Acts of the Apostles indicate—namely, as soon as his glory had passed by.

For after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, and the apostles spoke in the languages of all nations after the Holy Spirit had been sent down from heaven, many of those who had crucified Christ were pierced in their hearts. If they had known him, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. A partial blindness came upon Israel, as had been said: “I will cover you with my hand [my hand over you] until I pass by.”

Hence the Psalm says: “For day and night your hand has been heavy upon me.” He calls “day” the time when Christ performed divine miracles, and “night” the time when he died as a human being—when even those who had believed during the day stumbled.

[Col. 0740C]

This, then, is the meaning: “When I have passed by, then you will see my back.” When I have passed from this world to the Father, those whose type you bear will believe in me afterward.

For then they were pierced in their hearts and said, “What shall we do?” The apostles commanded them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ so that their sins might be forgiven.

The Psalm continues after saying, “Day and night your hand has been heavy upon me”—that is, so that I would not recognize him [so that I might recognize him]. For if they had known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

It then continues and joins this to what precedes: “I turned in my anguish when the thorn was fixed”—that is, when I was pierced in my heart.

[Col. 0740D]

Then he added: “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not conceal my guilt.” After they had seen the great crime in which they had crucified Christ, and after they had received the counsel to repent and receive forgiveness of sins in baptism, he says: “I said, ‘I will declare my transgression against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my heart.”

That this was a prophecy rather than an account of what the Lord said to Moses is sufficiently indicated by the event itself. Nothing is subsequently recorded as having taken place visibly concerning the rock or its cavern, the placing of his hand, or the vision of his back.

[Col. 0741A]

Immediately afterward, with an intervening clause, Scripture continues: “And the Lord said to Moses.” The Lord himself was, of course, also speaking the words above, and from that point Scripture connects what the Lord next says: “Cut for yourself two stone tablets, as the first ones were,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER 123. How the tablets that Moses was certainly going to break, although God foreknew it, are said not to be the work of a human being, while the later tablets, which were to remain so long in God’s tabernacle, are said to have been cut and written by a human being; from the same Book of Questions on Exodus

“And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.”

It was said of Moses that he wrote them, since shortly before God had said to him, “Write these words for yourself.”

[Col. 0741B]

But when he first received the law, whose tablets he threw down and broke, he is not said to have cut the stone tablets himself. Now he is told, “Cut for yourself two stone tablets”; nor had he then been told to write them, as he is now told.

Nor is he narrated as having written them himself, as Scripture now says: “He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words.”

But at that earlier time it was said: “And he gave Moses, as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, two tablets of testimony, stone tablets written with the finger of God.”

Then shortly afterward: “And Moses turned and descended from the mountain, and the two tablets of testimony were in his hands, stone tablets written on both their sides; on this side and on that side they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was God’s writing engraved on the tablets.”

[Col. 0741C]

A great question therefore arises: How are those tablets, which Moses was certainly going to break, although God foreknew it, said to be the work not of a human being but of God, and to have been written not by a human being but by the finger of God, while the later tablets, which were to remain so long and to be in God’s tabernacle and temple, were nevertheless, at God’s command, cut by a human being and written by a human being [were cut by a human being as well as written by a human being]?

Or perhaps the grace of God was signified in those earlier tablets—not a work of man. They became unworthy of that grace when they turned back in their hearts toward Egypt and made an idol; consequently they were deprived of that benefit, and Moses broke the tablets.

But by the later tablets were signified those who glory in their own works. Hence the Apostle says: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wanting to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God.”

[Col. 0741D]

Therefore the tablets sculpted by human work and written by human work are said [*dictae*; variant “given,” *datae*] to be theirs. Since they remained with them, they signified those who would glory in their own works, not in the finger of God—that is, in the Spirit of God.

Certainly, then, the repetition of the law signifies the New Testament. The earlier law signified the Old Testament, which was broken and abolished, especially because when the law is given a second time it is given without terror, unlike the first giving amid such a great tumult of fires, clouds, and trumpets that the people, terrified, said: “Let God not speak to us, lest we die.”

[Col. 0742A]

This signifies that there is fear in the Old Testament and love in the New.

How, then, is this question resolved: Why are the former the work of God, while these are the work of man; why are the former written by the finger of God, while these are written by a human being?

Or perhaps the Old Testament was more especially signified in the earlier tablets because there God commanded but the human being did not act.

For the law was established in the Old Testament to convict transgressors; it entered in so that transgression might abound. What was not fulfilled by love was not fulfilled by fear [variant: “which is not fulfilled except through love”].

Therefore it is called the work of God because God established the law and God wrote it. There is no work of man, because man did not obey God; rather, the law made him guilty.

In the second tablets, however, through God’s help a human being makes and writes the tablets, because the love of the New Testament fulfills the law. Hence the Lord says: “I have come not to abolish the law but to fulfill it.” And the Apostle says: “Love is the fulfillment of the law,” and, “faith working through love.”

Thus in the New Testament what was difficult in the Old became easy for the person who has faith working through love, while that finger of God—that is, the Spirit of God—writes the law inwardly in the heart, not outwardly on stone. Hence the Apostle says: “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts,” because the love of God, by which the commandment is truly fulfilled, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

[Col. 0742B]

This, therefore, is the meaning: the law was first given, in which the Old Testament is signified; it is solely the work of God and the writing of God’s finger. Of it the Apostle says: “Thus the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” The law, therefore, being holy and good, is God’s work, where the human being does nothing because he does not obey, but is instead burdened with guilt by the threatening and condemning law.

“For sin,” he says, “so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.”

But a person is blessed when this holy, just, and good commandment is also his work—that is, when he fulfills it—but through the grace of God.

## CHAPTER 124. The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit that will not be forgiven can be called by one name “impenitence,” that is, an impenitent heart; from a sermon to the people: What the unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is
Before all else, therefore, I admonish you to observe and understand that the Lord did not say, “Every blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven”; nor did he say, “Whoever speaks any word whatsoever against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven”; but rather, “Whoever speaks a word.” For if he had said the former, nothing at all would remain for us to discuss, since if every blasphemy and every word spoken against the Holy Spirit were not forgiven human beings, the Church would gain no one from any class of those who oppose Christ’s gift and the sanctification of the Church—whether pagans, Jews, or heretics of any kind, or even some uninstructed people within the Catholic Church itself. But far be it from the Lord to have said this; far be it, I say, from the Truth to have said that every blasphemy or every word spoken against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come.

He wished, rather, to exercise us through the difficulty of the question, not to deceive us through the facility [variant: difficulty or falsity] of the expression. Therefore, it is not necessary for anyone to suppose that every blasphemy and every word spoken against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness; but it is plainly necessary that there be some blasphemy and some word which, if spoken against the Holy Spirit, can never obtain pardon or forgiveness. For if we take it universally, who could be saved? But if, on the other hand, we suppose that there is none, we contradict the Savior.

There is, therefore, without doubt, some blasphemy and some word which, if spoken against the Holy Spirit, will not be forgiven. But the Lord wished us to ask what this word is; for that reason he did not state it explicitly. I repeat: he wished it to be sought, not denied. Scripture often speaks in such a way that, when something is said without defining whether it is meant wholly or partly, it is not necessary to understand that it can be done wholly but not partly.

The statement would have been wholly, that is, universally, expressed if it had said, “Every blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” or, “Whoever speaks that [whatever] word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” It would have been partly, that is, particularly, expressed if it had said, “A certain blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.” Since, therefore, the statement was expressed neither universally nor particularly—for it did not say, “Every blasphemy against the Spirit,” or, “A certain blasphemy,” but simply and indefinitely, “Blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven”—and since it did not say, “Whoever speaks any word whatsoever,” or, “Whoever speaks a certain word,” but indefinitely, “Whoever speaks a word,” we are not required to understand every blasphemy or every word. It is plainly necessary, however, to understand that the Lord intended some blasphemy and some word, although he did not wish to specify it, so that, by seeking, asking, and knocking, we might not regard as worthless whatever right understanding we may receive.

To make this clearer to you, consider what that same Lord said concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” For this was not said as though he wished it to be understood that the Jews would have been entirely without sin if he had not come and spoken to them. He found them full of sins and weighed down by them. Hence he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened.” What burdens were these, if not the loads of sins arising from transgressions of the law? For “the law entered in so that the trespass might increase.”

Since he himself also says elsewhere, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” how could they have had no sin if he had not come? Only because this statement, having been expressed neither universally nor particularly but indefinitely, does not compel us to understand every sin. Yet unless we understand that they had some sin which they would not have had unless Christ had come and spoken to them, we shall say—God forbid—that the statement is false [we would say that it was false].

He did not therefore say, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have had no sin,” lest the Truth should lie; nor did he state it definitely by saying, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had a certain sin,” lest pious inquiry should not be exercised sufficiently. Throughout the abundance of the holy Scriptures, we are nourished by what is clear and exercised by what is obscure. By the former, hunger is driven away; by the latter, distaste.

Since, therefore, it was not said, “They have [or would have] no sin,” let us not be disturbed when we recognize that the Jews would have remained sinners even if the Lord had not come. Yet because it was said, “If I had not come, they would not have had sin,” it is necessary to understand that, even if not every sin, they nevertheless acquired through the Lord’s coming some sin that they had not previously possessed.

That sin is surely the very fact that they did not believe in him when he was present and speaking to them, and, judging him to be an enemy because he spoke the truth, they even killed him. They certainly would not have had this sin—so great and horrifying—if he had not come and spoken to them.

Therefore, just as, when we hear there, “They would not have had sin,” we understand not every sin but some sin, so in today’s reading, when we hear, “Blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” we must understand not every blasphemy but a certain blasphemy; and when we hear, “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven,” we must understand not every word but a certain [word].

Indeed, even when he says, “Blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” we must necessarily understand not blasphemy against every spirit, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Even if he did not say this more plainly elsewhere, who would be so foolish as to understand anything else?

According to this rule of speech, another expression is understood in the same way: “Unless one is born again, of water and Spirit.” He did not say there, “and of the Holy Spirit,” yet this is what is understood.
