Nor, because he said, “of water and Spirit,” is anyone compelled to understand every spirit. Accordingly, when you hear, “Blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” just as you do not understand every spirit, so you ought not to understand blasphemy against every spirit.

I see that you now wish to hear what that blasphemy against the Spirit is which will not be forgiven, since it is not every blasphemy; and what that word is, since it is not every word, which, if spoken against the Holy Spirit, will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. I would already say [or, I would gladly say] what you are eagerly waiting to hear, but endure a few delays for the sake of greater care, until, with the Lord’s help, I have explained everything that arises.

The other two evangelists, Mark and Luke, when speaking about this matter, did not say “blasphemy” or “word,” so that we might understand not every blasphemy but a certain one, and not every word but a certain one. Since, therefore, the expression cannot be understood universally—for otherwise we would deprive pagans, Jews, heretics, and every kind of person who blasphemes the Holy Spirit through various errors and contradictions of the hope of forgiveness if they should correct themselves—it remains that, in the statement, “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever,” we must understand the person who blasphemes not in just any manner, but in such a manner that he can never be forgiven.

For just as, in the statement, “God tempts no one,” God must be understood as tempting no one not in every kind of temptation but in a certain kind, lest that other statement be false, “The Lord your God is testing you,” and lest we deny that Christ is God or declare the Gospel false where we read that he questioned a disciple in order to test him, although he himself knew what he was going to do—so there is a temptation that leads to sin, with which God tempts no one, and a temptation that tests faith, with which God also deigns to test.

Thus, when we hear, “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit,” we must not understand every kind of blasphemy, just as we do not understand every kind of temptation in the other passage.

Likewise, when we hear, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” we certainly do not understand one who believes in the manner in which the demons also believe and tremble, nor those baptized among whom Simon the Magician [Simon] was able to be baptized, though he could not be saved.

Therefore, just as, when he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” he was considering not all believers and baptized persons but some—namely, those established in the faith which, as the Apostle distinguishes it, works through love—so, when he said, “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever,” he was considering not every guilt of one who blasphemes the Holy Spirit, but a certain guilt by which whoever is bound will never be released by any forgiveness [will not be released].

What, too, are we to understand by his saying, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”? Can we include here even those of whom the Apostle says that they eat and drink judgment upon themselves, although they eat that very flesh and drink that very blood? Can we include Judas, the impious seller and betrayer of his master, even though he ate and drank with the other apostles [disciples] the sacrament of his flesh and blood, first prepared by his hands—as the evangelist Luke more explicitly shows? Did he remain in Christ, or Christ in him? Finally, so many who eat that flesh and drink that blood with a false heart, or who become apostates after eating and drinking them—do they remain in Christ, or Christ in them?

There is, assuredly, a certain manner of eating that flesh and drinking that blood, by which the one who eats and drinks remains in Christ, and Christ in him. Therefore, not in just any manner does one remain in Christ, and Christ in him, when one eats Christ’s flesh and drinks Christ’s blood, but in a certain manner—the manner, plainly, that he had in view when he said this.

So likewise, in the statement, “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever,” it is not in every manner of blasphemy that one becomes guilty of this unforgivable offense, but in a certain manner which the one who pronounced this true and fearful sentence wished us to seek and understand.

According to the measure of our capacity, insofar as we are permitted to see such things “through a mirror and in an enigma,” especially while we remain what we are, authority is suggested to us in the Father, birth in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit the communion of the Father and the Son; in the three there is equality.

Therefore, through what is common to the Father and the Son, he wished us to have communion both with one another and with them: through that gift which both possess as one, namely, through the Holy Spirit, God and the gift of God. For in this we are reconciled to the Divinity and take delight in it. What good would it do us to know anything good if we did not also love it? As we learn through truth, so we love through charity, so that we may know more fully and, having known, enjoy blessedly.

“Love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us”; and because sins alienated us from the possession of good people, “love covers a multitude of sins.”

The Father is therefore the truthful origin of the Son, who is Truth born from the truthful Father; and the Spirit is goodness poured forth from the good Father and the good Son. In all of them there is an undiminished divinity [goodness] and an inseparable unity.

First, therefore, as a gift of God’s goodness, the remission of sins comes into us from the beginning of faith, for the reception of eternal life, which will be given at the end. Through this benefit we are rescued from the power of darkness, and the prince of this world, who works in the children of unbelief, is cast out from our faith—not by any other force than the fellowship and bondage of sin.

In the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s people are gathered into one, the unclean spirit is cast out, the spirit that is divided against itself [has been divided against itself]. Against this gratuitous gift, against this grace of God, the impenitent heart speaks.

Impenitence itself, therefore, is the blasphemy against the Spirit which will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come. For against the Holy Spirit, through whom those who are baptized receive forgiveness of all their sins, and whom the Church received so that whoever’s sins it forgives may be forgiven, it speaks a very evil and exceedingly impious word, whether in thought or even with its tongue.

Although God’s patience leads such a person to repentance, he nevertheless, according to the hardness of his heart and his impenitent heart, stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, “who will render to each according to his works” [according to his deeds].

This impenitence—since, by some name or other, we can call both the blasphemy and the word against the Holy Spirit, which has no forgiveness forever—this impenitence, I say, was opposed by both the herald and the Judge when they said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

Against it the Lord God opened the mouth of evangelical preaching, and against it he foretold that the Gospel itself must be preached throughout the whole world. After he had risen from the dead, he said to his disciples: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

This impenitence plainly has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come, because repentance obtains forgiveness in this age that is effective in the age to come.

But this impenitence, or impenitent heart, cannot be judged so long as a person lives in this flesh. For no one is to be despaired of while God’s patience leads him to repentance, and while God does not take from this life the wicked person who does not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that he should turn back and live.

He is a pagan today: how do you know whether tomorrow he will become a Christian? He is an unbelieving Jew today: what if tomorrow he believes in Christ? He is a heretic today: what if tomorrow he follows Catholic truth? He is a schismatic today: what if tomorrow he embraces Catholic peace?

What if those whom you mark as belonging to any kind of error, and whom you now condemn as utterly hopeless, repent before they end this life and find true life?

Therefore, brothers, let what the Apostle says admonish you also in this matter: “Do not judge anything before the time.”

This is the blasphemy against the Spirit for which there is never any forgiveness—by which we understand not every blasphemy but a certain one, namely, the enduring hardness of an impenitent heart—which, as we have said, we have either stated, discovered, or shown as far as we think it can be shown. It cannot be detected in anyone, as long as he remains in this life.

This should not seem absurd because, when a person perseveres in hard impenitence to the end of this life and speaks for a long time and at length against this grace of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel nevertheless called the prolonged contradiction of an impenitent heart a brief “word,” saying: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

For although this blasphemy is extensive and woven together and prolonged through many words, Scripture nevertheless commonly calls many words a “word.” No prophet, indeed, spoke only one word, yet we read: “The word that came to this or that prophet.” And the Apostle says, “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and teaching”; he does not say “in words,” but “in the word.”

And holy James says: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only”; he too does not say “of words,” but “of the word,” although so many words from the holy Scriptures are read, spoken, and heard publicly and solemnly in the Church.

Therefore, just as, however long any one of us may labor in preaching the Gospel, he is called not a preacher of words but a preacher of the word; and however long any of you may listen carefully and earnestly to our preaching, you are called not a devoted hearer of words but a devoted hearer of the word—so, according to the manner in which Scripture speaks and ecclesiastical custom understands it, whoever throughout his entire life, however long it may be extended, speaks with an impenitent heart, whether with his mouth or merely in thought, whatever words he may utter against the forgiveness of sins that takes place in the Church, speaks a word against the Holy Spirit.

The reason that not only the word spoken against the Son of Man but every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings is that, wherever this sin of the impenitent heart against the Holy Spirit, through whom sins are loosed in the Church, is absent, all other sins are forgiven.

But how can that be forgiven which also prevents the forgiveness of other sins? All sins, therefore, are forgiven in those in whom this sin is absent, the sin that will never be forgiven. But in those in whom it is present, because it will never be forgiven, neither are the other sins forgiven, since it prevents the forgiveness of all of them by its bond.

It is not therefore because the one who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, while the one who speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son in the Trinity [“It is not therefore because whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, because in the Trinity…”]—a claim that no heretic has ever made—but because whoever resists truth and blasphemes the Truth, who is Christ, even after Christ had been so extensively preached among human beings that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—and that same Christ is the Son of Man—will be forgiven if he has not spoken that word of an impenitent heart against the Holy Spirit of whom it was said, “Unless one is born of water and Spirit,” and of whom it was likewise said, “Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven.”

That is, if he repents, he will receive through this gift the forgiveness of all sins, including the sin that he committed by speaking a word against the Son of Man, because to the sin of ignorance, or obstinacy, or any kind of blasphemy, he did not add the sin of impenitence against the gift of God and the grace of regeneration or reconciliation that takes place in the Church through the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, we must not accept what some people think: that the word spoken against the Son of Man is forgiven, while the word spoken against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven, because, on account of the flesh he assumed, Christ became the Son of Man, and by that flesh he is certainly less than the Holy Spirit, who in his own substance is equal to the Father and the only-begotten Son according to his divinity, according to which the only-begotten Son himself is also equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For if this had been said for that reason, all other blasphemy would surely have been passed over in silence, so that this alone would appear to be forgivable—the blasphemy spoken against the Son of Man, as though he were thought to be merely human. But when it has first been said, “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings”—which is also stated by another evangelist in this form: “All sins and blasphemies with which the children of human beings may blaspheme will be forgiven”—there is no doubt that the blasphemy spoken against the Father is also included in this general statement. Yet this alone is defined as unforgivable: the blasphemy spoken against the Holy Spirit.

Did the Father also take the form of a servant, by which he would be less than the Holy Spirit? Certainly not. Rather, after mentioning universally every sin and every blasphemy, he wished to express more prominently the blasphemy spoken against the Son of Man because, even if people were bound by that sin which he mentioned when he said, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin”—a sin that the Gospel according to John also shows to be exceedingly grave when it says of the Holy Spirit, promising that he would send him, “He will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment; concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me”—nevertheless, if such a person has not spoken the word of the impenitent heart against the Holy Spirit, even this sin spoken against the Son of Man will be forgiven.

At this point someone may ask whether only the Holy Spirit forgives sins, or whether the Father and the Son do so as well. We answer: the Father and the Son do so as well.

For the Son himself says concerning the Father: “If you forgive people’s sins, your Father will also forgive you your sins.” We too say to him in the Lord’s Prayer, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” and among the other things we ask this also, saying, “Forgive us our debts.”

Concerning himself he says: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…”

If, then, you say, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forgive sins, why is that impenitence which will never be forgiven said to belong only to blasphemy against the Spirit, as though the person bound by this sin of impenitence appeared to resist the gift of the Holy Spirit, through which gift the forgiveness of sins takes place?

These things are said in such a way that the Trinity’s operation is nevertheless understood to be inseparable: when the Father’s operation is mentioned, it is not to be understood as operating without the Son and the Holy Spirit; when the Son’s operation is mentioned, not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and when the Holy Spirit’s operation is mentioned, not without the Father and the Son. This is sufficiently known to those who believe rightly, or even to those who understand as much as they can.

For this reason, too, it is said of the Father, “He himself does the works”: because the origin even of the works is from him, from whom is the existence of the cooperating persons. The Son is born from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him, from whom the Son was born and with whom that same Spirit [the transmitted reading has ‘Christ’] is common.

This is why the Lord Jesus casts out demons in the Holy Spirit. It was not that he alone was unable to accomplish this, or that he assumed that aid as though it were insufficient for the task. Rather, it was fitting that the spirit divided against itself should be expelled by that very Spirit whom the Father and the Son possess in common, undivided in themselves [being undivided in themselves].

So also, since sins are not forgiven outside the Church, they had to be forgiven in that Spirit through whom the Church is gathered into one.

Finally, if someone outside the Church repents of his sins, yet has an impenitent heart with respect to this great sin, by which it is alien from the Church of God, what benefit does that repentance bring him, when by this sin alone he speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, being alien from the Church, which has received this gift so that forgiveness of sins may take place in it through the Holy Spirit?

Although the Trinity effects this forgiveness, it is nevertheless understood properly to belong to the Holy Spirit. For he is the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father,” and in whom we can also say to him, “Forgive us our debts.”

And by this we recognize, as the Apostle John says, “that Christ remains in us,” from the Spirit whom he gave us. The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.

For to him belongs the fellowship by which we become one body of the only Son of God. Hence it is written: “If there is therefore any exhortation in Christ, any comfort of love, any fellowship of the Spirit…”

On account of this fellowship, those into whom the Spirit first came spoke in the languages of all nations. For just as the fellowship of the human race is established through languages [the fellowship is more closely joined through languages], so it was necessary that the future fellowship of the children of God and members of Christ among all nations should be signified through the languages of all nations.

Thus, just as at that time the one who spoke in the languages of all nations appeared to have received the Holy Spirit, so now the one who is held in the bond of the Church’s peace [who is held in the bond of peace], which is spread throughout all nations, should recognize that he has received the Holy Spirit.

Hence the Apostle says: “Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

That he is the Spirit of the Father, the Son himself says: “He proceeds from the Father.” And elsewhere: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

That he is the Spirit of the Son, the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’”—that is, causing us to cry out. For we cry out because he pours love into our hearts, without which anyone who cries out cries in vain.

Hence he says again: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”

To whom, then, in the Trinity does this fellowship properly belong, if not to the Spirit who is common to the Father and the Son?

For the Holy Spirit does not dwell in anyone without the Father and the Son, just as the Son does not dwell without the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor the Father without them. The dwelling of those whose operation is inseparable is itself inseparable.

Yet they are often shown individually through signs supplied by creation, not through their substance itself. Just as, when syllables occupy successive portions of time, they are pronounced separately in speech, though they are not separated from one another by any intervals or moments of time; they can never be said simultaneously, even though they cannot exist except simultaneously.

But, as we have already said more than once, the forgiveness of sins—which overturns the divided spirit within itself and expels its kingdom—and the fellowship of the Church’s unity, outside which that forgiveness of sins does not take place, are, as it were, the proper work of the Holy Spirit, with the Father and the Son cooperating, because the Holy Spirit himself is in a certain manner the fellowship of the Father and the Son.

For the Father is not commonly possessed as Father by the Son and the Holy Spirit, because he is not the Father of both; nor is the Son commonly possessed as Son by the Father and the Holy Spirit, because he is not the Son of both. But the Holy Spirit is commonly possessed by the Father and the Son, because he is the one Spirit of both.

Whoever, therefore, is guilty of impenitence against the Spirit, in whom the unity and fellowship of the Church’s communion are gathered together, will never be forgiven, because he closes this fellowship against himself [has closed it against himself], where forgiveness is granted. And he will rightly be condemned with the spirit that is divided against itself, himself divided against the Spirit [the Holy Spirit], who is not divided against himself.

The occasion for this statement about blasphemy against the Spirit arose from the mention of the unclean spirit who is divided against himself. It had been said of the Lord that he cast out demons by the prince of demons. The Lord himself says that he casts out demons in the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit who is not divided against himself may conquer and expel the one who is divided against himself.

But that person remains in the other’s destruction who refuses, through impenitence, to pass into the peace of the one who is not divided against himself.

This is what Mark reports: “Amen, I say to you, all sins and blasphemies with which the children of human beings may blaspheme will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal sin.”

After saying these words of the Lord, he then added his own explanation, saying, “For they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit,’” to show that the occasion for the statement arose from this: they had said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. It was not because this itself was the blasphemy that is not forgiven—for this too is forgiven if proper repentance follows—but, as I have said, because it provided the occasion for the Lord to pronounce that statement, mentioning the unclean spirit whom the Lord showed to be divided against himself, in contrast with the Holy Spirit, who is not only not divided against himself but also makes undivided those whom he gathers together, by forgiving sins that are divided against themselves and dwelling in those whom he has cleansed.

Even if someone is so opposed to the truth that he resists God speaking not through the prophets but in his only Son—although, for our sake and so that he might speak to us in him, God wished him to be the Son of Man—he will be forgiven when, through repentance, he turns toward God’s kindness. God, not wishing the death of the wicked but rather that he should turn back and live, gave the Holy Spirit to the Church, so that whoever’s sins it forgives in him may have them forgiven.

But whoever becomes an enemy of this gift, so that he does not seek it through repentance but opposes it through impenitence, makes the sin unforgivable—not any sin whatsoever, but forgiveness itself, which he has despised or even attacked. Thus he speaks a word against the Holy Spirit when he never passes from dispersion to the gathering that received the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins.

Even if someone approaches this gathering through a wicked cleric who is nevertheless a Catholic minister—reprobate and false—but approaches with a sincere heart, he receives forgiveness of sins in the Holy Spirit himself. The Holy Spirit works in the holy Church even at this time, when it is threshed like a threshing floor containing chaff, in such a way that he neither rejects anyone’s genuine confession nor is deceived by anyone’s pretense. He avoids the reprobate in such a way that he gathers the good even through their ministry.

There is therefore one refuge, lest the blasphemy be unforgivable: the impenitent heart must be guarded against, and repentance must not be believed to profit in any other way than by holding fast to the Church, where forgiveness of sins is given and the fellowship of the Spirit is preserved in the bond of peace.

## CHAPTER CXXV. Concerning those who receive Communion daily and those who do so rarely, and also those who receive the Eucharist at the Lord’s Supper after the common meal; from the first book addressed to the Inquiries of Januarius.

Someone might say that the Eucharist should not be received every day. You will ask why. “Because,” he says, “one should choose the days on which a person lives more purely and more continently, so that he may approach so great a sacrament worthily. For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” [Col. 0752A].

Another argues the opposite. “Indeed,” he says, “if the wound of sin and the force of the disease are so great that such medicines must be postponed, then, by the authority of the bishop, each person ought to be removed from the altar in order to perform penance, and by that same authority be reconciled. For this is to receive unworthily: to receive at a time when one ought to be doing penance, rather than, whenever he pleases, either withdrawing himself from Communion or restoring himself to it by his own decision.

“But if the sins are not so great that a person ought to be judged excommunicated, he should not separate himself from the daily medicine of the Lord’s body.”

Perhaps the dispute is more rightly settled between them by one who urges them above all to remain in the peace of Christ. Let each person do what, according to his faith, he devoutly believes ought to be done. Neither of them dishonors the body and blood of the Lord; rather, let them strive together to honor the most health-giving sacrament [Col. 0752B].

For Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either place himself above the other, when one of them received the Lord joyfully into his house, while the other said, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Both honored the Savior in different and, as it were, opposite ways; both were wretched because of their sins, and both obtained mercy.

This comparison is also supported by the fact that, among the first people, the manna tasted in the mouth of each of the faithful according to his own desire. So, in the heart of each Christian, that sacrament by which the world has been subjected has its own taste. One, by honoring it, dares not receive it every day; the other, by honoring it, dares not omit it on any day 81. This [that] food does not wish to suffer contempt alone, just as manna does not wish to suffer loathing [Col. 0752C]. For this reason the Apostle also says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods with the special veneration that was due to it. Immediately after saying, “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” he adds, “not discerning the Lord’s body”—as is sufficiently clear at that very place in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, if it is carefully considered.

Suppose that a traveler happens to be in a place where those who persist in observing Lent do not wash on Thursday, nor relax their fast. “No,” he says, “I will not fast today.” The reason is asked. “Because,” he says, “this is not done in my homeland.” What else is this man attempting except to place his own custom above another’s custom? He will not be able to recite “[these things] this” to me from the Book of God. Either let him contend loudly against the whole Church—[wherever] it is spread—or he will show that the other acts contrary to the faith, while he himself acts according to the faith and according to the best customs of this place; or he will prove that the other violates them, while he himself observes them. In fact, they violate [their own] quiet and peace by quarrelling over a superfluous question.

Nevertheless, in matters of this kind I would prefer that he, in this man’s homeland, and this man, in the other’s homeland, should not shrink from what the others do. But if, while traveling in a foreign country where God’s people are more numerous, more frequent in attendance, and more fervent, he saw, for example, that the Eucharist was offered twice on Thursday of the final week of Lent, both in the morning and in the evening, and then, on returning to his own country, where the custom is for it to be offered at the end of the day, he were to insist that this was done wrongly and unlawfully because he himself had seen it done differently elsewhere, such childish thinking must be avoided in ourselves, tolerated [Col. 0753A] and corrected in our fellow believers.

—From the same Book I, addressed to the inquiries of the same Januarius.—

For these reasons—that is, either because of the faith or because of customs—what was being done wrongly ought to be corrected, or what was not being done ought to be instituted. For a change of custom itself, even when it is assisted by usefulness, disturbs people through its novelty. Consequently, a change that is not useful is unproductive and therefore harmful in its disturbance.

Nor should it therefore be thought that, because it is written, “Likewise also the cup after supper, saying …,” and so forth, the practice was instituted in many places of offering the Eucharist on that day after the meal. He could have called it “supper” because they had already received the body, so that afterward they might receive the cup. For elsewhere the Apostle says, “When you come together, therefore, it is not to eat the Lord’s supper,” calling this very reception of the Eucharist “the Lord’s supper.” This may have moved people more strongly to offer or receive the Eucharist on that day after they had already eaten, because the Gospel says, “While they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it,” after it had also said above, “When evening came, he was reclining with the twelve, and while they were eating he said, ‘One of you will betray me.’”

Afterward he gave them the sacrament, and it is perfectly clear when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord: they did not receive them fasting. Yet should the whole Church therefore be criticized because it is always received by those who are fasting? For it pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before [external] other foods [Col. 0753C]; for this reason that custom is observed throughout the world.

Nor, because the Lord gave it after the meal, should brothers therefore [ought] be going to assemble after lunch or dinner to receive that sacrament, or, as those whom the Apostle rebuked and corrected had done, mix this sacrament with their own meals. For the Savior, in order to commend the greatness of that mystery all the more forcefully, wished this final act to be impressed more deeply upon the hearts and memory of the disciples, from whom he was about to depart for his passion. Therefore he did not prescribe the order in which it should thereafter be received, so that he might preserve this place for the Apostles, through whom he was going to establish the Church.

For if he had instructed them that it should always be received after other foods, I believe that no one would have altered that custom. But when the Apostle speaks of this sacrament and says, “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another; if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment,” he immediately adds: “The remaining matters I will arrange when I come” [Col. 0753D]. From this it can be understood that, since it would have been too much for him to set out in the Epistle the entire order of observance, the order followed by the Church throughout the world was established by his direction, since it is not altered by any diversity of customs.

## CHAPTER CXXVI

What is intended by the observance of the Sabbath and the Moon in the celebration of Easter, and concerning Lent, or concerning the correspondence of Pentecost with the day on which the Law was given, from Book II addressed to the same Januarius.

You ask what the reason is that the anniversary day for celebrating the Lord’s Passion does not return to the same [day of the year] [Col. 0754A] as the day on which he is said to have been born, and then you add: “If this happens [is the case] because of the Sabbath and the Moon, what is the significance here of observing the Sabbath and the Moon?”

First, you ought to know that the Lord’s Nativity is not celebrated as a sacrament, but merely recalled in memory—that he was born. Accordingly, nothing was necessary except that the recurring day of the year on which the event itself occurred should be marked by devout festivity. A sacrament, however, is present in a celebration when the commemoration of an event is conducted in such a way that it is also understood to signify something, which must be received in holiness.

Thus we celebrate Easter not merely by recalling what was done [what happened]—that Christ died and rose again—but also by not omitting the other matters that attest [Col. 0754B] to its sacramental significance. For, as the Apostle says, “He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification,” and in that Passion and resurrection of the Lord a kind of passage from death to life was consecrated.

Indeed, those who know both languages say that the very name *Pascha* is not Greek, as it is commonly thought, but Hebrew. For it is not derived from *πάθειν* (*pathein*), “to suffer,” in Greek, but from the fact that, as I have said, a passage is made [from] from death to life; in the Hebrew language the term is said to mean “passage,” as those who know these matters report.

The Lord himself wished to allude to this when he said, “Whoever believes in me will pass from death to life.” The same Evangelist is understood especially to have wished to express this when, as the Lord was about to celebrate Easter with his disciples and had given them the mystical supper, he says: “When Jesus saw that the hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father” [Col. 0754C]. Thus a passage from this mortal life into another, immortal life—that is, from death to life—is commended in the Passion and resurrection of the Lord.

For us this passage is now accomplished through faith, which is for us unto the forgiveness of sins and the hope of eternal life, for those who love God and neighbor, since “faith works through love,” and “the righteous lives by faith.” But “hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience,” according to that faith, hope, and love by which we have begun to exist [Col. 0754D] under grace.

Already we have died with Christ and have been buried with him through baptism, as the Apostle says: “For our old self was crucified together with him on the cross.” And we have risen with him, because he also raised us together with himself and made us sit together in the heavenly places.

Hence the exhortation: “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth.” What follows, however, says 82: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” This sufficiently indicates what is meant: our passage from death to life, which takes place through faith, is now accomplished in the hope of what is to come, at the resurrection and glory at the end, when this corruptible thing—that is, this flesh in which we groan—puts on incorruption, and this mortal thing puts on immortality.

For now, indeed, we possess through faith the first fruits of the Spirit, but within ourselves we still groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body [Col. 0755A]. The redemption of our body remains, and while awaiting it we groan within ourselves. Hence the saying: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation.”

This renewal, then, of our life, and a certain passage from death to life—which first takes place through faith, so that we may rejoice in hope and be patient in tribulation—continues while our outward self is being corrupted but our inward self is being renewed day by day.

It is on account of this beginning of new life, and on account of the new person whom we are commanded to put on and the old person whom we are commanded to put off, that we purge out the old leaven, so that we may be a new lump, “because Christ our Pasch has been sacrificed” [Col. 0755B].

Because of this newness of life, therefore, the first month among the months of the year has been assigned to this celebration. For it is also called the month of new things.

Since, moreover, in the whole duration of the age a third period has now appeared, the resurrection extends over three days. The first period is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace, where the manifestation is now made of the sacrament previously hidden in prophetic mystery.

This is also signified by the lunar number. Since the number seven is accustomed to appear mystically in Scripture as signifying a certain perfection, Easter is celebrated in the third week of the Moon: the day falls between the fourteenth and the twenty-first.

There is another sacrament here as well. If it is obscure to you because you are less learned in such investigations, do not be distressed, nor think me better [Col. 0755C] because I learned these things in my boyhood studies: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

—From another work.—

There are two plausible opinions about the Moon; which of them is true, or whether either is true at all, I think a human being can know only not at all, or with the greatest difficulty.

When it is asked from where the Moon receives its light, some say that it has light of its own, but that half of its sphere is luminous and half dark. As it moves along its orbit, they say, it gradually turns toward the earth the same side that is luminous, so that it can be seen by us, and therefore it first appears as though horned.

For if you make a ball half white and half dark, and hold the dark side before your eyes, you see no whiteness. But when you begin to turn the white side toward your eyes, doing so gradually, you first see the horns of whiteness; then it gradually increases until the entire bright side is presented to your eyes and none of the other, dark side is visible [Col. 0755D]. If you continue turning it gradually, the darkness begins to appear and the brightness to diminish, until it returns again to the horns; finally it is turned entirely away from the eyes, and once more only that dark side can be seen.

They say that this is what happens when the Moon’s light is seen to increase up to the fifteenth lunar day, and then diminish again until the thirtieth, returning to the horns until no light at all appears in it.

According to this opinion, the Moon signifies the Church allegorically: the Church shines in part spiritually, while in part it is dark carnally. At times its spiritual aspect is visible to human beings in good works; at other times it lies hidden in the conscience and is known only to God. Then it appears to human beings through the body alone, as happens when we pray in the heart and seem to be doing almost nothing, although we are commanded to have our heart lifted not toward the earth but upward to the Lord [Col. 0756A].

Others, however, say that the Moon has no light of its own but is illuminated by the Sun. When it is together with the Sun, they say, it presents to us the side that is not illuminated, and therefore no light is visible in it. But when it begins to recede from the Sun, it is illuminated, including on the side that faces the earth; necessarily it begins at the horns, until it becomes full, opposite the Sun on the fifteenth day.

Then, as the Sun sets, it rises, so that whoever has watched the setting Sun, when he can no longer see it, will see the Moon rise after turning toward the east [Col. 0756B]. From that point, when it begins to draw near again, it turns toward us the side that is not illuminated, until it returns to the horns and then disappears altogether, because at that time the side that is illuminated is above, toward the sky, while toward the earth is the side that the Sun cannot irradiate.

According to this opinion also, therefore, the Moon is understood as the Church, because it does not possess its own light but is illuminated by the only-begotten Son of God, who in many places in the holy Scriptures is allegorically called the Sun.

Some heretics, not knowing him and unable to see him, attempt to turn the minds of the simple toward this bodily and visible sun, which is the common light of human beings and flies; and they turn away some who, so long as they cannot contemplate the inner light of truth with the mind, refuse to be content with the simple Catholic faith [Col. 0756C]. Yet this faith is the one salvation of the little ones, and by this one milk they reach, with sure strength, the firmness of more solid food.

Whichever of these two opinions is true, this at least is perfectly clear, and easily recognized by anyone who pays attention: the Moon does not increase before our eyes except by receding from the Sun, nor diminish except by approaching the Sun from the other side.

Now consider what we read in Proverbs: “The wise person remains like the Sun, but the fool changes like the Moon.” And who is the wise person who remains, except that Sun of righteousness of whom it is said, “The Sun of righteousness has risen for me,” and whom the impious, lamenting that he did not rise for them on the last day, will say: “The light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the Sun did not rise for us”?

God makes this bodily visible sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and he also sends rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous. Appropriate likenesses are always drawn from visible things to invisible things.

Who, then, is that fool who changes like the Moon, except Adam, in whom all sinned? For the human soul, turning away from the Sun of righteousness—that is, from the inner contemplation of unchangeable truth—turns all its powers toward earthly things, and becomes increasingly darkened in its inner and higher faculties [Col. 0756D].

But when it begins to return to that unchangeable wisdom, the more closely it approaches it in an attitude of devotion, the more the outward person is corrupted, while the inward person is renewed day by day. All that light of understanding which had been directed toward lower things is turned toward higher things and is, in a manner, withdrawn from earthly concerns, so that the soul may die more and more to this age and its life be hidden with Christ in God [Col. 0757A].

It therefore changes for the worse as it advances outward and casts its inner life away in its conduct; and this appears better to the earth—that is, to those who set their minds on earthly things—when “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” and “the one who acts wickedly is blessed.”

But it changes for the better when it gradually turns its attention and glory away from earthly things, which appear in this age, and turns them toward higher and inward things [and turns the higher things from the lower things]. This appears worse to the earth—that is, to those who set their minds on earthly things.

Hence those impious people, finally repenting fruitlessly, will also say among many other things: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach. We fools considered their life madness” [Col. 0757B].

Accordingly, 83 the Holy Spirit, drawing a likeness from visible things to invisible things and from bodily things to spiritual sacraments, wished that the passage from one life into another—the event called *Pascha*—should be observed from the fourteenth Moon. This was not only because of the third period mentioned above, since the third week begins from it, but also so that a likeness might be drawn from the Moon for the very turning from outward things to inward things.

It extends to the twenty-first because of the number seven itself, by which the totality of things is often signified and which is also attributed to the Church because of its likeness to totality. For this reason the Apostle John writes in Revelation to seven churches [Col. 0757C].

The Church, while it still exists in this mortality of the flesh, is signified in Scripture by the name of the Moon because of its very mutability. Hence the saying: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot at the upright in heart in the dark Moon.”

Before what the Apostle says comes to pass—“When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory”—the Church appears dark during the time of its pilgrimage, groaning amid many iniquities. At that time the ambushes of deceitful seducers are to be feared, and these he wished to be understood by the name of arrows.

Elsewhere, because of the most faithful messengers of the truth whom the Church continually brings forth everywhere, it is said: “The Moon is a faithful witness in heaven.”

And when the psalmist was singing of the Lord’s kingdom, he said: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the Moon is destroyed”—that is, abundance of peace will increase until it consumes every mutability of mortality [Col. 0757D].

Then the last enemy, death, will be destroyed, and whatever resists us because of the weakness of the flesh, on account of which we do not yet possess perfect peace, will be wholly consumed when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality.

For this reason also the walls of that city called Jericho—which is said to mean “Moon” in the Hebrew language—collapsed when the Ark of the Testament had been carried around them for the seventh circuit.

What else does the proclamation of the kingdom of heaven now accomplish, as the circling of the Ark signified, except that all the defenses of mortal life—that is, every hope of this age that resists hope of the future age—should be destroyed by the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit through free will? [Col. 0758A] For this reason, when the Ark circled them, those walls fell not through a violent blow but of their own accord.

There are also other testimonies of Scripture that present to us, through mention of the Moon, the signification of the Church, which in this mortality journeys in hardships and labors far from that Jerusalem whose citizens are the holy angels.

Nevertheless, fools who refuse to be changed for the better ought not therefore to think that these heavenly lights are to be worshiped merely because a likeness is sometimes drawn from them to represent divine mysteries; a likeness is drawn from every creature.

Nor should we therefore rush into the sentence of condemnation pronounced in the Apostle’s words against certain people “who worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” [Col. 0758B].

For just as we do not worship cattle, although Christ is called both the Lamb and the Calf; nor a wild animal, because he is called the Lion of the tribe of Judah; nor stones, because “the Rock was Christ”; nor Mount Zion, because the Church is represented in it—so neither do we worship the Sun or the Moon, although figures of the sacraments are taken from this heavenly creature, as from many earthly creatures, for mystical instruction.

We do not, therefore, infer from the Sun and Moon, according to annual or monthly periods, the outcomes of our actions, lest, dashed against the rocks of miserable servitude amid the dangerous storms of human life, we suffer shipwreck with respect to free will. Rather, to signify a matter sacramentally, we receive appropriate likenesses with the deepest religious devotion, just as we do from the rest of creation—from winds, sea, earth, birds, fish, cattle, trees, and human beings—using them abundantly in speech, but, by Christian freedom, very sparingly in the celebration of sacraments: for example, water, grain, wine, and oil [Col. 0758C].

Under the bondage of the former people, many things were also commanded to be celebrated which are handed down to us only for understanding.

But how great is the difference between observing the stars for practical purposes—adapting them to atmospheric conditions, as farmers and sailors do; marking the regions of the world and determining a course from one place to another, as ship pilots do, and as those do who travel through sandy deserts toward the inner regions of the South without any fixed or direct route [or straight route]; or commemorating certain stars to signify something useful in teaching through figurative representation—and the vanities of people who observe the stars for this purpose: not to discern atmospheric conditions, routes through regions, merely the numbers of times, or spiritual likenesses, but to seek what they regard as the already determined fated outcomes of events—who does not understand the difference? [Col. 0758D]

But let us now examine why, when we celebrate Easter, it is also observed that a Sabbath should occur. This is distinctive, or especially characteristic, of the Christian religion.

The Jews observe only the month of new things and the Moon, from the fourteenth through the twenty-first. But because their Easter, on which the Lord suffered, occurred in such a way that the Sabbath day lay between his death and resurrection, our fathers judged that something should be added, both so that our festival would be distinguished from the Jewish festival and because we must believe that this was not done without purpose by the one who exists before time, through whom time was made, who came in the fullness of time, and who had authority to lay down his life and to take it up again [Col. 0759A].

For this reason he awaited not a fated hour but an opportune hour for the sacrament he had undertaken to commend, when he said, “My hour has not yet come,” so that it might be observed by posterity in the annual celebration of his Passion.

For what we now undertake—as I said above—in faith and hope [we journey as strangers], and toward which we strive through love, is a kind of rest from every labor and every trouble, holy and perpetual. Our passage from this life is made into this [same] rest, a passage which our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to foreshadow [show] and consecrate by his Passion [Col. 0759B].

That rest contains not slothful inactivity but a certain ineffable tranquility of unencumbered action. For one rests from the works of this life at the end in such a way that one rejoices in the activity of the other life.

But because that activity is directed toward the praise of God, without labor of the limbs and without the anguish of cares, one does not pass into it [the same state] through rest in such a way that labor follows rest—that is, activity does not begin in such a way that rest ceases. We do not return to labors and cares; rather, what belongs to rest remains within activity: neither laboring in work nor wavering in thought.

Because, then, through rest one returns to the first life from which the soul fell into sin, rest is signified by the Sabbath [Col. 0759C].

That first life, which is restored to those returning from pilgrimage and receiving the first robe, is represented by the one Sabbath-day which we call the Lord’s Day.

Count the seven days and read Genesis: you will find the seventh without evening, because it signifies rest without end. The first life, therefore, was not eternal for the sinner, but the final rest is eternal. Accordingly, the eighth will also possess eternal blessedness, because that rest which is eternal is received by the eighth, not extinguished by it; otherwise it would not be eternal.

Thus the eighth will be the first in such a way that the first life is not taken away but made eternal.

The Sabbath, however, was commended to the former people to be celebrated through bodily rest, so that it might be a figure of 84 sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. Never [Nowhere] in Genesis do we read of sanctification on all the preceding days; only of the Sabbath is it said: “God sanctified the seventh day” [Col. 0759D].

Because, therefore, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us,” sanctification is mentioned on the seventh day, where rest is commended.

Since we cannot do good works unless assisted by his gift, as the Apostle says, “For it is God who works in us both to will and to act according to his good pleasure,” nor can we act and rest [rest] after all the good works we perform in this life unless we are sanctified and perfected for eternity by his gift, it is therefore said of God that, after he had made all his works “very good,” he rested on the seventh day from all the works he had made [Col. 0760A].

For he signified the future rest which he would give to [us] human beings after their good works.

Just as, when we act well, he is said to work in us, whose gift enables us to act well, so, when we rest, he is said to rest, [because it is he who grants that we rest]—for we do not rest beforehand.

Therefore, among all those ten commandments, only the commandment concerning the Sabbath is prescribed to be observed figuratively. We have accepted this figure as something to be understood, but not also to be celebrated through bodily rest.

Since spiritual rest is sanctified [signified] by the Sabbath, concerning which it is said in the Psalm, “Be still and see that I am the Lord [for I am God],” and to which people are called by the Lord himself when he says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me [because] for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” [Col. 0760B], we nevertheless observe the other commandments there properly, as commandments, [without any] each without figurative significance.

Accordingly, we understand—not inappropriately—that everything said figuratively in Scripture is useful for stirring up the love by which we strive toward rest, since the only commandment in the Decalogue prescribed figuratively is the one in which rest is commended: rest which is loved everywhere but found holy and certain in God alone.

The Lord’s Day, however, was declared not to the Jews but to Christians by the Lord’s resurrection, and from that time it began to possess its festival character [Col. 0760C].

The souls of all the saints are indeed in rest before the resurrection of the body, but they are not yet engaged in that activity by which they will be invigorated after receiving their bodies.

The eighth day, which is also the first, signifies such activity because it does not take away that rest but glorifies it. Difficulty does not return with the body from the body, because corruption does not return either. For “this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality.”

Therefore, although before the Lord’s resurrection the holy Fathers, filled with the prophetic Spirit, were by no means unaware of the sacrament of the eighth day, by which the resurrection was signified—for a Psalm is also written [inscribed], “For the eighth,” infants were circumcised on the eighth day, and in Ecclesiastes it is said, with reference to the two Testaments, “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight”—nevertheless it was reserved and hidden [it was hidden from them], and only the celebration of the Sabbath was handed down, because at that time there was the rest of the dead [Col. 0760D].

No one had yet risen [until Christ came]—he who, having risen from the dead, would die no more, and over whom death would have no further dominion. Thus, after such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body—so that it might go before, in the Head of the Church, what the body of the Church would hope for at the end—the Lord’s Day also, that is, the eighth, which is also the first, began to be celebrated.

The reason is also understood why, in the celebration of Easter, when they are commanded to kill and eat a sheep [a lamb], which most clearly prefigures the Lord’s Passion, they were not commanded to observe it in such a way that they should take care that a Sabbath occur and that it coincide with the third week of the month of new things, so that the Lord might rather mark by his Passion that same day—the Lord who had also come to declare the Lord’s Day, that is, the eighth day, which is also the first [Col. 0761A].

Consider, then, the most sacred three-day period: the crucified, the buried, and the raised. What the cross signifies we enact in the present life; what the burial and resurrection signify we undertake in faith and hope.

For now it is said to a human being: “Take up your cross and follow me.” The flesh is crucified when our members that are upon the earth are put to death: fornication, uncleanness, lust, greed, and other such things, concerning which he likewise says: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.”

Hence he also says of himself: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” Elsewhere he says: “Knowing that our old self was crucified together with him on the cross, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin” [Col. 0761B].

As long, therefore, as our works are directed toward destroying the body of sin, as long as the outward person is being corrupted so that the inward person may be renewed, it is the time of the cross.

These are good works, certainly, but they are still laborious; their reward is rest.

In the ancient Scriptures no time was prescribed for celebrating Easter except from the fourteenth Moon of the month of new things through the twenty-first. In the Gospel, however, since it is clear on which day the Lord was crucified, was in the tomb, and rose again, the observance of those actual days was also added through the councils of the Fathers, and it was established throughout the entire Christian world that Easter ought to be celebrated in this manner [Col. 0761C].

Lent, certainly, possesses the authority of fasting, both from the fasts of Moses and Elijah in the ancient books and from the Gospel, since the Lord fasted for the same number of days, demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets.

The Law is understood in the person of Moses, and the Prophets in the person of Elijah; between them he appeared gloriously on the mountain, so that it might stand out more clearly that which the Apostle says of him: “Having testimony from the Law and the Prophets.”

At what part of the year, then, could the observance of Lent more appropriately be established than immediately adjacent and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For in it this laborious life is signified, a life requiring self-restraint, so that we may fast from friendship with the world, which certainly never ceases to flatter deceptively, scatter the cosmetics of allurements around us, and boast [Col. 0761D].

I think that this life is represented by the number forty for the following reason. The number ten, in which the perfection of our blessedness exists—as it does in the number eight, because it returns to the first—when multiplied by four, appears to express that the creature, represented by the number seven, adheres to the Creator, in whom the unity of the Trinity is manifested, and who is to be proclaimed throughout the temporal world.

This world is bounded by the four winds, established by the four elements, and varied by the four seasonal cycles. Four times ten is completed in forty. But when forty is calculated through its parts, [it adds] added to the ten itself, it makes fifty, as though the reward of labor and self-restraint.

For it was not without purpose that the Lord himself spent forty days after his resurrection on this earth and in this life with his disciples; and after he ascended into heaven, when ten days had intervened, he sent the promised Holy Spirit when the day of Pentecost was complete [Col. 0762A].

That fiftieth day contains another sacrament: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and when one returns to the beginning, which is the eighth, also the first, fifty days are completed. These are celebrated after the Lord’s resurrection.

Now, as a figure not of labor but of rest and joy, the fasts are relaxed, and we pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection. Hence this practice is observed at the altar on all the Lord’s Days, and “Alleluia” is sung, signifying that our future activity will consist in nothing but praising God, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever 85 they will praise you” [Col. 0762B].

The fiftieth day is also commended in Scripture—not only in the Gospel, because the Holy Spirit came then, but also in the ancient books. For there too, after they had celebrated Easter by killing the lamb, fifty days are counted up to the day on which the Law was given on Mount Sinai to the servant of God Moses, written by the finger of God.

The true Pasch is celebrated, and after fifty days have intervened, the Holy Spirit is given for love. He is the finger of God, opposed to people who seek their own interests and therefore bear a harsh yoke and a heavy burden, finding no rest for their souls, because love does not seek what belongs to itself.

For this reason the temper of heretics is always restless [Col. 0762C]. The Apostle shows that they possess the endeavor of the magicians of Pharaoh when he says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, people corrupted in mind, disapproved with regard to the faith; but they will make no further progress. For their madness [folly] will be manifest to all, just as theirs was.”

Because through that corruption of mind they were [most restless] exceedingly wicked, they failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them. For when they failed, they said: “The finger of God is here.”

Just as the Holy Spirit, reconciled and appeased, grants rest to the gentle and humble in heart, so, when he is opposed and hostile to the harsh and proud, he torments them with restlessness.

That restlessness was signified by those very small flies, under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God” [here] [Col. 0762D].

Count, therefore, from the fourteenth day of the first month, on which Easter took place, to the third day of the third month, and you will find seventeen days of the first month, thirty of the second, and three of the third; these make fifty.

The Law is in the Ark; sanctification is in the Lord’s body, through whose resurrection future rest is promised to us. To receive that rest, love is inspired by the Holy Spirit.

“The Spirit had not yet been given,” because [when] Jesus had not yet been glorified. Hence that prophecy was sung: “Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the Ark of your sanctification.” Where there is rest, there is also sanctification. Therefore we have now received a pledge so that we may love and desire it.

All who are called to the kingdom [rest] of the other life, into which one passes from this life—the thing signified by Easter—are called in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0763A].

For this reason the number fifty, multiplied three times, with the triad itself added to heighten the sacrament, is also found in those great fish which the Lord, demonstrating the new life after his resurrection, commanded to be brought up on the right side. The nets were not torn, because then there will be no heretical restlessness.

Then the perfect and peaceful human being, purified in soul and body by the Lord’s pure words—silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold—will receive the denarius as his reward, so that there are seventeen.

In this number also, as in others that display multiple figures, a wonderful sacrament is found. Not without reason, moreover, the seventeenth Psalm alone is read in full in the Books of Kings, because it signifies that kingdom in which we will have no adversary [Col. 0763B].

Its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

For who is represented in David except the one who came according to the flesh from the seed of David? He still suffers enemies in his body, which is the Church.

Hence a voice sounded from heaven to that persecutor whom he struck down with his voice and, transferring him into his own body, in a certain manner consumed: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”

But when will this body of his be delivered from the hand of all its enemies, except when that final enemy, death, is also destroyed?

The number of the one hundred and fifty-three fish belongs to that time. For the seventeenth number itself, rising into a triangle, completes the sum of one hundred and fifty-three [Col. 0763C].

Add together all the intermediate numbers as you ascend from one to seventeen and you will find this: add two to one, and the result is three; add three, and the result is six; add four, and the result is ten; add five, and the result is fifteen; add six, and the result is twenty-one; continue adding the remaining numbers in this way, and, when the seventeenth itself is included, the result is one hundred and fifty-three.

These matters are held with the strongest authority from Scripture: Easter and Pentecost. For just as the consensus of the Church strengthened the observance of those forty days before Easter, so also it established that the eight days of the newly baptized should be distinguished from the others, that is, that the eighth should harmonize with the first.

The practice of singing “Alleluia” in the Church during those fifty days alone is not observed everywhere; in some places it is sung variously on other days as well, but during those days it is certainly [everywhere] sung.

Whether we pray standing both on those days and on all the Lord’s Days is observed everywhere, I do not know. Nevertheless, I have stated, as best I could, what practice the Church follows in this matter, and I think it is clear [Col. 0763D].

## CHAPTER CXXVII

### On those who cast lots by reading from the Gospel pages, from the same Book II addressed to Januarius

As for those who cast lots by reading from the Gospel pages: although it is preferable that they do this rather than rush to consult demons, nevertheless this practice also displeases me—to wish to turn the divine oracles, which speak for the sake of another life, toward secular business and the vanity of this present life.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII

### That in Genesis the day began with light, whereas now days are reckoned from the nights, from a sermon to the people at the Easter vigil

[Col. 0764A]

It must be explained why we keep vigil with such great solemnity especially on this night: no Christian doubts that the Lord Christ rose from the dead on the third day. The Gospel bears witness that this happened on this night. For there is no doubt that the whole day is reckoned from the preceding night—not according to the order of the days described in Genesis, although there too darkness came first. For “darkness was over the abyss” when God said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be; but because that darkness was not yet night—for day had not yet preceded it—God divided the day between light and darkness. First he called the light “day,” then the darkness “night,” and, from the appearance of light until the following morning, the day was counted as one day.

It is clear that those days began with light and, after the light had passed, each was brought to an end at morning. But after the human being, created from the light of righteousness, turned aside into the darkness of sin—and when Christ’s grace frees us from those darknesses—it came about that we now reckon days from nights, because we strive to come not from light to darkness but from darkness to light; and, with the Lord’s help, we hope this will happen, as the Apostle says: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light.”

Thus the day of the Lord’s Passion, on which he was crucified, followed its own night, which had already passed; and so it came to a close and was completed [Col. 0764C] up to the Parasceve, which the Jews also call the “pure supper.” Beginning the observance of the Sabbath at the beginning of that night, then the day of the Sabbath, itself beginning from its own night, ended in the evening of the night that was beginning, which belongs to the beginning of the Lord’s Day, since the Lord consecrated it by the glory of his resurrection.

It is therefore the memory of that night, belonging to the beginning of the Lord’s Day, that we now celebrate in this solemn observance. We spend awake the night on which the Lord rose, and we meditate upon that life of which we spoke shortly before, where there is neither death nor sleep, 86 the life which he began for us in his flesh and inaugurated by rising from the dead in such a way that he would no longer die and death would no longer rule over him.

For when those who loved him and sought him came at dawn to his tomb, they did not find his body [Col. 0764D] and received from the angels the reply that he had already risen, it is clear that he rose during the night whose final part was that dawn. By keeping watch a little longer for him as he rose, we offer him a hymn, so that we may reign with him by living without end.

But even if, perhaps, during these hours in which we conduct this vigil his body was still in the tomb and he had not yet risen, nevertheless our keeping vigil is not inappropriate, because he slept so that we might keep watch; he died so that we might live.

## CHAPTER CXXIX  
### How, according to the figure of Jonah, three days and three nights are reckoned in the Lord’s Passion, from the first book of the *Questions on the Gospel*, title 7

“For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.”

Take the part of the day of Friday on which he was buried, together with the preceding night, as one night and day; that is, count the entire day of the Sabbath, night and day; and then count the night of the Lord’s Day together with the day that was dawning. By taking a part for the whole, you thus have three days and three nights.

For when ten months of pregnancy are mentioned, nine are complete, but the beginning of the tenth is counted as the whole tenth month. Likewise, when one evangelist says that the Lord’s manifestation on the mountain took place “after six days,” while another says “after eight days,” the first counts the later part of the first day—on which the Lord promised that this would happen—and the earlier part of the final day—on which what he promised was fulfilled—as complete days. Thus you should understand [Col. 0765B] that the one who said “after six days” counted only the intervening days, whereas the other counted days that had been completed in their entirety.

For in Genesis the day begins with light and ends with darkness, signifying the human fall; now, however, it proceeds from darkness to light, as it is said that light shines from darkness [or: becomes clear from darkness], because the human being, freed from sins, arrives at the light of righteousness.

## CHAPTER CXXX  
### On the Providence of God

It can happen that, through a wicked person, divine providence both punishes and assists. For the impiety of the Jews both brought Judas to ruin and became a means of salvation for the Gentiles.

Likewise, it can happen that divine providence, through a good person, both condemns and helps, as the Apostle says: [Col. 0765C] “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life, but to others the fragrance of death unto death.”

But since every tribulation is either the punishment of the wicked or the training of the righteous—for the same threshing instrument crushes the chaff and separates the grain from the chaff, which is why tribulation receives its name—and since, again, peace and freedom from worldly troubles both benefit the good and corrupt the wicked, divine providence regulates all these things according to the merits of souls.

Nevertheless, the good do not choose for themselves the ministry of tribulation, nor do the wicked love peace. Therefore those through whom something they do not know is brought about receive not the reward of the justice that is referred to God, but the reward of their own ill will. Likewise, what harms someone even though good people wish to benefit that person is not counted against the good; rather, the reward of benevolence is attributed to their good intention.

Thus the rest of creation, according to the merits of rational souls, is either perceived or hidden, troublesome or beneficial. For since the supreme God administers well everything he has made, there is nothing disordered and nothing unjust in the universe, whether we know it or do not know it. The sinful soul is offended in a particular part of it. Yet because, according to its merits, the soul is placed where it is fitting for such a soul to be, and suffers what it is just for such a soul to suffer, the whole kingdom of God is not disfigured by any ugliness of its own.

Therefore, since we do not know everything that the divine order does well on our behalf, in our good will alone we act according to the law; in other respects we are acted upon according to the law, while the law itself remains unchangeable and governs all mutable things with the most beautiful ordering. [Col. 0766A] “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

### Why the wicked sometimes prosper and the good suffer  
### From the sermon *On the Providence of God*

Above all, we should believe what piety proclaims: that a judgment will plainly be revealed in the future. For now we see human prosperity and disaster shared indiscriminately by good and wicked alike, as though without any judgment; yet God’s justice—whose providence is so conspicuous even in small matters—cannot possibly leave greater matters drifting about indiscriminately without judgment.

What is greater, not only in human nature but also in angelic nature, than that the wicked should be punished with a just misery and the good should enjoy blessedness? Therefore, when things are now apparently well with a wicked person, this is a hidden punishment, a false happiness; and when things are badly with a good person, the reward of piety is not denied, but the endurance of piety is increased for greater rewards.

Again, when a wicked person sometimes suffers evil in this life, it is either correction or punishment for sins. When things are well with a good person, this is not the certain joy of the heavenly homeland, but merely some consolation in this dangerous pilgrimage.

If unbelieving impiety considered these and similar matters, it would not deny divine providence in the administration of human affairs, nor persist in its dark and deadly powers against the light and life of wisdom.

Let the unbelieving person consider something that cannot be claimed to have been instituted by human beings, lest he deny that God gives order to human affairs: the God who taught bees to arrange the cells of their honeycombs with such marvelous order. Who gave human beings the capacity to be offended by disordered things and to take delight in the order of things? Did they not find this within the nature of their own soul, which they did not make for themselves?

Why, then, does a person refuse to believe that God governs human affairs because he does not find order in human affairs, unless it is because he naturally knows how to prefer ordered things to disordered things? Does a human being therefore judge that ordering, rather than confusion, is more appropriate to divine works? Does God not have an ordered judgment concerning all human beings, who created in each person the sense of order? He certainly does; he certainly does. Let piety have no doubt, even if weakness cannot comprehend it.

We praise the works of craftsmen when we can inspect them; but we marvel at the works of engineers, and unless they are opened up and displayed, we wonder that they could have accomplished what seems impossible. Why, then, do we judge so rashly concerning God’s judgments? Why do we hasten to deny the order of divine work wherever we cannot see it, praising the Creator’s power in the leaves of trees but refusing to believe that it is present in human affairs? Why do we not rather believe that the order of human affairs proceeds in an inscrutable and hidden way—an order whose immensity we cannot comprehend and whose concealment we cannot penetrate?

Yet the orders of things established by God, visible things from which hidden things may be inferred, strike even the eyes of the impious. [Col. 0766D]

### What Solomon debated in Ecclesiastes concerning the good and evil things that are shared in this life  
### From Book XX of *The City of God*

Now, when not only are the good found amid evil and the wicked amid good, which seems unjust, but also evil frequently befalls the wicked and good befalls the good, the judgments of God become still more inscrutable and his ways unsearchable.

Although, therefore, we do not know by what judgment God either does or permits these things to happen—he in whom there is supreme power, supreme wisdom, and supreme justice, with no weakness, recklessness, or injustice—we nevertheless learn beneficially not to value highly either the good or the evil that we see shared by good and wicked alike, but to seek those good things that belong to the good and to flee most especially those evils that are proper to the wicked.

When we come to that judgment whose time is properly called the Day of Judgment, and sometimes the Day of the Lord, not only will everything judged then appear to be most just, but also everything judged from the beginning and everything that is still to be judged up to that time will be revealed as most just.
