There it will also become clear how just God’s judgment is when so many, indeed almost all, of God’s just judgments now escape the perception and understanding of mortals, even though in this matter the faith of the devout does not fail to recognize that what is hidden is just.

The most wise King Solomon of Israel, who reigned in Jerusalem, began the book called *Ecclesiastes*, which is also held by the Jews among the canon of the sacred writings, in this way: “Vanity of vanities; everything is vanity. What abundance does a person have from all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” As he connected other matters with this statement, recalling the troubles and errors of this life and the passing away of time, in which nothing solid and nothing stable is retained, he also lamented in a certain way, amid this vanity of things under the sun, that although there is an abundance of wisdom over folly, just as there is an abundance of light over darkness, and although the wise person’s eyes are in his head while the fool walks in darkness, nevertheless one fate overtakes them all in this life that is lived under the sun. In this way he signified the evils that we see shared by good and wicked alike.

He also says that the good suffer evil as though they were wicked, while the wicked obtain good things as though they were good, speaking as follows:

“There is,” he says, “a vanity that has occurred upon the earth: there are righteous people upon whom what happens to the wicked has come, as though it were the deed of the wicked; and there are wicked people upon whom what happens to the righteous has come, as though it were the deed of the righteous. I said that this too is vanity.”

The most wise man devoted this entire book to explaining this vanity, as much as seemed sufficient—not for any other reason than that we might desire the life that has no vanity beneath this sun, but truth beneath the one who made this sun.

In this vanity, then, would not a human being, made like that same vanity by the just and righteous judgment of God, fade away? Yet during the days of his vanity it makes a very great difference whether he resists or obeys the truth, and whether he is without true piety or shares in it—not for the sake of acquiring the good things or avoiding the evils of this life, which pass away in vanity, but for the sake of the future judgment, through which good things will remain without end for the good and evil things without end for the wicked.

Finally, this wise man concluded the book by saying: “Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole human being, because God will bring every work into judgment, including every neglected thing, whether good or evil.” [Col. 0768A]

What could have been said more briefly, more truthfully, or more beneficially? “Fear God,” he says, “and keep his commandments, because this is the whole human being.” Whoever exists is this: a keeper, certainly, of God’s commandments; for whoever is not this is nothing.

Such a person is not reformed according to the image of truth, but remains in the likeness of vanity, because God will bring every work—that is, everything done by a human being in this life—into judgment, whether good or evil; “including every neglected thing,” that is, even every person who here appears contemptible and therefore is not noticed, because God sees even that person, does not despise him, and does not pass him by when he judges.

## CHAPTER CXXXI  
### By what sayings the judgment of the Lord to take place at the end of the world is declared  
### Also from Book XX of *The City of God*

When the Savior rebuked the cities in which he had performed great miracles, but which had not believed, and preferred foreigners to them, he said: “Nevertheless I tell you: it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.”

Shortly afterward he said to another city: “Amen, I tell you: it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

Here he most clearly proclaims that the Day of Judgment will come. Elsewhere he says: “The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. The Queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here.”

Here we learn two things: that the judgment will come, and that it will come together with the resurrection of the dead. When he said these things concerning the Ninevites and the Queen of the South, he was undoubtedly speaking of the dead, whom he nevertheless foretold would rise on the Day of Judgment. He did not say “they will condemn” because they themselves would sit in judgment, but because this generation would rightly be condemned by comparison with them.

Again, elsewhere, when speaking of the present mingling of good and wicked people and their subsequent separation—which will certainly take place on the Day of Judgment—he used the example of wheat that had been sown and weeds that had been sown over it. Explaining this to his disciples, he said: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is [here] the world,” and so on up to the passage where he says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Here he did not name the judgment or the Day of Judgment, but he expressed it much more clearly through the events themselves and foretold that it would occur at the end of the world. Again he said to his disciples: “Amen, I tell you: you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

Here we learn that Jesus will judge together with his disciples. Hence elsewhere he said to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.”

Nor, because he said that they would sit upon twelve thrones, should we think that only twelve men will judge with him. For by the number twelve a certain entirety of the multitude of judges is signified, on account of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is usually signified. These two parts—three and four—multiplied one by the other produce twelve. For four times three and three times four are both twelve, as is any other numerical relationship of this twelve that may be found to apply to the matter.

Otherwise, since we read that Matthias the apostle was appointed in the place of Judas the betrayer, will the Apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them, have no place from which to judge? He clearly shows that he belongs with the other saints to the number of judges when he says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?”

The same reasoning applies to those who are to be judged in this number twelve. It does not follow that, because it was said “judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth among them, will not be judged, or that they will judge only that people and not the other nations as well.

When he says “in the regeneration,” he undoubtedly wishes the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the term “regeneration.” For our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption just as our soul has been regenerated through faith.

I pass over many things that appear to be spoken about the final judgment in such a way that, when carefully considered, they are found to be ambiguous or to pertain more properly to something else—whether to the Savior’s coming, by which throughout this whole period he comes in his Church, that is, gradually and little by little in his members, since the whole Church is his body, or to the destruction of earthly Jerusalem. For when he speaks about that event, he often speaks as though he were speaking about the end of the world and that final and great Day of Judgment. It is altogether impossible to distinguish the matters unless everything similarly said about this subject by the three evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke is compared with everything else.

One of them explains more obscurely what another sets forth more plainly, so that it becomes evident from what source statements concerning one and the same matter are drawn. I have made some effort to do this in a letter that I wrote in reply to the blessed-memory man Hesychius, bishop of the city of Salona. The title of that letter is *On the End of the World*.

## CHAPTER CXXXII  
### The differing opinions of three faithful servants who estimate the time of the Lord’s coming  
### From the letter to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, *On the End of the World*

The Lord’s coming must therefore be loved and awaited, as you piously exhort, declaring that great blessedness belongs to those who love his coming and adducing the Apostle’s testimony, whose words you quote as follows:

“From now on a crown of righteousness has been laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love the Lord’s coming.”

Then, as you recall from the Gospel, “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.” And the prophet says: “For behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth over the nations, but in you the Lord will appear, and his majesty will be seen in you.”

Likewise it is written: “Those who wait for the Lord will rejoice with strength; they will grow wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not hunger.” [Col. 0770A]

You say this with complete piety and truth, commending the blessedness of those who love the Lord’s coming. But those to whom the Apostle said, “Do not be quickly shaken in mind, as though the Day of the Lord were imminent,” also certainly loved the Lord’s coming. When the teacher of the Gentiles said this, he was not breaking them away from that love with which he wanted them to be inflamed. He therefore did not want them to believe those from whom they heard that the Day of the Lord was imminent, lest perhaps, when the time they believed he would come had passed and they did not see him come, they should suppose that the other promises made to them were also false and despair of the reward of their faith.

Therefore it is not the person who asserts that the Lord is near, nor the person who asserts that he is not near, who loves the Lord’s coming, but rather the one who, whether it is near or far off, awaits it with sincere faith, firm hope, and ardent love.

For if the Lord is loved all the more the more strongly one believes and proclaims that he will come sooner, then those who were saying that his coming was already imminent loved him more than those whom the Apostle forbade to believe them—or than the Apostle himself, who certainly did not believe this.

If, therefore, it is hidden when the entire world, from sea to sea, will be filled with the fruitfulness and growth of the Church, then undoubtedly it is hidden when the end will come; for it will not come before that.

But to disclose to you, as a holy man of God and a most sincere brother, what I think about this question: error must be avoided in either direction, insofar as a human being can avoid it—whether one believes that the Lord will come sooner or later than he actually will.

Yet I do not think that someone is in error when he knows that he does not know something, but when he thinks he knows what he does not know.

Let us therefore remove from our midst that wicked servant who says in his heart, “My master is delaying his coming,” and who dominates his fellow servants and joins them in feasting and drunkenness. This man undoubtedly hates his master’s coming.

With that wicked servant removed, let us place before our eyes three good servants, diligently and soberly caring for their master’s household, thirsting for his coming, awaiting it watchfully, and loving it faithfully. Suppose that one of them thinks the Lord will come sooner, another later, while the third confesses his ignorance about the matter.

Although all agree with the Gospel, since they all love the Lord’s manifestation and await it eagerly and watchfully, let us nevertheless see which one agrees with it more fully.

One says: “Let us keep watch and pray, because the Lord will come sooner.”

Another says: “Let us keep watch and pray, because this life is short, even though the Lord will come later.”

The third says: “Let us keep watch and pray, because this life is both short and uncertain, and we do not know the time when the Lord will come.”

The Gospel says: “Watch, keep awake, and pray, for you do not know when the time will be.”

I ask you: what else do we hear this third servant saying than what we hear the Gospel saying? All of them, out of their desire for the kingdom of God, want what the first thinks to be true; but the second denies it. The third does not deny any of these things, but confesses that he does not know which of them is speaking the truth.

Accordingly, if what the first predicted takes place, the second and the third will rejoice with him. For they all love the Lord’s manifestation, and both will rejoice that what they love has come sooner.

But if it does not happen, and what the second was saying begins to appear true, we must fear that, during the delay itself, those who had believed what the first said may become confused and begin to think not that the Lord’s coming is delayed, but that there will be no coming at all. You see how great the destruction of souls would be.

If they have such great faith that they turn to what the second predicted and faithfully and patiently await the Lord even while he delays, they will nevertheless be overwhelmed by the reproaches, insults, and mockery of enemies who turn many weak people away from the Christian faith by saying that the kingdom was promised to them as falsely as it had been falsely said that the Lord would come quickly. [Col. 0771B]

Those, however, who believe what the second says—that the Lord will come later—will not be disturbed in faith at all if this is found to be false and the Lord comes sooner; instead, they will enjoy unexpected joy.

Therefore the person who says that the Lord will come sooner speaks more desirably, but dangerously if he is mistaken. Would that it were true, because it will be painful if it is not true.

The person who says that the Lord will come later, yet believes, hopes for, and loves his coming, is certainly mistaken even about his delay—but he is happily mistaken. He will have greater patience if the matter turns out this way, and greater joy if it does not. Thus, among those who love the Lord’s manifestation, the first is heard more sweetly, while the second is trusted more safely.

The person who confesses that he does not know which of these things is true desires the one and endures the other; he is wrong in none of them, because he neither affirms nor denies any of them.

I ask you not to despise me as such a person. I too love you for affirming what you desire to be true, and the more I love what you promise, the more I do not want you to be mistaken, because I see how dangerous it would be if you were mistaken.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII  
### What the first resurrection and the second resurrection are  
### From Book XX of *The City of God*, among other passages and at the relevant place

“Amen, amen, I tell you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself [or: in himself personally], so he has granted the Son to have life in himself.”

He is not yet speaking about the second resurrection, that is, the resurrection of bodies, which will occur at the end, but about the first, which is now taking place. To distinguish it, he says: “The hour is coming, and now is.” This resurrection is not of bodies but of souls.

For souls too have their own death in impiety and sins. According to this death, those people were dead of whom the same Lord says: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead,” so that the dead in soul might bury the dead in body.

On account of these people, therefore, who are dead in soul through impiety and iniquity, he says: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” By “those who hear” he means those who obey, who believe, and who persevere to the end.

Here he makes no distinction between good and wicked people. For it is good for all to hear his voice and live toward a life of piety, passing from the death of impiety. Concerning this death the Apostle Paul says: “Therefore all have died, and he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again.”

All, therefore, have died in sins, no one whatsoever being excepted, whether through original sins or through sins added by the will, whether through ignorance or knowledge, by failing to do what is just. And for all the dead, one who was alive died—one who had no sin at all—so that those who live through the remission of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all on account of our sins and rose again on account of our justification.

Thus, believing in him who justifies the ungodly, we may be justified from impiety and, as though made alive from death, belong to the first resurrection [Col. 0772B], which is now taking place.

For only those who will be blessed forever belong to this first resurrection. To the second resurrection, about which he is about to speak, he will teach that both the blessed and the miserable belong. The first is an act of mercy; the second is an act of judgment.

For this reason it is written in the Psalm: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.” Concerning this judgment he then adds: “And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

Here he shows that he will come to judge in the flesh in which he came to be judged. For this is why he says, “because he is the Son of Man.” Then he continues with the passage under discussion:

“Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”

This is the judgment that shortly before he had designated as condemnation, as he does now, when he says: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but passes from death to life.” That is, by belonging to the first resurrection, through which one now passes from death to life, such a person will not come into condemnation, which he signified by the term “judgment,” just as in the present passage where he says, “Those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment,” that is, of condemnation.

Let the person who does not wish to be condemned in the second resurrection rise in the first.

“For the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live”—that is, they will not come into condemnation, which is called the second death. Into this death those who do not rise in the first resurrection, which is the resurrection of souls, will be cast after the second resurrection, which will be the resurrection of bodies.

The hour is coming—here he does not say “and now is”—because it will be at the end of the world, that is, at the final and greatest judgment of God, when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth.

He did not say, as he did concerning the first resurrection, “and those who hear will live.” For not all will live—that is, with the life which, because it is blessed, alone deserves to be called life. Of course, they could not hear and come forth from the tombs with their flesh rising again without possessing some kind of life.

But why will not all live? He teaches this in what follows: “Those who have done good,” he says, “to the resurrection of life”—these are the ones who will live. “But those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment”—these are the ones who will not live, because they will die the second death.

They did evil because they lived evilly; they lived evilly because they did not live again in the first resurrection, which is now taking place among souls, because they did not remain to the end in the first [resurrection], or in that in which they rose (*resurrexerunt*; variant *revixerant*, “had come alive again”) [syntax uncertain].

Therefore, just as there are two regenerations, of which I have already spoken above—one according to faith, which now takes place through baptism, and the other according to the flesh, which will take place through its incorruption and immortality in the great and final judgment—so there are also two resurrections.

The first is now taking place and is the resurrection of souls; it does not permit those who belong to it to enter the second death. The second is not taking place now but will occur at the end of the world; it is not the resurrection of souls but of bodies. Through the final judgment it will send some into the second death and others into that life which has no death.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV  
### The two resurrections and the thousand years  
### From Book XX of *The City of God*
The evangelist John likewise spoke of these two resurrections in the book called the Apocalypse, in such a way that its first resurrection, misunderstood by some of our people, was moreover turned into certain ridiculous fables. For in the book mentioned the apostle John says:

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a chain in his hand. And he seized that dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, [Col. 0773C] bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, shut him in, and set a seal over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were ended. After this he must be released for a short time.

“And I saw thrones, and those seated upon them, and judgment was given to them; and the souls of those who had been killed because of the testimony of Jesus and because of the word of God, and of those who had not worshiped the beast or his image, nor received his mark upon their forehead or upon their hand. And they reigned with Jesus for a thousand years. The rest of them did not live until the thousand years were ended. This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in this first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.”

Those who, because of these words of the book, supposed that the first resurrection would be bodily were especially moved, among other considerations, by the number of a thousand years—as though it were necessary that there should be, among the saints, a sabbath-rest of that kind for so long a period: namely, a holy rest after the labors of the six thousand years since humanity was created and, on account of the merit of that great sin, was cast from the blessedness of paradise into the hardships of this mortality. For since it is written, “One day with the Lord is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day,” after six thousand years, as though six days had been completed, a kind of seventh-day sabbath would follow in the final thousand years, for the celebration of this sabbath by the resurrection of the saints.

This opinion would be in some measure tolerable if some spiritual delights were believed to await the saints in that sabbath through the presence of the Lord. [Col. 0774A] For we too once held this view. But when they say that those who will then rise will devote themselves to exceedingly immoderate bodily banquets, in which there will be such quantities of food and drink that they will not merely observe no moderation but will exceed even the bounds of credulity itself, these things can in no way be believed except by the carnal. [90] Those who are spiritual call such believers χιλιασταί, using a Greek word which, rendered word for word, we might call “millenarians.” It would take too long to refute them point by point; rather, we must now show how this Scripture should be understood.

The Lord Jesus Christ himself says: “No one can enter the house of a strong man and seize his goods unless he first binds the strong man”—wishing the strong man to be understood as the Devil, [Col. 0774B] because he was able to hold the human race captive; while his goods, which he was going to seize, were to be his faithful people, whom the Devil possessed in various sins and acts of impiety.

Therefore, so that this strong man might be bound, the apostle saw in the Apocalypse an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a chain in his hand. “And he seized,” he says, “that dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.” This means that he restrained and curbed his power to deceive and possess those who were to be set free.

As far as occurs to me, the thousand years may be understood in two ways. Either this event takes place in the final thousand years—that is, in the sixth millennium of years, as though in the sixth day, whose latter periods are now passing—[Col. 0774C] after which there will follow the sabbath that has no evening, namely, the rest of the saints that has no end; and he therefore called the final part of this millennium, as of a day, which remained until the end of the age, “a thousand years,” according to the manner of speech by which a part is signified by the whole.

Or else he used “a thousand years” for all the years of this age, so that by a perfect number the fullness of time itself might be indicated. For the number one thousand gives the solid square of the number ten. Ten multiplied by ten is one hundred, which is also a square figure, but a plane one. In order for it to rise in height and become solid, one hundred is again multiplied by ten, producing one thousand.

Moreover, if one hundred is sometimes used for totality—as when the Lord promises the one who leaves everything and [Col. 0774D] follows him that he will receive a hundredfold in this age—and the Apostle, explaining this in a way, says, “As having nothing, yet possessing everything”; and if it had already been said, “The whole world is the wealth of a faithful man,” how much more may one thousand be used for totality, since it contains the solidity of the tenfold square? This also helps us understand what is read in the Psalm: “He has remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations”—that is, for all generations.

“And he cast him,” he says, “into the abyss.” Certainly, he cast the Devil into the abyss. By this name is signified the innumerable multitude of the ungodly, whose hearts, in their hostility toward the Church of God, are profoundly evil—not because the Devil was not already there, but because he is said to have been sent there for this reason: that, excluded from believers, he began to possess the ungodly more fully. [Col. 0775A] For the Devil possesses more completely the one who is not only alienated from God but also hates those who serve God without cause.

“And he shut him in,” he says, “and set a seal over him, so that he would no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were ended.” He “shut him in” means that he forbade him to go out, that is, to transgress the prohibition. By adding that he “set a seal,” he seems to me to have signified that God wished it to remain hidden who belong to the Devil’s portion and who do not. This is entirely hidden in the present age, because it is uncertain whether the one who appears to stand will fall, and whether the one who appears to lie fallen will rise.

[Col. 0775B] The Devil is prohibited and restrained by this bond and confinement from deceiving those nations which belong to Christ, whom he previously deceived or held captive. For God chose these nations before the foundation of the world to rescue them from the power of darkness and transfer them into the kingdom of the Son of his love, as the Apostle says.

For who among the faithful does not know that the Devil even now deceives the nations and drags them with him into eternal punishment—not, however, those predestined to eternal life? Nor should it disturb us that the Devil often deceives even those who, already regenerated in Christ, are walking in the ways of God. For “the Lord knows those who are his”; from among these he deceives no one into eternal condemnation. The Lord knows them as God, to whom even future events are not hidden—not as a human being sees another human being in the present, if indeed he sees him at all, since he does not see his heart and does not know what the other will later become, nor does that person know even himself.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. [Col. 0775C] On the binding and release of the Devil

The Devil, then, was bound and shut up in the abyss for this purpose: that he might no longer deceive the nations from which the Church is constituted, whom he had previously held deceived before the Church existed. [For it was not said, “so that he might not deceive anyone,” but, “so that he might no longer deceive the nations.”]

Nor was it said, “so that he might not deceive,” he says, “the nations,” in which the Church was undoubtedly intended to be understood. “Until the thousand years are ended,” he says—that is, either what remains of the sixth day, which consists of a thousand years, or all the years during which this age is thereafter to run its course.

Nor should we understand what he says—“so that he might not deceive the nations until the thousand years are ended”—as though afterward he were going to deceive those particular nations from which the predestined Church consists, [Col. 0775D] from deceiving whom he has been prevented by that bond and confinement.

Either this was said according to a manner of expression found several times in Scripture, such as that in the Psalm: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us.” For when he has had mercy, the eyes of his servants will certainly not cease to be directed toward the Lord their God.

Or else this is the order of the words: “And he shut him in and set a seal over him until the thousand years are ended.” What he inserted—“so that he might no longer deceive the nations”—is to be understood as free from the connection of this order and separately, as though it had been added afterward, so that the whole sentence would read: “And he shut him in and set a seal over him until the thousand years are ended, so that he might no longer deceive the nations”; that is, he shut him in until the thousand years were ended [Col. 0776A] for the purpose of preventing him from deceiving the nations.

“After this,” he says, “he must be released for a short time.” If being bound and shut in means that the Devil cannot deceive the Church, will his release therefore mean that he will be able to deceive it? Far from it. The Church, predestined and chosen before the foundation of the world, of which it was said, “The Lord knows those who are his,” will never be deceived by him. Yet it will exist even at the time when the Devil is to be released, just as it has existed from the time it was established, and it will exist at all times in its members, who succeed one another through birth and death.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. What should be answered to those who think that the resurrection applies only to bodies and not also to souls, from the same book, *The City of God*, Book XX, among other passages, and concerning this passage

[Col. 0776B] “This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in this first resurrection”—that is, who is a participant in it. The participant in it is the one who not only rises again from the death that exists in sins but also remains in that life into which he has risen.

“Over these,” he says, “the second death has no power.” It therefore has power over the others, concerning whom he said above: “The rest of them did not live until the thousand years were ended.” For throughout this entire interval of time, which he calls a thousand years, however long any of them lived in the body, he did not rise again from the death in which impiety held him, so as to become, by rising again, a participant in the first resurrection, and so that the second death would have no power over him.

There are those who think that resurrection can be spoken of only [91] with reference to bodies, and therefore insist that this first resurrection too will take place in bodies. “Those things which fall,” they say, “are the things that rise again. Bodies fall by dying, and corpses are even called *cadavera* from *cadere*, ‘to fall.’ Therefore,” they say, “there can be no resurrection of souls, but only of bodies.”

But what do they say against the Apostle, who calls it resurrection? For according to the inner, not the outer, person, those to whom he said, “If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on the things that are above,” had certainly already risen. Elsewhere he expressed the same thought in other words, saying: “As Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life.”

Hence also comes the saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.”

But when they say that no one can rise again [Col. 0776D] unless he has fallen, and therefore think that resurrection pertains to bodies and not to souls because it is bodies [Col. 0776C] that fall, why do they not hear: “Do not depart from him, lest you fall”; “He stands or falls before his own master”; and “Let the one who thinks that he stands beware lest he fall”? For I think that this fall, which must be guarded against, occurs in the soul, not in the body.

If, then, resurrection belongs to those who fall, and souls also fall, it must certainly be acknowledged that souls too rise again.

After saying, “Over these the second death has no power,” he added: “But they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.” This was not said only of bishops and presbyters, who in the Church are now properly called priests. Rather, just as we call all Christians “christs” because of the [Col. 0777A] mystical chrism, so we call all priests, because they are members of the one Priest.

Of these the apostle Peter says: “You are a holy people, a royal priesthood.”

It is true that, briefly and in passing, he also indicated that Christ is Lord, when he said, “Priests of God and of Christ,” that is, of the Father and of the Son. Yet, because of the form of a servant, just as he became the Son of Man, so Christ also became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. We have spoken of this matter more than once in this work.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. On Gog and Magog, whom the Devil, released near the end of the age, will incite to persecute the Church of God, from the same Book XX

“And when the thousand years are ended, Satan will be released from his prison [Col. 0777B] and will go out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and will draw them into battle. Their number is like the sand of the sea.”

He will deceive them then for the purpose of drawing them into this war. For even before this he deceived them by whatever means he could, through many different evils. “He will go out” means that he will burst forth from the hiding places of his hatred into open persecution.

This will be the final persecution, when the final judgment is imminent, which the holy Church—that is, the entire city of Christ—will suffer throughout the whole world from the entire city of the Devil, however large each may be upon the earth.

The nations whom he calls Gog and Magog should not be understood as though they were certain barbarians settled in some part of the earth—whether the Getae and Massagetae, as some suspect because of the first letters of these names, or some other foreigners [and those not legally separated from Roman authority] [Col. 0777C] and not lawfully separated from Rome.

For these nations are signified as existing throughout the whole world, since he said, “the nations that are at the four corners of the earth,” and then identified them as Gog and Magog. We have discovered that the interpretation of these names is: Gog, “roof”; Magog, “from the roof”—as though the house were one thing and the one who proceeds from the house another.

The nations, therefore, are those in which we understood above that the Devil was enclosed as in an abyss; and he himself somehow rises up and proceeds from them, [so that he is, as it were, the roof, himself roof; the wording is uncertain]—so that they are the roof, with him proceeding from the roof.

But if we refer both names to the nations, assigning neither one to the nations and the other to the Devil, then the nations themselves are “the roof,” because in them the ancient enemy is enclosed and, in a way, covered; and they will be “from the roof” when they burst forth from concealment into open hatred.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. [Col. 0777D] Whether the fire said to have descended from heaven and consumed them pertains to the final judgment of the ungodly, from the same book

When he says: “And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city,” this does not mean that they came or will come to one particular place, as though the camp of the saints and the beloved city were to exist in some single location. For this is none other than the Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world.

Therefore, wherever it will then exist—which means among all the nations, [Col. 0778A] as signified by the name “the breadth of the earth”—there will be the camp of the saints. Wherever the city beloved by God is, there it will be surrounded by all its enemies, since they too will be among all the nations together with it, by the terrible force of that persecution. That is, it will be confined within the straits of tribulation, pressed, hemmed in, and enclosed, yet it will not abandon its warfare, which is called by the name “camp.”

But when he says, “And fire descended from heaven and consumed them,” this should not be thought to be the final punishment, which will occur when it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” Then they themselves will be cast into the fire; fire will not descend from heaven [upon them].

Here, however, “fire from heaven” is rightly understood as coming from the very steadfastness of the saints, by which they will not yield to their persecutors so as to carry out their [Col. 0778B] will. Heaven is a firmament, and by the steadfastness of the saints they will be tormented with the most ardent zeal, because they will not be able to draw Christ’s saints over to the side of Antichrist. This will be the fire that consumes them, and it will be from God, because it is by God’s gift that the saints become inseparable; hence [they will be tormented], the enemies are tormented.

For just as it is said in a good sense, “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” so, conversely, it is said in an evil sense, “Zeal has seized an uninstructed people.” Then the fire will consume those opposed to it.

This may also refer, apart from the fire of that final judgment, to the plague by which the persecutors of the Church will be struck when Christ has already come—those whom he will find alive upon the earth, when he kills Antichrist with the breath of his mouth. If this has been called fire descending from heaven and consuming them, even that will not be the final punishment of the ungodly, [Col. 0778C] but the punishment they will suffer after the resurrection of their bodies.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. What the Apostle wrote to the Thessalonians, and concerning the manifestation of Antichrist, from the same Book XX of *The City of God*

“We beseech you, brothers,” he says, “by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by spirit or by word or by a letter purportedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand. Let no one deceive you in any way, for unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—the one who opposes and exalts himself [Col. 0778D] above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God—do you not remember that when I was still with you I used to tell you these things?

“And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation [92] of his presence—him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness among those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.

“And therefore God will send them [Col. 0779A] a working of error, so that they may believe the lie and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.”

There is no doubt that he said these things concerning Antichrist, and that the day of judgment—which he calls “the day of the Lord”—will not come unless the one whom he calls the apostate comes first, plainly one who has apostatized from the Lord God.

If this may properly be said of all the ungodly, how much more may it be said of this one? But in what temple of God he will sit [as God] is uncertain: whether in the ruins of the temple built by King Solomon or in the Church. For the Apostle would not call the temple of some idol or demon “the temple of God.”

For this reason some wish Antichrist to be understood in this passage not as the ruler himself but, in a certain sense, as his entire body—that is, the multitude of human beings belonging to him, together with their own ruler. [Col. 0779B] They think it more correct to say, as it is in Greek, not “in the temple of God,” but “into the temple of God he will sit,” as though he himself were the temple of God, which is the Church; just as we say, “he sits into a friend,” meaning “as a friend,” or according to some other expression of this kind.

But when he says, “And now you know what restrains him,” that is, what delays him and what causes his manifestation to be postponed until his own time, you know: because he said that they knew, he did not wish to state it openly. Therefore we, who do not know what they knew, desire, but are unable, to reach with difficulty what the Apostle meant.

This is especially so because what he added makes the meaning more obscure. For what does this mean: “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst, and then the lawless one will be revealed”?

I openly confess that I do not know at all what he meant. Yet I will not conceal the conjectures of people that I have either heard or read.

Some think that this was said of the Roman Empire, and that the Apostle Paul therefore did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the accusation of having wished evil upon the Roman Empire, which was hoped to be eternal. They think that by saying, “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work,” he intended Nero, whose deeds already appeared to be those of Antichrist.

Hence some suspect that Nero will rise again and become Antichrist. Others do not think that he was killed but rather that he was withdrawn so that he would be thought dead, and that he is being kept alive in the vigor of the age he possessed when he was believed to have perished, until he is revealed [Col. 0779D] at his appointed time and restored to the kingdom.

But the great presumption of those who hold such opinions seems exceedingly strange to me.

Nevertheless, what the Apostle says—“Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst”—may not unreasonably be believed to have been said of the Roman Empire, as though he had said: “Let the one who now rules continue to rule until he is removed from the midst,” that is, until he is taken away; and then the lawless one will be revealed, whom everyone acknowledges to be Antichrist.

Others, however, think that both what he says, “you know what restrains him,” and “the mystery of iniquity is at work,” were spoken only of the wicked and hypocritical people who are in the Church, until they reach such a number as will make a great people for Antichrist. This, they say, is the mystery of iniquity, because it appears hidden.

[Col. 0780A] The Apostle therefore exhorts the faithful to persevere steadfastly in the faith they hold, saying: “Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst”—that is, until the mystery of iniquity, which is now hidden, goes out from the midst of the Church.

They think that this mystery is also referred to in what the evangelist John says in his Letter: “Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. From this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

Thus, they say, just as before the end, in this hour which John calls the last, many heretics went out from the midst of the Church—whom he calls many antichrists—so at that time all who will belong not [Col. 0780B] to Christ but to that final Antichrist will go out from it, and then he will be revealed.

One person therefore conjectures one way, another another way, concerning the obscure words of the Apostle. Yet there is no doubt about what he said: Christ will not come to judge the living and the dead unless his adversary, Antichrist, first comes to deceive the dead in soul, although it already belongs to the hidden judgment of God that they will be deceived by him.

For his coming will be, as it was said, “according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders, and with every deceit of unrighteousness among those who are perishing.”

Then Satan will be released, and through that Antichrist he will work with all his power—marvelously indeed, but deceitfully.

It is commonly debated whether the expressions “signs [Col. 0780C] and lying wonders” were used because he will deceive mortal senses through phantasms, so that he will appear to do what he does not do; or because those very wonders, even if they are genuine wonders, will lead into falsehood those who believe them, since they do not know that they could have been performed only by divine power, being unaware of the Devil’s power—especially when he has received a power as great as he never before possessed.

For when fire fell from heaven and in one stroke consumed the household of the holy Job together with his immense flocks of sheep, and when a whirlwind rushed upon the house, overthrowing it and killing his children, these were not phantasms, although they were works of Satan, to whom God had granted that power.

For what reason, then, these are called “lying signs and wonders” will be made clear at that time. But whatever the reason for the expression, those who deserved to be deceived [Col. 0780D] will be deceived by these signs and wonders, “because,” he says, “they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.”

The Apostle did not hesitate to add: “Therefore God will send them a working of error, so that they may believe the lie.” God will send it because, by his just judgment, God will permit the Devil to do these things, although the Devil will act according to an unjust and evil purpose.

“So that all may be judged,” he says, “who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.”

Accordingly, those who have been judged will be deceived, and those who have been deceived will be judged. They are deceived by those judgments of God which are secretly just and justly secret, by which, from the beginning of the sin of rational creation, he has never ceased to judge. But those who have been deceived will be judged at the final and manifest judgment through Christ Jesus, who will judge most justly, though he was judged most unjustly.

## CHAPTER CXL. [Col. 0781A] What the same Apostle taught in his First Letter to the same people concerning the resurrection of the dead, from the same Book XX

But in this passage the Apostle was silent about the resurrection of the dead. Writing to the same people in his First Letter, however, he says:

“We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

“For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have already fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead [who are in Christ] will rise in Christ first. Then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ [93] in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

These apostolic words very clearly show that the resurrection of the dead will occur when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead.

It is often asked whether those whom Christ will find alive here—whose person the Apostle represented in himself and in those who were then living with him—will never die at all, or whether, at the very moment when they are caught up in the clouds with those who rise to meet Christ in the air, they will pass to immortality through death with astonishing speed. [Col. 0781C]

For it cannot be said that it is impossible for them, while being carried upward through the air, to die and come to life again within that interval.

What he says, “And so we shall always be with the Lord,” should not be understood as though he said that we would always remain with the Lord in the air, since the Lord himself certainly will not remain there, because in coming he will pass through it.

They will go to meet him as he comes, not as he remains there. Rather, “so we shall be with the Lord” means that we shall be in this condition, possessing everlasting bodies, wherever we shall be with him.

With regard to the interpretation that even those whom the Lord will find alive here will, within that brief interval, suffer death and receive immortality, the Apostle himself does not seem to compel us when he says, “All will be made alive in Christ,” while elsewhere, speaking of the [Col. 0781D] resurrection of bodies, he says: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.”

How, then, will those whom Christ finds alive here be made alive through immortality, if they do not die, when we see that the statement, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies,” was made for this very reason?

Or, if we are correct in saying that only those human bodies are sown which, by dying in some manner, return to the earth—as is also expressed in the divine sentence pronounced upon the transgressor, the father of the human race: “You are earth, and to earth you will go”—then it must be admitted that those whom Christ will find not yet departed from their bodies when he comes are not bound by either these words of the Apostle or those from Genesis.

For, being caught up in the clouds above, they are not sown, since they do not go into the earth or return to it, whether they experience no death at all or die briefly in the air.

But another difficulty arises from what the same Apostle said when speaking to the Corinthians about the resurrection of bodies: “We shall all rise again,” or, as other manuscripts have it, “We shall all sleep.”

Since resurrection cannot occur unless death has preceded it, and since in that passage “sleep” can mean nothing other than death, how will all either sleep or rise again [Col. 0782A] if so many whom Christ will find in the body will neither sleep nor rise again?

If, therefore, we believe that the saints who will be found alive when Christ comes and who will be caught up to meet him will, in that very rapture, leave their mortal bodies and immediately return to those same bodies made immortal, we will encounter no difficulty [Col. 0782B] in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies,” or where he says, “We shall all rise again,” or, “We shall all sleep.”

For they too will not be made alive through immortality unless, however briefly, they first die; and consequently they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which will be preceded by their sleep, brief though it will be, yet not nonexistent.

Why should it seem incredible to us that such a multitude of bodies might, in a sense, be sown in the air and immediately there revive in immortality and incorruption, when we believe what the same Apostle states most openly: that the resurrection will occur “in the twinkling of an eye,” and that the dust of the most ancient corpses will return, with such ease and immeasurable speed, to limbs destined to live without end?

Nor should we think that those saints will be exempt from the sentence pronounced [Col. 0782C] upon humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you will go,” if the bodies of those who die do not fall into the earth. Rather, just as they will die in the very rapture, so they will rise again while being carried into the air.

For “to earth you will go” [that is], you will go, having lost your life, into that which you were before you received life; that is, once lifeless, you will be what you were before you were made living.

For God breathed into the face of the earth the breath of life when the human being [had been made] was made a living soul—as though it were said: “You are animated earth, which you were not; you will be lifeless earth, as you were”—that is, what all dead bodies are before they decay, and what those bodies too will be if they die, wherever they die, when they are deprived of the life they will immediately receive again.

Thus they will go into the earth, [Col. 0782D] because they will be earth from living human beings, just as that which becomes ash goes into ash, that which becomes old goes into old age, that which is made into a potsherd from clay goes into a potsherd, and we speak similarly in six hundred other cases [“drying up,” uncertain reading].

But how what we now conjecture as best we can according to the limited powers of our reasoning will actually occur—that will rather be revealed then, so that we may know it.

If we wish to be Christians, we must believe that the resurrection of the dead will occur, and that it will be a resurrection in the flesh, when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. But our faith concerning this matter is not therefore vain merely because we are unable perfectly to comprehend how it will occur.

## CHAPTER CXLI. [Col. 0783A] On the coming of Elijah before the judgment, through whose preaching, as he discloses the secrets of Scripture, the Jews will be converted to Christ, from the same book of *The City of God*

When he had urged them to remember the law of Moses, foreseeing that for a long time yet they would not receive it spiritually as they ought, he immediately added:

“And behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite before the coming of the great and glorious day of the Lord, who will turn the heart of the father toward the son, and the heart of the human being toward his neighbor, lest perhaps, when I come, I strike the earth utterly [with a curse].”

It is widely celebrated [Col. 0783B] in the discourse and hearts of the faithful that through this great and wondrous prophet Elijah, when the law has been spiritually explained to the Jews at the end of time before the judgment, they will believe in the true Christ—that is, in our Christ.

It is not without reason that he is expected to come before the advent of the Savior who will judge, since he is also rightly believed to be alive even now. For he was snatched away from human affairs in a fiery chariot, as Holy Scripture most clearly testifies.

When he comes, therefore, to explain spiritually the law which the Jews now understand carnally, he will turn “the heart of the father toward the son,” that is, the heart of the fathers toward the sons. The Seventy translators used the singular in place of the plural; and the meaning is that the sons too will understand the law in the way the fathers understood it—that is, the Jews in the way the fathers, namely the prophets, understood it, among whom Moses himself was also included.

Thus the heart of the fathers will be turned toward the sons when the understanding of the fathers is brought to the understanding [Col. 0783C] of the sons; and the heart of the sons will be turned toward their fathers when the sons agree with what the fathers understood.

The Seventy said: “And the heart of the human being toward his neighbor.” The fathers and sons are indeed very close to one another. Yet in the words of the Seventy translators, who translated prophetically, another and even more excellent meaning may be found: namely, that Elijah will turn the heart of God the Father toward the Son—not by causing the Father to love the Son, but by teaching that the Father loves the Son, so that the Jews too may love the one whom they previously hated, the same Christ who is ours.

For God now has, toward the Jews, a heart turned away from our Christ, because they think this [namely, that he is neither God nor the Son of God]. His heart will therefore then be turned toward the Son with respect to them, when they themselves, with hearts converted, learn the Father’s love for the Son.

But what is better understood by what follows—“and the heart of the human being toward his neighbor”—than the heart of the human being toward the human Christ? Although our God exists in the form of God, he deigned to take the form of a servant and thereby became also our neighbor.

This, then, is what Elijah will do, “lest [94] perhaps,” he says, “I come and strike the earth utterly.” For those who understand earthly things are earth, as the carnal Jews have been until now. From this fault came those murmurs against God, because they think that evil people please him and that the one who serves God is laboring in vain.

## CHAPTER CXLII. Whether bodies can remain perpetually in the burning of fire, from the same book, *The City of God*, Book XXI
What, then, shall I show by which unbelievers may be convinced that human bodies, endowed with life and animation, can not only never be dissolved by death but also endure the torments of everlasting fires? For they do not wish us to refer this to the power of the Almighty; rather, they demand that they be persuaded by some example. If we answer them that there are indeed animals that are corruptible because they are mortal, yet live amid fires; that a certain kind of worm is also found in the springs of hot waters, whose heat no one can touch with impunity; and that those creatures not only exist there without any injury to themselves but cannot exist outside those waters, they will either refuse to believe us if we cannot demonstrate it, or, if we are able either to show the creatures themselves to their eyes or to inform them through reliable witnesses, they will still insist, with the same unbelief, that this is not sufficient as an example of the matter under discussion; [Col. 0784A] for they will say that these animals neither live forever nor live in those heats with pain. They thrive, they say, in conditions suited to their nature; those elements do not torment them—as though it were not more incredible to thrive in such things than to be tormented by them. It is remarkable to suffer in fires and yet live; but it is more remarkable to live in fires and not suffer. If the former is believed, why not the latter also?

## CHAPTER 143. Whether the destruction of the flesh necessarily follows bodily pain

“But,” they say, “there is no body that can suffer pain and yet cannot die.” And how do we know this? For, concerning the bodies of demons, who can be certain whether they suffer pain when they confess that they are afflicted by great torments? [Col. 0784B]

If the answer is that no earthly body—that is, no solid and visible body—exists of such a kind, or, to express the matter in a single term, that there is no flesh which can suffer pain and yet cannot die, what else is being said than what human beings have inferred from bodily sensation and experience? They know no flesh except mortal flesh, and this is their entire reasoning: whatever they have not experienced, they suppose cannot exist (the printed variant *posse* adds “to be possible”).

For what kind of reasoning is it to make pain an indication of death, when it is rather an indication of life? Even if we ask whether whatever feels pain can live forever, it is nevertheless certain that everything that feels pain is alive, and that pain cannot exist except in a living thing. It is therefore necessary that what suffers pain be alive; but it is not necessary that pain cause death. For pain does not kill every one of these mortal—and certainly destined-to-die—bodies, and the reason why some pain can kill them is that the soul is joined to the body in such a way that it yields and departs under the greatest pains. The very structure of the limbs and vital organs is so fragile that it cannot withstand the force that produces great or extreme pain. [Col. 0784C]

But at that time the soul will be joined to such a body and in such a manner that, just as the bond will not be dissolved by any length of time, so it will not be broken by any pain. Therefore, even if there is now no flesh that can endure the sensation of pain and yet cannot die, there will then be flesh of a kind that does not now exist, just as there will then be a kind of death that does not now exist. It will not be no death at all, but everlasting death, when the soul will be unable to live because it does not possess God, and unable to escape bodily pains by dying. [Col. 0784D]

The first death drives the unwilling soul from the body; the second death holds the unwilling soul in the body. Both deaths have this in common: the soul suffers against its will what it does not wish to suffer from its body. These objectors observe that there is now no flesh that can suffer pain and yet cannot die, but they fail to observe (the printed *[non]* is “not”) that there is nevertheless something greater than the body that possesses such a condition: the soul itself, whose presence gives the body life and governance, and which can suffer pain but cannot die. Behold, then, a thing has been found which possesses the sensation of pain and yet is immortal. [Col. 0785A]

This, therefore, will also exist then in the bodies of the damned which we now know to exist in the souls of all. If we consider the matter more carefully, the pain called bodily pain belongs more properly to the soul. It is the soul that suffers, not the body, even when the cause of its suffering arises from the body and it suffers in the place where the body is injured. Thus, just as we speak of bodies that sense and bodies that live, although sensation and life come to the body from the soul, so we speak of bodies that suffer pain, although pain cannot belong to the body except through the soul.

The soul therefore suffers pain with the body in the place where something occurs that causes it to suffer [the source has the difficult wording “in that place of it,” *in eo loco ejus*]. It also suffers pain when it is alone in the body and, while the body remains unharmed, is saddened by some cause that is even invisible. It suffers pain even when it is not situated in a body: for certainly that rich man suffered pain in the underworld when he said, “I am tormented in this flame.” But a body without a soul does not suffer pain, nor does an animated body suffer pain without the soul. [Col. 0785B]

If, therefore, an argument for death were correctly derived from pain—so that death could occur because pain could occur—then dying would belong more properly to the soul, to which suffering pain also belongs more properly. But when that which can suffer pain more intensely cannot die, what force is there (the variant *aufert* means “takes away,” for *affert*, “brings”) in the reason why we should believe that those bodies, because they will be in pain, will therefore also die?

The Platonists did indeed say: “From earthly bodies and dying limbs come fear and desire, pain and joy.” Hence Virgil says:

> From these—that is, from the dying limbs of the earthly body—  
> they fear and desire, suffer pain, and rejoice.

But in the fourteenth book of this work we proved that, according to them, souls purified from every stain of the body nevertheless possess a dreadful desire by which they begin again to wish to return to bodies. Wherever desire can exist, pain can certainly exist as well. For frustrated desire—whether because it does not reach what it was striving toward, or because it loses what it had attained—is transformed into pain. [Col. 0785C]

Therefore, if the soul, which either alone or chiefly suffers pain, nevertheless possesses a certain immortality proper to its condition, those bodies will not be able to die merely because they will suffer pain. Finally, if bodies cause souls to suffer pain, why can they inflict pain upon them but not death? Is it not because it does not follow that whatever causes pain also causes death? Why, then, is it incredible that fires should be able to inflict pain upon those bodies without causing death, just as the bodies themselves cause souls to suffer pain without thereby forcing them to die? Pain, therefore, is not a necessary proof of the death that is to come. [Col. 0785D]

## CHAPTER 144. That in extraordinary matters the supreme ground for belief is the omnipotence of the Creator, from the same book, *The City of God*, book XXI

Why, then, should God be unable both to raise the bodies of the dead and to torment the bodies of the damned with eternal fire, when he made the world—in heaven, on earth, in the air, and in the waters—full of innumerable miracles, although the world itself is undoubtedly a greater and more excellent miracle than everything with which it is filled? [Col. 0786A]

But these people with whom, or against whom, we are dealing believe both that there is a Lord by whom the world was made and that there are gods made by him, through whom the world is administered by him [the variant prints *administrantur hic*, literally “are administered here”]. They do not deny—or even praise—the powers that produce worldly miracles, whether spontaneous, or commanded by worship and ritual of whatever kind, or even magical. Yet when we set before them the remarkable power of other things—things that are neither rational animals nor spirits endowed with reason, such as those of which we have mentioned a few—they are accustomed to reply: “This is the power of nature; their nature is such; these are the natural properties of those things.” [Col. 0786B]

Thus their entire explanation of why flame makes Agrigentine salt flow and water crackle is that this is its nature. Yet this seems rather to be contrary to the nature which gave salt the property of dissolving not in fire but in water, and gave fire the property of scorching, not water (the variant *torrere* is “to scorch,” in place of *torrorem*, “scorching”). “But,” they say, “the natural power of this salt is such that it undergoes these contrary effects.” [Col. 0786C]

The same explanation is given of the Garamantian spring, where one channel is cold by day and hot by night, each condition causing discomfort to those who touch it. The same is said of another spring which is cold to those who touch it and, like other springs, extinguishes a lighted torch, but which nevertheless, in a different and marvelous way, lights the same torch again after it has been extinguished.

The same is said of asbestos, which, although it has no fire of its own, nevertheless burns so intensely when it receives fire from elsewhere that it cannot be extinguished. The same explanation is offered for the other things that it would be tedious to recount: although an unusual power contrary to nature seems to reside in them, no explanation is given for them other than that this is their nature.

That is indeed a brief explanation, I admit, and a sufficient answer. But since God is the author of all natures, why do they not allow us to give a stronger explanation when they refuse to believe something as though it were impossible, and, when they demand an explanation from us, we reply that it is the will of Almighty God? The variant *volunt* would read, “why are they willing [for us] to give” it. [Col. 0786D] He is called Almighty for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills. He was able to create so many things which, unless they were displayed before our eyes or reported by witnesses whose testimony is still believed today, would certainly be thought impossible (the variant *si non* reads “if not,” for *nisi*, “unless”; *esse* supplies “to be” after “impossible”).

I have mentioned not only things that are quite unknown among us, but also things that are well known: lime, which boils in water but is cold in oil; the lodestone, which by some imperceptible attraction does not move a straw but seizes iron; the flesh of the peacock, which does not rot, although Plato’s flesh has rotted; straw so cold that it prevents snow from melting, yet so hot that it compels fruits to ripen; and a bright fire which, according to its brightness, whitens stones by cooking them, but, contrary to that same brightness, darkens many things by burning them. [Col. 0787A]

There is also the fact that black stains become conspicuous in shining oil, while black lines are similarly impressed upon bright silver. There is the fact that coals, when fire is applied to them, are transformed into opposites: from the most beautiful wood they become foul, from hard things fragile, and from things that can rot they become incapable of rotting.

I have mentioned these things also because I read them in the histories of the writers belonging to those against whom we are arguing. I wished to show how many such things—and how many of their kind—they believe, without any explanation being supplied, in the writings of their learned authors, while they do not deign to believe us when we say that Almighty God will do what surpasses their experience and perception, even though we provide no explanation. [Col. 0787B]

For what better and more powerful explanation can be given of such matters than to assert that the Almighty is able to do them and is said to be going to do what is read as having been foretold there, where many other things were foretold that he is shown to have accomplished? He himself will do it because he foretold that he would do it—he who promised things thought impossible and brought it about that unbelieving nations should believe things that were incredible.

But if they reply that they do not believe what we say about human bodies that will always burn and never die because we know that the nature of human bodies was established in a very different way, so that the explanation given for those marvelous natures cannot be applied here—namely, that “this is the natural power” or “this is the nature of the thing,” since we know that this is not the nature of human flesh—we do have an answer from the sacred writings. [Col. 0787C]

Human flesh itself was established differently before sin: namely, so that it could never suffer death. After sin, however, it was established differently, as it became known in the misery of this mortality, so that it could not retain everlasting life. Thus it will be established differently in the resurrection of the dead from the way in which it is known to us.

## CHAPTER 145. Whether it is just that the duration of punishments should not be longer than the duration of sins

Some of those against whom we defend the City of God consider it unjust that anyone should be condemned to eternal punishment for sins, however great, committed in a short time—as though any justice of law had ever required that a person be punished for as long a period as the period during which he committed the offense for which he is punished. [Col. 0787D]

Tullius writes that there are eight kinds of punishment in the laws: damages, imprisonment, lashes, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, and slavery. Which of these is restricted to a brief period according to the swiftness of each person’s sin, so that the offense is punished for exactly as long as it took to commit it—unless perhaps retaliation? For retaliation ensures that each person suffers what he has done. Hence the law says: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.”

It can happen that someone loses an eye through the severity of punishment in as short a time as he himself took, through the wickedness of his sin, to take it from another. But if it is reasonable to punish with lashes the kiss imposed upon another man’s wife, is not the person who did it in a moment of time beaten for an immeasurable number of hours, and is not the brief sweetness of pleasure punished by prolonged pain? [Col. 0788A]

What of imprisonment? Is each person to be judged as deserving imprisonment only for as long as he took to commit the act for which he deserved to be bound, when a slave may most justly spend years in fetters because, through a word or blow passing in an instant (*transeunter*, the variant, means “transiently”), he either provoked or struck his master?

Moreover, when damages, disgrace, exile, and slavery are often imposed in such a way that no pardon releases them, do they not appear, in proportion to the course of this life, similar to eternal punishments? They cannot be eternal precisely because the life of those punished by them is not extended forever. Yet the sins that are punished by the longest penalties are committed in the briefest time. [Col. 0788B]

No one has ever maintained that the torments of the guilty should end as quickly as the homicide, adultery, sacrilege, or any other crime was committed; for such matters are measured not by the length of time but by the magnitude of impiety and iniquity.

When someone is punished with death for a serious crime, do the laws assess his punishment by the brief delay in which he is killed—or do they assess it by the fact that they remove him forever from the society of the living? The variant *leges breve existimant* reads: “do the laws regard his punishment as brief?” What happens in this mortal city when people are removed by the punishment of the first death is what happens in that immortal City when people are removed by the punishment of the second death. [Col. 0788C]

For just as the laws of this City do not make it possible for someone who has been killed to be restored to it, so the laws of that City do not allow anyone condemned by the second death to be restored to its eternal blessedness.

“How, then,” they say, “is what your Christ said true: ‘With what measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you,’ if a temporal sin is punished by eternal punishment?” They fail to observe that the measure was spoken not because of an equal span of time but because of reciprocity in evil—that is, so that the person who has done evil may suffer evil. Yet the same measure can properly be understood in relation to the matter about which the Lord was speaking when he said this, namely, judgments and condemnations. [Col. 0788D]

Thus, one who judges and condemns unjustly, if he is judged and condemned justly, receives according to the same measure, although not the same thing that he gave: he acted through judgment and suffers through judgment. Although he carried out an unjust condemnation, he suffers a just condemnation.

## CHAPTER 146. On the magnitude of the first transgression, because of which eternal punishment is owed to all who are outside the grace of the Savior, from book XXI of *The City of God*

Eternal punishment seems harsh and unjust to human feelings because, in this weakness of our mortal senses, we lack that sense of the highest and purest wisdom by which one could perceive how great a crime was committed in that first transgression. [Col. 0788D]

For the more a human being enjoyed God, the greater was the impiety with which he abandoned God. He became deserving of eternal evil because he destroyed within himself a good that could have been eternal. Hence the entire mass of the human race was condemned, because the one who first lost this good was punished together with the offspring rooted in him. [Col. 0789A]

No one is freed from this just and deserved punishment except by mercy and unmerited grace. Thus the human race is divided so that in some it may be demonstrated what merciful grace can accomplish, and in others what just retribution can accomplish.

Both would not be demonstrated in everyone. For if all remained in the punishments of just condemnation, the merciful grace of the redeemer would appear in no one. Again, if all were transferred from darkness into light, the truth of retribution would appear in no one—a truth that is manifested precisely because there are far more in the former condition than in the latter, so that it may be shown what was owed to all. [Col. 0789B]

If this were repaid to all, no one could reproach the justice of the one who justly exacts vengeance. But because so many are freed from it, there is reason for the greatest thanksgiving to be offered for the free gift of the one who liberates.

## CHAPTER 147

That punishment for crime after death is not a cause of purification, in the same place

The Platonists, although they do not wish any sins to remain unpunished, nevertheless think that all punishments are imposed for correction, whether inflicted by human or divine laws, whether in this life or after death, if someone is spared here or punished in such a way that he is not corrected here.

Hence Virgil’s famous statement, where, after saying of earthly bodies and dying limbs that souls:

> From these they fear and desire, suffer pain, and rejoice;  
> enclosed in darkness and a blind prison, they do not take in the breezes  
> (*Suscipiunt*; a variant reads *Respiciunt*, “look back upon”).

He then continues and says:

> And even when life has departed with its final light—

that is, when this life has left them on the last day—

> Yet not every evil has left the wretched, nor have all  
> the bodily plagues wholly departed. Deep within, it is necessary
