> that many things long congealed should grow in them  
> through wondrous means.  
>   
> Therefore they are disciplined by punishments and pay the penalties  
> of their former evils. Some are spread out, empty,  
> suspended upon the winds; for others, beneath the vast abyss,  
> the polluted crime is washed away or burned up in fire. [Col. 0789C]

Those who hold this view wish all punishments after death to be purifying punishments, so that, because the elements above the earth are water, air, and fire, whatever was contracted from earthly contamination may be cleansed through expiatory punishments by means of one of these elements.

Air is understood in the phrase “suspended upon the winds”; water in the phrase “beneath the vast abyss”; and fire is explicitly named when he says “burned up in fire.” [Col. 0789D]

We, however, also acknowledge that there are certain purifying punishments in this mortal life [the source has the variant “in mortal life”]—not punishments by which those who suffer them become no better, or even become worse, but punishments that are purifying for those who are corrected by being restrained through them.

All other punishments, whether temporary or eternal, are inflicted according to the way in which each person is handled by divine providence, either for sins—whether past sins or sins in which the person being punished still lives—or for the exercise and demonstration of virtues, through human beings and angels, whether good or evil.

For even if someone suffers some evil (*mali quid*; variant *aliquid*, “something”) through another person’s wickedness or error, the human being who, through ignorance or injustice, inflicts evil on someone does indeed sin; but God does not sin when, by a just though hidden judgment, he permits it to occur. [Col. 0790A]

Some suffer temporary punishments only in this life, others after death, and others both now and then; nevertheless, they suffer them before that most severe and final judgment. Not all who undergo temporary punishments after death come to the eternal punishments that will follow that judgment. For some things that are not forgiven in this age are forgiven in the age to come—that is, so that they will not be punished by the eternal punishment of the age to come, as we have already said above.

Very few, however, are those who suffer no punishments in this life but only afterward. Yet we ourselves have known and heard of some who, even into decrepit old age, never experienced so much as the lightest fever and led a tranquil life. [Col. 0790B]

## CHAPTER 148. On those who define that those who remain in the Catholic faith, even if they have lived extremely badly, are nevertheless to be saved because of the foundation of faith, from the same book XXI of *The City of God*

There are some (*autem*, “however,” appears in the printed text) who, because it is written, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved,” make this promise to those who persevere only in the Catholic Church, even if they live badly within it: they will supposedly be saved through fire on account of the merit of the foundation of which the Apostle says. [Col. 0790C]

> For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon [this] foundation (*hoc* is the printed variant) gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. But if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; yet he himself will be saved, but so as through fire.

They therefore say that a Catholic Christian of any kind of life has Christ as his foundation—a foundation that no heresy possesses, having been cut off from the unity of his body. For this reason they think that, because of this foundation, even if the Catholic Christian has lived badly, like someone who has built wood, hay, and straw upon it, he will be saved through fire; that is (the printed variant adds *est*, “is”), he will be liberated after the punishments of that fire by which the wicked will be punished at the final judgment. [Col. 0790D]

## CHAPTER 149. What it means to have Christ as one’s foundation, and to whom salvation through the burning of fire is promised, from the same book XXI
Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. He shows what it means to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood, not merely sacramentally but truly: for this is to remain in Christ, so that Christ may remain in him. For he said this as though he were saying: “Whoever does not remain in me, and in whom I do not remain, should not say or think that he eats my body or drinks my blood.” Therefore those who are not his members do not remain in Christ. But those who make themselves members of a prostitute are not members of Christ [Col. 0791A], unless they cease from that evil by repentance and return through reconciliation to this good.

“But,” they say, “Catholic Christians have Christ as their foundation, from whose unity [truth] they have not departed, even though they have built upon this foundation a life of whatever kind, however wicked, like wood, hay, and straw. Thus their right faith, through which Christ is the foundation, though with loss—for what has been built upon it will be burned up—can nevertheless perhaps eventually save them from the perpetuity of that fire.”

Let the apostle James answer them briefly: “If someone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him?” And who, they ask, is the person of whom the apostle Paul says, “But he himself will be saved, yet as through fire”? Let us inquire together who this person is. It is nevertheless most certain that he is not this person, lest we set the judgments of the two Apostles at odds, if one says, “Even if someone has evil works, faith will save him through fire,” while the other says, “If he does not have works, can faith save him?”

Let us therefore discover who can be saved through fire, if we first discover what it means to have Christ as one’s foundation. To understand this as quickly as possible from the comparison itself: nothing in a building is placed before its foundation. Whoever therefore has Christ in his heart in such a way that he does not place earthly and temporal things—even those that are lawful and permitted—before him has Christ as his foundation. But if he places such things before Christ, then, even if he appears to have faith in Christ, Christ is not his foundation, since such things are placed before him.

How much more, then, when someone despises saving commandments and commits what is unlawful: he is shown not merely to have failed to place Christ first, but to have placed him last, since he has disregarded Christ while he commanded or permitted these things, and has chosen to satisfy his desire through shameful acts contrary to Christ’s commands or permissions.

If a Christian loves a prostitute and, cleaving to her, becomes one body with her, he no longer has Christ as his foundation. But if someone loves his wife, and loves her according to Christ, who would doubt that Christ is his foundation? If, however, he loves her according to this world, carnally, in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God, even this, according to the apostle—or rather, through the apostle, Christ—allows by way of concession.

Such a man, therefore, may have Christ as his foundation. For if he places nothing of this affection and pleasure before Christ, even though he builds wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation, Christ is his foundation; and for this reason he will be saved through fire [Col. 0791D]. For the fire of tribulation will burn up such pleasures and earthly loves that are not condemnable because of the marital union. To this fire belong bereavements and whatever calamities take these things away. Accordingly, this building will be harmful to the one who built it, because he will no longer possess what he built upon it and will be tormented by the loss of those things in whose enjoyment he had rejoiced. Yet he will be saved through this fire by reason of the foundation, because, even if a persecutor were to propose to him the choice between possessing those things and possessing Christ, [he would freely profess that he preferred to possess Christ rather than those things]; he would not place them before Christ.

Observe in the apostolic words the person building upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones: “The unmarried man,” he says, “thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.” Observe another building wood, hay, and straw: “The married man,” he says, “thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.” “Each person’s work [whatever its quality] will become manifest; for the day of the Lord will declare it”—that is, the day of tribulation—“because,” he says, “it will be revealed in fire.”

He calls that same tribulation fire, as it is written elsewhere: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.” “And the fire will test the quality of each person’s work, whether someone’s work endures.” For the work built by one who thinks of the things of God, how he may please God, endures; and he will receive a reward for what he has built, that is, he will receive that for which he had been thinking. But if someone’s work burns, he will suffer loss, because he will not possess what he had loved. He himself, however, will be saved, because no tribulation has shaken him from the stability of that foundation—yet as through fire: for what he did not possess without an alluring love, he does not lose without burning grief.

Behold, as it seems to me, we have found a fire that condemns none of them, but enriches one, causes the other loss, and tests both. But if we want to understand that fire as the place about which the Lord will say to those on his left, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” so that those who build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation are also thought to be among them, and so that the good merit of the foundation frees them from that fire after a time imposed for their evil merits, what are we to think of those on the right, to whom he will say, “Come, blessed ones of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you”? Are they not those who built upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones?

But if both those on the right and those on the left must be sent into the fire of which it was said, “Yet as through fire,” if this is how it is to be understood, then both are to be tested by that fire—both those on the right and those on the left. For both are to be tested by the fire of which it was said: “The day will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work.”

If, then, the fire will test both, so that, if someone’s work endures—that is, if what he built upon the foundation has not been consumed by the fire—he receives a reward, while if someone’s work burns, he suffers loss, then clearly this is not that eternal fire. For only those on the left will be sent into that fire for final and perpetual condemnation. This fire, however, tests those on the right, but it tests some of them in such a way that it does not burn up or consume the building it finds constructed by them upon Christ the foundation; others it tests differently, namely, so that what they have built burns and they suffer loss from it, yet they are saved because they held Christ, firmly established as their foundation, with surpassing love.

But if they will be saved, then surely they will stand on the right and hear with the others: “Come, blessed ones of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you”—not on the left, where those who will not be saved will be, and therefore will hear: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” [Col. 0793A]. For no one will be saved from that fire, since all those people will go into eternal punishment, where “their worm does not die [will not die] and the fire is not quenched”; there they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.

After the death of this body, until we come to that final day of condemnation and reward which will occur after the resurrection of bodies, if the spirits of the dead are said to undergo a fire of such a kind that those who, during the life of this body, did not have such habits [and loves] as would cause their wood, hay, and straw to be consumed do not feel it, while others do feel it, who carried such buildings with them, whether only there, or both here and there, or perhaps so that here they may find a fire of passing tribulation consuming worldly things that are venial rather than damnable, even though they will not find it there—I do not refute this, because perhaps it is true.

For even the death of the flesh may belong to this tribulation, since it was conceived from the perpetration of the first sin, so that each person may feel, according to his building, the time that follows it [and according to each person’s building, in its own time, what each person has undergone; persecutions of the Church may also be included]. The persecutions by which the martyrs were crowned, and which all Christians suffer, test both buildings like fire. They consume some, together with the builders themselves, if they do not find Christ as their foundation in them; others they consume without the builders, if they do find Christ in them, because, although the builders will be saved with loss, they themselves will not be consumed on account of Christ’s [Col. 0793C] merit, which is found in the foundation and remains forever. Still other buildings they do not consume, because they find in them things that remain forever.

At the end of the world there will also be a tribulation during the time of Antichrist, such as has never occurred before. How many buildings there will then be—some golden, some made of hay—upon the excellent foundation that is Christ Jesus! That fire will test both kinds, bringing joy to some and loss to others, yet destroying neither, because it will find in them a stable foundation.

Whoever, however, places before Christ by loving carnally according to human custom—not a wife, whose bodily union he also uses for carnal pleasure, but the very ties called piety, which are remote from such pleasures—does not have him as his foundation, and therefore he will not be saved through fire [Col. 0793D]. Rather, he will not be saved because he cannot be with the Savior, who, speaking most plainly about this, says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me.”

But whoever loves these relationships carnally in such a way that he nevertheless does not place them before Christ the Lord, and would rather be without them than without Christ, if he is brought to such a point of testing, will be saved through fire, because the pain resulting from their loss must burn as much as the love had clung to them.

Moreover, whoever loves father, mother, sons, and daughters according to Christ, so that he counsels them toward attaining Christ’s kingdom and cleaving to him, or loves in them the fact that they are members of Christ, should not be thought to possess a love that will be found among the wood, hay, and straw destined for consumption. Rather, it will plainly be assigned to a building of gold, silver, and precious stones.

How, then, can he love them more than Christ, when he loves them for Christ’s sake?

—On the exposition of Psalm 80—

“Explain to us, then,” he says, “the wood, hay, and straw that people build upon the foundation: how do they not perish but are saved, yet as though through fire?”

That question is indeed obscure, brothers, but I shall speak briefly as I can. There are people who utterly despise this world, to whom whatever passes away in time is as nothing. They do not cling through any love to earthly possessions; they are chaste, holy, continent, righteous, perhaps even selling all they possess and distributing it to the poor, or possessing as though they did not possess, and using this world as though they did not use it [Col. 0794B].

But there are others who cling to things permitted because of human weakness, with a certain degree of affection. He does not seize another person’s estate, but loves his own in such a way that, if he loses it, he is troubled. He does not desire another man’s wife, but clings to and unites himself with his own so excessively that he does not observe the limit prescribed there in the tablets for the procreation of children. He does not take what belongs to another, but reclaims what is his, and goes to court with his brother.

To such people it is said: “It is already altogether a fault in you that you have lawsuits with one another.” Yet he commands that the lawsuits themselves be conducted in the Church and not brought before the public courts, while still calling them faults. For a Christian contends for earthly possessions more than is fitting for one to whom the kingdom of heaven has been promised. He does not raise his whole heart upward, but drags part of it toward the earth.

Finally, if the temptation to undergo martyrdom should come, what do those who have Christ as their foundation and build gold, silver, and precious stones say at such an opportunity? “It is good for me to depart and be with Christ.” They run eagerly, or are troubled not at all or only slightly by earthly frailty. But those who love their own possessions and their own houses are gravely disturbed: the hay, straw, and wood burn.

They therefore have wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation, but these are permitted things, not unlawful ones. For I say, brothers: Possess the foundation; cling to heaven; trample the earth. If you are such a person, you build nothing but gold, silver, and precious stones.

But when you say, “I love this possession; I fear that it may perish,” and loss threatens, and you are saddened, you do not in fact place it before Christ. For you love this possession in such a way that, if you are asked, “Do you want it or Christ?” and you are sad to lose it, you nevertheless embrace Christ more closely, whom you have placed in the foundation: you will be saved as through fire.

Hear another example: You cannot retain this possession unless you give false testimony. Not doing this is to place Christ in the foundation. For the Truth said: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.”

Therefore, if you love your possession but do not commit robbery for its sake, do not give false testimony for its sake, do not commit murder for its sake, do not swear falsely for its sake, and do not deny Christ for its sake—because you do not do these things for its sake—you have Christ as your foundation. Yet because you love it and are saddened if you lose it, you have placed upon the foundation not gold, silver, and precious stones, but wood, hay, and straw. You will therefore be saved when what you have built begins to burn, yet as though through fire [Col. 0795A].

Let no one who builds adulteries, blasphemies, sacrileges, idolatries, or perjuries upon this foundation think that he will be saved through fire, as though these were wood, hay, and straw. Rather, the person who builds love of earthly things upon the foundation of the heavenly kingdom—that is, upon Christ—will have the love of temporal things burned up, and he himself will be saved because of the soundness of the foundation.

“The enemies of the Lord lied to him,” saying, “I will go to the vineyard,” but did not go; “and their time will be not for a time, but forever.” And who are these people?

“And he fed them with the fat of wheat” [Psalm 80:17].

You know the fat of wheat from which many enemies who lied to him are fed. “And he fed them with the fat of wheat”: he mixed them with his sacraments. When he gave Judas the morsel, he fed him with the fat of wheat; and the enemy of the Lord lied to him, “and his time will be forever.”

“He fed them with the fat of wheat.” O ungrateful people! He fed them with the fat of wheat, and “satisfied them with honey from the rock.” In the wilderness he brought water from the rock, not honey. Honey is wisdom, holding first place in sweetness among the foods of the heart.

How many enemies of the Lord, therefore, while lying to the Lord, are fed not only with the fat of wheat but also with honey from the rock—with the wisdom of Christ! How many take delight in his word, in the knowledge of his sacraments, and in the explanation of his parables! How many take delight in it! And this honey is not from just any person, but from the rock; “and the rock was Christ.”

How many, then, are filled with this honey! They cry out and say, “It is sweet.” They say, “Nothing better, nothing sweeter, could be understood or spoken.” Yet the enemies of the Lord lied to him.

I do not wish to linger longer over painful matters. Although the psalm has ended on this terrifying note, nevertheless I beg you: let us return from its conclusion to its beginning: “Rejoice in God our helper.”

## CHAPTER 150. Against the persuasion of those who think that the sins in which they persisted while giving alms will not harm them; from the same Book XXI

It remains to answer those who say that only those who neglect to give alms worthy of their sins will burn in the eternal fire, because of what the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has not shown mercy.”

“Therefore,” they say, “whoever has shown mercy, even though he has not corrected his ruined ways but has lived wickedly and impiously amid his very almsgiving, will face a merciful judgment: either he will not be condemned at all, or after some time he will be freed from final condemnation.”

They think that Christ will distinguish the righteous from the wicked for no other reason than the giving or neglecting of alms, sending some into the kingdom and others into eternal punishment. And because they want to believe that the daily sins they never cease to commit—whatever their quality or magnitude—can be forgiven through almsgiving, they attempt to employ the prayer taught by the Lord himself both as an advocate and as a witness.

“For just as,” they say, “there is no day on which this prayer is not said by Christians, so there is no daily sin, whatever its kind, that is not forgiven through it, when we say, ‘Forgive us our debts,’ provided that we take care to do what follows: ‘As we also forgive our debtors.’ For the Lord did not say, ‘If you forgive people their sins, your Father will forgive you your daily minor sins,’ but, ‘He will forgive you your sins.’ Therefore, whatever their kind or magnitude, even if they are committed daily and the person’s life does not turn away from them for the better, they presume that forgiveness can be obtained through almsgiving.”

It is good, however, that these people remind us that worthy alms must be given for sins. For if they said that any kind of alms could obtain divine mercy for daily and serious sins, and for whatever amount of criminal habit, so that daily forgiveness would follow, they would see themselves asserting something absurd and ridiculous. They would thus be compelled to admit that a very wealthy man could redeem murders, adulteries, and every kind of wicked deed by spending ten small coins each day on alms.

If it is utterly absurd to say this, then, when we ask what alms are worthy for sins—those of which even that forerunner of Christ said, “Therefore produce worthy fruits of repentance”—surely we will not find them being performed by people who stab their lives to death through the continual perpetration of daily crimes.

First, because in taking away other people’s possessions they seize far more than they distribute in small amounts to the poor; from these gains they suppose that they feed Christ in order to believe that they have bought—or rather, are buying daily—the license to commit evil deeds, and so they commit such damnable [damnabilia] acts without fear.

If, for a single crime, they were to distribute everything to the needy members of Christ, it would be unable to benefit them unless they ceased from such deeds, possessing charity, which does not act wrongly.

Whoever therefore gives alms worthy of his sins first begins by giving them to himself. For it is unworthy that he should not do for himself what he does for his neighbor, when he hears God saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Let him also hear: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.”

If he does not give this alms to his soul—that is, does not make it pleasing to God—how can he be said to give worthy alms for his sins? For this too is written: “Whoever is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?”

Alms assist prayers. And certainly we must attend to what we read: “Son, if you have sinned, do not add to it again, and pray for your former sins, that they may be forgiven you.”

Alms must therefore be given so that, when we pray for former sins, we may be heard—not so that, while persisting in those sins, we may think that through alms we can purchase permission to do evil.

For this reason the Lord foretold that he would reckon with those on the right for the alms they had given, and with those on the left for the alms they had not given: to show by this how much alms avail for erasing former sins, not for committing perpetual sins with impunity.

Nor should those who refuse to change their lives for the better from their habitual crimes be said to give such alms. For even when he says, “When you did not do it for one of the least of mine, you did not do it for me,” he shows that they do not do it even when they think they are doing it.

If they were to give bread to a hungry Christian as to a Christian, surely they would not deny themselves the bread of righteousness, which is Christ himself, since God considers not to whom something is given but with what intention it is given.

Whoever therefore loves Christ in a Christian presents alms to him with the disposition with which he approaches Christ, not with the disposition by which he wishes to depart from Christ unpunished. For the more someone loves what Christ condemns, the more he abandons Christ.

What benefit is it to anyone to be baptized if he is not justified? Did not the one who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit [the Holy Spirit], he will not enter the kingdom of God,” also say, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven”?

Why do many, fearing the former, take care to be baptized, while, not fearing the latter, not many take care to be justified?

Thus, just as someone does not say “Fool” to his brother when, in saying this, he is not hostile to the brotherhood itself but to his sin—for otherwise he will be liable to the fire of Gehenna—so, conversely, someone who gives alms to a Christian does not give them to a Christian if he does not love Christ in him.

But he does not love Christ who refuses to be justified in [by] Christ. And just as, if someone is overtaken by this fault and says “Fool” to his brother—not wishing to remove his sin, but insulting him unjustly [is convicted by righteousness]—it is not enough for him to redeem this fault by giving alms unless he also adds the remedy of reconciliation that follows there.

For it follows there: “If, therefore, you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”

In the same way, it is not enough to give however much alms for whatever crime while remaining in the habit of committing crimes.

The daily prayer taught by Jesus himself, and therefore called [named] the Lord’s Prayer, does indeed erase daily sins when it is said each day: “Forgive us our debts,” because what follows is not only said but also done: “As we also forgive our debtors.”

But sins are committed; therefore it is said—not so that they may be committed because it is said. Through this prayer the Savior wished to show us that, however righteously we live amid the darkness and weakness of this life, we are not without sins for whose forgiveness we ought to pray, and that we ought to forgive those who sin against us so that we too may be forgiven.

The Lord therefore did not say, “If you forgive people their sins, your Father will forgive you your sins,” so that, trusting in this prayer, we might confidently commit daily crimes, whether through power, by which we would not fear human laws, or through cunning, by which we would deceive people themselves. Rather, he said it so that through this prayer we might learn not to think ourselves without sins, even if we were free from serious crimes, just as in the old law God also instructed the priests about this very matter through the sacrifices that he commanded them to offer first for their own sins and then for those of the people.

For the very words of so great a teacher and our Lord must be examined attentively. He did not say, “If you forgive people their sins, your Father will also forgive you sins of whatever kind,” but said, “Your sins.” For he was teaching the daily prayer and speaking, of course, to disciples who had been justified.

What, then, does “your sins” mean except sins without which even you who have been justified and sanctified will not be? When, therefore, those who seek an occasion for committing crimes daily through this prayer say that the Lord meant serious sins also, because he did not say “he will forgive you minor sins,” but “your sins,” we, considering the people to whom he was speaking and hearing the words “your sins,” ought to understand nothing other than minor sins, since serious sins no longer belonged to such people.

Nevertheless, even serious sins—from which a person must altogether depart after changing his ways for the better—are not forgiven through prayers unless what is said there is done: “As we forgive our debtors.”

For if minor sins, without which even the life of the righteous is not lived, are not forgiven in any other way, how much less will those entangled in many and serious crimes, even if they cease to commit them, obtain any pardon if they are inexorable in forgiving others what each has sinned against them, since the Lord says: “But if you do not forgive people [their sins], neither will your Father forgive you.”

For this is what the apostle James also means when he says: “Judgment without mercy is for the one who has not shown mercy.”

The servant to whom his master forgave ten thousand talents should also come to mind; afterward he ordered him to repay them because he had not pitied his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii.

Among those who are children of the promise and vessels of mercy, what the same Apostle says is therefore applicable. He adds accordingly: “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (superexultat misericordia judicio [judicium]). For even those who lived with such great holiness that they also receive others into eternal dwellings—those whom they made friends through the mammon of iniquity—were freed by mercy from the one who justifies the ungodly, assigning the reward according to grace, not according to debt.

The Apostle belongs to their number when he says: “I obtained mercy, so that I might be faithful.”

But those who are received by such people into the eternal dwellings must be acknowledged not to possess such character that their own life could suffice to free them without the assistance of the saints. Accordingly, mercy triumphs over judgment (superexultat misericordia judicio [judicium]) in them much more.

Yet no one should therefore think that a most wicked person, who has not been changed toward either a good or even a tolerable life, is received into the eternal dwellings because he has served the saints from the mammon of iniquity—that is, from money or riches that were acquired wickedly; or even if acquired well, not from true riches, but from what iniquity thinks are riches, since it does not know what the true riches are with which those who receive others into eternal dwellings abound.

There is therefore a certain mode of life, not so bad that generosity in almsgiving—by which the poverty of the righteous is supported and friends are made who will receive them into eternal dwellings—does not benefit those who live it toward attaining the kingdom of heaven; yet it is not so good that it is itself sufficient for attaining such blessedness, unless they obtain mercy through the merits of those whom they have made their friends.

I am accustomed to wonder that this saying of the Lord is also found in Virgil, where he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they too may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

A similar saying is: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.”

For when that poet was describing the Elysian fields, where they think the souls of the blessed dwell, he placed there not only those who were able to reach those seats by their own merits, but added the following words:

“And those who, by deserving well, made others remember them,”

that is, those who earned the favor of others and, by deserving it, made those others remember them.

It is altogether as though he were saying to them what frequently occurs among Christians, when a humble person commends himself to one of the saints and says, “Remember me,” and makes it possible for this to occur by deserving it.

But what this measure is, and what the sins are that so impede entrance into the kingdom of God yet nevertheless obtain forgiveness through the merits of holy friends, is exceedingly difficult to discover and most dangerous to define.

For my part, although I have labored at this matter up to the present time, I have not been able to discover them; and perhaps they remain hidden for this reason: lest the human sluggishness that wraps itself securely in such entanglements should grow slack in its zeal to advance toward avoiding all sins, if people knew what sins, and of what kind, they are for which—even while the sinners persist in them and do not adopt a better way of life—the intercession of the righteous must be sought and hoped for. They would not care to free themselves from such entanglements by the exertion of virtue, but would seek only to be freed by the merits of others whom they had made friends through the generosity of almsgiving from the mammon of iniquity.

But now, while the measure of venial iniquity is unknown—even if it persists—zeal to advance toward better things is applied more watchfully through prayer and earnest effort, and the care of making holy friends from the mammon of iniquity is not neglected.

This deliverance, however, whether it is accomplished through each person’s own prayers or through the intercession of the saints, has the effect that a person is not sent into the eternal fire, not that, once sent there, he is rescued after however long a time.

Even those who think that the passage about the good earth producing fruit—some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold—should be understood to mean that, according to the diversity of their merits, some saints will free thirty people, others sixty, and others one hundred, usually suppose that this will occur on the day of judgment, not after judgment.

When someone saw human beings perversely promising themselves impunity because, in this manner, all might appear able to share in deliverance, he is said to have answered most elegantly that it would be better to live well, so that each person might be found among those who will intercede for the liberation of others. Otherwise they might be so few that, when each had quickly reached his number—thirty, sixty, or one hundred—many would remain who could no longer be rescued from punishment through their intercession; and among them would be found anyone who, with utterly reckless presumption, promised himself the fruit of another’s labor.

## CHAPTER 151. On the eternal and unchangeable will; from Book XXII of *The City of God*

Many things are indeed done by the wicked against the will of God, but he possesses such great wisdom and such great power that everything that appears contrary to his will tends toward those outcomes, or ends, that he himself foreknew to be good and just.

Accordingly, when God is said to change his will, so that those toward whom he was gentle, for example, are met with his anger, they rather are changed than he is, and in what they suffer they encounter him as though he had been changed. It is like the sun changing for wounded eyes, and becoming in some way harsh, so that what was mild and pleasing becomes troublesome, while the sun itself remains in its own nature the same as it was.

The will of God is also called that which he produces in the hearts of those who obey his commands. Of this the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in us even to will.” In the same way, God’s righteousness is called not only that by which he himself is righteous, but also that which he brings about in a person whom he justifies. So too his law is called that which is rather the law of human beings, but which he gave [to human beings]. For the people to whom Jesus said, “In your law it is written,” were certainly human beings, while elsewhere we read: “The law of his God is in his heart.”

According to this will, by which we say that God wills what he has caused others to will—although they do not know what will happen—he wills many things and does not bring them about. For his saints wish many things to happen, inspired by a holy will from him, yet they do not happen. Thus they devoutly and piously pray for certain people, but he does not do what they pray for, even though he himself has produced in them, through his Holy Spirit, this will to pray.

Accordingly, when the saints, according to God, wish and pray that someone may be saved, we can, in that manner of speaking, say that God wills it and does not do it, meaning that we call him willing it who causes them to will it.

But according to that will of his which is eternal together with his foreknowledge, he has already done in heaven and on earth everything that he willed—not only what is past or present, but also what is future.

Before the time comes when he willed something to happen—something he foreknew and ordained before all times—we say, “It will happen when God wills.” But if we do not know not only the time when it will happen, but also whether it will happen, we say, “It will happen if God wills.” We do not mean that God will then have a new will that he did not previously possess, but that what has been prepared from eternity in his unchangeable will will then occur.

On this same will of God, from Psalm 110:

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.”

Search, inquire into, and investigate, if you can, all the wills of the Lord: in all of them you will always find his works to be great. For no will is more powerful than his will. When he permits something to be done against it, he demonstrates his mercy and his justice.

For just as he wills that a person not sin, so he wills to spare the sinner, so that he may return and live. Likewise, he wills to punish the one who persists in sins, so that the rebellious person may not escape the power of justice. Thus, whatever you choose, human being, God will not lack the means by which to fulfill his will concerning you.

Whether, therefore, he justifies the ungodly, rebukes the sluggish, patiently waits for the adversary, or abandons the one destined for punishment, he is always merciful, always just, always almighty.

## CHAPTER 152. On the possession of the saints’ eternal blessedness and the perpetual punishments of the ungodly; from the same Book XXII
Therefore, to pass over so many other matters, just as we now see fulfilled in Christ what he promised to Abraham, saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” so what he promised to that same seed will be fulfilled where he says through the prophet, “Those who were in the tombs will rise,” and where he says, “There will be a new heaven and a new earth, and they will not remember former things, nor will they come into their heart; but they will find joy and exultation in it. Behold, I will make Jerusalem an exultation and my people a joy; and I will exult in Jerusalem and rejoice in my people, and the voice of weeping will no longer be heard in it.” And through another prophet, what he foretold when he said to that same prophet: “At that time your people will be saved, everyone who is found written in the book; and many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth [or, as some have interpreted it, in the heap] will rise—these to eternal life, and those to eternal reproach and eternal confusion.” And elsewhere through the same prophet: “The saints of the Most High [God] will receive the kingdom, and they will possess it forever and ever.” And shortly afterward: “His kingdom,” he says, “is an everlasting kingdom.” I have set down other matters relevant to this in the twentieth book, or matters that I did not set down but are nevertheless written in the same Scriptures. These things too will come, just as those things came which unbelievers did not think would come. For the same God promised both, and foretold that both would come—the God whom the deities of the pagans dread, as even Porphyry, the most distinguished of the pagan philosophers [the pagans themselves], bears witness.

## CHAPTER 153. Against the wise men of the world, who think that earthly human bodies cannot be transferred to a heavenly dwelling; from the same Book XXII

But evidently learned and wise men, in opposition to the force of such great authority—which, as it foretold so long beforehand, has turned every kind of person toward believing and hoping in this—think that they argue cleverly against the resurrection of bodies. They say what Cicero recorded in the third book of *The Republic*. For when he asserted that Hercules and Romulus had been made gods from among all [human beings], he says that their bodies were not carried up into heaven: “For nature would not permit what was of the earth to remain anywhere but in the earth.” This is the great argument of the wise, whose thoughts the Lord knows, because they are futile.

If we were souls only—that is, spirits without any body—and lived in heaven, while knowing nothing of earthly animals, and it were said that we would one day be joined by some marvelous bond to earthly bodies in order to animate them, would we not argue much more forcefully, refusing to believe it, and say that nature does not permit an incorporeal thing to be bound by a bodily bond? And yet the earth is full of living souls to which these earthly limbs are joined and intertwined in a marvelous manner.

Why, then, by the will of that same God who made this living creature, could an earthly body not be raised into a heavenly body, if the soul—which transcends all these earthly things and is superior even to every heavenly body—could be bound to an earthly body? Could so tiny a particle of earth hold within itself something better than a heavenly body, so that it possessed sensation and life, while heaven would disdain to receive that particle as it senses and lives, or, having received it, would be unable to sustain it, even though it experiences and lives by something better than every heavenly body?

But this does not happen now because the time has not yet come when the one who willed it to happen appointed that it should happen. He has made what has already become commonplace through our sight far more wondrously than what these people do not believe. Why, indeed, do we not marvel more intensely that incorporeal souls, superior to heavenly bodies, are joined to earthly bodies than that bodies—although earthly, yet bodily—are raised to dwelling places that, though heavenly, are nevertheless corporeal? We do not marvel because we are accustomed to seeing the former and are ourselves the former, whereas we are not yet the latter and have not yet seen it.

For, certainly, when considered with sober reasoning, the divine work is found to be more wondrous when it in some way attaches corporeal things to incorporeal beings than when it joins bodies to bodies—although they are different, since the one are heavenly and the other earthly. Yet one day this will have been considered incredible.

## CHAPTER 154. On the resurrection of the flesh, which some do not believe although the world believes it; from the same Book XXII

Behold, the world has already believed that Christ’s earthly body was taken up into heaven, together with the resurrection of the flesh and the ascent to the heavenly dwelling places, while only a very few—both learned and unlearned—remain astonished. Learned and unlearned alike have now believed.

If they have believed something credible, let them see how foolish those are who do not believe it. But if something incredible has been believed, then it is itself incredible that what is incredible should have been believed in this way. Thus God, before either of these two incredible things occurred—namely, the eternal resurrection of our bodies and the fact that the world would believe so incredible a matter—foretold that both would occur.

We see that one of the two incredible things has already happened: the world believed what was incredible. Why, then, is it despaired of that the remaining thing should also come to pass—namely, that what the world believed to be incredible should occur—just as what was likewise incredible has already come to pass, namely, that the world should believe something so incredible? For both these incredible things—the one of which we see and the other of which we believe—were foretold in the same Scriptures through which the world believed.

## CHAPTER 155. That the world’s belief in Christ was the work of divine power, not human persuasion; and on Romulus’s false divinity; from the same Book XXII

And if the manner in which the world believed is considered, it is found to be even more incredible. Christ sent very few men—uneducated in the liberal disciplines and, so far as the learning of these people is concerned, entirely unpolished; untrained in grammar, unarmed with dialectic, and not puffed up with rhetoric—fishermen with the nets of faith, to the sea of this age. And so he caught from every kind of people so many fish, and fish all the more marvelous the rarer they were, including the philosophers themselves.

If you wish—indeed, because you ought to—let us add this third incredible thing to the other two. There are therefore three incredible things, which nevertheless have occurred:

It is incredible that Christ rose in the flesh and ascended into heaven with the flesh.

It is incredible that the world believed so incredible a thing.

It is incredible that men of no rank, the lowliest, very few, and uneducated, were able to persuade the world—and in it even the learned—of so incredible a thing so effectively.

Of these three incredible things, the first those with whom we are dealing refuse to believe. The second they are compelled to see, though they cannot find how it occurred if they do not believe the third. The resurrection of Christ, certainly, and his ascent into heaven with the flesh in which he rose, is now proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world.

If it is not credible, how has it already been believed throughout the entire world? If many noble, eminent, and learned people said that they had seen it and took care to spread abroad what they had seen, it is not surprising that the world believed them; but it is stubborn of these people still to refuse belief. If, however—as is true—the world believed a few obscure, insignificant, and uneducated people who said and wrote that they had seen it, why do a few exceedingly obstinate people who remain still refuse to believe the world, which already believes?

The world believed on account of the small number of obscure, lowly [weak], uneducated men because divinity itself persuaded it all the more wondrously through such contemptible witnesses. The utterances of those who persuaded—the marvelous things they proclaimed—were deeds, not words. For those who had not seen Christ rise in the flesh and ascend into heaven with it believed those who reported that they had seen this, not merely speaking but also performing miraculous signs.

They suddenly heard men whom they knew to have possessed only one, or at most two, languages speaking miraculously in the languages of all nations. They saw a man lame from his mother’s womb restored to health at their word in the name of Christ after forty years. They saw handkerchiefs taken from their bodies bring healing to the sick. They saw countless people suffering from various diseases, placed in orderly fashion along the road they were to travel, immediately receive healing when the shadow of those passing over them fell upon them. They saw many other astonishing deeds performed through them in the name of Christ [signs were performed], and finally they even saw the dead rise.

If they grant that these events were accomplished as they are read, behold, we add so many incredible things to those three incredible things. To make one incredible thing—that which is proclaimed about the resurrection of the flesh and the ascent into heaven—believable, we heap up such testimony from many incredible events, and still we do not bend the unbelievers, hardened with dreadful obstinacy, toward belief.

But if they do not believe that these miracles too were performed through Christ’s apostles so that people would believe them when they proclaimed Christ’s resurrection and ascension, this one great miracle is sufficient for us: the fact that the world believed without any miracles.

Let us also recall here what Cicero marvels at concerning the divinity believed of Romulus. I shall insert his words as they were written:

> “What is more remarkable in the case of Romulus,” he says, “is that the others who are said to have been made gods from men lived in less educated ages, when the explanation was readily invented, since the unlearned were easily driven to believe. But we see that Romulus lived less than seven hundred years ago, when letters and learning had already become ancient, and when that ancient error arising from the uncultivated life of human beings had been removed.”

A little later he speaks of the same Romulus in a way relevant to this point:

> “From this it can be understood,” he says, “that Homer lived many years before Romulus, so that, by the time of learned people and of an age itself educated, there was scarcely any room left for fabrication. Antiquity accepted fabricated stories, sometimes even crude ones; but this age, already cultivated and especially rejecting whatever cannot happen, repudiates them.”

Marcus Tullius Cicero, one of the most learned men and also the most eloquent of all, therefore says that Romulus’s divinity was remarkably believed because the times were already educated and would not accept the falsehoods of fables.

But it is very laughable to mention Romulus’s false divinity when we are speaking of Christ. Nevertheless, since Romulus lived approximately six hundred years before Cicero, and since that age is said already to have been cultivated by learning, so that it rejected everything that could not happen, how much more, six hundred years later, in Cicero’s own time and especially afterward under Augustus and Tiberius—in ages certainly more educated—would the human mind have mocked and rejected from its ears and heart the resurrection of Christ’s flesh and his ascent into heaven as something that could not happen, unless the divinity of truth itself—or the truth of his divinity—had shown, through the attesting signs of miracles, that it could happen and had happened?

Thus, despite so many and such great persecutions, which terrified and opposed it, the resurrection that had preceded in Christ and was afterward to follow in others into the new age, together with the immortality of the flesh, was believed with complete faith and proclaimed without fear. It was to spread more fruitfully throughout the world when it was sown in the blood of the martyrs.

For the earlier prophecies of the prophets were read, displays of power converged, and the new truth was commended to custom, though it was not contrary to reason, until the world—which had pursued it in fury—followed it in faith.

## CHAPTER 156. On the miracles performed so that the world might believe in Christ, and which do not cease to occur even though the world believes; from the same Book XXII

“Why,” they ask, “are those miracles which you proclaim to have occurred not performed now?”

I could indeed say that they were necessary before the world believed, in order that the world might believe. Whoever still seeks miracles in order to believe is himself a great miracle, since he does not believe while the world believes.

But they say this in order not to believe that those miracles were performed even then. From where, then, does it come that Christ is everywhere proclaimed as having been taken up into heaven with the flesh? How, in educated times that rejected everything impossible, did the world believe incredible things so astonishingly, without any miracles?

Will they perhaps say that these things were credible and therefore were believed? Why, then, do they themselves not believe? Our conclusion, therefore, is brief: either other incredible things, which nevertheless occurred and were seen, gave credibility to an incredible matter that was not seen; or else this matter was so credible that it needed no miracles to persuade people, in which case it exposes the excessive unbelief of these people.

I say this to refute the most empty-headed. For we cannot deny that many miracles were performed to attest that one great and saving miracle by which Christ ascended into heaven with the flesh in which he rose. Everything is recorded in the same most truthful books: both what was done and the reason why it was done, namely, so that it might be believed.

These events became known so that they might produce faith; through the faith they produced, they become known much more clearly. They are read publicly so that they may be believed, yet they would not be read publicly unless they had been believed.

Even now miracles are performed in his name, whether through his sacraments, through prayers, or through memorials of his saints. But they are not displayed with the same brilliance, so that they are not publicized with glory as great as that of the earlier miracles. The canon of the sacred Scriptures, which had to be established, causes those earlier miracles to be recited everywhere and to remain fixed in the memory of all peoples.

But wherever these later miracles occur, they are scarcely known throughout the whole city or whatever local community is involved. Often, even there, only a very few know of them while the others remain unaware—especially if the city is large. And when such events are reported elsewhere and to other people, the authority supporting them is not so great that they are believed without difficulty or doubt, even though faithful Christians report them to faithful Christians.

## CHAPTER 157. Whether all the bodies of the dead will rise according to the form of the Lord’s body; from the same Book XXII

Christ rose in the bodily measure in which he died. It is not permissible to say that, when the time of the resurrection of all comes, a size will be added to his body that he did not possess when he appeared to his disciples in the form in which they knew him, so that he might become equal to the tallest people.

But if we say that the larger bodies of some people must also be reduced to the measure of the Lord’s body, a great deal will perish from many bodies, although he himself promised that not even a hair would perish. It remains, therefore, that each person will recover the measure that he either possessed in youth, even if he died old, or would have possessed, even if he died before reaching it.

And what the Apostle mentioned concerning “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” should either be understood as having been said for another reason—that is, so that, when that Head is joined to the Christian peoples, the perfection of all the members may complete the measure of his age—or, if this was said about the resurrection of bodies, let us understand it as meaning that the bodies of the dead will rise neither below nor beyond the form of youth, but in that age and strength to which we know Christ attained here.

For the most learned men of this age have determined that youth extends to about thirty years; when its proper span has ended, a person begins to decline into the burdens of older and senile age. For this reason it was not said “into the measure of the body” or “into the measure of stature,” but “into the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.”

## CHAPTER 158. How the conformity of the saints to the image of the Son of God is to be understood; from the same Book XXII

What he also says—that those predestined are to be made conformed to the image of the Son of God—can be understood according to the inner person. For elsewhere he says to us: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind.” Therefore, where we are transformed so that we are not conformed to this age, there we are conformed to the Son of God.

It can also be understood in this way: just as he became like us in mortality, so we are to be made like him in immortality. This indeed also pertains to the resurrection of bodies.

But if these words too admonish us about the form in which bodies will rise, then, just as that measure, so this conformity must be understood not in terms of size but of age. Thus all will rise as great in body as they either were or would have been in the age of youth, although it will do no harm even if the form of an infant’s or an old person’s body remains, since there no weakness of mind or of the body itself will remain.

Therefore, even if someone insists that each person will rise in the bodily form in which he died, we should not engage in laborious contradiction with him.

## CHAPTER 159. Whether women’s bodies will be raised and remain in their own sex; from the same Book XXII

Some people, because it is said, “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age,” and “conformed to the image of the Son of God,” believe that women will not rise in the female sex but all in the male, since God made the man from clay alone and the woman from the man. But those seem to me to judge more wisely who do not doubt that both sexes will rise.

For there will be no sexual desire there, which is the cause of shame. Before they sinned, they were naked and were not ashamed—the man and the woman. The faults will therefore be removed from those bodies, while nature will be preserved. The female sex is not a fault but a nature, which then will indeed be free both from intercourse and from childbirth. Nevertheless, female members will remain—not adapted to their former use but to a new beauty, by which the desire of the one who looks will not be aroused, for no such desire will exist; rather, God’s wisdom and mercy will be praised. He both made what did not exist and freed from corruption what he had made.

For, at the beginning of the human race, when a woman was made by taking a rib from the side of the sleeping man, Christ and the Church had already to be prophetically signified by such an act. That sleep of the man was the death of Christ, whose lifeless side, hanging on the cross, was pierced by a spear, and from it flowed blood and water. We know these to be the sacraments by which the Church is built.

For Scripture also used this word when it did not say “formed” or “fashioned,” but “built her into a woman.” Hence the Apostle too speaks of “the building up of the body of Christ,” which is the Church.

The woman, therefore, is God’s creature, just as the man is; but the fact that she was made from the man commended their unity. And since Christ was to be made in that manner, as has been said, the Church was prefigured.

Therefore, the one who established both sexes will restore both.

Finally, when Jesus was questioned by the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, “Whose wife will she be among the seven brothers whom each successively had?”—since each wished to raise up offspring for the deceased, as the law had prescribed—he said:

> “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.”

And when there was an opportunity for him to say, “The woman you ask me about will be a man also, not a woman,” he did not say this. Instead he said:

> “For in the resurrection women will not marry, nor will men take wives, but they are like the angels of God in heaven.”

They will be equal to the angels in immortality and blessedness, not in flesh, nor in resurrection, which the angels did not need, since they could not die.

The Lord therefore denied that marriages would occur in the resurrection, not that women would exist there. He denied marriage precisely where such a question was being debated that he could have resolved it more easily by denying the female sex, if he had foreseen that it would not exist there. Rather, he affirmed that it would exist by saying “women will not marry,” which pertains to women, and “men will not take wives,” which pertains to men.

Therefore, those who here commonly marry or take wives will exist there, but they will not do these things there.

## CHAPTER 160. That in the resurrection of the dead the nature of bodies scattered in whatever ways must be restored whole; from the same Book XXII

Far be it from us to think that the omnipotence of the Creator cannot restore, for the resurrection and return to life of bodies, everything that beasts or fire has consumed and reduced to dust or ashes, that has been dissolved into moisture, or that has been exhaled into the air. Far be it from us to think that any recess or hidden place of nature can receive something withdrawn from our senses in such a way that it either escapes the Creator’s knowledge or eludes his power.

Cicero, a great authority among these people, wished to define God in this way: “He is,” he says, “a certain mind, released and free, separated from every mortal combination, perceiving and moving all things, and itself endowed with everlasting motion.” He found this in the teachings of the great philosophers.

To speak according to them, then, how can anything be hidden from one who perceives all things, or irrevocably escape one who moves all things?

Here, too, we must resolve a question that seems more difficult than the others: when the flesh of a dead person becomes the flesh of another living person, to which of them will it be restored in the resurrection?

Suppose someone, overcome by hunger and compelled by it, eats human corpses—a dreadful event that both ancient history attests to have happened occasionally and the unhappy experiences of our own times have demonstrated. Can anyone reasonably maintain that everything was completely digested through the lowest passages, with nothing from it changed and converted into his flesh, when the emaciation that was present and is no longer present sufficiently indicates what losses were replenished by that food?

I have already set down earlier certain points that will also help untie this knot. Whatever flesh hunger consumed was certainly exhaled into the air. We have said that God, in his omnipotence, can restore what has escaped.

That flesh, therefore, will be restored to the person in whom human flesh first began to exist. From the other person it is to be regarded as borrowed, like a loan, and must be returned to the one from whom it was taken, just as a debt is repaid. But the flesh of the person whom hunger had emptied [had emptied] will be restored to him by the one who can also recall what has been exhaled.

Even if it had perished in every possible way, and no material of it remained in any hidden recesses of nature from which the Omnipotent could restore it whenever he wished, it would still be possible for him to recreate it. But in view of the sentence of Truth, “Not a hair of your head will perish,” it is absurd to think that, while a person’s hair cannot perish, so much flesh eaten and consumed by hunger could have perished.

When all these matters have been considered and examined according to our limited ability, the following conclusion emerges: in the resurrection of the flesh, the size of each body will possess forever the measure that the innate constitution of that body had in its youth, whether that constitution was in the process of being completed or had already been completed. The appropriate beauty of all the limbs will also be preserved in their proportions.

If, in order to preserve that beauty, something is removed from some excessive size established in one part and distributed throughout the whole, so that it neither perishes nor disrupts the harmony of the parts anywhere, it is not absurd to believe that something may even be added to the body’s stature when it is distributed among all the parts so that they may preserve their beauty. For if it were excessive in one part, it would certainly not be beautiful.

Or, if it is maintained that each person will rise in the bodily stature in which he died, we should not resist contentiously, provided that all deformity, all weakness, all sluggishness, and all corruption are absent, together with anything else that would be unbefitting in that kingdom where the children of the resurrection and of the promise will be equal to the angels of God—if not in body, not in age, then certainly in blessedness.

Therefore, whatever was lost from living bodies or, after death, from corpses will be restored. Together with what remained in the graves, it will rise, changed from the old condition of an animal body into the newness of a spiritual body, clothed in incorruption and immortality.

Even if, through some grave accident or the savagery of enemies, it were completely crushed into dust and scattered into the air or waters, and nature allowed it, so far as possible, to be nowhere, it could in no way be withdrawn from the omnipotence of the Creator. Not even a hair of its head will perish.

The spiritual flesh will therefore be subject to the spirit, yet it will remain flesh, not spirit, just as the carnal spirit itself was subject to the flesh, yet remained spirit, not flesh.

We have an example of this matter in the deformity of our punishment. Those to whom the Apostle said, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people,” were not carnal according to the flesh but certainly according to the spirit.

A spiritual person is likewise so called in this life while still being carnal in body, and he sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind. But he will also be spiritual in body when that same flesh rises in such a way that what is written will be fulfilled: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body will rise.”

But what and how great is the grace of a spiritual body—since we have not yet experienced it—I fear that every statement made about it would be presumptuous.

—On the newness of the spiritual body, in which the flesh of the saints will be changed. From the same Book XXII of *The City of God*.—

When this promise is fulfilled, what will we be? What will we be like? What good things will we receive in that kingdom, since, when Christ died for us, we have already received such a pledge?

What will the human spirit be like when it has absolutely no fault—neither one beneath which it lies, nor one to which it yields, nor one against which it must at least contend laudably—perfected in the most peaceful virtue?

How great, how beautiful, how certain will knowledge of all things be there, without any error or labor, when the wisdom of God will be drunk from its own fountain, with complete blessedness and without any difficulty?

What will the body be like when it is wholly subject to the spirit and sufficiently enlivened by it, needing no nourishment of any kind? For it will not be an animal body but a spiritual one, possessing the substance of flesh, yet without any carnal corruption.

## CHAPTER 161. On the obstinacy of certain people who attack the resurrection of the flesh, which, as foretold, the whole world believes

As for the goods of the soul, which it will enjoy in the greatest blessedness after this life, distinguished philosophers do not disagree with us. They dispute about the resurrection of the flesh and deny it as far as they can.

But they have left many believers and very few deniers; and learned and unlearned alike, the wise of the world and the foolish, have turned with faithful hearts to Christ, who demonstrated in his own resurrection what seems absurd to these people.

The world believes what God foretold—God who also foretold that the world would believe this very thing. He was not compelled by the magic arts of Peter [Porphyry] to announce it so long beforehand with the praise of believers.

For he is the God whom, as I have already said several times and do not tire of recalling, the very deities dread, as Porphyry confessed and wished to prove through the oracles of his gods. Porphyry praised him so highly that he called him both God the Father and king.

Far be it from us to understand what he foretold in the way those people wish who did not believe with the world what he foretold that the world would believe. Why should it not instead be understood as the world was foretold so long beforehand that it would believe, rather than as the very few chatter who refused to believe with the world what it was foretold that the world would believe?

If they say that these things must be believed in another way lest, by saying that what was written is false, they do injury to that God to whom they bear such great testimony, they inflict an even greater injury upon him if they say that these things must be understood otherwise—not as the world believed them, the world whose future belief he praised, promised, and himself fulfilled.

But why [indeed] can he not make the flesh rise and live forever? Is it to be believed that he will not do this because it is evil and unworthy of God? We have already said much about his omnipotence, by which he does so many and such great incredible things.

If they wish to find something that the omnipotent cannot do, they have it plainly. I shall say it: he cannot lie.

Let us therefore believe what he can do, without believing that he can do what he cannot do. Thus, since they do not believe that he can lie, let them believe that he will do what he promised he would do. And let them believe it as the world believed it—the world whose future belief he foretold, whose future belief he praised, whose future belief he promised, and whose belief he has already shown to have occurred.

But from where do they demonstrate that this is evil [has been demonstrated]? There will be no corruption there, which is the evil of the body.

We have already discussed the order of the elements and have said enough about the other conjectures of human beings, including how great will be the ease of movement in an incorruptible body. In the thirteenth book, as I think, we sufficiently demonstrated this by comparison with the condition of present good health, which certainly cannot in any way be compared with immortality.

Let those who have either not read the earlier portions of this work or wish to recall what they read consult them.

## CHAPTER 162. How Porphyry’s definition is refuted by Plato’s own position; from the same Book XXII

“But Porphyry,” they say, “maintains that every body must be fled from if the soul is to be blessed.”

Therefore, since we have said that the body will be incorruptible, it is of no benefit if the soul will not be blessed unless it flees from every body.

I have already discussed this matter at the necessary length in the book mentioned. Here I shall recall only one point from it: let Plato, the teacher of all these people, amend his books and say that the gods he describes will flee from their bodies in order to be blessed—that is, that they will die. He said that these gods were enclosed in heavenly bodies, and yet that the god by whom they were made promised them immortality—that is, eternal continuance in those same bodies—so that they could be secure, not because their nature possessed this, but because his decision prevailed.

There he also overturns what they say: that because resurrection is impossible, it therefore must not be believed. For, according to the same philosopher, when the uncreated God promised immortality to the gods made by him—something impossible—he openly said that he would do what is impossible.

For Plato reports him speaking in this way:

> “Since you have come into being,” he says, “you cannot be immortal and indissoluble. Nevertheless, you will not be dissolved, nor will any fate of death destroy you, nor will they be more powerful than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetual existence than those bonds by which you have been joined.”

If those who hear these things are not merely absurd but also deaf, they nevertheless cannot doubt that, according to Plato, the god who made the gods promised something impossible to the gods made by him.

For one who says, “You cannot be immortal, but by my will you will be immortal,” says nothing other than: “What cannot happen, you will nevertheless be through my action.”

That God, therefore, will resurrect the flesh incorruptible, immortal, and spiritual—the God who, according to Plato, promised that he would do what is impossible.

Why, then, do they continue to proclaim that what God promised, and what the world believed when God promised it—the world which was itself promised to believe it—is impossible? We proclaim that God will do this, although even according to Plato God does impossible things.

Therefore, for souls to be blessed, the whole body need not be fled from. Rather, an incorruptible body must be received. And in what body will they rejoice more appropriately than in the one in which they groaned while it was corruptible?

For then they will not possess that dreadful desire which Virgil, following Plato, set down when he said:

> “And again they begin to wish to return into the body.”

As I have said, they will not have the desire to return to bodies when they have with them the bodies into which they desire to return; and they will possess them in such a way that they will never cease to have them and will never lay them aside through death, not even for the briefest moment.

## CHAPTER 163. On the contrary definitions of Plato and Porphyry, in which, if each yielded to the other, neither would depart from the truth; from the same Book XXII

Plato and Porphyry each made certain statements which, if they had been able to share them with one another, might perhaps have made them Christians.

Plato said that souls cannot exist forever without bodies. For this reason he also said that even the souls of the wise would return to bodies after however long a time.

Porphyry, however, said that the soul, once completely purified and returned to the Father, would never again return to the evils of this world.

Therefore, if Plato had granted Porphyry what he had seen to be true—namely, that even the most purified souls of the righteous and wise would return to human bodies—and if Porphyry had in turn granted Plato what he had seen to be true—namely, that holy souls would never return to the miseries of a corruptible body—then, instead of each saying only one of these things, both would say both. I think they would then see that it followed that souls would return to bodies and receive other bodies in which they would live blessedly and immortally.

For according to Plato even holy souls will return to human bodies; according to Porphyry holy souls will not return to the evils of this world.

Let Porphyry therefore say with Plato, “They will return to bodies.” Let Plato say with Porphyry, “They will not return to evils.” And let them agree that they will return to bodies in which they will suffer no evils.

Such bodies can only be those that God promises: blessed souls will be forever with their own eternal flesh [will make them remain].

I think that both of them would by now readily grant us this: since they acknowledged that the souls of the saints would return to immortal bodies, they would allow them to return to their own bodies, in which they endured the evils of this age and in which they worshiped God piously and faithfully so that they might be freed from those evils.

## CHAPTER 164. What Plato, Labeo, or even Varro might have contributed to the true belief in the resurrection, if their opinions had converged in one understanding; from the same book, chapter 28

Some of our people, because they love Plato for a certain remarkable elegance of speech and for some things he perceived truthfully, say that he also held a view somewhat like ours concerning the resurrection of the dead. Tully touches on this in such a way in his book *On the Republic* that he seems rather to assert that Plato was playing than to affirm that he wished to say it was true [or: “rather than, by affirming it, to say that it was true”]. For he introduces a man who had come back to life and reported certain things that accorded with Platonic discussions.

Labeo likewise says that two men died on the same day and met one another at a certain crossroads; then they were ordered to return to their bodies, and agreed among themselves that they would live as friends; and so it happened until they later died. But these authors narrated that a bodily resurrection had occurred of the sort experienced by those whom we know to have risen: they were restored to life, but not in such a way that they would no longer die afterward.

More remarkably, a certain Marcus Varro records the following in the books he composed *On the Race of the Roman People*; I thought his very words should be set down:

“Certain astrologers,” he says, “have written that there is, in the rebirth of human beings, something which the Greeks call *palingenesia* (παλιγγενεσία). They have assigned it a completion in a period of four hundred and forty years, so that the same body and the same soul which were once joined together in a human being would again return to the same conjunction.”
