This Varro—or those astrologers, whoever they were (for he did not disclose the names of those whose opinion he cited)—said something which, although it is false [Col. 0812B] (for once souls have returned to the same bodies they previously possessed, they will never afterward leave them), nevertheless tears down and destroys many of the arguments of that impossibility with which these people chatter against us.

For those who think—or thought—this did not consider it impossible that corpses dispersed into the air, into dust, into ash, into fluids, or into the bodies of animals that feed on them, or even of human beings themselves, should return again to what they had been.

Therefore, if Plato and Porphyry—or rather, whoever loves them and is still alive—agree with us that even holy souls will return to bodies, as Plato says, but will not return to any evils, as Porphyry says, so that what Christian faith proclaims follows from these positions, namely, that they will receive such bodies as will enable them to live happily forever without any evil [Col. 0812C]—let them also adopt this from Varro: that they will return to the same bodies in which they previously were. Then the entire question concerning the eternal resurrection of the flesh will be settled among them.

## CHAPTER 165. The nature of the vision by which the saints will see God in the future age; from the same book, book 22

Now let us see, insofar as the Lord deigns to help us, what the saints will do in immortal and spiritual bodies, with their flesh no longer living carnally but now living spiritually. 106 And what that activity—or rather, that rest and leisure—will be like, I do not know, if I wish to speak the truth. For I have never seen it through the bodily senses. But if I say that I have seen it with the mind, that is, with the intellect, what is our intellect, or how much is it, in comparison with that excellence?

There is the peace of God which, as the Apostle says, surpasses all understanding—whose understanding, unless it is ours, or perhaps even that of all the holy angels? Certainly not God’s. If, then, the saints are to live in the peace of God, they will surely live in that peace which surpasses all understanding, since there is no doubt that it surpasses ours. But if it surpasses even that of the angels, so that the one who said “all understanding” seems not to have excluded them, we must understand the saying in this sense: the peace of God, with which God Himself is at peace, cannot be known by us, or by any angel, in the manner in which God knows it. Thus it surpasses all understanding—obviously, all understanding except His own.

Yet because we too have become participants in His peace according to our measure, we shall possess, within ourselves, among ourselves, and with Him, as much peace as our highest capacity permits. In this way the holy angels know it according to their measure, whereas human beings now remain far below it, however greatly they may excel through progress of mind [profectu].

For we must consider what a great man was saying when he said: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part, until what is perfect comes; and now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face.” The angels already see in this way. They are also called our angels because, having been rescued from the power of darkness and having received the pledge of the Spirit, and having been transferred into the kingdom of Christ, we have already begun to belong to those angels with whom we shall share that holy and most sweet commonwealth which is itself the city of God, about which we have already written so many books.

Thus they are our angels, who are God’s angels, just as Christ is God’s and Christ is ours. They are God’s because they did not abandon God; they are ours because they have begun to have us as their fellow citizens.

Jesus said: “See that you do not condemn one of these little ones; for I tell you, their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Therefore, just as they see, so shall we see; but we do not yet see in that manner, because of what the Apostle said, as I mentioned shortly before: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face.”

This vision is therefore reserved for us as the reward of faith. The apostle John speaks of it: “When he appears,” he says, “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” The face of God must be understood as His manifestation, not as something resembling the bodily members that we possess and call by that name.

Therefore, when I am asked what the saints will do in that spiritual body, I do not say what I already see; I say what I believe, according to what I read in the Psalm: “I believed, and therefore I spoke.” I say, then, that they will see God in that very body [or: “I say that they will see”]. But whether they will see Him through the body, as we now see the sun, moon, stars, sea, earth, and the things upon it through the body, is no small question.

It is difficult to say that the saints will then have such bodies that they will not be able to close and open their eyes whenever they wish. It is more difficult to say that whoever closes his eyes there will not see God. For if the prophet Elisha, though absent in body, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts given to him by Naaman the Syrian—whom the prophet mentioned had cleansed from the deformity of leprosy—which the wicked servant had secretly thought he had done without his master seeing, how much more will the saints in that spiritual body see everything, not only when they close their eyes, but even things from which they are bodily absent?

Then that perfection will arrive of which the Apostle speaks: “We know in part,” he says, “and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished.” Then, to show by some comparison how far this present life is from the life that is to come—not merely the life of any people, but even of those who here possess outstanding holiness—he says:

“When I was a child, I understood as a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I also have been known.”

If, then, in this life—where the prophecy of remarkable human beings is to be compared with that life as a child is compared with a young man—Elisha nevertheless saw his servant receiving gifts in a place where he himself was not, will the saints, when what is perfect has come and the corruptible body no longer weighs down the soul but the incorruptible body impedes nothing, need their bodily eyes in order to see what is to be seen, when Elisha, although absent, did not need them in order to see his servant?

For, according to the translators of the Septuagint, these are the prophet’s words to Gehazi: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned from his chariot to meet you, and you received the money?” And as the presbyter Jerome translated it from the Hebrew: “Was not my heart,” he says, “present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?”

The prophet therefore said that he had seen this with his heart, aided, as no one doubts, in a wondrous way by divine power. But how much more will all possess that gift then, when God will be all in all?

Yet those bodily eyes will also have their own function and will remain in their proper place, and the spirit will use them through the spiritual body. For although that prophet did not need them in order to see someone absent, he did use them to see things present, which he could nevertheless have seen by the spirit even if he had closed them, just as he saw absent things in a place where he himself was not with them.

Far be it from us, therefore, to say that the saints in that life will not see God with closed eyes, when they will always see Him by the spirit. The question is whether they will also see Him through the eyes of the body when they have those eyes open.

For if, in the spiritual body, those eyes can do only as much as these eyes we now have can do, clearly God could not be seen through them. Their power, therefore, will be of a very different kind if through them that incorporeal nature will be seen which is not contained in a place but is wholly everywhere.

For when we say that God is in heaven and on earth—for He Himself says through the prophet, “I fill heaven and earth”—we are not saying that He has one part in heaven and another on earth. He is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, not at different times but in both places simultaneously; no bodily nature can do this.

The power of those eyes will therefore be far greater—not merely so that they see more sharply than snakes or eagles are said by some to see. For however sharp the sight of those animals may be, they can see nothing other than bodies. Rather, the power will be such that they can see incorporeal things as well.

Perhaps this great power of sight was granted for a time even to the eyes of the holy man Job in this mortal body, when he said to God: “I had heard you before by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and I waste away, and I regard myself as earth and ashes.”

Nothing here prevents us from understanding “the eye of the heart,” of which the Apostle says: “Having the eyes of your heart enlightened.” No Christian doubts that God is seen by these eyes when He is seen, if he faithfully accepts what that divine Teacher said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” But whether He will also be seen there with bodily eyes is what we are considering in this question.

The statement that is written, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God,” can be understood without any knot of difficulty as though it had said, “And every human being shall see Christ, the salvation of God”—He who was certainly seen in the body and will be seen in the body when He judges the living and the dead.

That He Himself is the salvation of God is also shown by many other testimonies of Scripture, but the words of that venerable old man Simeon make it especially clear. When he had taken the infant Christ into his hands, he said: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation.”

There is also what the aforementioned Job says, as it is found in copies translated from the Hebrew: “And in my flesh I shall see God.” He certainly prophesied the resurrection of the flesh, but he did not say, “through my flesh.” If he had said that, Christ God could have been understood, since He will be seen through the flesh and in the flesh. But now it can also be understood in this way: “In my flesh I shall see God [my Savior],” as though he had said, “I shall be in my flesh when I see God.”

Nor does the Apostle’s statement, “face to face,” compel us to believe that we shall see God through this bodily face, where bodily eyes are located, when we shall see Him continually by the spirit. For if there were not also a face of the inner person, the same Apostle would not say: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

Nor do we understand otherwise what is sung in the Psalm: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed.” For one draws near to God by faith, which clearly belongs to the heart, not to the body.

But because we do not know how many forms of approach the spiritual body will possess—for we are speaking about something we have not experienced—and no authority from the divine Scriptures occurs and comes to our aid concerning something that cannot be understood otherwise, what is written in the Book of Wisdom must necessarily happen to us: “The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans are uncertain.”

The reasoning of the philosophers, by which they argue that intelligible things are seen by the mind’s sight and sensible things—that is, corporeal things—by the bodily senses, so that the mind cannot contemplate intelligible things through the body, nor corporeal things by itself, would, if it could be certain for us, establish that God could in no way be seen through the eyes of even a spiritual body.

But both true reason and prophetic authority mock this reasoning. Who is so opposed to truth that he would dare to say that God does not know these corporeal things? Does He therefore have a body through whose eyes He can learn them?

Furthermore, what we said shortly before about the prophet Elisha surely indicates that corporeal things can be seen by the spirit, not through the body. When that servant received the gifts, the act certainly occurred bodily; nevertheless, the prophet saw it not through the body but through the spirit.

Therefore, since it is established that the spirit can see corporeal things, what if the power of the spiritual body will be so great that the spirit can also be seen through the body?

For each person knows his own life, by which he now lives in the body and animates and makes these earthly members living, through an inner sense and not through bodily eyes. Yet he sees the lives of others, although they are invisible, through the body. For how do we distinguish living bodies from nonliving ones unless we see both the bodies and the lives together, which we cannot see except through the body? We do not see lives without bodies with bodily eyes.

Therefore it can happen—and is highly credible—that we shall then see the bodies of the world, of the new heaven and the new earth, in such a way that we shall see, through the bodies we shall bear and the bodies we shall behold, God present everywhere and governing all corporeal things, with the clearest perception wherever we turn our eyes.

This will not be as now, when the invisible things of God are perceived intellectually through the things that have been made, “through a mirror, in an enigma,” and “in part,” when faith by which we believe has greater force in us than the appearance of corporeal things that we see with bodily eyes. Rather, just as we live among human beings who are alive and display vital movements, so that as soon as we look at them we do not believe that they are alive but see it, although we cannot see their life without their bodies, yet perceive that life in them through their bodies with every ambiguity removed [Col. 0817A].

In this way, wherever we direct those spiritual lights of our bodies, we shall also behold, through bodies, the incorporeal God who governs all things.

Either God will be seen through those eyes in such a way that, in their great excellence, they will possess something resembling the mind by which the incorporeal nature may also be perceived—a possibility that is difficult or impossible to demonstrate by any examples or testimonies of the divine Scriptures—or, what is easier to understand, God will be known and visible to us in such a way that He will be seen by each of us in our own selves, by one person in another, in Himself, in the new heaven and the new earth, and in every creature that will then exist; and He will also be seen through bodies in every body wherever the gaze of the spiritual body’s eyes is directed.

Our thoughts will also be open to one another. For then what the Apostle said will be fulfilled: “Do not judge anything before the appointed time”; and he immediately added: “Until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the thoughts of the heart; and then each person’s praise will come from God.”

## CHAPTER 166. The eternal happiness of the City of God and the perpetual Sabbath; from the same book, book 22 of *The City of God*

How great will that happiness be where there will be no evil, no good will remain hidden, and we shall devote ourselves to praising God, who will be all in all! For what else will be done there, where there will be neither any idleness to cease nor any need to be endured, I do not know. I am also reminded of the holy Song, where I read or hear: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you.”

All the members and inward parts of the incorruptible body, which we now see distributed among various necessary functions—for then there will be no such necessity, but complete security [or: “full, certain, secure”], everlasting happiness—will contribute to the praises of God.

For all those bodily harmonies whose numbers are now hidden, about which I have already spoken, will then not be hidden. They will be arranged inwardly and outwardly throughout the whole body and, together with the other things that will there appear great and wondrous, will kindle rational minds to praise so great an Artisan through delight in rational beauty [or: “will succeed”].

I do not dare rashly to define what movements of such bodies will occur there, because I cannot imagine them. Nevertheless, both movement and rest will be fitting, just as the appearance itself will be fitting, whatever it may be, since nothing unfitting will exist there.

Certainly, wherever the spirit wishes, the body will immediately be there; nor will the spirit wish anything that the body cannot suitably perform [decernere / decere]. There will be true glory, where no one will be praised through error or flattery. There will be true honor, which will be denied to no one who deserves it and bestowed on no one undeserving. Nor will any undeserving person seek it, since no one will be permitted to exist there except the deserving.

There will be true peace, where no one will suffer anything adverse, either from himself or from another. The reward of virtue will be the One who gave virtue and who promised to give Himself to it, than whom nothing better or greater can exist.

For what else is meant by what He said through the Prophet, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people,” except: “I will be what satisfies them; I will be whatever human beings rightly desire”—life, salvation, nourishment, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing?

The Apostle’s statement is also rightly understood in this way: “So that God may be all in all.” He Himself will be the end of our desires. He will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue. This gift, this love, this activity will surely belong to everyone, just as the common life itself will be eternal.

But what degrees of rewards, and also what ranks of honors and glories, will belong to those who merit them—who is capable of imagining, much less of expressing? Yet there is no doubt that such distinctions will exist. That blessed city will also regard as a great good within itself the fact that no inferior will envy anyone superior to him, just as the other angels now do not envy the archangels.

Each person will not wish to be what he has not received, although he will be bound to the one who has received it by the most peaceful bond of concord—just as, within the body, the eye does not wish to be the finger, while the peaceful structure of the whole flesh contains both members.

Thus one will have a gift less than another, but will also have this gift: that he does not wish for more. Nor will they therefore lack free choice, because sins will not be able to delight them. Rather, free choice will be more truly free because it will have been liberated from the delight of sin into an unchangeable delight in not sinning.

For the first free choice given to human beings when they were first created upright could avoid sinning, but could also sin. The final free choice will be more powerful because it will not be able to sin. Yet this too will be a gift of God, not a capacity belonging to nature by itself. For it is one thing to be God and another to be a participant in God. God cannot sin by nature; a participant in God receives from Him the ability not to sin.

The stages of the divine gift had to be preserved: first, free choice was given by which a human being could avoid sinning; finally, free choice by which he could not sin. The former belonged to the acquisition of merit, the latter to the reception of reward. But because this nature sinned when it could sin, it is liberated by more abundant grace so that it may be brought to that freedom in which it cannot sin.

Just as the first immortality was the ability not to die, which Adam lost by sinning, while the final immortality will be the inability to die, so the first free choice was the ability not to sin, while the final free choice will be the inability to sin.

Thus the will of piety and righteousness will be as incapable of being lost as the will of happiness. For by sinning we did not retain either piety or happiness, but we did not lose the will for happiness even when happiness itself was lost.

Surely God Himself is not to be denied free choice on the grounds that He cannot sin, is He? Therefore that city will possess one will common to all and inseparable within each person: a free will liberated from every evil, filled with every good, enjoying without failure the delight of eternal joys, forgetful of faults and punishments, yet not forgetful of its liberation, so that it may remain grateful to its Liberator.

Accordingly, with respect to rational knowledge, it will remember even its former evils; but with respect to the experience of suffering, it will be utterly forgetful. For even the most skilled physician knows nearly all diseases of the body insofar as they are known by medical art, but insofar as they are felt in the body he does not know many of them, because he has not suffered them himself.

Thus there are two kinds of knowledge of evils: one by which they do not escape the power of the mind, and another by which they cling to the senses of experience. Vices are known in one way through the teaching of wisdom and in another through the worst life of folly.

There are likewise two kinds of forgetfulness of evils: the educated and learned person forgets them in one way, and the person who has experienced and suffered them in another—the former if he neglects his knowledge, the latter if he is freed from misery.

According to the forgetfulness I placed second, the saints will not remember their former evils, for they will be free from all evils, so that those evils will be completely erased from their senses. Yet the power of knowledge, which will be great in them, will not leave hidden from them either their own past or the eternal misery of the damned.

Otherwise, if they are going to be unaware that they had once been miserable, how will they sing forever, as the Psalm says, “the mercies of the Lord”? Nothing will surely be more pleasing to that city than this song, sung to the glory of the grace of Christ, by whose blood we have been redeemed.

There it will be fulfilled: “Be still, and know that I am God.” This will truly be the greatest Sabbath, having no evening, which the Lord commended in the first works of the world, where we read: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works which he had made; and God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he rested from all his works which God began to make.”

For we ourselves will be the seventh day when we have been filled and perfected [or: restored] by His blessing and sanctification. There, resting, we shall see that He is God. We wished to be this ourselves when we fell away from Him, listening to the deceiver: “You shall be as gods.” We withdrew from the true God, through whose making we would have been gods by participation, not by desertion.

For what did we accomplish without Him except that, in His anger, we failed? Restored and perfected by a greater grace, we shall rest forever, seeing that He is God, with whom we shall be filled when He is all in all.

Even our good works are counted toward our attainment of this Sabbath when they are understood to belong more to Him than to us. For if we attribute them to ourselves, they will be servile, since it is said concerning the Sabbath: “You shall do no servile work on it.”

For this reason it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “I gave them my Sabbaths as a sign between me and them, so that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctify them” [or: “restore them”]. We shall rest perfectly and see perfectly that He is God [or: “Then we shall know perfectly, when we rest perfectly and see perfectly that He is God”].

This Sabbath-rest will become clearer if the succession of the ages is reckoned as a succession of days according to those divisions of time that appear to be expressed in Scripture. For seven ages are found: the first age is, as it were, the first day, from Adam to the Flood.

The second extends from there to Abraham—not by equality of periods of time but by the number of generations. From that point onward, as the evangelist Matthew determines, three ages follow until Christ’s coming, each marked by fourteen generations: the first from Abraham to David, the second from there to the deportation to Babylon, and the third from there to Christ’s birth according to the flesh.

Thus there are five ages in all. The sixth is now in progress and is not to be measured by any number of generations, because of what was said: “It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority.”

After this, as on the seventh day, God will rest, when He causes that same seventh day—which we ourselves shall be—to rest in God Himself.

It would now take too long to discuss each of these ages carefully. Yet this seventh age will be our Sabbath, whose end will not be evening, but the Lord’s Day, as it were an eternal eighth day, consecrated by Christ’s resurrection and prefiguring eternal rest not only for the spirit but also for the body.

There we shall rest and see; we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Behold what will exist at the end—without end. For what other end is ours except to arrive at the kingdom whose end there is none?

## CHAPTER 167. How Matthew can say that the centurion came to the Lord on behalf of his servant, when Luke says that he sent friends to Him; from book 2 of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 20

Let us see whether Matthew and Luke agree concerning the centurion’s servant. Matthew says: “A centurion came to him, asking him and saying, ‘My boy lies at home paralyzed.’” This seems to conflict with Luke’s statement:

“When he had heard about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and heal his servant. When they came to Jesus, they earnestly begged him, saying, ‘He is worthy that you grant this to him [or: ‘for him’], for he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.’ Jesus was going with them. And when he was already not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying, ‘Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. Therefore I did not consider myself worthy to come to you myself; but say the word, and my boy will be healed.’”

If this is how the event occurred, how can Matthew’s account be true? “A certain centurion came to him,” when he himself did not come but sent friends? Unless, by carefully observing the matter, we understand that Matthew did not entirely depart from the customary manner of speaking.

For we customarily say that someone has come even before he reaches the place to which he is said to have come. Hence we also say that someone has come a little way or a long way toward the place he is seeking to reach. More than this, we often say that the arrival itself, for the sake of which someone approaches, has taken place even when the person who arrives does not see the one at whom he arrives, as when he reaches someone through a friend whose favor he needs.

Custom has established this so firmly that even in ordinary speech those are called “approachers” who, through the intervention of suitable persons, reach by the arts of ambition the minds of powerful people who are, as it were, inaccessible.

If the arrival itself is customarily said to be accomplished through others, how much more can approach be accomplished through others? Approach often falls short of arrival, since someone may approach very closely and yet be unable to arrive.

Matthew therefore did not absurdly wish to say briefly, in a way intelligible even to ordinary people, that the centurion approached the Lord through others: “A centurion came to him.”

Nevertheless, we must also attend carefully to the profound mystical expression of the holy evangelist, in accordance with what is written in the Psalm: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened.” Since the centurion’s faith—the means by which one truly approaches Jesus—was praised by Jesus Himself, so that He said, “I have not found such great faith in Israel,” the discerning Evangelist wished to say that the centurion himself had approached Christ rather than those through whom he had sent his words.

Luke, for his part, disclosed the entire course of events precisely so that from this we might understand how the other evangelist, who could not lie, said that the centurion had approached.

For the woman who suffered from a flow of blood, although she touched the fringe of His garment, nevertheless touched the Lord more than the crowds who pressed against Him. Just as she touched the Lord more the more she believed, so the centurion approached the Lord more the more he believed.

The remaining matters in this chapter, which one evangelist relates and the other omits, are treated unnecessarily, since according to the rule established at the outset they are found to contain nothing contradictory.

## CHAPTER 168. How all four evangelists agree with one another in the miracle of the five loaves
This miracle, then, which all four evangelists record and which is thought to differ somewhat from the others, must be examined and discussed, so that from it we may also learn a rule for other similar expressions: by such diverse formulations the same meaning is nevertheless retained, and the same truth of events preserved. The examination should indeed begin, not with Matthew according to the order of the evangelists, but rather with John, by whom this account is expressed in such a way that he even gives the names of the disciples with whom the Lord discussed the matter. For he says:

“When Jesus, therefore, had lifted up his eyes and had seen that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip, ‘Where shall we buy bread, that these people may eat?’ Now he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do. Philip answered him, ‘Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive a little.’ One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, said to him, ‘There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish; but what are these among so many?’ Then Jesus said, ‘Have the people sit down’ (there was much grass in the place [the reading *mulum* is uncertain]). So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Then Jesus took the loaves and, when he had given thanks, distributed them to those who were seated; likewise also as much of the fish as they wanted. When they had been filled, he said to his disciples, ‘Gather up the fragments that remain, so that they may not be lost.’ So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves that remained after those who had eaten.”

Here we are not asking what John said about the kind of loaves: he did not omit that they were barley loaves, whereas the others omitted it. Nor are we asking what he did not say: that, besides the five thousand men, there were also women and children, as Matthew says. In questions of this kind it should now be entirely certain and regularly maintained that no one ought to be troubled when one evangelist says what another omits.

[Col. 0822B] Rather, the question is how everything they said can be true, so that, by recounting something different, one evangelist does not exclude another. For if the Lord, according to John’s account, after observing the crowds, asked Philip, testing him, from where food could be obtained for them, it may seem problematic how what the others recount can be true: that the disciples first said to the Lord that he should dismiss the crowds, so that they could go and buy food for themselves in the nearby places. According to Matthew, he answered them, “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat.” Mark and Luke agree with this, merely omitting the words, “They do not need to go away.”

It is therefore understood that after these words the Lord looked upon the multitude and said to Philip what John records, though the others omitted it.

[Col. 0822C] Next, what Philip answered in John is reported by Mark as having been answered by the disciples, wishing it to be understood that Philip also gave this answer on behalf of the others, although they could very commonly have used the plural number for the singular. What, then, did Philip say? “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for them, so that each might receive a little.” This is equivalent to Mark’s statement: “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give them something to eat?”

Mark alone records that the Lord said, “How many loaves do you have?” The others omitted this. What Andrew suggested in John concerning the five loaves and two fish, the others reported from the standpoint of the disciples, using the plural for the singular. Luke, moreover, compressed Philip’s answer and Andrew’s answer into one statement. When he says, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish,” he attributes this to Andrew’s answer; but when he adds, “Unless perhaps we should go and buy food for all this crowd,” he seems to refer to Philip’s answer, except that he says nothing about the two hundred denarii. Yet this may also be understood as part of Andrew’s statement. For when he had said, “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish,” he himself added, “But what are these among so many?” That is equivalent to saying, “Unless perhaps we should go and buy food for all this crowd.”

From this entire variety of wording, together with the agreement of the events and meanings, it is sufficiently clear that we are profitably taught to seek nothing in words except the intention of those speaking. All truthful narrators, whether they are recounting something about a human being, an angel, or God, ought to devote themselves to making that intention clear. Their intention can be expressed in different words without their disagreeing about the matter itself.

[Col. 0823A] Certainly, at this point we must not omit something that should also prepare the reader for other cases of this kind that may arise. Luke said that the people were ordered to sit down in groups of fifty; Mark, however, says groups of fifty and groups of one hundred [the supplied text has a variant: “and groups of one hundred”]. This does not cause difficulty here, because one mentioned a part and the other the whole. The one who reported groups of one hundred reported what the other omitted. There is therefore no contradiction.

Nevertheless, if one evangelist had mentioned only groups of fifty and another only groups of one hundred, it would seem highly contradictory, and it would not easily be recognized that both statements had been made, with one evangelist reporting one detail and the other the other detail. Yet, on closer consideration, who would not admit that both facts ought to have been discovered? I have said this because there are often matters of this kind which seem contradictory to those who pay little attention and judge rashly, although they are not.

## CHAPTER CLIX. How Matthew agrees with Mark concerning the staff, which Matthew says the Lord forbade them to carry, whereas Mark says that they were to carry only a staff; from the same book, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, II

It is likewise often asked how Matthew and Luke recorded that the Lord told the disciples not to carry even a staff, whereas Mark says: “And he commanded them to take nothing for the journey, except a staff”; and he himself continues, “no bag, no bread, nor money in their belt,” thereby showing that his account concerns the same episode as theirs, in which they said that a staff was not to be carried.

This is resolved by understanding that the staff which, according to Mark, was to be carried is mentioned with one meaning, and the staff which, according to Matthew and Luke, was not to be carried with another meaning. The same applies to the word “temptation.” Of one kind it is said, “God tempts no one”; of another, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.” The former is temptation toward deception; the latter is testing.

Similarly, the word “judgment” is understood in one way in the passage, “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment,” and in another way where it is said, “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.” The former judgment is condemnation; the latter is discernment.

There are many other words that do not have one single meaning. Placed suitably in different contexts, they are understood in different ways. Sometimes this is expressed with an explanation, as in the passage: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in malice, so that you may be mature in understanding.” This concise sentence could have been expressed as: “Do not be children, but be children.” Likewise: “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise.” What else does this mean than, “Let him not be wise, so that he may be wise”?

At other times such sayings are deliberately phrased so as to exercise the person who seeks their meaning, as in what he says to the Galatians: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another; for each one will bear his own burden.”

Unless the word “burden” is understood in different senses, one will undoubtedly think that the speaker contradicts himself, and this within a single statement, with the words placed so close together. For shortly before he said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” and afterward, “Each one will bear his own burden.”

But some burdens are those of sharing in weakness, while others are those of rendering an account to God for our actions. The former are shared with our brothers and sisters in order to support one another; the latter are borne individually by each person.

[Col. 0824B] In the same way, the staff is understood spiritually, as in the Apostle’s words, “I will come to you with a staff,” and bodily, as the staff we use for a horse or for some other need—not to mention the other figurative meanings of this word.

Both statements, then, must be understood as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles: that they should not carry a staff, and that they should carry nothing except a staff. For when, according to Matthew, he said to them, “Do not possess gold or silver or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff,” he immediately added, “For the worker is worthy of his food.”

From this he clearly showed why he did not want them to possess and carry these things: not because they are unnecessary for sustaining this life, but because he was sending them in such a way as to demonstrate that these things were owed them by the very people to whom they would proclaim the Gospel when those people believed—just as wages are owed to soldiers, fruit to those who plant a vineyard, and milk to shepherds of a flock.

Hence Paul says: “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not receive milk from the flock?” He was speaking there about the things necessary for preachers of the Gospel. A little later he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things? If others share in your authority over you, should we not do so even more? But we have not used this authority.”

From this it is clear that the Lord did not command these things as though evangelists ought not to live from anything other than what was supplied by those to whom they preached the Gospel. Otherwise the same Apostle would have acted against this command when he supported himself by the labor of his hands, so that he would not be a burden to anyone. Rather, the Lord gave them the authority by which they would know that these things were owed them.

When something is commanded by the Lord, failure to do it is disobedience. But when authority is granted, anyone may choose not to use it, just as anyone may relinquish what belongs to him by right.

In saying these things to the disciples, therefore, the Lord was doing what the Apostle later explained more openly: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel; but I have used none of these things.”

When he says that the Lord so ordained, but that he himself did not use the arrangement, he clearly shows that the authority to use these things was granted, not that a necessity of serving was imposed.

[Col. 0825A] In giving this ordinance—that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—the Lord was telling the apostles to go without anxiety, possessing and carrying none of the necessities of this life, whether great or small. For this reason he included the staff: to show that all things were owed by his faithful people to his ministers, who demanded no superfluities. By adding, “For the worker is worthy of his food,” he fully disclosed and clarified wherefore and why he was speaking of all these matters.

He therefore signified this authority by the name “staff” when he said that they should take nothing on the journey except a staff. For this might also have been stated briefly as: “Carry none of the necessities with you—not even a staff,” [variant: “nor a staff, except a staff alone”]. Thus the statement “nor a staff” may be understood to mean not even the smallest possessions; while the addition, “except a staff alone,” may be understood to mean that through the authority received from the Lord, signified by the name “staff,” even what they did not carry would not be lacking.

The Lord therefore said both things. But because one evangelist did not record both, it is thought that the one who said that the staff, used in one sense, was to be carried contradicts the one who said that the staff, used in another sense, was not to be carried. Once the explanation has been given, however, this should no longer be thought.

Likewise, when Matthew says that sandals were not to be carried on the journey, he forbids the anxiety that leads them to think they must carry them so that they will not be without them [variant: “so that they may not be lacking”]. The same is to be understood concerning two tunics: no one among them was to think anxiously that, besides the tunic he was wearing, he should carry another in case it were needed, since he could receive one by virtue of that authority [variant wording: “should think anxiously that he ought to carry another, when he could receive one through that authority”].

Therefore Mark, by saying that they were to be shod with sandals or light shoes (*soleae*), indicates that this footwear has some mystical significance: the foot is neither to be covered nor bare against the ground—that is, the Gospel must neither be concealed nor rest upon earthly advantages.

And when he does not forbid them to carry or possess two tunics, but more explicitly forbids them to put on two tunics, saying, “and they were not to put on two tunics,” what does he urge them to do except to walk not with duplicity but with simplicity?

There is no doubt, then, that the Lord said all these things, partly literally and partly figuratively, but that the evangelists inserted different elements into their writings: one this, another that; some things two or three of them, or all four, recorded alike. Yet not everything he said or did was written down in this way.

If anyone thinks that the Lord could not, in one discourse, place some sayings figuratively and others literally, let him examine the rest of his teaching [variant: “let him inspect it”]. He will see how rashly and unlearnedly he makes such a judgment. For, to mention one example that occurs to me for the moment, such a person might think that even the almsgiving and everything else commanded there should be understood figuratively, because the Lord instructs us not to let the left hand know what the right hand is doing.

I must again remind the reader of something that ought to be remembered, so that he will not need this reminder repeatedly: in different places in his discourses the Lord often repeated many things that he had already said elsewhere. Thus, if the order of the passages does not agree when compared with another evangelist, no one should suppose that one of them is thereby contradictory. He should understand that what had already been said in one place was said again elsewhere. This principle should be observed not only concerning sayings but also concerning actions.

There is nothing to prevent us from believing that the same action was performed again. But to slander the Gospel by refusing to believe that something was done again, when no one can prove that it could not have been done again, is sacrilegious folly.

## CHAPTER CLXX. Concerning the statement of Matthew and Mark that it happened after six days, whereas Luke says after eight; from the same book II, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

Matthew continues:

“Amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

[Col. 0826B] “And after six days Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother and led them up a high mountain privately,” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”

This vision of the Lord on the mountain, while Peter, James, and John were praying, where testimony was also borne to him from heaven by the Father’s voice, is recorded by three evangelists in the same order and with entirely the same meaning. The remaining details, however, differ according to their various modes of expression, without any difference in meaning, as we have shown in many passages above and as readers can observe for themselves.

As for Mark’s saying that this happened after six days, like Matthew, whereas Luke says after eight, those who are troubled by this should not be dismissed but instructed once the reason has been given.

When we say “after so many days,” we sometimes do not count the day on which we are speaking, nor the day on which the event we foretell or promise will occur; rather, we count the intervening days, after which the event will truly take place in full and complete form. Matthew and Mark did this. Excluding the day on which Jesus said these things and the day on which he displayed the vision mentioned on the mountain, they looked to the intervening days and said, “after six days.” Luke, however, counted the final days—the first and the last—and said, “after eight days,” using the manner of speech in which a part is mentioned for the whole.

Likewise, Luke says concerning Moses and Elijah: “And it happened, as they were departing from him, that Peter said to Jesus, ‘Master, it is good for us to be here,’” and so on. This should not be thought contrary to what Matthew and Mark have joined together, as though Peter suggested this while Moses and Elijah were still speaking with the Lord.

For they did not state that it happened at that time; rather, they omitted what Luke added—that Peter made his suggestion about making three tabernacles as Moses and Elijah were departing. Luke also added that, as they entered the cloud, a voice came from the cloud. The others did not say this, but neither did they contradict it.

## CHAPTER CLXXI. Concerning the alabaster jar of ointment: how Matthew and Mark, who say “two days before Passover,” do not conflict with John, who says “six days before”; from the same book II, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

“When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him with an alabaster jar of costly ointment and poured it over his head as he reclined,” and so on, up to the passage where he says: “What she has done will also be spoken of in memory of her.”

Let us now consider the woman and the costly ointment involved in the event that took place at Bethany. Although Luke records a similar event and the name of the person with whom the Lord was dining agrees—for he too says that the man was Simon—it is not contrary to the nature or custom of human beings that, if one person can have two names, two people can have one name.

It is more credible that this was a different Simon, not the leper, in whose house this event took place at Bethany. For Luke does not say that the event he narrates took place in Bethany. Although he does not mention the city or village where it happened, his account nevertheless does not appear to concern the same place.

I therefore think that nothing else should be understood except that the woman who was then a sinner, who came to Jesus’ feet, kissed them, washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, was not a different woman. To her the Lord, using the comparison of the two debtors, said that her many sins had been forgiven because she had loved much.

Rather, the same Mary had done this twice: once, namely, as Luke narrated, when she first approached with that humility and those tears and deserved the forgiveness of her sins.

Although John does not narrate the event in the same way as Luke, he nevertheless commended this same Mary when, having begun to speak about the raising of Lazarus, he mentioned her before he came to Bethany. He narrates it there as follows:

“There was,” he says, “a certain man who was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha, her sister. Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill.”

In saying this, John bears witness to Luke, who narrated that the event took place in the house of a certain Pharisee named Simon. Mary, therefore, had already done this.

But what she did again at Bethany is another event, one that does not belong to Luke’s narrative but is narrated jointly by three evangelists: John, Matthew, and Mark.

Let us therefore consider how this event agrees among these three—Matthew, Mark, and John. There is no doubt that they narrate the same event as having taken place at Bethany, where, as all three record, the disciples murmured against the woman, as though because of the destruction of the very costly ointment.

[Col. 0827D] Matthew and Mark say that the Lord’s head was anointed with the ointment, whereas John says that his feet were anointed. The rule we demonstrated in discussing the feeding of the crowds with five loaves shows that this is not contradictory.

There, because someone was found who recorded both groups of fifty and groups of one hundred sitting down, while another mentioned groups of fifty, it could not seem contradictory. It could have seemed contradictory if one had mentioned only groups of one hundred, just as another mentioned only groups of fifty; yet it had to be discovered that both things had occurred.

That example should have taught us, as I warned there, that even where individual evangelists record one of two events, we should understand that both occurred.

Here, therefore, let us understand that the woman anointed not only the Lord’s head but also his feet. Unless, perhaps, someone is so absurd and malicious that, because Mark records that the head was anointed after the alabaster jar had been broken, he denies that anything could have remained in the broken vessel with which she might also have anointed his feet.

But if he insists that it was broken in such a way that nothing remained, contending against the truth of the Gospel, how much better and more reverently may another insist that it was not broken in such a way as to pour out everything, contending in defense of the truth of the Gospel?

If that malicious critic is so stubbornly blind that he tries to break the harmony of the evangelists over the broken alabaster jar, let him first accept that the feet were anointed before the jar was broken, while it remained whole, and that afterward the head too was anointed when the breaking poured out the whole contents.

We recognize that provision is made for us in an orderly way from the head, but we also ascend in an orderly way from the feet to the head.

The remaining details of this event seem to me to present no difficulty. The others say that the disciples murmured over the pouring out of the costly ointment, whereas John mentions Judas. Since Judas was a thief, I think it is clear that by “the disciples” Judas himself is meant, according to the mode of expression we indicated in discussing Philip and the five loaves, in which the plural is used for the singular.

It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded by Judas when he said it, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the intention of all in words. But Judas said it because he was a thief, while the others did so out of concern for the poor. John, however, wished to mention only Judas, whose habitual practice of stealing he believed should be disclosed on this occasion.

## CHAPTER CLXXII. Concerning the hour of the Lord’s passion: how Mark, who says “the third hour,” and John, who says “about the sixth hour,” do not disagree; from book III of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, title XIII

If, then, Jesus was handed over to the Jews to be crucified at about the sixth hour, while Pilate was sitting on the tribunal, how was he crucified at the third hour, as some have thought who do not understand Mark’s words?

First, let us see at what hour he could have been crucified; then we shall see why Mark said that he was crucified at the third hour.

“It was about the sixth hour when he was handed over to be crucified, while Pilate was sitting,” as has been said, “on the tribunal.” It was not fully the sixth hour, but approximately the sixth—that is, the fifth hour had been completed and some portion of the sixth had begun.

They would never say “the fifth hour and a quarter,” or “the fifth hour and a third” [variant: “the fifth hour and a triens”], or “the fifth and a half,” or anything of this kind. Scripture has the custom of placing the whole for a part, especially in matters of time. Thus, concerning the eight days after which they say he went up the mountain, Matthew and Mark, looking to the intervening days, said “after six days.” This is especially clear because John spoke so carefully that he did not say “the sixth hour,” but “about the sixth hour.”

If he had not spoken in this way, but had simply said “the sixth hour,” we could understand the customary scriptural manner of placing the whole for a part, as I said: once the fifth hour had been completed and the sixth begun, the events they narrate concerning the crucifixion of our Lord were taking place, until, when the sixth hour was completed and he was hanging on the cross, darkness occurred, to which the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—bear witness.

Let us now ask why Mark said this. After recording that those who crucified him divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine who should take what, he followed this by adding: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him.”

He had already said, “And when they crucified him, they divided his garments.” The others likewise testify that the garments were divided after he had been crucified.

If, then, Mark wished to record the time when this event occurred, it would have been enough to say, “It was the third hour.” Why did he add, “and they crucified him,” unless he wished, by recapitulating, to indicate something that would be discovered when the Scripture itself was read in those times when it was known to the universal Church at what hour the Lord had been hung upon the tree, so that an error of this kind could be corrected or a falsehood refuted?

But because he knew that the Lord had been hung by the soldiers, not by the Jews, as John states most explicitly, he wished to show secretly that those who cried out for him to be crucified were more responsible for his crucifixion than those who, in fulfillment of their duty, performed the service assigned to them by their ruler.

It is therefore understood that it was the third hour when the Jews cried out for the Lord to be crucified. It is most truthfully shown that they crucified him at the moment when they cried out, especially since they did not wish to appear to have done this. For that reason they handed him over to Pilate, as their words sufficiently indicate according to John.

When Pilate had said to them, “What accusation do you bring against this man?” they answered him, “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” Pilate therefore said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews said, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.”

What they especially did not want to appear to have done, Mark shows that they did at the third hour, indicating most truthfully that the tongue of the Jews was more responsible for the Lord’s death than the hands of the soldiers.

Anyone who wishes to consider the matter without the harshness of impiety will easily see how appropriately Mark placed this reference to the third hour. Whoever reflects there will remember the hour at which the Jews crucified the Lord, although they wanted to shift the crime itself onto the Romans, whether their rulers or their soldiers, in the passage where the action of the soldiers is recorded.

For he says: “And when they crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them to determine who should take what.” Who did this except the soldiers, as John makes clear?

Therefore, lest anyone, turning away from the thought of so great a crime as committed by the Jews, should direct it toward those soldiers, Mark says: “It was the third hour, and they crucified him.” Thus the careful investigator will discover that those who cried out at the third hour for him to be crucified are rather found to have crucified him, although the soldiers’ hands hung him upon the tree.

He will also observe that what was done by the soldiers occurred at the sixth hour [variant: “is said to have occurred at the sixth hour”].

Some, however, wish the *parasceve* mentioned by John—“It was the Preparation, about the sixth hour”—to be understood as the third hour of the day [variant: “the third hour of the day”], when Pilate sat on the tribunal. In this way the third hour would appear to have been completed when he was crucified, and, while he was already hanging on the tree, another three hours would have elapsed, after which he gave up his spirit. From the hour when he died, namely the sixth hour of the day, darkness would have occurred until the ninth hour.

They say that on that day, which was followed by the Sabbath, there was the *parasceve* of the Jews’ Passover, and that the unleavened bread began with that same Sabbath. Nevertheless, the true Passover that was already being enacted in the Lord’s passion was not the Jews’ but the Christians’ Passover, whose preparation began—that is, whose *parasceve* occurred—at the ninth hour [variant: “from the ninth hour of the night”], when the Lord was being prepared for death at the hands of the Jews.

For *parasceve* means “preparation.” From that ninth hour of the night until his crucifixion, there occurred, according to John, the sixth hour of the *parasceve*, and according to Mark, the third hour of the day. Thus Mark did not recall and mention the hour at which the Jews cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him,” in a recapitulation, but said quite literally that it was the third hour at which the Lord was crucified on the tree.

What believer would not favor this solution to the question, provided that some point in time can be inferred from the ninth hour of the night, from which we can appropriately understand that the *parasceve* of our Passover—the preparation for Christ’s death—began?

For if we say that it began when the Lord was seized by the Jews, it was still the early part of the night. If it began when he was brought to the house of Caiaphas’ father-in-law, where he was also heard by the chief priests, the cock had not yet crowed, as we infer from Peter’s denial, which had already occurred when the cock was heard.

If, however, it began when he was handed over to Pilate, it is clearly written that it was already morning. It therefore remains for us to understand that this *parasceve* of Passover—the preparation for the Lord’s death—began when all the chief priests before whom he was first heard answered and said, “He is worthy of death.” This is found in Matthew and Mark, if, by recapitulation, we understand that they related later, in connection with Peter’s denial [the supplied text reads *cognitione*, with variant *negatione*], what had happened earlier.

It is not an unreasonable conjecture that, at the time when, as I said, they pronounced him worthy of death, it could have been the ninth hour of the night. From that hour until the hour when Pilate sat on the tribunal, it was approximately the sixth hour—not of the day, but of the *parasceve*, that is, of the preparation for the Lord’s sacrifice, which is the true Passover. Thus, when the sixth hour of that *parasceve* was complete—which corresponded to the third hour of the day—the Lord was hung upon the tree.

Whether this should rather be understood, or whether Mark recalled the third hour and wished especially to mention it as an indictment of the Jews at the Lord’s crucifixion, since they could be understood to have cried out for him to be crucified, so that we should regard them as having crucified him rather than those by whose hands he was hung upon the tree—just as the centurion approached the Lord more than those friends whom he sent—the question concerning the hour of the Lord’s passion has certainly been resolved. This question commonly provokes the shamelessness of contentious people and disturbs the ignorance of the weak.

## CHAPTER CLXXIII. Concerning the two criminals: how, despite the unequal accounts of Matthew and Mark, they do not differ in meaning; from book III of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

Matthew continues and says: “And the criminals who were crucified with him also insulted him.” Mark does not differ, saying the same thing in other words.

Luke, however, may seem to contradict them unless we remember a very customary mode of expression. Luke says:

“One of the criminals who were hanging there blasphemed him, saying, ‘If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.’ But the other answered and rebuked him, saying, ‘Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.’ And he said to Jesus, ‘Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.’ And Jesus said to him, ‘Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.’”

How, then, as Matthew says, did the criminals who were crucified with him insult him? Or, as Mark says, “Those who were crucified with him reviled him”? According to Luke’s testimony, one of them reviled him, while the other restrained him and believed in God.

We must understand that Matthew and Mark, briefly touching upon this passage, used the plural number for the singular, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read the plural statement, “They shut the mouths of lions,” although only Daniel is understood; and, “They were sawn in two,” although this is traditionally said concerning Isaiah alone [variant: “although it is related concerning Isaiah alone”].

In the psalm too, where it is said, “The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together,” the plural number is used for the singular, as the Acts of the Apostles explains. The kings are understood on account of Herod, and the rulers on account of Pilate; they used the testimony of that psalm.

Since pagans too are accustomed to slander the Gospel, let them observe how their own authors spoke of Phaedras, Medeas, and Clytemnestras, although there was only one of each.

What is more common, for example, than for someone to say, “The peasants are insulting me,” even if only one is insulting him? It would be contradictory to Luke’s explicit account if they had said that both criminals reviled the Lord; for then one person could not be understood under the plural number.

But when it is said “the criminals,” or “those who were crucified with him,” and the word “both” is not added, this could be said not only if both had acted, but also because one had done so. By the customary manner of speech, the singular may be signified through the plural number [the supplied wording is grammatically corrupt: “through the plural number [singular]”].

## CHAPTER CLXXIV. The evangelists report that the Lord appeared ten times after the resurrection, from the same book
We find, then, that in the four Evangelists it is mentioned ten times that the Lord was seen by human beings after the resurrection: once, by the women at the tomb; a second time, by the same women as they were returning from the tomb on the road; third, by Peter; fourth, by the two going to the village; fifth, by several in Jerusalem, where Thomas was not present; sixth, where Thomas saw him; seventh, at the Sea of Tiberias; eighth, on the mountain in Galilee, according to Matthew; ninth, as Mark says, finally, while they were reclining at table, since they were no longer on earth to dine with him; tenth, on that very day—not now on earth, but lifted up in a cloud—as he ascended into heaven. Mark and Luke mention this: Mark, indeed, after the appearance to them while they were reclining, continuing in such a way as to say, “And the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven”; Luke, however, omitting all that could have occurred during the forty days in which he dealt with the disciples, silently joins to the first day of his resurrection, when he appeared to several in Jerusalem, the final day on which he ascended into heaven, narrating as follows: “And he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them; and it happened that, while he blessed them, he was carried up into heaven” [“he departed from them and was carried up into heaven”]. Thus they saw him not only as they had seen him on earth, but also while he was being carried up into heaven.

Therefore, in the Gospel books he is mentioned as having been seen by all of them so many times before he ascended into heaven: nine times on earth, and once in the air as he ascended. But not everything was written down, as John acknowledges. His intercourse with them was frequent during the forty days before he ascended into heaven, though he did not appear to them continuously throughout all forty days. For John says that after the first day of his resurrection another eight days intervened, after which he appeared to them again; and then, for the third time, at the Sea of Tiberias, perhaps on the immediately following day. Nothing prevents us from supposing that afterward, whenever he wished, he appointed for them what he had also foretold earlier: that he would go before them to the mountain in Galilee [“that he might go before them to the mountain in Galilee”]; indeed, throughout those forty days he appeared as often as he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, as Peter says when he was preaching him to Cornelius and those who were with him: “We ate and drank together with him after he rose from the dead, for forty days.”

This does not mean that they ate and drank with him every day for forty days; for that would conflict with John, who inserted those eight days during which he was not seen by them, before he was manifested for the third time at the Sea of Tiberias. From that point onward, even if he appeared to them and dined with them every day, there is no contradiction; and perhaps for this reason it was said, “for forty days.” The four tens signify, in a mystery, either the whole world or the whole of the temporal age; for those first ten days, which included the eight days, may, according to the manner of Scripture, appropriately be counted as a whole by reference to a part.

Let what the apostle Paul says also be considered, to see whether it raises any difficulty: “He rose,” he says, “on the third day according to the Scriptures, and appeared to Cephas.” He did not say, “He appeared first to Cephas,” for that would conflict with what is read in the Gospel, namely, that he first appeared to the women. “Then,” he says, “to the Twelve”—at whatever time one may understand, but nevertheless on the very day of the resurrection; “then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once.” Whether these were gathered together with the eleven, with the doors shut because of fear of the Jews, so that when Thomas had gone out Jesus came to them, or whether it happened at any time after those eight days, there is no contradiction.

“Then,” he says, “he appeared to James.” We should not understand this to mean that he first appeared to James at that time, but rather that he appeared to him in some particular and individual manifestation. “Then to all the apostles”—not to them for the first time then, but now so that he might converse more familiarly with them until the day of his ascension. “Last of all,” he says, “as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me”; but this already occurred from heaven, after a considerable interval following his ascension.

Let us now examine what we had postponed: for what mystery, according to Matthew and Mark, did he command after rising, “I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me”? This too was fulfilled, though only after many other events had occurred, even though the command was given—as far as necessity is concerned, without prejudice to the possibility that either this alone or this first was expected to take place.

Undoubtedly, therefore, since these words are not the voice of the Evangelist narrating that this happened, but of the angel speaking by the Lord’s command, and afterward of the Lord himself, while the Evangelist narrates that this was said by the angel and by the Lord, they must be understood prophetically. For “Galilee” is interpreted either as “migration” or as “revelation.”

First, then, according to the meaning “migration,” what else should be understood by “He goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him,” except that the grace of Christ was going to migrate from the people of Israel to the Gentiles? The apostles, when preaching the Gospel to them, would in no way have been believed unless the Lord himself had prepared a way for them in human hearts; and this is meant by, “He will go before you into Galilee.”

But that, rejoicing, they would marvel as difficulties were broken through and overcome and a door was opened to them in the Lord through the illumination of believers—this is meant by, “There you will see him”; that is, there you will find his members; there you will recognize his living body in those who receive you.

According to the other interpretation, in which Galilee means “revelation,” this is not to be understood as referring to the form of a servant, but to that form in which he is equal to the Father—the form he promised in John to those who love him when he said, “And I will love him and show myself to him.” Certainly this does not refer merely to what they were already seeing, and which, even after rising with his scars, he later showed them not only to see but also to touch. Rather, it refers to that ineffable light by which he enlightens every human being coming into this world, according to which “he shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend him.”

He went before us to that place from which, when he came to us, he did not depart, and in which, going before us, he did not abandon us. That will be the revelation that is true Galilee: when we are like him, there we shall see him as he is. It will also be the more blessed migration from this age into that eternity, if we embrace his commandments in such a way that we may deserve to be separated to his right hand. For then the wicked will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life. They will migrate from here to there and will see him in a manner in which the ungodly do not see him. For “the wicked will be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord,” and “the ungodly will not see the light.”

“This is eternal life,” he says, “that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent”—as he will be known in that eternity, to which he will lead his servants through the form of a servant, so that, as free persons, they may contemplate the form of the Lord.

## CHAPTER CLXXV  
### How, in the three Evangelists, the gifts of active virtue shine forth, but in John’s Gospel the gifts of contemplative virtue; and how, since it is recognized by those capable of discerning this that it is not perfect but partial, it will remain thus until the perfect comes, from Book IV of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*

To the disciples also, by breathing upon them, he gave the Holy Spirit, so that no one would suppose that the Spirit who is consubstantial and coeternal with the Trinity belonged only to the Father and not also to the Son.

Finally, entrusting his sheep to Peter, who loved him and confessed that love three times, he says that he wishes that same John to remain until he comes. Here, too, it seems to me that he taught, in a profound mystery, this very dispensation of John’s Gospel, by which he is borne sublimely into the clearest light of the Word, where the equality and unchangeableness of the Trinity can be seen, and where it can be clearly recognized and understood in what distinctive way the human being differs from the others through whose assumption the Word became flesh—but only when the Lord himself comes. For that reason, it will remain until he comes.

It remains now in the faith of believers; then it will be contemplated face to face, when our life appears and we also appear with him in glory. But whoever thinks that it can happen to a human being still living this mortal life that, once every cloud of bodily and carnal imaginings has been removed and dispelled, he may possess the most serene light of unchangeable truth, and that, with his mind wholly withdrawn from the habits of this life, he may cling to it steadfastly and without deviation, does not understand either what he is seeking or whom he is seeking.

Let him rather believe the sublime and wholly trustworthy authority: as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord and walk by faith, not yet by sight. While perseveringly retaining and guarding faith, hope, and charity, let him look toward that vision, relying on the pledge of the Holy Spirit which we have received. The Spirit will teach us [teaches us] all truth, when God, who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, gives life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in us.

Before what is dead is given life, however, it is undoubtedly corruptible because of sin and weighs down the soul. And if at some point it rises above this cloud with which the whole earth is covered—that is, above this carnal darkness with which all earthly life is covered—it is touched, as it were, by a swift flash of lightning, and returns to its weakness, while the desire by which it may be lifted up again remains alive, but its purity is not sufficient for it to remain fixed there. The more capable a person is of this, the greater he is; the less capable, the lesser he is.

But if the human mind has not yet experienced anything of this kind, although Christ dwells in it through faith, it ought to devote itself to reducing and bringing to an end the desires of this age through the activity of moral virtue, walking, as it were, in the company of those three Evangelists, with Christ as mediator. Let it faithfully hold fast to him who is always the Son of God but for our sake became the Son of Man, so that his eternal power and divinity, accommodated to our weakness and mortality, might make for us, from what is ours, a way to himself and toward himself, with the joy of great hope.

Let Christ the King rule him, so that he may not sin; and if perhaps he should sin, let Christ the Priest make expiation for him. Thus, nourished in the activity of a good conduct and life, let him be lifted from earthly things on the wings of the twofold love, as on two strong wings, and let him be illuminated by Christ the very Word—by the Word who “was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”—although through a mirror and in an enigma, yet far more sublimely than through any bodily likeness.

Therefore, although in those three Evangelists the gifts of active virtue shine forth, while in John’s Gospel the gifts of contemplative virtue shine forth for those capable of discerning this [these things], nevertheless even this aspect of John’s Gospel, because it is partial, will remain thus until the perfect comes. “To one,” indeed, “is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit.” One has a taste for the day of the Lord; another drinks something more clearly from the breast of the Lord; another, lifted up to the third heaven, hears ineffable words. Yet all, as long as they are in the body, are away from the Lord; and for all the faithful who possess good hope, written in the book of life, what was said is reserved: “And I will love him and show myself to him.”

Nevertheless, during this pilgrimage, the more someone has advanced in understanding this matter, the more carefully he must guard against the devil’s vices, pride and envy. He should remember that this very Gospel of John, the more greatly it lifts us toward the contemplation of truth, the more greatly it commands us concerning the sweetness of charity. And because the commandment is most true and salutary, “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things,” the Evangelist who commends Christ far more highly than the others has him wash the disciples’ feet.

## CHAPTER CLXXVI  
### On the saying, “No one knows the Son except the Father,” from Book I of *Questions on the Gospel*
