When he said, “No one knows the Son except the Father,” he did not add, “and anyone to whom the Father wills to reveal him,” as he did when he said, “No one knows the Father except the Son,” adding, “and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

This should not be understood as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone, while the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son revealed him. Rather, it was said in such a way that we understand both the Father and the Son himself to be revealed through the Son. For he himself is the light of our mind, so that when the text later adds, “and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him,” we should understand this to refer not only to the Father but also to the Son.

The whole statement is explained by what follows: “For by his Word the Father declares himself” [“the Father himself is declared”]. The Word declares not only that which is declared through the Word, but also himself.

## CHAPTER CLXXVII  
### On the children sitting in the marketplace and calling to those who were unwilling either to humble themselves with John or to rejoice with Christ, where he teaches most beautifully what true restraint in food is, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospel*

Concerning the children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, he answered the propositions in reverse order. For when he says, “We mourned and you did not weep,” this refers to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But when he says, “We played the flute for you and you did not dance,” this refers to the Lord himself, who, by eating and drinking with the others, represented the joy of the kingdom.

But they were unwilling either to humble themselves with John or to rejoice with Christ, saying that the former had a demon, while the latter was a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.

When he adds, “And wisdom was justified by all her children,” he shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness does not consist either in abstaining or in eating, but in the evenness of spirit by which one endures poverty and exercises moderation amid abundance: not corrupting oneself, and taking or not taking at the proper time those things whose use is not blameworthy, but whose desire is.

It makes no difference at all what kind of food you take to meet the body’s need, provided that your kinds of food are suited to those with whom you must live. Nor does it matter greatly how much you take, since we see that some people’s stomachs are filled more quickly, yet they ardently, intolerably, and altogether shamefully crave the very little by which they are satisfied. Others, however, are satisfied by somewhat more, but endure deprivation more easily; even when food has been set before them ahead of the usual hour, they can look upon it calmly, without touching it, if this is timely, useful, or necessary.

It matters more, therefore, not what or how much food someone takes, in accordance with human custom, his own condition, and the necessity of his health, but with how much happiness and serenity of soul he can do without these things when he ought, or even must, do without them. Thus what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in the Christian’s soul: “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things [‘in all things and in all things’] I have been instructed, both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.” And also: “Neither, if we eat, will we abound, nor, if we do not eat, will we lack.” And again: “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy.” Since people commonly rejoice greatly in bodily feasts, he added, “in the Holy Spirit.”

Wisdom, therefore, is justified [also] by all her children, who understand that the appropriate times for using earthly things ought to vary, but that the ease of doing without such things and the love of enjoying eternal things ought not to vary with the times, but to be retained perpetually.

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII  
### On gluttony, even with the cheapest foods, from Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*

Whoever uses passing things more sparingly than is customary among those with whom he lives is either temperate or superstitious [Note: “He repeats this statement also in chapter 274, volume II.”]. But whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the limits and customs of the good people among whom he lives either signifies something or is morally corrupt. For in all such matters it is not the use of things but the lust of the user [“of the one using them”] that is at fault.

What, then, is suited to places, times, and persons must be carefully considered, lest we rashly condemn disgraceful behavior. It can happen that a wise person uses the most expensive food without any fault of craving [“desire”] or gluttony, while an unwise person burns with the most shameful flame of appetite for the cheapest food. Someone may more healthily prefer to eat fish in the manner of the Lord than lentils in the manner of Esau, Abraham’s grandson, or barley in the manner of beasts of burden.

Most animals are not therefore more self-controlled than we are because they use cheaper foods. In all such matters, what we do must be judged or approved not from the nature of the things we use, but from the reason for using them and the manner in which we desire them.

## CHAPTER CLXXIX  
### On the impossibility of fasting in the presence of the bridegroom, where he approves two kinds of fasting, one of tribulation and the other of joy, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospel*

Fasting is either in tribulation or in joy. In tribulation, it is practiced to appease God for sins; in joy, because bodily things delight us less in proportion as the nourishment of spiritual things is greater.

When, therefore, the Lord was asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered concerning both kinds of fasting. As for the fasting customarily practiced in tribulation, it is concerned with what he says: that the bridegroom’s sons will fast when the bridegroom has been taken away from them. Then they will be desolate, and will be in sorrow and mourning, until the joys of consolation are restored to them through the Holy Spirit.

Once they have received this gift, they will also most appropriately celebrate the other kind of fasting, which will take place through the joy of those already renewed into spiritual life. Before they receive it, he says that they are like old garments to which a new patch is unsuitably sewn—that is, some portion of teaching belonging to the discipline of the new life. If this is done, the teaching itself is somehow torn, because the portion concerning fasting from food is inappropriately imparted, whereas the teaching prescribes a general fast not merely from desire for food but from every joy in temporal pleasures.

Of this, as it were, a patch—that is, some part relating to food—he says should not be given to people still devoted to their old customs, because a kind of tearing seems to occur there as well, and because it does not suit their oldness. He also says that they are like old wineskins, which new wine—that is, spiritual commandments—would more easily burst than be contained by them.

They will be new wineskins when, after the Lord’s ascension, they are renewed by longing for his consolation through prayer and hope [“were renewed”]. For then they received the Holy Spirit; filled with him, they spoke in the languages of all the nations who were present and were said to be full of new wine. The new wine had already come to the new wineskins.

## CHAPTER CLXXX  
### On the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospel*

“A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.” This man is understood to be Adam in the human race. Jerusalem means “city of peace,” the heavenly city, from whose blessedness he fell. Jericho is interpreted as “moon” and signifies our mortality, because it is born, grows, ages, and dies.

The robbers are the devil and his angels, who stripped him of immortality and, after inflicting wounds by persuading him to sin, left him half-dead. For in that part by which a human being can understand and know God, he is alive [printed *visus*, “seen”; likely *vivus*, “alive”]; but in that part by which he wastes away and is weighed down by sins, he is dead. For this reason he is called half-dead.

The priest and the Levite, who saw him and passed by, signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, which could not provide salvation.

“Samaritan” is interpreted as “guardian,” and therefore the Lord himself is signified by this name. The binding of the wounds is the restraint of sins; the oil is the consolation of good hope, on account of the forgiveness granted for reconciliation to peace; the wine is an exhortation to work with the most fervent spirit.

His beast of burden is the flesh in which he deigned to come to us. To be placed upon the beast is to believe in Christ’s incarnation. The inn is the Church, where travelers returning from pilgrimage to their eternal homeland are refreshed.

The next day is the time after the Lord’s resurrection. The two denarii are either the two commandments of love, which the apostles received through the Holy Spirit in order to evangelize the others, or the promise of the present life and of the future life. For according to the two promises it was said: “He will receive seven times as much in this age, and in the age to come he will obtain eternal life.”

The innkeeper, therefore, is the apostle. What he spends beyond this is either the counsel expressed in the words, “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel,” or the fact that he also worked with his own hands so as not to burden any of the weak at the beginning of the Gospel, although he had the right to be nourished by the Gospel.

## CHAPTER CLXXXI  
### How Martha, receiving him into her house, signifies the Church as it now is, while Mary signifies it as it will be in the future, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospel*

That Martha received him into her house signifies the Church as it now is, receiving the Lord into its heart. Her sister Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and heard his word, signifies the same Church in the future age, where, ceasing from work and from the ministry required by necessity, it will enjoy wisdom alone.

Martha, therefore, is occupied with much service, because the Church is now exercised in such works. But when she complains that her sister does not help her, an occasion is provided for the Lord’s judgment, by which he shows that this Church is anxious and troubled about many things, although there is one necessary thing, to which one comes through the merits of this ministry.

He says that Mary chose the better portion, which will not be taken away from her. It is understood to be better because one advances toward it through the other—the ministry—and it will not be taken away. The ministry, however, although it is good, will be taken away when the need being served has passed.

# THE TREASURE OF SAINT EUGYPPius, AFRICAN ABBOT  
### From the works of Saint Augustine. Later volume.

[Col. 0839]

## CHAPTER CLXXXII. 1  
### On the man who asked his friend for three loaves at midnight, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*

The friend to whom one comes at midnight to borrow three loaves is certainly presented as a likeness according to which someone, placed in the midst of tribulation, asks God to grant him an understanding of the Trinity by which he may be consoled in the labors of the present life. But the comparison is from the lesser.

If a human friend rises from bed and gives, not because of friendship but because he is compelled by annoyance, how much more readily does God give, who without annoyance bestows most generously what is requested! Yet he wishes to be asked for this purpose: that those who ask may become capable of his gifts.

In the three loaves is also signified that the Trinity is of one substance. The friend whom the petitioner says has come from a journey and that he has nothing to set before him signifies the human appetite, which ought to obey reason. It was serving a temporal habit, which he calls a journey because of all things that pass with time.

But when the human being turns to God, that appetite too is recalled from its habit. If, however, the interior joy of spiritual teaching, by which the Trinity of the Creator is proclaimed, does not console him, great distress arises in the person whom mortal misery oppresses: he is commanded to abstain from those things that delight outwardly, while inwardly there is no refreshment from the joy of the Savior’s teaching. That very distress is midnight, which compels him to persist urgently in asking that he may receive the three loaves.

When he is told that the door is already shut from within and that his children are with him in bed, this signifies a time of famine of the word, when understanding is closed. Those who preached throughout the world, distributing evangelical wisdom as bread, are the children of the master of the house and are already in secret rest with the Lord.

Nevertheless, through prayer the one who longs for understanding succeeds in receiving it from God himself, even if there is no human being through whom wisdom may be preached.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII  
### On the bread, fish, and egg, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*

Concerning the bread, fish, and egg, to which he opposed the contrary things: stone, serpent, and scorpion.

The bread is understood as charity, because of its greater desirability and because it is so necessary that without it the other things are nothing, just as a table is poor without bread. Its opposite is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

The fish is understood as faith in invisible things, either because of the water of baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Since faith, battered by the waves of this world, is not broken, it is rightly compared to a fish. Its opposite he set forth as the serpent, because of the poisons of deceit that it first sowed by giving bad advice to the first human being.

In the egg is understood hope. For an egg is not yet a perfected offspring [*fetus perfectus*, “a perfect fetus”], but is hoped for as it is incubated. Its opposite he set forth as the scorpion, whose venomous sting must be feared from behind; just as the opposite of hope is looking backward, whereas hope for future things extends itself toward what lies ahead.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV  
### On what he said to the disciples, “Do not be lifted up on high,” and on the man with dropsy and the bent woman, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*

When he told the disciples that they should not be anxious about food, he said, “And do not be lifted up on high.” At first a person seeks these things to satisfy necessity; but when they have become abundant, he begins also to grow proud because of them.

This is like someone who has been wounded boasting that he has many plasters in his house, although it would be good for him if he had no wounds and needed not even one plaster.

Appropriately, he compared the man with dropsy to an animal that had fallen into a well, for the man suffered from fluid. Similarly, he compared the woman whom he said had been bound for eighteen years, and whom he released from that bondage, to an animal that is untied in order to be led to water.

We rightly compare the man with dropsy to the greedy rich person. Just as the former thirsts more the more he abounds in disordered fluid, so the latter desires such things more ardently the richer he is in wealth that he does not use well. The woman bent by illness so that she could not straighten herself signifies the soul weakened and oppressed by earthly opinions, so that it cannot think about divine things.

## CHAPTER CLXXXV  
### On the steward whom the Lord was removing from his stewardship, from the same Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*

In the case of the steward whom the Lord was removing from his stewardship and praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as something to imitate.

It is not permissible either to commit fraud in some way against our master in order to make alms from that very fraud, or to understand as debtors of God and our Lord those from whom we wish to be received into eternal dwellings. Rather, the just and holy are signified here: they admit into eternal dwellings those who have shared their earthly goods with them in their need. Concerning them he also says, “If anyone gives one of these a cup of cold water merely in the name of a disciple, he will not lose his reward.”

Conversely, these likenesses are also given so that we may understand this: if that man could be praised by the Lord whom he was defrauding, how much more must those please the Lord God who do such works according to his command!

Similarly, in the case of the unjust judge to whom the widow made repeated appeals, he drew a comparison with God the Judge, with whom the unjust judge is in no respect comparable.

As for the fact that he had the debtor write fifty measures instead of one hundred jars of oil, and eighty measures instead of one hundred measures of wheat, I think it has no other purpose than to indicate that what every Jew similarly does for priests and Levites should abound in the Church of Christ: that its righteousness should exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. Thus, while they gave tenths, these should give halves; just as Zacchaeus, not from his produce but from his actual possessions, either gave [“or certainly doubled”] or, by giving two tenths, surpassed the expenditures of the Jews.

“Mammon of iniquity” is the name the Lord gave to the money we possess for a time [“therefore”], because mammon is interpreted as “wealth.” Yet these are wealth only for the wicked, who place in them the hope and abundance of their blessedness. When the righteous possess them, they are indeed money, but they are not their wealth; their wealth is heavenly and spiritual. By spiritually supplying their need with these, and by excluding the poverty of misery, they will be enriched with an abundance of blessedness.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI. 2  
### On the one who is on the roof, the one who is in the field, and Lot’s wife, from Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*

What does the Lord mean when he says, “Let the one who is on the roof, with his vessels in the house, not come down to take them”?

The one who is on the roof is he who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually as though in the open air. His vessels in the house are the carnal senses, by which many people, using them to investigate the truth grasped by understanding, have gone completely astray.

For this spiritual person, these vessels are now idle in the house, because, with his mind raised above the body and placed, as it were, on the roof through the sharpness of understanding, he enjoys the clarity of wisdom as though beneath a completely open sky. Let him therefore beware lest, on the day of tribulation, he again take pleasure in carnal life, which is nourished through the bodily senses, and descend to take up such vessels.

What does the saying mean: “Likewise, let the one who is in the field not turn back”? The one who works in the Church and, like Paul and Apollos, plants and waters should not look back toward the worldly hope to which he has renounced himself.

What did Lot’s wife signify? Those who, in tribulation, look back and turn themselves away from the hope of the divine promise. For this reason she became a pillar of salt, so that, by warning people not to do this, she might, as it were, season their hearts, lest they become foolish.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII  
### On the two in bed, the two women grinding together, and the two in the field

Who are the two in bed that night, the two women grinding together, and the two in the field, concerning all of whom one of each pair will be taken and one left?

Three kinds of people seem to be signified here. The first consists of those who choose leisure and quiet, occupied neither with secular affairs nor with ecclesiastical affairs; their rest is signified by the name “bed.”

The second consists of those placed among the common people and governed by the more learned, conducting the affairs of this world. He signified them by the name of women because, as I have said, it is advantageous for them to be governed by the counsels of the experienced. He called them “grinding” because of the cycle and circuit of temporal affairs; yet he said that they were grinding together insofar as, from those very affairs and occupations, they provide what is useful to the Church.

The third consists of those who work in the ministry of the Church as in God’s field, concerning which the Apostle speaks of agriculture.

In each of these three classes there are again two kinds of people, distinguished according to the strength of their powers. Although all seem to belong to the members of the Church, when the temptation of tribulation arrives, some of those who are at leisure, some of those engaged in worldly affairs, and some of those who serve God in the Church remain, while others fall.

Those who remain are taken; those who fall are left. Thus, “one will be taken and one will be left” is not said as though it concerned two individual people, but two kinds of dispositions within each of the three classes of profession.

When he says “that night,” he means that tribulation. I think that the three classes who are taken are also represented by the three names of holy men whom the prophet Ezekiel declares alone would be able to deliver others: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

Noah seems to pertain to those through whom the Church is governed, just as the ark, which bore the figure of the Church, was governed by him upon the waters. Daniel, who chose a celibate life—that is, who despised earthly marriage—so that, as the Apostle says, he might live without anxiety, thinking about the things of God, signifies the class of those who are at leisure, yet are very strong in temptations, so that they may be taken.

Job, because he had a wife, children, and abundant earthly possessions, belongs to the class to which the mill is assigned; yet they must be very strong in temptations, as he was, for otherwise they could not be taken [“could not have been taken”].

I do not think that there are other classes of people of whom the Church consists besides these three, each possessing two distinctions because of being taken and left, although within each class many differences of pursuits and desires may be found, all nevertheless converging toward harmony and unity.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII  
### On the unjust judge whom the widow repeatedly petitioned, from the *Questions on the Gospels*
What is the reason that, in order to teach that one ought always to pray and not lose heart, he wished to set forth the parable of an unjust judge who, although he neither feared God nor respected human beings, nevertheless yielded to a widow’s persistent appeals and granted her justice, lest she finally weary him? For this is what he says: “Lest, by coming continually, she wear me out.”

The Lord presents parables either on the basis of some likeness—as in the case of that servant whose master forgave the debt which, when an account was rendered, he was found to owe, while he himself was unwilling even to grant his fellow servant a delay; and in the case of the moneylender, who, after forgiving two debtors what they owed, was loved more by the one to whom he had forgiven more; and in the case of the man who had two sons, the elder remaining near him in the field, while the younger lived riotously in a distant land—and innumerable examples of this kind. In these cases, insofar as they are similar, understanding is led toward the matter to which they are applied, whether to disclose a mystery or to seek truth; or else he proves something by the very dissimilarity, as in the saying that if God so clothes the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?

To this latter kind also belongs the parable of the servant whose master had announced that he would remove him from the stewardship. For that servant defrauded his master by falsifying the written accounts and reducing the debts of his master’s debtors by as much as seemed advantageous to him. The Lord in no way encourages us to defraud him; but, if someone provided for his future by committing fraud, the Lord says that he was commended by his master. How much more eagerly, then, should those who are commanded to make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, in order to act justly, provide for themselves for eternal life—as has been explained in its proper place.

To this kind also belongs the man who, not out of friendship but to escape annoyance, was roused while already asleep in order to lend three loaves to his friend. If he gave because he was compelled by annoyance, how much more will God, who loves his servants and urges them to ask, give good things to those who ask him?

Thus the former kind may be joined to these words: “As that happened, so also this”; while the latter may be expressed by: “If that is so, how much more this?” or, “If that is not so, how much less this?” Sometimes these formulations are obscure, and sometimes they are explicit.

Here, therefore, the unjust judge has been introduced not on the basis of likeness but of dissimilarity, so that the Lord might show how much more certain ought to be those who persistently entreat God, the fountain of justice and mercy—or, if something more excellent can be said or heard—when, with a most unjust judge, the petitioner’s persistence proved effective even in obtaining the fulfillment of her desire.

The widow herself may bear a likeness to the Church, which seems desolate until the Lord comes, although even now he secretly cares for her. But if it is asked why God’s elect pray to be avenged—a matter also said of the martyrs in the Apocalypse of John—when we are very plainly instructed to pray for our enemies and persecutors, it must be understood that the vengeance of the righteous consists in the destruction of all the wicked. They perish in two ways: either by conversion to righteousness, or by losing, through punishment, the power by which they now act against the good, for as long as it is advantageous to the good that they should possess even a temporary power.

Thus, even if all human beings were converted to God—including the enemies for whom we are commanded to pray—the devil, who works in the children of distrust, would nevertheless remain to be condemned at the end of the age. When the righteous desire that this end should come, although they pray for their enemies, they are nevertheless not unreasonably said to desire vengeance.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX. On the saying: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”

“Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath”—that is, pray that you may not be detained by some impediment, since in winter a person was hindered from traveling by rains or cold, and on the Sabbath, when it was not permitted to set out, one was likewise hindered from a journey. Or else it means: pray that on that day no one may be found either in sorrow or in joy over temporal affairs.

### CHAPTER CXC. On the camel that will pass through the eye of a needle; from Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*.

What does he mean when he says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God”? Here he calls “rich” one who is greedy for temporal things and proud of such possessions. Opposed to these rich people are the poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs.

This makes clear that all greedy people—even if they lack the resources of this world—belong to the class of rich people that has been rebuked. For afterward those who heard him said: “Who, then, can be saved?” They understood that those who are seized by the desire to possess such things are included in this number, even though they do not possess them, and the crowd of the poor is incomparably larger.

The meaning is that it is easier for Christ to suffer for lovers of the world than for lovers of the world to be converted to Christ. He wished himself to be understood under the name “camel,” because he humbled himself and carried burdens. For where is this more clearly understood than in the saying that is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things”?

By the “needle” he signifies pricks; by the pricks, the pains endured in his Passion. Thus he calls the eye of the needle the straits of the Passion.

When he says, “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God,” this should not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud, signified by the name of that rich man, will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride. Rather, it is possible for God—through his Word, as we see has happened and happens every day—to convert people from desire for temporal things to love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to saving humility.

### CHAPTER CXCI. On what is written about the Lord: “He pretended that he would go farther,” where he argues in various ways for true meanings against falsehood; from the same Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*.

What is written about the Lord—“He pretended that he would go farther”—does not pertain to falsehood. For not everything that we pretend is a lie; rather, it is a lie when we pretend something that signifies nothing. When our pretense, however, refers to some meaning, it is not a lie but a kind of figure of truth. Otherwise everything spoken figuratively by wise and holy men, or even by the Lord himself, would be judged false, because, according to the ordinary meaning, truth would not stand in such statements.

The man who had two sons, of whom the younger, after receiving his share of the inheritance, departed into a distant country, and the other details woven into that narrative, is not spoken of as though there really were some man who either experienced or did these things with his two sons. These things were invented to signify something far greater, more distant, and more exalted, and incomparably different, so that through that invented man the true God might be understood.

Just as sayings are invented without falsehood for the purpose of signifying something, so also actions may be invented for that purpose. Hence there is also the act of that same Lord when he sought fruit on a fig tree at a time when its fruit did not yet exist. There is no doubt that this search was not genuine; any human being could have known, whether by divinity or by the season, that the tree had no fruit.

Therefore, a fiction that refers to some truth is a figure; one that refers to nothing is a lie.

What, then, does it signify that the Lord pretended to go farther while he was accompanying the disciples and explaining the holy Scriptures to them, although they did not know whether he was the one? What should we think it means except that he indicated that people can arrive at knowledge of him through the duty of hospitality? Although he himself would afterward withdraw far from human beings, above all the heavens, he would nevertheless be with those who show hospitality to his servants. Thus, when they begin to say, “Lord, when did we see you as a stranger and bring you in?”—as though they meant the one who had gone far away—he will answer: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

Whoever has been instructed in the word and shares all good things with the one who instructs him keeps Christ from going farther away from him, as the Apostle says: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.” And in another passage, after saying, “Sharing in the needs of the saints,” he immediately added, “Pursuing hospitality.”

These people too had been instructed in the word while he explained the Scriptures to them. Because they pursued hospitality, they recognized in the breaking of bread the one whom they had not recognized in the exposition of the Scriptures. For “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.”

The Evangelist, saying, “But he himself pretended to go farther,” used the very word in which liars take excessive delight, so that they may lie with impunity—as though everything that is pretended were a lie—although very many things are truly invented in order that one thing may signify another. If Jesus had signified nothing else by pretending to go farther, it would rightly be judged a lie. But if it is correctly understood and referred to what he intended to signify, it is found to be a mystery.

Otherwise all things would be lies that, because of some likeness by which things are signified, are narrated as though they had happened when they did not happen. Hence there is that lengthy narrative about the two sons of one man: the elder who remained with his father, and the younger who traveled far away.

In this kind of invention, human beings have also attributed sayings and actions to irrational creatures and to things lacking sense, so that through such invented narratives, but with truthful meanings, they might convey more effectively what they wished.

This is found not only among authors of secular literature—for example, in Horace, where the mouse speaks to the wall and the weasel to the little fox—so that through an invented narrative a truthful meaning may be referred to the matter at hand; hence no one was so uneducated as to think that Aesop’s fables, which were composed for such an end, should be called lies.

It is found also in the sacred writings. In the Book of Judges, trees seek a king for themselves and speak to the olive, the fig tree, the vine, and the bramble. All this is certainly invented so that one may arrive at the intended matter through an invented narrative—not a deceptive one, but one bearing a truthful meaning.

I have said this because it is written about Jesus: “And he himself pretended to go farther,” lest anyone, like the Priscillianists, wishing to establish that lying is permitted, should even claim that Christ was a liar.

Whoever wishes to understand what that act of pretending foreshadowed should observe what he later accomplished by acting. For afterward he went farther, above all the heavens, and yet did not abandon his disciples. In order to signify this future event, divinely ordained, that present act was humanly invented; and therefore the meaning already placed in that fiction was truthful, because in his departure the truth of that meaning followed afterward. Let the person argue that Christ lied by pretending who denies that by his action he fulfilled what he signified.

It is not a lie when the truth is concealed by silence; it is a lie when falsehood is put forward in speech.

As for Jacob, who acted at his mother’s instigation so that he might appear to deceive his father, if the matter is examined carefully and faithfully, it is not a lie but a mystery. If we call these things lies, then all parables and figures that signify various matters—things not to be taken literally, but in which one thing is to be understood through another—will also be called lies. Far be such a judgment from us.

For whoever thinks this may also bring the same accusation against all the many figurative expressions, so that even what is called *metaphor*—that is, the transfer of a word from its proper subject to a nonproper subject—could by this reasoning be called a lie.

When we say that the crops “wave,” that the vines “bud,” that youth is “flowering,” or that hair is “white as snow,” those who judge these things to be lies will undoubtedly say so because we do not find waves, gems, flowers, or snow in the things to which we have transferred these words.

Likewise, “Christ is a rock,” and “the Jews have a heart of stone”; “Christ is a lion,” and “the devil is a lion”—and innumerable expressions of this kind—will be said to be lies.

What shall we say of the figurative expression that extends even to what is called *antiphrasis*, so that what is not present is said to abound, what is sour is called sweet, a grove is called *lucus* because it does not shine, and the Fates (*Parcae*) are so called because they do not spare?

Hence there is the saying in the holy Scriptures: “If he does not bless you to your face,” which the devil says to the Lord concerning holy Job and which is understood to mean “if he does not curse you.” By the same word, the fictitious accusation made by the slanderers against Naboth was named. For it was said that he had “blessed” the king—that is, cursed him.

All these modes of speech will be considered lies if figurative speech or action is counted as falsehood. But if it is not a lie when things signifying one another are referred to the understanding of truth, then not only what Jacob did or said to his father in order to receive the blessing, but also what Joseph said to his brothers as though mocking them, what David pretended when he acted insane, and other examples of this kind should not be judged lies. Rather, they are prophetic sayings and actions, to be referred to the understanding of things that are true.

They are covered with figurative garments for this reason: to exercise the understanding of the person who seeks reverently, and so that things openly exposed and easily grasped may not become cheap. Although we have learned elsewhere that certain things were stated openly and clearly, when those same things are drawn out of hidden places they are, in a way, renewed in our thought; and once renewed, they become sweet. They are not begrudged to learners because they are obscured in these ways; rather, they are commended, so that, as though withdrawn, they may be desired more ardently and, once desired, discovered more joyfully.

Nevertheless, true things—not false things—are spoken, because true things—not false things—are signified, whether by word or by deed. For the things that are signified are themselves, in a sense, spoken. They are considered lies because people do not understand that the things signified are true; instead, they believe that false things have been spoken.

To make this clearer by examples, consider what Jacob did. Certainly, he covered his limbs with the skins of young goats. If we seek only the immediate reason, we shall think that he lied, for he did this so that he might be thought to be someone he was not. But if this deed is referred to that for the sake of which it was truly performed, then the goatskins signify sins, while the one who covered himself with them signifies the one who bore not his own sins but the sins of others. A truthful signification, therefore, can in no way rightly be called a lie.

The same applies to speech as to action. For when his father said to him, “Who are you, my son?” he replied, “I am Esau, your firstborn.” If this is referred to those two twins, it will appear to be a lie. But if we understand here the one for whose signification these deeds and sayings were recorded, he is to be understood in his body (*corpore suo*), which is his Church. Speaking of this matter, he says: “When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, while you yourselves are cast outside, and people will come from the east and the west and the north and the south and recline in the kingdom of God; and behold, the last who were first, and the first who were last.”

Thus, in a certain sense, the younger brother took away the elder’s primacy and transferred it to himself. Since, therefore, such true things are signified so truthfully, what here should be thought to have been done or said falsely? For the things signified are not absent from the truth: they are past, present, or future. The signification is therefore undoubtedly true, and there is no lie.

But it is somewhat more appropriate that I explain why this seems to me a threefold method of arguing against those who wish to enlist the Scriptures as patrons of their lies. First, we should show that some things thought to be lies there are not lies, if they are correctly understood. Second, if there are any manifest lies there, they are not to be imitated. Third, against every opinion of those who think that it sometimes belongs to the duty of a good person to lie, we must hold absolutely in the teaching of religion that one must never lie.

For that pretense of Peter and Barnabas by which they compelled the Gentiles to Judaize was rightly rebuked and corrected—both so that it would not then cause harm and so that it would not provide posterity with an example for imitation. When the Apostle Paul saw that they were not walking rightly in accordance with the truth of the Gospel, he said to Peter before them all: “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

But as for what Paul himself did—retaining and practicing certain legitimate observances according to Jewish custom, so as not to show himself hostile to the law and the prophets—we must not believe that he did this deceitfully. His position on this matter is sufficiently well known: it had been established that Jews who then believed in Christ were not to be prohibited from observing their ancestral traditions, nor were Gentiles, when they became Christians, to be compelled to observe them.

Thus the sacraments known to have been divinely commanded were not to be shunned as though they were sacrileges; yet, once the New Testament had been revealed, they were not to be regarded as so necessary that those who converted to God without them could not be saved.

There were people who believed and taught this, even though they had already accepted the Gospel of Christ; and Peter and Barnabas had pretended to agree with them. Therefore they compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. To compel them meant to preach those observances as necessary, as though, even after the Gospel had been received, there were no salvation in Christ without them.

This was the error held by certain people; this was what Peter’s fear pretended; this was what Paul’s freedom rebuked.

When Paul says, “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all,” he did this through compassion, not through lying. A person becomes like the one whom he wishes to help when he helps with as much mercy as he would wish to receive if he himself were placed in the same misery. Thus he becomes like that person, not because he deceives him, but because he considers himself as though he were that person.

Hence there is also the saying of the same Apostle, already mentioned above: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself lest you also be tempted.”

For if, because he said, “I became as a Jew to the Jews and as one under the law to those under the law,” he is thought to have deceitfully adopted the sacraments of the old law, then he ought, by the same kind of lying, also to have adopted the idolatry of the Gentiles, because he said that he became “as one without the law to those without the law,” in order to win them. But he certainly did not do this. He did not sacrifice to idols anywhere or worship any images; rather, as a martyr of Christ, he openly showed them to be detestable and to be avoided.

A lie is a false signification accompanied by the will to deceive. But there is no false signification when one thing is signified by another and what is signified is nevertheless true, provided it is correctly understood.

There are examples of this kind in the Gospel even from the Savior, since the Lord himself deigned to be a prophet among the prophets. Such are the passages in which he says, concerning the woman who suffered from an issue of blood, “Who touched me?” and concerning Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?”

He asked as though he did not know what he certainly did know; and in this way he pretended not to know so that his apparent ignorance might signify something else. Since that signification was truthful, it was certainly not a lie.

For the woman who suffered from the issue of blood and the man who had been dead for four days signified those whom the one who in a certain way knew all things nevertheless did not know. The woman represented the type of the people of the Gentiles, concerning whom the prophecy had already been uttered: “A people whom I did not know served me.” Lazarus, removed from the living, lay as though in the place of which he says: “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”

Therefore, as though Christ did not know either who the woman was or where Lazarus had been placed, these matters were represented by the words of the questioner, and every lie was avoided through truthful signification.

### CHAPTER CXCII. On the eight kinds of lies; from the book *On Lying*.

The first kind is the capital lie, and one to be fled from far away: the lie told in religious teaching. No one should ever be brought to this lie under any condition.

The second is one told in order to harm someone unjustly; it is such that it benefits no one and harms someone.

The third benefits one person in such a way that it harms another, although it does not harm the other with bodily defilement.

The fourth is told solely from the desire to lie and deceive; it is pure [or: sheer] lying.

The fifth is told from the desire to please, through attractive speech.

After all these have been completely avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind, which harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if a person who knows where someone’s money is, when it is about to be unjustly taken away, pretends not to know.

The seventh likewise harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if a person unwilling to betray someone who is being sought for execution lies, not only about a just and innocent person but also about a guilty one, since it belongs to Christian discipline that one should neither despair of anyone’s correction nor close anyone’s path to repentance.

We have dealt sufficiently with these two kinds, which commonly provoke great controversy, and have shown what seems right to us: that these kinds too should be avoided by brave, faithful, and truthful men and women, who should honorably and courageously endure the disadvantages that follow.

Thus, when someone asks where a person is who has entrusted himself to another’s faith, one must not lie, but must answer more courageously: “I will neither betray him nor lie.”

This was done by Firmus, once bishop of the Church of Tagaste, firm in name and firmer in resolve. When, by order of the emperor, officers sent by him sought a man who had taken refuge with Firmus and whom he was hiding with all the care he could, he replied to those who were asking that he could neither lie nor betray the man. He endured many bodily tortures—for the emperors were not yet Christians—and remained firm in his decision.

Then, when he was brought before the emperor, he appeared so pitiable that the emperor himself readily granted pardon to the man whom Firmus had protected. What could be stronger or more steadfast than this?

The eighth kind of lie is one that harms no one and serves to protect someone from bodily defilement.

One must not, therefore, lie in religious teaching: it is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie.

One must not lie in the second way, because no one should be wronged.

One must not lie in the third way, because no one’s interests should be advanced through another’s injury.

One must not lie in the fourth way, because the desire to lie is itself vicious.

One must not lie in the fifth way, because even the truth should not be spoken merely to please human beings; how much less should one speak a lie, which is shameful in itself precisely because it is a lie?

One must not lie in the sixth way. For even the truth of testimony should not rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety. No one should be led to eternal salvation by the aid of a lie. A person should not be converted to good morals through the wicked morals of those converting him. For if this must be done to him, then, once converted, he too ought to do the same to others; and so he will be converted not to good but to wicked morals, when he is given for imitation, after his conversion, what was done for him in converting him.

Nor should one lie in the seventh way. No one’s temporal advantage or safety should be preferred to the completion of faith. Nor, if someone is so badly moved by our right actions that he becomes worse in spirit and much more distant from piety, should right actions therefore be abandoned. We must hold especially to that by which we ought to call and invite those whom we love as ourselves. We must drink with the strongest courage that apostolic saying: “To some we are the aroma of life leading to life, and to others the aroma of death leading to death”; and, “Who is sufficient for these things?”

Nor should one lie in the eighth way, because among goods chastity of mind is greater than bodily purity, and among evils what we ourselves do is greater than what we allow to be done.

Among these eight kinds, a person sins less by lying the more he rises toward the eighth; and sins more the farther he sinks toward the first. Whoever thinks that there is some kind of lie that is not a sin deceives himself disgracefully, considering himself an honest deceiver of others.

### CHAPTER CXCIII. Against those who produce from Scripture examples that seem to support their lying; from the book *Against Lying*, addressed to Consentium.

When examples of lying are brought forward from the holy Scriptures, either they are not lies but are thought to be so because they are not understood, or, if they are lies, they are not to be imitated, because they cannot be just.

But when it is written that God acted well toward the Hebrew midwives and toward Rahab, the prostitute of Jericho, this was not because they lied, but because they showed mercy toward the people of God. It was not their deceitfulness that was rewarded, but their benevolence—the kindness of their disposition, not the wickedness of their lying.

For just as it would not be astonishing or absurd if God wished to forgive earlier evil deeds because of later good deeds, so it is not astonishing that, at one time and in one matter, God, observing both things—that is, the deed performed mercifully and the deed performed deceitfully—rewarded the good and, because of that good, forgave the evil.

If sins committed because of carnal desire and not because of mercy are forgiven because of a later period of mercy, why should those committed because of mercy itself not rightly be forgiven? The sin that proceeds from the mind of the one doing harm is more serious than the one that proceeds from the mind of the one rendering assistance.

Accordingly, if the former is erased by a subsequent work of mercy, why should this lesser offense not be erased by the person’s own mercy—both preceding the sin and accompanying it when it is committed?

This may indeed appear to be so. Nevertheless, it is one thing to say, “I ought not to have sinned, but I will perform works of mercy by which I may erase the sin I committed earlier,” and another to say, “I ought to sin, because I cannot otherwise show mercy.” It is one thing, I say, to say, “Because we have already sinned, let us do good,” and another to say, “Let us sin so that good may come.” In the former case, the judgment against sin must be exhausted; in the latter, the teaching of sin must be avoided.

### CHAPTER CXCIV. Against various people who strive in various ways to excuse their sins, which he confirms can never remain unpunished; from the sermon *On Continence*.

In order that by our spirit we may put to death the works of the flesh, we are led by the Spirit of God, who grants self-restraint, by which we may curb, subdue, and conquer concupiscence. In this great battle, in which a person lives under grace, and, when fighting well with divine assistance, exults in the Lord with trembling, even vigorous combatants are not without certain wounds of sin—not even those who, though unconquered, put the works of the flesh to death. Because of these wounds, which must be healed daily, they truly say: “Forgive us our debts.” Against these same vices and against the devil, the prince and king of vices, they contend in that prayer with much greater vigilance and earnestness, lest his deadly suggestions have any power—suggestions by which he incites the sinner to excuse rather than accuse his sins—and so those wounds may not only fail to be healed but, even if they were not deadly, may be inflicted grievously and fatally. [Col. 0851C]

Here, therefore, an even more cautious self-restraint is necessary, by which the appetite of the proud person may be restrained: that appetite by which he takes pleasure in himself, does not want to be found guilty, and scorns, when he sins, to be convicted of having sinned. Instead of accepting the accusation of himself with saving humility, he seeks an excuse in ruinous self-exaltation. [Col. 0851D] To restrain this pride, that man whose words I have already quoted above and commended as best I could asked the Lord for self-restraint. For when he had said, “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of self-restraint around my lips, so that my heart may not turn aside to evil words,” he explained more clearly why he said this: “To excuse excuses in sins.”

For what is more evil than these words, by which an evil person denies that he is evil, even when convicted of an evil deed that he cannot deny? Since he cannot conceal what was done, nor call it a good deed, and sees that it is plainly evident that he did it, he seeks to attribute what he did to something else, as though he could thereby remove what he deserved. Unwilling to be guilty, he instead adds to his guilt; and, by excusing rather than accusing his sins, he does not understand that he is not removing punishment but forgiveness. [Col. 0852A]

Before human judges, since they can be deceived, it appears for a time to be of some use to cleanse by whatever deceitful defense one can devise what was wrongly done. Before God, however, who cannot be deceived, a deceptive defense must not be offered, but a truthful confession of sins. Some people who habitually excuse their sins complain that they are driven to sin by fate, as though the stars had decreed this and heaven had sinned first by making such decrees, so that afterward a human being might sin by committing such acts.

Others prefer to attribute their sins to Fortune, because they think they are buffeted by accidental events; yet they insist that they understand and affirm this not with the rashness of chance but with considered reasoning. [Col. 0852B] What madness, then, to attribute their arguments to reason while subjecting their actions to chance!

Others refer everything evil that they do to the devil, and do not wish to have even a share with him, although they can suspect that he secretly suggested evil to them, while they cannot doubt that they consented to those suggestions, from whatever source they came.

There are also those who extend their excuse into an accusation of God—wretched because of divine judgment, but blasphemous through their own madness. For they introduce, in opposition to Him, a rebellious substance of evil, which, they say, He could not have resisted unless He had mingled with that rebellious substance a part of His own substance and nature, to be contaminated and corrupted. They then say that they sin when the nature of evil prevails over the nature of God. [Col. 0852C]

This is the utterly impure madness of the Manichaeans, whose diabolical contrivances are very easily overthrown by the indisputable truth that confesses God’s nature to be undefiled and incorruptible. What kind of criminal contamination and corruption, indeed, should rightly not be believed of those who believe that God, who is supremely and incomparably good, can be contaminated and corrupted?

There are also those who accuse God in excusing their sins in this way: they say that sins please Him. “For if they displeased Him,” they say, “He would in no way permit them to occur, with His omnipotent power.” As if God had permitted sins to remain unpunished even in those whom He frees from eternal punishment by forgiving their sins! [Col. 0852D]

No one receives pardon for a deservedly heavier punishment unless he has paid some punishment of some kind, even if it is far less than he deserved. Thus the generosity of mercy is bestowed without leaving justice and discipline behind. Even the sin that appears to go unpunished has its attendant punishment: one grieves over what one has committed because of its bitterness, or fails to grieve because of blindness.

Therefore, just as you say, “Why does He permit these things if they displease Him?” so I say, “Why does He punish these things if they please Him?” And thus, just as I confess that these things would not occur at all unless they were permitted by the Omnipotent, so you must confess that what is punished by the Just One ought not to be done. By not doing what He punishes, we may deserve to learn from Him why He permits the existence of what He will punish.

“For the mature,” as it is written, “solid food belongs”: those who have made good progress already understand that it belonged rather to God’s omnipotence to permit evils arising from free choice and the will. [Col. 0853A] His goodness is so omnipotent that He can even bring good out of evils—whether by forgiving them, healing them, adapting and turning them to the benefit of the devout, or even by exacting the most just vengeance.

All these things are good and most worthy of the good and omnipotent God, yet they are not done except in relation to evils. What, then, is better or more powerful than the One who, while doing nothing evil, brings good even out of evils?

He hears those who have done evil crying to Him, “Forgive us our debts,” and He forgives. Their evils have harmed sinners; He comes to their aid and heals their sicknesses. Their enemies rage against His servants; from the rage of those enemies He makes martyrs. [Col. 0853B] Finally, He even condemns those whom He judges worthy of condemnation—although they suffer their own evils—and nevertheless He does what is good. For what is just cannot fail to be good. And just as sin is unjust, so the punishment of sin is just.

God did not lack the power to make a person who could not sin. Rather, He preferred to make one for whom it would lie within his power to sin if he wished, and not to sin if he did not wish: forbidding the one and commanding the other, so that first there might be the good merit of not sinning and afterward the just reward of being unable to sin. For at the end He will also make His saints such that they cannot sin at all.

Even now He has angels such as these, whom we love in Him in such a way that we fear none of them might become a devil by sinning. [Col. 0853C] We do not presume this of any righteous human being during the mortality of this present life; but we confidently believe that all will be such in the immortality of that life. For what good will the omnipotent God, who brings good even out of our evils, give when He has freed us from every evil?

## CHAPTER CXCV. On the Apostle’s statement, “With the mind I serve the law of God,” and so forth; from the same sermon *On Self-Restraint*

The Apostle does not say, “Each person is tempted by concupiscence,” but adds “his own,” so that whoever hears this may understand how he ought to cry out: “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against You.’” It would not have needed healing unless it had corrupted itself by sinning, so that its own flesh might lust against it—that is, the soul itself might resist itself in that part by which it has been weakened in the flesh. [Col. 0853D]

For the flesh desires nothing except through the soul. Yet the flesh is said to desire against the spirit when the soul, through carnal concupiscence, resists the spirit. In all this, we are the whole subject. The flesh itself, which dies when the soul departs, is our lowest part. It is not abandoned so as to be fled from, but is laid aside so as to be received again [variant: “is put off”]; and when received, it will never again be abandoned. “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body rises.”

Then the flesh will no longer desire against the spirit, when it too will be called spiritual, because it will be subjected to the spirit to be vivified forever—not merely without any resistance, but also without any need for bodily nourishment. [Col. 0854A] These two things, then, which now oppose each other within us, since we are present in both, let us pray and act that they may be reconciled.

We must not think that one of them is the enemy, but rather the vice by which the flesh desires against the spirit. When that vice has been healed, it too will no longer exist; both substances will be preserved, and there will be no conflict between them.

Let us hear the Apostle: “I know,” he says, “that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.” He says this because the vice of the flesh is not good within a good thing. When the vice ceases to exist, there will be flesh, but it will no longer be corrupted or vicious. Yet the same teacher first shows that the flesh belongs to our nature by saying, “I know that it does not dwell in me,” and then adding, “that is, in my flesh.” [Col. 0854B] He therefore says that his flesh is himself. It is not, then, itself our enemy; and when its vices are resisted, it is loved, because it is being healed.

No one has ever hated his own flesh, as the Apostle himself says. In another passage he says: “Thus I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

Let those who have ears hear: “Thus I myself”—I with my mind, I with my flesh—“but with my mind I serve the law of God, while with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” How, then, do I serve the law of sin with the flesh? Surely not by consenting to carnal desire. Far from it. Rather, I have within me movements of desire that I did not wish to have, yet did have; and by not consenting to them, I served the law of God with my mind and restrained my members from becoming weapons of sin.

Thus there are evil desires within us, and by not consenting to them we do not live evilly. There are sinful concupiscences within us, and by not obeying them we do not accomplish evil; but because we have them, we do not yet perfect the good. [Col. 0854C]

The Apostle shows both things: the good is not perfected here, because evil is desired in this way, and evil is not perfected here, because such desire is not obeyed. He shows the first when he says, “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not”; and the second when he says, “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh” [variant: “do not fulfill the desires of the flesh”].

For there he does not say that doing good is not present to him, but completing it; nor here does he say, “Do not have the desires of the flesh,” but, “Do not fulfill them.” Evil concupiscences therefore arise within us when what is not permitted becomes pleasing to us; but they are not fulfilled when, while the mind serves the law of God, the lusts are restrained.

The good is done when what is wrongly pleasing is not done because a good delight conquers it. [Col. 0854D] Yet the perfection of the good is not fulfilled so long as lust, while the flesh serves the law of sin, entices us, and, although restrained, is nevertheless stirred. For it would not need to be restrained unless it were stirred.

One day there will also be the perfection of the good, when evil has been brought to an end: the former will be supreme, and the latter will be nothing. If we think this should be hoped for in our present mortality, we are deceived. It will be then, when death no longer exists; and it will be there, where eternal life exists [variant: “In that age”].

In that age and in that kingdom there will be the supreme good and no evil, when there will also be the highest love of wisdom and no labor of self-restraint [variant: “where eternal life will be, there will be”].

## CHAPTER CXCVI. Whether the soul is one thing and the spirit another, or whether one thing is called by both names? From the book *On the Origin of the Soul to Victor Vincentius*

It remains to show how, although “spirit” is also properly used, it does not refer to the whole soul but to something belonging to it, as the Apostle says: “And may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole.” Or, much more explicitly, in the book of Job: “You have released my soul from my spirit.” Nevertheless, the whole soul is also called by this name, although this question seems much more to concern names than things.

For when it is established that there is something in the soul that is properly called spirit, and that, apart from this, the soul is properly so called, there is no longer any dispute about the things themselves—especially since I too say that what you say is properly called spirit is indeed spirit, namely, that by which we reason and understand, whenever these terms are distinguished in the way the Apostle says: “And may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole.” [Col. 0855A]

He also seems to call this spirit “mind” when he says, “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.” For the meaning is: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” What he there said by “mind” should therefore be understood here as “spirit.”

This is not as you suppose, namely, that the whole mind is called spirit, consisting of soul and spirit. I do not know where you have read that. We generally call our mind nothing other than our rational and intellectual faculty. Therefore, when the Apostle says, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” what else does he say except, “Be renewed in your mind”? The spirit of the mind is nothing other than the mind, just as the body of the flesh can be nothing other than the flesh. [Col. 0855B]

This too is written: “In the putting off of the body of the flesh,” where he calls the flesh “body.” Yet he also speaks in another way of the human spirit, which he entirely distinguishes from the mind. “If I pray in a tongue,” he says, “my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” [variant: “without fruit”]. But we are not now speaking of this spirit, which is distinct from the mind.

This spirit has its own equally difficult question. Scripture calls spirit by many names and in different senses. But concerning the spirit with which we reason, understand, and possess wisdom, we agree that it is also properly called spirit, while it is not the whole soul but something belonging to it. [Col. 0855C]

Nevertheless, if you deny that the soul is also spirit because its understanding is distinctly called spirit, you could deny that the whole seed of Jacob is called Israel, since, apart from Judah, the ten tribes that were then in Samaria were also distinctly called Israel [variant: “at that time”].

But why linger here any longer? Attend now to what more readily enables us to show that what is soul is also called spirit. You hear or read what is written concerning the Lord at His death: “And He bowed His head and gave up the spirit.” You want this to be understood as though a part signified the whole, rather than as meaning that what is soul can also be called spirit.

But, to prove my point more quickly, I will bring you yourself forward as a witness. [Col. 0855D] You defined spirit in such a way that animals appear not to have spirit but to have soul. They are called irrational because they do not possess the power of understanding and reason.

When you wished to admonish human beings to know their nature, you spoke in this way:

> “Since the good God created nothing without reason, and begot the human being himself—a rational animal, capable of understanding, possessed of reason, and lively in sensation—who distributes by prudent arrangement all things lacking reason.”

In these words of yours you sufficiently asserted what is entirely true: that the human being possesses reason and is capable of understanding. Animals lacking reason certainly do not possess this. Therefore, on the testimony of Scripture, you compared those who do not understand to beasts, which plainly do not possess understanding. [Col. 0856A] Elsewhere too it is written: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.”

Since this is so, consider also the words by which you defined and described spirit when you attempted to distinguish it from soul:

> “This soul,” you say, “which has its origin from the breath of God, could not exist without its own sensation and inward understanding; this is spirit.”

A little later:

> “Although the soul,” you say, “animates the body, nevertheless that which senses, understands, and is vigorous must be spirit.”

Again, a little later:

> “The soul,” you say, “will be one thing and the spirit another; wisdom is the soul’s sensation.”

These words sufficiently indicate what you think the spirit of a human being is: namely, our rational faculty, by which the soul senses and understands—not in the way the bodily senses perceive, but as that inward sense from which the word “judgment” is derived. [Col. 0856B]

By this we are undoubtedly superior to beasts, because they lack reason. Beasts therefore do not have spirit—that is, understanding, and the sense of reason and wisdom—but only soul.

It was said of them: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and let the earth bring forth a living soul.” Thus, so that you may know with complete clarity that what is soul is also called spirit in the manner of the divine Scriptures, the spirit of a beast is mentioned. [Col. 0856C]

Yet beasts certainly do not possess that spirit which your affection, distinguishing it from the soul, has defined. It is therefore clear that the soul of a beast could rightly be called spirit in the general sense of the word, just as we read in the book of Ecclesiastes:

> “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of human beings goes upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes downward into the earth?”

Likewise, in the account of the devastation of the Flood, it is written:

> “And all flesh that moved upon the earth died: birds, cattle, animals, wild beasts, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth; and every human being, and everything that has the spirit of life.” [Col. 0856D]

Here, with every ambiguity and evasive uncertainty removed, we understand that “spirit” is a general name for the soul.

The meaning of this name extends so widely that even God is called spirit. The airy breath, too, although corporeal, is called “the spirit of the storm” in the Psalm. Therefore I think that what is soul is also called spirit, according to the words: [Col. 0857A]

> “You take away their spirit, and they perish.”

And again:

> “Their spirit will go forth, and they will return to their earth”—that is, their body will return to its dust.

Thus, “soul” is called spirit because it is spiritual; “soul” is called soul because it animates the body, that is, gives it life.

I think that, reminded by the testimonies of the divine writings I have cited—where even the soul of a beast, which has no understanding, is read to be called spirit—you will not deny this any longer. Therefore, if you understand and appreciate what has been discussed concerning the incorporeal nature of the soul, you have no reason to be displeased that I said I knew it not to be a body but a spirit: for it is shown not to be a body, and it is called spirit in the general sense.

> “Bless the Lord, my soul; I will bless the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist.” [Col. 0857B]

The holy and spiritual soul itself encourages itself to praise the Lord, and, by its higher part, stirs up what is lesser within it. It is not one soul that speaks and another to which it speaks. Nor is this a voice of the flesh, which receives both life and sensation from the soul and cannot, without the soul, will or refuse anything.

Since the soul’s activities are twofold, being raised toward God by one function and inclined toward the flesh by another, if it serves the spirit well, it presides well over the flesh. By that part which clings to God, it invites even that part which clings to the body toward higher affections, granting those subject to it as much as is sufficient for salvation by a rational rule, lest it become so entangled in corruptible things that its dignity—by which it is subject to God alone—is diminished. [Col. 0857C]

The mind, then, the highest part of the soul, stirring itself in all its efforts, says: “Bless the Lord, my soul.”

## CHAPTER CXCVII. How Christ, the Head, sent the ancient righteous ahead like a hand before He was born; from the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*

Everything that we read in the holy Scriptures was written before the Lord’s coming for no other reason than to commend His coming and foreshadow the future Church—that is, the people of God among all nations, which is His body—together with all the saints who lived in this world before His coming, believing that He would come just as we believe that He has come.

For just as Jacob first extended a hand from the womb while he was being born, and by that hand held the heel of his brother who was being born before him, and then the head necessarily followed, and afterward the remaining limbs, so the head nevertheless precedes not only those limbs that followed but also the very hand that came first in birth, in dignity and power. Although not first in the time of appearance, it is first in the order of nature. [Col. 0857D]

In the same way, the Lord Jesus Christ, before He appeared in the flesh and, as it were, proceeded from the womb of His hidden purpose before human eyes as the mediator between God and human beings—the One who is God over all, blessed forever—sent ahead in the holy patriarchs and prophets a certain part of His body. Like a hand, it foretold that He would be born and also tripped up the proud people who preceded Him, by the bonds of the law as though by five fingers, because He did not cease to have His coming foretold and prophesied through the five divisions of the ages. [Col. 0858A]

In harmony with this, the one through whom the law was given wrote five books. Those who thought carnally and wished to establish their own righteousness were not filled with the blessing of Christ’s open hand; rather, they were held back by that hand when it was clenched and closed. Their feet were therefore bound, and they fell; but we have risen and have been set upright.

Although, as I have said, the Lord Christ sent ahead a certain part of His body in the saints who preceded Him in the time of His birth, He Himself is the Head of the body, the Church. All those saints belonged to that same body, of which He is the Head, by believing in Him whom they foretold. They were not severed by running ahead; rather, they were joined to Him by serving. [Col. 0858B]

For although a hand can be sent ahead of the head, its connection nevertheless remains beneath the head. Therefore everything written beforehand was written to instruct us; they were figures of us, and these things happened to them figuratively. They were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

What greater reason is there for the Lord’s coming than that God might show His love toward us, commending it most powerfully because, while we were still enemies, Christ died for us? This happened because the end of the commandment and the fullness of the law is love: that we should love one another; and, just as He laid down His life for us, so we should lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.

Since God first loved us and did not spare His only Son but handed Him over for us all, if we are reluctant to love, at least let us not be reluctant to return love. [Col. 0858C] For there is no greater invitation to love than to take the initiative by loving.

## CHAPTER CXCVIII. How Christian students should piously overlook the solecisms of certain priests; from the same book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*

When those who seem to excel other people in the art of speaking come to become Christians, we should grant them something more than we grant the uneducated. They must be diligently admonished to learn, clothed in Christian humility, not to despise those whom they discover to avoid faults of character more than faults of speech, and not to dare to compare their trained tongue with a pure heart, much less to prefer it, as they have been accustomed to do. [Col. 0858D]

Above all, such people must be taught to listen to the divine Scriptures, lest the solid style of their speech offend them because it is not inflated. Nor should they think that statements or deeds of human beings, wrapped and concealed in carnal coverings and recorded in those books, should not be unfolded and opened so that they may be understood, but should be received only according to the sound of the letters.

The usefulness of this hidden meaning—which is why such things are also called mysteries—and the value of the concealment of riddles in sharpening love of the truth and dispelling the sluggishness of distaste must be demonstrated by experience, when something that had been plainly set before them but had not moved them is drawn out through the unraveling of an allegory.

For such people it is especially useful to know that meanings should be preferred to words in the same way that the soul is preferred to the body. Hence they should prefer to hear more truthful rather than more eloquent speeches, just as they should prefer to have wiser rather than more handsome friends. [Col. 0859A]

They should also know that no voice reaches the ears of God except the affection of the soul. Thus they will not mock if they happen to observe certain bishops and ministers of the Church invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, or failing to understand and awkwardly distinguish the very words they pronounce. These things should certainly not be left uncorrected, so that the people may say “Amen” to what they plainly understand; nevertheless, they should be piously tolerated by those who have learned that just as a person is blessed by sound in the public forum, so he is blessed by intention in the Church.

Therefore that forensic expression, though it may sometimes be good diction, can never be called a blessing.

## CHAPTER CXCIX. On the humility of that hen whose gentle wings the proud refuse, becoming prey to birds; from the same book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*
