Let us consider what has been granted to us by Him who showed us an example, so that we might follow His footsteps. However much our articulated speech differs from the liveliness of our understanding, the mortality of our flesh differs even more greatly from the equality of God; and yet, when He was in the same form, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. [Col. 0859B]

Why did He do this, unless because He became weak for the weak in order to win the weak? Hear His imitator also saying elsewhere:

> “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ compels us, judging this: that one died for all.”

How would he have been ready to spend himself for their souls if he had been reluctant to bend down to their ears? [Col. 0859C]

For this reason He became a little one in our midst, like a nurse cherishing her children. Unless love invites us, is it pleasurable to mutter shortened and mutilated words? Yet people wish to have infants to whom they may offer such things, and it is sweeter for a mother to spit out small, chewed morsels into the mouth of her little son than to chew and swallow larger pieces herself.

Therefore let the thought of that hen never depart from our hearts: with languishing feathers she covers her tender young and, with a broken voice, calls her chirping chicks to herself. The proud, who refuse her gentle wings, become prey to birds. [Col. 0859D]

If understanding delights us in the innermost places of a most sincere heart, it also delights us to understand that the more diligently love descends to the lowest places, the more powerfully it returns to the innermost places through a good conscience, seeking nothing from those to whom it descends except their eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER CC. On changing our arrangements without grief when necessity arises; from the same book

If the omission of another task, to which you had already committed yourself as though it were more necessary, has broken your spirit, and for that reason you catechize sadly and without pleasure, you must consider—apart from the fact that we know we must act mercifully in everything we do with human beings and out of the duty of the sincerest love—that it is uncertain what we should do that is more useful, and what we should postpone or omit entirely. [Col. 0860A]

For we do not know what the merits of the people for whom we act are before God. What benefits them for the time being, we surmise rather by conjecture that is nonexistent, very slight, or highly uncertain than truly comprehend. Therefore we ought to arrange the tasks to be done according to our capacity. If we are able to complete them in the way we have arranged, we should not rejoice because it was pleasing to us, but because it pleased God that they be done in that way [variant: “if they were able to be completed, let us not rejoice because it was pleasing to us, but because it pleased God that they be done in that way”].

But if some necessity arises by which that arrangement of ours is disturbed, let us bend easily so that we may not be broken; let the one whom God has placed before our arrangement become our arrangement. For it is more just that we follow His will than that He follow ours. The order of tasks that we wish to maintain according to our judgment is indeed to be approved when better things take precedence. [Col. 0860B]

Why, then, do we grieve that human beings are preceded by the Lord God in something so much better, when by loving our own arrangement we desire to be disorderly? No one orders what is being done—or, according to the variant, “what he should do”—better than the person who is more ready not to do what divine power forbids than eager to do what human thought has planned, because “many thoughts are in the heart of a person.” But the counsel of God [variant: “of the Lord”] remains forever.

If sorrow seizes us because of some error or sin of ours, let us remember not only that a troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God, but also that just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin; and, “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice.” [Col. 0860C]

Therefore, just as, if we were endangered by a fire, we would certainly run to water by which it could be extinguished and would rejoice if someone offered it from nearby, so, if a flame of sin has arisen from our hay and we are consequently troubled, when an opportunity for a most merciful work is given, let us rejoice as though a fountain had been offered to us, so that what had flared up may be put out by it.

Unless perhaps we are so foolish that we think we should run more eagerly with bread to fill the stomach of a hungry person than with the word of God to instruct the mind of one who is eager to learn. Moreover, if doing this alone brought benefit, while not doing it caused no harm, we would unhappily reject a remedy offered in a danger—not now to the salvation of our neighbor, but to our own. [Col. 0860D]

But when these threatening words resound from the mouth of the Lord—“You wicked and lazy servant, you should have given my money to the money-changers”—what madness it is, merely because our sin troubles us, to wish to sin again by not giving the Lord’s money to one who wants and asks for it?

## CHAPTER CCI. How one who wishes to become a Christian should be catechized; from the same book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*
But let us suppose [“nevertheless, let us suppose”] that someone has come to us who wishes to be a Christian—one of the ordinary sort, though not a countryman but a townsman, such as you must necessarily encounter in considerable numbers at Carthage—and that, when asked whether he desires to be a Christian for some advantage in the present life or for the rest that is hoped for after this life, he has replied that it is for the future rest. Perhaps we would instruct him with an address such as this:

“Thanks be to God, brother. I congratulate you greatly and rejoice over you, because amid the many and so perilous storms of this world you have thought about some true and certain security. For even in this life people seek rest and security through great labors, but they do not find them because of misguided desires. They wish to rest in things that are restless and impermanent; and because these things are taken away in time [“because they are taken away from them in time”] and pass away, they drive people about with fears and pains and do not allow them to be at peace. Even if a man wishes to rest in riches, he becomes more proud rather than more secure.

“Truly, brother, that is the great and true blessedness which is promised to the saints in the age to come. All visible things, however, pass away, and all the splendor, pleasures, and curiosity of this age will perish; and they drag their lovers with them into destruction. From this destruction—that is, from everlasting punishments—the merciful God, wishing to free human beings if they are not themselves enemies to him and do not resist the mercy of their Creator, sent his only-begotten Son, that is, his Word, equal to himself, through whom he created all things.

“Remaining in his divinity and not departing from the Father, changed in no respect, yet by assuming humanity and appearing to human beings in mortal flesh, he came among them. Thus, just as through one man who was created first, namely Adam, death entered the human race because he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil, so that they transgressed God’s commandment, so through one man who is also God, Jesus Christ the Son of God, all who believe in him might enter eternal life, with all their former sins blotted out.

“For all that you now see being done in the Church of God and throughout the whole world under the name of Christ was foretold before the ages. As we read of these things, so also we see them, and by them we are built up in faith. Once a flood occurred over the whole earth, so that sinners might be destroyed; yet those who escaped in the ark were displaying a sacrament of the future Church, which now floats amid the waves of this age and is delivered from drowning through the wood of Christ’s cross.

“It was foretold to Abraham, the faithful servant of God, a single man, that a people would be born from him who would worship the one God among the other nations that worshiped idols; and everything foretold that would happen to that people came to pass [“had come to pass”] just as it had been foretold. Christ, the King of all the saints and God, was also prophesied among that people: he would come from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh which he assumed, so that all who imitated Abraham’s faith would also be sons of Abraham. And so it happened.

“Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, who belonged to that lineage. It was foretold through the prophets that he would suffer on the cross at the hands of that same Jewish people, from whose lineage he came according to the flesh; and so it happened. It was foretold that he would rise again, and he rose again. In accordance with the very prophecies of the prophets, he ascended into heaven and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples.

“It was foretold not only by the prophets but also by the Lord Jesus Christ himself that his Church would exist throughout the whole world, spread through the martyrdoms and sufferings of the saints. This was foretold when his name was still hidden from the nations and, where it was known, was mocked; yet these things were proclaimed and believed through the power of his miracles, whether those he performed himself or those he performed through his servants. Now we see that what was foretold has been fulfilled: even the kings of the earth who formerly persecuted Christians have been subjected to the name of Christ.

“It was also foretold that schisms and heresies would emerge from his Church and, under his name, would seek their own glory rather than Christ’s wherever they were able. And these things have been fulfilled. Will those things that remain, then, not come to pass? It is clear that just as these foretold things came to pass, so also those things will come to pass: whatever tribulations of the righteous still remain; and the day of judgment, which at the resurrection of the dead will separate all the ungodly from the righteous. It will separate not only those who are outside the Church but also the chaff of the Church itself, which must endure with the greatest patience until the final winnowing, and will consign it to the fire it deserves.

“Those who mock the resurrection, thinking that this flesh cannot rise because it decays, will rise again in it for punishment. God will show them that he who was able to make these bodies before they existed is able to restore them in an instant as they were.

“All the faithful, however, who are to reign with Christ will rise in the same body, yet in such a way that they will also deserve to be changed into angelic incorruption, becoming equal to the angels of God, as the Lord himself promised. They will praise him without any failing or weariness, living forever in him and from him, with such joy and blessedness as human beings can neither express nor conceive.

“Since you believe these things, beware of temptations, because the devil seeks those who will perish with him. Let that enemy not deceive you, whether through those who are outside the Church—pagans, Jews, or heretics—or through those whom you see living badly within the Catholic Church itself: those who are immoderate in the pleasures of belly and throat, or unchaste, or devoted to vain curiosities or unlawful practices, whether spectacles, remedies, or diabolical divinations; those devoted to the pomp [and] vainglory of greed and pride; or those living in any way that the law condemns and punishes.

“Rather, join yourself to the good. You will easily find them if you too are such that together you worship and love God freely, because he himself will be our entire reward, so that in that eternal life we may enjoy his goodness and beauty. He is not to be loved as something seen by the eyes, but as wisdom, truth, holiness, justice, charity, and whatever else is called by such names—not as these qualities exist in human beings, but as they exist in the very fountain of incorruptible and unchangeable wisdom.

“Therefore, join yourself to all whom you see loving these things, so that through Christ, who became man in order to be the mediator between God and human beings, you may be reconciled to God. Do not suppose that wicked people will enter the kingdom of heaven merely because they enter the walls of the Church; they will be separated at the proper time if they do not change for the better.

“Imitate the good, tolerate the wicked, love everyone, because you do not know what the person who is wicked today will be tomorrow [“what he will be tomorrow”]. Do not love their injustice, but love them for this reason: that they may attain justice. For the commandment given to us is not only love of God but also love of neighbor; on these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

“No one fulfills this commandment unless he has received the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is equal to the Father and the Son, because the Trinity itself is God. In this God all hope must be placed; it must not be placed in any human being, whoever he may be. For the one by whom we are justified is one thing, and those with whom we are justified are another.

“The devil tests us not only through desires but also through the terrors of insults, sufferings, and death itself. Whatever a person suffers for the name of Christ and for the hope of eternal life, and endures steadfastly, a greater reward will be granted him. For if he yields to the devil, he will be condemned with him; but works of mercy, together with devout humility, obtain from the Lord that he not permit his servants to be tested beyond what they can endure.”

## CHAPTER CCII  
### That the Apostle’s command, “Reprove sinners in the presence of all,” is not contrary to the Lord’s command, “Reprove him between yourself and him alone”; from the book *On Faith and Works*

The Lord forbids that what is holy be given to dogs. Yet the Apostle is not contrary to the Lord when he says, “Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear,” while the Lord says, “Reprove him between yourself and him alone.” Both must be done, as the differing weakness of those whom we undertake—not to destroy but to correct and heal—requires; one person must be healed in one way, another in another.

There is likewise a reason for concealing and tolerating the wicked in the Church, and again a reason for chastising, reproving, refusing admission, or removing them from communion. People go wrong when they do not observe the proper measure. Once they begin to incline too readily in one direction, they do not consider the other testimonies of divine authority by which they could be recalled from that purpose and brought to rest in the truth and moderation that are tempered from both sides. This occurs not only in the matter now under discussion but also in many others.

Some, observing the testimonies of the divine writings that teach the worship of one God, thought that the same person was the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Others, suffering as if from the opposite disease, paid attention to those passages by which the Trinity is declared but could not understand how God is one when the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is neither the Son nor the Father. They therefore thought that differences of substances had to be asserted.

Some, observing in Scripture the praise of holy virginity, condemned marriage. Others, again, pursuing those testimonies in which chaste marriage is commended, equated virginity with marriage. Some, when they read, “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat or drink wine,” and certain similar passages, judged God’s creation and whatever foods they wished to be unclean. Others, reading, “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving,” collapsed into gluttony and drunkenness, unable to rid themselves of their vices except by allowing vices of the opposite kind, equally great or greater, to take their place.

So also in the matter before us: some, observing the commands of severity by which we are admonished to reprove the disorderly, not to give what is holy to dogs, and to tear out from the body the heathen who contemptuously scandalizes the Church [“the member that causes scandal”], disturb the peace of the Church so greatly that they attempt to separate the weeds before the proper time. Blinded by this error, they are themselves separated from the unity of Christ. Such is the cause we have against the schism of Donatus.

This is not said to those who knew that Caecilianus had been attacked not with true but with slanderous charges and who, through a deadly shame, did not abandon their pernicious judgment. Rather, it is said to those to whom we say: “Even if those people had been wicked on whose account you are not in the Church, nevertheless you ought to have remained in the Church by tolerating those whom you were entirely unable to correct or separate.”

Others, on the contrary, placing themselves in danger, have seen that the mixture of good and wicked people in the Church is demonstrated or foretold, and have learned the commands of patience—which make us exceedingly firm, so that even if weeds seem to exist in the Church, neither our faith nor our charity is impeded, and so that, merely because we see weeds in the Church, we do not ourselves depart from the Church. Yet they think that the discipline of the Church should be abandoned, granting those in authority a most perverse security, as though their only responsibility were to say what must be avoided or done, while they need not care what anyone does.

We, however, consider it part of sound doctrine to regulate life and judgment by the testimonies on both sides: to tolerate dogs in the Church for the sake of the Church’s peace, but not to give what is holy to dogs where the Church’s peace is secure.

When, therefore, whether through the negligence of those in authority, through some excusable necessity, or through secret infiltrations, we find wicked people in the Church whom ecclesiastical discipline cannot correct or restrain, let no impious and destructive presumption rise in our hearts by which we think that we must separate ourselves from them so as not to be defiled by their sins. Let us not try to drag others after us, as though we were pure and holy disciples separated from the company of the wicked and from the bonds of unity.

Let those likenesses from Scripture, those divine utterances, or those most certain examples come to mind by which it has been demonstrated and foretold that the wicked would remain mixed with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that they would harm none of the good through unity and participation in the sacraments, provided that the good had not consented to their deeds.

When, however, those through whom the Church is governed possess the authority—without endangering peace—to exercise discipline against the wicked or impious, then let us not sleep again through indifference and sluggishness. We must be roused by the sharp goads of the precepts that pertain to severe correction, so that, directing our steps along the Lord’s way under his guidance and help, in accordance with both sets of testimonies, we may neither grow numb under the name of patience nor become cruel under the pretext of diligence.

## CHAPTER CCIII  
### That people must not be made falsely secure, as though they would not be condemned on account of their right faith even if they persisted in crimes; from the book *On Faith and Works*

Let us therefore take great care, with the help of the Lord our God, not to make people falsely secure by telling them that if they have been baptized in Christ, then, however they may have lived within that faith, they will attain eternal salvation.

Let us not make Christians like the Jewish proselytes to whom the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when you have made him, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves.” Rather, let us hold to the sound teaching of God our Master in both matters, so that Christian life may correspond to holy baptism; and let eternal life be promised to no one if either of these is lacking.

For the one who said, “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” also said, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Of them he says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Do what they say, but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

Their righteousness, then, consists in saying and not doing. Consequently, he wanted ours to be abundant beyond theirs in both saying and doing; if it is not, no one will enter the kingdom of heaven.

This does not mean that anyone should become so exalted that he dares not merely to boast before others but even to think within himself that he is without sin in this life. Yet unless there were certain sins so serious that they deserved even excommunication, the Apostle would not say: “When you and my spirit are assembled, hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus.”

For this reason he also says: “Otherwise I might mourn over many of those who sinned previously and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication that they committed.”

Again, unless there were certain sins that were not to be healed by the kind of humble repentance given in the Church to those who are specifically called penitents, but by certain medicines of correction, the Lord himself would not say: “Reprove him between yourself and him alone; and if he listens to you, you have gained your brother.”

Finally, unless there were certain sins without which this life does not pass, he would not have placed a daily remedy in the prayer that he taught us, so that we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

I have now explained, as I think, sufficiently what I understood concerning that whole opinion in which three questions were raised [“which they raised”]. The first concerns the mixture of the good and wicked in the Church, like wheat and weeds. We must take care not to think that these likenesses have been set forth—the likeness of the wheat and weeds, that of the unclean animals in the ark, or any others signifying the same thing—so that the discipline of the Church may sleep. Concerning the figure of the woman, it is said: “Her household’s ways are strict.” Rather, these likenesses were given so that no one might advance to such madness—more properly, rashness than severity in the name of diligence—as to presume to separate the good from the wicked through criminal schisms.

For these likenesses and prophecies did not give the good a recommendation of laziness, by which they should neglect what they ought to prohibit, but a recommendation of patience, by which they should endure, while preserving the sound doctrine of truth, what they are unable to correct.

Nor, because it is written that unclean animals also entered Noah’s ark, should those in authority therefore fail to prevent the most unclean people from wishing to enter baptism while leaping about—which is certainly milder [“than committing adultery”]. Rather, through this historical figure it was foretold that unclean people would exist in the Church for the sake of the principle of tolerance, not for the corruption of doctrine or the dissolution of discipline.

For the unclean animals did not enter the ark however they pleased, breaking through its structure; they entered through the structure intact, by one and the same door that the builder had made.

The second question concerns those who thought that only faith should be handed on to those seeking baptism and that, after they had already been baptized, they should then be taught about morals. But, unless I am mistaken, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that it belongs even more to the watchman’s responsibility, when all who seek the sacrament of the faithful listen more attentively and anxiously to everything that is said, not to remain silent about the punishment with which the Lord threatens those who live badly. Otherwise they would be guilty of the gravest crimes in the very baptism to which they come so that all guilt for their sins may be forgiven.

The third question is the most dangerous. Because it was insufficiently considered and not treated according to divine teaching, it seems to me to have given rise to that entire opinion in which salvation and eternal life are most wickedly and shamefully promised to those who live in crimes and disgrace—even if they continue to live in that manner—provided only that they believe in Christ and receive his sacraments. This contradicts the Lord’s clearest statement. When someone who desired eternal life asked him, he replied: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He then recalled which commandments: those by which such sins are avoided, although somehow eternal salvation is promised on the basis of faith without works—a dead faith.

I have discussed these three questions sufficiently, as I believe, and have demonstrated that the wicked are to be tolerated in the Church without neglecting ecclesiastical discipline; that those who seek baptism are to be catechized so that they not only hear and accept what they ought to believe but also how they ought to live; and that eternal life is to be promised to the faithful in such a way that no one thinks he can attain it through a dead faith, which cannot save without works, but through that faith of grace which works through love.

## CHAPTER CCIV  
### Who the prophets are of whom the Apostle says, “second, prophets”; from the book *Questions to Paulinus, Bishop of Nola*

Concerning the prophets, where the Apostle says, “God has appointed some in the Church as apostles, some as prophets,” I understand this as you yourself have written. In this passage, those are called prophets of whom Agabus was one, not those who prophesied that the Lord would come in the flesh.

We find evangelists whom we do not read to have been apostles, such as Mark and Luke. As for pastors and teachers, whom you especially wished us to distinguish, I think they are the same, as it also seemed to you: we should not understand some as pastors and others as teachers, but rather that, after first mentioning pastors, he added teachers in order to show that teaching belongs to the office of pastors.

For he does not say, “Some pastors, but others teachers,” although in the preceding expressions he distinguished the offices by the same form of speech, saying, “Some apostles, some prophets, and some evangelists.” Instead, he embraced the two names as referring to one office: “some pastors and teachers.”

## CHAPTER CCV  
### What are the supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings that the Apostle mentions to Timothy; from the same book addressed to Paulinus

Those terms are particularly difficult to distinguish where, writing to Timothy, he says: “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made.”

Many of our people think that *precationes* and *deprecationes* mean the same thing, and this has now become entirely prevalent through daily usage. Those who spoke Latin more precisely, however, used *precationes* when wishing for good things, and *deprecationes* when avoiding evils. They said that *precari* meant to wish for good things by praying, while *imprecari* meant to pray for evils—what is now commonly called cursing; *deprecari*, meanwhile, meant to drive away evils through prayer.

Let us rather follow the now customary manner of speaking. Whenever we find either *precationes* or *deprecationes*, which the Greeks call δεήσεις (*deēseis*, “supplications”), let us not think the text ought to be corrected.

Much could be said here that would not be objectionable, but I choose to understand these words as the whole or nearly the whole Church commonly does. Let us take *precationes* to mean those prayers that we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; *orationes* when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution—the whole petition being concluded by nearly the whole Church with the Lord’s Prayer; and *interpellationes*, or *postulationes*, as your manuscripts read, when the people are blessed. At that time the bishop [“bishops”], like advocates, commend those entrusted to them to the most merciful power through the laying on of hands.

When these things have been completed and so great a sacrament has been shared, thanksgiving concludes everything. The Apostle also commended it as the final element in these words.

The principal reason for saying this was that, after these matters had been touched upon and indicated briefly, no one should think the following command could be neglected: “For all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and charity.” No one should suppose—as human weakness of thought might lead one to do—that these prayers need not be offered for those through whom the Church was suffering persecution, since the members of Christ were to be gathered from every kind of human being.

Accordingly, he adds: “For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

And lest anyone should say that there could be a way of salvation through good conduct and the worship of the one almighty God without participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” Thus what he had said—“he desires all human beings to be saved”—is to be understood as accomplished in no other way than through the mediator: not through the God who was always the Word, but through the man Christ Jesus, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

## CHAPTER CCVI  
### On what Luke says, “Their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him,” and Mark says, “He appeared to them in another form”; from the same book *Questions to Paulinus*

Your inquiry concerning the Gospel often troubles many people: how, after his resurrection, the Lord—having risen in the same body—was both not recognized and recognized by certain men and women who had known him.

The first question usually raised is whether something happened in his body or rather in their eyes so that he could not be recognized. For when we read, “Their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him,” some impediment to recognition seems to have been placed in the eyes of those who were looking.

When, however, it is plainly said elsewhere, “He appeared to them in another form,” it was certainly in the body itself, whose form was different, that something occurred by which their eyes were held back by an impediment—that is, they experienced a delay in recognizing him.

Yet I wonder: since there are two features in the body by which someone’s appearance is recognized—its lineaments and its color—why does no one find it difficult that before the resurrection he was transfigured on the mountain so that his face became radiant like the sun, to such an extraordinary degree of brightness and change in the color of his body, while after the resurrection it is considered somewhat difficult that his features were changed so that he could not be recognized? And why should he not, by the same power, have restored after the resurrection his former features just as he had then restored the former color?

Indeed, those three disciples before whose eyes he was transfigured on the mountain would not have recognized him if someone of that appearance had come to them from elsewhere; but because they were with him, they retained complete certainty that it was he.

“But it was the very body in which he rose,” someone may say. What does that have to do with the matter? It was also certainly the very body in which he was transfigured on the mountain, and it was the same body he had as a young man as that in which he was born. Yet if someone who knew him only as an infant had suddenly seen him as a young man, he certainly would not have recognized him.

Or is the power of God unable to change features quickly when human age can change them through the passage of years?

## CHAPTER CCVII  
### On the sword that pierced Mary’s soul; from the same book *Questions*, addressed to Bishop Paulinus

Concerning Simeon’s words to the Lord’s virgin mother—“And your own soul a sword will pierce”—I said in another letter, a copy of which I have just sent, what seems to me to be the meaning; and this also appeared to you, among other matters.

As for what he added—“so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed”—I think it should be understood in this way: through the Lord’s passion both the plots of the Jews and the weakness of the disciples were exposed.

It is therefore credible that a tribulation is signified by the name of the sword, by which the mother’s soul was wounded through the experience of grief. That sword was in the mouth of the persecutors, of whom it is said in the psalm: “And a sword is in their mouth.” They were the sons of men “whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword.”

The iron that pierced Joseph’s soul also seems to me to signify severe tribulation. For it is plainly said: “Iron pierced his soul until his word came,” that is, he remained in severe tribulation until what he had foretold came to pass. From this he was regarded as great and was freed from that tribulation. But lest what came to pass—namely, that what he had foretold was fulfilled—be attributed to human wisdom, holy Scripture gives the glory to God and immediately adds: “The word of the Lord set him on fire.”

## CHAPTER CCVIII  
### In discussing baptism, he explains how “Whoever is not with me is against me” is not contrary to “Whoever is not against you is for you”; from Book One *On Baptism*
The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.” [Col. 0869C] Yet when the disciples reported to him that they had seen someone casting out demons in his name and had forbidden him because he was not following them, he said: “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you. For no one can do something in my name and then speak evil of me.”

If there was nothing to correct in that man, then let anyone who, established outside the communion of the Church, gathers in Christ’s name those separated from Christian fellowship be secure—and that saying will be false: “Whoever is not with me does not gather, but scatters” [“Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters”]. If, however, what the Lord’s disciples wished to do through ignorance was something that needed correction, as the Lord’s command “Do not forbid him” indicates, why did he himself forbid this prohibition, and [Col. 0869D] how will what he said there be true: “Whoever is not against you is for you”? In that action he was not against them but for them, since he was working healings through the name of Christ [variant: operabatur, “was working”].

Therefore, so that both statements may be true—as is also true of the one in which he says, “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters,” and of the one in which he says, “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you”—what remains to be understood except that this man had to be strengthened in reverence for so great a name, since he was not against the Church but for the Church? Yet he had to be blamed for his separation, in which, if he gathered, he would scatter. And if he should come to the Church, he would not receive there what he already possessed, but would correct the error in which he had gone astray.

For neither were the prayers of Cornelius, a gentile, unheard, nor were his almsgivings unaccepted. Indeed, he deserved both that an angel be sent to him and that he behold the one who was sent, through whom he could certainly have learned everything necessary without the intervention of any human being. But because whatever good he possessed in his prayers and almsgiving could not benefit him unless he were incorporated into the Church through the bond of Christian fellowship and peace, he was commanded to send for Peter, and through him he learned about Christ. Through him also he was baptized and joined to the Christian people and to the fellowship of communion, [Col. 0870B] to which he had been joined only by the similarity of his good works.

For he would have disastrously despised the good he did not yet possess, taking pride in what he did possess. Likewise, those who separate themselves from the fellowship of the others, violating charity and breaking the bond of unity, if they do none of what they received within that fellowship, are separated from it in every respect. Therefore, if someone whom they have joined to themselves wishes to come to the Church, he ought to receive everything that he did not receive.

But if they do some of the same things, they have not separated themselves from us in those matters; in that respect they remain held within the structure of the fabric, though in other respects they are torn away. Therefore, if they join someone to themselves, that person is connected to the Church in the respect in which they themselves are not separated from it:

> [Note: [Col. 0869D] Although the material placed in the margin seemed superfluous, we nevertheless added it, moved by religious scruple, lest we alter anything in so ancient a copy: “And therefore, if he wishes to come to the Church, he ought to receive everything that he did not receive. But if they do some of the same things, they have not separated themselves from us in those matters, and in that respect they remain held within the structure of the fabric, though in other respects they are torn away. Therefore, if they join someone to themselves, he is connected to the Church in the respect in which they themselves are not separated from it,” etc.]

And therefore, if he wishes to come to the Church, he is healed in the respect in which he had wandered, wounded and torn. Where he was connected while sound [sanus; uncertain variant: sana curare], he is not healed but recognized, lest, when we wish to heal what is diseased, we instead wound what is sound.

Thus those whom they baptize are healed of the wound of idolatry or unbelief, but they strike them with the more grievous wound of schism. The sword killed idolaters among the people of God, but a chasm in the earth swallowed schismatics. And the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.”

If someone were brought to a physician with a serious wound in some necessary part of his body, and the physician said, “He will die from this unless it is treated,” I do not think that those who brought him would be so foolish that, after considering and counting the other healthy members of his body, they would answer the physician: “Then do all these healthy limbs not suffice for his life, while that one wounded limb suffices for his death?” They certainly do not say this. Instead, they present him for treatment. Nor, because they present him for treatment, do they ask the physician to treat what is healthy as well; rather, they urgently apply medicine to that one place from which death threatens even though the other parts remain healthy, and from which death will come unless it is healed.

What benefit, then, is a sound faith, or perhaps the sacrament of faith alone sound, where the health of charity has been destroyed by the deadly wound of schism, and where, solely because charity has been destroyed, even those sound elements are dragged toward death? To prevent this, God’s mercy does not cease to act through the unity of his holy Church, so that they may come and be healed by the medicine of reconciliation and the bond of peace.

Let them not suppose that they are healthy merely because we say that they possess something sound; nor, conversely, let them suppose that what is sound must be treated merely because we have shown that something is wounded. Thus, in the soundness of the sacrament, since they are not against us, they are for us. But in the wound of schism, whatever they do not gather with Christ, they scatter.

Let them not exalt themselves over what they possess. Why do they direct such proud eyes toward the many things that are sound? Let them humbly look upon their wound, and attend not only to what is present but also to what is lacking. Let them see how many and how great things are of no benefit if one thing is missing. [Col. 0871B] And let them see what that one thing is—not by listening to me, but to the Apostle:

“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so that I move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing.”

What benefit, then, is it to them if they possess an angelic tongue in the sacred mysteries, and prophecy like Caiaphas and Saul, who at some time prophesied, although holy Scripture testifies that they were condemnable? What benefit is it if they not only know the sacraments but also possess them, as Simon Magus possessed them? What benefit is faith like that of the demons who confessed Christ? For they certainly believed when they said, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? We know who you are.” What benefit is it if they themselves distribute their possessions to the poor, as many do not only within the catholic faith but also in various heresies? What benefit is it if, when persecution arises, they hand their bodies over with us to the flames for the faith which they confess together with us?

Nevertheless, because they do these things while separated, not bearing with one another in love and not striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, they plainly do not possess charity. Even with all those things—which by themselves profit them nothing—they cannot attain eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER CCIX  
### He resolves the Donatists’ objection whether Christ’s baptism generates children in the Donatist party or does not generate them.

They seem, then, to ask with the greatest subtlety whether Christ’s baptism generates children in the Donatist party or does not generate them. If we agree that it generates them, they will assert that their Church is the mother, since it was able to generate children from Christ’s baptism; and since there must be one Church, they will consequently accuse us of not being the Church. But if we say, “It does not generate them,” they ask: “Why, then, are those who pass from us to you not reborn through baptism, when they were baptized among us, if they have not yet been born?”

It is as though baptism generated from the source from which it is separated, rather than from the source with which it is joined. It is separated from the bond of charity and peace, but it is joined in the one baptism. Therefore there is one Church, which alone is called catholic. Whatever belongs to it, among those separated from its unity in various communities, generates through the fact that it possesses in them what belongs to it; it is the Church itself that generates, not those communities.

For their separation [earum; variant eorum: “their separation”] does not generate; rather, what they retained from the Church generates. If they also abandon this, they generate nothing at all.

## CHAPTER CCX  
### That the same Church generates even Catholics who live badly, just as it generated Simon.

The Church therefore generates all in whom her sacraments are retained. Thus something of this kind can be generated anywhere, even though not all whom she generates belong to her unity—the unity that will save those who persevere to the end [or: “which perseveres to the end”].

For not only those belong to this category who are openly manifest through the sacrilege of separation, but also those who, bodily mingled within her unity, are separated from her by their evil way of life. Indeed, the Church herself had borne Simon Magus through baptism, yet he was told that he had no share in Christ’s inheritance. Did he lack baptism, the Gospel, or the sacraments? No; but because he lacked charity, he was born in vain, and it might perhaps have been better for him not to have been born.

Were those not born to whom the Apostle says: “As infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food”? Yet he calls them back from the sacrilege of schisms [from the sacrilege of schism], into which they were rushing [or: “had rushed”] because they were carnal:

“As infants in Christ,” he says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to receive it. Indeed, you are not even now able, for you are still carnal. For since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways? When one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I to Apollos,’ are you not human?“

Of these matters he had said above:

“I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. What I mean is this: each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

If these people had remained in this obstinacy and perversity, they would certainly have been born, but they would not have belonged, through the bond of peace and unity, to that Church from which they had been born.

## CHAPTER CCXI  
### Whether this remission of sins takes place among heretics; from the same book.

The Church herself therefore generates, both through her own womb and through the wombs of her maidservants, from the same sacraments as from the seed of her husband. For the Apostle does not say without reason that all those things took place figuratively. But those who are proud and are not joined to their lawful mother are like Ishmael, of whom it was said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

Those, however, who lovingly embrace the lawful wife of their father, from whom they were lawfully born, are like the sons of Jacob, though born of slave women, yet receiving the same inheritance.

Those who are born within, from the womb of that mother herself, in unity, but neglect the grace they have received, are like Esau, the son of Isaac, who was rejected, God bearing witness and saying: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”—although both were conceived from one intercourse and born from one womb.

They also ask whether sins are forgiven through baptism in the Donatist party. If we say that they are forgiven, they reply: “Then the Holy Spirit is there, because when the Lord breathed upon the disciples and gave him to them, he then followed by saying: ‘Baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained.’” And if this is so, they say, “Our communion is the Church of Christ.”

For the Holy Spirit does not effect the forgiveness of sins outside the Church. And if our communion is the Church of Christ, your communion is not the Church of Christ. For there is one Church, whoever she may be, of whom it is said: “My dove is one; she is the only one of her mother.” There cannot be as many Churches as there are schisms.

But if we say that sins are not forgiven there, they reply: “Then there is no true baptism there. Therefore those whom you receive from us ought to be baptized by you. Since you do not do this, you admit that you are not in the Church of Christ.”

We resist them in this matter by questioning them according to the Scriptures, so that they may answer for themselves what they ask of us. For I ask them to say whether sins are forgiven where charity is absent. Sins are the darkness of souls; for we hear John saying: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now.” No one would create schisms if he were not blinded by hatred of his brother.

If, then, we say that sins are not forgiven there, how is the person who is baptized among them reborn? For what is it to be reborn through baptism except to be renewed from the old condition? But how is someone renewed from the old condition if his past sins are not forgiven?

And if he has not been reborn, neither has he put on Christ. From this it follows that he would appear to require baptism again, since the Apostle says: “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” If he has not put him on, he should not be considered baptized into Christ.

But because we say that he was baptized into Christ, we confess that he put on Christ; and if we confess this, we confess that he was regenerated. If this is so, his sins were also forgiven.

How, then, does John say, “Whoever hates his brother remains in darkness until now,” if the forgiveness of sins has already taken place? Is there no hatred of brothers in schism? Who could say this, when the origin and persistence of schism have no other cause than hatred of one’s brother [fraternal hatred]?

They believe that they resolve this question for themselves when they say: “Then there is no forgiveness of sins in schism, and therefore no regeneration of the new person, and consequently no baptism of Christ.” But because we confess that Christ’s baptism exists there, we put this question to them for resolution: Was that Simon Magus truly baptized with Christ’s baptism?

They will answer, “Yes,” because they are compelled by the authority of holy Scripture. I ask, then, whether they admit that his sins were forgiven. They will certainly admit it. Again I ask why Peter said to him that he had no share in the lot of the saints.

They answer: “Because he sinned afterward, wishing to buy the gift of God with money, since he believed that the apostles were sellers of it.”

But if he approached baptism itself as a hypocrite, were his sins forgiven or not? Let them choose whichever they wish. Whichever they choose is sufficient for us. If they say that his sins were forgiven, how will the Holy Spirit, who shuns hypocrisy, have avoided the hypocrite if he effected forgiveness of sins in that hypocrite? If they say that his sins were not forgiven, I ask whether, if he afterward confessed his hypocrisy with a contrite heart and genuine sorrow, he would be judged in need of baptism again.

But to say this would be utter madness. Let them therefore admit that a person can be baptized with Christ’s true baptism and yet, while his heart persists in wickedness or sacrilege, prevent the abolition of his sins from taking place.

Thus they should understand that a person who, an enemy of Christ’s charity and peace, has received Christ’s baptism—which those who have separated themselves have not lost—in some heresy or schism, where his sins were not forgiven because of that sacrilegious crime, is not to be baptized again when he corrects himself and comes to the fellowship and unity of the Church. For reconciliation and peace themselves bring it about that the sacrament, which he received in schism and could not benefit him there, now begins to benefit him in unity unto the forgiveness of his sins.

If they say that, in the case of the hypocrite who approached baptism, his sins were indeed forgiven through the holy power of so great a sacrament at that very moment, but that the sacrament’s efficacy was immediately restored when the Holy Spirit came upon the baptized person so that the sins departed, and the persistence of his hypocrisy fled so that the sins returned, then both statements will be true: “As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ,” and “The Holy Spirit will flee from hypocrisy.”

That is, the holiness of baptism puts Christ on him, while the destructive power of hypocrisy strips Christ from him, just as when someone passes from darkness through light into darkness again. His eyes remain directed toward the darkness throughout, but the light can do nothing except illuminate him as he passes through it.

If they say that this happens, let them understand that the same thing happens in those who are outside the Church’s communion but are nevertheless baptized with the Church’s baptism. Wherever it exists, it is holy in itself. Therefore it does not belong to those who separate themselves, but to the one from whom they separate themselves.

It benefits them, nevertheless, to this extent: by its light they pass into the darkness of their dissension, while their sins immediately return—the sins that the holiness of baptism had forgiven at that moment—just as darkness returns when the light had dispelled it during their passage.

## CHAPTER CCXII  
### That sins are not forgiven without charity: proved by the servant whose debt the master had forgiven.

The Lord teaches most clearly in the Gospel that forgiven sins return where brotherly charity is absent. He speaks of the servant whom he found owing ten thousand talents and forgave everything when the servant pleaded with him. But when that servant did not take pity on his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, the master ordered him to repay what he had forgiven him.

The time at which forgiveness is received through baptism is therefore like the time for rendering an account, so that all debts found there may be forgiven. Yet that servant had not afterward lent his fellow servant the money he had owed him. When the fellow servant could not repay it, the servant did not take pity on him—even though the fellow servant owed him money—while he himself had been released from such a vast debt when rendering his account to his master.

He had not forgiven his fellow servant what the man owed him, and so he had approached the master to receive forgiveness. This is indicated by the words of the fellow servant: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you.” Otherwise he would have said: “You had already forgiven me this; why are you demanding it again?”

The Lord’s own words make this even clearer. He says: “When that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii.” He did not say, “to whom he had already forgiven a debt of one hundred denarii.” For if he had forgiven it, the fellow servant would not have owed it to him. Since he said “owed him,” it is evident that he had not forgiven it.

It would indeed have been better, and more fitting for someone who was about to render an account for so great a debt and was awaiting his master’s mercy, if he had first forgiven his fellow servant what was owed to him and then approached to render his account, where he would have to implore his master’s mercy.

Nevertheless, the fact that he had not yet forgiven his fellow servant did not prevent his master from forgiving him everything he owed at the time when he was to render his account. But what did it profit him, since, because he persisted in hatred, everything was immediately charged against him again?

So the grace of baptism is not prevented from forgiving all sins, even if hatred of a brother persists in the heart of the person whose sins are forgiven. The previous day is canceled, and whatever lies before it is canceled as well, including the very hour and moment before baptism and in baptism. From then onward, however, he immediately begins to be liable not only for the days, hours, and moments that follow, but also for those already past, since everything that was forgiven returns. Such things often occur in the Church.

## CHAPTER CCXIII  
### On baptizing someone in danger of death who harbors enmity.

It often happens that a person has an enemy whom he hates most unjustly, although we are commanded to love even unjust enemies and to pray for them. Then, suddenly endangered by death, he becomes distressed and asks for baptism. He receives it with such haste that the danger scarcely allows [admittat; printed ammittat, “loses”] time for the necessary interrogation of a few words—how much less for a lengthy exhortation by which that hatred might be driven from his heart, even if the person baptizing him knows of it.

Certainly such things continue to occur not only among us but also among them. What, then, are we to say? Are this man’s sins forgiven or are they not forgiven?

Let them choose whatever they wish. For if they are forgiven, they immediately return [immediately, i.e. at once]. The Gospel speaks and the truth cries out: whether they are forgiven or not forgiven, subsequent medicine is necessary. Yet if he survives, learns that this matter must be corrected, and corrects it, he is not baptized again, whether among them or among us.

Likewise, when schismatics or heretics possess and practice certain things in no other way than the true Church, when they come to us we do not correct them but rather approve them. For in the things in which they do not disagree with us, they are not separated from us. Nevertheless, because these things benefit them nothing as long as they remain schismatics or heretics—because of the other matters in which they disagree with the truth and because of the monstrous sacrilege of separation itself—we exhort them to come to the salvation of peace and charity, whether their sins have remained in them or have immediately returned after being forgiven.

We exhort them not merely so that they may possess something they did not possess, but so that what they possessed may also begin to benefit them.

## CHAPTER CCXIV  
### That the baptism of God and of the Church belongs to God and the Church wherever it is found; from the same book.

They therefore say to us in vain: “If you accept our baptism, what do we lack that makes you think we must be advised to join your communion?”

We answer: We do not accept your baptism—for that baptism is not the baptism of schismatics or heretics—but the baptism of God and of the Church, wherever it is found and wherever it is transferred. What belongs to you, however, is only what you wrongly believe, what you sacrilegiously practice, and the impious way in which you separate yourselves.

For even if you possess or believe all the other things truly—and yet persist in that same separation, against the bond of brotherly peace and against the unity of all the brothers who, throughout the whole world, have both been promised and have appeared, whose causes and hearts you could never in any way know or examine, so as rightly to condemn those who cannot be guilty merely because they trusted ecclesiastical judges rather than litigants—there is only this one thing that you lack: what the person who does not have charity lacks.

Why, then, do we need to rehearse this for you? Look for yourselves in the Apostle and see how much you lack. What difference does it make whether someone who does not have charity flies out, carried away by some wind of temptation, or remains inside the Lord’s harvest, only to be separated at the final winnowing? Yet even such people, if they have once obtained baptism, must not be born again.

## CHAPTER CCXV  
### That the Church gives birth, either through herself or through the womb of her maidservants, from the seed of her husband; with the examples of Esau and Asher.

The Church gives birth to all through baptism, whether among her own people—that is, from her own womb—or outside herself, from the seed of her husband [or: “whether from herself or from her maidservant”].

Esau too was born from a wife, but because of brotherly discord he was separated from the people of God. Asher, though born through the authority of a wife but from a maidservant, received the promised land because of brotherly concord.

Thus, in Ishmael’s case, the fact that his mother was a maidservant did not prevent his separation from the people of God; rather, brotherly discord prevented him. Nor did the authority of the wife benefit him, although he was more truly her son, since through her marital rights he had been conceived with the maidservant and born from the maidservant. So among these people, by the right of the Church—which exists in baptism—those who are born are born.

But if they are reconciled with their brothers through the unity of peace, they come to the promised land—not to be cast out again from their mother’s womb, but to be recognized in their father’s seed. If they persist in discord, they will belong to Ishmael’s cord.

Ishmael came first and Isaac afterward; Esau came first and Jacob afterward. This is not because heresy gave birth before the Church, or because the Church first gave birth to carnal or natural people and afterward to spiritual people. Rather, in the condition of mortality in which we are born from Adam, what is natural comes first and what is spiritual afterward.

From this natural understanding, because the natural person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit, all dissensions and schisms are generated. Those who persist in this understanding, the Apostle says, belong to the Old Testament—that is, to the desire for earthly promises, in which spiritual things are indeed represented, but the natural person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit.

## CHAPTER CCXVI  
### That the Church is an ancient reality, possessing in some a natural portion and in others a spiritual portion.

Whenever such people begin to exist in this life—people who, although already imbued with the divine sacraments according to the distribution of the ages, nevertheless think carnally and hope for and desire carnal things from God, whether in this life or after this life—they are natural people.

The Church, however, which is the people of God, is an ancient reality even during the pilgrimage of this life. In some people she possesses a natural portion, and in others a spiritual one. The Old Testament belongs to the natural; the New Testament to the spiritual. But in the earliest times both were hidden, from Adam until Moses.

From Moses onward the Old Testament was made manifest, and within it the New Testament was itself concealed, because it was signified secretly. Afterward, when the Lord came in the flesh, the New Testament was revealed, while the sacraments of the Old Testament came to an end. Yet such desires did not cease.

For among those who, through the sacrament of the New Testament, have already been born, the Apostle says that some are still natural and unable to perceive the things of God’s Spirit. Just as some spiritual people lived under the sacraments of the Old Testament, belonging to the New Testament that was then secretly hidden, so now many natural people live under the sacrament of the New Testament, which has already been revealed.

If they do not wish to advance toward perceiving the things of God’s Spirit, to which the apostolic word exhorts them, they will belong to the Old Testament. But if they advance, then even before they grasp those things, by that very progress and approach they belong to the New Testament. And if they are taken from this life before they become spiritual, guarded by the holiness of the sacrament, they are counted among the living, where our hope and portion is the Lord.

I find no more truthful understanding of what is written: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state,” since what follows says: “And in your book all shall be written.”

The same mother who gave birth to Abel, Enoch, Noah, and Abraham also gave birth to Moses and the prophets who came later, before the Lord’s coming. The same mother who gave birth to these also gave birth to the apostles, our martyrs, and all good Christians.

All appeared born at different times, but they are held together in the fellowship of one people. As citizens of the same city, they have experienced the labors of this pilgrimage; some are experiencing them now, and the rest will experience them until the end.

Again, the same mother who gave birth to Cain, Ham, Ishmael [Ismahel], and Esau also gave birth to Dathan and others like them within the same people. The same mother also gave birth to Judas the pseudo-apostle, Simon Magus, and the other pseudo-Christians down to the present day, stubbornly hardened in a natural disposition—whether they are mingled within the unity or openly dissent through separation.

## CHAPTER CCXVII  
### How the Church generates good and evil people, like Rebecca bearing twins through herself.

When such people are evangelized and instructed in the sacraments by spiritual persons, Rebecca gives birth to them through herself, as she gave birth to Esau. But when such people are generated within the people of God through those who do not proclaim the Gospel chastely, they are born not through Sarah but through Hagar [“through Sarah, but through Hagar”].

Likewise, when good spiritual people are generated through carnal evangelists or baptizers, Leah or Rachel gives birth to them by marital right, but through the womb of maidservants.

But when good believers are generated through spiritual people in the Gospel—those who either advance into the disposition of spiritual maturity, or do not cease striving toward it, or fail to do so only because they cannot—they are born into the new life and the New Testament from Sarah’s womb, as Isaac was, or from Rebecca’s, as Jacob was.

Therefore, whether they seem to be inside or are openly outside, what is flesh is flesh. Whether the chaff remains in its barrenness on the threshing floor or is lifted outside by the wind of temptation, what is chaff is chaff. Whoever is separated from the unity of that Church which is without stain or wrinkle is separated from it, even if he is mingled with the congregation of the saints in carnal hardness.

Yet no one is to be despaired of, whether he appears to be such a person inside or opposes the Church more openly outside. Spiritual people, however, and those who are piously striving to become spiritual, do not go outside. For even when they seem to be expelled through some perversity or necessity of human beings, they are tested there more than if they remained inside, provided that they do not in any way rise up against the Church but are firmly rooted in the solid rock of unity through the strongest strength of charity. [Col. 0879A]

This is what is meant by the statement concerning Abraham’s sacrifice: “But he did not divide the birds.”

## CHAPTER CCXVIII  
### That the Lord did not reveal to Cyprian his judgment concerning baptism, which he later disclosed through a plenary council, so that Cyprian’s charity might appear more fully; from the same book.

There remain great testimonies in the letters of the blessed martyr Cyprian. Let me now turn to him, since these people flatter themselves carnally through his authority, while they are spiritually destroyed by his charity.

In those days, before the judgment of a plenary council had confirmed, through the agreement of the whole Church, what ought to be followed in this matter, it seemed right to him, together with nearly eighty of his fellow bishops from the African churches, that everyone who had been baptized outside the communion of the catholic Church ought to be baptized again when coming to the Church.

Because this was not correct, the Lord evidently did not reveal the truth to so great a man for this reason: so that his piety, humility, and charity in wisely preserving the peace of the Church might be made manifest.

He therefore penetrated less deeply and failed to perceive the hidden secret of the sacrament. But if he had known all the sacraments and did not have charity, he would be nothing.

Yet although he perceived that matter less fully, he nevertheless guarded charity humbly, faithfully, and courageously, and deserved to reach the crown of martyrdom. Thus, if any mist arising from human weakness had crept [inrepserant; variant irrepserat] into his clear mind, it was driven away by the glorious brightness of his shining blood.

For the Lord Jesus Christ himself did not speak without reason when he called himself the vine and said that his own, as branches in the vine, were cut off and removed from the vine as useless branches that bore no fruit.

What is the fruit except that new offspring of which he also says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”? That is the charity without which the other things are of no benefit.

The Apostle also says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control.” All these begin from charity and, through their remaining conjunction, form something like a marvelous cluster.

Nor did the same Lord add without reason: “Every branch in me that bears fruit, my Father prunes, so that it may bear more fruit.” For even those who excel in the fruit of charity may still possess something requiring pruning; the farmer does not leave it uncultivated.

Thus, although that holy man held a view about baptism different from the truth of the matter—a truth later examined and established through the most careful consideration—he remained within catholic unity. What he lacked was compensated by the abundance of charity and cleansed by the sickle of his passion.

## CHAPTER CCXIX  
### That just as what belongs to the devil within must be exposed, so what belongs to Christ outside must be recognized; from Book IV On Baptism.

Thus, just as what belongs to the devil must be reproved within, so what belongs to Christ must be acknowledged outside. Does Christ not have his own outside the unity of the Church, while the devil has his own within the unity of the Church? This may perhaps be said of human beings, so that, just as the devil has none of his own among the holy angels, God has none of his own outside the communion of the Church. But with regard to this Church, which still bears the mortality of the flesh so long as it is a pilgrim away from the Lord, the devil has been permitted to mix in weeds—that is, wicked people—and this permission has been granted because of the Church’s pilgrimage, so that the rest of that homeland which the holy angels enjoy might be desired more ardently.

But this cannot be said of the sacraments. For just as they can possess and administer them not for their salvation but for their destruction—since the interior weeds have been destined for the fire—so too the exterior weeds, which received them from those who departed from within, still possess them because those who departed did not lose them. This is undoubtedly made clear when they return and the sacraments are not restored to them, since sometimes some of those very people who had departed return.

Nor should anyone say: “What grain of wheat do the weeds have?” For if this is so, the condition is equal both within and outside, at least in this respect. Grains of wheat are found among the exterior weeds as well as among the interior ones. When the question concerns the sacrament[s], however, the question is not whether the weeds possess some grain of wheat, but whether they possess anything of heaven. For both the exterior and the interior weeds receive, together with the wheat itself, the common rain, which is heavenly and sweet. Even if the weeds grow sterilely from it, so too the Gospel sacrament of Christ is divine and sweet; nor should it be condemned because of the sterility of those upon whom it rains, even outside.

## CHAPTER CCXX

### That true baptism cannot succeed itself in the way in which true faith succeeds false faith; from the same fourth book *On Baptism*.

We have already shown sufficiently that, with regard to baptism consecrated by evangelical words, the error of either the giver or the recipient is irrelevant, whether that person thinks differently about the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit from what heavenly teaching indicates. For many carnal and merely natural people are baptized even within the Church, although the Apostle plainly says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God”; and, after they have already received baptism, he says that they are still natural.

According to a carnal understanding, a soul devoted to bodily senses cannot think of God except in a carnal manner. Hence many who make progress after baptism—and especially those baptized as infants or children—when their understanding becomes increasingly serene and illuminated, as the inner person is renewed day by day, mock, reject with abhorrence, and confess that they are abandoning their former opinions about God, together with the phantasms by which they had been deceived [or: “were deceived”]. Yet they are not for that reason judged not to have received baptism, nor are they said to have received a baptism corresponding to the nature of their error. Rather, in them the integrity of the sacrament is honored, while the vanity of the mind is corrected, even if that vanity had become entrenched and had perhaps been skillfully defended through many controversies.

Therefore, even a heretic who is plainly outside, if he received evangelical baptism there, did not receive a baptism corresponding to the error by which he is blinded. Consequently, if he comes to his senses and sees that what he had wrongly held must be abandoned, he must not at the same time abandon the good that he had received. Nor, because his error must be condemned, should Christ’s baptism in him therefore be repudiated.

For it is already sufficiently evident from those within who happen to be baptized while holding false opinions about God that the truth of the sacrament must be distinguished from the error of the person who believes wrongly, although both can be found in one and the same person. Therefore, when someone established in some error outside the Church has nevertheless been baptized with the true sacrament, and is restored to the unity of the Church, true baptism cannot succeed true baptism in the way that true faith succeeds false faith. The same thing cannot succeed itself, because it cannot depart.

Heretics therefore come to the Catholic Church so that what is evil in them may be corrected, not so that God’s good gift may be repeated.

Someone may say: “Then is there no difference if two people are established in equal error and wickedness, with neither their life nor their heart changed, and one of them is baptized outside while the other is baptized within?” I acknowledge that there is a difference. The one who is baptized outside is worse—not because he is baptized, but because he is outside. It is also an evil, neither negligible nor small, to belong to that division, provided that the one baptized within did not wish to remain within for some earthly or temporal advantage, but preferred the unity of the Church spread throughout the whole world to the cutting apart of schisms. Otherwise, he too must be counted among those who are outside.

Let us therefore posit two people of this sort: one, for example, holding about Christ what Photinus held and being baptized in his heresy outside the communion of the Catholic Church; the other holding the same opinion but being baptized within the Catholic Church, believing that this was itself the Catholic faith. I do not yet call the latter a heretic, unless, after the doctrine of the Catholic faith has been made known to him, he prefers to resist it and chooses what he had previously held. Before that occurs, it is clear that the one outside is worse. Thus, in the one, the false opinion alone must be corrected; in the other, the division as well. But in neither of them must the truth of the sacrament be repeated.

If, however, someone holds the same opinion as the first, knows that it is a heresy separated from Catholic unity, and wishes to be baptized within the Catholic unity where this doctrine is taught and learned for the sake of some secular advantage—or, having been baptized within it, refuses to leave it for that reason—he must be regarded not merely as separated but as all the more criminal, insofar as he adds the deceit of pretense to heretical error and division from unity.

Accordingly, the more dangerous and crooked a person’s depravity is, the more urgently and diligently it must be corrected. Yet if that person possesses anything sound—especially if it is not his own but God’s—his depravity does not make it something to be regarded as nothing, condemned in the same manner, or attributed to his depravity rather than to the generosity of the One who, even to a soul fornicating away from him and following after its lovers, gave his own bread, wine, oil, and other provisions or adornments. These things belong neither to the soul itself nor to its lovers, but to the One who, in pity for it, willed everywhere to admonish it toward whom it should return.  
[Col. 0882A]

## CHAPTER CCXXI

### On the heretic of good morals and the criminal who is Catholic; from the same fourth book *On Baptism*.

Let us posit a chaste, continent, non-greedy heretic who does not serve idols, welcomes strangers, ministers to the needy, is no one’s enemy, is not quarrelsome, is patient and tranquil, envies no one, is sober and frugal. No one can doubt that, merely because he is a heretic, he will not possess the kingdom of God.

Let us posit another person who is a fornicator, impure, lustful, greedy, or even more openly devoted to idols; a sorcerer, contentious, quarrelsome, jealous, hot-tempered [or: “rash”], seditious, envious, drunk, and a glutton, but Catholic. Will he, merely because he is Catholic, possess the kingdom of God while committing the acts about which the Apostle concludes: “These things I proclaim to you, as I proclaimed them before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God”? If we say this, we deceive ourselves. For God’s word does not deceive us: it neither keeps silent nor spares us, nor does it mislead us through any flattery.

That is why it also says elsewhere: “But know this, recognizing that every fornicator, or impure person, or greedy person—for greed is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words.” We therefore have no grounds for complaining about the Lord’s word. It says altogether plainly and openly that those who live badly do not belong to the kingdom of God.
