We must not flatter a Catholic surrounded by all these vices, nor dare promise him, because he is a Christian and a Catholic, an impunity that divine Scripture does not promise.

Nor, if he possesses even one of the things just mentioned, should we promise him fellowship in that heavenly homeland. For in writing to the Corinthians the Apostle lists them individually, and in each individual item it is implied that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idol-servants, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God.”

He does not say: “Those who have all these vices together will not possess the kingdom of God”; rather, “Neither this one nor that one,” so that you understand in each individual case that none of them will possess the kingdom of God. Therefore, just as heretics will not possess the kingdom of God, so the greedy will not possess the kingdom of God.

There is indeed no doubt that the punishments by which those who will not possess the kingdom of God will be tormented differ according to the diversity of their crimes, some being more severe than others, so that in the eternal fire there may be different torments of punishment corresponding to the unequal weight of sins. For the Lord himself did not say without reason: “It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for you on the day of judgment.”

## CHAPTER CCXXII

### That the water of baptism saves within the Church and condemns outside the Church; from the fifth book *On Baptism*.

There are also some among those who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or in the superstitions of the gentiles; yet even there the Lord knows who are his. For in that ineffable foreknowledge [of God], many who appear to be outside are within, and many who appear to be within are outside.

From all those who are, so to speak, inwardly and secretly within is constituted that enclosed garden, sealed fountain, well of living water, and paradise with the fruit of trees. Their divinely granted gifts are partly proper to them—for example, tireless charity in the present age and eternal life in the future—and partly shared with the wicked and perverse, as are all the other things that include the holy mysteries.

This now gives us a simpler and more accessible way to consider that ark of which Noah was the builder and pilot [or: “captain”]. For Peter says: “In Noah’s ark a few, that is, eight human souls, were saved through water; and baptism, in a corresponding form, now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience.”

Therefore, if there appear to human beings to be baptized within the Catholic unity people who renounce the world with words alone and not in their deeds, how do they belong to the mystery of this ark, since there is in them no appeal of a good conscience? Or how are they saved through water if, making bad use of holy baptism, they appear to be within yet persevere to the end of their lives in shameful and ruined conduct? Or how were those not saved through water whom Cyprian himself records as having been admitted straightforwardly into the Church in the past with the baptism they had received in heresy?

The unity of the ark itself saved them, and no one is saved in it except through water. For he himself says: “The Lord is powerful in his mercy to grant pardon and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who were admitted straightforwardly into the Church and fell asleep in the Church.” If not through water, how are they in the ark? If not in the ark, how are they in the Church? But if they are in the Church, then certainly they are in the ark; and if in the ark, certainly through water.

It can therefore happen that some baptized outside are, through God’s foreknowledge, more truly reckoned baptized within, because there the water begins to benefit them for salvation. For they cannot otherwise be said to have been saved in the ark except through water. Conversely, some who appear to have been baptized within may, through that same foreknowledge of God, more truly be reckoned baptized outside. For by making bad use of baptism they die through the water, something that at that time happened to no one except one who was outside the ark.

Certainly it is clear that what is called within and outside in the Church must be understood as referring to the heart, not the body, since all who are in the unity of the ark in heart are saved through that same water, while all who are outside in heart—whether or not they are also outside in body—die through it as adversaries of unity.

Thus, just as it was not another water but the same water that saved those placed in the ark and destroyed those placed outside the ark, so it is not another baptism but the same baptism through which good Catholics are saved and bad Catholics or heretics perish.

## CHAPTER CCXXIII

### That there are many wolves lying in wait within and many sheep wandering outside, yet the Lord knows who are his; and concerning Saint Cyprian and the Apostle Peter, from the sixth book *On Baptism*.

Even those slower of heart, so far as I think, understand that Christ’s baptism cannot be violated by any perversity of a human being, whether giver or recipient. It was for no other reason that, in those times when this question was being debated against a useful custom, with disputants arguing while preserving charity and unity, it seemed to certain distinguished bishops of Christ—among whom blessed Cyprian stood out especially—that Christ’s baptism could not exist among heretics or schismatics, except that the sacrament was not distinguished from the effect or use of the sacrament. Since its effect and use, liberation from sins and uprightness of heart, were not found among heretics, the sacrament itself was thought not to exist there.

But when they turned their eyes toward the multitude of interior chaff, and saw that those who are perverse and live ruinously within the unity itself appeared unable either to give or to possess remission of sins—for it was said not to wicked but to good sons, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they will be retained”—it became sufficiently clear to the shepherds of the Catholic Church spread throughout the world that such people nevertheless possess, give, and receive the sacrament of baptism. Later, the original custom was confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.

Thus the sheep that had wandered outside, and had received the Lord’s mark outside from its deceitful plunderers, comes to the salvation of Christian unity: it is corrected from error, freed from captivity, and healed from its wound. Yet the Lord’s mark is recognized rather than rejected, since many wolves also imprint it upon wolves—wolves who appear to be within but are shown by the fruits of their conduct, in which they persist to the end, not to belong to that one sheep which is also one among many.

According to God’s foreknowledge, just as many sheep wander outside, so many wolves lie in wait within. Yet among them the Lord knows who are his. They hear no voice except that of the shepherd, even when he cries out through people like the Pharisees, of whom it was said: “Do whatever they say.”

For just as a spiritual person, possessing the end of the commandment—that is, charity—from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, may, because of the body that is still corruptible and burdens the soul, see something less clearly and think differently; and God, when he wills, will reveal it to him while he remains in that same charity—so in a carnal and perverse person something good and useful may be found that comes from elsewhere, not from that person himself.

For just as something requiring cleansing is found on a fruitful branch, so that it may bear more fruit, so a grape may hang even on a barren and dry reed, or on one that has been tied up. Therefore, just as it is foolish to cherish the refuse of a fruitful branch, while the person who does so rightly does not reject his fruit wherever it may be hanging, so anyone cut off from unity who rebaptizes because Cyprian thought that those coming from heretics ought to be baptized again avoids what deserves praise in so great a man, pursues what deserves correction, and does not attain even what he pursues.

For while he vehemently detested, out of zeal for God, those who had separated themselves from unity, he also judged that they had been separated from baptism itself. These people, however, considering it a small crime that they themselves have been separated from Christ’s unity, insist that his baptism was not there either and that it departed with them. They are therefore so far from Cyprian’s fruitfulness that they do not even equal his refuse.

Again, whoever lacks charity and enters upon the ruined paths of the worst conduct appears to be within while actually being outside; and the fact that he does not repeat Christ’s baptism among heretics does nothing to aid his sterility, since he is not fertilized by what is his own but is burdened with the fruit of another.

It can happen, however, that someone is vigorous in the root of charity, and thinks most rightly about the matter on which Cyprian thought otherwise, and yet that more things are fruitful in Cyprian than in this person, while more things require cleansing in this person than in Cyprian.

We therefore not only in no way compare bad Catholics with blessed Cyprian, but do not easily equate even good Catholics with him. The devout mother Church counts him among the rare and few men of outstanding grace. Nevertheless, these people recognize Christ’s baptism even among heretics, whereas he thought otherwise; and through him, seeing less clearly in this matter yet remaining most firmly in unity, it was more clearly demonstrated to heretics by what sacrilegious crime the bond of peace was broken.

For the blind Pharisees, although they sometimes said what ought to be done, were not to be compared with the Apostle Peter, although he sometimes said what ought not to be done. Not only is the barrenness of these people not to be compared with his flourishing vigor, but the fruit of others is not to be equated with Cyprian’s abundance.

No one now compels the gentiles to Judaize, and yet no one who has progressed as far as possible in the Church today should for that reason be compared with Peter’s apostleship.

Therefore, while rendering the reverence due and offering the honor appropriate to the peaceful bishop and glorious martyr Cyprian as far as I am able, I nevertheless dare to say that he thought differently about baptizing schismatics or heretics from what the truth later revealed—not on my own authority, but on the judgment of the universal Church, strengthened and confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.

Likewise, while venerating Peter according to his merit, the foremost of the apostles and the most eminent of martyrs, I nevertheless dare to say that he did not act rightly in compelling the gentiles to Judaize. I say this too not on my own authority, but on the saving teaching of the Apostle Paul, retained and preserved throughout the Church.

In discussing Cyprian’s opinion, therefore, though far below Cyprian’s merits, I say that both the good and the wicked can possess, give, and receive the sacrament of baptism: the good beneficially and salvifically, the wicked harmfully and punitively. Yet in both it remains equally complete, and its equal integrity in every respect is not affected by how wickedly one of the wicked possesses it, just as it is not affected by how well one of the good possesses it. Accordingly, it makes no difference how wickedly one gives it, just as it makes no difference how well another gives it; and likewise it makes no difference how wickedly one receives it, just as it makes no difference how well another receives it. For in itself, both among those who are not equally just and among those who are not equally unjust, it is equally holy.

## CHAPTER CCXXIV

### That under the same baptism sins are forgiven because of the bond of charity, under which they were retained because of the sacrilege of division; and concerning the praise of Saint Cyprian; from the same book.

As has been said, it makes no difference to the holiness of baptism how wickedly someone possesses it or how wickedly someone gives it. A person who is separated can give it, just as a separated person can possess it; but just as it is harmful for him to possess it, so it is harmful for him to give it.

The one to whom he gives it, however, can receive it salvifically if he receives it without himself being separated. This happened to many: with a Catholic disposition and a heart not alienated from the unity of peace, they were driven by some pressing danger of death to enter the presence of a heretic, received Christ’s baptism from him without any perversity, and, whether they died or were rescued, did not remain with those to whom they had never passed over in heart.

But if the recipient himself received it while separated, he receives it more harmfully in proportion as the good he receives is greater and he receives it badly; and it contributes more to the separated person’s destruction in proportion as it could contribute to his salvation if he were joined to unity.

Therefore, if he is corrected from that perversity and turns away from separation to Catholic peace, his sins are forgiven under the same baptism that he had received. They had been retained under that baptism because of the sacrilege of division, but are forgiven because of the bond of charity. For what is holy in both the just person and the unjust person remains always holy; it is neither increased by anyone’s righteousness nor diminished by anyone’s unrighteousness.

Since this is so, what does it matter to this truth—so evident—that many fellow bishops agreed with Cyprian in that opinion and issued their own statements corresponding to it, except that the charity of that man toward Christ’s unity may become increasingly known? If he had remained alone in holding this opinion, with no one agreeing with him, it might have appeared that he had recoiled from the crime of schism merely because he could find no companions in error. But although so many agreed with him, he nevertheless remained, together with others who thought differently, in the unity of the Catholic whole; he preserved that most holy bond not through fear of solitude but through love of peace.

## CHAPTER CCXXV

### That the sacrament of baptism is equal in the wicked and in the good; from the sixth book.

It can therefore happen that someone is worse than a gentile, and yet Christ’s sacrament is not only present in him but is no worse than in a holy and just person. For although, so far as that person is concerned, it did not save him but was violated by his mind and will, nevertheless, so far as the sacrament itself is concerned, it remained whole and inviolate even with its despiser and repudiator.

Were not the inhabitants of Sodom gentiles, that is, pagans? The Jews, then, were worse than they, and the Lord says to them: “It will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.” The prophet also says to them: “You justified Sodom”—that is, in comparison with you, Sodom was justified.

Yet were the divine sacraments that existed among the Jews for that reason such as the Jews themselves were? The Lord himself also received them, sent the lepers whom he had cleansed to perform them, and an angel stood beside Zechariah as he ministered and announced to him that his sacrifice in the temple had been heard.

These same sacraments existed both among the good people of that time and among wicked people worse than gentiles, since in wickedness they were ranked above the Sodomites. Yet those sacraments remained whole and divine in both groups.

Our holy teachers did not disapprove even of whatever divine and upright element the gentiles were able to possess in their teachings, although the gentiles were detestable because of their superstitions, idolatry, pride, and other ways of life, and unless they were corrected they were destined to be punished by divine judgment.

The Apostle Paul, when speaking about God among the Athenians, also bore witness that some of them had said something of this kind. If they had come to Christ, that element would certainly have been recognized in them, not condemned.

Saint Cyprian too uses such witnesses against those same gentiles. For when speaking about the magi, he says: “Their chief, however, is Sosthenes” [*Hostanos*, Ed. Ben.], “who denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels stand beside his throne” [Note: “See Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*.”]. Plato agrees with this in like manner: while preserving belief in one God, he says that the others are angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus likewise speaks of one God and confesses him to be incomprehensible and beyond estimation.

If these people had come to receive Christian salvation, they would certainly not have been told, “You possess this evil,” or, “You possess this falsehood.” Rather, it would rightly have been said to them: “Although this is whole and true in you, it would nevertheless benefit you nothing unless you came to Christ’s grace.”

If, then, something divine can be found and rightly approved even among gentiles, although their salvation must still be granted by Christ, we ought not to be so disturbed—even if heretics are worse—that we wish to correct what in them belongs to their evil while refusing to acknowledge what in them belongs to Christ’s good.

## CHAPTER CCXXVI

### That those who wish to excuse themselves by Cyprian’s charity are condemned; from the seventh book *On Baptism*.

The Catholic Church as a whole more truly judged that heretics or schismatics who had already received Christ’s baptism where they came from should be admitted into Catholic communion with that baptism, after being corrected from their error and rooted and grounded in charity. Thus, with regard to the sacrament of baptism, what was lacking is not added; rather, what was present becomes beneficial.

Blessed Cyprian indeed says: “When the body that is corruptible no longer burdens the soul, and earthly habitation no longer weighs down the understanding occupied with many thoughts, he serenely perceives the truth that he merited to attain through charity” [Alternate text: “And blessed Cyprian indeed: ‘Now, when the corruptible body no longer burdens the soul, nor earthly habitation weighs down the understanding occupied with many thoughts, he perceives more serenely the truth that he merited to attain through charity.’”].

May he therefore assist us by his prayers while we labor in the mortality of this flesh, as though in a cloud of darkness, so that, with the Lord’s gift, we may imitate his good qualities as far as we can.

But if he thought differently in some matter and persuaded certain brothers and fellow bishops of it—something which he now sees, with the One whom he loved revealing it, while we are far below his merits—then, nevertheless, following in our weakness the authority of the Catholic Church, of which he himself is an outstanding and beloved member, we set forth the matter against heretics and schismatics. They have been cut off from the unity that he maintained, withered away from the charity in which he flourished, and fallen from the humility in which he stood. He condemns and rejects them all the more because he knows that they seek to scrutinize what he wrote in order to lie in wait for him, while refusing to imitate what he did for the sake of peace.

So too those who call themselves Christian Nazarenes and circumcise their flesh in the Jewish manner—heretics by birth, deriving from that error from which Peter was recalled by Paul—still persist in it to this day.

Therefore, just as those people, after Peter had been crowned with the glory of martyrdom as chief among the apostles, remained cut off from the Church in their perversity, so these people, after Cyprian had been received into the lot of the saints through the abundance of his charity and the glory of his suffering, acknowledge themselves exiles from unity, and, on the basis of their accusations, set a citizen of unity against the homeland of unity.

## CHAPTER CCXXVII

### That, just as among the worst Catholics who have been corrected baptism does not begin to be present where it was lacking, but to benefit where it was present, so it is also among heretics; from the same seventh book *On Baptism*.

Here our Lord God shows us, through the peaceful bishop Cyprian and those who agreed with him, how greatly Catholic unity must be loved: in what they thought differently, they tolerated those who held another opinion until God should reveal that matter also, rather than separating themselves from them through wicked schism.

Here the mouths of the Donatists are entirely closed, even if we say nothing about the Maximianists. For if the wicked contaminate the good within unity, Cyprian himself found no Church with which he could associate. But if the wicked do not stain the good within unity, the sacrilegious Donatist has no cause for separation.

Now many others who perform the works of the flesh—works such that those who do them will not possess the kingdom of God—both possess and give baptism. Heretics, too, possess and give it; they are numbered among those works, and because they did not lose it by departing, they were able to give it by remaining. Yet such people give it to such people as fruitlessly and uselessly as those other fathers of theirs, since they will not possess the kingdom of God.

And just as, when those people are corrected, baptism does not begin to be present where it was lacking, but to benefit where it was present, so it is also with heretics. Therefore Cyprian and those who thought with him could not prescribe against the Catholic Church, which they did not wish to cut off.

We are not alarmed that they thought differently, because together with them we venerate Peter. We rejoice that they did not withdraw from unity, because together with them we are built upon the Rock.

## CHAPTER CCXXVIII

### What the outer darkness is; from the book *On the Grace of the New Testament*, addressed to Honoratus.

With reverent fear, therefore, which endures forever and ever, let every descendant of Israel fear God. Let them fear the one whom they love—not by setting their minds on lofty things, but by associating with the lowly—and let them work out their own salvation with fear and trembling [variant: “by working”]. For it is God who works in them both the willing and the working, according to his good will. This is the righteousness of God; this is what God gives to a human being when he justifies the ungodly. The proud Jews, ignorant of this righteousness of God and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to the righteousness of God.

By this pride they are cast down so that the humble wild olive may be grafted in; and they will go into the outer darkness, about which you asked, although many come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. For at present they are in the external darkness, from which correction must not be despaired of; but if they despise correction, they will go into the outer darkness where there will be no opportunity for correction. For God is light, and there are no darknesses in him at all—but this is the light of the heart, not of the eyes that are in the flesh, nor altogether such as the appearance of this visible light is imagined to be, although there too there is seeing, but in a very different and utterly dissimilar way. For what sort of light is love itself? Who could explain it in words? What example drawn from things accessible to the bodily senses could demonstrate it?

Or perhaps love is not light? Hear the apostle John. He himself said what I have just recalled: “God is light, and there are no darknesses in him”; and again he says, “God is love.” Therefore, if God is light and God is love, love itself is assuredly the light that is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. He also says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now.”

These are the darknesses into which the devil and his angels advanced through their great pride. For love is not jealous and is not puffed up; it is not jealous because it is not puffed up. For where inflation comes first, jealousy immediately follows, since pride is the mother of envy. The devil and his angels, therefore, turned away from the light and warmth of love and advancing too far into pride and envy, became torpid as though in icy hardness; and for this reason, figuratively speaking, they are placed in the north.

Hence, when the devil lay upon the human race, the future grace of the Savior is spoken of in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its fragrances flow.” Rise, you who fell, who lie upon those subject to you, who press down those whom you possess; rise, so that those whose souls you have bent down by pressing upon them may be lifted up when relieved of your burden. “And come, south wind,” he says, invoking the spirit of grace, blowing from the south as though from a warm and luminous quarter, “and let the fragrances flow.”

Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ in every place.” For this reason it is also said in a certain psalm: “Turn again our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south”—that is, the captivity in which they were held under the devil as under the north wind, where, as iniquity abounded, they had grown cold and had in a certain sense frozen. For this reason the Gospel also says: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold.”

But when the south wind blows, the ice melts and torrents flow—that is, when sins have been forgiven, peoples hasten to Christ in love. Hence it is also written elsewhere: “As ice in fair weather, so your sins will be dissolved.”

Therefore a rational creature, whether in an angelic spirit or in a human soul, was made in such a way that it cannot itself be the good by which it becomes blessed. But if its mutability turns toward the immutable good, it becomes blessed; if it turns away, it is wretched. Its turning away is its vice, and its turning toward the good is its virtue.

Nature, then, is not evil, because the creature is a spirit of rational life, even when deprived of the good by participation in which it is blessed. That is, even when vicious, it is better than the body that is highest among bodies—namely, this light perceived by the eyes of the flesh, since that too is a body. Every incorporeal nature is superior to any body, not by bulk—for bulk belongs only to bodies—but by a certain power by which it surpasses every image that the mind revolves after drawing it from bodily senses.

Yet just as among bodies those that are lower—such as earth and water, and air itself—become better through participation in what is better, when they are illuminated by light and invigorated by warmth, so incorporeal rational creatures become better through participation in the Creator himself when they cleave to him in the purest and holiest love. If they are entirely deprived of this, they will grow dark and, in a certain sense, harden.

Accordingly, unbelieving human beings are darkness; when they turn to God through faith, they become light after a certain preliminary illumination. If, by progressing in this, they pass from faith to sight, so that they become worthy to behold what they believe—just as so great a good can be beheld—they will receive the perfect image of God. To such people the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

The devil and his angels, however, are the outer darkness for unbelieving human beings. They have turned away still farther from that love and advanced into their own deed and obstinacy. Since at the final judgment Christ will say to those whom he distinguishes at his left hand, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” he says that these wicked spirits, together with those who are to be joined and condemned with them, will go into the outer darkness—that is, into the punitive fellowship of the devil and his angels.

The opposite of this punishment is what is said to the good servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Thus, to the extent that the outer darkness is outer, the inner light is inner.

These things must not be imagined through intervals of space by some empty fantasy. Spatial regions are occupied only by bodily masses [variant: “by the mass of a body”]. This is not the spirit of life; it is not the rational soul; still less is it God, the most benevolent Creator and most just Ruler of all. These things are said to draw near or become distant, to enter or go out, according to wills and affections.

But because they delight in evil works—that is, in works of darkness—and because punishment that torments will follow, the Lord, when he says “the outer darkness,” adds also: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” He does this so that such people may not foolishly imagine that, in that punishment too, they will enjoy pleasures like those in which the wicked here delight when they grow dark through unbelief and injustice.

For because they willingly and unjustly make use of good things, they will justly be tormented against their will by evil things. Thus the outer darkness may also be understood as bodily punishments. The body is external to the soul; accordingly, the soul’s evils—by which the mind, turned away from the light of love, delights in sins—are the outer darkness. The body’s evils, however, by which it will be tormented eternally to the end, are also the outer darkness. These alone are feared by those who are still held by slavish fear.

For if they were allowed to continue forever, without punishment, to roll and entangle themselves in those outer things that consist in sins, they would certainly never wish to draw near to God, to be illuminated, and to cleave to him through love, where there is a reverent fear enduring forever and ever. This fear does not torment; rather, it makes the soul cling more tenaciously to that good which, if it abandons it, will fall.

## CHAPTER CCXXIX  
### What are the breadth, length, height, and depth mentioned by the Apostle; from the book *On the Grace of the New Testament*

Rightly, therefore, the hearts of those who are filled will live forever and ever. For Christ is the life who dwells in their hearts—meanwhile through faith, and afterward through sight. For now they see “through a mirror, in an enigma,” but then “face to face.”

Accordingly, love is now exercised in good works of affection, stretching itself out in every direction as far as it can to provide assistance; and this is the breadth. Now it endures adversity with patience and perseveres in what it has held truthfully; and this is the length. It does all this in order to obtain the eternal life promised to it on high; and this is the height.

This love, however, arises from what is hidden, where we have been founded and rooted, so to speak—where the reasons for God’s will are not investigated, by whose grace we have been saved, not from works of righteousness that we ourselves have done, but according to his mercy.

For he brought us forth willingly by the word of truth; and this will of his lies hidden. Fearing, in a certain sense, the depth of this secret, the Apostle cries: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” This is the depth.

“Height” is a common term for what is high and what is deep. When it is said of what is high, the eminence of sublimity is commended; when it is said of what is deep, the difficulty of investigation and knowledge is meant. Hence it is also said to God: “How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.” And again: “Your judgments are like a great abyss.”

This, then, is the passage of the Apostle that you placed among the matters to be investigated: “For this reason,” he says, “I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, so that, rooted and founded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God.”

Pay careful attention to everything. “For this reason,” he says, “I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” You ask, “For what reason?” He had said above: “For this reason I ask that you not grow weak in my tribulations for you.” Thus he wishes them not to grow weak in the tribulations that he was enduring for their sake, and for this reason he bowed his knees before the Father.

He then continues and says what he wishes them not to grow weak for: “That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit.” These are the riches of which he says: “O the depth of riches!” For they have hidden causes; before any merits preceded, what do we have that we did not receive?

Then he continues and adds what he desires: “That Christ,” he says, “may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person.” This is the life of hearts by which we live forever and ever, from the beginning of faith to the end of sight: “so that,” he says, “rooted and founded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints.”

This is the fellowship of a certain divine and heavenly commonwealth. Here the poor are filled—not seeking their own interests, but those of Jesus Christ; that is, not pursuing private advantages, but attending to the common good, where the salvation of all is concerned. For concerning the bread with which such people are filled, the Apostle says in one place: “Because we, though many, are one bread and one body.”

What, then, are they to comprehend? “What is,” he says, “the breadth”—as I have already said, in good works by which goodwill is extended as far as loving one’s enemies; “and the length,” so that hardships may be endured patiently for the sake of this breadth; “and the height,” so that for these things one may hope for the eternal reward that is above, rather than for anything changing and temporal; “and the depth,” from which the free grace of God arises according to the secret and hidden character of his will.

For there we have been rooted; there we have been founded—rooted with reference to cultivation, founded with reference to building. Since this does not come from a human being, the same Apostle says elsewhere: “You are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building.”

All this, then, while in our present pilgrimage faith works through love, will in the age to come be perfected and complete love, without any endurance of evils. It will not believe by faith what it does not see, nor desire through hope what it does not possess; rather, it will contemplate eternally the unchangeable appearance of truth. Its peaceful work without end will be to praise what it loves and to love what it praises.

After this he proceeds to say: “And to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God.”

In this mystery the figure of the cross is displayed. Since Christ died because he willed to die, he died in the manner he willed. Therefore he did not choose such a kind of death without reason, unless it was also so that in it he might become the teacher of breadth, length, height, and depth.

The breadth is represented by the wood fixed transversely above; this pertains to good works, because there the hands are extended. The length is represented by what is visible from that wood down to the earth; for there, in a certain sense, one stands—that is, persists and perseveres—which is attributed to patience.

The height is represented by the part of the wood that remains above the transverse beam, toward the head of the crucified one; for this is the expectation of heavenly things on the part of those who hope well.

But the part of the wood that is not seen, fixed and hidden, from which the whole structure rises, signifies the depth of free grace. In investigating this, the understanding of many is worn down as they attempt to explore it, until at last it is said to them: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?”

The hearts, therefore, of the poor who are filled will live forever and ever—that is, the hearts of those who burn with humble love, who do not seek their own interests but rejoice in the fellowship of the saints.

## CHAPTER CCXXX  
### Whether parents harm baptized infants when they try to heal them through sacrifices to demons, and, if they do not harm them, how the faith of parents benefits them when they are baptized, since the parents’ unbelief cannot harm them

You ask me whether parents harm their baptized infants when they try to heal them through sacrifices to demons; and, if they do not harm them, how the faith of the parents benefits them when they are baptized, since the parents’ faithlessness cannot harm them.

Here I answer that the power of that sacrament—namely, saving baptism—is so great within the holy structure of the body of Christ that one who has once been generated through another’s carnal pleasure, once regenerated through another’s spiritual will, can thereafter not be bound by the chain of another’s iniquity, since he gives it no consent by his own will.

“For the soul of the father is mine,” he says, “and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it shall die.” The infant himself does not sin when his parents, or anyone else, quite unknown to him, bring upon him the sacrileges of demons.

But for this reason he drew from Adam what the grace of that sacrament was to remove: he was not yet a separately living soul—that is, another soul concerning which it could be said, “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine.”

Once, therefore, a human being has become different in himself from the one who generated him, he is not held guilty by another’s sin without his own consent. His origin carried guilt because, when what he inherited was committed, he was one with the person from whom he inherited it.

But one person does not inherit from another when each is living his own individual life; for there is already a basis for saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die.”

In order that the infant may be regenerated through the service of another’s will, when he is offered for consecration, one Spirit accomplishes this—the Spirit from whom the one offered is regenerated. For it is not written, “Unless one has been reborn from the will of parents,” or “from the faith of those who offer or minister,” but: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit.”

Water, therefore, supplying outwardly the sacrament of grace, and the Spirit, working inwardly the benefit of grace—releasing the bond of guilt and reconciling the good of nature—regenerate in the one Christ the person generated from the one Adam.

Thus the regenerating Spirit in the adults who offer the infant, and in the infant who is offered and reborn, is common to them. Therefore, through the fellowship of one and the same Spirit, the will of those who offer benefits the infant who is offered.

But when adults sin against an infant, offering him and attempting to bind him with the sacrilegious bonds of demons, the soul of both is not common, so that they can also share a common guilt. Guilt is not communicated through another’s will in the same way that grace is communicated through the unity of the Holy Spirit.

For the one Holy Spirit can be in this person and in that person, even if they do not know one another, by whom the grace common to both is present. But the human spirit cannot belong both to this person and to that person, so that, when one sins and the other does not sin, there is nevertheless a common guilt.

Accordingly, an infant once generated from the flesh of his parents [variant: *generantis*, “of one begetting”] can be regenerated by the Spirit of God, so that the bond contracted from them may be released. But one who has once been regenerated by the Spirit of God cannot be regenerated from the flesh of his parents so that the bond once released may be contracted again.

Therefore, once received, the grace of Christ is not lost by the infant except through his own impiety, if, with advancing age, he becomes so wicked. Then he will also begin to have sins of his own, which are not removed by regeneration but healed by another remedy.

Nevertheless, parents, or whatever adults attempt to bind baptized children or any baptized infants by the sacrilege of demons, are rightly called spiritual murderers. In those infants they do not indeed carry out a killing, but, as far as lies within them, they become killers.

It is rightly said to them, when they are restrained from this crime: “Do not kill your children.” For the Apostle says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” This is not because the Spirit can be extinguished, but those who act in such a way as to wish him extinguished are deservedly called, so far as it lies within them, his extinguishers.

If sacraments did not possess a certain likeness to the realities of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness the names of the realities themselves are often applied to the sacraments.

Thus, just as, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood, so the sacrament of faith is faith.

To believe is nothing other than to have faith. Accordingly, when it is answered that an infant believes who does not yet possess the disposition of faith, the answer means that he has faith because of the sacrament of faith, and that he turns toward God because of the sacrament of conversion; for the answer itself belongs to the celebration of the sacrament.

Thus concerning baptism itself the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death.” He does not say, “We signified a burial,” but says plainly, “We were buried.” The sacrament of so great a reality, therefore, he named by the term of that same reality.

Thus, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of that faith already makes him faithful. For just as the answer “to believe” is given, so he is also called faithful—not by assenting to the reality with his own mind, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.

When the person begins to understand, he will not repeat that sacrament; rather, he will understand it and will conform his will harmoniously to its truth.

As long as he cannot do this, the sacrament will be effective for his protection against hostile powers. It will be so effective that, if he departs from this life before attaining the use of reason, through that sacrament, with the love of the Church commending him, he will be delivered by Christian assistance from the condemnation that entered the world through one human being.

Whoever does not believe this and thinks it impossible is certainly an unbeliever, even if he possesses the sacrament of faith. Far better is the infant who, although he does not yet have faith in his thoughts, nevertheless does not oppose the sacrament he beneficially receives with the obstacle of an opposing thought.

## CHAPTER CCXXXI  
### Whether the apostles were baptized; from the letter to Seleuciana

I do not know what kind of heart a person has who says that the apostles were baptized but denies that Peter was baptized.

When it is said that Peter did penance, care must be taken lest it be thought that he did so in the manner of those who in the Church are properly called penitents. Who could tolerate our thinking that the first of the apostles should be numbered among such penitents?

He repented of having denied Christ, as his tears show; for it is written: “Because he wept bitterly.” For they had not yet been strengthened by the Lord’s resurrection, nor by that coming of the Holy Spirit which appeared on the day of Pentecost, nor by that inspiration which the Lord manifested after he rose from the dead, when he breathed upon their faces and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore it can rightly be said that, when Peter denied the Lord, the apostles had not yet been baptized—not with water, but with the Holy Spirit. He said this to them after he had risen and had lived among them: “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, which you are also going to receive not many days from now.”

Some manuscripts have: “But you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” Whether it is said, “You will be baptized,” or, “You will begin to be baptized,” makes no difference to the matter.

For manuscripts in which *Baptizaberis* (“you will be baptized,” singular) or *Incipietis baptizari* (“you will begin to be baptized”) is found are corrupt; this is very easily demonstrated from the Greek manuscripts.

But if we say that they were not baptized with water, we must fear that we may be seriously mistaken about them and give human beings authority to despise baptism. Apostolic discipline commends baptism as something not to be despised to such an extent that Cornelius the centurion and those who were with him, even after they had received the Holy Spirit, were baptized.

In the same way, for the ancient righteous, if they were not circumcised, it was not counted as sin; but after God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised, failure to do so became a grave sin.

So too, after the Lord Christ gave his Church, in place of circumcision of the flesh, holy baptism as the sacrament of the New Testament, and said most clearly, “If someone has not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” we must no longer ask when each person was baptized. Rather, whenever we read that people belong to the body of Christ, which is the Church, we must understand them to be baptized and to belong to the kingdom of heaven—unless perhaps they were overtaken by the urgency of martyrdom and were killed for refusing to deny Christ before they were baptized; to them martyrdom itself was reckoned in place of baptism.

But can we say this of the apostles, who had so ample a period in which to be baptized that they even baptized others?

Not everything that happened, however, is found written down; nevertheless, what happened is proved by other evidence. It is written when the Apostle Paul was baptized, but it is not written when the other apostles were baptized. Nevertheless, we too must understand that they were baptized, just as it is written when the communities of the churches in Jerusalem and Samaria were baptized.

When the other communities of the nations to whom the apostles sent letters were baptized, this is certainly not written; yet we have no doubt that they too were baptized, because of the Lord’s saying: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Two things are written about the Lord: that he baptized more people than John, and that he himself did not baptize, but his disciples did. This enables us to understand that he did indeed baptize through the presence of his majesty, though he did not baptize with his own hands. The sacrament of baptism belonged to him; the ministry of baptizing belonged to the disciples.

Thus, when John the evangelist says in his Gospel, “After this Jesus and his disciples went into the land of Judea, and there he remained with them and baptized,” shortly afterward, speaking of him, he says: “When Jesus therefore learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John”—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples—“he left the land of Judea and went again into Galilee.”

At that time, therefore, when he left Jerusalem with his disciples and went into Judea, remaining there with them, he baptized not by himself but through his disciples. We understand that they had already been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some think, or, what is more credible, with Christ’s baptism.

For he would not have shrunk from the ministry of baptizing in order to have baptized servants through whom he could baptize others, since he did not shrink from that memorable ministry of humility when he washed their feet. When Peter asked him to wash not only his feet but also his hands and head, he answered: “The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet; rather, he is wholly clean.” From this it is understood that Peter had already been baptized.

## CHAPTER CCXXXII  
### That it is beneficial for the proud or those who sin secretly to fall into some open and manifest sin; from Book XIV of *The City of God*

In the case of an obvious and open sin, where something has been done that God had forbidden, the devil would not have captured the human being [variant: “deceived”] unless that person had already begun to please himself.

For this reason, the statement “You will be like gods” was also pleasing: they could have become better by cleaving through obedience to the highest and true Principle, rather than by arrogantly becoming their own principle. Created gods are gods not through their own truth but through participation in the true God.

By desiring more, the human being became less. While choosing to be sufficient for himself, he fell away from the one who truly suffices for him.

That evil, therefore, by which a human being, pleasing himself as though he too were light, turns away from the light that, if it pleased him, would also make him light—that evil, I say, came first in secret, so that this evil that has now been perpetrated openly might follow.

For it is true what is written: “Before a fall the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.” The fall that occurs secretly plainly precedes the fall that is manifest, while the former is not thought to be a fall.

Who considers exaltation a fall, when already there is in it the defect by which the exalted person has been abandoned? Yet who does not see a fall when there is an evident and indisputable transgression of a commandment?

For this reason God prohibited that act; once it had been committed, no imagined claim of righteousness could defend it. Therefore I dare to say that it is beneficial for the proud to fall into some open and manifest sin, so that those who had fallen by pleasing themselves may come to displease themselves.

Peter’s self-displeasure when he wept was healthier than his self-pleasure when he presumed. The sacred psalm says this too: “Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek your name, O Lord”—that is, that you may please them when they seek your name, since they had pleased themselves by seeking their own.

But there is a worse and more condemnable pride: that by which even in manifest sins a refuge of excuse is sought, as with those first human beings. One of them said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate”; and the other said: “The woman whom you gave to be with me—she gave me from the tree, and I ate.” Nowhere here is there a request for pardon; nowhere an appeal for healing.

## CHAPTER CCXXXIII  
### On the Trinity, from the letter to Consentius
The composition of carnal thought and its vain fabrication—once true reason begins to undermine it—we immediately hasten to shatter within us (with the help and illumination of him who does not wish to dwell in our hearts together with such idols) and to drive these things, as it were, out of our faith, so that we do not permit even a particle of such fantasies to remain there. Therefore, unless faith had preceded in our hearts and clothed us with piety—through the reasoning of an argument by which, admonished from without and with the truth shining inwardly, we perceive these things to be false—would we not hear the things that are true to no purpose? And so, since faith performed what belonged to it, the reasoning that followed discovered something of what it was seeking. Thus true reason, by which we understand what we believe, and faith itself in things not yet understood, are without doubt to be preferred to false reasoning. For it is better, although not yet seen, to believe what is true than to suppose that you see as true what is false. Faith has, in fact, eyes of its own, by which it somehow sees that what it does not yet see is true, and by which it most certainly sees that it does not yet see what it believes. Moreover, one who already understands by true reason what he had previously only believed is plainly to be preferred to one who still desires to understand what he believes.

[Col. 0898A] But if he does not even desire this, and thinks that things which ought to be understood are merely to be believed, he does not know what purpose faith serves. For pious faith does not wish to exist without hope and without love. Thus a faithful person ought to believe what he does not yet see in such a way that he both hopes for and loves the vision.

With respect to visible things of the past, which have passed away in time, there is faith alone, since they are not hoped for as still to be seen, but are believed as having occurred and been completed. Such is the fact that Christ died once for our sins and rose again, and no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him. Things that do not yet exist but are future—for example, the resurrection of our spiritual bodies—are believed in such a way that they are also hoped for as things to be seen, but they cannot now be displayed in any way.

Things that exist in such a manner that they neither pass away nor are destined to be future, but remain eternal, are partly invisible, such as justice and wisdom, and partly visible, such as Christ’s already immortal body. Invisible things, however, are seen when understood; consequently, they too are seen in a manner appropriate to them, and when seen they are far more certain than those things touched by the bodily senses. They are called invisible, therefore, because they cannot in any way be seen by these mortal eyes.

Those permanent things that are visible can, if they are displayed, also be perceived by these mortal eyes, just as the Lord displayed himself to the disciples after his resurrection, and also afterward to the apostle Paul and to the deacon Stephen. Accordingly, we believe these permanent visible things in such a way that, even if they are not displayed, we hope that one day we shall see them. Nor should we attempt to comprehend them by reasoning and understanding except insofar as, because they are visible, we may think of them more distinctly as different from invisible things. And when we imagine by thought what they are like, we know well enough that they are not known to us.

For I can think of Antioch, which I do not know, but not in the same way as I think of Carthage, which I do know: my thought fabricates an image of the former, while it recalls the latter. Nevertheless, I have no doubt either about what I believed concerning the former on the testimony of many witnesses or about what I believed concerning the latter from my own sight.

Justice, however, wisdom, and whatever is of this kind, we do not imagine in one way and contemplate in another. Rather, we perceive these invisible things, once understood by the simple attention of mind and reason, without any bodily forms or masses, without any outlines or shapes of limbs, without any local boundaries or dimensions or limitless spaces. We also perceive the very light by which we distinguish all these things—a light in which it becomes sufficiently clear to us what we believe without knowing, what we retain as known, what bodily form we remember, what we fabricate in thought, what the bodily senses reach, what the mind imagines as resembling a body, and what intelligence contemplates as certain and utterly unlike all bodies.

[Col. 0898D] This light, in which all these things are judged, is not diffused in every direction through local spaces, nor does it illuminate our mind with something like the visible radiance of the sun or of any bodily light. Rather, it shines invisibly, ineffably, and yet intelligibly. It is as certain to us as it makes certain for us the things that we perceive according to it.

Since, then, there are three kinds of things that are seen, the first is bodily: this heaven and this earth, and whatever bodily sense perceives and touches in them. The second is like bodily things: those things that, conceived in the spirit, we imagine—whether remembered or forgotten—and contemplate as if they were bodies. Such are also the visions that, whether in dreams or in some mental ecstasy, are presented to us with something like local dimensions. The third is distinct from both: it is neither a body nor does it possess any likeness to a body, as is wisdom, which is perceived when understood by the mind, and in whose light all these things are judged truly.

[26] In which of these kinds should we believe the Trinity we wish to know to exist? Surely either in one of them or in none. If in one, then certainly in that which is superior to the other two, as wisdom is. But if its gift is in us, and is less than that supreme and unchangeable wisdom called the wisdom of God, I think that we ought not to conceive the giver as inferior to his gift.

If some splendor of that wisdom is in us, which is called our wisdom, however much of it we can grasp “through a mirror and in an enigma,” we must distinguish it from all bodies and from all likenesses of bodies. But if the Trinity is to be thought to exist in none of these kinds, and is invisible in such a way that it is not even seen by the mind, we ought all the more not to hold the opinion that it resembles bodily things or images of bodily things.

For it surpasses bodies not by the beauty of mass or by size, but by the dissimilarity and disparity of its nature. And if it is distinct from comparison with the good qualities of our mind—such as wisdom, justice, love, chastity, and other things of this kind, which we certainly do not measure by bodily mass, nor represent in thought as though they had bodily forms, but, when we understand them rightly, behold in the light of the mind without any corporeality or likeness of corporeality—how much more distinct is it from comparison with all bodily qualities and quantities?

The Apostle nevertheless testifies that it is not wholly foreign to our understanding when he says: “For his invisible things, from the foundation of the world, are clearly perceived and understood through the things that have been made, and also his eternal power and divinity.” Since this same Trinity made both body and soul, it is without doubt superior to both.

The soul, especially the human soul, rational and intellectual, which was made in his image, may perhaps be raised, with his help, toward understanding its creator, provided that it does not overcome our thoughts and understandings but that, by mind and understanding, we are able to apprehend its chief possession—that is, the mind and understanding itself. But if it fails within itself and succumbs to itself, let it be content with pious faith while it is a pilgrim away from the Lord, until what was promised to humanity comes to pass, through him who is able, as the Apostle says, to do above what we ask and understand.

It remains, therefore, that we believe the Trinity to be of one substance, in such a way that the essence itself is nothing other than the Trinity itself. However far we may progress in this life toward seeing it, what we shall see will be “through a mirror and in an enigma.” When we have begun to possess the spiritual body promised in the resurrection, whether we see it with the mind or, in a wondrous manner—for the grace of the spiritual body is ineffable—even with the body, we shall nevertheless see it according to our capacity, not through intervals of place, nor as smaller in one part and greater in another, since it is not a body and is wholly present everywhere.

As for what you wrote in your letter—that it seemed to you, or rather that it had seemed to you, that nothing living according to substance exists in justice, and that for this reason you could not yet conceive God, that is, a living nature, as resembling justice, because, as you say, justice does not live in itself but in us, or rather we live according to it, while justice itself does not live in itself at all—consider this, so that you may answer yourself: whether it can rightly be said that the very life by which everything lives that we not falsely call living does not itself live.

I think it would seem absurd to you that one should live by means of life while life itself did not live. But if life itself especially lives, by which everything that lives lives, recall, I beg you, whom divine Scripture calls dead souls. You will certainly find that they are unjust, impious, and unbelieving. For although the bodies of the impious live through them—of those concerning whom it is said that “the dead bury their dead”—and although unjust souls are thereby understood not to be without some kind of life, since their bodies could not otherwise live through them unless they possessed some sort of life, from which souls are wholly unable to be deprived and on account of which they are rightly called immortal, nevertheless they are called dead after losing justice for no other reason than that, although the life of souls is immortal in the limited sense in which living beings live, justice is a truer and greater life: as it were, the life of lives. When souls are in bodies, the bodies themselves are alive, although they cannot live by themselves.

Therefore, if souls cannot help but live to some degree even in themselves, since bodies live through them and die when abandoned by them, how much more must true justice be understood to live already in itself, since souls live through it in such a way that, when it is lost, they are called dead, although they do not cease to live with whatever limited life they possess?

That justice which lives in itself is undoubtedly God, and it lives unchangeably. As this life, although it exists in itself, also becomes life for us when we in some measure become participants in it, so, although it exists as justice in itself, it also becomes justice for us when, by cleaving to it, we live justly. And we are just in greater or lesser measure according as we cleave to it more or less.

Accordingly, it is written concerning the only-begotten Son of God, who is certainly the Father’s wisdom and justice and who always exists as such in himself, that he was made for us by God “wisdom, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption,” so that, as it is written, “the one who glories, let him glory in the Lord.”

You yourself saw this, indeed, when you added and said: “Unless perhaps only that justice which is God, and not human equity, is being asserted as justice.” It is plainly so: that supreme God is true justice, or that true God is supreme justice. To hunger and thirst for it is our justice in this pilgrimage, and to be filled with it afterward is our complete justice in eternity.

Let us not, then, conceive God as resembling our justice; rather, let us conceive ourselves as becoming more like God in proportion as we are able to become more just through participation in him. If, therefore, we must beware of thinking that God resembles our justice—for the light that illuminates is incomparably superior to the light that is illuminated—how much more must we beware of believing him to be inferior to, and in some way less splendid than, our justice?

What else is justice, when it is in us—or any virtue by which one lives rightly and wisely—than the beauty of the inner person? And certainly it is according to this beauty, more than according to the body, that we were made in the image of God.

Hence we are told: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.”

If, therefore, we say—or know, or desire—that the mind is beautiful not in mass, nor in parts separated by their locations as bodies are either perceived or conceived, but in an intelligible virtue such as justice, and if according to this beauty we are transformed into the image of God, then the beauty of God himself, who transformed and transforms us into his image, must certainly not be imagined in any bodily mass. For this reason he must be believed to be incomparably more beautiful to the minds of the just inasmuch as he is incomparably more just.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIV. 27. On the Unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are first in the Trinity

Those who have said that our Lord Jesus Christ is not God, or is not true God, or is not one and the only God with the Father, or is not truly immortal [or is not immortal], have been refuted by the clearest testimonies of the divine writings and by their harmonious voice. Among these are the following: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

For it is clear that we understand the Word of God to be the only Son of God, concerning whom John later says: “And the Word was made flesh,” referring to his birth through the incarnation, which took place in time from a Virgin. In the statement “And the Word was God,” he declares not only that he is God but also that he is of the same substance as the Father, because, after saying “And the Word was God,” he adds: “He was in the beginning with God.”

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For he does not say “all things” except of things that were made—that is, of the whole creation. Hence it plainly appears that he himself was not made through whom all things were made. And if he was not made, he is not a creature; but if he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance that is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God.

And if the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a made substance. If he is a made substance, then all things were not made through him; but if all things were made through him, then he is of one and the same substance with the Father.

Therefore he is not only God but true God. The same John says this most plainly in his Epistle: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.”

[Col. 0902A] From this it is also consequently understood that the apostle Paul did not speak only of the Father when he said, “who alone has immortality,” but of the one and only God, which is the Trinity. For eternal life itself is not mortal according to any mutability. Therefore, because the Son of God is eternal life, he too is understood with the Father where it is said: “He alone has immortality” [“who alone has immortality”]. We too, having become participants in that eternal life, are made immortal according to our measure. But the eternal life itself, of which we become participants, is one thing, and we, who live forever through participation in it, are another.

For even if he had said: “Whom the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will display at his proper times, who alone has immortality,” the Son should not for that reason be understood as separated from him. For when the Son himself speaks elsewhere in the voice of Wisdom—for he himself is the wisdom of God—and says, “I alone traversed the circuit of heaven,” he did not separate the Father from himself. How much less, then, is it necessary to understand as spoken only of the Father, to the exclusion of the Son, the statement “He alone has immortality”?

It is said in this manner: “That you keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will display at his proper times, who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever.”

In these words neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit is expressly named, but rather “the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords,” who is the one, only, and true God—the Trinity.

Unless perhaps what follows disturbs this interpretation, since he said: “Whom no human being has seen or can see.” Yet this too is understood to pertain to Christ according to his divinity, which the Jews did not see, although they saw and crucified his flesh. Divinity cannot in any way be seen by human sight, but it is seen by that sight by which those who see are no longer human beings but something beyond human beings.

Thus the one God, the Trinity, is rightly understood as the blessed and only powerful one who displays the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ at his proper times. For “he alone has immortality” is said in the same sense as “who alone does wondrous things.”

I should like to know of whom they understand the statement to have been made. If of the Father alone, how then is it true that the Son himself says: “Whatever things the Father does, these the Son also does likewise”? Is anything more wondrous among wondrous things than to raise and give life to the dead? Yet the same Son says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wishes.”

How, then, does the Father alone perform wondrous things, when these words permit us to understand neither the Father alone nor the Son alone, but plainly the one, true, and only God—that is, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

[Col. 0903A] Likewise, when the same apostle says: “For us there is one Father, God, from whom are all things, and we are in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him,” who could doubt that he is speaking of all created things, just as blessed John says: “All things were made through him”?

I therefore ask of whom he speaks elsewhere when he says: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever” [amen]. If he means the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that individual functions are assigned to the individual persons—“from him,” from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit [“from him,” that is, from the Father; “through him,” that is, through the Son; “in him,” that is, through the Holy Spirit]—it is evident that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, since he concludes in the singular: “To him be glory for ever and ever.”

For when he began this thought, he did not say: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of the Father,” or “of the Son,” or “of the Holy Spirit,” but “of the wisdom and knowledge of God.” “How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.”

But if they wish this to be understood of the Father alone, how then are all things through the Father, as it is said here, and all things through the Son, as in the Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says, “and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” and as in John’s Gospel: “All things were made through him”?

For if some things are through the Father and others through the Son, then not all things are through the Father, nor all things through the Son. But if all things are through the Father and all things are through the Son, then the same things are through the Father as through the Son. The Son is therefore equal to the Father, and the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. For if the Father made even one thing—the Son—which the Son himself did not make, then all things were not made through the Son; but all things were made through the Son.

He himself, therefore, was not made, so that together with the Father he might make all things that were made.

Nor was the Apostle silent about the Word himself; rather, he said most plainly: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized”—here expressly calling the Father God, just as elsewhere: “The head of Christ is God.”

Likewise, testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit have been collected, by which those before us who discussed these matters made abundant use, because the Holy Spirit too is God and not a creature. If he is not a creature, he is not merely a god—for human beings too have been called gods—but he is also true God.

Therefore he is wholly equal to the Father and the Son, consubstantial and coeternal in the unity of the Trinity. This is especially clear in the passage where it is evident that the Holy Spirit is not a creature: we are commanded not to serve the creature but the Creator—not in the manner in which we are commanded through love to serve one another, which in Greek is δουλεύειν, but in the manner in which service is rendered to God alone, which in Greek is λατρεύειν. Hence those who offer such service to images, which is due to God, are called idolaters.

According to this service it is said: “You shall worship the Lord your God and him alone shall you serve.” For this distinction is found more clearly in the Greek text; it has λατρεύσεις, “you shall serve.”

[Col. 0904A] But if we are forbidden to serve a creature with such service, since it is said, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him alone shall you serve,” and since the Apostle condemns those who “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator,” then the Holy Spirit is certainly not a creature, since all the saints offer him this kind of service. The Apostle says: “For we are the circumcision, who serve the Spirit of God,” which in Greek is λατρεύοντες, “serving.”

Many Latin manuscripts also read: “who serve the Spirit of God”; but all, or nearly all, the Greek manuscripts have this reading. In some Latin copies, however, we find not “we serve the Spirit of God,” but “we serve God by the Spirit.”

But those who err in this and refuse to yield to the weightier authority—do they also find the following passage varying among the manuscripts? “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?”

What could be more insane and sacrilegious than for anyone to dare say that the members of Christ are the temple of a lesser creature, according to their own view, than Christ? For elsewhere he says: “Your bodies are members of Christ.” If, then, what are members of Christ are a temple of the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit is not a creature. For to him whose temple we offer our body, we must necessarily owe that service which is owed to God alone, and which in Greek is called λατρεία, “worshipful service.”

Accordingly, he goes on to say: “Therefore glorify God and bear him in your body.”

### CHAPTER CCXXXV. That the only-begotten Son of God is said to be less than the Father according to the form of a servant, while in the form of God he is equal to the Father, from the same book, title 7

By these and similar testimonies of the divine Scriptures—which, as I have said, those before us used more extensively to overthrow such calumnies or errors of the heretics—the unity of our faith and the equality of the Trinity are made known.

But because many things in the holy books are said on account of the incarnation of the Word of God, which took place for the restoration of our salvation, so that the man Christ Jesus might be the mediator between God and human beings, in such a way as to signify, or even most openly demonstrate, that the Father is greater than the Son, people who examined or considered the whole sequence of the Scriptures less carefully went astray. They tried to transfer to Christ’s substance—which was eternal before the incarnation and is eternal—the things said of Christ Jesus according to his humanity.

They say that the Son is less than the Father because it is written, in the Lord’s own words: “The Father is greater than I.”

But the truth shows that, according to this mode of being, the Son is also less than himself. For how was he not also made less than himself, when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”? He did not take the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father.

If, then, he took the form of a servant without losing the form of God, and if the same only-begotten Son of God exists both in the form of a servant and in the form of God—in the form of God equal to the Father, and in the form of a servant the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—who does not understand that in the form of God he is greater even than himself, while in the form of a servant he is less even than himself?

Scripture therefore not improperly says both things: that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood with reference to the form of God, the latter with reference to the form of a servant, without any confusion. This rule for resolving the question throughout all the holy Scriptures is drawn from one chapter of the Epistle of the apostle Paul, where this distinction is commended more clearly.

He says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being.”

The Son of God is therefore equal by nature to God the Father, but less in appearance or condition. In the form of a servant, which he took, he is less than the Father; in the form of God, in which he existed even before taking this form, he is equal to the Father.

In the form of God he is the Word through whom all things were made; in the form of a servant he was made from a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law.

Accordingly, in the form of God he made the human being; in the form of a servant he was made human.
