For if the Father had made the human being without the Son, it would not have been written: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.” Therefore, because the form of God took the form of a servant, he is both God and human: both God, on account of the one who took the servant’s form, and human, on account of the human nature taken.

For neither of them was changed or transformed into the other through that assumption: neither was divinity changed into a creature so as to cease to be divinity, nor was the creature changed into divinity so as to cease to be a creature.

### CHAPTER CCXXXVI. On the subjection by which the Son is said to be subjected to the Father, from the same book.

But what the Apostle says—“When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him”—was said either to prevent anyone from supposing that Christ’s form, which was assumed from human creation, would later be changed into divinity itself—or, to express it more precisely, into the Deity, which is not a creature but the incorporeal and immutable unity of the Trinity, a nature consubstantial and coeternal with itself. Or, if anyone insists—as some have understood it—that the words “the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him” mean that this subjection will be the creature’s change and transformation into the very substance or essence of the Creator, so that what had been the substance of a creature becomes the substance of the Creator, he certainly concedes at least this point, about which there can be no doubt: that this had not yet happened when the Lord said, “The Father is greater than I.” For he said this not only before he had ascended into heaven, but even before he had suffered and risen from the dead.

But those who think that his human nature will be changed and transformed into the substance of the Deity, and that the words “Then the Son himself also will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him” mean that then the Son of Man himself, and the human nature assumed by the Word of God, will be changed into the nature of him who subjected all things to him, think that this will occur when, after the day of judgment, he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father. Accordingly, even on this view, the Father is still greater than the form of a servant, which [because] was received from the Virgin. [Col. 0905D]

And if some assert that the man Christ Jesus has already been changed into the substance of God, they certainly cannot deny that the nature of man still remained in him when, before his passion, he said, “For the Father is greater than I.” Hence there is no hesitation that this was said in the sense that the Father is greater than the form of a servant, while the Son in the form of God is equal to the Father.

Nor should anyone, when he hears the Apostle say, “When he has said that all things have been subjected to him, it is clear that it is excepted that one who subjected all things to him,” understand this of the Father in such a way as to suppose that the Father subjected all things to the Son but that the Son himself did not subject all things to him. For the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. Otherwise the Father himself did not subject all things to himself either; rather, the Son subjected them to him who handed the kingdom over to him, and who abolishes every principality, every authority, and every power. These words are spoken of the Son: “When he has handed over” (29), he says, “the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality, every authority, and every power.” For it is he who subjects all things who abolishes them.

Nor should we think that Christ will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father in such a way as to take it away from himself. For some foolish talkers have believed this as well. When it is said, “He will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father,” he himself is not separated, because together with the Father he is one God. [Col. 0906A]

But the word “until,” placed in the text, deceives those who are careless about the divine Scriptures and eager for disputes. For the text continues: “For he must reign until he has placed his enemies under his feet,” as though, once he has placed them there, he would not reign. They do not understand that this is said in the same way as: “His heart is established; he will not be moved until he sees over his enemies.” For he will not, after seeing them, then be moved.

What, then, does “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” mean? It does not mean that God the Father does not now possess the kingdom; rather, it means that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, will lead all the righteous in whom he now reigns—those who live by faith—to the vision which the same Apostle calls “face to face.” Thus it is said: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father,” as though one were saying, “When he has led believers to the contemplation of God and the Father.” [Col. 0906B]

For he says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son [and no one knows the Father except the Son], and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” The Father will be revealed by the Son when he has abolished every principality, every authority, and every power—that is, when the administration of likenesses through angelic principalities, authorities, and powers is no longer necessary.

In the person of these beings, it is not improperly understood that the Song of Songs says to the bride: “We will make for you likenesses of gold, with silver ornaments, until the king is at his couch,” that is, until Christ is in his secret place, because “our life [your life] is hidden with Christ in God.” “When Christ,” he says, “our life [your life], appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.” [Col. 0906C]

Before this happens, “we now see through a mirror in an enigma,” that is, through likenesses; then, however, “face to face.” For this contemplation is promised to us as the end of all our actions and the eternal perfection of our joys. We are children of God, and “it has not yet appeared what we shall be”; but “we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

What he said to his servant Moses—“I am who I am”; and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’”—this we shall contemplate when we see [live] forever. For he says: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” [Col. 0906D]

This will happen when the Lord comes and “brings to light the things hidden in darkness,” when the darkness of this mortality and corruption has passed away. Then will be our morning, of which it is said in the Psalm: “In the morning I shall stand before you and contemplate.”

I understand “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” as referring to this contemplation—that is, when he has led the righteous, in whom the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, now reigns through faith, to the contemplation of God and the Father. [Col. 0907A]

If I am mistaken here, let the one who understands better correct me; I see no other explanation. For we will seek nothing else when we have attained that contemplation, which is not present now, so long as our joy is in hope. “Hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience,” until “the king is at his couch.”

Then what is written will take place: “You will fill me with joy in your presence.” That joy requires nothing further, because there will be nothing further to require. The Father will be shown to us, and he will be sufficient for us. Philip rightly understood this when he said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us”; but he did not yet understand that he could say the very same thing in another way: “Lord, show us yourself, and it is enough for us.” [Col. 0907B]

To make him understand this, the Lord answered him: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” But because he wanted Philip to live by faith before he could see that reality, he continued and said: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Contemplation is the reward of faith, and by faith hearts are cleansed for that reward, as it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.” That hearts are cleansed for this contemplation is proved especially by the saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

And because this is eternal life, the Lord says in the Psalms: “I will satisfy him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.” [Col. 0907C]

Whether, therefore, we hear, “Show us the Son,” or, “Show us the Father,” it amounts to the same thing, because neither can be shown without the other. For they are one, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one.”

Indeed, because of this inseparability, sometimes one person of the Trinity alone is named—either the Father alone or the Son alone—as the one who will fill us with joy in his presence. Yet the Spirit of both, that is, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is not separated from them. This Spirit is properly called the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive; that is, those who love the world. [Col. 0907D]

For this is the fullness of our joy, beyond which there is nothing: to enjoy the Triune God, in whose image we were made.

For this reason Scripture sometimes speaks of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness. He is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son. The Father alone is likewise sufficient because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit. And the Son is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does he mean when he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, so that he may be with you forever—the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive,” that is, those who love the world? “For the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God.” [Col. 0908A]

Yet it may still appear that the words “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate [so that he may be with you forever]” were said as though the Son alone were not sufficient. But elsewhere he speaks of the Spirit as though he alone were entirely sufficient: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.”

Is the Son, then, separated from this, as though he himself did not teach all truth? Or as though the Holy Spirit fulfills what the Son was less able to teach? Let them say, then, if they please, that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Son, whom they are accustomed to call less than him. [Col. 0908B]

Or, because it was not said, “He alone,” or, “No one except him will teach you all truth,” do they therefore allow that the Son is believed to teach together with him?

The Apostle, then, separated the Son from knowledge of the things of God when he said: “Thus no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God.” From this these perverse interpreters could now say that the Son also does not know the things of God unless the Holy Spirit teaches him, as a greater teaches a lesser—although the Son himself attributed so much to the Spirit that he said: “Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you.” [Col. 0908C]

He said this not because of any inequality between the Word of God and the Holy Spirit, but because the presence of the Son of Man among them was an impediment to the coming of the one who was not lesser, since he had not emptied himself as the Son had done by taking the form of a servant. [Col. 0908D]

## CHAPTER CCXXXVII. 30 That it was beneficial for believers that Christ ascended to the Father in the form of a servant. From the same book, title 9.

It was therefore necessary that the form of a servant be removed from their eyes. While they saw it, they thought that Christ was nothing more than what they saw.

This is also the meaning of what he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.” That is: “For this reason I must go to the Father, because while you see me in this way, you judge from what you see that I am less than the Father; and, occupied with the creature and the form assumed by me, you do not understand the equality that I have with the Father.” [Col. 0909A]

This is also the meaning of: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.” Touching is like bringing knowledge to its conclusion. Therefore he did not want the focused attention of their hearts to find its end in him, so that what was seen might be regarded as the whole reality.

His ascension to the Father meant that he would be seen as equal to the Father, so that there the vision sufficient for us would reach its completion.

## CHAPTER CCXXXVIII. How the Son will hand over the kingdom to the Father. From the same book, title 10.

For the manifestation of the Trinity, certain things are said with the individual persons named, although they are not to be understood as separated from the others [separately: nevertheless they are not to be understood as separated from the others], because of the unity of that same Trinity and the one substance and Deity [divinity] of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0909B]

Our Lord Jesus Christ will therefore hand the kingdom over to God and the Father, without being separated from him or from the Holy Spirit, because he will lead believers to the contemplation of God, where there is the end of all good actions, eternal rest, and joy that will not be taken away from us.

This is signified by what he says: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

What does “I came out from the Father” mean except: “Not in the form in which I am equal to the Father, but in another form—that is, in the assumed creature—I appeared as lesser”?

And what does “I came into this world” mean except: “I displayed to the eyes of sinners who love this world the form of a servant, which I received by emptying myself”? [Col. 0909C]

And what does “Again I leave the world” mean except: “I remove from the sight of those who love the world what they saw”?

And what does “I go to the Father” mean except: “I teach my faithful to understand me as equal to the Father”?

Those who believe this will be considered worthy of being led from faith to sight, that is, to the vision itself. In this sense he is said to hand the kingdom over to God and the Father as the one who leads them there.

His faithful, whom he redeemed by his blood, are called his kingdom; for them he now intercedes. But then, making them cleave to himself there, where he is equal to the Father, he will no longer ask the Father for them. For he says: “The Father himself loves you.” In the respect in which he is lesser, he asks; but in the respect in which he is equal, he is heard together with the Father. [Col. 0909D]

Accordingly, when he says, “The Father himself loves you,” he does not separate himself from the Father. Rather, this is to be understood according to what I recalled above and sufficiently explained: that often one person of the Trinity is named in such a way that the others are also understood to be present.

Thus it is said, “The Father himself loves you,” with the Son and the Holy Spirit also understood—not because the one who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all does not love us now, but because God loves us as we shall be, not as we are. For those whom he loves, he preserves forever in the state he loves.

This will occur when he hands the kingdom over to God and the Father—the one who now intercedes for us—so that he no longer asks the Father for us, because the Father himself loves us.

And by what merit except faith, by which we believe before we see what is promised? Through faith we arrive at sight, so that he loves us as those whom he loves us to become, not as those whom he hates because we are what we are; and he exhorts us and grants that we should not always wish to remain such. [Col. 0910A]

## CHAPTER CCXXXIX. In what distinction the Son is to be understood as now equal to the Father and now lesser. From the same book, title 11.

Once this rule for understanding the Scriptures concerning the Son of God is known—namely, that we distinguish what sounds in them according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, from what is said according to the form of a servant, which he assumed, in which he is less than the Father—we will not be troubled as though the statements of the holy books were contradictory and opposed to one another.

For according to the form of God, the Son is equal to the Father, as is the Holy Spirit, because neither of them is a creature, as we have already shown. According to the form of a servant, however, he is less than the Father, because he himself said: “The Father is greater than I.” [Col. 0910B]

He is less than himself, because it was said of him: “He emptied himself.”

He is less than the Holy Spirit, because he himself said: “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.”

And he performed miracles by him when he said: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.”

And through Isaiah he says what he himself read in the synagogue and showed, without any uncertainty, to have been fulfilled concerning him.

## CHAPTER CCXL. In what sense the Son is said not to know the day and hour which the Father knows. From the same book, title 11.

According to the form of God, everything the Father has belongs to him: “All that is yours is mine,” he says, “and mine is yours.”

According to the form of a servant, however, the teaching is not his, but that of the one who sent him. And concerning the day and hour: “No one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.” [Col. 0910C]

He does not know this in the sense that he causes others not to know it; that is, he did not know it in such a way as to disclose it to the disciples at that time. This is like what was said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God,” meaning, “Now I have caused you to know,” since Abraham himself also became known to himself through that testing.

For he was certainly going to tell the disciples at the appropriate time about what was still future, speaking of it as though it had already occurred: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends; for the servant does not know his master’s will, but I have called you friends because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you.”

He had not yet done this, but because he was certainly going to do it, he spoke as though he had already done it. For he said to them: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” Among these things the day and hour are also understood.

The Apostle likewise says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” He was speaking to people who could not grasp higher matters concerning Christ’s Deity. To them he says shortly afterward: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh.” [Col. 0910D]

Thus, among them he did not know what they could not know through him, and he said that he knew only what they needed to know through him. In short, among the mature he knew what among children he did not know. For there he says: “We speak wisdom among the mature.” [Col. 0911A]

By this same manner of speech, anyone is said not to know what he conceals, just as a pit is called blind because it is hidden. For Scripture does not speak in any manner that is absent from ordinary human usage, since it speaks to human beings.

According to the form of God it was said: “Before all the hills he begot me,” that is, before all the heights of created things; and: “Before the morning star I begot you,” that is, before all temporal things.

According to the form of a servant, however, it was said: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (31), because according to the form of God he said: “I am the truth,” and according to the form of a servant: “I am the way.”

Because he is the firstborn from the dead, he made a way for his Church to the kingdom of God, to eternal life, of which he is the head, and also to the immortality of the body. Therefore he was created “at the beginning of God’s [his] ways,” in his works. [Col. 0911B]

For according to the form of God he is the beginning, and in this beginning God made heaven and earth; but according to the form of a servant he is the Bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber.

According to the form of God he is the firstborn of every creature; he himself is before all things, and all things hold together in him. According to the form of a servant he is the head of the body, the Church.

According to the form of God he is the Lord of glory; from this it is clear that he glorifies his saints. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.” [Col. 0911C]

It was said of him that he justifies the ungodly; it was said of him that he is righteous and the one who justifies. Therefore, if those whom he justified he also glorified, the one who justifies also glorifies—the one who, as I said, is the Lord of glory.

According to the form of a servant, however, when the disciples were anxiously concerned about his glorification, he answered: “To sit at my right or left is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

But what has been prepared by his Father has also been prepared by the Son himself, because he and the Father are one.

We have already shown, through many forms of divine speech, that in this Trinity statements concerning each individual person are also made concerning all, because of the inseparable operation of one and the same substance.

Thus concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “When I go away, I will send him to you.” He does not say, “We will send him,” but speaks as though the Son alone were going to send him, and not the Father as well, although elsewhere he says: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you; but the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will declare all things to you.” [Col. 0911D]

Here again it is said as though the Son would not also send him, but only the Father.

Therefore, just as in these passages, so also in the words “for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” he wished it to be understood that he prepared the seats of glory together with the Father for those whom he wished.

Someone may say: When he spoke about the Holy Spirit, he said that he himself would send him in such a way that he did not deny that the Father would send him; and elsewhere he spoke of the Father sending him in such a way that he did not deny that he himself would send him. But here he plainly says, “It is not mine to give,” and then attributes the preparation to the Father.

But this is what we established beforehand: that it was said according to the form of a servant. We are therefore to understand “It is not mine to give you” as though it meant: “It is not within human power to give this.” From this it is understood that he gives it in the capacity in which he is God and equal to the Father. [Col. 0912A]

“It is not mine,” he says, “to give”—that is, “I do not give these things by human power, but they have been prepared by my Father.” Yet understand this: if everything the Father has is mine, then this too is mine, and I prepared these things together with the Father.

I also ask how we should understand the statement: “If anyone does not hear my words, I will not judge him.” Perhaps here he said, “I will not judge him,” in the same sense as “It is not mine to give.”

But what follows? “For I did not come,” he says, “to judge the world, but to save the world.” Then he adds: “Whoever rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him.” At this point we would understand the Father, unless he added: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.” [Col. 0912B]

What, then? Will the Son no longer judge, because he said, “I will not judge him”? Nor will the Father, but only the word that the Son spoke?

On the contrary, listen further to what follows: “For I have not spoken from myself, but the Father who sent me gave me a command—what I should say and what I should speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life. Therefore the things I speak, I speak just as the Father told me.”

If, then, the Son does not judge, but the word that the Son spoke judges—and the word that the Son spoke judges because the Son did not speak from himself, but the Father who sent him gave him a command concerning what he should say and speak—then the Father certainly judges, whose Word is what the Son spoke; and that very Word of the Father is the Son himself. [Col. 0912C]

For the Father’s commandment is not one thing and the Father’s Word another. He called the Father’s Word itself a commandment.

Let us therefore see whether perhaps, when he says, “I have not spoken from myself,” he wished this to be understood: “I have not been born from myself.” For if the Father’s Word speaks, he speaks himself, because he himself is the Father’s Word.

He often says, “The Father gave me,” wishing it to be understood that the Father begot him—not that, as though he already existed but did not possess something, the Father gave him something, but that the Father gave him existence by giving him what he has; to beget him was to cause him to be.

For unlike a creature, the Son of God—before the incarnation and the assumption of a creature—the only-begotten one through whom all things were made, is not one thing and does not possess another. Rather, he himself is what he possesses. [Col. 0912D]

This is stated more clearly in the passage—if anyone is capable of grasping it—where he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself.” For he did not give life to one who already existed but did not possess it, since he himself is life.

Thus “he gave the Son to have life in himself” means: “He begot the Son to be immutable life,” which is eternal life.

Since, then, the Word of God is the Son of God, and the Son of God is true God and eternal life, as John says in his Epistle, what else do we recognize here when the Lord says: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day”? He says that this word is the Father’s Word, and that the Father’s commandment is this same Word, and that this commandment itself is eternal life: “And I know,” he says, “that his commandment is eternal life.” [Col. 0913A]

I therefore ask how we are to understand: “I will not judge, but the word that I have spoken will judge.” From what follows, it appears to have been said as though he were saying: “I will not judge, but the Father’s Word will judge.” The Father’s Word, however, is the Son of God himself.

Is this to be understood as: “I will not judge, but I will judge”? How can this be true except in this sense: “I will not judge by human authority, because I am the Son of Man; but I will judge by the authority of the Word, because I am the Son of God”?

Or, if the statements “I will not judge” and “I will judge” seem contradictory and opposed, what shall we say about the passage where he says: “My teaching is not mine”?

How is it “mine,” and how is it “not mine”? He did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but, “My teaching is not mine.” The teaching he called his own he also called not his own. [Col. 0913B]

How is this true except that he called it his own in one respect and not his own in another: his own according to the form of God, not his own according to the form of a servant?

For when he says, “It is not mine but belongs to the one who sent me,” he makes us return to the Word himself. The Father’s teaching is the Father’s Word, who is the only Son.

What does he also mean by: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me”? How is it belief in him, and how is it not belief in him? How can this apparent contradiction and opposition be understood?

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “does not believe in me (32) but in him who sent me,” unless you understand it in this way: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in what he sees, lest our hope be placed in a creature, but in the one who assumed a creature, in which he would appear to human eyes, and thus cleanse hearts by faith so that they might contemplate him equal to the Father.” [Col. 0913C]

Therefore, by directing the believers’ attention to the Father and saying, “He does not believe in me but in him who sent me,” he did not wish to separate himself from the Father, that is, from the one who sent him. Rather, he wished people to believe in him in the way they believe in the Father, to whom he is equal.

Elsewhere he plainly says: “Believe in God, and believe in me”—that is, “As you believe in God, believe also in me, because I and the Father are one God.”

Thus, just as here he seems to have taken human faith away from himself and transferred it to the Father by saying, “He does not believe in me but in him who sent me,” while certainly not separating himself from the Father, so also with the words “It is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” I think it is now clear in what respect each statement is to be understood.

The same applies to: “I will not judge,” although he will judge the living and the dead. But because he will not judge by human authority, he returns to the Deity and lifts human hearts upward, for the sake of raising which he descended. [Col. 0913D]

Textual-apparatus register: At [Col. 0906A], *quae [quia]* means “which [because].” At [Col. 0906B], the alternate reading is *cum autem omnia ei subjecta fuerint, manifestum quia praeter eum qui illi subjecit omnia*: “when all things have been subjected to him, it is clear that [the exception is] the one who subjected all things to him.” At [Col. 0906D], *a Patre [meo]* means “by the Father [by my Father],” and *neque Patrem quis novit nisi Filius [et nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius]* means “nor does anyone know the Father except the Son [and no one knows the Father except the Son].” At [Col. 0907A], *vita nostra [vestra]* means “our life [your life]”; *scimus [enim]*, “we know [indeed]”; and *quod [quid] erimus*, “what [what, with an alternate form] we shall be.” At [Col. 0907B], *videbimus [vivemus] in aeternum* means “we shall see [we shall live] for ever.” At [Col. 0907C], *spes autem [enim]* means “but hope [for hope],” and *sicut [et ipse] ait*, “as [he himself] says.” At [Col. 0908A], *frui [scilicet]* means “to enjoy [namely].” At [Col. 0909B], *non aliis separatis intelliguntur [separatim: non tamen aliis separatis intelligentur]* means “they are not understood with the others separated [separately: nevertheless, they will not be understood with the others separated],” and *deitatem [divinitatem]* means “Deity [divinity].” At [Col. 0909C], *quo minor [est] Pater* means “in the respect in which he is less than [is] the Father.” At [Col. 0910A], *ut tales [nos] amet* means “that he may love such [us].” At [Col. 0911A], *quod [quo] dicitur fossa caeca* means “by which [by which, with an alternate form] a pit is called blind.” At [Col. 0911B], *Dei [suarum]* means “of God [his].” At [Col. 0911C], *ipsos [hos]* means “them [these],” and *Dominus [est] gloriae*, “the Lord [is] of glory.” At [Col. 0912B], *Imo [potius]* means “indeed [rather].” At [Col. 0913A], *Ego non judicabo, [sed] verbum quod locutus sum judicabit* means “I will not judge, [but] the word that I have spoken will judge”; *quoniam [quia]* means “because [because, with an alternate form].” At [Col. 0913C], *secundum quid [qualiter]* means “in what respect [how].”

## CHAPTER CCXLI. How the sending of either the Son or the Holy Spirit is to be understood. From Book II of *On the Trinity*, title 5.

But, when refuted on these points, they turn to the argument that “the one who sends is greater than the one who is sent.” Therefore, the Father is greater than the Son, because the Son repeatedly declares that he was sent by the Father; and he is also greater than the Holy Spirit, because Jesus said of him, “Whom the Father will send in my name.” The Holy Spirit, then, is less than both, because the Father sends him, as we have mentioned, [Col. 0914A] and the Son also sends him when he says, “But if I depart, I will send him to you.”

In this question I first ask: from where and to where [or: in what manner] was the Son sent? “I came forth,” he says, “from the Father and came into this world.” Therefore, to come forth from the Father and to come into this world is to be sent. What, then, does the same evangelist mean when he says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him”? Then he adds: “He came to his own.” He was certainly sent there where he came. But if he was sent into this world because he came forth from the Father and came into this world, and if he was in this world, then he was sent there where he already was.

For what is written in the Prophet, where God says, “I fill heaven and earth”—if this was said of the Son, as some wish to understand him as speaking either to the prophets or in the prophets—to where was he sent, if not there where he was? He was everywhere, since he says, “I fill heaven and earth.” But if this was said of the Father, where could he be without his Word and without his Wisdom, which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly”? Nor could he anywhere be without the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if God is everywhere, his Holy Spirit is everywhere also. The Holy Spirit, then, was sent there where he already was.

The one who could not find a place to which he might go from the presence of God, and who says, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present,” wishing God to be understood as present everywhere, first mentioned his Spirit. For he says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” Therefore, if both the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent there where they already were, we must ask how this mission is to be understood, whether of the Son or of the Holy Spirit. For the Father alone is nowhere said to have been sent.

Concerning the Son, the Apostle writes: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law.” He says, “He sent his Son, made of a woman.” What Catholic does not know that by this expression he intended to signify, in the Hebrew manner of speaking, not the loss of virginity but the distinction of sex? When, therefore, he says, “God sent his Son, made of a woman,” he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely by being made of a woman. In that he was born from God, he was already in this world; but in that he was born from Mary, he came sent into this world.

Accordingly, he could not have been sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit—not only because, when the Father sent him, that is, made him from a woman, the Father is understood not to have done this without his Spirit, but also because the Gospel states this most plainly and explicitly. When the Virgin Mary asked the angel, “How will this happen?” the angel replied: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Matthew likewise says: “She was found to have conceived in her womb from the Holy Spirit.” Moreover, in the prophet Isaiah Christ himself may be understood to speak of his future coming: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.”

Perhaps someone may compel us to say that the Son was also sent by himself, because that conception and birth from Mary was the work of the Trinity, by whose creation all things are created. “How, then,” he asks, “did the Father send him, if he sent himself?”

I answer him first by asking him to say, if he can, how the Father sanctified him, if he sanctified himself. For the same Lord says both things: “The Father sanctified and sent him into this world. You say, ‘He blasphemes,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” Elsewhere he says: “And for their sake I sanctify myself.”

Again I ask how the Father handed him over, if he handed himself over. The apostle Paul says both things. He says of the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.” Elsewhere he says of the Savior himself: “He loved me and handed himself over for me.”

I believe that, if he understands these matters correctly, he will answer that the will of the Father and the Son is one, and their operation inseparable. Let him therefore understand that incarnation and birth from the Virgin, in which the Son is understood to have been sent, were accomplished by one and the same inseparable operation of the Father and the Son—not, of course, with the Holy Spirit separated from it, of whom it is appropriately [or: plainly] said: “She was found to have conceived in her womb from the Holy Spirit.”

Even if we ask the question in this way, what we are saying may perhaps become clearer. How did God send his Son? Did he order him to come, and did he come in obedience to the one giving the order? Or did he entreat him, or merely admonish him? Whatever the case may be, it was done by the Word. The Word of God, however, is the Son of God himself. Therefore, when the Father sent him by the Word, it was by the Father and his Word that he was made to be sent.

Thus the same Son was sent by the Father and by the Son, because he himself is the Word of the Father. Who would clothe himself in so sacrilegious an opinion as to think that a temporal Word was made by the Father so that the eternal Son might be sent and appear in the flesh in time? Rather, in the very Word of God, which “was in the beginning with God, and was God,” that is, in the very Wisdom of God, there existed without time the time at which it was fitting for him to appear in the flesh.

Therefore, since the Word existed without any beginning of time—in the beginning—and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, without any time there existed in that very Word the time at which the Word would become flesh and dwell among us. When that fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman—that is, made in time—so that the incarnate Word might appear to human beings. What was to take place in time existed without time in the very Word: namely, the time in which it would take place. For the order of times exists without time in the eternal Wisdom of God.

Since, therefore, it had been brought about by the Father and the Son that the Son should appear in the flesh, the one who appeared in that flesh was appropriately said to have been sent; while the one who did not appear in it was said to have sent him. For those things that are performed outwardly before bodily eyes arise from the inward ordering of spiritual nature, and therefore are appropriately said to be sent.

The form of the humanity assumed, moreover, belongs to the person of the Son, and not also to the Father. Therefore, the invisible Father, together with the invisible Son who was with him, is said to have sent that same Son by making him visible—as though he had been made visible in such a way that he ceased to be invisible with the Father; that is, as though the invisible substance of the Word had been changed and transformed into visible creation and passed over into it. In that case, the Son would be understood to have been sent by the Father in such a way that he was merely sent and was not also found to be sending with the Father.

But when the form of a servant was received in such a way that the form of God remained unchangeable, it is clear that what appeared in the Son was brought about by the Father and the Son, neither of whom appeared—that is, the same Son was sent by the invisible Father together with the invisible Son. Why, then, does he say, “I did not come of myself”? This was said according to the form of a servant, just as it was said, “I judge no one.”

If, then, the one who is inwardly always hidden from mortal eyes in spiritual nature is said to have been sent insofar as he appeared outwardly in bodily creation, it is now readily understandable why the Holy Spirit is also said to have been sent.

For a certain form of creation came into being in time in which the Holy Spirit might be visibly manifested: either when he ascended upon the Lord himself in bodily form like a dove [or: “descended upon the Lord himself in bodily form like a dove”], or when, after ten days had passed following his ascension, on the day of Pentecost, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a powerful wind being carried along, and tongues divided as if by fire appeared to them and rested upon each one of them.

This operation, visibly expressed and offered to mortal eyes, was called the sending of the Holy Spirit—not because his substance itself appeared, for he too is invisible and unchangeable, like the Father and the Son, but so that human hearts, stirred by outward visible manifestations, might be turned from the temporal manifestation of the one who came to the hidden eternity of the one who is always present.

## CHAPTER CCXLII. On the one true God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—from Book VI of *On the Trinity*, title 9 [Col. 0916C]

On the testimony of the Lord, we say that the Father is one true God, the Son is one true God, and the Holy Spirit is [one] true God; and together, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, the Trinity itself together—are not three true gods but one true God.

Or, since he added, “And Jesus Christ whom you sent,” should “one true God” be understood, so that the order of the words is: “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the one true God”? Why, then, did he remain silent about the Holy Spirit?

Is it because it follows that wherever the One is named, the Holy Spirit—cleaving to the One in such peace that through this peace the two are one [or: “through it the two are one”]—is thereby also understood as that very peace, even though he is not mentioned? The Apostle likewise seems in one passage almost to omit the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, he is understood there when he says: “All things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s”; and again: “The head of the woman is the man, the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God.”

But if God is understood only as all three together, how is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ—when Christ is in the Trinity, so that the Trinity exists? Or is what the Father is together with the Son the head of what the Son is alone? The Father together with the Son is God, whereas Christ is the Son alone—especially since the Word, already made flesh, is speaking according to the humility [or: humanity] of his condition. According to this humility, the Father is also greater, as he says: “For the Father is greater than I.” Thus the very fact that he is God—something he has in common with the Father and by which he is one with the Father—is the head of the human Mediator, who is Christ alone.

For if we rightly call the mind the principal part of a human being, as though it were the head of human substance, although a human being is human together with the mind, why should it not be much more fittingly and much more truly said that the Word, together with the Father, who is God with him, is the head of Christ, even though Christ cannot be understood apart from the Word made flesh?

## CHAPTER CCXLIII. On the Apostle’s statement that the man is the image of God and the woman the glory of the man, from Book XII of *On the Trinity*, title 7 [Col. 0917A]

If, then, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and the one who is renewed is the new human being, renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him, no one doubts that the human being was made according to the image of the one who created him—not according to the body, nor according to any other part of the soul, but according to the rational mind, in which the knowledge of God can exist.

According to this renewal, we also become children of God through the baptism of Christ; and by putting on the new human being, Christ, we are certainly clothed through faith. Who, then, would exclude women from this fellowship, since they are fellow heirs with us of grace, and since the same Apostle says elsewhere:

“For you are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Have believing women, then, lost the sex of their bodies? No. But because they are renewed according to the image of God where there is no sex, the human being was made according to the image of God where there is no sex—that is, in the spirit of the mind.

Why, then, should a man not cover his head because he is the image and glory of God, while a woman should cover hers because she is the glory of the man—as though the woman were not renewed in the spirit of her mind, which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him?

But because she differs from the man in bodily sex, that part of reason which is directed toward governing temporal matters could rightly be represented by her bodily covering, so that the image of God remains only in that part by which the human mind clings to the contemplation or consultation of eternal principles. It is evident that not only men but also women possess this part.

Therefore, in their minds the common nature is recognized, while in their bodies the distribution of that one mind is symbolized.

## CHAPTER CCXLIV. What was discussed and what was established by the reasoning of the preceding fourteen books, from Book XV of *On the Trinity*, title 3 [Col. 0917D]

But since the necessity of discussion and reasoning compelled us, over fourteen books, to say many things which we cannot view all together at once, so that we may refer them by a swift act of thought to the point we wish to grasp, I shall do, insofar as the Lord helps me, what I can: whatever I brought to an understanding through argument in the individual volumes, I shall collect briefly, removing the argument itself, and place before the mind, as though under one view, not the way in which each matter persuaded us, but the conclusions themselves that were established.

This is so that the later matters may not be so far removed from the earlier ones that the contemplation of what follows causes us to forget what preceded; or, if it does, so that what has slipped from memory may quickly be recovered by rereading.

In the first book, the unity and supreme equality of that highest Trinity is demonstrated according to the holy Scriptures.

In the second, third, and fourth books, the same subject is treated. But the careful investigation of the mission of the Son and of the Holy Spirit occupied three books, and it was demonstrated that the one who is sent is not thereby less than the one who sends [or: “that the sender is not thereby greater than the one who is sent”], because one sent and the other was sent. For the Trinity, which is equal in every respect, operates inseparably, being likewise in its nature unchangeable, invisible, and present everywhere.

In the fifth book, the discussion concerns those who think that the Father and the Son do not have the same substance because they suppose that everything said of God is said according to substance. Therefore, because generating and being generated, or being begotten and being unbegotten, are different, they argue that the substances are different.

It is demonstrated that not everything said of God is said according to substance. “Good” and “great,” and whatever else is said in relation to God himself, are said according to substance; but things are also said relatively—that is, not in relation to himself, but to something that he is not. Thus he is called Father in relation to the Son, or Lord in relation to the creation that serves him.

When something relative—that is, something referring to what he himself is not—is said of him in time, as in “Lord, you have become our refuge,” nothing happens to him by which he is changed; rather, he remains altogether unchangeable in his nature or essence.

In the sixth book, the manner in which Christ is called by the Apostle’s mouth “the power of God and the wisdom of God” is discussed. The question is deferred for more careful reconsideration: whether the one from whom Christ was begotten is not himself Wisdom but only the Father of his Wisdom, or whether Wisdom begot Wisdom.

Whichever of these alternatives might be the case, the equality of the Trinity appeared in this book also: not a triple God but a Trinity, nor as though the Father and Son were something double in comparison with the Holy Spirit as something single, since the three are not anything more than one of them.

It was also discussed how the statement of Hilary the bishop might be understood: “Eternity in the Father, form in the image, use in the gift.”

In the seventh book, the question that had been deferred is explained. God who begot the Son is shown to be not merely the Father of his own power and wisdom but himself also power and wisdom. The same is true of the Holy Spirit. Yet there are not three powers or three wisdoms together, but one power and one wisdom, just as there is one God and one essence.

Then the question was considered how three persons are said to be one essence, or, by certain Greeks, three substances are said to be one essence. It was found that this is said from the necessity of expression, so that the three whom we truthfully confess to be three—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—might be expressed by one name when the question is asked what they are.

In the eighth book, with a rational explanation also supplied, it is made clear to those who understand that, in the substance of Truth, the Father is not greater than the Son, nor are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit alone; nor are any two in the same Trinity anything greater than one; nor are all three together anything greater than each individually.

Then, through the truth that is perceived by understanding, through the supreme good from which every good derives, and through the justice for which the just soul is loved even by a soul that is not yet just, I urged that the nature which is not only incorporeal but also unchangeable—namely, God—be understood insofar as this can be done.

And through the love that is called God in the holy Scriptures, by which the Trinity also began, to some extent, to appear to those who understand, there appeared the lover, the beloved, and the love.

In the ninth book, the discussion reached the image of God, which is the human being, according to the mind. In it a certain trinity is found: the mind, the knowledge by which it knows itself, and the love by which it loves itself and its knowledge. These three are shown to be equal to one another and to belong to one essence.

In the tenth book, this same matter was treated more carefully and subtly, and the discussion was brought to the point where a more evident trinity was found in the mind: namely, memory, understanding, and will.

But since it was also discovered that the mind could never exist in such a way that it did not remember itself, understand itself, and love itself—although it does not always think of itself, and when it does think, it does not by that same thought distinguish itself from bodily things—the discussion of the Trinity of which the mind is an image was deferred, so that a trinity might also be found in bodily visions themselves and the reader’s attention might be exercised more distinctly in it.

Therefore, in the eleventh book the sense of sight was selected. In it what could also be recognized as having been found in the other four bodily senses, even if it had not been stated, was examined. Thus the trinity of the outward human being first appeared in things perceived externally: in the body that is seen, in the form impressed from it upon the gaze of the one seeing, and in the intention of the will that joins the two.

But it became clear that these three are not equal to one another and do not belong to one substance.

Then, in the mind itself, as though introduced by the things sensed externally, another trinity was found, in which the same three appeared to belong to one substance: the bodily image that exists in memory, the formation that arises when the gaze of the thinker is turned toward it, and the intention of the will that joins the two.

This trinity was therefore found to belong to the outward human being because it was introduced from bodies, which are perceived externally.

In the twelfth book, wisdom was seen to require distinction from knowledge [or: “wisdom from wisdom”]. In that which is properly called knowledge, because it is inferior, a certain trinity of its own kind had first to be sought. Although this already belongs to the inner human being, it should not yet be called or considered the image of God.

This is pursued in the thirteenth book through the commendation of the Christian faith.

In the fourteenth book, the discussion concerns the true wisdom of the human being—that is, wisdom granted as a gift of God through participation in God himself, and distinguished from knowledge. The discussion reaches the point where the Trinity appears in the image of God, which is the human being according to the mind. The mind is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created the human being in his own image, and thus it perceives wisdom, where there is contemplation of eternal things.

## CHAPTER CCXLV. On the Holy Spirit, who is understood to be equal to the Father and the Son, is called the Spirit of both, and is understood under the name of love, although each person in the Trinity is love; from Book XV of *On the Trinity*, titles 17, 18, and 19 [Col. 0920A]

Now the Holy Spirit must be discussed, insofar as God grants us the ability to see. According to the holy Scriptures, the Holy Spirit is neither the Father’s alone nor the Son’s alone, but belongs to both; [et: and] therefore he signifies to us the common love by which the Father and the Son love one another.

[Col. 0920B] Yet, in order to exercise us, the divine word has caused us to inquire with greater diligence—not about matters readily at hand, but about those that must be sought in secret and brought forth from secrecy. Scripture therefore did not say, “The Holy Spirit is love.” Had it said this, it would have removed no small part of the present question. Instead, it said, “God is love,” so that it remains uncertain—and therefore must be investigated—whether God the Father is love, or God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit, or God himself as Trinity.

For we shall not say that God is called love merely because love itself is some substance worthy of the name of God, but because it is God’s gift, just as it was said to God, “For you are my patience.” This was certainly not said because our patience is God’s substance, but because it comes to us from him, as is read elsewhere: “For my patience is from him.”

[Col. 0920C] The very language of Scripture easily refutes this interpretation. “You are my patience” has the same sense as “Lord, my hope,” and “My God, my mercy,” and many similar expressions. It was not said, “Lord, my love,” or “You are my love,” or “[Tu: You,] God, are my love”; rather, it was said, “God is love,” just as it was said, “God is Spirit.” Whoever does not distinguish this should seek understanding from the Lord, not an explanation from us, for we can say nothing clearer.

God, then, is love. But whether this means the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself—for the Trinity too is not three gods but one God—is the question. Yet earlier in this book I also argued that the Trinity, which is God, must not be understood from those three things that we have shown to exist in our mind’s trinity as though the Father were the memory of all three, the Son the understanding of all three, and the Holy Spirit the love of all three: as though the Father did not understand or love himself, but the Son of God understood him and the Holy Spirit loved him; as though the Father remembered only himself and them, while the Son neither remembered nor loved himself, but the Father remembered him and the Holy Spirit loved him, while he himself understood only himself and them; and likewise as though the Holy Spirit neither remembered nor understood himself, but the Father remembered him and the Son understood him, while he himself loved only himself and them.

[Col. 0920D] Rather, all three, and each one individually, must possess all these things in his own nature, and these things must not be distinct in them as memory, understanding, and affection—or love—are distinct in us. Instead, there is one reality capable of accomplishing all these things, just as wisdom itself is; and it exists in each one’s nature in such a way that whoever possesses it is what he possesses, as an immutable and simple substance.

[Col. 0921A] If this has been understood, and if, insofar as we have been permitted to see or conjecture concerning such great matters, it has become clear that it is true, I do not know why, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each called wisdom, while all together they are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit should not likewise each be called love, while all together they are one love. For in the same way the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, while all together they are one God.

Nevertheless, it is not without reason that in this Trinity only the Son is called the Word of God; only the Holy Spirit is called God’s gift; and only the Father is called the one from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally. I added “principally” because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father too gave this to the Son—not to one who already existed and did not yet possess it, but whatever he gave to the Only-Begotten Word, he gave by begetting him. Thus he begot him in such a way that the common gift would also proceed from him, and the Holy Spirit would be the Spirit of both.

[Col. 0921B] This distinction within the inseparable Trinity must therefore not be passed over casually but examined carefully. For this is why the Word of God is also properly called the wisdom of God, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom as well.

If, then, one of these three is to be properly called love, what is more fitting than that this should be the Holy Spirit? In that simple and supreme nature, substance is not one thing and love another; rather, the substance itself is love, and love itself is substance, whether it is in the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Yet the Holy Spirit is properly called love, just as the term “law” sometimes signifies all the words of the holy Scriptures of the Old Testament taken together.

[Col. 0921C] For when the Apostle cites the prophet Isaiah, saying, “In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people,” he nevertheless prefaced it with, “It is written in the law.” And the Lord himself said, “In their law it is written: They hated me without cause,” although this is read in a Psalm. At other times, however, “law” properly denotes the law given through Moses, as in the statement, “The Law and the Prophets were until John,” and, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.” Here “Law” properly means the law given from Mount Sinai.

[Col. 0921D] The Psalms too are signified by the name “Prophets”; nevertheless, elsewhere the Savior himself said, “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms should be fulfilled.” Here he wished the name “Prophets” to be understood as excluding the Psalms. Thus “law” is used universally when the Prophets and Psalms are included, and it is also used properly for the law given through Moses. Likewise, “Prophets” is used collectively together with the Psalms, and it is also used properly apart from the Psalms.

[Col. 0922A] Many other examples could show that terms for things are used both universally and properly of particular things, unless the obviousness of the matter made a lengthy discussion inappropriate. I have said this so that no one may think that we improperly call the Holy Spirit love because God the Father and God the Son can also be called love. Just as we properly call the only Word of God by the name “Wisdom,” although the Holy Spirit and the Father himself are universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name “love,” although the Father and the Son are also universally love.

The Word of God—that is, the Only-Begotten Son of God—is plainly called the wisdom of God by the Apostle, who says, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” But where the Holy Spirit is called love we discover if we carefully examine the words of the Apostle John.

[Col. 0922B] After saying, “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God,” he immediately continued: “Everyone who loves is born of God; whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”

Here he made clear that he had called God that love which he had said was from God: therefore love from God is God. But because the Son of God too is born from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, it is rightly asked which of them we should understand to be called here “God love.” The Father alone is God in such a way that he is not from God. Therefore love, which is God in such a way that it is from God, is either the Son or the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0922C] But in what follows, after mentioning the love of God—not the love by which we love him, but by which he loved us and sent his Son as deliverer for our sins—and after exhorting us to love one another, so that God might remain in us, since he had called God love, he immediately wished to speak more openly about this matter: “By this,” he said, “we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.”

Therefore the Holy Spirit, of whom he gave us, causes us to remain in God and God in us; and love accomplishes this. He, then, is God love. Finally, shortly afterward, when he had repeated this very point and said, “God is love,” he immediately added, “Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” This corresponds to what he had said above: “By this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” He, therefore, is signified where it is read, “God is love.”

[Col. 0922D] God the Holy Spirit, then, who proceeds from God, when he has been given to a human being, kindles that person with love of God and neighbor; and he himself is love. For a human being has no means of loving God except from God. Hence, shortly afterward, he says, “We love because he first loved us.” The Apostle Paul likewise says, “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

[Col. 0923A] No gift of God is greater than this. It alone distinguishes the children of the eternal kingdom from the children of eternal perdition. Other gifts are given through the Holy Spirit, but without love they are of no benefit. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon each person in such measure as to make that person a lover of God and neighbor, he is not transferred from the left hand to the right.

Nor is the Spirit properly called a gift except on account of the love which, if someone does not possess, makes that person—though he speaks in the tongues of human beings and angels—“a sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal.” If he has prophecy, and knows all mysteries and all knowledge; if he has all faith, so as to move mountains; if he distributes all his possessions; and if he hands over his body to be burned, it profits him nothing.

[Col. 0923B] How great, then, is that good without which such great goods bring no one to eternal life! But love itself—or charity, for both are names of one reality—if possessed by someone who does not speak in tongues, who does not have prophecy, who does not know all mysteries and all knowledge, who does not distribute all his possessions to the poor—either because he has nothing to distribute or because some necessity prevents him—and who does not hand over his body to be burned, if no such trial of suffering is present, brings him to the kingdom.

Thus love makes faith useful; without love faith can indeed exist, but it cannot benefit. Therefore the Apostle Paul says, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” In this way he distinguishes it from the faith by which even demons believe and tremble.

[Col. 0923C] The love that is from God and is God is therefore properly the Holy Spirit. Through him the love of God is poured into our hearts, and through this love the entire Trinity dwells in us. Accordingly, since the Holy Spirit is God, he is rightly also called the gift of God. What should this gift properly be understood to be except love, which brings us to God, and without which no other gift of God brings us to God?

Or must it also be proved that the Holy Spirit is called the gift of God in the sacred writings? If this too is expected, we have in the Gospel according to John the words of the Lord Christ: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist then continued: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

[Col. 0923D] Paul the Apostle also says, “We were all given to drink of one Spirit.” But whether this water, which is the Holy Spirit, was called the gift of God is the question. Just as here we find that this water is the Holy Spirit, so elsewhere in the same Gospel we find that this water was called God’s gift.

For when the Lord was speaking with the Samaritan woman, to whom he had said, “Give me a drink,” and she had replied that Jews did not associate with Samaritans, Jesus answered her and said, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The woman said to him, “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep; from where, then, do you have living water?” and so forth.

[Col. 0924A] Jesus answered and said to her, “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst. Rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.”

Since this living water, as the Evangelist explained, is the Holy Spirit, there can be no doubt that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God. Here the Lord says, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” For what does he say there? [nam quod ibi ait: “for what he says there,” an alternative reading] “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Here he says, “It will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.”

The Apostle Paul likewise says, “Grace is given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” And to show that Christ’s gift is the Holy Spirit, he continued: “Therefore it says, ‘He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings.’”

[Col. 0924B] It is well known that the Lord Jesus, after he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, gave the Holy Spirit, and those who believed [crediderunt: “believed,” an alternative reading], when they had been filled with him, spoke in the languages of all nations.

The fact that he says “gifts,” not “gift,” should not trouble us. He took this testimony from [ex: “from,” an alternative reading] the Psalm. In the Psalm it reads: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among human beings.” Thus many copies read, especially the Greek ones; and this is how we have it translated from the Hebrew.

The Apostle therefore said “gifts,” like the prophet, rather than “gift.” But while the Prophet said, “You received gifts among human beings,” the Apostle preferred to say, “He gave gifts to human beings,” so that from the two expressions—one prophetic and the other apostolic, since both possess the authority of the divine word—the fullest sense might be conveyed. Both are true: he both gave to human beings and received among human beings.

[Col. 0924C] He gave to human beings as their head gives to his members; and he received among human beings, himself likewise receiving in his members. On account of these members he cried from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” And concerning these members he said, “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.” Christ himself therefore both gave from heaven and received on earth.

Moreover, the prophet and the Apostle both used the plural “gifts” for this reason: through the gift that is the Holy Spirit, many gifts that are proper to particular individuals are distributed among all the members of Christ. For not every individual possesses all of them; some have one and others another, although all possess the gift itself from which the particular gifts are distributed—that is, the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0924D] For after mentioning many gifts elsewhere, Paul says, “All these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing his own gifts to each one as he wills.” The same expression is also found in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where it is written, “God bearing witness by signs and wonders, various powers, and distributions [distributionibus: “distributions,” an alternative reading; the source also has divisionibus, “divisions] of the Holy Spirit.”

And here, after saying, “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings,” what does the statement that he ascended mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth? “He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.” And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers.

[Col. 0925A] This shows why they are called “gifts,” as he says elsewhere: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” and so forth. Here he added, “For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.”

This is the house which, as the Psalm sings, is built after captivity. For those who have been rescued from the devil, by whom they were held captive, are used to build the body of Christ; and this house is called the Church. He himself took captivity captive because he conquered the devil. And so that the members of the holy Head who were destined to come might not be dragged with him into eternal punishment, he bound him first with the chains of justice and then with those of power.

The devil himself, then, is the captivity that was taken captive by him who ascended on high and gave gifts to human beings—or received them among human beings.

[Col. 0925B] The Apostle Peter, as we read in the canonical book in which the Acts of the Apostles are written, was speaking about Christ when the Jews were cut to the heart and said, “What then shall we do, brothers? Show us.” He said to them, “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Again, in the same book, we read that Simon Magus wished to give money to the Apostles so that he might receive from them the power by which [qua: “by which,” an alternative reading; the source also has quia, “because”] the Holy Spirit would be given through the laying on of their hands. Peter said to him, “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be acquired with money.”

[Col. 0925C] Elsewhere in the same book, when Peter was speaking to Cornelius and those who were with him, announcing and preaching Christ, Scripture says: “While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were hearing the word. And the faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the gift of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations.” For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.

When Peter later gave an account to the brothers who were in Jerusalem concerning what he had done—namely, that he had baptized the uncircumcised—because the Holy Spirit had come upon them before they were baptized, thereby removing the knot of this question, and because those who heard of this were troubled, he said, among other things: “When I began to speak to them, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as upon us in the beginning. And I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.’ If, therefore, he gave them an equal gift, just as he gave it to us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God from giving them the Holy Spirit?”

[Col. 0925D] There are many other testimonies of Scripture that jointly attest that the Holy Spirit is the gift of God, insofar as he is given to those who through him love God. But it would be too lengthy to collect them all; and what is enough for those for whom what we have said is not enough?

They should certainly be reminded that, since they now see that the Holy Spirit has been called the gift of God, when they hear “the gift of the Holy Spirit,” they should recognize the kind of expression found in the phrase, “in the stripping off of the body of flesh.” Just as “body of flesh” means nothing other than flesh, so “gift of the Holy Spirit” means nothing other than the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0926A] He is therefore the gift of God insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given. In himself, however, God exists even if he is given to no one, because he was coeternal with the Father and the Son before he was given to anyone. Nor is he inferior to those who give him merely because they give him. He is given as God’s gift in such a way that he also gives himself as God.

It cannot be said that he is not master of his own power, of whom it was said, “The Spirit breathes where he wills,” and of whom the apostolic statement already mentioned above says, “All these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing his own gifts to each one as he wills.” There is no subordination of the one given and domination of those who give; rather, there is harmony between the one given and those who give.

Therefore, as holy Scripture proclaims, “God is love”: that love which is from God and works in us so that we may remain in God and he in us—and we know this because he has given us of his Spirit—is itself the God who is love.

[Col. 0926B] Furthermore, if no gift of God is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more consistently than that he himself is the love that is called both God and from God? And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably demonstrates the communion of them both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called love who is the Spirit common to both?

This is more soundly believed or understood: in that Trinity the Holy Spirit is not the only one who is love, but he is not without reason properly called love, on account of what has been said. Likewise, he is not the only Spirit or the only holy one in that Trinity, since the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy—something piety does not doubt. Yet he is not improperly called the Holy Spirit in a particular sense.

[Col. 0926C] Because he is common to both, he is properly called by that name which both possess in common. Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit alone were love in that Trinity, the Son would be found to be not only the Father’s Son but also the Son of the Holy Spirit. For in countless passages the Only-Begotten Son of God the Father is said and read to be the Son, yet the Apostle’s statement about God the Father would also be true: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.” He did not say “of his Son,” although had he said this, he would have spoken most truly, just as he spoke most truly when he said it many times; rather, he said, “of the Son of his love.”

[Col. 0926D] The Son, therefore, would also be the Son of the Holy Spirit if the love of God in that Trinity were none other than the Holy Spirit. But since this is utterly absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not the only one who is love there; rather, on account of the matters I have sufficiently discussed, he is properly called by this name.

What is said, “the Son of his love,” should be understood as meaning nothing other than “his beloved Son,” or, finally, “the Son of his substance.” For the love of the Father, which exists in his ineffably simple nature, is nothing other than that very nature and substance—as we have often said already, and do not tire of repeating. Consequently, the Son of his love is none other than the one begotten from his substance.

## CHAPTER CCXLVI

### The Heretic’s Question Against Those Who Said That God’s Only-Begotten Son Is the Son of Will Rather Than of the Father’s Substance; from Book XV on the Trinity

[Col. 0927A] A certain man gave a sharp answer to a very cunning heretic who asked whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. If he were said to have begotten him unwillingly, an utterly absurd misery would follow concerning God; but if he were said to have done so willingly, the heretic would immediately conclude, as though by an invincible argument, that the Son was not of nature but of will.

That man, however, most vigilantly asked him in return whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly.
