If he answered “unwillingly,” the misery would follow which it would be utter madness to believe concerning God; but if he said “willingly,” the reply would be made to him: “Then he too is God by his will, not by nature.” What remained, then, except that he should fall silent and see himself bound by his own question with an insoluble bond?

[Col. 0927B] But if a particular person in the Trinity is properly to be called God’s will, this name is more fitting for the Holy Spirit, just as is the name “love.” For what else is love than will?

In this book, then, I have discussed the Holy Spirit according to the holy Scriptures in a manner sufficient for the faithful, who already know that the Holy Spirit is God, of no other substance and no less than the Father and the Son. In the earlier books, according to those same holy Scriptures, we taught that this too is true.

We also gave such admonition as we could concerning the creature made by God to those who demand an account of such matters, so that they might perceive his invisible attributes through the things that have been made, as far as they could understand them, and especially through the rational or intellectual creature made in the image of God. Through this creature, as through a mirror, they might, if they were able, discern the Trinity who is God in our memory, understanding, and will.

[Col. 0927C] Whoever vividly perceives these three, divinely established by nature in his mind, and perceives how great is that faculty within him by which the eternal and immutable nature can also be remembered, contemplated, and desired—for he remembers through memory, gazes upon through understanding, and embraces through love—certainly discovers the image of that supreme Trinity.

Toward remembering, seeing, and loving that supreme Trinity—so that he may remember it, contemplate it, and delight in it—he ought to direct everything that he lives. Yet, lest he compare this image, made by that same Trinity and deteriorated through its own fault, with the Trinity itself in such a way as to think it similar in every respect, but rather that he should discern a great dissimilarity even within whatever likeness exists, I have offered as much admonition as seemed sufficient.

## CHAPTER CCXLVII

### The Resemblances of the Divine Trinity That Could in Some Measure Be Found in the Nature of the Mind Made in the Image of God

[Col. 0927D] Certainly, as far as I was able, I have taken care to indicate through this resemblance—in an enigma, by conjecture, not yet face to face—how God the Father and God the Son, that is, God the Begetter, somehow spoke everything that he substantially possesses in his coeternal Word, and how his Word itself, who is God and who substantially possesses neither more nor less than what exists in the one who truthfully, not falsely, begot the Word, might be signified by the memory and understanding of our mind.

[Col. 0928A] To memory I assign everything that we know, even when we are not thinking about it. To understanding I assign, in its own particular way, a certain formation of thought. For when we discover what is true by thinking, this is what we are said [dicimus: “we say,” an alternative reading] especially to understand; and we again leave this in memory.

But there is a more hidden depth of our memory, where we also discover this truth when we first think about it. There an inner word is begotten, which belongs to no language: knowledge from knowledge, vision from vision, and understanding appearing in thought from understanding that had already existed in memory but lay hidden.

Yet thought itself would not return to the things it had left in memory while considering other things unless it possessed a kind of memory of its own.

[Col. 0928B] Concerning the Holy Spirit, I have shown nothing in this enigma that appeared similar to him except our will, or love, or affection, which is a more powerful form of will. For our will, naturally present in us, has various affections according as things are placed before it or come upon it—things by which we are attracted or offended.

What, then? Shall we say that our will, when it is rightly ordered, does not know what it desires or what it avoids? But if it knows, then it certainly possesses a kind of knowledge of its own, which cannot exist without memory and understanding. Or should anyone be heeded who says that love does not know what it is doing, when it does not act wrongly?

[Col. 0928C] Just as understanding therefore exists in that primary memory, so love exists there too—in the memory in which we find prepared and stored what we can reach by thinking. For we find these two things there when, by thinking, we discover ourselves: both understanding something and loving what was there, even when we were not thinking about it.

And just as memory exists in the understanding formed by thought, so love exists there as well. This true word, which we speak inwardly without the language of any nation, is spoken when we have come to know. For unless it returns through remembering, it does not return to anything; and unless it loves, the gaze of our thought does not wish to return.

Thus love joins together the vision established in memory and the vision formed from it in thought, as though joining parent and offspring.

## CHAPTER CCXLVIII

### The Three Things in the Image of God—Memory, Understanding, and Love—Belong to One Person, Because Being Is Not the Same for Him as Possessing These Things; from the Same Book

[Col. 0928D] When these things exist in one person, as in a human being, someone may say to us: “These three—memory, understanding, and love—belong to me, not to themselves; they act as they do not for themselves but for me. Indeed, I act through them: I remember through memory, understand through understanding, and love through love.”

[Col. 0929A] When I turn the eye of my thought toward my memory, and thus say in my heart what I know, and a true word is begotten from my knowledge, both are mine—knowledge, certainly, and the word. I know; I say in my heart what I know. And when, by thinking, I find something in my memory, I find that I already understand and love something. Understanding and love were there even before I thought about it, but I find my understanding and my love in my memory, through which I understand and love—not that memory itself does so.

Likewise, when my thought remembers and wishes to return to the things it had left in memory, so as to see them as understood and speak of them inwardly, it is my memory that remembers, and my will that wishes, not theirs.

My love too, when it remembers and understands what it ought to seek and what it ought to avoid, remembers through my memory, not its own, and understands through my understanding, not its own, whatever it loves intelligently.

This can be stated briefly: “I remember through all three; I understand through all three; I love through all three. I am neither memory, nor understanding, nor love, but I possess these.”

[Col. 0929B] These things, then, can be said by one person who possesses the three, but who is not himself the three.

In that supreme simplicity of nature, however, which is God—although God is one—there are nevertheless three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Trinity itself is one thing, and the image of the Trinity in another thing is another. Because of this image, both the image and that in which these three exist are called an image, just as both a tablet and what is painted upon it are called an image; but because of the painting that is in it, the tablet too is called by the name “image.”

## CHAPTER CCXLIX

### How True Unity Exists in the Trinity of God, and How True Trinity Exists in That Unity; from the Same Book, Title 23

[Col. 0929C] In that supreme Trinity, which incomparably surpasses all things, there is such inseparability that, although a trinity of human beings cannot be called one human being, in that Trinity one God both is called and truly is one God. Nor, conversely, is that Trinity such as this image—the human being who possesses those three—is, for this image is one person, whereas the Trinity consists of three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

[Col. 0929D] Although human memory—especially that memory which animals do not possess, namely, memory in which intelligible things are contained in such a way that they have not entered it through the bodily senses—has, in this image of the Trinity, some likeness of the Father, incomparably unequal though it is; and although human understanding, formed through the activity of thought when what is known is spoken and becomes the word of the heart belonging to no language, has, in its great dissimilarity, some likeness of the Son; and although human love, proceeding from knowledge and joining memory and understanding as something common to parent and offspring, has in this image some likeness—though very unequal—of the Holy Spirit, who is understood neither as parent nor as offspring:

nevertheless, just as in this image of the Trinity these three are not one human being but belong to one human being, so in the supreme Trinity itself, of which this is the image, those three do not belong to one God, but are one God; and they are three, not one person.

[Col. 0930A] This is wondrously ineffable, or ineffably wondrous: this image of the Trinity is one person, while the supreme Trinity itself consists of three persons. Yet that Trinity of three persons is more inseparable than this Trinity of one person. For it exists in the nature of Divinity—or, better, Deity—and is what it is: unchangeable and always equal within itself. It never was nonexistent or different, nor will it ever be nonexistent or different.

But these three things that exist in the unequal image, although they are not separated by places—for they are not bodies—are nevertheless separated from one another in this present life by degrees of greatness. For although there are no masses there, we nevertheless see that in one person memory is greater than understanding, while in another the reverse is true [in alio autem e contrario: “in another, conversely,” an alternative reading]; in another, these two are surpassed by the greatness of love, whether those two are equal to one another or unequal.

[Col. 0930B] Thus, in various ways, two are overcome by one, one by two, and one by one; the greater overcome the lesser. Even when they have become equal to one another, after being healed of every weakness, the nature of the immutable reality will still not be equaled by that reality which will not be changed through grace—for a creature is not equal to the Creator—and when it is healed of every weakness, it will be changed.

But when the vision promised to us face to face comes, we shall see this Trinity—which is not only incorporeal but also supremely inseparable and truly immutable—much more clearly and certainly than we now see its image, which is what we are.

[Col. 0930C] Yet those who, in this mirror and enigma, see as far as they are permitted to see in this life are not merely those who behold in their own mind the things we have arranged and commended. They are those who see it as an image, so that they may refer, in whatever way they can, what they see to the one whose image it is. Through the image that they see by contemplating it, they also see by conjecture that reality itself, since they cannot yet see face to face.

For the Apostle did not say, “Now we see in a mirror,” but, “Now we see through a mirror.”

## CHAPTER CCL

### Why the Holy Spirit Was Given Twice; from the Same Book, Title 26
Then, in that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown—or even asked—whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both. For Holy Scripture calls the Spirit the Spirit of both. He is the one of whom the Apostle says: “But because you are sons [of God], God sent [Col. 0930D] the Spirit of his Son into our hearts [yours].” And he is the one of whom the same Son says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” By many other testimonies of the divine utterances it is likewise proved that the Spirit—properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity—is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

The Son himself also says of him: “Whom I will send to you from the Father”; and elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name.” That he proceeds from both is taught as follows: the Son himself says, “He proceeds from the Father”; and when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, he breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” thereby showing that he also proceeds from himself. It is the same power that went out from him [went forth from him], as we read [Col. 0931A] in the Gospel, “and healed them all.”

What, then, was the reason that after his resurrection he first gave the Holy Spirit on earth and afterward sent him from heaven? I think it was because through this gift love is poured into our hearts, by which we love God and our neighbor, according to those two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Signifying this, the Lord Jesus gave the Holy Spirit twice: once on earth, because of love of neighbor, and again from heaven, because of love of God. And even if some other explanation is offered for the Spirit’s being given twice, we must nevertheless [Col. 0931B] have no doubt that it was the same Spirit who was given when Jesus breathed upon them—the one of whom he immediately afterward said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” where this Trinity is especially commended.

He, therefore, is also the one who was given from heaven on the day of Pentecost, that is, ten days after the Lord ascended into heaven. How, then, can the one who gives the Holy Spirit not be God? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God! For none of his disciples gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid their hands; they themselves did not give him. The Church still preserves this practice in its appointed leaders.

## CHAPTER CCLI. Why the Holy Spirit was given twice; from a sermon on the Lord’s Ascension

Many people have offered many explanations of why he gave the Holy Spirit twice. Like human beings, they investigated the matter and said something that was not contrary to the faith: one this, [Col. 0931C] another that, each explanation remaining within the rule of truth. If I say that I know why he gave him twice, I shall be lying to you. Whoever claims to know what he does not know is rash; whoever denies knowing what he does know is ungrateful.

Therefore I confess to you that I am still seeking the reason why the Lord gave the Holy Spirit twice. I desire to reach something more certain. May the Lord help me, through your prayers, so that what he deigns to grant may not remain unspoken to you. Thus I do not know what I should think—still not knowing, still not holding it as certain—as firmly as I hold the fact that he gave him. Yet I shall not keep silent about what I think. If this is the reason, may the Lord confirm it; if there is another that appears more truthful, may the Lord grant it.

I therefore think—I think that the Holy Spirit was given twice so that the two commandments of love might be commended. There are two [Col. 0931D] commandments, but love is one: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, 40 and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend. One love and two commandments; one Spirit and two gifts.

For one love was not given first and another afterward, since the love by which we love our neighbor is not different from that by which we love God. It is not, therefore, another love: with the love by which we love our neighbor, we also love God. But because God is one thing and our neighbor another, they are loved with one love, although those who are loved are not one and the same.

Since, then, the great love of God is to be commended first, and love of neighbor is second, but one begins from the second [Col. 0932A] in order to reach the first—for “if you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God, whom you do not see?”—perhaps for this reason, instructing us in love of neighbor, while visible on earth and a neighbor to those near him, he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing upon their faces; and from heaven he sent the Holy Spirit again, because of that love which is in heaven.

Receive the Holy Spirit on earth, and love your brother; receive him from heaven, and love God. For what you received on earth is also from heaven: Christ gave it on earth, but what he gave is from heaven. He gave it because he descended from heaven; here he found someone to whom he could give, but from there he brought what he gave.

What, then, brothers? Perhaps I should also recall how love pertains to the Holy Spirit. Listen to Paul: “And not only so,” [Col. 0932B] he says, “but we glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance character, character hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts.” Why, then, did you take credit for anything? Why did you presume as though it were your own? “For what do you have that you did not receive?” Therefore, from where could it come except from what follows: “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us”?

This love is possessed only within the unity of the Church. Those who divide themselves do not have it, as the Apostle Jude says: “These are the ones who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit.” Therefore they flow apart, because they do not have the bond of love.

## CHAPTER CCLII. What was discussed in a sermon to the people concerning the difference between the Son’s generation and the Holy Spirit’s procession [Col. 0932C]; from the same book, title 27

Since in that coeternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable, and inseparable Trinity it is exceedingly difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let what we said on this subject in a sermon delivered to the ears of the Christian people—and afterward committed to writing—suffice for the present for those who cannot extend their understanding any further.

Among other things, after I had taught through testimonies of the holy Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, I said: “If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’? Why do you think, except that he is accustomed to refer to him even what belongs to him, since he himself is from him? Hence also comes the statement: ‘My teaching is not mine, but [Col. 0932D] his who sent me.’ If, then, the teaching is understood here to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more ought the Holy Spirit there to be understood also to proceed from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

“From the one from whom the Son has his being God—for he is God from God—he surely has also this: that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Son, as he proceeds from the Father, is something he has from the Father.

“Here, too, insofar as it can be understood by those such as we are, we can in some measure understand why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born but rather to proceed. For if he too were called a son, he would necessarily be called the Son of both; and that is utterly absurd [Col. 0933A]. A son belongs to no two persons except a father and a mother. But far be it from us to imagine anything of this kind between God the Father and God the Son.

“For even a human son does not proceed simultaneously from father and mother. When he proceeds into the mother from the father, he does not at that moment proceed from the mother; and when he proceeds from the mother into this light, he does not at that moment proceed from the father. The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both. Nevertheless, the Father gave this to the Son: that the Spirit should proceed from the Son as he proceeds from the Father.

“For we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Accordingly, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son also to have life in himself, so he gave him to have life proceeding from him, just as it proceeds from the Father [Col. 0933B] himself.”

I transferred these words from that sermon into this book, addressing the faithful, not unbelievers. But if they are too weak to contemplate this image and to see how true those things are which exist in their mind—how the three are not so constituted that they are three persons, but all three belong to the human being, who is one person—why do they not believe concerning that supreme Trinity, which is God, what is found in the sacred writings, rather than demand that a perfectly clear explanation be given to them, an explanation that cannot be grasped by the human mind, which is slow and weak?

And surely, once they have firmly believed the holy Scriptures as utterly truthful witnesses, they should act by praying, seeking, and living well, so that they may understand—that is, so that, insofar as it can be seen, what is held by faith may be seen by the mind. Who [Col. 0933C] could forbid this? Indeed, who would not exhort them to it?

If, however, they think that these things must be denied because they are unable to see them with blind minds, then those who have been blind from birth ought also to deny that the sun exists. The light therefore shines in the darkness; and if the darkness does not comprehend it, let them first be enlightened by God’s gift so that they may become believers and begin to be light in comparison with unbelievers. Upon this foundation let them be built up, so that they may see what they believe and at some time be able to see it.

For there are things believed in such a way that they can no longer be seen at all. Christ will not be seen again on the cross; but unless one believes that this happened and was seen in such a way that it is no longer hoped for as something future and to be seen, one does not reach Christ as he will be seen without end.

As for [Col. 0933D] that supreme, ineffable, incorporeal, and immutable nature, which is to be discerned in some manner through understanding, the human mind nowhere exercises its powers better—provided that the rule of faith guides it—than in that which the human being possesses by his own nature better than the other animals, and better even than the other parts of his soul: namely, the mind itself. To it a certain sight of invisible things has been granted, and to it, as it presides honorably in a higher and inward place, all things are reported for judgment even by the bodily senses. Nothing is superior to it that should govern it in subjection, except God.

Yet amid all these things, many of which I have now said, I dare to profess that I have said nothing worthy of the ineffability of that supreme Trinity. Rather, I confess: “His knowledge has become too wonderful for me; it has grown too strong, and I have not been able to attain to it” [Col. 0934A].

O my soul, where do you feel yourself to be? Where do you lie, or where do you stand, until the one who has shown mercy toward all your iniquities heals all your diseases? Surely you recognize that you are in that inn to which the Samaritan brought the man he found half-dead from the many wounds inflicted by robbers.

And yet you have seen many true things—not with those eyes by which colored bodies are seen, but with the eyes for which the one who said, “Let my eyes see equity,” was praying. You have indeed seen many true things and distinguished them from that light by which, while it shone upon you, you saw them. Lift your eyes to the light itself and fix them upon it, if you can. Thus you will see the difference between the birth of God’s Word and the procession of God’s gift, on account of which the only-begotten Son [Col. 0934B] said that the Holy Spirit was not born from the Father—for otherwise he would be his brother—but proceeded.

Thus, since he is a certain consubstantial communion of the Father and the Son, the Spirit of both, he is called the Spirit of both, but not, God forbid, the Son of both. But to see this clearly and distinctly, you cannot fix your inward sight there—I know it; you cannot. I speak the truth; I speak to myself: I know what I cannot do.

Nevertheless, that light itself shows you those three things within yourself in which you could recognize the image of the supreme Trinity, which you are not yet able to contemplate with a steady gaze. It shows you that the true Word exists within you when it is generated from your knowledge—that is, when we say what we know—even if we neither utter nor think a voice signifying the language of any nation. Rather, our thought is formed from what we know, and in the mind of the thinker the image is exceedingly like the thought that memory held. These two, as it were parent and offspring, are joined by a third, namely, the will or love.

This will [Col. 0934C] proceeds from thought—for no one wills what he is entirely ignorant of, either as to what it is or what kind of thing it is—yet it is not the image of knowledge. Thus a certain distinction between generation and procession is suggested in this intelligible matter, since to behold something in thought is not the same as to desire it or even to enjoy it by the will. Whoever can do so sees and distinguishes this.

You too were able—though you could not and cannot explain in adequate language what you scarcely saw amid the clouds of bodily likenesses that never cease to assail human thoughts. But that light, which is not what you are, also showed you that those incorporeal likenesses of bodies are one thing, and that the truth which we contemplate by understanding after rejecting them is another. That light has shown these and other similarly certain things to your inward eyes.

What, then, is the reason why you cannot see [Col. 0934D] that light itself with a fixed gaze, except weakness? And what caused that weakness in you, except iniquity? Who, then, heals all your diseases except the one who shows mercy toward all your iniquities?

## CHAPTER CCLIII. That all teaching concerns either things or signs, and that the thing to be enjoyed is the Trinity, God; from the book *On Christian Doctrine*

All teaching concerns either things or signs; but things are learned through signs. Here I have properly called [Col. 0935A] “things” those that are not employed to signify something, such as wood, stone, an animal, and other things of this kind—not, however, that wood which we read Moses placed in the bitter waters so that they might lose their bitterness, nor that stone which Jacob placed beneath his head, nor that animal which Abraham sacrificed in place of his son. These are indeed things, but they are also signs of other things.

There are other signs whose entire use consists in signifying, such as words. No one uses words except in order to signify something. From this it is understood what I call signs: namely, things employed to signify something. Therefore every sign is also a thing; for what is no thing is absolutely nothing. But not every thing is also a sign.

Thus, in this division between things and signs, [Col. 0935B] when we speak of things, we speak in such a way that, even if some of them can be employed to signify something, they do not disrupt the division by which we first discussed things and afterward signs. We should remember that, in the case of things, what must now be considered is what they are, not what else they signify besides themselves.

Some things, then, are to be enjoyed; others are to be used; and others both enjoy and use. Those that are to be enjoyed make us blessed. By those that are to be used we are assisted and, as it were, supported as we strive toward blessedness, so that we may reach and cling to those things that make us blessed.

We, who both enjoy and use, are placed between the two. If we wish to enjoy those things that are to be used, our [Col. 0935C] course is impeded and sometimes even diverted, so that, hindered by love of inferior things, we are delayed or even recalled from obtaining those things that are to be enjoyed.

To enjoy is to cling to something in love for its own sake. To use is to refer what has come into use to the attainment of what is loved, provided that it ought to be loved. For illicit use should rather be called misuse or abuse.

Suppose, then, that we were travelers who could live happily only in our homeland, and that we were miserable in our traveling and desired to end our misery by returning home. We would need either land or sea vehicles, which we would use in order to reach the homeland that was to be enjoyed. But if the pleasantness of the journey and the movement of the vehicles themselves delighted us, and we turned toward enjoying the things we ought to have used, we would not want to bring the journey quickly to an end. Entangled in a perverse pleasure, we would be alienated from our homeland, whose sweetness would make us blessed.

So, in this life of mortality, [Col. 0935D] while traveling away from the Lord, if we wish to return to our homeland, where we can be blessed, we must use this world, not enjoy it, so that “the invisible things of God, being understood through the things that have been made, may be seen”—that is, so that from bodily and temporal things we may grasp the eternal and spiritual.

The things, therefore, that are to be enjoyed are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—the same Trinity, one supreme thing common to all who enjoy it, if indeed it is a “thing,” and not rather the cause of all things, if indeed it is also a cause. It is not easy to find a name appropriate to such excellence, except that it is better said in this way: this Trinity is one God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things [Col. 0936A].

Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each God, and together they are one God; each of them is complete substance, and together they are one substance. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. The Father is only Father, the Son only Son, and the Holy Spirit only Holy Spirit.

The three have the same eternity, the same immutability, the same majesty, and the same power. In the Father there is unity, in the Son equality, and in the Holy Spirit the concord of unity and equality. These three are one: all are equal because of the Father, all are joined because of the Son, and all are one because of the Holy Spirit.

Have we said or uttered anything worthy of God? Indeed, I feel that I have intended to say nothing else. But [Col. 0936B] if I did say something, it is not what I intended to say. How do I know this except because God is ineffable? Yet what has been said by me, if it were ineffable, would not have been said. Accordingly, God cannot even be called ineffable, because when this is said, something is said, and there arises a kind of conflict of words: if that is ineffable which cannot be said, then that which can even be called ineffable is not ineffable.

This conflict of words should be avoided by silence rather than settled by speech. Yet although nothing worthy can be said about God, he has accepted the service of the human voice and has willed that we rejoice in his praise through our words. This is also why he is called “God.” He is not truly known in the sound of these two syllables, but nevertheless, whenever this sound reaches the ears of those who know the Latin language, it moves them to think of an exceedingly exalted and immortal nature [Col. 0936C].

For when the one God of gods is thought of—even by those who imagine, invoke, and worship other gods, whether in heaven or on earth—he is thought of in such a way that their thought attempts to reach something than which nothing better or higher exists.

## CHAPTER CCLIV. On the purification of the mind for enjoying that light which, while offering itself to us as the way, was foolishly thought by the proud to have acted as a human being, caring for opposites and likenesses; from the same book, book I

Since, therefore, we must enjoy that truth which lives immutably, and since in it the Trinity, God, is the author and creator of the universe and provides for the things it created, the mind must be purified, so that it may both perceive [Col. 0936D] that light and cling to it once perceived.

We should regard this purification as a kind of walking and, as it were, a voyage to our homeland. We do not move toward the one who is present everywhere by distances of place, but by good purpose and good conduct. We could not do this unless Wisdom itself deigned to accommodate itself to our great weakness and gave us an example of how to live, in no other way than in a human being, since we too are human.

But when we come to Wisdom, we act wisely; when Wisdom comes to us, it is thought by proud human beings to have acted foolishly. When we come to Wisdom, we recover strength; when Wisdom comes to us, it is regarded as weak. Yet “the foolishness of God is wiser [Col. 0937A] than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.”

Since Wisdom itself is our homeland, it also made itself the way to our homeland. And although it is everywhere present to a sound and pure inner eye, it deigned to appear even to the bodily eyes of those whose inner eye was weak and unclean.

Because the world could not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God “through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.” It is therefore not by coming across distances of place, but by appearing in mortal flesh to mortals, that he is said to have come to us. He came to where he already was, because he was in this world, and the world was made through him.

But because human beings, shaped by the desire to enjoy the creature in place of the Creator, were conformed to this world and most appropriately called by the world’s name, they [Col. 0937B] did not know him. Therefore the evangelist said: “And the world did not know him.” Thus the world could not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God. Why, then, did he come when he was already here? Because it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

How did he come? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” When we speak, what we hold in our mind enters the mind of the hearer through bodily ears. The word we carry in our heart becomes sound and is called speech. Yet our thought is not converted into that same sound; remaining whole within itself, it assumes the form of a voice by which it may enter the ears without any corruption through alteration.

So the Word of God, without being changed, nevertheless became flesh so that he might dwell among us. And just as [Col. 0937C] treatment is a way to health, so this treatment undertook to heal and restore sinners.

As physicians, when they bind wounds, do so not disorderly but appropriately, so that a certain beauty may also accompany the usefulness of the bandage, so the medicine of Wisdom, through assuming humanity, was adapted to our wounds, healing some by opposites and others by likenesses.

When someone treats a bodily wound, he applies certain opposites—for example, something cold to something hot, or something dry to something moist, or something else of that kind. He also applies certain likenesses, such as a piece of linen, or something round to a round wound, or something oblong to an oblong wound; and he fits the bandage itself not identically to every member but similarly to similar members.

So the Wisdom of God, healing the human being, presented itself for healing: itself [Col. 0937D] the physician, itself the medicine. Since the human being fell through pride, Wisdom applied humility for healing. We were deceived by the serpent’s wisdom; we are freed by the foolishness of God.

Just as that wisdom was called wisdom but was foolishness to those who despised God, so what is called foolishness is wisdom to those who conquer the devil. We misused immortality so as to die; Christ used mortality well so that we might live. Disease entered through the woman’s corrupted soul; salvation proceeded through the woman’s intact body.

To the same class of opposites belongs the fact that our vices are healed even by the example of Christ’s virtues. The likenesses applied as bandages to our members and wounds are these: [Col. 0938A] the man born through a woman freed human beings deceived through a woman; being mortal, he freed mortals; and through death, the dead.

## CHAPTER CCLV. Whether a human being ought to enjoy or use himself, and concerning the divinely established rule of love; from the same book

There is a major question whether human beings ought to enjoy themselves, use themselves, or do both. We have been commanded to love one another. But the question is whether a human being ought to be loved for his own sake or for the sake of something else. If for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for the sake of something else, we use him.

It seems to me, however, that he must be loved for the sake of something else. For that in which the blessed life is established is to be loved for its own sake. Even if its reality is not yet present, its hope consoles us in the present age. “Cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being.”

Nor ought anyone to enjoy himself, if you observe clearly [Col. 0938B] that he ought not to love himself for his own sake, but for the sake of that [thing] which is to be enjoyed. A human being is best when his entire life proceeds toward immutable life and he clings to it with his whole affection. But if he loves himself for his own sake, he does not refer himself to God; turning toward himself, he does not turn toward anything immutable. Therefore, with some defect, he already enjoys himself, since he is better when he clings and binds himself wholly to the immutable good than when he relaxes from it even toward himself.

If, then, you ought not to love yourself for your own sake but for the sake of that [thing] in which the most rightful end of your love lies, another human being should not be angry if you love him also for God’s sake. This is the divinely established rule of love: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” he says, but God “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” so that you may direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your entire understanding toward him, from whom you have the very things you direct [Col. 0938C] toward him.

When he says “with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind,” he leaves no part of our life that ought to be vacant and, as it were, make room for us to wish to enjoy another thing. Whatever else comes into the mind to be loved must be carried there where the whole force of love is running.

Whoever therefore rightly loves his neighbor ought to act with him so that he too may love the Lord God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind. For by loving him as himself, he refers all love of himself and of the other person to [Col. 0938D] that love of God, which permits no stream to be drawn away from it and diminished by diversion.

Not everything that is to be used should be loved, but only those things that either, through some fellowship with us, are referred together with us to God—such as a human being or an angel—or, when referred to us, need God’s beneficence through us, such as the body. The martyrs certainly did not love the crime of their persecutors, although they used it to gain God’s favor.

## CHAPTER CCLVI. 43. On the four things that are to be loved, on the necessity of having an ordered love, and on providing for those joined to us by circumstance; from the same book

Since, then, four things are to be loved—one that is above us, another that we are, a third that is beside us [Col. 0939A] and a fourth that is beneath us—no commands needed to be given concerning the second and fourth. However far a human being departs from the truth, love of himself and love of his body remain in him.

The fugitive soul acts so as to rule itself and its body, rather than be ruled by the immutable light that rules all things. Therefore it cannot help loving both itself and its body. It considers itself to have achieved something great if it can also dominate its companions, that is, other human beings. For in a vicious soul there is a desire to seek more and to claim for itself, as though owed to it, what belongs properly to God alone.

Such love of oneself is better called hatred. It is unjust, because a person wants what is beneath him to serve him, while he himself refuses to serve what is above him. It is therefore rightly said: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” [Col. 0939B]. Thus the soul becomes weak and is tormented by the mortal body. It must love the body and be weighed down by its corruption.

The body’s immortality and incorruption arise from the soul’s health. The health of the soul consists in clinging most firmly to what is superior, namely, the immutable God. But when a person also desires to dominate those who are naturally his equals, that is, human beings, it is utterly intolerable pride.

No one therefore hates himself; on this point there has been no controversy with any sect. Nor does anyone hate his own body. The Apostle is right when he says: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” And those who say that they would prefer to be entirely without a body are completely mistaken. They do not hate their body but its corruptions and burden.

They do not therefore wish to have no body at all, but an incorrupt and exceedingly swift [entirely sound] [Col. 0939C] body. They think that if it were such, it would not be a body, because they think that the soul is something of this kind.

As for those who appear to pursue their bodies through abstinence and labors, if they do this rightly, they do not act so as not to have a body, but so that they may have one subjected and ready for necessary works. They seek to extinguish desires that misuse the body—that is, habits and inclinations of the soul toward enjoying inward things—through a kind of laborious service of the body.

They do not meanwhile kill themselves but take care of their health. Those who do it perversely, however, wage war against their body as though it were a natural enemy. They are deceived by what they read: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other.”

This [Col. 0939D] is said concerning an unruly carnal habit, against which the spirit desires—not in order to destroy the body, but so that, once its desire, that is, its evil habit, has been subdued, it may make the body subject to the spirit, as the natural order requires.

After the resurrection the body will be wholly subject to the spirit in supreme tranquility and will live immortally. This must also be practiced in the present life, so that the carnal habit may be changed for the better and no longer resist the spirit with disordered movements.

Until this occurs, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh”: the spirit does not resist through hatred but through authority, because it wishes what it loves to be subject to what is better; nor does the flesh resist through hatred, but through the bond of habit, which has grown old through the propagation of our ancestors and has taken root by the law of nature.

The spirit therefore acts in subduing [Col. 0940A] the flesh so as to dissolve the evil habit’s quasi-perverse agreements and bring about the peace of a good habit.

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend.” The end of the commandment, therefore, is love, and it is twofold: of God and of neighbor.

If you understand “yourself” as your whole self—that is, soul and body—and “your neighbor” as his whole self—that is, his soul and body, since a human being consists of soul and body—then no category of things to be loved has been omitted from these two commandments.

Since love of God comes first, and [Col. 0940B] the measure of this love is prescribed in such a way that all other things flow into it, nothing seems to have been said about love of yourself. But when it says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” love of yourself by yourself has also been included.

The person who lives rightly and devoutly is the one who is an accurate assessor of things. Such a person has an ordered love, so that he does not love what should not be loved, fail to love what should be loved, love more what should be loved less, love equally what should be loved either less or more, or love less or more what should be loved equally.

Every sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; and every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake. God, however, is [Col. 0940C] to be loved for his own sake, and God must be loved more than any human being.

Everyone ought to love God more than himself. Likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our body, because all these things must be loved for God’s sake. Another human being can enjoy God together with us, but the body cannot, since the body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God.

Everyone is to be loved equally. But since you cannot benefit everyone, you must especially provide for those who, because of the circumstances of place, time, or any other matter, are more closely joined to you, as though by lot.

For if you had an abundance of something that ought to be given to someone who lacked it, but it could not be given to two people, and two persons came to you, neither of whom surpassed the other either in need or in some relationship to you, you could do nothing more just than [Col. 0940D] choose by lot to whom what could not be given to both should be given.

So, among human beings whom you cannot benefit all alike, you should regard it as a matter of lot, according to how closely each person happens at that time to be attached to you.

Among all those who can enjoy God with us, some we love because we help them; some because they help us; some because we both need their help and assist them in their need; and some because we neither confer any advantage upon them nor expect them to confer one upon us.

Nevertheless, we ought to wish that all should love God with us, and everything by which we help them or are helped by them must be referred to that one end.

## CHAPTER CCLVII. [Col. 0941A] 44. On the beginning of the ways according to Solomon; from the same book
When you enjoy a human being in God, enjoy God rather than the human being; for you enjoy the one by whom you are made blessed, and you will rejoice that you have reached the one in whom you place your hope of arriving. Hence Paul says to Philemon: “Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord.” If he had not added “in the Lord,” but had merely said, “Let me enjoy you,” he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him.

Although *frui* is also used in a closely related sense for “to use with love” [and, conversely, for “to use with delight”], whenever what is loved is present, it necessarily brings delight with it. If you pass through that delight and refer it to the thing in which one ought to remain, you use it, and are said to enjoy it only abusively, not properly. But if you cleave to it and remain in it, placing the end of your happiness in it, then you are said to enjoy it truly and properly. This must be done only in that Trinity—that is, in the supreme and unchangeable Good.

See how, when Truth itself and the Word through whom all things were made nevertheless became flesh so that he might dwell among us, the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way.” For he who wished to offer himself not only as the possession of those arriving, but also as the way for those coming, wished to assume flesh as the beginning of the ways.

Hence there is also the saying: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways,” so that those who wished to come might begin from there. Therefore the Apostle, although he was still walking on the way and following God, who called him, toward the prize of the heavenly calling, had nevertheless already passed beyond the beginning of the ways: forgetting what lay behind and stretching forward to what lay ahead, he no longer needed that from which the journey must nevertheless be undertaken and begun by all who desire to reach the truth and remain in eternal life. For he says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” That is: through me one comes; to me one arrives; in me one remains.

When one arrives at him himself [one also arrives at the Father himself], because the one who is equal to him is recognized through the Equal One, with the Holy Spirit binding and, as it were, gluing us together, so that we may remain in the supreme and unchangeable Good.

From this it is understood that no thing ought to hold us on the way, because even the Lord himself, insofar as he deigned to be our way, did not wish to hold us fast, but to have us pass through, lest we cling weakly to temporal things, although they were undertaken and accomplished by him for our salvation. Rather, we should hasten eagerly through them, so that we may deserve to be carried onward and arrive at that very one who freed our nature from temporal things and placed it at the right hand of the Father.

Of all the matters mentioned above, then, since we are dealing with things, this is the final conclusion: the fullness and end of the Law and of all the divine Scriptures is to be understood as the love of the thing that is to be enjoyed, and of the thing that can enjoy that same thing with us. For no command is needed in order that each person love himself.

Therefore, so that we might know and be capable of this, the whole temporal dispensation was established through divine providence for our salvation. We ought to use it—not with the sort of abiding love and delight appropriate to a dwelling-place, but with a passing love, as one loves a road, vehicles, or any other instruments; or, if something more fitting can be said, we should love the things by which we are carried because of that to which we are being carried.

Whoever, then, thinks that he has understood the divine Scriptures, or any part of them, in such a way that this understanding does not build the twofold love of God and neighbor, has not yet understood them. But whoever draws from them a meaning useful for building this love, even if he does not say what the person whom he is reading can be shown to have intended in that passage, is not deceived in a harmful way, nor is he altogether lying.

For the person who lies has within him the will to say what is false. Hence we find many who wish to lie, but no one who wishes to be deceived. Since a person knowingly does the one and unknowingly suffers the other, it is sufficiently clear that, in one and the same matter, the person who is deceived is better than the person who lies, since it is better to suffer injustice than to commit it.

Everyone who lies, however, acts unjustly. If it seems to anyone that a lie is sometimes useful, it may also seem that injustice is sometimes useful. For no one who lies keeps faith in the very matter about which he lies: he wants the person to whom he is lying to trust him, yet by lying to him he does not keep faith with him. But every violator of faith is unjust. Either, then, injustice is sometimes useful—which cannot be—or a lie is always useless.

Whoever, however, perceives in the Scriptures something other than the person who wrote them without lying is deceived. Nevertheless, as I began to say, if he is deceived in a meaning by which he builds love, which is the end of the commandment, he is deceived as someone would be who, leaving the road through error, nevertheless went across the field to the same destination to which that road leads.

He must still be corrected, and it must be shown how useful it is not to leave the road, lest through the habit of straying he be compelled to go even farther across or astray. For by rashly asserting that the person whom he is reading did not mean what he says, he often runs into other matters that he cannot connect with that interpretation. If he agrees that these are true and certain, then what he had understood cannot be true; and somehow it happens that, by loving his own interpretation, he begins to be more offended by Scripture than by himself.

If this evil is allowed to spread, it will overthrow him. For “we walk by faith, not by sight.” But faith will falter if the authority of the divine Scriptures wavers. When faith falters, love itself also grows weak. For if someone falls away from faith, he must also fall away from love. He cannot love what he does not believe to exist. But if he both believes and loves, living rightly and obeying the precepts of good conduct, he brings it about that he also hopes to reach what he loves.

## CHAPTER CCLVIII

That when faith and hope depart, love remains; that a temporal thing becomes worthless when it arrives, whereas an eternal thing is loved more ardently; from the same book.

These, then, are the three things in whose service all knowledge and prophecy stand: faith, hope, and love. Faith is succeeded by sight, which we shall see; hope is succeeded by blessedness itself, which we shall attain. But love will rather increase when those two depart.

For if by believing we love what we do not yet see, how much more will we love it when we begin to see it? And if by hoping we love that which we have not yet reached, how much more will we love it when we have reached it?

There is this difference between temporal and eternal things: a temporal thing is loved more before it is possessed, but becomes worthless when it arrives, for it does not satisfy the soul when eternity is its true and certain dwelling-place. An eternal thing, however, is loved more ardently once attained than while desired.

No one who desires it is permitted to think more highly of it than it actually is, so that it becomes worthless to him when he finds less than he expected. Rather, as much as each person is able to expect while coming toward it, so much more will he find upon arriving.

A person, then, supported by faith, hope, and love, and holding them unshakably, does not need the Scriptures except for instructing others. Thus many people, through these three things, live even in solitude without books. In them, I think, what was said has already been fulfilled: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished [destroyed].”

Through these things, as through instruments, such an edifice of faith, hope, and love has arisen in them that, possessing something perfect, they do not seek what exists only in part. Perfect, indeed, insofar as this life permits; for in comparison with the life to come, the life of no just or holy person here is perfect.

“Faith, hope, and love, these three remain,” he says; “but the greatest of these is love,” because when each person has reached eternal things, with those two departing, love will remain more abundant and more certain.

Therefore, when someone has recognized that the end of the commandment is love “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith,” he should approach the interpretation of all the divine Scriptures confidently, referring every understanding to these three things.

When he said “love,” he added “from a pure heart,” so that nothing other than what ought to be loved might be loved. He then added “a good conscience” because of hope: the person in whom there is the scruple of a bad conscience despairs of reaching what he believes and loves.

Third, he says, “and an unfeigned faith.” For if our faith is free from falsehood, then we neither love what ought not to be loved nor, by living rightly, hope that our hope will in any way be deceived.

## CHAPTER CCLIX

Natural and given signs; from Book II of *On Christian Teaching*.

When I was writing about things, I first warned that no one should attend to anything in them except what they are, and not also to whether they signify something else besides themselves. Conversely, when discussing signs, I say that no one should attend to what they are, but rather to the fact that they are signs—that is, to what they signify.

A sign is a thing which, besides the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into thought from itself. Thus, when we see a footprint, we think that the animal whose footprint it is has passed by; when we see smoke, we recognize that fire lies beneath it; when we hear the voice of a living creature, we perceive the state of its mind; and when a trumpet sounds, soldiers know that they ought either to advance or to retreat, or to do whatever else the battle requires.

Some signs, then, are natural and others given. Natural signs are those which, without any will or desire to signify, cause something other than themselves to be known from themselves. Such is smoke, signifying fire. It does not do this because it wishes to signify fire; rather, by observing and noting experienced things, one recognizes that fire lies beneath it, even if only smoke is visible.

The footprint of a passing living creature also belongs to this category. Likewise, the face of an angry or sorrowful person signifies a state of mind, even without the will of the person who is angry or sorrowful; or, if some other movement of the mind is revealed by the face as its indicator, it is revealed even though we are not acting in order to reveal it.

Given signs, on the other hand, are those which living beings give to one another in order to display, as far as they can, the movements of their minds, or any sensations or thoughts they may have. We have no reason for signifying—that is, for giving a sign—except to bring forth and transfer into another’s mind what the person giving the sign has in his own mind.

We have therefore decided to examine and discuss this kind of sign insofar as human beings are concerned, since the signs given by God, which are contained in the holy Scriptures, were made known to us through human beings who wrote them down.

## CHAPTER CCLX

That among all signs words hold the chief place, but that, because of the sin of pride, they could not be common to all nations; from the same book.

All signs are very few in comparison with words. Words have plainly gained primacy among human beings for signifying whatever is conceived in the mind, if a person wishes to reveal it.

The Lord also gave a sign through the fragrance of the ointment with which his feet were anointed; by the sacrament of his body and blood, tasted beforehand, he signified what he wished; and when the woman was healed by touching the fringe of his garment, that too signified something.

But the countless multitude of signs by which human beings express their thoughts is constituted in words. For I could state in words all those signs whose kinds I have briefly touched upon, whereas I could in no way state words through those signs. But because spoken sounds pass away immediately when the air has been struck, and remain no longer than they are sounding, signs of words were established through letters.

Thus voices are displayed to the eyes, not in themselves, but through certain signs belonging to them.

These signs, then, could not be common to all nations because of a certain sin arising from human discord, when each person seizes primacy for himself. The sign of that pride is the tower raised toward heaven, where the impious were made to have not only discordant minds but also discordant voices.

As a result, the divine Scripture—which relieves such great diseases of human wills—originated in one language, through which it could suitably be spread throughout the world, but became known among the nations by being disseminated far and wide through the various languages of translators for their salvation. Those who read it seek nothing else than to discover the thoughts and will of those by whom it was written, and through them the will of God, according to which we believe such people spoke.

But people are deceived by many and varied obscurities and ambiguities when they read rashly, understanding one thing in place of another. In some passages they cannot even discover what they might suspect falsely, so dense a darkness covers certain obscure statements.

I do not doubt that all this was divinely provided in order to humble pride through labor and to recall the intellect from boredom. For things easily discovered generally become worthless to the mind.

## CHAPTER CCLXI

That Scripture, through a certain likeness, more sweetly stirs the mind; for example, the passage from the *Song of Songs*: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep”; from the same book.

What is it, I ask, that makes this less pleasing to a listener? Suppose someone says that holy and perfect persons are those by whose life and conduct the Church of Christ cuts away from every kind of superstition those who come to her and, through imitation of the good, incorporates them into herself, as it were; that these good faithful persons and true servants of God, laying down the burdens of the world, came to the holy washing of baptism, and then, rising from it through the conception of the Holy Spirit, brought forth the fruit of the twofold love—that is, love of God and neighbor.

What is it, then, that makes this less pleasing to a listener than when someone expounds the passage in the *Song of Songs* with the same meaning, where the Church is addressed, when she is praised as a beautiful woman:

“Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren”?

Does a person learn anything different from this than he would learn if he heard the same thing in the clearest words, without the aid of this likeness? And yet, somehow, I look upon the saints with greater sweetness when I see them as the teeth of the Church, as it were: cutting people away from their errors and transferring them into her body, their hardness softened, as though they had been bitten and chewed.

I also recognize most joyfully the sheep shorn of the burdens of the world, as though they had laid aside their fleeces, ascending from the washing—that is, from baptism—and all producing twins: the two commandments of love. I see that none is barren of this holy fruit.

But why I should see this more sweetly than if no such likeness had been drawn from the divine books, although the thing and the knowledge are the same, is difficult to say, and is another question.

For now, however, no one doubts that things are more willingly learned through likenesses, and that what has been sought with some difficulty is found much more gratifyingly. Those who do not find at all what they seek suffer hunger; those who do not seek because they have things readily available often waste away through boredom. In both conditions, weakness must be avoided.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, has arranged the holy Scriptures magnificently and beneficially, so that in their clearer passages he might meet hunger, while in their obscurer passages he might wipe away boredom. For scarcely anything is drawn from those obscurities that is not found stated with complete clarity elsewhere.

Above all, therefore, it is necessary to be converted by the fear of God, in order to learn his will and what he commands us to desire and to avoid. This fear must necessarily bring to mind our mortality and future death, and, as though our flesh had been nailed down, fasten every movement of pride to the wood of the cross.

Next, one must be softened by piety and must not contradict Scripture, whether it is understood and strikes at some of our faults, or is not understood, as though we could know better and give better commands than it. Rather, we must think and believe that what is written there is better and truer, even if it remains hidden, than anything we can know through ourselves.

After these two stages—fear and piety—one comes to the third stage, that of knowledge, which I have now begun to discuss. Every student of the divine Scriptures exercises himself in this stage, finding nothing in them other than that God must be loved for God’s sake, and the neighbor for God’s sake; God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; and the neighbor as oneself—that is, so that the whole love of the neighbor, just as our own love, may be referred to God.

We treated these two commandments in the preceding book when we were discussing things.

It is therefore necessary first for each person to discover in the Scriptures that he is entangled in love of this world—that is, of temporal things—and is far removed from such love of God and such love of neighbor as Scripture itself prescribes. Then the fear by which he thinks about God’s judgment, and the piety by which he can do nothing but believe and yield to the authority of the holy books, compel him to mourn for himself.

For this knowledge makes a person of good hope not boastful but sorrowful. Through this disposition he obtains, by persistent prayers, the consolation of divine assistance, so that he is not broken by despair.

## CHAPTER CCLXII

Concerning proper and transferred signs: the example that “ox” properly indicates an animal, but by transfer indicates an Evangelist; from the same book.

What is written is not understood for two reasons: either it is concealed by unfamiliar signs or by ambiguous signs.

Signs are either proper or transferred. They are called proper when they are employed to signify the things for which they were established. Thus, when we say “ox,” we understand an animal, which all speakers of the Latin language among us call by this name.

They are transferred when the things themselves that we signify by their proper words are used to signify something else. Thus, we say “ox,” and by these two syllables we understand the animal that is customarily called by this name; but then, through that animal, we understand an Evangelist, whom Scripture signified when the Apostle interpreted it [saying]: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.”

## CHAPTER CCLXIII

Concerning ignorance of things, which makes figurative expressions obscure when we are ignorant of the natures of animals, stones, plants, or other things; from the same book.

Ignorance of things makes figurative expressions obscure when we are ignorant of the natures of animals, stones, plants, or other things that are often placed in Scripture for the sake of some likeness.

Consider what is known about the serpent: when attacked, it exposes its whole body while protecting its head. How greatly this illuminates the meaning of the Lord’s command that we should be clever as serpents! We should offer our body to our persecutors in place of our head, which is Christ, lest Christian faith be denied in us, as though the head were killed, if we spare the body and deny God.

Or consider the serpent which, constricted by the narrowness of a cave, is said to shed its old skin and receive new strength. How well this agrees with imitating the serpent’s cleverness and stripping off the old person, as the Apostle says, so that we may put on the new; and with stripping him off through narrow passages, as the Lord says: “Enter through the narrow gate.”

Thus knowledge of the serpent’s nature illuminates the many likenesses that Scripture customarily draws from this creature. In the same way, ignorance of certain animals, which Scripture likewise frequently mentions through likenesses, greatly obstructs the understanding. The same is true of stones, plants, and whatever else is held by roots.

Knowledge of the carbuncle, which shines in darkness, illuminates many obscure passages of books wherever it is used because of a likeness. Ignorance of the beryl or the diamond, however, often closes the doors of understanding.

There is no other reason why it is easy to understand that the olive branch carried by the dove returning to the ark signifies perpetual peace, except that we know both that the gentle touch of oil is not easily spoiled by another liquid and that the tree itself remains perpetually green.

Many people, however, because they are ignorant of hyssop and do not know what power it has either for cleansing the lungs or, as is said, for penetrating rocks with its roots, cannot understand at all why it is said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.”

## 47 CHAPTER CCLXIV

Concerning ignorance of numbers, which causes many things not to be understood; from the same book.

Ignorance of numbers also causes many things placed figuratively and mystically in the Scriptures not to be understood. A naturally gifted mind, so to speak, cannot help being moved by the question of what it means that Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for forty days. The figurative knot of this action cannot be untied without knowledge and consideration of this number.

For forty contains four times ten, as though the knowledge of all things were woven into the cycles of time. The cycles of days and years are completed through the number four: daily cycles through the periods of morning, midday, evening, and night; yearly cycles through the months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Since we live in time, we must abstain and fast from delight in temporal things for the sake of eternity, in which we wish to live. Even the course of time itself impresses upon us the teaching that temporal things are to be despised and eternal things desired.

Moreover, the number ten signifies the knowledge of the Creator and creation. The Trinity is the Creator, while the number seven indicates creation, because of life and body. For life too has three parts, which is why God is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; while in the body four elements are most clearly apparent, from which it is constituted.

Thus, in this number ten, as it is disclosed to us temporally—that is, multiplied by four—we are instructed to live chastely and continently, abstaining from delight in temporal things. This is what it means to fast for forty days [we are instructed]. The Law, represented by Moses, teaches this; prophecy, represented by Elijah, teaches it; and the Lord himself teaches it. As though he had testimony from the Law and the Prophets, he appeared between them on the mountain, while three disciples looked on in amazement.

Next it is asked how the number fifty arises from the number forty, a number that is not lightly sacred in our religion because of Pentecost; and how, when it is multiplied by three—because of the three periods, before the Law, under the Law, and under grace, or because of the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and when the Trinity itself is added in a more exalted way, it may refer to the mystery of the most purified Church and arrive at the hundred and fifty-three fish which the nets, cast toward the right side after the Lord’s resurrection, began to enclose.

Thus, through many other forms and patterns of numbers, certain likenesses are placed secretly in the holy books; because of ignorance of numbers, they remain closed to readers.

## CHAPTER CCLXV

Concerning ignorance of musical matters; from the same book.

Ignorance of certain musical matters also closes and conceals not a few things. The distinction between the psaltery and the lyre has indeed disclosed some figures of things not without harmony. And among learned people it is reasonably asked whether the ten-stringed psaltery has some musical law that requires so great a number of strings.

Or, if it does not, whether the number itself should for that very reason be received as more sacred, perhaps because of the Decalogue of the Law. If this number too is investigated, it must be referred only to the Creator and creation, or to the number ten itself, as explained above.

That number associated with the building of the temple, when it is mentioned in the Gospel—namely, forty-six years—seems to sound with some musical significance. When it is referred to the construction of the Lord’s body, for which reason the temple was mentioned, it compels certain heretics to confess that the Son of God was clothed not falsely but truly in a human body.

We find that both number and music are honorably placed in many passages of the holy Scriptures. We must not listen to the errors of pagan superstitions, which invented nine Muses as the daughters of Jupiter and Memory. Varro refutes them, and I do not know whether anyone among them could be more learned or more curious about such matters.

He says that some city—I do not remember its name—commissioned three craftsmen to make three statues of the Muses each, intending to place them as a gift in the temple of Apollo. Whoever among the craftsmen had made the more beautiful figures, the city would buy those from him in preference to the others.

It happened that the works of all three craftsmen were equally beautiful and pleased the city, so that all nine were purchased and dedicated in Apollo’s temple. Varro says that the poet Hesiod later supplied them with names.

Jupiter, therefore, did not beget nine Muses; three craftsmen created three each. And the city had not commissioned three craftsmen because it had seen the Muses in dreams, or because all of them had displayed themselves to the eyes of someone. Rather, it was easy to recognize that every sound, which is the material of songs, has a threefold nature.

Sound is produced either by the voice, as in those who sing with their throats without an instrument; or by breath, as in trumpets and flutes; or by percussion, as in lyres and drums and all other instruments that produce sound through striking.

But whether what Varro reported is so or not, we must not, because of the superstition of the profane, flee from music if we are able to seize from it anything useful for understanding the holy Scriptures. Nor, if we discuss something about lyres and instruments that can assist in grasping spiritual matters, should we turn toward their theatrical frivolities.

We should not refuse to learn letters merely because the pagans say that Mercury is their god, or because they dedicated temples to Justice and Virtue and preferred to worship in stones what ought to be carried in the heart. For that reason we must not flee justice and virtue.

Indeed, whoever is a good and true Christian should understand that the truth belongs to his Lord wherever he finds it. By gathering it together and recognizing it, he should reject even in the sacred writings the superstitious fictions, and should grieve over and beware of those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God, and so forth.

## CHAPTER CCLXVI

Concerning the signs of superstition, by which fellowship with demons is perniciously acquired; from the same book.

There are two kinds of disciplines practiced even among pagan peoples: one concerned with things established by human beings; the other with things they have observed as already accomplished or divinely established.

That which belongs to human institutions is partly superstitious and partly not. Superstitious is whatever has been instituted by human beings for making and worshiping idols, or for worshiping as God a creature or any part of a creature, or for consultations and certain agreements concerning signs made and ratified with demons—such as the devices of magical arts, which poets are accustomed rather to mention than to teach [Col. 0949D]. Of this kind, though in a somewhat more permissibly foolish form, are the books of haruspices and augurs.

To this class also belong all amulets and remedies condemned even by the medical profession, whether in incantations, or in certain marks called characters, or in hanging and tying various objects, or even in dancing them about in some fashion—not for regulating bodies, but for certain signs, either hidden or even manifest, which they call “natural” by a milder name, so that they may seem not to involve superstition but to provide benefit through nature. Such are earrings worn at the upper part of each ear; little rings made from [ostrich] bones and placed on the fingers; or when someone tells a person suffering from hiccups to hold the left thumb with the right hand.

To these are added thousands of utterly empty observances: if some limb has twitched; if, while friends are walking together, a stone, a dog, or a child passes between them; and the belief that stepping on a stone—as though it were a breaker [or plunderer] of friendship—is less troublesome than striking an innocent child on the cheek when he happens to pass between people walking together. Yet it is amusing that children are sometimes defended against dogs; for some people are so superstitious that they even dare to strike a dog that has passed between them—and not without punishment. For, as a result of this useless remedy, the dog sometimes quickly sends its striker to a real physician.

These too belong to the same category: stepping on the threshold when passing in front of one’s own house; returning to bed if someone sneezes while putting on his shoes; returning home if, while setting out, one stumbles; and, when clothing has been gnawed by mice, trembling more at the suspicion of future harm than grieving over the present damage.

Hence Cato’s witty saying: when a certain man consulted him and said that mice had gnawed his shoes, he replied that this was not a portent, but that it would truly have been a portent if mice had been gnawed by the shoes.

Nor should those who are called genethliaci—now commonly called “mathematicians,” because of their consideration of birth dates—be separated from this kind of pernicious superstition. These opinions, therefore, which are based on certain signs of things established by human presumption, must also be referred to those same supposed agreements and compacts with demons.

For this is why, by some hidden divine judgment, people greedy for evil things are handed over, according to the deserts of their desires, to be mocked and deceived—mocked and deceived by transgressing angels, to whom this lowest part of the world has been subjected, according to the most beautiful order of things, by the law of divine providence.
