Through these illusions and deceptions it happens that, by these superstitious and pernicious forms of divination, many things past and future are foretold, and events occur just as they are foretold; and many things happen to those who observe them in accordance with their observances. Entangled in these practices, they become more curious and insert themselves ever more deeply into the many snares of the most pernicious error.

Divine Scripture did not silently pass over this kind of fornication of the soul, nor did it deter the soul from it merely by denying that such things should be followed because their practitioners call them false. Rather, it also says: “If they tell you something, and it comes to pass, do not believe them.” For it is not the case that, because the image of the dead Samuel made a true prediction to King Saul, the sacrileges by which that image was presented are therefore less detestable; nor, because the ventriloquist woman in the Acts of the Apostles gave true testimony to the Lord’s apostles, did the apostle Paul spare that spirit, rather than cleanse the woman by expelling the demon that possessed her.

All such arts, therefore—whether belonging to foolish or harmful superstition—established through a certain pestilential fellowship between human beings and demons, like agreements of an unfaithful and deceitful friendship, must be wholly rejected [Col. 0951A] and shunned by a Christian. “Not that an idol is anything,” says the Apostle, “but because what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become partners with demons.”

What the Apostle said about idols and about sacrifices offered in their honor must also be understood of all imaginary signs that lead either to the worship of idols, or to the worship of a creature and its parts as God, or to the care of remedies and other observances. These things have not been divinely established for the love of God and neighbor as public institutions; rather, through private desires for temporal things, they scatter the hearts of miserable people.

In all these disciplines, therefore, the fellowship of demons must be feared and avoided. They seek nothing with their prince, the devil, except to close and bar our return [Col. 0951B].

Just as, concerning the stars that God created and ordered, human beings have established deceptive conjectures, so also concerning certain things that are born or that exist in any manner through the administration of divine providence, many people have committed to writing many conjectures based on human suspicions, as though these had been established according to a rule. This applies if unusual events occur—for example, if a mule gives birth or something is struck by lightning. All these things have only as much power as they have been bound, through the presumption of human minds, as though by a common language agreed upon with demons. Yet they are all full of pestilential curiosity, tormenting anxiety, and deadly servitude.

They were not noticed because they had power; rather, by noticing and marking them, people made them seem to have power. Therefore different things happen to different people, according to their thoughts and presumptions. Those spirits who wish to deceive arrange such things for each person according to the kinds of suspicions and agreements by which they see that person entangled.

For example, the single figure of the letter X, marked crosswise, has one meaning among the Greeks and another among the Latins—not by nature, but by the convention and agreement governing its meaning. Therefore someone who knows both languages, if he wishes to communicate something in writing to a Greek, does not use this letter with the meaning it has when he writes to a Latin. Likewise, βῆτα (*bēta*), with one and the same sound, is the name of a letter among the Greeks but the name of a vegetable among the Latins. And when I say *lege* (“read” or “choose”), a Greek understands one thing in these two syllables and a Latin another.

Therefore, just as all these signs move the minds of people according to the agreement of each community, and because the agreements differ they move them differently—and people did not agree upon them because they already possessed power to signify, but they possess power because people agreed upon them—so also those signs by which a pernicious fellowship with demons is acquired have power according to each person’s observances. This is most clearly shown by the practice of augurs, who, both before observing signs and after they have observed and secured them, take measures not to see the birds’ flights or hear their cries, because none of these are signs unless the observer’s agreement is added.

## CHAPTER CCLXVII [Col. 0952A]

### On knowledge of propositions, implications, definitions, divisions, and partitions; from the same book

There remain those matters that pertain not to the senses of the body but to the reasoning of the mind, where the disciplines of disputation and number hold sway.

The discipline of disputation is exceedingly useful for penetrating and resolving all kinds of questions found in the holy Scriptures. Only the desire to quarrel and a certain childish display of deceiving one’s opponent must be avoided.

There are many things called *σοφίσματα* (*sophismata*), false conclusions of reasoning, which often imitate the truth so closely that they deceive not only the slow-witted but even intelligent people who are insufficiently attentive.

Someone once proposed this argument to a person with whom he was speaking: “What I am, you are not.” The other agreed, for it was true in one respect—or at least true because the first man was crafty and the other simple. Then the first added: “But I am a human being.” When the other had also conceded this, he drew the conclusion: “Therefore you are not a human being.”

Scripture, I think, detests this kind of deceptive conclusion in the passage where it says: “One who speaks sophistically is hateful.” Although even speech that is not deceptive, but that pursues verbal ornament more abundantly than dignity permits, is called sophistic.

There are also genuinely valid implications whose propositions are false, and which follow from the error of the person with whom one is dealing. A good and learned person introduces such implications so that the person whose error they follow, becoming ashamed, may abandon that same error; for if he wishes to remain in it, he will necessarily be forced to retain even the propositions he condemns.

The Apostle was not asserting truth when he said: “Neither has Christ been raised,” followed by: “Our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty,” and then the other statements that are wholly false, since Christ has been raised, and the preaching of those who proclaimed this was not empty, nor was the faith of those who believed it. Yet these false statements followed with complete validity from the proposition that there is no resurrection of the dead. Once these false statements are rejected—for they would be true if the dead do not rise—it follows that there is a resurrection of the dead.

Since, therefore, implications can be valid not only when their propositions are true but also when they are false, it is easy to learn the truth of implications even in those schools that exist outside the Church. But the truth of propositions must be sought in the holy ecclesiastical books [Col. 0952D].

The truth of implications itself was not established by human beings; it was observed and recorded by them so that they might learn or teach it. For it exists perpetually in the order of things and has been divinely established.

Just as someone who narrates the order of times does not himself compose it, and someone who displays the positions of places or the natures of animals, plants [or serpents], or stones does not display things established by human beings; and just as someone who demonstrates the stars and their movements does not demonstrate something established by himself or by any human being—so also someone who says, when the consequent is false, that the antecedent must be false, speaks the truth. He does not make it so; he merely demonstrates that it is so.

This is the rule underlying the passage about the Apostle that we mentioned. The antecedent is: “There is no resurrection of the dead,” which was said by those whose error the Apostle wished to destroy. From that prior proposition—“There is no resurrection of the dead”—there necessarily follows: “Neither has Christ been raised.” But this consequent is false, for Christ has been raised. Therefore the antecedent is also false, namely: “There is no resurrection of the dead.” Therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.

The whole argument is expressed briefly as follows: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised. But Christ has been raised; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.”

That, by removing the consequent, the antecedent is also necessarily removed was not established by human beings; they merely demonstrated it. This rule concerns the truth of implications, not the truth of propositions.

In this case, however, since the discussion concerns the resurrection, both the rule of implication is true and the proposition reached in the conclusion is itself true.

In the case of false propositions, the truth of the implication works as follows. Suppose we grant that someone has said: “If a snail is an animal, it has a voice.” Once this has been granted, and once it has been proved that a snail does not have a voice, then, because removal of the consequent removes the antecedent, the conclusion follows: “A snail is not an animal.” This proposition is false, but, given the false premise, the implication of the conclusion is valid.

The truth of a proposition therefore has force in itself; the truth of an implication depends upon the opinion or concession of the person with whom one is dealing. As we said above, something false is introduced through a valid implication so that the person whose error we wish to correct may regret having conceded the antecedents whose consequent he sees must be rejected.

From this it is easy to understand that, just as true implications can arise from false propositions, false conclusions can also arise from true propositions.

Suppose, for example, that someone proposes: “If that man is just, he is good,” and this is conceded. Then he adds: “But he is not just,” which is also conceded, and draws the conclusion: “Therefore he is not good.” Although all these propositions may be true, the rule of the conclusion is not valid. For just as, when the consequent is removed, the antecedent is necessarily removed, so when the antecedent is removed the consequent is not necessarily removed.

It is true to say: “If he is an orator, he is a human being.” But if from this proposition we assume: “He is not an orator,” it does not follow that we may conclude: “Therefore he is not a human being.”

It is therefore one thing to know the rules of implications and another to know the truth of propositions. In the former one learns what follows, what does not follow, and what is contrary.

What follows is: “If he is an orator, he is a human being.”

What does not follow is: “If he is a human being, he is an orator.”

What is contrary is: “If he is a human being, he is a quadruped.”

Here, therefore, the implication itself is being judged. But in the truth of propositions, the propositions themselves must be considered in their own right, not their connection. When true and certain propositions are joined to uncertain propositions by a valid implication, the uncertain propositions must also become certain.

Some people boast when they have learned the truth of implications, as though they had thereby learned the truth of propositions themselves. Others, by contrast, often retain a true proposition but wrongly disparage themselves because they do not know the laws of conclusion.

The person who knows that there is a resurrection of the dead is better than the person who knows that, if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ been raised.

Likewise, the science of defining, dividing, and partitioning, although it is often applied to false things, is not itself false. Nor was it established by human beings; it was discovered in the order of things.

The fact that poets use it in their fictions, and false philosophers or heretics—that is, false Christians—in their erroneous opinions, does not make it false that, in defining, dividing, or partitioning, one must not include anything that does not belong to the matter itself, nor omit anything that does belong to it.

This remains true even if the things being defined or distributed are not true. For even falsehood itself is defined when we say that a falsehood is a signification of a thing that is not as it is signified, or something of that kind. This definition is true, although a falsehood itself cannot be true.

We can also divide falsehood by saying that there are two kinds of false things: one consisting of things that cannot exist at all; the other consisting of things that do not exist, although they could exist.

Someone who says that seven and three are eleven says something that cannot exist at all. But someone who says that it rained on the Calends of January, although it did not happen, says something that could have happened.

The definition and division of false things can therefore be completely true, although the false things themselves are certainly not true.

## CHAPTER CCLXVIII [Col. 0954C]

### That no one should boast about eloquence, which is employed not so that we may understand but so that we may express what we have understood; from the same book

There are also certain rules of more extensive disputation, which is now called eloquence. These rules are no less true, although falsehoods can also be made persuasive through them. Since they can also serve truth, the faculty itself is not blameworthy; the perversity of those who misuse it is.

For it was not established by human beings that an expression of charity should win over the listener, or that a brief and clear account should easily convey what it intends, or that variety should hold the attention without causing weariness, or that other observations of this kind should have their effect. These principles are true whether applied to false or true causes. Yet insofar as they cause something to be known or believed, or move the mind to seek or avoid something, they were discovered because they are so, rather than instituted so that they might be so.

When this branch of learning is studied, it should be employed more to express what has been understood than to produce understanding. The discipline of conclusions, definitions, and distributions, however, greatly assists understanding, provided that there is no error by which people imagine that, once they have learned these things, they have learned the truth of the blessed life.

It often happens that people more easily grasp the things for whose attainment these disciplines are learned than they grasp the extremely intricate and thorny rules of such instruction.

It is as if someone wishing to give instructions for walking should advise that the rear foot must not be lifted until the forward foot has been placed, and should then describe in minute detail how the joints and knees ought to move. He would be speaking truly, and walking cannot occur otherwise. Yet people more easily walk by doing these things than they notice them while doing them or understand them when hearing them explained. Those who cannot walk care even less about these matters, since they cannot attend to them through experience.

So, in many cases, an intelligent person recognizes more quickly that a conclusion is invalid than he grasps its rules. A dull person does not recognize the invalidity, and understands even less what is prescribed about it. In all these matters, the spectacles of truth themselves often give more pleasure than they provide assistance in disputing or judging—unless perhaps they make minds more practiced without making them more malicious or more inflated; that is, unless they lead people to delight in deceiving others through plausible speech and questioning, or to imagine that, by learning these things, they have attained something great by which they may place themselves above the good and innocent.

## CHAPTER CCLXIX

### That the discipline of number was not established by human beings but rather investigated and discovered, and that it should be referred to the praise of God, from whom truth comes; from the same book

The discipline of number makes it clear even to the dullest person that it was not established by human beings but rather investigated and discovered.

For it is not the case that, just as Virgil wished the first syllable of *Italia* to be pronounced short, and it thereby became short, someone can bring it about, whenever he wishes, that three times three is not nine, or that three times three cannot form a square figure, or that three times three is not triple in relation to the number three, sesquialterate in relation to six, and double in relation to no number—for intelligible number has no half.

Whether numbers are considered in themselves, or applied to the laws of figures, sounds, or other movements, they possess immutable rules. These rules were not established by human beings in any way; they were discovered by the insight of intelligent people.

Yet whoever loves all these things so much that he wishes to boast of himself among the unlearned, rather than seek the source of the truths whose truth he has merely perceived—and the source of certain things that are not only true but also immutable, whose immutability he has not grasped—and who, proceeding from the appearance of bodies to the human mind, finds that the mind itself is mutable, sometimes learned and sometimes unlearned, and yet, between the immutable truth above him and the mutable things beneath him, turns everything else toward the praise and love of the one God, from whom he knows all things to be—such a person may seem learned, but in no way is he wise.

For this reason, it seems to me salutary to instruct diligent and intelligent young people who fear God and seek the blessed life that they should not dare to follow securely any disciplines practiced outside the Church of Christ as though these would lead them to the blessed life. Rather, they should judge them soberly and carefully.

If they find disciplines instituted by human beings, varying because of the different wills of their founders, and unknown because of the suspicions of those who err—especially if they also involve an established partnership with demons through certain signs resembling agreements and compacts—they should wholly reject and detest them. They should also withdraw their zeal from the superfluous and luxurious institutions of human beings.

Those human institutions that serve the fellowship of people living together, however, they should not neglect, since the necessity of this life requires them.

But among the other disciplines found among the nations, apart from the history of things—whether of the past or of the present—belonging to the bodily senses, to which the experiments and conjectures of useful bodily arts may also be assigned, and apart from the reasoning of disputation and number, I think there is nothing useful. In all these matters one must observe: “Nothing in excess,” especially in those matters that concern the bodily senses and are bounded by times and places.

## CHAPTER CCLXX [Col. 0956B]

### That a Christian, leaving Egypt, should carry away the useful disciplines of the philosophers of this age as riches, as possessions belonging to him, for his use

As for those called philosophers, if they have perhaps said anything true and suited to our faith—especially the Platonists—not only need they not be feared, but what belongs to our use must also be claimed from them as from unjust possessors.

For, just as the Egyptians possessed not only idols and heavy burdens, which the people of Israel would detest and flee, but also vessels and ornaments of gold and silver, and clothing, which that people, as they departed from Egypt, secretly claimed for themselves for better use—not by their own authority, but at God’s command, with the Egyptians unknowingly supplying what they themselves were not using well—so all the disciplines of the nations contain not only false and superstitious fictions and heavy burdens of unnecessary labor, which each of us, under Christ’s leadership, must abominate and avoid when departing from fellowship with the nations, but also liberal disciplines better suited to the service of truth, and certain extremely useful moral teachings.

Among them are also found some truths concerning the worship of the one God. These truths are like their gold and silver—not things they themselves instituted, but things they extracted from certain veins, as it were, of divine providence, which has been infused everywhere. Since they misuse these truths perversely and unjustly in the service of demons, when a Christian separates himself in spirit from their miserable fellowship, he ought to take them from them for the proper use of proclaiming the Gospel.

Their clothing too—that is, human institutions, but institutions adapted to human society, without which we cannot live in this life—may be accepted and possessed so that it can be turned to Christian use.

For what else did many of our good and faithful people do? Do we not see with how much gold, silver, and clothing Cyprian, that most gracious teacher and most blessed martyr, came out of Egypt? How much Lactantius? How much Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary? To say nothing of the living, how much did countless Greeks carry away?

The most faithful servant of God, Moses, had done this before them, for it is written that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

The superstitious custom of the nations—and especially in those times when, having shaken off Christ’s yoke, it was persecuting Christians—would never have lent Christians the disciplines it possessed as useful if it had suspected that they would be turned to the worship of the one God, by which the empty worship of idols would be destroyed. Yet they gave their gold, silver, and clothing to the people of God as they departed from Egypt, not knowing how what they gave would be returned in the service of Christ.

There is no doubt that what took place in Exodus was a figure prefiguring this, as I say without prejudice to another or equal or better interpretation.

But once the student of the divine Scriptures has been instructed in this way, when he begins to approach them for careful investigation, he should never cease to think of the apostolic saying: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

Thus he will understand that, although he may come out of Egypt rich, he cannot be saved unless he celebrates the Passover. “Our Passover has been sacrificed: Christ.” Nothing does Christ’s sacrifice teach us more than what he himself cries out, as if to those whom he sees laboring in Egypt under Pharaoh:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy [or gentle], and my burden is light.”

To whom does this apply except to the gentle and humble in heart, whom knowledge does not puff up but love builds up?

Let them therefore remember those who at that time celebrated the Passover symbolically through the shadows of things to come, when they were commanded to mark the doorposts with the blood of a lamb. They were commanded to mark them with hyssop.

This herb is lowly and gentle, and nothing is stronger or more penetrating than its roots, so that, rooted and grounded in love, we may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth—that is, the cross of the Lord.

Hyssop also has purifying power, lest, as knowledge puffs him up, the swollen breast should proudly breathe over the riches carried away from Egypt.

“You shall sprinkle me with hyssop,” he says, “and I shall be clean; you shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. You shall make me hear joy and gladness.”

He then adds what follows in order to show that hyssop signifies purification from pride: “The humbled bones shall rejoice.”

How much smaller is the quantity of gold, silver, and clothing that the people carried away from Egypt compared with the riches they later acquired at Jerusalem, which are displayed especially in King Solomon. So great is all the knowledge gathered from the books of the nations when compared with knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

For whatever a person learns outside them, if it is harmful, is condemned there; if it is useful, it is found there. And when someone finds there everything useful that he has learned elsewhere, he will find there much more abundantly what is learned nowhere else at all, but only in the marvelous height and marvelous humility of those Scriptures.

Therefore, equipped with this instruction, when unknown signs no longer impede him, let the reader approach the ambiguous signs in Scripture to examine and discuss them as one who is gentle and humble in heart, gently subjected to Christ and bearing a light burden, grounded and rooted and built up in love, so that knowledge cannot puff him up.

## CHAPTER CCLXXI [Col. 0958A]

### On ambiguous signs and distinctions; by way of example, how the passage “In the beginning was the Word” and the Apostle’s “I do not know what to choose” should be distinguished; from Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*

A person whose mind is in a condition to be instructed through us should know that ambiguity in Scripture occurs either in literal words or in figurative words. We demonstrated these categories in the second book.

But when literal words make a passage ambiguous, one must first see whether we have made a wrong division or pronunciation. When careful attention has perceived that it is uncertain how the passage should be divided or pronounced, one should consult the rule of faith received from the clearer passages of Scripture and from the authority of the Church. We discussed this sufficiently when we were speaking about things in the first book.

If both—or even all, if there are several—of the possible divisions accord with the faith, the text of the passage itself must next be consulted, by examining the preceding and following parts that placed the ambiguity in the middle, so that we may see which of the several apparent meanings it supports and allows to be connected with it.

Now consider the examples.

There is the heretical division:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was,”

so that the meaning is: “This Word was in the beginning with God,” while the speaker refuses to confess that the Word was God.

But this must be refuted by the rule of faith, which instructs us concerning the equality of the Trinity, so that we say:

“And God was the Word,”

and then add:

“This was in the beginning with God.”

The ambiguity of the division in the other passage does not resist the faith on either side and must therefore be judged by the text itself. The Apostle says:

“And what I should choose I do not know; but I am compelled by two alternatives, having a desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is far better, but to remain in the flesh is necessary for you.”

It is uncertain whether the words “having a desire” belong with “I am compelled by two alternatives,” or whether they should be joined to what follows:

“Having a desire to depart and to be with Christ.”

But since the words “for that is far better” follow, it appears that he says he has a desire for the better of the two possibilities: although he is compelled by two alternatives, he has a desire for one and a necessity for the other—namely, a desire to be with Christ and a necessity to remain in the flesh.

This ambiguity is decided by the one following word *enim* (“for”), which some translators omitted. They were led by that omission to a meaning in which he seemed not only to be compelled by two alternatives but also to have a desire for both.

The passage should therefore be divided as follows:

“And what I should choose I do not know, but I am compelled by two alternatives.”

This division is followed by:

“Having a desire to depart and to be with Christ.”

And as though someone were asking why he has a desire for this rather than the other, he says:

“For that is far better.”

Why, then, is he compelled by two alternatives? Because there is a necessity to remain, which he adds in these words:

“To remain in the flesh is necessary for you.”

Where ambiguity cannot be resolved either by the rule of faith or by the text itself [Col. 0959A], it does no harm to divide the passage according to whichever of the meanings presented is chosen.

For example, in the passage addressed to the Corinthians:

“Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. Receive us; we have wronged no one.”

It is uncertain whether the passage should be understood as:

“Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit,”

meaning that a person should be holy both in body and in spirit;

or as:

“Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh; and, in spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God: receive us.”

Such ambiguities of division are therefore within the reader’s discretion.

## CHAPTER CCLXXII [Col. 0959B]

### On ambiguous pronunciations; by way of example, how “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” should be pronounced; from the same book
Whatever we have said about ambiguous divisions must likewise be observed in ambiguous pronunciations. For these too, unless they are impaired by the reader’s excessive carelessness, are corrected either by the rules of faith, or by the connection of the preceding or following words; and if neither of these is applied for their correction, they will nevertheless remain doubtful, so that, however the reader pronounces them, he is not at fault.

For unless faith recalls us—that faith by which we believe that the Lord will not accuse his elect, and that Christ will not condemn his elect—the passage may be pronounced in this way: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” so that the answer might follow as though to a question: “God, who justifies”; and then the question might be asked again: “Who is the one who condemns?” and the answer given: “Christ Jesus, who died.” Since it would be utterly foolish to believe this, it should be pronounced so that an inquiry comes first and a question follows. [Col. 0959C]

The ancients said that an inquiry and a question differ in this respect: many answers can be given to an inquiry, but to a question the answer is either “no” or “yes.” Thus it should be pronounced so that, after the inquiry in which we say, “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?”, what follows is uttered in the tone of someone asking a question: “God, who justifies?”—so that the silent answer is “No.” Likewise, let us inquire: “Who is the one who condemns?” and let us again ask: “Christ Jesus, who died, or rather who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us?”—so that everywhere the silent answer is “No.” [Col. 0959D]

But in the passage where he says, “What then shall we say?”—because those who were not pursuing righteousness attained righteousness—unless, after the inquiry expressed by “What then shall we say?”, the answer is added, “Because the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness,” the following text will not cohere.

However one may pronounce what Nathanael said—“Can anything good come from Nazareth?”—whether affirming it, so that only the words “From Nazareth?” belong to the question, or asking the whole statement with doubt, I do not see how the distinction can be determined. Neither sense, however, impedes the faith. [Col. 0960A]

There is also ambiguity in the uncertain sound of syllables, and this certainly belongs to pronunciation. For what is written, “My *os* [mouth/bone] was not hidden from you, which you made in secret,” does not make clear to the reader whether *os* is pronounced with a shortened or lengthened vowel. If it is shortened, it is understood from the word for “bones”; if lengthened, it is understood from the word for “mouth,” in the singular number. Such matters, however, are judged by examining the preceding language. For in Greek it is not *stoma* (στόμα, “mouth”) but *osteon* (ὀστέον, “bone”) that is found.

Hence ordinary speaking usage is often more useful for conveying things than grammatical correctness. I would rather have someone say, with a barbarism, “My bone was not hidden from you,” than have the meaning become less clear merely because the expression is more properly Latin.

Sometimes, however, the doubtful sound of a syllable is determined by a neighboring word belonging to the same sense. Such is the Apostle’s statement: “I warn you, as I said before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.” If he had said only, “I warn you,” and had not added “as I said before,” we would have had to return to the text in the earlier language to discover whether the middle syllable of *praedico* should be lengthened or shortened. But now it is clear that it must be lengthened: he does not say *sicut praedicavi* (“as I preached”), but *sicut praedixi* (“as I said before”). [Col. 0960B]

Not only these, but also those ambiguities that do not concern division or pronunciation must be considered in the same way. Such is the passage to the Thessalonians: “Therefore we were comforted, brothers, in you.” For it is doubtful whether the meaning is “O brothers” or “these brothers.” Neither alternative conflicts with the faith, but the Greek language does not have these cases in identical form; therefore, on consulting it, the expression is determined to be vocative: “O brothers.” [Col. 0960C]

If the translator had wished to say, “Therefore we received consolation, brothers, in you,” he would have adhered less closely to the words, but the meaning would have been less doubtful. Or, certainly, if he had added *our*, scarcely anyone would doubt that the case was vocative on hearing, “Therefore we were comforted, our brothers, in you”; but this is now permitted only with greater danger.

The same thing occurred in the passage to the Corinthians, where the Apostle says: “Every day I die, by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus.” For one translator says, “Every day I die; I swear by your glory,” because in Greek the oath-word *nē* (νὴ) is explicit and has no ambiguous sound. [Col. 0960D]

Thus, as far as the books of divine Scripture are concerned, ambiguity in proper words is found only very rarely and with great difficulty—ambiguity that is not resolved either by the context itself, through which the writer’s intention becomes known, or by comparison of translations, or by examination of the earlier language.

## CHAPTER CCLXXIII  
### On ambiguities in translated words, in which he warns beforehand that figurative speech must not be taken literally; from the same book

The ambiguities of translated words, which must now be discussed, demand no small degree of care and diligence. For at the outset one must beware of taking figurative speech literally. This is also the point of the Apostle’s statement: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” [Col. 0961A]

When something said figuratively is understood as though it had been said literally, the understanding becomes carnal. No death of the soul can more appropriately be called such than when what distinguishes it from beasts—namely, understanding—is subjected to the flesh by following the letter.

For one who follows the letter treats translated words as though they were proper words, and does not refer what is signified by the proper word to another meaning. If, for example, that person hears “Sabbath,” he understands nothing except one day out of the seven that recur in continuous succession. When he hears “sacrifice,” he does not extend his thought beyond what is customarily performed with animal victims and earthly fruits.

This, then, is the miserable slavery of the soul: to take signs for realities and to be unable to raise the eye of the mind beyond bodily creation in order to drink in the eternal light. Yet this slavery differed greatly from the practice of the other nations among the Jewish people, since they were so subjected to temporal things that one God alone was commended to them in everything. Although they observed signs of spiritual realities in place of those realities themselves, not knowing to what they referred, they nevertheless had this implanted in them: that through such slavery they were pleasing the one God of all, whom they did not see. The Apostle writes that this observance existed as the guardianship of children under a pedagogue. [Col. 0961B]

Therefore those who clung stubbornly to such signs could not endure the Lord’s rejection of them when the time of their revelation had come. Their rulers consequently devised accusations because he healed on the Sabbath, and the people, bound to those signs as though they were realities, did not believe that the one who refused to observe them as they were observed by the Jews was God or had come from God. [Col. 0961C]

But those who believed—including the people from whom the first Church at Jerusalem was formed—showed clearly how useful it had been to be guarded under a pedagogue in that manner: the signs imposed for a time bound those who served the worship of the one God, maker of heaven and earth, to the conviction of those who observed them.

## CHAPTER CCLXXIV  
### He establishes this method for discovering whether an expression is proper or figurative: whatever appears harsh or almost disgraceful to the inexperienced when spoken or done by God or the saints should without doubt be understood figuratively; from the same book

The method by which one discovers first whether an expression is proper or figurative must therefore be demonstrated. The method is this: whatever in divine speech cannot properly be referred either to moral uprightness or to the truth of faith should be recognized as figurative. [Col. 0961D]

Moral uprightness concerns loving God and one’s neighbor; the truth of faith concerns knowing God and one’s neighbor. Each person’s hope lies in his own conscience, according to how he senses that he is progressing in the love and knowledge of God and of his neighbor. These matters were discussed in the first book.

But since it is easy for the human race to judge sins not by the impulses of desire itself but rather by its own customs, it generally happens that each person considers only those things blameworthy which the people of his religion and time have been accustomed to censure and condemn, and considers worthy of approval and praise only those things permitted by the custom of those among whom he lives. [Col. 0962A]

Consequently, if Scripture either commands something that conflicts with the custom of its hearers, or condemns something that does not conflict with it, they may think the expression figurative once the authority of the word has already taken hold of their minds.

Scripture, however, commands nothing except love, and condemns nothing except desire, and in this way forms human conduct. Likewise, if an erroneous opinion has already occupied someone’s mind, people consider anything Scripture asserts otherwise to be figurative. Scripture, however, asserts only the catholic faith concerning past, future, and present things: it narrates past things, foretells future things, and demonstrates present things.

All these things serve to nourish and strengthen the same love and to conquer and extinguish desire. By “love” I mean the movement of the soul toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. By “desire” I mean the movement of the soul toward enjoying oneself, one’s neighbor, or any bodily thing, not for God’s sake. [Col. 0962B]

What uncontrolled desire does in order to corrupt its own soul and body is called *flagitium* (“shameful vice”); what it does in order to harm another is called *facinus* (“crime”). These are the two kinds of all sins, though shameful vices come first. When they have emptied the soul and brought it into a kind of poverty, one leaps—or rushes [*prosilitur*]—into crimes, either to remove obstacles to the vices or to seek aids for them.

Likewise, what love does to benefit itself is called *utilitas* (“advantage”); what it does to benefit one’s neighbor is called *beneficentia* (“benevolence”). Advantage comes first, since no one can benefit another from what he does not possess. The more the kingdom of desire is destroyed, the more love increases. [Col. 0962C]

Whatever harsh or almost savage thing is read in Holy Scripture, whether in deed or word, as proceeding from God or his saints, serves to destroy the kingdom of desire. If it speaks plainly, it should not be referred elsewhere as though it had been said figuratively. Such is the Apostle’s statement:

“You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works: eternal life to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious and distrust the truth but believe iniquity. Tribulation and anguish upon every soul of a person who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek.”

This is addressed to those in whom the kingdom of desire itself is overturned because they have wished to conquer it. [Col. 0962D]

When the kingdoms of desire are overthrown in the person whom they had dominated, the expression is plain: “Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified [*suam*, ‘their’] flesh with passions [*vitiis*, ‘vices’] and desires.” Yet here too certain words are used figuratively, such as “the wrath of God” and “they have crucified.” But there are not so many of them, nor are they arranged in such a way that they conceal the meaning or create an allegory or riddle, as I call a properly figurative expression.

When Jeremiah is told, “See, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, destroy, devastate, and demolish,” there is no doubt that the whole expression is figurative and must be referred to the end we have described. [Col. 0963A]

Whatever appears disgraceful to the inexperienced—whether it is merely said or also done—when it proceeds either from God or from people whose holiness is commended to us, is wholly figurative; its hidden meanings must be laid open for the nourishment of love.

Whoever uses passing things more restrictively than the customs of those among whom he lives require is either temperate or superstitious. Whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the limits of the customs of the good people among whom he lives either signifies something or is committing a disgraceful act. In all such matters, it is not the use of things but the desire of the user [*utentis*] that is at fault.

No sober person would believe that the Lord’s feet were anointed by a woman with precious perfume in the manner customary among luxurious and wicked people, whose banquets we detest. For “good fragrance” is a good reputation: whoever follows Christ’s footsteps by works of good conduct pours over his feet, as it were, the most precious fragrance. [Col. 0963B]

Thus what is generally a disgraceful act in other persons is, in a divine or prophetic person, a sign of some great reality. The union with a prostitute is one thing in depraved conduct and another in the prophecy of the prophet Hosea. Nor, because bodies are disgracefully exposed at the banquets of drunkards and lechers, is it therefore disgraceful to be naked in a bath.

## CHAPTER CCLXXV  
### On the general rule of justice, “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another,” which, when referred to the commandment of the twofold love, removes all shameful vices and crimes

Moved by the innumerable variety of customs, certain people—sleeping, so to speak, though not sunk in the deep sleep of folly and yet unable to awaken into the light of wisdom—thought that justice did not exist in itself, but that each nation considered its own custom just. [Since customs differ among all nations, while justice ought to remain unchanging,] they concluded that it was manifest that justice existed nowhere. [Col. 0963C]

They failed to understand, not to mention many other matters, that the rule “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” cannot in any way be altered by any difference among the nations.

When this principle is referred to the love of God, all shameful vices perish; when it is referred to the love of one’s neighbor, all crimes perish. No one wishes his dwelling to be corrupted; therefore he ought not to corrupt God’s dwelling—namely, himself. No one wishes to be harmed by anyone; therefore he himself ought not to harm anyone. [Col. 0963D]

Thus, once the tyranny of desire has been overthrown, love reigns by the most just laws: love of God for God’s sake, and love of oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER CCLXXVI  
### Further on figurative expressions that are not understood, which must be examined until interpretation leads to the kingdom of love

In figurative expressions, therefore, the following rule must be observed: what is read must be examined with careful consideration until interpretation leads to the kingdom of love. If the passage already sounds proper, it should not be considered a figurative expression.

If it is a command forbidding a shameful vice or crime, or commanding advantage or benevolence, it is not figurative. But if it appears to command a shameful vice or crime, or to forbid advantage or benevolence, it is figurative. [Col. 0964A]

“Unless you eat,” he says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” This appears to command a crime or a shameful vice; it is therefore a figure, commanding participation in the Lord’s passion [*passioni*, “passion”] and the sweet and beneficial storing in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

Scripture says, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.” Here it unquestionably commands benevolence. But what follows—“For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head”—might make you think that a crime of malevolence is being commanded. [Col. 0964B]

Do not hesitate, therefore, to understand it figuratively. Since it can be interpreted in two ways—one toward harming, the other toward providing—let love recall you instead to benevolence, so that you understand the burning coals to be the burning groans of repentance by which the pride of the person who is grieved to have been the enemy of one who comes to his misery’s aid is healed.

Likewise, when the Lord says, “Whoever loves his soul will lose it,” we must not think that he forbids the advantage by which each person ought to preserve his soul. Rather, “he will lose his soul” is figurative: he should destroy and lose the use that his soul now has—namely, the perverse and disordered use by which it is inclined toward temporal things so that it does not seek eternal things.

It is written, “Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner.” The second part of this statement appears to forbid benevolence, for it says, “Do not receive the sinner.” Understand, therefore, that “sinner” is figuratively used for “sin,” so that you do not receive his sin. [Col. 0964C]

## CHAPTER CCLXXVII  
### What we must know in observing the principles for understanding Scripture: some commands are given to everyone generally, others to particular classes of persons, as in “Give your daughter,” and similar passages; from the same book

It often happens that whoever is—or thinks he is—in a higher condition of spiritual life considers figurative whatever is commanded to those in lower conditions. For example, if someone has embraced a celibate life and has castrated himself for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, he may insist that whatever the holy books command concerning loving and governing a wife must be understood not properly but figuratively.

Likewise, whoever has decided to preserve his virgin daughter unmarried may attempt to interpret as a figurative expression the statement, “Give your daughter, and you will have accomplished a great work.” [Col. 0964D]

This too, therefore, must be included among the principles for understanding Scripture: we must know that some things are commanded to everyone generally, while others are commanded to each particular class of persons, so that medicine may reach not only the general condition of health but also the particular weakness of each member. What cannot be raised to a better class must be cared for within its own class.

## CHAPTER CCLXXVIII  
### How one and the same thing can be understood by analogy in a good or an evil sense; from the same book

But since similar things appear in many ways, we must not suppose that, if a certain thing signifies something by analogy in one passage, we should always believe that it signifies the same thing. [Col. 0965A]

The Lord used leaven in condemnation when he said, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” and in praise when he said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened.”

Observation of this variety has two forms. Things signify one thing and another either by signifying opposites or merely by signifying different things. They signify opposites when the same thing is presented by analogy now in a good sense and now in an evil one, as in the example of leaven just mentioned.

The lion signifies Christ where it is said, “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered,” but it signifies the devil where it is written, “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” [Col. 0965B]

The serpent is good in the statement, “Be as wise as serpents,” but evil in the statement, “The serpent deceived Eve by its cunning.”

Bread is good in the statement, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven,” but evil in the statement, “Gladly eat hidden breads.”

There are many other examples of this kind. The examples I have mentioned bear meanings that are by no means doubtful, since examples ought to be cited only when they are clear.

There are, however, passages in which it is uncertain in which sense they should be understood, such as: “The cup in the Lord’s hand is full of unmixed wine; it is mixed.” For it is uncertain whether this signifies God’s wrath—not extending to the final punishment, that is, to the dregs—or rather the grace of the Scriptures passing from the Jews to the Gentiles, because “he inclined from this to that,” while the observances that the Jews understand carnally remain with them, since “its dregs have not been emptied.” [Col. 0965C]

## CHAPTER CCLXXIX  
### On things that are placed not with opposite but merely with different meanings; from Book III of the same work

When the same thing is presented not with an opposite but merely with a different meaning, water is an example. It signifies a people, as we read in the Apocalypse, and it signifies the Holy Spirit, as in the statement, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” It may also signify one thing or another according to the passages in which water occurs. [Col. 0965D]

So too with other things: each of them signifies not only two different things but sometimes many, according to the context of the passage in which it is found.

Where things are presented more clearly, we must learn there how they are to be understood in obscure passages. For the statement addressed to God, “Take up armor and shield, and rise to my help,” cannot be understood better than from the passage where we read, “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will.”

Yet we must not therefore conclude that whenever we read “shield” as a protection we should understand nothing except God’s good will. For it is also said, “The shield of faith, with which,” he says, “you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.” [Col. 0966A]

Nor, again, should we therefore attribute only faith to this kind of spiritual armor, since elsewhere the breastplate is also called faith: “Put on,” he says, “the breastplate of faith and love.”

When, from the same words of Scripture, not one but two or more meanings are perceived, even if it is hidden what the writer intended, there is no danger, provided that any one of those meanings can be shown from other passages of the Holy Scriptures to agree with the truth.

Nevertheless, the person who investigates divine utterances should strive to arrive at the author’s intention—the intention of the one through whom the Holy Spirit produced that Scripture. Whether he succeeds in this, or draws from those words another meaning that does not rightly conflict with the faith and has testimony from any other passage of the divine utterances, the author may perhaps have seen the very meaning we are seeking in those same words; and certainly the Spirit of God, who worked through him, foresaw it. Indeed, he provided that it would occur to the reader or hearer, because it rests upon the truth. [Col. 0966B]

For what could have been provided more generously and abundantly by divine providence in the divine utterances than that the same words should be understood in several ways, with other equally divine testimonies confirming them?

But where a meaning is drawn whose certainty cannot be established by certain testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, it remains for that meaning to become more clearly evident once an account has been given—even if the person whose words we seek to understand perhaps did not perceive it.

This practice, however, is dangerous. It is much safer to walk through the divine Scriptures, whose figurative words are veiled, in such a way that either what emerges from them is free of controversy or, if controversy exists, it is settled by witnesses found and applied from the same Scripture wherever they occur. [Col. 0966C]

## CHAPTER CCLXXX  
### On the modes of expression whose understanding he declares necessary for resolving the obscurities of Scripture; from the same book

The learned should know that our authors employed all the modes of expression that grammarians call by the Greek term *tropous* (Τρόπους, “tropes”) more extensively and abundantly than those who have not learned these matters elsewhere can imagine or believe.

Those who know these tropes recognize them in the sacred writings, and their knowledge assists them to some extent in understanding them. But it is not appropriate to teach them here to the unlearned, lest we appear to be teaching grammar. I do urge them, however, to learn these matters elsewhere, although I already gave this warning above—in the second book, where I discussed the necessary knowledge of languages. [Col. 0966D]

For the letters from which grammar itself takes its name—*grammata* (γραμματά), as the Greeks call letters—are signs of sounds and belong to the articulated voice with which we speak.

In the divine books one finds not only examples of these tropes, as of all things, but also the names of some of them, such as *allegory* (ἀλληγορία), *enigma* (αἴνιγμα), and *parable* (παραβολή).

Although nearly all the tropes that are learned through the liberal art are also found in the speech of those who have never listened to grammarians and are content with the language used by ordinary people, who does not say, “May you thus flourish”? The trope involved—*quorum* [*qui*], “of which/which”—is called *metaphor* (μεταφορά). [Col. 0967A]

Who does not speak of a “fishpond,” even one that contains no fish and was not made for fish, although it nevertheless received its name from fish? This trope is called *catachresis* (κατάχρησις).

It would take too long to pursue the others in this way, since ordinary speech extends even to them. They are all the more remarkable because they signify contrary to what is said. Such is the figure called *irony* (εἰρωνεία) or *antiphrasis* (ἀντίφρασις).

Irony indicates by pronunciation what it wishes to be understood, as when we say to someone doing evil things, “You are doing good things.”

Antiphrasis, however, signifies the contrary not through the speaker’s tone of voice, but either through words whose origin is contrary—as when a grove is called *lucus* because it scarcely gives light—or because something has come to be customarily called by a certain name even though the name is not contrary, as when we ask to receive something that is not there and are answered, “There is plenty.”

Or we make what we say understood in the contrary sense by adding words, as when we say, “Beware of him, because he is a good man.” [Col. 0967B]

What uneducated person does not say such things, even without knowing what these tropes are or what they are called? Knowledge of them is necessary for resolving the ambiguities of Scripture because, when a meaning taken according to the proper sense of the words is absurd, we must ask whether what we do not understand may have been said by one trope or another. In this way many things that were hidden have been discovered.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXI  
### On Tyconius’s seven rules, by which he says students are greatly assisted in understanding the Scriptures; from Book III of *Christian Doctrine*
First, concerning the Lord and his body: in this rule, knowing that the head and body—namely, Christ and the Church—are sometimes made known to us as one person (for [Col. 0967C] it was not without reason said to the faithful, “Therefore you are Abraham’s offspring,” since Abraham’s offspring is one, namely Christ), we should not hesitate when the transition is made from the head to the body or from the body to the head, while nevertheless remaining within one and the same person. For one person speaks, saying, “As a bridegroom he placed a turban upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament”; yet it must certainly be understood which of these two expressions applies to the head and which to the body—that is, which to Christ and which to the Church.

The second concerns the Lord’s divided body, although it ought not really to have been called this. For what will not be with the Lord forever is not truly the Lord’s body; it should rather have been called the Lord’s true and mixed body, or true and pretended body, or something else of the kind. For [Col. 0967D] hypocrites are not to be said to be with him not only eternally but even now, although they appear to belong to his Church. Hence this rule could also have been called “concerning the mixed Church.” It requires an attentive reader whenever Scripture, although already speaking to others, appears to speak as though to the very persons to whom it was speaking before, or to speak about them when it is already speaking about others—as though the bodies of both groups were one, because of their temporary mixture and participation in the sacraments.

This applies to the Song of Songs: “I am dark and beautiful, like the tents of Kedar”; and, she says, “I am beautiful, like the skins of Solomon.” She did not say, “I was dark like the tents of Kedar, and I am beautiful like the skins of Solomon,” but said that she was both [Col. 0968A], because of the temporal unity within one net of good and evil fish. The tents of Kedar belong to Ishmael, who will not be heir with the son of the free woman.

Thus, when God says of the good part, “I will lead the blind by a way they do not know, and they shall tread paths they do not know; I will make darkness light before them and crooked things straight,” and adds, “I will do these things and will not abandon them,” he immediately speaks of the other part, which is badly mixed with it: “But they have turned back,” although by these words others are now signified. But since they are presently one, he speaks as though of the same persons of whom he had been speaking. They will not, however, always be one; for this is that servant mentioned in the Gospel whose lord, when he comes, will divide him and appoint his portion with the hypocrites.

The third rule [Col. 0968B] concerns promises and the law. It can also be called, in another way, “concerning the spirit and the letter,” as we called it when we wrote a book on this subject. It may likewise be called “concerning grace and commandment.” Yet this seems to me more a great question than a rule to be applied for resolving questions. The Pelagians, because they did not understand it, either founded their heresy or drew upon—and increased—it [*auxerunt* is an alternative reading for *hauserunt*, “drew upon”].

Tychonius worked well at explaining this matter, but not completely. For, discussing faith and works, he said that works are given to us by God in accordance with the merit of faith, but that faith itself is from us in such a way that it is not from God. He did not heed the Apostle’s words: “Peace to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.” But he had not yet encountered this heresy which arose in our time [Col. 0968C] and greatly exercised us, so that we might defend against it the grace of God which is through our Lord Jesus Christ. In accordance with what the Apostle says—“There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you”—it made us much more watchful and diligent, so that we might notice in the holy Scriptures what escaped Tychonius, who was insufficiently attentive and insufficiently alert against an opponent: namely, that faith itself is also a gift from the one who apportions to each person the measure of faith.

From this teaching it was said to some: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” Who, then, would doubt that both are God’s gifts if he faithfully and intelligently hears that both have been granted? There are many other testimonies by which this is shown, but that is not our present subject [Col. 0968D]; elsewhere and on many other occasions we have dealt with it.

Tychonius’s fourth rule concerns “the Species and the Genus.” He calls it this because he wants the species to be understood as the part and the genus as the whole of which that part is a species—just as each city is certainly a part of the entire community of nations. He calls the city the species and all nations the genus. Nor need we here employ the subtle distinction taught by dialecticians, who argue with great precision about the difference between a part and a species.

The same reasoning applies if something of this kind is found in the divine utterances not concerning each individual city but concerning each province, nation, or region. For Scripture does not merely say something about Jerusalem or about a city of one of the nations—whether Tyre, Babylon, or any other [Col. 0969A]—which exceeds its own scope and applies rather to all nations. It also says something about Judea, Egypt, Assyria, or any other nation containing many cities, although it is not the whole world but a part of it; what is said exceeds that nation’s scope and agrees rather with the whole of which it is a part—or, as Tychonius calls it, with the genus of which it is a species.

Hence these expressions have even entered common usage, so that ordinary uneducated people understand what is established specifically and what generally in any imperial command. The same occurs with individuals. For what is said about Solomon exceeds his scope and becomes clear as referring rather to Christ or to the Church, of which Solomon was a part.

The species is not always exceeded: often [Col. 0969B] things are said that plainly fit it—or perhaps fit it exclusively. But when Scripture passes from species to genus, while seeming still to speak about the species, the reader’s attention must remain alert, lest he seek in the species what he can find more fully and certainly in the genus.

It is easy to understand the following words of the prophet Ezekiel as referring to that house of Israel of which the Apostle says, “See Israel according to the flesh” [Col. 0969C]: “The house of Israel dwelt in the land and defiled it by its way, by its idols, and by its sins. Its way became before my face like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman; and I poured out my anger upon them, and scattered them among the nations, and dispersed them through the regions. According to their ways and according to their sins I judged them.” The carnal people of Israel both did and suffered all these things, and what follows may likewise be understood as applying to that people.

But when he begins to say, “And I will sanctify my holy name, that great name which has been profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord,” the reader must now pay attention to how the species is exceeded and the genus joined to it. For he continues:

“When I am sanctified in you before their eyes, I will take you from the nations, gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your idols. I will cleanse you, and I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take the heart of stone [Col. 0969D] from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and I will make you walk in my statutes, observe my judgments, and perform them. You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers; you shall be my people, and I shall be your God. I will cleanse you from all your uncleannesses.”

Anyone who observes understands without doubt that this was prophesied concerning the New Testament. It concerns not only that one nation in its remnant, of which it is written elsewhere, “If the number of the children of Israel is like the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved,” but also the other nations promised to their fathers, who are likewise our fathers. Here the washing of regeneration was promised, which we now see granted to all nations [Col. 0970A].

The same is apparent in what the Apostle says when commending the grace of the New Testament so that it might stand out in comparison with the Old: “You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” He recognized and perceived that this was drawn from the passage where the prophet says: “I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; I will take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”

Hence the Apostle says, “on tablets of fleshly hearts.” He wished the heart of flesh to be distinguished from the heart of stone by a life that feels, and by that sentient life he signified understanding. Thus Israel becomes spiritual—not one nation, but all the nations promised to the fathers in their offspring, which is Christ.

This spiritual Israel is distinguished from that carnal Israel, which is one nation, by the novelty of grace [Col. 0970B] rather than by ancestral nobility, and by mind rather than by nation. Yet the prophetic height, while speaking about or to the one, secretly passes over to the other; and when it is already speaking about or to the latter, it still appears to speak about or to the former. Scripture does not begrudge us its meaning as though with hostile intent, but exercises our heart medicinally.

Therefore, when it says, “I will bring you into your own land,” and shortly afterward, as though repeating the same statement, says, “You shall dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers,” we must understand this not carnally, as it applies to carnal Israel, but spiritually, as it applies to spiritual Israel.

The Church without stain or wrinkle, gathered from all nations and destined to reign eternally with Christ, is itself the land of the blessed, the land of the living. It is to be understood as [Col. 0970C] the land given to the fathers when it was promised to them by God’s certain and immutable will. For by the firmness of the promise or predestination it has already been given, although the fathers believed that it would be given in its own time. The Apostle says the same of God’s grace, which is given to the saints, when writing to Timothy: “Not according to our works, but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages, but has now been manifested through the coming of our Savior.”

He said that grace was given when there were not yet those to whom it would be given, because in God’s arrangement and predestination what would occur in its own time had already been accomplished; he says that this was manifested.

These words can also be understood of the land of the future age, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth [Col. 0970D] in which the unjust will not be able to dwell. Therefore it is rightly said to the godly that this land is theirs, since it will in no respect belong to the impious. It too was given when it was established that it would be given.

Tychonius gives as his fifth rule the rule “concerning Times.” By this rule the quantity of time hidden in the holy Scriptures can often be discovered or inferred. He says that this rule operates in two ways: either through the trope *synecdoche* or through established numbers.

The trope *synecdoche* makes the whole understood from a part or the part from the whole. Thus one evangelist says that something happened “after eight days,” while another says “after six days,” when, on the mountain, with only three disciples present, the Lord’s face shone like the sun and his garments like snow. Both statements [Col. 0971A] concerning the number of days could not be true unless the one who said “after eight days” is understood to have counted as whole days the final part of the day on which Christ foretold that it would happen together with the first part of the day on which he fulfilled it, while the one who said “after six days” counted all the complete days, but only the intervening ones.

This manner of speaking, in which the whole is signified by a part, also resolves the question concerning Christ’s resurrection. The final part of the day on which he suffered, unless it is taken for the whole day—that is, with the preceding night added—and the night during whose final part he rose, unless the whole day is taken with the day dawning on Sunday added, cannot yield the three days and three nights during which he foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth.

By established numbers [Col. 0971B] he means those which divine Scripture commends with particular prominence, such as seven, ten, and twelve, and whatever other numbers there are which diligent readers readily recognize. Such numbers are often used for the whole of time. Thus “Seven times a day I praise you” means nothing other than “His praise is always in my mouth.”

The same applies when they are multiplied by ten, as with seventy and seven hundred. Thus Jeremiah’s seventy years can spiritually be understood as the whole period during which the Church is among strangers. The same applies when numbers are multiplied by themselves: ten times ten is one hundred, and twelve times twelve is one hundred forty-four. This number signifies the totality of the saints in the Apocalypse.

It is therefore clear [Col. 0971C] that these numbers are not used merely to resolve questions about times; their meanings extend more widely and branch into many matters. For the number in the Apocalypse does not concern times but people.

Tychonius calls the sixth rule “recapitulation,” which he discovered with sufficient vigilance amid the obscurities of Scripture. Certain things are spoken as though they followed in temporal order or were narrated in continuous sequence, while the narrative secretly returns to earlier matters that had been omitted. Unless this is understood through the rule of recapitulation, one goes astray.

Thus in Genesis it is said: “And the Lord God planted a paradise in [Eden] [Col. 0971D], toward the east, and there he placed the man whom he had formed. And God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful in appearance and good for food.” This seems to say that the trees were made after God had placed the man in paradise. Yet, after briefly mentioning both matters—namely, that God planted the paradise and placed there the man whom he had formed—the narrative returns by recapitulation and tells what it had omitted: how the paradise was planted, namely, because God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful in appearance and good for food.

It then adds: “And the tree of life in the midst of the paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil,” followed by the river by which the paradise was watered, divided into four sources and four rivers. This entire account belongs to the establishment of the paradise. When it has finished this, it repeats what it had already said—and what in fact followed—and says: “And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the [Col. 0972A] paradise,” etc.

It was after these things had been made that the man was placed there, as the order itself now demonstrates. The things described above did not occur after the man had been placed there, as they may be thought to have occurred unless recapitulation is carefully understood at that point, by which the narrative returns to what had previously been omitted.

Likewise, in the same book, when the generations of Noah’s sons were being recalled, it says: “These are the sons of Ham in their tribes, according to their languages, in their lands, and in their nations.” After the sons of Shem have also been enumerated, it says: “These are the sons of Shem in their tribes, according to their languages, in their lands, and in their nations.” It then adds concerning them all: “These are the tribes of the sons of Noah, according to their generations and according to their nations. From these the islands of the nations were scattered over the earth after the flood.”

Then it says: “And the whole earth [Col. 0972B] had one language and one voice among all.” This addition appears to mean that, at the time when they had already been scattered over the earth, even among the islands of the nations there had been one language common to all. That plainly contradicts the preceding words, where it says, “according to their languages.” For the individual tribes that formed the individual nations could not already be said to have their own languages when there was one language common to all.

Accordingly, the words “And the whole earth had one language and one voice among all”—that is, one language for everyone—were added by recapitulation, as the narrative secretly returned in order to explain how they had been divided from one common language into many. Immediately afterward the building of the tower [Col. 0972C] is narrated, where, by divine judgment, this punishment for their pride was inflicted upon them. After that event they were scattered over the earth according to their languages.

Recapitulation occurs even more obscurely in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “On the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire rained from heaven and destroyed them all. So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. In that hour, whoever is on the roof and has his belongings in the house must not go down to take them; and whoever is in the field likewise must not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife.”

Are these instructions to be observed when the Lord has been revealed, so that no one looks back—that is, seeks the life he has renounced? Or rather are they to be observed at the present time, so that, when the Lord is revealed, each person may receive recompense for what he has preserved or despised? Yet because it says [Col. 0972D], “In that hour,” people think that these things are to be observed when the Lord has been revealed, unless the reader’s understanding is alert to perceive the recapitulation, aided by another passage of Scripture which, even in the time of the apostles, cried out: “Children, it is the last hour.”

The period itself, therefore, during which the Gospel is preached until the Lord is revealed, is the hour in which these things must be observed, because the Lord’s revelation itself belongs to that same hour, which will end on the day of judgment.

Tychonius’s seventh and final rule is likewise concerning the devil and his body. He too is the head of the impious, who are in a certain sense his body and will go with him into the punishment of eternal fire, just as Christ is the head of the Church, which is his body and will be with him [Col. 0973A] in everlasting kingdom and glory.

Therefore, just as in the first rule, which he calls “concerning the Lord and his body,” one must remain watchful in order to understand, when Scripture speaks about one and the same person, what applies to the head and what to the body, so in this final rule something is sometimes said about the devil that can be recognized as applying not to him but rather to his body. His body consists not only of those who are manifestly outside, but also of those who belong to him and are nevertheless temporarily mixed with the Church, until each person departs this life or the chaff is separated from the grain by the final winnowing.

What is written in Isaiah—“How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, the morning star?” etc.—is said under the figure of the king of Babylon concerning the same person or to the same person, and in the very context [Col. 0973B] of the discourse is clearly understood of the devil. Yet what is said there, “He is crushed upon the earth who sends to all nations,” does not entirely apply to the head himself. For although the devil sends his angels to all nations, it is his body, not he himself, that is crushed upon the earth—unless it is because he is in his body, which, when crushed, becomes like dust scattered by the wind from the face of the earth.

All these rules, except the one called “concerning Promises and the Law,” make one thing understood from another. This is proper to tropical expression, which extends more widely than, in my view, anyone can wholly comprehend. Wherever something is said as though it were one thing so that another may be understood, even if the name of that trope is not found in the art of speaking, the expression is tropical.

When this occurs where it customarily occurs [Col. 0973C], understanding follows without difficulty. But when it occurs where it is not customary, one labors to understand it; some do so more, others less, just as the gifts of God are greater or lesser in human talents, or as aids are granted more or less abundantly.
