Therefore, just as with proper words, which we discussed above, things must be understood as they are said, so with transferred expressions that produce tropical speech—where one thing must be understood from another—we have dealt sufficiently, as it seemed appropriate, up to this point. Those devoted to sacred literature must be admonished not only to know the kinds of expression found in the holy Scriptures and to observe carefully and retain in memory how something is customarily said in them, but also—and this is the chief and most necessary matter—to pray that they may understand. For in the writings to which they devote themselves they read that [Col. 0973D] “the Lord gives wisdom, and from his face come knowledge and understanding”; from him they have received even their study, if it is furnished with piety.

## Chapter 282. On the Apostle’s statement, “Death has been swallowed up in victory”; from the book of Questions

It is often asked what is meant by the statement, “Then will be fulfilled what is written: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’” The sting of death is sin, but the strength of sin is the law.

I think that in this passage death signifies the carnal habit which resists the good will through the pleasure of temporal things. For it would not be said, “Where is your contention?” unless its contention [Col. 0974A] had resisted and opposed us. The same is described elsewhere: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do what you wish.”

Through perfect sanctification, therefore, it comes about that every carnal appetite is subjected to our enlightened and vivified spirit—that is, to the good will. Just as we see ourselves deprived of many childish pleasures which, when we were children, tormented us most bitterly if they were denied us, so we must believe that the same will happen with every carnal pleasure when perfect holiness has restored the whole person.

For now, as long as there is in us something that resists the good will, we need God’s help through good people and good angels, so that, until our wound is healed, it may not trouble us so greatly [Col. 0974B] as to destroy even the good will. We have deserved this death through sin. Sin was entirely within free choice when, in paradise, no pain caused by the denial of pleasure resisted the good will of the human being.

For example, if someone has never found hunting pleasurable, he is entirely free to decide whether he wants to hunt or not, and he is not tormented by anyone who forbids it. But if he has abused this freedom and gone hunting against the command of the one who forbade it, pleasure gradually creeps in and mortifies the soul, so that, if he wishes to abstain, he cannot do so without distress and anguish, although in complete health he had previously not engaged in it.

Thus the sting of death is sin, because sin produced a pleasure capable of resisting the will and of being restrained only with pain. Since this pleasure [Col. 0974C] arises from the soul’s decline and has made it worse, it is rightly called death [or, according to the alternative reading, “we call it death”].

The strength of sin is the law, because the things prohibited by the law are committed with far greater wickedness and shamefulness than if they were prohibited by no law. Death, then, will be swallowed up in victory when, through sanctification in every part of the human being, the pleasure of spiritual things has been perfected and carnal pleasure has been restrained.

## Chapter 283. On the forty-six years of the Temple’s construction; from Homily 10 on the Gospel according to John

The Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” And the Lord said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews did not understand this mystery and said, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and you say that in three [Col. 0974D] days you will raise it up?”

The Jews were not speaking of the time spent on Solomon’s building, but of the time spent on Ezra’s, whose completion had been forbidden by the neighboring nations. They were carnal and understood carnal things; he was speaking spiritually. Who could understand which temple he meant? But we need not search far, for the evangelist disclosed it to us and said which temple he meant: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” But, the evangelist says, “he was speaking about the temple of his body.” It is clear that the Lord was killed and rose again after three days.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] For this commentary, see Cyprian, in his little book *Against the Jews*, and the corrections of the distinguished Desiderius Erasmus concerning both Augustine and Cyprian; [Col. 0974D] Rotterdam. Also see Cornelius Agrippa, *On the Excellence of the Female Sex*.]

What, then, does the number forty-six signify? [Col. 0975A] For the moment, you heard yesterday that Adam signifies the whole world through four Greek letters representing four Greek words. If you write these four words one beneath another—that is, the names of the four parts of the world, east, west, north, and south, which constitute the whole world, from whose four winds the Lord says he will gather his elect when he comes for judgment—if, then, you take these four Greek names, ἀνατολή, meaning east; δύσις, meaning west; ἄρκτος, meaning north; and μεσημβρία, meaning south:

**Ἀνατολή, δύσις, ἄρκτος, μεσημβρία**

the initial letters of the words spell **Adam**.

How, then, do we find the number forty-six there? Because Christ’s flesh was from Adam. The Greeks count numbers by letters [Col. 0975B]. What we call the letter *a*, they call in their language ἄλφα, and it is called α in their numerals, signifying one. Where they write beta, β—their *b*—it signifies two in their numerals. Where they write gamma, γ, it signifies three. Where they write delta, δ, it signifies four. Thus they have numerical values for all their letters. The letter we call *m*, which they likewise call *mu*, μ, signifies forty; for they call it μῦ, τεσσαράκοντα (“forty”).

Now observe what numerical value these letters have, and there you will find the temple built in forty-six years. Adam has ἄλφα, which is one; he has δέλτα, which is four—making five; he has ἄλφα again, which is one—making six; and he has μῦ, which is forty—making forty-six.

My brothers, this too was said [Col. 0975C] by our predecessors, and this number, forty-six, was found in the letters. Since our Lord Jesus Christ received his body from Adam but did not derive sin from Adam, he took from him a bodily temple, not iniquity, which must be driven from the temple. The Jews crucified the very flesh that he had taken from Adam—for Mary was from Adam, and the Lord’s flesh was from Mary—and he was to raise in three days that flesh which they were about to kill on the cross.

They destroyed the temple built in forty-six years, and he raised it again in three days.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] This statement concerning human conception and formation is not Augustine’s, as is shown by a marginal note added by a scribe in an ancient copy; nor does it seem to be Eugippius’s. The marginal inscription reads: “We have excerpted this from an anonymous book of 153 Questions on account of the present passage.” Let the reader investigate, since we do not have the leisure to discover from where it must now be extracted.]

Six, nine, twelve, ten, and eighteen together make forty-five; add the one itself, and they make forty-six. Multiplied by six, these make two hundred seventy-six.

Human conception is said to proceed and reach completion in this manner: during the first six days it has something like the appearance of milk; during the following nine days it is changed into blood; then during twelve days it becomes solid; during the remaining eighteen it is formed until the complete outlines of all the limbs are present; thereafter, during the remaining time up to birth, it increases in size.

Thus there are forty-five days, with one added to signify the total. For six, nine, twelve, and eighteen combined make forty-two. With the one added, as stated, they make forty-six. When this number is multiplied by the six, which governs the structure as its principal number, the result is two hundred seventy-six—that is, nine months and six days. These are counted from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which day the Lord is believed to have been conceived, because on that day he also suffered, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, on which day he was born [Col. 0976A].

It is therefore not unreasonable that the temple, which signified his body, is said to have been built in forty-six years, so that as many days were spent in the perfection of the Lord’s body as years were spent in the construction of the temple.

Nor is it without reason that, in the building of the Lord’s body—in whose figure he said that the temple destroyed by the Jews would be raised by him in three days—the number six itself is understood to have been set in place of a year. For they said, “This temple was built in forty-six years”; and forty-six [Col. 0976B] times six equals two hundred seventy-six. This number of days completes nine months and six days, which are counted as ten months for women who give birth—not because all reach the sixth day after the ninth month, but because the perfection of the Lord’s body is found to have been brought to birth after that many days, as the authority preserved by the Church received from the tradition of the predecessors.

For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which he also suffered. The new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed either before or afterward, corresponds to the Virgin’s womb in which he was conceived, where no mortal had been sown.

He is traditionally said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. From that day to the other, when the days are counted, two hundred [Col. 0976C] seventy days are found; these contain the number six forty-six times, the number of years in which the temple was built. By that number of sixes the Lord’s body was perfected, and, destroyed by the passion of death, he raised it in three days. For he was speaking about the temple of his body, as is declared by the Gospel’s most evident and strongest testimony.

## Chapter 284. On the ten virgins; from Book 84 of Questions
Among the parables spoken by God, the one concerning the ten virgins customarily exercises those who inquire into it deeply. Many have indeed drawn from it many interpretations that are not contrary to the faith; but it is necessary to labor over how an exposition may correspond to all its parts. I have also read in a certain writing, among those called apocryphal [Col. 0976D], something that is not contrary to the catholic faith. Yet, when I consider all the parts of this similitude, it seems to me less suited to this passage. Nevertheless, I dare not rashly judge anything concerning that exposition, lest perhaps it is not its incongruity that has caused me difficulty, but my own slowness in failing to find its correspondence. What, however, seems to me not absurdly applicable here, I shall explain as briefly and carefully as I can.

When our Lord was secretly asked by his disciples about the consummation of the age, among the many things [Col. 0977A] he said, he also said this: “Then the kingdom of heaven will be likened to ten virgins,” and so forth. The [number] ten of the virgins, of whom five are admitted and five excluded, signifies the distinction between the good and the wicked. Therefore, if the name “virginity” is honorable, why is it common to those who are admitted and those who are excluded? Moreover, what is signified by the number five in each group? And what the oil signifies seems remarkable. Likewise, why do the wise not share with those who ask, when it is not lawful to envy those who are so perfected that they are received by the bridegroom—by which name, without any doubt, the Lord Jesus Christ is signified—and when one ought to be merciful in giving from what one possesses, as that saying of the same Lord prescribes: “Give to everyone who asks”? What [Col. 0977B], moreover, can be given in such a way that it is insufficient for both groups? These matters especially increase the difficulty of the question, although, when the other details are also carefully considered so that everything converges upon one interpretation, and nothing said about one part obstructs another, great caution must be exercised.

It therefore seems to me that the five virgins signify continence divided into five parts, from the allurements of the flesh. For the desire of the mind must be restrained from the pleasure of seeing, from the pleasure of hearing, from the pleasure of smelling, tasting, and touching. But because this continence is practiced partly before God, so that he may be pleased in the inward joy of conscience, and partly before human beings, merely so that human glory may be enjoyed, five are called wise and five foolish. Both, however, are virgins, because both practice continence, although they rejoice in different sources of stimulation [Col. 0977C].

They are lamps, moreover, because works performed according to this continence are carried in the hands; for it is said: “Let your works shine before human beings.” “All of them took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.” It must therefore be understood that those of whom he is speaking are reckoned under the name of Christ. For those who are not Christians cannot go out to meet Christ the bridegroom. But the five foolish, after taking their lamps, did not take oil with them.

Many, although they hope greatly in Christ’s goodness, nevertheless have no joy although they live continently [do not live continently], they have no joy except in human praise. They therefore do not have oil with them; for I think that joy itself is signified by the oil: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” But whoever does not rejoice because he is pleasing inwardly [Col. 0977D] to God does not have oil with him.

The wise, however, took oil with them in their vessels, together with their lamps—that is, they placed the joy of good works in their heart and conscience. Thus the Apostle also exhorts us: “Let a person examine himself,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.”

While the bridegroom delayed, they all fell asleep, because from both kinds of continent people—whether those who rejoice before God or those who rest content in human praise—people die during this interval, until the resurrection of the dead takes place at the Lord’s coming.

At midnight—that is, when no one knows or expects it—for the Lord himself says: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows,” and the Apostle says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night,” by which it is signified that, when he comes [will come], he will be entirely hidden [Col. 0978A]—there was a cry: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; rise to meet him.” “In the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, we shall all rise.” Therefore all those virgins arose and prepared their lamps—that is, the accounts they would have to render of their works. For we must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, so that there each person may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

The foolish said to the wise: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.” For the deeds of those whose conduct is supported by the praise of others fail when that praise is withdrawn; and by habit one always seeks the source from which the mind is accustomed to rejoice. Thus people seek to have before God, who examines the heart, the testimony of human beings, who do not see the heart.

But what did the wise answer [Col. 0978B]? “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.” For each person will render an account for himself, and no one is helped before God by another’s testimony, since the secrets of the heart are visible to him. Scarcely is anyone sufficient even for himself, so that his conscience may testify on his behalf. “For who can boast that he has a clean heart?” This [from there] is what the Apostle says: “It is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself.” Therefore, since each person can scarcely, or not at all, pronounce a true judgment about himself, how can he judge another, when no one knows what is happening in a human being except the person’s spirit?

“Go instead to those who sell and buy some for yourselves.” They should not be thought to have offered advice, but rather to have recalled their crime indirectly. For flatterers [Col. 0978C] sell oil: by praising either what is false or what they do not know, they lead souls into error; and by procuring vain joys for them as though for foolish people, they receive from them some payment—whether food, money, honor, or some other temporal advantage. They do not understand what has been said: “Those who call you happy lead you into error.” It is better to be rebuked by a righteous person than to be praised by a sinner. “The righteous,” he says, “will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but the oil of the sinner will not fatten my head.” 60”

“Go therefore to those who sell and buy some for yourselves”—that is: Let us see whether those who are accustomed to sell you praise and lead you into error, so that you seek glory not before God but from human beings, will help you.

While they went to buy, the bridegroom came—that is, while they inclined themselves toward external things and, being accustomed to rejoice, sought joys [Col. 0978D] because they did not know inward joys, he came who judges. Those who were ready—that is, those whose conscience bore good testimony before God—entered with him into [to] the wedding feast, that is, where the pure soul is joined to God’s eternal Word to be made fruitful.

The door was shut—that is, after those who have been changed into angelic life had been admitted. “We shall all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed.” Access to the kingdom of heaven was closed. For after the judgment there is no place for prayers or merits.

Finally, the other virgins also came, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” It is not said that they bought oil; and therefore they must be understood, when no joy from the praise of others remained, to have returned amid distress [Col. 0979A] and great afflictions to imploring God. But great is the severity after judgment of the one whose ineffable mercy was bestowed before judgment. Thus he answered: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you”—in accordance with that principle that God’s art, that is, God’s wisdom, does not admit into his joy those who appeared to perform something according to his commandments not before God but in order to please human beings.

And so he concludes: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour”—not merely the day and hour of that final time when the bridegroom will come, but each person is ignorant of the day and hour of his own sleep. Whoever is found ready until sleep—that is, until death, which is owed to everyone—will also be found ready when that voice sounds at midnight by which all will awaken.

As for the statement that the virgins came out to meet the bridegroom, I think it should be understood in such a way that the one called the bride is constituted from those very virgins. It is as though, when all Christians are running together into the Church, the children are said to run together [Col. 0979B] to their mother, while the one called mother is constituted from those assembled children.

For now the Church is betrothed, and she is a virgin who is to be led to the wedding—that is, while she restrains herself from worldly corruption. At that time she will marry, when, after all mortality has passed away, she enjoys immortal union: “I have betrothed you,” he says, “to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.” He says, “You,” a virgin, concluding from the plural to the singular. Therefore they may be called both virgins and a virgin. Why they were said to be five has, as I think, been explained.

“Now we see in a riddle, but then face [Col. 0979C] to face; and now in part, but then in full.” That we now discern something in Scripture in a riddle and in part, yet in accordance with the catholic faith, comes from that pledge received by the virgin Church at the humble coming of her bridegroom. At his final coming, when he comes in glory, she will marry, since then she will behold him face to face. For he has given us the pledge of the Spirit, as the Apostle says. Therefore this exposition does not claim to discern anything certain except what accords with the faith, nor does it prejudice other interpretations that may likewise accord with the faith.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXV. On Lent and Pentecost; from the same book [Col. 0979D]

All wisdom and discipline [All discipline of wisdom] that pertains to the instruction of human beings consists in distinguishing the Creator from the creature, worshiping him as ruler, and acknowledging the creature as subject.

God is the Creator, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are. Therefore the Trinity is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The creature, however, is partly invisible, as the mind, and partly visible, as the body. The number three is assigned to the invisible part. Therefore we are commanded to love the Lord threefold: with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind.

The number four is assigned to the body, because of its most evident nature—that is, hot and cold, moist and dry. Therefore the number seven is assigned to the whole of creation.

Consequently, all discipline that distinguishes and differentiates the Creator and the creature [Col. 0980A] is indicated by the number ten. As long as this discipline is represented temporally by bodily movements, it consists in believing. Through the authority of things done and things that will come and pass away, it nourishes the little ones, as with milk, so as to make them fit for contemplation—which does not come and pass away but always remains.

In that contemplation, when a person has been instructed in things divinely done or to be done temporally for the salvation of human beings, things that are still proclaimed as future, if he perseveres in faith, hopes for what has been promised, and diligently strives to fulfill with tireless love what divine authority commands, he will rightly conduct the life of this necessity and this age, which is commended by the number forty.

For the number ten, which signifies the whole of discipline, multiplied four times—that is, multiplied [Col. 0980B] by the number assigned to the body—because administration is carried out through bodily movements, by which faith was said to consist, produces the number forty. Thus it also obtains the stable wisdom that needs no time, which is commended by the number ten, so that ten is added to forty.

For the equal parts of the number forty, taken together, reach fifty. The number forty has these equal parts: forty taken once, twenty taken twice, ten taken four times, eight taken five times, five taken eight times, four taken ten times, and two taken twenty times. Thus one, two, four, five, eight, ten, and twenty, taken together, produce fifty.

Therefore, just as the number forty, when its equal parts are calculated, produces an additional [Col. 0980C] ten and becomes fifty, so the time of faith—of things done and to be done for our salvation—when lived with equity of life, obtains an understanding of stable wisdom, so that discipline may be strengthened not only by believing but also by understanding.

For this reason the Church as it now exists, although we are sons of God, nevertheless, before what we shall be appears, lives amid labors and afflictions, and in it the righteous person lives by faith: “For unless you believe,” he says, “you will not understand.” This is the time when we groan and grieve, awaiting the redemption of our body, which is celebrated in Lent.

But we know that when he appears [will have appeared], we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. When the ten is added to the forty, so that we may deserve not only to believe what pertains to faith but also to understand the manifest truth, that Church in which there will be no sorrow, no mixture of evil people, and no iniquity, but joy, peace, and gladness, is prefigured by the celebration of Pentecost.

Therefore, after our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead, when forty days had been completed with his disciples—namely, the temporal dispensation [Col. 0980D] pertaining to faith signified through this number—he ascended into heaven. When another ten days had been completed, he sent the Holy Spirit, so that, for the contemplation not of human and temporal things but of divine and eternal things, the ten might be added to the forty as a kind of breath and fire of love and charity. Therefore this whole period [Col. 0981A], that is, the number of fifty days, must now be marked by a celebration of joy.

The Lord the Father also signifies these two periods—one of labor and anxiety, the other of security, joy, and charity—by nets cast into the sea. Before the Passion, a net is said to have been cast into the sea, and they caught so many fish that they could scarcely draw it to shore, and the nets were torn. They were not cast on the right side, for the Church of this age has many wicked people; nor on the left, for it also has good people; but indiscriminately, to signify the mingling of the wicked and the good. The fact that the nets were torn signifies that, with charity violated, many heresies arose [came into existence].

After the resurrection, however, when he wished to foreshow the Church of the future [Col. 0981B] age, in which all will be perfect and holy, he commanded that the nets be cast on the right side. They caught enormous fish, one hundred and fifty-three in number, and the disciples marveled that, although the fish were so large, the nets were not torn.

Their size signifies the greatness [image] of wisdom and righteousness. The number, however, signifies that discipline which we have said is perfected both through temporal dispensation and through eternal rebirth and commended by the number fifty.

Since at that time bodily aids will not be necessary, and faith and wisdom will be held in the mind—for we have said that the number three is assigned to the mind—we multiply fifty by three, and it produces one hundred and fifty. The Trinity is added to this number, because all this perfection is consecrated in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0981C]. Thus one hundred and fifty-three is produced, the number of fish found to have been caught on the right side.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXVI. On what the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens”; from the same book

Because the observance of the Old Testament involved fear, it could not be signified more clearly that charity is the gift of the New Testament than in this passage, where the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” This is understood to be the law of Christ by which the Lord himself commands that we love one another. He assigned such weight to this commandment that he said: “By this it is known that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

The duty of this love is to bear one another’s burdens [Col. 0981D]. But this duty [which] is not eternal will indeed lead to eternal blessedness, in which there will be no burdens of ours that we are commanded to bear for one another. Now, while we are in this life—that is, on this road—let us bear one another’s burdens, so that we may reach the life that is free from every burden [may be able to reach].

As some who have devoted themselves to such knowledge have written about deer, when they cross a strait to islands in search of pasture, they arrange themselves so that they carry on one another the burdens of their heads, which they bear on their antlers. Thus the one behind stretches forward over the neck of the one in front and places his head there. Since there must be one who leads the others and has no one before him to whom he can bow [Col. 0982A] his head, they are said to do this in turns: when the one leading becomes tired from the burden of his head, he returns behind all the others, and the one whose head he had carried while leading takes his place. Thus, bearing one another’s burdens, they cross the strait until they come to the stability of land.

Perhaps Solomon had this nature of deer in mind when he said: “The deer of friendship and the fawn of your graces shall converse with you.” For nothing proves a friend so much as bearing a friend’s burden.

Yet we would not bear one another’s burdens if the time of both persons’ weakness were the same, or if the kind of weakness were the same. Rather, different times and different kinds of weakness make it possible for us to bear one another’s burdens.

For example, you will bear your brother’s anger when you are not angry with the guilty person [Col. 0982B], so that, in turn, when anger has overtaken you, he may support you by his gentleness and tranquility [his own]. This example concerns different times among those bearing their burdens, although the weakness itself is not different, since in both cases anger is borne by one another.

For a different kind of weakness, another example should be considered. Suppose one person has overcome loquacity in himself but has not yet overcome stubbornness, while another is still talkative but is no longer stubborn. The former ought to bear the latter’s loquacity, and the latter the former’s stubbornness, until that weakness in one and this weakness in the other are healed through charity.

For equal weakness in two people, if it occurs at the same time, does not allow them to tolerate one another when it is directed against each other. For example, two people who are angry with each other may agree and tolerate one another against some third person, although they should not be said to tolerate one another [Col. 0982C] [but rather to console one another]. Similarly, those who are sad about the same matter support one another more and, as it were, lean upon one another than if one were sad and the other rejoicing.

But if they are sad against each other, they cannot tolerate one another at all. Therefore, in such emotions, a little of the sorrow itself must be taken upon oneself, so that the other may be freed through you [through some part of yourself] from whatever causes it; and it must be taken up in such a way that it contributes to help, not to an equality of misery—just as a person bends down who extends a hand to one lying on the ground. He does not throw himself down so that both may lie there, but bends only enough to raise up the one who is lying.

Nothing makes this dutiful labor of bearing the burdens of others willingly undertaken except when we consider how much the Lord endured for us. Therefore the Apostle, admonishing [Col. 0982D] us, says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.”

Earlier he had said: “Not each looking to his own interests, but to those of others.” He joined to this saying what follows: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.” The point is that, just as Christ, in becoming the Word made flesh and dwelling among us, although he was without sin, took upon himself our sins and did not attend to what was his own but to what was [ours], so we too, in imitation of him, should willingly bear one another’s burdens.

This thought is joined by another: he took on a human being, whereas we are human beings, and we should consider that the distress, whether of mind or body, which we see in another human being [Col. 0983A] we too have been able, or may be able, to experience. Therefore let us show to the person whose weakness we wish to bear what we would wish him to show us if we happened to be in that condition and he were not.

This is relevant to what the Apostle himself says: “I have become all things to all people, that I might win all.” He means that he considered that he too might have been subject to the vice from which he desired to free another. He did this through compassion, not by lying, as some suppose—especially those who, in defending lies [Col. 0983B] that they cannot deny, seek the protection of some great example.

Furthermore, we must also consider that there is no human being who cannot possess some good that you do not yet possess, even if it is hidden in him, and in that respect he may unquestionably be superior. This thought is useful for crushing and subduing pride, lest, because certain of your own goods are conspicuous and apparent, you therefore think that another possesses none that are hidden and perhaps of greater weight, by which he surpasses you without your knowing it.

For the Apostle does not command us to deceive ourselves or merely to flatter others when he says: “Do nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility of mind consider one another superior to yourselves.” We should not understand this to mean that we should pretend to consider another superior when we do not so consider him; rather, we should [Col. 0983C] truly consider that there may be something hidden in another by which he is superior to us, even if the good by which we seem superior to him is not hidden.

These thoughts, which depress pride and increase charity, make us bear our brothers’ burdens not only with an even temper but also most willingly. In no way should a judgment be passed upon an unknown person, and no one is known except through friendship. Therefore we bear the faults of friends more firmly, because their good qualities delight and hold us.

No one’s friendship should therefore be rejected if he presents himself for friendship—not so that he should be received immediately, but so that his admission may be desired and he may be treated in such a way that he can be received. We may say that a person has been received into friendship when we dare to pour out [Col. 0983D] all our plans to him.

If someone does not dare to offer himself for friendship because some temporal honor or dignity of ours holds him back, we must go down to him and offer him, with a certain courtesy and humility of spirit, what he himself does not dare to seek. Yet, although more rarely, it sometimes happens that the faults of the person whom we wish to receive into friendship become known to us before his good qualities. Offended and in a certain sense repelled by them, we abandon him and do not proceed to investigate his good qualities, which may be more deeply hidden.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, who wishes us to become his imitators, admonishes us to tolerate his weaknesses, so that through the endurance of charity [Col. 0984A] we may be led to certain healthy qualities in whose enjoyment we may rest. For he says: “The healthy do not need a physician, but the sick.”

Therefore, if for the sake of Christ’s charity we ought not to drive from our hearts even one who is perhaps sick in every respect, since he can be healed through the Word of God, how much less should we reject someone who may seem entirely sick to us merely because, at the first entrance into friendship, we could not tolerate certain wounded parts of him?

What is worse, we dare to pass a rash prejudicial judgment concerning the whole person, with resentment in our hearts, not fearing what has been said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged”; and: “In the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

Often the good qualities appear first. Even then, a rash judgment of benevolence must be avoided, lest, when you have considered the whole [Col. 0984B] person good, the faults that later appear find you secure and unprepared and offend you more severely; so that you hate more bitterly the one whom you had rashly loved—which is a wickedness.

For even if none of his good qualities had preceded, and the faults that appeared later had stood out first, they nevertheless ought to have been tolerated until you had dealt with him in all the ways by which such things are customarily healed. How much more, then, when good qualities preceded and, as pledges, ought to bind us to tolerate what comes later?

This, therefore, is the law of Christ: that we bear one another’s burdens. By loving Christ, we easily endure the weakness of another, even one whom we do not yet love for his own good qualities. For we consider that the Lord whom we love died for that person.

The Apostle Paul impressed this charity upon us when he said: “And the weak brother will perish [Col. 0984C] through your knowledge, for whom Christ died.” Thus, if we love that weak person less because of the fault by which he is weak, let us consider him in the one who died for him. Not loving Christ, however, is not weakness but death.

Therefore, with immense care and after imploring God’s mercy, we must consider whether we are neglecting Christ because of a weak person, when we ought to love the weak person because of Christ.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXVII. On the Pelagian heresy, from the book *On Heresies*, addressed to the deacon Quodvultdeus

The heresy of the Pelagians is at the present time the most recent of all, having arisen from the monk Pelagius. Coelestius followed him [Col. 0984D] as teacher so closely that their followers are also called Coelestians.

They are such enemies of God’s grace—by which we were predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, and by which we are rescued from the power of darkness so that we may believe in him and be transferred into his kingdom, on account of which he said, “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father,” and by which charity is poured into our hearts so that faith may work through love—that they believe a human being can fulfill all the divine commandments without this grace.

Yet, if this were true, the Lord would seem to have said in vain: “Without me you can do nothing.”

Finally, when Pelagius was rebuked by the brothers because he attributed nothing to the help of God’s grace for fulfilling his commandments [Col. 0985A], he yielded to their correction only so far as not to place grace before free will, but, with faithless cunning, to place it beneath free will. He said that grace is given to human beings so that they may more easily fulfill through grace what they are commanded to do through free will.

By saying “so that they may more easily,” he plainly wished it to be believed that human beings can, though with greater difficulty, fulfill the divine commands without divine grace.

They say that the grace of God, without which we can do no good, consists only in free will, which our nature received from him without any preceding merits of its own. God assists it only through his law and teaching, so that we may learn what we ought to do and what we ought to hope for—not so that, through the gift of his Holy Spirit, we may do what we have learned ought to be done.

Thus they confess that knowledge is given to us divinely [Col. 0985B], by which ignorance is driven away, but deny that charity is given, by which one lives piously. In this way, although knowledge is God’s gift, and without charity it puffs up, charity itself is not God’s gift, even though it builds up so that knowledge does not puff up.

They also destroy the prayers offered by the Church, whether for unbelievers and those who resist God’s teaching, that they may be converted to him, or for the faithful, that faith may be increased in them and that they may persevere in it.

For they insist that human beings do not receive these things from God but possess them from themselves, saying that the grace of God by which we are freed from impiety is given according to our merits. Pelagius, fearing that he would be condemned in the episcopal judgment at Palestine, was indeed compelled to condemn this doctrine; but it is found that he taught it in his later writings.

They also proceed [Col. 0985C] to say that the life of the righteous in this age has absolutely no sin, and that the Church of Christ is perfected in this mortality so as to be entirely without spot or wrinkle—as though it were not Christ’s Church that cries out to the Lord throughout the whole world: “Forgive us our debts.”

They also deny that little children, born carnally according to Adam, contract the contagion of [ancient] death at their first birth. For they assert that they are born entirely without any bond of original sin, so that there is absolutely nothing that ought to be forgiven them at a second birth.

They say that they are baptized for this reason: so that, having been adopted through regeneration, they may be admitted to the kingdom of God and transferred from good to better, not released through this regeneration from any evil obligation of an earlier state. For even if they are not baptized, they promise them a certain eternal and blessed life of their own outside [Col. 0985D] the kingdom of God.

They also say that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died in body; and that he died not by the merit of guilt but by the condition of nature.

Other objections are also made against them, but these are the principal ones, from which it is understood that the others, whether all or nearly all, depend.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXVIII. 63 Likewise, on the same Pelagian heresy, from the sermon *To the People*
Those two petitions—“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and “Do not lead us into temptation”—when they are brought forward against the Pelagians, what do you think they reply? I shuddered, my brothers, when I heard it. I did not hear it with my own ears, but our holy brother and fellow bishop Urban, who was once presbyter here and is now bishop of Sicca, reported it after returning from the city of Rome. There, when he had disputed—or reported that he had disputed—with someone who held such views, and when he was pressed by the weight of the Lord’s Prayer—for he pressed him and said:

“If it is in our power not to sin, and if it is in our power to overcome all temptations to sin by the strength of our will alone, why do we say to God, ‘Do not lead us into temptation’?”

What do you think the man replied? “We ask God,” he said, “‘Do not lead us into temptation,’ lest we suffer some evil that is not in our power: lest I fall from a horse, break my leg, be killed by a robber, or suffer something of that kind. For these things,” he said, “are not in my power. But to overcome the temptations of my sins—if I wish, I can; and I can do so without God’s help.”

You see, brothers, how malignant the heresy is; you see how you all recoil from it. Beware lest you be captured. I know the cunning and evasions of impious men who have turned away from the truth; and because they have already fallen into their own opinions and are unwilling to be defeated, see, I beg you, how he found something to say: that we therefore say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” lest something happen to us that is not in our power, namely, according to bodily temptation.

Therefore the Lord said, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation.” Did he mean: “Watch and pray lest you break your foot, or lest your head ache, or lest you suffer loss”? He did not mean this. What did he mean? What he said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.” “I have prayed,” he says—God to a human being, the Lord to a servant, the teacher to a disciple, the physician to a sick person—“I have prayed for you.” For what? “That it may not fail.” What? Your hand, your foot, your eye, your tongue, some paralysis, that is, a dissolution of the limbs? No, but “that your faith may not fail.”

According to these men, it is in our power that our faith should not fail. Why, then, is God asked to grant us the ability to ask for what they say we ought not to ask from the eternal Majesty, but ought to possess in our own power?

My brothers, our blessings—which we pronounce over you—they empty, annul, and destroy. You have heard me, I believe, my brothers, when I say: “Turned toward the Lord, let us bless his name; may he grant us perseverance in his commandments, that we may walk in the straight path of his instruction, please him in every good work,” and other things of this kind. “All this,” they say, “has been placed entirely in our power.”

Then we wish such things for you in vain. Let us defend ourselves and you, lest we bless without cause and you subscribe “Amen” without cause. My brothers, your “Amen” is your written affirmation; it is your consent; it is your assent. Let us beware lest some of them condemn both us and you.

Let us defend ourselves by the apostle Paul. Let us see whether he wished such things for his people. Listen to what he said; listen to the kind of things we pray over you. Hear what he said in one place. I will state the matter briefly. You, new heretic, whoever you are who hear me—if you are present—what do you say?

“You say that we have such power not to sin that we can accomplish this without the help of divine grace.”

“That is what you say.”

“Then,” he says, “we have the power not to sin without God’s help?”

“Certainly,” he says. “Our free will is sufficient for this.”

“What, then, is the meaning of what the Apostle says when writing to the Corinthians? ‘We pray to God that you do no evil’” [2 Cor. 13:7]. You have paid attention; you have heard; you have understood. Since the statement is perfectly clear, without doubt you have understood what the Apostle prayed: “We pray to God that you do no evil.” He could have said: “We admonish you not to do evil; we teach you not to do evil; we command and instruct you not to do evil.” If he had said this, he would certainly have spoken correctly, because our will does accomplish something—for our will does not accomplish nothing—but it is not sufficient by itself.

Nevertheless, he preferred to say, “We pray,” in order to commend grace itself, so that they might understand that, when they do not do something evil, they avoid evil not by their own will alone, but fulfill what has been commanded with God’s help.

Therefore, brothers, when a command is given, recognize the freedom of the will; when what is commanded is requested in prayer, recognize the benefit of grace. You have both in the Scriptures: a command is given, and what is commanded is prayed for. Pay attention to what I am saying.

A command is given so that we may understand: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, without understanding.” You have heard that this is commanded. Ask that you may be able to fulfill what is commanded.

“How,” you ask, “do I ask?”

Hear from Scripture what has been commanded to you: “Do not be like a horse or a mule, without understanding.” Because it is commanded, you have recognized the will. Hear that it is prayed for, so that you may recognize grace: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.”

We are commanded to have wisdom. I read that it is commanded.

“Where do you read this?” he asks.

“Hear: ‘You who are foolish among the people, understand; and you fools, become wise at last.’” [Ps. 93:8]

Do you see how God has commanded us to become wise? Is wisdom therefore in our power? I have already said: I heard the command and recognized the will. Hear the prayer, so that you may recognize grace.

The wisdom that has been commanded to us is at issue. Let us hear what the apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone” [Jas. 1:5].

Self-control is commanded to us. Where is it commanded? The Apostle says to Timothy: “Control yourself” [2 Tim. 4:5]. It is a command; it is an instruction. It must be heard and carried out. But unless God helps, we remain incapable. We do indeed strive to act by our will, and the will makes some effort; but power must not presume upon itself unless weakness is helped. Certainly it is commanded: “Control yourself.”

Hear another passage of Scripture: “And since I knew that no one can be self-controlled unless God grants it—and it was itself wisdom to know whose gift this was—what did I do?” he says. “I approached the Lord and pleaded” [Wis. 8:21].

Why go through many examples, my brothers? Whatever is commanded to us must be prayed for, so that it may be fulfilled. But this does not mean that we should lie on our backs as though we were helpless and say, “May God rain food down upon our faces,” so that we do not wish to do anything at all; and when the food has been rained down upon our mouths, say, “God may even swallow it for us.”

We too must do something; we must study; we must strive; and in whatever we have been able to do, we must give thanks; for what we have not been able to do, we must pray.

When you give thanks, you take care not to be condemned as ungrateful. When you ask for what you do not yet have, you take care not to remain empty because you are obstructed.

Consider these things, therefore, my brothers. If someone comes to you and says, “What are we to do, then, if we have no power unless God gives everything? Then God will not crown us, but will crown himself”—you already see that this comes from that vein. It is a vein, but it contains poison; it has been struck by a serpent and is not healthy.

This is what Satan is doing today: through the poisons of heretics he is driving people out of the Church, just as at that time, through the serpent’s poison, he drove them from paradise.

Let no one say that he was absolved by the bishops. He was absolved; but the confession itself, as a correction, was the reason he was absolved, because what he had said before the bishops appeared Catholic, whereas the bishops who absolved him did not know what he had written in his books. Perhaps he has been corrected. We must not despair of a person who perhaps preferred to join himself to the Catholic faith and fled for refuge to its grace and help. Perhaps this has happened. Yet it is not the heresy that has been absolved, but a man who denies the heresy.

## CHAPTER CCLXXXIX

### God saves the world because of grace and judges it because of free will; from the letter to Valentinus

I therefore appeal to you, brothers, as the Apostle appealed to the Corinthians, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you.

First, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Afterwards, however, as the apostle Paul writes, God will judge the world when he comes, as the whole Church confesses in the Creed: “To judge the living and the dead.”

If, then, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free will, how does he judge the world?

The Apostle forbids this, saying: “Let no one glory in man” [1 Cor. 3:21]; and elsewhere: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” [1 Cor. 1:31].

But those heretics, thinking that they make themselves righteous by themselves—as though God had not given this to them, but they had given it to themselves—certainly glory not in the Lord but in themselves. To such people the Apostle says: “For who makes you different?” [1 Cor. 4:7]

He says this because, from that mass of perdition which came into being through Adam, no one is distinguished so as to be made a vessel for honor rather than dishonor except by God. But because a carnal and vainly inflated person, on hearing “Who makes you different?”, could reply either aloud or in thought, “My faith makes me different; my prayer makes me different; my righteousness makes me different,” the Apostle immediately confronts his thoughts and says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” [1 Cor. 4:7]

Those who think that they are justified by themselves, and therefore glory in themselves rather than in the Lord, boast as though they had not received these things.

They say that God’s grace is given according to our merits. This is utterly false—not because there is no merit, whether good in the godly or evil in the ungodly; otherwise, how would God judge the world? Rather, the mercy and grace of God convert a person. Of this the Psalm says: “My God, his mercy will precede me” [Ps. 58:10], so that the ungodly may be justified—that is, may become righteous from being ungodly—and begin to possess good merit, which the Lord will crown when the world is judged.

This is the very question concerning the grace of God that led people who did not understand to suppose that the apostle Paul said: “Let us do evil, so that good may come.” Hence the apostle Peter says in his second letter:

“Therefore, beloved, while you await these things, strive to be found by him unstained and unblemished in peace, and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him. He speaks of these things in all his letters, in which there are some matters difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” [2 Pet. 3:14–16].

Beware, therefore, of what so great an Apostle says so fearfully. Wherever you realize that you do not understand, meanwhile believe the divine utterances, because both the free will of man exists and the grace of God exists, without whose help free will can neither turn toward God nor advance in God.

Pray that what you piously believe you may also understand wisely. For free will itself exists for this purpose also, namely, that we may understand wisely. If we did not understand and become wise by free will, Scripture would not command us, saying: “Understand, therefore, you who are foolish among the people, and you fools, become wise at last” [Ps. 93:8].

By the very fact that we are commanded and instructed to understand and become wise, our obedience is required; and there can be no obedience without free will. But if free will could accomplish this by itself, without the help of grace, so that we might understand and become wise, it would not be said to God: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” [Ps. 118:73]. Nor would it be written in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” [Luke 24:45]. Nor would the apostle James say: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” [Jas. 1:5].

Therefore, beloved, whoever says, “My will is sufficient for me to perform good works,” declines to the right. But those who think that a good life must be abandoned when they hear God’s grace preached in such a way that it is believed and understood that grace makes human wills themselves good from being evil, and also preserves the wills it has made good—and who therefore say, “Let us do evil, so that good may come”—decline to the left.

For this reason he said to you: “Do not turn aside either to the right or to the left” [Deut. 5:32; 17:11]. That is: do not defend free will in such a way that you attribute good works to it without God’s grace; and do not defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works. May the grace of God itself turn this away from you.

Presenting the words of such people, the Apostle says: “What shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, so that grace may abound?” [Rom. 6:1] And to the words of those who err and do not understand God’s grace he answered as he ought: “Certainly not!” [Rom. 6:2] For if we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?

Nothing could be said more briefly or better. What more useful thing does God’s grace confer on us in this present evil age than that we should die to sin? Thus the person who wishes to live in sin apart from that grace through which we die to sin will be found ungrateful even toward grace itself.

## CHAPTER CCXC

### Those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; from the same book

When it is said, “Do not do this” and “Do not do that,” and when the divine admonitions require the exercise of the will for doing or not doing something, they sufficiently demonstrate that free will exists.

Let no one, therefore, blame God in his heart. Let each person blame himself when he sins. Nor, when he does something according to God, should he remove it from his own will. For when he does it willingly, then it should be called a good work, and then the reward of the good work should be hoped for from him of whom it is said: “He will repay each one according to his works” [Rom. 2:6].

Those who know the divine commandments are deprived of the excuse that people customarily make from ignorance. But even those who do not know God’s law will not be without punishment: “For those who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” [Rom. 2:12].

It does not seem to me that the Apostle said this as though he were indicating that those who do not know the law will suffer something worse in their sins than those who know it. For to perish seems worse than to be judged.

But when he was speaking of Gentiles and Jews—because the former are without the law, whereas the latter received the law—who would dare say that Jews who sin under the law will not perish if they have not believed in Christ, since it was said of them, “They will be judged by the law”? No one can be delivered without faith in Christ. Thus they will be judged in such a way that they perish.

For if the condition of those who do not know the law is worse than that of those who know God’s law, how will what the Lord says in the Gospel be true? “The servant who does not know his master’s will and does things worthy of blows will receive few blows; but the servant who knows his master’s will and does things worthy of blows will receive many blows” [Luke 12:47–48].

There he shows that the person who knows sins more seriously than the person who does not know. Yet one must not therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance and seek an excuse there. For it is one thing not to have known and another to have been unwilling to know.

The will is indeed condemned in the one of whom it is said: “He was unwilling to understand so as to act well” [Ps. 35:4]. But even that ignorance which belongs not to those who are unwilling to know, but to those who are simply ignorant, does not excuse anyone so completely that he will not burn in eternal fire. If someone did not believe because he had not heard at all what he ought to believe, perhaps he will burn more mildly.

For it was not said without reason: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that do not know you” [Ps. 78:6]; and what the Apostle says: “When he comes in flaming fire to take vengeance on those who do not know God” [2 Thess. 1:8].

Nevertheless, so that we may possess knowledge itself, lest someone say, “I did not know; I did not hear; I did not understand,” the human will is called to account where it is said: “Do not become like a horse or a mule, in which there is no understanding” [Ps. 31:9]. Yet worse appears to be the case of the one about whom it is said: “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey” [Prov. 29:19].

When a person says, “I cannot do what is commanded, because I am overcome by my desire,” he no longer has an excuse from ignorance, nor does he blame God in his heart; rather, he recognizes and grieves over his evil in himself.

Yet the Apostle says to him: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” [Rom. 12:21]. And certainly, when one is told, “Do not be overcome,” the freedom of his will is being called to account without doubt. To will and not to will belong to one’s own will.

But we must fear lest all these divine testimonies—and whatever others there are, which without doubt are very numerous—be understood in defense of free will in such a way that no place is left for God’s help and grace in a pious life and good conduct, for which an eternal reward is owed. Then the wretched human being, when he lives and acts well—or rather, thinks that he lives and acts well—might dare to glory in himself rather than in the Lord and place the hope of right living in himself, so that Jeremiah the prophet’s curse might follow him:

“Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, strengthens the flesh of his arm, and whose heart turns away from the Lord” [Jer. 17:5].

Understand this prophetic testimony, brothers. Because the prophet did not say, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in himself,” someone might think that “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” was said so that no one should place hope in another person, but in himself.

Therefore, to show that he had admonished a person not to place hope even in himself, after saying, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man,” he immediately added: “And makes flesh his arm.”

He used “arm” for the power of acting. By “flesh,” however, human weakness is to be understood. Thus the person who thinks that his weak and feeble power—that is, human power—is sufficient for him to act well “makes flesh his arm,” and does not hope for help from the Lord.

For this reason he added: “And his heart turns away from the Lord.” Therefore, let us not place our hope for acting well in man, making the flesh of our arm our strength; let our heart not turn away from the Lord, but let it say to him: “Be my helper; do not abandon me” [Ps. 26:9].

Let us remember him saying: “Turn, and you will live” [Ezek. 18:32]; and to him it is said: “Convert us, O God” [Ps. 79:4]. Let us remember God saying: “Cast away from yourselves all your ungodliness” [Ezek. 18:31], while he himself justifies the ungodly. Let us remember him himself saying: “Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit” [Ezek. 18:31], while he says: “I will give you a new heart, and I will give you a new spirit” [Ezek. 36:26].

How, then, is what he says—“Make yourselves”—the same as what he says—“I will give you”? Why does he command, if he himself is going to give? Why does he give, if a human being is going to make? Is it not because he gives what he commands, when he helps the person to whom he commands, so that he may do it?

Free will is always in us, but it is not always good. For either it is free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good.

But God’s grace is always good. Through it a person who previously possessed an evil will becomes a person of good will. Through it also the good will itself, which has already begun to exist, is increased and grows so great that it can fulfill the divine commandments that it wills [what it can], when it wills very fully and perfectly.

This is the purpose of what is written: “If you will, you will keep the commandments” [Sir. 15:15]: a person who wills but cannot should recognize that he does not yet will fully, and should pray to possess as much will as is sufficient for fulfilling the commandments. Thus he is helped to do what is commanded.

It is useful to will when we are able, and it is useful to be able when we will. For what benefit is there if we will what we cannot do, or do not will what we can?

The Pelagians think they know something important when they say: “God would not command what he knew a human being could not do.” Who does not know this? But he commands certain things that we cannot do so that we may learn what we ought to ask from him. For faith itself obtains through prayer.

Finally, the same one who said, “If you will, you will keep the commandments,” says somewhat later in the same book of Ecclesiasticus:

“Who will place a guard over my mouth and a prudent seal upon my lips, lest I perhaps fall because of them, and my tongue destroy me?” [Sir. 22:27]

Certainly he had already received the commandments: “Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit” [Ps. 33:14]. Since what he said is true—“If you will, you will keep the commandments”—why does he ask that a guard be placed over his mouth?

He is like the one who says in the Psalm: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth” [Ps. 140:3]. The commandment of God and his own will are not sufficient for him, since, if he wills, he will keep the commandments.

There are many commandments of God against pride. He already knows them, and if he wills, he will observe them. Why, then, does he say shortly afterward: “Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughty eyes” [Sir. 23:4]?

The Law had already said to him: “You shall not covet” [Exod. 20:17]. Let him therefore will and do what is commanded, since, if he wills, he will keep the commandments. Why does he continue and say: “Turn coveting away from me” [Sir. 23:5]?

Against lust God has given many commandments. Let him do them, because, if he wills, he will keep the commandments. What does it mean that he cries out to God: “May the appetite of the belly and sexual intercourse not seize me” [Sir. 23:6]?

If we were saying these things to him at present, he would rightly answer us: “From this prayer of mine, in which I ask these things from the Lord, understand how I said, ‘If you will, you will keep the commandments.’ It is certain that we keep the commandments if we will to do so; but because the will is prepared by the Lord, we must ask him to grant that we may will as much as suffices for us to do by willing.”

It is certain that we will when we will. But he makes us will the good, of whom I quoted shortly before that the will is prepared by the Lord; of whom it is said: “The steps of a man will be directed by the Lord, and he will will his way” [Ps. 36:23]; of whom it is said: “He who works in you both to will” [Phil. 2:13].

It is certain that we do when we do. But he makes us do, granting the will the most effective strength—he who said: “I will make you walk in my statutes, and you will observe and do my judgments” [Ezek. 36:27].

When he says, “I will make you do,” what else does he say but: “I will remove from you the heart of stone, from which you did not do, and I will give you a heart of flesh, from which you will do”? And what is this but: “I will remove the hard heart, from which you did not do, and I will give you an obedient heart, from which you will do”?

He makes us do, to whom a person says: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth.” For this is to say: “Make me set a guard over my mouth.” The person who said, “I have set a guard over my mouth” had already received this benefit from God [Ps. 38:2].

Therefore, whoever wishes to do God’s commandment and cannot already possesses a good will, but it is still small and weak. He will be able when he possesses a great and strong will.

When the martyrs fulfilled those great commandments, they did so with a great will, that is, with great love. Concerning this love the Lord himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” [John 15:13].

Hence the Apostle says: “The one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” For “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; you shall not steal; you shall not covet,” and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Rom. 13:8–9]. Love does no evil to one’s neighbor. Therefore, love is the fullness of the law.

The apostle Peter did not yet possess this love when, out of fear, he denied the Lord three times. “Fear is not in love,” as the evangelist John says in his Letter, “but perfect love casts out fear” [1 John 4:18].

Nevertheless, although small and imperfect, love was not absent when he said to the Lord: “I will lay down my life for you” [John 13:37]. He thought that he could do what he sensed he willed. And who had begun to give him this love, though small, except the one who prepares the will and, by cooperating, perfects what he begins by working? For he himself works so that we may will, beginning the work; and he cooperates with those who will, perfecting it.

For this reason the Apostle says: “I am confident that the one who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ” [Phil. 1:6].

Therefore, so that we may will, he works without us; but when we will, and will in such a way that we do, he cooperates with us. Nevertheless, without him—whether working so that we may will or cooperating with us when we will—we are powerless for works of piety.

It is said of him working so that we may will: “For it is God who works in you both to will” [Phil. 2:13]. Of him cooperating with us when we already will and do by willing, it is said: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” [Rom. 8:28].

What does “all things” mean except even those terrible and savage sufferings? That burden which is heavy for weakness becomes light for love. For the Lord said that his burden was light to people such as Peter was when he suffered for Christ, not such as he was when he denied Christ.

Commending this love—that is, the will burning with the most ardent divine love—the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” [Rom. 8:35] and so forth.

## CHAPTER CCXCI

### The hardening of the heart occurs because of preceding evils; from the same book

It is written in the Proverbs of Solomon: “As the movement of water, so is the heart of a king in the hand of God; wherever he wills, he will incline it” [Prov. 21:1].

And in Psalm 104 it is said concerning the Egyptians what God did to them: “And he turned their heart, so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants” [Ps. 104:25].

In the apostolic writings also, see what is written in the Letter of the apostle Paul to the Romans: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity” [Rom. 1:24]. A little later: “Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions” [Rom. 1:26]. Again, a little later: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do things that are improper” [Rom. 1:28].

And in his Second Letter to the Thessalonians he says concerning certain people: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God sends them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” [2 Thess. 2:10–12].

By these and similar testimonies of the divine utterances—which it would take far too long to recall in their entirety—it is sufficiently revealed, as I think, that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes, whether toward good according to his mercy or toward evil according to their merits, by his judgment, sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just.

It must be firmly and immovably fixed in your hearts that there is no unrighteousness with God. Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that people are led astray, dulled, or hardened in heart by God, do not doubt that their evil merits preceded this, so that they suffer these things justly. Otherwise you will fall into that saying of Solomon: “The folly of a man perverts his ways, and he blames God in his heart” [Prov. 19:3].

Grace, however, is not given according to human merits; otherwise grace would no longer be grace, because it is called grace precisely because it is given freely.

If God is powerful enough to work even in the hearts of the wicked—whether through good angels, evil angels, or by whatever other means—according to the merits of those whose wickedness he himself did not make, but which was either inherited originally from Adam or grew through their own will, what wonder is it if he works through the Holy Spirit in the hearts of his elect for good? He made those very hearts good from being evil.

But people may imagine whatever good merits they please, which they think precede their justification by God’s grace. They do not understand that, when they say this, they are doing nothing other than denying grace. But, as I said, let them imagine this concerning adults; what will they say concerning infants?

Certainly the Pelagians find no answer. They cannot identify any will in the receiving of grace whose merit they might say preceded it. Moreover, we see infants sometimes resisting with tears when they are baptized and receive the divine sacraments—something that would be counted against them as a great sin of impiety if they were already using free will.

And yet grace is plainly present even in those who resist, with no good merit preceding it. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

Sometimes this grace is granted to the children of unbelievers, when by the hidden providence of God they somehow come into the hands of the godly. Sometimes the children of believers do not obtain it, because some obstacle prevents help from reaching those in danger.

These things occur through the hidden providence of God, whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable. Observe what the Apostle had said before making this statement. He was speaking of Jews and Gentiles when he wrote to the Romans, that is, to Gentiles, and said:

“For just as you once did not believe God, but now have received mercy through their unbelief, so they too have now not believed through the mercy shown to you, so that they also may receive mercy. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” [Rom. 11:30–32].

And when he considered what he had said, marveling at the certain truth but great profundity of his statement, he immediately exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” [Rom. 11:33]

Because perverse people did not consider these inscrutable judgments and unsearchable ways—being inclined to criticize but incapable of understanding—they supposed and loudly claimed that the Apostles were saying: “Let us do evil, so that good may come.” God forbid that the Apostles should say this.

But people who did not understand thought that this was being said when they heard the Apostle say: “The law entered in so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded still more” [Rom. 5:20].

Grace, of course, acts so that those who had done evil may now do good, not so that they may persist in evil and think that good should be repaid to them.

They should not therefore say: “Let us do evil, so that good may come,” but: “We did evil, and good came; now let us do good, so that in the age to come we may receive good for good, we who in this age receive good for evil.”

For this reason it is written in the Psalm: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” [Ps. 100:1].

At first, therefore, the Son of Man did not come into the world in order to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. This was because of mercy. Afterwards, however, he will come in judgment to judge the living and the dead.

Although even at the present time salvation itself does not occur without judgment, it occurs through a hidden judgment. For this reason he said: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” [John 9:39].

Therefore, refer such matters to the hidden judgments of God when you see, in one and the same condition—which all infants certainly share, since they inherit evil from Adam—that one is helped so as to be baptized while another is not helped and dies in that state of bondage; that one, after being baptized, is left in this life, although God foreknew that he would become ungodly, while another, after being baptized, is snatched from this life lest wickedness change his understanding.

Do not ascribe injustice or folly in these matters to God, with whom is the fountain of justice and wisdom. Rather, as I exhorted you at the beginning of this sermon, walk in what you have attained. God will reveal this also to you—if not in this life, certainly in the next—for nothing is hidden that will not be revealed.

When, therefore, you hear the Lord saying, “I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray” [Ezek. 14:9], and what the Apostle says, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” [Rom. 9:18], believe that evil merits preceded the one whom he permits to be led astray or hardened.

But in the one on whom he has mercy, faithfully and without doubt recognize the grace of God, who does not repay evils with evils, but good with evils.

Do not therefore remove free will from Pharaoh because God says in many places, “I hardened Pharaoh,” or “I have hardened,” or “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.” For this does not mean that Pharaoh himself did not harden his own heart. Indeed, this too is read concerning him when the dog-fly [Greek: κυνόμυια, *kunómuia*] was removed from the Egyptians. Scripture says: “And Pharaoh hardened his heart, even at this time, and he was unwilling to let the people go” [Exod. 8:32].

Thus both God hardened him by a just judgment and Pharaoh himself by free will.

Be certain, therefore, that your labor will not be in vain if, advancing in a good purpose, you persevere to the end. For God, who now does not repay those whom he delivers according to their works, will then repay each one according to his works.

God will certainly repay evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good; and good for good, because he is good and just. Only evil for good will he not repay, because he is not unjust.

He will therefore repay evil for evil—punishment for injustice; he will repay good for evil—grace for injustice; and he will repay good for good—grace for grace.

## CHAPTER CCXCII

### He distinguishes two conditions: “To be able not to sin” and “Not to be able to sin”; likewise concerning death; from the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, addressed to Valentinus and the monks.

[Col. 0996B] What, then, will be freer than free choice when it will not be able to serve sin—a reward of merit that was also destined for humanity, just as it was made for the holy angels? But now, since the good merit has been lost through sin, in those who are delivered the gift of grace has been made that which was destined to be the reward of merit. Therefore these two distinctions must be examined carefully and watchfully: “to be able not to sin” and “not to be able to sin”; “to be able not to die” and “not to be able to die”; “to be able not to abandon the good” and “not to be able to abandon the good.”
