The first human being was able not to sin, was able not to die, and was able not to abandon the good. Are we then going to say that one who possessed such free choice was unable to sin? Or that one to whom it was said, “If you sin, you shall die the death,” was unable to die? Or that he was unable to abandon the good, when he abandoned it by sinning and therefore died?

The first freedom of the will, then, was the ability not to sin; the last will be much greater: the inability to sin. The first immortality was the ability not to die; the last will be much greater: the inability to die. The first was the power of perseverance—the ability not to abandon the good; the last will be the happiness of perseverance—the inability to abandon the good.

Does the fact that the latter goods will be more excellent and better mean that the former were either nothing or insignificant? The helps themselves must likewise be distinguished: one kind of help is that without which something does not happen, and another is the help by which something happens. For without nourishment we cannot live; yet, when nourishment is available, it does not make someone live who has wished to die. The help of nourishment, therefore, is something without which life does not occur, but not something by which we are made to live. Happiness, however, which a person does not possess, makes him happy immediately when it is given. It is a help not only without which something does not happen, but also by which it happens—the very reason for which it is given. Therefore this help is both that by which something happens and that without which it does not happen: if happiness is given to a person, he immediately becomes happy; and if it is never given, he will never be happy. Nourishment, on the other hand, does not necessarily make a person live, although without it he cannot live.

Thus the first human being, who had received in the good in which he was created upright the ability not to sin, the ability not to die, and the ability not to abandon that very good, was given the help of perseverance—not a help by which he would persevere, but one without which, through free choice, he could not [or: would not be able to] persevere. Now, however, the saints predestined by the grace of God for the kingdom of God are given not such a help of perseverance, but one of such a kind that perseverance itself is bestowed upon them—not merely so that without this gift they cannot persevere, but also so that through this gift they can do nothing except persevere.

For he not only said, “Without me you can do nothing”; he also said, “You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.” By these words he showed that he had given them not only righteousness but also perseverance in it. For since Christ appoints them to go, bear fruit, and have their fruit remain, who would dare to say, “Perhaps it will not remain”? “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable”—but this refers to those who are called according to his purpose. Since, therefore, Christ intercedes for these people so that their faith may not fail, it will unquestionably not fail to the end; and thus it will persevere to the end, and the end will find it remaining, not otherwise.

A greater freedom is necessary against so many and such great temptations, which were not present in paradise, strengthened and fortified by the gift of perseverance. Thus the world, with all its attractions, terrors, errors, and torments, is overcome. The martyrdoms of the saints have demonstrated this. That man, with no one terrifying him, and even in opposition to the command of the terrifying God, did not stand by free choice amid such great happiness and such great ease of not sinning. These others, however—not merely while the world terrified them, but while it raged to prevent them from standing—stood firm in faith. He saw the present goods that he was going to abandon; they did not see the future goods that they were going to receive. From where did this come, except from him who granted them the mercy by which they became faithful, from whom they received not the spirit of fear, by which they would yield to their persecutors, but the spirit of power, love, and self-control, by which they overcame everything that threatened, everything that enticed, and everything that tormented them?

Thus, to that man, the free will with which he was created was given without any sin, and he made it serve sin. In these others, however, the will had been enslaved to sin; it was liberated by him who said, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.” Through this grace they receive such great freedom that, although as long as they live here they struggle against the desires of sins and some of those desires creep upon them, for which they say daily, “Forgive us our debts,” they nevertheless no longer serve sin, which leads to death. Concerning this sin the apostle John says, “There is sin leading to death; I do not say that one should pray for it.”

Since this sin has not been specified, many different views may be held about it. For my part, I say that it is abandoning, even unto death, the faith that works through love. They no longer serve this sin—not as free people by their first creation, as that man was, but liberated by the grace of God through the second Adam. Through this liberation they have free choice by which they serve God, not by which they are taken captive by the devil. For, having been liberated from sin, they became servants of righteousness; in it they will stand to the end, through the gift of perseverance bestowed by him who foreknew and predestined them, called them according to his purpose, justified them, and glorified them.

[Col. 0998A] But when these things are said even of the saints who will persevere, as though it were uncertain whether they will persevere, they must be heard in no other way by those for whom it is useful not to think highly of themselves but to fear. For who among the multitude of believers, while living in this mortality, would presume that he is among the number of the predestined? This must be kept hidden here, where pride must be avoided so carefully that even the apostle, lest he become exalted, was struck with a powerful blow through an angel of Satan. Hence it was said to the apostles, “If you remain in me,” by the one who certainly knew that they would remain; and through the prophet, “If you are willing and obey me,” although he himself certainly knew in whom he was working the willing. Many similar statements are made. For the sake of this useful secrecy, lest anyone become exalted, but so that all—even those who are running well—may fear while it remains hidden who will reach the goal, we must believe that some of the sons of perdition, not having received the gift of persevering to the end, begin to live in the faith that works through love, live faithfully and justly for some time, and afterward fall. If this had happened to none of them, people would retain that most salutary fear, by which the vice of pride is suppressed, until they reached the grace of Christ through which one lives piously; thereafter they would already be secure that they would never fall away from him. But such presumption is not useful in this place of temptation, where weakness is so great that security can produce pride.

In the end, this too will come to pass—but then what already exists in the angels will also exist in human beings, when no pride will be possible.

### CHAPTER CCXCIII. That grace neither prevents correction, nor correction denies grace; from the same book

If sometimes we refrain from correcting someone out of fear that the person might thereby perish, why do we not also correct out of fear that the person might thereby perish even more? For we do not possess a greater compassion than the blessed apostle, who says: “Correct the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone; see that no one repays evil for evil.” Here we should understand that evil is repaid for evil when the person who ought to be corrected is not corrected but is neglected through a perverse dissimulation.

He says, “Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear.” This must be understood of sins that are not hidden, lest he be thought to have spoken contrary to the Lord’s command. For the Lord says, “If your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him.” Yet he carries the severity of correction so far as to say, “If he does not even listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.” And who loved the weak more than the one who became weak for all and was crucified for all through that very weakness?

Since this is so, grace neither prevents correction, nor does correction deny grace. Therefore righteousness must be commanded in such a way that grace from God—by which what is commanded may be done—is sought in faithful prayer. Both must be done in such a way that just correction is not neglected and that all these things are done with love, because love neither commits sin nor covers over a multitude of sins.

### CHAPTER CCXCIV. Concerning predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge, whereas foreknowledge can exist without predestination; from the book addressed to Prosper

Predestination is something that cannot exist without foreknowledge, whereas foreknowledge can exist without predestination. By predestination God foreknew those things that he himself was going to do; hence it is said, “He made the things that were to be.” But he is also able to foreknow things that he does not himself do, such as all sins. For although there are some sins that are also punishments of sins—hence it is said, “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting”—the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment.

Therefore God’s predestination, which is directed toward the good, is, as I have said, a preparation of grace; grace, however, is the effect of predestination itself. When God promised Abraham the faith of the nations in his seed, saying, “I have appointed you the father of many nations,” and the Apostle says, “Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the seed,” he did not promise on the basis of the power of our will but on the basis of his own predestination. For he promised what he himself was going to do, not what human beings were going to do. For although human beings do the good things that pertain to the worship of God, he himself makes them do what he has commanded; they do not make him do what he has promised. Otherwise, for God’s promises to be fulfilled, the matter would lie not in God’s power but in that of human beings, and what was promised by God would be rendered to Abraham by them.

Abraham, however, did not believe in this way. He believed while giving glory to God, because he was powerful to do what he had promised. The text does not say “to foretell,” nor does it say “to foreknow,” for he can foretell and foreknow the actions of others. Rather, it says, “He is powerful also to do,” and thus the actions are not those of others but his own.

Or perhaps God promised Abraham the good works of the nations in his seed, so that he promised what he himself does; but he did not promise the faith of the nations, which human beings make for themselves, except that, in order to promise what he himself does, he foreknew that human beings would make it? The Apostle certainly does not speak in this way. God promised Abraham sons who would follow the footsteps of his faith, as he states most clearly. But if he promised the works of the nations, then surely he did not promise faith, since there are no good works except from faith: “The righteous shall live by faith,” “whatever is not from faith is sin,” and “without faith it is impossible to please God.”

Nevertheless, for God to fulfill what he promised would still lie in human power. Unless a person does what belongs to the human being—which God does not give—he will not do what God gives. That is, unless a person has faith from himself, God does not fulfill what he promised, so that works of righteousness may be given by God. Consequently, for God to fulfill his promises would lie not in God’s power but in that of human beings.

But if truth and piety forbid us to believe this, let us believe with Abraham that he is powerful to do what he promised. He promised Abraham sons, and they cannot be such if they do not have faith; therefore he himself gives faith also.

When the Apostle says, “Therefore it is from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace,” I am astonished that people prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise.

“But God’s will concerning me is uncertain,” someone says. What, then? Is your own will concerning yourself certain? Do you not fear: “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall”?

Since both are uncertain, why does a person entrust his faith, hope, and love to what is firmer rather than to what is weaker?

“But when it is said, ‘If you believe, you will be saved,’ one of these is required and the other is offered: what is required lies in human power, and what is offered lies in God’s power.”

Why are both not in God’s power—both what he commands and what he offers? For he is asked to give what he commands, and believers ask that their faith be increased. They pray for unbelievers, that faith may be given to them. Thus both in its growth and in its beginning faith is God’s gift.

The statement “If you believe, you will be saved” is said in the same way as “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Here too one of two things is required and the other is offered. “If by the Spirit,” he says, “you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Thus putting to death the deeds of the flesh is required, while living is offered.

Would it then be acceptable to say that putting to death the deeds of the flesh is not God’s gift, or to refuse to acknowledge it as God’s gift because we hear it required of us with the reward of life offered if we do it? Far be this from the participants in and defenders of grace. This is the damnable error of the Pelagians, whose mouths the Apostle immediately closed by adding: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.” He did this so that we would not believe that we put to death the deeds of the flesh through our own spirit and not through God’s Spirit.

He was speaking of this Spirit of God also where he says, “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one individually as he wills.” Among these things, as you know, he named faith as well.

Therefore, just as putting to death the deeds of the flesh is God’s gift, yet is required of us with the promised reward of life, so faith too is God’s gift, although it is required of us with the promised reward of salvation when it is said, “If you believe, you will be saved.” These things are commanded to us and are shown to be God’s gifts so that it may be understood that we do them and that God makes us do them, as he says most clearly through the prophet Ezekiel. For what is clearer than where he says, “I will cause you to do it”?

Attend to the passage of Scripture itself, and you will see that God promises that he will cause them to do what he commands them to do [or: “what he commands to be done”]. He does not, however, remain silent there about their merits—evil merits—by which he shows that he repays evil with good, precisely by making them thereafter possess good works, when he himself makes them do the divine commandments.

All this reasoning by which we defend that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord is truly grace—that is, that it is not given according to our merits—is asserted most clearly by the testimonies of the divine writings. Nevertheless, it is resisted by those who think that, unless they assign to themselves something that they first give in order that it may be repaid to them, they are being restrained from every pursuit of piety.

This argument sometimes struggles with adults who already exercise the freedom of the will. But when it comes to infants and to the mediator himself between God and human beings, the human assertion of preceding merits collapses entirely. For infants are not distinguished from the rest by any preceding good merits so that they might belong to the liberator of human beings; nor was he, although he too was human, made the liberator of human beings by any preceding human merits.

Who could accept the claim that infants are baptized and depart from this life during infancy on account of their future merits, while other infants who are not baptized die at the same age because their future merits too were foreknown—but evil ones—not because God rewards or condemns their good or evil life, but because they had no life at all?

The Apostle fixed a boundary that human, or—to speak more mildly—careless suspicion must not cross. He says, “We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.” He says “has done,” and does not add, “or was going to do.”

But I do not know how this idea entered the minds of such men: that merits of infants which will never come to exist should be punished or honored. Why is it said that a person is to be judged according to what he has done through the body, when many things are done by the mind alone, not through the body or any bodily member, and often things so great that such thoughts deserve the most just punishment? I say nothing of the words of the fool in his heart, “There is no God.”

What, then, does “according to what he has done through the body” mean except “according to what he has done during the time when he was in the body,” so that by “through the body” we understand “during the time of the body”? After the body, no one will be in the body except at the final resurrection—not to acquire any merits, but to receive rewards for good merits and suffer punishments for evil ones.

### CHAPTER CCXCV. That the door of the word is opened when the heart of the hearer is opened so that he may believe; from the same book

How is the door of the word opened except when the understanding of the hearer is opened so that he may believe, and, once faith has begun, admit what is preached and discussed for the building up of sound teaching, rather than, with the heart closed through unbelief, reject and repel what is said?

Thus he also says to the Corinthians: “I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” What else can be understood here except that, when the Gospel was first preached there through him, many believed and many adversaries of that same faith arose? This accords with the Lord’s words: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father,” and, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.”

The door, therefore, is opened in those to whom it has been given; the many adversaries are from among those to whom it has not been given.

Likewise, in the second Epistle, the same Apostle says to the same people: “When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit because I did not find Titus, my brother; but, taking leave of them, I went out into Macedonia.” From whom did he take leave except from those who had believed, in whose hearts the door had been opened to him as he preached the Gospel?

But observe what he adds: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, a fragrance of death unto death; to others, a fragrance of life unto life.”

See from where this most zealous soldier and unconquered defender of grace gives thanks: he gives thanks because the apostles are the good fragrance of Christ to God, both among those who are saved by his grace and among those who perish by his judgment. But lest this provoke too much anger against those who understand it poorly, he himself gives warning when he adds and says, “And who is sufficient for these things?”

But let us return to the opening of the door, by which the Apostle signified the beginning of the hearers’ faith. What else does “praying together also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word” mean except the clearest demonstration that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift? For it would not be requested from him in prayer unless it were believed to be granted by him.

This gift of heavenly grace had descended upon that seller of purple to whom, as Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, God had opened her understanding, and she attended to the things being spoken by Paul. In this way she was called so that she might believe.

God does what he wills in human hearts, either by helping or by judging, so that through them also what his hand and counsel predestined to be done may be fulfilled.

Therefore they said that even that which we established by the testimony of the books of Kings and Chronicles—namely, that when God wills something to happen which ought to happen only through willing human beings, he inclines their hearts so that they will it, since he himself inclines them, the one who works within us in a wondrous and ineffable way the willing itself—does not pertain to the question under discussion.

What else is this than to say nothing and yet contradict? Unless perhaps they think that God inclines human wills in order to establish earthly kingdoms, but does not incline, for the attainment of the heavenly kingdom, the wills of those whose wills he wills to incline.

Yet, as I think, the following was said concerning the kingdom of heaven, not concerning an earthly kingdom: “Incline my heart to your testimonies”; or, “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he will delight in his way”; or, “The will is prepared by the Lord”; or, “I will give them another heart, and I will give them a new spirit.”

Let them also hear this: “I will put my spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes.” Let them hear: “The steps of a man are corrected by the Lord.” Let them hear: “Every person seems righteous to himself, but the Lord directs the hearts.” Let them hear: “As many as were appointed to eternal life believed.” Let them hear these and whatever other statements I have not mentioned, by which it is shown that God prepares and turns human wills toward the kingdom—even the kingdom of heaven—and toward eternal life.

Consider, then, what it means for us to believe that God works human wills to establish earthly kingdoms, while human beings work their own wills in order to obtain the kingdom of heaven.

### CHAPTER CCXCVI. That grace precedes faith and grants perseverance; from the book On the Gift of Perseverance

Grace, then, also precedes faith. Otherwise, if faith precedes grace, the will undoubtedly precedes it as well, since faith cannot exist without the will. But if grace precedes faith, since it precedes the will, it certainly precedes every obedience and also love, by which alone one truly and pleasantly obeys God.

Grace works all these things in the person to whom it is given and whose every one of these things it precedes. What remains among these goods is perseverance [to the end]. It would be useless to ask the Lord for it daily if the Lord did not work it through his grace in the person whose prayer he hears.

See now how far from the truth it is to deny that perseverance to the end of this life is God’s gift, when he himself gives this life an end whenever he wills. If he gives it an end before an impending fall, he makes the person persevere to the end.

But the generosity of God’s goodness is even more wondrous and evident to the faithful in that this grace is given also to infants, whose age does not permit obedience to be given.

God undoubtedly foreknew that he would give these gifts of his to whomever he gives them, and he prepared them in his foreknowledge. Those whom he predestined, he also called—with that calling which I am never reluctant to mention, concerning which it is said, “The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.” For to arrange in his foreknowledge, which cannot be deceived or changed, the works that he himself is going to do is precisely, and nothing else, to predestine.

### CHAPTER CCXCVII. That if original sin did not exist, infants would be subject to no evil; from the third book Against Julian

You therefore think in vain that there is no offense in infants because an offense cannot exist without the will, and no will exists in them. This is correctly said concerning each person’s own sin, not concerning the contagion of the original sin of the first human being.

If that contagion did not exist, infants would certainly be bound by no evil, and under the great power of the just God they would suffer nothing evil either in body or in soul.

Yet this too took its beginning from the evil will of earlier human beings. Thus, unless there is an evil will, there is no origin of anyone’s sin.

If you understand these things, you will confess simply and truthfully Christ’s grace toward infants. You will not be forced to say the most impious and absurd things: either that infants ought not to be baptized—which perhaps you will say later—or that so great a sacrament is a mockery in them, so that they are baptized in the Savior but not saved; redeemed by the liberator but not liberated; washed in the bath of regeneration but not cleansed; exorcized and exsufflated but not rescued from the power of darkness.

Let their price be the blood that was poured out for the remission of sins, yet let them be cleansed by the remission of no sin!

You say all this because you are afraid to say that they should not be baptized, lest not only the faces of your men be smeared with spittle, but the heads of your little women be battered with sandals.

We certainly say that the reason the one who is born is under the devil until he is reborn in Christ is the contagion arising from sin. But you who deny this should at least look at what is evident: why do some infants suffer from a demon, unless perhaps you will deny either that demons themselves exist or that infants are under the devil? Nor will the Gospel remind you, where perhaps for your sake the Lord asked what he knew, so that the boy’s father might answer that his son had been grievously afflicted by a demon from infancy, so that he could not be expelled by Christ’s disciples.

Behold, I do not say that marriage is the reason infants are under the devil, as you falsely accuse me of saying. Marriage has its own order, its own blessing, and its own goodness, which even when sin entered it could not lose.

But you—why is that infant under the devil, at least the one who is manifestly tormented by the devil, so that at times he even dies from the torment itself? Answer, if you can.

You do not want anyone to undergo punishment for another’s sins, lest it become credible from this that the contagion of sins can also pass from those who beget to those who are born.

But this splendid dialectician, evidently, will not let me escape. You will question me directly and briefly: “In infants, should I regard the guilty act or nature as responsible?” And you answer both alternatives: “If the act, show what they have done; if nature, show who made them.”

As though an evil act could make anyone guilty without making a nature guilty as well. The one who is guilty by an act is a human being; but a human being is nature. Thus, just as adults are guilty through the act of sin, minors are guilty through the contagion of their elders: the former through what they do, the latter through those from whom they derive their origin.

Therefore, in infants there is the good that they are human beings—something they would not exist as at all unless the one who is supremely good had created them. But if they drew no evil from their origin, they would never be born with bodily or other defects.

For God, who is the creator of souls, is also the creator of bodies. He certainly does not inflict defects upon human nature in its very creation without cause. For it cannot be said of the countless infants who are born with such a great variety of defects in soul and body that what the Lord said concerning the man born blind applies to them: that this happened neither because of his own sin nor because of his parents’ sin, but so that the works of God might be manifested in him.

Many are never healed at all, but die with the same defects, whether at whatever age or in infancy itself. Some infants, even after being reborn, either retain the evils with which they were born or acquire evils of this kind.

Far be it from us to say that this happens undeservedly. Rather, let us understand from this that their rebirth benefits them for the age to come, while the arrangement of this age, because of the beginning of human pride through which humanity defected from God, is carried out through the various evils of human beings, under a grievous yoke upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all.

### CHAPTER CCXCVIII. That when Julian acknowledges the remedy, he must also acknowledge the disease; from the same book

You eloquently place conjugal chastity, as though in the middle, between the wanton and the continent. It is indignant that the former have committed illicit acts, while it is astonished that the latter have even despised what is licit. It has been allotted the region of the furthest boundary: it curses the barbarism of those rushing beyond it and venerates the radiance of those shining above it. With modest hands it both comforts those who are burning and praises those who do not need such a remedy.

I take great pleasure in this most eloquent truth. But I ask you: surely, as you say—and you say it most eloquently and truthfully—conjugal chastity praises the continent because they do not need the remedy that it recognizes itself to have needed, namely, as the Apostle says, that one who does not exercise self-control should marry.

Why, then, when I say that this desire is a disease, do you deny it, although you nevertheless confess that it requires a remedy? If you acknowledge the remedy, acknowledge the disease; if you deny the disease, deny the remedy.

I ask you: yield at last to the truth speaking through your own mouth. No one provides a remedy for health.

### CHAPTER CCXCIX. Concerning the desire of the flesh against the spirit, and of the spirit against the flesh; from the same book

71 Recall what the Apostle writes to the Galatians—certainly baptized people. “Walk by the Spirit,” he says, “and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” He does not say, “Do not have them,” because they could not avoid having them; rather, he says, “You will not fulfill them,” that is, you will not complete their works by the consent of the will.

“For the flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things that you want.”

See whether this is not what he says to the Romans: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want—that I do.”

Then he adds and says to the Galatians: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the law.” See whether this is not what he says to the Romans: “It is no longer I who do it”; and, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person”; and, “Let sin not reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires.”

For if the desires are not obeyed—desires that must exist in the flesh of sin and in this body of death—what the Apostle forbids to be fulfilled will not be completed, when he says, “You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh.”

These are the very works concerning which he continues and says [“all in a wonderful way”]: “The works of the flesh are evident: fornications, impurities, debaucheries, the worship of idols, and so forth.” If, therefore, the desires of the flesh are not consented to, although they are enacted as movements, they will nevertheless not be completed in works.

Accordingly, when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things that we want, neither are the desires of the flesh completed, although they occur, nor are our good works completed, although they occur.

For just as the desire of the flesh is completed when the spirit consents to it in evil works, so that it no longer desires against the flesh but acts together with it, our good works will also then be completed when the flesh consents so fully to the spirit that it itself no longer desires against the spirit.

This is what we want when we desire the perfection of righteousness; this is what we must continually intend to want. But because we cannot accomplish it in this corruptible flesh, he says to the Romans: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good” [“I intend not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, but I do not find how to accomplish the good”]. Or, as the Greek manuscripts have it: “To will is present with me, but not to accomplish the good”—that is, accomplishing the good is not present with me.

He does not say “to do,” but “to accomplish the good.” For doing good is not following the desires; accomplishing the good is not having the desires. Therefore, what is said to the Galatians, “You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” corresponds conversely to what is said to the Romans, “I do not find how to accomplish the good.”

For neither are those desires completed in evil when the consent of our will does not join them, nor is our will completed in good as long as the movement of those desires—which we do not consent to—remains.

This very conflict, in which even baptized people contend as in an arena when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—where the spirit does a good work by not consenting to evil desire, yet does not complete it because it does not extinguish the evil desires themselves, and the flesh produces an evil desire, yet does not complete it because the spirit does not consent to it and the flesh itself does not reach condemned works—this conflict is shown briefly to belong not to Jews or to any others, but plainly to faithful Christians who labor in this struggle by living well.

He says to the Romans: “Therefore it is I myself who with the mind serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.”

If this is the condition of the body of this death—a condition that certainly did not exist in paradise, in that body of life—it is unquestionably evident enough where infants derive the bondage of sin when they are born carnally, a bondage that is not dissolved except when they are reborn spiritually.

For they do not derive it from the work by which God made human nature, but from the wound inflicted upon human nature by its enemy—not the enemy who, according to the Manichaeans, springs from an evil nature that God did not create, but the angelic enemy who was once good through God’s work and became evil through his own work. He first wounded and cast himself down, so that, having been struck down, he might strike down others and inflict a wound through the evil persuasion of transgression. Hence the human race, even in those who walk in God’s way, would limp.

### CHAPTER CCC. Against Pelagian objections and conclusions, under fifteen headings: responses of Saint Augustine from the book addressed to the bishops Paul [Col. 1006D] and Eutropius, On the Perfection of Righteousness.

First of all, he says, let the person who denies that a human being can exist without sin be asked what sort of sin is in question: one that can be avoided, or one that cannot be avoided. If it is one that cannot be avoided, it is not sin. If it is one that can be avoided, then a person can exist without the sin that can be avoided; for no reason or justice permits even calling something sin that cannot be avoided in any way.

We reply that sin can be avoided if human nature, having been corrupted, is healed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For nature is not healthy to the extent that a person either does not see through blindness what ought to be done, or fails through weakness to accomplish it, while “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh,” so that people do not do what they wish.

Again, he says, it must be asked whether sin is a matter of will or necessity. If it is a matter of necessity, it is not sin; if it is a matter of will, it can be avoided. We reply as above; and in order that we may be healed, we call upon him to whom it is said in the Psalm: “Deliver me from my necessities.”

Again, he says, it must be asked what sin is: natural or accidental. If it is natural, it is not sin; but if it is accidental, it can depart; and what can depart can be avoided; and what can be avoided is something without which a person can exist.

We reply that sin is not natural, but that, especially because our nature has been corrupted, free choice is insufficient for avoiding sin unless grace through Jesus Christ our Lord comes to its aid and heals it. Thus we have become by nature children of wrath.

Again, he says, it must be asked what sin is: an act or a thing. If it is a thing, it must have an author; and if it is said to have an author, someone other than God will appear to be introduced as the author of some thing. But if it is impious to say this, and it is necessary to confess that every sin is an act, not a thing, then, if it is an act—or rather, because it truly is an act—it can be avoided.

We reply that sin is indeed called and is an act, not a thing. But lameness in the body is likewise an act, not a thing, since the thing is the foot itself, or the body, or the person who limps because the foot is defective. Yet one cannot avoid lameness unless one has a healed foot. The same can happen in the inner person, through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord.

The defect itself by which a person limps is neither the foot, nor the body, nor the person, nor lameness itself—for lameness is certainly absent when the person is not walking—although the defect by which lameness occurs when the person walks is present. Let him therefore ask what name he wishes to give that defect: whether he wants to call it a thing, or an act, or rather an evil quality of a thing, by which the act becomes deformed.

So also, in the inner person, the mind is a thing, robbery is an act, and greed is a defect—that is, a quality according to which the mind is evil even when it does nothing by which it serves its greed, even when it hears, “You shall not covet,” and condemns itself, yet remains greedy. Nevertheless, it is renewed—that is, healed—through faith day by day, and this occurs only through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord.

Again, he says, it must be asked whether a person ought to be without sin. Without doubt, he ought. If he ought, he can; if he cannot, then neither ought he to be. And if a person ought not to be without sin, then he ought to be with sin; nor will sin be sin if it is established that it ought to be present. But if even this is absurd to say, it is necessary to confess that a person ought to be without sin, and it is established that a person ought to do nothing other than what he can.

We reply with the same analogy by which we already replied above. When we see a lame person who can be healed, we rightly say: “This person ought to be without lameness.” And if he ought to be, he can be; yet when he wishes, he cannot immediately do so. He can only do so once treatment has been applied, he has been healed, and medicine has assisted his will.

This occurs in the inner person with respect to sin, as his lameness, through the grace of the one who came “not to call the righteous, but sinners,” because “it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill.”

Again, he says, it must be asked whether it has been commanded that a person be without sin. Either he cannot be without sin, and therefore it has not been commanded; or, because it has been commanded, he can be without sin. For why would something be commanded that could not possibly be done?

We reply that it is most appropriately commanded that a person walk with straight steps, so that, when he recognizes that he cannot do so, he may seek the medicine which, for healing the inner person’s lameness of sin, is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Again, he says, it must be asked whether God wants a person to be without sin. Without doubt he does, and without doubt it is possible. For who is so insane as even to doubt that something can happen which he does not doubt God wants to happen?

We reply that if God did not want a person to be without sin, he would not have sent his Son to heal people from their sins. This occurs in those who believe and profess [profitentibus, “profess”; proficientibus, “make progress”], through the renewal of the inner person day by day, until perfect righteousness comes, like complete health.

Again, he says, it must be asked how God wants a person to be: with sin or without sin. Without doubt, he does not want the person to be with sin. One must consider how great the impiety and blasphemy would be to say that a person can be with sin, which God does not want, while denying that a person can be without sin, which God does want—as though God had created someone to be able to be what he does not want and unable to be what he does want, and to exist contrary to his will rather than according to it.

We have already replied above, but I see that something must be added: “We have been saved in hope,” but “hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience.” Then righteousness [erit, “will be”] will be complete when health is complete; health will be complete when love is complete—for “love is the fullness of the law”; and love will be complete when we see him as he is. Nothing will be added to love when faith has arrived at vision.

Again, he says, it must be asked through what a person comes to be with sin: through the necessity of nature or through free choice. If through the necessity of nature, he is without guilt; if through free choice, it must be asked from whom he received that free choice. Without doubt, from God. But what God gave is certainly good; this cannot be denied. By what reasoning, then, is it proved to be good if it is more inclined toward evil than toward good? For it is more inclined toward evil than toward good if, through it, a person can be with sin but cannot be without sin.

We reply that it was through free choice that the person came to be with sin, but then a punitive corruption followed, which transformed freedom into necessity. Hence faith cries out to God: “Deliver me from my necessities.” Under these necessities we either cannot understand what we wish, or, although we understand it, we wish for it but are unable to accomplish it. For freedom itself is promised to believers by the Liberator: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.” Nature, overcome by judgment [judicio; or vitio, “defect”] into which the will fell, lost its freedom.

For this reason another Scripture says: “By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved.” Just as the healthy do not need a physician but the sick do, so the free do not need a liberator, but slaves do, so that gratitude for freedom may say to him: “You have saved my soul from necessities.” For true freedom is itself health, which would not have perished if the will had remained good.

But because the will sinned, the harsh necessity of possessing sin followed the sinful will, until the whole weakness is healed and such freedom is received that, as it is necessary for the will to remain happily in the life of blessedness, so there is also a voluntary and blessed necessity of living well and never sinning.

Therefore, he says, God made the human being good, and, besides making him good, also commanded him to do good. How impious it would be to confess that the human being is evil, although he was neither made evil nor commanded to be evil, and to deny that he can be good, although he was made good and was commanded to do good.

We reply: Since God, not the human being, made the human being good, God—not the human being himself—restores him so that he may be good. He does this by delivering the willing, believing, and calling person from the evil that the person himself inflicted upon himself. This takes place as the inner person is renewed day by day by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that the outer person may rise on the last day to eternal life rather than punishment.

Again, he says, it must be asked in how many ways every sin consists. In two, unless I am mistaken: either those things are done which are forbidden, or those things are not done which are commanded. Everything that is forbidden can certainly be avoided, just as everything that is commanded can be accomplished; for something would be forbidden or commanded in vain if it could neither be avoided nor fulfilled. How, then, shall we deny that a person can be without sin, when we must confess that he can avoid everything that is forbidden and accomplish everything that is commanded?

We reply that there are many divine commandments in the holy Scriptures, and it would be too laborious to recall them all. But the Lord, “consummating and abbreviating his word upon the earth,” said that the Law and the Prophets depend upon two commandments, so that we might understand that whatever else has been divinely commanded finds its fulfillment in these two and must be referred to them: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

“On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole Law and the Prophets depend.” Therefore, whatever we are forbidden by God’s law and whatever we are commanded to do is forbidden and commanded so that we may fulfill these two. Perhaps the general prohibition is, “You shall not covet,” and the general command is, “You shall love.”

The apostle Paul briefly joined both together in one passage. The prohibition is: “Do not be conformed to this age”; the command, however, is: “But be transformed in the renewal of your mind.” The former pertains to not coveting, the latter to loving; the former to self-restraint, the latter to righteousness; the former to turning away from evil, the latter to doing good. By not coveting, we strip off the old nature; by loving, we put on the new.

But no one can be self-controlled unless God grants it, and “the love of God is poured into our hearts,” not by ourselves, “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.” This happens day by day in those who progress by willing, believing, and calling upon God, “forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead.”

For this reason the law commands these things: when a person fails to fulfill them, he should not exalt himself, swollen with pride, but, exhausted, should flee to grace. Thus, by terrifying him, the law leads him to love Christ in the role of a pedagogue.

Again, he says, it must be asked how a person cannot be without sin: by will or by nature. If by nature, it is not sin; if by will, the will can very easily be changed by the will.

We reply, warning that one must consider how great the presumption is in saying not only that the will can change—which, with God’s grace assisting, must not be denied—but that it can do so very easily, when the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another [sibi, ‘to each other’], so that you do not do the things you wish.” He does not say, “They oppose one another so that you do not wish to do what you can do,” but “so that you do not do the things you wish.”

Why, then, has the desire of the flesh—which is certainly blameworthy and corrupt, and is nothing other than the desire for sin, which the same Apostle commands not to reign in our mortal body—not been changed by that will which the Apostle clearly expressed when he said, “so that you do not do the things you wish,” if the will can easily be changed by the will?

We do not thereby accuse the nature either of the soul or of the body, which God created and which is wholly good. Rather, we say that it has been corrupted by its own will and cannot be healed without the grace of God.

Again, he says, it must be asked: if a person cannot be without sin, whose fault is it—his own or someone else’s? If it is the person’s own fault, how can it be the person’s fault if this condition is something that cannot be avoided?

We reply that it is the person’s fault that he is not without sin because it was by the human will alone that he came into this necessity, although this necessity cannot be overcome by the human will alone.

Again, he says, it must be asked: if human nature is good—as no one but Marcion or a Manichaean will dare deny—how is it good if it cannot be without evil? For who would doubt that every sin is evil?

We reply that human nature is good and that it can be without evil. For this is why we cry out, “Deliver us from evil”: this deliverance is not completed as long as “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul.” But grace works through faith so that at some point it may be said: “Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the Law, because the Law, by prohibiting, increases the desire for sin unless the Spirit pours out love; and love will then be full and perfect when we see face to face.

And this, he says, must also be said: God is certainly just; this cannot be denied. God imputes every sin to the human being. I think this too must be confessed, because whatever is not imputed as sin is not sin, even if there is some sin that cannot be avoided. How, then, is God called just if he is believed to impute to someone what cannot be avoided?

We reply that long ago the cry was raised against the proud: “Blessed is the one to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” For he does not impute it to those who faithfully say to him: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” And he justly does not impute it, because it is just that which he says: “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

Sin occurs when love is either absent where it ought to be, or is less than it ought to be, whether this can be avoided by the will or cannot. If it can, the present will causes it; if it cannot, the former will caused it. Yet it can be avoided—not when the proud will is praised, but when the humble will is assisted.

After this, the author of these writings introduces himself as though disputing with another person. He has himself questioned and has the questioner say to him: “Give me a person without sin.” He replies: “I give you one who can be so.” Again the questioner says to him: “Who is he?” He replies: “You yourself.”

“If you say,” he continues, “‘I cannot be so,’ the response must be: ‘Whose fault is that?’ If you say, ‘Mine,’ it must be said: ‘How is it your fault if you yourself cannot?’”

Again, he has himself questioned and told: “You yourself are without sin, since you say that a person can be without sin?” He replies: “If I am not without sin, whose fault is that?” If the questioner says, “Yours,” the response must be: “How is it mine if I cannot be without sin?”

We reply that there should be no dispute with them over these words, because he did not dare to say that any person—or himself—was without sin, but answered only that a person could be without sin. This we too do not deny. The question is when and through whom this can happen.

For if it is already the case, then it would not be necessary for every faithful soul placed in this body of death to pray and say, “Forgive us our debts,” once all past sins had been forgiven in holy baptism. Whoever tries to persuade Christ’s faithful members that this prayer should not be made professes nothing other than that he himself is not a Christian.

Moreover, if a person can be without sin by himself, then Christ died for nothing. But Christ did not die for nothing. Therefore a person cannot be without sin, even if he wishes to be, unless he is aided by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This is being brought about now in those who are progressing, and will be fulfilled completely when the contest with death has been removed and love, nourished by believing and hoping, has been perfected by seeing and possessing.

Next he undertakes to establish his position by divine testimonies. Let us examine carefully what these are.

## CHAPTER CCCI  
### Where the commandments can be fulfilled in perfection, and what it means to be delivered from the body of death; or how the whole generality of righteousness is signified by the names fasting, almsgiving, and prayer; from the same book

“These are the testimonies,” he says, “by which it is proved that a person has been commanded to be without sin.”

To this we reply: The question is not whether it has been commanded—which is entirely clear—but whether that very command, whose existence is established, can be fulfilled in this body of death, where “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things we wish.”

Not everyone who ends this life is delivered from this body of death. Rather, the person is delivered who has received grace in this life and, so as not to receive it in vain, has performed good works. For it is one thing to depart from this body—which the final day of life compels all human beings to do—and another thing to be delivered from this body of death, which God’s grace alone grants to his holy and faithful people through Jesus Christ our Lord.

After this life, the reward that brings completion is given, but only to those who have acquired the merit of that same reward in this life. No one will reach the fullness of righteousness after departing from this life unless he has pursued it here by hungering and thirsting for it: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.”

Therefore, as long as we are pilgrims away from the Lord and “walk by faith, not by sight”—whence it is said, “The righteous person lives by faith”—our righteousness during this pilgrimage is to strive now, by the uprightness and perfection of our course, toward that perfection and fullness of righteousness in which love will already be full and perfect in the vision of its beauty.

We do this by disciplining our body and subjecting it to servitude; by cheerfully and wholeheartedly practicing almsgiving, both in granting benefits and in forgiving sins committed against us; by persevering without ceasing in prayer; and by doing these things within sound teaching, through which upright faith, firm hope, and pure love are built up.

This is our righteousness now, by which we run, hungering and thirsting, toward the perfection and fullness of righteousness, so that afterward we may be satisfied with it.

Therefore, when the Lord had said in the Gospel, “Do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them”—so that we would not measure our course by the end of human glory—he did not proceed in explaining righteousness beyond these three things: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer.

By fasting he signified every form of bodily discipline; by almsgiving, every act of goodwill and beneficence, whether giving or forgiving; and by prayer, every rule of holy desire.

For through bodily discipline the desire that ought not to be restrained merely but ought not to exist at all is curbed. It will not exist in that perfection of righteousness where there will be no sin whatsoever; yet even now, in the use of things that are permitted and lawful, it often displays its lack of moderation.

In true beneficence, by which the righteous person cares for a neighbor, things are sometimes done that cause harm even though they were thought to be beneficial. And at times, through weakness—when one does not sufficiently meet the needs of others, or when what is expended in kindness and labor makes little progress in them—weariness creeps in and darkens the cheerfulness in which God loves the giver. It creeps in more strongly the less a person has progressed, and less strongly the more he has progressed.

## CHAPTER CCCII  
### He says that the commandment concerning love of God is perfectly fulfilled in the life to come, and explains the testimonies by which a person is commanded to be perfect, or when the Church is glorious

Therefore, let all who are perfect understand this—that is, let all who run perfectly understand that we are not yet perfect, so that we may be perfected there toward which we now run in perfection. When “that which is perfect” has come, “that which is partial” will be abolished: it will no longer be partial but complete, because the reality of faith and hope will succeed—not something that is believed and hoped for, but something that is seen and possessed.

Love, however, which is greater than these three, will not be taken away but increased and fulfilled, contemplating what it believed and obtaining what it hoped for.

In the fullness of this love that commandment will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” For while there remains some carnal desire that must be curbed by self-restraint, God is not loved with the whole soul. The flesh does not desire without the soul, although the flesh is said to desire, because the soul desires in a carnal manner.

Then the righteous person will be without any sin whatsoever, because no law in his members will resist the law of his mind. Rather, with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind he will love God, which is the first and greatest commandment.

Why, then, should this perfection not be commanded to a person, although no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run correctly if one does not know where one must run. And how would one know if it were not shown by commandments?

Let us therefore run so that we may attain it. For all who run correctly [current, “running”; currunt, “run”] will attain it—not as in a theatrical contest, where everyone runs but only one receives the prize. Let us run by believing, hoping, and desiring; let us run by disciplining our body; let us cheerfully and wholeheartedly give alms by doing good and forgiving evil; and let us pray that the strength of those who run may be assisted.

Thus let us hear the commandments of perfection, lest we neglect to run toward the fullness of love.

With these points established, let us carefully hear the testimonies that the person to whom we are replying has set forth as though we ourselves had produced them.

In Deuteronomy: “But you shall be perfect before the Lord your God.” Also there: “And there shall be no one incomplete among the children of Israel.”

Likewise the Savior in the Gospel: “Be perfect, because your Father who is in heaven is perfect.”

Likewise the Apostle in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: “Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfect.”

Likewise in the Letter to the Colossians: “Correcting every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ.”

Likewise in the Letter to the Ephesians: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, so that it might be holy and immaculate.”

Hence blessed David also says: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain? The one who walks without spot and practices righteousness.”

And elsewhere: “And I shall be immaculate with him.”

And elsewhere: “Blessed are the immaculate in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.”

Likewise in Solomon: “The Lord loves holy hearts, and all the immaculate are acceptable to him.”

Some of these testimonies encourage those who are running to run perfectly; others recall the very end toward which they must strive by running.

A person who walks without spot may also reasonably be understood not as one who is already perfect, but as one who runs irreproachably toward perfection itself, free from damnable crimes and not neglecting to cleanse even venial sins through almsgiving.

For our entrance—that is, our journey by which we strive toward perfection—is cleansed by a pure prayer. Prayer is pure when one truthfully says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive.” Thus, while what is not imputed is not reproved, our course toward perfection is held to be without reproach—that is, without spot. When we arrive [venerimus, “we arrive”; pervenerimus, “we shall have arrived”] at that perfection, there will no longer be anything at all to be cleansed through forgiveness.

But it is one thing to be without sin, which in this life is said only of the Only-Begotten; it is another thing to be without blame, which could be said even in this life of many righteous people. For there is a certain manner of good life concerning which no just complaint can be made even amid this human existence.

Who could justly complain about a person who wishes evil upon no one, faithfully cares for those whom he can help, and does not retain a desire for vengeance against anyone’s injuries, so that he can truthfully say, “As we also forgive our debtors”?

Yet precisely by truthfully saying, “Forgive as we also forgive,” he declares that he is not without sin. Hence he says: “There was no iniquity in my hands, but my prayer was pure.” His prayer was pure because the person who truly granted forgiveness was not unjustly asking for it.

“For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy; but mercy triumphs over judgment.” If this were not so, what hope would there be, since, when the just King sits upon the throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin?

Then, through his mercy, the righteous, fully and perfectly cleansed, will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun.

Then the Church will be fully and perfectly without “spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind,” because then it will truly be glorious. For when he not only said that he would present the Church to himself without spot or wrinkle but added “glorious,” he sufficiently indicated when it would be without spot, wrinkle, or anything of that kind—namely, when it would be glorious.

It should not be said that she is glorious now, amid so many evils, so many scandals, such a mixture of wicked people, and so many insults from the impious, merely because kings serve her, where the danger and temptation are greater. Rather, she will be glorious then, when what the same Apostle says is fulfilled: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

For since the Lord himself, according to the form of a servant by which the Mediator joined himself to the Church, was not glorified until after the glory of the resurrection [or: except by the glory of the resurrection]—“The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”—how can his Church be said to have been glorious before his resurrection?

Therefore he now cleanses her by the washing of water, cleansing her past sins in the word and driving away from her the dominion of evil angels. Then, perfecting her healings, he makes her meet that glorious state, without spot and wrinkle.

“For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he will also glorify.”

I think this mystery is signified in the words: “Behold, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third [day] I am completed”—that is, perfected. He said this in the person of his body, which is the Church of God, assigning distinct and ordered times, and also signifying them in his own resurrection over the course of three days.

I also think there is a difference between being upright in heart and being pure in heart. The upright in heart reaches forward toward what lies ahead, forgetting what lies behind, so that by an upright course—that is, with upright faith and intention—he may arrive where the pure in heart dwells.

Thus each phrase must be assigned to its proper meaning where it says: “Who ascends the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? One innocent in hands and pure in heart.” The innocent in hands will ascend, and the pure in heart will stand: the former pertains to action, the latter to the end.

There, too, what is said must be understood more deeply: “Good is the substance of the one who has no sin in his conscience.” For then the substance will truly be good—that is, true riches—when all poverty has passed away, that is, when every weakness has been consumed.

But now let a person turn away from sin as he progresses and departs from it; let him be renewed day by day; let him direct his hands toward works of mercy; let him cleanse his heart from every sin; and let him show mercy, so that what remains may be forgiven.

This is understood beneficially and without vain or empty boasting in what Saint John said: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask we shall receive from him.”

In this passage he seems to have warned us not to let our heart condemn us in the very prayer and petition. That is, when we begin to say, “Forgive us as we also forgive,” we must not be pierced by the realization that we are not doing what we say, nor must we lose the confidence to ask because we do not dare to say what we are not doing.

## CHAPTER CCCIII  
### On the Apostle’s statement, “Judgment from one offense unto condemnation”; from the Letter of Reply to Hilary’s Questions

Since, therefore, in both cases—that is, in judgment and in grace—the same principle applies with respect to one offense and many offenses, let them tell us why he said that judgment proceeds from one offense to condemnation, but grace from many offenses to justification.

Or let them agree that it was said in this way because two persons are established in this matter: Adam, from whom the carnal generation exists, and Christ, from whom the spiritual generation [regeneratio, “regeneration”] exists. But because the former is merely human, while the latter is both God and human, regeneration does not dissolve only the one offense that comes from Adam, in the way that generation binds through that one offense.

For the former generation needs only the connection of one offense for condemnation. Whatever people subsequently add through their evil works does not belong to that generation but to human conduct. This regeneration, however, is not sufficient merely to dissolve the offense that is inherited from Adam; it also removes whatever is subsequently added through the wicked works of human conduct. Therefore, “judgment from one offense unto condemnation,” but “grace from many offenses unto justification.”

For if “death reigned through the one” because of one offense—the offense from which infants are cleansed through baptism—much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Much more, certainly, will they reign in life, because it will be the reign of eternal life. Death, however, passes through them temporarily; it will not reign eternally.

Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings—condemnation from which infants are to be liberated through the sacrament of baptism—so also through one act of righteousness justification came upon all human beings unto life.

He said “all” in both places, not because all human beings come to the grace of justification in Christ, since so many who are alienated from it die eternally, but because all who are reborn are reborn unto justification only through Christ, just as all who are born are born unto condemnation only through Adam.

For no one [est, “is”] exists in that generation except Adam, and no one exists in this regeneration except Christ. Therefore he says “all” and “all.” He later calls the same people “many,” adding: “For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one human being the many will be constituted righteous.”

Who are these “many,” if not those whom he had just called “all”? Observe how he emphasizes “one” and “one”—that is, Adam and Christ: the former unto condemnation, the latter unto justification.

Christ came in the flesh long after Adam, so that we may know that the ancient righteous, whoever they were who could exist, were liberated only through the same faith by which we are liberated: the faith, namely, in Christ’s incarnation, which was foretold to them just as it was proclaimed to us [facta annuntiatur, “is proclaimed as having occurred”].

For this reason he calls Christ a human being, although he is also God, so that no one might think that the ancient righteous could be liberated through Christ as God alone—that is, through the Word who was in the beginning—and not also through faith in his incarnation, by which Christ is called human as well.

This statement cannot be overthrown, the one in which he says elsewhere: “Through one human being came death, and through one human being the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.” He is certainly speaking of the resurrection of the righteous, where there is eternal life, not of the resurrection of the wicked, where there will be eternal death. Therefore he says “will be made alive,” because the others will be condemned.

For this reason, in the ancient sacraments, circumcision was commanded to be performed on infants on the eighth day, because Christ—in whom the stripping away of carnal offense takes place, which circumcision signifies—rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day after the seventh day of the Sabbath.

This, then, was also the faith of the ancient righteous. Hence the Apostle says: “Having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’; and we also believe, therefore we speak.” He would not have said “the same spirit of faith” unless he were reminding us that the ancient righteous also possessed the same spirit of faith, namely, faith in Christ’s incarnation.

But because what was future was foretold to them and what has now occurred is proclaimed to us, and because what is veiled in the time of the Old Testament is revealed in the time of the New Testament, the sacraments were varied, so that some belonged to the Old Testament and others to the New. The faith itself, however, is not varied but one, because “just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.”

## CHAPTER CCCIV  
### Against what the Pelagians said: that what lacks substance cannot change or weaken human nature; from the book *On Nature and Grace*
First, he says, it must be discussed whether nature is said to have been weakened and altered through sin. Therefore, he says, I think that above all it must be asked what sin is: whether it is some substance, or altogether a name lacking substance,^[76] by which not a thing, not an existing entity, not some body, but an act wrongly performed is expressed. Then he adds: I believe that this is so. And if it is so, he says, how could something lacking substance have weakened or altered human nature?

Do you see where this argument is heading and toward what it is stretching out its hand? It is attempting to make the statement altogether seem pointless: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins.” For how will he save them where there is no illness? The sins from which the Gospel says Christ’s people are to be saved are not substances, and according to this man they cannot corrupt them.

O brother, it is good that you remember you are a Christian. Perhaps it would have been enough to believe these things; nevertheless, since you wish to argue—and this is not harmful, indeed it is beneficial, provided that the firmest faith comes first—let us not suppose that human nature cannot be corrupted by sin. Rather, believing the divine Scriptures, let us accept that it has been corrupted by sin and inquire how this could have happened.

Since we have now learned that sin is not a substance, is it not evident—leaving other examples aside—that not eating is also not a substance? For one withdraws from a substance, since food is a substance; but abstaining from food is not a substance. Yet if the substance of the body abstains altogether from food, it grows so weak, is so impaired by the disturbance of its health, so drained of strength, and so weakened and broken by exhaustion that, if it somehow continues to live, it can scarcely be restored to the food from which abstinence has corrupted it.

So sin is not a substance, but God is a substance, indeed the supreme substance, and the only true food of a rational creature. By withdrawing from him through disobedience, and through weakness no longer being able to receive and enjoy him as it ought, hear how the Psalm says: “My heart was struck like grass and withered, because I forgot to eat my bread.”^[The printed text reads *munducare*; the context requires *manducare*, “to eat.”]

## CHAPTER CCCV. Concerning Samuel and the Pythoness, from the book addressed to Dulcitius on Eight Questions

Your sixth proposition concerns whether, according to the history of the Book of Kings, the pythoness summoned the prophet Samuel himself from the underworld.

The blessed Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, once asked me this. Read below what I answered him.

“Again,” I said, “you ask whether the unclean spirit that was in the pythoness could have caused Samuel to appear to Saul and speak with him. But it is a much greater miracle that Satan himself, the prince of all unclean spirits, was able to speak with God and ask that the most righteous man Job be put to the test; he also asked that the apostles be tested.

“Or, if this does not pose a difficult question because the truth that is everywhere present speaks through whatever creature it wishes to whatever creature it wishes, and because it is not therefore a matter of great merit for the one to whom God speaks—for what matters is what he says: an emperor also does not speak with many innocent people for whose safety he provides with the greatest foresight, while he speaks with many guilty people whom he orders to be killed—then, if there is no question here, let there be no question about how an unclean spirit could also have spoken with the soul of a holy man. For God the Creator and Sanctifier is certainly far greater than all the saints.

“But if the difficulty is that an evil spirit was permitted to raise the soul of a righteous man and, as it were, summon it from the hidden dwelling places of the dead, is it not more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple? However he did that, the manner in which Samuel was raised is likewise hidden—unless perhaps someone should say that the devil had an easier license to take up the living Lord from wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling.

“If that Gospel event does not disturb us because the Lord wished and permitted it to happen without any diminution of his power and divinity—just as he permitted himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean and were performing the devil’s works—then it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy prophet, not unwillingly and not under the domination or subjugation of magical power, but willingly and obediently, should consent to the hidden dispensation of God, which was concealed from the pythoness and Saul, and allow itself to be shown to the king’s sight in order to strike him with the divine sentence.

“For why should the soul of a good man, if summoned by evil living people and if it should come, seem to lose its dignity, when good people who are still alive often come when summoned by the wicked and do among them what their duty requires, preserving the fairness and unshaken dignity of their virtue, while dealing with their vices according to the use or necessity of present circumstances?

“Nevertheless, there may be another, easier solution and more straightforward interpretation: perhaps we should not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but rather that some phantom and imaginary illusion was produced by the devil’s machinations. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel because images are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“Thus everything that is painted or fashioned from some material—metal, wood, or any other substance suitable for such work—and even things seen in dreams, are commonly called by the names of the things whose images they are. Who, after all, would hesitate to call a painted man a man? When we look at a portrait of each individual, we readily use each person’s proper name. For example, looking at a panel or a wall, we say, ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the Simois River; that is Rome,’ although they are nothing other than painted images.

“Thus, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures fashioned from metal, which God commanded to be placed above the Ark of the Covenant to signify a great reality, are nevertheless called nothing other than cherubim. Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine’ or ‘of Simplicianus,’ but ‘I saw Augustine’ or ‘Simplicianus,’ even though at the time when he saw such a thing we were unaware of it. So obvious is it that it is not the men themselves but their images that are seen.

“Pharaoh too said that in his dream he had seen ears of grain and cattle, not images of ears of grain or of cattle. If, then, it is plainly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and his ministers into ministers of righteousness.
