“Now, if it troubles us how true predictions could also have been made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may likewise seem surprising how the demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize. For when God wishes someone to learn the truth even through the lowest and infernal spirits—truth, that is, concerning temporal matters and matters belonging to this mortal life—it is easy and not unfitting that the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance by foreknowing the evil that threatens them, should by the hidden arrangement of his mysteries grant even such spirits some power of divination, so that they may announce to human beings what they hear from the angels.

“They hear only as much as the Lord and Ruler of all either commands or permits. Thus the pythonic spirit in the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to act as an evangelist. Yet such spirits mix falsehoods with the truth they have been able to know, announcing it not so much to instruct as to deceive. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel foretold Saul’s death, it also said that he would be with him—which is certainly false.

“For we read in the Gospel that the good are separated from the evil by a great interval after death, when the Lord testifies that a great chasm had been fixed between that proud rich man, already suffering torments in the underworld, and the man covered with sores who had lain at his gate and was already established in rest.

“Or, if Samuel said to Saul, ‘You will be with me,’ so that this referred not to equality of happiness but to a common condition of death—that both were human beings and both could die, and that the dead man was foretelling death to the living—your prudence, I think, sees that under either interpretation this reading can be given a meaning that is not contrary to the faith.

“Unless perhaps, through a deeper and more extended inquiry—which exceeds either my strength or the limits of the available time—it may finally be discovered whether or not a human soul, after departing this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear to the sight of the living, even bearing the bodily features, so that it can not only be seen but recognized; and, if this is possible, whether even the soul of a righteous person, not compelled by magical rites but graciously consenting to appear in obedience to the more hidden commands [or mysteries] of the supreme law, can do so.

“If it should become clear that this is impossible, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the treatment and exposition of this Scripture; rather, once the other has been excluded, an imaginary representation [or likeness] of Samuel, produced by a diabolical ritual, should be understood.

“But whether that can happen or cannot happen, the deceit of Satan and his cunning operation in producing images nevertheless keeps watch in many forms to deceive human senses. Therefore, while proceeding cautiously so as not to prejudge more careful investigations, let us nevertheless rather suppose that something of this sort was done through the agency of that evil pythoness, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise and explain something further.”

These are the things I then wrote in reply concerning the pythoness and Samuel.

[Note: This sentence seems to have been added either by Eugyppius or by someone else.]

That I did not say without reason that we should cautiously suppose an image of Samuel to have been presented through the agency of the evil pythoness—“so as not to prejudge more careful investigations”—was made clear by a later inquiry of mine, when I found in the book of Ecclesiasticus, where the fathers are praised in order, that Samuel himself was praised in such a way that he was said to have prophesied even after his death.

But if this book too is rejected on the authority of the Hebrews, because it is not in their canon, what shall we say about Moses? He certainly is read as having died in Deuteronomy and as having appeared to the living in the Gospel with Elijah, who did not die.

## CHAPTER CCCVI. To whom sacrifice is beneficial, and concerning the place of the martyrs where someone is buried, from the book addressed to Bishop Paulinus, On Care for the Dead

You wrote to me asking whether it benefits anyone after death that his body be buried near the memorial of some saint.

Certainly it does. For you say that it seems to you that the movements of religious and faithful hearts, when they arrange such things for their own people, are not empty. You add that it cannot be without significance that the whole Church customarily prays for the dead, so that from this it may also be inferred that a person benefits after death if, through the faith of his relatives in burying his body, a place is provided for him in which the aid of the saints appears to have been sought in this way as well.

But when these things are so, how is this not contrary to what the Apostle says: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil”? You indicate that you do not sufficiently see the answer.

By this apostolic judgment, he warns that before death one must do what can be beneficial after death—not at the time when each person must already receive what he did before death.

The question is resolved in this way: through a certain manner of life, while one lives in this body, one acquires the condition that these things may help the dead. Accordingly, according to what they have done through the body, the dead are helped by what is religiously done for them after the body.

There are some whom these things do not help at all: either because their merits were so evil that they are not worthy even of such assistance, or because their merits were so good that they have no need of such assistance. The manner of life that each person led through the body therefore determines whether whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body will help or not help him.

For if no merit by which these things might help has been acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life. Thus it happens that neither does the Church, or the care of the living for the dead, expend religious devotion uselessly, nor does each person fail to receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil, since God renders to each according to his works.

For the ability of what is expended to benefit someone after the body has been acquired in the life that he lived in the body.

The provision of a place for burying bodies near the memorial of the saints is therefore an expression of good human affection toward the dead. For if there is some religious significance in burying them, there cannot be none in considering where they are to be buried.

But when such consolations of the living are sought, through which their pious affection for their own may become evident, I do not see what help this gives the dead except that, when the living remember where the bodies of those they love have been placed, they may commend them in prayer to the same saints as patrons who have received them and may assist them before the Lord.

This could indeed be done even if they could not bury them in such places. The reason that memorials and monuments are given to the distinguished tombs of the dead is not otherwise than that they recall to memory those whom death has removed from the eyes of the living, so that they are not also removed from their hearts by forgetfulness, and, by reminding them, cause them to be thought of.

The name “memorial” itself shows this most clearly; and a “monument” is so called because it admonishes the mind—that is, reminds it. For this reason the Greeks call what we call a memorial or monument μνημεῖον (*mnēmeion*), because in their language the memory by which we remember is called μνὴμη (*mnēmē*).

When the mind therefore recalls where the body of a beloved person has been buried, and the place of a venerable martyr comes to mind, the affection of the one who remembers and prays commends the beloved soul to that martyr. This is what the faithful offer to the dead whom they love, and it is without doubt beneficial to those who, while living in the body, earned the right for such things to benefit them after this life.

Even if some necessity prevents bodies from being buried at all, or from being buried in such places, the prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The Church has undertaken to offer them for all the dead within the Christian and Catholic fellowship, even without naming them individually, in a general commemoration, so that those who lack parents, children, relatives, or friends to do these things for them may have them offered by the one common pious mother.

But if these prayers, offered for the dead with right faith and piety, were absent, I think that their spirits would gain no benefit, however much their lifeless bodies were placed in holy locations.

When, therefore, a faithful mother desired that the body of her faithful deceased son be placed in the basilica of a martyr, if she believed that his soul would be helped by the martyr’s merits, this belief itself was a kind of prayer, and whatever benefit resulted came from it. Likewise, when she returned in thought to the same tomb and commended her son more and more in her prayers, it was not the location of the dead body but the living affection of the mother, awakened by the place, that helped the spirit of the deceased.

For the thought both of who had been commended and to whom he had been commended—or, as the variant reads, of who was to be commended—certainly touched the religious mind of the one praying, not without fruit.

Those who pray also use the members of their bodies in ways appropriate to prayer: they bend their knees, stretch out their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground. They may do whatever else they visibly do, although their invisible will and the intention of their heart are known to God, who does not need these signs in order for the human mind to be opened to him.

Rather, by such actions a person arouses himself to pray and lament more humbly and fervently. Somehow, although these bodily movements cannot occur without a movement of the mind preceding them, when the same actions are again performed outwardly and visibly, the inward and invisible movement that produced them is strengthened. Thus the affection of the heart, which preceded the actions so that they might occur, grows because they have occurred.

Nevertheless, if someone is so restrained or even bound that he cannot perform these actions with his limbs, that does not mean that the inner person does not pray, or that he does not lie prostrate before God’s eyes in the most secret chamber where he is inwardly pierced with compunction.

So too, although it matters greatly where someone places the body of his dead relative for whom he is beseeching God—for the preceding affection chose a holy place, and when the body has been placed there, the remembered holy place renews and increases the affection that came before—it nevertheless follows that, even if the religious mind cannot bury the one it loves where it has chosen, it must in no way cease the necessary prayers of commendation.

Wherever the flesh of the dead person lies—or even if it does not lie anywhere—the spirit must be granted rest. When it departed from the body, it took with it the sense by which it can know what condition each person is in, whether good or evil. Nor does it expect its life to be helped by the flesh to which it itself had given life, which it removed when it departed and will restore when it returns.

For it is not the flesh that earns for the spirit, but the spirit that earns for the flesh, even the merit of the resurrection—whether it will rise again for punishment or for glory.

## CHAPTER CCCVII. That the dead are often thought to appear to the living in dreams, from the same book

Certain visions are reported that seem to introduce a question not to be neglected in this discussion. It is said that some dead people have appeared to the living, either in dreams or in some other way, to people who did not know where their bodies lay unburied; and that, by showing them the places, they warned them to provide the burial that had been denied them.

If we answer that these things are false, we shall seem shamelessly to oppose the writings of certain believers and the testimony of those who affirm that such things have happened to them. But it must be answered that the dead should not therefore be thought to perceive such things merely because they appear in dreams to say, indicate, or request them.

The living also often appear to the living while they are asleep, even though the people who appear do not know that they are appearing; and afterward they hear from those who say that they saw them in dreams, doing or saying something.

If, then, someone can see me in a dream indicating something that has happened, or even foretelling something that will happen, while I am entirely unaware of it and have absolutely no concern not only for what he is dreaming but whether, while I am asleep, he is awake, or while I am awake, he is asleep, or whether we are both awake or both asleep at the same time when he sees the dream in which he sees me, why should it be surprising if the dead, without knowing or perceiving such things, are nevertheless seen in dreams by the living and say something that the living recognize as true after awakening?

I would therefore believe that through angelic operations—whether permitted from above or commanded—it happens that the dead seem in dreams to say something about the burial of their bodies, although the deceased to whom those bodies belonged are wholly unaware of it.

This sometimes happens beneficially, either as some kind of consolation for the living to whom those dead belong, whose images appear to the dreamers, or so that through such warnings humane concern in burial may be commended to humankind. Although burial does not help the dead, it is nevertheless culpably neglected through irreligious carelessness.

At other times, however, people are led into great errors by deceptive visions, and it is just that those who experience such things should suffer them. For example, someone might dream what poets falsely report that Aeneas saw in the underworld; the image of some unburied person might appear to him and speak the sort of words that Palinurus is said to have spoken. On awakening, he might find that person’s body in the place where, according to what he heard in the dream, it lay unburied, having been warned and asked to bury what he found.

And because he discovers this to be true, he might believe that the dead are buried so that their souls may pass to places from which, as he dreamed, the law of the underworld prevents the souls of the unburied from departing.

Does he not, by believing this, stray very far from the path of truth?

Human weakness is such that when someone sees a dead person in a dream, he supposes that he is seeing the person’s soul; but when he similarly dreams of someone alive, he does not doubt that neither the person’s soul nor his body appeared to him, but only the likeness of a human being. Yet the likenesses of dead people who are unaware of it could appear to sleepers in the same way—not their souls.

When we were certainly at Milan, we heard that a debt was being demanded from someone on the basis of a bond belonging to his deceased father, although the debt had already been paid by the father without the son’s knowledge. The man began to grieve most bitterly and to wonder why his father, when dying, had not told him what he owed, especially since he had also made a will.

Then, when he was excessively anxious, his father appeared to him in a dream and indicated where the canceled bond had been placed. When the young man found it and produced it, he not only repelled the accusation of a false debt but also recovered his father’s promissory note, which the father had not received when the money was paid.

Here it is certainly thought that the man’s soul had taken care of his son and had come to him while he slept, teaching him what he did not know so that he might be freed from great distress.

But at almost the same time when we heard this—that is, while we were staying at Milan—Eulogius, the rhetorician of Carthage, who had been my student in that same art, later told me that, while he was assigning Cicero’s rhetorical books to his students, he was reviewing the passage he was going to teach the following day and encountered a difficult place. Unable to understand it, he could scarcely sleep because of his anxiety.

That night, while he was dreaming, I explained to him what he did not understand—or rather, not I, but my image, while I was unaware of it and was doing or dreaming something else far away across the sea, with no concern at all for his anxieties.

I do not know how such things happen. But however they happen, why should we not believe that a person sees a dead man in a dream in the same way that he sees a living man? In both cases, neither person knows or cares who is dreaming of his image, or where or when it is being dreamed.

Some waking visions are also similar to dreams, such as those experienced by people whose senses are disturbed—for example, by the fevered or by those who are raging in any kind of madness. They too speak with themselves as though they were speaking with people who were truly present, and they do so with both absent and present people whose images they perceive, whether living or dead.

But just as those who are living do not know that they are seen by such people or that they are speaking with them—for in reality they are not present and are not speaking, but the disturbed people suffer such imaginary visions—in the same way those who have departed this life appear to people in such conditions as though they were present, although they are absent, and they themselves are entirely unaware whether anyone is seeing them imaginatively.

Something similar also occurs when people are withdrawn from bodily sensation more deeply than in sleep and are occupied by such visions. Images of the living and the dead appear to them as well. But when they are restored to their senses, those who hear them say that they saw dead people believe that they were truly with them. They do not notice that, in the same way, images of certain living people who were absent and unaware were also seen by them.

The spirits of the dead are therefore in a place where they do not see whatever is done or happens to human beings in this life. How, then, do they see their own tombs or their own bodies, whether they lie cast aside or buried? How do they share in the misery of the living, when either they themselves are suffering evils, if they have acquired such merits, or are resting in peace, as was promised to Josiah, where they endure no evil either by suffering it or by sharing in the suffering of others, having been freed from all the evils that they endured by suffering and sharing in suffering while they lived here?

Someone may say: If the dead have no concern for the living, how did the rich man who was tormented in the underworld ask Abraham his father to send Lazarus to his five brothers, who were not yet dead, and warn them not to come to the same place of torment?

But did the fact that the rich man said this mean that he knew what his brothers were doing or what they were suffering at that time? Thus he had concern for the living even though he had no knowledge at all of what they were doing, just as we have concern for the dead even though we certainly do not know what they are doing. For if we had no concern for the dead, we would certainly not beseech God on their behalf.

## CHAPTER CCCVIII. Whether the martyrs should be believed to participate in human affairs through the benefits conferred by their prayers, from the same book

Accordingly, it must be acknowledged that the dead do not know what is happening here while it is happening. Later, however, they may hear from those who go from here to them by dying—not everything, but what those who are permitted to remember such things are also permitted to disclose, and what those to whom they disclose it ought to hear.

The dead may also hear something from the angels who are present at the events taking place here, insofar as the One to whom everything is subject judges that each of them ought to hear it.

For if there were no angels who could be present at the places of the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: “It happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom.” Those whom God wished to take from here to there could therefore be present now in one place and now in the other.

The spirits of the dead can also, through the revelation of God’s Spirit, learn certain things that happen here—things which it is necessary for them to know [and which it is not necessary for them not to know]—not only things present or past but also things future. While they lived here, the prophets likewise knew not everything, but what God’s providence judged should be revealed to them.

Divine Scripture also testifies that some of the dead may be sent to the living, just as, conversely, Paul was caught up from among the living into paradise.

This also resolves the question of how the martyrs, through the very benefits granted to those who pray, can indicate that they participate in human affairs if the dead do not know what the living are doing.

We have heard, not through uncertain rumors but through reliable witnesses, that the confessor Felix, whose dwelling-place you piously love, appeared not only through the effects of benefits but also to human sight itself when Nola was being attacked by the barbarians.

Yet such things are provided by divine power in a manner very different from the customary order assigned to each kind of creature. The fact that water was suddenly changed into wine when the Lord wished it does not mean that we should fail to distinguish what water can do according to its proper order among the elements from the rarity—or rather, the singularity—of that divine work.

Nor, because Lazarus was raised, should we conclude that every dead person rises whenever he wishes, or that a lifeless person is awakened by a living person in the same way that a sleeping person is awakened by someone who is awake.

The limits of human affairs are therefore one thing, and the signs of divine power another. Some things occur naturally, others miraculously, although God is present to nature so that it may exist, and nature is not absent from miracles.

We should not therefore suppose that any of the dead can participate in the affairs of the living merely because the martyrs are present to heal or assist certain people. Rather, we should understand that the martyrs participate in the affairs of the living through divine power precisely because, by their own nature, the dead cannot participate in the affairs of the living.

Nevertheless, this question has overcome the powers of my understanding: how do the martyrs assist those whom it is certain they help through their intercession? Do they themselves appear simultaneously in many different places separated by great distances—whether at the places where their memorials are, or elsewhere, wherever they are felt to be present?

Or, while they are removed from all human intercourse in a place suited to their merits, do they nevertheless pray generally for those who supplicate according to their needs, just as we pray for the dead, to whom we are certainly not present and whose location or activities we do not know?

Does almighty God, who is present everywhere, neither confined among us nor distant from us, hear the prayers of the martyrs and, through angelic ministries spread everywhere, provide people with such consolations as he judges ought to be provided amid the misery of this life? And does he, wherever, whenever, and however he wishes—especially through the memorials of the martyrs, because he knows that this is useful to us for building up the faith of Christ, for whose confession they suffered—commend their merits by his marvelous and ineffable power and goodness?

This matter is too lofty for me to reach and too hidden for me to investigate. Therefore I do not dare to determine which of these two possibilities is correct—or whether perhaps both are correct: that sometimes these things occur through the martyrs’ own presence, and sometimes through angels assuming the role of the martyrs.

I would rather inquire of those who know such things. For it is not the case that no one knows them; rather, some may think they know and yet not know.

For the gifts of God are given differently to different people, according to the Apostle, who says that “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the benefit of all.”

## CHAPTER CCCIX. Again, concerning offerings or almsgiving for the dead, from the same book

Since these things are so, let us not suppose that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except what we solemnly beseech God to grant on their behalf through sacrifices at the altar, prayers, or almsgiving.

These things do not benefit everyone for whom they are performed, but only those who, while they lived, acquired the merit that such things should benefit them. But because we cannot distinguish who these people are, we ought to perform these acts for all the regenerate, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to come may be omitted.

It is better that these things remain in excess for those whom they neither harm nor help than that they be lacking for those whom they do help.

Nevertheless, each person performs these acts more diligently for his own relatives, so that his own may perform them similarly for him.

Whatever is spent on burying the body is not a means of salvation but an act of humanity, according to the affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh. Therefore one ought to care as much as possible for the flesh of a neighbor when the one who governed it has departed from it.

And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh perform these acts, how much more ought those who believe that the dead body will nevertheless rise and remain in eternity perform them, so that such a duty may also in some way be a testimony to that faith?

As for being buried near the memorials of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the dead only in that the affection of the one commending him to the martyrs’ protection is thereby increased in prayer.

## CHAPTER CCCX. Concerning the Lord’s saying, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” and so forth, from Book I of *The Sermon on the Mount*
“You have heard that it was said [to the ancients], ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

Thus the lesser righteousness is not to commit adultery through bodily intercourse; but the greater righteousness of the kingdom of God is not to commit adultery in the heart. Whoever does not commit adultery in the heart much more easily takes care not to commit adultery in the body. Therefore the one who gave this command confirmed that commandment; for he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.

It should certainly be considered that he did not say, “Everyone who lusts after a woman,” but, “Whoever looks at a woman [Col. 1027B] in order to lust,” that is, who looks at her with this purpose and intention, namely, to lust after her. This is no longer merely to be tickled by the pleasure of the flesh, but plainly [fully] to consent to lust, so that the unlawful desire is not restrained but, if the opportunity is given, is satisfied.

For there are three things by which sin is completed: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Suggestion occurs either through memory or through the bodily senses, when we see, hear, smell, taste, or touch something. If it is pleasing to take delight in it, the unlawful pleasure must be restrained. For example, when we are fasting and, on seeing food, the palate’s appetite rises: this happens only through pleasure, yet we do not consent to it, and by the authority of the ruling reason we restrain it. But if consent has taken place, the sin is complete—known [however] to God in our heart [Col. 1027C], even if it does not become known to human beings through an outward act.

These stages, then, are like the action of the serpent: suggestion comes from the serpent, that is, from what is slippery and shifting—namely, from the temporal movement of bodies. For even if such images move within the soul, they have been drawn from the body externally. And if some hidden bodily movement, apart from these five senses, touches the soul, it too is temporal and slippery. Therefore, the more secretly it slips in so as to touch thought, the more appropriately it is compared to a serpent.

These three things, as I began to say, resemble that event written in Genesis: suggestion and a kind of persuasion come, as it were, from the serpent; pleasure is in the carnal appetite, as in Eve; and consent is in the reason, as in the man. Once these things have occurred, the human being is most justly driven out of paradise—that is, from the most blessed [Col. 1027D] light of righteousness—into death.

For the one who persuades does not compel; and all natures are beautiful in their own order and according to their own degrees. But one must not descend from higher things, in which the rational mind has been ordered, to lower things. No one is compelled to do this; and therefore, if someone does it, he is punished without a legitimate defense, since he does not commit it unwillingly.

Nevertheless, before habit is formed, pleasure is either absent or so slight as to be almost nonexistent. To consent to it is nevertheless a great sin when the pleasure is unlawful. Once someone has consented, he commits sin in the heart. But if it also proceeds into action, the desire appears to be satisfied and extinguished. Afterwards, when the suggestion returns, a greater pleasure is kindled, [Col. 1028A] though it is still much less than the pleasure that repeated actions turn into habit.

It is exceedingly difficult to overcome this habit. Yet even habit itself can be conquered, if one does not abandon oneself and does not shrink from Christian military service (*militiam*, evidently misread in the source as *malitiam*), with Christ as guide and helper. Thus the man is again subjected to Christ and the woman to the man, returning to their original peace and order.

Just as one reaches sin through three stages—suggestion, pleasure, and consent—so sin itself has three forms: in the heart, in action, and in habit. These are like three deaths: the first, as though in the house [Col. 1028B], when lust is consented to in the heart; the second, already brought outside, as though beyond the gate, when consent proceeds into action; and the third, when the mind is pressed down by the force of evil habit, like an earthly mass, as though already rotting in a tomb. Anyone who reads the Gospel recognizes that the Lord raised these three kinds of dead.

Perhaps such a person also considers the differences in the very voice of the one who raises them: in one place he says, “Girl, arise”; elsewhere, “Young man, I say to you, arise”; elsewhere, “[81] He groaned in spirit and wept,” and then groaned again and afterward cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come outside.”

Therefore, by the name “adulterers,” who are mentioned in this chapter, every carnal and lustful desire must be understood. For since Scripture so frequently calls idolatry fornication, and the apostle Paul calls greed idolatry, who could doubt that every evil desire is rightly called fornication? The soul, neglecting the higher law by which it is governed, is corrupted as though prostituted for a price through the shameful pleasure of lower [Col. 1028C] natures.

Therefore, whoever feels that carnal pleasure is rebelling against his right will through sinful habits, whose untamed violence drags him into captivity, should recall, as far as he can, what peace he has lost by sinning, and should cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ [our Lord].”

For when he cries out that he is wretched, he implores the Consoler’s help through mourning. Nor is the recognition of one’s own wretchedness a small step toward blessedness. Hence: “Blessed [also] are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”

## CHAPTER CCCXI. On the Lord’s saying, “Give to everyone who asks”; how this is not contrary [Col. 1028D] to the saying, “Do not give to a sinner”

“Give,” he says, “to everyone who asks you”—not everything to everyone who asks—so that you give what you can give honorably and justly. For what if someone should ask for money with which he intends to kill an innocent person? What if, finally, he should ask for sexual violation? But not to pursue the many examples that are innumerable, one should certainly give what, as far as a human being can know or believe, harms neither oneself nor another.

To the person to whom you justly deny what he asks, the justice itself should be explained, so that you do not send him away empty-handed. Thus you will give to everyone who asks you, although you will not always give what he asks; and sometimes you will give something better, when you correct the person asking you for something unjust.

As for what he says, “Do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you,” [Col. 1029A] this should be referred to the disposition of the mind. For God loves a cheerful giver. Everyone who receives borrows, even if he himself is not going to repay; since God restores more to the merciful, everyone who bestows a benefit lends at interest.

## CHAPTER CCCXII. How the saying “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people” is to be understood; and what the left hand is; from the same book

Purity of heart is like an eye by which God is seen. We must care for this eye as greatly as the dignity of that which can be seen through such an eye demands.

Yet, when this eye has been purified to a considerable degree, it is difficult for some dirt not to steal in from those things that commonly accompany our good actions [Col. 1029B]—for example, human praise. Certainly, not to live rightly is harmful; but to live rightly and not wish to be praised—what else is this than to be hostile to human affairs, which are all the more wretched the less human right conduct is pleasing?

Therefore, if those among whom you live do not praise you when you live rightly, they are in error. But if they do praise you, you are in danger—unless you have a heart so simple and pure that you do not do what is right for the sake of human praise, and that you rejoice more for those who praise what is right, because they delight in what is good, than for yourself because you live rightly, even if no one praised you.

You should understand your praise to be useful to those who praise you only when they honor not yourself in your good life but God, whose most holy temple is everyone who lives well. Thus what David says may be fulfilled [Col. 1029C]: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the gentle hear and rejoice” [“Let the meek hear and rejoice”].

Therefore, it belongs to a pure eye not to look toward human praise in doing what is right, nor to refer what you do rightly to such praise—that is, not to do something rightly for the reason that you may please human beings. For then one will also be pleased to simulate goodness, if attention is paid [is paid] (*attendentur* [*attenditur*]) only so that a person may praise him. Since a human being cannot see the heart, he can also praise what is false. Those who do this—that is, who pretend to goodness—are double-minded.

A person therefore has a simple heart, that is, a pure heart, only if he rises above human praise and looks solely to the one whom he seeks to please when he lives rightly, the one who alone examines the conscience. Whatever proceeds from the purity of that conscience is all the more praiseworthy the less it desires human praise [Col. 1029D].

“Take care,” he says, “to perform your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.” That is, take care not to live justly with the intention of being seen by people, and not to establish your good in their seeing you. Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven—not if you are seen by human beings, but if you live justly for the purpose of being seen by them.

For where, then, is what was said at the beginning of this discourse: “You are the light [*lux*, ‘light’] of the world”? “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Thus let your light shine before people, so that they may see [Col. 1030A] your good works.” But he did not end there; he added: “And let them glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

Here, however, because he condemns this if it is [if the end is there] the end in itself of right actions—that is, if we do what is right for the sole purpose of being seen by people—after saying, “Take care to perform your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them,” he added nothing else. From this it is apparent that he did not prohibit doing what is right before people, but prohibited doing what is right before people for the purpose of being seen by them—that is, making this one’s object and placing the end of one’s intention there.

For the apostle also says, “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ,” while elsewhere he says, “Please people [all people] in all things, just as [also] I please all people [Col. 1030B] in all things.” Those who do not understand these statements think them contradictory. But he said that he did not please people because he was not doing what was right in order to please people, but in order to please God, to whose love he wished to turn human hearts precisely by pleasing people.

Thus he rightly said that he did not please people, because in that very matter he looked toward pleasing God. And he rightly commanded that people should be pleased—not so that this should be sought as the reward of right actions, but because one could not please God without offering oneself as an example to those whom one wanted to be saved. No one can imitate a person who has not pleased him in any way.

Just as someone would speak sensibly if he said, “In this work by which I am seeking a ship, I am not seeking the ship but my homeland,” [Col. 1030C] so the apostle could appropriately say: “In this work by which I please people, I do not please people but God,” because I do not seek this in itself, but refer it to the purpose that those whom I wish to be saved may imitate me.

He says the same concerning the offering made for the saints: “I do not seek the gift, but I inquire [seek: *requiro*] after the fruit” [“I do not seek your gift, but I seek the fruit”]. That is, “I am not seeking your gift as such, but your fruit.” For this could show how much they had advanced toward God: they willingly did [offered] what was sought from them not for the joy of receiving [82] gifts, but for the fellowship of charity.

Those, therefore, receive their reward who give alms for no other reason than to be glorified by people—not if they happen to be glorified by people, but if they give for the purpose of being glorified [Col. 1030D], as was discussed above. Human praise ought not to be sought by the person doing what is right; it ought to follow the person doing what is right, so that it may benefit those who can also imitate what they praise, not so that the person who is praised may think that this brings him some benefit.

“But when you give alms, let your left hand not know [be unaware of] what your right hand is doing.” Nothing seems more appropriately signified by the left hand than the very pleasure of praise; the right hand, on the other hand, signifies the intention of fulfilling the divine commandments. When the desire for human praise mingles with the conscience of one giving alms, the left hand becomes conscious of the work of the right.

Therefore, “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing,” that is, let the desire for human praise not mingle with your conscience when, in giving alms, you strive to fulfill the divine command.

“Let your alms [Col. 1031A] be in secret” [“in concealment”]. What is “in secret” except in the good conscience itself, which cannot be displayed to human eyes or disclosed in words, since many people tell many lies?

Therefore, if the right hand acts inwardly and in secret, everything outward that is visible and temporal belongs to the left hand. Let your alms therefore be in your conscience itself. Many people give alms with good will even when they do not possess money—or anything else that can be given to the needy. Others give outwardly but do not give inwardly: through ambition or for the sake of some temporal thing, they wish to appear merciful. In such people only the left hand should be considered to be working.

Others occupy a middle position between these two groups: they give alms with an intention directed toward God [Col. 1031B], yet some desire for praise or for some fragile and temporal thing inserts itself into this excellent will. But our Lord forbids the left hand to work alone much more vehemently when he also forbids it to mingle with the works of the right hand. Thus we must take care not only not to give alms out of a mere desire for temporal things, but also not to attend to God in this work in such a way that the desire for external advantages mingles with or attaches itself to that attention.

For the matter at hand is the purification of the heart. Unless it is simple, it will not be pure. But how will it be simple if it serves two masters, and does not purify its vision through a single intention directed toward eternal things, but also clouds it with love of mortal and fragile things?

“Let your alms be in secret” [“in concealment”] [Col. 1031C], “and your Father who sees in secret will repay you”—entirely right and entirely true. For if you await a reward from the one who alone examines the conscience, the conscience itself should be sufficient for you as the means of earning the reward.

## CHAPTER CCCXIII. Why one should pray when God knows what we need; from the same book

It may be asked whether one should pray by actions or by words. What need is there for prayer itself if God already knows what we need? The answer is that the very attentiveness of prayer calms and purifies our heart and makes it more receptive to receiving the divine gifts that are spiritually poured into us.

God does not hear us because of the ambition of our prayers. He is always ready to give us his light—not visible but intelligible and spiritual. But we are not always ready to receive it, when we are turned [inclined] (*declinamur* [*inclinamur*]) toward other things [Col. 1031D] and held in darkness by desire for temporal matters.

In prayer, therefore, the heart turns toward the one who is always ready to give, provided that we are able to receive what he gives. In this turning, the inward eye is purified, as those things are excluded that were desired temporally, so that the vision of the simple heart may bear the simple light that shines divinely, without setting or change. It can not only bear that light but also remain in it—not merely without distress but with ineffable joy, through which the blessed life is truly received [perfected].

## CHAPTER CCCXIV. On the distinction between temptation and being led into temptation; and how the devil stood before God or asked that Job be tempted; from the same book

The sixth petition is: “And do not lead us into temptation.” [Col. 1032A] Some manuscripts have “do not bring us into temptation,” which I think has the same meaning; for the one Greek expression, **ἐνέγκῃς** [more fully, **εἰσενέγκῃς**], has been translated into Latin in both ways.

Many, however, pray in this form: “Do not allow us to be led into temptation,” thereby explaining how “bring us into temptation” is to be understood. God does not himself lead someone into temptation; rather, he permits the person whom he has abandoned in respect of his help to be led into it. By a most hidden order, and for causes corresponding to that person’s merits—often also manifest causes—God judges the one whom he abandons worthy of being allowed to be led into temptation.

To be led into temptation, however, is one thing, and to be tempted is another. No one can be approved without [Col. 1032B] temptation, whether in relation to himself, as it is written, “What does one who has not been tempted know?” or in relation to others, as the apostle says: “You did not despise your trial in my flesh.”

For he recognized that they were steadfast because they had not turned away from charity on account of the tribulations that had happened to the apostle according to the flesh. We are known to God before all temptations, since he knows all things before they happen.

Therefore, what is written, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him,” uses the expression “to know” in the sense of “to make you know.” In the same way we call a day joyful because it makes people joyful, and cold sluggish because it makes people sluggish. There are innumerable expressions of this kind, found either in ordinary speech, in the language of teachers, or in the holy Scriptures.

Heretics who oppose the Old Testament [Col. 1032C], failing to understand this, regard as a defect of ignorance the statement about which it is said, “The Lord your God is testing you,” as though the Gospel did not also say concerning the Lord: “He was saying this to test him,” although he himself knew what he was going to do.

For if he knew the heart of the person he was testing, what did he wish to discover by testing him? Clearly, the purpose was that the person being tested should become known to himself and condemn his own despair when the crowds had been filled with the Lord’s bread—he who had thought that they did not have anything to eat.

We do not therefore pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation. It is as though someone who must be tested by [Col. 1032D] fire does not pray that he may never come into contact with fire, but that he may not be burned.

“The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, but the temptation of tribulation tests righteous people.” Joseph was tempted by the enticement of sexual violation, but he was not led into temptation. Susanna was tempted, but she too was not led or brought into temptation. There were many others of both sexes.

But Job above all: when those heretical enemies of the Old Testament wished, with sacrilegious speech, to mock his admirable steadfastness in the Lord his God, they especially brandish the fact that Satan asked that he be tempted. For they ask inexperienced people, who are entirely incapable of understanding such matters, how Satan could have spoken with God.

They do not consider—for they cannot, being blinded by superstition and contentiousness—that God does not [83] occupy one place with the bulk of a body, being in one place and not in another, or having one part here [Col. 1033A] and another elsewhere. Rather, he is present everywhere in majesty, undivided, complete everywhere.

If they understand corporeally what is said, “Heaven is my throne [seat], and earth is the footstool of my feet”—to which the Lord also testifies when he says, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet”—what wonder is it if the devil, established on earth, stood before the feet of God and spoke something in his presence?

For when will they understand that there is no soul, however perverse, that is in any way capable of reasoning, in whose conscience the Lord does not speak? Who wrote the natural law [Col. 1033B] in human hearts except God? Concerning this law the apostle says:

“When the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, they, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.”

Therefore, if every rational soul—even one blinded by desire—nevertheless thinks and reasons, then whatever is true in its reasoning must not be attributed to the soul itself but to the light of truth, by which it is illuminated, however faintly and according to its capacity, so that it perceives something true in reasoning.

What wonder is it, then, if the devil’s soul, perverted by evil desire, is said to have heard—when it wished to tempt the just man—whatever truth it conceived concerning him from the voice of God himself, that is, from the voice of Truth itself?

Whatever is false is attributed to that desire by which the devil received his name. Yet [although: *quanquam* (*quamvis*)] God [Col. 1033C] has often spoken through a bodily and visible creature, both to the good and to the wicked, as the Lord and ruler of all things, ordering them according to the merits of each matter—for example, through angels who also appeared to human beings, and through prophets saying, “Thus says the Lord.”

What wonder is it, then, if God is said to have spoken with the devil, though not in the devil’s own thought, but through some creature suited to such an act?

Nor should they think that it is a mark of dignity, or a merit of righteousness, that God spoke with him, since he spoke with an angelic soul, though foolish and desirous—just as if he were speaking with a human soul that was foolish and desirous. Or let them explain how God spoke with that rich man [Col. 1033D] whose utterly foolish desire he wished to rebuke when he said: “Fool, this night your soul is required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”

Certainly the Lord himself says this in the Gospel, to whom these heretics, whether they wish to or not, bow their necks.

But if they are troubled by the fact that Satan asked God that a righteous man be tempted, I will not explain why it happened; I will compel them to explain why the Lord himself said in the Gospel to his disciples: “Behold, Satan asked to sift you like wheat.” And to Peter he said: “But I have prayed that your faith may not fail.”

When they explain this to me, they will at the same time explain to themselves what they ask me. If they cannot explain it, let them not rashly condemn in another book what they cannot understand without taking offense in the Gospel [Col. 1034A].

Temptations therefore come through Satan, not by his own power but by the Lord’s permission, either so that human beings may be punished for their sins or, through God’s mercy, tested and exercised. It matters greatly into what kind of temptation each person falls.

Judas, who betrayed the Lord, did not fall into the same kind of temptation as Peter when, terrified, he denied the Lord.

There are also human temptations, I believe, when someone, with a good intention but still according to human frailty, makes a mistake in some decision or becomes irritated with a brother out of zeal for correcting him, but somewhat more than Christian tranquility permits. Concerning these the apostle says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” He also says: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear, but with the temptation he will also make a way out [a favorable outcome], so that you may be able to endure.” [Col. 1034B]

In this statement he sufficiently shows that we should not pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation. We are led into it if temptations of such a kind occur as we cannot bear. But whether dangerous temptations—into which it is harmful to be brought or led—arise from prosperous temporal circumstances or from adverse ones, no one is broken by the distress of adversity if he is not captivated by the pleasure [love] of prosperity.

## CHAPTER CCCXV. On the sevenfold Spirit, the seven beatitudes, and the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer

It also seems to me that the number seven in these petitions corresponds to that other number seven [Col. 1034C] from which this whole discourse proceeded.

If the fear of God is that by which the poor in spirit are blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, let us ask that God’s name be sanctified among human beings, with holy fear enduring forever and ever.

If piety is that by which the meek are blessed, because they will possess the earth as an inheritance, let us ask that his kingdom come—either into us ourselves, so that we may become meek and not resist him, or from heaven to earth, in the glory of the Lord’s coming, when we will rejoice and be praised, as he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

“In the Lord,” says the prophet, “my soul shall be praised; let the gentle [meek] hear and rejoice.”

If knowledge is that by which those who mourn are blessed, because they will be comforted, let us pray that his will may be done [Col. 1034D] as in heaven and on earth. For when the body, like earth, has consented in complete and total peace to the spirit, like heaven, we will not mourn. There is no other mourning of this present time except when these things struggle against one another and compel us to say: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” and to bear witness to our mourning with a tearful voice: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”

If fortitude is that by which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, because they will be satisfied, let us pray that our daily bread be given to us today. Strengthened and sustained by it, we shall be able to come to that fullest satisfaction.

If counsel is that by which the merciful are blessed, because God will have mercy on them, let us forgive our debtors and pray that our debts also may be forgiven to us.

If understanding is that by which the pure in heart are blessed, because they will see God, let us pray not to be led into temptation, lest we have a double heart by failing to seek the simple good to which we refer all that we do, while at the same time pursuing temporal and earthly things.

Temptations arising from things that seem burdensome and calamitous to human beings have no power over us if those temptations do not have power that arise through the allurements of things that people regard as good and joyful.

If wisdom is that by which the peacemakers are blessed, because they will be called sons of God, let us pray to be delivered from evil. For this very deliverance will make us free—that is, sons of God—so that by the spirit of adoption we may cry, “Abba, Father.”

## CHAPTER CCCXVI. [84] On fasting and washing the face or anointing the head; from the same book

“When you fast,” he says, “do not become like the hypocrites, who look gloomy, for they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.

“But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will repay you.”

These commands clearly direct all our intention toward inward joys, lest, by seeking a reward outwardly, we conform ourselves to this age and lose the promise of a much more substantial and enduring blessedness—the inner blessedness to whose image God chose us to be conformed, the image of his Son [his own]. [Col. 1035C]

In this chapter it must especially be noted that ostentation can exist not only in the splendor and display of bodily things, but also in mournful filth itself; and it is more dangerous when it deceives under the name of service to God.

Someone who shines through excessive bodily grooming, dress, or the splendor of other things is easily convicted by those very things of pursuing the pomp of the world. Nor does anyone deceive through a false appearance of holiness. But when someone, in his profession of Christianity, attracts the eyes of people to himself through unusual squalor and filth—doing so willingly and not suffering it from necessity—it can be inferred from his [that person’s: *hujus* (*ejus*)] other actions whether he does this out of contempt for excessive adornment or out of some ambition.

For the Lord also commanded that wolves should be avoided beneath sheep’s clothing: “You will know them,” he says, “by their fruits.” “For by their fruits,” he says, “you will know them.” [Col. 1035D]

When [Col. 1035D], through certain temptations, the very things [namely] that they have obtained or wish to obtain by means of this covering begin to be taken away from them or denied to them, then it must appear whether there is a wolf in sheep’s clothing or a sheep in its own clothing.

A Christian ought not therefore to please human eyes with excessive adornment because impostors often adopt a modest and necessary appearance in order to deceive the unwary. Nor should those sheep put aside their skins if wolves sometimes hide themselves beneath them.

It is therefore commonly asked what is meant by the statement: “When you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting.” No one could rightly command that, although we wash our face as part of daily custom [Col. 1036A], we should also have anointed heads when we fast. If everyone admits that this would be disgraceful, the command to anoint the head and wash the face must be understood as referring to the inner person.

To anoint the head therefore refers to joy; to wash the face refers to purity. Thus the person who rejoices inwardly in mind and reason anoints the head. We rightly understand the head as that which is preeminent in the soul and by which the other parts of the human being are plainly governed and directed. This is done by the person who does not seek joy outwardly, in order to rejoice carnally in human praise.

The flesh, which ought to be subject, is in no way the head of the whole human nature. “No one,” as the apostle says when he commands love for one’s wife, “has ever hated his own flesh.” But “the head of the woman is the man,” and the head of the man is [Col. 1036B] Christ.

Let the inner person therefore rejoice in his fasting, by which he turns away from the world’s pleasure through fasting so as to be subject to Christ, who, according to this command, desires to have an anointed head. In this way he will also wash his face—that is, purify his heart—with which he will see God, without a veil interposed because of weakness contracted from filth, but firm and stable because he is pure and simple.

“Wash yourselves,” he says; “be clean. Remove wickedness from your souls and from before my eyes.”

Our face must therefore be washed of those impurities by which God’s sight is offended. For with unveiled face, contemplating the glory of God, we will be transformed into the same image.

Often, too, thought about the necessities belonging to this life wounds and soils our inner eye, and very often doubles [makes double] (*conduplicat* [*cor duplicat*]) the heart [Col. 1036C], so that we do not perform the things we appear to do rightly among human beings with the heart commanded by the Lord. That is, we do not do them because we love those people, but because we wish to obtain some advantage from them on account of the necessities of the present life.

We ought to do good to them for the sake of their eternal salvation, not for the sake of our temporal advantage. Therefore, let God incline our heart toward his testimonies, and not toward profit.

For “the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

But whoever looks after a brother for the sake of his own necessity in this life does not serve charity. He does not look after the person whom he ought to love as himself; he looks after himself—or rather, he does not even look after himself, since by this he creates for himself a double heart, which prevents him from seeing God. In that vision alone there is certain and perpetual [Col. 1036D] blessedness.

## CHAPTER CCCXVII. On the Lord’s saying, “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?”; from the same book

“The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness?”

This passage should be understood so that we recognize that all our works are clean and pleasing in God’s sight if they are done with a simple heart—that is, with a heavenly intention and with charity as their end, since charity is also the fullness of the law [Col. 1037A].

Here, then, we must understand the eye as the very intention with which we do whatever we do. If that intention is pure and upright, and looks toward what ought to be looked toward, all our works that we perform according to it must be good.

He called all these works the whole “body,” because the apostle also calls certain works our members, disapproving of them and commanding that they be put to death when he says: “Put to death therefore your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, greed, and other such things.”

It is therefore not what someone does [but with what intention he does it] that must be considered. This is the light in us, because it is clear to us that we do what we do with a good intention. For everything that is made manifest is light.

The actions themselves that proceed from us into human society have an uncertain [Col. 1037B] outcome, and therefore he called them darkness. For when I extend money to a needy person who asks for it, I do not know what he will do or suffer as a result. It may happen that he does something evil with it or suffers some evil because of it—something that I did not want to happen when I gave it, nor did I give it with that intention.

Therefore, if I did with a good intention what was known to me when I did it, it is called light; and my action is illuminated, whatever its outcome may be. Since that outcome is uncertain and unknown, it is called darkness.

But if I acted with a bad intention, even the light itself is darkness. It is called light because each person knows with what intention he acts [85], even when he acts with a bad intention. Yet this light itself is darkness, because the simple intention is not directed toward heavenly things but declines toward lower [Col. 1037C] things, and through its double heart it produces something like a shadow.

Therefore, if the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness? That is, if the very intention of the heart with which you do what you do—and which is known to you—is soiled and blinded by desire for earthly and temporal things, how much more so is the action itself, whose outcome is uncertain, dirty and dark?

For even if what you do without a right and pure intention turns out well for someone, you are judged according to how you did it, not according to how it turned out for that other person.

## CHAPTER CCCXVIII. On the prohibition against anxiety about the following day; from the same book
Do not therefore be anxious about tomorrow [Do not think about tomorrow]. For “tomorrow” is spoken of only in time, where the future succeeds the past in turn. Therefore, when we do something good, let us think not of temporal things but of eternal things; then that work will be good and perfect. “Tomorrow,” he says, “will be anxious for itself”—that is, when the necessity itself begins to press upon you, you will then obtain food, drink, or clothing, as may be required. For these things will be present, because your Father knows that we need all these things. “Sufficient for the day,” he says, “is its own evil”—that is, it is enough that the necessity itself will compel us to obtain these things. I think it is called “evil” for the following reason: it is penal for us, for it belongs to that frailty and mortality which we deserved by sinning.

Do not therefore add anything more burdensome to this temporal punishment of necessity, so that you suffer not only the lack of these things but also serve God for the sake of satisfying that lack. Here one must be especially careful lest, when we see a servant of God making provision that these necessities not be lacking either to himself or to those entrusted to his care, we judge him to be acting against the Lord’s command and to be anxious about tomorrow. The Lord himself, although angels ministered to him, nevertheless, for the sake of example—so that no one afterward might be scandalized when he observed one of his servants procuring these necessities—was willing to have a money-box containing funds from which whatever was needed for necessary uses could be supplied. The keeper and thief of that money-box, as it is written, was Judas, who betrayed him.

The apostle Paul likewise may seem to have thought about tomorrow when he said: “Now concerning the collections being made for the saints: as I instructed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set aside at home, storing up whatever he has been pleased to give, so that collections may not be made when I come.” From these and similar passages of Scripture it is sufficiently clear that our Lord does not disapprove if someone, in the human manner, makes provision for such things, but only if someone serves God for their sake, so that in his works he regards not the kingdom of God but the acquisition of these things.

This whole command, then, is brought back (redigitur) [or directed (dirigitur)] to the following rule: even when making provision for these things, we are to think of the kingdom of God; but in the service of the kingdom of God we are not to think about these things. For even if these things should sometimes be lacking—which God often permits for our training—not only do they not weaken our purpose, they also strengthen it once it has been tested and proved. “For we glory,” he says, “in tribulations.” [Cols. 1037D–1038C]

## CHAPTER 319. How “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” is to be understood; and concerning the speck in a brother’s eye and the beam not seen in one’s own eye; from the same book, On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount [Cols. 1038C–1041C]

“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment with which you have judged, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.”

In this passage, I think nothing else is commanded to us except that we interpret in the better sense those actions concerning which it is uncertain with what intention they are performed. For what is written—“You will know them by their fruits”—was said of manifest acts, which cannot be performed with a good intention. Such are sexual violations, blasphemies, thefts, drunkenness, and similar acts, concerning which we are permitted to judge, since the Apostle says: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are within that you judge?”

But concerning kinds of food—since any human food can be taken without fault, with a good intention and a simple heart, without the defect of desire—the same Apostle forbade those who abstained from such foods to judge those who ate meat and drank wine: “Let the one who eats,” he says, “not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.” There too he says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls.”

Regarding such matters, which can be done with a good, simple, and magnanimous spirit, although they can also be done with an evil spirit, those people, being human, wanted to pass judgment upon the hidden things of the heart—matters of which God alone is judge. To this also belongs what he says elsewhere: “Do not judge anything before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate [and he will illuminate] the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the intentions of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God [the Lord].”

There are therefore certain intermediate acts whose intention we do not know, because they can be performed both well and badly; it is rash to judge them, especially so as to condemn them. The time will come for these acts to be judged, when God [the Lord] illuminates the hidden things of darkness and reveals the intentions of the heart.

The same Apostle says elsewhere: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, while those of others follow after.” By “manifest” he means those concerning which it is clear with what intention they are performed. These go before to judgment, that is, if judgment follows upon them, it is not rash. Those other sins follow afterward, namely, those that are hidden, because they too were not concealed at their proper time. The same must be understood of good works, for he adds: “Similarly, good works are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden.”

Let us therefore judge what is manifest, but leave judgment concerning what is hidden to God, since these things too—whether evil or good—cannot remain concealed when the time comes for them to be revealed.

There are two circumstances in which we must avoid rash judgment: when it is uncertain with what intention something was done [has been done], or when it is uncertain what the person who now appears either evil or good will become. Thus, if someone complained of stomach trouble and did not wish to fast, and you, not believing him, attributed this to the vice of gluttony, you would judge rashly. Likewise, if you recognized manifest gluttony and drunkenness, and reproached him as though he could never be corrected or changed, you would likewise judge rashly.

Let us therefore not reprove what we do not know with what intention it was done; nor let us reproach manifest acts in such a way that we despair of recovery. Thus we shall avoid the judgment of which it is now said: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”

What he says may nevertheless cause difficulty: “For with the judgment with which you have judged, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you have measured, with that same measure it will be measured back to you.” If we have judged with rash judgment, will God therefore judge us rashly also? Or if we have measured with an unjust measure, is there an unjust measure with God by which it will be measured back to us?

I think that the word “measure” signifies judgment itself. God in no way judges rashly or repays anyone with an unjust measure. Rather, this was said because the very rashness with which you punish another is itself that by which you must be punished (eadem ipsa [est ei qua]); unless perhaps one should suppose that injustice harms the person against whom it proceeds but does nothing to the person from whom it proceeds. On the contrary, it often harms not at all the one who suffers the injury, but necessarily harms the one who commits it.

What harm did the injustice of the persecutors do to the martyrs? It harmed the persecutors themselves greatly. Even if some of them were corrected, nevertheless, at the time when they were persecuting, their own wickedness blinded them. So too rash judgment often harms not at all the person rashly judged, but the rashness itself necessarily harms the person who judges rashly.

I think this same rule is signified by the saying: “Everyone who strikes with the sword will die by the sword.” How many strike with the sword and yet do not die [by] the sword—as Peter himself did not? But lest anyone suppose that he escaped such punishment through the forgiveness of sins, although nothing could be more absurd than to think that Peter could have suffered a greater punishment by the sword than by the cross, which he did suffer, what will he say about the thieves who were crucified with the Lord? One of them, who deserved forgiveness, received it after he had been crucified; the other did not deserve it at all.

Or perhaps all those whom they had killed had been crucified, and therefore they themselves deserved to suffer this? It is ridiculous to think so. What else, then, does the saying “Everyone who strikes with the sword will die by the sword” mean except that the soul dies by the very sin it commits?

Since the Lord here warns us about rash and unjust judgment, he wants us to do whatever we do with a simple heart directed toward the one God. Many acts are of uncertain intention, and it is rash to judge them. Those judge most rashly concerning uncertain matters, and reproach most readily, who love to blame and condemn more than to amend and correct. This vice is either pride or envy.

He then appropriately adds and says: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?” For example, suppose that he sinned through anger, while you reproach him out of hatred. How great, then, is the difference between a speck and a beam—as great, so to speak, as the difference between anger and hatred. Hatred is anger that has grown old, as though through age itself it had acquired such strength that it deserved to be called a beam.

It may happen that if you are angry with someone, you wish him to be corrected; but if you hate someone, you cannot wish him to be corrected. How, then, do you say to your brother, “Let me remove the speck from your eye,” when there is a beam in your own eye? “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to remove the speck from your brother’s eye”—that is, first drive hatred away, and then you will be able to correct the person whom you love.

He rightly says, “Hypocrite.” To accuse vices is the duty of good and benevolent men. When wicked people do so, they play another’s part, like hypocrites, who conceal under a role what they are and display in that role what they are not.

By the name “hypocrites,” therefore, understand pretenders. Their kind is truly one that must be greatly avoided and is burdensome: although they undertake every accusation of vice out of hatred and envy, they also want to appear to be comforters. Therefore we must watch carefully and piously, so that whenever necessity compels us to reprove or rebuke someone, we first consider whether the vice is one we have never had, or one of which we have already been freed.

If we have never had it, let us consider that we too are human and could have had it. But if we have had it and no longer have it, let the memory of our common weakness touch us, so that mercy, not hatred, precedes our reproach or rebuke—whether it proves effective for the correction of the person for whom we do it, or for his corruption, since the outcome is uncertain. At least we shall then be secure in the simplicity of our own eye.

But if, on examining ourselves, we discover that we are in the same vice as the person whom we were preparing to reprove, let us neither reprove nor rebuke him. Instead, let us groan together with him (congemiscamus) [the variant reads cavendum, “it must be avoided”], and invite him not to obey us but to strive together with us.

The Apostle’s saying also belongs here: “I became as a Jew to the Jews, in order to win the Jews; to those under the law, as though I were under the law—although I myself am not under the law—in order to win those under the law; to those without the law, as though I were without the law—although I am not (non sim) [was not (essem)] without the law of God, but am in the law of Christ—in order to win those without the law; I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that I might win all.”

He certainly did not act through pretense, as some wish to understand it, thereby protecting their detestable hypocrisy with the authority of so great an example. Rather, he did this through love, by which he regarded the weakness of the person whom he wished to help as though it were his own. He indicates this beforehand when he says: “Although I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win more.”

To understand that this is done not through pretense but through love, by which we sympathize with weak human beings as people who are ourselves, listen to his warning elsewhere: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.” This cannot happen unless each person regards the weakness of another as his own, so that he may bear it calmly until the one whose salvation he is seeking is freed from it.

Rebukes should therefore be used rarely and [in] great necessity. Even then, we must insist that not we but God [the Lord] be served through them. For this is the end: that we do nothing with a divided heart, removing from our own eye the beam of envy, wickedness, or pretense, so that we may see to remove the speck from our brother’s eye.

## CHAPTER 320. How “the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him” is to be understood; from the book On the Presence of God [Cols. 1041D–1043A]

Thus God dwells in every individual as in his temples, and in all of them gathered together into one as in his temple. As long as this temple, like Noah’s ark, is tossed about in this world, what is written in the psalm comes to pass: “The Lord inhabits the flood.” This may also appropriately be understood on account of the many peoples of the faithful in all nations, whom Revelation signifies under the name of “waters”: “The Lord inhabits the flood.”

It continues: “And the Lord will sit as King forever”—clearly in his temple, established now in eternal life after the turbulence of this world.

God, therefore, who is present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, toward which he is kind and gracious through his favor. Yet, while dwelling in them, he is received more fully by some and less fully by others.

Regarding our Head, the Apostle says: “For in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily.” This does not mean “bodily” because God is corporeal [or: because God is a body]. Rather, he either used the word metaphorically, as though God had dwelt in a handmade temple not bodily but figuratively—that is, through signs that prefigured what was to come. For he calls all those observances “shadows of things to come,” using the word metaphorically; and, as it is written, the supreme God does not dwell in handmade temples.
