Or “bodily” was certainly said because God dwells in the body of Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, as in a temple. Hence, when the Jews asked for a sign and he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” the Evangelist, explaining what this meant, adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

What, then, is the distinction between the Head and the other members? Is it that, although the Godhead dwells in any member, however eminent—as in some great prophet or apostle—it does not dwell in that member as it does in the Head, who is Christ, in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells?

In our own body, too, every member possesses all the senses, but not to the same extent as the head, in which all five are present in full: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; in the other members, only touch is present.

Or, beyond the fact that the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells in that body as in a temple, is there some other distinction between that Head and the excellence of any member? Certainly there is. Through a singular assumption of that man, one person was made with the Word. Of none of the saints could it be said, or can it be said, or will it be said: “The Word became flesh.” No saint, however great his excellence in grace, received the name “only-begotten,” so that what the Word of God himself is before the ages might be said together with the man he assumed.

That assumption, therefore, is unique, and cannot in any way be shared with any holy human beings, however outstanding in wisdom and holiness. Here the evidence of divine grace is sufficiently clear and unmistakable. For who would be so sacrilegious as to dare affirm that any soul could, through the merit of free will, bring it about that another person should be Christ? For it to belong to the person of the only-begotten Word—how could a single soul have deserved this through free will, which is given commonly and naturally to all, unless singular grace had granted it? It is right to proclaim that grace; it is wrong to wish to judge it.

If, to the extent of our abilities and as the Lord helps us, we have treated these matters properly, then, when you extend your thought to God’s being present everywhere—not dispersed everywhere through spatial distances, as though by some mass or extension, but wholly present everywhere—turn your mind away from all images of bodies that human thought customarily turns over.

Wisdom is not conceived in this way, nor justice, nor finally love, of which it is written: “God is love.”

When you think about his dwelling, think of unity and the congregation of the saints, especially in heaven. He is said to dwell there especially because there his will is perfectly accomplished in those in whom he dwells. Then think of him on earth, where he dwells while building his house, which is to be dedicated at the end of the age.

Think also of Christ our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, equal to the Father, and likewise the Son of Man, in which respect the Father is greater than he. Thus you may not doubt that he is wholly present everywhere: as God, and in the same temple of God as the indwelling God, and in some place in heaven because of the condition of his true body.

## CHAPTER 321. On appointing as bishop a man who is the husband of one wife; from the book On the Good of Marriage [Cols. 1043A–1043D]

What food is for the health of the body, intercourse is for the propagation of the race, and neither is without bodily pleasure. The different practices of the fathers were caused only by the difference of the times.

It was therefore necessary for the non-carnal prophets also to engage in carnal intercourse, just as it was necessary for the non-carnal apostles also to eat bodily food.

Those who understood more keenly judged that an administrator of the Church could not be ordained unless he were the husband of one wife. They also judged that a man who had taken another wife while a catechumen or pagan could not be ordained.

The issue concerns a sacrament, not sin. For all sins are forgiven in baptism. Yet the one who said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin,” and, “Let her do what she wishes; she does not sin if she marries,” made it sufficiently clear that marriage is no sin.

But on account of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman who has been violated while still a catechumen cannot, after baptism, be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it was not unreasonably thought that a man who had exceeded the singular number of wives had not committed some sin, but had lost a certain sacramental standard—not one necessary for the merit of a good life, but one required as the sign of ecclesiastical ordination.

Accordingly, just as the many wives of the ancient fathers signified our future Churches from all nations, subject to one man, Christ, so our bishop who is the husband of one wife signifies the unity from all nations, subject to one man, Christ. This unity will be perfected when he reveals the hidden things of darkness, and so forth.

At present, however, hidden dissensions are manifest even among those who, while preserving love, are destined to be one and in one. Then, certainly, there will be none. Therefore, just as it was not permitted to serve two or more masters, so to pass from a living husband into another marriage was not permitted then, is not permitted now, and will never be permitted.

To apostatize from the one God and go over to another’s adulterous superstition is always evil. Nor did our saints, for the sake of more numerous offspring, do what Cato the Roman is said to have done: while still alive, hand over his wife to another household to fill it with children. In our marriages, the holiness of the sacrament is worth more than the fertility of the womb.

## CHAPTER 322. On nocturnal emission; from the same book [Cols. 1044A–1044B]

The law establishes many things in the sacraments and shadows of future realities.

Thus a certain material [as it were] formlessness in the seed—which, once formed, is to produce the human body—was established as a sign of a formless and uneducated life. Since a human being must be cleansed from this formlessness by the form and training of instruction, purification was commanded as a sign of this very thing after the emission of seed.

For one does not sin in dreams, and yet purification was commanded even in that case. Or, if someone thinks this is a sin, supposing that it occurs only as the result of some desire of this kind—which is certainly false—are women’s customary menstrual periods also sins? Yet the same ancient law commanded that women be purified from them, solely because of that material formlessness which is added, as it were, to the construction of the body when conception takes place.

Thus, when it flows in an unformed state, the law wished it to signify an undisciplined soul flowing indecently and dissolutely, without the form of discipline; it signifies that the soul ought to be formed when the law commands such bodily flow to be purified.

Finally, is dying a sin? Or is burying the dead not also a good work of humanity? Yet purification was commanded for this as well, because when life has departed from a dead body, that is not sin, but it signifies the soul’s abandonment by righteousness.

## CHAPTER 323. On the virtue of the soul, whether hidden or manifest; from the same book [Cols. 1044B–1044D]

Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the soul. The virtues of the soul are sometimes manifested in action and sometimes lie hidden in a disposition. Thus the virtue of martyrdom was outstanding [appeared] and became visible through enduring sufferings. But how many possess that same virtue of soul while lacking the temptation through which what is within them, before God, might also come forth before human beings?

The usefulness of drinking wine was relaxed for Timothy’s body in such a way that the disposition of continence remained in his soul. For this is the disposition by which something is done when there is need; when it is not done, it can be done, but there is no need.

Was there therefore no virtue of continence in Christ regarding food and drink, as there was in John the Baptist, so that it could be said: “Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine”? Are such things not also said about his household, our fathers, with respect to another kind of use of earthly things, namely intercourse: “Behold, men who are lustful and impure, lovers of women and of wantonness”?

Wisdom was justified by her children, who perceive that the virtue of continence must always exist as a disposition of the soul, but must be manifested in action according to the opportunity afforded by circumstances and times.

When someone says in an evil conversation to a continent person who refuses marriage, “Are you therefore better than Abraham?”, let him reply: “I am not better, but the chastity of the unmarried is better than the chastity of marriage.” Abraham had one of these in use and both in disposition. He lived chastely in marriage; he could also have lived chastely without marriage, but at that time it was not appropriate.

For my part, I more easily refrain from the marriage which Abraham used than I would use marriage in the way Abraham used it. What I am doing now he would have done better, if it had been necessary to do it then.

## CHAPTER 324. “No one has ascended into heaven,” and, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness”; from the first book On the Baptism of Infants [Cols. 1045A–1046B]

“No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

“This,” he says, “is how the spiritual generation will take place: earthly people will become heavenly. They will not be able to attain this unless they become my members. Thus the one who descended ascends, because no one ascends except the one who descended.”

Unless, therefore, all are changed and lifted up into the unity of Christ, so that Christ who descended himself ascends—since he regards no other body as his body, that is, his Church, than himself, because the saying “The two will be one flesh” is more truly understood of Christ and the Church—they will not be able to ascend at all. For “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

Although the Son of Man became so on earth, he did not consider his divinity, by which he remained in heaven while descending, unworthy of the name “Son of Man,” just as he deigned to call his flesh “the Son of God.” This was so that they would not be understood as two Christs, one God and the other man, but as one and the same God and man: God, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God”; man, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Accordingly, because of the distinction between divinity and weakness, the Son of God remained in heaven while the Son of Man walked on earth. But because of the unity of person, by which the two substances are one Christ, the Son of God also walked on earth, and that same Son of Man remained in heaven.

Faith in the more credible realities is therefore made stronger by believing the incredible ones. If the divine substance, so much more distant and exalted by an incomparable difference, could for our sake assume human substance in such a way that one person was made, so that the Son of Man, who was on earth through the weakness of the flesh, was also in heaven through the participation of the flesh in divinity, how much more credible is it that other holy and faithful human beings become one Christ with the man Christ? Thus, when all who ascend through this grace and fellowship of his ascend, the one Christ himself ascends into heaven who descended from heaven.

So too the Apostle says: “Just as in one body we have many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ.” He did not say, “So also are Christ’s”—that is, the body or members of Christ—but “so also is Christ,” calling the Head and the body one Christ.

Great and wondrous is this condescension. Since it cannot occur except through the forgiveness of sins, he goes on to say: “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

We know what happened in the wilderness. Many were dying from the bites of serpents. Then the people, confessing their sins, pleaded with the Lord through Moses to remove this poison from them. Accordingly, at the Lord’s command, Moses lifted up a bronze serpent in the wilderness and instructed the people that anyone who had been bitten by a serpent should look at the lifted-up serpent. Those who did so were immediately healed.

What is the lifted-up serpent except the death of Christ, in the manner of signification by which the effect is signified through the agent producing it? Death came from the serpent, which persuaded the human being to commit the sin by which he would die. But the Lord did not transfer sin into his flesh as though it were the serpent’s poison. He nevertheless transferred death, so that there might be, in the likeness of sinful flesh, punishment without guilt; hence, in sinful flesh, both guilt and punishment might be abolished.

Therefore, just as the person who looked at the lifted-up serpent was healed from the poison and freed from death, so now the person who is conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death through faith and his baptism is freed from sin through justification and from death through resurrection. This is what he says: “So that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

## CHAPTER 325. Whether the resurrection of Lazarus or of Christ corresponds to the future resurrection; from the book Response against Six Questions of the Pagans [Cols. 1046B–1047D]

It is therefore not the resurrection of Lazarus but rather that of Christ which corresponds to the promised resurrection, because Lazarus rose in such a way that he would die again, whereas Christ, as it is written of him, “having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him.” This too was promised for the resurrection (resurrectionis) [to those who will rise (resurrecturis)] at the end of the age and reign with him forever.

The difference between Christ’s birth and ours likewise has no bearing on the difference of resurrection: he was born without the seed of a man, whereas we were created from a man and a woman. Just as this does not bear upon the difference denoted by mortalis [mortis], “of death”—for his death was not therefore unreal because he was born without male seed—nor does it matter that the flesh of the first human being arose differently from ours. He was created from the earth without parents, whereas we come from parents; yet this contributed nothing to a difference in death, so that he should die in one way and we in another.

Just as differing birth does not affect the difference of death, neither does it affect the difference of resurrection. Nor should unbelievers [people] be unwilling [are unwilling] to believe what is written about the first human being. Let them investigate, or at least observe if they are able, how many kinds of animals are produced from the earth without parents, yet reproduce by mating offspring like themselves. Despite the difference in their births, there is no difference in the nature of those produced from the earth and those produced through their mating. They live in the same way and die in the same way, although they were born differently.

Similarly, it is not absurd that bodies which arose differently should rise in the same way. People of this kind, unable to discern with respect to what a difference matters and with respect to what it does not, insist that wherever they have noticed some difference in origins, all subsequent things must also differ.

Such people might suppose that oil made from fat ought not to float on water as olive oil does, because the origins of the two are very different: one flows from wood and the other from flesh.

As for the difference that Christ’s body rose on the third day without being dissolved by decay and putrefaction, whereas ours, after a long time, will be restored from a certain confusion from which [into which] they will have departed after being dissolved, both are impossible for human ability but both are exceedingly easy for divine power.

Just as the ray of our eye does not reach what is near more quickly and what is far more slowly, but travels equal distances with equal speed, so, when the resurrection of the dead occurs in the twinkling of an eye, as the Apostle says, through the omnipotence of God and his ineffable command, it is just as easy to raise recent bodies as corpses that have dispersed over a long period.

These things are incredible to some because they have not experienced them, although all the nature of things is so full of miracles that things seem not wonderful because of some easy investigation of reason but because of familiarity through repeated observation. For this reason they seem worthy neither of consideration nor inquiry.

But I, and with me everyone who strives to perceive the invisible things of God through the things that have been made, admire no less—and perhaps more—the fact that in one tiny grain of seed all the things we praise in a tree lay hidden, as though woven together, than that the vast expanse of this world, which absorbs human bodies as they dissolve, will restore them wholly and intact for the future resurrection.

How is it contrary that Christ ate after his resurrection while there will be no need for food in the promised resurrection? We read that angels also took such food in the same manner, not in a fictitious apparition but in the clearest reality, and yet not from necessity but from power.

The thirsty earth absorbs water in one way; the burning ray of the sun absorbs it in another. The former does so from need, the latter through power.

Will the body of the future resurrection therefore have imperfect happiness if it cannot take food? Or will it have imperfect happiness if it needs food?

Let the person who posed these questions know that after his resurrection Christ showed scars, not wounds, to those who doubted. For their sake also he wished to take food and drink, not once but repeatedly, lest they suppose that he was not a body but a spirit, and that he appeared to them not solidly but imaginatively.

Those scars would then have been false if no wounds had preceded them. Yet they would not have existed either if he had not wished them to exist. For the sake of a definite dispensation, however, he wished to show to those whom he was building up in unfictitious faith not something else in place of something else, but that the very one whom they had seen crucified had risen.

What, then, does the objection mean: “If he did this for the sake of the unbeliever, he fabricated it”? It is as though some brave man, fighting for his country, received many grievous wounds and then said to a very skilled physician, who was able to heal them so that no scars would appear, that he preferred to be healed in such a way that the traces of the wounds would remain on his body as titles of his glory. Would the physician therefore be said to have fabricated the scars? Although by his art he could have made them absent, for a definite reason he instead uses his art to make them present. They could be proved false in only one way, as I said above: if no wounds had been healed.

## CHAPTER 326. “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person,” and so forth; from the first book of Questions on the Gospel [Cols. 1048A–1048B]

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person,” and the rest, signifies that some will believe in such a way that they cannot endure the labors of continence and will return to the world.

The statement “He takes with him seven other spirits” is understood to mean that when someone has fallen from righteousness, he will also possess pretense. For when carnal desire has been expelled through repentance from its customary activities, if it does not find pleasures in which to rest, it returns more avidly and again occupies the human mind—provided that, after it had been forced out, negligence followed [if, when it had been expelled, neglect of righteousness followed], so that the word of God was not introduced as an inhabitant into the cleansed house through sound teaching.

And because such a person will not only possess those seven vices that are opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy that he possesses the virtues themselves, therefore that desire returns with seven other spirits more wicked than itself—that is, with the sevenfold pretense itself—so that the final condition of that person is worse than the first.

## CHAPTER 327. On the resources for building a tower; from Book II of Questions on the Gospel, title 21
## The Cost of Building a Tower; the Strength Required to Attain Christ’s Discipleship

The cost of building a tower, and the strength required to attain Christ’s discipleship: and the ten thousand who are to fight against a king who has twenty thousand, fighting with Christ’s simplicity against the devil’s duplicity—that is, against his deceits and frauds—are found in the resolve of one who renounces everything that belongs to him. [Col. 1048C] For he concludes in this way: “Thus, therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.” [Note: *claudit*, “closes”; variant: *concludit*, “concludes.”]

Among all these things, temporal life itself must also be understood. One ought to possess it for a time in such a way that it does not hinder one from attaining the eternal, if he has threatened to take it away. Just as, concerning the unfinished tower, he deterred them by the reproach of those who said, “This man began to build and was not able to finish,” so, in the case of the king with whom one must fight, he condemned that peace itself when he said: “While he is still far away, sending a delegation, he asks for the terms of peace.” [Col. 1048D] He thereby signified also the threats of temptations impending from the devil: people who do not renounce everything they possess are unable to withstand them and make peace with him by consenting to commit sins.

To build the tower, then, and to fight against that king, is to be Christ’s disciple; but to have the resources for completing the tower and to have ten thousand strong enough to confront the king’s twenty thousand is to renounce everything that belongs to one.

## CHAPTER 328. In what providential arrangement [dispensation] of God the Scriptures of the Old Testament were translated from Hebrew into Greek, so that they might become known to all nations; from Book XVIII of *The City of God*

One of the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt also desired to know and possess the sacred Scriptures. After the magnificent and very short-lived power of Alexander of Macedon, who was also called the Great—a power by which he had subdued all Asia, indeed almost the whole world, partly by force and arms and partly by terror, and during which he entered and conquered Judaea among the other regions of the East—when Alexander died, his companions divided that vast kingdom among themselves, not intending to possess it peacefully but rather having dispersed it and laying everything waste through wars. Egypt then began to have Ptolemaic kings. [Col. 1049A] The first of these, the son of Lagos, transferred many captives from Judaea to Egypt.

His successor was another Ptolemy, called Philadelphus. He allowed all those whom his predecessor had brought there, after they had been subjugated [*subigatos*, “subdued”; variant: *subjugatos*, “subjugated”], to return free. In addition, he sent royal gifts to the temple of God and requested from Eleazar, then the high priest, that the Scriptures be given to him. He had certainly heard them proclaimed by report as divine, and for that reason he desired to possess them in the very distinguished library he had established. [Col. 1049B]

When that same high priest had sent him the Hebrew Scriptures, Ptolemy afterward requested translators as well. Seventy-two men were given to him, six from each of the twelve tribes, highly learned in both languages—Hebrew, that is, and Greek. Their translation has now, by established usage, come to be called the Septuagint.

It is related that there was in their words such a marvelous, astonishing, and wholly divine agreement that, when they sat separately to perform this work—for Ptolemy had decided to test their reliability in this way—not one of them differed from another in any word that had the same meaning and equivalent force, or in the order of the words. Rather, it was as though there were one translator: what they all translated was one and the same, because in truth there was one Spirit in them all. [Note: *sederent* and *sederint* both refer to their sitting separately; the variant changes the imperfect subjunctive to the perfect.]

For this reason they had received so marvelous a gift from God: the authority of those Scriptures was commended in this manner as well, not as though they were human writings but as divine writings, which would later benefit the nations who were to believe. [Col. 1049C] We now see that this has come to pass. [Note: The printed *sicut erant*, “as they were,” affirms their divine character; the variant *tanquam* means “as/as though.”]

## CHAPTER 329. On the authority of the Septuagint translators, which, without dishonoring the Hebrew style, is to be preferred to all other translators; from the same book

Although there were other translators who transferred those sacred writings from Hebrew into Greek—Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, as well as the translation whose author is not known and which, for that reason, without the translator’s name, is called the Fifth Edition—the Church nevertheless received the Septuagint as though it alone existed. [Col. 1049D] The Christian peoples of Greece use it, and most of them do not even know whether any other translation exists. [Note: After *sicut etiam illa* (“as also that [translation]”), the source supplies *est*, “is.”]

From this Septuagint translation, what the Latin churches possess was also translated into Latin. Yet in our own times there has been our presbyter Jerome, a very learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated those same Scriptures into Latin not from Greek but from Hebrew. [Note: The source supplies *est* after *interpretatum* to complete “was translated.”]

Although the Jews admit that his scholarly labor is accurate, while they maintain that the Septuagint translators made many errors, the Church of Christ nevertheless judges no one preferable to the authority of so many men, chosen for this very work by Eleazar, then the high priest. [Col. 1050A] For even if one divine Spirit had not appeared among them, but the seventy learned men had compared their translations with one another in the human manner, so that what pleased everyone would remain, no single translator ought to have been preferred to them.

But since such a sign of divinity appeared in them, whoever else translates those Scriptures truthfully from Hebrew into any other language either agrees with those seventy translators, or, if he seems not to agree with them, a prophetic profundity must be believed to be present there. The Spirit who was in the prophets when they spoke those words was the same Spirit in the seventy men when they translated them. By divine authority that Spirit could cause them to say something else, as though one prophet had spoken both versions, because the same Spirit spoke both; and it could express the same meaning differently, so that, for those who understood rightly, the identical sense would become clear without identical words. It could also omit something [*praetermitteret*, “he might omit”; variant: *praetermittere*, “to omit”] or add something [*adderet*, “he might add”; variant: *addere*, “to add”], so that this too might show that the work was not a human servitude bound to the translator’s words, but rather a divine power that filled and governed the translator’s mind. [Col. 1050B] [Note: The printed *erat*, “was,” has the variant *etiam*, “also.”]

Some people thought that the Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint translation should be corrected from the Hebrew manuscripts. Nevertheless, they did not dare remove what the Hebrews did not have [*non habent*, “they do not have”; variant: *non habebant*, “they did not have”], but the Septuagint had supplied. They merely added what was found in the Hebrew manuscripts but absent from the Septuagint, and marked these additions at the beginnings of the same verses with certain signs made in the form of stars. These signs are called *asterisks* (*ἀστερίσκους*).

What the Hebrews do not have but the Septuagint does have, they likewise marked at the beginnings of the verses with horizontal strokes, as uncial letters are written. Many manuscripts containing these marks have been circulated everywhere, including among the Latins. [Col. 1050C]

But what has not been omitted or added, yet has been expressed differently—whether it produces another sense, though one that is not incompatible, or appears to explain the same sense in another way—cannot be discovered without examining both sets of manuscripts.

If, then, as we ought, we look for nothing else in those Scriptures except what the Spirit of God spoke through human beings, whatever is in the Hebrew manuscripts and not found among the Septuagint translators was something the Spirit of God did not wish to say through these translators but through those prophets. Whatever is found in the Septuagint but not in the Hebrew manuscripts, the same Spirit preferred to say through these translators rather than through those prophets, thereby showing that both groups were prophets. [Col. 1050D] [Note: The printed *ea*, “those things,” has the variant *hoc*, “this.”]

For in this manner the one Spirit said one thing through Isaiah, another through Jeremiah, and another through yet another prophet; or said the same thing differently through one prophet and another, as he willed. Whatever is found in both, the one and same Spirit wished to say through both—but in such a way that the former preceded by prophesying, while the latter followed by interpreting prophetically. For just as there was one Spirit of peace among the former, who spoke truthfully and concordantly [*concordia*, “concordant things”; variant: *concordantia*, “things agreeing”], so the same one Spirit appeared among the latter, who did not consult one another and yet interpreted everything as though with one mouth.

## CHAPTER 330. What is to be understood concerning the destruction of the Ninevites, whose announcement extends over forty days in the Hebrew text but is compressed into three days in the Septuagint; from the same book

[Note: The printed *de cujus denuntiationi* has irregular syntax (“concerning whose announcement,” with a mismatched case); the variant *cujus denuntiatio in* reads “whose announcement in ...”.]

Someone may say: “How will I know what the prophet Jonah said to the Ninevites: ‘Three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown,’ or ‘Forty days’?” For who does not see that both statements could not have been made at that time by the prophet who had been sent to the city with the threat of impending destruction? [The printed *terrae comminutionem*, “the crushing of the earth,” is corrupt in this construction. The variant *terrere comminatione*, “to terrify by a threat,” supplies the sense used here.] If its destruction was to occur on the third day, then certainly not on the fortieth; but if on the fortieth, then certainly not on the third.

If, therefore, I am asked which of these Jonah said, I think it was rather what is read in the Hebrew: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” [Col. 1051B] The Septuagint translators, who translated much later, could have said something else that nevertheless pertained to the matter and converged upon one and the same meaning, although under another signification. They could thereby admonish the reader, without rejecting either authority, to rise above the history and seek the things for whose signification the history itself was written.

Those events took place in the city of Nineveh, but they also signified something that exceeded the limits of that city. In the same way, what happened when the prophet himself was in the belly of the sea creature for three days signified another person who was to remain for three days in the depths of hell—the Lord of all the prophets. [Note: The source supplies *illa*, “those [events],” after “were done.”]

Therefore, if that city is rightly understood as a prophetic figure of the Church of the nations, overthrown through repentance so that it would no longer be what it had been, then, since this was accomplished through Christ in the Church of the nations, of which Nineveh bore the figure, whether the period was forty days or three days, Christ himself was signified in both cases.

He was signified by the forty days because he spent that number of days with his disciples after his resurrection [*resurrectionem*, “resurrection”; variant adds *suam*, “his own”] and then ascended into heaven; by the three days because he rose on the third day. Thus the Septuagint translators—and those same prophets [*idemque*; variant: *iidemque* (alternative plural spellings here, “and the same men”)]—seem to have awakened from sleep the reader who wished to cling to nothing but the history of past events, urging him to search out the depth of prophecy. In a certain sense they said: “Seek him in the forty days; in him you will also be able to find the three days. You will find the one in his ascension and the other in his resurrection.” [Col. 1051D]

For this reason both numbers could most appropriately signify Christ: one was spoken through the prophet Jonah, the other through the prophecy of the Septuagint translators, yet by one and the same Spirit.

I avoid length, so as not to demonstrate this through many examples in which the Septuagint translators are thought [The source supplies *putantur*, “are thought.”] to differ from the Hebrew truth but, when rightly understood, are found to agree. Thus I too, following as far as I can in the footsteps of the apostles—for they also placed prophetic testimonies from both sources, that is, from the Hebrews and from the Septuagint—have judged that both authorities should be used, since both are one and divine. [Note: The source repeats *ex*, “from,” before the Septuagint, alongside the preceding “from the Hebrews.”]

## CHAPTER 331. On what the Apostle says: “Every sin that a person [Col. 1052A] commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” From a sermon on this subject

The question in the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Corinthians, where he says, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body,” I do not know whether it can be fully resolved, although, with the Lord’s help, something probable may be said about it. For it is exceedingly profound.

Earlier in the same Epistle the Apostle says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.” A little later he says: “Do you not know that [Col. 1052B] your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? By no means! Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute is one body with her? For, he says, ‘The two will be one flesh’; but the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit. Flee fornication.”

There he then adds: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body.”

Since, therefore, he had first enumerated in this chapter many terrible sins of human beings, through which they would not receive the kingdom of God, although these sins can be perpetrated by human beings only through the body—and since he said that [Col. 1052C] this body, already belonging to the faithful, is the temple of the Holy Spirit whom we have from God, and affirmed that the very members of our body are members of Christ, concerning which he says by way of accusation and, as it were, questioning, “Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” and answers himself, “By no means!”—then he continues and says: “Do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute is one body with her? For the two, he says, will be one flesh; but the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit.” He concludes: “Flee fornication.”

Yet he himself then follows by saying: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.”

It is as though the sins he had enumerated—“Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, [Col. 1052D] nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God”—could not all these crimes and disgraceful acts be committed or practiced except through the body. What sane person would deny this?

The Apostle was dealing with and defending this whole passage because of the body itself, which had been bought at a great price, that is, by the precious blood of Christ, and made the temple of the Holy Spirit by God, so that it might not be polluted by such disgraceful acts but might rather be preserved inviolate as God’s dwelling place.

Why, then, did he wish to add something from which a difficult question would arise? Why did he say, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication [Col. 1053A] sins against his own body,” when fornication itself, or other sins of this kind—which cannot be committed except through the body and resemble disgrace and fornication—are carried out and practiced only through that very body?

What of this? Could anyone—leaving aside the other sins mentioned above—be a thief, a drunkard, a reviler, or a rapacious person without the operation of this body? Even idolatry and greed cannot reach their use and enjoyment without the body’s service. What, then, does this mean: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body”?

First, because a person is constituted in this body, whatever he may wickedly desire with the mind alone cannot be said to be done by him outside this body, since it is clear that [Col. 1053B] he does it with bodily sensation and bodily understanding, while still enclosed by this body.

The same is true of what is written in the Psalm: “The wicked person said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’” The blessed Apostle certainly could not separate this from bodily action in the passage where he says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.” For the wicked person could say, “There is no God,” only while constituted in the body.

I will say nothing of the fact that, in another Epistle, the same Teacher of the nations says: “The works of the flesh are manifest,” and lists them: “fornications, impurities, debaucheries, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, and things like these.” He says: “I warn you, as [Col. 1053C] I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Do the other things he inserted there—rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, envies, and heresies—not seem to us to occur outside the body? Yet the Teacher of the nations attributes these things to the works of the flesh, in faith and truth.

What, then, does this mean: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body,” while naming only the sin of fornication he says, “But the one who commits fornication sins against his own body”?

It is apparent even to anyone slow and dull-witted [*obtunso*; variant: *obtuso* (both “dull,” alternative forms)] what a difficult question this is. If the Lord should graciously illuminate and reveal something of it to our pious intention, we may be able to say something reasonable. [Note: After “dull,” *quam*, “how,” has the variant *quae*, “what/which,” introducing the difficult question.]

It seems that the blessed Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking, either wished to exaggerate [Col. 1053D] the evil of fornication above all other sins—which, although committed through the body, do not bind and subject the human mind to carnal desire in the same way—or else, in the solitary act of bodily fornication, the immense force of lust mingles the mind with the body itself, fastening and binding it to the body in a certain sense.

At that moment and in the experience of so great a disgrace, a person is permitted to think of or attend to nothing else except what takes possession of the mind and subjects it as a captive—the submersion and, as it were, absorption of lust and carnal desire—so that this seems to be the meaning of the statement: “But the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” For then the heart of the fornicator becomes, [Col. 1054A] in a special and intimate way, the body’s slave, especially during the very moment of that most wicked act. [Note: The printed *servum*, “slave,” is accusative; the variant *servus* is nominative.]

The Apostle, wishing to emphasize more forcefully that this evil must be avoided, says: “Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” And, cursing and detesting the thought, he answers: “By no means!” He continues: “Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute is one body with her? For the two, he says, will be one flesh.”

Could this be said of the various other crimes of human beings? In all the other kinds of wickedness, the human mind is free both to perform one particular act and, at that very time, to wander elsewhere in thought. But during the actual act and moment of fornication, the mind is not free to think of anything else.

Thus [Col. 1054B] the whole person is absorbed by and in the body itself, so that it can no longer be said that the mind belongs to itself. Rather, the whole person may be said to be flesh, “a spirit that goes away and does not return.”

Thus we can understand the statement: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” As I said, the Apostle seems to have wished to exaggerate the evil of fornication to such an extent that, in comparison with this fornication, he judged all other sins to be outside the body, even though they are carried out through the body. He said that only in this evil of fornication does a person sin against his own body, because the body’s pleasure, through a greater heat of lust than any other, holds a person as its slave and makes him captive.

Let this be said concerning the specific fornication of the body. But because fornication is condemned and named in the sacred writings [Col. 1054C] not only specifically but also generally, let us attempt, with God’s help, to say something probable about this as well.

General fornication is plainly revealed in the Psalm, where it says: “For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you.” Immediately afterward it adds how this general fornication can be avoided and escaped: “But for me, it is good to cling to God.” [Note: After *adjunxit*, “he added,” the source supplies *enim*, “for.”]

From this we can readily understand that general fornication of the human soul consists in one’s not clinging to God but clinging to the world. Hence the blessed apostle John says: “If anyone has loved the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” The apostle James says: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?”

[Col. 1054D] In brief, it has been defined that the one who has love of the world cannot possess love of God, and that the one who wishes to be a friend of the world is an enemy of God.

To this also belongs what the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will stand by the one and despise the other.” He concludes: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.”

This, then, is general fornication of the soul, as has been said: it contains absolutely everything by which one does not cling to God while clinging to the world. Thus we may also understand, according to this general fornication, what the Apostle says: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication [Col. 1055A] sins against his own body.”

For if the human soul does not fornicate by clinging to the world, but clings to God, then whatever other sins—entirely alien to carnal desire—a person may incur through the frailty of mortality, whether through ignorance, negligence, forgetfulness, or lack of understanding, this is what is meant by “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body.” No sin of bodily or temporal desire can be found in such a case; therefore any such sin is rightly said to be outside the body.

But if, by clinging to the world, a worldly person distances himself from God and fornicates away from God, he sins against his own body. For the [Col. 1055B] human mind is drawn and distracted by carnal sensation and understanding toward every temporal and carnal thing, serving the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

Thus, as far as I can see, without prejudice to the faith, the evil of both kinds of fornication—the specific and the universal—can be understood in this one passage of so great and eminent a Teacher, where he says: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.”

Either the Apostle has exaggerated the specific fornication by which a person is rightly understood to sin against his own body, because nowhere else is the whole person so devoted to the body’s pleasure and so ineffably—or inevitably—fastened to it; thus, in comparison with this great evil, the other sins appear to be outside the body, even when they are carried out through the body.

It is like [Col. 1055C] the force of a commanding lust found uniquely in fornication: it subjects a person to its condition and makes him the body’s own wretched slave [*servum*, “slave,” accusative; variant: *servus*, nominative], especially during the very moment of its most filthy operation, so that the human mind is free neither to think nor to attend to anything besides what it is doing in the body itself.

But if the Apostle also wished to signify general fornication, on account of which he seems to have said, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body,” then it should be received and understood in this way: whenever someone does not cling to God but has clung to the world, loving and desiring all temporal things, he is rightly said to sin against his own body. That is, he has become devoted and subjected to every carnal desire, like a person wholly [Col. 1055D] enslaved to the creature and alienated from the Creator through that pride which is the beginning of every sin. As it is written, the beginning of human pride is apostasy from God.

Anyone who is alien to this general evil of fornication, however, may incur some other sin as a still corruptible and mortal human being. This is understood to be “outside the body,” that is, outside and separate from the evil of every bodily and temporal desire, as has often been said.

Only through the evil of carnal and general desire does the soul fornicate entirely away from God. Bound and fastened to bodily and temporal desires and pleasures, it sins against its own body; serving this universal desire, it is bent toward [Col. 1056A] the world and alienated from God. This is what is meant by the statement: “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God.”

For this reason the blessed John warns us to avoid the evil of general fornication, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of worldly life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world will pass away, and its desire. But the one who does the will of God remains forever, just as he remains forever.”

This love of the world, which contains within itself the world’s universal desire, is general fornication. Through it the mind sins against its own body, because it continually serves all human bodily, visible, and temporal desires and pleasures, [Col. 1056B] having been abandoned and forsaken by the Creator of all things.

## CHAPTER 332. On the knowledge of God

Everything past no longer exists; everything future does not yet exist. Therefore everything past and future is absent. But with God nothing is absent. Therefore with God there is neither past nor future; everything is present with God. [Note: *deesse*, “to be absent,” has the variant *deest*, “is absent.”]

### On the threefold power

Everything that exists has one aspect by which it subsists, another by which it is distinguished, and another by which it is fitting or harmonious. Every creature, therefore, both exists in some manner and is very far removed from what is altogether nothing, and its parts are mutually harmonious.

Its cause must likewise be threefold: by which it exists, by which it is this particular thing, and by which it is harmonious with itself. We call God the cause of the creature, that is, its author. [Col. 1056C]

There must therefore be a Trinity, than which perfect reason can discover nothing more excellent, more intelligent, or more blessed. Consequently, when truth is sought, there can be no more than three kinds of questions: whether something exists at all; whether it is this or something else; and whether it should be approved or disapproved.

### On God and the creature

What is unchangeable is eternal, for it is always of the same kind. What is changeable, however, is subject to time, since it is not always of the same kind; and therefore it is rightly not called eternal. What changes does not remain; what does not remain is not eternal.

There is therefore a distinction between immortal and eternal: everything eternal is immortal, but not everything immortal can, with sufficient precision, be called eternal. For even if something always lives, nevertheless, if it undergoes change, it is not properly called eternal, because it is not always of the same kind. Yet it may rightly be called immortal, because it always lives. Sometimes, however, what is immortal is also called eternal. [Col. 1056D] [Note: *idque*, “and that,” has the variant *ideoque*, “and therefore.” In the next sentence *tamen*, “nevertheless,” has the variant *si*, “if.”]

But what both undergoes change and is said to live by the presence of a soul, when it is not itself a soul, cannot in any way be understood as immortal, and still less as eternal. For when something is properly called eternal, neither is anything past, as though it had passed away, nor anything future, as though it did not yet exist; rather, whatever is, simply is. [Note: The printed *in aeterno*, “in the eternal,” is corrected to *aeternum*, “eternal,” without *in*.]

### On the place of God; from the book *Eighty-Seven Questions*

[Col. 1057A]

God is not in any place. Whatever is in a place is contained by a place; whatever is contained by a place is a body. God is not a body; therefore he is not in any place.

Yet because he exists and is not in a place, all things are rather in him than he is anywhere; nevertheless, they are not in him in such a way that he himself is a place. [Bracketed interpolation: “as he himself is somewhere, yet thus in him”; the enclosed words seem redundant. EDIT.]

For place exists in space, which is occupied by the length, breadth, and height of a body; God is nothing of this kind. Therefore all things are in him, but he is not a place.

Nevertheless, the temple of God is improperly called God’s place—not because he is contained by it, but because he is present to it. Nothing is better understood by this than a pure soul.

## CHAPTER 333. On the providence of God; from the book *Eighty-Four Questions*

[Col. 1057B]

It can happen that, through an evil person, divine providence both punishes and assists. For the impiety of the Jews both brought Judas to ruin and became salvation for the nations.

Likewise, it can happen that, through a good person, divine providence both condemns and assists, as the Apostle says: “To some we are the aroma of life leading to life, but to others the aroma of death leading to death.”

But since every tribulation is either the punishment of the wicked or the training of the righteous—for the same tribulation both cuts down the chaff and separates the grain from the chaff, which is why it received the name “tribulation”—and since peace and freedom from worldly troubles both enrich the good and corrupt the wicked, divine providence regulates all these things according to the merits of souls.

Nevertheless, the good do not choose for themselves the ministry of tribulation, nor do the wicked love peace. Therefore even those through whom something is done that they themselves do not know receive not the reward of the justice that is referred to God, but the reward of their own ill will. Likewise, it is not imputed to good people if, while they wish to benefit someone, that person is harmed; rather, the reward of benevolence is assigned to their good intention.

So too the rest of creation is, according to the merits of rational souls, either perceived or hidden, moderate [troublesome], or beneficial.

Since the supreme God administers well everything he has made, there is nothing disordered in the universe and nothing unjust, whether we know it or do not know it. [Col. 1057C] The sinful soul is offended in some particular part; nevertheless, because it is there according to its merits, where it is fitting for such a soul to be, and suffers what it is just for such a soul to suffer, the universal kingdom of God is not disfigured by any ugliness of its own.

Therefore, since we do not know everything that the divine order does well concerning us, we act according to the law only in our good will; in everything else we are acted upon according to the law. The law itself remains unchangeable and governs all changeable things with the most beautiful ordering. [Col. 1057D]

Glory, therefore, to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.

## CHAPTER 334. On what is written: “Found in appearance as a human being”; from the same book
We speak of *habitus* in many ways: either of the habit of the mind, as when the apprehension of some discipline is strengthened and firmly established through practice; or of the habit of the body, according to which we say that one person is more full-bodied and stronger than another—a condition more properly usually called *habitudo*; or of those things that are externally fitted to our limbs, according to which we speak of someone as clothed, shod, armed, and so forth.

In all these kinds, since this noun is derived from the verb *habere*, “to have,” it is clear that *habitus* is said of something that happens to someone in such a way that he can also not have it. For instruction happens to the mind; bodily substance and strength to the body; and clothing and weapons, there is no doubt, come upon our limbs. Thus a mind can be uninstructed if instruction does not come to it; a body thin and languid, without the substance of its inward parts and strength; a person naked without clothing; unarmed without weapons; and barefoot without footwear. *Habitus*, therefore, is said of something that comes to us [*accidit*] so that it may be possessed.

Nevertheless, there is this distinction: some things that happen to us so as to produce a *habitus* are not changed by us, but themselves change us, while remaining intact and unshaken in themselves—as wisdom, when it comes to a person, is not itself changed but changes the person, making him wise instead of foolish.

Other things happen in such a way that they both change and are changed, as food: it loses its own form and is changed into our body, while we, nourished by food, are changed from thinness and weakness into strength and vigor.

There is a third kind, when the things themselves that happen to us are changed in order to produce a *habitus*, and are in a certain manner formed by those to whom they produce the *habitus*, as with clothing. For when a garment has been cast aside or put away, it does not have the form it assumes when it is put on and fitted to the limbs. Once clothed, therefore, it receives a form that it did not have when it was removed, while the limbs themselves remain in their own condition both when they are clothed and when they are unclothed.

There may also be a fourth kind, when the things that happen in order to produce a *habitus* neither change those to whom they happen nor are themselves changed by them, as with a ring on a finger, if one does not examine the matter too subtly. Yet this kind is either nonexistent, if one investigates carefully, or altogether extremely rare.

When, therefore, the Apostle was speaking of the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as concerns his divinity, according to which he is true God, he said that he was equal to the Father. It was not for him an act of robbery—that is, an attempt to seize something alien—if, while always remaining in that equality, he did not wish to be clothed in man and appear to human beings as a man. Rather, “he emptied himself,” not changing his own form but taking the form of a servant; neither converted nor transformed into a man, with his unchangeable stability lost, but by taking up a true man, so that he himself, the one who received him, was made in the likeness [*similitudinem*] of men—not for himself, but for those to whom he appeared in man—“found in appearance as a man,” that is, found as a man by having man.

For God could not be found as man by those who had an unclean heart and could not see the Word with the Father, unless he assumed what they could see and through which they might be led to that inner light. This *habitus*, however, is not of the first kind: for the human nature, remaining in itself, did not change the nature of God. Nor is it of the second: man did not change God, nor was he changed by him. Nor is it of the fourth: man was not assumed in such a way that he neither changed God nor was changed by him. Rather, it belongs to the third kind, for he was assumed in such a way that he was changed [into something better, and formed by him] ineffably, and in a manner more exalted and more closely joined than clothing is when it is put on by a man.

By this term, therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he had said, “made in the likeness [*similitudinem*] of men”: not by transformation into a man, but by *habitus* he was made [found], when he was clothed with man, uniting and in a certain manner conforming him to himself, so that he might associate him with immortality and eternity.

The Greeks call that *habitus* which consists in the acquisition of wisdom and discipline **ἕξις** (*hexis*); but the kind according to which we speak of someone as clothed or armed they call rather **σχῆμα** (*schēma*). From this it is understood that the Apostle spoke of this kind of *habitus*, since the Greek copies read **σχήματι** (*schēmati*), which we have in Latin as *habitu*.

By this term it ought to be understood that the Word was not changed by the assumption of man, just as the limbs are not changed when clothed by a garment, although that assumption united the one assumed ineffably to the one who assumed him. But insofar as human words can be fitted to ineffable realities, so that God may not be understood as changed when he assumes human weakness, it was chosen that this assumption should be called **σχῆμα** in Greek and *habitus* in Latin.

## Chapter 335. On nourishment, from the same book

What is it that receives the thing that it changes, as an animal receives food? What is it that is received and changed, as food itself is? What is it that is received and not changed, as light is received by the eyes and sound by the ears? But the soul receives these through the body.

What, then, is received by the soul through itself and changed into itself, as another soul, which it makes like itself by receiving it into friendship? And what is received through itself and not changed, as truth?

Therefore it must be understood both what was said to Peter, “Kill and eat,” and what is said in the Gospel, “And the life was the light of men.”

## Chapter 336. On the statement, “It repents me that I made man,” from the same book

Holy Scripture, raising us from an earthly and human sense to a divine and heavenly one, descended even to those expressions used among themselves by the custom of the most foolish people. Thus the men through whom the Holy Spirit spoke did not hesitate to place most appropriately in their books even the names of those emotions that our mind experiences—emotions which anyone who understands more wisely already knows to be most distant from God.

For example, since it is exceedingly difficult for a human being to exact something without anger, they judged that God’s vengeance, which is altogether without such disturbance, should nevertheless be called “anger.” Likewise, because men are accustomed to guard the chastity of marriage through jealous concern, they called that providence of God by which it is commanded and brought about that the soul not be corrupted, and not, as it were, prostitute itself by following other gods, the “jealousy of God.”

So also the hand of God means the power by which he acts; the feet of God, the power by which he extends himself to preserve and govern all things; the ears or eyes of God, the power by which he perceives and understands all things; the face of God, the power by which he manifests and makes himself known; and so forth.

This is so because we, to whom the speech is addressed, ordinarily work with our hands, walk with our feet, reach wherever the mind directs, perceive bodily things with our ears, eyes, and other bodily senses, and become known through the face—together with anything else that belongs to this sort of rule.

In the same way, then, because we ordinarily do not undertake to change something begun and transfer it into something else except through repentance, although divine providence appears, to those who contemplate it with a serene mind, to administer [to be administering] all things in the most certain order, nevertheless, in a manner most suited to humble human understanding, those things that begin to exist and do not continue as long as they were expected to continue are said to have been taken away, as though through [God’s] repentance.

## Chapter 337. On the statement, “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines”

The number ten can signify the knowledge of the whole. If this is referred to inward and intelligible things, which are signified by the number six [is signified by the number six], it becomes as though ten times six, which is sixty. If it is referred to earthly and corruptible things, which can be signified by the number eighty, there are ten times eight, which is eighty.

The queens, therefore, are souls reigning over intelligible and spiritual things; the concubines are those who receive the reward of earthly things. Of these it is said, “They have received their reward,” while the maidens have no number, that is, no determinate knowledge, and can be endangered by various doctrines, so that the number mentioned may signify a certain and indisputable confirmation of knowledge.

### On eternal times

It may be asked how the Apostle Paul could have said, “before eternal times.” For if they are times, how are they eternal? Unless perhaps he meant “before all times.” For if he had said “before times” and had not added “eternal,” it could be understood as meaning before certain times that themselves had other times preceding them. But he preferred to say “eternal” rather than “all,” perhaps because time did not begin from time.

Or did he signify the age by “eternal times”? The difference between that and time is that the former is stable, whereas time is changeable.

## Chapter 338. On man made in the image and likeness of God, from the same book

Since Holy Scripture mentions an inner and an outer man, and distinguishes them so clearly that the Apostle said, “Even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet the inner man is renewed day by day,” it may be asked whether one of these was made in the image and likeness of God. For it would be foolish to ask, “Which one of these?” Who, after all, doubts that one should rather speak of the one who is renewed than of the one who is corrupted?

But whether both were made so is a major question. For if the outer man is Adam and the inner man is Christ, both are well understood. Yet since Adam, although he was made good by God, did not remain so, but by loving carnal things became carnal, it may not absurdly appear that this very condition consisted in his lacking the image of God and losing the likeness, and that therefore he himself is renewed and is also the inner man.

How, then, is he the outer man? Is it according to the body, so that the inner man is according to the soul, and the inner man is the resurrection and renewal that now takes place through the death of the former life—that is, sin—and through the regeneration of the new life—that is, righteousness? Scripture likewise calls these two men one old, whom we ought to strip off, and the other new, whom it reminds us must be put on.

Again, it calls the former the image of the earthly man, because he is borne according to the sin of the first man, who is Adam; and the other the image of the heavenly man, because he is borne according to the righteousness of the second man, who is Christ.

The outer man, who is now being corrupted, will be renewed in the future resurrection, when he has paid the debt of this death that he owes to nature under that law which was given in paradise through a commandment.

But how it is not inappropriate to say that the body too was made in the likeness of God is easily understood by anyone who carefully attends to the statement, “And God made all things very good.” No one doubts that he himself is supremely good in the first place.

Things can be said to be like God in many ways: some according to virtue and wisdom, because in him there is virtue and wisdom not feigned [not made]; others insofar as they merely live, because he supremely and primarily lives; others insofar as they exist, because he supremely and primarily is.

Therefore things that merely exist, yet neither live nor possess wisdom, are not perfect but have only a slight likeness to him, because they too are good in their proper order, while he is good above all, from whom they are good. But all things that live and do not possess wisdom participate somewhat more in his likeness. For whatever lives also exists, but not everything that exists also lives.

Those, moreover, that possess wisdom are so close to that likeness that among creatures nothing is nearer. For that which participates in wisdom both lives and exists; but whatever lives must exist, whereas it need not possess wisdom.

Since, therefore, man can participate in wisdom according to the inner man, in that respect he is made in the image [of God], so that no intervening nature forms him; and therefore nothing is more closely joined to God. For he possesses wisdom, lives, and exists; and there is no creature better than this.

But if the outer man is understood as that life by which we sense through the body, by means of the five most familiar senses that we share with animals—for even this life can be assailed by troublesome and perceptible persecutions and corrupted—it is not without reason that this man too is said to participate in the likeness of God, not merely because he lives, which is also evident in beasts, but even more because he turns toward the mind that governs him and which wisdom illumines—something impossible in beasts, which lack reason.

The human body also, since among the bodies of earthly animals it alone is not stretched prone and prostrate upon its belly, but, though visible, is raised upright for contemplating the heavens, which are the beginning of visible things, may rightly be considered more than the other bodies of animals to have been made in the image and likeness of God. This is so although it is recognized as living not by itself but through the presence of the soul. For it is good not only because it exists and insofar as it exists, but also because it is such that it is suited for contemplating the heavens.

Nevertheless, since a human being is not properly called such without life, perhaps the outer man is more correctly understood as both the body together with the life that exists in bodily sensation, rather than as the body alone or that life alone.

Nor is it unintelligently distinguished that one thing is the image and likeness of God—who is also called the Son—and another is made according to the image and likeness of God, as we understand man to have been made.

There are also those who understand, not without reason, that two things are indicated by the words “image” and “likeness,” since, if there were only one reality, they argue that one name would have been sufficient. They wish the mind to have been made according to the image, since it is formed by truth itself without any intervening substance. The mind is also called “spirit”—not the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, but the spirit of man.

For the Apostle distinguishes them in this way: “No one knows what is taking place in a man except the spirit of man; and no one knows what is taking place in God except the Spirit of God.” Again, concerning the human spirit he says, “He will save your spirit, soul, and body.” This spirit too was made by God, like the rest of creation.

For it is written in Proverbs: “Know in this way that the Lord knows the hearts of all, and that he himself knows everything who formed the spirit of all.” Therefore this spirit is understood, without any doubt, to have been made according to the image of God; in it there is an understanding of truth, for it clings to truth without any intervening creature.

They wish the rest of man to have been made according to the likeness, because every image is indeed similar, but not everything that is similar is properly an image—although it may perhaps be called one by an abuse of language.

In such matters, however, we must beware of thinking that anything should be asserted too dogmatically. This point must certainly be safeguarded: since every body is extended through spatial dimensions, no one should believe that anything of this kind is the substance of God. For a thing that is smaller in part than in its entirety is not compatible with the dignity of the soul—how much less with the majesty of God!

## Chapter 339. On the statement in the Gospel, “In one house two will be divided against three, and three against two.” From the exposition of Psalm 44

“Gird your sword around your thigh, O most mighty.”

Your sword—what is it but your word? With that sword he struck down enemies; with that sword he divided son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law.

We read these things in the Gospel: “I have not come to send peace, but a sword”; and, “There will be five in one house against two, and two against three, and three against two will be divided”—that is, son against his father, daughter against her mother, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.

Christ brought about this division by that sword. And truly, brothers, we see this even in daily examples. A young man wishes to serve God, but his father is displeased; they are divided against each other. The one promises an earthly inheritance, while the other loves a heavenly one; the former promises one thing, the latter chooses another. Let the father not think that an injury has been done to him: God alone has been preferred to him. Yet he quarrels with his son who wishes to serve God. But that spiritual sword, which separates, is stronger than carnal nature, which unites.

This also happens with a daughter against her mother, and much more with a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. For sometimes a daughter-in-law and mother-in-law are found in one house, one heretical and the other Catholic [heretical and Catholic]; and where this sword is received with strength, we do not fear rebaptism. A daughter could be divided against her mother, and a daughter-in-law cannot be divided against her mother-in-law?

This also took place generally in the human race: the son was divided against the father, for we were once sons of the devil. It was said to unbelievers, “You are from your father the devil.” Whence came all our unbelief, if not from the father, the devil? Not because he created us, but because we imitated him.

Now you see the son divided against the father. That sword came; he renounces the devil, finds another father, and finds another mother. The former, offering himself for imitation, begot him for destruction; the two parents whom we have found beget us for earthly life.

The son was divided against the father, and the daughter was divided against her mother. That people from among the Jews who believed was divided against the Synagogue. The daughter-in-law too was divided against her mother-in-law: the people coming from the Gentiles is called the daughter-in-law because Christ is the bridegroom and the Son of the Synagogue.

For from where was the Son of God born according to the flesh? From that Synagogue. He who left father and mother and clung to his wife so that the two might be one flesh—this is attested not by our conjecture but by the Apostle, who says, “This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church.”

In a certain sense he left the Father—not that he left him altogether, as though by separation, but for the assumption of human flesh. How did he leave him? Because, “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

How did he leave his mother as well? The Jewish people, that Synagogue clinging to its ancient sacraments. This too belongs to the same figure, where he says, “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” For he was teaching within, while they were standing outside. See whether the Jews are not still in this condition: Christ teaches in the Church, while they stand outside.

What, then, is the mother-in-law? The mother of the bridegroom. The mother of the bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, is the Synagogue. Therefore his daughter-in-law is the Church, which, coming from the Gentiles, did not consent to carnal circumcision and was divided against its mother-in-law.

## Chapter 340. On Pharaoh’s magicians and why they performed certain miracles, like Moses the servant of God. From the book of Questions

We should not be disturbed when miracles are often performed through magical arts that resemble the miracles performed through the holy servants of God, as it is written in Exodus that Pharaoh’s magicians performed certain things similarly to what Moses did.

We should not, therefore, be amazed at this, because everything that is visibly done can also, not unreasonably, be believed capable of being done through the lower powers of this air. But the difference is that, when the saints do such things in the name of God, God commands the lower creature through the higher ranks of the whole order of things.

When evil people perform similar things through evil arts, they are handed over to their own devices when they are heard by demons. They are worthy to be deceived by such an answer, so that what they appear to obtain as a benefit becomes a punishment for them, when the lower powers privately display certain miracles to them in order to keep them under their control. Yet this occurs by permission of divine providence, so that each person receives what is appropriate to the merits of his soul.

Every soul exercises authority partly over a certain private domain of its own and is partly restrained and governed by the laws of the whole, as by public laws. Since, therefore, every visible thing in this world has an angelic power appointed over it, as Holy Scripture testifies in several places, that power acts concerning the thing over which it has been placed [as though by private right], while in another respect it is compelled to act publicly.

For the whole is more powerful than the part, since even what it does privately there is permitted to do only to the extent allowed by the law of the whole.

A soul is more purified in piety the less it delights in what is private to itself and the more it contemplates the law of the whole, obeying it devotedly and willingly. For the law of the whole is divine wisdom.

But the more a soul rejoices in what is private to itself, and, neglecting God—who presides usefully and salubriously over all souls—wishes to be a god to itself or to others insofar as it can, cherishing its own power over itself or others rather than God’s power over all, the more filthy it becomes and the more it is compelled, as a punishment, to serve the divine laws as public laws.

Therefore, the more the human soul, having abandoned God, delights in its own honors or power, the more it is subjected to powers of the kind that rejoice in what is private to themselves and desire to be honored by human beings as gods. By divine law they are often granted permission to provide even something in the way of miracles to those whom they have subjected to themselves according to their merits, exercising that private right in those matters over which they have been appointed at the lowest, though nevertheless most orderly, level of the powers.

But when the divine law, as a public law, commands, it certainly overcomes private license, although that private license itself would not exist without the permission of universal divine power.
