Therefore it happens that the holy servants of God, when it is useful for them to possess this gift, command the lower powers according to the public and, in a certain sense, imperial law—that is, according to the power of the supreme God—to perform certain visible miracles. For in them God himself commands, he whose temple they are and whom, having despised their private power, they love with the utmost ardor.

In magical acts of obtaining things, however, the powers produce an effect, to entice and deceive those to whom they grant such things, so that they may subject them to themselves. They do this through the prayers and rites of the magicians, by a private right granting what they are permitted to grant to those who honor them, serve them, and preserve certain agreements made with them in their sacraments.

And when magicians appear to command, they frighten lower powers through the names of higher ones, and display certain visible things which, because of the weakness of the flesh, seem great to people unable to contemplate eternal things—things which the true God himself grants to those who love him.

God permits all this while justly governing everything, so that according to their desires and choices he distributes their forms of servitude and freedom.

And if at some time, through an invocation of the supreme God, they obtain something for their evil desires, whence that [their] grace is called not grace—for the Apostle does not say without reason, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts.” For in some people, the ease with which their sins are perpetrated is the punishment for the preceding sins of others.

When the Lord says, “Satan cannot cast out Satan,” lest anyone, using the names of certain lower powers and having cast out a demon, should think the Lord’s statement false, he should understand that it was said because in this way Satan also spares the body, or the bodily senses, so that he may dominate the will of that very person with a greater triumph through the error of impiety.

In this way Satan does not go out but rather enters into the innermost parts, so that he may work in the person as the Apostle says: “According to the prince of the power of this air, who now works in the children of unbelief.”

He did not disturb or torture their bodily senses, nor batter their bodies; rather, he reigned in their will—or rather, in their desire.

When the Lord says that false prophets will perform many signs and wonders, so that, if possible, they may deceive even the elect, he certainly warns us to understand that even wicked people can perform certain miracles—*quali* [*qualibus*] *sanctificare non possunt* (“they cannot sanctify”: an evidently corrupt construction, and therefore uncertain); the Benedictine edition reads, “such as the saints cannot perform”—and yet for that reason they are not to be considered more highly placed before God.

The magicians of Egypt were not more acceptable to God than the people of Israel merely because that people could not do what they did, although Moses, through the power of God, could do greater things.

But such gifts are not granted to all saints lest the weak be deceived by a most destructive error, thinking that greater gifts consist in such deeds than in works of righteousness, by which eternal life is obtained.

For this reason the Lord forbids the disciples to rejoice in such things when he says, “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice because your names are written in heaven.”

When magicians therefore perform things of the kind that saints sometimes perform, these things do indeed appear visibly to be the same, but they are done with a different purpose and under a different right. The magicians act while seeking their own glory; the saints act while seeking the glory of God. The magicians act through certain powers granted permissions in their own order, as through private transactions or benefits; the saints act through a public administration, at the command of him to whom every creature is subject.

A possessor is compelled to give a horse to a soldier in one way, but hands it over to a purchaser in another, or gives it or lends it to anyone else.

And just as many wicked soldiers, whom imperial discipline condemns, frighten certain possessors with the standards of their emperor and extort from them something that has not been publicly commanded, so sometimes wicked Christians, or schismatics, or heretics, through the name of Christ, or through Christian words or sacraments, exact something from powers that have been commanded to yield to the honor of Christ.

When such powers yield at the command of wicked people, they yield in order to lead human beings astray, whose error delights them.

Accordingly, magicians perform miracles in one way, good Christians in another, and wicked Christians in yet another: magicians through private contracts; good Christians through public justice; wicked Christians through the signs of public justice.

Nor is it surprising that these signs have power when they are used by such people. Even when they are usurped by outsiders who have not at all enrolled their name in this service, they have power because of the honor of the most excellent emperor.

Among these was the man about whom the disciples reported to the Lord that he was casting out demons in his name, although he did not follow along with them.

When such powers do not yield to these signs, God himself secretly prevents it when he judges that this is just and useful. For no spirits dare in any way to despise these signs. They tremble whenever they see them, but, unknown to human beings, something else is divinely commanded:

either so that the wicked may be confounded when they ought to be confounded, as we read concerning the sons of Sceva in the Acts of the Apostles, to whom the unclean spirit said, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize; but who are you?”;

or so that the good may be admonished to advance in faith and may be able to do such things not boastfully but beneficially;

or so that the gifts of the members of the Church may be distinguished, as the Apostle says: “Are all powers? Do all possess the gift of healing?”

For these reasons, therefore, as has been said, it is often divinely commanded, unknown to human beings, that when these signs are applied such powers should not obey the will of men.

But so that the wicked may often harm the good temporarily, they receive power over them for the greater benefit of the good, namely, for the exercise of patience.

Therefore the [Christian] soul should always remain watchful amid its tribulations, following the will of its Lord, lest by resisting God’s ordering it acquire for itself a heavier judgment.

For what the Lord himself, acting as a man, said to Pontius Pilate, he could also have said to Job concerning the devil: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.”

It is not, therefore, the will of the one whose malice grants power over the good, but the will of the one from whom this power is granted, that ought to be most precious to us. For “tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

## Chapter 341. Against the mathematicians [astrologers], from the same book

The ancients did not call those people astrologers who are called so now, but those who investigated the numbers of times through the motion of the heavens and the stars. Of them it is most rightly said in Holy Scripture: “Again, these too ought not to be forgiven. For if they know [will be able to know] so much as to estimate the age, how did they not more readily find its Lord?”

For the human mind, judging from visible things, can recognize that it is itself better than all visible things. Yet when it also acknowledges, because of its deficiency and progress in wisdom, that it is changeable, it finds [found] above itself unchangeable truth. Clinging to it, as it is said, “My soul clung after you,” it becomes blessed, finding inwardly even the Creator and Lord of all visible things. It does not seek visible things externally, even heavenly things—things that either are not found or are found in vain with great labor—unless, from the beauty of things that are outside, it discovers the craftsman who is within, who first works superior beauties in the soul and then inferior beauties in the body.

Against those who are now called astrologers, who wish to subject our actions to heavenly bodies and sell us to the stars, while taking from us the very price for which we are sold, nothing shorter or truer can be said than that they cannot give an answer except after receiving horoscopes.

In horoscopes, however, they mark divisions such as they say the zodiacal circle has—three hundred and sixty of them. They say that the motion of the heavens proceeds through fifteen divisions in one hour, so that fifteen divisions rise in the length of time occupied by one hour. They say that each of these divisions contains sixty minutes. But the minutes of minutes they do not find in the horoscopes by which they claim to foretell the future.

The conception of twins, however, since it occurs through one act of intercourse, as the physicians testify—whose discipline is much more certain and evident—takes place within so small a point of time that it does not extend to two minutes of minutes.

Whence, then, such great diversity in the actions, events, and wills of twins, who must have the same horoscope of conception, and to an astrologer are given one horoscope for both, as though for a single person?

If they wish to rely upon horoscopes at birth, they are refuted by the twins themselves, who are often delivered from the womb one after the other in such a way that the interval of time again comes down to minutes of minutes—minutes which they never accept as something to be dealt with in their horoscopes and cannot deal with.

When it is said that they have predicted many true things, this happens because people do not retain in memory their falsities and errors. Attending only to what has occurred according to their answers, they forget what has not occurred, and they remember what comes about not through that nonexistent art but through some obscure chance of events.

If they wish to attribute this to their skill, let them say that they can skillfully divine even from written sheets of parchment, from which a lot often emerges according to the will of chance. If a verse predicting the future often emerges by chance from books, not through an art, what wonder is it if some prediction of future things emerges from the soul of someone speaking, not by art [but by chance]?

## Chapter 342. On the Word

“In the beginning was the Word,” which in Greek is called **Λόγος** (*Logos*). In Latin it signifies both *Reason* and *Word*. But in this passage we interpret it better as “Word,” so that it may signify not only a relation to the Father but also the operative power by which things were made through the Word.

“Reason,” however, is rightly called reason even if nothing is done through it.

### On the statement, “Without him nothing was made,” and on the two prepositions *de* and *ex*. From the book *On the Nature of the Good*.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing—that is, nothing was made without him.

For we must not listen to the ravings of those who think that, in this passage, “nothing” is to be understood as “something,” and who suppose that someone can be compelled to adopt such an absurdity because the word “nothing” has been placed at the end of the sentence. “Therefore,” they say, “it was made; and consequently, because it was made, this ‘nothing’ is something.” They have lost their senses through their eagerness to contradict, and do not understand that it makes no difference whether one says, “Without him was made nothing,” or, “Without him nothing was made”; for even if the words were arranged in the latter order, “Without him nothing was made,” they could still say that this “nothing” is something, because it was made.

For when something truly is something, what difference does it make whether one says, “Without him the house was made,” or, “Without him the house was made,” provided that one understands that something was made without him—namely, the thing that is a house? Thus, since it is said, “Without him nothing was made,” and since “nothing” is certainly not something, whenever the expression is used in its true and proper sense—whether one says, “Without him was made nothing,” or, “Without him nothing was made,” or, “Nothing was made”—it makes no difference.

But who would wish to argue with people who can say of this very phrase, “It makes no difference”: “Therefore it makes some difference, because this ‘nothing’ is something”? Those whose brains are sound see plainly that, when I said “it makes no difference,” the same thing is understood as would be understood if I said, “Nothing makes a difference.”

But if they ask someone, “What did you do?” and he replies that he did nothing, they will immediately slander him by saying: “Then you did something, because you did nothing; for this ‘nothing’ is something.”

The Lord himself also has this word at the end of a sentence, where he says: “And in secret I have spoken nothing.” Let them read that and be silent.

Since God made all things that he did not beget from himself but made through his Word—not from things that already existed, but from things that did not exist at all, that is, from nothing—the Apostle says: “Who calls things that are not as though they were.” More plainly, it is written in the Book of Maccabees: “I beseech you, my son, look upon heaven and earth and all that is in them; see and know that the Lord God did not make us from things that already existed.” And in the Psalm it is written: “He spoke, and they were made.” It is clear that he did not beget these things from himself, but made them by his Word and command.

Since he did not make them from himself, he made them from nothing; for there was nothing else from which he could make them. Of this the Apostle speaks most clearly: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.”

“From him” does not mean the same as “out of his substance.” What is “of him” may be said to be “from him”; but not everything that is “from him” is rightly said to be “of him.” Heaven and earth are from him, because he made them; but they are not of him, because they are not made from his substance.

For example, if a man begets a son and builds a house, both the son and the house are from him; but the son is of him, whereas the house is of earth and wood. This is because he is a man, who cannot also make something from nothing.

God, however, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, did not need any material that he himself had not made to assist his omnipotence.

When we hear that all things are from him, through him, and in him, we must understand all natures that exist naturally. For sins are not from him: they do not preserve nature but corrupt it. Holy Scripture testifies in many ways that sins arise from the will of those who sin, especially in the passage where the Apostle says:

“Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to the hardness of your heart and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.”

Yet, although all things that God created are in God, they do not defile him who sins. Of his wisdom it is said: “It reaches all things because of its purity, and nothing defiled enters into it.” For just as we must believe God to be incorruptible and unchangeable, so consequently we must also believe him incapable of being defiled.

## CHAPTER 343  
### On the Lord’s body after the resurrection, from the letter to Consentius, who had consulted him on the same matter

You ask whether the Lord’s body now has bones and blood, or the other features of flesh. What if you added: “And clothing as well?” Would that not enlarge the question? Why else, except that we can scarcely conceive without corruption those things that we know to be corruptible in the ordinary course of our present life, although certain examples of divine miracles have already been given from which we may infer greater things?

If the clothing of the Israelites could remain unworn for so many years in the desert; if the dead skin of their footwear could endure for so long without decay, God can everywhere preserve, for as long as he wishes, the incorruptible condition of any bodies whatsoever.

Accordingly, I believe that the Lord’s body is in heaven as it was on earth when he ascended into heaven. When the disciples doubted his resurrection and thought that what they saw was not a body but a spirit, he said to them, as we read in the Gospel:

“See my hands and my feet; touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have.”

Just as he was handled by their hands when he was on earth, so he was conveyed before their eyes when he went into heaven. There the angelic voice sounded: “He will come in the same manner as you see him going into heaven.”

Let faith be present, and no question will remain—unless perhaps one asks about blood. For when he said, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh,” he did not add “blood.” Therefore let us not inquire about what he did not add to mention, and, if you please, let the question be brought to an end briefly.

Perhaps, however, once blood has been introduced as an occasion for inquiry, a more troublesome investigator will press us and say: “If there is blood, why not also phlegm? Why not yellow bile and black bile, by which medical science also teaches that the nature of flesh is regulated by four humors?”

But whatever anyone adds, let him beware of adding corruption, lest he corrupt the soundness and purity of his faith. From the habitual course of things that they have experienced, human weakness measures divine works that it has not experienced, and thinks itself clever in its chatter when it says: “If there is flesh, there is blood; if there is blood, there are the other humors; therefore there is also corruption.”

By the same reasoning one might say: “If there is a flame, it burns; if it burns, it scorches; if it scorches, then the fire must also have burned the bodies of the three men whom the impious king cast into the furnace.”

But if anyone who understands divine works rightly does not doubt that a miracle occurred in the case of those three men, why should we not believe that the one who made those bodies was able to make that body incapable of being corrupted by fire—indeed, incapable of being corrupted by fire, hunger, disease, old age, or any other force by which corruption ordinarily weakens human bodies?

If someone says that incorruptibility was not added to the flesh of those three men against the fire, but that the power to corrupt was taken away from the fire itself, why should we fear that he could not make flesh incapable of being corrupted who made fire incapable of corrupting?

For if that event is understood not as a change in the flesh but as a change in the fire, it is much more marvelous: at the same time the fire did not burn the human bodies, because it was unable to harm them, and yet it burned the wood of the furnace, so that it was able to blaze.

Those who do not believe even these things distrust divine power excessively, and our present discussion is neither with them nor addressed to them. But those who believe these things should infer from them, in whatever way they can, the other things that they faithfully seek.

Divine power, then, which made fire incapable of corrupting, can remove from this visible and tangible nature of bodies whatever qualities it wishes, while allowing certain others to remain. Consequently, it can also establish mortal limbs in stable strength, while their bodily features remain but the corruption of mortality is extinguished: so that decay is absent, appearance remains, movement remains, weariness is absent; the ability to eat remains, the necessity of hunger is absent.

It is therefore certain, and in no way should it be doubted, that the body of Christ—which, although it did not experience the corruption of decay in the tomb, whence it is written, “You will not permit your holy one to see corruption,” could nevertheless be pierced by a spear—now exists wholly in incorruption.

What was sown in the dishonor of suffering and death is now in the glory of eternal life; what could be crucified in weakness now reigns in power; and what was an animal body, because it was taken from Adam, is now spiritual, because it has been inseparably joined to a spirit.

## CHAPTER 344  
### On the animal body and the spiritual body, addressed to the same Consentius

The Apostle said: “An animal body is sown; a spiritual body will rise.”

Therefore, just as an animal body is not a soul but a body, so we must not think that a spiritual body is a spirit rather than a body.

Who, moreover, would dare to suppose either that Christ’s body did not rise spiritual, or that, if it rose spiritual, it was no longer a body but a spirit? The disciples’ opinion refutes this, for when they saw him and thought that they were seeing a spirit, he said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have.”

That flesh was therefore already a spiritual body, yet it was not a Spirit but a body, no longer to be dissolved and separated from the soul by death. The animal body, likewise, when it was animated by God’s breath as man was made a living soul, would itself have become spiritual without the intervention of death, had transgression not inflicted upon it, through the sin previously committed, the punishment that God would have given as the crown of preserved righteousness.

Thus the Lord Christ came through us to us, finding us sinners though he was righteous, by means, so to speak, of the bed of our humility, but not with the disease of our iniquity. For he appeared to us through what is animal—that is, through a mortal body—although, if he had wished, he could have come at first with an immortal body.

But because it was necessary for us to be healed through the humility of the Son of God, he descended to the level of our weakness and displayed the merit and reward of our faith through the power of his resurrection. Therefore the Apostle continues and says: “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.”

This may be understood either as referring to the first Adam, who was formed from dust, and the last Adam, who was born of the Virgin; or as being fulfilled in every human being, so that the first Adam is the human being in a mortal body, while the last Adam is that same person in an immortal body.

Nevertheless, he wished there to be this difference between a living soul and a life-giving spirit: in the former there is an animal body, in the latter a spiritual body. For the soul does live in an animal body, but it does not give life to the extent of removing corruption.

In a spiritual body, however, because it adheres perfectly to the Lord and is one spirit with him, it gives life in such a way as to make the body spiritual, consuming all corruption and fearing no separation: “And we,” he says, “are changed.”

This change must without doubt be understood as a change for the better, because all will rise again, both the righteous and the unrighteous. But, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.” He calls judgment eternal punishment, as in another passage: “Whoever does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged.”

Therefore those who will rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruption which cannot suffer the corruption of pain. That belongs to the faithful and the saints. These, however, will be tormented by perpetual corruption, because “their fire will not be quenched, and their worm will not die.”

What, then, does this distinction mean: “The dead will rise incorruptible, and we will be changed,” except that all will rise incorruptible, but the righteous among them will also be changed into that incorruption which no corruption whatsoever could harm?

Accordingly, those who will not be changed into it will indeed rise incorruptible in the integrity of their limbs, but they will nevertheless be corrupted by the pain of punishments when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” From hearing this evil, the righteous person will not be afraid.

After saying, “We will be changed,” as though we were asking how this would happen or what sort of change it would be, he adds: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality.”

In my opinion, there is no need to doubt the meaning of the statement, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” because the corruption and mortality of flesh and blood will not be there. It is according to these qualities that he names flesh and blood in this passage.

Thus, to give an example that occurs to me for the moment, Scripture says: “Lest the tempter tempt you and our labor be in vain,” and here the devil is understood as the tempter, as though God did not tempt at all. Elsewhere Scripture says of him: “He himself tempts no one.” This statement is not contrary to the one that says: “The Lord your God is testing you.”

The question is resolved when we recognize that the word “temptation” has different meanings: one kind is the temptation of deception, another the temptation of testing. According to the former, the tempter is understood to be none other than the devil; according to the latter, God tests.

Likewise, when it is said both “Flesh will possess the kingdom of God” and “Flesh will not possess the kingdom of God,” the meaning of this term must be distinguished, and there will be no question. For flesh, understood according to its substance—as in the statement, “A spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have”—will possess the kingdom.

But flesh understood according to corruption will not possess it. This was explained when it was said, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” and immediately added: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption,” as, I think, we have discussed sufficiently.

## CHAPTER 345  
### Whether the features of bodies are formed individually by God the Creator, and concerning the question of the soul; from the same letter, or from two letters, to Optatus

As to your question whether the features of bodies are formed individually by God the Creator, it will not trouble you if, insofar as the human mind is able, you understand the power of divine activity.

For how could we deny that God is even now at work in all things that are created, when the Lord says: “My Father is working until now”?

Therefore, the cessation of the seventh day must be understood as applying to the creation of the natures themselves, not to the administration of those natures, which are said to have been created. Since, then, the nature of things is governed by the Creator, and all things are born according to their appointed orders, places, and times, God is working until now.

For if God does not now form these things, how is it written: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you”? How also can this be understood: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven,” unless perhaps we are to believe that the grass is clothed by God but bodies are not formed by God?

When he said, “He clothes,” he plainly indicated not a past arrangement but a present operation.

There is also the Apostle’s statement about seeds, which I mentioned above: “You do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, such as wheat or one of the others. But God gives it a body as he wills.”

He did not say “brings forth” or “arranged,” but “gives,” so that we may understand the Creator to apply the effectiveness of his wisdom to forming the things that arise daily at their appointed times. Of this wisdom it is said: “It reaches mightily from end to end.” He did not say “he arranged all things,” but “he arranges all things gently.”

It is a great matter even to have a slight understanding of how mutable and temporal things are formed not by mutable and temporal movements of the Creator, but by an eternal and stable power.

You also ask me whether that breath of God in Adam is itself the soul. I answer briefly: either the soul was made by that breath, or, if it is that breath itself, it too was made.

For God speaks of the soul through the prophet Isaiah, where he says: “I made every breath.” That he intends souls is sufficiently indicated by what follows: “Because of sin I grieved him a little”—that is, the breath itself—and the rest, which cannot be understood except of the human soul.

In this question we must be especially careful not to believe that the soul is not a nature made by God but God’s own substance, like the only-begotten Son, who is his Word, or some portion of God; as though that nature and substance by which God is could be changeable. Anyone who feels that he has a soul cannot fail to recognize that the soul is changeable.

As for the soul’s origin, by which it comes to be in the body—whether it derives from that one soul which was first created when man was made a living soul, or whether individual souls are likewise made individually—I did not know then, and I still do not know.

A person should not be ashamed to confess that he does not know what he does not know, lest, while pretending to know, he never become worthy to know.

Who, moreover, denies that God is the creator and maker not merely of one soul but of every soul, except someone who most openly resists his words? For without any ambiguity he says through the prophet: “I made every breath,” evidently wishing souls to be understood, as the words that follow make clear: “He did not make only the one breath that he breathed into the first man whom he formed from the earth; he made every breath, and he is still making them.”

Nevertheless, the question remains whether he makes every breath from that one breath, just as he makes every human body from that one body, or whether he makes new bodies from one body but new souls from nothing.

For who makes the kinds of things corresponding to their origins even from seeds, except the one who made the seeds themselves without seeds?

But when a matter that is obscure by nature exceeds our limited capacity, and clear divine Scripture does not come to our aid, human conjecture presumptuously attempts to define something. According to the lives that they begin to possess as their own, we say that new human beings are born, whether in soul or in body. But according to original sin, they are born old; for this reason they are renewed through baptism.

I have not yet discovered anything certain in the canonical Scriptures about the origin of the soul.

Those who assert that souls are newly made without any propagation place among the testimonies by which they try to establish their position the two passages I mentioned shortly before: “Who forms the spirit of man within him,” and “Who formed their hearts one by one.”

You see how those who resist them can respond: it is uncertain whether, when he forms, he forms from something else or from nothing.

One testimony, however, seems especially important: the passage in Solomon’s book, Ecclesiastes: “And the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it.”

The easiest response is that the body returns to the earth from which the first human body was made, and the spirit returns to God by whom the first human soul was made.

For, they say, just as our body, although it was propagated from that first body, nevertheless returns to the place from which the first body itself was made, so our soul, although propagated from that soul, does not return to nothing, because it is immortal, but returns to the one by whom the first soul itself was made.

Accordingly, the statement that the spirit of each person returns to God who gave it does not resolve this exceedingly obscure question, because whether it comes from that one soul or from nothing else, God certainly gave it.

Likewise, those who defend the propagation of souls with thoughtless rashness think that, among the other testimonies they believe support their cause, none can be produced that is clearer or more explicit than what is written in Genesis: “All the souls that entered Egypt with Jacob, who came out from his thighs.”

By this apparently most evident testimony, they may believe that souls are propagated from parents into children, since it seems to be said plainly that souls themselves came out from Jacob’s thighs, not merely the bodies of his sons.

In the same way they wish to understand as a part standing for the whole what Adam said when his wife was shown to him: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” For he did not say, “and soul of my soul.”

But it may be that, when flesh is named, both are understood, just as here souls are named, while bodies in the sons are also intended.

Yet this testimony certainly does not suffice as a clear and manifest solution to the question—not even if it were read in the feminine gender, “who came out from his thighs,” so that we understood souls as those who came out. It would still not suffice, because it is shown by a certain manner of speech that the word “soul” alone can signify the body: what contains is signified by what is contained.

Thus someone says, “The wines crown,” when the wine vessels are crowned; for the wine is contained, while the vessel contains it.

In the same way, we call the basilica containing the people “the church,” although the people are properly called the Church. Thus, by the name “Church”—that is, the people who are contained—we signify the place that contains them.

Likewise, since souls are contained in bodies, the bodies of the sons may be understood through the souls that are named. In this way the statement in the Law that a person is defiled if he enters upon a dead soul—that is, upon the corpse of the deceased—is better understood: by “dead soul” the dead body that contained the soul is meant.

For even when the people, that is, the Church, are absent, the place is nevertheless still called a church.

This would be the response if, as I said, the feminine form had been used: “who came out from Jacob’s thighs,” that is, “the souls who came out.” But since the masculine form is used—“who came out from Jacob’s thighs”—who would not prefer to understand it as meaning: “all the souls of those who came out from his thighs,” that is, the souls of human beings?

Thus it may also be understood that, according to the body alone, the men came out from the thighs of their father, while the souls belonged to them; through the number of those souls, so many human beings are understood.

Therefore, if you can assert the newness of souls without any propagation in such a way that, by a sound argument not alien to the Catholic faith, they may nevertheless be shown to be subject to the sin of the first man, assert what you think as best you can.

But if you cannot make them alien to propagation in any other way than by making them free from every bond of sin at the same time, refrain entirely from such an argument. For the remission of sins in the baptism even of little children is not false; it is not said merely in words, but truly accomplished.

But so that your affection may also hear from me some definite conclusion on this question: whatever the origin of souls may be—whether they are propagated from that one soul or from no other—the soul of the Mediator certainly did not draw any sin from Adam; this must not be doubted.

For if no soul is propagated from another, while all are held under the condition of propagated sinful flesh, how much less should we believe that a soul could come by propagation from a sinful soul, when his flesh came from a virgin, conceived not through lust but through faith, so that he might exist in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not in sinful flesh?

But if the other souls are held liable because of the sin of the first sinful soul, because they were propagated from it, then surely the soul that the Only-Begotten joined to himself either did not draw sin from it, or was not drawn from it at all.

For the one who took away our sins could not have been unable to draw a soul for himself without sin; nor could he who created a new soul for the flesh which he made from earth without a parent have been unable to create a new soul for the flesh which he took from a woman without a man.

For I confess that I still have not discovered how the soul draws sin from Adam. Hence it must not be doubted that the soul itself is not drawn from Adam; but this is something I must investigate more carefully than assert rashly.

When certain considerations rightly compel us to doubt about a question, we should not therefore also doubt whether we ought to doubt. For concerning doubtful matters we must doubt without hesitation.

You see how the Apostle does not hesitate to doubt concerning himself whether he was caught up into the third heaven in the body or outside the body: “Whether this or that,” he says, “I do not know; God knows.”

Since, then, as long as I do not know, I cannot say whether my soul came into this life by propagation or without propagation, although I do not doubt that in either case it was made by the supreme and true God, why should I not be permitted to say: “I know that my soul subsists through God’s work and is wholly God’s work; whether it came by propagation, as the body did, or outside propagation, as the soul given to the first man did, I do not know; God knows”?

Which of these two do you want me to confirm? I could do so if I knew.

If you yourself know, then you see that I am more eager to learn what I do not know than to teach what I do know. But if you do not know, as I do not, pray, as I do, that the Teacher who said to his disciples, “Do not wish to be called Rabbi by men, for one is your Teacher, Christ,” may teach us, whether through one of his servants or through himself—provided that he knows it is advantageous for us to know such things. For he knows not only what to teach but also what it is advantageous for us to learn.

I confess my desire to your affection: I do wish to know what you ask; but I would much more desire to know, if it were possible, when the one desired by all nations will appear and when the kingdom of the saints will come, than to know from where I began to come into this world.

Yet when his disciples, our Apostles, asked him who knows all things about that matter, they received the answer: “It is not yours to know the times that the Father has placed in his own power.”

What if he also knows that it is not ours to know this—since he certainly knows what it is useful for us to know?

I know from him that it is not ours to know the times that the Father has placed in his own power. But whether it is ours to know the origin of souls, which I do not yet know—that is, whether knowing it pertains to us—I do not even know.

For if I knew at least this, that it is not ours to know, I would not merely refrain from affirming it while I remain ignorant; I would also cease asking about it. But although it is so obscure and profound that I must guard more against the rashness of teaching than I possess eagerness to learn, I would nevertheless like to know it, if I could.

And although it is far more necessary to know what that holy man said—“Make known to me, Lord, my end”—for he did not say “my beginning”—I wish that, as far as this question is concerned, my beginning were nevertheless hidden from me.

Yet I am not ungrateful to my Teacher even concerning that beginning of mine. I know that the human soul is a spirit, not a body, and that it is rational or intellectual. I know that it is not God’s nature, but rather a creature that is mortal in some respect, insofar as it can be changed for the worse and alienated from the life of God, by participation in which it becomes blessed; and immortal in some respect, because it cannot lose the capacity of perception by which, after this life, it may fare well or ill.

I also know that the soul did not deserve to be enclosed in the flesh because of deeds committed before the flesh; but neither does that mean that it exists in a human being without the stain of sin, even if, as Scripture says, his life on earth were only one day.

Accordingly, I know that no one is born from Adam through the succession of generation without sin; therefore even little children must be born again through the grace of regeneration in Christ.

These many and substantial things concerning the beginning or origin of our souls—in which there are many matters belonging to that knowledge that are established by faith—I rejoice that I have learned and affirm that I know.

Therefore, if I do not know whether, in the origin of souls, God makes them for human beings by propagation, although I do not doubt that he makes them, I choose to know this rather than not know it. But as long as I cannot do so, I prefer to doubt about it rather than rashly confirm as certain something that might be contrary to a matter about which I perhaps ought not to doubt.

You, then, my good brother, since you consult me and wish me to define one of these alternatives—whether the other souls are made individually by the Creator from that one man, by propagation as bodies are, or without propagation, as the soul of that one man was—I ask you to allow me also to ask how the soul of sinners draws sin originally from the source from which it itself is not drawn originally.

For we likewise do not deny that all souls draw original sin from Adam, lest we rush, in detestable fashion, into the detestable heresy of Pelagius.

If you do not know the answer to what I ask, patiently allow us both to remain ignorant of what you ask and of what I ask. But if you already know the answer to my question, then, once you have taught me this also, I will answer what you wish me to answer, fearing nothing further on that point.

I therefore ask you not to be angry because I could not confirm what you ask. I was able to demonstrate what it is that you are asking; when you find the answer, do not hesitate to confirm what you were asking.

I thought that this should be written to your holiness, since you already regard the propagation of souls as something to be rejected, almost as though you were certain.

But if I had been writing in reply to those who assert it, I might perhaps have shown how they are ignorant of what they think they know, and how great a reason they have to fear asserting it.

## CHAPTER 346  
### That the baptized are delivered not from common death but from eternal punishment, from which he also says that the first human beings were delivered through the Lord’s blood; why David, after his sin was forgiven, fulfilled what God had threatened through the prophet; and concerning the mystery of the twenty-year number, or concerning the question of the soul stated above

From Book II *On the Baptism of Little Children*, near the end.

By no means, then, would the outstanding patience of one who undergoes or despises death for the sake of justice be praised, if death were not a great and exceedingly grievous affliction. Whoever conquers fear of it through faith wins great glory for faith itself and a just reward. Hence it is not astonishing both that bodily death would not have befallen humanity had sin not come first, and that such a punishment should follow sin; and, after the forgiveness of sins, that death should still befall the faithful, so that the strength of justice may be exercised in conquering its fear.

[Col. 1078A] For the flesh that was first made was not sinful flesh; in it humanity refused to preserve justice amid the delights of paradise. Therefore God decreed that, after its sin, the propagated sinful flesh should strive through labors and hardships to receive justice. For this reason Adam, having been expelled from paradise, dwelt opposite Eden—that is, opposite the seat of delights—to signify that sinful flesh, which had not preserved obedience amid delights before it became sinful flesh, was to be instructed through labors, which are contrary to delights.

Thus, just as those first human beings, afterward living justly—whereby they are rightly believed to have been freed through the Lord’s blood from the ultimate punishment—nevertheless did not in that life merit being restored to paradise, so sinful flesh, even if a person has lived justly in it after his sins have been forgiven, does not immediately merit escaping that death which it drew from the succession of sin.

[Col. 1078B] Something of this sort has been intimated to us concerning the patriarch David in the Book of Kings. When the prophet had been sent to him and, because of the sin he had committed, threatened him with evils that would befall him through God’s anger, David earned forgiveness by confessing his sin. The prophet replied that his disgrace and crime had been forgiven him; nevertheless, what God had threatened followed, so that he might be humbled by his son.

Why, then, is it not said here also: “If God had threatened this because of that sin, why, when the sin was forgiven, did he fulfill what he had threatened?” Unless the most correct answer is this: the forgiveness of that sin was granted so that sin might not prevent the man from attaining eternal life; but the fulfillment [effect] of the threat followed so that human piety might be exercised and tested in that humility. [Col. 1078C] Thus God both inflicted bodily death on humanity because of sin and, after the forgiveness of sins, did not remove it, in order to exercise justice.

Let us therefore hold fast the unwavering confession of faith. There is one, and only one, who was born without sin, in the likeness of sinful flesh; who lived without sin in the flesh, amid the sins of others; and who died without sin, because of our sins. Let us not turn aside either to the right or to the left. To turn aside to the right is to deceive oneself by saying that one is without sin; to turn aside to the left is, through some perverse and depraved security, to surrender oneself to sins as though with impunity.

For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right—he alone who is without sin and can erase our sins—but the ways that are on the left, with sins, are perverse. [Col. 1078D] Those young men of twenty years likewise prefigured the new people who entered the promised land; they are said to have turned aside neither to the right nor to the left.

The age of twenty, however, is not to be compared with the innocence of little children. Rather, unless I am mistaken, this number foreshadows and echoes some mystical meaning. The Old Testament excels in the five books of Moses, while the New Testament is preeminent through the authority of the four Gospels. Multiplied by one another, these numbers arrive at twenty: four times five, or five times four, is twenty.

Such a people, as I have said, instructed in the kingdom of heaven through the two Testaments, the Old and the New, will enter that land of promise, turning neither to the right through proud presumption of justice nor to the left through complacent [Col. 1079A] love of sin. There we shall no longer hope that sins will be forgiven us, nor fear that they will be punished in us. We have been freed by that Redeemer who, though not sold under sin, redeemed Israel from all his iniquities, whether committed in anyone’s individual life or inherited from origin.

For those who, even if they did not wish openly to express in their writings that little children need the forgiveness of sins, nevertheless confessed that redemption was necessary for them, did not yield little to the authority and truth of the divine Scriptures. For, using another word—one likewise drawn from Christian instruction—they said nothing else at all.

Nor should those who read, hear, and hold the divine writings faithfully doubt that from that flesh which first became [Col. 1079B] sinful flesh through the will of sin, and from which thereafter, through succession, the transmission of iniquity and death passed to all, sinful flesh was propagated—except for the one likeness of sinful flesh, which nevertheless would not exist unless sinful flesh existed.

As for the soul: whether it too was propagated in the same manner and is bound by guilt that must be forgiven—for we cannot say that only the flesh of a child, and not also the soul, needs the help of a Savior and Redeemer, or that it is excluded from the thanksgiving expressed in the Psalms, where we read and say, “Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his rewards, who is merciful to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption”—or whether, though not propagated, it nevertheless needs forgiveness of that sin and its own redemption simply because it is joined to sinful flesh and burdened [Col. 1079C] with it; with God, through his supreme foreknowledge, judging that those who have not yet been born, who have done nothing by their own lives, whether good or evil, do not merit release from this guilt;

[Col. 1079D] and how God, even if he does not create souls by transmission, is nevertheless not the author of that same guilt, on account of which the sacrament of redemption is necessary also for the soul of a child—this is a great question and calls for another discussion. Yet, in my judgment, it should be approached with this restraint: cautious inquiry should be praised rather than precipitous assertion condemned.

For when an exceedingly obscure matter is being discussed, without the certain and clear testimony of divine authorities to assist us, human presumption ought to restrain itself, doing nothing by inclining to either side. Even if I do not know how any of these alternatives can be demonstrated and explained, I nevertheless believe that, if humanity could not remain ignorant of this matter without loss of the promised salvation, the divine utterances would here too provide the clearest authority.

## CHAPTER 347  
### What the sins of the unwilling are; from the book *Questions on the Book of Numbers*

Since it is rightly asked how the sins that are committed unwillingly are to be expiated, it is also rightly asked what these sins of the unwilling are: whether they are those committed by people who are unaware, or whether something can properly be called the sin of an unwilling person when he is compelled to do it.

[Col. 1080A] For this too is commonly said to be done against one’s will. Yet the person certainly wills the reason for which he does it—for example, if someone does not wish to swear falsely but does so because he wishes to live, when someone threatens him with death unless he swears falsely. He therefore wishes to do it because he wishes to live. He does not desire to swear falsely for its own sake, but in order to live by swearing falsely.

[Col. 1080B] If this is so, I do not know whether such sins can be called the sins of the unwilling, of the sort that are said here to require expiation. For, if the matter is carefully considered, perhaps no one wishes to sin itself; rather, it is done for the sake of something else, which the sinner does will. All people who knowingly do what is not permitted would wish it to be permitted. To such an extent does no one desire sin for its own sake, but rather for the sake of what results from it.

If this is so, these are not the sins of the unwilling, except insofar as they are the sins of the unaware, which are distinguished from the sins of the willing.

## CHAPTER 348  
### On the statement, “Fathers shall not die for their sons,” and on the statement, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the sons”; from the book *Questions on Deuteronomy*

“Fathers shall not die for their sons, and sons shall not die for their fathers; each shall die in his own sin.” Here not only the prophets said this; the Law also says that each person is to be put to death for his own fault, not for that of his father or his son.

What, then, is meant by the statement elsewhere that God repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation? Is this understood of sons not yet born, on account of original sin, which the human race also drew from Adam? Here, however, the distinction concerns sons already born, so that each dies in his own sin.

[Col. 1080C] For one who was already born when his father sinned does not draw anything from his father [textual variant: “from the father”]. Moreover, since the passage also says, “to those who hate me,” it is clear that this condition too can be changed if the children do not imitate the deeds of their parents.

That other punishment, too, is repaid from Adam temporally, because all die on account of it; but it is not repaid eternally to those who have been spiritually regenerated by grace and have remained in that state to the end.

[Col. 1080D] Nevertheless, it may reasonably be asked: if the sins of the fathers are repaid upon the sons, upon those who hate God, why to the third and fourth generation—either with the first and second omitted, or without continuing into the remaining generations so long as impiety and imitation of evil parents persist? Or did he wish, through this number—since the number seven is understood—to signify universality? If so, why did he not rather use the number seven itself and say “to the seventh generation,” so that everyone would be understood, since in this way he would have indicated more clearly the reason for the perfection of this number?

For this number is said to be perfect because it consists of these two numbers: three, the first complete odd number, and four, the first complete even number. Hence I think that the prophetic statement repeatedly found—“For three transgressions and for four I will not turn away”—has the same meaning: it signifies all transgressions rather than merely three or four.

## CHAPTER 349  
### That, following the Lord’s example, temporal well-being is to be despised; and what resurrection is commended by the example of Job’s sons; also concerning Job’s endurance and the Lord’s faith; and that the veil of the Temple was not a wall, as some maintain. From the book *On the Grace of the New Testament*

[Col. 1081A] Humanity brought death upon itself and upon the Son of Man; but the Son of Man, by dying and rising again—an object of human reproach and the people’s rejection even unto death—brought life to humanity.

He wished to suffer this in the sight of his enemies, so that they might think him abandoned and thereby the grace of the New Testament might be commended. Through this grace we learn to seek another happiness, which is now possessed in faith but will later be possessed in appearance. For, as the Apostle says, “While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Therefore now we live in hope, but then in reality.

[Col. 1081B] Finally, he did not wish to reveal his resurrection—which, unlike ours, did not need to be postponed for a long time—in the example of his flesh so that we might learn what we ought to hope for in our own flesh, to strangers, but to his own people. I call them strangers not by nature but by vice, which is always contrary to nature.

He therefore died in the sight of human beings and rose again in the sight of the children of human beings, because death belonged to humanity, while resurrection belonged to the Son of Man. For just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ.

Accordingly, to exhort his faithful by the example of his flesh to despise temporal things for the sake of eternal happiness, he endured his persecutors and their savagery even unto death, while they arrogantly mocked him as defeated and crushed.

But when he raised his flesh and restored it to the sight and touch of his disciples, and ascended into heaven while they watched, he built them up and showed with the clearest truth what they ought to expect and what they ought to preach.

[Col. 1081C] Those from whom he had endured such evils even unto death, however, he left in the belief that they had conquered and destroyed him, boasting of this as though it were true. Thus anyone among them who wished to be saved with eternal salvation had to believe in the resurrection of that dead man, which those who had seen it proclaimed with signs as witnesses—and for whose proclamation they did not hesitate to endure similar sufferings.

Therefore James, one of his apostles, in his Epistle, when exhorting the faithful who remained in this life after Christ’s passion and resurrection, distinguished the dispensation of the Old and New Testaments and said: “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end.”

[Col. 1081D] He did not say this so that they would patiently endure temporal evils in order to have restored to them what we read was restored to Job. Job was healed from that wound and putrefaction, and everything he had lost was restored to him twofold.

Here too the faith of the resurrection was commended. For his sons were not restored twofold, but the same number was given back, signifying that those whom he had lost would rise again. Thus they too, joined to the former sons, would not be found excluded from the restoration of the double portion.

Therefore, so that we would not hope for such a reward when we suffer temporal evils, James did not say, “You have heard of Job’s endurance and his end,” but, “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end.” It is as though he said: “Endure temporal evils as Job did; but for this endurance do not hope for temporal goods, which were restored to him in increased measure. Rather, hope for eternal goods, which preceded in the Lord.”

[Col. 1082A] Job, then, belonged to those fathers who cried out and were saved. When he says, “But I,” he sufficiently indicates what kind of salvation he wishes us to understand by their being saved: the salvation in which he himself was certainly forsaken. This does not mean that they were excluded from eternal salvation; rather, what was to be revealed in Christ was then hidden.

In the Old Testament there is a veil, which is removed when someone passes from it to Christ. When Christ was crucified, the veil of the Temple was also torn, signifying what the Apostle said concerning the veil of the Old Testament: that in Christ it is abolished.

## CHAPTER 350  
### What is to be loved; from the book *Eighty-Four Questions*

[Col. 1082B] Since whatever does not live does not fear, and no one would persuade us to be deprived of life so that we might also be free from fear, we ought to love living without fear. But since a life without fear, if it also lacks understanding, is not to be desired, we ought to love living without fear and with understanding.

Is that alone to be loved? Or is love itself also to be loved? Indeed it is, since without it the other things are not loved. But if love is loved for the sake of other things that ought to be loved, it is not rightly said to be loved. For to love is nothing other than to desire some thing for its own sake.

Should love, then, be desired for its own sake, when, if what is loved is absent, love is an unmistakable misery? Further, since love is a certain movement, and no movement exists except toward something, when we ask what ought to be loved, we are asking what that thing is toward which we ought to move.

[Col. 1082C] Therefore, if love is to be loved, not every love is to be loved. There is also a shameful love by which the mind pursues things inferior to itself; this is more properly called desire, namely, the root of all evils. Consequently, we ought not to love what can be taken away from love while love remains and enjoys it.

The love of what, then, should be loved, except of that which cannot be absent while it is being loved? That is what it means to possess nothing other than to know as it ought to be known. Gold and every body, however, are not possessed in the same way as they are known. They therefore ought not to be loved.

And since something can be loved without being possessed—not only things that ought not to be loved, such as a beautiful body, but also things that ought to be loved, such as the happy life—and, conversely, something can be possessed without being loved, such as chains, it is rightly asked whether someone can fail to love what is nothing other than knowing when he possesses it—that is, when he knows it.

[Col. 1082D] Yet we see some people learning numbers, for example, for no other reason than that through the discipline they may become wealthy or please people, and, once they have learned it, they direct it toward the same end they had set for themselves while learning it. Since possessing any discipline is nothing other than knowing it, it can happen that someone possesses something whose possession is identical with knowing it, and yet does not love it.

Nevertheless, no one can perfectly possess or know a good that he does not love. Who can know how great is the good he does not enjoy? He does not enjoy it if he does not love it. Therefore the person who does not love does not possess what ought to be loved, even though someone who does not possess it may be able to love it.

[Col. 1083A] No one, then, knows the happy life as it ought to be known and remains miserable. For if it is to be loved as it is, then knowing it is the same as possessing it.

Since this is so, what else is living happily than possessing something eternal through knowing it? For the eternal is the one thing in which it is right to trust, which cannot be taken away from the one who loves it; and possessing it is the same as knowing it.

Of all things, the most excellent is what is eternal. Therefore we cannot possess it except through that by which we are more excellent, namely, the mind. Whatever is possessed by the mind is possessed through knowing; and no good is perfectly known unless it is perfectly loved.

Nor, just as the mind alone can know, can it alone love. Love is a certain desire, and we see that the other parts of the soul also contain desire. If that desire consents to the mind and reason, it will rest in such peace and tranquility that the mind may contemplate what is eternal.

[Col. 1083B] Therefore the soul ought also to love with its other parts this great reality that must be known by the mind. And since what is loved must necessarily affect the one who loves it, it follows that, when what is eternal is loved in this way, it makes the soul eternal [variant: affects the soul with eternity]. Hence the happy life is that which is eternal.

[Col. 1083C] What, then, is eternal, which can affect the soul with eternity, except God? Love of things that ought to be loved is better called charity or devotion. Therefore, with all the powers of our thought, we must consider that most salutary commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and what the Lord Jesus said: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

## CHAPTER 351  
### On nurturing charity; from the same book

I call charity the movement of the soul by which it loves things that are not to be despised in comparison with the lover himself—that is, what is eternal and what can love the eternal itself.

God, therefore, and the soul by which these things are loved, are properly called charity: most pure and perfected if nothing else is loved. I also prefer that this be called devotion. But when God is loved more than the soul, so that a person prefers to belong to God rather than to himself, then the soul is truly and supremely cared for, and consequently the body also, without our troubling ourselves through any desire, but simply taking what is readily available and offered.

[Col. 1083D] The poison of charity is hope of acquiring or retaining temporal things. Its nourishment is the diminution of desire; its perfection is the absence of desire. The sign of its progress is the reduction of fear; the sign of its perfection is the absence of fear. For desire is the root of all evils, and perfected love casts out fear.

Therefore whoever wishes to nourish charity should devote himself to diminishing desires. Desire is love of acquiring or possessing temporal things. The beginning of its diminution is fear of God, who alone cannot be feared without love.

For one strives toward wisdom, and nothing is truer than what has been said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

There is no one who does not flee pain more than he seeks pleasure. We see even the most savage beasts deterred from the greatest pleasures by fear of pain; when this has become their habitual condition, they are called tamed and domesticated.

[Col. 1084A] Since human beings possess reason, and since, when reason serves desire through a pitiable perversion, it suggests that people can avoid being feared by concealing their crimes and devises the cleverest deceptions for hiding secret sins, it follows that people who are not yet delighted by the beauty of virtue are harder to tame than wild animals unless they are deterred from sinning by the punishments truly proclaimed through holy and divine men, and unless they acknowledge [or: decree] that what they conceal from human beings cannot be concealed from God.

[Col. 1084B] To make God feared, one must persuade people that everything is governed by divine providence—not so much through arguments, since whoever can follow arguments can also perceive the beauty of virtue, but through examples, whether recent ones if any arise, or examples from history, especially those that, under the direction of divine providence itself, have received outstanding religious authority in either the Old or the New Testament.

At the same time, one must speak both of the punishments of sinners and of the rewards of those who act rightly.

When some habit of not sinning has made what was thought burdensome seem easy, the sweetness of piety should begin to be tasted and the beauty of virtue commended, so that the freedom of charity may stand out above servitude to fear. Then the faithful, who have already received the preceding sacraments of regeneration—which necessarily move them profoundly—must be taught the difference between two human beings: the old and the new, the outward and the inward, the earthly and the heavenly. That is, they must learn the difference between one who pursues carnal and temporal goods and one who pursues spiritual and eternal goods.

[Col. 1084C] They must also be warned not to expect from God perishable and transitory benefits, which wicked people can also possess in abundance, but firm and everlasting benefits. To receive these, everything that is considered good in this world, as well as its evils, must be utterly despised.

The Lord’s outstanding and unique example must be set before them. Although he showed by so many miracles that he possessed such great power over things, he despised what the inexperienced consider great goods and endured what they consider great evils. To prevent anyone from daring to undertake this way of life and discipline any less because he honors it all the more, it must be shown, from the promises and exhortations of the Lord and from the multitude of those who imitated him—apostles, martyrs, and countless saints—that these things are not to be despaired of.

[Col. 1084D] Once the allurements of carnal pleasures have been overcome, one must beware lest the desire to please people creep in and take their place, whether through some miraculous deeds, difficult continence or endurance, some act of generosity, or in the name of knowledge or eloquence. This is also a form of the desire for honor.

Against all these things, let the passages written in praise of charity and concerning the emptiness of boasting be brought forward. Let people be taught how shameful it is to wish to please those whom one would not wish to imitate. For either they are not good, and there is nothing great in being praised by the wicked; or they are good, and they ought to be imitated.

But those who are good are good through virtue, and virtue does not desire what lies in the power of other people. Therefore whoever imitates the good desires the praise of no human being; whoever imitates the wicked is unworthy of praise.

[Col. 1085A] If, however, you wish to please people so that you may benefit them by leading them to love God, then you are no longer desiring this, but something else. Yet whoever wishes to please still needs fear: first, lest by secretly sinning he be counted by the Lord among hypocrites; then, if he seeks to please through good deeds and, in hunting for this reward, loses what God is going to give.

Once this desire has been conquered, pride must be guarded against. It is difficult for someone who no longer wishes to please people and considers himself full of virtues to deem himself worthy of fellowship with them.

Therefore fear is still necessary, lest even what he seems to possess be taken away from him and he be sent, bound hand and foot, into the outer darkness.

[Col. 1085B] Consequently, fear of God not only begins but also perfects the wise person. The wise person is one who supremely loves God and his neighbor as himself. What dangers and difficulties must be feared on this journey, and what remedies ought to be used, is another question.

## CHAPTER 352  
### A sermon on the praise of charity

[Col. 1085C] The person whose heart is full of charity comprehends, without any error, the manifold abundance and vast teaching of the divine Scriptures, and guards it without any labor. The Apostle says: “The fullness of the law is charity”; and elsewhere: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfailing faith.”

What is the end of the commandment, then, except the fulfillment of the commandment? And what is the fulfillment of the commandment except the fullness of the law? Therefore what he said there—“The fullness of the law is charity”—he also said here: “The end of the commandment is charity.”

There can be no doubt that a human being in whom charity dwells is the temple of God. John says: “God is charity.”

When the Apostles said these things and commended to us the excellence of charity, they could only belch forth what they had eaten. The Lord himself fed them with the word of salvation, with the word of charity—which is himself, the living bread that came down from heaven. He said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another”; and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

[Col. 1085D] He came through the mockery of the cross to destroy the corruption of the flesh and, through the newness of his death, to dissolve the oldness of the bond of our death. By a new commandment he made the human being new.

It was an old thing for a human being to die; but, so that this might not always prevail in humanity, a new thing occurred: God died. Yet because he died in the flesh, not in divinity, through the eternal life of his divinity he did not permit the destruction of the flesh to be eternal.

Therefore, as the Apostle says: “He died for our sins, and rose again for our justification.” The one who brought the newness of life against the oldness of death himself sets the new commandment against the old sin.

Therefore, if you wish to extinguish the old sin, extinguish desire through the new commandment and embrace charity [textual variant: “punish charity”]. For just as desire is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all good things.

[Col. 1086A] Charity securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances, because we love God and our neighbor. The one heavenly Teacher teaches us and says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.”

If, then, you do not have time to search through all the sacred pages, to unfold all the folds of the sayings, and to penetrate all the secrets of Scripture, hold fast to charity, on which everything depends. In this way you will hold what you have learned there; you will also hold what you have not yet learned.

For if you know charity, you know something on which even what you perhaps do not know depends. In what you understand in the Scriptures, charity is evident; in what you do not understand, charity is hidden. Therefore the person who holds charity in his conduct holds both what is evident and what is hidden in the divine sayings.

[Col. 1086B] Therefore, brothers, pursue charity, the sweet and salutary bond of minds, without which the rich person is poor, and with which the poor person is rich.

In adversity it endures; in prosperity it exercises restraint; amid harsh sufferings it is strong; in good works it is cheerful; in temptation it is most secure; in hospitality it is most generous; among true brothers it is most joyful; among false ones it is most patient.

In Abel it was pleasing through sacrifice; in Noah it was secure through the Flood; in Abraham’s pilgrimage it was most faithful; in Moses amid injuries it was most gentle; in David amid tribulations it was most meek.

[Col. 1086C] Among the three youths it innocently gazed upon the gentle flames; among the Maccabees it bravely endured the savage flames. In Susanna it was chaste toward her husband; in Anna, after her husband; in Mary, apart from a husband. In Paul it was free to rebuke; in Peter, humble in obedience; in Christians, humane in confession; in Christ, divine in forgiveness.

But what greater or richer thing can I say about charity than the praises the Lord thunders through the mouth of the Apostle, pointing out the supreme way and saying:

“If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.

“Charity is patient; charity is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not dishonored, does not seek its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never falls.”

[Col. 1086D] How great is this! It is the soul of the letters, the power of prophecy, the salvation of the sacraments, the foundation of knowledge, the fruit of faith, the wealth of the poor, the life of those who are dying.

What is so magnanimous as to die for the ungodly? What is as kind as loving even one’s enemies? It alone is not exalted by its own happiness, because it is not puffed up; it alone is not stung by an evil conscience, because it does not act wrongly.

Amid reproaches it is secure; amid hatred it is beneficent; amid anger it is peaceful; [Col. 1087] amid ambushes it is innocent; amid iniquities it groans; in truth it breathes freely.

What is stronger than it—not in repaying injuries, but in taking no account of them? What is more faithful—not to vanity, but to eternity [variant: truth]?

For this reason it bears all things in the present life, because it believes all things concerning the future life; and it endures all that is inflicted here, because it hopes for all that is promised there. Rightly, therefore, it never falls.

[Col. 1088] Pursue charity, then, and, thinking of it in holiness, bring forth the fruit of justice. Whatever richer words than I have been able to speak you may discover in its praises, let them appear in your conduct. For a sermon of old age ought not only to be weighty but also brief.
