## Paschasius the Deacon

[Col. 1149] Preliminary Matter and Preface, 9–10.

### *On the Holy Spirit*, Book I, 11

**Chapter I.** That we ought to believe in the Holy Spirit, but, with the preposition *in* omitted, believe the Catholic Church.

**Chapter II.** That Christ was created by the Holy Spirit, as God, and not begotten. *Ibid.*

**Chapter III.** The unity to be asserted by prophetic testimonies, 12.

**Chapter IV.** Concerning the Trinity, and that even the liberal disciplines have dealt with the three Persons. *Ibid.*

**Chapter V.** When the Son is called the face of the Father, he is acknowledged as coeternal with the Father, 13.

**Chapter VI.** That the Spirit of the Father is the Holy Spirit himself, 14.

**Chapter VII.** Concerning the finger of God, 16.

**Chapter VIII.** That the divinity of the Holy Spirit is not impaired because he appears to be neither begotten nor unbegotten, 17.

**Chapter IX.** That the Holy Spirit perfects charisms and bestows them, 18.

**Chapter X.** In the Acts of the Apostles the assertion of the Trinity is repeated; there Christ is also affirmed to have been sent against the Novatians to grant repentance, 20.

**Chapter XI.** It is proper to God to sanctify the creature, 21.

**Chapter XII.** The Holy Spirit is not local, 22.

### Book II, 25

**Chapter I.** That no rational creature can be infused into a cognate creature. *Ibid.* [Col. 1150]

**Chapter II.** Whether, according to the opinion of the unlearned, the Holy Spirit was incarnate like the Son, since he too came upon Mary; or whether only the Son was begotten from the Virgin, 26.

**Chapter III.** Macedonius’s objection, by which he impiously asserts the Holy Spirit to be a more excellent creature, 27.

**Chapter IV.** Macedonius, asserting duality, denies that the Holy Spirit has a proper person, 28.

**Chapter V.** The objection that the statement we read—“Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit”—likewise testifies that water and the Holy Spirit are creatures, 32.

**Chapter VI.** Where it is asked whether the designation “Holy Spirit” is considered a surname or a name. *Ibid.*

**Chapter VII.** It is demonstrated by clear testimonies that the Holy Spirit specially fills the prophets and is equally believed and called God, 33.

**Chapter VIII.** Where it is demonstrated that the temple of God is the temple of the Holy Spirit, 35.

**Chapter IX.** Where God gave the Gentiles repentance unto life against the Novatians; the order of the reading itself shows that this God is the Holy Spirit, 36.

**Chapter X.** Where, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, the Holy Spirit is declared to be God through the distributions of powers, 37.

**Chapter XI.** It must be observed that, just as he says there is one God, so he says there is one Holy Spirit—a statement that could in no way be made of a creature belonging to the common people, or of one who divides among individuals as he wills. *Ibid.*

**Chapter XII.** Where he says that those who have become the temple of the Holy Spirit ought to advance in such a way that they may deserve to carry God in their body, 38.

**Chapter LI.** Where they say that sacrifice is offered to the Father alone, 386.

**Chapter LII.** Where they say that the Son had no work in common with the Father, 387.

**Chapter LIII.** Where they say that only the Father is called the Most High. *Ibid.*

**Chapter LIV.** Where they say that the Son called himself the beginning, 388.

**Chapter LV.** Where it is said: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” *Ibid.*

**Chapter LVI.** Where they say that the Apostle testifies that Christ did not know himself according to the flesh. *Ibid.*

**Chapter LVII.** Where they say that the Son will descend from heaven at the command and voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, 389. [Col. 1153]

**Chapter LVIII.** Where they say that only the Father is adored by the faithful, 390.

**Chapter LIX.** Where they say that the Son gave thanks to the Father. *Ibid.*

**Chapter LX.** Where they say that the Son was established king by the Father on Mount Zion, 391.

**Chapter LXI.** Where they say that the Son is lower than the Father both in power and in nature, 392.

**Chapter LXIII.** Where they say that the Son is not coeternal with the Father, 393.

**Chapter LXIV.** Where they say that the Father made the Son, but the Son made all things. *Ibid.*

**Chapter LXVI.** Where they say that only the Father dwells in inaccessible light. *Ibid.*

**Chapter LXVII.** Where they say that the Son, unlike the Father, is not perfect, 395.

**Chapter LXVIII.** Where they say: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,” 396.

**Chapter LXX.** Where they say: “The Father, from whom are all things, and the Son, through whom are all things,” 397.

**Chapter LXXI.** Where they say: “If the Father and the Son are one God, then first the Word and afterward God.” *Ibid.*

**Chapter LXXII.** Where they say: “If the Father and the Son are one God, then God was named first, and afterward Father,” 398.

**Chapter LXXIII.** Where they say that the Son and the Father are not called one God—he having been born from the Father before the times and afterward from the Virgin, 399.

# Table of Chapters Contained in the Two Volumes of Eugippius

As arranged by the author himself.

## In the Earlier Volume
[Col. 1155] [Col. 1155]

## Chapter One

**On the statement of the apostle James:** “If anyone keeps the whole law but offends in one point, he has become guilty of all”; while he likewise says, “We all offend in many things”; and on charity and the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The complete book addressed to the presbyter Jerome. 561

**Chapter II.** On the four virtues mentioned above, which he distinguished in the preceding book. In the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, while discussing them, he referred them all to the one commandment of charity. 570

**Chapter III.** Whether the virtues by which one strives toward eternity will come to an end when they have led one to eternal things. From Book XIV of *On the Trinity*, among other passages. 571

**Chapter IV.** On the four affections which Cicero called disturbances, others passions, and which Virgil thinks are present in human beings on account of the flesh, although the devil too is not without them, despite being without flesh; and on the fact that he approves the saints, whose love is rightly ordered, as possessing all these affections rightly ordered. From Book XIV of *The City of God*. 572

**Chapter V.** On the five bodily senses. From Book X of the *Confessions*. 575

**Chapter VI.** A beautiful and extended discourse on those same five bodily senses. From Book X of the *Confessions*. 577

**Chapter VII.** On the mediator’s sacrament for the purification of souls. From Book X of the *Confessions*, among other passages, and at the relevant place. 583

**Chapter VIII.** On the same sacrament. From Book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 15. 584

**Chapter IX.** On miracles performed by magical arts. From Book III of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6. 585

**Chapter X.** On the original causes of natural creatures, which the Creator implanted in the world. From Book III of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8. 588

**Chapter XI.** On the simplicity of our Savior, which meets and corresponds to our doubleness. From Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3. 589

**Chapter XII.** On the mediator toward death, the devil, and the mediator toward life, Christ Jesus. From the same Book IV. 591

**Chapter XIII.** On the ease of the deceptions by which unclean spirits deceive human beings. From the same Book IV, chapter 11. Ibid.

**Chapter XIV.** On false and deceptive purifications. From the same Book IV. 592

**Chapter XV.** On those who promise themselves purification by their own virtue. From the same Book IV. Ibid.

**Chapter XVI.** On the mediator’s sacrament, on the faith by which we believe things accomplished in time, and on the truth that makes them eternal. From Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 18. Ibid.

**Chapter XVII.** That some testimonies foretold Christ as coming, while others testified that he had come. From Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19. 594

**Chapter XVIII.** On the same sacrament of the mediator. From Book I of *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*. Also, how many kinds of apostleship there are, or what the name “apostleship” means; and how we can know who is sent by God. From the *Book of Responses to Orosius*. Ibid.

**Chapter XIX.** What Plato, if he were questioned while alive, might answer concerning the Christian religion, which teaches the mind to cleave to unchangeable truth—that is, to God—and which, coming to the aid of all the various diseases with different remedies appropriately suited to the teaching, also proclaims universally, “Do not love the world”; and how the Church deals with Gentiles, heretics, schismatics, and Jews. From the book *On True Religion*. 595

**Chapter XX.** How fittingly the wisdom of God, Christ, assisted human beings through his humanity: having been born, he commended to the disciple the mother whom, while speaking to the crowds and turning water into wine, he had denied, but whom he acknowledged from the cross. His entire life was a discipline of morals, so that no sin is committed except when people desire what he despised or flee what he endured; and on the various modes of teaching. From the book *On True Religion*. 599

[Col. 1156]

**Chapter XXI.** He reproves the pleasure-loving, the curious, and the proud, appropriately assigning to each the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of life—three things shown to be avoided by the author of life in each of the three kinds of temptation. From the book *On True Religion*. 601

**Chapter XXII.** That it is better to be conquered by a human being than by a vice; and that bodily relationships are not to be loved in a merely carnal manner. But when one cannot benefit all whom one loves equally, one becomes unjust unless one prefers to benefit those who are closer. From the same book, *On True Religion*. Ibid.

**Chapter XXIII.** That the law of God is a certain lofty discipline, which commands those who desire to know it to follow a twofold order, one part of which is life and the other learning; and that in both parts it gives commands to the young. From Book II of *On Order*. 605

**Chapter XXIV.** On the serpent’s speech to Eve and on the incantations of the Marsians. From Book XI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 607

**Chapter XXV.** That God, for those who follow him out of love, has fortified the way of authority sevenfold. He also explains the apostle’s statement, “For neither death nor life cannot separate us from the love of God.” And that, most beneficially, authority should precede reasoning in the Church. From the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*. 608

**Chapter XXVI.** On the beginning of Genesis, and, from that same beginning, that a manifold exposition of meanings is more beneficial, provided it is not contrary to the faith. From Book XII of the *Confessions*. 610

**Chapter XXVII.** The beginning of the book *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 614

**Chapter XXVIII.** Against those who say, “Was Moses there when God made heaven and earth, so that he should be believed?” From Book XI of *The City of God*, chapter 4. 618

**Chapter XXIX.** That those who bring accusations concerning the age of the world can be refuted by consideration of the world’s location. From the same Book XI. 619

**Chapter XXX.** That angels too can be understood as signified and created under the name “light.” From the same Book XI. 621

**Chapter XXXI.** Against those who say that the world was made so that souls which had sinned previously might be enclosed in it; where he proves Origen to have erred from his books called *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*). From Book XI of *The City of God*. 622

**Chapter XXXII.** On the same error and on eternal fire. From the book *Response to the Questions of the Presbyter Orosius*. 623

**Chapter XXXIII.** How the statement “Every creature groans and travails until now” should be understood; and the statement in Job, “The stars are not clean before him”; and that what the blind man who was healed said—“God does not hear sinners”—is not true. From the same book, *Response to the Presbyter Orosius*. 625

**Chapter XXXIV.** Likewise, from the book *On Heresies*, on Origen’s error. 628

**Chapter XXXV.** Against those who introduced cycles of recurring revolutions. From Book XII of *The City of God*. 629

**Chapter XXXVI.** Against the statement, “How did the devil first acquire an evil will, when he had been created good by God?” Likewise from Book XII of *The City of God*. 631

**Chapter XXXVII.** That the devil, from the very beginning of creation, apostatized from his Creator through pride, because envy is born from pride, and through envy he became a murderer. From Book XI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 635

**Chapter XXXVIII.** How the statement in Isaiah, “How Lucifer fell from heaven,” and the statement in Ezekiel, “You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of paradise,” should be understood. From the same book. 635

**Chapter XXXIX.** Against those who ask why God created the human being whom he knew beforehand would sin. From the same book. 637

**Chapter XL.** On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. From Book VIII of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 642

**Chapter XLI.** Likewise on the same tree; from the same book. 643

**Chapter XLII.** On the twofold work of God’s providence, and on the same double operation of divine governance in the human being himself. From the same book. 646

**Chapter XLIII.** That the eternal divinity, moved neither by time nor by place, moves creation; and on the order of natures—what he has placed above what, and what he has subjected to what. From Book VII of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 647

**Chapter XLIV.** That both the divine speech to Adam and the divine walking in paradise should without hesitation be understood as occurring not through God’s own substance but through a created thing subject to him. Likewise from Book VIII of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 650

**Chapter XLV.** On the question of Methuselah’s years. From the *Questions on Genesis*. 651

**Chapter XLVI.** On the statement that the angels of God had intercourse with the daughters of human beings. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter XLVII.** On Noah’s ark: whether it could have carried all the animals together with their food. From the same book. 652

**Chapter XLVIII.** That God’s reconsideration of changing things is an unchangeable principle; and on the dimensions of the ark, in which the human body is plausibly measured on account of Christ’s body. From Book XV of *The City of God*. Ibid.

**Chapter XLIX.** How the statement “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” should be understood. From Book XI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 654

**Chapter L.** How Adam was not deceived, as the apostle says, although the same apostle calls him a transgressor. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LI.** On the creation of the first human being and on causal principles; or how fifteen years were added to King Hezekiah’s life, although it had been foretold that he would not live. From Book VI of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. 656

**Chapter LII.** On the star that the Magi followed, a servant of Christ and not a portent governed by fate. From Book II *Against Faustus*. 661

**Chapter LIII.** On commandments for carrying out life and commandments for signifying life, in the twofold love and in circumcision. From Book VI *Against Faustus*. 662

**Chapter LIV.** Why, in the Old Testament, certain foods of flesh were forbidden—because they signified either souls or doctrines. From the same book. 662–663

**Chapter LV.** On unleavened bread, the Feast of Booths, and other matters; and on the prohibition of a linen-and-wool garment, or the forbidden yoking together of an ox and a donkey. From the same book. 663

**Chapter LVI.** How the statement “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” should be understood. From Book XI *Against Faustus*. 664

**Chapter LVII.** On the six days in Genesis and the six ages; or on the woman made from the side of the sleeping man. From Book XII *Against Faustus*. 668–669

**Chapter LVIII.** That Cain and Abel prefigured two peoples; and on the statement, “Whoever kills Cain shall pay sevenfold vengeance”; or on the sign that God placed upon Cain. From the same book. 669

**Chapter LXIX.** That the statement “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” can be understood in different ways. From Book XV of *The City of God*. 671

**Chapter LX.** On the number seven as rest and eight as resurrection. That, just as the floodwaters rose fifteen cubits, so the water of baptism, through the depth of its heavenly mystery, surpasses every height of the proud; or on the sending out of the raven and the dove. From Book XII *Against Faustus*. 674

**Chapter LXI.** On God’s commands to Noah after the flood, and on the bow appearing in the clouds; or on Noah’s nakedness, which his son Ham mocked and which is recognized as having prefigured the Jewish people. From the same book. 675

**Chapter LXII.** On Abraham’s departure from his land; on Joseph, who was sold and honored; and on Israel’s departure from Egypt. Book XII *Against Faustus*. 676

**Chapter LXIII.** That certain sins are made manifest by punishment, which proves certain sins to have been hidden. From Book XIII *Against Faustus*. 681

**Chapter LXIV.** On the statement, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” Book XIV *Against Faustus*. Ibid.

**Chapter LXV.** On Moses’ statement, “You will see your life hanging before you, and you will not believe in your life.” From Book XVI *Against Faustus*. 684

**Chapter LXVI.** That the Sabbath rest can also be understood in the Lord’s burial; and that circumcision on the eighth day, performed on the genital member, signified the stripping away of mortality, from which our race was stripped when the Lord rose on the first day, which is also the eighth. From the same book. 685

**Chapter LXVII.** He says that the pagans imposed the names of their gods not only on days but also on months; for among the people of God, whether the Sabbath, circumcision, or distinctions among sacrifices, these were figures of our realities. From Book XVIII *Against Faustus*. 686

**Chapter LXVIII.** That “Eye for eye” is not contrary to “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek,” and so forth. From Book IX *Against Faustus*. 687

**Chapter LXIX.** How the apostle’s statement “In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” should be understood. From Book XXI *Against Faustus*. 689

**Chapter LXX.** On the same apostle’s statement, “God has tempered the body.” From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXI.** From the example of Abraham concealing his wife: when a person has something he can do, he should not put God to the test. From Book XXII *Against Faustus*. 690

**Chapter LXXII.** What realities Jacob’s four wives prefigured. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXIII.** On Judah’s act, when he had intercourse with his daughter-in-law. From the same book. 694

**Chapter LXXIV.** On David’s sin with the wife of Uriah the Hittite. From the same book. 697

**Chapter LXXV.** On Solomon’s initial goodness and subsequent wickedness. From the same book. 698

**Chapter LXXVI.** On the calf’s head being burned, scattered into water, and given to the people to drink. From the same book. 699

**Chapter LXXVII.** On raising up offspring for a deceased brother. From the same book. 700

**Chapter LXXVIII.** On the statement that clean and unclean birds entered the ark. From the *Questions on Genesis according to the Literal Meaning*, among other passages and at the relevant place. 703

**Chapter LXXIX.** What the Lord’s statement “I will not again curse the ground” means. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXX.** What is meant by “From the hand of his brother I will require the life of the human being.” From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXXI.** Ham, who sinned, is cursed not in his own person but in his son. From the same book. 704

**Chapter LXXXII.** “The whole earth had one language”: this is said by recapitulation. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXXIII.** How Sarah, although she spent several days with the king of Egypt, is not believed to have been defiled by intercourse with him. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXXIV.** How the eternal character of the statement “I will give you the land as an eternal possession” is to be understood. From the same book. Ibid.

**Chapter LXXXV.** “I knew that he would command his sons after him to keep the ways of the Lord.” From the same book. 705

**Chapter LXXXVI.** “Going down I will see whether they have been utterly destroyed according to the cry that has come to me; but if not, I will know.” From the same book. Ibid.

# Life of Saint Severinus

[Col. 1167]

## Erratum

[Col. 1167]

Through a typographical error, the following little work was placed after the indices, although it should have preceded them. We wish also to inform the reader that numbers 5 and 6, which intervened between Eugyppius’s letter and the panegyric of Saint Severinus, were intentionally omitted, since they contained a letter of Paschasius that had long ago been published among the works of that deacon.

[Col. 1167]

# Life of Saint Severinus, Apostle of Noricum, by Eugyppius

(C)

[Col. 1167]

## Letter of Eugyppius to the Deacon Paschasius

### 1

To the holy and deservedly venerable lord Paschasius, Eugyppius sends greetings in the Lord.

Nearly two years ago—namely, during the consulship of Importunus [Note: [Col. 1167] Others call him Opportunus. He was sole consul in the year of Christ 509, which was the eighteenth year of the emperor Anastasius.]—a letter from a certain noble layman, addressed to a certain presbyter, was brought to us for reading. It contained the life of the monk Basilicus [Note: [Col. 1167] Belfortius and Bassus. Concerning Mount Titas, or Titanus, where the village now called Saint Marino is situated, we shall speak on 3 September, in connection with the Life of Saint Marinus.], who had once lived in the monastery of the mountain called Titas, above Ariminum [Note: [Col. 1168] A celebrated place on the Adriatic, named from the river of the same name.], and afterward died in the region of Lucania—a man well known both to many others and to me. When I learned that some people were making copies of this letter, I began to consider the matter privately and also to tell religious men that the miracles celebrated through the divine works of blessed Severinus ought not to be concealed.

### 2

When the author of the aforementioned letter learned this, he more readily instructed me to send him some information about the same Saint Severinus, so that, equipped with it, he might write a little book of his life that would benefit the memory of posterity. Compelled, therefore, by this request, I immediately composed a memorandum filled with several indications [Col. 1168], drawn from the very familiar and daily reports of our elders. I did so with no small sorrow of heart, considering it unjust that, while you were still alive, a layman should have to ask us to undertake this work. To him, indeed, the form and style of the work could be entrusted only with some presumption, lest, polished merely by secular literature, he should compose the life in such language that the ignorance of many would greatly suffer from it; and lest the marvelous events that had long lain hidden in a kind of silent night should, so far as we are concerned, fail to shine because of an obscure exposition inaccessible to those ignorant of the liberal arts.

But I shall seek no light beyond the flame of that little lamp, since you shine like the sun. I ask only that you do not cover the rays of your expertise with some cloud of excuse, namely by accusing me of ignorance. Do not, I beg you, strike me with such harsh words when you say: “Why do you expect water from a flint?” I am no longer expecting it from the flint of secular speech, but from you, who, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, will refresh us from that firmest rock with the honey of the discourse that flows from you. From it, directing toward me the nectarous taste of your sweetest promise, you command me to send a memorandum, or indications of the life of the often-mentioned Severinus [Col. 1169A], so that, until they may deserve to pass into the little book of your composition, they will not offend the mind of the one reviewing them.

For whoever seeks an architect to build a house carefully prepares the necessary material. If a mass resembling walls is assembled out of unworked pieces while the craftsman delays, one cannot be said to have built with stones when no structure of the master has entered it at all and no proper supports have been laid beneath the foundations. So I too, barely preparing precious material for your talent in a most humble composition, should not be thought to have written what I wish, when there is no construction of liberal discipline and no ornament of grammatical elevation.

It plainly possesses the sure foundation of faith alone, by which it is established that the holy man shone with wondrous virtues. This foundation I offer to be laid by the hands of your speech [Col. 1169B], so that from the summit of your work I may render to Christ the praises due to him.

### 3

I also ask that you deign to append the benefits of his virtues and the remedies of his healings that were accomplished by divine power either on the journey or here, at the memorial of that most blessed Father. Since your son Deogratias, a faithful bearer of the message, knows these things very well, we commend them to you for communication in words, hoping that we shall continually call him “bearer” also because of the completion of your work. Thus, just as this most faithful servant of God, rich in such great virtues, is raised to the glory of the saints by his merits through Christ’s grace, so may he be consecrated to human memory by your writings.

Certainly, the homeland from which he originated perhaps necessarily requires us to begin there, as is customary, when weaving the beginning of a life [Col. 1169C]. Although I confess that I possess no clear evidence about it, I shall nevertheless not remain silent about what I have learned from you concerning what should be held on this matter.

### 4

Since many priests and spiritual men, as well as noble and religious laymen, whether natives or coming to him from distant regions, often hesitated among themselves, asking what nation the man belonged to whom they saw shining with such great virtues—and since no one at all dared to inquire of him—finally a certain presbyter named Pirmenius [Note: [Col. 1169D] Belfortius reads Pygmenius; Braunerus, Primenius.], a noble man of Italy and one possessing every authority, who had taken refuge with him when the patrician Orestes was unjustly killed [Note: This commander of the army, created by the emperor Julius Nepos, rebelled against him and made his own son Momyllus, also called Augustulus, emperor on 31 October 475. Odoacer, summoned into Italy by Orestes’ enemies, killed him and his brother Paul, and exiled Augustulus to Campania in 476, in the consulship of Basiliscus II and Armatus.], fearing Orestes’ murderers because he was said to have been like a father to the slain man, after many days of intimacy broke forth, as though speaking for everyone, and asked him as follows [Col. 1169D]:

“Holy lord, from what province has God deemed it worthy to grant such a light to these regions?”

The man of God first replied with cheerful wit: “If [Col. 1170A] you think I am a fugitive, prepare a ransom that you can offer for me when I am sought.”

Then he immediately added seriously [Note: [Col. 1169D] Baronius the elder reads this seriously.]: “What benefit is there for a servant of God in revealing his place or his origin, when by keeping silent he can more holily avoid boasting—which is left-handed [Note: The Latin *sinistra* here carries both the literal sense “left” and the moral sense “sinister” or “wrong”—], since, without its knowledge, I desire to accomplish the good work through Christ’s gift, by which I may deserve to become a companion of the right hand and be enrolled as a citizen of the heavenly homeland? If you truly know that I desire that homeland, although unworthy, why is it necessary for you to know the earthly one that you are asking about?

“Nevertheless, know that the God who granted you to become a priest also commanded me to be present among these people in their peril.”

At this response the presbyter fell silent, and no one before or afterward presumed to question the blessed man on this matter. His speech, however, testified that he was entirely Latin [Note: Henri Canisius’s edition inserts here *Africanum* (“an African”), a word absent from the manuscript of Belfortius and from Baronius and seemingly unnecessary. Braunerus suspects *Romanum* (“a Roman”); Baronius favors this. Aventinus writes that he was born in Africa, as we have said.]: [Col. 1170B] yet it is established that he had gone to a certain desert region of the East in the fervor of a more perfect life. From there he afterward came, compelled by a divine revelation, to the towns of Riparian Noricum [Note: Riparian Noricum is all the territory lying along the bank of the Danube from the Inn, the boundary of Raetia and Vindelicia, as far as the Pannonians.] near Upper Pannonia, which were being afflicted by the frequent incursions of barbarians, just as he himself was accustomed to relate [Note: [Col. 1170D] Baronius closes the sentence here.], in a more secretive manner, as though he were speaking about someone else. He mentioned certain cities of the East and indicated that he had marvelously passed through the dangers of an immense journey.

These, then, are the only things I have always heard whenever discussion arose about the homeland of blessed Severinus, even while he himself was alive. The indications of his wondrous life, recorded in the memorandum attached to this letter and set out under the chapters presented above, will, as I requested, become clearer through the instruction of your book. It remains only that you do not cease to join your prayers to his, and that you do not cease to ask pardon for me.

# Here Begins the Life of Saint Severinus

## Chapter One

Saint Severinus foretells various things in Noricum and comes to the aid of those in distress.

### 7. 

At the time when Attila, king of the Huns, died [Note: In the year 454], both Pannonias and the other regions bordering the Danube were thrown into confusion by uncertain circumstances. First, great struggles arose among his sons over possession of the kingdom; swollen with the disease of unjust domination, they made their father’s death the occasion of their own crime [Note: Of these, as Jordanes writes in *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 50, almost the entire population was, through unrestrained lust, [depraved]. The elder was called Ellac, or Chabas by others. He engaged in a memorable battle with his brother Aladaric, in which the power of the Huns was completely broken. Velser, book II of *Bavarian Affairs*.].

At that time, therefore, the most holy servant of God, Severinus, came from the regions of the East and lived in the vicinity of Noricum Ripense and Pannonia, in a town called Asturis [Note: Sur., Baron., Har., Casturis. Lazius has *Castuns* and *Casturis*, that is, as he says, “Augustan Forts,” an audacious conjecture, as Velser judges. Petrus de Natalibus and Ferrarius [read] *Astaris*. In the *Notitia Imperii*, under the commander of Pannonia I and Noricum Ripense, there is *Austuris*; Ortelius calls it *Astura*. Aventinus, book II of the *Annals*, says that the town of Astura, on the border of Noricum Ripense and Pannonia, perished at this time—namely, in the days of Severinus. Cuspinianus, in his *Description of Austria*, in the *Life of Saint Coloman*, wishes it to be Stokeraw. Guido Pancirolo, in his commentary on the *Notitia Imperii*, chapter 83, makes it a town of Moesia. He says that it was called *Asutas* by Stephanus. We do not find that word in Stephanus, but we do find Ἄσυρα (*Asyra*) and Ἄσυρον (*Asyron*), a city of Asian Mysia toward the Troad.], living according to evangelical and apostolic doctrine. Endowed with every form of piety and chastity, he fulfilled his venerable purpose in the Catholic faith through holy works.

Thus strengthened by such practices, he blamelessly pursued the crown of the heavenly calling. One day he went, as usual, to the church. After summoning the priest, the clergy, and the citizens, he began, with complete humility of spirit, to warn them that they should ward off the imminent ambushes of the enemy by prayers, fasts, and works of mercy. But their stubborn minds, inclined toward carnal desires, tested the prophecies of the preacher at the peril of their unbelief.

The servant of God then returned to the lodging where he had been received by the church’s custodian. Revealing the day and hour of the impending destruction, he said: “I am hastening away from this obstinate town, which will perish all the sooner” [Col. 1171B].

From there he withdrew to the neighboring town called Commagenis [Note: Petrus de Natalibus has *Commagonis*. Velser has *Comagenis*, presumably from *castris*; Antoninus has *Comagenas* in his *Itinerary*. Cuspinianus says it was called Kaumberg, Lazius Holenburg. Ferrarius writes that this town was then surrounded by a hostile siege [Col. 1172D]; plainly incorrectly, as is clear from this passage.].

The town was guarded with the strictest security by barbarians stationed inside it who had entered into treaty with the Romans; no one was readily granted permission either to enter or to leave. Yet, because the servant of God was unknown, they neither questioned nor rejected him. As soon as he had entered the church, therefore, he urged all who despaired of their own safety to arm themselves with fasting, prayers, and almsgiving. He set before them examples of ancient deliverance, by which divine protection had wonderfully rescued God’s people against everyone’s expectation.

When they hesitated to believe his promise of universal safety at that very moment of danger, the old man who had earlier received so great a guest at Asturis [Col. 1171C] arrived. After being anxiously questioned by the gatekeepers, he showed by his clothing and speech the destruction of his town, adding that it had been destroyed by the barbarians on the very day when a certain man of God had foretold it.

When they heard this, the guards anxiously replied: “Could he perhaps be the one who promises us God’s help when all hope is lost?” As soon as they recognized the servant of God in the church, the old man fell at his feet and declared that he had been saved through his merits, so that he would not suffer destruction together with the other townspeople.

### 8. 

When the inhabitants of the aforesaid town heard this, they asked forgiveness for their unbelief and obeyed the holy instructions of the man of God. Devoting themselves to fasting, they gathered in the church for three days and chastised their former errors with groans and lamentations.

On the third day, as the solemnity of the evening sacrifice was being completed, a sudden earthquake occurred [Col. 1172A]. The barbarians living inside the town were so terrified that they compelled the Romans to open the gates for them quickly. All of them fled as they went out [Note: The Belfort manuscript has *conciti* (“hurriedly”). Braunerus thinks that these barbarians were remnants of Attila’s army; others think they were Boii.]. Believing themselves surrounded by the siege of the neighboring enemy, and thrown into still greater terror by divine intervention and confused by the darkness of night, they cut one another down with their own swords.

Thus, when the adversaries had been consumed by such mutual slaughter, the people, saved by divine protection, learned through the holy man to fight with heavenly weapons.

### 9. 

At the same time, the city called Favianis was suffering under a severe famine [Note: Cuspinianus writes that it was called *Flavabis* in the Gothic language, like *Batabis*, now Batavia. Velser thinks it was *Castra Fabiana*, perhaps from the cohort Fabia or Fabiana. From *Fabianis*, with the final syllables cut away at both ends and *A* changed into *E*, he derives *Wien*, otherwise *Vindobona*, now the capital of Austria. Georgius Brunus does not approve this in his *Theatre of Cities*, but offers nothing more certain.]. Its inhabitants believed that their only remedy would be to invite the man of God from the aforementioned town of Commagenis by religious prayers.

Foreseeing that they would come to him, he hesitated whether or not to go with them [Col. 1172B], but was admonished by the Lord to accompany them. When he arrived, he began to urge the citizens, saying: “You will be able to free yourselves from the destruction of so great a famine through the fruits of repentance.”

While they were advancing in such practices, the most blessed Severinus learned by divine revelation that a certain widow named Procula had hidden a great quantity of grain. He brought her forward and vehemently rebuked her.

“Why,” he said, “though born of the noblest ancestry, do you make yourself a slave to greed and a bondservant of avarice, which, as the Apostle teaches, is the service of idols? Behold, while the Lord mercifully provides for his servants, you will have nothing to do with what you have wrongly acquired—unless, perhaps, by throwing into the waters of the Danube the grain said to have been withheld [reading uncertain], you intend to show humanity to fish, which you have denied to human beings. Therefore, help yourself rather than the poor from what you still think you are keeping for Christ while he is hungry” [Col. 1172C].

Terrified by great fear when she heard this, the woman began willingly to distribute to the poor what she had preserved.

Not long afterward, many rafts from the regions of Rhaetia, heavily laden with merchandise, unexpectedly appeared on the bank of the Danube. They had been frozen for many days in the thick ice of the river Eni [Note: Some have *Aeni*, but *Oeni* is better. He distinguishes the Rhaetians from the Noricans, and says that the river joins the Danube at Batavia. Velser and the Belfort manuscript have *Rheni*, incorrectly.] [Note: Another reading: “had been tied together.”]. At God’s command they were immediately released and brought abundant food to those suffering from famine.

Then everyone began continually to praise God, the giver of an unexpected remedy. They had believed that they would perish from the evil of the prolonged famine, but now acknowledged that the rafts had arrived outside the proper season, released from the cold of the ice through the prayers of the servant of God.

## CHAPTER II. He foretells or obtains victory and other things.

### 10. 

At the same time, barbarian marauders, taking advantage of an unexpected incursion, carried off as captives whatever men and animals they had found outside the walls [Col. 1173A]. Thus many of the citizens flocked tearfully to the man of God and reported the disaster that had befallen them, while also displaying evidence of the recent plundering.

He questioned Mamertinus. Then he asked the tribune [Note: Aventinus makes him a governor; Velser rightly rejects this.] who was afterward ordained bishop [Note: These words were absent from Surius’s manuscript. Velser suspects a gloss, since at nearly the same time Mamertus, bishop of Vienne in Gaul, was living, concerning whom we shall speak on 2 May. Lazius makes Mamertinus the first bishop of Vienna in Austria and confirms this by the authority of an old chronicle; in Velser’s judgment, not very solidly.] whether he had any armed men with him with whom he could pursue the brigands more vigorously.

He replied: “I have very few soldiers, and therefore I do not dare to engage such a great multitude of enemies. But if your Reverence commands it, although we lack the aid of weapons, we believe that through your prayer we shall become victorious.”

The servant of God said: “Even if the soldiers are unarmed, they will now be armed from among the enemy. For neither human numbers nor strength are required where God is proved to be the defender in all things. Go quickly in the name of God; go confidently. Since the Lord mercifully goes before you, each weak man will appear strongest. The Lord will fight for you, and you will be silent. Go, then, without delay, observing this above all: bring to me unharmed all the barbarians whom you capture.”

They went out, and at the second mile they found the aforesaid robbers beside a stream called Dicuntia [Note: Surius has *Taguntia*; the Belfort manuscript *Gyguntia*; Raderus *Jaguntia* or *Dicuntia*; Staibano *Tiguntius*]. The robbers suddenly turned and fled, and the soldiers seized all their weapons. The others they bound and brought captive to the servant of God, as he had commanded.

After releasing them from their bonds and restoring them with food and drink, he addressed them briefly: “Go and tell your accomplices not to dare approach this place again out of greed for plunder. For they will immediately be punished by the judgment of heavenly vengeance, since God fights for his servants. He is accustomed to protect them by divine power in such a way that the enemy’s weapons inflict no wounds upon them but instead supply them with arms.”

After dismissing the barbarians, he himself rejoiced in the miracles of Christ. He promised that, through Christ’s mercies, the town would never again experience the plunder of enemies, provided only that the citizens allowed neither prosperity nor adversity to draw them away from the work of God.

### 11. 

Afterward, Blessed Severinus withdrew to a more remote place called ad Vineas [Note: The Belfort manuscript has *Ad Juncas*. Lazius testifies that ruins of a cell still existed in the district of Siferinga and that the district took its name from Saint Severinus. Cuspinianus says that he purchased there a villa where the traces of Severinus’s cell were preserved, in his memory. It lies a great mile from Vienna. Lazius says that there had been a larger monastery at a place called Heyligstat, that is, “holy place,” from the habitation of saints there. Saint Leopold later removed stones from there for the construction of the cloister at Neuburg, as we shall say on 15 November in his Life. Ferrarius writes that this monastery of Saint Severinus was built by the king of the Rugians.]. Content with a small cell, he was compelled by divine revelation to return to the aforesaid town. Although the quiet of the cell delighted him, he nevertheless obeyed God’s commands and built a monastery not far from the city [Col. 1174A]. There he began to train many in a holy purpose, instructing the souls of his hearers more by deeds than by words.

He himself often withdrew to a secluded dwelling called Purgum by the inhabitants [Note: Cuspinianus interprets it as Burckensdorf; but his claim that the Rugian king Flaccitheus lived there is unsupported. Staibano and Eugenius write that the saint withdrew here into solitude, to a place called Burgum.], five miles from Favianis, so that, avoiding the crowds of people who were accustomed to come to him, he might cling immediately to God in continual prayer.

But the more eagerly he desired to live in solitude, the more frequently he was warned by revelations not to deny his presence to afflicted peoples. Thus his merit advanced each day, and the fame of his virtues increased. Spreading far and wide, it revealed in him the signs of heavenly grace.

For good things cannot remain hidden when, according to the Savior’s saying, neither can a lamp be concealed under a bushel nor a city set on a mountain be hidden [Col. 1174B].

Among the other great gifts that the Savior had granted him, he received above all the gift of abstinence and subdued his flesh by very frequent fasts. He taught that a body nourished with excessive food would immediately bring destruction upon the soul.

He wore no footwear at all. Even in midwinter, when those regions are numbed by severe frost, he was always content to walk barefoot, giving a singular example of endurance. The Danube itself bears witness to the severity of that cold, for it was so often frozen by excessive ice that it even provided a solid crossing for wagons.

Yet, though exalted by God’s grace through such virtues, he confessed his profound humility, saying: “Do not think that what you see is the achievement of my merit; it is rather an example for your salvation. Let human presumption cease; let the haughtiness of pride be restrained. We are chosen so that we may do some good, as the Apostle says: ‘He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight.’ Pray, rather, for me, that the Savior’s gifts may advance me not toward an accumulation of condemnation but toward an increase of justification.”

He used to say these and similar things with tears, teaching people by the marvelous example of his humility. Fortified by the foundation of this virtue, he shone with such splendor of divine grace that even heretical enemies honored him with the greatest reverence.

### 12. 

The king of the Rugians, Flaccitheus [Note: Other manuscripts have *Flacitheus*, *Flaciteus*, or *Flacitheus*; Irenicus has *Flactitetus*.], began to waver at the very beginning of his reign. He had the Goths of Lower Pannonia violently hostile to him and was terrified by their innumerable multitude [Note: After Attila’s death they received settlements in Pannonia from the Romans. Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 50.].

In his dangers he therefore consulted the most blessed Severinus as a heavenly oracle. When he was in the greatest distress, he came to him and lamented that he had requested passage to Italy from the Gothic leaders and had no doubt that they would kill him because his request had been denied.

The man of God then gave him this response:

“If one Catholic faith united us, you ought rather to have consulted me concerning eternal life. But since you ask only about present safety, which we share, listen to the instruction you need. You will not be disturbed either by the numbers or by the hostility of the Goths, because, once they depart, you will soon reign in safety with the prosperity you desire. Only do not neglect the admonitions of my humility.

“Do not, then, disdain to seek peace even with the least of men, and never rely upon your own strength. ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and turns his heart away from the Lord,’ says Scripture. Learn, therefore, to avoid ambushes, not to set them. You will pass from this life peacefully in your bed.”

When he departed joyfully after receiving this oracle, word reached him that a band of marauders and barbarians had captured some of the Rugians. He immediately sent to consult the man of God.

Severinus warned him, by holy commands and through a revelation from the Lord, not to pursue the robbers, saying: “If you follow them, you will be killed. Take care not to cross the river and, through rashness, fall into the ambushes prepared for you in three places [Col. 1175C]. For a faithful messenger will soon arrive and inform you of all these things.”

Then two of the captives fled from the enemy’s settlements and reported in order everything that the most blessed man had foretold, Christ having revealed it to him.

Thus, when the ambushes of the adversaries had been frustrated, Flaccitheus, whose fortunes increased with greater prosperity, ended his life in complete tranquility.

### 13. 

After this, a certain man of Rugian race, crushed for twelve years by an unbelievable pain in his bones, had lost all soundness in his limbs. His unbearable torment had become widely known to his neighbors through its very duration.

Since no variety of remedy had helped, his widowed mother finally brought her son, placed in a vehicle, to the holy man. She threw him down before the monastery gate and, amid continual weeping, begged that her only son be restored to her unharmed.

But the man of God, perceiving that great things were being demanded of him, was moved to tears and said: “Why am I oppressed by a deceptive opinion? Why am I thought capable of what I cannot do? It is not within my power to grant such great things. Nevertheless, I shall offer counsel as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord.”

He then ordered the woman to give something to the poor according to her means [Col. 1176A]. Without delay, she quickly removed the garment she was wearing and hastened to distribute it among the needy.

When the man of God heard this, he admired her fervor and again instructed her to cover herself with her own garments, saying: “When your son goes away with you, healed by the Lord, you will fulfill your vows by your deeds.”

He then prescribed, as usual, a fast of several days. After pouring out prayers to God, he immediately healed the sick man and sent him home walking on his own feet.

Later, whenever the man attended the crowded markets, he displayed an astonishing miracle before everyone’s eyes. Some would say: “Look, that is the man who had been broken by bodily corruption.” Others, however, absolutely denied that he was the same person, and a pleasant dispute arose among them.

From the time when health was restored to the man who had been given up for lost, the entire nation of the Rugians began to visit the servant of God and offer him thankful service, asking his help for their illnesses [Col. 1176B]. Many from other peoples, too, to whom the fame of so great a miracle had reached, desired to see Christ’s soldier.

### 14. 

With the same devotion, even before this event certain barbarians, as they were traveling toward Italy, turned aside to him in order to obtain his blessing. Among them was Odovacar, who later ruled Italy [Note: The Belfort manuscript has *Odovacar*; Jordanes, *Odovacer*. Elsewhere he is called *Odobagar* and *Otachar*; Aventinus has *Odagrius* and *Odacer* [Col. 1176D], commonly Odoacer, who became king of Italy in the year 476.].

At that time he came as a tall young man dressed in the most wretched clothing. When he bent down so that the crown of his head would not touch the low roof of the cell, he learned from the man of God that he would become glorious.

When Odovacar was taking his leave, Severinus said to him: “Go to Italy; go, now covered with the poorest hides, but soon destined to bestow many and great gifts upon many.”

## CHAPTER III. Contempt is avenged; he gathers relics and refuses honors.

### 15. 

King Felectheus, also called Fava, son of the aforementioned Flaccitheus [Note: Elsewhere he is called Feletheus, and by Paul the Deacon, book I, chapter 19, Feletheus and Feva. Velser and Lazius, book XII of *The Roman Republic*, read *Fethia*; others have Febanus, Filitheus, Favia, Favianus, and Felteus. The Belfort manuscript has Seva; Braunerus also Faba. Raderus has Feletus; Petrus de Natalibus Feuba; Staibano Feletrus, Selettus, and calls his wife Lisa.], followed his father’s diligence and began, at the beginning of his reign, frequently to visit the holy man.

His savage and harmful wife, named Gisa, was always holding him back from remedies of clemency. Among the other contaminations of her wickedness, she also attempted to rebaptize certain Catholics. But out of reverence for Saint Severinus, since her husband would not consent, she quickly abandoned her sacrilegious intention.

Nevertheless, she burdened the Romans with harsh conditions and even ordered some to be carried away to the Danube. One day, after coming from a nearby village of Favianis, she ordered several men to be brought to her from there, intending to condemn them to the servitude of the most degrading labor.

The man of God sent to her and asked that she release them. But, blazing with the torches of feminine fury, she ordered an exceedingly harsh reply to be brought back:

“Pray for yourself, servant of God, as you hide in your little cell; let us dispose of our slaves as we wish.”

When the man of God heard this, he said: “I trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, because she will be compelled by necessity to accomplish what she has rejected through wicked intention” [Col. 1177A].

Swift punishment followed, bringing down the proud woman’s spirit. She had confined certain barbarian goldsmiths under strict guard in order to manufacture royal ornaments [Note: Aventinus, with his usual recklessness, calls them Roman goldsmiths and embroiderers. He says that Severinus interceded for them and that Gisa’s son was afflicted by illness and healed through Severinus’s prayers.].

On the very day when the queen had despised the servant of God, the young son of the aforesaid king, a small boy named Fridericus, entered their prison in a childish impulse.

The goldsmiths placed a sword against the child’s breast and said that if anyone attempted to enter among them without the prescribed oath [Note: The Belfort manuscript and Baronius add “under protection.”], they would first pierce the royal child and then kill themselves. They had no hope of preserving their own lives, since they had been worn down by prolonged imprisonment.

When the cruel and impious queen heard this, she tore her garments in grief and cried out:

“O servant of God, Severinus, are injuries inflicted by your God avenged in this way? Did you seek this punishment for my contempt through your outpoured prayers, so that you might take vengeance in my own flesh?”

Running about in deep anguish and lamentable mourning, she confessed that she was being struck by the vengeance of the present wound because of the crime of contempt that she had committed against the servant of God.

She immediately dispatched horsemen to seek forgiveness and sent away the Romans whom she had carried off that day, for whose release she had scorned the petitioner. The goldsmiths, upon receiving an oath, immediately released the child and were themselves likewise set free.

When the most reverend servant of Christ heard this, he gave immense thanks to the Creator, who sometimes delays the requests of those who ask so that, as faith, hope, and charity grow, greater things may be granted while lesser things are requested.

The power of the Almighty and Savior had brought this about: while the savage woman had subjected free men to servitude, she was compelled to restore servants to freedom [Col. 1177C].

After these things had been wonderfully obtained, the queen immediately hurried with her husband to the servant of God. She showed him her son, whom she confessed had been rescued from the brink of death through his prayers, and promised never again to oppose his commands.

### 16. 

The servant of God, who had also been endowed with the great grace of prophecy, was especially diligent in ransoming captives. He applied himself earnestly to restoring to genuine freedom those oppressed under barbarian rule.

Meanwhile, after redeeming a certain man together with his wife and children, he ordered him to cross the Danube and seek an unknown man at the barbarians’ market [Note: Velser remarks that this does not mean a public marketplace but a pagan village; both are expressed by the same German word, *Marckt*]. Through divine revelation Severinus had learned so much about the man that he could even indicate the signs of his stature, the color of his hair, the appearance of his face, and the style of his clothing. He also showed in which part of the market the man would be found, adding that, whatever the person found might say to him, he should return and report it promptly to the servant of God.

The man set out and, to his amazement, found everything just as the man of God had foretold.

Questioned by the very man whom he had been amazed to find, he heard him say: “Do you think I can find someone who, for whatever payment he wishes, will take me to the man of God whose fame is spread everywhere? For a long time now I have been earnestly calling upon the holy martyrs whose relics I carry, asking that I may at last be released from such service, unworthy though I am. Until now I have endured it not through rash presumption but through religious necessity.”

The messenger then presented him to the man of God. Severinus received with due honor the relics of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius [Note: They are commemorated on 19 June] and placed them in the basilica that he had built in the monastery, entrusting them to the ministry of priests.

In that place he gathered the sacred relics of many martyrs. Yet he always obtained them only when revelation went before him, knowing that the adversary often creeps in under the name of holiness.

### 17. 

When he was asked to accept the honor of the episcopate [Note: Staibano and Eugenius write that Odoacer offered him a bishopric. Who reports this?], he closed the matter with a prepared answer, saying that it was enough for him that, deprived of the solitude he desired, he had come to that province by divine direction in order to serve the frequent crowds of the afflicted.

Nevertheless, while giving the monks a rule of life, he urged them with anxious care to cling to the footsteps of the blessed fathers, by which instruction in holy conduct might be acquired. They should take care lest anyone who had abandoned parents and the world should, by looking back, desire the allurements of worldly pomp that he had avoided. For this reason he set before them the terrible example of Lot’s wife.

He also reminded them that, through fear of God, the incitements of lust must be put to death. He asserted that the fires of bodily pleasure could be overcome in no other way than by being extinguished through the grace of God in a fountain of tears.

## CHAPTER IV. He helps captives and the afflicted; he corrects sacrilegious persons.

### 18. 

A certain man named Maurus was the sacristan of the monastery’s basilica. Blessed Severinus had redeemed him from the hands of the barbarians.

One day the man of God said to him: “Beware lest you go anywhere today; otherwise you will not escape the danger that threatens.”

Against the command of so great a Father, however, and persuaded by a certain secular man, Maurus went out at midday to gather apples two miles from Favianis. The barbarians soon carried him captive across the Danube together with his persuader.

At that hour, while the man of God was reading in his cell, he suddenly closed his book and said: “Quickly seek Maurus.” When he was found nowhere, Severinus himself immediately crossed the waters of the Ister and hastened after the robbers [Col. 1178D], whom the common people called Scamaros [Note: The Belfort manuscript has *Scameras*. Velser writes that this is not the name of a people but of a type of brigandage.].

Unable to endure his venerable presence, they humbly returned the captives whom they had taken.

### 19. 

While the upper towns of Noricum Ripense still stood and scarcely any fortress avoided barbarian incursions [Note: Surius has *intraret* (“entered”), and Velser does not entirely reject it.], the reputation of Saint Severinus blazed so brightly that the individual fortresses vied with one another to invite him to them for the sake of their defenses [Col. 1179A]. They believed that nothing adverse could happen to them in his presence.

This was not without the grace of a divine gift, so that everyone was terrified by his instructions as though by heavenly oracles and was educated in good works by his example.

The holy man was also invited by the devotions of the inhabitants to a fortress called Cucullis [Note: Surius has *Cocullis*; Petrus de Natalibus *Cocullo*; Lazius *Catullus*, which he thinks is now called Tuln; Staibano and Eugenius say that this took place at Favianis.]. I cannot remain silent about a great miracle that occurred there, which, however, [I learned] from the report of Marcianus, afterward our priest, through whose account we learned the astonishing miracles of that same place [Note: Other copies have *Majorani* and *Majoriani*. Lazius and Velser rightly criticize Marcianus for asserting from this passage that he became bishop of the monastery of Saint Severinus at Favianis [Col. 1180D], immediately after Mamertinus.].

A portion of the people was attached to abominable sacrifices. When the man of God discovered this sacrilege, he addressed the people at length and urged the priest of the place to proclaim a three-day fast. He also ordered candles to be brought from every household, which each person affixed with his own hand to the walls of the church [Col. 1179B].

After the psalmody had been completed in the customary manner, the man of God urged the priest and deacon, at the hour of the sacrifice, to pray with him to the common Lord with complete eagerness of heart, so that he might reveal the light of his knowledge for distinguishing the sacrilegious.

Thus, while he prayed with many and abundant tears and with his knees fixed to the ground, most of the candles brought by the faithful were suddenly lit by divine power. The remaining candles, belonging to those who had been infected by the aforesaid sacrileges and had denied them in their desire to remain hidden, remained unlit.

Those who had placed them, once they had been exposed by divine judgment, immediately cried out and revealed the secrets of their hearts through their confessions. All of them, by the testimony of their own candles, openly acknowledged their sacrileges.

O merciful power of the Creator! While it inflamed the candles and the souls, the fire that was kindled in the candles shone back upon the senses. Visible light melted the wax into flames, and invisible light dissolved the hearts of the confessors into tears.

Who would believe that those whom sacrilegious error had entangled afterward shone more brightly in good works than those whose candles had been divinely kindled?

### 20. 

At another time, in the territory of the same fortress, great numbers of locusts settled and consumed the crops, devastating everything with their destructive bites.

Struck by this plague, the priests and other inhabitants immediately approached Saint Severinus with the most earnest prayers and said:

“To remove the severity of so great a plague, we ask for the proven aid of your prayers, which we recently saw to be of great power with the Lord in the miracle of the kindled candles” [Col. 1179D].

He addressed them with still greater religious seriousness:

“Have you not read what divine authority commanded the sinful people through the prophet: ‘Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping’? And shortly afterward: ‘Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the people, sanctify the Church,’ and the other words that follow.

“Fulfill these commands, so that by worthy works you may easily escape the evil of the present time. Let no one go out to the field, as though he intended by human effort to prevent the locusts, lest the divine indignation be provoked still further.”

Without delay, therefore, everyone gathered in the church, and each person in his proper order sang psalms as usual. Every age and sex, including those unable to pray with the voice, offered prayer to God through tears. Almsgiving did not cease, and whatever good works the present necessity required were fulfilled, as the servant of God had commanded.

While everyone was occupied in such practices, a very poor man abandoned the work of God that had begun and went out to inspect his own crop, which lay very small among the fields of others. Throughout the day, in great anxiety, he drove away as best he could the cloud of locusts that hung overhead. Then he entered the church intending to receive communion.

But the dense mass of locusts devoured his small crop, surrounded as it was by the abundant crops of his neighbors [Col. 1180B]. The locusts were driven from those territories that night by divine command [Note: The Belfort manuscript has “having been expelled”]. Thus it was proved how powerful faithful prayer is.

In the morning, the man who had rashly violated and despised the holy work went out again to his field, falsely confident. He found it completely stripped bare by the locusts. Greatly amazed that all the surrounding sowings remained intact, he returned to the fortress with lamentable cries.

When he had reported what had happened, everyone went out to see such a miracle. There they saw that the locusts’ bites had marked out the stubborn man’s crop as though along a straight measuring line.

He then fell at everyone’s feet and, with an outpouring of lamentation, asked through their intercession for forgiveness of his offense.

Taking this as an opportunity for admonition, the man of God taught everyone to learn obedience to almighty God, whose commands even the locusts obey.

But the aforesaid poor man tearfully pleaded that he could obey the commands thereafter if any hope of living remained to him.

The man of God then addressed the others:

“It is right that the man who has given you an example of humility and obedience by his own punishment should, through your generosity, receive food for the present year.”

Thus, through the contribution of the faithful, the very poor man was corrected and enriched. He learned how much loss unbelief brings and how great a benefit divine generosity grants to those who worship God.

## CHAPTER V. He performs various other miracles.

### 21. 

Near the town called Juba [Note: The Belfort manuscript has *Juvao*. Lazius interprets it as *Juvavo* and *Juvaviam*, but Velser rejects this. Petrus de Natalibus and Staibano have *Joviaco*.], one day, when they entered the basilica in summer to celebrate the evening solemnity, they found no fire with which to light the lamps. They were unable to draw forth a flame by striking stones together as usual. They delayed so long in repeatedly striking iron against stone that the time of the evening service was passing.

But the man of God prayed intently with his knees fixed to the ground. Immediately, before the eyes of the three spiritual men who were then present, the candle held in the hand of Saint Severinus himself was lit [Col. 1181A].

By its light, the evening sacrifice was completed according to custom, and thanks were given to God in all things.

Although the aforementioned holy man wished to conceal this miracle from those who had witnessed it, as he also concealed many great works accomplished through him by divine power, the glory of so great a virtue could not remain hidden. Instead, it splendidly kindled the faith of the others.

### 22

It also happened that a certain woman of the same place, afflicted by a prolonged illness, lay half-dead, with her funeral rites already prepared. Her relatives, with mournful silence, suppressed the funeral lamentations by a certain cry of faith, and laid her body, already almost lifeless, before the door of the holy man’s cell. Seeing that the entrance was blocked by the bier, the man of God said to them: “What is it that you have wished to do?” They replied: “That through your prayer the lifeless woman may be restored to life.”

Then he himself, bursting into tears, exclaimed: “Why do you ask great things of a little man? I recognize that I am wholly unworthy; would that I might deserve to find pardon for my sins!” And they said: “We believe that, if you pray, she will revive.”

Then Saint Severinus immediately poured forth tears and prostrated himself in prayer. When the woman at once rose again, he addressed them: “Do not attribute any of this to my deeds. The fervor of your faith has obtained this grace. And this happens in many places and among many peoples, so that it may be recognized that there is one God, who performs wonders in heaven and on earth, raising the lost to salvation and restoring the dead to life.”

After the woman had recovered her health, on the third day she began, according to the custom of the province, to perform agricultural work with her own hands.

[Note: Belfort reads *opus agrale*; others read *sacrale*.]

### 23

There was a municipality called Quintanis, situated in the Second Rhaetia on the bank of the Danube; on the opposite side a small river called the Businca approached it.

[Note: The *Notitia Imperii*, under the governor of Rhaetia I and II, has “Prefect of the First Flavian Ala of the Rhaetians at Quiotavis.” Antoninus calls it Quintianas. It is now said to be called Kuntzen; Cuspinianus calls it Cuntzing. It is a village on the right bank of the Danube, above Batava.]

[Note: Velser discusses the boundaries of the Rhaetias in Book I of his *Rerum Augustanarum*, and Cluverius in Book V of *Ancient Germany*. They think that the Second Rhaetia was enclosed by Lake Brigantia and the River Inn.]

This stream, swollen by the frequent inundation of the overflowing Danube, occupied parts of the fort, since it had been founded on level ground. The inhabitants of the place also had a church constructed outside the walls from wood. It projected outward on a suspended extension, supported by stakes driven deeply into the ground and by branches; in place of a floor, it had a smooth joining of planks. Whenever the river exceeded its banks, the overflowing water covered it.

The faith of the people of Quintanis therefore summoned Saint Severinus there. When he arrived during a time of drought, he asked why the planks appeared exposed, with their coverings stripped away. The inhabitants replied: “Because, through the frequent inundation of the river, whatever has been laid above them is immediately swept away.”

But he said: “Let a floor now be laid over the planks in the name of Christ; for from now on you will see the river restrained by a heavenly command.”

When the floor had been completed, the man of God himself took an axe, went down below, and, after praying, struck the posts. Then, making the sign of the venerable cross toward the river water, he said: “May my Lord Jesus Christ not allow you to pass beyond this sign of the cross.”

From that time onward, whenever the river rose according to its custom and surrounded the neighboring area as it usually did, it remained so far below the church’s floor that it never at all passed beyond the sign of the holy cross that the man of God had impressed.

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads *Businca*. Velser’s manuscript reads *Quintana*, although Velser himself prefers Surius’s reading, *Quintanica*.]

### 24

It happened that the presbyter of the fort mentioned above, a highly revered man named Silvinus, was dying. After his body had been placed on a bier in the church, they spent the night keeping the customary vigil and singing psalms. As dawn was already increasing, the man of God asked all the weary presbyters and deacons to withdraw for a little while, so that after the labor of the vigil they might refresh themselves somewhat in sleep.

When they had gone out, the man of God asked the church doorkeeper, named Maternus, whether everyone had departed as he had instructed. When Maternus replied that all had gone, Severinus said: “Not at all; someone is hiding here.”

Then the church’s doorkeeper searched the enclosure a second time and testified that no one remained inside. But the soldier of Christ, since the Lord had revealed it to him, said: “I do not know who it is, but someone is hiding here.”

When he searched more carefully for the third time, he found a consecrated virgin who had hidden herself in a more secluded place. The aforementioned doorkeeper rebuked her: “Why did you think that your presence could remain concealed there, while the servant of God was lying here?”

She replied: “Love of devotion persuaded me to do this. When I saw everyone being sent outside, I thought that the servant of Christ, after invoking the divine majesty, would raise the dead man who was present.”

After the aforementioned virgin had gone out, the man of God, together with the presbyter, the deacon, and the two doorkeepers, bowed down in prayer and begged with abundant tears that divine power might display its customary work.

When the prayer was finished, the blessed man addressed the corpse: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, holy presbyter Silvinus, speak with your brothers.”

At once the dead man opened his eyes.

The man of God could scarcely persuade those present to remain silent for joy. Then he said to him again: “Do you wish us to ask the Lord to grant that you may remain longer in this life for the service of his servants?”

But he replied: “By the Lord I adjure you: do not keep me here any longer and deprive me of the everlasting rest in which I already saw myself to be.”

Immediately, after prayer had been offered again, he died and rested.

This deed, through the adjuration of Saint Severinus, was kept so secret that it could not be known before his death. Nevertheless, I learned what I have related from the testimony of the subdeacon Marcus and the doorkeeper Maternus. For the presbyter and the deacon, who had witnessed so great a miracle and had sworn before the holy man that they would reveal what they had seen to no one, are known to have died before him.

[Note: Lazius sometimes calls him Silvinus and sometimes Silvius, and makes him a bishop consecrated by Severinus, although Severinus himself was only a presbyter. Velser rightly reproves that author’s ignorance of ecclesiastical matters and his bad faith, since he presents these things as though drawn from Eugyppius. Aventinus writes that a church still exists at Quintanis, or Kunsen, where Saint Sylvinus, a priest of the Vindelici and a friend of Severinus, is buried. Raderus, in Volume II of *Holy Bavaria*, calls him Blessed; but his memory is faulty, since in Volume I he wrote that only a presbyter and a deacon were present at this miracle.]

## CHAPTER VI. He helps captives, the poor, and the afflicted.

### 25

Thus blessed Severinus, rich in such gifts through the grace of Christ, had undertaken, by the innate compassion within him, so great a care for captives and the needy that almost all the poor throughout the various towns and forts were fed through his efforts. He ministered to them with such joyful concern that he believed himself to be satisfied and abounding in every good only when he saw the bodies of the needy being sustained.

Although he himself was not weakened by the continuous fasts of successive weeks, he nevertheless considered himself afflicted by the hunger of the wretched.

When many observed his pious generosity toward the poor, they endured the pressures of famine under the harsh rule of the barbarians, yet most devoutly gave a tenth of their crops to the poor. Although this commandment was well known to everyone from the Law, they kept it with such devotion that they seemed to hear it from the mouth of an angel present among them.

The man of God also felt the cold intensely in the nakedness of the poor. For he had received from God in a special way the strength to remain vigorous and cheerful in a very cold region, disciplined by wondrous abstinence.

As we have said, he sent letters exhorting the presbyters of Noricum to give the tithes by which the poor might be fed.

[Note: Velser interprets “Noricum” as Mediterranean Noricum whenever “Ripense” is not added.]

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads “the peoples.”]

When, following this custom, they had sent him a considerable supply of clothing for distribution, he asked those who had come whether a similar contribution would also be sent from the city of Tiburnia.

[Note: Surius, Lazius, and others interpret this as Tigurina, Tiberina, or Tiberia; some understand it as Regensburg, or Reginoburg, but not very plausibly, since in Eugyppius’s time Tiburnia was the metropolis of Noricum, while Regensburg was a city of the Second Rhaetia. Aventinus makes it the town of Saint Vitus in Carinthia and says that traces of Tiburnia still exist there. Ptolemy has the Norican city Τεουρνία (*Teournía*); perhaps Τεουρτία (*Teourtía*) was written for Teburnia or Tiburnia. Cluverius thinks it was the town of Villach on the Drava. Velser considers the word *Tiburnia* suspect; it existed in the manuscript of Belfort and is retained by Braunerus. Teurnia is listed among the towns of Noricum, and by Linius in Book III, chapter 24.]

When they replied that a contribution would immediately come from there as well, the man of God did not indicate that they would come, but foretold that their offering, delayed, would be given to the barbarians.

Not long afterward, therefore, the citizens of Tiburnia, fighting the Goths who were besieging them in various engagements, scarcely having entered into a treaty, among other things also offered to the enemy the contribution that had already been gathered into one collection and that they had undertaken to send to the servant of God, just as he had foretold.

### 26

The citizens of Lauriacum, once frequently admonished by Saint Severinus, had delayed giving the tithes of their crops to the poor.

[Note: Others write *Laureacum*. It is now said to be a small village under the jurisdiction of the town of Enns, still retaining the ancient name Lorch. Lauriacum is mentioned by Antoninus in the *Itinerary* and in the *Notitia Imperii*, which places there the prefect of the Second Legion and subsequently also mentions the prefect of the Lauriacensian fleet. Velser considers it a work of Marcus Aurelius, or rather of Aurelian, in Book III of his *Boian Affairs*.]

When famine pressed upon them, and the ripening grain was already turning yellow, the nearby means of relief were plainly visible. But when the unexpected blight of rust appeared and damaged the crops, they soon came to him, prostrated themselves, and confessed the punishment of their disobedience.

The soldier of Christ comforted them with spiritual words, saying: “If you had offered tithes to the poor, you would not only have enjoyed an eternal reward, but also would have been able to abound comfortably in present goods. But because you chastise your fault by confessing it, I promise, relying on the Lord’s compassion, that the present rust will not utterly destroy the crops with such force. Only let your faith not waver henceforth.”

This promise made the citizens more ready from that day onward to pay their tithes. Then, as he was accustomed to do, he instructed the local official to proclaim a fast. When it had been completed, a gentle rain removed the danger threatening the harvest.

### 27

The town called Patavis was situated between two rivers, namely the Inn and the Danube. There blessed Severinus had founded a small cell in the usual manner with a few men, because the citizens repeatedly asked him to come there, especially on account of the constant incursions of the Alamanni, whose king, Gibuldus, loved him with the greatest reverence.
