[Note: We discussed him on January 7 in the Life of Saint Valentine. The correct form is *Batava*, according to the *Notitia Imperii*, under the governor of Rhaetia: “Tribune of the New Cohort of the Batavi at Batavis.”]

[Note: Their power was then considerable in Greater Germany. From there they advanced also into Rhaetia and even into Belgica, where they were shortly afterward defeated in a memorable battle by Clovis, king of the Franks, at the town of Tolbiac, in the year of Christ 496.]

At one time Gibuldus eagerly came to see him.

[Note: From this one may infer Aventinus’s bad faith, since he writes that Gibuldus merely pretended to come in order to visit Severinus.]

The saint went out to meet him so that his arrival would not burden that city, and he addressed the king with such firmness that the latter began to tremble violently in his presence. Later he told his armies that he had never been shaken by such trembling, whether in warfare or through any other fear.

When he offered the servant of God the choice of obtaining whatever he wished, the most compassionate teacher asked him instead to restrain his people from ravaging Roman territory and gladly to release the captives whom his men had taken.

The king then decided to send someone from his own people to carry out this task as quickly as possible. Immediately the deacon Amantius was sent; he followed the king without delay and, keeping watch before his door, was unable for many days to gain an audience.

As he was returning in the deepest sorrow because the matter for which he had been sent had not been accomplished, a certain man appeared to him bearing the likeness of Saint Severinus. Frightening him with a threatening summons, he ordered him to follow.

Terrified but hastening after him, Amantius reached the king’s door. At once the guide who had gone before him vanished from the astonished man’s sight.

The king’s messenger then asked the deacon where he was from and what he hoped to obtain. He briefly explained the matter, presented the letters to the king, received the king’s reply, and returned.

After being dismissed, he brought back nearly seventy captives, together with the king’s welcome promise: once he had carefully traveled through the province, he would release as many captives as he found there.

For this purpose Saint Lucillus the presbyter was later sent and brought back a great number of wretched people from captivity.

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads *Lucellus*. Lazius makes him bishop of Batava, and then of Faviana, without an authority. Aventinus calls him Bishop Lucillus.]

## CHAPTER VII. He foretells various things through the divine Spirit.

### 28

During the period when the Roman Empire still stood, soldiers from many towns were maintained at public expense to guard the frontier. When this practice came to an end, the military units were likewise disbanded. Nevertheless, some men continued from the Batavian frontier to Italy, to bring the last pay to their comrades, whom no one had recognized as having been killed by the barbarians on the journey.

[Note: Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 18. He says that he had become a horse and, among other animals, had carried provisions for the soldiers—what is called *retica*, because it is carried to the Rhaetians. Vives says that *retia* and *reticulum* denote a kind of sack in which travelers were accustomed to carry bread, meat, and apples. Velser instead reads *Rhaetica*, because it was carried to the Rhaetias, and thinks that the pay was conveyed at the same time. Indeed, Augustine is speaking there of Italy.]

One day, while Saint Severinus was reading in his cell, he suddenly closed the book and began to weep with a deep sigh. He ordered the young men standing nearby to hurry to the river, which, he affirmed, was at that very hour being stained with human blood. Immediately it was reported that the bodies of the aforementioned soldiers had been carried onto the bank by the force of the river.

### 29

A certain presbyter named Paulinus came to Saint Severinus, as his fame spread ever more widely.

[Note: The men of Regensburg begin their catalogue of bishops with this Paulinus. Conrad of the Mountain of Maidens is said to have been the first to write it. Velser refutes this, with our Raderus agreeing. This is clear from what was said above in chapter 6.]

After spending several days in the company of the blessed man, when he wished to return, Paulinus heard Severinus say to him: “Venerable presbyter, hasten, because soon the dignity of the episcopate will adorn you, though, as we believe, you resist the desires of the peoples.”

As soon as he returned to his homeland, the words of the one who had foretold this were fulfilled. For the citizens of Tiburnia, which is the metropolis of Noricum, compelled that man to accept the primacy of the highest priesthood.

### 30

Outside the walls of the town of Batava, at a place called Boitro across the River Inn, where Severinus himself had built a small cell for a few monks, the relics of martyrs were being sought.

[Note: Lazius reads *Boiotro*. This seems to be the place Ptolemy calls Boiodurum in Table 5 of Europe, chapter 14, and assigns to Vindelicia, since the Inn flows between Batava and Boiodurum and forms the boundary between Noricum and Vindelicia. Antoninus and the *Notitia Imperii* have *Boiodorum*; the Peutinger Table has *Bolodorum*. It is now called Instat, as though one said “the city of the Inn.” There is a small river there called Boiter or Boitra, which preserves the ancient name. A church dedicated to Saint Severinus is still seen there and preserves the memory of the cell mentioned here.]

When the presbyters pressed forward, asking that they be sent to bring the relics to the sanctuary, blessed Severinus gave them this warning:

“Although all buildings constructed by mortal labor perish, these buildings nevertheless must be abandoned more quickly than the others. Therefore no labor should be undertaken to obtain the relics of the saints, because the blessing of Saint John will be brought to them of its own accord.”

Meanwhile, the citizens of the aforementioned town approached the blessed man humbly and asked him to go to Fava, the prince of the Rugians, to seek permission for them to engage in commerce.

[Note: *Favam* seems to be the correct reading.]

He replied: “The time of this town is approaching when it will remain deserted, like the other earlier forts abandoned by their inhabitants. Why, then, is it necessary to provide merchandise for places where a merchant will no longer be able to appear?”

When they replied that they ought not to be despised but should be supported by the customary government, a certain presbyter, filled with a diabolical spirit, added: “Go, I beg you, holy father, go quickly, so that during your absence we may rest for a little while from fasts and vigils.”

At these words the man of God was overcome by immense tears, because the priest had burst into ridiculous foolishness before everyone who heard him. For open buffoonery testifies to hidden sins.

The brothers therefore asked the holy man why he was weeping so. He replied: “I see that, while we are absent, a most grievous blow will immediately befall this place, and the shrines of Christ”—which, he said, he was compelled to express only with groans—“will overflow with human blood. Indeed, this place itself will be violated, for they were speaking in the baptistery.”

He therefore went down by boat to his ancient and greatest monastery, near the walls of the town of Faviana, which was more than one hundred miles away.

[Note: This is reckoned at approximately forty German miles between Passau and Vienna.]

As soon as he had departed, Chunimundus, accompanied by a few barbarians, attacked the town of Batava, just as the saint had foretold. Since almost all the inhabitants were occupied in the harvest, he killed the forty men of the town who had remained behind to guard it.

He also killed that presbyter who had spoken so sacrilegiously against the servant of Christ in the baptistery when the priest, fleeing to the same place, was overtaken by the pursuing barbarians. For the enemy of truth had come there in vain, having offended God, to the very place where he had acted so shamelessly.

[Note: Aventinus makes him a bishop and interprets—or rather corrupts—the joke previously directed against the saint as follows: “Go, then, wherever among the nations you wish,” he said, “for if you remain here longer, we shall all perish from hunger, as you threaten.”]

[Note: Jornandes reads *Hunimundus*; Belfort reads *Humibundus*. He was king of the Suebi.]

### 31

Thus, while the most holy Severinus was reading the Gospel in the monastery at Faviana, he rose after completing his prayer and immediately ordered a small boat to be prepared. To those who were present and wondered at this, he said: “Blessed be the name of the Lord; we must go to meet the relics of the blessed martyrs.”

Without delay they crossed the Danube. On the farther bank of the river they found a man sitting there and earnestly begging them to be taken to the servant of God, to whom he had long wished to come after hearing of him through widespread report.

When the servant of Christ had been pointed out to him, the man humbly offered him relics of Saint John the Baptist, which he had kept with him for many years.

The servant of God received them with due reverence and, as he had foretold, consecrated the basilica of Saint John by the spontaneously bestowed blessing, through the ministry of priests.

### 32

Severinus was also warned by his customary revelation concerning the inhabitants of a town called Jopia, situated more than seventy miles from Batava.

[Note: Aventinus, Hundius, and others read *Juvavia*, which is now Salzburg. The manuscript of Belfort reads *Lubianum*. Raderus reads *Topia*.]

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads “twenty.”]

He sent to them Moderatus, the church’s cantor, instructing him to order all the inhabitants to leave that settlement without delay, for they would soon perish if they disobeyed the command.

Some doubted such a great prophecy; others utterly refused to believe it. Severinus therefore sent again a certain Quintasius.

[Note: Belfort reads *Quintarius*.]

Weeping, he said to him: “Go more quickly and warn them that, if they remain there this night, they will be captured without delay.”

He also ordered Saint Maximus, a presbyter of spiritual life, to be warned with greater urgency, so that he at least might leave the despisers behind and hasten to be rescued by heavenly mercy. The servant of God said that he was deeply troubled on his behalf, lest by delaying the saving command he should fall into the impending destruction.

[Note: Belfort reads *Maximianus*. Lazius and Aventinus, without tables or witnesses, make him a bishop. Raderus, in Volume I of *Holy Bavaria*, calls him a saint and martyr.]

The man sent above therefore went and carried out his orders. While the others remained wavering in disbelief, the messenger of the man of God would not in any way consent to the presbyter’s wish to retain him and offer him hospitality.

That night the Heruli unexpectedly attacked at once, devastated the town, and carried away many captives. They hanged the aforementioned presbyter on a gallows.

[Note: Lazius attributes this incursion to the Alamanni; Aventinus to the Heruli, Alamanni, and other German peoples. Paul the Deacon mentions it in Book I, chapter 20. In chapter 9 he lists the Heruli among the peoples related to Odoacer’s ancestors. Braunerus attributes the sack of Juvavia itself to Odoacer.]

[Note: Aventinus adds: “Together with him they slaughtered more than fifty-five fellow priests, and hurled them headlong from the caves in the rocks where they had fled, as is still shown. They are said to have been buried in the church of Saint Amandus, now Saint Margaret’s. Bruschius also discusses them in his account of Patavia and says that those caves are still shown at Salzburg near Saint Peter’s. Braunerus agreed, as we said above.”]

When the servant of God heard this, he grieved deeply that those who had been warned had paid no attention.

### 33

A certain man from Noricum, named Maximinus, regularly visited the servant of God.

[Note: He is called Maximus below.]

Because of the familiarity he had formed with the holy man, he stayed several days in his monastery. There he was informed in Severinus’s presence that his homeland would suddenly suffer a grave disaster.

After receiving letters addressed to Saint Paulinus the bishop, he returned with all haste.

The aforementioned bishop, instructed by the contents of the letters, strongly warned all the dioceses and forts in his own writings that they should meet the impending destruction by observing the three-day fast prescribed in the letters of the man of God.

When they had fulfilled the command, the fast ended, and behold: a very large host of Alamanni savagely devastated everything. Yet the forts experienced no danger, for the faithful armor of the fast and the praiseworthy humility of heart had confidently armed them against the ferocity of the enemy.

## CHAPTER VIII. He aids those in danger, the sick, and the needy.

### 34

After this, a certain leper from the territory of Milan went to Saint Severinus, drawn by the fame of the saint. He humbly implored remedies for his health, and Severinus commended him to his monks, imposing a fast upon them. The man was immediately cleansed by the grace of God.

When he had recovered his health and was being urged to return to his homeland, he cast himself at the feet of the holy man and begged not to be forced to return to his own people. He desired, that is, to escape the leprosy of sins as he had escaped that of the flesh and to end his life in that same place with a praiseworthy death.

The man of God greatly admired his religious disposition. By paternal authority he ordered a few monks to remain with him in continual prayer, observing frequent fasts with him, so that the Lord might grant him whatever was necessary.

Thus fortified by such remedies, within the space of two months he was released from the bonds of mortal life.

### 35

At the same time, the inhabitants of Quintanis, exhausted by the frequent incursions of the Alamanni, abandoned their homes and migrated to the town of Batava.

But this refuge did not escape the notice of the same barbarians. For this reason they were inflamed all the more, believing that they could plunder the populations of the two towns in a single attack.

Blessed Severinus, however, applying himself more earnestly to prayer, repeatedly exhorted the Romans with saving examples. He foretold that, with God’s present help, the enemy would indeed be overcome, but that after the victory those who disregarded his warnings would perish.

Thus all the Romans, strengthened by the holy man’s prophecy and relying on the promised victory, drew up their battle line against the Alamanni. They were fortified not so much by material weapons as by the prayers of the holy man.

When the Alamanni had been defeated and put to flight in the battle, the man of God addressed the victors:

“My sons, do not attribute the triumph of this present battle to your own strength. Know that you have now been freed by God’s protection, so that from here you may depart after a short interval, as though a brief truce had been granted.

“Gather with me, therefore, and descend to the town of Lauriacum.”

Thus the man of God, full of compassion, admonished them. But when the people of Batava hesitated to leave their native soil, he added:

“Although the town to which we are going must also soon be abandoned when barbarism advances, let us nevertheless all depart from here together now.”

Many followed those admonitions. Some were found to be obstinate, and the sword of the enemy did not fail to punish those who despised them.

For all who remained there contrary to the prohibition of the man of God paid the penalty of their contempt when the Thuringi invaded that same week: some were slaughtered, and others were led into captivity.

[Note: Velser prefers *Turcilingi*, who lived not far from there and were the ancestors of Odoacer.]

### 36

After the destruction of the towns in the upper part of the Danube, the people who had obeyed Saint Severinus’s warnings migrated into the town of Lauriacum. He fortified them by constant exhortations, warning them not to rely on their own strength, but to devote themselves to prayers, fasts, and almsgiving and to arm themselves instead with spiritual weapons.

One day the man of God ordered all the poor to assemble in a single basilica, intending to distribute oil as necessity required. In those regions this commodity was exceedingly difficult to obtain, being brought only by the transport of merchants.

As though to receive a blessing, therefore, a larger crowd of needy people gathered. The precious foodstuff provided by the oil increased both the crowd and the number of those asking for it.

Then, after completing his prayer and making the sign of the cross, blessed Severinus uttered for all to hear his customary words from Holy Scripture: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

He then began with his own hand to fill the vessels brought by the assistants. The faithful servant imitated his Lord, who had come not to be served but to serve; following the Savior’s footsteps, he rejoiced as the supply increased, pouring with his right hand while his left knew nothing of the service.

When the poor people’s vessels had been filled, nothing diminished in the hands of those who were distributing it.

While those standing around silently marveled at so great a benefit of God, one of them, named Biennius, was terrified by great fear and cried out: “My lord, this cauldron of oil is increasing here and overflowing like a spring!”

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads “the wisest.”]

As soon as the miraculous power had been disclosed, the most welcome liquid ceased to flow. Immediately the servant of Christ exclaimed to him: “What have you done, brother? You have obstructed the benefit of many. May the Lord Jesus Christ forgive you.”

Thus once a widow, weighed down by debts, was instructed by the command of the prophet Elisha to fill as many vessels as possible from the small amount of oil she possessed. When she had done this, and her son was still asking for vessels, as soon as she reported that no vessels remained, the oil stopped.

### 37

At the same time Maximus of Noricum, whom we mentioned above, inflamed by the warmth of faith, tried to come to blessed Severinus in the middle of winter, when the roads of that region are closed by rigid frost. His journey was a bold undertaking—or rather, as later became clear, one of fearless devotion.

He hired many companions to carry around their necks clothing intended for captives and the poor, which the religious collection of the Noricans had gathered.

[Note: This clearly shows that Paulinus, the bishop of this Maximus—or Maximinus, as he is called in number 33—was not the bishop of Regensburg; nor was Tiburnia Regensburg.]

They advanced until they reached the highest summits of the Alps. There such a great quantity of snow fell throughout the night that, enclosing them as though they were sunk in a vast pit, it surrounded them beneath the protection of a great tree.

When they had entirely abandoned hope for their lives, the leader of the companions saw in sleep a man standing in the likeness of the man of God and saying to him: “Do not be afraid; continue toward the place where you began.”

Immediately encouraged by this revelation, they began to advance more by faith than by their feet. Suddenly, by divine command, a bear of enormous size appeared from the side, as though to show them the way. The animal customarily hid itself in caves during winter; it now opened the desired route.

For approximately two hundred miles it showed them the road they desired, turning neither to the left nor to the right. It went ahead of them at precisely the distance necessary to prepare a path with its fresh tracks.

[Note: Belfort reads “recent track.”]

Thus the beast proceeded through the desolation of the wilderness and did not abandon the men who were carrying aid to the needy. It led them as far as it could, with a kindness almost human, to the dwellings of men; then, having completed its task, it turned aside in another direction.

By performing so great a service as their guide, it showed what human beings ought to do for human beings and how much charity they ought to extend, since a savage beast had shown a road to men in despair.

When word was brought to the servant of God that those men had arrived, he said: “Blessed be the name of the Lord. Let those enter whom the bear opened a road to come here.”

When they heard this, they were filled with astonishment, for they marveled that the man of God related what had happened in his absence.

## CHAPTER IX. He is a protection to many against enemies and revered by barbarians.

### 38

The citizens of Lauriacum and the fugitives from the upper forts appointed scouts to suspicious locations and took every possible human precaution against the enemy.

But the servant of God, warned by divine inspiration, prepared them with prophetic foresight, instructing them to enclose within the walls all the supplies sufficient for their poverty, so that the savage attack of the enemy, finding no human provisions, would immediately be compelled by hunger to abandon its monstrous acts of cruelty.

He testified to this for three days.

[Note: The manuscript of Belfort reads “for four days.”]

As evening was already falling, he sent a monk named Valens to Saint Constantius, the bishop of that place, and to the others living there, saying: “Keep a stricter watch tonight, stationing guards along the walls according to custom, and beware of the ambushes of the approaching enemy.”

But they insisted that, according to the scouts, they had perceived absolutely nothing adverse.

The herald of Christ nevertheless did not cease to warn them. When they doubted, he cried out in a loud voice that they would be captured that very night unless they faithfully obeyed his commands, repeatedly saying: “Stone me if I have lied.”

At last they were compelled to keep watch on the walls. After completing the customary psalmody at the beginning of the night, they began to maintain a very numerous watch.

A heap of hay lying nearby was accidentally set alight by the torch of an unwilling bearer; it gave the city light but did not set it on fire.

At this, everyone began shouting. The enemy, who had been concealed in the woods, was suddenly terrified by the brightness and the shouting. Thinking that they had been detected in advance, they remained quiet.

When morning came, they surrounded the city and ran about everywhere. Finding no provisions, they plundered the herd of animals belonging to a certain man who, despite the servant of God’s prophecy, had obstinately refused to protect his possessions. Then they withdrew.

After they had departed, the citizens left through the gates and found, not far from the walls, ladders lying on the ground. The barbarians had thrown them down during the night, intending to destroy the city, but had been disturbed by the shouts of the watchmen.

Therefore the aforementioned citizens humbly asked the servant of Christ for pardon, confessing that their hearts were harder than stones. By what had now happened before their eyes, they recognized that prophetic grace had been active in the holy man.

The entire disobedient population would have been taken captive in a single attack had not the customary prayer of the man of God preserved it in freedom, as the Apostle James testifies: “The constant prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.”

39. Feletheus, king of the Rugians, also called Fava, hearing that the survivors of all the towns which had escaped the barbarians’ swords had betaken themselves to Lauriacum under the protection of the servant of God, came with an army, intending suddenly to seize them and settle them in the towns subject to him and nearby—among which was Favianis—which were separated from the Rugians only by the Danube. [Note: [Col. 1191D] It does not, however, follow from this that a royal residence of the Rugians stood there, as Lazius wrote; for the Rugians still lived beyond the Danube, while they either possessed certain towns in Noricum as tributaries or protected them against other barbarians in return for an agreed payment.]

Therefore everyone was greatly alarmed, and they humbly approached Saint Severinus, asking him to go out to meet the king and soften his mind. Hastening throughout the whole night, he met him at dawn at the twentieth mile from the city.

The king, immediately terrified at his arrival, declared that he was greatly distressed by Severinus’s fatigue and asked the reason for his sudden journey. The servant of God replied:

“Peace be with you, excellent king. I come as Christ’s envoy, to seek pardon for your subjects. Recall the grace and remember the divine benefits by which your father often felt himself assisted. For throughout all the days of his reign he never dared to undertake anything without consulting me. By not resisting wholesome counsels, he recognized through repeated successes how much an obedient spirit could accomplish, and how greatly it benefits conquerors not to grow proud of their victories.”

The king said: “I shall not allow this people, for whom you approach as a kindly advocate, to be laid waste by the savage plundering of the wicked Alamanni or Thuringians [Note: [Col. 1192D] Velserus prefers ‘Turcilingi’], slaughtered by the sword, or reduced to servitude, since we have towns and fortresses in which they ought to be settled.”

The servant of Christ replied firmly:

“Were these people rescued from the repeated devastation of raiders by your bow and sword, and not rather preserved by God’s gift so that they might for a short while serve you? Therefore, excellent king, do not reject my counsel. Entrust these subjects to my faith, lest they be devastated by the compulsion of so great an army rather than transferred. For I trust in my Lord that he who made me share in their calamities will make me capable of leading them to the promised places.”

When the king heard this, he was softened by the moderate arguments and returned with his army. Thus the Romans whom Saint Severinus had taken under his protection departed from Lauriacum under peaceful arrangements and lived in friendly alliance with the Rugians.

Severinus himself, dwelling at Favianis in his ancient monastery, did not cease either to admonish the peoples or to foretell the future, asserting that all of them would migrate into the Roman province without suffering any loss of liberty.

40. At the same time, King Odovacar sent Saint Severinus friendly letters, humbly offering him whatever he might consider worth hoping for, mindful of the prophecy by which Severinus had once declared that he would become king.

Thus, invited by such great appeals, the saint asked that a certain exiled Ambrosius be released. Odovacar gladly obeyed his command.

On another occasion, while many nobles were praising the aforementioned king before the holy man with the human flattery customary on such occasions, Severinus asked which king they were exalting with such praises. When they replied, “King Odovacar,” he said:

“Odovacar, upright and whole, will reign for thirteen and fourteen years”—that is, for thirteen complete years and into the fourteenth. Then, indicating the end of his reign, [Note: [Col. 1192D] Velserus suspects that something is missing here] he added that they would soon prove the truth of what he had foretold.

## CHAPTER X  
### He cures illnesses, foretells dangers, and averts them

41. Saint Severinus came when he had been humbly summoned by the townspeople of Comagena, among whom he had first become known. When his arrival became known, one of the nobles of King Feletheus crossed the Danube and threw at his feet his adolescent son, who had long been afflicted with illness and for whom he was already preparing a funeral. Weeping, he said:

“I believe, man of God, that through you I can swiftly obtain divine healing for my son.”

After prayer had been offered, the boy—who had been brought half-dead—immediately rose, to his father’s amazement, and at once returned home in perfect health.

42. A certain elephantiasis sufferer named Telo [Note: [Col. 1192D] Surius has “Thegio”], summoned from distant regions by the miracles of Saint Severinus, came asking to be cleansed through his prayers. Having received the customary instruction, he was ordered to implore God, the giver of every grace, continually and with tearful supplication.

What more is needed? Through the prayers of the blessed man, that same leper was cleansed by divine assistance. As he changed his conduct for the better, he also merited a change in his complexion, proclaiming far and wide the great deeds of the eternal King both by his own voice and through the voices of many others.

43. Bonosus likewise, a monk of blessed Severinus, barbarian by birth and devoted to his responses, was greatly afflicted by weakness of the eyes. He asked that healing be granted him through Severinus’s prayer, distressed that newcomers and outsiders should experience the assistance of saving grace while no help of any kind was being offered to him.

The servant of God said to him:

“My son, it is not good for you to have clear sight in your bodily eyes and to display the bright vision of the outward eye. Pray rather that your inner vision may be strengthened.”

Thus instructed by such counsels, he took pains to see more with his heart than with his body. He merited, without any weariness, to persevere wonderfully and continually in prayer, and, remaining nearly forty years in the monastery’s vigils, he passed to the Lord with the same ardor of faith with which he had entered religious life.

44. At the place called Boitro, mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1193D] Surius has “Barotro”; Belfort has “Bolotlo,” incorrectly], the humble teacher found three monks of his monastery stained by the foulness of pride. Since he had rebuked each of them for his offenses and found that they persisted in their ruin, he prayed that the Lord, receiving them into the adoption of sons, would deign to chastise them with a father’s scourge.

Before he had finished his prayer with streaming tears, at one and the same moment those monks were seized and tormented by a demon. In pitiable voices they confessed their obstinacy, the arrogance of their breasts, and the pride of their hearts.

Let no one consider this cruel or harmful, since such persons were handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, as the blessed Apostle teaches, “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” [Note: [Col. 1193D] Paulinus relates this in his Life of Saint Ambrose, 7 December.] For Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, when he discovered that a servant of Stilicho was the author of false letters, said that he ought to be handed over to Satan, so that he would not dare to commit such acts in the future. At that very moment, while the words were still in the priest’s mouth, an unclean spirit seized the man and began to tear him apart. [Note: [Col. 1193D] This is related in Dialogue I, chapter 5, and in Book IV of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 5 [Col. 1194D].]

Severus Sulpicius also reports, on the testimony of Postumianus, that a man remarkable for great virtues and miracles, in order to drive from his heart the empty vanity of boasting into which he had fallen, begged that the devil be permitted to exercise power over him for five months, so that he might become like those whom he himself had healed. A little later he says:

“Accordingly, seized by a demon and held in chains, he endured everything that the possessed ordinarily suffer. At last, in the fifth month, he was healed—not only of the demon, but, what was more useful and desirable for him, of the vanity of exaltation.”

The man of God therefore assigned the aforementioned monks to the brothers for forty days of severe ascetic remedies. When these had been completed, he prayed over them, delivered them from the power of the demon, and granted them not only bodily health but also health of mind. After this deed, reverence for the holy man increased, and a greater fear of discipline took hold of the others.

45. He had sent the monk Marcianus, who later became the priest in charge of our monastery, to Noricum with his brother Renatus. When the third day was passing, he said to the brothers:

“Pray, dearest ones, because at this hour a serious tribulation is pressing upon Marcianus and Renatus; nevertheless, they will soon be delivered from it by Christ’s help.”

Then the monks immediately wrote down what he had said. When the two returned many months later and indicated the day and hour of the danger at which they had escaped from the barbarians, they confirmed that it was exactly as the monks had recorded it.

46. Likewise, the most blessed Severinus suddenly ordered a monk named Ursus to undertake forty days of stricter fasting, meeting the coming calamity with abstinence from food and lamentation. He said:

“Bodily danger threatens you; you will expiate it through the remedies of a little bread and water, with God’s protection.”

On the fortieth day, a deadly pustule appeared on the fasting man’s arm, and he immediately entered and humbly showed it to Severinus. The holy servant of God said to him:

“Do not fear the danger foretold to you forty days ago.”

Then, at once drawing the sign of the cross over it with his own hand, he caused the deadly pustule to vanish, to the amazement of those present.

It is enough to have related this one instance of healings among his own household, so as to avoid the weariness of an overly long work. For, often, when Christ revealed the illnesses of his monks to him, he foretold them and healed them with the same gifts by which he had foreseen them.

47. The spiritual teacher lived no farther away from his disciples’ cell, persevering continually in prayer and abstinence. With them, however, he solemnly completed the morning prayers and the psalmody proper to the beginning of the night; he completed the remaining periods of prayer in the small oratory where he lived.

There he was often instructed by heavenly revelations. By God’s grace he foretold many future events, and, learning the hidden matters of many people, he brought them to light when necessary. He provided remedies for each person according to the nature of the illness.

His bed was a single hair shirt spread on the floor of the oratory. At all times he used the same garment that he wore, even when resting. He never broke his fast before sunset except on an appointed feast. During Lent, content with one meal a week, he remained radiant with the same cheerful expression. He mourned the sins of others as though they were his own and moderated them by whatever means he could.

## CHAPTER XI  
### He foretells his death, instructs his people and kings with admonitions, and dies

48. After many struggles and prolonged battles, when blessed Severinus perceived through the Lord’s revelation that he was about to depart from this world, he sent word to the aforementioned Rugian king Fava and his most cruel wife, named Gisa, to come to him.

After exhorting the king with saving admonitions—urging him to conduct himself toward his subjects in such a way that he would continually remember that he must render an account to the Lord for the state of his kingdom—and after fearlessly warning him in other words, [Note: [Col. 1194D] Staibanus writes that he took the queen’s hand, incorrectly, as is clear] he extended his hand and pointed to the king’s breast. Then he challenged the queen with these questions:

“Gisa, do you love this soul more, or gold and silver?”

When she replied that she preferred her husband to all riches, the man of God wisely said:

“Then cease to oppress the innocent, lest their affliction destroy your power even more; for you often undermine the king’s gentleness.”

She replied:

“Why do you regard us in this way, servant of God?”

He answered:

“I, a humble man who am already about to depart to the Lord, solemnly warn you to refrain from wicked deeds and to dignify your conduct with pious works. Until now, by the Lord’s providence, your kingdom has prospered; from this point onward, see to yourselves.”

Instructed sufficiently by these admonitions, the king and his wife took their leave and departed.

49. Then the saint did not cease to address his people with the sweetness of charity concerning the nearness of his departure—indeed, he had never previously ceased to do so.

“Know, brothers,” he said, “that just as the children of Israel were rescued from the land of Egypt, so all the people of this land must be freed from the unjust domination of the barbarians. For all of them, emigrating from these towns with their possessions, will reach the Roman province without being taken captive.

“But remember the command of the holy patriarch Joseph, whose testimony I, unworthy and most insignificant, bring before you: ‘The Lord will surely visit you, and you shall carry my bones away with you from here.’ This will not benefit me, but you.

“For these places, now crowded with inhabitants, will be reduced to such a vast solitude that the enemy, expecting to find an abundance of gold, will even dig up the graves of the dead.”

The truth of this prophecy was confirmed by the course of present events. Therefore the Father of the holiest character prudently ordered that his little body be raised, so that, when the general migration of the people occurred, the undivided community of the brothers whom he had gathered might depart and remain united in one bond of holy fellowship through the memory of him.

50. More than two years beforehand, he also indicated by this sign the day on which blessed Severinus would depart from the body.

On the day of Epiphany, when the holy presbyter Lucillus anxiously informed him that on the following day he would celebrate with annual solemnity the day of deposition of his abbot, Saint Valentinus, formerly bishop of Raetia [Note: [Col. 1195D] We discussed him on 7 January], that same servant of God replied:

“If blessed Valentinus has entrusted you with celebrating these solemn rites, then I too leave you, for observance on that same day, the duties of my vigils, since I shall be departing from the body.”

Trembling at these words, Lucillus, an aged man, commended himself to him even more earnestly, as though he would be the first to depart. Severinus added:

“This will happen, holy presbyter, just as you have heard; for what the Lord has decreed will not pass away through human will.”

51. Moreover, when Fridericus received from his brother, the Rugian king Fava, one of the few towns that remained on the bank of the Danube—Favianis, beside which Saint Severinus lived, as I have related—Fridericus came to him, as was customary, to pay his respects.

The soldier of Christ began to speak to him at length about his own departure, declaring solemnly:

“Know that I shall soon depart to the Lord. Therefore, warned in advance, take care that, after my departure, you do not attempt to touch any of the things entrusted to me or lay hands upon the property of the poor and captives, lest, God forbid, you experience divine indignation for such presumption.”

Struck by this unexpected admonition, Fridericus said:

“Why do you confound us with such a warning, when we do not wish to be deprived of such great protections and when it is fitting that we should contribute something to your holy generosity, which is known to all, rather than take anything away? Thus, as did our father Flaccitheus, we may deserve to be fortified by your prayer; he learned by experience that he had always been helped by the merits of your holiness.”

Severinus replied:

“Whatever the occasion, if you wish to harm my cell, you will experience here and pay in the future a vengeance which I do not desire for you.”

Then Fridericus promised to observe the servant of Christ’s admonitions and returned home.

The most gracious teacher, however, did not cease to address his disciples from moment to moment, saying:

“I trust in the grace of my Christ Jesus that, while you persevere in his work and remain joined together in peaceful fellowship in memory of me, he will grant you the goods of eternal life and will not deny you the consolations of the present life.”

52. On the Nones of January he began to be lightly afflicted by pain in his side. After it had lasted for three days, in the middle of the night he ordered the brothers to be present. He admonished them concerning his death and strengthened them with paternal instruction, earnestly and wonderfully continuing in these words:

“Dearest sons in Christ, you know that blessed Jacob, when the condition of death was approaching, ordered his sons to be present and, rewarding each one with the words of prophetic blessing, disclosed the mysteries of future events.

“But we, insignificant and lukewarm, unequal to such great holiness, do not dare to claim this prerogative for ourselves. Nevertheless, I shall not be silent about one thing suitable to humility. I shall send you to the examples of our ancestors; as you contemplate the end of their way of life, imitate their faith.

“For Abraham, when called by the Lord, obeyed in faith and went out to a place he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out without knowing where he was going.

“Therefore imitate the faith of this blessed patriarch; imitate his holiness. Despise your earthly homeland and always seek the heavenly one. I trust in the Lord that eternal gains will come to me through you.

“For I see that you have increased my joy by the fervor of your spirit, that you love justice, cherish the bonds of fraternal charity, devote yourselves to chastity, and preserve the rule of humility. As far as human judgment can see, I confidently praise and approve these things.

“But pray that what is worthy in human eyes may be confirmed by the judgment of eternal discernment, because God does not see as man sees. For, as the divine word declares, he searches all hearts and knows beforehand the thoughts of every mind.

“Therefore pray continually that the Lord may enlighten the eyes of your hearts and open them, as blessed Elisha prayed, so that you may recognize how many aids of the saints surround us and how many helps are prepared for the faithful. For our God draws near to those who supplicate him.

“Let unceasing prayer not be lacking among those engaged in spiritual warfare. Let those who were not ashamed to commit sin not be ashamed to do penance. Let sinners not be ashamed to mourn, if somehow the offense against divine judgment may be appeased by the flood of your tears, since God has deigned to call a contrite spirit a sacrifice.

“Let us therefore be humble in heart, tranquil in mind, avoiding every offense and always mindful of the divine commandments. Let us know that the name of monk, the title of religion, and the appearance of piety do not benefit us if we are found degenerate and rejected in our observance of the commandments.

“Therefore, dearest sons, let your conduct agree with the commitment you have undertaken. It is a great crime for a layman to pursue sins; how much more so for monks, who, fleeing the world’s flatteries as though they were a savage beast, have preferred Christ to every affection, and whose walk and dress are believed to be evidence of virtue?

“But why do I delay you any longer, dearest sons, with the speech of a long discourse? It remains for me to pursue you with the final prayer of the blessed Apostle, who says:

“‘And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to preserve you and to give you an inheritance among those who are sanctified.’

“To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.”

53. After this edifying address, he ordered them all to approach him in turn for his kiss. Having received the sacrament of communion, he strictly forbade them to weep. Then, extending his hand, he marked his whole body with the sign of the cross and ordered them to sing psalms.

While they hesitated, overcome by grief, he himself began the psalm:

“Praise the Lord in his holy places; let every spirit praise the Lord.”

On 8 January, while we could scarcely answer him because of our tears, he rested in the Lord at this verse.

After he had been buried, our elders, believing that what he had foretold concerning the migration, like many other things, could not pass unrealized, prepared a small wooden chest, so that when the foretold migration of the people occurred they might fulfill the command of the prophet.

## CHAPTER XII  
### The body of Saint Severinus is transferred to Italy

54. When Fridericus learned of the death of blessed Severinus, he, being poor and impious and ever more savage in barbarian greed, believed that the clothing assigned to the poor and certain other things ought to be taken away.

Adding sacrilege to this crime, he ordered the silver chalice and the other vessels used in the altar service to be removed. When these had been placed upon the sacred altars, and the appointed steward did not dare extend his hands to such an act, Fridericus compelled a soldier named Avicianus [Note: [Col. 1197C] Surius has “Avicianum”] to plunder the objects mentioned.

Although he carried out the command unwillingly, he was immediately and continually tormented by trembling in all his limbs and was also seized by a demon. He therefore quickly corrected his error by adopting better counsel. Taking up the commitment of a holy vocation, he was enlisted in the heavenly army in the solitude of an island and exchanged his military service for another kind of service.

Fridericus, however, forgetful of the holy man’s warning and prophecy, stripped the monastery of all its possessions and left only the walls, which he could not transfer across the Danube.

But the announced vengeance soon overtook him. For within a month he was killed by Fridericus, his brother’s son, and lost both his plunder and his life.

Therefore King Odoacer brought war upon the Rugians. After defeating them, driving Fridericus into flight, and capturing his father Fava as well, he transferred him to Italy together with the wicked wife mentioned above, namely Gisa. [Note: [Col. 1197C] This happened in the year 487, during the consulship of Boethius. What is related here also refutes Irenicus, who says in Book V of the *Exegesis of Germany*, chapter 14, that Feletheus died without children and left his kingdom to Gisa; that she married Sunia and bore Hunulfus; and that Odoacer became king of Italy.]

55. Later, when the same Odoacer heard that Fridericus had returned to his own territory, he immediately sent his brother Aonulfus with many armies [Note: [Col. 1197D] Surius has “Brauner”; Sigonius, “Onulfum”; Aventinus, “Anulfum”; Staibanus, “Mulfum”]. Fridericus fled again before him and went to King Theodoric, who at that time was staying at Nova, a city of the province of Moesia [Note: [Col. 1197D] Shortly afterward, namely in the year 489, he invaded Italy and defeated Odoacer in several battles]. [Note: [Col. 1197D] Others have “Novas”; Staibanus has “Nonas,” incorrectly. The *Notitia Imperii* has several places called Novae or situated near Novae. This one was located on the Danube in Lower Moesia. At that time Theodoric was regarded as governing part of Lower Moesia and Riparian Dacia.]

Aonulfus, warned by his brother’s command, ordered all the Romans to migrate to Italy. Then all the inhabitants, as though led out of the house of Egyptian bondage, were delivered from the daily barbarity of incessant plundering, and they recognized the prophecies of Saint Severinus.

Mindful of his command, our venerable presbyter Lucillus, while everyone was being compelled to depart by Count Pierius [Note: [Col. 1197D] Surius and Staibanus have “Pigerius.” He appears to have been a military count, not, as Aventinus maintains, governor of Vindelicia and Noricum], ordered the place of burial to be opened after first celebrating evening psalmody with the monks.

When it had been opened, such a fragrance of sweetness came upon all who stood around that, overcome by immense joy and wonder, we fell prostrate upon the ground.

Then, humanly expecting to find the bones of the corpse disarticulated—for the sixth year since his deposition had elapsed [Note: [Col. 1197D] This migration occurred after Feletheus was captured in 487 and before the war moved by Theodoric in 489; therefore in 487, or rather 488. It may consequently be inferred that Saint Severinus died in 482, six years earlier, and not in 494, as Hundius wrote. Braunerus also thinks that Saint Antony, who will be discussed on 28 December, migrated from Noricum to Italy at this time [Col. 1198C]—we found the body intact.

We gave immense thanks for this miracle to the Creator of all, because the saint’s corpse, in which there had been no spices and which no embalmer’s hand had touched, had remained unharmed, together with its beard and hair, until that time.

The linen wrappings were therefore changed, and the body was enclosed in a coffin prepared long beforehand. It was soon carried away on a cart drawn by horses, while all the provincials accompanied us on the same journey. They had left the towns along the bank of the Danube and received various settlements in different regions of Italy as the destinations of their migration.

The little body of the saint was carried, after passing through many regions, to a fortress called Mount Feletem. [Note: [Col. 1198C–D] It is not sufficiently clear which fortress this was. In the territory of the Veneti and the Carni there is Feltria, by the Piave River, an episcopal city of ancient name. Was the body of Saint Severinus carried there? Or rather into Umbria, part of which is called Montefeltro between the rivers Conca and Marecchia, where there is a town on a high hill commonly called San Leo, formerly Mons Feratratus—perhaps Feretretus, in Greek μόντης φεράντης? Staibanus writes that the saint’s remains were carried to Monte Seletum; Eugenius, to Siletum.]

56. At the same time, many people afflicted with various illnesses, and some oppressed by unclean spirits, immediately experienced the healing of divine grace.

Then a certain mute man was brought to that fortress by the compassion of his relatives. When he had reached the oratory cheerfully, where the little body of the holy man still remained placed upon the cart, he shut the door of his mouth and prayed in the chamber of his heart. At once his tongue was released for prayer and uttered praise to the Most High.

When he returned to the lodging where he was accustomed to stay, he was questioned according to custom. Having been prompted by gestures and signs, he replied in a clear voice that he had prayed and offered praise to God.

Those who knew him were terrified when he spoke. They ran shouting to the oratory and informed the holy presbyter Lucillus, and us who were with him, without knowing what had happened. Then, all exulting with joy, we gave thanks to divine mercy.

57. Thus the illustrious woman Barbaria [Note: [Col. 1198D] Baronius has “Barbara”] venerated blessed Severinus with religious devotion. She had known him very well through reputation or letters, together with her former husband.

When she heard after his death that the saint’s little body had been brought to Italy with great toil and had not yet been committed to the earth, she repeatedly invited our venerable presbyter Marcianus [Note: [Col. 1198D] Eugenius has “Martinus”] and the entire community by letter.

Then, with the authority of Saint Gelasius, pontiff of the Roman See, and with the people of Naples coming out to meet the funeral procession with reverence, the body was in part placed in a mausoleum at the fortress of Lucullanum by the hands of Saint Victor, bishop; the mausoleum had been built by the aforementioned woman. [Note: [Col. 1198D] These two words, “in part,” were absent from the Belfort manuscript.]

58. During this celebration, many afflicted by various illnesses, whose enumeration would be lengthy, immediately recovered their health.

Among them was a venerable handmaid of God named Processa, a citizen of Naples. When she was suffering from a most severe illness, drawn by the miraculous power of the holy corpse, she hurried to meet it on the road. Having entered beneath the vehicle carrying the venerable body, she was immediately freed from every illness of her limbs.

59. Then a certain blind man named Laodicius [Note: [Col. 1198D] Others have “Laodicius”] was startled by the unexpected loud singing of the people and anxiously asked his companions what was happening.

When they replied that the body of a certain Saint Severinus was passing by, he was moved with compunction and asked to be led to the window of the house in which he was staying. From there, a healthy person could see from a distance the multitude singing and the vehicle carrying the saint’s body.

When he leaned intently against the window and prayed, he immediately saw, identifying each one, all his acquaintances and neighbors. When this had happened, everyone who heard of it offered thanks to God with tearful joy.

60. Marinus, likewise, the primicerius (chief officer) [Note: [Col. 1198D] Surius and Belfort add “of the singers”] of the holy Church of Naples, was unable to recover his health after a dreadful headache. He placed his head against the vehicle and soon lifted it free from the pain. Mindful of that benefit, he came every year on the day of the saint’s deposition and offered God a devoted sacrifice with thanksgiving.

Let these reports of miracles and acts of power be sufficient concerning the countless benefits performed at his arrival, for many others know more of them. A monastery built at that same place in memory of the blessed man continues to this day. Through his merits many possessed by demons have been healed, and many afflicted by various illnesses have received—and continue to receive—health, through the working of God’s grace, to whom be honor and glory throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO THE LIFE OF SAINT SEVERINUS, OR BASNAGE’S OBSERVATIONS ON THE AUTHOR OF THAT LIFE

(*Canisius, Treasury of Monuments*)

[Col. 1199]

1. Aventinus said that Eugyppius was born at Batavis in Noricum. Velserus criticized him on this account, since, even if that abbot of Lucullanum had lived for some time in Noricum, it is not established that Noricum was his homeland.

But how did it become established for Velserus that Eugyppius had lived in Noricum? Was it because he wrote the Life of Severinus, the Apostle, as they call him, of that region? Eugyppius certainly recorded much about Severinus from the very well-known and daily reports of the elders, but he does not say that he learned this tradition while living in Noricum.

Velserus attacks Trithemius, Baronius, and the others because they did not distinguish two Eugyppii: one an Italian, who composed the Life of Severinus in the year 511; the other an African, who, at the command of Bishop Redux or Residux, excerpted a *Treasury of Sentences* from Augustine in the year 582.

We, however, can attack Velserus, Miraeus, Bollandus, Rosweyde, and the others who make two Eugyppii, while vindicating Baronius.

Sigebert of Gembloux provided the occasion for the error. He writes:

“Eugyppius, abbot, at the urging of Redux, bishop of Naples, extracting passages from Augustine’s books, gave a volume of great usefulness to the virgin Proba and, through the hands of Redux the bishop, presented it to the Church of Naples. He lived in the time of Pelagius II and the emperor Tiberius Constantius”—that is, in the year 582.

Miraeus adds a note so that the two Eugyppii may be distinguished more easily, one Italian and the other African.

But it can easily be proved against Sigebert that this Eugyppius did not write in the time of Pelagius II at the command of Redux. Rather, he wrote at the beginning of the sixth century and is therefore the same Eugyppius as the author of the Life of Severinus, who composed this Life two years after the consulship of Importunus—that is, in the year 511.

2. First, that Eugyppius who is called African and distinguished from our Eugyppius dedicated to the virgin Proba the *Treasury of Sentences* excerpted from Augustine. Sigebert himself asserts this.

But the virgin Proba lived at the beginning of the sixth century, and Cassiodorus spoke of her as already dead, referring to her as his kinswoman. [The source’s numbering reads “2o” and continues the second argument.]

Second, Cassiodorus often recommended the *Treasury* of Eugyppius for repeated reading. Writing around the year 560, he said:

“It is fitting,” he remarked, “that you should necessarily read the work of the presbyter Eugyppius, whom we ourselves had seen.”

Cassiodorus had seen Eugyppius; therefore Eugyppius had already died when that learned Senator wrote. Cassiodorus wanted his *Treasury* to be read from the year 560 onward. Therefore that *Treasury* was not written at the command of Redux in the year 582, after Cassiodorus’s death.

Third, the author of the *Treasury* himself, contrary to Sigebert, asserts that he did not write it at the command of Redux, bishop of Naples, but while professing the monastic life, at the urging of his lord abbot Marinus and the other holy brothers. For so says the prologue to that work, which Sigebert had not read.

Fourth, Redux contributed his own labor so that the *Treasury* of Eugyppius, composed long before by the abbot of Lucullanum, might be accurately copied and deposited in the Church of Naples, never to be removed from it. This occurred under the emperor Tiberius, in the third year after the consulship of that same Augustus, in the fifteenth indiction, while the Lombards were besieging the city of Naples, as stated in the conclusion or subscription of Redux himself in the manuscript which he had arranged to be written and which the most learned Mabillon published after Labbeus.

Eugyppius therefore wrote his *Treasury* at the beginning of the sixth century, while the virgin Proba was still alive and before Cassiodorus had arranged his divine Readings. He composed it at the same time that our Eugyppius was writing the Life of Severinus.

But how could two Eugyppii of the same name have been abbots of Lucullanum at the same time? From this you may conclude that the author who published the Life of Severinus and excerpted the *Treasury* from Augustine was one and the same.

Nevertheless, Redux ordered that this *Treasury* be copied more than sixty years later and thereafter, so that it might be preserved in the Church of Naples. Mabillon conjectures, however, that the manuscript subsequently came into his own possession in the library of Saint-Germain.

### 3.

Eugyppius did not write a history of the Heruli and of their settlements in Noricum, as Lazius asserted; rather, he composed the Life of Severinus, who had brought the peoples of Noricum to the Christian faith, from the daily reports of his elders. Eugyppius was distressed that he, a layman, wished to undertake this work, lest, being polished only in secular literature, he should write such a life in a style hampered by the ignorance of many.

Thus, in his sorrow, he urged Paschasius the deacon [Col. 1200C] to render the Life, richly adorned, into written form; and, so that Paschasius might give whatever assistance he could, Eugyppius attached to it a memorandum (*commemoratorium*) filled with various indications. But after reading the memorandum, Paschasius withdrew his hand from the tablet—that is, he declined the task—for he praised the work as already completed. “You have expressed more simply what you were asking me to narrate,” Paschasius said; “you have explained it more easily. We have judged that nothing should be added to your labor by our own efforts.”

Those who believe, therefore, that the Life of Severinus was composed by Paschasius at Eugyppius’s request are mistaken. From the letter published by Canisius, it is indeed clear that Eugyppius asked this of Paschasius, since he distrusted himself in such matters; but from Paschasius’s own reply, which is read in Velser, it is demonstrated most clearly that the Life of Severinus now extant is the work of Eugyppius.

### 4.

As for the Life of Severinus, it was published by Velser without the letter to Paschasius; and that letter, although highly relevant to the matter, was omitted from the latest edition of Velser’s works—a surprising decision [Col. 1200D]. Had Velser himself read it, he would not have denied so categorically that Severinus was an African, nor would he have attacked those who asserted this.

For Eugyppius writes thus to Paschasius: “Yet his speech proved him to be an African, a wholly Latin man.” It is true that he came to Noricum from the regions of the East, as Velser noted. Nevertheless, he had not been born in the East. Eugyppius resolves the difficulty in his letter to Paschasius, where he indicates that Severinus had fled to a certain wilderness of the East and, departing from there, had come to the towns of Riparian Noricum.

Moreover, what Eugyppius related about Severinus—at least most of it—is found in Cuspinianus’s description of Austria, in Aventinus’s *Annals*, and in Lazius’s *Commentaries on Severinus*.

**END OF THE SIXTY-SECOND VOLUME**
